Initially created: 2025-12-17T09:25:39.237+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Annals of Emperor Wǔ, Volume One
Grand Ancestor Emperor Wǔ,
a native of Qiáo in Péiguó,
bore the surname Cáo,
with the given name Cāo,
and the courtesy name Mèngdé.
He was a descendant of Cān, the Chancellor of Hàn.
During the reign of Emperor Huán,
Cáo Téng served as Zhōngchángshì and Dàchángqiú,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Fèitíng.
His adopted son Sōng succeeded him,
and rose to the position of Tàiwèi.
No one could ascertain the full details of his origins.
Sōng begat the Grand Ancestor.
The Grand Ancestor was quick-witted in his youth,
and possessed stratagems,
but he was also fond of chivalry and unrestrained,
not applying himself to serious occupations.
Therefore, people of his time did not consider him extraordinary;
only Qiáo Xuán of Liángguó and Hé Yōng of Nányáng saw him differently.
Xuán said to the Grand Ancestor:
"The world is about to fall into chaos.
If it is not a talent destined for the age, it cannot be saved.
As for the one who can bring peace,
will it be you?"
At twenty,
he was nominated as Xiàolián and became a Láng,
appointed as the Northern Commandant of Luòyáng,
then promoted to Magistrate of Dùnqīu,
and subsequently summoned and appointed Yìláng.
At the end of Guānghé,
the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out.
He was appointed Qídūwèi
to suppress the bandits in Yǐngchuān.
He was promoted to Chancellor of Jìnán.
The state had over ten counties,
and many chief officials were sycophantic towards the imperial relatives,
their corruption widespread.
He consequently impeached and dismissed eight of them;
he prohibited illicit cults,
and criminals fled,
making the entire commandery orderly.
After a long time,
he was summoned back to be the Administrator of Dōngjùn;
he did not take the post,
claiming illness and returning to his hometown.
Soon after,
Wáng Fēn, the Inspector of Jìzhōu, Xǔ Yōu of Nányáng, Zhōu Jǐng of Péiguó, and others allied with prominent heroes,
plotting to depose Emperor Líng
and install the Marquis of Héfěi.
They informed the Grand Ancestor,
but the Grand Ancestor rejected them.
Fēn and his allies subsequently failed.
Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì of Jīnchéng killed the Inspector and Administrator and rebelled,
with a host of over a hundred thousand,
causing unrest throughout the realm.
The Grand Ancestor was summoned to be Diǎnjūn Xiàowèi.
At this time, Emperor Líng died,
the crown prince ascended the throne,
and the Empress Dowager held court.
Grand General Hé Jìn conspired with Yuán Shào to execute the eunuchs,
but the Empress Dowager would not agree.
Jìn then summoned Dǒng Zhuó,
intending to intimidate the Empress Dowager with him.
Before Zhuó arrived, Jìn was killed.
When Zhuó arrived,
he deposed the emperor as the King of Hóngnóng and enthroned Emperor Xiàn,
causing great chaos in the capital.
Zhuó recommended the Grand Ancestor as Xiāoqí Xiàowèi,
wishing to consult with him on matters.
The Grand Ancestor then changed his name,
and secretly traveled east.
Upon leaving the pass,
he passed through Zhōngmóu,
where he was suspected by the Tíngzhǎng
and apprehended and brought to the county seat.
Someone in the city secretly recognized him
and pleaded for his release.
Zhuó subsequently killed the Empress Dowager and the King of Hóngnóng.
The Grand Ancestor arrived at Chénliú,
distributed his family wealth,
and gathered a righteous army,
intending to execute Zhuó.
In the twelfth month of winter,
he first raised his army at Jǐwú.
This was the sixth year of Zhōngpíng.
In the first month of spring of the first year of Chūpíng,
General of the Rear Yuán Shù, Inspector of Jìzhōu Hán Fù,
Inspector of Yùzhōu Kǒng Zhòu,
Inspector of Yǎnzhōu Liú Dài,
Administrator of Hénèi Wáng Kuāng,
Administrator of Bóhǎi Yuán Shào, Administrator of Chénliú Zhāng Miǎo, Administrator of Dōngjùn Qiáo Mào,
Administrator of Shānyáng Yuán Yí,
and Chancellor of Jìběi Bào Xìn
all simultaneously raised armies,
each with tens of thousands of men,
and nominated Shào as their盟zhǔ (alliance leader).
The Grand Ancestor acted as General Fènwǔ.
In the second month,
Zhuó heard that armies were rising
and consequently moved the Son of Heaven to the capital at Cháng'ān.
Zhuó remained garrisoned in Luòyáng,
and then burned the palaces.
At this time, Shào was garrisoned in Hénèi;
Miǎo, Dài, Mào, and Yí were garrisoned at Suānzǎo;
Shù was garrisoned in Nányáng;
Zhòu was garrisoned in Yǐngchuān;
Fù was in Yè.
Zhuó's army was strong,
and Shào and the others dared not advance.
The Grand Ancestor said:
"We have raised a righteous army to punish the tyrannical rebels.
The great host has already assembled,
why do you gentlemen hesitate?
If Dǒng Zhuó had heard of the eastern armies rising,
relied on the prestige of the imperial house,
and held the strategic dangers of the Two Zhōu,
he would have faced the world from the east;
though he acted without principle,
he would still be a formidable threat.
Now, he has burned the palaces,
and coerced the Son of Heaven to move.
The realm is shaken,
not knowing where to turn.
This is the time of Heaven's destruction of him.
A single battle will pacify the world,
this opportunity must not be lost."
He then led his troops west,
intending to seize Chénggāo.
Miǎo dispatched General Wèi Zī with a portion of his troops to follow the Grand Ancestor.
Upon reaching the Biàn River in Xíngyáng,
they encountered Zhuó's general Xú Róng.
They fought disadvantageously,
and many soldiers were killed or wounded.
The Grand Ancestor was struck by a stray arrow,
and the horse he was riding was wounded.
His younger cousin Hóng gave his horse to the Grand Ancestor,
who was able to escape by night.
Róng saw that the Grand Ancestor had few troops,
and had fought fiercely all day.
He thought that Suānzǎo would not be easy to attack,
so he also withdrew his troops.
When the Grand Ancestor arrived at Suānzǎo,
the combined armies numbered over a hundred thousand,
but they spent their days feasting and holding grand gatherings,
without planning to advance.
The Grand Ancestor rebuked them,
and then offered a plan, saying:
"Gentlemen, listen to my plan.
Have Bóhǎi lead the Hénèi troops to the Mèngjīn Pass,
the generals at Suānzǎo hold Chénggāo,
occupy Àocāng,
block Huányuán and Tàigǔ,
thus fully controlling these strategic points;
have General Yuán lead the Nányáng army to garrison Dān and Xī,
enter Wǔguān,
to shake Sānfǔ. All should build high ramparts and deep moats,
and not engage in battle,
but increase their feigned troops,
to show the world their military strength,
and by righteousness punish the rebellious.
This can swiftly pacify the realm.
Now our armies are moved by righteousness,
but you are hesitant and do not advance,
losing the hopes of the world.
I am secretly ashamed for you gentlemen!"
Miǎo and the others could not use his plan.
As the Grand Ancestor's troops were few,
he went with Xiàhóu Dūn and others to Yángzhōu to recruit soldiers.
Inspector Chén Wēn and Administrator Zhōu Xīn of Dānyáng gave him over four thousand men.
Returning to Lóngkàng,
many of his soldiers rebelled.
Upon reaching Zhì and Jiànpíng,
he gathered over a thousand more men,
and advanced to garrison in Hénèi.
Liú Dài was hostile towards Qiáo Mào;
Dài killed Mào,
and appointed Wáng Gōng to lead as Administrator of Dōngjùn.
Yuán Shào conspired with Hán Fù to enthrone Liú Yú, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, as emperor,
but the Grand Ancestor rejected this.
Shào also once obtained a jade seal,
and while sitting with the Grand Ancestor, he raised it towards his elbow.
The Grand Ancestor smiled at this, but was displeased.
In the spring of the second year,
Shào and Fù then enthroned Yú as emperor,
but Yú ultimately dared not accept.
In the summer, fourth month,
Zhuó returned to Cháng'ān.
In the autumn, seventh month,
Yuán Shào coerced Hán Fù,
and took Jìzhōu.
Bandits like Yú Dú, Bái Rào, and Suī Gù (Suī,
pronounced like Shēnsuí) from Hēishān,
numbering over a hundred thousand, plundered Wèijùn and Dōngjùn.
Wáng Gōng could not defend against them.
The Grand Ancestor led his troops into Dōngjùn,
attacked Bái Rào at Púyáng,
and defeated him.
Yuán Shào then memorialized the Grand Ancestor as Administrator of Dōngjùn,
governing from Dōngwǔyáng.
In the third year, in spring,
Tàizǔ's army was stationed at Dūnqiū.
Dú and others attacked Dōngwǔyáng.
Tàizǔ then led his troops west into the mountains,
and attacked Dú and the others' original encampment.
When Dú heard of this,
he abandoned Wǔyáng and returned.
Tàizǔ intercepted and attacked Suī Gù,
and also attacked the Xiongnú Yú Fúluó at Nèihuáng.
All were decisively defeated.
In summer, fourth month,
Sītú Wáng Yǔn and Lǚ Bù together killed Zhuó.
Zhuó's generals Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì, and others killed Yǔn and attacked Bù.
Bù was defeated,
and exited Wǔguān to the east.
Jué and the others seized control of the court.
The Qīngzhōu Yellow Turbans, numbering a million, entered Yǎnzhōu,
killed Zhèng Suì, the Chancellor of Rènchéng,
and moved into Dōngpíng.
Liú Dài wished to attack them.
Bào Xìn remonstrated, saying:
"Now the bandits number a million,
the common people are all terrified,
and the soldiers have no fighting spirit.
They cannot be opposed.
Looking at the bandit multitude, they follow each other in groups,
their army has no baggage train,
relying solely on plunder for resources.
It would be better now to conserve the strength of our officers and men,
and first establish a strong defense.
If they wish to fight, they cannot;
if they attack, they also cannot.
Their momentum will certainly dissipate.
Afterwards, select the elite,
occupy their vital points,
and attack them, and they can be defeated."
Dài did not heed him,
and consequently engaged in battle,
and was indeed killed by them.
Xìn then, with provincial officials Wàn Qián and others, went to Dōngjùn to welcome Tàizǔ to govern as Yǎnzhōu Mù.
He then advanced his troops and attacked the Yellow Turbans east of Shòuzhāng.
Xìn fought bravely and died in battle,
but they barely managed to defeat them.
They sought Xìn's body but could not find it,
so the multitude carved wood into Xìn's likeness,
sacrificed to it, and wept.
They pursued the Yellow Turbans to Jìběi.
They begged for surrender.
In winter,
he accepted the surrender of over three hundred thousand soldiers,
and over a million men and women.
He recruited the elite among them,
who were called the Qīngzhōu Army.
Yuán Shù and Shào had a rift.
Shù sought aid from Gōngsūn Zàn.
Zàn sent Liú Bèi to garrison Gāotáng,
Dān Jīng to garrison Píngyuán,
and Táo Qiān to garrison Fāgān,
to put pressure on Shào.
Tàizǔ and Shào met and attacked them,
defeating all of them.
In the fourth year, in spring,
the army was at Juànchéng.
Jīngzhōu Mù Liú Biǎo cut off Shù's supply route.
Shù led his army into Chénliú,
and encamped at Fēngqiū.
The remaining bandits of Hēishān and Yú Fúluó and others assisted him.
Shù sent his general Liú Xiáng to garrison Kuāngtíng.
Tàizǔ attacked Xiáng.
Shù came to his rescue,
and engaged in battle,
decisively defeating him.
Shù retreated to defend Fēngqiū.
He then besieged it,
but before the encirclement was complete,
Shù fled to Xiāngyì.
He pursued him to Tàishòu,
where he breached the canal and flooded the city.
Shù fled to Nínglíng.
He pursued him again,
and Shù fled to Jiǔjiāng.
In summer,
Tàizǔ returned his army to Dìngtáo.
Quē Xuān of Xiàpí gathered several thousand people,
and proclaimed himself Son of Heaven;
Xúzhōu Mù Táo Qiān raised an army with him,
took Huá and Fèi in Tàishān,
and plundered Rènchéng.
In autumn,
Tàizǔ campaigned against Táo Qiān,
capturing over ten cities.
Qiān remained in his city and dared not sally forth.
That year,
Sūn Cè, at Yuán Shù's behest, crossed the Yangtze,
and within a few years established control over Jiāngdōng.
In the first year of Xīngpíng, in spring,
Tàizǔ returned from Xúzhōu.
Previously,
Tàizǔ's father Sōng,
after retiring from office, returned to Qiáo.
During Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion,
he sought refuge in Lángyá,
and was harmed by Táo Qiān.
Therefore, Tàizǔ was determined to seek revenge by campaigning east.
In summer,
he ordered Xún Yù and Chéng Yù to defend Juànchéng,
and again campaigned against Táo Qiān,
capturing five cities,
and then plundered the land as far as Dōnghǎi.
Upon returning, he passed Tán.
Qiān's general Cáo Bào and Liú Bèi were stationed east of Tán,
intercepting Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ attacked and defeated them,
then attacked and captured Xiāngbēn.
Many were killed and devastated wherever he passed.
At this time, Zhāng Miǎo and Chén Gōng rebelled and welcomed Lǚ Bù,
and all the commanderies and counties responded.
Xún Yù and Chéng Yù held Juànchéng.
The two counties of Fàn and Dōng'ā held firm.
Tàizǔ then led his army back.
When Bù arrived,
he attacked Juànchéng but could not take it.
He then encamped west at Púyáng.
Tàizǔ said:
"Bù suddenly gained a province,
but instead of occupying Dōngpíng,
cutting off the roads of Kàngfù and Tàishān, and using the dangerous terrain to intercept me,
he encamped at Púyáng.
I know he is incapable of achieving anything."
He then advanced his army and attacked him.
Bù sent out troops to battle,
first assaulting the Qīngzhōu Army with cavalry.
The Qīngzhōu Army fled.
Tàizǔ's formation was disrupted.
He charged out through the fire,
fell from his horse,
and burned his left palm.
Sīmǎ Lóu Yì helped Tàizǔ back onto his horse,
and he then withdrew.
Before reaching the camp,
the generals, not having seen Tàizǔ,
were all terrified.
Tàizǔ then exerted himself to encourage the army,
ordered the army to quickly prepare siege equipment,
and advanced to attack again,
remaining in a standoff with Bù for over a hundred days.
Locusts arose,
the common people suffered a great famine,
and Bù's provisions also ran out.
Each then withdrew.
In autumn, ninth month,
Tàizǔ returned to Juànchéng.
Bù arrived at Chéngshì,
was defeated by Lǐ Jìn, a man of that county,
and encamped east at Shānyáng.
Thereupon, Shào sent someone to persuade Tàizǔ,
wanting to form an alliance.
Tàizǔ had just lost Yǎnzhōu,
and his army's provisions were exhausted.
He was about to agree.
Chéng Yù stopped Tàizǔ,
and Tàizǔ followed his advice.
In winter, tenth month,
Tàizǔ arrived at Dōng'ā.
That year, a *hú* of grain cost over five hundred thousand cash.
People ate each other.
Therefore, new recruits among officials and soldiers were discharged.
Táo Qiān died,
and Liú Bèi succeeded him.
In the second year, in spring,
he attacked Dìngtáo.
Wú Zī (吳資), the Administrator of Jìyīn (濟陰), defended the Southern City,
which was not yet taken.
Coincidentally, Lǚ Bù (呂布) arrived,
and was again defeated.
In summer,
Lǚ Bù's generals Xuē Lán (薛蘭) and Lǐ Fēng (李封) were stationed at Jùyě (鉅野).
Tàizǔ (太祖) attacked them.
Lǚ Bù went to aid Xuē Lán.
Xuē Lán was defeated,
and Lǚ Bù fled.
So, Xuē Lán and others were beheaded.
Lǚ Bù then came from Dōngmín (東緡) with Chén Gōng (陳宮) leading over ten thousand men to battle.
At that time, Tàizǔ's troops were few,
so he set an ambush
and unleashed a surprise attack,
utterly routing them.
Lǚ Bù fled during the night.
Tàizǔ again attacked,
taking Dìngtáo,
and dispatched troops to pacify the various counties.
Lǚ Bù fled east to Liú Bèi (劉備).
Zhāng Miǎo (張邈) followed Lǚ Bù,
sending his younger brother Zhāng Chāo (張超) to guard Yōngqiū (雍丘) with their family.
In autumn, eighth month,
Yōngqiū was besieged.
In winter, tenth month,
the Son of Heaven appointed Tàizǔ as the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
In the twelfth month,
Yōngqiū collapsed,
and Zhāng Chāo committed suicide.
Zhāng Miǎo's (張邈) three clans were exterminated.
Zhāng Miǎo went to Yuán Shù (袁術) to ask for aid,
but was killed by his own followers.
Yǎnzhōu was pacified,
and so he advanced east to conquer Chén (陳) territory.
That year,
Cháng'ān (長安) fell into chaos,
and the Son of Heaven moved east.
He was defeated at Cáoyáng (曹陽),
crossed the river, and reached Ānyì (安邑).
In the first year of Jiàn'ān (建安), spring, first month,
Tàizǔ's army reached Wǔpíng (武平).
Yuán Sì (袁嗣), the Chancellor of Chén (陳) appointed by Yuán Shù, surrendered.
Tàizǔ intended to welcome the Son of Heaven.
Some of the generals were doubtful,
but Xún Yù (荀彧) and Chéng Yù (程昱) advised him to do so.
So, he sent Cáo Hóng (曹洪) with troops to welcome him from the west.
The General of the Imperial Guard, Dǒng Chéng (董承), and Yuán Shù's general Cháng Nú (萇奴) defended the passes,
preventing Cáo Hóng from advancing.
The Yellow Turbans of Rǔnán (汝南) and Yǐngchuān (潁川), Hē Yí (何儀), Liú Pì (劉辟), Huáng Shào (黃邵), Hē Màn (何曼), and others,
each with tens of thousands of followers,
initially responded to Yuán Shù,
and then attached themselves to Sūn Jiān (孫堅).
In the second month,
Tàizǔ advanced and attacked them, defeating them.
Liú Pì (劉辟) and Huáng Shào (黃邵) and others were beheaded.
Hē Yí (何儀) and all his followers surrendered.
The Son of Heaven appointed Tàizǔ as General Who Establishes Virtue (Jiàndé Jiāngjūn, 建德將軍).
In summer, sixth month,
he was promoted to General Who Quells the East (Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn, 鎮東將軍)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Fèitíng (費亭侯).
In autumn, seventh month,
Yáng Fèng (楊奉) and Hán Xiān (韓暹) brought the Son of Heaven back to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Yáng Fèng separately encamped at Liáng (梁).
Tàizǔ then arrived at Luòyáng,
defending the capital.
Hán Xiān fled.
The Son of Heaven granted Tàizǔ the authority of the Imperial Axe (Jiéyuè, 節鉞)
and appointed him to oversee the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū Shì, 錄尚書事).
Luòyáng was ruined and desolate.
Dǒng Zhāo (董昭) and others advised Tàizǔ to make Xǔ (許) the capital.
In the ninth month,
the imperial carriage left Huányuán (轘轅) and proceeded east.
Tàizǔ was appointed General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn, 大將軍)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔpíng (武平侯).
Since the Son of Heaven's move west,
the imperial court had become increasingly chaotic.
It was only now that the ancestral temples, altars of soil and grain, and ceremonial institutions were finally established.
When the Son of Heaven was moving east,
Yáng Fèng (楊奉) from Liáng (梁) wanted to intercept him,
but failed.
In winter, tenth month,
the Duke attacked Yáng Fèng.
Yáng Fèng fled south to Yuán Shù.
He then attacked Yáng Fèng's encampment at Liáng (梁)
and captured it.
Thereupon, Yuán Shào (袁紹) was made Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi, 太尉).
Yuán Shào was ashamed to be ranked below the Duke
and refused to accept.
The Duke then firmly declined
and yielded the General-in-Chief position to Yuán Shào.
The Son of Heaven appointed the Duke as Grand Minister of Works (Sīkōng, 司空)
and acting General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn, 車騎將軍).
That year, based on the proposals of Zǎo Zhī (棗祗), Hán Hào (韓浩), and others,
the system of military-agricultural colonies (túntián, 屯田) was first implemented.
Lǚ Bù attacked Liú Bèi,
taking Xiàpí (下邳).
Liú Bèi came to seek refuge.
Chéng Yù advised the Duke, saying:
“I observe that Liú Bèi possesses heroic talent and greatly commands the hearts of the people.
He will ultimately not remain subservient to others.
It would be better to deal with him early.”
The Duke said:
“This is a time for gathering heroes.
To kill one man and lose the hearts of all under Heaven
is unacceptable.”
Zhāng Jì (張濟) fled from Guānzhōng (關中) to Nányáng (南陽).
When Zhāng Jì died,
his nephew Zhāng Xiù (張繡) took command of his forces.
In the second year, spring, first month,
the Duke arrived at Wǎn (宛).
Zhāng Xiù surrendered,
but then regretted it
and rebelled again.
The Duke fought him,
but his army was defeated.
He was struck by a stray arrow.
His eldest son Cáo Áng (曹昂) and nephew Cáo Ānmín (曹安民) were killed.
The Duke then led his troops back to Wǔyīn (舞陰).
Zhāng Xiù led his cavalry to raid them.
The Duke attacked and defeated them.
Zhāng Xiù fled to Ráng (穰)
and joined Liú Biǎo (劉表).
The Duke said to his generals:
“When I accepted Zhāng Xiù's surrender,
I failed to immediately secure hostages,
which led to this outcome.
I know why I was defeated.
All of you, observe:
from now on, I will not be defeated again.”
Then he returned to Xǔ (許).
Yuán Shù intended to declare himself emperor in Huáinán (淮南),
and sent an envoy to Lǚ Bù.
Lǚ Bù seized the envoy
and submitted his letter.
Yuán Shù was enraged
and attacked Lǚ Bù,
but was defeated by Lǚ Bù.
In autumn, ninth month,
Yuán Shù invaded Chén (陳).
The Duke went east to campaign against him.
When Yuán Shù heard that the Duke was personally coming,
he abandoned his army and fled,
leaving his generals Qiáo Ruí (橋蕤), Lǐ Fēng (李豊), Liáng Gāng (梁綱), and Lè Jiù (樂就).
When the Duke arrived,
he attacked and defeated Qiáo Ruí (橋蕤) and the others,
beheading them all.
Yuán Shù fled across the Huái (淮) River.
The Duke returned to Xǔ (許).
When the Duke returned from Wǔyīn (舞陰),
the various counties of Nányáng (南陽) and Zhānglíng (章陵) rebelled again for Zhāng Xiù.
The Duke sent Cáo Hóng (曹洪) to attack them,
but he was unsuccessful.
He returned to garrison Yè (葉),
and was repeatedly harassed by Zhāng Xiù (張繡) and Liú Biǎo (劉表).
In winter, eleventh month,
the Duke personally campaigned south,
arriving at Wǎn (宛).
Liú Biǎo's general Dèng Jì (鄧濟) occupied Húyáng (湖陽).
He attacked and captured it,
taking Dèng Jì (鄧濟) alive.
Húyáng (湖陽) surrendered.
He attacked Wǔyīn (舞陰)
and took it.
In the spring, the first month of the third year,
Gōng returned to Xǔ.
The position of Jūnshī Jìjiǔ was first established.
In the third month,
Gōng besieged Zhāng Xiù at Ráng.
In the summer, the fifth month,
Liú Biǎo dispatched troops to rescue Xiù,
in order to cut off Gōng's rear supply lines.
When Gōng was about to withdraw,
Xiù's troops came to pursue,
and Gōng's army could not advance.
They set up continuous camps and moved forward gradually.
Gōng wrote a letter to Xún Yù, saying:
"The rebels are pursuing us.
Though we advance only a few *lǐ* a day,
I have a plan.
When we reach Ānzhòng,
we will surely defeat Xiù."
Upon reaching Ānzhòng,
Xiù and Biǎo's troops joined forces to defend a strategic pass.
Gōng's army was attacked from both front and rear.
Gōng then secretly dug a tunnel through the pass at night,
moved all the baggage trains through,
and set up surprise troops.
At dawn,
the rebels thought Gōng had fled,
and sent their entire army to pursue.
Gōng then unleashed his surprise troops, both infantry and cavalry, to attack from both sides,
and inflicted a great defeat upon them.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
Gōng returned to Xǔ.
Xún Yù asked Gōng:
"Earlier, you predicted the rebels would surely be defeated.
How did you know?"
Gōng replied:
"The barbarians blocked our return path
and forced us to fight in a death trap.
That is how I knew we would win."
Lǚ Bù again sent Gāo Shùn to attack Liú Bèi on Yuán Shù's behalf.
Gōng dispatched Xiàhóu Dūn to rescue him,
but he was unsuccessful.
Bèi was defeated by Shùn.
In the ninth month,
Gōng marched east to conquer Bù.
In the winter, the tenth month,
Péngchéng was sacked,
and its chancellor, Hóu Xié, was captured.
Gōng advanced to Xiàpī,
where Bù personally led his cavalry to intercept and attack.
Bù's forces were greatly defeated,
and his valiant general, Chéng Lián, was captured.
Gōng pursued them to the city walls.
Bù was afraid
and wished to surrender.
Chén Gōng and others thwarted his plan,
sought help from Shù,
and urged Bù to fight.
Bù fought again and was defeated,
so he returned and held firm in defense.
Gōng attacked but could not take the city.
At this time, Gōng had been fighting continuously,
his soldiers were exhausted,
and he wished to return.
Following the advice of Xún Yōu and Guō Jiā,
he then diverted the Sī and Yí rivers to flood the city.
After more than a month,
Bù's generals Sòng Xiàn and Wèi Xù and others seized Chén Gōng
and surrendered the city.
Bù and Gōng were captured alive
and both were executed.
Zāng Bà, Sūn Guān, Wú Dūn, Yǐn Lǐ, and Chāng Xī of Tàishān each gathered their followers.
When Bù defeated Liú Bèi,
Bà and the others all followed Bù.
After Bù's defeat,
Bà and the others were captured.
Gōng treated them generously
and then ceded the two prefectures of Qīng and Xú, those attached to the sea, to their charge,
dividing Lángyá, Dōnghǎi, and Běihǎi into the commanderies of Chéngyáng, Lìchéng, and Chānglǜ.
Earlier,
when Gōng was governor of Yǎnyhōu,
he appointed Bì Chén of Dōngpíng as a *biéjià*.
When Zhāng Miǎo rebelled,
Miǎo seized Chén's mother, younger brother, wife, and children.
Gōng courteously dismissed Chén,
saying:
"Your elderly mother is there,
you may go."
Chén bowed deeply, showing no disloyalty.
Gōng praised him
and shed tears for him.
After he left,
he then fled back to Miǎo.
When Bù was defeated,
Chén was captured alive.
Everyone feared for Chén,
but Gōng said:
"If a man is filial to his parents,
how can he not also be loyal to his lord?
He is exactly what I seek."
He appointed him as Chancellor of Lǔ.
In the spring, the second month of the fourth year,
Gōng returned to Chāngyì.
Zhāng Yáng's general Yáng Chǒu killed Yáng.
Suī Gù then killed Chǒu,
and submitted his followers to Yuán Shào,
stationing them at Shèquǎn.
In the summer, the fourth month,
Gōng advanced his army to the Yellow River,
and sent Shǐ Huàn and Cáo Rén to cross the river and attack them.
Gù left Yáng's former chief clerk Xuē Hóng and the Grand Administrator of Hénèi, Miáo Shàng, to guard the rear,
while he personally led troops north to meet Shào and seek help.
He encountered Huàn and Rén at Quǎnchéng.
In the ensuing battle,
Gù's forces were greatly defeated,
and Gù was slain.
Gōng then crossed the Yellow River
and besieged Shèquǎn.
Hóng and Shàng led their followers to surrender,
and were enfeoffed as marquises.
Gōng's army returned to Áocāng.
He appointed Wèi Zhǒng as Grand Administrator of Hénèi,
entrusting him with affairs north of the Yellow River.
Earlier,
Gōng had recommended Zhǒng as a *xiàolián*.
When Yǎnyhōu rebelled,
Gōng said:
"Only Wèi Zhǒng will not abandon me."
When he heard that Zhǒng had fled,
Gōng angrily said:
"If Zhǒng doesn't flee south to Yuè or north to Hú,
I will not let you go!"
After taking Shèquǎn,
Zhǒng was captured alive.
Gōng said:
"It is solely for his talent!"
He released him from his bonds and employed him.
At this time, Yuán Shào had already absorbed Gōngsūn Zàn,
and controlled the territory of four prefectures,
with an army of over one hundred thousand.
He was about to advance his army to attack Xǔ.
His generals believed he was irresistible,
but Gōng said:
"I know Shào's character.
He has great ambition but little wisdom,
a fierce exterior but a timid heart,
is envious and critical but lacks authority.
His army is numerous but his planning is unclear;
his generals are arrogant and his commands are not unified.
Though his territory is vast
and his provisions abundant,
it is just enough to serve as tribute for me."
In the autumn, the eighth month,
Gōng advanced his army to Líyáng,
and sent Zāng Bà and others into Qīngzhōu to defeat Qí, Běihǎi, and Dōng'ān.
Yú Jìn was left to guard the Yellow River.
In the ninth month,
Gōng returned to Xǔ
and divided his troops to guard Guāndù.
In the winter, the eleventh month,
Zhāng Xiù led his followers to surrender
and was enfeoffed as a marquis.
In the twelfth month,
Gōng's army was at Guāndù.
Yuán Shù, since his defeat at Chén,
gradually became distressed.
Yuán Tán sent a messenger from Qīngzhōu to invite him.
Shù wanted to pass north through Xiàpī.
Gōng sent Liú Bèi and Zhū Líng to intercept him.
Coincidentally, Shù died of illness.
Chéng Yù and Guō Jiā, hearing that Gōng had sent Bèi,
said to Gōng:
"Liú Bèi must not be let go."
Gōng regretted it
and pursued him, but could not catch him.
Before Bèi went east,
he secretly plotted rebellion with Dǒng Chéng and others.
Upon reaching Xiàpī,
he then killed the Inspector of Xúzhōu, Chē Zhòu,
and raised troops to station at Pèi.
Liú Dài and Wáng Zhōng were sent to attack him
but failed.
The Grand Administrator of Lújiāng, Liú Xún, led his followers to surrender
and was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Dǒng Chéng (董承) and others' plot was revealed,
and all were executed.
Gōng (公) was about to personally lead an eastern expedition against Liú Bèi (劉備).
All the generals said:
“The one who contends with Gōng for control of the realm
is Yuán Shào (袁紹).
Now Yuán Shào is about to come, but you abandon him and go east;
if Yuán Shào attacks from the rear,
what then?”
Gōng said:
“Indeed, Liú Bèi
is a hero among men.
If we do not attack him now,
he will surely become a future menace.
Although Yuán Shào has great ambitions,
he is slow to act;
he will surely not move.”
Guō Jiā (郭嘉) also advised Gōng.
So, Gōng attacked Liú Bèi to the east,
defeated him,
and captured his general Xiàhóu Bó (夏侯博) alive.
Liú Bèi fled to Yuán Shào.
Gōng captured his wife and children.
Liú Bèi’s general Guān Yǔ (關羽) was stationed at Xiàpī (下邳).
Gōng again advanced and attacked him.
Guān Yǔ surrendered.
Chāng Xī (昌豨) rebelled and sided with Liú Bèi.
Gōng again attacked and defeated him.
Gōng returned to Guāndù (官渡).
Yuán Shào ultimately did not sally forth.
In the second month,
Yuán Shào sent Guō Tú (郭圖), Chúnyú Qióng (淳于瓊), and Yán Liáng (顏良) to attack Liú Yán (劉延), the Tàishǒu (太守) of Dōngjùn (東郡), at Báimǎ (白馬).
Yuán Shào led his army to Líyáng (黎陽),
intending to cross the river.
In summer, the fourth month,
Gōng went north to relieve Liú Yán.
Xún Yōu (荀攸) advised Gōng, saying:
“Now our troops are few and no match for them.
Only by dividing their forces can we succeed.
When Gōng reaches Yánjīn (延津),
if you pretend to cross the river and attack their rear,
Yuán Shào will surely send forces west to respond.
Then, with light troops, attack Báimǎ,
taking them by surprise.
Yán Liáng can be captured.”
Gōng followed his advice.
Yuán Shào heard that troops were crossing,
and immediately divided his forces to respond in the west.
Gōng then led his army, marching quickly day and night towards Báimǎ.
When he was still more than ten *lǐ* away,
Yán Liáng was greatly alarmed,
and came out to meet the attack.
Gōng ordered Zhāng Liáo (張遼) and Guān Yǔ to advance.
They attacked and defeated (Yán Liáng’s forces),
and beheaded Yán Liáng.
Thus, the siege of Báimǎ was lifted.
Gōng moved its inhabitants,
and followed the river west.
Yuán Shào then crossed the river to pursue Gōng’s army,
reaching south of Yánjīn.
Gōng gathered his troops and encamped at the foot of the southern slope.
He sent men to ascend the rampart to observe,
and they reported:
“There are about five or six hundred cavalry.”
A moment later,
they reported again:
“The cavalry has increased,
and the infantry are countless.”
Gōng said:
“Do not report again.”
Then he ordered his cavalry to dismount and release their horses.
At this time,
the Báimǎ baggage train was on the way.
The generals thought the enemy cavalry was numerous,
and suggested returning to defend the camp.
Xún Yōu said:
“This is how we bait the enemy!
How can we leave it?”
Yuán Shào’s cavalry general Wén Chǒu (文醜) and Liú Bèi’s general arrived one after another with five or six thousand cavalry.
The generals again reported:
“We should mount our horses.”
Gōng said:
“Not yet.”
A moment later,
more cavalry arrived,
some splitting off to target the baggage train.
Gōng said:
“Now we can.”
So, all mounted their horses.
At that time, his cavalry numbered less than six hundred.
Gōng then unleashed his troops to attack,
utterly defeating them,
and beheaded Wén Chǒu.
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu were both famous generals of Yuán Shào.
In two battles,
both were captured.
Yuán Shào’s army was greatly shaken.
Gōng returned his army to Guāndù.
Yuán Shào advanced and secured Yángwǔ (陽武).
Guān Yǔ fled back to Liú Bèi.
In the eighth month,
Yuán Shào gradually advanced his camps,
setting up fortifications along the sand dunes,
stretching for tens of *lǐ* east and west.
Gōng also divided his camps to match them,
but was unsuccessful in combined engagements.
At that time, Gōng’s army numbered less than ten thousand,
with two or three tenths wounded.
Yuán Shào again advanced to Guāndù,
constructing earthworks and tunnels.
Gōng also built them internally,
to counter them.
Yuán Shào shot into the camp,
arrows falling like rain.
Those who walked had to carry shields (over their heads).
The troops were greatly afraid.
At this time, Gōng was short on provisions.
He wrote a letter to Xún Yù (荀彧),
discussing his intention to return to Xǔ (許).
Xún Yù believed that:
“Yuán Shào has gathered all his forces at Guāndù,
wishing to decide the victory or defeat with Gōng.
Gōng is using his utmost weakness against the utmost strength.
If you cannot control him,
you will certainly be taken advantage of.
This is the greatest opportunity for the realm.
Moreover, Yuán Shào
is merely a hero among commoners.
He can gather people but cannot employ them.
With Gōng’s divine might and sagacity, supported by great providence,
what direction could fail to succeed!”
Gōng followed his advice.
Sūn Cè (孫策), hearing that Gōng and Yuán Shào were locked in a stalemate,
then plotted to raid Xǔ.
Before he could carry it out,
he was killed by assassins.
The surrendered bandit Liú Pì (劉辟) and others from Rǔnán (汝南) rebelled and sided with Yuán Shào.
They plundered the area around Xǔ.
Yuán Shào sent Liú Bèi to assist Liú Pì.
Gōng sent Cáo Rén (曹仁) to attack and defeat them.
Liú Bèi fled,
and Gōng then destroyed Liú Pì’s encampment.
Yuán Shào's thousands of grain carts arrived.
Gōng used Xún Yōu's strategy,
sending Xú Huáng and Shǐ Huàn to intercept and attack them.
They inflicted a great defeat,
burning all the carts.
Gōng and Shào had been locked in a stalemate for months.
Although there had been battles and generals slain,
his forces were few and their provisions exhausted,
leaving the soldiers weary and fatigued.
Gōng said to the logistics officers:
"In fifteen days, I will defeat Shào for you;
you will no longer have to toil."
In the tenth month of winter,
Shào sent carts laden with grain,
ordering Chún Yú Qióng and five others to lead over ten thousand soldiers to escort them.
They encamped forty *lǐ* north of Shào's main camp.
Shào's strategist, Xǔ Yōu, was greedy,
and Shào could not satisfy him,
so he defected,
and consequently persuaded Gōng to attack Qióng and his group.
Those around Gōng were suspicious,
but Xún Yōu and Jiǎ Xǔ advised Gōng to agree.
Gōng then left Cáo Hóng to guard the camp,
and personally led five thousand infantry and cavalry by night.
They arrived at dawn.
Qióng and his men saw Gōng's small force
and arrayed themselves outside the camp gate.
Gōng immediately attacked them.
Qióng retreated to defend his camp,
and Gōng then assaulted it.
Shào sent cavalry to rescue Qióng.
Some of Gōng's men said,
"The enemy cavalry are drawing near.
Please divide our forces to resist them."
Gōng angrily replied,
"The enemy is at our backs,
yet you report this now!"
The soldiers all fought to the death,
utterly defeating Qióng and his group,
and beheading them all.
When Shào first heard of Gōng's attack on Qióng,
he said to his eldest son, Tán:
"Let him attack Qióng and his group.
I will attack and capture his camp.
Then he will surely have nowhere to return!"
He then sent Zhāng Hé and Gāo Lǎn to attack Cáo Hóng.
When Hé and his group heard that Qióng was defeated,
they promptly surrendered.
Shào's army was utterly routed.
Shào and Tán abandoned their army and fled,
crossing the river.
They were pursued but could not be caught.
All of Shào's baggage, documents, treasures,
and his remaining troops were captured.
Gōng collected documents from Shào's camp,
finding letters from Xǔ and from within his own army,
and burned them all.
Many prefectures in Jìzhōu raised their cities and towns in surrender.
Previously,
during the reign of Huán Dì, a yellow star appeared in the regions of Chǔ and Sòng.
Yīn Kuí (Kuí
is an ancient form of the character *kuí*,
as seen in *Sān Cāng*) of Liáodōng,
skilled in astronomy,
said that fifty years later, a true man would arise between Liáng and Pèi,
whose might would be irresistible.
By this time, exactly fifty years had passed,
and Gōng defeated Shào,
becoming unrivaled under heaven.
In the fourth month of summer in the sixth year,
Gōng deployed his troops along the river,
attacking Shào's army at Cāngtíng.
He defeated them.
Shào returned,
reassembled his scattered soldiers,
and subjugated the rebellious prefectures and counties.
In the ninth month,
Gōng returned to Xǔ.
Before Shào's defeat,
he had sent Liú Bèi to raid Rǔnán,
and the Rǔnán bandits Gòng Dū and others responded to him.
Cài Yáng was sent to attack Dū,
but he was unsuccessful
and defeated by Dū.
Gōng marched south to campaign against Bèi.
When Bèi heard that Gōng was personally leading the army,
he fled to Liú Biǎo,
and Dū and his group all dispersed.
In the first month of spring in the seventh year,
Gōng's army was at Qiáo.
He issued an order saying:
"I raised my righteous army
to eliminate tyranny and chaos from the world.
The people of my old homeland
have almost all perished,
and I can walk all day within the state
without seeing anyone I know,
which fills me with sorrow and grief.
Since I raised this righteous army,
any generals and soldiers who died without heirs—
find their relatives to adopt as heirs,
grant them land,
provide them with oxen from the government,
and establish teachers to educate them.
For those who survive, erect temples
so they may worship their ancestors.
If their spirits have awareness,
what regrets would I have after my hundredth year?"
He then proceeded to Jùnyí,
repaired the Suīyáng Canal,
and sent an envoy with a grand offering to sacrifice to Qiáo Xuán.
The army advanced to Guāndù.
After Shào's army was defeated,
he fell ill and vomited blood,
dying in the fifth month of summer.
His youngest son, Shàng, succeeded him.
Tán proclaimed himself General of Chariots and Cavalry,
encamping at Líyáng.
In the ninth month of autumn,
Gōng campaigned against them,
fighting continuously.
Tán and Shàng were repeatedly defeated and retreated,
holding firm in defense.
In the third month of spring in the eighth year,
Gōng attacked their outer wall,
and they came out to fight.
Gōng attacked
and inflicted a great defeat.
Tán and Shàng fled by night.
In the fourth month of summer,
Gōng advanced to Yè.
In the fifth month, he returned to Xǔ,
leaving Jiǎ Xìn to garrison Líyáng.
On the day *jǐyǒu*,
he issued an order saying:
"The *Sīmǎ Fǎ* states, 'A general who dies in battle is to be granted peace.'
Hence, Zhào Kuò's mother
begged that Kuò not be held accountable.
This indicates that in ancient times, if a general
had his army defeated outside,
his family would suffer punishment within the state.
Since I started appointing generals for campaigns,
I have only rewarded achievements and not punished transgressions,
which is not a national standard.
Therefore, let it be ordered that when generals embark on campaigns,
those whose armies are defeated will be held accountable,
and those who suffer losses will be dismissed from their official positions and ranks."
In the seventh month of autumn,
he issued an order saying:
"Fifteen years
have passed since the beginning of the chaos and warfare.
Those born since then have not seen the customs of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and deference,
which I deeply lament.
Therefore, let each commandery and kingdom cultivate literary studies.
Counties with over five hundred households should establish schools,
selecting the most outstanding talents from their local areas to teach them,
hoping that the Way of the Former Kings will not be abandoned
and that there will be benefits for the world."
In the eighth month,
Gōng campaigned against Liú Biǎo,
his army stationed at Xīpíng.
When Gōng departed from Yè and headed south,
Tán and Shàng contended for Jìzhōu.
Tán was defeated by Shàng
and fled to defend Píngyuán.
Shàng pressed his attack severely,
so Tán sent Xīn Pí to request surrender and ask for aid.
All the generals were doubtful,
but Xún Yōu advised Gōng to agree.
Gōng then withdrew his army.
In the tenth month of winter,
he arrived at Líyáng,
arranging a marriage between his son Zhěng and Tán.
When Shàng heard that Gōng was heading north,
he abandoned Píngyuán and returned to Yè.
Lǚ Kuàng and Lǚ Xiáng of Dōngpíng rebelled against Shàng,
encamped at Yángpíng,
and led their forces to surrender,
for which they were enfeoffed as marquises.
In the ninth year, in the spring, first month,
he crossed the Jì Hé,
and blocked the Qí Shuǐ into the Bái Gōu to open up a grain route.
In the second month,
Yuán Shàng again attacked Tán,
leaving Sū Yóu and Shěn Pèi to guard Yè.
The Duke advanced his army to the Huán Shuǐ,
and Sū Yóu surrendered.
Upon arrival,
he attacked Yè,
building earth mounds and digging tunnels.
The Chief of Wǔ'ān, Yǐn Kǎi, was stationed at Máo Chéng,
opening up the grain route to Shàngdǎng.
In the summer, fourth month,
the Duke left Cáo Hóng to attack Yè,
and personally led a force to attack Yǐn Kǎi,
defeating him and returning.
Yuán Shàng's general Jǔ Hú was guarding Hándān,
and the Duke attacked and captured it as well.
Hán Fàn, the Magistrate of Yìyáng, and Liáng Qí, the Chief of Shè, surrendered their counties,
and were granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
In the fifth month,
the earth mounds and tunnels were destroyed,
an encirclement was formed,
and the Zhāng Shuǐ was diverted to flood the city;
more than half of the people in the city died of starvation.
In the autumn, seventh month,
Yuán Shàng returned to relieve Yè.
All the generals thought,
"This is an army returning home,
each man will fight for himself,
it is better to avoid them."
The Duke said,
"If Shàng comes via the main road,
we should avoid him;
if he comes along the western mountains,
he will be our captive."
Yuán Shàng indeed came along the western mountains,
and set up camp overlooking the Fǔ Shuǐ.
At night, he sent soldiers to attack the encirclement.
The Duke counter-attacked, defeated them, and put them to flight,
and then encircled Yuán Shàng's camp.
Before the encirclement was complete,
Yuán Shàng was afraid,
and sent the former Inspector of Yùzhōu, Yīn Kuí, and Chén Lín to beg for surrender.
The Duke refused,
and tightened the encirclement.
Yuán Shàng fled at night,
and took refuge in Qí Shān.
The Duke pursued and attacked him.
His generals Mǎ Yán and Zhāng Yǐ, among others, surrendered on the battlefield,
and Yuán Shàng's army suffered a great rout.
Yuán Shàng fled to Zhōngshān.
All his baggage was captured,
including Yuán Shàng's seals, ribbons, credentials, and battle axes.
The Duke had Yuán Shàng's surrendered men show these to their families,
and the people in the city were demoralized.
In the eighth month,
Shěn Pèi's nephew, Róng, opened the eastern gate of the city he was guarding at night to let in troops.
Shěn Pèi counter-attacked,
was defeated,
and captured alive.
He was then executed,
and Yè was pacified.
The Duke personally offered sacrifices at Yuán Shào's tomb,
and wept until his tears flowed;
he comforted Yuán Shào's wife,
returned her family's treasures,
gave her various silks and cotton,
and provided her with grain.
Originally,
Yuán Shào and the Duke had both raised armies.
Yuán Shào asked the Duke,
"If things don't go well,
which region can we rely on?"
The Duke said,
"What do you think?"
Yuán Shào said,
"I would occupy the land south of the Hé,
block the north with Yān and Dài,
and combine the forces of the Róng and Dí tribes.
Then I would face south to contend for the world.
Would that be sufficient?"
The Duke said,
"I would employ the wisdom and strength of the whole world,
and govern it with the Way.
There is nothing that cannot be achieved."
In the ninth month,
an order was issued, saying:
"Héběi has suffered from the calamity of the Yuán clan.
Let them not pay this year's rent and taxes!"
The laws against powerful magnates engaging in annexation were strengthened,
and the common people were joyful.
The Son of Heaven appointed the Duke as Governor of Jìzhōu,
but the Duke declined and returned to Yǎnzhōu.
While the Duke was besieging Yè,
Yuán Tán seized Gānlíng, Ānpíng, Bóhǎi, and Héjiān.
When Yuán Shàng was defeated,
he returned to Zhōngshān.
Yuán Tán attacked him,
and Yuán Shàng fled to Gù'ān,
where he consolidated his forces.
The Duke sent a letter to Yuán Tán,
reproaching him for breaking his promise,
and ended their marriage alliance,
sending his daughter back.
Only then did he advance his army.
Yuán Tán was afraid,
evacuated Píngyuán,
and fled to Nánpí for protection.
In the twelfth month,
the Duke entered Píngyuán,
and gradually pacified the various counties.
In the tenth year, in the spring, first month,
he attacked Yuán Tán,
defeated him,
beheaded Yuán Tán,
and executed his wife and children.
Jìzhōu was pacified.
An order was issued, saying:
"Those who were complicit in the evil of the Yuán clan,
shall be given a fresh start."
The people were forbidden from private vengeance,
and elaborate funerals were prohibited,
all were to conform to the law.
In this month,
Yuán Xī's chief generals Jiāo Chù and Zhāng Nán, among others, rebelled and attacked Yuán Xī and Yuán Shàng.
Yuán Xī and Yuán Shàng fled to the Wūhuán of the Three Commanderies.
Jiāo Chù and others surrendered their counties,
and were enfeoffed as Marquises.
When Yuán Tán was first being suppressed,
people fleeing without breaking the ice were
ordered not to be allowed to surrender.
Shortly after,
a fugitive came to the gate to surrender.
The Duke said to him,
"To listen to you would be to violate the order;
to kill you would be to execute a surrenderer.
Go home and hide yourself well,
do not be captured by officials."
The man departed weeping;
later, he was indeed captured.
In the summer, fourth month,
Zhāng Yàn, the bandit leader of Hēishān, led his more than ten thousand followers to surrender,
and was enfeoffed as a Marquis.
Zhào Dú and Huò Nú of Gù'ān, among others, killed the Inspector of Yōuzhōu and the Administrator of Zhuō Jùn.
The Wūhuán of the Three Commanderies attacked Xiānyú Fǔ at Kuǎngpíng.
In the autumn, eighth month,
the Duke marched against them,
beheaded Zhào Dú and others,
then crossed the Lù Hé to relieve Kuǎngpíng,
and the Wūhuán fled out of the pass.
In the ninth month,
an order was issued, saying:
"Partisanship and forming factions
are abhorred by the ancient sages.
I hear that in Jìzhōu,
fathers and sons belong to different factions,
and mutually slander and praise each other.
In the past, Zhí Bùyí had no elder brother,
yet people said he stole his brother's wife;
Dìwǔ Bóyú married three orphaned women,
yet people said he beat his father-in-law;
Wáng Fèng usurped power,
yet Gǔ Yǒng compared him to Shēn Bó;
Wáng Shāng offered loyal advice,
yet Zhāng Kuāng called him a deviant: these are all cases of calling white black,
deceiving Heaven and misleading the ruler.
I wish to rectify customs,
and if these four evils are not eliminated,
I consider it a disgrace."
In the winter, tenth month,
the Duke returned to Yè.
Originally,
Yuán Shào had appointed his nephew Gāo Gàn as Governor of Bìngzhōu.
When the Duke captured Yè,
Gāo Gàn surrendered,
and was then made Inspector.
When Gāo Gàn heard that the Duke was campaigning against the Wūhuán,
he rebelled with his province,
arrested the Administrator of Shàngdǎng,
and raised an army to guard Húguān Kǒu.
The Duke sent Yuè Jìn and Lǐ Diǎn to attack him,
and Gāo Gàn returned to defend Húguān Chéng.
In the eleventh year, in the spring, first month,
the Duke marched against Gāo Gàn.
When Gāo Gàn heard this,
he left his subordinate general to guard the city,
and fled into the Xiongnú territory,
seeking aid from the Chányú,
but the Chányú did not accept him.
The Duke besieged Húguān for three months,
and captured it.
Gāo Gàn then fled to Jīngzhōu,
where the Commandant of Shàngluò, Wáng Yǎn, captured and beheaded him.
In the eighth month of autumn,
Duke Cáo Cāo campaigned eastward against the pirates led by Guǎn Chéng.
Upon reaching Chúnyú,
he dispatched Lè Jìn and Lǐ Diǎn to attack and defeat them.
Chéng fled into a sea island.
Xiāngbēn, Tán, and Qī of Dōnghǎi were carved out and added to Lángxié.
Chānglǜ Commandery was abolished.
The Wūhuán of the Three Commanderies, taking advantage of the chaos under Heaven,
broke into Yōuzhōu
and seized over one hundred thousand Hàn households.
Yuán Shào had made all their chieftains and powerful figures Xúdān yú,
and gave his own daughters (familial progeny)
to them as wives.
Tàdùn, the Xúdān yú of Liáoxī, was especially strong,
and was favored by Shào.
Therefore, Shàng and Xī (brothers) relied on him
and frequently raided the border regions, causing harm.
The Duke was about to campaign against them,
so he dug canals.
From Hū River, it entered Gū River,
(Gū pronounced gū.)
named Pínglǔqú (Pacifying the Barbarians Canal);
and another from Jūhékǒu (Jū pronounced jū.)
was dug into Lùhé,
named Quánzhōuqú,
to connect to the sea.
In the twelfth month, and then the second month of spring,
the Duke returned to Yè from Chúnyú.
On the dīngchǒu day,
an order was issued, saying:
"I raised an army of righteousness to punish the violent and rebellious
nineteen years ago.
Every campaign has been victorious.
How could this be my achievement alone?
It is the strength of the worthy gentry and officials.
Although the realm is not yet entirely settled,
I ought to settle it together with the worthy gentry and officials.
How can I alone enjoy the fruits of their labor?
How can I be at ease with that!
Therefore, swiftly determine merits and confer enfeoffments."
Thereupon, over twenty meritorious officials were greatly enfeoffed,
all becoming marquises.
The rest received enfeoffments in due order,
and the orphans of those who died in service were also reinstated,
with varying degrees of awards.
When about to campaign north against the Wūhuán of the Three Commanderies,
all the generals said:
"Yuán Shàng
is a mere fugitive.
The barbarians are greedy and disloyal.
How can they be used by Shàng?
If we now campaign deep into their territory,
Liú Bèi will surely persuade Liú Biǎo to attack Xǔ.
If, by any chance, something unexpected happens,
the matter will be regrettable."
Only Guō Jiā reasoned that Biǎo would surely not trust Bèi,
and urged the Duke to proceed.
In the fifth month of summer,
he reached Wúzhōng.
In the seventh month of autumn,
there was a great flood,
and the coastal road was impassable.
Tián Chóu requested to serve as a local guide,
and the Duke followed his advice.
He led the army out through Lúlóngsài.
The road beyond the pass was broken and impassable,
so they cut through mountains and filled valleys for over five hundred lǐ.
Passing by Báitán,
crossing Pínggāng,
and traversing Xiānbēitíng,
they headed east towards Liǔchéng.
Before reaching it by two hundred lǐ,
the barbarians then became aware of their approach.
Shàng, Xī, and Tàdùn, along with Lóubān (Xúdān yú of Liáoxī), Néngchénzhī (Xúdān yú of Yòuběipíng), and others, led tens of thousands of cavalry to intercept the army.
In the eighth month,
they ascended Báilángshān,
and suddenly encountered the barbarians.
Their forces were very numerous.
The Duke's baggage train was at the rear,
and few soldiers were armored.
Those around him were all frightened.
The Duke ascended a height,
and observed that the barbarian formation was not in order.
Thereupon, he unleashed his troops to attack them,
making Zhāng Liáo the vanguard.
The barbarian forces collapsed dramatically,
and Tàdùn and the famous kings below him were beheaded.
Over two hundred thousand Hú and Hàn surrendered.
Sùpúwán (Xúdān yú of Liáodōng), and the powerful figures of Liáoxī and Běipíng,
abandoned their people and fled with Shàng and Xī to Liáodōng.
Their forces still numbered several thousand cavalry.
Initially,
Gōngsūn Kāng, the Grand Administrator of Liáodōng, relied on his distant location and remained disobedient.
After the Duke defeated the Wūhuán,
some advised the Duke to immediately campaign against him,
saying the Shàng brothers could be captured.
The Duke said:
"I am about to make Kāng behead and send the heads of Shàng and Xī.
There is no need for troops."
In the ninth month,
the Duke led his army back from Liǔchéng.
Kāng immediately beheaded Shàng, Xī, Sùpúwán, and others,
and sent their heads.
Some generals asked:
"The Duke returned, and Kāng then beheaded and sent Shàng and Xī.
Why was this?"
The Duke said:
"He has always feared Shàng and the others.
If I pressured him, they would unite their strength.
If I relaxed, they would plot against each other.
That was the natural course of events."
In the eleventh month, he reached Yìshuǐ.
Pǔfùlú, the acting Xúdān yú of the Wūhuán of Dàijùn, and Nàlóu, the acting Xúdān yú of the Wūhuán of Shàngjùn,
brought their famous kings to offer congratulations.
In the first month of spring of the thirteenth year,
the Duke returned to Yè and
constructed the Xuánwǔ Pond to train his navy.
The Hàn court abolished the offices of the Three Excellencies
and established the Chancellor and the Imperial Censor.
In the sixth month of summer,
the Duke was appointed Chancellor.
In the seventh month of autumn,
the Duke campaigned south against Liú Biǎo.
In the eighth month,
Biǎo died.
His son, Cóng, succeeded him,
stationed in Xiāngyáng, while Liú Bèi was stationed in Fán.
In the ninth month,
the Duke arrived at Xīnyě,
and Cóng surrendered.
Bèi fled to Xiàkǒu.
The Duke advanced to Jiānglíng
and issued an order to the officials and common people of Jīngzhōu,
granting them a new beginning.
He then rewarded those in Jīngzhōu who had submitted,
fifteen becoming marquises.
Wén Pìn, Liú Biǎo's grand general, was made Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià,
and was allowed to command his original troops.
Famous scholars from Jīngzhōu, such as Hán Sōng and Dèng Yì, were appointed to office.
Liú Zhāng, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, began to answer calls for service
and sent troops to supply the army.
In the twelfth month,
Sūn Quán attacked Héfèi for Bèi.
The Duke campaigned against Bèi from Jiānglíng,
reaching Bāqiū.
He dispatched Zhāng Xī to relieve Héfèi.
When Quán heard that Xī had arrived,
he fled.
The Duke arrived at Chìbì
and engaged Bèi in battle,
but was unsuccessful.
Thereupon, a great plague broke out,
and many officials and soldiers died.
So he withdrew his army.
Bèi then gained control of Jīngzhōu
and the various commanderies south of the river.
In the third month of spring of the fourteenth year,
the army reached Qiáo.
Light boats were constructed,
and the navy was repaired.
In the seventh month of autumn,
he entered the Huái River from the Wō River,
emerged at Féishuǐ,
and garrisoned Héfèi.
On the xīnwèi day,
an order was issued, saying:
"Since recently,
the army has frequently campaigned.
Some have encountered epidemics,
and officials and soldiers have died and not returned,
leaving their families grieving and desolate,
and the common people scattered.
How could a benevolent person take pleasure in this?
It is out of necessity.
Let those families of the deceased who have no foundation or means to support themselves
not have their stipends cut off by the government.
Let the chief officials care for them, comfort them, and console them,
to fulfill my intentions."
Chief officials for the commanderies and counties of Yángzhōu were appointed,
and the Sháopí agricultural colonies were opened.
In the twelfth month,
the army returned to Qiáo.
In the spring of the fifteenth year,
an order was issued, saying:
"From antiquity, the rulers who received the Mandate of Heaven and those who restored it
have never failed to obtain virtuous and sagely gentlemen to govern the realm with them!
When they obtained the virtuous,
they often did not come from prominent families.
Could it be merely by chance encounters?
It is that those above did not seek them.
Today, the realm is not yet settled,
this is precisely an urgent time to seek the virtuous.
'Méng Gōngchuò would be excellent as an elder in Zhào and Wèi,
but cannot be a Grand Master in Téng and Xuē.'
If only the incorruptible could be employed,
then how could Qí Huán have become hegemon of his age!
Are there perhaps not today those who wear coarse clothes but carry jade (i.e., hide their talent) and fish by the Wèi River?
And are there perhaps not those who 'stole their sister-in-law' and 'accepted gold' but have not yet encountered a Bù Zhī?
You gentlemen, assist me in widely exalting the humble and obscure;
only talent shall be recommended.
I will obtain and employ them."
In winter,
the Bronze Sparrow Terrace (Tóngquè Tái) was constructed.
In the first month of spring of the sixteenth year,
the Son of Heaven commanded Gōng’s (i.e., Cáo Cāo’s) heir-apparent Pī to be the Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng,
established a staff for him,
and made him the Vice Chancellor.
Shāng Yào and others from Tàiyuán rebelled with Dàlíng.
Xiàhóu Yuān and Xú Huǎng were dispatched to besiege and defeat them.
Zhāng Lǔ occupied Hànzhōng.
In the third month,
Zhōng Yáo was dispatched to attack him.
Gōng ordered Yuān and others to go out from Hédōng to meet with Yáo.
At this time, the various generals in Guānzhōng suspected Yáo intended to attack them directly,
so Mǎ Chāo, along with Hán Suì, Yáng Qiū, Lǐ Kān, Chéng Yí, and others, rebelled.
Cáo Rén was dispatched to suppress them.
Chāo and others garrisoned Tóngguān.
Gōng admonished his generals:
"The soldiers west of the pass are elite and fierce,
so hold fast to your fortifications and do not engage them in battle."
In the seventh month of autumn,
Gōng campaigned west,
and camped opposite Chāo and others across the pass.
Gōng held them off urgently,
but secretly dispatched Xú Huǎng, Zhū Líng, and others to cross the Púbǎnjīn at night,
and establish a camp west of the river.
Gōng himself crossed north from Tóngguān.
Before he had fully crossed,
Chāo rushed the boats in a fierce attack.
Staff officer Dīng Fěi then released cattle and horses to bait the rebels.
The rebels scrambled to seize the cattle and horses,
and Gōng was thus able to cross,
and follow the river to construct a covered walkway southward.
The rebels retreated,
and blocked the mouth of the Wèi River.
Gōng then set up many feigned troops,
secretly transported soldiers by boat into the Wèi,
built pontoon bridges,
and at night,
divided his troops to establish camps south of the Wèi.
The rebels attacked the camps at night,
but the hidden troops ambushed and defeated them.
Chāo and others camped south of the Wèi,
and sent an envoy to request a peace treaty by ceding the territory west of the river.
Gōng did not permit it.
In the ninth month,
he advanced his army and crossed the Wèi.
Chāo and others repeatedly challenged them to battle,
but again Gōng did not permit it;
they insisted on ceding land
and requested to send hostages.
Gōng followed Jiǎ Xǔ’s plan
and feigned agreement.
Hán Suì requested to meet with Gōng.
Gōng and Suì's father were of the same age in their being selected as Xiàolián,
and Gōng was also a contemporary of Suì.
Therefore, they met on horseback and conversed for a long time,
without discussing military affairs,
but only speaking of old acquaintances in the capital,
clapping hands and laughing joyfully.
After they parted,
Chāo and others asked Suì:
"What did Gōng say?"
Suì replied:
"He said nothing."
Chāo and others became suspicious of him.
Another day,
Gōng again wrote a letter to Suì,
with many deletions and alterations,
as if Suì had revised and corrected it;
Chāo and others grew even more suspicious of Suì.
Gōng then set a day for a decisive battle,
first sending light troops to provoke them.
After battling for a long time,
he then unleashed his elite cavalry to attack from both sides,
greatly defeating them,
and beheading Chéng Yí, Lǐ Kān, and others.
Suì, Chāo, and others fled to Liángzhōu.
Yáng Qiū fled to Āndìng.
Guānzhōng was pacified.
Some generals asked Gōng:
"Initially,
the rebels guarded Tóngguān,
and the road north of the Wèi was blocked.
Why did you not attack Féngyì from Hédōng, but instead held Tóngguān,
and then spent many days before crossing north?
What was the reason?"
Gōng replied:
"The rebels were guarding Tóngguān.
If I had entered Hédōng,
the rebels would certainly have moved to guard all the fords,
making the Xi River impossible to cross.
Therefore, I massed troops towards Tóngguān;
when the rebels sent all their forces to guard the south,
the defenses of the Xi River were weakened,
thus the two generals were able to take the Xi River at will.
Then I led my army to cross north.
The rebels could not contend with me for the Xi River
because of the armies of the two generals there.
Linking chariots and erecting palisades
to form a covered walkway southward,
this was both to make ourselves impregnable
and to show weakness.
Crossing the Wèi to build a strong fort,
and not emerging when the barbarians arrived,
this was to make them arrogant;
thus the rebels did not build camps but sought to cede land.
My agreeing to their terms
was to comply with their wishes,
to make them feel secure and unprepared,
and thereby to conserve the strength of my soldiers and officers.
To strike them suddenly,
this is what is called 'a sudden thunderclap leaves no time to cover the ears.'
The changes in military strategy
are indeed not confined to one path."
At first,
whenever a division of the rebels arrived,
Gōng would show joy.
After the rebels were defeated,
the generals asked him the reason.
Gōng replied:
"Guānzhōng is vast and remote.
If the rebels had each relied on dangerous terrain,
campaigning against them
would not have allowed pacification in less than one or two years.
Now they have all gathered.
Although their numbers are great,
none submit to each other,
and the army has no true leader.
They can be eliminated in one swift blow,
making the task relatively easy.
This is why I rejoiced."
In the tenth month of winter,
the army campaigned north from Cháng'ān against Yáng Qiū,
besieging Āndìng.
Qiū surrendered,
his titles were restored,
and he was left to pacify his people.
In the twelfth month,
he returned from Āndìng,
leaving Xiàhóu Yuān to garrison Cháng'ān.
In the first month of spring of the seventeenth year,
Gōng returned to Yè.
The Son of Heaven commanded that Gōng be allowed to perform the ritual bow without his name being called,
not hasten when entering court,
and ascend the hall wearing his sword and shoes,
following the precedent of Xiāo Hé.
Mǎ Chāo’s remaining followers, Liáng Xīng and others, were garrisoned in Lántián.
Xiàhóu Yuān was sent to attack and pacify them.
Dàngyīn, Cháogē, and Línglǜ from Hénèi commandery;
Wèiguó, Dùnqū, Dōngwǔyáng, and Fāgàn from Dōngjùn commandery;
Yǐngtáo, Qǔzhōu, and Nánhé from Jùlù commandery;
Rènchéng from Guǎngpíng commandery;
and Xiāngguó, Hándān, and Yìyáng from Zhào commandery were detached to augment Wèijùn commandery.
In the tenth month of winter,
Gōng campaigned against Sūn Quán.
In the first month of spring of the eighteenth year,
the army advanced to Rúxūkǒu,
attacked and broke Quán’s camp west of the river,
and captured Quán’s commander Gōngsūn Yáng.
Then he led his army back.
An imperial edict merged fourteen prefectures
and restored the Nine Provinces.
In the fourth month of summer,
he arrived at Yè.
On the day Bǐngshēn of the fifth month,
the Son of Heaven sent the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Xī Lǜ, bearing the imperial staff, to issue an edict formally appointing Gōng as Wèi Gōng,
saying: "I, being without virtue,
suffered early from misfortune and calamity,
displaced to the western lands,
and moved to Táng and Wèi.
At this time,
like a tattered banner,
the ancestral temples lacked sacrifices,
and the altars of soil and grain had no proper position;
many villains coveted power,
dividing the various Huá (i.e., China).
Among the people of the entire realm,
I had none,
and thus the mandate of my High Ancestor was about to fall to the ground.
I therefore
Rising early and napping,
grief and dread shook My heart.
I said:
“My ancestors and My father,
My capable and upright predecessors,
who among them could have helped My person?”
Then Heaven's will was inspired,
and it brought forth
the prime minister (chéngxiàng),
who guards and governs Our imperial house (huángjiā),
and greatly helps in times of difficulty.
I truly rely on him.
Now I shall bestow upon you the rites and ceremonies;
listen respectfully to My command.
In the past, when Dǒng Zhuó first stirred up national calamity,
the regional lords (qúnhòu) abandoned their positions to plot against the royal house (wángshì).
You then stepped forward,
first initiating military action.
This was your loyalty to this
dynasty (cháo).
Later, when the Yellow Turbans (huángjīn) rebelled and overturned the natural order,
invading Our three provinces (sānzhōu)
and extending their reach to the common people,
you again cut them down to pacify the Eastern Summer (dōngxià).
This, too, was your merit.
When Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng usurped authority and gave commands,
you then initiated a punitive expedition,
successfully overcoming their rebellion,
and consequently moved the capital to Xǔdū,
creating Our imperial domain (jīngjī).
You established officials and designated sacrificial sites,
without losing the old customs,
whereby Heaven, Earth, ghosts, and spirits found peace.
This, too, was your merit.
When Yuán Shù usurped power and rebelled,
running rampant in Huáinán,
he was awed and deterred by your divine might,
and you used your great and manifest strategies.
In the battle of Qíyáng,
Qiáo Ruí was decapitated.
Your formidable might advanced south,
and Shù consequently perished.
This, too, was your merit.
Turning the spears to campaign in the east,
Lǚ Bù was executed.
While returning
in your chariot,
Zhāng Yáng died,
Suī Gù confessed his crimes,
and Zhāng Xiù submitted.
This, too, was your merit.
When Yuán Shào rebelled against the natural order,
plotting to endanger the state (shèjì),
relying on
his numerous forces,
he raised troops to invade internally.
At this time,
the royal army (wángshī) was small and weak,
the world was disheartened,
and no one had firm resolve.
You upheld the great principles,
your sincerity piercing the white sun.
You unleashed your
martial fury,
employed your divine strategies,
and reached Guāndù,
annihilating the enemy hordes,
thereby saving Our state (guójiā) from perilous collapse.
This, too, was your merit.
Leading the army across the Hóng
River (hé),
you pacified and settled the four provinces.
Yuán Tán and Gāo Gàn
were both executed.
Sea pirates fled,
and the Black Mountain (hēishān) bandits submitted.
This, too, was your merit.
The three Wūhuán tribes
had caused chaos for two generations.
Yuán Shàng relied on them,
forcibly occupying the region north of the frontier.
You tied horses and hung chariots (over precipices),
and in a single campaign, you destroyed them.
This, too, was your merit.
Liú Biǎo was treacherous
and failed to provide
tribute services.
When the royal army (wángshī) set out,
your prestige and might preceded it.
A hundred cities (bǎichéng) and eight commanderies (bājùn)
folded their arms and knelt in submission.
This, too, was your merit.
Mǎ Chāo and Chéng Yí,
in their evil alliance,
occupied the banks of the Hé (Yellow River) and Tóng (Pass),
seeking to achieve their desires.
You annihilated them south of the Wèi (River),
presenting tens of thousands of severed heads.
Thus, the border regions were pacified,
and the Rong and Di (barbarians) were reconciled.
This, too, was your merit.
The Xiānbēi and Dīnglíng,
through multiple interpreters, arrived.
The Chányú (shànyú) and the báiyú (rulers of allied tribes)
requested to be appointed officials and perform their duties.
This, too, was your merit.
You have the merit of pacifying the world,
and furthermore, your manifest virtue
spreads throughout the realm (hǎinèi),
proclaiming excellent customs.
You widely disseminated diligent teachings,
and carefully managed punishments and prisons.
Officials have no harsh policies,
and the people harbor no evil intentions.
You honored and elevated the imperial
clan (dìzú),
and restored interrupted lineages.
Former virtues and past merits
were all duly recognized.
Even Yī Yǐn, who reached unto August Heaven,
and Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng), whose light shone across the four seas,
compared to you, are insignificant.
I have heard that the former kings (xiānwáng) concurrently established illustrious virtues,
bestowing upon them lands,
and dividing among them populations,
exalting their honors and insignia,
and providing them with ritual objects,
thereby protecting the royal house (wángshì)
and assisting
its generations.
In the time of King Chéng of Zhōu (Zhōu Chéng),
when Guǎn and Cài caused unrest,
learning from the difficulty and remembering past merits,
he then ordered Duke Kāng of Shào (Shào Kāng Gōng) to grant Duke Tàigōng of Qí (Qí Tàigōng) authority
from the east to the sea,
from the west
to the Hé (Yellow River),
from the south to Mùlíng,
and from the north to Wúdì.
The five marquises (wǔhóu) and nine earls (jiǔbó)
were indeed permitted to be levied by him,
and he inherited the position of Grand Tutor (tàishī) for generations,
to serve as a bulwark in the east.
And when
King Xiāng (Xiāng Wáng) reigned,
there were also the Chǔ people who did not perform their royal duties.
He again commanded Duke Wén of Jìn (Jìn Wén Gōng) to be elevated as a marquis and earl,
bestowing upon him two chariots, tiger warriors (hǔbēn), battle-axes (fūyuè), black millet wine (jùchàng), and bows and arrows,
greatly opening up
Nányáng,
to be the permanent covenant lord (méngzhǔ).
Therefore, the Zhōu house (Zhōu shì) did not collapse;
it relied on these two states.
Now, you have displayed great and manifest virtue,
clearly protecting My person,
responding to Heaven's mandate,
and propagating your grand achievements.
Across the nine regions (jiǔyù),
none have failed to follow and obey.
Your merits are higher than those of Yī and Zhōu (Duke of Zhōu),
yet your reward is lower than those of Qí and Jìn.
I am greatly ashamed of this.
I, with My insignificant
person,
am placed above the myriad people.
Forever thinking of the difficulties,
it is like treading on a deep abyss of ice.
Were it not for your rescue,
I would be incapable.
Now, I grant you the ten commanderies of Hédōng,
Hénèi, Wèijùn, Zhàoguó, Zhōngshān, Chángshān, Jùlù, Ānpíng, Gānlíng, and Píngyuán in Jìzhōu,
and enfeoff you as Duke of Wèi (Wèi Gōng).
I bestow upon you black soil,
wrapped in white grass;
and I grant you a turtle shell for divination,
to establish a grand altar to the gods of earth and grain (zhǒngshè).
In the past, in the Zhōu house (Zhōu shì),
Duke Bì (Bì Gōng) and Duke Máo (Máo Gōng) served as high ministers (qīngzuǒ) within,
while Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng) and Duke of Shào (Shào Gōng) served as Grand Tutors and Grand Protectors, going out to be the two
regional lords (bó).
You are indeed suited for both internal and external responsibilities;
therefore, you shall continue to lead Jìzhōu as governor (mù) in your capacity as prime minister (chéngxiàng).
Furthermore, I confer upon you the Nine Bestowals (jiǔxī).
Listen respectfully to My command.
Because you
manage the rites and laws,
serving as a model for the people,
enabling them to live securely in their occupations,
without changing their aspirations,
I therefore bestow upon you one grand chariot (dàlù) and one war chariot (rónglù),
and two teams of black stallions.
You encourage
devote yourselves to the fundamentals,
the diligent people labor from dawn to dusk.
Grain and silks are abundantly accumulated,
and great enterprises flourish.
Therefore, We bestow upon you, Lord, the robes of a Gǔnmiǎn,
accompanied by scarlet slippers.
You, Lord, earnestly uphold
humility and deference,
thereby inspiring the people to act.
The young and old are courteous,
and those above and below are all harmonious.
Therefore, We bestow upon you, Lord, the music of Xuānxián,
and the dance of Liùyì.
You, Lord, assist in propagating transforming influences,
which
spread to the four directions.
Distant peoples change their ways,
and Huáxià is enriched.
Therefore, We bestow upon you, Lord, a vermilion gate for your residence.
You, Lord, refine your wisdom and foresight,
considering what is difficult for the Emperor.
You appoint officials according to their talents and employ the worthy,
and all good men are certainly promoted.
Therefore, We bestow upon you, Lord, a Nàbì for ascending.
You, Lord, hold the balance of the state,
maintaining a serious demeanor in the center.
The slightest evil,
none is not suppressed and repelled.
Therefore, We bestow
upon you, Lord, three hundred Hǔbēn warriors.
You, Lord, diligently enforce the heavenly punishments,
making known the guilt of offenders.
Those who violate regulations and disrupt order,
none are not executed.
Therefore, We bestow upon you, Lord, one Fúyuè
each.
You, Lord, soar like a dragon and gaze like a tiger,
surveying the eight directions.
You suppress and punish rebellious factions,
and break the enemy's spirit throughout the four seas.
Therefore, We bestow upon you, Lord, one crimson bow,
one hundred crimson arrows,
ten black bows,
and
one thousand black arrows.
You, Lord, take gentleness and respect as your foundation,
and filial piety and brotherly love as your virtues.
Your intelligence, trustworthiness, and profound sincerity
have moved Our thoughts.
Therefore, We bestow upon you, Lord, one jug of Jùchàng,
accompanied by a Guīzàn.
The state of Wèi is to establish a chancellor and below him, all the high ministers and various officials,
all following the system of the vassal kings in the early Hàn dynasty.
Go forth with reverence,
and respectfully obey Our command!
Examine and care for your
people,
and at all times fulfill your many duties,
so as to complete your illustrious virtue,
and respond to and glorify the excellent mandate of Our High Ancestor!
In autumn, the seventh month,
the altars of Wèi (Shèjì) and the ancestral temple (Zōngmiào) were first established.
The Son of Heaven betrothed the Duke's three daughters to be Guìrén,
the youngest to await her age in the state.
In the ninth month,
Jīnhǔtái was constructed,
and a canal was dug to divert the Zhāng River into the Báigōu to connect with the Yellow River.
In winter, the tenth month,
Wèijùn was divided into eastern and western parts,
and a Dūwèi was appointed for each.
In the eleventh month,
Shàngshū, Shìzhōng, and the Six Ministers were first established.
Mǎ Chāo was in Hànyáng,
again causing trouble with the Qiāng and Hú.
The Dī king, Qiānwàn, rebelled and joined Chāo,
stationing his forces at Xīngguó.
Xiàhóu Yuān was sent to suppress him.
In the nineteenth year, spring, the first month,
the Jìtián was first ploughed.
Zhào Qú of Nán'ān and Yǐn Fèng of Hànyáng, among others, attacked Chāo,
executing his wife and children.
Chāo fled to Hànzhōng.
Hán Suì moved to Jīnchéng,
entered the territory of the Dī king Qiānwàn,
and led more than ten thousand Qiāng and Hú cavalry to battle Xiàhóu Yuān.
He attacked,
and was greatly defeated.
Suì fled to Xīpíng.
Yuān and his generals attacked Xīngguó,
and massacred its inhabitants.
Āndōng and Yǒngyáng Commandaries were abolished.
When Wúqiū Xìng, the Administrator of Āndìng, was about to take office,
the Duke admonished him, saying:
"If the Qiāng
and Hú wish to communicate with Zhōngguó,
they should naturally send people here.
Be very careful not to send anyone there.
Good people are hard to find,
and they will certainly instruct the Qiāng and Hú to make unreasonable requests,
thereby seeking self-interest.
If you do not comply, it will be seen as disregarding the wishes of foreign tribes;
if you comply, it will be of no benefit."
When Xìng arrived,
he sent Commander Fàn Líng to the Qiāng territory.
Líng indeed instructed the Qiāng
to request themselves to be appointed as subordinate Dūwèi.
The Duke said:
"I foresaw that it would be so.
This is not because I am a sage,
but merely because I have experienced many more matters."
In the third month,
the Son of Heaven granted the Duke of Wèi a position above that of all other vassal kings,
and bestowed upon him a golden seal,
a red sash, and a Yuǎnyóuguān.
In autumn, the seventh month,
the Duke launched an expedition against Sūn Quán.
Earlier,
Sòng Jiàn of Lǒngxī declared himself King Pínghàn of Héshǒu,
gathered a multitude in Báohǎn,
changed the era name,
and established a hundred officials,
for over thirty years.
Xiàhóu Yuān was sent from Xīngguó to suppress him.
In winter, the tenth month,
Báohǎn was sacked,
Jiàn was executed,
and Liángzhōu was pacified.
The Duke returned from Héféi.
In the eleventh month,
Empress Fú Shì of Hàn was accused of having written a letter to her father, the former Commandant of Cavalry, Wán,
stating that the Emperor resented the Duke because of Dǒng Chéng's execution,
with words that were extremely offensive.
When this was discovered,
the Empress was deposed and died,
and all her brothers were executed.
In the twelfth month,
the Duke arrived at Mèngjīn.
The Son of Heaven commanded the Duke to establish a Máotóu,
and to place bells and bell-stands in his palace.
On the Yǐwèi day,
an order was issued, stating:
"Indeed, men of good conduct may not necessarily be capable of advancement,
and men capable of advancement may not necessarily possess good conduct.
Was Chén Píng truly of upright conduct?
Was Sū Qín truly trustworthy?
Yet Chén Píng established the Hàn dynasty,
and Sū Qín saved the weak state of Yān.
From this, it can be said,
if a man has a particular shortcoming,
how can he be discarded?
If officials consider this principle clearly,
then no talent will be left neglected,
and no official duties will be left undone."
It also said:
"Indeed, punishment [Xíng]
is the very life of the common people.
Yet some of those in the army who administer justice are not the right persons,
and are entrusted with matters of life and death for the three armies.
We greatly fear this.
Therefore, select those who are clear and knowledgeable in law and reason,
and let them be responsible for administering justice."
Thereupon, Lǐcáo Yuànshǔ were established.
In the twentieth year, spring, the first month,
the Son of Heaven elevated the Duke's second daughter to be Empress.
The commandaries of Yúnzhōng, Dìngxiāng, Wǔyuán, and Shuòfāng were abolished.
Each commandary was to have one county administering its people,
and these were combined to form the Xīnxīng Commandary.
In the third month,
Gōng marched west to campaign against Zhāng Lǔ.
Upon reaching Chéncāng,
he intended to enter Dī from Wǔdū.
The Dī people blocked the road,
so he first dispatched Zhāng Hé, Zhū Líng, and others to attack and break through.
In the summer, fourth month,
Gōng departed from Chéncāng, passed through Sàn Guān,
and reached Héchí.
The Dī King Dòu Mào, with over ten thousand men,
relied on the treacherous terrain and refused to submit.
In the fifth month,
Gōng attacked and slaughtered them.
The generals from Xīpíng and Jīnchéng, Qū Yǎn, Jiǎng Shí, and others together beheaded Hán Suí and sent his head.
In the autumn, seventh month,
Gōng arrived at Yángpíng.
Zhāng Lǔ sent his younger brother Wèi and general Yáng Áng and others to hold Yángpíng Guān,
building fortifications along the mountains for over ten *lǐ*.
Unable to overcome them in attack,
Gōng then withdrew his army.
When the bandits saw the main army retreating,
their defenses became lax.
