Gōng secretly dispatched Xiè and Gāo Zuò and others to take advantage of the treacherous terrain and launch a night raid,
greatly defeating them.
They beheaded their general Yáng Rèn,
and advanced to attack Wèi.
Wèi and others fled in the night,
and Lǔ retreated in disarray to Bāzhōng.
Gōng's army entered Nánzhèng,
seizing all of Lǔ's treasuries and precious goods.
Bā and Hàn all surrendered.
Hànníng Commandery was renamed Hànzhōng;
Anjáng and Xīchéng of Hànzhōng were divided to form Xīchéng Commandery,
with a Grand Administrator appointed;
Xī and Shàngyōng Commanderies were divided,
with Commandery Commandants appointed.
In the eighth month,
Sūn Quán besieged Héféi,
but Zhāng Liáo and Lǐ Diǎn attacked and defeated him.
In the ninth month,
the Bā Seven-Surnamed Yi King Pú Hú and the Cóngyì Marquis Dù Huò led the Bā Yi and Cóng people to submit.
Consequently, Bājùn was divided,
with Pú Hú made Grand Administrator of Bādōng,
and Dù Huò made Grand Administrator of Bāxī,
both enfeoffed as Marquises of a Fief.
The Emperor ordered Gōng to act on his behalf to enfeoff and appoint marquises and administrators.
In the winter, tenth month,
the ranks from Mínghào Hóu down to Wǔ Dàfū were first established.
Together with the old ranks of Lièhóu and Guānnèi Hóu, there were six ranks in total,
to reward military merits.
In the eleventh month,
Lǔ, with his remaining forces, surrendered from Bāzhōng.
Lǔ and his five sons were all enfeoffed as Marquises of a Fief.
Liú Bèi attacked Liú Zhāng,
seized Yìzhōu,
and then occupied Bāzhōng;
Zhāng Hé was sent to attack him.
In the twelfth month,
Gōng returned from Nánzhèng,
leaving Xiàhóu Yuān to garrison Hànzhōng.
In the spring of the twenty-first year, second month,
Gōng returned to Yè.
On the *rén yín* day of the third month,
Gōng personally plowed the ceremonial field.
In the summer, fifth month,
the Emperor promoted Gōng to the rank of Wèi Wáng.
Pǔ Fùlú, the acting Chányú of the Wūhuán of Dàijùn, and their marquis kings came to court.
The Emperor ordered a royal daughter to be a princess,
with a bath-and-food fief.
In the autumn, seventh month,
Hūchúquán, the Southern Chányú of the Xiōngnú, brought his eminent kings to court.
They were treated with the courtesy due to guests,
and then remained in Wèi,
with Yòuxián Wáng Qù Bēi sent to supervise their state.
In the eighth month,
Dàlǐ Zhōng Yáo was made Xiàngguó.
In the winter, tenth month,
the army was mustered,
and then a campaign was launched against Sūn Quán.
In the eleventh month, the army reached Qiáo.
In the spring of the twenty-second year, first month,
the King's army was stationed at Jūcháo.
In the second month,
the army advanced and garrisoned Hǎoxī on the west bank of the Jiāng.
Quán built fortifications at Rúxūkǒu to resist,
so the King pressed his attack,
and Quán retreated.
In the third month,
the King withdrew his army,
leaving Xiàhóu Dūn, Cáo Rén, Zhāng Liáo, and others to garrison Jūcháo.
In the summer, fourth month,
the Emperor ordered the King to display the Emperor's banners and insignia,
and to be escorted with royal clearings when coming and going.
In the fifth month,
the Pàn Gōng was built.
In the sixth month,
Jūnshī Huá Xīn was made Yùshǐ Dàfū.
In the winter, tenth month,
the Emperor ordered the King to wear a crown with twelve pendants,
ride in a golden-rooted carriage,
drawn by six horses,
and have five seasonal outrider carriages,
and appointed Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng Pī as the Crown Prince of Wèi.
Liú Bèi sent Zhāng Fēi, Mǎ Chāo, Wú Lán, and others to garrison Xiàbiàn;
Cáo Hóng was sent to resist them.
In the spring of the twenty-third year, first month,
Hàn Tàiyī Lìng Jí Běn, along with Shǎofǔ Gěng Jì and Sīzhí Wéi Huàng and others, rebelled,
attacked Xǔ,
and burned the camp of Chéngxiàng Zhǎngshǐ Wáng Bì.
Wáng Bì, along with Yǐngchuān Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiàng Yán Kuāng, suppressed and beheaded them.
Cáo Hóng defeated Wú Lán,
beheading his generals Rèn Kuí and others.
In the third month,
Zhāng Fēi and Mǎ Chāo fled to Hànzhōng.
Qiáng Duān of the Yīnpíng Dī beheaded Wú Lán
and sent his head.
In the summer, fourth month,
Wúchén Dī and others from the Wūhuán of Dàijùn and Shànggǔ rebelled.
Yānlíng Hóu Zhāng was sent to attack and defeat them.
In the sixth month,
an order stated:
"In ancient times, those who were buried
were always placed in barren and desolate land.
His own mausoleum is planned to be on the western plateau of the Xīmén Bào Shrine,
using the high ground as its base,
neither sealed nor planted with trees.
According to the *Zhōu Lǐ*, the supervisor of tombs managed the land for public graves.
All marquises were located to the left and right in front,
while ministers and grandees were behind;
the Hàn system also referred to these as 'accompanying mausoleums'.
Those of his grandees, ministers, and meritorious generals
should accompany the longevity mausoleum.
Its burial ground should be greatly expanded
to accommodate them sufficiently."
In the autumn, seventh month,
the army was mustered,
and then marched west to campaign against Liú Bèi.
In the ninth month,
the army reached Cháng'ān.
In the winter, tenth month,
the Wǎn defending general Hóu Yīn and others rebelled,
seized the Grand Administrator of Nányáng,
kidnapped and plundered officials and commoners,
and held Wǎn.
Initially,
Cáo Rén was campaigning against Guān Yǔ,
stationed at Fánchéng.
This month, Rén was ordered to besiege Wǎn.
In the spring of the twenty-fourth year, first month,
Rén stormed Wǎn,
beheading Hóu Yīn.
Xiàhóu Yuān battled Liú Bèi at Yángpíng,
and was killed by Bèi.
In the third month,
the King departed from Cháng'ān through Xié Gǔ,
stationed his army at Zhēyào overlooking Hànzhōng,
and then reached Yángpíng.
Liú Bèi, relying on the treacherous terrain, resisted defensively.
In the summer, fifth month,
the army was withdrawn to Cháng'ān.
In the autumn, seventh month,
his consort, Lady Biàn, was made Queen.
Yú Jìn was sent to assist Cáo Rén in attacking Guān Yǔ.
In the eighth month,
the Hàn River overflowed,
flooding Yú Jìn's army.
The army was destroyed,
Yú Jìn was captured by Guān Yǔ,
who then besieged Cáo Rén.
Xú Huàng was sent to rescue him.
In the ninth month,
Xiàngguó Zhōng Yáo was dismissed for his subordinate Xīcáo Yuàn Wèi Fèng's rebellion.
In the winter, tenth month,
the army returned to Luòyáng.
Sūn Quán sent an envoy to submit a memorial,
offering to campaign against Guān Yǔ.
The King marched south from Luòyáng to campaign against Guān Yǔ.
Before he arrived,
Xú Huàng attacked Guān Yǔ,
defeated him,
and Guān Yǔ fled,
lifting the siege on Cáo Rén.
The King's army was at Mópí.
In the spring of the twenty-fifth year, first month,
he arrived at Luòyáng.
Sūn Quán attacked and beheaded Guān Yǔ,
and sent his head.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
the king died in Luòyáng
at the age of sixty-six.
His dying injunctions said:
"The world is not yet stable,
so the ancient rites cannot yet be followed.
Once the burial is complete,
all are to remove their mourning attire.
Those who are leading troops or garrisoned
are not to leave their garrisons or divisions.
Officials are each to diligently perform their duties.
For the interment, use everyday clothes,
and do not include gold, jade, or precious treasures."
He was posthumously granted the title Wǔ Wáng.
In the second month, on the *dīngmǎo* day,
he was buried at Gāolíng.
The commentary says: At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
the world was in great chaos,
and powerful heroes rose up simultaneously.
Yuán Shào, in particular, dominated four provinces
and was so mighty that none could rival him.
Tàizǔ (Wǔ Dì) planned and strategized,
conquering the realm.
He embraced the methods of Shēn Bùhài and Shāng Yāng,
and encompassed the extraordinary stratagems of Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ.
He appointed officials and assigned talents
according to their individual capabilities.
He suppressed personal feelings and relied on calculations,
not dwelling on past grievances.
Ultimately, he was able to control the imperial machinery
and achieve great accomplishments,
solely because his brilliant strategies were superior.
Indeed, he can be called an extraordinary person,
a hero surpassing his age.
Emperor Wén's taboo name was Pī,
and his courtesy name was Zǐhuán.
He was the Crown Prince of Emperor Wǔ.
In the winter of the fourth year of Zhōngpíng,
he was born in Qiáo.
In the sixteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
he was made Commandant of the Palace Gate and Vice Chancellor.
In the twenty-second year,
he was established as the Crown Prince of Wèi.
When Tàizǔ died,
he succeeded him as Chancellor and King of Wèi.
He honored the Queen as the Queen Dowager.
The twenty-fifth year of Jiàn'ān was changed to the first year of Yánkāng.
In the second month of the first year,
on the *wángxū* day,
Jiǎ Xǔ, the Grand Master of the Palace, was made Grand Commandant;
Huá Xīn, the Imperial Censor, was made Chancellor;
and Wáng Lǎng, the Chief Justice, was made Imperial Censor.
Four Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate and four Palace Attendants were appointed.
Eunuchs serving as officials were not allowed to exceed the rank of director of any office.
This was recorded in a golden tablet
and stored in a stone chamber.
Originally,
in the fifth year of Xīpíng of the Hàn dynasty,
a yellow dragon was seen in Qiáo.
Guānglù Dàfū Qiáo Xuán asked the Grand Astrologer Shàn Yáng:
"What omen is this?"
Yáng replied:
"Later, a king will rise in this state.
Within fifty years,
it will be seen again.
Celestial events always have corresponding phenomena;
this is its manifestation."
Yīn Dēng of Nèi Huáng silently recorded this.
Forty-five years later,
Dēng was still alive.
In the third month,
a yellow dragon was seen in Qiáo.
Upon hearing of it, Dēng said:
"Shàn Yáng's words,
are they not now proven true!"
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Xiàhóu Dūn, the former General of the Vanguard, was made Grand General.
The *Huì Mò* and *Fúyú* Chányú, and the kings of *Yānqí* and *Yútián*, all sent envoys to offer tribute.
In the summer, on the *dīngsì* day of the fourth month,
Ráozhōuyán County reported seeing a white pheasant.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
Grand General Xiàhóu Dūn died.
In the fifth month, on the *wùyín* day,
the Son of Heaven commanded the King to posthumously honor his imperial ancestor, the Grand Commandant, as Grand King,
and Lady Dīng as Grand Queen.
His son, Ruì, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔdé.
In this month,
the mountain bandits Zhèng Gān and Wáng Zhào from Fèngyì led their followers to surrender,
and were all enfeoffed as marquises.
Huáng Huá of Jiǔquán and Zhāng Jìn of Zhāngyè, among others, seized their respective governors and rebelled.
Sū Zé, the Governor of Jīnchéng, attacked and
executed Jìn.
Huá surrendered.
In the sixth month, on the *xīnhài* day,
troops were drilled in the eastern suburbs.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the expedition to the south began.
In the autumn, on the *gēngchén* day of the seventh month,
an order was issued, stating:
"Xuānyuán had the 'Clear Terrace' assembly,
and Fàngxūn had the 'Crossroads Chamber' inquiry,
all for the purpose of widely seeking opinions from below.
All officials and functionaries,
you must diligently offer earnest remonstrances in your respective duties.
Generals and commanders should present military laws;
court gentlemen should clarify systems and regulations;
regional governors should explain governmental affairs;
and scholars should examine the Six Arts.
I will examine all of them."
Sūn Quán sent an envoy to offer tribute.
Shǔ general Méng Dá led his forces to surrender.
The Dī King Yáng Pú of Wǔdū led his clansmen to pledge allegiance,
settling in Hànyáng Commandery.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the army arrived at Qiáo.
A grand feast was held for the Six Armies and the elders and common people of Qiáo in the eastern part of the city.
In the eighth month,
Shíyì County reported phoenixes gathering.
In the winter, on the *guǐmǎo* day of the tenth month,
an order was issued, stating:
"Among the generals who went on expeditions,
some of the fallen soldiers have not yet been collected and buried.
I am deeply saddened by this.
Inform the commanderies and states to provide coffins and to conduct the funeral rites,
(The character *huì* is pronounced *wèi*.)
sending them to their families.
The government will arrange sacrifices."
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
the King traveled to Qǔlí.
The Hàn Emperor, seeing that the popular sentiment was with Wèi,
summoned his high ministers and noblemen,
and offered sacrifices at the high temple.
He sent Zhāng Yīn, concurrently Imperial Censor, bearing the imperial staff and seal to formally abdicate.
The edict stated:
"Listen, O King of Wèi! In ancient times, Emperor Yáo abdicated to Yú Shùn,
and Shùn likewise bestowed it upon Yǔ.
Heaven's mandate is not constant;
it only devolves upon the virtuous.
The Hàn Way has declined,
and the world has lost its order.
Down to my own person,
great chaos has prevailed.
Numerous villains have committed acts of rebellion,
overturning the realm.
It is thanks to the divine might of Wǔ Wáng
that this difficulty across the four directions was saved.
He cleansed our central land,
thereby securing our ancestral temples.
It is not I alone who benefited,
but the entire realm that received his blessings.
Now, O King, you respectfully continue the previous achievements,
bringing glory to your virtues,
expanding the great enterprise of culture and martial prowess,
and illuminating the grand achievements of your father.
Imperial spirits send auspicious signs,
and gods and men declare omens.
You are truly a bright talent,
granted this mandate by your mentor.
All say that your measure conforms to that of Yú Shùn.
Following our ancient Tang precedent,
I respectfully cede my position to you.
Alas!
Heaven's calendar count rests upon your person.
Hold fast to the Mean,
and Heaven's blessing will last eternally.
May you respectfully follow the great ritual,
receive homage from these myriad states,
and reverently uphold Heaven's mandate."
Thereupon, an altar was built at Fányáng.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the King ascended the altar and took the throne,
with all officials in attendance.
When the ceremony was complete,
he descended the altar,
observed the burning sacrifice to complete the ritual, and returned.
Yánkāng was changed to Huángchū,
and a general amnesty was declared.
In the eleventh month, on the day *Guǐyǒu*, of the first year of the Huángchū era,
the ten thousand households of Shānyáng Commandery, Hénèi, were granted to the Hàn Emperor, who was enfeoffed as Shānyáng Gōng.
He was to observe the Hàn calendar,
perform suburban sacrifices with the rites due to the Son of Heaven,
and in his memorials to the throne, he was not to address himself as a subject.
When there were matters concerning the Imperial Ancestral Temple in the capital,
he was to be sent sacrificial meat.
His four sons were enfeoffed as列侯 (Lièhóu, marquises of various ranks).
The imperial ancestor Tàiwáng (Grand King) was posthumously honored as Tàihuángdì (Grand Emperor),
and the late Wǔwáng (King Wǔ) as Wǔhuángdì (Emperor Wǔ).
The empress dowager was honored as Huángtàihòu (Empress Dowager).
All adult males were granted one rank of nobility,
and those who succeeded their fathers, or were filial and brotherly and diligent in farming, were granted two ranks.
The Hàn feudal lords were made Chóngdé Hóu,
and the 列侯 (Lièhóu) were made Guānzhōng Hóu.
Fányáng Tíng in Yǐngyīn was renamed Fánchāng Xiàn.
The enfeoffments and promotions varied in degree.
Xiàngguó (Chancellor) was changed to Sītú (Minister of the Masses),
Yùshǐ Dàfū (Grandee Secretary) to Sīkōng (Minister of Works),
Fèngcháng (Grand Master of Ceremonies) to Tàicháng (Grand Minister of Ceremonies),
Lángzhōng Lìng (Chief of the Palace Gentlemen) to Guānglù Xūn (Superintendent of the Palace Gate),
Dàlǐ (Grand Judge) to Tíngwèi (Grand Judge),
and Dànóng (Grand Minister of Agriculture) to Dàsīnóng (Grand Minister of Agriculture).
Many
commanderies, kingdoms, counties, and settlements were renamed.
Hūchúquán, the Southern Chányú of the Xiōngnú, was again granted a Wèi seal and ribbon.
He was also bestowed a green-canopied carriage, imperial chariot, precious sword, and jade *jué*.
In the twelfth month,
the construction of Luòyáng Palace began.
On the day *Wùwǔ*, the emperor journeyed to Luòyáng.
That year,
Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi Dài Líng admonished the emperor not to hunt frequently,
which greatly angered the emperor.
Dài Líng’s death penalty was commuted by one degree.
In the spring, the first month of the second year,
sacrifices were made to Heaven and Earth, and at the Míngtáng.
On the day *Jiǎxū*,
the emperor hunted to Yuán Líng,
and dispatched an envoy to sacrifice to Hàn Shìzǔ with the grand offering.
On the day *Yǐhài*,
the emperor offered sacrifices to the sun in the eastern suburbs.
An initial order was issued that commanderaries and kingdoms with a population of over 100,000
should recommend one *xiàolián* annually.
Those who were outstanding
were not to be constrained by household registration.
On the day *Xīnsì*,
the households and territories of the Three Ducal Ministers were divided,
and one son or younger brother of each was enfeoffed as a 列侯 (Lièhóu).
On the day *Rénwǔ*,
Yǐngchuān Commandery was granted a one-year exemption from land tax.
Xǔ Xiàn was renamed Xǔchāng Xiàn.
The eastern part of Wèi Commandery was made Yángpíng Commandery,
and the western part was made Guǎngpíng Commandery.
An imperial edict stated:
“In the past, Zhòngní, endowed with the talent of a great sage,
and possessed of the capacity of an emperor,
lived at the end of the declining Zhōu dynasty,
but lacked the destiny to receive the mandate.
In the courts of Lǔ and Wèi,
he taught and transformed the people along the Zhū and Sì rivers.
With sorrow and
restlessness,
he wished to humble himself to preserve the Way,
and degrade his person to save the world.
At that time, the kings and dukes ultimately could not employ him.
So he withdrew and studied the rites of the Five Dynasties,
and performed the deeds of an uncrowned king.
He compiled the Chūnqiū based on the history of Lǔ,
and rectified the *yǎ* and *sòng* with the Grand Music Master.
Thus, after a thousand years,
none fail to revere his writings in their compositions,
or look up to his sagacity to form their plans.
Alas!
He can be called a great sage born for his age,
and a teacher and model for myriad generations.
In this time of great chaos in the world,
all rituals have fallen into disrepair.
The temple at his old residence
is ruined and unrestored.
The descendants of Bāochéng
are extinct and uncontinued.
At Quēlǐ, the sounds of lectures and recitations are no longer heard.
The positions for seasonal sacrifices are not seen.
How can this be called honoring ritual and repaying merit,
or a great virtue that must be sacrificed to for a hundred generations?
Therefore, let Counselor Kǒng Xiàn be enfeoffed as Zōngshèng Hóu,
with a hundred households,
to attend to the sacrifices for Kǒngzǐ.”
An order was issued to Lǔ Commandery to repair and rebuild the old temple,
and to station a hundred households of officials and soldiers to guard it.
Furthermore, extensive buildings were to be constructed outside it to house scholars.
In the third month,
Gōngsūn Gōng, the Administrator of Liáodōng, was promoted to Chēqí Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry).
The five-zhu coin was reinstated for the first time.
In the summer, the fourth month,
Chēqí Jiāngjūn Cáo Rén was made Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General).
In the fifth month,
Zhèng Gān rebelled again.
Cáo Rén was dispatched to suppress and execute him.
On the day *Gēngzǐ* of the sixth month,
sacrifices were made to the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers for the first time,
and all other deities were likewise sacrificed to in their proper order.
On the day *Dīngmǎo*,
Lady Zhēn passed away.
On the last day of the month, *Wùchén*,
there was a solar eclipse.
The officials proposed dismissing the Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant).
An imperial edict stated:
“Calamities and anomalies
are intended to rebuke the sovereign,
not to shift blame to his chief ministers.
How can this be the meaning of Yǔ and Tāng blaming themselves?
Let all officials each perform their duties.
Should there be future celestial or terrestrial disasters,
the Three Ducal Ministers shall not be impeached again.”
In the autumn, the eighth month,
Sūn Quán sent an envoy with a memorial,
and also sent Yú Jìn and others back.
On the day *Dīngsì*,
Tàicháng Xíng Zhēn was dispatched with the imperial insignia to appoint Sūn Quán as Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General),
enfeoff him as Wúwáng (King of Wú),
and grant him the Nine Bestowments.
In the winter, the tenth month,
Yáng Biāo was appointed Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Glorious Splendor).
Due to the high price of grain,
the five-zhu coin was abolished.
On the day *Jǐmǎo*,
Dàjiāngjūn Cáo Rén was made Dàsīmǎ (Grand Marshal).
In the twelfth month,
the emperor undertook an eastern tour.
That year, Língyún Tái was constructed.
In the spring, the first month, on the first day, *Bǐngyín*, of the third year,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the day *Gēngwǔ*,
the emperor journeyed to Xǔchāng Palace.
An imperial edict stated:
“Today’s *jì* (recommendations) and *xiào* (filial candidates)
are the *gòngshì* (recommended scholars) of antiquity.
Even a village of ten households
is sure to have loyal and trustworthy individuals.
If we limit the age for selecting officials,
then Lǚ Shàng and Zhōu Jìn would not have been prominent in past generations.
Let the selections made by commanderies and kingdoms
not be restricted by age.
Scholars who are well-versed in classical arts,
and officials who are proficient in laws and regulations,
shall all be tested and employed.
The authorities shall rectify those who fail to act truthfully.”
In the second month,
the kings of Shànshàn, Qiūcí, and Yútián each sent envoys with tribute.
An imperial edict stated:
“When the Western Rong came,
and the Dǐ and Qiāng came to pay homage,
the *Shī* and *Shū* praised them.
Recently, the foreign barbarians of the Western Regions have all offered allegiance and submitted.
Let envoys be sent to comfort and reward them.”
After this, the Western Regions were opened up,
and the Wùjǐ Xiàowèi (Commandant of Wùjǐ) was established.
On the day *Yǐchǒu* of the third month,
Qí Gōng Ruì was made Píngyuán Wáng.
The emperor’s eleven younger brothers, including Yānlíng Gōng Zhāng, were all made kings.
It was decreed for the first time that the secondary sons of enfeoffed kings should be Húi Gōng,
the secondary sons of heirs apparent to kings should be Tínghóu,
and the secondary sons of dukes should be Tíngbó.
On the day *Jiǎxū*,
Imperial Prince Lín was made Hédōng Wáng.
On the day *Jiǎwǔ*,
the emperor journeyed to Xiāngyì.
In the summer, the fourth month, on the day *Wùshēn*,
Juànchéng Hóu Zhí was made Juànchéng Wáng.
On the day *Guǐhài*,
the emperor returned to Xǔchāng Palace.
In the fifth month,
the eight commanderies of Jīng, Yáng, and south of the Yangtze River were made Jīngzhōu,
because Sūn Quán was leading them as governor.
The commanderies north of the Yangtze River in Jīngzhōu were made Yǐngzhōu.
In the intercalary month,
Sūn Quán defeated Liú Bèi at Yílíng.
Initially,
when the emperor heard that Liú Bèi’s army was moving east,
and engaging Sūn Quán,
having erected palisades and connected camps for over seven hundred *lǐ*,
he said to his ministers:
“Liú Bèi does not understand military strategy.
How can there be a seven-hundred *lǐ* camp that can resist the enemy!
‘To encamp across open plains, wetlands, dangerous passes, and difficult terrain makes one vulnerable to capture by the enemy.’
This is a military taboo.
Sūn Quán’s report on his victory will arrive today.”
Seven days later,
the news of Liú Bèi’s defeat arrived.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
there was a great locust plague in Jìzhōu.
The people suffered from famine.
Shàngshū Dù Jī was dispatched with the imperial insignia to open granaries to relieve them.
In the eighth month,
the Shǔ Grand General Huáng Quán led his troops and surrendered.
In the ninth month, on the *jiǎwǔ* day,
an edict stated:
"Women interfering in government
is the root of chaos.
From now on,
ministers are forbidden to report matters to the empress dowager.
Families of the empress dowager's clan are not permitted to hold the office of regent,
nor shall they arbitrarily receive titles of fiefdoms.
This edict shall be transmitted to later generations.
Should anyone violate it,
the whole realm shall execute them."
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Empress Guō was established.
All men in the realm were granted two ranks of nobility.
Widows, widowers, the severely infirm, and the poor who could not sustain themselves were granted grain.
In winter, the tenth month, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Mount Shǒuyáng's eastern side was designated as the Shòulíng tomb,
and a final decree was issued, stating:
"According to ritual,
when a ruler ascends the throne, a temporary coffin is prepared
(*bēi*, pronounced *fú lì*).
This means not forgetting death in life.
In ancient times, Yáo was buried in Gǔlín,
with trees planted all around.
Yǔ was buried in Kuàijī,
and farmers did not alter their fields.
Therefore, being buried in mountains and forests
is in harmony with mountains and forests.
The custom of elaborate burial mounds and tree-planting
is not from high antiquity,
and I have no use for it.
The Shòulíng tomb shall take the mountain as its body,
without elaborate mounds or planted trees,
without establishing a sleeping hall,
creating an imperial park,
or constructing a spirit path.
Indeed, burial (*zàng*)
means concealment (*cáng*),
desiring that people cannot see it.
Bones have no knowledge of pain or itching;
a tomb is not a dwelling for the spirit.
Ritual does not prescribe tomb sacrifices,
desiring that the living and the dead should not be defiled.
Coffins should be sufficient to allow bones to decay,
and grave clothes sufficient to allow flesh to decay, nothing more.
Therefore, I am arranging this barren and infertile mound,
wishing that after a change of dynasties, its location will be unknown.
Do not use reeds or charcoal;
do not bury gold, silver, copper, or iron.
Only use pottery vessels,
in accordance with the ancient meaning of clay carriages and straw effigies.
The coffin's joints need only be lacquered three times.
For the mouth-filling offering, do not use pearls or jade.
Do not use pearl shrouds or jade caskets;
these are all practices of ignorant commoners.
Jì Sūn was buried with precious jade,
and Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) intervened step by step to prevent it,
likening it to exposing the corpse in the wilderness.
Sòng Gōng was buried lavishly,
and gentlemen called Huá Yuán and Lè Jǔ disloyal,
considering it abandoning their lord to evil.
Emperor Wén of Hàn's tomb was not desecrated because
Bàlíng had nothing to seek;
Emperor Guāngwǔ's tomb was excavated because
Yuánlíng had burial mounds and planted trees.
The preservation of Bàlíng
was due to the merit of Shìzhī;
the excavation of Yuánlíng
was the fault of Emperor Míng.
Thus, Shìzhī's loyalty benefited his lord,
while Emperor Míng's love harmed his parent.
Loyal subjects and filial sons
should reflect on the words of Zhòngní (Confucius), Qiūmíng (Zuo Qiuming), and Shìzhī,
and take warning from Huá Yuán, Lè Jǔ, and Emperor Míng,
focusing on what ensures the security of their lord and the peace of their parents,
so that their spirits may be safe for ten thousand generations.
This is the loyalty and filiality of sages and worthies.
From ancient times until now,
there has never been a country that did not perish,
nor a tomb that was not excavated.
Since the chaos of war,
none of the Hàn imperial tombs have escaped excavation,
even to the extent of burning and taking jade caskets and gold threads,
with the bones utterly destroyed.
This is like the punishment of being burned;
is it not deeply grievous!
Calamity comes from lavish burials and elaborate mounds.
'Sāng and Huò serve as a warning to me,'
is this not clear?
As for empresses and noblewomen below,
who do not follow the king to his domain,
they shall all be buried west of the ravine upon their death.
Their location has already been designated.
Shùn was buried in Cāngwú,
and his two consorts did not follow him.
Yánlíng buried his son
far away in Yíng and Bó.
If souls have spirits,
there is nowhere they cannot go.
The space of one ravine
is not too far.
If anyone violates this current edict,
and presumptuously makes alterations or changes,
I shall be massacred underground,
massacred again and again,
dead and dead again.
Subjects who thus slight their deceased lord and father
are disloyal and unfilial.
If the deceased has consciousness,
they will not bless you.
This edict shall be stored in the ancestral temple,
with copies in the Department of State Affairs, the Imperial Secretariat, and the Three Ducal Offices."
That month,
Sūn Quán rebelled again.
Yǐng Prefecture was restored as Jīng Prefecture.
The Emperor personally led a southern expedition from Xǔchāng,
and all the armies advanced in concert.
Quán defended by the river.
In the eleventh month, on the *xīnchǒu* day,
the imperial retinue proceeded to Wǎn.
On the *gēngshēn* day, the last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
That year,
the Língzhī Pond was dug.
In the fourth year, spring, the first month,
an edict stated:
"Since the chaos of war,
military conflict has not ceased,
and the people of the realm
have been slaughtering each other.
Now that the realm is initially settled,
anyone who dares to privately seek revenge shall have their entire clan executed."
The Southern Inspection Terrace was built in Wǎn.
In the third month, on the *bǐngshēn* day,
the imperial retinue returned from Wǎn to Luòyáng Palace.
On the *kuǐmǎo* day,
the moon encroached upon the central large star of the Heart constellation.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Grand Marshal Cáo Rén passed away.
That month, there was a great plague.
In summer, the fifth month,
pelicans gathered at Língzhī Pond.
An edict stated:
"These are what the poets called 'birds of defiled marshes.'
The 'Cáo poem' criticized Duke Gōng for keeping gentlemen at a distance and associating with petty men.
Are there now wise and sagely scholars in low positions?
If not, why have these birds come?
Let us broadly select outstanding virtues, abundant talents, and independent gentlemen from across the realm,
to answer the criticism of the 'Cáo people'."
In the sixth month, on the *jiǎxū* day,
Zhāng, King of Rènchéng, passed away in the capital.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Grand Commandant Jiǎ Xǔ passed away.
Venus was seen in daylight.
That month, there were heavy rains.
The Yī and Luò rivers overflowed,
killing people
and destroying homes.
In autumn, the eighth month, on the *dīngmǎo* day,
Court Steward Zhōng Yáo was appointed Grand Commandant.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
a hunting expedition was held in Xíngyáng,
and then an eastern tour was made.
Rewards were given for merits in the campaign against Sūn Quán,
and various generals and others received promotions in rank and increases in households.
In the ninth month, on the *jiǎchén* day,
the imperial retinue proceeded to Xǔchāng Palace.
In the fifth year, in spring, the first month,
it was first ordered that only in cases of謀反 (móufǎn) and大逆 (dànì) could people report on each other;
all other accusations were not to be heard or judged.
Anyone who dared to falsely accuse another
would be punished with the crime they alleged.
In the third month,
the Emperor returned to Luòyáng Gōng (Luòyáng Palace) from Xǔchāng (Xǔchāng).
In summer, the fourth month,
the Grand Academy (Tàixué) was established,
and methods for testing and evaluating the Five Classics (Wǔjīng) were instituted.
Doctors of the Gǔliáng (Gǔliáng) Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) were appointed.
In the fifth month,
the relevant officials suggested that the Duke-Ministers (gōngqīng) should hold court on the朔 (shuò) and望 (wàng) days (the first and fifteenth of the lunar month),
and then present their doubts about affairs,
listen to decisions on major policies,
and discuss what was gained and lost.
In autumn, the seventh month,
the Emperor went on an eastern tour,
visiting Xǔchāng Gōng (Xǔchāng Palace).
In the eighth month,
a naval force was formed.
The Emperor personally commanded the Dragon Boat,
cruising along the Cài (Cài) and Yǐng (Yǐng) Rivers,
floating on the Huái (Huái) River,
and visiting Shòuchūn (Shòuchūn).
All officers, soldiers, and common people in the Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu) region
who had committed crimes punishable by five years of imprisonment or less
were pardoned and released.
In the ninth month,
he then reached Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng),
pardoned the two prefectures of Qīng (Qīng) and Xú (Xú),
and replaced various generals and governors.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
Tàibái (Venus) was seen in daylight.
The Emperor returned to Xǔchāng Gōng (Xǔchāng Palace).
In the eleventh month, on the day Gēngyín,
due to famine in Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu),
envoys were dispatched to open granaries and provide relief.
On the last day of the month, Wùshēn,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the twelfth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"The rituals instituted by the former kings
were to manifest filial piety in serving ancestors.
The greatest were the suburban and communal sacrifices (jiāoshè),
followed by ancestral temples (zōngmiào),
the three luminaries (sānchén) and five elements (wǔxíng),
and famous mountains and great rivers (míngshāndàchuān).
Things not of this category
were not included in the sacrificial canon.
In later generations, during times of decline and chaos,
people excessively believed in shamans and scribes (wūshǐ),
to the extent that within palaces
and between doors and windows,
nothing was not consecrated.
How deeply deluded this was!
From now on,
any who dare to establish sacrifices not in the canon,
or utter words of shamans and invocators,
shall all be judged as practicing unorthodox ways (zuǒdào),
and this shall be written into the statutes."
In this year, the Tiānyuān Chí (Heavenly Abyss Pond) was dug.
In the sixth year, in spring, the second month,
envoys were dispatched to travel from Xǔchāng (Xǔchāng) eastward as far as Pèijùn (Pèijùn),
to inquire about the people's sufferings and hardships,
and to provide relief and loans to the poor.
In the third month,
the Emperor visited Shàolíng (Shàolíng),
and opened the Tǎolǔ Qú (Tǎolǔ Canal).
On the day Yǐsì,
he returned to Xǔchāng Gōng (Xǔchāng Palace).
Liáng Xí (Liáng Xí), the Inspector of Bìngzhōu (Bìngzhōu), attacked the Xiānbēi (Xiānbēi) leader Kēbǐnéng (Kēbǐnéng),
and decisively defeated him.
On the day Xīnwèi,
the Emperor led a naval force on an eastern campaign.
In the fifth month, on the day Wùshēn,
he visited Qiáo (Qiáo).
On the day Rénxū,
Yínghuò (Mars) entered Tàiwēi (Tàiwēi).
In the sixth month,
Cài Fāng (Cài Fāng) and other soldiers of Lìchéng Jùn (Lìchéng Commandery) rebelled with the commandery,
killing the Administrator Xú Zhì (Xú Zhì).
Túnqí Xiàowèi (Colonel of Cavalry) Rèn Fú (Rèn Fú), and Bùbīng Xiàowèi (Colonel of Infantry) Duàn Zhāo (Duàn Zhāo) were sent with the Inspector of Qīngzhōu (Qīngzhōu) to suppress them;
those who were coerced or forced, and those who fled,
were all pardoned.
In autumn, the seventh month,
Imperial Prince Jiàn (Jiàn) was enfeoffed as Dōngwǔyáng Wáng (Prince of Dōngwǔyáng).
In the eighth month,
the Emperor then led the naval force from Qiáo (Qiáo), entered the Huái (Huái) River via the Wō (Wō) River,
and traveled by land to Xú (Xú).
In the ninth month,
the Dōngxún Tái (Eastern Inspection Terrace) was constructed.
In winter, the tenth month,
the Emperor visited the old city of Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng),
observing the troops from the riverbank.
There were over a hundred thousand soldiers,
with banners and flags stretching for hundreds of lì.
This year was extremely cold,
the waterways froze,
and the boats could not enter the river,
so he returned.
In the eleventh month,
Dōngwǔyáng Wáng (Prince of Dōngwǔyáng) Jiàn (Jiàn) passed away.
In the twelfth month,
the Emperor traveled from Qiáo (Qiáo) through Liáng (Liáng),
and sent an envoy with a Grand Sacrifice (Tàiláo) to offer sacrifices to the late Hàn (Hàn) Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Qiáo Xuán (Qiáo Xuán).
In the seventh year, in spring, the first month,
the Emperor was about to visit Xǔchāng (Xǔchāng),
but the south gate of Xǔchāng (Xǔchāng) city collapsed without cause.
The Emperor found this ominous,
and consequently did not enter.
On the day Rénzǐ,
the Emperor returned to Luòyáng Gōng (Luòyáng Palace).
In the third month,
the Jiǔhuá Tái (Nine Glories Terrace) was constructed.
In summer, the fifth month, on the day Bǐngchén,
the Emperor's illness became critical.

He summoned the Zhōngjūn Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-chief of the Central Army) Cáo Zhēn (Cáo Zhēn), Zhènjūn Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-chief Who Guards the Army) Chén Qún (Chén Qún), Zhēngdōng Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-chief Who Conquers the East) Cáo Xiū (Cáo Xiū), and Fǔjūn Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-chief Who Pacifies the Army) Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (Sīmǎ Xuānwáng),
and all received the imperial will to assist the heir.
He sent the concubines,淑媛 (shūyuàn),昭儀 (zhāoyí), and those below them, back to their families.
On the day Dīngsì,
the Emperor passed away in the Jiāfú Diàn (Jiāfú Palace),
at the age of forty.
In the sixth month, on the day Wùyín,
he was buried at Shǒuyáng Líng (Shǒuyáng Mausoleum).
From the embalming to the burial,
everything was carried out according to the final rites.
Originally,
the Emperor loved literature,
and made writing his priority.
He personally compiled nearly a hundred chapters.
He also had various scholars compile classics and commentaries,
categorized them by type,
totaling over a thousand chapters,
known as the Huánglǎn (Huánglǎn).
A review states: Wéndì (Wéndì) was naturally endowed with literary talent;
he would put pen to paper and compose finished essays.
He was broadly knowledgeable and had a strong memory,
and was proficient in various arts.
If he had also possessed a magnanimous disposition,
and been spurred by sincere fairness,
with aspirations fixed on the Dao,
and could have expanded his virtuous heart,
then how distant from him
would the wise rulers of antiquity have been!
Annals of Emperor Míng (Míngdì Jì) 3
Emperor Míng (Míng Dì), personal name Ruì (Ruì),
courtesy name Yuánzhòng (Yuánzhòng),
was the Crown Prince of Wéndì (Wéndì).
From birth, Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ) loved him,
and always kept him close.
At the age of fifteen,
he was enfeoffed as Wǔdé Hóu (Marquis of Wǔdé).
In the second year of Huángchū (Huángchū), he became Qí Gōng (Duke of Qí),
and in the third year, Píngyuán Wáng (Prince of Píngyuán).
Because his mother was executed,
he was not yet established as the heir.
In the seventh year, in summer, the fifth month,
when the Emperor was gravely ill,
he was then established as the Crown Prince.
On the day Dīngsì,
he ascended the imperial throne,
and proclaimed a general amnesty.
The Empress Dowager was honored as Tàihuáng Tàihòu (Grand Empress Dowager),
and the Empress as Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager).
All ministers received varying noble titles and ranks.
On the day Guǐwèi,
his mother, Lady Zhēn (Zhēn Fūrén), was posthumously honored as Wénzhāo Huánghòu (Empress Wénzhāo).
On the day Rénchén,
his imperial younger brother Ruí (Ruí) was enfeoffed as Yángpíng Wáng (Prince of Yángpíng).
In the eighth month,
Sūn Quán (Sūn Quán) attacked Jiāngxià Jùn (Jiāngxià Commandery),
but the Administrator Wén Pìn (Wén Pìn) held firm.
The court deliberated sending troops to relieve him,
but the Emperor said:
"Quán (Quán) is skilled in naval warfare.
The reason he dares to disembark and attack by land
is likely to catch us unprepared.
Now he is stalemated with Pìn (Pìn).
The advantage in attack and defense is doubled,
and he will ultimately not dare to stay long."
Previously, Shìyùshǐ (Imperial Censor) Xún Yǔ (Xún Yǔ) had been sent to comfort the border regions.
When Yǔ (Yǔ) arrived,
he dispatched soldiers from the counties he had passed through in Jiāngxià (Jiāngxià), along with a thousand infantry and cavalry from his retinue, to light fires on the mountains.
Sūn Quán (Sūn Quán) then retreated.
On the xīn sì day,
imperial prince Jiǒng was made Prince of Qīnghé.
Wú generals Zhūgě Jǐn and Zhāng Bà, among others, attacked Xiāngyáng.
Grand General of the Garrison, Sīmǎ Xuānwáng, campaigned against them and defeated them,
beheading Bà.
Grand General of the Expedition to the East, Cáo Xiū, also defeated their detached force at Xúnyáng.
Merits were assessed and rewards bestowed, each according to their distinctions.
In the winter, tenth month,
Prince Jiǒng of Qīnghé died.
In the twelfth month,
Grand Commandant Zhōng Yáo was appointed Grand Tutor.
Grand General of the Expedition to the East, Cáo Xiū, was appointed Grand Marshal.
Grand General of the Central Army, Cáo Zhēn, was appointed Grand General.
Minister of Works, Huá Xīn, was appointed Grand Commandant.
Minister of Education, Wáng Lǎng, was appointed Minister of Works.
Grand General of the Guarded Army, Chén Qún, was appointed Minister of Education.
Grand General of the Garrison, Sīmǎ Xuānwáng, was appointed Grand General of Agile Cavalry.
In the spring, first month of Tàihé元年 (the first year of Tàihé),
Emperor Wǔ was worshipped in the suburban sacrifice to match Heaven.
Emperor Wén was worshipped in the ancestral temple (Míngtáng) to match the Supreme Lord.
The southern part of Jiāngxià was divided,
and the Commander of Jiāngxià Southern Commandery was established.
Qū Yīng of Xīpíng rebelled,
killing the Magistrate of Línqiāng and the Chief of Xīdū.
Generals Hǎo Zhāo and Lù Pán were dispatched to campaign against and execute him.
In the second month, on the xīn wèi day,
the Emperor ploughed the ceremonial field.
On the xīn sì day,
a sleeping temple for Empress Wénzhāo was established in Yè.
On the dīng hài day,
the morning sun was worshipped in the eastern suburbs.
In the summer, fourth month, on the yǐ hài day,
Wǔzhū coins were put into circulation.
On the jiǎ shēn day,
construction of the ancestral temple began.
In the autumn, eighth month,
the moon was worshipped in the western suburbs.
In the winter, tenth month, on the bǐng yín day,
military drills were conducted in the eastern suburbs.
The King of Yānqí sent his son to serve as a hostage.
In the eleventh month,
Empress Máo Shì was established.
Men throughout the empire holding noble titles were granted two ranks.
The poor, widows, orphans, and the solitary who could not support themselves were granted grain.
In the twelfth month,
the Empress's father, Máo Jiā, was enfeoffed as a Marquis.
The Administrator of Xīnchéng, Mèng Dá, rebelled.
An imperial edict commanded Grand General of Agile Cavalry, Sīmǎ Xuānwáng, to campaign against him.
In the spring, first month of the second year,
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng attacked and captured Xīnchéng,
beheaded Dá,
and sent his head.
Shàngyōng, Wǔlíng, and Wūxiàn from Xīnchéng were separated to form Shàngyōng Commandery,
and Xīxiàn was made Xī Commandery.
Shǔ Grand General Zhūgě Liàng invaded the border.
Officials and common people of the three commanderies of Tiānshuǐ, Nán'ān, and Āndìng rebelled in response to Liàng.
Grand General Cáo Zhēn was dispatched to oversee Guānyòu,
and simultaneously advanced troops.
General of the Right, Zhāng Hé, engaged Liàng at Jiētíng,
thoroughly defeating him.
Liàng retreated in defeat,
and the three commanderies were pacified.
On the dīng wèi day,
the Emperor traveled to Cháng'ān.
In the summer, fourth month, on the dīng yǒu day,
he returned to Luòyáng Palace.
Imprisoned individuals, except those sentenced to special death or worse, were pardoned.
On the yǐ sì day,
merits for campaigning against Liàng were assessed,
and enfeoffments and increased stipends were granted, each according to their distinctions.
In the fifth month,
there was a great drought.
In the sixth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"Honoring Confucianism and valuing learning is the foundation of the kingly teaching.
Recently, some Confucian officials have been unfit for their positions.
How then can the sage's way be proclaimed and elucidated?
Therefore, select highly qualified Doctors,
those whose talents are suitable for being Court Attendants or Palace Attendants.
Instruct and order the commanderies and states
to recommend scholars with classical learning as the priority."
In the autumn, ninth month,
Cáo Xiū led various armies to Wǎn,
and battled Wú general Lù Yì at Shítíng,
suffering a defeat.
On the yǐ yǒu day,
imperial prince Mù was made Prince of Fányáng.
On the gēng zǐ day,
Grand Marshal Cáo Xiū died.
In the winter, tenth month,
an imperial edict commanded the Dukes, Ministers, and close officials to each nominate one excellent general.
In the eleventh month,
Minister of Works Wáng Lǎng died.
In the twelfth month,
Zhūgě Liàng besieged Chéncāng.
Cáo Zhēn dispatched General Fèi Yào and others to resist him.
Gōngsūn Yuān, nephew of Gōngsūn Gōng, Administrator of Liáodōng,
forcibly seized Gōng's position,
and Yuān was subsequently made Administrator of Liáodōng.
In the summer, fourth month of the third year,
Prince Lǐ of Yuánchéng died.
In the sixth month, on the guǐ mǎo day,
Prince Mù of Fányáng died.
On the wù shēn day,
the Grand Chamberlain of the High Ancestor was posthumously honored as Emperor Gāo,
and his wife, Lady Wú, was posthumously honored as Empress Gāo.
In the autumn, seventh month,
an imperial edict stated:
"According to the Rites,
if the Queen has no heir,
a son from a collateral branch is chosen to succeed the main lineage.
Then he should inherit the legitimate succession and uphold public righteousness,
how can he still care for his private relatives?
Emperor Xuān of Hàn, succeeding Emperor Zhāo,
conferred an imperial title upon his deceased father.
Emperor Āi, supported from a feudal domain,
and Dǒng Hóng and others cited the perished Qín,
deluding and misleading the court of the time.
They both honored Emperor Gōng
and established a temple in the capital,
and also favored the feudal concubine,
allowing her to compare with Chángxìn,
placing her in the front hall according to the ancestral rites,
and placing her four positions in the eastern palace.
Such presumptuous extravagance knew no bounds,
and neither men nor spirits provided protection.
Instead of punishing the loyal and upright remonstrances of Shī Dān,
they brought about the disaster of Dīng and Fù's destruction.
From then on,
this practice was followed in succession.
In ancient times, the 'inverse sacrifice' of Duke Wén of Lǔ
was a crime initiated by Xiàfù.
The 'improper measure' of the state of Sòng
was criticized by Huá Yuán.
Let the Dukes, Ministers, and relevant officials
deeply take warning from the actions of previous generations.
If a future successor, by some chance, comes from a feudal lord to uphold the great succession,
he must clearly understand the meaning of 'being a successor to another.'
Anyone who dares to be a sycophant, misleading the current monarch,
falsely establishing an illegitimate title to interfere with the legitimate succession,
calling his father an 'Emperor'
and his mother an 'Empress,'
then the high ministers
shall execute them without pardon.
This shall be written on golden tablets,
stored in the ancestral temple,
and recorded in the legal statutes."
In the winter, tenth month,
the Viewing Terrace of Píngwàng was renamed the Viewing Terrace for Hearing Cases.
The Emperor often said,
"Prisons
are the lifeblood of the world."
Whenever judging major cases,
he would often go to the terrace to personally listen.
Initially,
the ancestral temple in Luòyáng was not yet completed,
and the spirit tablets were in the Yè temple.
In the eleventh month,
the temple was finally completed.
The Grand Herald, Hán Jì, was sent with a staff of authority to welcome the spirit tablets of Emperor Gāo, Emperor Tài, Emperor Wǔ, and Emperor Wén from Yè.
On the jí chǒu day of the twelfth month, they arrived,
and the spirit tablets were respectfully placed in the temple.
On the guǐ mǎo day,
King Pōdiào of Dà Yuèzhī sent an envoy with tribute.
Pōdiào was made "King Pōdiào of Dà Yuèzhī, Close to Wèi."
In the spring of the fourth year, in the second month, on the day rénwǔ,
an edict stated:
"The refinement or plainness of the world
changes with education.
Since the military unrest,
classical studies have been abandoned,
and later generations, eager for advancement,
do not follow the classics and injunctions.
Is it that guidance has not been sufficient,
or that those promoted are not recognized for their virtue?
Let officials and clerks who are proficient in one classic
and capable of governing the people
be examined by the Eruditists,
and those who achieve the highest grades
be immediately employed.
As for those who are superficial and do not devote themselves to the fundamental principles of the Dao,
all shall be dismissed."
On the day wùzǐ,
an edict commanded Grand Tutor Sān Gōng: to engrave Wén Dì's Diǎn Lùn on stone,
and erect it outside the temple gate.
On the day guǐsì,
Cáo Zhēn, the Grand General, was made Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ);
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng, the Cavalry General of Píqi, was made Grand General;
and Gōngsūn Yuān, the Administrator of Liáodōng, was made General of Chariots and Cavalry.
In the summer, fourth month,
Grand Tutor Zhōng Yáo passed away.
In the sixth month, on the day wùzǐ,
the Grand Empress Dowager passed away.
On the day bǐngshēn,
Shàngyōng Commandery was abolished.
In the autumn, seventh month,
Empress Dowager Wǔxuān Biàn Hòu was interred at Gāolíng.
An edict commanded Grand Marshal Cáo Zhēn and Grand General Sīmǎ Xuānwáng to attack Shǔ.
In the eighth month, on the day xīnsì,
an eastern tour was undertaken,
and envoys were sent with special oxen to sacrifice to the Central Marchmount.
On the day yǐwèi,
the imperial retinue arrived at Xǔchāng Palace.
In the ninth month,
there was heavy rain;
the Yī, Luò, Hé, and Hàn rivers overflowed.
An edict commanded Zhēn and others to return their armies.
In the winter, tenth month, on the day yǐmǎo,
the imperial retinue returned to Luòyáng Palace.
On the day gēngshēn,
an order stated:
"For crimes not punishable by death, redemption is permitted, with different rates."
In the eleventh month,
Tàibái offended Suìxīng.
In the twelfth month, on the day xīnwèi,
Empress Wénzhāo Zhēn Hòu was reburied at Cháoyánglíng.
On the day bǐngyín,
an edict commanded the Gōngqīng to recommend virtuous and upright individuals.
In the spring of the fifth year, first month,
the Emperor plowed the sacrificial field.
In the third month,
Grand Marshal Cáo Zhēn passed away.
Zhūgě Liàng encroached upon Tiānshuǐ,
and an edict commanded Grand General Sīmǎ Xuānwáng to resist him.
From the tenth month of last winter until this month, there was no rain.
On the day xīnsì,
a great rain ceremony was held.
In the summer, fourth month,
Kēbǐnéng, the King by Virtue of Fùyì of the Xiānbēi, led his people and Érchán, a great elder of the Dīnglíng, to Yōuzhōu to present tribute horses.
The Protector of the Xiōngnú, Zhōnglángjiàng, was re-established.
In the autumn, seventh month, on the day bǐngzǐ,
as Liàng had retreated,
titles and ranks were increased according to their differences.
On the day yǐyǒu,
Imperial Prince Yīn was born,
and a general amnesty was granted.
In the eighth month,
an edict stated:
"In ancient times, feudal lords paid homage and made visits,
which served to strengthen kinship and harmonize the myriad states.
The former emperor issued an order
not to allow the kings to reside in the capital,
because a young ruler was on the throne
and the empress dowager was regent,
guarding against subtle changes gradually,
which concerned prosperity and decline.
I have not seen the kings for twelve years,
and such a long-held sentiment,
how can it not arouse longing!
Let all kings and noble lords of the imperial clan each bring one legitimate son to court.
Hereafter, if there is a young ruler and empress dowager in the palace,
it shall be as per the former emperor's order,
which is to be clearly stated and recorded in the orders."
In the winter, eleventh month, on the day yǐyǒu,
the Moon offended the Great Star of Xuānyuán.
On the day wùxū, the last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the twelfth month, on the day jiǎchén,
the Moon offended Zhènxīng.
On the day wùwǔ,
Grand Commandant Huá Xīn passed away.
In the spring of the sixth year, second month,
an edict stated:
"The ancient emperors and kings
enfeoffed feudal lords
to serve as screens and bulwarks for the royal house.
Does the Shī Jīng not say,
'Those who cherish virtue will be peaceful,
the scions of the clan are as city walls'?
Qín and Hàn succeeded Zhōu,
some were strong and some weak,
both losing their balance.
The Great Wèi founded its enterprise,
and the kings established their states,
but the timing was suitable,
and there was no fixed system,
which is not
Therefore, the enfeoffment of the feudal kings shall be changed,
all commanderies becoming states."
In the third month, on the day guǐyǒu,
an eastern tour was undertaken.
Wherever it passed, the aged, widows, and orphans were visited and enquired after,
and given grain and silk.
On the day yǐhài,
the Moon offended the Great Star of Xuānyuán.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day rénbǎo,
the imperial retinue traveled to Xǔchāng Palace.
On the day jiǎzǐ,
new fruits were first presented at the temple.
In the fifth month,
Imperial Prince Yīn passed away,
and was posthumously enfeoffed and given the posthumous title Ānpíng Āi Wáng.
In the autumn, seventh month,
Dǒng Zhāo, the Commandant of the Guards, was made Minister of Education (Sītú).
In the ninth month,
the imperial retinue traveled to Mópí,
managed Xǔchāng Palace,
and constructed the Jǐngfú and Chéngguāng Halls.
In the winter, tenth month,
Tián Yù, the General who Subdues Barbarians, led his troops to attack Zhōu Hè, an Wu general, at Chéngshān,
and killed Hè.
In the eleventh month, on the day bǐngyín,
Tàibái was seen in daylight.
A comet appeared in Yì,
near the general star of Tàiwēi.
On the day gēngyín,
Chén Sī Wáng Zhí passed away.
In the twelfth month,
the imperial retinue returned to Xǔchāng Palace.
In the spring of the first year of Qīnglóng, first month, on the day jiǎshēn,
a green dragon was seen in a well at Mópí in Jiá.
In the second month, on the day dīngyǒu,
the imperial retinue traveled to Mópí to observe the dragon,
whereupon the reign year was changed;
Mópí was renamed Lóngpí,
and men were granted two ranks of nobility,
and widows, orphans, and the solitary were exempted from this year's taxes and levies.
In the third month, on the day jiǎzǐ,
an edict commanded the Gōngqīng to each recommend one virtuous and upright scholar.
In the summer, fifth month, on the day réngshēn,
an edict commanded that the late Grand General Xiàhóu Dūn, Grand Marshal Cáo Rén, and General of Chariots and Cavalry Chéng Yù be sacrificed to in the ancestral temple of Tàizǔ.
On the day wùyín,
Běihǎi Wáng Ruí passed away.
In the intercalary month, on the first day gēngyín,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the day dīngyǒu,
imperial clan women who were not daughters of kings were all re-enfeoffed as Yìzhǔ.
An edict commanded that mountains and rivers in various commanderies and states not included in the sacrificial canon should not be sacrificed to.
In the sixth month,
the Jūshì chamber of Luòyáng Palace caught fire.
Bùdùgēn, a great elder of the Bǎisài Xiānbēi, privately communicated with Kēbǐnéng, a great elder of the rebellious Xiānbēi.
Bì Guǐ, the Inspector of Bìngzhōu, submitted a memorial,
proposing to send out troops to awe Kēbǐnéng externally
and suppress Bùdùgēn internally.
The Emperor, after reviewing the memorial, said:
"Bùdùgēn is believed to have been enticed by Kēbǐnéng,
and has self-doubt.
Now if Guǐ sends out troops,
it will only cause the two tribes to be startled and unite as one.
How can this awe or suppress them?"
He urgently commanded Guǐ
that the troops sent out must not cross the frontier or pass Gōuzhù.
Before the imperial edict arrived,
Guǐ had advanced his troops and encamped at Yīnguǎn,
and sent Generals Sū Shàng and Dǒng Bì to pursue the Xiānbēi.
Kēbǐnéng sent his son with over a thousand cavalry to meet Bùdùgēn's tribe,
and encountered Shàng and Bì.
They fought at Lóufán,
and the two generals were [defeated and] killed.
Bùdùgēn's tribe all rebelled and left the frontier,
uniting with Kēbǐnéng to raid the border.
General of Valiant Cavalry Qín Lǎng was sent to lead the central army to suppress them,
and the captives then fled to Mòběi.
In the autumn, ninth month,
Hú Bó Jū Zīzhí and other great elders of the Bǎisài Xiōngnú of Āndìng rebelled.
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng sent General Hú Zūn and others to pursue and suppress them,
defeating and subjugating them.
In the winter, tenth month,
Dài Hú Ālángní and other great elders of Bùdùgēn's tribe submitted to Bìngzhōu,
and Lǎng withdrew his troops.
In the twelfth month,
Gōngsūn Yuān beheaded and sent the heads of Zhāng Mí and Xǔ Yàn, envoys sent by Sūn Quán,
whereupon Yuān was made Grand Marshal and Duke of Lèlàng.
In the second year, spring, second month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
Tàibái (Venus) encroached upon Yínghuò (Mars).
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"The whip is used as an official punishment
to correct sloth and idleness,
but lately many have died innocently from it.
Let the regulations for the whip and rod be reduced,
and this be established in the law."
In the third month, on the *gēngyín* day,
the Duke of Shānyáng (山陽) passed away.
The Emperor wore plain mourning clothes and expressed sorrow,
sending an envoy with imperial credentials to oversee the funeral arrangements.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
a great amnesty was declared.
In summer, fourth month,
a great epidemic occurred.
The Chónghuá (崇華) Hall suffered a disaster (fire).
On the *bǐngyín* day,
an edict commanded the relevant officials to sacrifice a grand offering at Wéndì (文帝) Temple.
The Duke of Shānyáng was posthumously honored as Hàn Xiàoxiàn Huángdì (漢孝獻皇帝),
and buried with Hàn (漢) rites.
In this month,
Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) emerged from Xié Gǔ (斜谷),
stationing his troops in Wèinán (渭南).
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (司馬宣王) led various armies to resist him.
An edict was sent to Xuānwáng (宣王), stating:
"Just hold fast to your fortifications and resist to blunt his vanguard.
If he cannot achieve his ambitions by advancing,
and has no one to fight by retreating,
if he delays for long, his provisions will run out,
and with no spoils to plunder,
he will surely flee.
When he flees, pursue him.
Wait for the weary with the rested;
this is the way to complete victory."
In the fifth month,
Tàibái (Venus) was seen in daylight.
Sūn Quán (孫權) entered Húkǒu (湖口) on Cháo Hú (巢湖),
advancing towards the new city of Héféi (合肥).
He also dispatched generals Lù Yì (陸議) and Sūn Sháo (孫韶), each leading over ten thousand men, into the Huái (淮) and Miǎn (沔) rivers.
In the sixth month,
General who Conquers the East, Mǎn Chǒng (滿寵), advanced his troops to resist him.
Mǎn Chǒng (滿寵) wanted to evacuate the defenders of the new city
and lead the enemy to Shòuchūn (壽春).
The Emperor did not approve,
saying:
"In the past, Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武) sent troops to occupy Luèyáng (略陽) by force,
and eventually defeated Wěi Xiāo (隗囂).
The late Emperor established Héféi (合肥) in the east,
guarded Xiāngyáng (襄陽) in the south,
and secured Qí Shān (祁山) in the west.
The bandits were repeatedly defeated beneath these three cities
because these places must be contested.
Even if Sūn Quán (孫權) attacks the new city,
he will surely not be able to capture it.
Command all generals to hold fast.
I will personally go to campaign against him.
By the time I arrive,
I fear Sūn Quán (孫權) will have fled."
In autumn, seventh month, on the *rén yín* day,
the Emperor personally took the imperial dragon boat on an eastern expedition.
Sūn Quán (孫權) attacked the new city.
General Zhāng Yǐng (張穎) and others resisted and fought bravely.
Before the Emperor's army was even several hundred *lǐ* away,
Sūn Quán (孫權) fled,
and Lù Yì (陸議), Sūn Sháo (孫韶) and others also retreated.
The assembled officials believed that the Grand General was still in a standoff with Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) and had not yet resolved it,
so the imperial carriage should proceed west to Cháng'ān (長安).
The Emperor said:
"With Sūn Quán (孫權) having fled,
Zhūgě Liàng's (諸葛亮) courage is broken.
The Grand General will control him,
so I have no worries."
He then advanced his army to Shòuchūn (壽春),
recorded the merits of the various generals,
and bestowed appropriate rewards.
In the eighth month, on the *jǐwèi* day,
a grand military review was held,
and a feast was given to the Six Armies.
Envoys with imperial credentials were sent to commend and reward the various armies at Héféi (合肥) and Shòuchūn (壽春).
On the *xīnsì* day,
the imperial procession returned to Xǔchāng (許昌) Palace.
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (司馬宣王) and Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) were in a standoff,
surrounding each other for many days.
Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) repeatedly challenged them to battle,
but Xuānwáng (宣wáng) held firmly to his camp and did not respond.
Eventually, Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) died,
and his army retreated.
In winter, tenth month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
the moon encroached upon Zhèn Xīng (鎮星) (Saturn) and Xuānyuán (軒轅).
On the *wùyín* day,
the moon encroached upon Tàibái (Venus).
In the eleventh month,
an earthquake occurred in the capital,
coming from the southeast.
There was a rumbling sound,
and roof tiles shook.
In the twelfth month,
an edict commanded the relevant officials to review and revise the death penalty,
reducing capital crimes.
In the third year, spring, first month, on the *wùzǐ* day,
Grand General Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (司馬宣王) was appointed Grand Commandant.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Shuòfāng (朔方) Commandery was re-established.
A great epidemic occurred in the capital.
On the *dīngsì* day,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
On the *yǐhài* day,
a meteor fell in Shòuguāng (壽光) County.
In the third month, on the *gēngyín* day,
Empress Wéndé Guō Hòu (文德郭后) was buried.
Her tomb was constructed on the west side of the Jiàn (澗) Stream at Shǒuyáng Líng (首陽陵),
according to her final wishes.
At this time,
extensive repairs were made to Luòyáng (洛陽) Palace.
Zhāoyáng (昭陽) and Tàijí (太極) Halls were built,
and Zǒngzhāng Guān (總章觀) was constructed.
The common people missed their farming seasons.
Upright officials Yáng Fù (楊阜), Gāo Tánglóng (高堂隆), and others repeatedly remonstrated,
and although their advice was not always followed,
they were always treated with generosity and tolerance.
In autumn, seventh month,
Chónghuá (崇華) Hall in Luòyáng (洛陽) suffered a disaster (fire).
In the eighth month, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
Imperial Prince Fāng (芳) was enfeoffed as King of Qí (齊),
and Xún (詢) as King of Qín (秦).
On the *dīngsì* day,
the imperial procession returned to Luòyáng (洛陽) Palace.
Officials were ordered to rebuild Chónghuá (崇華) Hall,
renaming it Jiǔlóng (九龍) Hall.
In winter, tenth month, on the *jǐyǒu* day,
Zhōngshān (中山) King Yǎn (兗) passed away.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Tàibái (Venus) was seen in daylight.
In the eleventh month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
the imperial procession journeyed to Xǔchāng (許昌) Palace.
In the fourth year, spring, second month,
Tàibái (Venus) was again seen in daylight.
The moon encroached upon Tàibái (Venus),
and also encroached upon one star of Xuānyuán (軒轅),
entering Tàiwēi (太微) and then exiting.
In summer, fourth month,
Chóngwén Guān (崇文觀) was established,
and those skilled in writing were summoned to fill its positions.
In the fifth month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
Minister of Education Dǒng Zhāo (董昭) passed away.
On the *dīngsì* day,
the Sùshèn (肅慎) people presented *kǔ* arrows.
In the sixth month, on the *rénshēn* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Yǒuyú (有虞) clan drew images [of punishments] and the people did not offend.
The Zhōu (周) people set aside punishments and did not use them.
I am at the end of a hundred kings,
looking back at the customs of the ancient times—
how distant they are!
Laws and decrees multiply,
and offenders become more numerous.
Punishments increase,
yet wickedness cannot be stopped.
Previously, when reviewing capital punishment statutes,
many were abolished,
with the intention of saving the lives of the people.
This was my utmost intention.
Yet in commanderies and states, deaths in prison
still exceeded several hundred in a single year.
Is it that my moral instruction is impure,
leading the people to treat crimes lightly,
or that harsh laws still exist,
creating traps for them?
Let the relevant officials discuss cases and delay executions,
striving for leniency and simplicity.
Regarding those who request imperial grace,
sometimes their plea has not yet been issued, but the case is already reported as decided,
which is not the way to fully understand the truth and exhaust the facts.
Let the Grand Judge and all prison officials throughout the realm,
for all capital cases that have been thoroughly examined and decided,
unless it is for rebellion or intentional homicide,
promptly inform their close relatives.
If there are those who request imperial grace,
have their requests submitted along with the case documents,
and I will consider how to spare them.
Let this be proclaimed throughout the empire
to make my intention clear."
In autumn, seventh month,
King Gāogōulí (高句驪) Gōng (宮) beheaded the envoy Hú Wèi (胡衞) and others, sent by Sūn Quán (孫權),
and presented their heads to Yōuzhōu (幽州).
On the day jiǎyín (甲寅),
Tài Bái (太白) trespassed against the main star of Xuānyuán (軒轅).
In winter, tenth month, on the day jǐmǎo (己卯),
the procession returned to Luòyáng (洛陽) Palace.
On the day jiǎshēn (甲申),
a comet appeared in Dà Chén (大辰).
On the day yǐyǒu (乙酉),
it appeared again in the east.
In the eleventh month, on the day jǐhài (己亥),
a comet was seen,
trespassing against Huànzhě Tiānjì Xīng (宦者天紀星).
In the twelfth month, on the day guǐsì (癸巳),
Sīkōng (司空) Chén Qún (陳羣) passed away.
On the day yǐwèi (乙未),
the emperor proceeded to Xǔchāng (許昌) Palace.
In the spring of the first year of Jǐngchū (景初), first month, on the day rénchén (壬辰),
Shānchí (山茌) County reported seeing a yellow dragon.
(Chí (茌) is pronounced as shìlí (仕狸) in reverse.)
Thereupon, officials concerned submitted a memorial,
believing that Wèi (魏) had obtained the Earth Mandate,
and it was appropriate to designate the month of jiànchǒu (建丑) as the first month.
In the third month,
the calendar was fixed, and the year was changed to begin in the fourth month of Mèngxià (孟夏).
The favored color was yellow,
sacrificial animals were white,
in military affairs, black-headed white horses were ridden,
a large crimson banner was erected,
and in court, a large white banner was erected.
The Tàihé (太和) calendar was renamed the Jǐngchū (景初) calendar.
Although the designation of the first, middle, and last months of spring, summer, autumn, and winter differed from the regular year,

as for the suburban sacrifices, welcoming the qi (氣), summer sacrifices, autumn sacrifices, winter sacrifices, imperial tours, hunting expeditions, solstices, equinoxes, and the beginning and end of seasons, promulgating seasonal ordinances, the timing of mid-season qi (氣), and respectfully assigning tasks to the people,
all followed the regular year's dǒujiàn (斗建) as the sequence of the calendar.
In the fifth month, on the day jǐsì (己巳),
the procession returned to Luòyáng (洛陽) Palace.
On the day jǐchǒu (己丑),
a general amnesty was granted.
In the sixth month, on the day wùshēn (戊申),
there was an earthquake in the capital.
On the day jǐhài (己hài),
Shàngshūlìng (尚書令) Chén Jiǎo (陳矯) was made Sītú (司徒),
and Shàngshū Yòupúshè (尚書右僕射) Wèi Zhēn (衞臻) was made Sīkōng (司空).
On the day dīngwèi (丁未),
Wèiyáng (魏陽) from Wèixīng (魏興), Ānfù (安富) from Xī (錫) Commandery, and Shàngyōng (上庸) were separated to establish Shàngyōng (上庸) Commandery.
Xī (錫) Commandery was abolished,
and Xī (錫) County was assigned to Wèixīng (魏興) Commandery.
Officials concerned submitted a memorial: Wǔ Huángdì (武皇帝) restored order from chaos,
becoming Wèi Tàizǔ (魏太祖), and the music used was the Wǔshǐ (武始) dance.
Wén Huángdì (文皇帝) responded to Heaven's mandate,
becoming Wèi Gāozǔ (魏高祖), and the music used was the Xiánxī (咸熙) dance.
The Emperor initiated reforms and brought about governance,
becoming Wèi Lièzǔ (魏烈祖), and the music used was the Zhāngbīn (章斌) dance.
The temples of the Three Ancestors
shall never be destroyed for ten thousand generations.
As for the other four temples,
when the familial relationship became distant, they were to be successively abolished,
following the system of the ancestral temples of Hòujì (后稷), Wén (文), and Wǔ (武) of Zhōu (周).
In autumn, seventh month, on the day dīngmǎo (丁卯),
Sītú (司徒) Chén Jiǎo (陳矯) passed away.
Sūn Quán (孫權) dispatched General Zhū Rán (朱然) and twenty thousand men to besiege Jiāngxià (江夏) Commandery.
The Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州), Hú Zhì (胡質), and others attacked them,
and Rán (然) retreated.
Earlier,
Quán (權) had sent envoys across the sea to communicate with Gāogōulí (高句驪),
intending to attack Liáodōng (遼東).
Múqiū Jiǎn (毋丘儉), Governor of Yōuzhōu (幽州), was ordered to lead various armies, Xīanbéi (鮮卑), and Wūhuán (烏丸) to garrison the southern border of Liáodōng (遼東).
An imperial edict summoned Gōngsūn Yuān (公孫淵).
Yuān (淵) raised an army and rebelled.
Jiǎn (儉) advanced his army to suppress him,
but continuous rain for ten days caused the Liáo Shuǐ (遼水) to swell greatly.
An edict ordered Jiǎn (儉) to withdraw his army.
Kòulóudūn (寇婁敦), Chányú (單于) of Wūhuán (烏丸) of Yòuběipíng (右北平), Wáng Hùliú (王護留), Governor of Wūhuán (烏huán) of Liáoxī (遼西), and others residing in Liáodōng (遼東),
led their tribes and subjects to attach themselves to Jiǎn (儉) and join the imperial court.
On the day jǐmǎo (己卯),
an edict pardoned all officials, soldiers, and common people of Liáodōng (遼東) who had been coerced by Yuān (淵) and unable to surrender.
On the day xīnmǎo (辛卯),
Tài Bái (太白) appeared in daylight.
After Jiǎn's (儉) return, Yuān (淵) then established himself as King of Yān (燕),
appointed all officials,
and proclaimed the first year of Shàohàn (紹漢).
An edict ordered the four provinces of Qīng (青), Yǎn (兗), Yōu (幽), and Jì (冀) to greatly build seagoing ships.
In the ninth month,
the people of the four provinces of Jì (冀), Yǎn (兗), Xú (徐), and Yù (豫) suffered from floods.
Shìyùshǐ (侍御史) were dispatched to inspect and rescue those who had drowned or lost property,
opening granaries in affected areas.
On the day gēngchén (庚辰),
Empress Máo (毛) passed away.
In winter, tenth month, on the day dīngwèi (丁未),
the moon trespassed against Yínghuò (熒惑).
On the day guǐchǒu (癸丑),
the mourning Empress Máo (毛) was buried in Mǐnlíng (愍陵).
On the day yǐmǎo (乙卯),
the Wēisù (委粟) Mountain south of Luòyáng (洛陽) was established as the Round Mound (圜丘).
In the twelfth month, on the day rénzǐ (壬子), the Winter Solstice occurred,
and sacrifices began.
On the day dīngsì (丁巳),
the four counties of Línjǔ (臨沮), Yíchéng (宜城), Jìngyáng (旍陽), and Qí (邔) from Xiāngyáng (襄陽) were separated,
and a Southern Duwei (都尉) of Xiāngyáng (襄陽) was established.
(Qí (邔) is pronounced as qí jǐ (其己) in reverse.)
On the day jǐwèi (己未),
officials concerned memorialized that Wénzhāo Huánghòu (文昭皇后) should have a temple established in the capital.
Ruòyè (鄀葉) County of Xiāngyáng (襄陽) Commandery was assigned to Yìyáng (義陽) Commandery.
In the second year, spring, first month,
an edict ordered Tàiwèi (太尉) Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (司馬宣王) to lead his forces to campaign against Liáodōng (遼東).
In the second month, on the day guǐmǎo (癸卯),
Dàzhōng Dàfū (大中大夫) Hán Jì (韓暨) was made Sītú (司徒).
On the day guǐchǒu (癸丑),
the moon trespassed against the outer star of Xīn (心),
and also against the central main star of Xīn (心).
In summer, fourth month, on the day gēngzǐ (庚子),
Sītú (司徒) Hán Jì (韓暨) passed away.
On the day rén yín (壬寅),

the ten counties of Xiāo (蕭), Xiāng (相), Zhúyì (竹邑), Fúlí (符離), Qí (蘄), Zhì (銍), Lóngkàng (龍亢), Shānshāng (山桑), Xiáo (洨), and Hóng (虹) from Pèi (沛) Kingdom were separated to form Rǔyīn (汝陰) Commandery.
Sòng (宋) County and Kǔ (苦) County of Chén (陳) Commandery were all assigned to Qiáo (譙) Commandery.
Pèi (沛), Zhùqiū (杼秋), Gōngqiū (公丘), Fēngguó (豐國) and Guǎngqī (廣戚) from Péngchéng (彭城),
these five counties, were combined to form Pèi (沛) Kingdom.
(Xiáo (洨) is pronounced hújiāo (胡交) in reverse.
Hóng (虹) is pronounced jiàng (絳).)
On the day gēngxū (庚戌),
a general amnesty was granted.
In the fifth month, on the day yǐhài (乙亥),
the moon trespassed against the outer star of Xīn (心),
and also against the central main star.
In the sixth month,
Húnu (狐奴) County of Yúyáng (漁陽) Commandery was abolished,
and Ānlè (安樂) County was re-established.
In autumn, eighth month,
the Qiāng (羌) kings Mángzhōng (芒中) and Zhùyì (注詣) of Shāodāng (燒當) rebelled.
The Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州) led various commanderies to attack them,
beheading Zhùyì (注詣).
On the day guǐchǒu (癸丑),
a comet was seen in the constellation Zhāng (張).
On the day bǐngyín (丙寅),
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (司馬宣王) besieged Gōngsūn Yuān (公孫淵) at Xiāngpíng (襄平),
greatly defeating him,
and sending Yuān's (淵) head to the capital.
All commanderies east of the sea were pacified.
In winter, eleventh month,
for the merits in suppressing Yuān (淵),
Tàiwèi (太尉) Xuānwáng (宣王) and others below him received varying increases in their fiefs and noble titles.
Originally,
the Emperor discussed sending Xuānwáng (宣王) to suppress Yuān (淵),
raising forty thousand soldiers.
All ministers who debated thought forty thousand soldiers were too many,
and the expenses would be difficult to provide.
The Emperor said:
"For a campaign four thousand lǐ (里) away,
although it is said to rely on strategy,
it should also rely on strength,
and one should not calculate the expenses. "
So he proceeded with forty thousand men.
When Xuānwáng (宣王) arrived in Liáodōng (遼東),
continuous rain prevented timely attack.
Some ministers thought Yuān (淵) could not be defeated quickly,
and suggested ordering Xuānwáng (宣王) to return.
The Emperor said:
"Sīmǎ Yì (司馬懿) handles changes in critical situations,
and capturing Yuān (淵) can be awaited on a fixed date. "
In the end, everything happened as planned.
On the day rényǐ (壬午),
Sīkōng (司空) Wèi Zhēn (衞臻) was made Sītú (司徒),
and Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉) Cuī Lín (崔林) was made Sīkōng (司空).
In the intercalary month,
the moon trespassed against the central main star of Xīn (心).
In the twelfth month, on the day yǐchǒu (乙丑),
the Emperor fell ill and was not well.
On the day xīnsì (辛巳),
an Empress was established.
All men in the empire with noble titles were granted two ranks,
and the widowed, orphaned, and solitary received grain.
Yān Wáng (燕王) Yǔ (宇) was made Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍),
but was dismissed on the day jiǎshēn (甲申),
and Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (武衞將軍) Cáo Shuǎng (曹爽) replaced him.
Earlier,
in the third year of Qīnglóng (青龍),
a peasant's wife in Shòuchūn (壽春) claimed to be sent by a celestial deity,
commanded to be Dēngnǚ (登女),
who would protect the imperial house,
remove evil, and bestow blessings.
She gave people water to drink,
and also used it to wash sores,
and many were cured.
Therefore, a residence was established in the inner palace,
and an imperial edict praised her,
showing her great favor and preference.
When the Emperor fell ill,
drinking her water had no effect,
so she was executed.
In the spring, the first month of the third year, on the *dìnghài* day,
Grand Commandant Sīmǎ Xuānwáng returned to Hénèi.
The Emperor summoned him by relays of horses.
He was led into the inner bed-chamber,
and the Emperor, holding his hand, said:
“My illness is severe.
I entrust my affairs after death to you, my lord.
You should assist my young son with Cáo Shuǎng.
Having been able to see you, my lord,
I have no regrets!”
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng bowed his head, weeping.
On the same day,
the Emperor passed away in the Jiāfú Palace,
at the age of thirty-six.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
he was buried in Gaopíng Mausoleum.
A commentary says: Emperor Míng was resolute and discerning,
acting according to his own will,
and indeed possessed the utmost bearing of a ruler of men.
At that time, the common people were impoverished and exhausted,
and the four seas were in disarray.
Instead of first diligently following the example of the Illustrious Ancestor [Cáo Cāo],
and expanding the great foundation,
he hastily emulated Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdì,
constructing palaces and halls.
Compared to far-reaching plans,
was this not ill-advised?
Annals of the Three Young Emperors, Part Four
Qí Wáng, personal name Fāng,
courtesy name Lánqīng.
Emperor Míng had no sons,
and adopted Wáng Fāng and Qín Wáng Xún.
Court affairs were kept secret,
so no one knew their origins.
In the third year of Qīnglóng,
he was made Qí Wáng.
On the *dìnghài* day, the first day of the first month of the third year of Jǐngchū,
the Emperor became severely ill,
and thereupon established him as Crown Prince.
On that very day,
he ascended the imperial throne,
and a general amnesty was declared.
The Empress was honored as the Empress Dowager.
General-in-Chief Cáo Shuǎng and Grand Commandant Sīmǎ Xuānwáng assisted in governing.
An imperial edict stated:
“I, with my humble person,
have inherited this grand enterprise,
and am forlorn in my grief,
with no one to turn to.
The General-in-Chief and Grand Commandant have received the final command [from the late emperor],
to assist my person.
The Minister over the Masses, Minister of Works, Chief Minister, and Grand Counselor shall lead all officials
to bring peace to the state.
They, along with all the high ministers and grandees, should exert their utmost efforts
to fulfill my intentions.
All ongoing construction projects of palaces and halls
are to be halted according to the late emperor’s will.
All official male and female slaves aged sixty and above
are to be freed and become commoners.”
In the second month,
envoys from the Western Regions, through multiple interpreters, presented fire-proof cloth.
An edict commanded the General-in-Chief and Grand Commandant to personally test it and display it to all officials.
On the *dīngchǒu* day, an edict stated:
“The Grand Commandant embodies the Way and is upright,
having devoted loyalty for three reigns.
In the south, he captured Méng Dá;
in the west, he defeated the Shǔ barbarians;
in the east, he annihilated Gōngsūn Yuān.
His achievements overshadow all within the seas.
Formerly, King Chéng of Zhōu established the office of senior tutors;
more recently, Emperor Xiǎnzōng of Hàn greatly honored Déng Yǔ.
The reason for such esteemed treatment of outstanding individuals
is certainly out of respect.
Therefore, let the Grand Commandant be made Grand Tutor,
retaining his staff of authority and command of all military affairs as before.”
In the third month,
Mǎn Chǒng, General Who Attacks the East, was made Grand Commandant.
In the summer, sixth month,
due to the officials and common people of Dōngtà County in Liáodōng having crossed the sea to reside in Qíjùn commandery,
the former Zòngchéng was established as Xīntà County to accommodate the resettled people.
In the autumn, seventh month,
the Emperor began to personally attend court
and listen to the reports of the high ministers.
In the eighth month,
a general amnesty was declared.
In the winter, tenth month,
Huáng Quán, General Who Guards the South, was made General of Chariots and Cavalry.
In the twelfth month,
an edict stated:
“Our Illustrious Ancestor, Emperor Míng, departed from the world in the first month.
His ministers and sons forever recall the sorrow of that anniversary.
Therefore, the Xià calendar shall be reinstated.
Although this deviates from the late emperor’s principle of unifying the three calendar systems,
this is also a change permissible by rites and regulations.
Moreover, the Xià calendar, in terms of numerology, aligns with the celestial positive.
Therefore, the month of *jiànyín* shall be the first month of the first year of Zhèngshǐ,
and the month of *jiànchǒu* shall be the twelfth month after it.”
