Nánshēnzé county reported the descent of sweet dew.
Wú sent envoys Jì Zhì and Hóng Qiú to request peace.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict stated:
“The Grand Counselor, the King of Jìn, broadly displayed divine foresight,
and his glory covered the four seas;
he demonstrated martial prowess,
and his might overshadowed distant lands,
his influence and transforming power flowed,
extending universally without boundary.
He pitied and cared for the region south of the Jiāng,
striving to save and nurture them,
halting military action and valuing benevolence,
showing them his might and virtue.
Wherever his civil pronouncements reached,
they submitted to his influence and looked up to him,
sending envoys to offer tribute,
to demonstrate their surrender and obedience,
presenting precious and rare treasures,
joyfully expressing their intentions.
Yet the King, in his utmost humility,
returned all of them,
which is not the way to comfort those who have newly submitted,
nor to accede to their sincere wishes.
All the offerings presented by Sūn Hào
shall be returned
and given to the King,
to conform to ancient rites.”
The King firmly declined, and it was stopped.
It was also decreed that the King of Jìn wear a crown with twelve streamers,
erect the emperor’s banners and standards,
have a clear-the-way escort when going out and coming in,
ride in a golden-wheeled carriage drawn by six horses,
be provided with five seasonal auxiliary carriages,
have *máotóu* and *yúnhǎn* (military standards) displayed,
have eight rows of dancers and musicians,
and set up *zhōngjù* (bell stands) and palace screens.
The King’s consort was promoted to Queen,
the Heir Apparent to Crown Prince,
and the titles of princes, princesses, and royal grandsons remained as before.
The titles of princes, princesses, and royal grandsons remained as before.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
In autumn, in the eighth month, on the *xīnmǎo* day,
the Grand Counselor, King Wén of Jìn, passed away.
On the *rénchén* day,
Yán, the Crown Prince of Jìn, inherited the enfeoffment and assumed the position,
taking charge of all government affairs.
All regalia and official documents
were to be as before.
In this month,
Xiāngwǔ county reported seeing a giant,
over three *zhàng* tall,
with footprints three *chǐ* and two *cùn* long,
white-haired,
wearing a yellow unlined garment,
a yellow turban,
and leaning on a staff.
He called himself Wáng Shǐ, saying:
“There will now be great peace.”
In the ninth month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
Sī Tú Hé Céng was appointed Grand Chancellor of Jìn.
On the *guǐhài* day,
Piaòqí Jiāngjūn Sīmǎ Wàng was appointed Sī Tú,
Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn Shí Bāo was appointed Piaòqí Jiāngjūn,
and Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn Chén Qiān was appointed Chēqí Jiāngjūn.
On the *yǐhài* day,
King Wén of Jìn was buried.
In the intercalary month, on the *gēngchén* day,
Kāngjū and Dàyuān presented famous horses,
which were returned to the Grand Counselor’s Residence,
to manifest the achievement of attracting all nations and reaching the distant.
In the twelfth month, on the *rénxū* day,
the Mandate of Heaven had ended forever,
and the cosmic reckoning now rested with Jìn.
An imperial edict instructed the dukes and high officials to prepare rituals and set up an altar in the southern suburbs,
and to send an envoy to present the Emperor’s seals and ribbons, and a written decree,
ceding the throne to the Heir King of Jìn,
following the precedents of Hàn and Wèi.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
an envoy was sent to present the decree.
He then moved his residence to Jīnyǒng City,
and finally resided in Yè,
being twenty years old at the time.
A commentary states: In ancient times, the world was considered public,
and only the virtuous were elevated.
Later generations established hereditary positions,
appointing the eldest son by the principal wife as heir.
If the legitimate heir failed to continue the line,
then it was appropriate to choose a virtuous person from a collateral branch,
like Wén and Xuān of the Hàn dynasty.
This is an unchangeable, constant standard.
However, Míng Dì was unable to do this.
His emotions were bound by private affection,
and he raised an infant,
to whom he passed the great office.
His trust was not exclusive,
and he inevitably involved collateral relatives.
This ultimately led to the extermination of Cáo Shuǎng
and the dethronement of Qí Wáng.
The Duke of Gāoguì was intelligent and accomplished early on,
fond of inquiry and eloquent in speech.
He indeed possessed the elegant demeanor of Wén Dì.
However, his rashness and unrestrained temper
led him to great misfortune.
Chénliú Wáng respectfully faced south as ruler,
while the prime ministers governed.
He looked up to and followed previous precedents,
yielding and abdicating.
He then enjoyed being enfeoffed in a large state
and became a guest of Jìn.
Compared to Shānyáng,
his favor was even greater.
The Yì Jīng states:
“The male occupies his proper position outside,
the female occupies her proper position inside.
When male and female are in their proper positions,
it is the great righteousness of Heaven and Earth.”
The wise kings of ancient times
all understood the system of empresses and consorts,
conforming to the virtue of Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, with the two consorts Pín and Guī,
the way of Yú prospered;
with Rèn and Sì as consorts to Jī,
the Zhōu house flourished.
Rise and fall, survival and demise,
are always due to this.
The Chūnqiū states that the Son of Heaven has twelve daughters (concubines),
and feudal lords have nine daughters (concubines).
Examining this against common sense,
it is an unchangeable principle.
Yet in later ages, extravagance and license
indulged their extravagant desires,
leading to resentment among men and women,
disturbing the harmony.
Only beauty was valued,
not intrinsic virtuousness.
Therefore, moral education declined, and the great principles were destroyed and forgotten.
Is this not regrettable!
Alas,
those who possess states and families
should forever take this as a lesson!
According to the Hàn system,
the emperor's paternal grandmother was called Tài Huáng Tàihòu,
the emperor's mother was called Huáng Tàihòu,
and the emperor's principal consort was called Huánghòu.
The other inner palace officials had fourteen ranks.
Wèi adopted the Hàn laws;
the titles for empress mothers
were all according to the old system.
From the rank of Fūrén downwards,
there were periodic increases and decreases.
When Tài Zǔ founded the state,
he first appointed a Wáng Hòu.
Below her were five ranks: Fūrén,
Zhāoyí,
Yú,
Rónghuá,
and Měirén.
Wén Dì added Guìpín, Shúyuàn, Xiūróng, Shùnchéng, and Liángrén.
Míng Dì added Shúfēi, Zhāohuá, and Xiūyí;
and abolished the Shùnchéng official.
During the Tàihé era, Fūrén was again appointed
and elevated above Shúfēi.
From Fūrén downwards, there were twelve ranks in total: Guìpín and Fūrén
ranked next to the empress,
and their stipends were not specified.
Shúfēi ranked as prime minister (Xiàngguó),
and her stipend was comparable to that of a feudal king (Zhūhóu Wáng).
Shúyuàn ranked as censor-in-chief (Yùshǐ Dàfū),
and her stipend was comparable to that of a county duke (Xiàn Gōng).
Zhāoyí ranked as a county marquis (Xiàn Hóu).
Zhāohuá ranked as a district marquis (Xiāng Hóu).
Xiūróng ranked as a pavilion marquis (Tíng Hóu).
Xiūyí ranked as a Marquees of the Imperial Domain (Guānnèi Hóu).
Yú ranked as a Zhong Èrqiānshí.
Rónghuá ranked as a Zhēn Èrqiānshí.
Měirén ranked as a Bǐ Èrqiānshí.
Liángrén ranked as a Qiānshí.
Empress Wǔxuān, née Biàn,
was from Kāiyáng, Lángyá.
She was the mother of Wén Dì.
Originally from a courtesan family,
at age twenty, Tài Zǔ took her as a concubine in Qiáo.
Later, she followed Tài Zǔ to Luòyáng.
When Dǒng Zhuó caused chaos,
Tài Zǔ secretly left Luòyáng dressed as a commoner to avoid danger.
Yuán Shù spread false news of Tài Zǔ's death.
At that time, all of Tài Zǔ's attendants who were in Luòyáng wanted to return home.
The Empress stopped them, saying:
“Cáo Jūn's fate is yet unknown.
If you return home today,
and if he is alive tomorrow,
what face will you have to see him again?
Even if disaster has struck,
what hardship is there in dying together!”
They consequently followed the Empress's words.
Tài Zǔ heard of this and praised her.
In the early Jiàn'ān era,
Lady Dīng was deposed,
and the Empress was made his second wife.
For all his sons who had lost their mothers,
Tài Zǔ ordered the Empress to raise them.
When Wén Dì was made Crown Prince,
the palace attendants around him congratulated the Empress, saying:
“The General has been made Crown Prince,
and everyone in the world is delighted.
Your Majesty should open your storerooms to bestow rewards.”
The Empress said:
“The King himself chose Pī because he is older
and therefore made him heir.
I am only fortunate to have avoided the fault of failing to teach him.
Why should I give extravagant rewards?”
The attendants returned
and reported everything to Tài Zǔ.
Tài Zǔ was pleased and said:
“To not change one's expression in anger
and not lose one's composure in joy,
this is truly the most difficult thing.”
In the twenty-fourth year,
she was appointed Queen (Wáng Hòu).
The imperial edict stated:
“Lady Biàn
has raised all the sons
with the virtue of a mother.
Now she is promoted to Queen.
The Crown Prince and the feudal lords will attend her,
all officials will offer congratulations,
and capital crimes within the state will be reduced by one degree.”
In the twenty-fifth year,
Tài Zǔ died.
Wén Dì ascended the throne as King
and honored the Empress as Queen Mother (Wáng Tàihòu).
When he became emperor,
he honored her as Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu)
and called her Yǒngshòu Gōng.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he honored the Empress Dowager as Grand Empress Dowager (Tài Huáng Tàihòu).
During the Huángchū era,
Wén Dì wanted to posthumously enfeoff the Empress Dowager's parents.
Shàngshū Chén Qún memorialized, saying:
“Your Majesty, by your sage virtue, has responded to the cosmic shift and received the mandate.
You have founded an enterprise and reformed the system,
which should serve as an eternal model for later generations.
According to the texts of the classics,
there is no system of women being granted territory or titles.
In the rites,
a woman takes her title from her husband.
Qín violated ancient law,
and the Hàn dynasty followed suit,
which is not the excellent institution of the former kings.”
The Emperor said:
“This argument is correct.
Do not implement it.
Let this edict be recorded and stored in the palace archives
to serve as an eternal model for later generations.”
However, in the spring of the fourth year of Tàihé,
Míng Dì posthumously honored the Empress Dowager's grandfather Guǎng as Kāiyáng Gōng Hóu,
and her father Yuǎn as Jìng Hóu.
Her grandmother Zhōu was enfeoffed as Yángdū Jūn and
(Jìng) Hóu Fūrén.
All were granted seals and ribbons.
In the fifth month of that year,
the Empress died.
In the seventh month,
she was interred together with Tài Zǔ in Gāolíng.
Initially,
the Empress Dowager’s younger brother, Bǐng (秉),
was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dūxiāng (都鄉) for his meritorious service.
In the seventh year of Huángchū (黃初) (226 CE), he was advanced to Marquis of Kāiyáng (開陽),
with an income of one thousand two hundred households,
and served as General Zhaoliè (昭烈將軍).
After Bǐng (秉) died,
his son Lán (蘭) succeeded him.
He was talented and learned from a young age,
serving as Fengchē Dūwèi (奉車都尉) and Yoují Jiāngjūn (游擊將軍),
and was granted Sanqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
After Lán (蘭) died,
his son Huī (暉) succeeded him.
Later, Bǐng’s (秉) peerage was divided,
and Lán’s (蘭) younger brother Lín (琳) was enfeoffed as a Liehou (列侯),
rising to the rank of Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉).
Lán’s (蘭) granddaughter, the daughter of Lóng (隆), became the Empress of Gāoguì Xiānggōng (高貴鄉公).
Lóng (隆), as the Empress’s father, was made Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
with the rank of Tèjìn (特進),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Suīyáng Xiāng (睢陽鄉).
His wife, Lady Wáng (王), was enfeoffed as Xiǎnyáng Xiāngjūn (顯陽鄉君).
Lóng’s (隆) former wife, Lady Líu (劉), was posthumously enfeoffed as Shùnyáng Xiāngjūn (順陽鄉君),
because she was the Empress’s birth mother.
Lín’s (琳) daughter later became the Empress of Chénlíu Wáng (陳留王).
At that time, Lín (琳) had already died,
so his wife, Lady Líu (劉), was enfeoffed as Guǎngyáng Xiāngjūn (廣陽鄉君).
Empress Wénzhāo Zhēn (文昭甄皇后) was
a native of Wújí (無極) in Zhōngshān (中山).
She was the mother of Emperor Míng (明帝).
She was a descendant of the Hàn (漢) Grand Protector, Zhēn Hán (甄邯),
and her family had held official positions with a salary of two thousand bushels for generations.
Her father, Yì (逸),
was the Prefect of Shàngcài (上蔡).
The Empress lost her father when she was three years old.
Later, the world was in military turmoil,
and compounded by famine,
the common people all sold their gold, silver, pearls, jade, and other precious objects.
At that time, the Empress’s family had a large store of grain,
and they used a considerable amount to buy these items.
When the Empress was over ten years old,
she spoke to her mother, saying:
“Now the world is in chaos, and we are buying many treasures.
An ordinary man is innocent,
but possessing a jade disc makes him guilty.
Moreover, everyone around us is hungry and distressed.
It would be better to use the grain to relieve our relatives and neighbors,
thus widely extending our benevolence.”
The whole family praised her words,
and immediately followed her advice.
During the Jiàn’ān (建安) period (196-220 CE),
Yuán Shào (袁紹) took her as wife for his second son, Xī (熙).
Xī (熙) went out to govern Yōuzhōu (幽州),
and the Empress remained to care for her mother-in-law.
When Jìzhōu (冀州) was pacified,
Emperor Wén (文帝) took the Empress at Yè (鄴).
She was favored and
gave birth to Emperor Míng (明帝) and Princess Dōngxiāng (東鄉公主).
In the first month of the first year of Yánkāng (延康) (220 CE),
Emperor Wén (文帝) ascended the throne as King.
In the sixth month,
he campaigned south,
and the Empress remained in Yè (鄴).
In the tenth month of the first year of Huángchū (黃初) (220 CE),
the Emperor ascended the imperial throne.
After he ascended the throne,
the Duke of Shānyáng (山陽公) offered his two daughters to be consorts in Wèi (魏).
Empress Guō (郭后), Lady Lǐ (李), and Lady Yīn (陰貴人) were all loved and favored,
and the Empress became increasingly disheartened
and uttered words of complaint.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and in the sixth month of the second year (221 CE),
he sent an envoy to bestow death upon her.
She was buried in Yè (鄴).
When Emperor Míng (明帝) ascended the throne,
the relevant officials memorialized to posthumously grant her an honorific title.
They sent Sīkōng (司空) Wáng Lǎng (王朗), holding the insignia of authority, to offer a memorial and perform a Grand Sacrifice at her tomb,
and also separately established a sleeping temple (ancestral shrine).
In the third month of the first year of Tàihé (太和) (227 CE),
one thousand households from the Ānchéng (安城) township of Wèichāng (魏昌) in Zhōngshān (中山) were
posthumously enfeoffed to Yì (逸),
who was given the posthumous title Marquis Jìng (敬侯);
his eldest grandson Xiàng (像) inherited the title.
In the fourth month,
when the ancestral temple was first being constructed,
a jade seal was unearthed,
measuring one cun and nine fen square.
Its inscription read:
“The Son of Heaven longs for his loving mother.”
Emperor Míng (明帝) changed his countenance because of this,
and offered a Grand Sacrifice at the temple.
He also once dreamed of the Empress,
and so he ranked the closeness and status of her maternal relatives,
bestowing favors accordingly.
The rewards accumulated to tens of thousands;
Xiàng (像) was made Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng (虎賁中郎將).
In this month,
the Empress’s mother died.
The Emperor wore mourning clothes (sīfú) to attend the funeral,
and all the officials joined him.
In the eleventh month of the fourth year (230 CE),
because the Empress’s old tomb was low and humble,
Xiàng (像) was made acting Tàiwèi (太尉),
and, holding the insignia of authority, went to Yè (鄴)
to make a solemn announcement to Hòutǔ (后土).
In the twelfth month,
she was reinterred at Cháoyáng Líng (朝陽陵).
Upon Xiàng’s (像) return,
he was promoted to Sanqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
In the spring of the second year of Qīnglóng (青龍) (234 CE),
the Empress’s brother Yǎn (儼) was posthumously honored as Ānchéng Xiāng Mùhóu (安城鄉穆侯).
In the summer,
the Wú (吳) bandits invaded Yángzhōu (揚州).
Xiàng (像) was appointed Fúbō Jiāngjūn (伏波將軍),
and, holding the insignia of authority, supervised the various generals in the eastern expedition.
Upon his return,
he was reinstated as Shèshēng Xiàowèi (射聲校尉).
In the third year (235 CE), he died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍),
re-enfeoffed in Wèichāng Xiàn (魏昌縣),
and given the posthumous title Marquis Zhēn (貞侯);
his son Chàng (暢) succeeded him.
Chàng’s (暢) younger brothers Wēn (溫) and Yàn (豔) were also enfeoffed as Liehou (列侯).
In the fourth year (236 CE),
Yì (逸) and Yǎn’s (儼) original enfeoffments were both changed to Wèichāng Hóu (魏昌侯),
with their posthumous titles remaining as before.
Yǎn’s (儼) principal wife, Lady Líu (劉), was enfeoffed as Dōngxiāng Jūn (東鄉君),
and Yì’s (逸) principal wife, Lady Zhāng (張), was posthumously enfeoffed as Ānxǐ Jūn (安喜君).
In the summer of the first year of Jǐngchū (景初) (237 CE),
the relevant officials discussed and finalized the Seven Ancestral Temples.
In the winter,
they further memorialized, saying:
“Verily, when emperors and kings rise,
there are both rulers who receive the Mandate,
and also sagely consorts who are in harmony with the divine spirit.
Only then can their generations prosper
to accomplish the imperial enterprise.
In ancient times, Gāoxīnshì (高辛氏) divined that the sons of his four consorts would all possess the realm,
and Emperor Zhì (帝摯), Táotáng (陶唐), Shāng (商), and Zhōu (周) successively rose.
The Zhōu (周) people traced back to Hòujì (后稷)
to match him with August Heaven,
and in recounting the origins of their kingship,
they based it on Jiāngyuán (姜嫄).
They specially established a palace temple [for her],
where she was honored and offered sacrifices generation after generation.
This is what the 'Rites of Zhōu' (周禮) refers to as, 'Playing the 'Yīzé' (夷則),
singing the 'Zhōnglǚ' (中呂),
and dancing the 'Dàhù' (大濩),
to honor the ancestral mother.'
The poet praised her, saying:
‘The first to give birth to the people,
it was Jiāngyuán (姜嫄).’
This speaks of the foundation of royal transformation,
the origin of the people’s birth.
It also says: ‘The secret temple is silent and profound,
how substantial and grand!
Resplendent is Jiāngyuán (姜嫄),
her virtue is unswerving.’
The 'Shī' (詩) (Classic of Poetry) and 'Lǐ' (禮) (Book of Rites) describe the flourishing of the Jī (姬) clan,
whose beauty was thus.
The Great Wèi (魏) corresponds to the era [of Yú (虞)],
and its imperial Way has been greatly enhanced,
flourishing over three generations.
The number of its ancestral temples
is indeed the same as that of Zhōu (周).
Now, Empress Wǔxuān (武宣皇后) and Empress Wéndé (文德皇后) are each matched with an unending prosperity.
As for Empress Wénzhāo (文昭皇后), she received the celestial spiritual token,
gave birth to a brilliant sage,
her accomplishments benefited the common people,
and her virtue filled the universe,
opening the way for all future generations.
This is where the Way and transformation arise.
Her sleeping temple’s special sacrifices
are also like Jiāngyuán’s (姜嫄) secret temple.
However, the regulation for its perpetual preservation has not yet been established.
We fear that the principle of acknowledging merit and repaying virtue
might be neglected throughout the myriad generations,
which is not how one manifests filiality and sets an example for later generations.
The Wénzhāo (文昭) Temple should be perpetually honored with sacrifices and music,
just like the ancestral temple,
establishing a permanent, unperishing canon,
to spread the wind of sagely goodness.”
Thereupon, this discussion, along with the deliberation on the Seven Ancestral Temples,
was engraved on golden tablets
and stored in a golden cabinet.
The Emperor constantly thought of his maternal uncle.
Chàng was still young.
Towards the end of the Jǐngchū reign,
Chàng was made Archer-Captain,
and additionally, an Attendant Official.
A grand mansion was specially built for him,
and the imperial carriage personally visited it.
Also, in his back garden, a temple was built for the Emperor's mother,
and the district was named Wèiyáng Lǐ,
to commemorate his mother.
In the first month of the third year of Jiāpíng,
Chàng died.
He was posthumously granted the title of General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and given the posthumous epithet Gōng Hóu.
His son, Shào, succeeded him.
In the sixth year of Tàihé,
Míngdì's beloved daughter, Shú, died.
Shú was posthumously enfeoffed and given the epithet Píngyuán Yì Gōngzhǔ,
and a temple was built for her.
The Empress's deceased collateral grandnephew, Huáng, was taken and interred with her.
Huáng was posthumously enfeoffed as a Liehou.
The Empress's father, Guō Shì's collateral younger brother, Dé, was made his successor,
to carry on the Zhēn clan name.
Dé was enfeoffed as Píngyuán Hóu,
inheriting the Princess's rank.
During the Qīnglóng reign,
the Empress's collateral elder brother's son, Yì, and three of her younger brothers
were all enfeoffed as Liehou.
Yì repeatedly submitted memorials on current affairs,
and his highest official position was Colonel of Yueqi.
During the Jiāpíng reign,
Chàng's two sons were again enfeoffed as Liehou.
The Empress's elder brother Yǎn's granddaughter became the Empress of Qí Wáng.
Since the Empress's father had already passed away,
her mother was enfeoffed as Guǎngyuè Xiāng Jūn.
Empress Wéndé Guō Shì was
a native of Guǎngzōng, Ānpíng.
Her ancestors had been long-term officials.
When the Empress was young, her father Yǒng marveled at her, saying:
"This is truly the queen among my daughters."
Thus, he gave her the courtesy name Nǚwáng.
She lost both parents early
and was displaced by chaos and turmoil,
ending up in the household of Hóu of Tóngdī.
When Tàizǔ was Duke of Wèi,
she was able to enter the Eastern Palace.
The Empress possessed wisdom and resourcefulness,
and from time to time offered advice and proposals.
When Wéndì was designated as heir,
the Empress had a role in it.
When the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
she became a Fūrén,
and upon his enthronement,
she became a Guìpín.
The death of Empress Zhēn was due to the Empress's favor.
In the third year of Huángchū,
as she was about to ascend to the position of Empress,
Wéndì wanted to establish her as Empress.
Zhàn Qián, a Zhonglang, submitted a memorial, stating:
"In ancient times, when emperors and kings governed the world,
they did not just rely on external assistance,
but also had internal support.
The reasons for order or chaos,
and the rise or fall of prosperity, followed from this.
Thus, Xīlíng married Huáng,
and Yīng É descended to Guī,
both renowned for their virtue and wisdom,
their fragrant reputations flowing down through ancient times.
Jié fled to Náncháo,
disaster stemming from Mòxǐ;
Zhòu used the Cannon Roasting punishment,
to please Dájǐ.
Therefore, sagely and wise rulers carefully establish their principal empresses,
always choosing from the noble and ancient families of previous generations,
selecting those who are virtuous and refined to govern the six palaces,
reverently serve the ancestral temples,
and diligently cultivate internal education.
The Yìjīng says:
'When the family is in order, the world is at peace.'
From the internal to the external,
this was the excellent tradition of the former kings.
The Chunqiu records Zōngrén Xìnxià, stating
that there is no rite for making a concubine a principal wife.
Qí Huán swore an oath at Kuíqiū,
also saying, 'Do not make a concubine a wife.'
Now, the palace favorite
often rides in a carriage second only to the Emperor.
If she is elevated to Empress due to affection,
causing a lowly person to become suddenly powerful,
I fear that in later generations, subordinates will disrespect superiors,
and improper extravagance will become widespread,
with chaos originating from the top."
Wéndì did not heed this,
and consequently established her as Empress.
The Empress lost her brothers early,
so her collateral elder brother Biǎo succeeded Yǒng.
He was appointed Commandant of Chariots.
The Empress's distant relative Liú Fěi married into another state.
When the Empress heard of this,
she issued an edict saying:
"All relatives' marriages
should naturally be with households of similar standing in their hometowns.
They must not, by relying on power,
forcibly marry people from other regions."
The Empress's sister's son Mèng Wǔ returned to his hometown
and sought a minor wife.
The Empress stopped him.
She then issued an edict to all families, saying:
"Currently, there are few women in the world.
They should be married to soldiers and officers.
One must not, through connections, take them as concubines.
You should all be cautious yourselves;
do not become the first to be punished."
In the fifth year,
the Emperor campaigned in the east.
The Empress remained at the Yǒngshǐ Terrace in Xǔchāng.
At that time, there was continuous rain for over a hundred days,
and many city towers were damaged.
Officials requested that she move residences.
The Empress said:
"Formerly, when Chǔ Zhāowáng went on an excursion,
Zhēnjiāng remained on Jiàntái.
The Jiang River rose,
and an envoy came to escort her, but without an imperial tally,
she refused to leave
and drowned.
Now the Emperor is far away.
Fortunately, I do not yet have such a misfortune,
but to move residences just like that,
how can I?"
None of the officials dared to speak again.
In the sixth year,
the Emperor campaigned against Wú in the east.
When he reached Guǎnglíng,
the Empress remained at Qiáo Palace.
At that time, Biǎo stayed behind to guard the palace.
He wanted to block the water to catch fish.
The Empress said:
"The water should be open for transport and grain.
Moreover, there is little timber.
If the servants are not around,
you will again privately take official bamboo and wood to build a dam.
What the Commandant of Chariots lacks now,
is it fish?"
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
he honored the Empress as Empress Dowager,
residing in Yǒng'ān Palace.
In the fourth year of Tàihé,
an edict enfeoffed Biǎo as Ānyáng Tíng Hóu.
He was further promoted to Xiāng Hóu,
with an increase of five hundred households to his previous fief, for a total of five hundred households.
He was promoted to Central Camp General.
Biǎo's son, Xiáng, was made Cavalry Commandant.
In the same year,
the Emperor posthumously granted the Empress Dowager's father Yǒng the title Ānyáng Xiāng Jìng Hóu,
and her mother Dǒng the title Dū Xiāng Jūn.
Biǎo was promoted to Zhāodé General,
granted a golden seal and purple ribbon,
with the rank of Special Advance.
Biǎo's second son, Xùn, was made Cavalry Commandant.
When Mèng Wǔ's mother died,
and he wanted a lavish burial
and to build an ancestral hall,
the Empress Dowager stopped him, saying:
"Since the period of chaos and turmoil,
no tombs have been left undisturbed;
this is all due to lavish burials.
The Shǒuyáng Tomb can serve as an example."
In the spring of the third year of Qīnglóng,
the Empress Dowager died in Xǔchāng.
Due to the mourning period, the imperial tomb construction was completed.
On the Gēngyín day of the third month,
she was buried west of Shǒuyáng Tomb.
The Emperor promoted Biǎo to Guānchīn Hóu,
increasing his fief by five hundred,
for a total of one thousand households.
Xiáng was promoted to Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
In the fourth year,
Yǒng was posthumously re-enfeoffed as Guānchīn Jìng Hóu,
and his wife Dǒng as Tángyáng Jūn.
The Empress's elder brothers Fú, Dū, and Chéng were posthumously enfeoffed and given epithets: Fú as Liánglǐ Tíng Dài Hóu,
Dū as Wǔchéng Tíng Xiào Hóu,
and Chéng as Xīnlè Tíng Dìng Hóu.
Envoys were sent to present the imperial edicts
and offer sacrificial cattle.
When Biǎo died,
his son Xiáng succeeded him.
Furthermore, Biǎo's title was divided to enfeoff Xiáng's younger brother Shù as a Liehou.
When Xiáng died,
his son Zhāo succeeded him.
Míng Dào Máo Huánghòu
was from Hénèi.
In the middle of the Huángchū era,
she was chosen to enter the Eastern Palace.
When Emperor Míng was the Prince of Píngyuán,
she was favored by him,
and they shared a carriage whenever they went out.
When he ascended the throne to become emperor,
she was made Guìbīn.
In the first year of Tàihé,
she was established as empress.
The empress's father, Jiā,
was appointed Qí Dūwèi,
and her younger brother, Zēng,
was Lángzhōng.
Initially,
when Emperor Míng was a prince,
he had first taken Lady Yú of Hénèi as his consort.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Lady Yú was not established as empress,
and Empress Dowager Biàn comforted and encouraged her.
Lady Yú said,
"The Cáos have a habit of establishing the low-born,
and none have ever been chosen based on righteousness.
However, the empress manages internal affairs,
and the sovereign oversees external governance.
Their paths rely on each other to succeed.
If one cannot begin well,
one cannot expect a good end.
This will likely lead to the demise of the state and the loss of ancestral sacrifices!"
Lady Yú was then dismissed and returned to Yègōng.
Jiā was promoted to Fèngchē Dūwèi,
and Zēng to Qí Dūwèi,
receiving lavish favors and gifts.
Shortly thereafter,
Jiā was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Bó Píng Xiāng
and promoted to Guānglù Dàfū,
and Zēng became Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Jiā had originally been a supervisor of carriage artisans.
Having suddenly become wealthy and noble,
Emperor Míng ordered his court officials to gather at Jiā's home for a banquet.
His demeanor and actions were exceedingly boorish.
When he spoke, he always referred to himself
as "this marquis."
People at the time found this amusing.
Later, Jiā was further promoted to the position of Tèjìn,
and Zēng was transferred to Sànqí Shìláng.
In the third year of Qīnglóng,
Jiā died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Guānglù Dàfū,
re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānguó,
his stipend was increased by 500 households,
totaling 1,000 households,
and he was given the posthumous title of Jiéhóu.
In the fourth year,
the empress's mother, Xià, was posthumously enfeoffed as Yěwáng Jūn.
When the Emperor favored Empress Guō Yuán,
the empress's affection and favor waned daily.
In the first year of Jǐngchū,
the Emperor was strolling in the imperial garden,
and summoned court ladies of the Cairen rank and above for a banquet of extreme revelry.
Empress Yuán said,
"It would be proper to invite the Empress,"
but the Emperor refused.
He then forbade his attendants,
from divulging anything.
The empress learned of it.
The next day,
when the Emperor saw the empress,
she said,
"Yesterday's banquet in the northern garden,
was it enjoyable?"
The Emperor believed his attendants had leaked the information,
and killed more than ten people.
He then ordered the empress to commit suicide,
but still conferred a posthumous title
and buried her in Mǐnlíng.
Zēng was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì,
and later moved to become Yǔlín Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng and Yuánwǔ Diǎnnóng.
Míng Yuán Guō Huánghòu
was from Xīpíng,
a prominent clan in the Héyòu region for generations.
In the middle of the Huángchū era,
her native commandery rebelled,
and she was consequently taken into the palace.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
she was greatly favored
and appointed Fūrén.
Her uncle Lì was appointed Qí Dūwèi,
and her cousin Zhī became Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng.
When the Emperor was critically ill,
she was then established as empress.
When the Prince of Qí ascended the throne,
he honored the empress as Huáng Tàihòu,
residing in Yǒngníng Gōng.
The empress dowager's father, Mǎn, was posthumously enfeoffed and given the title Xīdū Dìnghóu,
and Lì's son Jiàn inherited his peerage.
The empress dowager's mother, Dù, was enfeoffed as Hépáng Jūn.
Zhī was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì and Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
Lì
to Xuāndé Jiāngjūn,
and all were enfeoffed as marquises.
Jiàn's elder brother, Dé,
was adopted into the Zhēn clan.
Both Dé and Jiàn became Zhènhù Jiāngjūn,
were enfeoffed as marquises,
and were in charge of the imperial guard.
During the time of the three young and weak rulers,
the imperial regents governed.
All major decisions regarding appointments and dismissals
were first reported to the empress dowager before being implemented.
When Qiū Jiǎn, Zhōng Huì, and others rebelled,
they all claimed to be acting under her decree as their justification.
She died on the twelfth day of the twelfth month of the fourth year of Jǐngyuán.
In the second month of the fifth year,
she was buried west of Gāopínglíng.
Commentary: Although the families of Wèi empresses and consorts
were said to be rich and noble,
none were like those of the decadent Hàn, who seized power they did not possess
and manipulated court politics.
Learning from the past and changing course
was commendable in this regard.
Reconsidering Chén Qún's deliberations
and Zhàn Qián's discussions,
they are indeed sufficient to serve as a model for a hundred kings
and provide a standard for future generations.
Biography of Dǒng, the Two Yuán, and Liú, Part Six
Dǒng Zhuó, courtesy name Zhòngyǐng,
was from Líntáo, Lǒngxī.
In his youth, he enjoyed chivalry
and once traveled among the Qiāng people,
where he befriended all the prominent chiefs.
Later, he returned to farm in the countryside,
and when some prominent chiefs came to visit him,
Zhuó returned with them
and slaughtered his farming ox to feast and revel with them.
The chiefs were moved by his gesture
and, upon returning, gathered
over a thousand various livestock to present to Zhuó.
In the late reign of Emperor Huán of Hàn,
he was appointed Yǔlín Láng from a good family in the Six Commanderies.
Zhuó possessed talent and martial prowess,
with strength rarely matched.
He carried two quivers
and could shoot arrows while riding swiftly left and right.
He served as Jūnsīmǎ,
and, accompanying Zhōnglángjiàng Zhāng Huàn, he campaigned in Bìngzhōu, achieving merit.
He was appointed Lángzhōng
and granted nine thousand bolts of silk,
which Zhuó distributed entirely among his officers and soldiers.
He was promoted to Guǎngwǔ Lìng,
Dūwèi of the Northern part of Shǔjùn,
and Wùjǐ Xiàowèi of the Western Regions,
but was dismissed.
He was summoned and appointed Cìshǐ of Bìngzhōu and Tàishǒu of Hédōng.
He was promoted to Zhōnglángjiàng
to suppress the Yellow Turbans,
but his army was defeated, and he was punished.
When Hán Suì and others rose in Liángzhōu,
he was again made Zhōnglángjiàng
to resist Suì in the west.
At Wàngyuánxiá North,
he was surrounded by tens of thousands of Qiāng and Hú people,
and his provisions were exhausted.
Zhuó pretended he wanted to catch fish,
damming the water that they would cross on their return path to form a pond.
He allowed the water to accumulate for dozens of *lǐ*,
then secretly moved his army past the dam and breached it.
By the time the Qiāng and Hú learned of it and gave chase,
the water was already deep
and impassable.
At that time, of the six armies that advanced into Lǒngxī,
five were defeated.
Zhuó alone returned with his entire force intact,
stationing them in Fúfēng.
He was appointed Qián Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Xiānghóu,
then summoned to be Bìngzhōu Mù.
Emperor Líng (Língdì) passed away.
The Young Emperor (Shàodì) ascended the throne.
The Grand General Hé Jìn (Hé Jìn) and the Colonel-Director of Retainers, Yuán Shào (Yuán Shào), conspired to execute all the eunuch officials,
but the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) did not consent.
Hé Jìn (Hé Jìn) then summoned Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) to lead troops to the capital,
and secretly ordered him to submit a memorial stating:
“The Palace Regular Attendants Zhāng Ràng (Zhāng Ràng) and others have seized favor and ridden on privilege,
corrupting the entire realm.
In the past, Zhào Yāng (Zhào Yāng) raised the troops of Jìnyáng (Jìnyáng)
to expel the wicked men beside the lord.
I shall immediately beat the bells and drums and proceed to Luòyáng (Luòyáng),
to immediately suppress Zhāng Ràng (Zhāng Ràng) and the others.”
He intended to use this to coerce the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu).
Before Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) arrived,
Hé Jìn (Hé Jìn) was defeated.
The Palace Regular Attendants Duàn Guī (Duàn Guī) and others kidnapped the Emperor and fled to Xiǎopíngjīn (Xiǎopíngjīn).
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) then led his forces to welcome the Emperor at Běimáng (Běimáng)
and returned to the palace.
At this time, Hé Jìn's (Hé Jìn) younger brother, the General of Cavalry and Chariots Miáo (Miáo), was killed by Hé Jìn's (Hé Jìn) troops.
The divisions of Hé Jìn (Hé Jìn) and Miáo (Miáo) had no one to belong to,
and all went to Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó).
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) also sent Lǚ Bù (Lǚ Bù) to kill the Colonel Who Holds the Gilded Mace, Dīng Yuán (Dīng Yuán),
and seized his troops.
Thus, the military power in the capital was solely in Dǒng Zhuó's (Dǒng Zhuó) hands.
Before this,
Hé Jìn (Hé Jìn) had dispatched the Cavalry Commandant Bào Xìn (Bào Xìn) of Tàishān (Tàishān) to recruit troops wherever he went.
When he happened to arrive,
Bào Xìn (Bào Xìn) said to Yuán Shào (Yuán Shào):
“Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) commands powerful troops
and has ulterior motives.
If we do not deal with him early,
we will be controlled by him.
While he has just arrived and is tired,
we can attack him and capture him.”
Yuán Shào (Yuán Shào) feared Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó)
and dared not act.
Bào Xìn (Bào Xìn) then returned to his hometown.
Subsequently, due to a prolonged drought,
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) engineered the dismissal of Sīkōng (Sīkōng) Liú Hóng (Liú Hóng) and took his place.
Soon after, he was promoted to Tàiwèi (Tàiwèi),
and was granted the imperial insignia, battle-axe, and the Tiger Guards.
He then deposed the Emperor as the King of Hóngnóng (Hóngnóng).
Soon after, he also killed the King and Empress Dowager Hé (Hé Tàihòu).
He enthroned the youngest son of Emperor Líng (Língdì), the King of Chénliú (Chénliú),
who became Emperor Xiàn (Xiàndì).
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) was promoted to Xiàngguó (Xiàngguó),
enfeoffed as the Marquis of Méi (Méi Hóu),
given the privilege of not stating his name when announced for an audience,
and allowed to wear a sword and shoes in court.
He also enfeoffed Dǒng Zhuó's (Dǒng Zhuó) mother as the Lady of Chíyáng (Chíyáng Jūn),
and appointed a household steward and assistant.
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó), having led elite troops,
arrived precisely during a great disorder in the imperial house,
and was able to exclusively decide on depositions and enthronements,
controlling the military arsenal and armor,
and national treasures,
his might shaking the world.
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) was cruel and inhumane by nature,
and he used harsh punishments to threaten the masses.
Even for a minor grievance, he would retaliate,
so people could not protect themselves.
He once sent troops to Yángchéng (Yángchéng).
It happened to be the Shè (Shè) festival in the second month.
The people were all at their respective Shè (Shè) altars.
He ordered all the men's heads to be cut off,
harnessed their chariots and oxen,
loaded their women and valuables,
tied the severed heads to the carriage shafts,
and returned to Luòyáng (Luòyáng) in a long procession.
He claimed to have attacked bandits and made great gains,
and shouted "Long live!"
Upon entering, he opened the Yángchéng (Yángchéng) city gates,
burned the heads,
and took the women and armored soldiers as maids and concubines.
He even committed atrocities against palace women and princesses.
His villainy was thus.
Initially,
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) trusted the Minister Zhōu Bì (Zhōu Bì),
the Colonel of the City Gate Wǔ Qióng (Wǔ Qióng), and others.
He appointed Hán Fù (Hán Fù), Liú Dài (Liú Dài), Kǒng Zhòu (Kǒng Zhòu), Zhāng Zī (Zhāng Zī), Zhāng Miǎo (Zhāng Miǎo), and others, whom they recommended, to govern provinces and commanderies.
But when Hán Fù (Hán Fù) and the others reached their posts,
they all gathered their armies to attack Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó).
When Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) heard of this,
he believed that Zhōu Bì (Zhōu Bì) and Wǔ Qióng (Wǔ Qióng) were secretly colluding and betraying him,
so he executed them all.
Wáng Kuāng (Wáng Kuāng), the Administrator of Hénèi (Hénèi),
sent Tàishān (Tàishān) troops to station at Hèyángjīn (Hèyángjīn),
intending to scheme against Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó).
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) sent a diversionary force, pretending to cross at Píngyīn (Píngyīn),
while secretly sending elite troops to cross north of Xiǎopíng (Xiǎopíng).
They encircled and attacked their rear,
routing them completely north of the ford,
where almost all were killed.
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) was fearful and uneasy due to the concurrent uprisings of the heroes in Shāndōng (Shāndōng).
In the second month of the first year of Chúpíng (Chúpíng),
he moved the Son of Heaven's capital to Cháng'ān (Cháng'ān).
He burned the palaces and residences in Luòyáng (Luòyáng),
completely excavated the imperial tombs,
and took their treasures.
When Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) reached the Western Capital,
he became the Grand Tutor (Tàishī),
and was honored with the title “Father of the Nation” (Shàngfù).
He rode in a golden-wheeled chariot with a green canopy,
with images of claws painted on both sides,
which people at the time called the Gānmó (Gānmó) chariot.
Dǒng Zhuó's (Dǒng Zhuó) younger brother Mín (Mín) was made General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn)
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Hù (Hù Hóu);
his nephew Huáng (Huáng) was made Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Colonel of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Xiàowèi) in command of troops.
His entire clan, both close and distant, were arrayed in the imperial court.
The grandees and ministers, upon seeing Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó),
would pay obeisance before his chariot,
but Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) showed no courtesy.
He summoned and called upon all officials from the Three Ducal Ministers and Grand Ministers downwards to come personally to Dǒng Zhuó's (Dǒng Zhuó) residence to report on affairs.
He constructed the fort of Méiwù (Méiwù),
as high as the city walls of Cháng'ān (Cháng'ān),
accumulating grain for thirty years' storage.
He said that if his endeavor succeeded,
he would dominate the world,
and if it failed,
guarding this would be enough to live out his old age.
He once visited Méi (Méi) to inspect the fort.
The grandees and ministers, and all below them, gathered to bid him farewell outside Hèngmén (Hèngmén).
(Hèng is pronounced Guāng.)
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) had already set up tents for drinking.
He lured several hundred rebels from Běidì (Běidì) to surrender.
While they were seated, he first cut out their tongues,
or cut off their hands and feet,
or gouged out their eyes,
or boiled them in a cauldron.
While they were not yet dead,
they writhed and rolled among the cups and tables.
All who were present trembled with fear and dropped their spoons and chopsticks,
but Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) ate and drank as usual.
The Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ), observing the astral phenomena,
said there would be a high minister executed.
The former Grand Tutor (Tàiwèi) Zhāng Wēn (Zhāng Wēn), then Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi),
had always been at odds with Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó).
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) harbored resentment towards him.
Seizing upon a celestial anomaly,
and wishing to avert misfortune,
he sent people to claim that Zhāng Wēn (Zhāng Wēn) had colluded with Yuán Shù (Yuán Shù),
and then had him flogged to death.
His laws were harsh and cruel,
his judgments swayed by love and hate, leading to excessive punishments.
People falsely accused each other,
and thousands died unjustly.
The common people wailed,
and communicated with glances on the roads.
He completely smashed the bronze statues and bell stands,
and destroyed the Wǔzhū (Wǔzhū) coins.
He then cast smaller coins,
which were five parts of the old size,
without inscriptions,
with rough rims and no clear edge,
and unpolished.
Consequently, currency became cheap while goods became expensive,
with one hú (hú) of grain costing several hundred thousand.
From then on, money was no longer used.
In the fourth month of the third year,

the Minister of Works (Sītú) Wáng Yǔn (Wáng Yǔn), the Imperial Secretary (Shàngshū Púshè) Shìsūn Ruì (Shìsūn Ruì), and Dǒng Zhuó's (Dǒng Zhuó) general Lǚ Bù (Lǚ Bù) conspired to execute Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó).
At this time,
the Son of Heaven had just recovered from an illness,
and a grand assembly was held at the Wèiyáng (Wèiyáng) Palace.
Lǚ Bù (Lǚ Bù) dispatched the Cavalry Commandant (Qí Dūwèi) Lǐ Sù (Lǐ Sù) and others from the same commandery,
leading over ten personal guards,
to falsely wear the uniforms of imperial guards and guard the side gate.
Lǚ Bù (Lǚ Bù) carried an imperial edict.
When Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) arrived,
Lǐ Sù (Lǐ Sù) and the others attacked Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó).
Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) cried out in surprise, asking where Lǚ Bù (Lǚ Bù) was.
Lǚ Bù (Lǚ Bù) said,
“There is an imperial edict!”
and then killed Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó),
exterminating his three familial clans.
The Chief Clerk Tián Jǐng (Tián Jǐng) rushed forward to Dǒng Zhuó's (Dǒng Zhuó) corpse,
and Lǚ Bù (Lǚ Bù) also killed him.
In total, three people were killed,
and no one else dared to move.
The literati and common people of Cháng'ān (Cháng'ān) all celebrated,
and all those who had flattered Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) were imprisoned and executed.
Initially,
Dǒng Zhuó's (Dǒng Zhuó) son-in-law, the Colonel-Protector (Zhōnglángjiàng) Niú Fǔ (Niú Fǔ), commanded troops and was separately stationed at Shǎn (Shǎn).
He sent out commandants Lǐ Què (Lǐ Què), Guō Sì (Guō Sì), and Zhāng Jì (Zhāng Jì) to plunder the various counties of Chénliú (Chénliú) and Yǐngchuān (Yǐngchuān).
After Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) died,
Lǚ Bù (Lǚ Bù) sent Lǐ Sù (Lǐ Sù) to Shǎn (Shǎn),
intending to execute Niú Fǔ (Niú Fǔ) by imperial edict.
Niú Fǔ (Niú Fǔ) and the others fought Lǐ Sù (Lǐ Sù),
Lǐ Sù (Lǐ Sù) was defeated and fled to Hóngnóng (Hóngnóng),
and Lǚ Bù (Lǚ Bù) executed Lǐ Sù (Lǐ Sù).
Later, some of Niú Fǔ's (Niú Fǔ) camp soldiers rebelled and escaped during the night.
The camp was in a panic.
Niú Fǔ (Niú Fǔ) thought they had all rebelled,
so he took gold and treasures,
and fled alone with five or six trusted associates, including Hú Chì'ér (Hú Chì'ér).
They scaled the city wall and crossed the river to the north.
Hú Chì'ér (Hú Chì'ér) and the others coveted his gold and treasures,
so they beheaded him and sent his head to Cháng'ān (Cháng'ān).
When Guō Jǐ, etc., returned,
Fǔ had already been defeated.
The troops had nowhere to rely on,
and desired to scatter and return home.
Since there was no edict of amnesty,
and hearing that people in Cháng'ān intended to exterminate all people from Liángzhōu,
they were worried and fearful, not knowing what to do.
Adopting Jiǎ Xǔ's strategy,
they then led their troops west,
collecting soldiers wherever they went.
By the time they reached Cháng'ān,
their forces numbered over ten myriad,
and together with Dǒng Zhuó's former officers Fán Chóu, Lǐ Méng, Wáng Fāng, etc., they besieged the city of Cháng'ān.
The city fell in ten days.
They fought with Lǚ Bù within the city,
and Lǚ Bù was defeated and fled.
Guō Jǐ and the others unleashed their soldiers to plunder the old and young of Cháng'ān,
killing all of them.
The dead were strewn about in disorder.
They executed those who had killed Dǒng Zhuó,
and Wáng Yǔn's corpse was displayed in the marketplace.
Dǒng Zhuó was buried in Méi,
but a great wind and violent rain shook Dǒng Zhuó's tomb,
water flowed into the burial chamber,
and his coffin was swept away.
Guō Jǐ was made Chēqí Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry) and Chíyáng Hóu (Marquis of Chíyáng),
and held the positions of Sīlì Xiàowèi (Colonel Director of Retainers) and Jiǎ Jié (Acting Imperial Envoy with Credentials).
Guō Sì was made Hòujiāngjūn (General of the Rear) and Měiyáng Hóu (Marquis of Měiyáng).
Fán Chóu was made Yòujiāngjūn (General of the Right) and Wànnián Hóu (Marquis of Wànnián).
Guō Jǐ, Guō Sì, and Fán Chóu monopolized the court government.
Zhāng Jǐ was made Piàojì Jiāngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry) and Píngyáng Hóu (Marquis of Píngyáng),
and garrisoned Hóngnóng.
In that year,
Hán Suì, Mǎ Téng, and others surrendered,
and led their troops to Cháng'ān.
Hán Suì was appointed Zhènxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the West),
and sent back to Liángzhōu.
Mǎ Téng was appointed Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the West),
and garrisoned Méi.
Shìzhōng (Court Attendant) Mǎ Yǔ, together with Jiànyì Dàfū (Grandee Remonstrant) Zhǒng Shào and Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng (Left Commander of the Central Army) Liú Fàn, etc., conspired,
intending to have Mǎ Téng attack Cháng'ān,
while they acted as internal confederates,
to execute Guō Jǐ and the others.
Mǎ Téng led his troops to Chángpíng Guān (Chángpíng Pass),
but Mǎ Yǔ and the others' plot was leaked,
and they fled to Huáilǐ.
Fán Chóu attacked Mǎ Téng,
Mǎ Téng was defeated and fled,
returning to Liángzhōu;
then Fán Chóu attacked Huáilǐ,
and Mǎ Yǔ and the others all died.
At that time, the common people of the Sān Fǔ (Three Commanderies) still numbered several hundred thousand households.
Guō Jǐ and the others unleashed their soldiers to rob and plunder,
attacking and pillaging cities and towns.
The people suffered from hunger and hardship,
and within two years, they were almost entirely devoured by each other.
The various generals vied for power,
and consequently, Fán Chóu was killed,
and his troops were absorbed.
Guō Sì and Guō Jǐ became increasingly suspicious of each other,
and fought battles within Cháng'ān.
Guō Jǐ held the Son of Heaven hostage in his camp,
burned palaces, halls, and city gates,
plundered official temples and bureaus,
and seized all imperial carriages, robes, and articles for his household.
Guō Jǐ sent the Gōngqīng (Dukes and Ministers) to Guō Sì to request peace,
but Guō Sì arrested all of them.
They attacked each other for several months,
and tens of thousands died.
Guō Jǐ's general Yáng Fèng, together with Guō Jǐ's army officer Sòng Guǒ, etc., plotted to kill Guō Jǐ.
The plot was leaked,
and they then led their troops to rebel against Guō Jǐ.
Guō Jǐ's troops rebelled,
and his strength gradually weakened.
Zhāng Jǐ brokered a reconciliation from Shǎn,
and the Son of Heaven was then able to escape,
reaching the area between Xīnfēng and Bálíng.
Guō Sì again wanted to coerce the Son of Heaven back to the capital, Méi.
The Son of Heaven fled to Yáng Fèng's camp,
and Yáng Fèng attacked and defeated Guō Sì.
Guō Sì fled to Nánshān,
and Yáng Fèng and General Dǒng Chéng escorted the Son of Heaven back to Luòyáng.
Guō Jǐ and Guō Sì regretted letting the Son of Heaven go,
and again allied with each other,
overtaking the Son of Heaven at Cáoyáng in Hóngnóng.
Yáng Fèng urgently summoned the former Báibō (White Wave) leaders Hán Xiān, Hú Cái, Lǐ Lè, etc., from Hédōng to join forces,
and engaged Guō Jǐ and Guō Sì in a great battle.
Yáng Fèng's army was defeated,
and Guō Jǐ and the others unleashed their troops to kill the Gōngqīng and all officials,
and plundered palace women, bringing them into Hóngnóng.
The Son of Heaven fled to Shǎn,
crossed the Yellow River to the north,
lost his baggage train,
and proceeded on foot.
Only the Empress and noble consorts followed,
reaching Dàyáng,
where they stayed in a commoner's house.
Yáng Fèng, Hán Xiān, etc., then made the Son of Heaven take up residence in Ānyì,
riding in an ox-cart.
Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) Yáng Biāo, Tàipú (Grand Coachman) Hán Róng, and more than ten close ministers followed.
Hán Xiān was made Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the East), Hú Cái Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the West), and Lǐ Lè Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the North),
all holding political power with Yáng Fèng and Dǒng Chéng.
Hán Róng was sent to Hóngnóng
to establish peace with Guō Jǐ, Guō Sì, etc.,
and to return the plundered palace women, Gōngqīng, and all officials,
as well as several imperial carriages and horses.
At this time, locusts arose,
and there was a drought and no grain for the year.
The imperial retinue ate dates and vegetables.
The various generals were unable to lead themselves,
there was chaos above and below,
and provisions were exhausted.
Yáng Fèng, Hán Xiān, and Dǒng Chéng then escorted the Son of Heaven back to Luòyáng.
They exited Jī Guān,
descended the Zhǐ Dào (Zhǐ Road),
and Zhāng Yáng met them along the way with food,
and was appointed Dàsīmǎ (Grand Marshal).
The details are in Zhāng Yáng's biography.
When the Son of Heaven entered Luòyáng,
the palaces and chambers were all burned down,
the streets and alleys were overgrown,
and officials cleared thorns and brambles
to reside among the ruined walls.
The various zhōus and jùns each held troops for self-defense,
and none came to his aid.
Hunger and poverty became increasingly severe,
and officials from Shàngshū Láng (Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat) downwards
went out to gather firewood and forage for themselves,
some even starving to death among the walls.
Tàizǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Wèi) then welcomed the Son of Heaven to the capital, Xǔ.
Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng were unable to uphold the royal law,
and each fled,
pillaging between Xú and Yáng,
and were killed by Liú Bèi.
Dǒng Chéng followed Tàizǔ for over a year,
then was executed.
In the second year of Jiàn'ān,
Yèzhě Púyè Péi Mào was dispatched to lead the generals west of the pass to execute Guō Jǐ,
exterminating his three familial relations.
Guō Sì was attacked by his general Wǔ Xí,
and died in Méi.
Zhāng Jǐ, suffering from hunger,
went to Nányáng to plunder,
and was killed by the people of Ráng.
His nephew Zhāng Xiù took over his troops.
Hú Cái and Lǐ Lè remained in Hédōng,
Hú Cái was killed by his enemies,
and Lǐ Lè died of illness.
Hán Suì and Mǎ Téng returned to Liángzhōu on their own,
and again plundered each other.
Later, Mǎ Téng entered to become Wèiwèi (Minister of the Guards),
and his son Mǎ Chāo led his troops.
In the sixteenth year,
Mǎ Chāo, along with the generals of Guānzhōng and Hán Suì, etc., rebelled.
Tàizǔ campaigned against and defeated them.
The details are in Wǔ Jì.
Hán Suì fled to Jīnchéng,
and was killed by his general.
Mǎ Chāo occupied Hànyáng,
and Mǎ Téng was executed, his three familial relations exterminated.
Zhào Qú and others raised a righteous army to attack Mǎ Chāo,
Mǎ Chāo fled to Hànzhōng to join Zhāng Lǔ,
and later fled to Liú Bèi,
dying in Shǔ.
Yuán Shào, courtesy name Běnchū,
was a native of Rúyáng in Rǔnán.
His great-great-grandfather Yuán Ān
served as Hàn Sītú (Minister of Works).
From Yuán Ān downwards, four generations held the position of Sān Gōng (Three Excellencies),
thus his influence overshadowed the entire realm.
Yuán Shào had a handsome appearance and an imposing demeanor,
and was able to humble himself before scholars,
many of whom attached themselves to him.
Tàizǔ had befriended him in his youth.
He served as Dàjiāngjūn Yuàn (Aide to the General-in-Chief), then Shìyùshǐ (Palace Assistant Imperial Censor),
and gradually rose to Zhōngjūn Xiàowèi (Colonel of the Central Army),
and then Sīlì (Director of Retainers).
When Emperor Líng collapsed,
the Empress Dowager's brother, the General-in-Chief Hé Jìn, conspired with Yuán Shào to execute all the eunuchs.
The Empress Dowager did not consent.
Thereupon, Dǒng Zhuó was summoned,
intending to intimidate the Empress Dowager with him.
The Palace Attendants and Yellow Gate Attendants heard of this,
and all went to Hé Jìn to apologize,
offering to be placed as he wished.
At that time, Yuán Shào urged Hé Jìn that he could decide the matter then and there,
repeating this several times,
but Hé Jìn did not permit it.
He ordered Yuán Shào to dispatch civil and military officials to Luòyáng to inspect and oversee all the eunuchs.
He also ordered Yuán Shào's younger brother, the Colonel of the Tiger Guards, Yuán Shù, to select two hundred gentle and steady Tiger Guards,
who were to enter the Forbidden Palace
to replace the armed Yellow Gate Attendants guarding the gates.
The Regular Palace Attendant Duàn Guī and others falsely issued an edict from the Empress Dowager,
summoning Hé Jìn for consultation.
They then killed him,
and chaos ensued in the palace.
Yuán Shù led the Tiger Guards to burn the Qīngsuǒ Gate of Jiādé Hall in the Southern Palace,
intending to force Duàn Guī and others out.
Duàn Guī and the others did not come out,
instead kidnapping the Emperor and the Emperor's younger brother, the King of Chénliú, and fleeing to Xiǎopíngjīn.
Yuán Shào, having already executed Xǔ Xiāng, the Colonel Director of Retainers appointed by the eunuchs,
then marshaled his troops to arrest all the eunuchs,
killing them all regardless of age.
Some beardless individuals were mistakenly killed,
to the point that they had to expose their bodies to prove themselves before being spared.
Some eunuchs who had acted virtuously and maintained their conduct were still implicated.
Such was the extent of the indiscriminate killings.
Over two thousand people died.
They urgently pursued Duàn Guī and others.
Duàn Guī and the others all threw themselves into the river and died.
The Emperor was able to return to the palace.
Dǒng Zhuó summoned Yuán Shào,
and discussed deposing the Emperor
and establishing the King of Chénliú.
At this time, Yuán Shào's uncle Yuán Kuí was the Grand Tutor.
Yuán Shào feigned agreement,
saying:
"This is a major affair;
I should discuss it with the Grand Tutor first."
Dǒng Zhuó said:
"The Líu clan is not worth preserving."
Yuán Shào did not respond,
but held his sword horizontally, made a long bow, and departed.
Once Yuán Shào had left,
he fled to Jìzhōu.
The Palace Attendant Zhōu Bì, the Colonel of the City Gates Wǔ Qióng, and the Palace Counselor Hé Yǒng, among others,
were all renowned scholars.
Dǒng Zhuó trusted them,
but they secretly sided with Yuán Shào,
and thus persuaded Dǒng Zhuó, saying:
"The great matter of deposing and establishing an emperor
is not something ordinary people can handle.
Yuán Shào did not understand the larger situation and fled out of fear,
not because he had other intentions.
If you pursue him urgently now,
the situation will surely turn into a rebellion.
The Yuán clan has extended favors for four generations,
and their household retainers and former officials are spread throughout the empire.
If he gathers heroes and assembles a multitude,
and heroes rise because of him,
then Shāndōng will no longer be yours.
It is better to pardon him,
appoint him as a Commandery Administrator;
then Yuán Shào will be pleased to be cleared of his crime,
and there will surely be no trouble."
Dǒng Zhuó considered this to be true,
and thereupon appointed Yuán Shào as the Administrator of Bóhǎi
and enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Dāngxiāng.
Yuán Shào then raised an army in Bóhǎi,
intending to execute Dǒng Zhuó.
The details are found in the Chronicle of Wǔ.
Yuán Shào proclaimed himself General of Chariots and Cavalry,
presiding over the alliance.
He and Hán Fù, the Inspector of Jìzhōu, sought to enthrone Líu Yú, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, as Emperor.
They dispatched envoys to present a memorial to Líu Yú,
but Líu Yú dared not accept it.
Later, Hán Fù's army at Ānpíng
was defeated by Gōngsūn Zàn.
Gōngsūn Zàn then led his troops into Jìzhōu,
under the pretext of attacking Dǒng Zhuó,
but secretly intending to attack Hán Fù.
Hán Fù felt insecure.
When Dǒng Zhuó moved west into the passes,
Yuán Shào returned his army to Yánjīn.
Taking advantage of Hán Fù's panic,
he sent Gāo Gàn from Chénliú and Xún Chén from Yǐngchuān, among others, to persuade Hán Fù, saying:
"Gōngsūn Zàn is advancing south on his victory,
and various commanderies are responding to him.
General Yuán (Chēqí) has led his army eastward;
his intentions are unclear.
We secretly fear for your generalship."
Hán Fù said:
"What should I do?"
Xún Chén said:
"Gōngsūn Zàn leads the troops of Yān and Dài;
their vanguard is irresistible.
The Yuán clan is a hero of this age
and will surely not submit to you.
Jìzhōu is a vital resource
of the empire.
If two heroes combine their forces,
and their armies clash at the city walls,
ruin and demise can be awaited momentarily.
The Yuán clan is your old acquaintance,
and also your ally.
As for a plan for you now,
nothing is better than to offer Jìzhōu to the Yuán clan.
If the Yuán clan obtains Jìzhōu,
then Gōngsūn Zàn will be unable to contend with them
and will surely show great respect to you.
With Jìzhōu falling into the hands of a close friend,
you will have the reputation of yielding to a worthy person,
and your person will be as secure as Mount Tài.
We hope you will not hesitate!"
Hán Fù was always timid,
and thus agreed to this plan.
Hán Fù's Chief Clerk Gěng Wǔ, Assistant Inspector Mǐn Chún, and Registrar Lǐ Lì remonstrated with Hán Fù, saying:
"Although Jìzhōu is humble,
it has a million armored soldiers
and enough grain for ten years.
Yuán Shào is a lone guest with a poor army,
reliant on us for his survival;
he is like an infant in the palm of our hand.
If we cut off his sustenance,
he can be starved to death immediately.
Why do you wish to give the province to him?"
Hán Fù said:
"I was an old subordinate of the Yuán clan,
and my talent is not as good as Běnchū's (Yuán Shào's courtesy name).
To yield by evaluating one's virtue
is what the ancients valued.
Why are you gentlemen alone distressed by this?"
His supervisors Zhào Fú and Huàn requested to resist with troops,
but Hán Fù again did not listen.
Thereupon, he yielded to Yuán Shào,
and Yuán Shào thus took charge of Jìzhōu as its Inspector.
His supervisor Jǔ Shòu (Jǔ is pronounced like Zū)
persuaded Yuán Shào, saying:
"General, at a young age you ascended to the court,
and your fame spread throughout the seas.
When the occasion arose to depose and establish an emperor,
your loyalty and righteousness surged forth.
Riding alone, you fled,
causing Dǒng Zhuó to be filled with fear.
Crossing the river northward,
Bóhǎi bowed to you.
Raising the troops of one commandery
and gathering the multitude of Jìzhōu,
your prestige shakes Héshuò,
and your name is weighty throughout the empire.
Although the Yellow Turbans cause chaos
and the Black Mountain bandits are rampant,
if you lead your army eastward,
Qīngzhōu can be pacified.
Returning to attack the Black Mountain bandits,
Zhāng Yàn can be exterminated.
Turning your forces northward,
Gōngsūn Zàn will surely perish.
Threatening the Róng and Dí,
the Xiongnú will surely submit.
Spanning north of the great river,
uniting the lands of four provinces,
gathering heroes' talents,
commanding a million troops,
welcoming the Emperor to the Western Capital,
restoring the ancestral temples in Luòyì,
issuing commands to the empire
to punish those not yet subdued –
with this, who can contend with you?
Within a few years,
this achievement will not be difficult."
Yuán Shào joyfully said:
"This is my heart's desire."
He immediately memorialized to appoint Jǔ Shòu as Supervisor of the Army and General Who Manifests Awe.
Dǒng Zhuó sent the Commandant of the Guards Húmǔ Bān and the Grand Architect Wú Xiū to deliver an imperial edict to Yuán Shào,
but Yuán Shào ordered Wáng Kuāng, the Administrator of Hénèi, to kill them.
When Dǒng Zhuó heard that Yuán Shào had gained control of Guāndōng,
he executed all of Yuán Shào's clan, including the Grand Tutor Yuán Kuí.
At this time,
many heroes and chivalrous men attached themselves to Yuán Shào,
all eager to avenge him.
Provinces and commanderies rose up in droves,
all adopting his name.
Hán Fù, filled with fear,
requested to leave Yuán Shào
and went to rely on Zhāng Miǎo.
Later, Yuán Shào sent an envoy to Zhāng Miǎo
for some discussions,
whispering to Zhāng Miǎo.
Hán Fù was present
and believed he was being plotted against.
Soon after, he rose and went to the latrine to commit suicide.
Initially,
the Son of Heaven's enthronement was not Yuán Shào's intention.
When he was in Hédōng,
Shào sent Guō Tú from Yǐngchuān as an envoy there.
When Tú returned, he persuaded Shào to welcome the Son of Heaven to the capital at Yè,
but Shào did not agree.
Coincidentally, Tàizǔ welcomed the Son of Heaven to the capital at Xǔ,
recovered the lands south of the Yellow River,
and all of Guānzhōng submitted.
Shào regretted this,
and wanted Tàizǔ to move the Son of Heaven to the capital at Juànchéng to be closer to himself,
but Tàizǔ refused.
The Son of Heaven made Shào Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
then transferred him to Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yè (Yè Hóu),
but Shào declined the marquisate.
A short while later,
he defeated Gōngsūn Zàn at Yìjīng,
and absorbed his forces.
He sent his eldest son Tán to be in Qīngzhōu.
Jǔ Shòu admonished Shào:
"This will certainly be the beginning of disaster."
Shào did not listen,
saying:
"I want my sons to each occupy a province."
He also made his middle son Xī the Governor of Yōuzhōu,
and his nephew Gāo Gàn the Governor of Bìngzhōu.
With several hundred thousand troops,
he appointed Shěn Pèi and Féng Jì to command military affairs,
Tián Fēng, Xún Chén, and Xǔ Yōu as strategists,
and Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu as generals.
He selected one hundred thousand elite soldiers
and ten thousand cavalry,
and was about to attack Xǔ.
Before this,
Tàizǔ had sent Liú Bèi to Xúzhōu to resist Yuán Shù.
After Shù died,
Bèi killed the Inspector Chē Zhòu,
and led his army to garrison at Pèi.
Shào sent cavalry to assist him.
Tàizǔ sent Liú Dài and Wáng Zhōng to attack him,
but they did not succeed.
In the fifth year of Jiàn'ān [200 CE],
Tàizǔ personally campaigned against Bèi in the east.
Tián Fēng advised Shào to attack Tàizǔ from behind,
but Shào declined, citing his son's illness,
and would not permit it.
Fēng struck the ground with his staff and said:
"To encounter such a rare opportunity,
and lose the chance due to an infant's illness,
what a pity!"
Tàizǔ arrived,
and defeated Bèi;
Bèi fled to Shào.
Shào advanced his army to Líyáng,
and sent Yán Liáng to attack Liú Yán at Báimǎ.
Jǔ Shòu again admonished Shào:
"Liáng is impetuous and narrow-minded;
though fierce and brave, he cannot be entrusted alone."
Shào did not listen.
Tàizǔ rescued Yán,
fought with Liáng,
and defeated and beheaded Liáng.
Shào crossed the river,
camped south of Yánjīn,
and sent Liú Bèi and Wén Chǒu to challenge.
Tàizǔ attacked and defeated them,
beheaded Chǒu,
and in two battles,
captured Shào's major generals.
Shào's army was greatly shaken.
Tàizǔ returned to Guāndù.
Jǔ Shòu again said:
"The northern army is numerous but not as resolute and strong as the south,
the south is sparse in provisions but not as wealthy as the north;
the south's advantage lies in a quick battle,
the north's advantage lies in a prolonged engagement.
It would be best to endure slowly and persistently,
extending it for months and days."
Shào did not comply.
His camps gradually advanced,
approaching Guāndù,
and they engaged in battle.
Tàizǔ's army was at a disadvantage,
and retreated to its fortifications.
Shào built high towers
and raised earthen mounds,
shooting into the camp,
causing all in the camp to cover themselves with shields;
the troops were greatly terrified.
Tàizǔ then built stone-throwing carts,
attacked Shào's towers,
and destroyed them all.
Shào's troops called them 'Thunderclap Carts' (Pīlì Chē).
Shào dug tunnels,
intending to ambush Tàizǔ's camp.
Tàizǔ immediately dug long trenches inside to resist them,
and also sent surprise troops to raid Shào's supply carts,
greatly defeating them,
and burning all his grain.
Tàizǔ and Shào were stalemated for a long time,
the common people were exhausted,
many defected and sided with Shào,
and the army's provisions ran short.
At this time, Shào sent Chún Yú Qióng and others with more than ten thousand troops north to meet the supply carts.
Jǔ Shòu advised Shào:
"You should send General Jiǎng Qí to form a separate supporting force outside,
to cut off Cáo Gōng's raids."
Shào again did not comply.
Qióng encamped at Wūcháo,
forty *lǐ* from Shào's army.
Tàizǔ then left Cáo Hóng to guard,
and personally led five thousand infantry and cavalry to secretly attack Qióng under the cover of night.
Shào sent cavalry to rescue them,
but they were defeated and fled.
He defeated Qióng and the others,
and beheaded them all.
When Tàizǔ returned,
before reaching his camp,
Shào's generals Gāo Lǎn and Zhāng Hé led their forces to surrender.
Shào's army completely collapsed;
Shào and Tán fled across the river with single horses.
The remaining troops feigned surrender,
and were all buried alive.
Jǔ Shòu did not cross the river with Shào,
was captured by others,
and brought to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ treated him generously.
Later, he plotted to return to the Yuán clan,
and was killed.
Initially,
when Shào marched south,
Tián Fēng advised Shào, saying:
"Cáo Gōng is skilled in warfare,
ever-changing and unpredictable.
Although his troops are few,
he cannot be underestimated;
it is better to hold out for a long time.
Your Excellency occupies strong mountains and rivers,
commands the forces of four provinces,
befriends heroes externally,
and cultivates agriculture and warfare internally.
Then select your elite forces,
divide them into surprise troops,
and repeatedly emerge from weak points,
to harass Hénán.
If they rescue their right, attack their left;
if they rescue their left, attack their right.
Make the enemy exhaust themselves running about,
and the people unable to pursue their livelihoods peacefully.
We will not be tired, but they will already be exhausted.
In less than two years,
you can win by merely sitting still.
Now you abandon the strategy of absolute victory,
and decide success or failure in a single battle.
If it does not go as you wish,
regret will be too late."
Shào did not listen.
Fēng pleaded earnestly,
and Shào became furious,
believing he was demoralizing the troops,
and put him in chains.
After Shào's army was defeated,
someone said to Fēng:
"You will surely be highly regarded."
Fēng said:
"If the army had been victorious,
I would surely be spared.
Now that the army is defeated,
I will certainly die."
When Shào returned,
he said to his attendants:
"I did not heed Tián Fēng's words,
and indeed became a laughingstock."
He then killed him.
Shào was outwardly magnanimous and refined,
with a sense of propriety,
showing no joy or sorrow in his expression,
but inwardly he was often suspicious and harmful;
these were all examples of this.
Many cities and towns in Jìzhōu rebelled,
but Shào attacked and subdued them again.
After his army's defeat, he fell ill,
and in the seventh year,
died of grief.
Yuán Shào loved his youngest son, Shàng,
who was beautiful in appearance.
He wished to make him his successor but had not openly declared it.
Shěn Pèi and Féng Jì contended for power with Xīn Píng and Guō Tú.
Pèi and Jì sided with Shàng,
while Píng and Tú sided with Tán.
The multitude considered Tán to be the eldest,
and wished to establish him.
Pèi and others, fearing that if Tán were established, Píng and others would harm them,
and also mindful of Shào's original intention,
then enthroned Shàng to succeed Shào.
When Tán arrived,
he was not established,
and he proclaimed himself General of Chariots and Cavalry.
From this, Tán and Shàng developed a rift.
Tài-zǔ campaigned north against Tán and Shàng.
Tán's army was at Líyáng.
Shàng gave Tán few troops,
but sent Féng Jì to accompany Tán.
Tán requested more troops,
but Pèi and others deliberated and decided not to provide them.
Tán was enraged
and killed Jì.
Tài-zǔ crossed the river and attacked Tán.
Tán sent an urgent message to Shàng.
Shàng wanted to divide his troops to reinforce Tán,
but feared that Tán would then seize his forces.
So he ordered Shěn Pèi to guard Yè,
and Shàng personally led troops to assist Tán,
confronting Tài-zǔ at Líyáng.
From
the ninth month to the second month,
a great battle was fought below the city.
Tán and Shàng were defeated and retreated,
entering the city to defend.
Tài-zǔ was about to besiege them,
but they escaped by night.
He pursued them to Yè,
collected their wheat,
captured Yīn'ān,
and led his army back to Xǔ.
Tài-zǔ campaigned south against Jīngzhōu,
and his army reached Xīpíng.
Tán and Shàng then raised armies and attacked each other.
Tán was defeated and fled to Píngyuán.
Shàng pressed the attack severely.
Tán sent Xīn Pí to Tài-zǔ to request aid.
Tài-zǔ then returned to assist Tán,
arriving at Líyáng in the tenth month.
Shàng heard that Tài-zǔ was coming north,
abandoned Píngyuán, and returned to Yè.
His generals Lü Kuàng and Lü Xiáng rebelled against Shàng and surrendered to Tài-zǔ.
Tán secretly carved general's seals again and presented them to Kuàng and Xiáng.
Tài-zǔ knew of Tán's deceit,
but married his daughter to him to pacify him,
and then led his army back.
Shàng sent Shěn Pèi and Sū Yóu to guard Yè,
and again attacked Tán at Píngyuán.
Tài-zǔ advanced his army to attack Yè.
When he reached the Huán Shuǐ,
fifty *lǐ* from Yè,
Yóu intended to be an internal respondent.
His plot was exposed,
and he fought Pèi within the city.
He was defeated
and fled to Tài-zǔ.
Tài-zǔ then advanced and attacked it,
digging tunnels.
Pèi also dug trenches inside to counter them.
Pèi's general Féng Lǐ opened a sally port,
letting in more than three hundred of Tài-zǔ's soldiers.
Pèi became aware of it,
and from atop the city wall, he struck the wooden gate of the sally port with large stones.
The gate closed,
and all who had entered were lost.
Tài-zǔ then besieged it,
constructing a trench
forty *lǐ* in circumference.
Initially, he made it shallow,
appearing as if it could be crossed.
Pèi looked at it and laughed,
not coming out to contend for advantage.
Tài-zǔ dug it overnight,
making it two *zhàng* wide and deep,
and diverted the Zhāng Shuǐ to flood it.
From the fifth month to the eighth month,
more than half the people in the city died of starvation.
Shàng heard that Yè was in distress
and led an army of over ten thousand men to relieve it.
He approached from the Xī Shān,
reaching Yángpíng Tíng to the east,
seventeen *lǐ* from Yè.
He overlooked the Fú Shuǐ
and lit fires to signal the city.
The city also lit fires in response.
Pèi led troops out from the north of the city,
intending to meet Shàng and break the siege.
Tài-zǔ attacked them directly,
and they were defeated and returned.
Shàng was also defeated and fled,
making camp along the Qū Zhāng.
Tài-zǔ then surrounded him.
Before the encirclement was complete,
Shàng was afraid
and sent Yīn Kuí and Chén Lín to beg for surrender,
but he was not listened to.
Shàng fled back to Lànkǒu.
Tài-zǔ advanced and besieged him urgently again.
His generals Mǎ Yán and others surrendered during the battle.
The army greatly disintegrated,
and Shàng fled to Zhōngshān.
Tài-zǔ seized all his baggage and supplies,
obtaining Shàng's seals, ribbons, credentials, and clothing,
which he displayed to his family.
The people in the city were disheartened and collapsed.
Pèi's nephew Róng, who was guarding the east gate,
opened the gate at night to let in Tài-zǔ's troops.
He fought Pèi within the city
and captured Pèi alive.
Pèi's words and demeanor were resolute and heroic,
and he never showed signs of wavering,
so that all who saw him sighed in admiration.
He was then executed.
Gāo Gàn surrendered with Bīngzhōu,
and Tài-zǔ reinstated Gàn as Inspector.
While Tài-zǔ was besieging Yè,
Tán captured Gānlíng, Ānpíng, Bóhǎi, and Héjiān,
and attacked Shàng at Zhōngshān.
Shàng fled to Gù'ān to join Xī,
and Tán seized all of his forces.
Tài-zǔ was about to attack him.
Tán then captured Píngyuán
and Bèinánpí,
and established his own camp at Lóngcòu.
In the twelfth month,
Tài-zǔ's army reached his gate,
but Tán did not come out.
He fled by night to Nánpí,
and encamped along the Qīnghé.
In the first month of the tenth year,
Tài-zǔ attacked and captured it,
executing Tán and Tú and others.
Xī and Shàng were attacked by their generals Jiāo Chù and Zhāng Nán,
and fled to the Wūhuán in Liáoxī.
Chù proclaimed himself Inspector of Yōuzhōu,
rallied the prefects and magistrates of various commanderies,
turned away from the Yuán clan and towards the Cáo clan,
arrayed tens of thousands of soldiers,
killed a white horse to make an oath,
and declared:
"Those who disobey shall be executed!"
No one dared to speak,
and each in turn drank the blood.
When it came to Assistant Administrator Hán Héng,
he said:
"I have received great kindness from Lord Yuán and his sons.
Now that they are defeated and ruined,
my wisdom was insufficient to save them,
and my courage was insufficient to die for them,
which is a failure in righteousness.
If I were to turn north to serve the Cáo clan,
that is something I cannot do."
Everyone present changed color for Héng.
Chù said:
"Indeed, when undertaking a great enterprise,
one must establish great righteousness.
Whether the enterprise succeeds or fails
does not depend on one person.
Héng's aspiration may be fulfilled
to encourage loyal service to one's lord."
Gāo Gàn rebelled,
seized the Administrator of Shàngdǎng,
and raised an army to defend Húkǒu Guān.
Lè Jìn and Lǐ Diǎn were sent to attack him,
but had not yet captured it.
In the eleventh year,
Tài-zǔ campaigned against Gàn.
Gàn then left his generals Xià Zhāo and Dèng Shēng to defend the city,
and personally went to the Xiongnu Chányú to seek aid,
but failed.
He fled alone with a few horsemen,
intending to flee south to Jīngzhōu.
The Commandant of Shàngluò captured and executed him.
In the twelfth year,
Tài-zǔ went to Liáoxī to attack the Wūhuán.
Shàng and Xī fought the Wūhuán resisting army,
were defeated and fled to Liáodōng.
Gōngsūn Kāng lured and executed them,
sending their heads.
Tài-zǔ highly esteemed Hán Héng's integrity
and repeatedly invited him to serve, but he did not come,
and died at home.
Yuán Shù, courtesy name Gōnglù,
was the son of Sìkōng Fèng,
and a cousin of Shào.
He was known for his chivalrous spirit.
He was nominated as Xiàolián,
appointed as Lángzhōng,
and served various internal and external posts.
Later, he became Zhé chōng Xiàowèi and Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng.
When Dǒng Zhuó was about to depose the emperor,
he appointed Shù as Hòujiāngjūn.
Shù also feared Dǒng Zhuó's calamity,
so he fled to Nányáng.
At that time, Sūn Jiān, the Grand Administrator of Chángshā, killed Zhāng Zī, the Grand Administrator of Nányáng.
Shù was then able to occupy that commandery.
Nányáng had a population of several millions,
but Shù indulged in extravagance and desires,
exacting limitless taxes and levies,
which caused great suffering to the people.
Already having a rift with Shào,
and also being at odds with Liú Biǎo, he allied with Gōngsūn Zàn in the north.
Shào, being at odds with Zàn, allied with Liú Biǎo in the south.
Thus, the brothers were estranged,
discarding close allies for distant ones.
He led his army into Chénliú.
Tàizǔ and Shào combined forces and attacked,
greatly defeating Shù's army.
Shù fled with his remaining troops to Jiǔjiāng,
killed Chén Wēn, the Inspector of Yángzhōu,
and took charge of his province.
He appointed Zhāng Xūn, Qiáo Ruí, and others as great generals.
When Lǐ Quē entered Cháng'ān,
he sought to ally with Shù for support,
appointing Shù as Zuǒjiāngjūn,
enfeoffing him as Yángzháihóu,
and granting him the imperial credential (jié).
He dispatched Tàifù Mǎ Rìdī to bestow the appointment during his inspection tour.
Shù seized Rìdī's jié
and detained him, refusing to let him go.
At that time, Chén Guī, the Chancellor of Pèi and a native of Xiàpī,
was a nephew of the former Tàiwèi Qiú.
Shù and Guī were both descendants of noble families
and had been friends in their youth.
Shù wrote to Guī, saying:
"In the past, when Qín lost its government,
heroes across the land competed to seize it,
and those combining wisdom and courage ultimately received their due.
