Now, the affairs of the world are in chaos,
and there is again a tendency to disintegrate.
Truly, this is the time for heroes and extraordinary men to act.
Since you and I are old friends,
how could you not side with me?
If we accomplish great things,
you will truly be my heart and core."
Guī's middle son, Yìng, was then in Xiàpī.
Shù coerced and took Yìng as a hostage,
intending to force Guī to join him.
Guī replied in a letter, saying:
"At the end of Qín, it was tyrannical and indulged its desires,
spreading cruelty throughout the land
and inflicting poison upon the people.
The lower classes could not endure their lives,
and thus it collapsed.
Although it is now a degenerate age,
there is no chaos as harsh and tyrannical as that of the fallen Qín.
General Cáo, with his divine might, has risen in due time,
restoring the established laws and institutions.
He will surely quell the wicked and malicious,
and pacify and stabilize the land,
which is truly an auspicious sign.
I believe that you should unite your strength and heart
to assist the Hàn court,
but instead, you are plotting rebellion
and inviting disaster upon yourself.
How lamentable!
If you are deluded but know how to repent,
you might still escape.
I, as an old acquaintance,
therefore present my honest feelings.
Although it may be unpalatable to your ears,
it is an act of brotherly kindness.
If you wish me to serve my private interests and flatter you,
I would rather die than commit such a transgression."
In the winter of Xīngpíng 2nd year (195 CE),
the Emperor was defeated at Cáoyáng.
Shù gathered his subordinates and said:
"Now the Liú clan is weak,
and the world is in turmoil.
My family has served as prime ministers for four generations,
and the people look to us.
I wish to respond to Heaven and follow the people.
What are your opinions, gentlemen?"
None dared to answer.
The Chief Clerk Yán Xiàng stepped forward and said:
"In ancient times, from Hòujì to King Wén of Zhōu,
accumulated virtue and merit,
possessing two-thirds of the world,
yet still served Yīn.
Though your lordship's family has prospered for generations,
it is not as glorious as the Zhōu.
Although the Hàn court is weak,
it is not as tyrannical as King Zhòu of Yīn."
Shù remained silent and displeased.
He used the auspicious omen from Zhāng Jiǒng of Hénèi
and subsequently usurped the imperial title,
appointing the Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng as the Governor of Huáinán.
He established public ministers (gōngqīng)
and offered sacrifices in the northern and southern suburbs.
His extravagance and indulgence grew worse.
His hundreds of concubines all wore brocade and silk,
and leftover meat and grain abounded,
while his soldiers suffered from cold and hunger.
The area between the Jiāng and Huái rivers became completely desolate,
and people resorted to cannibalism.
Shù was first defeated by Lǚ Bù,
then by Tàizǔ.
He fled to his subordinates Léi Báo and Chén Lán in the mountains,
but was again rejected by them.
Anxious and fearful, he did not know what to do.
He intended to return the imperial title to Shào
and wished to go to Qīngzhōu to join Yuán Tán,
but fell ill and died on the way.
His wife and children sought refuge with Liú Xūn, the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng, who was Shù's former subordinate.
Sūn Cè defeated Xūn,
and they were again taken into custody.
Shù's daughter entered Sūn Quán's palace,
his son Yào was appointed Lángzhōng,
and Yào's daughter was also married to Quán's son, Fèn.
Liú Biǎo, courtesy name Jǐngshēng,
was a native of Gāopíng, Shānyáng.
He was famous in his youth,
known as one of the Eight Gentlemen (Bā Jùn).
He was over eight feet tall,
with a very imposing appearance.
He served as Dàjiāngjūn Yuàn and then Běijūn Zhōnghòu.
When Emperor Líng died,
he replaced Wáng Ruì as the Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
At this time, troops rose in Shāndōng,
and Biǎo also gathered his forces in Xiāngyáng.
When Yuán Shù was in Nányáng,
he allied with Sūn Jiān,
intending to attack and seize Biǎo's province.
He sent Sūn Jiān to attack Biǎo.
Sūn Jiān was struck by a stray arrow and died,
and his army was defeated.
Shù was subsequently unable to defeat Biǎo.
Lǐ Quē and Guō Sì entered Cháng'ān
and sought to ally with Biǎo for support.
They appointed Biǎo as Zhènnán Jiāngjūn and Governor of Jīngzhōu,
enfeoffed him as Chéngwǔhóu,
and granted him the imperial credential (jié).
When the Son of Heaven resided in Xǔ,
Biǎo, although sending envoys to offer tribute,
secretly allied with Yuán Shào in the north.
The Director of Personnel (zhìzhōng) Dèng Xī advised Biǎo against this,
but Biǎo did not listen.
Dèng Xī then resigned due to illness and withdrew,
remaining in retirement for the rest of Biǎo's life.
Zhāng Jì led his troops into Jīngzhōu territory
and attacked Rángchéng.
He was struck by a stray arrow and died.
Biǎo's officials and subordinates all offered congratulations.
Biǎo said:
"Jì came out of desperation.
The host was discourteous,
leading to an armed clash.
This was not the Governor's intention.
I accept condolences,
not congratulations."
He sent people to take in Jì's troops;
the troops rejoiced upon hearing this
and subsequently submitted.
Zhāng Xiàn, the Grand Administrator of Chángshā, rebelled against Biǎo.
Biǎo besieged him for years but could not take the city.
Xiàn died of illness,
and Chángshā then set up his son, Yì.
Biǎo subsequently attacked and annexed Yì,
taking Línglíng and Guìyáng in the south,
and occupying the Hànchuān region in the north.
His territory spanned several thousand lì,
with over a hundred thousand armored soldiers.
Táizǔ was then holding out against Yuán Shào at Guāndù.
Shào sent someone to ask for help,
but Biǎo, though promising it, did not send any,
nor did he assist Táizǔ.
He wished to preserve the region between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers
and observe the changes in the world.
Hán Sōng, a Cóngshì Zhōngláng, and Liú Xiān, a Biéjià, advised Biǎo, saying:
"Heroes contend,
and two mighty ones are locked in a standoff.
The fate of the world
rests with the General.
If the General wishes to achieve something,
he should take advantage of their exhaustion;
if not,
he must certainly choose whom to follow.
The General commands an army of a hundred thousand,
yet sits idly by, watching.
To see the virtuous and not assist them,
to seek peace and not achieve it –
these two grudges will surely fall upon the General,
and the General will not be able to remain neutral.
Given Cáo Gōng's wisdom and brilliance,
all the talented and virtuous men in the world rally to him.
His forces will certainly defeat Yuán Shào,
and then he will raise an army and advance towards the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
We fear the General will be unable to resist him.
Therefore, our plan for the General
is none other than to present the province to Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng will surely value the General's virtue highly;
you will long enjoy blessings and good fortune,
and pass them down to your descendants.
This is a foolproof strategy."
Biǎo's great general Kuǎi Yuè also urged Biǎo,
but Biǎo was irresolute.
So, he dispatched Sōng to Táizǔ to observe the true state of affairs.
Upon Sōng's return,
he strongly reported Táizǔ's might and virtue
and advised Biǎo to send his son as a hostage.
Biǎo suspected Sōng had turned to speak for Táizǔ.
He was furious
and wanted to kill Sōng.
He interrogated and killed Sōng's attendants,
and finding that Sōng had no other intentions,
he stopped.
Although Biǎo appeared refined on the outside,
his heart was full of suspicion and jealousy.
All such incidents were of this kind.
Liú Bèi fled to Biǎo,
and Biǎo treated him generously,
but could not employ him.
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
Táizǔ campaigned against Biǎo.
Before he arrived,
Biǎo died of illness.
Initially,
Biǎo and his wife loved their youngest son Cóng
and wished to make him heir.
Cài Mào and Zhāng Yǔn formed a faction for him,
and so the eldest son Qí was sent out as the Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià.
The populace then installed Cóng as the successor.
Qí and Cóng thus became enemies.
Yuè, Sōng, and the Eastern Chief Clerk Fù Xùn, among others, persuaded Cóng to surrender to Táizǔ.
Cóng said:
"Now, with you gentlemen, we hold the entire territory of Chǔ,
maintaining our late lord's legacy,
to observe the world.
Why should this not be possible?"
Xùn replied:
"Rebellion and obedience have a general principle;
strength and weakness have a fixed tendency.
For a subject to resist his lord is
rebellion;
for the newly established Chǔ to resist the state is
a force that cannot match;
for Liú Bèi to oppose Cáo Gōng is
also unmatched.
All three are shortcomings,
and to attempt to withstand the vanguard of the King's army
is the path to certain destruction.
How do you assess yourself compared to Liú Bèi?"
Cóng said:
"I am not his equal."
Xùn said:
"Indeed, if Liú Bèi is insufficient to resist Cáo Gōng,
then even holding the land of Chǔ is
insufficient to sustain yourself;
indeed, if Liú Bèi is sufficient to resist Cáo Gōng,
then Bèi will not be subservient to the General.
I urge the General not to waver."
When Táizǔ's army reached Xiāngyáng,
Cóng surrendered the province.
Bèi fled to Xiàkǒu.
Táizǔ appointed Cóng as the Inspector of Qīngzhōu and enfeoffed him as a Liehóu.
Kuǎi Yuè and fifteen other nobles (hóu) were also enfeoffed.
Yuè became the Guānglùxūn;
Sōng,
the Dàhónglú;
Xī,
the Shìzhōng;
Xiān,
the Shàngshūlìng;
and many others attained high offices.
Commentary says: Dǒng Zhuó was savage, cruel, and merciless,
tyrannical and inhumane.
Since the beginning of written history,
such a person has probably never existed.
Yuán Shù was extravagant, indulgent, and unrestrained;
his glory did not last his lifetime;
he brought it upon himself.
Yuán Shào and Liú Biǎo
both possessed imposing presence and distinguished bearing,
and were renowned in their time.
Biǎo strode across the south of Hàn;
Shào soared like a hawk over the north of the Yellow River.
However, both were outwardly magnanimous but inwardly suspicious,
fond of strategizing but indecisive,
had talent but could not employ it,
heard good advice but could not accept it.
They abolished the legitimate heir and established a concubine's son,
abandoned ritual and indulged in affection,
leading to their descendants' downfall
and the collapse of their states.
This was not misfortune.
In the past, Xiàng Yǔ disregarded Fàn Zēng's counsel,
thereby losing his royal enterprise.
Shào's killing of Tián Fēng was
far worse than Yǔ's!
Biographies of Lǚ Bù and Zhāng Miǎo, Chapter 7
Lǚ Bù, courtesy name Fèngxiān,
was a native of Jiǔyuán, Wǔyuán Commandery.
He was known for his martial prowess in Bīngzhōu.
The Inspector Dīng Yuán, serving as a Qí Dūwèi,
stationed in Hénèi,
appointed Bù as his Master of Records
and greatly favored and trusted him.
When Emperor Líng died,
Yuán led his troops to Luòyáng.
He conspired with Hé Jìn to eliminate the palace eunuchs,
and was appointed Zhí Jīnwǔ.
When Jìn was defeated,
Dǒng Zhuó entered the capital
and was about to cause chaos.
He wished to kill Yuán
and annex his troops.
Because Bù was trusted by Yuán,
Zhuó lured Bù into killing Yuán.
Bù cut off Yuán's head and presented it to Zhuó.
Zhuó appointed Bù as Qí Dūwèi,
greatly cherished and trusted him,
and swore to be father and son.
Bù was skilled with the bow and horse,
and his physical strength surpassed others.
He was known as the Flying General.
He was gradually promoted to Zhōnglángjiàng
and enfeoffed as a Dūtíng Hóu.
Zhuó, feeling that he treated people with no courtesy,
feared others would plot against him.
He always used Bù as his personal guard in his movements.
However, Zhuó was by nature stubborn and narrow-minded.
When angry, he would not consider consequences.
Once, slightly displeased,
he drew a hand-halberd and threw it at Bù.
Bù, agilely, dodged it.
He apologized to Zhuó,
and Zhuó's anger also subsided.
From then on, Bù secretly resented Zhuó.
Zhuó often made Bù guard his private chambers.
Bù had a private affair with Zhuó's maidservant,
and fearing discovery,
he felt uneasy.
Formerly,
Sītú Wáng Yǔn, seeing that Lǚ Bù was a robust man from his province,
treated him with great hospitality.
Later, Lǚ Bù went to Wáng Yǔn
and described how Dǒng Zhuó had nearly killed him.
At that time, Wáng Yǔn and Púyè Shìsūn Ruì were secretly plotting to execute Dǒng Zhuó,
so Wáng Yǔn informed Lǚ Bù and asked him to be an inside accomplice.
Lǚ Bù said,
"What about our father-son relationship?"
Wáng Yǔn said,
"You yourself are surnamed Lǚ;
you are not truly of his flesh and blood.
Now you are worried about dying and have no time to spare,
so what 'father-son relationship' are you talking about?"
Lǚ Bù then agreed,
and personally stabbed Dǒng Zhuó to death.
The account is in Dǒng Zhuó's biography.
Wáng Yǔn appointed Lǚ Bù as Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn,
granted him the jié,
and accorded him ceremonial treatment equal to the Sān Sī,
advancing him to Wēn Hóu,
and they together managed court affairs.
After Lǚ Bù killed Dǒng Zhuó,
he feared and hated the people from Liángzhōu,
and the people of Liángzhōu all resented him.
Because of this, Lǐ Quē and others banded together and returned to attack Cháng'ān city.
Lǚ Bù could not resist,
and Lǐ Quē and the others then entered Cháng'ān.
Six shùn after Dǒng Zhuó's death,
Lǚ Bù was also defeated.
Leading several hundred cavalry, he exited Wǔguān,
intending to go to Yuán Shù.
Lǚ Bù considered his killing of Dǒng Zhuó to be an act of vengeance for Yuán Shù,
and wished to be rewarded by him.
Yuán Shù disliked his fickle nature,
and refused to accept him.
He went north to Yuán Shào,
who, with Lǚ Bù, attacked Zhāng Yàn at Chángshān.
Zhāng Yàn had over ten thousand elite soldiers
and several thousand cavalry.
Lǚ Bù had a fine horse named Chìtù.
He often, with his close associates Chéng Lián and Wèi Yuè, broke through the enemy lines and charged into their formations,
thereby defeating Zhāng Yàn's army.
However, Lǚ Bù sought to increase his troops,
and his officers and soldiers engaged in looting,
which made Yuán Shào wary and resentful of him.
Lǚ Bù sensed his intention,
and asked Yuán Shào to leave.
Yuán Shào feared that Lǚ Bù would return to harm him,
and sent brave men to ambush and kill Lǚ Bù at night,
but they failed.
When the matter became known,
Lǚ Bù fled to Hénèi,
and joined Zhāng Yáng.
Yuán Shào ordered his troops to pursue him,
but all feared Lǚ Bù,
and none dared to approach him.
Zhāng Miǎo, courtesy name Mèngzhuó,
was a native of Shòuzhāng, Dōngpíng.
In his youth, he was known for his chivalry,
helping the poor and aiding those in urgent need,
sparing no expense from his family fortune;
many scholars pledged their allegiance to him.
Tàizǔ and Yuán Shào were both friends with Zhāng Miǎo.
He was summoned to the ducal household and,
due to his high merit, was appointed Qí Dūwèi,
then promoted to Chénliú Tàishǒu.
During Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion,
Tàizǔ and Zhāng Miǎo were the first to raise an army of righteousness.
In the Battle of Biànshuǐ,
Zhāng Miǎo sent Wèi Zī with troops to follow Tàizǔ.
After Yuán Shào became the alliance leader,
he showed signs of arrogance,
and Zhāng Miǎo justly criticized him.
Yuán Shào ordered Tàizǔ to kill Zhāng Miǎo,
but Tàizǔ refused,
reproaching Yuán Shào, saying:
"Mèngzhuó
is a close friend.
His right and wrong should be tolerated.
The world is not yet settled,
so it is not appropriate for us to harm each other."
Zhāng Miǎo knew this
and respected Tàizǔ even more.
When Tàizǔ marched against Táo Qiān,
he instructed his family, saying:
"If I do not return,
go and rely on Mèngzhuó."
Later, when he returned
and saw Zhāng Miǎo,
they wept in each other's presence.
Their intimacy was thus.
When Lǚ Bù left Yuán Shào to join Zhāng Yáng,
he visited Zhāng Miǎo, and before parting,
they clasped hands and swore an oath together.
Yuán Shào heard of this
and was greatly resentful.
Zhāng Miǎo feared that Tàizǔ would eventually attack him on Yuán Shào's behalf,
and his heart was uneasy.
In the first year of Xīngpíng (194 CE),
Tàizǔ again campaigned against Táo Qiān.
Zhāng Miǎo's younger brother Zhāng Chāo,
together with Tàizǔ's general Chén Gōng, and the officers Cóngshì Zhōngláng Xǔ Sì and Wáng Kǎi, conspired to rebel against Tàizǔ.
Chén Gōng persuaded Zhāng Miǎo, saying:
"Now heroes are rising in unison,
and the world is fragmented.
With your forces spanning a thousand lǐ
in a land of four battles,
brandishing your sword and looking around,
you are indeed worthy of being a hero.
Yet you are controlled by others,
is this not contemptible?
Now the provincial army is campaigning in the east,
and its territory is empty.
Lǚ Bù is a valiant warrior,
skilled in battle with no equal.
If we temporarily welcome him
to jointly govern Yǎnzhōu,
observe the world's situation,
and await changes in the times,
this would also be a moment of strategic brilliance."
Zhāng Miǎo agreed.
Tàizǔ had initially sent Chén Gōng to lead troops and garrison Dōngjùn.
Chén Gōng then used his troops to welcome Lǚ Bù from the east to be the Yǎnzhōu Mù,
occupying Púyáng.
All the commanderies and counties responded,
except for Juànchéng, Dōng'ē, and Fàn, which held out for Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ led his army back
and fought Lǚ Bù at Púyáng.
Tàizǔ's army was at a disadvantage,
and they were stalemated for over a hundred days.
At this time, there was a drought, locusts, and little grain;
people resorted to cannibalism.
Lǚ Bù moved east to garrison Shānyáng.
Within two years,
Tàizǔ recovered all the cities
and defeated Lǚ Bù at Jùyě.
Lǚ Bù fled east to Liú Bèi.
Zhāng Miǎo followed Lǚ Bù,
leaving Zhāng Chāo to guard his family at Yōngqiū.
Tàizǔ attacked and besieged it for several months,
then massacred it,
executing Zhāng Chāo and his family.
Zhāng Miǎo went to Yuán Shù to request aid, but before it arrived,
he was killed by his own soldiers.
Liú Bèi attacked Yuán Shù in the east,
and Lǚ Bù raided and captured Xiàpéi.
Liú Bèi returned to Lǚ Bù.
Lǚ Bù sent Liú Bèi to garrison Xiǎopèi.
Lǚ Bù proclaimed himself Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yuán Shù sent his general Jì Líng and others with thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Liú Bèi.
Liú Bèi sought help from Lǚ Bù.
Lǚ Bù's generals said to Lǚ Bù:
"General, you have always wanted to kill Liú Bèi;
now you can use Yuán Shù's hand."
Lǚ Bù said:
"Not so.
If Yuán Shù defeats Liú Bèi,
he will connect with the generals north of Tài Shān,
and I will be surrounded by Yuán Shù;
I cannot but save him."
He then prepared a thousand infantry and two hundred cavalry,
and rushed to Liú Bèi's aid.
When Jì Líng and the others heard that Lǚ Bù had arrived,
they all withdrew their troops and dared not attack again.
Lǚ Bù set up camp about one lǐ southwest of Pèi,
and sent an attendant to invite Jì Líng and others.
Jì Líng and the others also invited Lǚ Bù to feast together.
Lǚ Bù said to Jì Líng and the others:
"Xuándé
is my younger brother.
My brother is being besieged by you gentlemen,
so I have come to save him.
My nature is not to enjoy starting fights,
but only to enjoy resolving them."
Lǚ Bù ordered a sentry to erect a halberd in the middle of the camp gate.
Lǚ Bù said:
"Gentlemen, watch me shoot the small branch of this halberd.
If I hit it with one shot, you gentlemen must withdraw.
If I miss, you can stay and fight it out."
Lǚ Bù raised his bow and shot the halberd,
hitting the small branch precisely.
All the generals were astonished
and said,
"General's divine might!"
The next day, they celebrated again,
and then each departed.
Yuán Shù desired to ally with Lǚ Bù,
so he sought Lǚ Bù's daughter for his son.
Lǚ Bù agreed.
Yuán Shù sent his envoy Hán Yìn to inform Lǚ Bù of his imperial claim,
and also to request to bring the bride home.
Chén Guī, the Administrator of Pèi, feared that if Yuán Shù and Lǚ Bù were to marry,
Xú and Yáng would unite,
which would become a national disaster.
So he went to persuade Lǚ Bù, saying:
"Cáo Gōng welcomes the Son of Heaven,
assists in national governance,
and his awe-inspiring power is destined to rule the age,
soon to conquer the four seas.
General, you should cooperate with him in strategy and planning,
to secure the safety of Tài Shān.
Now, if you marry Yuán Shù,
you will bear the name of unrighteousness in the world,
and surely face a danger like stacked eggs."
Lǚ Bù also resented Yuán Shù for not having accepted him initially.
His daughter was already on her way,
but he called her back, broke off the marriage,
put Hán Yìn in shackles,
and displayed his head in Xǔ market.
Chén Guī wanted to send his son Chén Dēng to meet Tài Zǔ,
but Lǚ Bù refused to dispatch him.
It happened that an envoy arrived
and appointed Lǚ Bù as General of the Left.
Lǚ Bù was greatly pleased,
immediately allowed Chén Dēng to go,
and also ordered him to present a memorial of thanks.
When Chén Dēng met Tài Zǔ,
he described Lǚ Bù as courageous but devoid of strategy,
and fickle in his allegiance,
suggesting he should be dealt with early.
Tài Zǔ said:
"Lǚ Bù is
a wolf cub with a wild heart,
truly difficult to keep for long.
Without you, no one could fathom his true nature."
He immediately increased Chén Guī's salary to two thousand dàn of grain,
and appointed Chén Dēng as Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
Upon their farewell,
Tài Zǔ held Chén Dēng's hand and said:
"The affairs of the east
are now entrusted to you."
He ordered Chén Dēng to secretly gather troops and serve as an internal informant.
At first,
Lǚ Bù used Chén Dēng to request the governorship of Xú Zhōu.
When Chén Dēng returned,
Lǚ Bù was angry,
drew his戟 (jǐ) and chopped at a table, saying:
"Your father advised me to cooperate with Cáo Gōng
and break off the marriage with Gōnglù.
Now, I have gained nothing of what I sought,
yet you and your father are both prominent and honored.
I have been sold out by you!
Tell me, what did you say to him?
What was your reasoning?"
Chén Dēng showed no change of expression,
and calmly explained:
"I told Cáo Gōng: 'Treat the General as if raising a tiger;
you must feed it its fill of meat,
otherwise it will devour people.'
Cáo Gōng said: 'What you say is not so.
It is like raising a hawk;
when hungry, it is useful,
but when full, it will fly away.'
That is what he said."
Lǚ Bù's anger then subsided.
Yuán Shù was enraged,
and allied with Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng,
sending his grand general Zhāng Xūn to attack Lǚ Bù.
Lǚ Bù said to Chén Guī:
"The arrival of Yuán Shù's army
is your doing.
What should we do about it?"
Chén Guī said:
"Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng, with Yuán Shù,
are merely an ad hoc army.
Their strategy is not predetermined,
and they cannot sustain each other.
Zǐ Dēng's assessment of them
is like 'chickens tied together' (lián jī),
unable to perch together,
they can be separated."
Lǚ Bù adopted Chén Guī's plan,
sent someone to persuade Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng
to join forces with him to attack Yuán Shù's army,
promising Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng
all military provisions they possessed.
Thereupon, Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng agreed,
and Zhāng Xūn was utterly defeated.
In the third year of Jiàn'ān,
Lǚ Bù again rebelled for Yuán Shù,
sending Gāo Shùn to attack Liú Bèi at Pèi,
and defeated him.
Tài Zǔ sent Xiàhóu Dūn to rescue Liú Bèi,
but he was defeated by Gāo Shùn.
Tài Zǔ personally marched against Lǚ Bù,
and upon reaching his city,
sent Lǚ Bù a letter,
explaining the advantages and disadvantages.
Lǚ Bù wanted to surrender,
but Chén Gōng and others, feeling their guilt was too deep,
thwarted his plan.
Lǚ Bù sent someone to seek help from Yuán Shù,
(Yuán Shù) personally led over a thousand cavalry to battle,
was defeated and fled,
returning to hold the city,
not daring to sally forth.
Yuán Shù also could not provide aid.
Although Lǚ Bù was fierce and brave,
he was without strategy and full of suspicion,
unable to control his factions,
only trusting his various generals.
Each general had their own intentions and suspected each other,
hence they were often defeated in battle.
Tài Zǔ besieged him with trenches for three months,
and those above and below became disaffected.
His generals Hóu Chéng, Sòng Xiàn, and Wèi Xù seized Chén Gōng,
and led their forces to surrender.
Lǚ Bù ascended the White Gate Tower with his subordinates.
The siege was urgent,
so he surrendered.
He was then captured alive.
Lǚ Bù said:
"The bonds are too tight,
loosen them a little."
Tài Zǔ said:
"When binding a tiger, one must not be gentle."
Lǚ Bù pleaded:
"Your Excellency's only concern is me.
Now that I have submitted,
there is no need to worry about the world.
If Your Excellency leads the infantry,
and lets me lead the cavalry,
then the world will not be difficult to pacify."
Tài Zǔ showed a doubtful expression.
Liú Bèi stepped forward and said:
"Does Your Excellency not recall Lǚ Bù's dealings with Dīng Jiànyáng and Grand Tutor Dǒng?"
Tài Zǔ nodded.
Lǚ Bù then pointed at Liú Bèi and said:
"This fellow is the most untrustworthy."
Thereupon, Lǚ Bù was strangled to death.
Lǚ Bù, along with Chén Gōng, Gāo Shùn, and others, were all beheaded and their heads sent to Xǔ,
and then they were buried.
When Tài Zǔ captured Chén Gōng,
he asked Chén Gōng if he wanted his old mother and daughter to live.
Chén Gōng replied:
"I have heard that those who govern the world with filial piety do not sever people's kin,
and those who extend benevolence across the four seas do not cut off people's sacrifices.
My old mother is in your care,
not mine."
Tài Zǔ summoned and cared for his mother for the rest of her life,
and married off his daughter.
Chén Dēng,
whose courtesy name was Yuánlóng,
had a great reputation in Guǎnglíng.
He also rendered meritorious service by attacking Lǚ Bù from two sides,
and was promoted to Fúbō Jiāngjūn.
He died at the age of thirty-nine.
Later, Xǔ Sì and Liú Bèi were both seated with Liú Biǎo, the Jīngzhōu Mù.
Liú Biǎo and Liú Bèi discussed the people of the world,
and Xǔ Sì said:
"Chén Yuánlóng is a man of the lakes and seas,
with an untamed heroic spirit."
Liú Bèi said to Liú Biǎo:
"Is what Master Xǔ says right or wrong?"
Liú Biǎo said:
"If I say it is wrong,
this gentleman is a good scholar,
and I should not speak falsely;
if I say it is right,
Yuánlóng's name is highly esteemed throughout the world."
Liú Bèi asked Xǔ Sì:
"When you speak of his heroic spirit,
did anything happen?"
Xǔ Sì said:
"In the past, during the chaos, I passed through Xiàpī
and saw Yuánlóng.
Yuánlóng had no regard for the duties of host and guest,
and for a long time did not speak with me.
He himself went up onto a large bed to sleep,
and made the guest sleep on a lower bed."
Liú Bèi said:
"You have the reputation of a national worthy,
and now the world is in great chaos,
the Emperor has lost his place.
I hoped that you would be concerned for the country and forget your home,
with the intention of saving the world.
Yet you ask about fields and houses,
and your words are not worth adopting.
This is what Yuánlóng deplored,
so how could he have spoken with you?
If it were a person of low character,
wanting to sleep on a hundred-foot tower,
he would have made you sleep on the ground.
Why just between the upper and lower beds?"
Liú Biǎo laughed heartily.
Liú Bèi then said:
"As for Yuánlóng's literary and martial courage and ambition,
one must seek them in antiquity.
It is difficult to compare with him in a hurry."
Zāng Hóng, whose courtesy name was Zǐyuán,
was a native of Shèyáng in Guǎnglíng.
His father, Mín,
successively served as Xiōngnú Zhōnglángjiàng and Taishou of Zhōngshān and Tàiyuán,
and was famous wherever he served.
Zāng Hóng was physically imposing and
exceptionally distinct from other people.
He was recommended as Xiaolian and appointed as a Lang.
At that time, three-office Langs were selected to fill county magistrate positions;
Zhào Yù of Lángyá became the magistrate of Jǔ,
Liú Yáo of Dōnglái became the magistrate of Xiàyì,
Wáng Lǎng of Dōnghǎi became the magistrate of Zīqiū,
and Zāng Hóng became the magistrate of Qīu.
At the end of the Língdì era,
he abandoned his office and returned home.
The Taishou, Zhāng Chāo, invited Zāng Hóng to serve as Gōngcáo.
When Dǒng Zhuó killed the Emperor
and plotted to endanger the imperial altars,
Zāng Hóng persuaded Zhāng Chāo, saying:
"You, My Lord, have for generations received imperial favor,
and your brothers all hold major commanderies.
Now the imperial house is about to be imperiled,
and the treacherous minister has not yet been executed.
This is truly the time for loyal and righteous men of the realm to repay kindness and dedicate their lives.
Now your commandery's territory is still intact,
and the officials and common people are prosperous.
If we beat the drums,
we can raise twenty thousand men.
Using these to punish and eliminate the national traitor
and to take the lead for the world
is the greatest righteousness."
Zhāng Chāo assented to his words,
and went west with Zāng Hóng to Chénliú
to discuss the matter with his elder brother Miǎo.
Miǎo also had such intentions,
and they met at Suānzǎo.
Miǎo said to Zhāng Chāo:
"I heard that my younger brother, as a commandery governor,
exercises governance, education, authority, and kindness
not through his own will,
but always relies on Zāng Hóng.
Who is Hóng?"
Zhāng Chāo said:
"Hóng's talent, strategy, and wisdom surpass me.
I love him greatly;
he is a remarkable man in the realm."
Miǎo then summoned Zāng Hóng to an audience
and, after speaking with him, found him greatly exceptional.
He introduced him to Liú Yǎnzhōu Gōngshān and Kǒng Yùzhōu Gōngxù,
both of whom became close with Zāng Hóng.
So they set up an altar,
and were about to swear an oath together.
The various provincial and commandery governors deferred to each other,
none daring to take the lead.
They all collectively nominated Zāng Hóng.
Zāng Hóng then ascended the altar, held the plate, and drank the blood, swearing the oath:
"The Han dynasty is unfortunate,
the imperial order has lost its discipline.
The treacherous minister Dǒng Zhuó seized the opportunity to wreak havoc,
bringing disaster upon the Supreme One [the Emperor]
and cruelty to the common people.
We greatly fear the ruin of the imperial altars
and the destruction of the four seas.
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Dài, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Zhòu, Chénliú Taishou Miǎo, Dōngjùn Taishou Mào, Guǎnglíng Taishou Chāo, and others,
have gathered righteous armies
and all rush to the national crisis.
All of us, our allies,
will unite our hearts and exert our strength
to fulfill our duty as ministers.
We shall lose our heads and sacrifice our lives,
with absolutely no second thoughts.
If anyone violates this oath,
may his life be forfeit,
and may he leave no descendants.
Heaven above and Earth below,
and the bright spirits of our ancestors,
all truly bear witness to this!"
Zāng Hóng's words and demeanor were impassioned,
and tears flowed down his face.
Those who heard his words,
even common soldiers and servants,
were all roused,
and everyone desired to fulfill their duty.
After a while,
none of the armies dared to advance first,
and their provisions ran out, and the troops dispersed.
Zhāng Chāo sent Zāng Hóng to consult with Grand Marshal Liú Yú.
He encountered the troubles of Gōngsūn Zàn.
Upon reaching Héjiān,
he met with the conflict between Yōu and Jì provinces,
and his mission could not be delivered.
However, Yuán Shào saw Zāng Hóng
and also found him remarkably distinguished,
and established a bond of friendship with him.
Coincidentally, the Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu, Jiāo Hé, died,
and Yuán Shào made Zāng Hóng act as governor of Qīngzhōu to pacify its people.
Zāng Hóng was in the province for two years,
and the bandits fled.
Yuán Shào praised his ability
and transferred him to be Taishou of Dōngjùn,
governing Dōngwǔyáng.
Tàizǔ (Cáo Cāo) besieged Zhāng Chāo at Yōngqiū.
Zhāng Chāo said:
"I only rely on Zāng Hóng;
he will surely come to save me."
The crowd thought that Yuán and Cáo were currently on good terms,
and that since Zāng Hóng was employed by Yuán Shào,
he would certainly not ruin their good relations and invite disaster
by coming from afar to respond to this.
Zhāng Chāo said:
"Zǐyuán
is a righteous man of the world,
and will never betray his principles.
I only fear that he might be prohibited and restrained
and unable to reach me."
When Zāng Hóng heard this,
he indeed went barefoot, wailing,
and also assembled the troops under his command.
He also requested troops and horses from Yuán Shào,
seeking to rescue Zhāng Chāo,
but Yuán Shào ultimately did not consent.
Zhāng Chāo was subsequently exterminated with his clan.
Zāng Hóng therefore resented Yuán Shào
and completely ceased communication with him.
Yuán Shào raised an army and besieged him,
but could not overcome him for a year.
Yuán Shào ordered Chén Lín, a fellow townsman of Zāng Hóng, to write to Zāng Hóng,
explaining the consequences (of his actions) and
reminding him of their past kindness and righteousness.
Zāng Hóng replied: "Though separated by distance, I think of you,
and it arises even in my dreams.
Fortunately, we are but a short distance apart,
yet due to our differing paths and principles,
we cannot see each other.
This sorrow and regret
is indeed heartfelt!
A few days ago, you did not forget me,
and I was honored to receive your elegant gifts,
discussing prosperity and misfortune,
with sincere concern for both public and private matters.
The reason I did not immediately reply
is partly because my learning is shallow and my talent
dull,
insufficient to compose a rebuttal;
also because you, my friend, carry your concubine,
rest your shoulders with your host,
your family is in Dōngzhōu,
and I am an enemy.
To serve someone in this way,
even if I were to bare
my inner feelings,
and caused my liver and gall to fall.
Yet, as one estranged and guilty,
whose sweet words are viewed with suspicion,
and who cannot save himself from start to finish,
how can I feel compassion for others?
Moreover, with your talent,
having thoroughly studied the classics and
records,
how could you be ignorant of the Great Way
and not understand my intentions?
Yet, you still repeated your words,
from which I know that your words, Sir,
truly did not come from your heart,
but were meant to
avert disaster.
If you insist on calculating advantages and disadvantages,
and debating right and wrong,
discussions of right and wrong
fill the world.
To elaborate further would not clarify anything;
to say nothing would cause no harm.
You also spoke of injuring the principle of severing ties by formal announcement,
which is not something I can bear to do.
Therefore, I discarded paper and brush,
and made no reply whatsoever.
I also hoped that you would discern my heart from afar,
knowing that my decision
was final,
and would not be altered again.
Receiving your letter again,
citing ancient and modern examples,
a jumbled six pages,
though I wished not to speak,
how could I refuse?
I am a man of humble standing.
Originally, due to military service,
the bandits seized a great prefecture.
My lord's kindness was profound, his generosity ample.
How could I happily return today to face the blade myself?
Each time I ascend the city walls to marshal the troops,
gazing at
my lord's banners and drums,
feeling moved by the friendship of old comrades,
stroking my bowstring and grasping arrows,
I cannot help but feel tears streaming down my face.
Why is this?
I believe that in assisting my lord,
I have
nothing to regret.
My lord's treatment of me
surpassed all others.
At the beginning of my appointment,
I believed I would ultimately accomplish great things,
and together we would uphold the imperial house.
How could I have known that the Son of Heaven was displeased,
my home prefecture was invaded,
the Prefectural Administrator encountered the peril of Yǒulǐ,
and Chénliú devised a scheme to raise troops?
With plans delayed,
I lost the name of loyalty and filial piety,
and by taking up my staff and turning my back,
I damaged the bond of friendship.
Weighing these two,
between being compelled to act,
losing the name of loyalty and filial piety, and damaging the bond of friendship,
the gravity of these paths differs,
and the closeness and estrangement
are distinct.
Thus, I immediately wiped away my tears and announced the severance.
If my lord had shown a little compassion for his old friend,
with those remaining sitting respectfully,
and those departing restraining themselves,
not eagerly pursuing a departing friend
but relying on
punishment and execution
to support himself,
then I would have upheld the resolve of Jì Zhá
and there would be no battle today.
How can I prove this?
In the past, Zhāng Jǐngmíng personally ascended the altar, drank blood,
received his mission
and rushed about,
ultimately causing Hán Mù to yield his seal,
and my lord gained territory.
Thereafter, simply because he submitted a memorial to the court,
was granted a noble title and a lineage,
in a short span of time,
he was not granted
clemency for his transgressions,
but suffered the calamity of annihilation.
Lǚ Fèngxiān pursued Zhuó and then came to seek refuge.
When he requested troops but did not obtain them,
what crime was it to announce his departure?
Yet he was again attacked and stabbed,
brought to the brink of
death.
Liú Zǐqí served as an envoy for too long.
When he asked to resign but was not permitted,
fearing coercion and yearning for his family,
he sought to return through deception.
He could be said to have a will towards loyalty and filial piety,
without harming the hegemonic path;
yet,
he was promptly felled beneath the banner,
and received no leniency.
Although I am not clever,
and have always been unable to foresee the beginning and end,
or perceive the subtle and know the obvious,
I secretly surmise my lord's
intentions.
Does he truly believe these three sons deserved death,
and that their punishment was justified?
Rather, he simply desires to unify Shāndōng,
increase his troops to attack his enemies,
and fears that his warriors will be suspicious
and he will have no means to deter
or encourage them.
Therefore, he suppressed and abrogated imperial decrees to elevate his own authority,
so that those who admire righteousness are honored,
and those awaiting release are executed.
This is my lord's advantage,
not the wish of wandering strategists.
Therefore, I take warning from predecessors,
and will fight to the death in my distress.
Although I am most foolish,
I have also heard the words of a gentleman.
This is truly not my heart's desire.
It is my lord who invited
it.
All the reasons I abandoned my homeland
and pledged allegiance to this city
are precisely because a gentleman's departure
does not suit an enemy state.
Thus, I incurred my lord's wrath,
and have been under attack for a prolonged period.
Yet you, Sir, invoke this principle to guide me,
is this not words alike but intentions different,
not what a gentleman would consider gain or loss?
I have heard this:
righteousness does not abandon one's kin,
loyalty does not disobey one's lord.
Therefore, I align with my home prefecture in the east as a familial support,
and aid the Prefectural Administrator in the center to secure the state.
With one action,
I achieve two benefits to demonstrate loyalty and filial piety.
How can this be wrong?
But you, Sir, wish me to disregard my roots and ruin my family,
to equate my lord and my superior.
As for my lord and me,
by age, he is
my elder brother;
by relationship, he is a true friend.
When our paths diverge, to announce my departure
to secure my lord and kin
can be called proper.
If it were as you say,
then Bāosū should have sacrificed his life for Wǔ Yuán,
and not
cried out to the Qín court.
To merely concern oneself with averting disaster,
is to be ignorant that one's words contradict reason.
Perhaps, Sir, seeing the city besieged and unrelieved,
and no relief troops
arriving,
you are moved by the bond of marriage
and the goodwill of a lifetime,
believing that bending one's principles to survive
is better than upholding righteousness and being overthrown.
In the past, Yàn Yīng did not lower his aspirations before the sharp
blade,
and the Southern Historian did not distort his writing to save his life.
Therefore, their images are enshrined in paintings,
and their names live on for posterity.
What more for me, who holds a strong golden city,
marshals the strength of its soldiers and civilians,
expends three years'
provisions
as one year's supply,
aids the distressed and supplements the lacking,
to please all under Heaven?
How could I plan to build a house and then return to farming?
I only fear that when the autumn wind raises dust,
Bóguī's horse
will turn south,
Zhāng Yáng and Fēiyàn will
exert their strength to cause trouble,
and the northern frontier will report urgent danger,
while close subordinates present their sincerity to request leave.
My lord should take heed of people like
us,
turn back his banner and withdraw his troops,
and muster his forces in Yèyuán.
How could he fittingly prolong his mighty wrath,
and display his power beneath my city walls?
You, Sir, mock me for relying on Hēishān to
rescue,
do you alone not remember how the Huángjīn (Yellow Turbans) united?
Moreover, those like Fēiyàn have all received the King's mandate.
In the past, Gāozǔ captured Péng Yuè at Jùyě;
Guāngwǔ laid
the foundation at Lǜlín,
and eventually was able to soar like a dragon and achieve restoration,
thus completing the imperial enterprise.
If one can assist the lord and promote reform,
what is there to dislike?
Furthermore, I personally received the imperial edict,
and
am engaged in this endeavor.
Go, Kǒngzhāng!
You seek profit beyond the borders,
while Zāng Hóng dedicates his life to his lord and kin;
you entrust yourself to a covenant leader,
while Zāng Hóng made his name in Cháng'
ān.
You say I will die and my name will perish,
but I also laugh at you, for you will live and die without renown.
How sorrowful!
Though our roots are the same, our branches diverge.
Strive on, strive on!
What more
is there to say!
Shào saw Hóng's letter,
knew he had no intention of surrendering,
and increased his troops to attack urgently.
Inside the city, grain and provisions were exhausted,
and there was no strong rescue from outside.
Hóng knew he would not escape,
and called his officers and soldiers, saying:
"The Yuán clan is without principle,
their schemes are rebellious,
and they will not rescue Hóng, the prefectural commander.
For the sake of righteousness,
Hóng cannot but die.
Now, gentlemen, you are innocent and will suffer this calamity in vain!
You should, before the city falls,
take your wives and children out."
The officers, soldiers, and common people all wept, saying:
"Your Excellency and the Yuán clan originally had no enmity or grievances,
but now, for the sake of the imperial court's prefectural commander,
you have brought yourself to this plight.
How can the officers and common people bear to abandon Your Excellency and leave?"
Initially, they still dug up rats and boiled tendons and horns.
Later, there was nothing left to eat.
The chief clerk reported three dòu of rice in the inner kitchen,
and requested that it be divided to make thin gruel.
Hóng sighed, saying:
"What is the point of eating this alone!"
He had thin gruel made,
which the multitude shared and drank.
He killed his beloved concubine to feed the officers and soldiers.
The officers and soldiers all shed tears,
none able to look up.
Seven or eight thousand men and women died leaning against each other,
none deserting.
When the city fell,
Shào captured Hóng alive.
Shào had always been close to Hóng,
so he grandly displayed curtains and banners,
and gathered all his generals to see Hóng,
saying:
"Zāng Hóng,
how could you betray me like this!
Are you subdued today?"
Hóng knelt on the ground and glared, saying:
"The Yuán clan has served the Hàn,
with four generations and five dukes;
they can be said to have received great favor.
Now that the royal house is in decline,
you have no intention of supporting it,
but wish to seize the opportunity,
hoping for the unhoped-for,
killing many loyal and virtuous people to establish treacherous power.
I personally heard you call Zhāng Chénliú your elder brother,
so my lord Hóng should also be your younger brother.
We should unite our efforts
to eliminate harm for the country.
Why do you hold your troops and watch others be slaughtered?
It is a pity that my strength is weak,
and I cannot wield my blade to avenge the world.
How can I be called subdued!"
Shào originally cherished Hóng,
and intended to make him submit
and pardon him;
but seeing Hóng's stern words,
he knew he would never be used by him,
and so killed him.
Chén Róng, a man from Hóng's district, was a young scholar,
who admired Hóng and
followed him as the Commander of Dōngjùn;
before the city fell,
Hóng sent him out.
Shào ordered him to be present,
and when he saw Hóng about to die,
he stood up and said to Shào:
"General, you are undertaking a great enterprise,
wishing to eliminate tyranny for the world,
yet you specifically prioritize executing the loyal and righteous.
How can this accord with Heaven's will!
Zāng Hóng was appointed as a prefectural commander.
How can you kill him!"
Shào was ashamed,
and his attendants had him dragged out,
saying:
"You are not Zāng Hóng's companion.
Why do you act like this in vain!"
Róng looked back and said:
"Indeed, benevolence and righteousness are not constant;
he who practices them is a jūnzi (gentleman),
he who turns his back on them is a xiǎorén (petty person).
Today, I would rather die on the same day as Zāng Hóng
than live on the same day as the General!"
He was then killed.
There was no one among those seated with Shào who did not sigh,
and they secretly said to each other:
"How could two martyrs be killed in one day!"
Before this,
Hóng had sent two sīmǎ (commanders) out
to seek aid from Lǚ Bù;
by the time they returned,
the city had already fallen,
and they all died fighting the enemy.
A review says: Lǚ Bù possessed the valor of a roaring tiger,
but lacked the strategy of an eminent hero.
He was frivolous, cunning, and inconsistent,
caring only for profit.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been one like him who was not eradicated.
In the past, Hàn Guāngwǔ erred with Páng Méng,
and recently Wèi Tàizǔ was also misled by Zhāng Miǎo.
To know men is to be discerning,
but even emperors find it difficult.
This is indeed true!
Chén Dēng and Zāng Hóng both possessed heroic spirit and noble integrity.
Dēng died prematurely,
his achievements unfulfilled.
Hóng, with weak troops against a strong enemy,
failed to establish his fierce resolve.
What a pity!
Biographies of the Two Gōngsūn, Táo, and Four Zhāng, Chapter 8
Gōngsūn Zàn, courtesy name Bóguī,
was a native of Lìngzhī, Liáoxī Commandery.
(Lìng has the sound of Lángdìng fan.
Zhī has the sound of Qí'ér fan.)
He served as a clerical assistant in the commandery's gate-house.
He had a handsome appearance
and a loud voice.
The Administrator Hóu thought highly of him,
and gave him his daughter in marriage.
He was sent to Zhuō Commandery to study the Classics with Lú Zhí.
Later, he again became a commandery official.
When Administrator Liú was summoned to the Court of the Commandant of Justice for an offense,
Zàn drove his carriage
and personally served as a servant.
When Liú was exiled to Rìnán,
Zàn prepared rice and meat,
and offered a sacrifice to his ancestors on Běimáng mountain,
raising his goblet and wishing:
“Once I was a son,
now I am a subject.
I must go to Rìnán.
The miasma of Rìnán
may prevent my return,
so I bid farewell to my ancestors here.”
He bowed twice, full of emotion, and stood up.
Those who witnessed it at the time were all moved to tears.
Liú was pardoned on the way and returned.
Zàn was recommended as Xiaolián and became a Lang,
then appointed Chief of Liáodōng Shǔguó.
Once, he rode out of the frontier with several tens of horsemen.
He encountered several hundred Xiānbēi horsemen.
Zàn retreated into an empty pavilion,
and made an oath with his followers, saying:
“If we don’t charge them now,
we will all die.”
Zàn then personally took up a spear
with blades at both ends,
galloped out and stabbed the Hu,
killing and wounding several tens of them.
He also lost half of his followers,
but managed to escape.
The Xiānbēi were deterred and chastened,
and thereafter dared not re-enter the frontier.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Zhuō.
During the Guānghé era,
rebels rose in Liáng Province.
Three thousand Yōuzhōu cavalry were dispatched,
and Zàn was provisionally appointed Inspector-General with authority to act,
and ordered to lead them.
When his army reached Jìzhōng,
Zhāng Chún of Yúyáng instigated Qiū Lìjū and others of Wúhuán from Liáoxī to rebel.
They plundered Jìzhōng,
proclaimed themselves generals,
and plundered officials and people, attacking various cities in Yòuběipíng and Liáoxī Shǔguó.
Wherever they went, they caused devastation.
Zàn led his forces,
pursued and attacked Chún and others with success,
and was promoted to Cavalry Commandant.
The Wúhuán King Tānzhì of Shǔguó led his people to surrender to Zàn.
He was promoted to Colonel-Director,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng,
and advanced his troops to Shǔguó,
engaging in combat with the Hu for five or six years.
Qiū Lìjū and others plundered Qīng, Xú, Yōu, and Jì provinces,
all four provinces suffering their depredations,
and Zàn was unable to repel them.
The court deliberated, considering that the Imperial Clan Secretary Liú Bó'ān of Dōnghǎi possessed virtue and righteousness,
and had previously served as Inspector of Yōu Province,
where his benevolence and trustworthiness were widely known,
and the Róng and Dí tribes were attached to him.
If he were to be sent to pacify them,
it could be settled without expending much effort.
Thus, Liú Yú was appointed Governor of Yōu Province.
Upon Yú’s arrival,
he sent envoys into the Hu territory,
informing them of the advantages and disadvantages,
and demanding they send Chún’s head.
Qiū Lìjū and others, hearing of Yú’s arrival,
were pleased
and each sent interpreters to submit.
Zàn, resentful of Yú’s success,
secretly sent men to intercept and kill the Hu envoys.
The Hu, knowing his intentions,
secretly went to Yú.
Yú petitioned to disband all garrisoned troops,
leaving only Zàn with ten thousand infantry and cavalry stationed in Yòuběipíng.
Chún then abandoned his wife and children,
fled into Xiānbēi territory,
and was killed by his retainer Wáng Zhèng,
who sent his head to Yú.
Zhèng was enfeoffed as a Liehou.
Yú, for his merits, was immediately appointed Grand Commandant
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāngbēn.
Meanwhile, Dǒng Zhuó arrived in Luòyáng,
and promoted Yú to Grand Marshal
and Zàn to General of Martial Might,
enfeoffing him as Marquis of Jì.
When the allied armies of Guāndōng rose up,
Dǒng Zhuó abducted the emperor and moved the capital west.
He summoned Yú to be Grand Tutor,
but the roads were blocked,
and the imperial mandate could not reach him.
Yuán Shào and Hán Fú deliberated,
believing that the young emperor was controlled by treacherous ministers,
and the world had no one to whom its heart could turn.
Yú,
being a renowned member of the imperial clan
and the hope of the people,
was then put forward to be emperor.
Envoys were sent to Yú,
but Yú ultimately refused to accept.
Shào and others again urged Yú to take charge of the affairs of the Secretariat,
and to issue imperial decrees and grant enfeoffments.
Yú again refused to listen,
but still maintained alliance with Shào and others.
Yú’s son, Hé, was a Gentleman-in-Waiting
in Cháng'ān.
The Son of Heaven yearned to return east
and had Hé pretend to escape from Dǒng Zhuó,
secretly making his way out through Wǔguān to Yú,
ordering him to bring troops to escort the emperor.
On his way, Hé passed by Yuán Shù,
to whom he explained the Son of Heaven’s intention.
Shù, desiring Yú as an ally,
detained Hé and would not let him go,
promising that once troops arrived, they would all go west together,
and had Hé write a letter to Yú.
Upon receiving Hé’s letter,
Yú dispatched several thousand cavalry to Hé.
Zàn knew Shù had ulterior motives
and did not want to send troops,
trying to stop Yú,
but Yú would not be dissuaded.
Zàn feared Shù would hear and resent him,
so he also sent his younger cousin Yuè to lead a thousand cavalry to Shù to form an alliance,
but secretly instructed Shù to seize Hé
and appropriate his troops.
From this, the rift between Yú and Zàn deepened.
Hé escaped from Shù and came north,
but was again detained by Shào.
At this time,
Shù sent Sūn Jiān to garrison Yángchéng to resist Dǒng Zhuó.
Shào sent Zhōu Áng to seize that position.
Shù sent Yuè and Jiān to attack Áng,
but they did not win,
and Yuè was hit by a stray arrow and died.
Zàn angrily said:
“My brother died,
and the disaster originated with Shào.”
He then moved his army to Pánhé,
intending to seek revenge on Shào.
Shào, fearful,
bestowed the seal and ribbon of the Administrator of Bóhǎi, which he himself wore, upon Zàn’s younger cousin Fàn,
and sent him to the commandery,
hoping to forge an alliance.
Fàn then used the Bóhǎi troops to assist Zàn,
defeating the Yellow Turban rebels in Qīng and Xú provinces,
and his army grew stronger.
He advanced his army to Jièqiáo.
He appointed Yán Gāng as Inspector of Jì Province,
Tián Kǎi as Inspector of Qīng Province,
and Shàn Jīng as Inspector of Yǎn Province,
and set up various commanderies and counties.
Shào’s army was in Guǎngchuān.
He ordered his general Qū Yì to lead the vanguard and fight Zàn.
Yán Gāng was captured alive.
Zàn’s army was defeated and fled to Bóhǎi.
He and Fàn returned together to Jì.
To the southeast of the main city, they built a small city,
close to Yú,
and gradually their resentment and animosity towards each other grew.
Gōngsūn Zàn feared Yuān Yǔ might cause trouble,
so he raised an army to attack Yǔ.
Yuān Yǔ was defeated by Gōngsūn Zàn
and fled to Jūyōng.
Gōngsūn Zàn attacked and captured Jūyōng,
seizing Yuān Yǔ alive,
and took him back to Jì.
Around that time, Dǒng Zhuó died.
The Son of Heaven sent the envoy Duàn Xùn to increase Yuān Yǔ's territory
and to oversee six provinces;
Gōngsūn Zàn was promoted to Former General
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yì.
Gōngsūn Zàn falsely accused Yuān Yǔ of intending to claim the imperial title
and coerced Duàn Xùn into beheading Yuān Yǔ.
Gōngsūn Zàn then memorialized Duàn Xùn as Inspector of Yōuzhōu.
Gōngsūn Zàn became arrogant and conceited,
remembering faults and forgetting kindness,
and caused harm to many.
Yuān Yǔ's subordinates Xiānyú Fǔ of Yúyáng, Qí Zhōu, Cavalry Commandant Xiānyú Yín, and others,
led the provincial troops, intending to avenge Yuān Yǔ.
Because Yán Róu of Yānguó had always been trusted and benevolent,
they jointly recommended him as Commandant of the Wūhuán.
Yán Róu recruited and enticed the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi,
gathering tens of thousands of Hú and Hàn people.
They battled Zōu Dān, Gōngsūn Zàn's appointed Administrator of Yúyáng, north of Lù,
and utterly defeated him,
beheading Dān.
Yuán Shào also sent Qū Yì and Yuān Yǔ's son, Yuān Hé,
leading troops to join Fǔ and jointly attack Gōngsūn Zàn.
Gōngsūn Zàn's army suffered several defeats,
and he fled back to Yìjīng to make a strong defense.
He surrounded it with ten layers of moats,
and on the inner banks of the moats, he built walls,
all five or six *zhàng* high,
with towers on top of them.
The central moat was built as the main fortification,
especially high at ten *zhàng*,
where he resided.
He accumulated three million *hú* of grain.
Gōngsūn Zàn said:
"I once thought that affairs of the world could be settled with a wave of the hand.
Looking at it today,
it is not something I can decide.
It is better to cease hostilities,
work hard in farming and accumulate grain.
The art of war says,
one hundred towers are unassailable.
Now I have a thousand layers of towers and palisades.
When this grain is
exhausted, I will fully understand the affairs of the world."
He intended to wear out Yuán Shào with this.
Yuán Shào sent generals to attack him,
but for years they could not capture it.
In the fourth year of Jiàn'ān,
Yuán Shào fully mobilized his army to besiege him.
Gōngsūn Zàn sent his son to seek help from the Hēishān bandits,
and also wished to personally lead his elite cavalry to break out directly,
along the southwest mountains,
to rally the Hēishān forces,
to rampage through Jìzhōu,
and cut off Yuán Shào's rear.
His Chief Clerk, Guān Jìng, advised Gōngsūn Zàn, saying:
"Today, your general's officers and men
have all crumbled and fallen apart.
The reason they can still hold together
is out of concern for their homes, elders, and children,
and with you, General, as their leader.
If you, General, hold firm for a prolonged period,
Yuán Shào will eventually have to retreat himself.
After he retreats,
forces from all directions can certainly be reunited.
If you, General, abandon them and leave now,
the army will lack a stable command.
The danger to Yìjīng
can be expected to arrive immediately.
If you, General, lose your base
and are isolated in the wilderness,
what can you achieve!"
Gōngsūn Zàn then stopped and did not sally forth.
When the relief arrived,
he wanted to attack Yuán Shào from both inside and outside.
He sent someone to write a letter to his son,
setting a date for the troops to arrive,
and to raise a fire as a signal.
Yuán Shào's scouts obtained the letter
and raised a fire on schedule.
Gōngsūn Zàn thought the relief army had arrived
and sallied forth to battle.
Yuán Shào set an ambush
and utterly defeated him.
He returned to his defenses.
Yuán Shào dug tunnels,
breaching his towers,
Gōngsūn Zàn knew he was doomed to defeat,
killed all his wives and children,
then committed suicide.
Xiānyú Fǔ led his troops to uphold the imperial mandate.
gradually reaching the Central Fortification.
and overseen the six commanderies of Yōuzhōu.
Tàizǔ and Yuán Shào were stalemated at Guāndù.
Yán Róu sent envoys to Tàizǔ to receive orders
and was promoted to Protector of the Wūhuán.
Xiānyú Fǔ personally went to Tàizǔ
and was appointed General of the Left Who Crosses the Liao,
enfeoffed as a Marquis of a Pavilion,
and sent back to pacify his home province.
When Tàizǔ captured Nánpí,
Yán Róu led his contingent and the Xiānbēi to present famous horses to support the army,
and joined the campaign against the Wūhuán of the three commanderies.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as a Marquis Within the Passes.
Fǔ also led his troops to join.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
Fǔ was appointed General of Tiger's Teeth,
and Yán Róu as General Who Crosses the Liao.
Both were advanced to be enfeoffed as Marquis of a County,
and held the special rank of *Tèjìn*.
Táo Qiān, courtesy name Gōngzǔ,
was a native of Dānyáng.
In his youth, he was fond of learning,
became a scholar,
served as an official in his province,
was nominated as *Màocái*,
appointed as Magistrate of Lú,
promoted to Inspector of Yōuzhōu,
then summoned to be appointed Gentleman-Consultant,
and participated in the military affairs of General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhāng Wēn
in the western campaign against Hán Suì.
At that time, the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out in Xúzhōu,
and Táo Qiān was appointed Inspector of Xúzhōu.
He attacked the Yellow Turbans
and routed them.
During Dǒng Zhuó's chaos,
prefectures and commanderies raised armies.
The Son of Heaven resided in Cháng'ān,
and communications in all directions were cut off.
Táo Qiān sent envoys to discreetly offer tributes.
He was promoted to General Who Pacifies the East and Governor of Xúzhōu,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Lìyáng.
At that time,
the people of Xúzhōu were prosperous and numerous,
with abundant grain,
and many refugees sought refuge with him.
However, Táo Qiān abandoned the right path and acted on his impulses: Zhào Yù of Yáxié, Administrator of Guǎnglíng,
a renowned scholar of Xúfāng,
was alienated due to his loyalty and uprightness;
while Cáo Hóng and others,
slanderous and malicious minor figures,
were personally trusted by Táo Qiān.
His administration and justice were out of harmony,
and many good people suffered from it,
leading to gradual chaos.
Quē Xuān of Xiàpī declared himself Son of Heaven.
Táo Qiān initially allied with him for plunder and raids,
but later killed Quē Xuān
and absorbed his forces.
In the fourth year of Chūpíng,
Tàizǔ campaigned against Táo Qiān,
attacking and capturing over ten cities,
and fought a great battle at Péngchéng.
Táo Qiān's army was defeated and fled,
with tens of thousands dead,
causing the Sì River to cease flowing.
Táo Qiān retreated and defended Tán.
Tàizǔ, low on provisions, withdrew his army.
In the first year of Xīngpíng,
he again campaigned eastward,
conquering and pacifying various counties in Lángxié and Dōnghǎi.
Táo Qiān was afraid
and wanted to flee back to Dānyáng.
At that time, Zhāng Miǎo rebelled and welcomed Lǚ Bù,
so Tàizǔ returned to attack Bù.
That year,
Táo Qiān died of illness.
Zhāng Yáng, courtesy name Zhìshū,
was a native of Yúnzhōng.
He was appointed to Bìngzhōu for his martial bravery,
serving as a military commandant (wǔměng cóngshì).
In the late reign of Emperor Líng,
when the world was in turmoil,
the emperor, favoring the lesser eunuch Jiǎn Shuò, appointed him Colonel-in-Chief of the Western Garden Army (Xīyuán Shàngjūn Xiàowèi),
to command the capital region,
intending to use him to control the four directions.
He summoned heroes from across the empire to serve as his subordinates.
Tàizǔ (Cáo Cāo) and Yuán Shào, among others, were all appointed colonels (xiàowèi)
under him.
Dīng Yuán, the Inspector of Bìngzhōu, dispatched Yáng with troops to Jiǎn Shuò,
where he served as acting commandant (jiǎ sīmǎ).
After Emperor Líng's death,
Jiǎn Shuò was killed by Hé Jìn.
Yáng was again dispatched by Hé Jìn
to return to his home province to recruit soldiers,
gathering over a thousand men.
He then remained in Shàngdǎng,
attacking mountain bandits.
When Hé Jìn was defeated,
Dǒng Zhuó caused unrest.
Yáng then led his troops to attack the Administrator of Shàngdǎng at Húguān,
but failed to take it.
He plundered various counties,
and his forces grew to several thousand men.
Troops from the east of the mountains (Shāndōng) rose up,
intending to punish Dǒng Zhuó.
Yuán Shào arrived at Hénèi,
and Yáng joined him.
He then, along with the Xiongnu Chányú Yúfúluó, garrisoned at Zhāngshuǐ.
The Chányú wished to defect,
but Shào and Yáng refused to follow him.
The Chányú seized Yáng and departed with him.
Shào sent his general Qū Yì to pursue and attack them south of Yè,
defeating them.
The Chányú took Yáng to Líyáng,
where he attacked and defeated the army of Gěng Zhǐ, the General Who Crosses the Borders (Dùliáo Jiāngjūn),
and his forces recovered their strength.
Dǒng Zhuó appointed Yáng as General Who Establishes Righteousness (Jiànyì Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Hénèi.
When the Son of Heaven was in Hédōng,
Yáng led troops to Ānyì,
where he was appointed General Who Pacifies the State (Ānguó Jiāngjūn)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Jìnyáng.
Yáng wanted to escort the Son of Heaven back to Luòyáng,
but the other generals disagreed.
Yáng returned to Yěwáng.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān (196 CE),
Yáng Fèng, Dǒng Chéng, and Hán Xiān escorted the Son of Heaven back to the old capital,
but their provisions were exhausted.
Yáng provided provisions along the way,
and they successfully reached Luòyáng.
He said to the generals:
"The Son of Heaven should be shared by the empire.
Since there are already high ministers (gōngqīng) and grand officials (dàchén),
I, Yáng, should defend against external dangers.
Why should I meddle in the capital?"
He then returned to Yěwáng.
He was then appointed Grand Commander (Dàsīmǎ).
Yáng had always been on good terms with Lǚ Bù.
When Tàizǔ besieged Lǚ Bù,
Yáng wished to rescue him
but could not.
So he sent troops to the east market,
creating a distant show of force.
His general, Yáng Chǒu,
killed Yáng to surrender to Tàizǔ.
Yáng's general, Suī Gù, killed Yáng Chǒu,
took his forces,
and intended to join Yuán Shào in the north.
Tàizǔ sent Shǐ Huàn to intercept and attack him,
defeating him at Quǎnchéng,
beheading Suī Gù,
and seizing all his forces.
Gōngsūn Dù, courtesy name Shēngjì,
was originally from Xiāngpíng, Liáodōng.
Dù's father, Yán,
avoided officials and resided in Xuántú,
where he appointed Dù as a county official.
At that time, Gōngsūn Yù, the Administrator of Xuántú,
had a son named Bào,
who died young at the age of eighteen.
Dù's childhood name was Bào,
and he was the same age as Yù's son.
Yù saw him and was fond of him,
sending him to a teacher to study
and arranging a marriage for him.
Later, he was recommended for his virtuous conduct,
appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Láng),
and gradually promoted to Inspector of Jìzhōu,
but was dismissed due to rumors.
Xú Róng, from the same commandery, who was a Commandant (Zhōngláng Jiāng) under Dǒng Zhuó,
recommended Dù as Administrator of Liáodōng.
Dù started as a minor official in Xuántú,
and was looked down upon by the Liáodōng Commandery.
Previously,
Gōngsūn Zhāo, the Protector-General of the Dependent States (Shǔguó), served as Magistrate of Xiāngpíng,
and summoned Dù's son Kāng to be a petty officer (wǔzhǎng).
When Dù arrived in office,
he arrested Zhāo,
flogged him to death in the market of Xiāngpíng.
Prominent local magnates and powerful families in the commandery, such as Tián Sháo, who had previously treated him without favor,
were all executed according to the law.
Over a hundred families were wiped out,
and the commandery was filled with terror.
He campaigned eastward against Gāogōulí,
and westward attacked Wūhuán,
extending his authority overseas.
In the first year of Chūpíng (190 CE),
Dù, knowing that central China was in chaos,
said to his trusted officials Liǔ Yì and Yáng Yí, among others:
"The Hàn dynasty is about to end.
We should plan to become kings with you gentlemen."
At that time, a large stone,
over a zhàng in length,
with three small stones beneath it serving as feet, appeared in the Shèlǐ district of Xiāngpíng.
Someone told Dù:
"This is an auspicious sign like the 'Stone Crown' of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
and the district name is the same as your late father's.
The She (earth god altar) governs the land,
indicating that you will surely possess land,
with three dukes to assist you."
Dù was even more pleased.
Lǐ Mǐn, the former Administrator of Hénèi,
well-known in the commandery,
disliked Dù's actions,
and fearing harm,
he took his family and went to sea.
Dù was furious,
dug up Mǐn's father's tomb,
opened the coffin and burned the corpse,
and executed his clan.
He divided Liáodōng Commandery into Liáoxī and Zhōngliáo Commanderies,
and appointed administrators.
He crossed the sea to seize the counties of Dōnglái,
and established an Inspector of Yíngzhōu.
He appointed himself Marquis of Liáodōng and Provincial Shepherd (Píngzhōu Mù),
and posthumously enfeoffed his father Yán as Marquis of Jiànyì.
He erected temples for the two Hàn ancestors,
and, acting on imperial authority, set up altars at the south of Xiāngpíng city,
offered sacrifices to Heaven and Earth in the suburbs,
performed the plowing ceremony (jítián),
trained troops,
rode in the phoenix chariot (luánlù),
with nine streamers (jiǔliú),
and cavalry adorned with yak tails (máotóu yǔqí).
Tàizǔ appointed Dù as General of Martial Prowess (Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn)
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yǒngníng Township.
Dù said:
"I am king of Liáodōng,
what 'Yǒngníng' is this?"
He stored the seals and sashes in the armory.
When Dù died,
his son Kāng succeeded him,
and enfeoffed his younger brother Gōng as Marquis of Yǒngníng Township.
This was the ninth year of Jiàn'ān (204 CE).
In the twelfth year (207 CE),
Tàizǔ campaigned against the Wūhuán of the three commanderies
and massacred Liǔchéng.
Yuán Shàng and others fled to Liáodōng,
but Kāng beheaded Shàng and sent his head.
The details are in the biography of Wǔ (Wǔ Jì).
Kāng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāngpíng
and appointed General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn).
When Kāng died,
his sons Huǎng and Yuān were both young,
so the populace established Gōng as Administrator of Liáodōng.
When Emperor Wén (Cáo Pī) ascended the throne,
he sent an envoy to officially appoint Gōng as General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn) with the authority to use imperial credentials (jiǎjié),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Píngguō;
he posthumously granted Kāng the title of Grand Commander (Dàsīmǎ).
Initially,
Gōng suffered from yin wasting and became a eunuch,
weak and unable to govern the state.
In the second year of Tàihé,
Yuān coerced Gōng and seized his position.
When Míngdì ascended the throne, he appointed Yuān as Yángliè Jiāngjūn and Liáodōng Tàishǒu.
Yuān sent envoys south to communicate with Sūn Quán,
exchanging bribes and gifts.
Quán dispatched envoys Zhāng Mí and Xǔ Yàn,
carrying gold, jade, and precious treasures,
to enthrone Yuān as King of Yān.
Yuān, however, feared that Quán was too distant to rely upon,
and also coveted the goods.
He lured the envoys to him,
then beheaded Mí and Yàn, sending their heads to Míngdì.
Míngdì then appointed Yuān as Dàsīmǎ,
enfeoffed him as Lèlàng Gōng,
and he retained his credentials and command of the prefecture as before.
When the envoy arrived,
Yuān arrayed his armed forces in a military formation
to meet the envoy.
He also frequently spoke ill of the state's guests in front of his retainers.
In the first year of Jǐngchū,
an imperial decree was sent, with Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ Wúqiū Jiǎn and others, to summon Yuān.
Yuān consequently mobilized his troops
and met them at Liáosuì,
where he fought with Jiǎn and the others.
Jiǎn and his forces were unsuccessful and returned.
Yuān then declared himself King of Yān,
and established a full complement of officials.
He sent an envoy with credentials,
falsely conferring the Xīanbéi Dānchán seal,
to enfeoff and appoint border people,
and entice the Xiānbēi,
who then encroached upon and harassed the north.
In the spring of the second year,
Tàiwèi Sīmǎ Xuānwáng was sent to conquer Yuān.
In the sixth month,
the army reached Liáodōng.
Yuān sent generals Bēi Yǎn and Yáng Zuò with tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry to garrison Liáosuì,
encircling it with trenches for over twenty *li*.
When Xuānwáng's army arrived,
he ordered Yǎn to engage in battle.
Xuānwáng sent General Hú Zūn and others to attack and defeat them.
Xuānwáng ordered the army to dig through the encirclement,
leading his troops southeast,
but then rapidly turned northeast,
marching directly to Xiāngpíng.
Yǎn and his forces, fearing Xiāngpíng was unguarded,
fled during the night.
All the armies advanced to Shǒushān,
where Yuān again sent Yǎn and others to meet the army in a desperate fight.
They were attacked again,
and utterly defeated.
The army then advanced to the city walls,
and established an encircling trench.
It happened to rain continuously for over thirty days,
and the Liáo River swelled,
allowing supply boats to sail directly from Liáokǒu to the city walls.
When the rain cleared,
earthen mounds and siege towers were erected,
and stone-throwing crossbows were used to shoot into the city.
Yuān was in dire straits.
Provisions ran out,
people resorted to cannibalism,
and many died.
General Yáng Zuò and others surrendered.
On the night of bingyin in the eighth month,
a large meteor, tens of *zhàng* long,
fell from the northeast of Shǒushān to the southeast of Xiāngpíng city.
On renwu,
Yuān's forces collapsed.
He, with his son Xiū, led a few hundred cavalry and broke through the encirclement, fleeing southeast.
The main army pursued them fiercely,
and at the spot where the meteor had fallen,
Yuān and his son were beheaded.
The city was breached,
and the heads of the Xiāngguó and thousands of others were taken.
Yuān's head was sent to Luòyáng.
Liáodōng, Dàifāng, Lèlàng, and Xuántú were all pacified.
Initially,
strange occurrences frequently plagued Yuān's household:
a dog, wearing a turban and crimson clothes, went up to the roof;
during cooking, a small child was steamed to death in the甑 *zèng* (steamer).
In the north market of Xiāngpíng, raw meat appeared,
each piece several *chǐ* long,
with heads, eyes, mouths, and beaks,
but no hands or feet, yet it moved.
The divination said:
"Having form but no completion,
having body but no sound,
its state will perish."
Starting from when Gōng took control of Liáodōng in the sixth year of Zhōngpíng,
to Yuān, it was three generations,
a total of fifty years before its destruction.
Zhāng Yān,
a native of Zhēndìng, Chángshān,
originally had the surname Chǔ.
When the Yellow Turbans rose,
Yān gathered young men into bandit groups,
roaming and attacking in the mountains and marshes.
He returned to Zhēndìng
with over ten thousand followers.
Zhāng Niújiǎo of Bólíng also raised a force,
calling himself Jiāngbīng Cóngshì,
and joined with Yān.
Yān deferred to Niújiǎo as their leader,
and together they attacked Yǐngtáo.
Niújiǎo was struck by a flying arrow.
Wounded and near death,
he ordered his followers to serve Yān,
declaring:
"You must take Yān as your commander."
After Niújiǎo died,
the followers served Yān,
so he changed his surname to Zhāng.
Yān was swift and agile, surpassing others,
hence his army called him Fēiyàn (Flying Swallow).
Thereafter, his following gradually expanded.
The valleys of Chángshān, Zhàojùn, Zhōngshān, Shàngdǎng, and Hénèi were all connected.
His minor chieftains, Sūn Qīng and Wáng Dāng,
each with their own units, followed Yān,
and their numbers reached a million,
known as Hēishān (Black Mountain).
Língdì was unable to conquer them,
and the prefectures north of the Yellow River suffered their depredations.
Yān sent a messenger to the capital to offer surrender,
and Yān was appointed Píngnàn Zhōnglángjiāng.
After this,
Dǒng Zhuó moved the Son of Heaven to Cháng'ān,
and conflicts frequently erupted throughout the land.
Yān then allied his forces with various powerful figures.
When Yuán Shào and Gōngsūn Zàn contended for Jìzhōu,
Yān sent his general Dù Cháng and others to assist Zàn,
and fought with Shào.
They were defeated by Shào,
and their forces gradually dispersed.
When Tàizǔ was about to pacify Jìzhōu,
Yān sent an envoy to request assistance for the royal army,
and was appointed Píngběi Jiāngjūn.
He led his forces to Yè,
was enfeoffed as Ānguó Tínghóu,
and granted five hundred households.
Yān died,
and his son Fāng succeeded him.
Fāng died,
and his son Róng succeeded him.
Zhāng Xiù,
a native of Zǔlì, Wǔwēi,
was a nephew of the Agile Cavalry General, Jì.
When Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì caused chaos in Liángzhōu,
Qū Shèng of Jīnchéng attacked and killed Liú Jùn, the Prefect of Zǔlì.
Xiù, then a county official,
stealthily sought an opportunity to kill Shèng,
and the commandery considered it a righteous act.
Thereupon, he gathered young men
and became a local hero in the district.
When Dǒng Zhuó was defeated,
Jì, along with Lǐ Quē and others, attacked Lǚ Bù
to avenge Dǒng Zhuó.
The account is in Dǒng Zhuó’s biography.
Xiù followed Jì,
and through military merits, gradually rose to the rank of General Who Establishes Loyalty,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xuānwēi.
Jì was stationed at Hóngnóng.
His soldiers were starving, so
he attacked Ráng to the south,
where he was struck and killed by a stray arrow.
Xiù took command of his forces
and stationed them at Wǎn,
allying with Liú Biǎo.
Tàizǔ marched south,
encamping at Yùshuǐ,
and Xiù and his forces surrendered.
Tàizǔ took Jì’s widow as a consort,
which Xiù resented.
Tàizǔ, hearing of his displeasure,
secretly plotted to kill Xiù.
The plot was leaked,
and Xiù launched a surprise attack on Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ’s army was defeated,
and his two sons perished.
Xiù returned to secure Ráng,
and Tàizǔ attacked it for several years,
but could not conquer it.
When Tàizǔ resisted Yuán Shào at Guāndù,
Xiù followed Jiǎ Xǔ’s plan
and again surrendered with his forces.
The account is in Jiǎ Xǔ’s biography.
When Xiù arrived,
Tàizǔ held his hand
and feasted with him joyfully.
He arranged for his son, Jūn, to marry Xiù’s daughter,
and appointed Xiù General Who Manifests Martial Might.
During the Battle of Guāndù,
Xiù fought valiantly and rendered meritorious service,
for which he was promoted to General Who Breaks the Qiāng.
He followed in the defeat of Yuán Tán at Nánpí,
and his enfeoffment was again increased to a total of two thousand households.
At this time, the population of the empire had diminished,
with only one-tenth remaining,
and none of the generals had been enfeoffed with a thousand households,
yet Xiù received an exceptionally large amount.
He followed in the campaign against the Wūwán at Liǔchéng,
but died
before reaching it.
His posthumous title was Marquis Dìng.
His son, Quán, inherited the title,
but was executed for plotting rebellion with Wèi Fěng,
and the marquisate was abolished.
Zhāng Lǔ, courtesy name Gōngqí,
was a native of Fēng, Pèiguó.
His grandfather, Líng,
traveled as a sojourner to Shǔ
and studied the Dao in the Míng Mountains,
creating Daoist texts to delude the common people.
Those who received the Dao from him gave five dou of rice,
hence he was popularly called the "Rice Bandit."
After Líng died,
his son, Héng, continued his Way.
After Héng died,
Lǔ again continued it.
Liú Yān, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, appointed Lǔ as Chief Commandant of Righteous Volunteers,
and with Zhāng Xiū, Chief Commandant of a Separate Department, led troops to attack Sū Gù, the Administrator of Hànzhōng.
Lǔ then attacked Xiū, killed him,
and seized his forces.
After Yān died,
his son, Zhāng, succeeded him.
Because Lǔ was disobedient,
Zhāng killed all of Lǔ’s mother’s family.
Lǔ then occupied Hànzhōng,
teaching the people with the Way of Ghosts,
and styled himself
"Master and Lord" (Shī Jūn).
Those who came to learn the Dao
were initially all called
"Ghost Soldiers" (Guǐ Zú).
Once they believed in the main Way they had received,
they were called
"Libationers" (Jìjiǔ).
Each led a group of people,
the largest being called Chief Grand Libationer (Zhìtóu Dà Jìjiǔ).
All were taught sincerity and not to cheat.
If ill, they would confess their transgressions.
In general, it was similar to the Yellow Turbans.
All the Libationers established "righteous lodges" (yìshè),
similar to today’s relay stations.
They also provided "righteous rice and meat" (yìmǐròu),
hanging them in the righteous lodges,
for travelers to take according to their hunger.
If they took too much,
the Way of Ghosts would make them ill.
For those who broke the law,
there were three pardons
before punishment was administered.
No senior officials were appointed;
all governance was handled by the Libationers,
and the people, both Han and non-Han, found it convenient and joyful.
He held Bā and Hàn for nearly thirty years.
In the late Hàn dynasty,
the imperial court lacked the strength to campaign,
so it condescended to honor Lǔ by appointing him General of the Household Who Guards the People,
and Administrator of Hànníng,
merely accepting his tributes.
When a jade seal was found in the ground by the people,
his subordinates wanted to enthrone Lǔ as King of Hànníng.
Yán Pǔ of Bāxī, Lǔ’s Grand Clerk of Merits, admonished Lǔ, saying:
"The people of Hànchuān
number over a hundred thousand households.
The land is rich and fertile,
and it is naturally fortified on all four sides.
If you assist the Son of Heaven,
you will be like Huán of Qí and Wén of Jìn.
At a lesser extent, like Dòu Róng,
you will not lose wealth and nobility.
Now, you have received imperial authorization to appoint and dismiss,
and have the power to act independently;
there is no need to be a king.
I hope you will not claim the title for now,
lest you bring disaster upon yourself."
Lǔ followed his advice.
During the rebellions of Hán Suì and Mǎ Chāo,
tens of thousands of families from Guānxī fled through the Zǐwǔ Valley to him.
In the twentieth year of Jiàn'ān [215 CE],
Tàizǔ departed from Sànguān through Wǔdū to campaign against him,
reaching Yángpíng Pass.
Lǔ wanted to surrender Hànzhōng,
but his younger brother, Wèi, refused,
