leading tens of thousands of men to resist and hold the pass firmly.
Tàizǔ attacked and broke through,
then entered Shǔ.
When Lǔ heard that Yángpíng had fallen,
he was about to bow down and surrender.
Pǔ again said:
"If you go now under duress,
your merit will surely be light.
It is better to rely on Dù Hù and Pú Hú to resist,
and then commit yourself;
your merit will surely be great."
Thereupon, he fled to Nánshān and entered Bāzhōng.
His attendants wanted to burn all the treasures and storehouses,
but Lǔ said:
"I originally intended to surrender to the state,
but my intentions were not yet clear.
My current flight is to avoid the sharp edge [of the enemy],
not out of malice.
The treasures and storehouses
belong to the state."
So he sealed them up and left.
Tàizǔ entered Nánzhèng
and greatly praised this action.
Moreover, knowing Lǔ’s original good intentions,
he sent someone to comfort and persuade him.
Lǔ brought out his entire family,
and Tàizǔ met him, appointing him General Who Guards the South,
treating him with the courtesy due to a guest,
enfeoffing him as Marquis of Lángzhōng,
with ten thousand households.
He enfeoffed Lǔ’s five sons and Yán Pǔ and others
all as marquises.
He arranged for his son, Péngzǔ, to marry Lǔ’s daughter.
When Lǔ died,
he was posthumously titled Marquis Yuán.
His son, Fù, inherited the title.
Commentary states: Gōngsūn Zàn defended Jīng,
but merely sat and waited for his extermination.
Dù was cruel and unrestrained,
Yuān continued his savage ways,
merely enough to bring ruin upon their clans.
Táo Qiān was muddled and confused, dying of worry.
Zhāng Yáng was beheaded by his subordinates.
All of them occupied and held commanderies and prefectures,
yet were not even as good as commoners;
indeed, there is nothing commendable to say about them.
Yàn, Xiù, and Lǔ abandoned banditry,
were listed among meritorious ministers,
escaped peril and destruction,
and preserved their ancestral sacrifices,
which was certainly better than those others.
Biographies of the Xiàhóu and Cáo Clans, Volume Nine
Xiàhóu Dūn (夏侯惇), courtesy name Yuánràng (元讓),
was a native of Qiáo (譙), Péiguó (沛國).
He was a descendant of Xiàhóu Yīng (夏侯嬰).
At the age of fourteen,
when he was studying with a teacher,
someone insulted his teacher.
Dūn killed him,
and from this he became known for his fierce spirit.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) first raised an army,
Dūn often served as a subordinate general,
accompanying him on campaigns.
When Tàizǔ served as the General Who Spreads Martial Might,
he appointed Dūn as Sīmǎ (司馬),
and he was separately garrisoned at Báimǎ (白馬).
He was promoted to Colonel Who Breaks the Ranks,
and held the post of Administrator of Dōngjùn (東郡).
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Táo Qiān (陶謙),
he left Dūn to guard Púyáng (濮陽).
Zhāng Miǎo (張邈) rebelled and welcomed Lǚ Bù (呂布).
Tàizǔ’s family was in Juānchéng (鄄城),
so Dūn led a light force to confront him,
and happened to meet Bù,
engaging in battle.
Bù retreated,
then entered Púyáng,
and attacked Dūn’s army, capturing their supplies and baggage.
Bù sent a general who feigned surrender,
and together they seized Dūn,
demanding treasures and goods.
Dūn’s army was shaken with fear.
Dūn’s general Hán Hào (韓浩) then marshaled his troops and garrisoned them at the gate of Dūn’s camp,
summoning the military officers and all the generals,
ordering them to don their armor and remain at their posts without moving.
Only then did the various camps stabilize.
He then went to Dūn’s location
and sternly rebuked those holding Dūn hostage, saying:
“You villains
dare to seize the Great General.
Do you still hope to live?!
Moreover, I have received orders to suppress bandits.
How can I, for the sake of one general,
let you go free?!”
Then, shedding tears, he said to Dūn:
“What can be done about the laws of the state?!”
He quickly summoned soldiers to attack those holding the hostage.
The hostage-takers, in a panic, kowtowed,
saying,
“We only want to ask for provisions and then leave!”
Hào repeatedly reprimanded them,
and then executed them all.
After Dūn was freed,
Tàizǔ heard of it
and said to Hào:
“Your action here can serve as a law for ten thousand generations.”
He then issued an order that
from now on, if there were hostage-takers,
all should be attacked simultaneously,
without regard for the hostage.
From this, hostage-taking ceased.
When Tàizǔ returned from Xúzhōu (徐州),
Dūn followed him to campaign against Lǚ Bù
and was hit by a stray arrow,
wounding his left eye.
He again held the posts of Administrator of Chénliú (陳留) and Jìyīn (濟陰),
was promoted to General Who Establishes Martial Might,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāo’ān Township (高安鄉).
At that time, there was a great drought,
and locusts arose.
Dūn therefore dammed the Tàishòu (太壽) River to create a reservoir,
personally carrying earth,
leading his officers and soldiers to encourage the planting of rice.
The people benefited from this.
He was then transferred to hold the post of Intendant of Hénán (河南尹).
When Tàizǔ pacified Hébĕi (河北),
Dūn served as the Great General guarding the rear.
After Yè (鄴) was captured,
he was promoted to General Who Quells Waves,
retaining his post as Intendant as before,
and was permitted to act expediently
without being constrained by regulations.
In the twelfth year of Jiàn’ān (建安),
in recognition of Dūn’s previous and subsequent merits,
his enfeoffment was increased by one thousand eight hundred households,
making a total of two thousand five hundred households including the previous ones.
In the twenty-first year,
after returning from campaigning against Sūn Quán (孫權),
Dūn was made Area Commander of twenty-six armies,
and stationed at Jūcháo (居巢).
He was bestowed with entertainers and famous singers,
with an order saying:
“Wèi Jiàng (魏絳), for his merits in harmonizing with the Rong (戎),
still received the music of bells and chimes,
how much more so for the General!”
In the twenty-fourth year,
when Tàizǔ’s army was at Mópbēi (摩陂),
he summoned Dūn to always ride with him,
showing special intimacy and respect,
entering and exiting his private chambers.
None of the other generals could compare to this.
He was appointed Front General,
and supervised all armies returning to Shòuchūn (壽春),
then moved his garrison to Zhàolíng (召陵).
When Wéndì (文帝) ascended the throne as King,
he appointed Dūn as Great General.
He died a few months later.
Although Dūn was in the army,
he personally welcomed teachers and received instruction.
He was by nature pure and frugal,
always distributing any surplus wealth,
and if it was insufficient, he drew funds from the government.
He did not manage property.
His posthumous title was Zhōnghóu (忠侯, Loyal Marquis).
His son Chōng (充) succeeded him.
The Emperor, reflecting on Dūn’s merits,
wished for his descendants to all be marquises.
He divided Dūn’s fief of one thousand households
and bestowed upon Dūn’s seven sons and two grandsons the title of Marquis Within the Passes.
Dūn’s younger brother Lián (廉) and his son Máo (楙) had already been enfeoffed as Marquises.
Earlier,
Tàizǔ had given his daughter in marriage to Máo;
she was the Princess of Qīnghé (清河).
Máo successively held positions such as侍中 Shìzhōng (侍中), Shàngshū (尚書), and General Who Guards the West and General Who Suppresses the East,
and was granted imperial authority.
When Chōng died,
his son Yì (廙) succeeded him.
When Yì died,
his son Shào (劭) succeeded him.
Hán Hào
was from Hénèi (河內).
Shǐ Huàn (史渙) of Péiguó and Hào were both prominent for their loyalty and bravery.
Hào reached the rank of Central Protector of the Army,
and Huàn reached the rank of Central Leader of the Army.
Both commanded the imperial guards
and were enfeoffed as Marquises.
Xiàhóu Yuān (夏侯淵), courtesy name Miàocái (妙才),
was a cousin of Dūn.
When Tàizǔ was living at home,
he once had a matter involving county officials.
Yuān took the blame for a serious crime,
and Tàizǔ rescued him,
so he was spared.
When Tàizǔ raised his army,
Yuān followed as a Separate Department Sīmǎ (司馬) and Cavalier Commandant,
and was promoted to Administrator of Chénliú (陳留) and Yǐngchuān (潁川).
When Tàizǔ fought against Yuán Shào (袁紹) at Guāndù (官渡),
Yuān served as Acting Colonel Supervising the Army.
After Shào was defeated,
Yuān was appointed to supervise military provisions for Yǎn (兗), Yù (豫), and Xúzhōu (徐州).
At that time, military food was scarce,
but Yuān continuously transported supplies,
and the army recovered.
When Chāng Xī (昌狶) rebelled,
Yú Jìn (于禁) was sent to attack him.
Before he could subdue him,
Yuān was again sent to combine forces with Jìn.
They then attacked Xī,
subduing more than ten of his strongholds,
and Xī surrendered to Jìn.
When Yuān returned,
he was appointed Colonel of the Army.
When the Yellow Turban rebels Xú Hé (徐和) and Sīmǎ Jù (司馬俱) from Jǐnán (濟南) and Lè’ān (樂安) attacked cities
and killed chief officials,
Yuān led troops from Tàishān (泰山), Qí (齊), and Píngyuán (平原) Commanderies to attack them,
decisively defeating them,
executing Hé,
pacifying all the counties,
and collecting their grain to supply the soldiers.
In the fourteenth year,
Yuān was made Acting Leader of the Army.
When Tàizǔ returned from campaigning against Sūn Quán,
he ordered Yuān to supervise the generals in attacking Léi Xù (雷緒), who had rebelled in Lújiāng (廬江).
Xù was defeated.
Yuān then served as Acting Protector of the Army Who Conquers the West,
supervising Xú Huǎng (徐晃) in attacking bandits in Tàiyuán (太原).
They captured more than twenty strongholds,
executed the bandit leader Shāng Yào (商曜),
and razed his city.
He followed Tàizǔ in campaigning against Hán Suì (韓遂) and others,
fighting at Wèinán (渭南).
He also supervised Zhū Líng (朱靈) in pacifying Yúmí (隃糜) and Qiān Dǐ (汧氐).
He met with Tàizǔ at Āndìng (安定)
and secured the surrender of Yáng Qiū (楊秋).
In the 17th year [of Jiàn'ān],
Tàizǔ then returned to Yè.
He appointed Yuān as acting Protector-General of the Army (hùjūn jiāngjūn),
supervising Zhū Líng, Lù Zhāo, and others to garrison Cháng'ān,
and attack and defeat the Nánshān bandit Líu Xióng,
who surrendered his followers.
Yuān besieged Suí and Chāo's remaining partisans, Líang Xīng, in Hù,
captured it,
beheaded Xīng,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Bóuchāngtíng.
Mǎ Chāo besieged Wéi Kāng, Inspector of Líangzhōu, in Jì,
and Yuān went to relieve Kāng.
Before he arrived,
Kāng was defeated.
When he was over two hundred lì from Jì,
Chāo came to meet him in battle,
and Yuān's army was at a disadvantage.
The Dī of Qían rebelled,
and Yuān withdrew his army.
In the 19th year [of Jiàn'ān],
Zhào Qú, Yǐn Fèng, and others plotted to attack Chāo.
Jìang Qī raised an army in Lǔchéng to respond to them.
Qú and others tricked Chāo
into going out to attack,
and then killed all of Chāo's wives and children.
Chāo fled to Hànzhōng,
and then returned to besiege Qíshān.
They urgently sought help.
The generals debated, wanting to wait for Tàizǔ's orders.
Yuān said:
"The Duke is in Yè,
a round trip of four thousand lì.
By the time he replies,
they will certainly have been defeated.
This is not a matter for a leisurely pace."
So he set out,
ordering Zhāng Hé to lead five thousand infantry and cavalry as the vanguard,
entering through the narrow pass of Chéncāng.
Yuān personally supervised the provisions from the rear.
When Hé reached the Wèishǔi river,
Chāo's generals, with several thousand Dī and Qiāng, met Hé.
Before the battle,
Chāo fled,
and Hé advanced to seize Chāo's military equipment.
When Yuān arrived,
all the counties had already surrendered.
Hán Suí was in Xiǎnqīn.
Yuān wanted to surprise him,
but Suí fled.
Yuān seized Suí's military provisions,
and pursued him to Líuèyángchéng.
When he was over twenty lì from Suí,
the generals wanted to attack him.
Some said they should attack the Dī of Xīngguó.
Yuān believed that Suí's troops were elite,
and Xīngguó's city was strong;
an attack would not quickly succeed.
It would be better to attack the various Qiāng of Chánglí.
Many of the Chánglí Qiāng were in Suí's army,
and they would surely return to rescue their families.
If [Suí] abandoned the Qiāng and stood alone, he would be isolated.
If he rescued Chánglí, the government troops could engage in open battle,
and victory would be certain.
Yuān then left a supervising general to guard the baggage train,
and with light infantry and cavalry, went to Chánglí.
He attacked and burned the Qiāng camps,
slaying and capturing many.
The various Qiāng who were in Suí's army
each returned to their tribes.
Suí indeed went to relieve Chánglí,
and confronted Yuān's army.
The generals saw Suí's large force
and were apprehensive. They wanted to set up camp and dig trenches before fighting.
Yuān said:
"We have fought for a thousand lì.
If we now construct camps and trenches,
our officers and men will be exhausted,
and we cannot last long.
Although the bandits are numerous,
they are easy to deal with."
Then he beat the drums,
and utterly routed Suí's army,
capturing his banners and standards.
He returned to Líuèyáng,
and advanced to besiege Xīngguó.
Dī King Wànqiān fled to Mǎ Chāo,
and the rest of his followers surrendered.
He then attacked the Túcá of Gāopíng,
who all scattered and fled.
He seized their grain, cattle, and horses.
Tàizǔ then granted Yuān the privilege of holding the imperial 'Jié' (credentials).
Originally,
Sòng Jiàn of Páohǎn, taking advantage of the chaos in Líangzhōu,
proclaimed himself King Pínghàn, Leader of the Rivers (Héshǒu Pínghàn Wáng).
Tàizǔ sent Yuān to lead the various generals to attack Jiàn.
When Yuān arrived,
he besieged Páohǎn.
After more than a month, he captured it,
and beheaded Jiàn and those he had appointed, from Chancellor downwards.
Yuān separately dispatched Zhāng Hé and others to pacify Héguān,
cross the Hé river, and enter Xiǎohuángzhōng.
All the Qiāng west of the Hé river surrendered,
and Lǒngyòu was pacified.
Tàizǔ issued an order saying:
"Sòng Jiàn has caused rebellion for over thirty years.
Yuān extinguished him in one fell swoop,
striding like a tiger through Guānyòu,
with no one to oppose him.
Confucius (Zhòngní) said: 'I am not as good as him.'"
In the 21st year [of Jiàn'ān],
his enfeoffment was increased by three hundred households,
making a total of eight hundred households.
He then attacked the Dī and Qiāng of Wǔdū in Xiàbiàn,
seizing over ten myriad hú of Dī grain.
When Tàizǔ marched west against Zhāng Lǔ,
Yuān and the various generals, marquises, and kings of Líangzhōu,
met Tàizǔ at Xiūtíng.
Whenever Tàizǔ met with the Qiāng and Hú,
he used Yuān to intimidate them.
When Lǔ surrendered,
and Hànzhōng was pacified,
Yuān was appointed acting Protector-General (dūhù jiāngjūn),
supervising Zhāng Hé, Xú Huǎng, and others to pacify Bājùn.
Tàizǔ returned to Yè,
leaving Yuān to guard Hànzhōng,
and then appointed Yuān as General Who Conquers the West (zhēngxī jiāngjūn).
In the 23rd year [of Jiàn'ān],
Líu Bèi's army was at Yángpíngguān.
Yuān led his generals to resist him,
and they faced each other for several years.
In the first month of the 24th year [of Jiàn'ān],
Bèi burned the surrounding deer antlers at night.
Yuān sent Zhāng Hé to guard the eastern perimeter,
and personally led light troops to guard the southern perimeter.
Bèi provoked Hé to battle,
and Hé's army was at a disadvantage.
Yuān divided half of his troops to assist Hé,
but was then ambushed by Bèi.
Yuān was killed in battle.
He was given the posthumous title of Mǐnhóu.
Initially,
although Yuān often won battles,
Tàizǔ always warned him, saying:
"A general must sometimes show caution,
and not rely solely on bravery.
A general should be founded on courage,
but act with wisdom and strategy.
One who only knows how to rely on courage
is merely a match for a common soldier."
Yuān's wife
was Tàizǔ's younger sister-in-law.
His eldest son, Héng,
married the daughter of Tàizǔ's brother, the Marquis Āihóu of Hǎiyáng.
His favor and prestige were especially high.
Héng inherited the peerage
and was later enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānníngtíng.
During the Huángchū era,
his second son, Bà, was granted a title.
During the Tàihé era,
Bà's four younger brothers were granted titles,
all as Marquises within the Pass (guānnèi hóu).
Bà,
during the Zhèngshǐ era, served as Protector-General Who Attacks Shǔ (tǎoshǔ hùjūn) and General of the Right (yòujiāngjūn).
He was advanced to Marquis of Bóuchāngtíng,
and was always well-regarded by Cáo Shuǎng.
Upon hearing of Shuǎng's execution,
he became suspicious of himself
and fled into Shǔ.
Due to Yuān's past merits, Bà's son was pardoned
and exiled to Lèlàng Jùn.
Bà's brother, Wēi,
rose to the position of Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
Wēi's brother, Huì,
was Administrator of Lè'ān.
Huì's brother, Hé,
was Prefect of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn).
After Héng's death,
his son Jī succeeded him
as Colonel of the Tiger's Stance (hǔbēizhōnglángjiàng).
After Jī's death,
his son Bāo succeeded him.
Cáo Rén
zì Zǐxiào, was a younger cousin of Tàizǔ.
In his youth, he loved archery, horsemanship, hawking, and hunting.
Later, as heroes rose together,
Rén also secretly gathered young men,
obtaining over a thousand followers.
They roamed between the Huái and Sì rivers,
and then joined Tàizǔ as a Major of a Separate Command,
acting as Colonel of the Sharp Edge.
When Tàizǔ defeated Yuán Shù,
Rén's contributions in beheadings and captures were considerable.
Following Tàizǔ in the campaign against Xúzhōu,
Rén often commanded the cavalry,
serving as the army's vanguard.
He separately attacked Lǚ Yóu, a general under Táo Qiān,
defeating him.
He then returned to join the main army at Péngchéng,
where Táo Qiān's army was greatly defeated.
Following the attack on Fèi, Huá, Jìmò, and Kāiyáng,
Táo Qiān dispatched separate generals to reinforce various counties.
Rén attacked and defeated them with his cavalry.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Lǚ Bù,
Rén separately attacked Jùyáng,
capturing it,
and taking Lǚ Bù's general Liú Hé alive.
After Tàizǔ pacified the Yellow Turbans
and welcomed the Son of Heaven to the capital at Xǔ,
Rén had several meritorious achievements
and was appointed Grand Administrator of Guǎngyáng.
Tàizǔ valued his courage and strategy,
and did not allow him to take up his post in the commandery,
instead making him a Counsellor Remonstrant overseeing cavalry.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Zhāng Xiù,
Rén separately pacified the surrounding counties,
capturing over three thousand men and women.
When Tàizǔ's army returned,
they were pursued by Zhāng Xiù,
and the army suffered a disadvantage.
The officers and soldiers lost morale.
Rén rallied and encouraged his officers and men with great enthusiasm.
Tàizǔ was impressed by this,
and subsequently defeated Zhāng Xiù.
Tàizǔ and Yuán Shào were long stalemated at Guāndù.
Shào sent Liú Bèi to pacify the strong counties,
and many people responded by joining him.
South of Xǔ,
the officials and common people were unsettled.
Tàizǔ was concerned about this.
Rén said:
"The south assumes that the main army is currently preoccupied,
and therefore cannot come to their aid.
Liú Bèi is threatening them with strong forces,
so their defection is to be expected.
Bèi has only recently taken command of Shào's troops
and has not yet mastered their use.
If we attack him, he can be defeated."
Tàizǔ approved of his words,
and so sent him to lead cavalry to attack Bèi.
He defeated and routed him,
and Rén fully recovered all the rebellious counties before returning.
Shào sent his separate general Hán Xún to cut off the western road.
Rén attacked Xún at Jīluòshān,
greatly defeating him.
Because of this, Shào no longer dared to divide his troops.
Rén then, with Shǐ Huàn and others, intercepted Shào's supply wagons,
burning his grain stores.
After Héběi was pacified,
he followed in besieging Húguān.
Tàizǔ issued an order saying:
"When the city is taken,
all its inhabitants shall be buried alive."
It did not fall for several months.
Rén said to Tàizǔ:
"When besieging a city, one must show it an escape route,
thus opening a path to life for them.
Now, if Your Lordship declares that they will all surely die,
people will defend themselves to the death.
Moreover, the city is strong and has abundant provisions.
If we attack, our soldiers will be wounded,
and if we maintain the siege, it will drag on for a long time.
Now, to have our troops stalled beneath a strong city,
attacking enemies who are resolved to die,
is not a good strategy."
Tàizǔ followed his advice,
and the city surrendered.
Thereupon, considering Rén's past and present merits,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūting.
Following the pacification of Jīngzhōu,
Rén was appointed Acting General who Conquers the South
and stationed at Jiānglíng
to resist the Wú general Zhōu Yú.
Yú came to attack with tens of thousands of troops.
When his vanguard, numbering several thousand, first arrived,
Rén ascended the city wall to observe them.
He then recruited three hundred men
and sent his subordinate general Niú Jīn to meet them in challenge.
The enemy was numerous,
and Jīn's troops were few,
so they were soon surrounded.
The Chief Clerk, Chén Jiǎo, was also on the city wall.
Seeing Jīn and his men on the verge of being overwhelmed,
everyone around him turned pale.
Rén, full of furious spirit,
told his attendants to bring his horse.
Jiǎo and others together tried to restrain him.
They said to Rén:
"The enemy is numerous and strong;
they cannot be resisted.
Even if we abandon a few hundred men, what does it matter?
But for Your General to rush into it himself!"
Rén did not respond,
but donned his armor, mounted his horse,
and led dozens of brave cavalrymen from his immediate command out of the city.
When they were about a hundred paces from the enemy,
they approached a ditch.
Jiǎo and others thought Rén would stop at the ditch
to show support for Jīn.
But Rén directly crossed the ditch and charged forward,
plunging into the enemy's encirclement,
whereupon Jīn and his men were able to escape.
As the remaining troops had not all gotten out,
Rén again charged back in,
extracting Jīn's soldiers.
Only a few of them were lost,
and the enemy then retreated.
When Jiǎo and others first saw Rén charge out,
they were all terrified.
But when they saw Rén return,
they exclaimed:
"General, you are truly a man from heaven!"
The entire army admired his bravery.
Tàizǔ was even more impressed by him
and transferred his enfeoffment to Marquis of Ānpíngtíng.
When Tàizǔ attacked Mǎ Chāo,
Rén was appointed Acting General who Pacifies the West
to oversee various generals in resisting at Tóngguān,
and defeated Mǎ Chāo at Wèinán.
When Sū Bó and Tián Yín rebelled,
Rén was appointed Acting General of Valiant Cavalry
and overall commander of seven armies to attack Yín and others,
defeating them.
Rén was again appointed Acting General who Conquers the South,
granted an imperial staff,
stationed at Fán,
and garrisoned Jīngzhōu.
When Hóu Yīn rebelled in Wǎn
and gathered several thousand people from the surrounding counties,
Rén led various armies to attack and defeat Hóu Yīn,
beheading him.
He then returned to garrison Fán,
and was immediately appointed General who Conquers the South.
When Guān Yǔ attacked Fán,
the Hàn River suddenly overflowed.
Yú Jìn and his seven armies were all submerged,
and Jìn surrendered to Yǔ.
Rén, with several thousand men and horses, defended the city.
Only a few sections of the city wall remained above the water.
Yǔ approached the city by boat,
surrounding it several layers deep.
Internal and external communication was cut off,
provisions were running out,
and relief forces did not arrive.
Rén encouraged his officers and men,
showing them that death was certain.
Moved by this, the officers and men all remained unwavering.
When Xú Huǎng's relief force arrived,
the water also receded slightly.
Huǎng attacked Yǔ from the outside,
and Rén was able to break through the encirclement and emerge.
Yǔ retreated.
Cáo Rén (曹仁) in his youth did not maintain proper conduct.
When he grew older and became a general,
he strictly upheld the laws and regulations.
He always kept the code of law by his side,
and acted according to it.
When Yānlíng Hóu (鄢陵侯) Cáo Zhāng (曹彰) campaigned north against the Wūhuán (烏丸),
Emperor Wén (文帝), then in the Eastern Palace,
wrote a letter to admonish Cáo Zhāng (曹彰), saying:
"As a general upholding the law,
should you not be like the General Who Campaigns South?"
When Emperor Wén (文帝) ascended the throne,
he appointed Cáo Rén (曹仁) as Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍),
Grand Administrator of military affairs in Jīng (荊), Yáng (揚), and Yì (益) Provinces.
He was advanced to the title of Chén Hóu (陳侯),
with an additional two thousand households,
bringing the total to three thousand five hundred households.
Cáo Rén's (曹仁) father, Cáo Chì (曹熾), was posthumously granted the谥 (shì) of Chén Mù Hóu (陳穆侯),
and ten households were assigned to guard his tomb.
Later, Cáo Rén (曹仁) was recalled to garrison Wǎn (宛).
When Sūn Quán (孫權) sent his general Chén Shào (陳邵) to occupy Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
an imperial edict ordered Cáo Rén (曹仁) to attack him.
Cáo Rén (曹仁) and Xú Huǎng (徐晃) attacked and defeated Chén Shào (陳邵),
then entered Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
He ordered General Gāo Qiān (高遷) and others to resettle the people from south of the Hàn (漢) River who had come to submit to the north of the Hàn (漢) River.
Emperor Wén (文帝) sent an envoy to immediately appoint Cáo Rén (曹仁) as Dà Jiāngjūn (大將軍).
He further ordered Cáo Rén (曹仁) to move his garrison to Línyǐng (臨潁),
and promoted him to Dà Sīmǎ (大司馬).
He was again made Grand Administrator of all armies, stationed at Wūjiāng (烏江),
and then returned to garrison Héféi (合肥).
In the fourth year of Huángchū (黃初) (223 CE), he passed away,
and was posthumously granted the谥 (shì) of Zhōng Hóu (忠侯).
His son, Cáo TàI (曹泰), succeeded him,
and held office up to Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn (鎮東將軍).
He was granted authority to use a staff with a _jié_ (節),
and was transferred to the title of Nínglíng Hóu (甯陵侯).
After Cáo TàI (曹泰) passed away,
his son, Cáo Chū (曹初), succeeded him.
Cáo TàI's (曹泰) younger brothers, Cáo Kǎi (曹楷) and Cáo Fàn (曹範), were also granted separate fiefs,
and both became Liehóu (列侯).
Niú Jīn (牛金) held office up to Hòujiāngjūn (後將軍).
Cáo Rén's (曹仁) younger brother, Cáo Chún (曹純),
initially served as a Counselor of the Palace and participated in military affairs under the Minister of Works,
and commanded the Tiger and Leopard Cavalry in the siege of Nánpí (南皮).
Yuán Tán (袁譚) sallied forth to battle,
and many soldiers died.
Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) wanted to ease the attack,
but Cáo Chún (曹純) said:
"Now we have marched a thousand _li_ into enemy territory;
if we advance but cannot overcome them,
retreating will certainly cause us to lose prestige.
Moreover, with our forces deep in enemy territory,
it is difficult to sustain for long.
If they win, they will be arrogant;
if we fail, we will be fearful.
Using our fear against their arrogance,
we can surely overcome them."
Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) approved of his words,
and so pressed the attack,
and Yuán Tán (袁譚) was defeated.
Cáo Chún's (曹純) cavalry cut off Yuán Tán's (袁譚) head.
When campaigning north against the three commanderies,
Cáo Chún's (曹純) cavalry captured Dányú Dūn (單于頓).
For his accumulated merits, he was enfeoffed as Gāolíng Tínghóu (高陵亭侯),
with three hundred households.
Following the campaign in Jīng (荊) Province,
he pursued Liú Bèi (劉備) at Chángbǎn (長坂),
capturing his two daughters and baggage train,
and gathering his scattered soldiers.
He then advanced to subdue Jiānglíng (江陵),
and followed Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) back to Qiáo (譙).
In the fifteenth year of Jiàn'ān (建安) (210 CE), he passed away.
When Emperor Wén (文帝) ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the谥 (shì) of Wēi Hóu (威侯).
His son, Cáo Yǎn (曹演), succeeded him,
and held office up to Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍).
During the Zhèngyuán (正元) period, he was advanced to the title of Pínglè Xiānghóu (平樂鄉侯).
After Cáo Yǎn (曹演) passed away,
his son, Cáo Liàng (曹亮), succeeded him.
Cáo Hóng (曹洪), courtesy name Zǐlián (子廉),
was a paternal cousin of Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ).
When Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) raised a righteous army to attack Dǒng Zhuó (董卓),
upon reaching Xíngyáng (滎陽),
he was defeated by Dǒng Zhuó's (董 Zhuó) general Xú Róng (徐榮).
Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) lost his horse,
and the rebels pursued him very closely.
Cáo Hóng (曹洪) dismounted
and offered his horse to Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ).
Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) politely refused,
but Cáo Hóng (曹洪) said:
"The world can do without Cáo Hóng (曹洪),
but it cannot do without you, my lord."
He then followed on foot to the Biàn (汴) River.
The water was too deep to cross,
so Cáo Hóng (曹洪) followed the river and found a boat,
and crossed with Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ).
They returned and fled to Qiáo (譙).
Chén Wēn (陳溫), the Inspector of Yáng (揚) Province, had always been on good terms with Cáo Hóng (曹洪).
Cáo Hóng (曹洪) led over a thousand of his household troops
to Chén Wēn (陳溫) to recruit soldiers,
obtaining two thousand elite soldiers from Lújiāng (廬江).
He went east to Dānyáng (丹楊) and obtained several thousand more,
and met Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) at Lóngkàng (龍亢).
When Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) campaigned in Xú (徐) Province,
Zhāng Miǎo (張邈) raised a rebellion in Yǎn (兗) Province and welcomed Lǚ Bù (呂布).
At that time, there was a great famine.
Cáo Hóng (曹洪) led his troops ahead,
first occupying Dōngpíng (東平) and Fàn (范),
gathering grain to supply the army.
Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) attacked Zhāng Miǎo (張邈) and Lǚ Bù (呂布) at Púyáng (濮陽).
Lǚ Bù (呂布) was defeated and fled.
Cáo Hóng (曹洪) then occupied Dōng'ē (東阿),
and went on to attack more than ten counties, including Jìyīn (濟陰), Shānyáng (山陽), Zhōngmóu (中牟), Yángwǔ (陽武), Jīng (京), and Mì (密).
He captured them all.
For his accumulated merits, he was appointed Yīngyáng Xiàowèi (鷹揚校尉),
and promoted to Yángwǔ Zhōnglángjiàng (揚武中郎將).
When the Emperor established the capital at Xǔ (許),
Cáo Hóng (曹洪) was appointed Jiànyì Dàfū (諫議大夫).
He was separately dispatched to campaign against Liú Biǎo (劉表),
defeating Liú Biǎo's (劉表) detached generals at Wǔyáng (舞陽), Yīnyè (陰葉), Dǔyáng (堵陽), and Bówàng (博望).
For his merits,
he was promoted to Lìfēng Jiāngjūn (厲鋒將軍),
and enfeoffed as Guómíng Tínghóu (國明亭侯).
He successively followed in campaigns,
and was appointed Dūhù Jiāngjūn (都護將軍).
When Emperor Wén (文帝) ascended the throne,
he was made WèI Jiāngjūn (衞將軍),
then promoted to Piàojí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍),
advanced to the title of Yěwáng Hóu (野王侯),
with an additional thousand households,
bringing the total to two thousand one hundred households.
His rank was Đặcjìn (特進);
later he was transferred and enfeoffed as Dūyáng Hóu (都陽侯).
Initially,
Cáo Hóng (曹洪) was wealthy but stingy.
When Emperor Wén (文帝) was young, he had borrowed from him without success,
and always resented it.
Consequently, on the pretext of a guest in Cáo Hóng's (曹洪) household committing a crime,
he was imprisoned and sentenced to death.
All the officials pleaded for him, but none could succeed.
Empress Dowager Biàn (卞太后) said to Empress Guō (郭后):
"If Cáo Hóng (曹洪) dies today,
tomorrow I will command the Emperor to depose the Empress."
Thereupon, she tearfully pleaded repeatedly,
and Cáo Hóng (曹洪) was finally spared, though stripped of his office, rank, and land.
Cáo Hóng (曹洪) was a meritorious minister of the late emperor,
and many people at the time felt discontent over his treatment.
When Emperor Míng (明帝) ascended the throne,
Cáo Hóng (曹洪) was appointed Hòujiāngjūn (後將軍),
and re-enfeoffed as Lèchéng Hóu (樂城侯),
with a thousand households.
His rank was Đặcjìn (特進),
and he was again appointed Piàojí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍).
In the sixth year of Tàihé (太和) (232 CE), he passed away,
and was posthumously granted the谥 (shì) of Gōng Hóu (恭侯).
His son, Cáo Fù (曹馥),
succeeded as Marquis.
Initially,
Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) had divided households from Cáo Hóng's (曹洪) fief to enfeoff his son Cáo Zhèn (曹震) as a Liehóu (列侯).
Cáo Hóng's (曹洪) paternal cousin, Cáo Yú (曹瑜),
was careful, prudent, and respectful,
and held office up to WèI Jiāngjūn (衞將軍),
and was enfeoffed as a Liehóu (列侯).
Cáo Xiū
styled Wénliè, was a distant nephew of Tài-zǔ.
When the world was in chaos,
his clan scattered to their various home villages.
When Xiū was a little over ten years old,
his father died.
He alone, with a single guest, carried the coffin, feigned a burial,
and took his elderly mother,
crossing the Jiāng to Wú.
Because Tài-zǔ had raised an army for righteousness,
he changed his name, moved to Jīngzhōu,
and secretly traveled north to return
and meet Tài-zǔ.
Tài-zǔ said to his attendants:
“This is the thousand-li colt of my family.”
He had him reside with Wén-dì,
and treated him as a son.
He often accompanied him on campaigns
and was made to lead the Hǔbào Cavalry as a palace guard.
When Liú Bèi sent his general Wú Lán to garrison Xiàbiàn,
Tài-zǔ sent Cáo Hóng to attack him,
appointing Xiū as Cavalry Commandant,
to participate in Hóng's military affairs.
Tài-zǔ said to Xiū:
“Although you are a staff officer,
you are in fact the commander.”
Hóng, hearing this order,
also entrusted matters to Xiū.
Bèi sent Zhāng Fēi to garrison Gùshān,
intending to cut off the army's rear.
The multitude debated, full of doubt.
Xiū said:
“If the bandit truly intends to cut off the road,
he should ambush and move secretly.
Now he first makes a show of strength;
this means he cannot do it.
We should, while his forces are not yet gathered,
swiftly attack Lán.
If Lán is defeated, Fēi will naturally flee.”
Hóng followed this advice,
advanced his troops to attack Lán,
and thoroughly defeated him.
Fēi indeed fled.
When Tài-zǔ recaptured Hànzhōng,
the various armies returned to Cháng’ān,
and Xiū was appointed Central Leader of the Army.
When Wén-dì ascended the throne,
he was made General Leader of the Army.
Recording his past and present achievements,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngyáng Tíng.
When Xiàhóu Dūn died,
Xiū was made General Who Guards the South,
granted an imperial staff, and made Supervisor of All Military Affairs.
The emperor's carriage personally saw him off;
the emperor even dismounted from his carriage and clasped his hand in farewell.
Sūn Quán sent a general to garrison Lìyáng.
When Xiū arrived,
he attacked and defeated him.
He also separately dispatched troops to cross the Jiāng
and burn several thousand homes in the bandit's Wúhú camp.
He was promoted to General Who Conquers the East,
governor of Yángzhōu,
and advanced in enfeoffment to Marquis of Ānyáng Xiāng.
When the emperor attacked Sūn Quán,
Xiū was made Grand General Who Conquers the East,
granted a yellow battle-axe,
and given command of Zhāng Liáo and others, as well as over twenty armies from various prefectures and commanderies.
He attacked Quán's grand general Lǚ Fàn and others at Dòngpǔ
and defeated them.
He was appointed Minister of Yángzhōu.
When Míng-dì ascended the throne,
he was advanced in enfeoffment to Marquis of Chángpíng.
When the Wú general Shěn Dé garrisoned Wǎn,
Xiū attacked and defeated him,
beheading Dé.
Wú generals Hán Zōng, Zhái Dān, and others, one after another, led their troops to surrender to Xiū.
His enfeoffment was increased by four hundred households,
making a total of two thousand five hundred households.
He was promoted to Grand Marshal,
continuing to supervise Yángzhōu as before.
In the second year of Tàihé,
the emperor attacked Wú from two directions.
He sent Sīmǎ Xuān-wáng down the Hànshǔi,
while [Xiū] supervised the various armies heading towards Xúnyáng.
The bandit general feigned surrender,
and Xiū advanced deeply.
The battle went unfavorably,
and he retreated to encamp at Shítíng.
The army was alarmed by night;
the soldiers were in disarray,
abandoning much armor, weapons, and baggage.
Xiū submitted a memorial apologizing for his offense.
The emperor sent Cavalry Commandant Yáng Jì to comfort and appease him,
and his gifts and honors were even more generous.
Xiū subsequently developed a carbuncle on his back and died.
His posthumous title was Zhuàng-hóu.
His son Zhào succeeded him.
Zhào possessed talent and bearing appropriate for his generation,
serving as Palace Attendant and Cavalry Commandant.
When Míng-dì was seriously ill,
he was discussing with Yān-wáng Yǔ and others about matters concerning his successor.
The emperor's intention soon changed,
and he ordered Zhào to return to his residence as a marquis.
He died during the Zhèngshǐ period.
He was posthumously granted the title of General of the Guards.
His son Xìng succeeded him.
Initially,
Wén-dì divided three hundred households from Xiū's fief to enfeoff Zhào's younger brother Zuǎn as a 列侯 (lièhóu).
Later, he became General Who Destroys Wú.
When he died,
he was posthumously granted the title of General of the Vanguard.
Cáo Zhēn
styled Zǐdān, was a distant nephew of Tài-zǔ.
When Tài-zǔ raised his army,
Zhēn's father Shào recruited followers,
but was killed by the provincial and commandery authorities.
Tài-zǔ pitied Zhēn for being an orphan at a young age,
took him in and raised him along with his own sons,
and had him reside with Wén-dì.
Once, while hunting,
he was pursued by a tiger.
He turned and shot the tiger,
and it fell at the sound of the shot.
Tài-zǔ was impressed by his fierce courage
and made him lead the Hǔbào Cavalry.
He attacked the bandits of Língqiū
and defeated them,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Língshòu Tíng.
As a Major-General, he led troops to attack Liú Bèi's detached general at Xiàbiàn,
defeated him,
and was appointed General of the Central Guard.
He followed to Cháng’ān
and was appointed Central Leader of the Army.
At this time,
Xiàhóu Yuān had died at Yángpíng,
and Tài-zǔ was worried.
He appointed Zhēn as Protector-General Who Conquers Shǔ,
and had him supervise Xú Huǎng and others in defeating Liú Bèi's detached general Gāo Xiáng at Yángpíng.
Tài-zǔ personally went to Hànzhōng
to withdraw the various armies,
and sent Zhēn to Wǔdū to welcome Cáo Hóng and others back to garrison Chéncāng.
When Wén-dì ascended the throne,
Zhēn was made General Who Guards the West,
granted an imperial staff, and made Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Yōng and Liáng prefectures.
Recording his past and present achievements,
he was advanced in enfeoffment to Marquis of Dōngxiāng.
When Zhāng Jìn and others rebelled in Jiǔquán,
Zhēn sent Fèi Yáo to attack and defeat them,
beheading Jìn and others.
In the third year of Huángchū, he returned to the capital.
Zhēn was made Grand General of the Upper Army,
Supervisor of All Military Affairs inside and outside the court,
and granted an imperial staff and battle-axe.
With Xiàhóu Shàng and others, he campaigned against Sūn Quán,
attacked the garrison at Niúzhǔ,
and defeated it.
He was then appointed Grand General of the Central Army,
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant.
In the seventh year,
Wén-dì was seriously ill.
Zhēn, along with Chén Qún, Sīmǎ Xuān-wáng, and others, received the imperial edict to assist in governing.
When Míng-dì ascended the throne,
he was advanced in enfeoffment to Marquis of Shàolíng,
and promoted to Grand General.
Zhūgě Liàng besieged Qíshān.
The three commanderies of Nán'ān, Tiānshuǐ, and Āndìng responded to Liàng.
The Emperor dispatched Zhēn to oversee the various armies garrisoned at Méi.
He dispatched Zhāng Hé to attack Liàng's general, Mǎ Sù,
and thoroughly defeated him.
The people of Āndìng, led by Yáng Tiáo and others, took their officials and people and held Yuèzhīchéng.
Zhēn advanced his army and besieged them.
Tiáo said to his followers,
"Since the Grand General himself has come,
I wish to surrender early."
He then bound himself and came out.
All three commanderies were pacified.
Zhēn, believing that Liàng had been chastened at Qíshān,
and that his next sally would definitely be from Chéncāng,
ordered Generals Hǎo Zhāo and Wáng Shēng to guard Chéncāng
and fortify its walls.
The next spring,
Liàng indeed besieged Chéncāng,
but with preparations made, he could not overcome it.
His enfeoffment was increased,
making it 2,900 households in total.
In the fourth year,
he had an audience in Luòyáng,
was promoted to Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ),
and was granted the privilege of wearing a sword and shoes into the palace hall
and not needing to hurry when entering court.
Zhēn said,
"Shǔ has repeatedly invaded our borders,
it is fitting to attack them now.
With several routes entering simultaneously,
a great victory can be achieved."
The Emperor agreed to his plan.
When Zhēn was about to depart for the western expedition,
the Emperor personally came to see him off.
Zhēn departed from Cháng'ān in the eighth month,
entering southward via the Zǐwǔ Route.
Sīmǎ Xuánwáng sailed up the Hànshǔi River,
planning to meet at Nánzhèng.
The various armies either followed the Xié Gǔ Route
or entered via Wǔwēi.
At that time, there was heavy continuous rain for over thirty days,
and in some places the plank roads were cut off.
An imperial edict ordered Zhēn to return his army.
When young, Zhēn, along with his kinsman Cáo Zūn and fellow townsman Zhū Zàn, served Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
Zūn and Zàn died early,
and Zhēn pitied them.
He requested to divide a portion of his enfeoffment to grant to Zūn and Zàn's sons.
The imperial edict stated:
"The Grand Marshal has the benevolence of Shú Xiàng in caring for orphans,
and he deeply values the enduring friendship of Yàn Píng.
A gentleman helps others achieve their good.
We permit Zhēn to divide his fief to grant Zūn and Zàn's sons the title of Guānnèi Hóu,
each with one hundred households."
Whenever Zhēn embarked on campaigns,
he shared hardships with his officers and soldiers.
If military rewards were insufficient,
he would always distribute his family wealth.
Soldiers and commoners alike were willing to serve him.
When Zhēn fell ill and returned to Luòyáng,
the Emperor personally visited his residence to inquire about his illness.
After Zhēn passed away,
he was posthumously granted the title Yuánhóu.
His son, Cáo Shuǎng, succeeded him.
The Emperor, reflecting on Zhēn's merits,
issued an edict saying:
"The Grand Marshal upheld loyalty and integrity,
assisting two generations of emperors.
Internally, he did not rely on the favor of his relatives;
externally, he did not act arrogantly towards scholars of humble background.
He can be said to have been capable of maintaining his prosperity and position,
and to have embodied diligence and humility in his virtue.
Let all five of Zhēn's sons – Xī, Xùn, Zé, Yàn, and Ái – all be enfeoffed as Marquises (Liè Hóu)."
Initially,
Emperor Wén had divided two hundred households from Zhēn's fief
and enfeoffed Zhēn's younger brother, Cáo Bīn, as a Marquis (Liè Hóu).
Cáo Shuǎng, courtesy name Zhāobó,
was, in his youth, considered cautious and steady as a member of the imperial clan.
When Emperor Míng was in the Eastern Palace,
he was very fond of him.
Upon his accession,
he was made a Palace Attendant (Sànqí Shìláng),
and progressively promoted to Colonel of the City Gate (Chéngmén Xiàowèi),
with the additional title of Palace Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì),
and then transferred to General of the Martial Guard (Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn).
He received extraordinary favor and treatment.
When the Emperor was gravely ill,
he summoned Shuǎng into his bedchamber,
appointed him Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn),
granted him the imperial insignia (jiéyuè),
made him Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn Shì),
and oversaw the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
He, along with Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Sīmǎ Xuánwáng, received the imperial edict to assist the young emperor.
After Emperor Míng's death,
King Qí ascended the throne.
Shuǎng was given the additional title of Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng),
his title was changed to Marquis of Wǔ'ān,
with an enfeoffment of twelve thousand households,
and he was granted the privilege of wearing a sword and shoes into the palace hall,
not needing to hurry when entering court,
and not being called by his name when announced.
Dīng Mì devised a plan
to have Shuǎng inform the Son of Heaven
and issue an edict to transfer Xuánwáng to Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
Outwardly, this was to honor him with a grand title,
but inwardly, it was to ensure that memorials submitted to the Imperial Secretariat
would first pass through him,
allowing him to control their importance.
Shuǎng's younger brother Xī was Central Army Commander (Zhōng Lǐngjūn),
Xùn was General of the Martial Guard (Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn),
Yàn was Palace Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Lecturer (Shìjiǎng).
All his other younger brothers
served as Marquises (Liè Hóu) and accompanied him.
They entered and exited the forbidden palace freely.
Their power and favor were unsurpassed.
Hé Yàn of Nányáng, Dèng Yáng, Lǐ Shèng, Dīng Mì of Pèiguó, and Bì Guǐ of Dōngpíng all had reputations
and sought advancement at the time.
Emperor Míng, considering them frivolous and ostentatious,
had all suppressed and dismissed them.
However, when Shuǎng took power,
he reinstated and promoted them,
entrusting them as his close confidants.
Yáng and others wished Shuǎng to establish his prestige throughout the empire,
and urged him to attack Shǔ.
Shuǎng followed their advice,
and Xuánwáng's attempts to stop him were ineffective.
In the fifth year of Zhèngshǐ,
Shuǎng went west to Cháng'ān,
raising a large army of sixty to seventy thousand men,
and entered via Luògǔ.
At this time,
the supply transport in Guānzhōng and by the Dī and Qiāng peoples could not meet the demand.
Many cattle, horses, mules, and donkeys died,
and the people and barbarians wailed along the roads.
After entering the valley and traveling several hundred *lǐ*,
the bandits fortified themselves in the mountains,
and the army could not advance.
Shuǎng's military advisor Yáng Wěi explained the situation to Shuǎng,
stating that they should return immediately,
otherwise they would be defeated.
Yáng and Wěi argued in front of Shuǎng.
Wěi said,
"Yáng and Shèng are going to ruin the affairs of the state;
they should be executed."
Shuǎng was displeased,
and then withdrew his army.
Initially,
Sshǎng, considering Xuān Wáng's advanced age and high virtue,
always served him,
not daring to act independently.
But when Yàn and others were promoted and employed,
they all championed and supported him,
persuading Sshǎng that with such heavy authority, it was inappropriate to delegate it to others.
So he appointed Yàn, Yáng, and Mì as Shàngshū.
Yàn managed appointments,
Guǐ was Sīlì Xiàowèi,
Shèng was Hénán Yǐn,
and few matters subsequently went through Xuān Wáng.
Xuān Wáng then feigned illness to avoid Sshǎng.
Yàn and others monopolized power,
jointly dividing hundreds of qǐng of mulberry fields from the Diǎnnóng departments of Luòyáng and Yěwáng,
and destroying imperial bathing lands to make them their own property.
They used their influence to secretly seize government goods,
and through connections, sought control over zhōu and jùn.
Officials, seeing their formidable power,
dared not oppose their will.
Yàn and others had long-standing grievances with the Tíngwèi Lú Yù.
Taking advantage of a minor transgression by Yù's subordinate,
they framed Yù severely under the law,
ordering the relevant official to first confiscate Yù's seal and sash,
and only then report it.
Such was their display of power.
Sshǎng's food, drink, carriages, and clothing
mimicked those of the emperor;
rare treasures from the Shàngfāng department
filled his home;
his wives and concubines overflowed the inner courtyard.
He also secretly took seven or eight of the previous emperor's talented women,
as well as thirty-three imperial officials, artisans, musicians, and daughters of respectable families,
all as entertainers.
He forged an imperial edict
to send fifty-seven talented women to Yè Tái,
instructing the previous emperor's fú to train them as performers.
He arbitrarily took musical instruments from the Tàilè and
forbidden weapons from the Wǔkù.
He built a secret chamber
with richly adorned windows on all sides,
where he often met with Yàn and others,
drinking and making merry.
Xī considered this a great source of worry
and repeatedly admonished him to stop.
He also wrote three essays
expounding on how arrogance, extravagance, and excess lead to disaster and ruin.
The language and intent were very earnest,
but he dared not directly criticize Sshǎng,
instead using the pretext of cautioning his younger brothers to show them to Sshǎng.
Sshǎng knew they were directed at him,
and was very displeased.
Sometimes, when Xī's admonitions were not accepted,
he would weep and withdraw.
Xuān Wáng secretly made preparations for this.
In the winter of the ninth year,
Lǐ Shèng was appointed Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
He went to visit Xuān Wáng.
Xuān Wáng claimed to be gravely ill,
showing him his emaciated form.
Shèng could not detect the deception,
believing it to be true.
In the first month of the tenth year,
the imperial carriage went to pay respects at Gāopíng Líng,
and Sshǎng and his brothers all followed.
Xuān Wáng marshaled his troops,
first securing the Wǔkù,
then deploying to the pontoon bridge over the Luò Shuǐ.
He presented a memorial concerning Sshǎng, saying:
"When I returned from Liáodōng,
the late emperor commanded Your Majesty, Qín Wáng, and me to ascend the imperial bed,
and holding my arm,
expressed deep concern for the future of the state.
I said, 'The two ancestors also entrusted the future to me,
(and expressed concern for it) but this is what Your Majesty has personally witnessed;
there is nothing to worry about.
Should anything go awry,
I shall serve your enlightened edict with my life.'
Huángmén Lìng Dǒng Jī and others,
and the talented women who attended the emperor's illness,
all heard and knew this.
Now the Grand General Sshǎng has abandoned the entrusted mandate,
disrupting the national institutions.
Internally, he presumes imperial prerogatives;
externally, he monopolizes authority.
He has dismantled various camps
and seized all forbidden weapons.
Key official positions
are all filled with his confidants.
The palace guards,
old retainers from previous generations, have all been dismissed,
and he wishes to appoint new people to serve his private schemes.
His power base is entrenched and complex,
and his wanton behavior grows daily.
In addition to this,
he has appointed Huángmén Zhāng Dāng as Dūjiān,
who specializes in illicit dealings,
spying on the Emperor,
observing the imperial succession,
sowing discord between the two empresses,
and harming the imperial family.
The realm is in turmoil,
people are filled with fear and apprehension.
Your Majesty merely sits as a temporary occupant;
how can you long be secure?
This is not the original intention of the late emperor when he commanded Your Majesty and me to ascend the imperial bed.
Although I am old and infirm,
how dare I forget to speak frankly?
When Zhào Gāo indulged to the extreme,
the Qín dynasty was destroyed;
when Lǚ and Huò were promptly eliminated,
the Hàn dynasty lasted forever.
This is a great lesson for Your Majesty,
and the time for me to fulfill my mandate.
Tàiwèi chén Jì and Shàngshū Lìng chén Fú, etc.,
all believe that Sshǎng has a disloyal heart
and that his brothers should not command troops or guard the palace,
and they have presented this to the Yǒngníng Palace.
The Empress Dowager has commanded me to act as per the memorial.
I have immediately ordered the relevant officials and the Huángmén Lìng to dismiss Sshǎng, Xī, and Xùn's officers and soldiers,
so they may await return to their residences,
and not to delay the imperial carriage.
Anyone who dares to cause delay
will be dealt with according to military law.
I have exerted myself despite my illness
to lead troops to garrison the Luò Shuǐ pontoon bridge,
to observe any extraordinary developments."
When Sshǎng received Xuān Wáng's memorial,
he did not comprehend it
and was so distressed he knew not what to do.
Dàsīnóng Pèiguó Huán Fàn, hearing of the military action,
did not answer the Empress Dowager's summons.
He forged an imperial edict to open the Píngchāng Gate,
seized swords and halberds,
gathered the gate guards,
and rushed south to Sshǎng.
Xuān Wáng knew this
and said:
"Fàn devises strategies,
but Sshǎng will surely be unable to use Fàn's plan."
Fàn persuaded Sshǎng to take the imperial carriage to Xǔchāng
and summon outside forces.
Sshǎng and his brothers hesitated, undecided.
Fàn earnestly told Xī:
"On this day,
can your household ever again seek poverty and low status?
Moreover, if an ordinary man holds one hostage,
he can still hope to live.
Now you are with the Son of Heaven;
if you issue a command to the world,
who would dare not respond?"
Yet Xī could not accept it.
Shìzhōng Xǔ Yǔn and Shàngshū Chén Tài persuaded Sshǎng
to quickly surrender and admit guilt.
Sshǎng then sent Yǔn and Tài to Xuān Wáng,
admitting guilt and asking for death.
Only then was Xuān Wáng's memorial allowed to pass.
Consequently, Sshǎng and his brothers were spared,
returning to their residences as marquises.
Earlier,
Zhāng Dāng had privately given Sshǎng the talented women he had selected, such as Zhāng and Hé.
Suspecting illicit relations,
Zhāng Dāng was arrested and punished.
Dāng revealed Sshǎng's and Yàn's secret conspiracy for rebellion,
stating they had been practicing military drills
and intended to act in the third month.
Thereupon, Yàn and others were arrested and imprisoned.
The assembled gōngqīng and court officials deliberated,
concluding that
"According to the principle of the Chūnqiū,
'When the lord's kin harbors no rebellion, then he is punished if he does rebel.'
Sshǎng, as a collateral relative,
had always received extraordinary favor,
personally receiving the late emperor's clasped-hand final edict,
entrusting him with the realm.
Yet he harbored evil intentions
and disregarded the entrusted mandate.
Instead, he conspired with Yàn, Yáng, and Dāng to plot against the imperial throne.
Fàn, as an accomplice,
shares the same guilt.
All are guilty of great treason and unrighteousness."
Thereupon, Sshǎng, Xī, Xùn, Yàn, Yáng, Mì, Guǐ, Shèng, Fàn, Dāng, and others
were all executed
and their three clans exterminated.
During the Jiāpíng era,
to continue the merits of meritorious subjects,
Zhēn's great-grandson Xī was enfeoffed as Xīnchāng Tínghóu,
with three hundred households,
to continue Zhēn's lineage.
Yàn
was the grandson of Hé Jìn.
His mother, Lady Yǐn,
was a fūren of Tàizǔ.
Yàn grew up in the palace,
and moreover married a princess.
He was famous in his youth for his talent and brilliance,
fond of Lǎo-Zhuāng teachings,
and wrote dozens of essays, rhapsodies, and treatises, including the Dàodélùn.
Xiàhóu Shàng, courtesy name Bórén,
was a nephew of Yuān.
Emperor Wén was close friends with him.
When Tài Zǔ pacified Jìzhōu,
Shàng served as a military commander (jūnsīmǎ),
leading cavalry to participate in campaigns.
Later he became Literary Aide to the General of the Five Bureaus (wǔguānjiāng wénxué).
When the state of Wèi was first established,
he was promoted to Imperial Household Secretary (huángmén shìláng).
When the Hú of Dàijùn rebelled,
Yānlíng Hóu Zhāng was sent to subdue them.
Shàng was appointed to assist Zhāng in military matters.
After pacifying Dàidì,
he returned.
When Tài Zǔ died in Luòyáng,
Shàng, bearing a staff of authority (chíjié),
escorted the coffin back to Yè.
His previous achievements were recorded,
and he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Pínglíng Tíng,
appointed Regular Cavalier Attendant (sǎnqí chángshì),
and promoted to Central Army Commander (zhōnglǐngjūn).
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Pínglíng Xiāng,
promoted to General Who Conquers the South (zhēngnán jiāngjūn),
given command of Jīngzhōu as its Inspector (cìshǐ),
and granted an imperial staff of authority (jiǎjié) to supervise all military affairs in the south.
Shàng reported:
“Liú Bèi’s detached army is at Shàngyōng.
The mountain roads are treacherous and difficult.
They do not anticipate us.
If we send a surprise force to advance secretly,
catching them off guard,
we will surely defeat them.”
He then led his forces to attack and defeat Shàngyōng,
pacifying three commanderies and nine counties,
and was promoted to Grand General Who Conquers the South (zhēngnán dàjiāngjūn).
Although Sūn Quán nominally submitted,
Shàng further strengthened his offensive preparations.
Quán indeed later harbored disloyal intentions.
In the third year of Huángchū (222 CE),
the imperial carriage traveled to Wǎn.
Shàng was ordered to lead his forces with Cáo Zhēn to jointly besiege Jiānglíng.
Quán’s general Zhūgě Jǐn’s army confronted Shàng’s army across the river.
Jǐn crossed to an islet in the river
and divided his navy in the middle of the river.
At night, Shàng took many oil-boats,
leading over ten thousand infantry and cavalry,
secretly crossed downstream,
attacked Jǐn’s forces,
and burned their boats along both banks of the river.
Attacking by both land and water,
he defeated them.
Before the city could be captured,
a great plague occurred,
and an imperial edict ordered Shàng to withdraw all his forces.
His fief was increased by six hundred households,
making a total of one thousand nine hundred households.
He was granted a ceremonial axe (jiǎyuè)
and advanced to the rank of Governor (mù).
Jīngzhōu was devastated and desolate,
bordering the Mányí to the west,
and with the Hàn River forming its border with Wú.
Many of its old inhabitants lived south of the river.
Shàng opened a road from Shàngyōng,
extending over seven hundred lí westward.
Many mountain people and Mányí submitted to him.
Within five or six years,
several thousand households surrendered and became adherents.
In the fifth year (224 CE),
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Chānglíng Xiāng.
Shàng had a beloved concubine who was greatly favored,
and her favor overshadowed that of his principal wife.
His principal wife
was a daughter of the Cáo clan.
Therefore, Emperor Wén sent someone to strangle her.
Shàng was grief-stricken,
fell ill, and became disoriented.
After burying the concubine,
he could not bear missing her,
and so he exhumed her to look at her again.
Emperor Wén heard of this and angrily said,
“Dù Xí’s belittlement of Shàng
was indeed justified.”
However, as an old minister,
his imperial favor did not wane.
In the sixth year (225 CE),
Shàng’s illness became critical,
and he returned to the capital.
The Emperor visited him repeatedly,
holding his hand and weeping.
When Shàng died,
he was posthumously titled Dào Hóu.
His son Xuán succeeded him.
Additionally, three hundred households from Shàng’s fief were
granted to Shàng’s younger brother Fèng to hold the title of Marquis within the Pass (guānnèi hóu).
Xuán, courtesy name Tàichū,
was famous in his youth.
At twenty, he became Regular Cavalier and Imperial Household Secretary (sǎnqí huángmén shìláng).
Once, when he was granted an audience,
he was seated next to Máo Zēng, the Empress’s younger brother.
Xuán was ashamed of this
and showed his displeasure on his face.
Emperor Míng resented him for this
and demoted him to Supervisor of the Feathered Forest (yǔlín jiān).
At the beginning of Zhèngshǐ (240 CE),
Cáo Shuǎng assisted in governing.
Xuán
was the son of Shuǎng’s paternal aunt.
He was successively promoted to Regular Cavalier Attendant (sǎnqí chángshì) and Central Protector of the Army (zhōnghùjūn).
The Grand Tutor Sīmǎ Xuānwáng asked about current affairs.
Xuán deliberated, saying:
"Now, appointing officials and employing talent,
is the handle of the state.
Therefore, the selection and evaluation of officials is exclusively the domain of the Táigé,
this being the duty of the superiors.
Filial piety resides in the villages and alleys,
and the assessment of excellence or inferiority is entrusted to the local people,
this being the duty of the inferiors.
If one wishes for pure governance and careful selection,
it lies in clarifying these distinctions,
and not allowing them to overlap.
Why is this?
If superiors exceed their duty,
then there is a fear that those they appoint will not be fundamental (to their duties),
and a path for leveraging influence and seeking rapid advancement will open.
If inferiors overstep theirs,
then there is a fear that 'heavenly ranks' (inherent virtues) will be externally exploited,
and many avenues for manipulation and power will emerge.
Now, if 'heavenly ranks' are externally exploited,
this means commoners wield the handle of deliberation (power to influence appointments).
If there are many avenues for manipulation and power,
this is the origin of disorder.
Since the Zhōngzhèng officials of the Zhōujùn came to assess and evaluate official talents,
many years have passed.
Yet, amidst the vast complexity and confusion,
we have not heard of order being established.
Is this not because the distinctions are confused and overlapping,
and each has lost its essential function?
If we were to let the Zhōngzhèng merely examine conduct and rank individuals,
and those whose conduct is equitable according to their rank,
could then be appointed to office.
Why is this?
Now, if filial piety is manifest within one's household,
how could one not be loyal and respectful in office?
If benevolence and magnanimity are praised by one's extended family,
how could one not be astute in governance?
If righteous judgment is practiced in one's community,
how could one not be competent in discharging responsibilities?
For these three types of qualities,
if assessed by the Zhōngzhèng,
even if they do not occupy specific official titles (yet),
their suitability for office can be known.
Conduct has degrees of significance,
and comparisons have levels of superiority and inferiority,
then the categories of appointments,
would also be clearly and distinctly separated.
Why must we make the Zhōngzhèng interfere with the mechanism of selection and evaluation from below,
and those who hold the reins of power rely on others from above,
leading to mutual encroachment between superiors and inferiors,
thereby creating confusion and disorder?
Moreover, the Táigé, overseeing those below,
assesses performance and verifies shortcomings.
Among the various officials,
each has their own supervisor.
They are examined day and night;
nothing is more thorough than this.
But opinions from the villages and alleys,
are arbitrarily decided by personal bias.
If this causes skilled administrators to lose their positions,
and the populace is alarmed and dismayed,
how can we expect customs to be pure and tranquil?
Is that even possible?
The Tiāntái is distantly removed (from the local populace),
and beyond the grasp of the common people's intentions.
Those who manage to reach it,
are instead those who are close at hand.
Who among them would not embellish themselves to achieve their desires?
If there is a path to achieve one's desires,
then those who cultivate their own households,
are already not as good as those who make themselves known in their local communities.
Those who make themselves known in their local communities,
are already not as good as those who seek recognition from the Zhōubāng.
If a path for advancement is indeed opened up,
and we worry about superficial embellishment departing from fundamental truth,
even if we sternly admonish the Zhōngzhèng,
and enforce with penalties,
it will still be of no benefit.
How would this compare to making each (level of official) adhere to its own duty,
with supervisors presenting their subordinates' abilities and shortcomings to the Táigé,
and the Táigé, based on the supervisors' ranking of abilities and shortcomings,
and incorporating the ranking of moral conduct from the local communities,
then propose their comparative ranks,
without allowing for bias?
The Zhōngzhèng would only examine their conduct,
distinguish their superiority and inferiority,
and carefully determine their categories,
without allowing them to be promoted or demoted (by the Zhōngzhèng themselves).
The Táigé would then synthesize all of this.
If, in their selection,
there should be any confusion or error,
then the responsibility for it would lie with the appropriate officials.
The rankings made by supervisors,
and the categories proposed by the Zhōngzhèng,
would then be used comparatively according to their respective ranks.
If they prove unsuitable,
the responsibility would lie externally (with the supervisors/Zhōngzhèng).
In this way, internal and external assessments would be mutually informed,
success and failure would have their respective places,
and they would mutually scrutinize each other.
Who then could deceive or embellish?
This would stabilize people's hearts and align matters with reason,
and thus could perhaps calm customs and carefully select official talent."
He further submitted:
"In ancient times, the establishment of offices
was to aid and nourish the multitude of living beings,
and to govern the people and affairs.
Therefore, rulers and chiefs were appointed to oversee them.
The head of this oversight,
should be singular and specialized.
Singularity ensures stable official duties and peace between superiors and inferiors.
Specialization ensures well-executed professions and uncomplicated affairs.
Now, if affairs are simplified and professions well-executed,
and superiors and inferiors are at peace with each other, yet things remain ungoverned,
such a situation has never existed.
The ancient kings established ten thousand states;
although the details cannot be fully investigated,
yet they divided territories and demarcated boundaries,
with each guarding its own land and borders.
This was not a system of multiple layers of entanglement and constraint.
Furthermore, examining the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties' five ranks,
there were only differences in size, status, and nobility,
and no cases where rulers appointed officials, and subjects served the people, yet there were two systems mutually constraining each other.
Now, if the official system is not unified,
then professions are not well-executed.
If professions are not well-executed,
how can affairs be simplified?
If affairs are not simplified,
how can the people be tranquil?
If the people are not tranquil,
then wickedness and evil will simultaneously arise,
and deceit and trickery will proliferate.
The ancient kings understood this,
and therefore specialized their official duties and unified their governance.
Beginning with the Qín era,
they did not emulate the Way of the sages.
They used private means to control official duties,
and deceit to treat those below.
Fearing that administrators would not perform well,
they established supervisors to oversee them.
Fearing that these supervisors might be lenient or biased,
they established inspectors to correct them.
Administrators and supervisors mutually constrained each other,
and supervisors and inspectors mutually monitored each other.
People harbored ulterior motives,
and superiors and inferiors pursued different objectives.
The Hàn Dynasty inherited this legacy,
and was unable to rectify it.
With the rise of the Wèi house,
time was insufficient to address it daily.
Although the institutions of the five ranks are difficult to fully restore at once,
rough standards can be established to unify the system of governance.
Today's chief officials,
all govern officials and people.
They are additionally burdened by Jùnshǒu,
and further encumbered by Cìshǐ.
If what the commanderies oversee,
is only a broad overview,
then it is the same as what the provinces do;
there is no need for this duplication.
It is advisable to abolish the Jùnshǒu,
and only appoint Cìshǐ.
If the Cìshǐ's duties remain, supervision will not be neglected.
The tens of thousands of commandery officials,
could return to their agricultural pursuits,
thereby reducing administrative burden and expenditure,
enriching wealth and growing grain;
this is the first point.
Talented individuals from large counties,
are all capable of serving as Jùnshǒu.
Disputes of right and wrong,
always give rise to different opinions.
If one complies, there is peace;
if one adheres to one's own view, there is contention.
Now, the beauty of a seasoned broth,
lies in combining different flavors.
The benefit of superiors and inferiors,
lies in their ability to assist each other.
To have peace only through compliance,
is like a zither and lute producing a single note.
If we sweep away and eliminate this,
then offices will be fewer and affairs simpler;
this is the second point.
Moreover, officials who interfere with commanderies,
whose duty is to supervise various counties,
often protect their factions and relatives,
and old acquaintances from their hometowns.
If any are not up to par,
and are hindered due to public duty,
the people's distress and hardship,
arise from this.
If all these functions are combined,
then the root of disorder will naturally be blocked;
this is the third point.
Now, inheriting a state of decline and hardship,
the people are emaciated and withered.
Capable talents are few,
and those capable of undertaking responsibilities are scarce.
Good officials in commanderies and counties,
often not just one.
When a [jùn] receives a [xiàn] and it is established,
its most crucial [post] is at the bottom.
However, the most highly selected officials
must first be sufficient in the [jùn].
These are the officials who are close to the people,
exclusively controlling the grassroots.
Officials are the lifeblood of the people,
yet they are often obstinate and vulgar.
Now, if we consolidate them,
more officials will be selected from the pure and good to staff positions,
the great transformation will spread,
and the people and all things will attain peace.
This is the fourth point.
The system should be established such that a [xiàn] of ten thousand households
is named a [jùnshǒu],
one with five thousand or more [households]
is named a [dūwèi],
and those with fewer than one thousand households,
the [lìng] and [zhǎng] remain as before.
From [zhǎng] and above,
evaluations and promotions will be based on performance,
and they will be promoted according to their ability.
The territory they govern will also increase.
This is a way to advance talent and display merit.
If a regular system is fixed,
then official talent will have a hierarchy,
and administrative achievements will be clear and brilliant.
This is the fifth point.
If the [jùnshǒu] are abolished,
all [xiàn] will directly report,
affairs will not be obstructed,
and officials will not be delayed.
The style of the Three Dynasties,
though not necessarily attainable,
a simple and unified transformation
might possibly be achieved.
Benefiting the people and saving expenses
lies in this. "
He also believed:
"The alternation of refinement and simplicity
is like the successive emergence of the four seasons.
A sagely ruler embodies the Way of Heaven and governs all things,
and must address abuses to achieve smooth functioning.
When the times are excessively simple, adorn them with rituals;
when the times are excessively extravagant, remedy them with simplicity.
Now, succeeding the end of a hundred kings,
with the lingering influences of [Qín] and [Hàn],
the customs are overly elaborate.
It is appropriate to greatly reform them to meet the people's expectations.
Currently, the regulations stipulate that from dukes and marquises downwards,
and officials with ranks from [dàjiāngjūn] upwards,
all may wear brocade, damask, gauze, fine silk, and ornaments of gold and silver filigree.
From these downwards,
garments of mixed colors
are common even among the common people.
Although there are distinctions in rank between superiors and inferiors,
each showing a difference,
yet the regulations for court officials
are already comparable to the [zhìzūn] (emperor),
and the colors black and yellow
are already common among the lower ranks.
To desire that markets do not sell ostentatious colors,
merchants do not trade in rare goods,
and artisans do not create carved objects,
is impossible.
Therefore, it is appropriate to greatly address the root cause,
to measure against ancient laws,
and regarding the appropriateness of refinement and simplicity,
to take the middle standard
as the basis for ritual norms.
Carriages, attire, and insignia
should all adhere to simplicity,
prohibiting and eliminating the extravagant practices of later customs.
This would ensure that families of officials at court
and households with status
no longer have brocade decorations,
no mixed-color garments,
and no delicate and elaborate objects.
From the top down,
the distinctions in simplicity
would merely indicate levels,
not allowing for more than one or two distinctions.
As for rewards for merit and virtue,
and special favors bestowed by imperial grace,
all should be reported to the appropriate authorities
before they are worn or used.
The transformation of the lower ranks by the upper ranks
is like wind bending grass.
If the teaching of simplicity arises from the imperial court,
then the desire for extravagance will naturally disappear among the lower ranks."
[Xuān Wáng] replied in a letter:
"Examining officials and selecting personnel,
abolishing redundant offices,
and reforming dress codes
are all excellent.
As for honoring local communities for their conduct
and the court evaluating affairs,
the general thrust is as you indicated.
However, there has been an inherited custom for a long time,
and it is ultimately difficult to change.
During the [Qín] dynasty, there were no [cìshǐ],
only [jùnshǒu] and chief officials.
Although the [Hàn] imperial house had [cìshǐ],
they merely upheld the six articles [of impeachment].
Therefore, a [cìshǐ] was called a [chuánchē] (inspector with a traveling carriage),
and their subordinates were called [cóngshì] (attendants).
They had no fixed administrative seat,
and their officials did not become permanent subjects.
Later, they gradually changed to become regular government offices.
In the past, [Jiǎ Yì] also worried about dress codes.
Even though [Hàn Wén] himself wore dark coarse silk,
he still could not make everyone, high and low, satisfied.
I fear that these three matters
will have to await virtuous and capable individuals before they can be resolved."
[Xuán] then wrote again:
"Although [Hàn Wén] himself wore dark coarse silk,
he did not reform the laws and regulations.
Internally and externally, there were garments that overstepped boundaries,
and favored ministers received unlimited gifts.
From this perspective,
it seems he merely sought personal renown,
not truly intending to bring order to governance.
Now, if dukes and marquises are appointed to govern the world,
following the path of antiquity,
they will usher in a period of great governance,
suppressing the superfluous and correcting the fundamental.
If regulations are established by the superior,
then transformation will spread among the multitude.
When it is appropriate to make changes,
to harbor a diligent heart,
so that on the day they are issued,
the response from below is like an echo following a sound—
to still show excessive humility,
saying 'await virtuous and capable individuals,'
this is like [Yī] and [Zhōu] not correcting the established practices of [Yīn] and [Jī].
I humbly do not understand."
A little later,
he became General Who Conquers the West,
granted a Staff of Authority to supervise all military affairs in Yōng and Liáng Provinces.
He and Cái Sáng together launched the campaign of Luògǔ,
which people at the time ridiculed.
When Cái Sáng was executed,
Xuán was summoned to be Grand Herald.
Several years later, he was transferred to Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Xuán felt repressed by Cái Sáng
and was inwardly discontent.
Lǐ Fēng, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, although long favored and treated closely by Grand General Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng,
privately held affection for Xuán.
He then allied with Zhāng Jī, Grand Master of Brightness, father of the empress,
planning to assist Xuán in governing.
Fēng already wielded power internally,
his daughter was married to a prince,
and he and Jī were both from Fèngyì.
Therefore, Jī trusted him.
Fēng secretly ordered his younger brother, Yǎnzhōu Provincial Governor Yì, to request an audience at court,
intending for him to bring troops,
and combine forces to start an uprising.
When Yì requested an audience,
it was not granted.
In the second month of the sixth year of Jiāpíng,
when the nobles were to be formally honored,
Fēng and others intended to use the emperor's presence at the imperial pavilion,
where troops would be stationed at all gates,
to execute the Grand General
and replace him with Xuán,
making Jī General of Agile Cavalry.
Fēng secretly told Sū Shuò, the Supervisor of Yellow Gates; Yuèn Dūn, the Prefect of Yǒngníng Palace Office; Liú Xián, the Household Commander of Attendant Retainers, and others:
“You gentlemen, residing within the palace,
have committed many unlawful acts.
The Grand General is stern and upright,
and has spoken of this repeatedly.
Zhāng Dāng can serve as a warning.”
Shuò and the others all promised to obey.
The Grand General vaguely heard of their plot
and invited Fēng to meet him.
Fēng, unaware, went,
and was immediately killed.
The matter was reported to the authorities,
who arrested Xuán, Jī, Shuò, Dūn, Xián, and others and sent them to the Court of Judicial Review.
Zhōng Yù, the Grand Judge, reported:
“Fēng and others plotted to coerce the Supreme One,
and wished to execute the Chief Minister.
This is a great rebellion and utterly lawless.
I request they be judged according to the law.”
Thereupon, the high officials, court ministers, and the Court of Judicial Review convened to deliberate,
and all agreed that
“Fēng and others each received extraordinary favor,
and managed vital secrets.
Jī enjoyed the honor of an imperial relative and the empress’s family,
Xuán was a descendant of a family that served the court for generations,
and all held high positions.
Yet they harbored malicious intentions
and conspired for heinous rebellion,
colluding with eunuchs
and giving them treacherous plans.
Fearing heavenly might,
they dared not plot openly,
but intended to coerce the sovereign and intimidate the emperor,
to indulge their deceitful cruelty.
They plotted to execute a virtuous assistant
and wished to set up another.
This would overturn the imperial capital
and endanger the state.
What Yù has reported aligns with the codes and statutes.
Let Yù be informed to proceed.”
An imperial edict stated:
“Qí Princess Regent,
the late emperor’s beloved,
let her three sons be spared death.”
Thereupon, Fēng, Xuán, Jī, Dūn, Xián, and others all had their three clans exterminated.
Their remaining relatives were exiled to Lèlàng Commandery.
Xuán had a broad and generous mind.
When he was brought to the Eastern Market for execution,
his expression did not change,
and his demeanor was composed,
at forty-six years old.
During the Zhèngyuán era,
to continue the lineage of meritorious officials,
Shàng’s collateral great-grandson Běn was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chānglíng Pavilion,
with three hundred households,
to maintain Shàng’s posterity.
Previously,
Xǔ Yǔn of Gāoyáng, Central Army Commander, was close friends with Fēng and Xuán.
Before this, someone had fraudulently forged an imperial edict a foot and an inch long,
appointing Xuán as Grand General
and Yǔn as Grand Commandant,
both to jointly oversee the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
Someone, before dawn, rode a horse and handed the imperial tablet to Yǔn’s gate guard,
saying,
“There is an edict,”
and then galloped away.
Yǔn immediately threw the document into a fire and burned it,
without presenting it to Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng.
Later, when Fēng and others’ plot was discovered,
Yǔn was transferred to General Who Guards the North,
granted a Staff of Authority to supervise all military affairs north of the Yellow River.
Before he could depart,
he was accused of squandering official property,
arrested and handed over to the Court of Judicial Review,
exiled to Lèlàng,
and died on the way.
