Qīnghé Wáng Jīng was also known as a famous scholar from Jìzhōu along with Yǔn.
During the Gānlù era, he served as Imperial Secretary,
and was executed for involvement in the matter of Gāoguì Xiānggōng.
When Jīng first became a commandery governor,
Jīng’s mother told Jīng:
“You are a son of a farming family,
now you have reached an official position of two thousand *shí*.
Such excess is inauspicious.
You should stop now.”
Jīng could not follow her advice,
served as provincial governor in two provinces, and as Colonel Director of Retainers,
eventually leading to his downfall.
Yǔn’s friend, Cuī Zàn of the same commandery,
also once warned Yǔn about being too prominent in life.
Commentary says: The Xiàhóu and Cái clans
were united by marriage for generations.
Thus, Dūn, Yuān, Rén, Hóng, Xiū, Shàng, Zhēn, and others were all highly esteemed at the time due to their kinship and close ties.
They contributed greatly to the establishment and achievements of the state,
and all rendered effective service.
Cái Sáng, however, had meager virtue but held a high position,
and was drowned in extravagance and excess.
This is indeed what is described in the *Great Changes*
and what Daoists caution against.
Xuán was renowned in his generation
for his discerning standards and broad-mindedness.
However, he was deeply entangled with Cái Sáng, both publicly and privately.
His position and honor were such,
yet he was never heard to rectify Cái Sáng’s wrongs
or recommend virtuous talents.
Judging by this,
how could he be spared?
Biography of Xún Yù, Xún Yōu, Jiǎ Xǔ, Chapter Ten
Xún Yù, courtesy name Wénruò,
was from Yǐngyīn, Yǐngchuān.
His grandfather, Shú,
courtesy name Jìhé,
was Prefect of Lánglíng.
During the reigns of Emperors Shùn and Huán of Hàn,
he was well-known in his time.
He had eight sons,
who were called the Eight Dragons.
Yù’s father, Gǔn,
was Chancellor of Jìnán.
His uncle, Shuǎng,
was Minister of Works.
Xún Yù, when he was young,
Hé Yóng of Nányáng found him extraordinary
and said:
"He is a talent fit for a king's advisor."
In the first year of Yǒnghàn,
he was nominated as Xiàolián
and appointed as Shǒugōnglìng.
During Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion,
he sought to be assigned to an external post.
He was made Kàngfǔlìng,
but he then abandoned his office and returned home,
telling the elders:
"Yǐngchuān
is a land of four battles.
Whenever there is upheaval in the realm,
it is always a target for military conflict.
It would be best to leave it quickly;
do not stay long."
Many of the villagers, attached to their homeland, hesitated.
At that time, Hán Fù of the same commandery, the Shepherd of Jìzhōu, sent cavalry to welcome and establish them,
but none followed.
Only Xún Yù led his clan to Jìzhōu.
However, Yuán Shào had already seized Fù's position
and treated Yù with the rites due to an honored guest.
Yù's younger brother Xún Chén, and Xīn Píng and Guō Tú from the same commandery,
were all employed by Shào.
Yù judged that Shào would ultimately be unable to accomplish great things.
At that time, Tàizǔ was Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn,
stationed in Dōngjùn.
In the second year of Chūpíng,
Yù left Shào and joined Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased and said:
"You are my Zǐfáng!"
He made him Sīmǎ,
at which time he was twenty-nine years old.
At this time,
Dǒng Zhuó's power overshadowed the realm.
Tàizǔ asked Yù about him.
Yù said:
"Zhuó's tyranny is extreme;
he will surely end in chaos
and be unable to achieve anything."
Zhuó sent Lǐ Quē and others out of the pass to Guāndōng.
They plundered and ravaged everywhere they went,
reaching Yǐngchuān and Chénliú before returning.
Many of the villagers who remained were killed or captured.
The following year,
Tàizǔ assumed the post of Yǎnxzhōu Mù.
Later, he became Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn,
and Yù always accompanied him as Sīmǎ.
In the first year of Xīngpíng,
Tàizǔ campaigned against Táo Qiān
and appointed Yù to oversee affairs in his absence.
Coincidentally, Zhāng Miǎo and Chén Gōng rebelled in Yǎnxzhōu
and secretly welcomed Lǚ Bù.
When Bù arrived,
Miǎo sent Liú Yì to inform Yù, saying:
"General Lǚ has come to assist Lord Cáo in attacking Táo Qiān.
His army's provisions should be supplied quickly."
The people were bewildered.
Yù knew that Miǎo was causing trouble,
so he immediately mustered troops and prepared defenses,
and quickly summoned Xiàhóu Dūn, the Administrator of Dōngjùn.
Meanwhile, all the cities in Yǎnxzhōu had responded to Bù.
At that time, Tàizǔ had taken all his forces to attack Qiān,
leaving few defending troops.
Moreover, many of the commanding generals and high officials were secretly conspiring with Miǎo and Gōng.
When Dūn arrived,
that night he executed dozens of conspirators,
and the populace was then settled.
Guō Gòng, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, led tens of thousands of troops to the city gates.
Some said he was in league with Lǚ Bù,
and the people were greatly afraid.
Gòng requested to see Yù.
Yù intended to go.
Dūn and others said:
"My lord,
you are the guardian of a province.
Going will certainly be dangerous;
you must not."
Yù said:
"Gòng and Miǎo and the others were not previously allied.
His arrival is sudden,
so his plans must not yet be settled.
While they are unsettled, persuade him.
Even if he does not join us,
we can make him remain neutral.
If we show suspicion first,
he will become angry and firm up his plans."
When Gòng saw that Yù had no fear,
he thought Juànchéng would not be easy to attack,
and so he withdrew his troops.
Yù also conspired with Chéng Yù
to persuade Fàn and Dōng'ā,
ultimately saving the three cities
to await Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ returned from Xúzhōu to attack Bù at Púyáng,
and Bù fled eastward.
In the summer of the second year,
Tàizǔ's army was at Chéngshì,
and there was a great famine;
people ate each other.
Táo Qiān died,
and Tàizǔ wished to immediately seize Xúzhōu
and then deal with Bù upon his return.
Yù said:
"In the past, Gāozǔ secured Guānzhōng
and Guāngwǔ held Hénèi.
Both established deep roots and a solid base to control the realm.
Advancing, they were sufficient to defeat enemies;
retreating, they were sufficient to hold their ground.
Thus, although they faced difficulties and defeats, they ultimately achieved great success.
General, you initially began your enterprise in Yǎnxzhōu,
pacifying the troubles in Shāndōng,
and the common people all pledged their loyalty and submitted willingly.
Moreover, the Hé and Jǐ rivers
are vital strategic locations in the realm.
Although they are now ravaged and damaged,
they are still easy to secure for self-preservation.
This is also your Guānzhōng and Hénèi, General,
and it must be secured first.
Now, having defeated Lǐ Fēng and Xuē Lán,
if you divide your troops to strike Chén Gōng in the east,
Gōng will certainly not dare to look westward.
In the interim, you can muster troops to harvest the ripe wheat,
and gather food and store grain.
With one decisive action, Bù can be defeated.
After defeating Bù,
you can then ally with Yángzhōu in the south
to jointly attack Yuán Shù,
thereby dominating Huái and Sì.
If you abandon Bù and go east,
leaving too many troops will not be effective,
while leaving too few troops will cause the people to all seek refuge in cities,
unable to gather firewood or forage.
Bù will take advantage of the emptiness to raid and pillage,
making the people's hearts even more precarious.
Only Juànchéng, Fàn, and Wèi might be preserved;
the rest will not be yours.
This means losing Yǎnxzhōu.
If Xúzhōu cannot be secured,
where will you return, General?
Moreover, although Táo Qiān is dead,
Xúzhōu is not easily taken.
Having learned from their defeat of the previous year,
they will be fearful and seek alliances,
mutually supporting each other.
Now the east has all harvested its wheat,
and they will certainly fortify their walls and clear the fields to await you, General.
If you attack but cannot breach their defenses,
and raid but gain nothing,
within ten days,
your army of a hundred thousand will be self-defeated before battle.
When you previously attacked Xúzhōu,
your might and punishments were truly implemented.
Their sons and brothers, remembering the shame of their fathers and elder brothers,
will surely each defend themselves,
with no thought of surrender.
Even if you manage to defeat them,
you still cannot possess it.
Indeed, there are cases where one abandons this to take that.
It is acceptable to exchange a large one for a small one,
it is acceptable to exchange safety for danger,
and it is acceptable to temporarily weigh the current situation without worrying about the instability of the foundation.
But now,
none of these three benefits apply.
I hope, General, you will consider this carefully."
Tàizǔ then stopped.
He harvested a large amount of wheat,
and again fought Bù,
dividing his troops to pacify the various counties.
Bù was defeated and fled,
and Yǎnxzhōu was thus pacified.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān,
Tàizǔ defeated the Huángjīn.
Emperor Xiàn of Hàn returned to Luòyáng from Hédōng.
Tàizǔ deliberated on welcoming the emperor and establishing the capital at Xǔ.
Some argued that Shāndōng was not yet pacified,
and that Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng had only recently brought the Son of Heaven to Luòyáng.
They were connected to Zhāng Yáng in the north,
and could not be quickly controlled.
Xù exhorted Tàizǔ, saying:
“In the past, when Jìn Wén (Duke Wén of Jìn) received King Xiāng of Zhōu, the feudal lords followed him.
When Gāozǔ mourned the Righteous Emperor with white garments during his eastern campaign, the hearts of the world returned to him.
Since the Son of Heaven was in exile,
you, General, were the first to raise a righteous army.
Only because Shāndōng was in turmoil
were you unable to rush far to Guān Yòu.
However, you still dispatched generals and commanders,
braved dangers to send envoys.
Although you resisted difficulties from without,
your heart was always with the imperial house.
This is your long-cherished ambition, General, to bring order to the world.
Now the imperial carriage has returned,
the Eastern Capital is overgrown with weeds and brambles.
Righteous scholars have thoughts of preserving the foundation,
and the common people feel sorrow in remembrance of the past.
If you can seize this opportunity,
to uphold the sovereign and follow the aspirations of the people,
that is a great conformity to the Way;
to uphold utmost impartiality to subdue heroes,
that is a great strategy;
to foster grand righteousness to attract talented individuals,
that is great virtue.
Even if there are rebels in the world,
they will certainly not be able to cause harm,
that is clear.
How dare Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng cause trouble!
If the situation is not settled in time,
the four quarters will develop their own intentions.
Even if you deliberate later,
it will be too late.”
Tàizǔ then went to Luòyáng
and welcomed the Son of Heaven to make Xǔ the capital.
The Son of Heaven appointed Tàizǔ as Grand General [Dà Jiāngjūn],
and promoted Xù to Hàn Palace Attendant [Hàn Shìzhōng]
and Acting Grand Master of Scribes [Shǒu Shàngshū Lìng].
He often remained in the court, holding important responsibilities.
Even when Tàizǔ was campaigning abroad,
all military and state affairs were planned with Xù.
Tàizǔ asked Xù,
“Who can replace you in devising strategies for me?”
Xù named
“Xún Yōu and Zhōng Yáo.”
Before this,
Xù had recommended strategists,
advancing Xī Zhìcái.
After Zhìcái’s death,
he again advanced Guō Jiā.
Tàizǔ considered Xù discerning of people,
and all those he advanced proved competent.
Only Yán Xiàng, as Governor of Yángzhōu,
and Wéi Kāng, as Governor of Liángzhōu,
later met with defeat and ruin.
Since Tàizǔ welcomed the Son of Heaven,
Yuán Shào harbored inward resentment.
After Shào annexed the Hèshuò region,
the world feared his strength.
Tàizǔ was then troubled by Lǚ Bù in the east
and resisting Zhāng Xiù in the south.
Zhāng Xiù defeated Tàizǔ’s army at Wǎn.
Shào grew even more arrogant
and wrote a letter to Tàizǔ,
its tone rebellious and disrespectful.
Tàizǔ was greatly enraged,
his demeanor and actions changed from the usual.
Everyone thought it was because of his defeat at the hands of Zhāng Xiù.
Zhōng Yáo asked Xù about this.
Xù said,
“My lord’s intelligence
would certainly not dwell on past failures;
he must have other concerns.”
Then he went to see Tàizǔ and questioned him.
Tàizǔ then showed Shào’s letter to Xù,
saying,
“Now I intend to punish the unrighteous,
but my strength is insufficient.
What should I do?”
Xù said,
“In ancient times, those who succeeded or failed,
if they truly possessed the talent,
though weak, would surely become strong.
If they were not the right person,
though strong, they would easily become weak.
The rise and fall of Liú and Xiàng [Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ]
are enough to illustrate this.
Now, the only one contending with you, my lord, for the world
is Yuán Shào.
Shào appears outwardly magnanimous but is inwardly jealous;
he appoints people but distrusts them in his heart.
You, my lord, are enlightened and unconstrained,
employing talent as appropriate.
This is a victory of tolerance.
Shào is slow and indecisive,
missing opportunities.
You, my lord, can make great decisions
and adapt to changes without fixed methods.
This is a victory of strategy.
Shào commands his army with laxity and leniency,
laws and regulations are not established.
Although his soldiers are numerous,
they are in fact difficult to use.
Your laws and regulations, my lord, are clear,
rewards and punishments are certainly enforced.
Although your soldiers are few,
they all vie to fight to the death.
This is a victory of military prowess.
Shào relies on his family’s hereditary influence,
calmly embellishing his intelligence
to gain fame and reputation.
Therefore, many scholars of limited ability who like to ask questions flock to him.
You, my lord, treat people with utmost benevolence,
sincerely and not for superficial show.
You conduct yourself with caution and frugality,
yet spare no expense for those who have rendered meritorious service.
Therefore, loyal, upright, and effective scholars from across the world all wish to be employed by you.
This is a victory of virtue.
Indeed, with these four victories assisting the Son of Heaven
and upholding righteousness in your campaigns,
who would dare not follow?
What can Shào’s strength amount to!”
Tàizǔ was pleased.
Xù said,
“If Lǚ Bù is not defeated first,
Héběi will also not be easy to conquer.”
Tàizǔ said,
“Indeed.
What troubles me,
furthermore, is the fear that Shào might invade Guānzhōng,
stir up the Qiāng and Hú,
and entice Shǔhàn in the south.
Then I would be alone, with Yǎn and Yù, resisting five-sixths of the world.
What should a general do?”
Xù said,
“There are dozens of generals in Guānzhōng,
but none can unite them.
Only Hán Suí and Mǎ Chāo are the strongest.
Seeing that Shāndōng is currently embroiled in conflict,
they will certainly each gather their forces to protect themselves.
If you now treat them with kindness and virtue,
and send envoys to form an alliance,
although this stalemate cannot last long in peace,
it will be enough to keep them inactive
while you pacify Shāndōng.
Zhōng Yáo can be entrusted with the affairs of the west.
Then you will have no worries.”
In the third year,
after Tàizǔ had defeated Zhāng Xiù,
captured Lǚ Bù in the east,
and pacified Xúzhōu,
he then confronted Yuán Shào.
Kǒng Róng said to Xún Yù:
“Shào has vast territory and strong troops;
Tián Fēng and Xǔ Yōu
are men of wisdom and stratagem,
who devise plans for him;
Shěn Pèi and Féng Jì
are loyal ministers,
who manage his affairs;
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu
are exceptionally brave,
leading his forces: it will probably be difficult to defeat him!”
Xún Yù replied:
“Though Shào’s army is numerous, its discipline is not orderly.
Tián Fēng is rigid and offends his superiors,
Xǔ Yōu is greedy and undisciplined.
Shěn Pèi is dictatorial and lacks strategy,
Féng Jì is resolute but self-willed.
If these two are left in charge of subsequent matters,
and Xǔ Yōu’s family violates the law,
they will certainly not be able to let it go,
and if they do not let it go,
Xǔ Yōu will surely cause trouble.
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu
are merely brave as individuals;
they can be captured in a single battle.”
In the fifth year,
he fought continuously with Yuán Shào.
Tàizǔ held Guāndù,
and Shào besieged him.
Tàizǔ’s army provisions were almost exhausted,
so he wrote to Xún Yù,
discussing his desire to retreat to Xǔ to draw Shào out.
Xún Yù said:
“Though the army’s provisions are scarce now,
it is not as dire as Chǔ and Hàn were between Xíngyáng and Chénggāo.
At that time, Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ were both unwilling to retreat first,
for whoever retreated first would lose momentum.
You, Sire, with one-tenth of the enemy’s forces,
have held your ground defensively,
blocking their throat and preventing their advance,
for half a year already.
Their situation is evident and their strength exhausted;
a change is bound to occur.
This is the time to employ a surprise attack;
it must not be missed.”
Tàizǔ then stayed his ground.
He then used surprise troops to attack Shào’s detached camp,
beheading his general Chúnwú Qióng and others,
and Shào retreated.
Shěn Pèi, because Xǔ Yōu’s family acted unlawfully,
arrested his wife and children,
and Xǔ Yōu, enraged, defected from Shào;
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu met their end on the battlefield;
Tián Fēng was executed for his remonstrances: all as Xún Yù had predicted.
In the sixth year,
Tàizǔ moved his troops to Ānmín in Dōngpíng to gather provisions.
Provisions were scarce,
insufficient to withstand the forces north of the Yellow River.
He wished to take advantage of Shào’s recent defeat
to attack Liú Biǎo in the interim.
Xún Yù said:
“Now that Shào has been defeated,
his followers are disaffected.
It is advisable to take advantage of his weakened state
to completely pacify him;
but to turn your back on Yǎnzōu and Yùzhōu,
and lead a distant army to Jiānghàn,
if Shào gathers his remaining forces
and takes advantage of the vacuum to attack from behind,
then your cause, Sire, will be lost.”
Tàizǔ then again camped on the Yellow River.
Shào fell ill and died.
Tàizǔ crossed the Yellow River,
attacked Shào’s sons Tán and Shàng,
while Gāo Gàn and Guō Yuán invaded Hédōng,
causing alarm in Guān Yòu.
Zhōng Yáo led Mǎ Téng and others to defeat them.
The account is in Zhōng Yáo’s biography.
In the eighth year,
Tàizǔ recognized Xún Yù’s merits, both past and present,
and presented a memorial to enfeoff Xún Yù as Marquis of Wànsuìtíng.
In the ninth year,
Tàizǔ captured Yè,
and was appointed Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Someone advised Tàizǔ,
“It is appropriate to restore the ancient system of nine provinces (jiǔ zhōu).
Then Jìzhōu’s jurisdiction will be vast,
and the world will submit.”
Tàizǔ was about to follow this,
but Xún Yù said:
“If this is done,
then Jìzhōu will gain Hédōng, Féngyì, Fúfēng, Xīhé, Yōu, and Bìng,
taking from many.
Previously, when you, Sire, defeated Yuán Shàng
and captured Shěn Pèi,
the whole country was shocked,
and everyone feared they would not be able to retain their lands
and control their troops.
Now, if they are made to belong to Jìzhōu,
they will all be agitated.
Moreover, many are advising the generals in Guān Yòu to adopt a strategy of closing the passes;
now, hearing this,
they will think that they will inevitably be dispossessed in turn.
Should an uprising occur,
even with those who are (good at defending) [good at keeping order],
they will coerce each other into wrongdoing,
then Yuán Shàng will escape his death,
and Yuán Tán will harbor disloyalty,
Liú Biǎo will then secure the region between Jiāng and Hàn,
and the world will not be easy to conquer.
I beg you, Sire, to quickly lead your troops to first pacify the lands north of the Yellow River,
then restore the old capital,
and move south to Jingzhou,
demanding the unpaid tributes.
Then everyone in the world will understand your intention,
and people will feel secure.
When the world is completely pacified,
then discuss the ancient system.
This is a long-term benefit for the state.”
Tàizǔ then dropped the proposal for the nine provinces.
At this time, Xún Yōu was often the chief strategist.
Xún Yù’s elder brother, Xún Yǎn, as Supervisor of the Army Commandant, defended Yè,
and oversaw affairs north of the Yellow River.
When Tàizǔ was campaigning against Yuán Shàng,
Gāo Gàn secretly dispatched troops to attack Yè.
Xún Yǎn detected this in advance,
and executed them all,
being enfeoffed as a marquis for his merit.
Tàizǔ gave his daughter in marriage to Xún Yù’s eldest son, Xún Yùn,
who was later known as Princess Ānyáng.
Xún Yù and Xún Yōu were both highly esteemed,
yet they were modest and frugal,
distributing their stipends and gifts to their relatives and old acquaintances,
leaving no surplus wealth in their homes.
In the twelfth year,
Xún Yù’s fief was again increased by a thousand households,
totaling two thousand households.
Tàizǔ was about to attack Liú Biǎo,
and asked Xún Yù for his strategy.
Xún Yù said:
“Now that Huáxià is pacified,
the southern lands know of their impending difficulty.
You can openly march towards Wǎn and Yè, while secretly advancing lightly,
to catch them by surprise.”
Tàizǔ then set out.
Coincidentally, Liú Biǎo died of illness.
Tàizǔ proceeded directly to Wǎn and Yè as Xún Yù had advised,
and Liú Biǎo’s son, Liú Cóng, surrendered the province.
In the seventeenth year,
Dǒng Zhāo and others suggested that Tàizǔ should be promoted to Duke of the State,
and be granted the Nine Bestowments (Jiǔ Cì) to manifest his extraordinary achievements,
and secretly consulted Xún Yù about this.
Xún Yù believed that Tàizǔ originally raised a righteous army to restore the imperial court and pacify the nation,
upholding sincere loyalty
and practicing humility and deference;
a gentleman loves people with virtue,
and this would not be appropriate.
Tàizǔ was consequently displeased.
When he was campaigning against Sūn Quán,
he presented a memorial requesting Xún Yù to visit the army at Qiáo,
and then detained Xún Yù there,
appointing him as Attendant Officer and Grand Master of Remonstrance with Imperial Authority,
to participate in the Prime Minister’s military affairs.
When Tàizǔ’s army reached Rúxū,
Xún Yù fell ill and remained in Shòuchūn,
where he died of distress,
aged fifty.
He was posthumously granted the title Marquis Jìng.
The following year,
Tàizǔ indeed became Duke of Wèi.
Xún Yùn,
the heir to the marquisate,
rose to the office of Hǔbēn Zhōngláng Jiàng.
Initially,
Emperor Wén and Píngyuán Hóu Zhí were both considered as potential successors,
and Emperor Wén had shown deference to Xún Yù in his actions.
When Xún Yù died,
Xún Yùn also had a good relationship with Cáo Zhí,
but was not on good terms with Xiàhóu Shàng,
which greatly angered Emperor Wén.
Xún Yùn died young,
leaving sons Xún Hán and Xún Yì.
(Yì, pronounced like 'yì'.)
Due to their maternal kinship, they were still favored and well-treated.
Xún Yùn's younger brother, Xún Yǔ,
was Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Xún Yǔ's younger brother, Xún Shēn,
was Dàjiàngjūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Both were well-known
and died young.
Xún Shēn's younger brother, Xún Yǐ,
served as Sīkōng during the Xiánxī era.
Xún Hán, Xún Yùn's son,
succeeded him as Sànqí Chángshì,
and was promoted to the peerage of Guǎngyáng Xiānghóu.
He died at the age of thirty.
His son, Xún Yūn, succeeded him.
Xún Yì rose to the office of Zhōnglǐngjūn
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title Zhēn Hóu
and posthumously appointed Piàojí Jiāngjūn.
His son, Xún Kǎi, succeeded him.
Xún Yì's wife
was the younger sister of Sīmǎ Jǐng Wáng and Wén Wáng.
Both kings were on good terms with her.
During the Xiánxī era,
when the five ranks of nobility were established,
Xún Yì, for his distinguished service in the former court,
had Xún Kǎi enfeoffed as Nándùn Zǐ.
Xún Yōu, courtesy name Gōngdá,
was Xún Yù's paternal cousin's son.
His grandfather, Xún Tán,
was the Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
Xún Yōu was orphaned young.
When Xún Tán died,
his former clerk, Zhāng Quán, requested to guard Xún Tán's tomb.
Xún Yōu, at thirteen,
suspected him
and said to his uncle, Xún Qú:
"This clerk has an unusual expression;
he is likely up to mischief!"
Xún Qú realized this
and questioned him,
and indeed, he was a murderer on the run.
From then on, Xún Yōu was regarded as extraordinary.
When Hé Jìn held power,
he summoned over twenty famous scholars from within the seas, including Xún Yōu.
Upon arrival, Xún Yōu
was appointed Huángmén Shìláng.
During the turmoil of Dǒng Zhuó,
the Guāndōng armies rose,
and Dǒng Zhuó moved the capital to Cháng'ān.
Xún Yōu, along with Yìláng Zhèng Tài, Hé Yóng, Shìzhōng Zhǒng Jí, and Yuèqí Xiàowèi Wǔ Qióng, plotted, saying:
"Dǒng Zhuó is lawless,
worse than Jié and Zhòu.
The whole empire resents him.
Though he commands strong troops,
he is actually just a common man.
Now, let us directly assassinate him to appease the people,
then secure the Xiáo and Hán passes,
support the emperor's mandate,
and issue commands to the world.
This would be an act worthy of Huán and Wén."
The plot was almost complete when it was discovered.
Hé Yóng and Xún Yōu were arrested and imprisoned.
Hé Yóng, overwhelmed by fear, committed suicide.
Xún Yōu remained composed in speech and eating,
and happened to be released when Dǒng Zhuó died.
He abandoned his office and returned home,
then was again recruited by the ducal mansion,
and was recommended as a 'high talent' (gāodì).
He was promoted to Rèncéng Xiàng,
but did not take up the post.
Xún Yōu, considering Shǔ Hàn to be rugged and secure,
with a prosperous population,
requested to be appointed Grand Administrator of Shǔ Jùn.
The road was cut off, preventing him from reaching it,
so he stayed in Jīngzhōu.
Tàizǔ welcomed the Son of Heaven to the capital at Xǔ
and sent a letter to Xún Yōu, saying:
"Now the world is in great chaos,
a time for wise men to exert their minds,
yet you are observing the changes in Shǔ Hàn;
is this not too long?"
Thereupon, Xún Yōu was summoned as Grand Administrator of Rǔnán,
and then entered the court as Shàngshū.
Tàizǔ had long heard of Xún Yōu's reputation
and was greatly pleased after speaking with him.
He said to Xún Yù
and Zhōng Yáo:
"Gōngdá
is no ordinary man.
If I can plan affairs with him,
what worries can there be in the world?"
He appointed him as his strategist (jūnshī).
In the third year of Jiàn'ān (198 CE),
he accompanied Tàizǔ in the campaign against Zhāng Xiù.
Xún Yōu said to Tàizǔ:
"Zhāng Xiù and Liú Biǎo rely on each other to be strong,
but Zhāng Xiù, as a roving army, depends on Liú Biǎo for provisions.
Liú Biǎo cannot supply him,
so they are bound to separate.
It is better to slow down our army and wait for this to happen;
he can then be enticed to surrender.
If we press him hard,
they will certainly aid each other."
Tàizǔ did not follow this advice
and advanced his army to Ráng,
engaging in battle.
Zhāng Xiù was in dire straits,
and Liú Biǎo indeed came to his rescue.
The army suffered a defeat.
Tàizǔ said to Xún Yōu:
"Not following your advice led to this."
He then set up a surprise attack and fought again,
achieving a great victory.
That year,
Tàizǔ marched from Wǎn to campaign against Lǚ Bù,
reaching Xiàpī.
Lǚ Bù was defeated, retreated, and held fast in defense.
The siege failed to dislodge him,
and after continuous battles,
the soldiers were exhausted.
Tàizǔ wanted to return.
Xún Yōu and Guō Jiā advised him, saying:
"Lǚ Bù is brave but lacks strategy.
He has been defeated in all three battles,
and his morale is low.
The army depends on its commander.
If the commander's spirit is low, the army will have no will to fight.
Chén Gōng is intelligent but slow.
Now, while Lǚ Bù's spirit has not recovered
and Chén Gōng's plan is not yet set,
press the attack urgently.
Lǚ Bù can be captured."
So, they diverted the Yí and Sì rivers to flood the city.
The city walls collapsed,
and Lǚ Bù was captured alive.
Later, he accompanied Tàizǔ to relieve Liú Yán at Báimǎ.
Xún Yōu devised a plan to kill Yán Liáng.
The account is in the Wǔ Jì.
After Tàizǔ captured Báimǎ and returned,
he sent the baggage train along the Yellow River westward.
Yuán Shào crossed the river in pursuit
and unexpectedly encountered Tàizǔ.
All the generals were afraid
and urged Tàizǔ to return and hold the camp.
Xún Yōu said:
"This is how we can capture the enemy;
why abandon it?"
Tàizǔ looked at Xún Yōu and smiled.
He then used the baggage train as bait for the enemy.
The enemy rushed to seize it,
and their formation fell into disorder.
Then, he launched his cavalry and infantry to attack,
routing them greatly
and beheading their cavalry commander Wén Chǒu.
Tàizǔ then faced Yuán Shào at Guāndù.
As their army's food supply was almost exhausted,
Xún Yōu said to Tàizǔ:
"Yuán Shào's supply convoy will arrive day or night.
Its commander Hán is eager and underestimates the enemy;
we can attack and defeat him."
Tàizǔ asked:
"Who can be sent?"
Xún Yōu replied:
"Xú Huǎng can."
So, Xú Huǎng and Shǐ Huàn were dispatched to intercept and defeat them,
burning their baggage.
At that time, Xǔ Yōu surrendered
and reported that Yuán Shào had sent Chúnyú Qióng and others with over ten thousand troops to escort the grain convoy,
and that the general was arrogant and the soldiers lazy,
so they could be ambushed.
Everyone doubted this.
Only Xún Yōu and Jiǎ Xǔ urged Tàizǔ
Tàizǔ then left Xún Yōu and Cáo Hóng to guard
and personally led the attack, defeating them
and beheading Chúnyú Qióng and the others.
Yuán Shào's generals Zhāng Hé and Gāo Lǎn burned their siege towers and surrendered.
Yuán Shào then abandoned his army and fled.
When Zhāng Hé arrived,
Cáo Hóng was suspicious and dared not accept him.
Xún Yōu said to Cáo Hóng:
"Zhāng Hé's advice was not taken,
and he came here out of anger.
Why do you hesitate?"
So, he accepted him.
In the seventh year,
he followed in the campaign to attack Yuán Tán and Yuán Shàng at Líyáng.
The following year,
Tàizǔ was campaigning against Liú Biǎo,
and Tán and Shàng were fighting over Jìzhōu.
Tán sent Xīn Pí to beg for surrender and assistance.
Tàizǔ was about to grant it,
and sought the opinions of his subordinates.
Many of his subordinates believed that Liú Biǎo was strong
and should be pacified first,
while Tán and Shàng were not a cause for concern.
Xún Yōu said:
"The world is currently in turmoil,
yet Liú Biǎo sits and holds the region between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
It is clear he lacks ambition for the four directions.
The Yuán clan occupies territory spanning four provinces,
with a hundred thousand armored soldiers.
Yuán Shào gained the support of the populace through his magnanimity.
If his two sons were to live in harmony and maintain their established legacy,
then the difficulties of the world would never cease.
Now, however, the brothers are at odds.
This situation cannot allow both to survive.
If one is absorbed, their strength will be concentrated,
and a concentrated strength would be difficult to defeat.
By taking advantage of their discord,
the world will be settled.
This opportunity must not be missed."
Tàizǔ said:
"Excellent."
He then agreed to a peace alliance with Tán,
and proceeded to return and attack Shàng, defeating him.
Later, Tán rebelled,
and he followed in executing Tán at Nánpí.
When Jìzhōu was pacified,
Tàizǔ officially enfeoffed Xún Yōu, saying:
"My military strategist Xún Yōu,
since first assisting me,
has followed me in every campaign.
All previous victories against the enemy
were due to Xún Yōu's strategies."
Thereupon, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Língshù Tíng.
In the twelfth year,
an order was issued to widely commend merits and grant enfeoffments.
Tàizǔ said:
"Loyal, upright, and secretly strategizing,
bringing peace both internally and externally –
this is Xún Yù.
Gōngdá is next."
His stipend was increased by four hundred households,
bringing the total to seven hundred households,
and he was transferred to become Zhōngjūnshī.
When the state of Wèi was first established,
he became Shàngshūlìng.
Xún Yōu was profound, meticulous, and possessed strategic foresight.
Since following Tàizǔ in campaigns,
he always formulated strategies behind the scenes.
People of his time, and even his own sons and nephews, did not know what he said.
Tàizǔ often praised him, saying:
"Gōngdá is outwardly foolish but inwardly wise,
outwardly timid but inwardly brave,
outwardly weak but inwardly strong.
He does not boast of his good deeds,
nor does he flaunt his achievements.
His wisdom can be attained,
but his 'foolishness' cannot.
Even Yán Zǐ and Níng Wǔ could not surpass him."
When Emperor Wén was in the Eastern Palace,
Tàizǔ said to him:
"Xún Gōngdá
is a model teacher for others.
You should treat him with utmost courtesy and respect."
Once, when Xún Yōu was ill,
the Heir Apparent visited him to inquire about his health,
and bowed alone by his bed.
Such was the respect and distinction he received.
Xún Yōu was good friends with Zhōng Yáo.
Zhōng Yáo said:
"Whenever I plan something,
I ponder it repeatedly,
and consider it to be beyond improvement;
but when I consult Gōngdá,
he always surpasses my expectations."
Gōngdá devised a total of twelve extraordinary strategies throughout his life,
and only Zhōng Yáo knew of them.
Zhōng Yáo was compiling them but had not finished
when he died,
so the world was unable to hear them all.
Xún Yōu followed in the campaign against Sūn Quán,
and died on the way.
Tàizǔ wept whenever he spoke of him.
His eldest son, Jī,
had a similar character to Xún Yōu,
but died young.
His second son, Shì, succeeded him,
but had no son,
so the lineage ended.
During the Huángchū era,
Yuán Shào enfeoffed Xún Yōu's grandson, Biāo, as Marquis of Língshù Tíng,
with three hundred households.
Later, he was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Qiūyáng Tíng.
During the Zhèngshǐ era,
Xún Yōu was posthumously given the title Jìng Hóu.
Jiǎ Xǔ, courtesy name Wénhé,
was a native of Gūzāng, Wǔwēi.
In his youth, few people recognized his talent,
only Yán Zhōng of Hànyáng considered him exceptional,
saying that Jiǎ Xǔ possessed the extraordinary qualities of Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng.
He was recommended as Xiàolián and became a Láng.
Due to illness, he resigned his office.
While returning west to Qǐan,
he encountered rebellious Dī tribesmen on the road.
Dozens of fellow travelers were all captured.
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"I am the grandson of Duke Duàn.
You should bury me separately,
and my family will surely pay a handsome ransom."
At that time, the Grand Commandant Duàn Jiǒng,
who had long served as a frontier general,
had a fearsome reputation in the western lands.
Thus, Jiǎ Xǔ used this to intimidate the Dī.
The Dī indeed did not dare to harm him,
made an alliance, and sent him away,
while all the others died.
Jiǎ Xǔ was not actually Duàn Jiǒng's nephew;
he used this expediently to accomplish his goal.
Such instances were common for him.
When Dǒng Zhuó entered Luòyáng,
Jiǎ Xǔ, as a secretary to the Grand Commandant, was made Píngjīn Dūwèi,
and later promoted to Tǎolǔ Xiàowèi.
Dǒng Zhuó's son-in-law, Colonel Niu Fǔ, was stationed at Shǎn,
and Jiǎ Xǔ was in Niu Fǔ's army.
After Dǒng Zhuó's defeat,
Niu Fǔ also died.
The troops were terrified,
and commanders Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì, Zhāng Jì, and others wanted to disband
and secretly return to their hometowns.
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"I hear that there is discussion in Cháng'ān to execute all the people from Liángzhōu.
If you gentlemen abandon your troops and travel alone,
even a mere headman of a post station could capture you.
It would be better to lead your troops west,
gather soldiers wherever you go,
attack Cháng'ān,
and avenge Duke Dǒng.
If it succeeds by chance,
you can support the imperial court and conquer the world.
If it does not succeed,
it will not be too late to flee."
The multitude agreed.
Lǐ Jué then attacked Cháng'ān from the west.
The account is in Dǒng Zhuó's biography.
Later, Jiǎ Xǔ became Zuǒ Féngyì.
Lǐ Jué and others wanted to enfeoff him for his achievements.
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"This was merely a scheme to save our lives;
what achievement is there?"
He firmly declined the offer.
They also wanted to make him Shàngshū Púshè.
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"The Shàngshū Púshè is the chief of officials,
looked up to by the world.
My name is not well-established,
nor is it sufficient to command people's respect.
Even if I were to disregard honor and profit,
what would happen to the imperial court?"
They then appointed Jiǎ Xǔ as Shàngshū,
in charge of elections.
He rectified many matters,
and Lǐ Jué and others respected him but also feared him.
He left office during his mother's mourning period,
and was later appointed Guānglù Dàfū.
When Lǐ Jué and Guō Sì fought in Cháng'ān,
Lǐ Jué again asked Jiǎ Xǔ to be Xuānyì Jiāngjūn.
When Lǐ Jué and others reconciled
and released the Son of Heaven,
and protected the high ministers,
Jiǎ Xǔ played a significant role.
After the Son of Heaven had departed,
Jiǎ Xǔ returned his official seal and ribbon.
At this time, General Duàn Wēi was stationed at Huáyīn.
He was from the same commandery as Jiǎ Xǔ,
so Jiǎ Xǔ left Lǐ Jué and sought refuge with Duàn Wēi.
Jiǎ Xǔ was already well-known,
and was highly regarded by Duàn Wēi's army.
Duàn Wēi secretly feared that his position would be usurped,
but outwardly treated Jiǎ Xǔ with utmost courtesy,
which made Jiǎ Xǔ feel even more uneasy.
Zhāng Xiù was in Nányáng.
Xǔ secretly allied with Xiù.
Xiù sent someone to welcome Xǔ.
When Xǔ was about to depart,
someone said to Xǔ,
"Wēi has treated you generously,
why are you leaving him?"
Xǔ replied,
"Wēi is naturally suspicious,
and is wary of me.
Although he treats me generously,
it cannot be relied upon.
In time, I will be plotted against.
My departure will surely please him,
and he will hope that I will establish a powerful alliance outside,
so he will surely treat my wife and children well.
Xiù has no strategist,
and also wishes to have me,
so my family and I will both be safe."
Xǔ then went.
Xiù treated him with the courtesy due to a revered elder.
Wēi indeed treated Xǔ's family well.
Xǔ advised Xiù to form an alliance with Liú Biǎo.
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) later campaigned against him.
One morning, he withdrew his army.
Xiù pursued him personally.
Xǔ said to Xiù,
"Do not pursue them.
If you pursue, you will surely be defeated."
Xiù did not listen.
He advanced his troops and engaged in battle,
suffered a great defeat, and returned.
Xǔ said to Xiù,
"Quickly pursue them again.
If you fight again, you will surely win."
Xiù apologized, saying,
"I did not heed your words,
and this is what happened.
Now that I have already been defeated,
why should I pursue again?"
Xǔ said,
"The military situation has changed.
If you go quickly, it will surely be advantageous."
Xiù believed him,
so he gathered his scattered troops and went in pursuit.
They fought a great battle,
and indeed returned victorious.
He asked Xǔ,
"I pursued a retreating army with elite troops,
and you said I would surely be defeated.
I attacked a victorious army with defeated troops,
and you said I would surely conquer.
Everything was as you said,
but why was it contradictory and yet both proved true?"
Xǔ said,
"This is easy to understand.
Although the General is skilled in warfare,
you are no match for Cáo Gōng.
Although his army had just retreated,
Cáo Gōng would surely personally command the rear guard.
Although your pursuing troops were elite,
since the general was no match,
and their soldiers were also sharp,
I therefore knew you would surely be defeated.
Cáo Gōng attacked you without any miscalculation.
He retreated before exhausting his strength,
so there must have been some domestic issue.
Having already defeated you,
he would surely advance his light troops quickly.
Even if he left his generals to guard the rear,
though those generals are brave,
they are also no match for you, General.
Therefore, even using defeated troops, you would surely win the battle."
Xiù then submitted.
After this,
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) resisted Yuán Shào at Guāndù.
Shào sent people to recruit Xiù,
and also sent a letter to Xǔ to form an alliance.
Xiù wished to agree to it.
Xǔ, openly in Xiù's presence, said to Shào's envoy,
"Go back and thank Yuán Běnchū.
If brothers cannot tolerate each other,
how can he tolerate the nation's finest talents?"
Xiù was startled and fearful, saying,
"How could it come to this!"
He secretly said to Xǔ,
"If this is the case,
where should we go?"
Xǔ said,
"It is better to follow Cáo Gōng."
Xiù said,
"Yuán is strong and Cáo is weak.
Moreover, we are enemies with Cáo.
How can we follow him?"
Xǔ said,
"This is precisely why you should follow him.
Cáo Gōng serves the Son of Heaven to command the world;
this is the first reason why you should follow him.
Shào is strong and powerful.
If we join him with our small force,
he will surely not value us highly.
Cáo Gōng's forces are weak,
and he will surely be pleased to have us;
this is the second reason why you should follow him.
A person with the ambition of a hegemon king
will naturally set aside private grievances
to display his virtue to all beneath Heaven;
this is the third reason why you should follow him.
I hope the General will have no doubts!"
Xiù followed his advice,
and led his troops to surrender to Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ).
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) saw him,
was delighted,
and took Xǔ's hand, saying,
"It is you who makes me trusted and respected throughout the world."
He appointed Xǔ as Zhí Jīn Wú,
enfeoffed him as Dū Tíng Hóu,
and transferred him to Jì Zhōu Mù.
As Jì Zhōu was not yet pacified,
he remained to participate in the military affairs of the Sī Kōng.
Yuán Shào besieged Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) at Guāndù.
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ)'s provisions were almost exhausted.
He asked Xǔ what plan he had,
Xǔ said,
"Your brilliance surpasses Shào's,
your courage surpasses Shào's,
your use of men surpasses Shào's,
and your decisiveness surpasses Shào's.
Having these four advantages, yet being undecided for half a year,
is merely due to your desire for absolute safety.
If you decisively seize the moment,
you can settle it in an instant."
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) said,
"Excellent."
He then combined his troops and went out,
besieging and attacking Shào's camp over thirty *lǐ* away,
and defeated it.
Shào's army suffered a great rout,
and the area north of the Yellow River was pacified.
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) assumed the title of Jì Zhōu Mù
and transferred Xǔ to be Tài Zhōng Dà Fū.
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) defeated Jīng Zhōu,
and wished to proceed downstream along the river to the east.
Xǔ admonished him, saying,
"Your Lord (Míng Gōng) previously defeated the Yuán clan,
and now you have taken Hàn Nán.
Your prestige is widely known,
and your military power is already great.
If you rely on the abundance of the old Chǔ,
to reward your officers and soldiers,
and comfort the common people,
enabling them to settle down and enjoy their work,
then Jiāng Dōng will submit without exhausting your forces."
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) did not listen,
and his army subsequently gained no advantage.
Later, Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) fought Hán Suí and Mǎ Chāo at Wèi Nán.
Chāo and others sought to cede territory in exchange for peace,
and also requested to send hostages.
Xǔ believed that this could be falsely agreed to.
He was again asked for a plan.
Xǔ said,
"Simply sow discord among them."
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) said,
"I understand."
He consistently adopted Xǔ's strategy.
The details are in the Wǔ Jì.
In the end, Suí and Chāo were defeated;
this was Xǔ's original plan.
At this time,
Wén Dì was the Wǔguān Jiāng,
while Línzī Hóu Zhí's talent and fame were flourishing.
Each had their own partisans,
and there was a discussion about seizing the succession.
Wén Dì sent someone to ask Jiǎ Xǔ for advice on how to secure his position.
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"I wish for the general to broaden and elevate his virtue,
personally undertake the duties of a simple scholar,
diligently, morning and evening,
and not deviate from the filial path.
This is all."
Wén Dì followed his advice,
and deeply disciplined himself.
Tài Zǔ once also dismissed his attendants and asked Jiǎ Xǔ,
but Jiǎ Xǔ remained silent and did not reply.
Tài Zǔ said:
"I speak with you, yet you do not answer,
why is this?"
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"I was just thinking of something,
hence I did not immediately answer."
Tài Zǔ said:
"What were you thinking of?"
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"I was thinking of Yuán Běnchū and Liú Jǐngshēng and their sons."
Tài Zǔ laughed heartily,
and thereupon the crown prince was decided.
Jiǎ Xǔ, considering himself not an old official of Tài Zǔ,
and his strategies deep and far-reaching,
feared being suspected,
so he kept his doors closed, maintaining self-restraint.
He had no private dealings,
and in the marriages of his sons and daughters,
he did not ally with high-ranking families.
Those in the realm who discussed wisdom and strategy deferred to him.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
he appointed Jiǎ Xǔ as Tàiwèi,
advanced his peerage to Wèishòu Xiānghóu,
increased his stipend by three hundred households,
making it eight hundred households in total.
He also divided two hundred households from his fief,
and enfeoffed his youngest son Fǎng as a Lièhóu.
His eldest son Mù was made Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
The Emperor asked Jiǎ Xǔ:
"I wish to conquer those who do not obey in order to unify the realm.
Which should I attack first, Wú or Shǔ?"
He replied:
"Those who conquer take military power first;
those who establish foundations value moral transformation.
Your Majesty has received the abdication in accordance with the times,
and governs all under Heaven.
If you pacify them with civil virtue and await their changes,
then it will not be difficult to pacify them.
Wú and Shǔ, though small countries,
rely on the obstruction of mountains and rivers.
Liú Bèi has heroic talent,
Zhūgě Liàng is skilled in governing the state,
Sūn Quán understands the realities,
Lù Yì sees military situations.
They hold strategic passes and guard important points,
and navigate the rivers and lakes.
None are easy to defeat quickly.
The way of employing troops
is to ensure victory before battle,
and to assess the enemy and evaluate generals.
Thus, no strategy will be overlooked.
I humbly estimate among your officials,
none are a match for Bèi or Quán.
Even if you use heavenly might to approach them,
I do not see a situation of complete certainty.
In the past, Shùn wielded shields and axes, and the Miáo submitted.
I believe that at present, civil means should precede military ones."
Wén Dì did not accept this.
Later, the campaign of Jiānglíng was launched,
and many soldiers died.
Jiǎ Xǔ died at the age of seventy-seven,
and was posthumously named Sù Hóu.
His son Mù succeeded him,
and served successively as Jùnshǒu.
After Mù died,
his son Mó succeeded him.
The commentary says: Xún Yù was pure, elegant, and refined,
possessing the demeanor of a king's aide,
yet his sharp perception and foresight
could not fully realize his ambitions.
Xún Yōu and Jiǎ Xǔ,
they were almost flawless in their calculations and strategies,
adept at adapting to changing circumstances,
perhaps comparable to Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng!
Biographies of Yuán, Zhāng, Liáng, Guó, Tián, Wáng, Bǐng, Guǎn, Chapter Eleven.
Yuán Huàn, courtesy name Yàoqīng,
was a native of Fúlè, Chénjùn.
His father Pāng,
served as Hàn Sītú.
At that time, many noble sons overstepped the laws,
but Huàn was pure and quiet,
his every action was in accordance with propriety.
The commandery appointed him Gōngcáo,
and all the corrupt officials in the commandery voluntarily resigned.
Later, he was invited to the public offices,
recommended as an outstanding talent,
and promoted to Shìyùshǐ.
He was appointed Qíao Lìng,
but did not take office.
When Liú Bèi was Yùzhōu,
he recommended Huàn as Màocái.
Later, he fled to the area between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
and was appointed by Yuán Shù.
Whenever Shù consulted him,
Huàn always gave righteous counsel,
Shù could not resist him,
but respected him and dared not fail to treat him with courtesy.
After a while,
Lǚ Bù attacked Shù at Fùlíng,
and Huàn went to join him,
and was subsequently detained by Bù.
Bù had initially been friendly with Liú Bèi,
but later they became estranged.
Bù wanted Huàn to write a letter insulting Bèi,
but Huàn refused.
He was pressed repeatedly,
but he would not agree.
Bù became furious,
and threatened Huàn with soldiers, saying:
"Do it and live,
don't do it and die."
Huàn's expression did not change,
he smiled and replied:
"Huàn has heard that only virtue can humiliate a person,
not insults.
If he is truly a gentleman,
he will not be ashamed by your words, General.
If he is truly a petty person,
he will echo your intentions, General.
Then the humiliation will be here, not on him.
Furthermore, my service to General Liú in the past
is like my service to you today, General.
If one day I leave here,
and then insult you, General,
would that be acceptable?"
Bù was ashamed and stopped.
When Bù was executed,
Huàn was able to return to Tài Zǔ.
Huàn said:
"Indeed, weapons
are instruments of ill omen,
to be used only when there is no other choice.
Encourage with morality,
conquer with benevolence and righteousness,
and simultaneously pacify their people and eliminate their harms.
If this is done,
then one can die with them and live with them.
It has been over ten years since the great chaos,
and the people's desire for peace
is stronger than being hung upside down,
yet the turmoil has not ceased,
why is this?
Perhaps the administration has lost its way!
Huàn has heard that enlightened rulers are good at saving the world,
thus when the world is chaotic, they bring order with righteousness;
when the times are deceitful, they suppress it with simplicity.
When times change and circumstances shift,
governing a state differs,
and one must not fail to observe this.
As for the establishment or modification of systems,
this is not necessarily the same for ancient and modern times.
However, universal love for all under Heaven and restoring them to the righteous path,
even if chaos is pacified by military means, it is aided by virtue,
this is truly the unchanging way of all kings.
Your Lordship is enlightened and surpasses the world.
That which the ancients used to win the people,
Your Lordship has already diligently applied.
That which causes the people to be lost today,
Your Lordship has already taken warning from.
The entire realm relies on Your Lordship,
to escape the disaster of peril and death.
However, the people do not yet know righteousness.
If Your Lordship instructs them accordingly,
then the realm will be exceedingly fortunate!"
Tài Zǔ deeply accepted this.
He was appointed Pèi Nánbù Dūwèi.
At that time, newly recruited people were used to open up military-agricultural colonies,
but the people were unhappy
and many fled.
Huàn reported to Tài-zǔ, saying:
"People cherish their homes and are loath to move;
they cannot be drastically changed.
It is easy to act in accordance with them,
and difficult to act against them.
It is advisable to follow their wishes:
only those who are willing should be taken,
and those who are unwilling should not be forced."
Tài-zǔ followed his advice,
and the common people were greatly pleased.
He was transferred to become the Chancellor of Liáng.
Huàn always instructed the various counties:
"Be sure to care for the [zhòng] (the poor) and the elderly,
and distinguish filial sons and chaste wives.
It is often said, 'When the world is well-governed, rites are elaborate;
when the world is chaotic, rites are simplified.'
It all depends on discretion.
Although the present is turbulent,
it is difficult to transform with rites.
Nevertheless, it depends on how we conduct ourselves."
In governance, he emphasized instruction and education,
acted only after careful consideration,
was gentle and soft on the outside but decisive on the inside.
He left office due to illness,
and the common people missed him.
Later, he was summoned to be Grand Master of Remonstrance and Ritual Libationer of the Chancellor's Army.
He received many gifts before and after,
all of which he dispersed completely.
His family had no savings,
and he never inquired about property.
When in need, he would take from others,
not acting with scrupulous scrutiny.
However, people of his time respected his purity.
When the state of Wèi was first established,
he became the Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and acted as Grandee Secretary.
Huàn spoke to Tài-zǔ, saying:
"Now that the great difficulties under Heaven have been removed,
employing both civil and military means
is the way to lasting stability.
I believe we should widely collect books and documents,
illuminate the teachings of the ancient sages,
to influence the people's perceptions,
and make everyone within the seas eagerly turn towards virtue.
Then, those distant people who do not submit can be attracted by civilizing virtue."
Tài-zǔ approved of his words.
At that time, there was a rumor that Liú Bèi had died,
and all the officials offered congratulations;
but Huàn, having once recommended Bèi as an official,
alone did not offer congratulations.
After several years in office, he died.
Tài-zǔ wept for him,
and bestowed two thousand *hú* of grain.
One order said,
"Give one thousand *hú* of grain from the grand granary to the family of the Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary."
Another order said,
"Give one thousand *hú* of grain from by the wall to the family of Yào-qīng."
Outsiders did not understand its meaning.
The order explained:
"The grain from the grand granary
is according to official regulations;
the grain from by the wall
is for an old friend."
Also, the Emperor heard about Huàn's past resistance against Lǚ Bù,
and asked Huàn's younger cousin, Mǐn:
"How was Huàn's courage or timidity?"
Mǐn replied:
"Huàn appeared gentle and mild,
but when facing great crises
and difficult dangers,
even Bēn and Yù could not surpass him."
Huàn's son, Kǎn,
was also pure, refined, and modest,
inheriting his father's demeanor.
He successively held positions as Commander of a commandery and Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
Earlier,
Huàn's younger cousin, Bà,
was dutiful and capable in administration.
In the early Wèi period, he served as Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and was equally famous with Hé Kuí from the same commandery at that time.
And Bà's son, Liàng,
and Kuí's son, Zēng,
again shared renown and friendship with Kǎn.
Liàng was firm, upright, learned, and principled.
He detested Hé Yàn, Dèng Yáng, and others,
writing essays to criticize them sharply.
He rose to the positions of Administrator of Hé-nán and Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
Bà's younger brother, Huī,
was known for his scholarly simplicity.
Encountering the chaos under Heaven,
he sought refuge in Jiāo-zhōu.
The Minister of Education invited him,
but he did not go.
Huī's younger brother, Mǐn,
possessed martial skills and was fond of hydraulic engineering.
His official position reached River Embankment Usher.
Zhāng Fàn,
courtesy name Gōng-yí,
was from Xiū-wǔ, Hé-nèi.
His grandfather, Xīn,
was Minister of Education of Hàn.
His father, Yán,
was Grand Commandant.
The Grand Tutor Yuán Wěi wanted to marry his daughter to Fàn,
but Fàn declined and did not accept.
He was by nature tranquil and fond of the Way,
indifferent to fame and gain,
and did not accept any summons for office.
His younger brother, Chéng,
courtesy name Gōng-xiān,
was also well-known.
He was summoned for his uprightness,
appointed Gentleman-Consultant,
and transferred to Commander of Yī-què.
When Dǒng Zhuó caused unrest,
Chéng wanted to gather a multitude to join the world in punishing Zhuó.
Chéng's younger brother, Zhāo, who was then a Gentleman-Consultant,
happened to come from Cháng-ān
and said to Chéng:
"Now, if you want to punish Zhuó,
your numbers are no match.
Moreover, to initiate a plan on a whim
and fight with common people from the fields,
when the soldiers are not accustomed to command
and the troops are not trained,
it will be difficult to succeed.
Zhuó, relying on his troops but lacking righteousness,
certainly cannot last long.
It is better to choose a lord to follow,
wait for the opportune moment to act,
and then you can achieve your ambition."
Chéng agreed with this,
so he resigned his seal and sash, traveled incognito back home,
and, with Fàn, sought refuge in Yáng-zhōu.
Yuán Shù prepared rites to invite them,
but Fàn claimed illness and did not go.
Shù did not force him.
He sent Chéng to meet him.
Shù asked:
"In the past, when the Zhōu dynasty declined,
there were the hegemonies of Huán and Wén.
When Qín lost its government,
Hàn succeeded and employed it.
Now, with my extensive territory
and numerous soldiers and people,
I wish to seek the fortune of Duke Huán of Qí
and emulate the footsteps of Emperor Gāo-zǔ.
What do you think?"
Chéng replied:
"It depends on virtue, not on strength.
If one can use virtue to unify the desires of all under Heaven,
even with the resources of a commoner,
one can achieve the accomplishments of a hegemon or king.
This is not difficult.
But if one merely presumptuously emulates,
and acts inopportunely,
abandoned by the multitude,
who can raise him up?"
Shù was displeased.
At this time,
Tài-zǔ was about to campaign against Jì-zhōu.
Shù again asked:
"Now Cáo-gōng, with his meager few thousand troops,
intends to contend against a force of one hundred thousand.
This can be called not knowing one's own strength!
What do you think?"
Chéng then said:
"Although Hàn's virtue has declined,
Heaven's mandate has not changed.
Now Cáo-gōng holds the Son of Heaven to command all under Heaven.
Even contending against a million troops is acceptable."
Shù's expression changed, showing displeasure,
and Chéng left.
Tài-zǔ平Jì-zhōu,
sent an envoy to welcome Fàn.
Fàn remained in Péng-chéng due to illness,
and sent Chéng to meet Tài-zǔ.
Tài-zǔ recommended him for the position of Jiàn-yì Dà-fū.
Fàn's son Líng and Chéng's son Jiǎn were captured by bandits in Shān-dōng.
Fàn went directly to the bandits to plead for his two sons.
The bandits returned Líng to Fàn.
Fàn expressed his gratitude, saying:
"Gentlemen, you have been generous in returning my son.
While it is human nature to love one's own child,
I pity Jiǎn for being so young,
so I request to exchange Líng for him."
The bandits were moved by his words,
and returned both sons to Fàn.
When Tài-zǔ returned from Jīng-zhōu,
Fàn was able to meet him in Chén.
He was appointed Yì-láng
and participated in the Chéng-xiàng's military affairs,
and was greatly respected.
When Tài-zǔ went on campaigns,
he often ordered Fàn and Bǐng Yuán to stay behind,
to guard with the heir apparent.
Tài-zǔ told Wén-dì:
"In all your actions, you must consult these two."
The heir apparent treated them with the respect due to his elders.
He provided relief to the poor and destitute,
leaving nothing for himself.
All orphans and widows, both within and outside the family, turned to him.
He never refused gifts,
but also never used them.
When he left,
he returned them all.
He died in the seventeenth year of Jiàn-ān.
When the state of Wèi was first established,
Chéng served as Chéng-xiàng Cān-jūn Jì-jiǔ and concurrently Zhào-jùn Tàishǒu,
and his governance and transformation were widely effective.
When Tài-zǔ was about to go on a western campaign,
he summoned Chéng to participate in military affairs.
He died of illness upon reaching Cháng-ān.
Liáng Mào, courtesy name Bó-fāng,
was a native of Chāng-yì, Shān-yáng.
He was fond of learning in his youth,
and his discussions and arguments were always based on classical texts,
which he used to determine right and wrong.
Tài-zǔ appointed him Sī-kōng Yuàn,
and he was recommended as a high-ranking talent,
then appointed Shì-yù-shǐ.
At that time, Tài-shān had many bandits.
Mào was made Tài-shān Tàishǒu.
Within a month,
over a thousand families carrying their infants arrived.
He was then transferred to be Lè-làng Tàishǒu.
Gōng-sūn Dù was in Liáo-dōng,
and he arbitrarily detained Mào,
not allowing him to take up his post,
but Mào ultimately did not yield.
Dù said to Mào and his generals:
"I hear that Cáo-gōng is campaigning far away,
and Yè has no defenses.
Now I wish to take thirty thousand infantry
and ten thousand cavalry
directly to Yè.
Who can stop me?"
All the generals said:
"Indeed."
He then looked at Mào and said:
"What do you think?"
Mào replied:
"Recently, the empire was in great chaos,
and the altars of soil and grain were on the verge of collapse.
The General commanded an army of one hundred thousand,
and sat idly watching the outcome.
Is this how a subject should behave?
Cáo-gōng was concerned about the nation's peril and ruin,
and pitied the suffering of the common people.
He led a righteous army to punish the wicked for the world.
His achievements are high and his virtue widespread;
he can be said to be unparalleled.
It is because the empire has just been settled
and the people have only just begun to find peace
that he has not yet held the General accountable for his offenses!
Yet the General now wishes to raise an army and head west.
The outcome of survival or destruction
will be decided in less than a morning.
General, please consider this carefully!"
When the generals heard Mào's words,
they were all shaken.
After a long while,
Dù said:
"Lord Liáng is right."
Later, he was summoned and promoted to Wèi-jùn Tàishǒu and Gān-líng Xiàng,
and achieved success wherever he served.
When Wén-dì was Wǔ-guān Jiàng,
Mào was selected as Cháng-shǐ,
and then promoted to Zuǒ-jūn-shī.
When the state of Wèi was first established,
he was promoted to Shàng-shū Pú-yè,
and later served as Zhōng-wèi Fèng-cháng.
While Wén-dì was in the Eastern Palace,
Mào again served as Tài-zǐ Tài-fù,
and was greatly respected.
He died in office.
Guó Yuān, courtesy name Zǐ-ní,
was a native of Gài, Lè-ān.
He studied under Zhèng Xuán.
Later, he, along with Bǐng Yuán, Guǎn Níng, and others, fled to Liáo-dōng to escape the chaos.
After returning to his homeland,
Tài-zǔ appointed him Sī-kōng Yuàn-shǔ.
In public court discussions,
he always spoke frankly and with stern countenance,
without any private agenda upon his retreat.
Tài-zǔ wanted to widely establish military agricultural colonies (tún-tián)
and made Yuān supervise these affairs.
Yuān repeatedly presented proposals for improvements and disadvantages,
surveyed the land to settle the people,
allocated officials according to the population,
and clarified the laws of merit and labor.
Within five years, granaries were full,
and the people eagerly encouraged each other to work happily.
When Tài-zǔ campaigned in Guān-zhōng,
he made Yuān Jū-fǔ Cháng-shǐ,
to oversee remaining affairs.
Tián Yín and Sū Bó rebelled in Hé-jiān.
After Yín and others were defeated,
there were still remnants of their faction,
all of whom were subject to execution.
Yuān believed they were not the principal instigators
and requested that they not be executed.
Tài-zǔ agreed,
and over a thousand people were saved thanks to Yuān.
According to old practice, in documents reporting on defeated bandits,
the number (of captured or killed) was exaggerated tenfold.
However, when Yuān reported the number of heads,
it was the actual figure.
Tài-zǔ asked him why.
Yuān said:
"When campaigning against external enemies,
exaggerating the number of slain and captured
is meant to display great military might
and also to show it to the people.
Hé-jiān is within our borders,
and Yín and others rebelled.
Although we achieved victory and gained merit,
I am privately ashamed of it."
Tài-zǔ was greatly pleased,
and promoted him to Wèi-jùn Tàishǒu.
At that time, there were those who sent anonymous letters to slander.
Tài-zǔ detested this
and wanted to absolutely know the culprit.
Yuān requested to keep the original letter
without revealing it.
The letter frequently quoted the "Èr Jīng Fù."
Yuān instructed his Gōng-cáo, saying:
"This commandery is large,
and now it is in the imperial capital,
yet there are few learned people.
Select some intelligent young men
whom I wish to send to a teacher."
The Gōng-cáo selected three people.
When they were about to be sent, Yuān summoned them for an audience
and instructed them:
"What you have learned is insufficient.
The 'Èr Jīng Fù'
is a book of extensive knowledge.
People of this world overlook it,
and few have a teacher for it.
You can seek out someone who can read it and learn from them."
He also secretly conveyed his intention.
Within ten days, someone who could read it was found,
and he then went to receive instruction.
An official then requested him to write a memorial,
and by comparing it with the anonymous letter,
it matched the handwriting of the letter writer.
He was arrested and interrogated,
and the full truth was uncovered.
Yuān was promoted to Tài-pú.
Holding the position of a high minister,
he dressed simply and ate plainly.
His salary and gifts he distributed to his old friends and relatives,
maintaining himself with reverence and frugality.
He died in office.
Tián Chóu 字 Zǐtài,
a native of Wúzhōng, Yòuběipíng.
He loved to read
and was skilled at swordsmanship.
In the first year of Chūpíng (190 CE),
volunteer armies arose,
and Dǒng Zhuó moved the Emperor to Cháng'ān.
Liú Yú, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, sighed and said:
“Rebellious ministers create chaos,
the imperial court is scattered and adrift.
The four seas are suddenly in disarray,
and no one has a firm resolve.
I am a kinsman of the imperial house, an elder,
and cannot allow myself to be like the common crowd.
Now I wish to serve as an envoy and demonstrate my loyalty as a minister;
how can I find a man who will not disgrace the mission?”
The multitude all said:
“Although Tián Chóu is young,
many praise his exceptional talent.”
Chóu was then twenty-two years old.
Yú then prepared a formal reception to meet him,
and was greatly pleased with him.
He then appointed him as an attendant official,
and provided him with a carriage and cavalry.
As he was about to depart,
Chóu said:
“Now the roads are blocked,
and bandits and rebels roam freely.
To act as an official envoy
will make one a target for all.
I wish to travel privately,
only aiming to reach my destination.”
Yú agreed to this.
Chóu then returned home,
personally selected his family retainers and twenty young, brave, strong men who wished to follow, and they all set off together.
Yú personally went out to bid them farewell and sent them off.
After taking to the road,
Chóu then ascended the Western Pass,
exited the frontier,
skirted the north,
went directly to Shuòfāng,
followed a secluded path,
and finally reached Cháng'ān to deliver the message.
An imperial edict appointed him as a Cavalry Commandant.
Chóu believed that the Son of Heaven was still in distress and not yet settled,
and he should not accept such an honor and favor.
He firmly declined and did not accept.
The court highly esteemed his righteousness.
The Three Excellencies all invited him,
but he did not accept any of them.
Upon receiving a report,
he rushed back.
Before he arrived,
Yú had already been killed by Gōngsūn Zàn.
When Chóu arrived,
he paid his respects and offered sacrifices at Yú’s tomb,
presented the memorial and report,
wept, and then left.
Zàn was furious when he heard of this,
and put out a reward for Chóu.
When Chóu was captured, Zàn said to him:
“Why did you weep at Liú Yú’s tomb,
but did not send the memorial and report to me?”
Chóu replied:
“The Hàn dynasty is in decline,
and people harbor divergent ambitions.
Only Lord Liú maintained his loyalty and integrity.
The content of the memorial and report
would not be pleasing to you, General,
and I feared it was not what you would enjoy hearing,
so I did not present it.
Moreover, General, you are now undertaking a great enterprise to achieve your desires.
Having already destroyed an innocent ruler,
you now seek to retaliate against a minister who upheld righteousness.
If you truly carry out this act,
then the scholars of Yān and Zhào will all leap into the Eastern Sea and die;
how could anyone bear to follow you, General?”
Zàn admired his reply
and released him without executing him.
He detained him in the army camp,
forbidding his old acquaintances from communicating with him.
Someone persuaded Zàn, saying:
“Tián Chóu is a righteous man.
If you cannot treat him with courtesy,
and instead imprison him,
I fear you will lose popular support.”
Zàn then released Chóu.
Chóu returned north,
leading his entire clan and several hundred followers,
and swore an oath by sweeping the ground, saying:
“If I do not avenge my lord,
I cannot stand in this world!”
He then entered the Xúwú Shān mountains,
built settlements in deep, dangerous, yet open and flat areas, and resided there,
personally farming to support his parents.
The common people came to him,
and within a few years, there were over five thousand households.
Chóu said to the elders:
“Gentlemen, you have not considered me unworthy,
and have come from afar to join me.
Though many have established settlements,
there is no unified leadership,
which I fear is not the way to lasting peace.
I wish to recommend and select a worthy elder to be your leader.”
They all said:
“Good.”
They unanimously nominated Chóu.
Chóu said:
“Our being here now
is not merely for temporary safety;
we are planning a great undertaking
to avenge and wash away our shame.
I secretly fear that before our aspirations are realized,
frivolous individuals will harass each other,
seeking momentary pleasure,
without deep foresight or long-term planning.
I have a humble plan;
I wish to implement it with you all.
Is that acceptable?”
They all said:
“Acceptable.”
Chóu then established laws concerning murder, injury, theft, and disputes.
The heaviest penalty was death,
the next was punishment for a crime,
totaling over twenty articles.
He also instituted rites for marriage and weddings,
promoted schools and teaching,
and put these into practice among the populace.
Everyone found them convenient,
to the point where nothing was picked up from the roads.
The northern border tribes were all convinced by his authority and trustworthiness.
The Wūwán and Xiānbēi both sent interpreters as envoys to offer tribute and gifts.
Chóu welcomed and appeased them all,
ordering them not to be bandits.
Yuán Shào repeatedly sent envoys to invite him,
and even immediately bestowed upon him a general’s seal,
thereby offering him the chance to pacify and control his subordinates.
Chóu refused to accept them all.
After Shào’s death,
his son Shàng also invited him,
but Chóu still did not go.
Tián Chóu 常 Cháng had always resented that the Wūhuán had frequently plundered and killed the officials of his commandery.
He wished to attack them, but lacked the strength to do so.
In the twelfth year of Jiàn'ān,
Tàizǔ marched north to campaign against the Wūhuán.
Before he arrived,
he first sent an envoy to summon Tián Chóu,
and also ordered Tián Yù to convey his intentions.
Tián Chóu instructed his retainers to quickly prepare for travel.
His retainers said to him:
“Previously, Yuán Gōng admired you,
and offered you appointments five times,
but you, out of principle, did not yield;
now, Cáo Gōng sends an envoy once and you act as if you fear not being able to reach him in time.
Why is this?”
Tián Chóu smiled and replied:
“This is not something you would understand.”
So he followed the envoy to the army,
where he was appointed as Sīkōng Hùcáo Yuàn,
and granted an audience for counsel.
The next day, an order was issued, saying:
“Tián Zǐtài is not one whom I should treat as a subordinate.”
He was immediately nominated as a Máocái,
and appointed as the Magistrate of Tiáolìng.
He did not proceed to his post,
but instead followed the army to Wúzhōng.
At that time, it was summer, and there were heavy rains.
The coastal areas were low-lying,
muddy and impassable.
The barbarians also blocked key paths,
preventing the army from advancing.
Tàizǔ was troubled by this,
and consulted Tián Chóu.
Tián Chóu said:
“This road
is always underwater during autumn and summer;
it is too shallow for carriages and horses,
and too deep for boats and ships.
It has been a difficulty for a long time.
The former administrative seat of Běipíng Commandery was at Pínggāng,
and the road passed through Lúlóng,
reaching Liǔchéng.
Since Jiànwǔ,
it has been ruined and cut off,
for nearly two hundred years,
but there is still a small path that can be followed.
The barbarians will now assume that the main army will either advance from Wúzhōng
or retreat if it cannot advance,
and they will be lax and unprepared.
If we silently turn back the army,
pass through Lúlóngkǒu, traverse the danger of Báitán,
and emerge into unoccupied territory,
the path will be short and convenient.
Catching them off guard,
Tàdùn’s head can be taken without a battle.”
Tàizǔ said:
“Excellent.”
Thereupon, he led the army back,
and erected a large wooden marker by the water and roadside, saying:
“It is now hot summer,
the roads are impassable.
We shall await autumn and winter,
and then advance the army again.”
The barbarian scouts saw this,
and truly believed that the main army had departed.
Tàizǔ ordered Tián Chóu to lead his followers as guides,
ascend Mount Xúwú,
pass through Lúlóng,
cross Pínggāng,
and ascend Báilángduī.
When they were over two hundred *lǐ* from Liǔchéng,
the barbarians were finally alarmed.
The *Chányú* personally took to the field,
and Tàizǔ engaged him in battle,
achieving a great victory,
pursuing the fleeing enemy
to Liǔchéng.
When the army returned within the pass,
rewards were discussed and titles conferred.
Tián Chóu was enfeoffed as a Tínghóu,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
Tián Chóu considered that he had initially been in a difficult situation,
and led his followers in escape.
His righteous aspirations had not been established,
yet he benefited from it,
which was not his original intention.
He firmly declined.
Tàizǔ knew his sincerity,
and agreed not to force him.
When the head of Yuán Shàng was sent from Liáodōng,
an order was issued that
“anyone in the three armies who dares to weep for him shall be executed.”
As Tián Chóu had once been summoned by Yuán Shàng,
he went to mourn and offer sacrifices.
Tàizǔ did not question him.
Tián Chóu brought all his family members and three hundred clansmen to reside in Yè.
Tàizǔ bestowed upon Tián Chóu carriages, horses, grain, and silk,
all of which he distributed among his clan and acquaintances.
Upon returning from the campaign against Jīngzhōu,
Tàizǔ recalled Tián Chóu’s outstanding merits,
and regretted having previously accepted Tián Chóu’s refusal.
He said:
“This was fulfilling the will of one man,
but diminishing the great statutes of the royal law.”
Thereupon, he again offered Tián Chóu his previous title.
Tián Chóu submitted a memorial expressing his sincerity,
swearing by his death.
Tàizǔ did not listen,
and wished to appoint him,
doing so several times,
but he ultimately refused.
The officials impeached Tián Chóu for being stubborn and contrary to the Way,
and for merely upholding trivial principles,
suggesting he should be dismissed from office and punished.
Tàizǔ considered the matter grave,
and deliberated for a long time.
He then convened the heir apparent and the high ministers for a broad discussion.
The heir apparent equated Tián Chóu with Zǐwén who declined emoluments,
and Shēn Xū who avoided rewards,
suggesting that his integrity should be honored by not taking away his right to decline.
The Shàngshūlìng Xún Yù and Sīlì Xiàowèi Zhōng Yáo also believed it was acceptable to agree.
Tàizǔ still wished to enfeoff him.
Tián Chóu had always been on good terms with Xiàhóu Dūn.
Tàizǔ said to Xiàhóu Dūn:
“Please go and explain the situation to him with emotion.
Just speak as if it is your own suggestion;
do not reveal my intention.”
Xiàhóu Dūn stayed overnight with Tián Chóu,
following Tàizǔ’s instructions.
Tián Chóu surmised Tàizǔ’s intention,
and did not speak further.
As Xiàhóu Dūn was leaving,
he patted Tián Chóu’s back and said:
“Master Tián,
His Lord’s intentions are earnest;
can you truly not consider them?”
Tián Chóu replied:
“How can you speak so wrongly!
Chóu
is merely a man who abandoned righteousness and fled.
To have received grace and been saved
is already exceedingly fortunate.
How could I sell the pass of Lúlóng
in exchange for rewards and emoluments?
Even if the state were to pardon Chóu,
would Chóu not be ashamed in his heart?
General, you who know Chóu so well,
still persist in this manner.
If it absolutely cannot be avoided,
I beg to commit suicide by slitting my throat before you.”
Before he finished speaking,
tears streamed down his face.
Xiàhóu Dūn reported everything to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ sighed, knowing he could not be swayed,
and thereupon appointed him as Yìláng.
He died at the age of forty-six.
His son had also died young.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he honored Tián Chóu’s virtue and righteousness,
and bestowed upon Tián Chóu’s descendant, his great-grandson Xù, the title of Guānnèi Hóu,
to maintain his lineage.
Wáng Xiū (王脩), courtesy name Shúzhì (叔治),
was a native of Yínglíng (營陵) in Běihǎi (北海).
At the age of seven, he lost his mother.
His mother had died on the day of the Shè (社) festival.
The following year, when his neighbors held the Shè festival,
Xiū (脩) was deeply moved remembering his mother,
and his grief was profound.
When the neighbors heard of this,
they ceased their festival for him.
At twenty,
he traveled to Nányáng (南陽) for study,
staying at Zhāng Fèng's (張奉) house.
Fèng's (奉) entire household fell ill,
and there was no one to look after them.
Xiū (脩) personally attended to and cared for them,
and only left after they recovered.
During the Chūpíng (初平) era,
Kǒng Róng (孔融) of Běihǎi (北海) summoned him and appointed him Registrar (主簿),
and later Magistrate (令) of Gāomì (高密).
The Sūn (孫) clan of Gāomì (高密) had always been powerful and chivalrous,
and their retainers often broke the law.
When some commoners robbed each other,
the bandits entered the Sūn (孫) clan's residence,
and the officials were unable to apprehend them.
Xiū (脩) led officials and commoners to surround the residence.
The Sūn (孫) clan resisted,
and the officials and commoners, intimidated, dared not approach.
Xiū (脩) ordered the officials and commoners:
"Anyone who dares not attack will be equally guilty!"
The Sūn (孫) clan, fearing,
then surrendered the bandits.
From this, the powerful and influential were subdued.
He was recommended as Xiàolián (孝廉),
but Xiū (脩) deferred to Bǐng Yuán (邴原),
which Róng (融) did not permit.
At that time, the world was in chaos,
so he ultimately did not take up the position.
Shortly after,
there were rebels in the commandery.
When Xiū (脩) heard that Róng (融) was in distress,
he rushed to Róng (融)'s aid by night.
When the rebellion first broke out,
Róng (融) said to his attendants:
"The only one who would brave this danger to come
is Wáng Xiū (王脩)!"
No sooner had he spoken than Xiū (脩) arrived.
He was again appointed Chief Clerk (功曹).
At that time, Jiāodōng (膠東) was plagued by many bandits,
so Xiū (脩) was again ordered to serve as Magistrate of Jiāodōng (膠東).
Gōngshā Lú (公沙盧), a man from Jiāodōng (膠東), was strong and influential.
He built his own encampments and trenches,
and refused to respond to levies and conscriptions.
Xiū (脩) alone, leading a few horsemen, rode directly into his gate,
and cut down Lú (盧) and his brothers.
The Gōngshā (公沙) clan was shocked and dared not move.
Xiū (脩) appeased the rest,
and from then on, banditry largely ceased.
Whenever Róng (融) was in difficulty,
even if Xiū (脩) was on leave at home,
he always came to his aid.
Róng (融) often relied on Xiū (脩) to escape danger.
When Yuán Tán (袁譚) was in Qīngzhōu (青州),
he appointed Xiū (脩) as Chief Clerk (治中從事).
The Supervisor of the Household (別駕), Liú Xiàn (劉獻), frequently slandered Xiū (脩).
Later, Xiàn (獻) was due to be executed for an offense,
but Xiū (脩) interceded for him,
and he was spared.
