People at the time greatly praised this.
Yuán Shào (袁紹) also appointed Xiū (脩) as Magistrate of Jìmò (即墨),
and later he again served as Tán's (譚) Supervisor of the Household (別駕).
When Shào (紹) died,
Tán (譚) and Shàng (尚) had a rift.
Shàng (尚) attacked Tán (譚),
and Tán's (譚) army was defeated.
Xiū (脩) led officials and commoners to rescue Tán (譚).
Tán (譚) joyfully said:
"The one who forms my army
is Supervisor Wáng (王別駕)!"
When Tán (譚) was defeated,
Liú Xún (劉詢) raised an army in Luòyīn (漯陰),
and all the cities responded.
Tán (譚) sighed and said:
"Now the entire province has revolted,
is it because of my lack of virtue?"
Xiū (脩) said:
"Though the Administrator of Dōnglái (東萊), Guǎn Tǒng (管統), is across the sea,
this man will not revolt.
He will surely come."
After more than ten days,
Tǒng (統) indeed abandoned his wife and children and came to Tán's (譚) aid.
His wife and children were killed by bandits.
Tán (譚) then appointed Tǒng (統) as Administrator of Lè'ān (樂安).
Tán (譚) again wanted to attack Shàng (尚).
Xiū (脩) admonished him, saying:
"For brothers to attack each other
is the path to defeat and ruin."
Tán (譚) was displeased,
but he recognized Xiū's (脩) integrity.
Later, he again asked Xiū (脩):
"What is the plan?"
Xiū (脩) replied:
"Brothers
are like left and right hands.
It is like a man about to fight, who cuts off his right hand,
and then says, 'I will surely win.'
Is such a thing possible?
If one abandons brothers and does not show affection,
who in the world will show affection to him?
There are often slanderers
who will sow discord between them
to seek momentary gain.
I wish you, my lord, would cover your ears and not listen to them.
If you execute a few sycophants,
and restore your kinship and harmony
to resist the four directions,
you can roam freely throughout the world."
Tán (譚) did not listen,
and proceeded to attack Shàng (尚),
seeking help from Tàizǔ (太祖).
After Tàizǔ (太祖) defeated Jìzhōu (冀州),
Tán (譚) again rebelled.
Tàizǔ (太祖) then led his army to attack Tán (譚) at Nánpí (南皮).
Xiū (脩) was then transporting grain in Lè'ān (樂安).
Hearing that Tán (譚) was in dire straits,
he led his troops and several dozen subordinates to Tán's (譚) aid.
When he reached Gāomì (高密),
he heard of Tán's (譚) death.
He dismounted and cried out:
"Without a lord, where shall I return?"
He then went to Tàizǔ (太祖)
and begged to collect and bury Tán's (譚) body.
Tàizǔ (太祖), wishing to observe Xiū's (脩) intentions,
remained silent and did not respond.
Xiū (脩) again said:
"I received great kindness from the Yuán (袁) clan.
If I can collect Tán's (譚) body,
and then suffer execution,
I will have no regrets."
Tàizǔ (太祖) praised his righteousness
and allowed it.
He appointed Xiū (脩) as Superintendent of Military Grain (督軍糧),
and he returned to Lè'ān (樂安).
After Tán's (譚) defeat,
all the cities submitted,
except for Guǎn Tǒng (管統) in Lè'ān (樂安), who did not obey.
Tàizǔ (太祖) ordered Xiū (脩) to bring Tǒng's (統) head.
Xiū (脩), considering Tǒng (統) a loyal minister of a fallen state,
released him from his bonds
and sent him to Tàizǔ (太祖).
Tàizǔ (太祖) was pleased and pardoned him.
The Yuán (袁) clan's administration was lenient,
and many in positions of power accumulated wealth.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) captured Yè (鄴),
he confiscated the properties and assets of Shěn Pèi's (審配) household, amounting to tens of thousands.
When Nánpí (南皮) was captured,
Xiū's (脩) house was searched;
there was less than ten hù (斛) of grain,
and several hundred rolls of books.
Tàizǔ (太祖) sighed and said:
"A scholar does not gain fame without reason."
He then courteously appointed him Clerk to the Grand Minister of Works (司空掾),
acting Colonel Director of Metals (司金中郎將),
and promoted him to Administrator of Wèijùn (魏郡).
In his administration,
he curbed the strong and supported the weak,
and made rewards and punishments clear,
and the common people praised him.
When the state of Wèi (魏) was established,
he became Grand Minister of Agriculture (大司農郎中令).
Tàizǔ (太祖) discussed implementing corporal punishment,
but Xiū (脩) believed it was not yet feasible,
and Tàizǔ (太祖) adopted his suggestion.
He was transferred to become Minister of Ceremonies (奉尚).
Later, Yán Cái (嚴才) rebelled,
and with several dozen followers, attacked the Yèmén (掖門) gate.
When Xiū (脩) heard of the disturbance,
before his carriage and horses arrived,
he immediately led his subordinates on foot to the palace gate.
Tàizǔ (太祖), observing from the Tóngjuè (銅爵) Terrace,
said:
"The one coming is surely Wáng Shúzhì (王叔治)."
Chancellor Zhōng Yáo (鍾繇) said to Xiū (脩):
"It is an old custom that
when there is trouble in the capital,
the Nine Ministers each stay in their respective offices."
Xiū (脩) replied:
"If one eats their salary,
how can one avoid their danger?
Staying in one's office, though customary,
is not the righteousness of rushing to danger."
Shortly after,
he died in office from illness.
His son, Zhōng (忠),
rose to the positions of Administrator of Dōnglái (東萊) and Cavalier-in-Ordinary (散騎常侍).
Initially,
Xiū (脩) recognized Gāo Róu (高柔) when he was barely twenty,
and regarded Wáng Jī (王基) as extraordinary in his childhood.
Both eventually achieved great distinction,
and the world praised him for his discerning judgment of people.
Bǐng Yuán
had the courtesy name Gēnjǔ and was a native of Zhūxū, Běihǎi.
While young, he and Guǎn Níng were both known for their integrity and lofty aspirations,
and they both refused invitations from the provincial and commandery administrations.
When the Yellow Turbans arose,
Yuán led his family into the sea,
residing on Mount Yùzhōu.
At that time, Kǒng Róng was the Administrator of Běihǎi
and recommended Yuán for his virtue.
Yuán, seeing the Yellow Turbans were flourishing,
then went to Liáodōng.
He and Liú Zhèng, who was from the same commandery, both possessed courage, strategy, and heroic spirit.
Gōngsūn Dù, the Grand Administrator of Liáodōng, feared and detested them and wanted to kill them.
He arrested all of Zhèng's family,
but Zhèng managed to escape.
Dù announced to all the counties:
"Anyone who dares to hide Zhèng will be considered guilty of the same crime."
Zhèng, in dire straits,
went to seek refuge with Yuán.
Yuán hid him for over a month.
At that time, Tàishǐ Cí of Dōnglái was about to return,
so Yuán entrusted Zhèng to him.
Soon after, he said to Dù:
"General, the other day you wanted to kill Liú Zhèng,
considering him a harm to yourself.
Now that Zhèng has left,
is not your harm removed?"
Dù said:
"Indeed."
Yuán said:
"You feared Zhèng
because of his intelligence.
Now that Zhèng has escaped,
his intelligence will be put to use.
Why still detain Zhèng's family?
It would be better to pardon them
and avoid increasing resentment."
Dù then released them.
Yuán also provided funds and transportation for Zhèng's family,
and they all returned to their home commandery.
While Yuán was in Liáodōng,
hundreds of families came to reside with him within a year.
The voices of scholars pursuing knowledge
and teaching
were ceaseless.
Later, he was able to return,
and Tàizǔ appointed him as a Clerk for the Minister of Works.
Yuán's daughter died young,
and at that time Tàizǔ's beloved son, Cāngshū, also passed away.
Tàizǔ wished to have them buried together,
but Yuán declined, saying:
"Joint burial
is not in accordance with ritual.
The reason I am able to gain the favor of Your Illustrious Lord,
and the reason Your Lord treats me as you do,
is because I can uphold the traditional principles without changing them.
If I were to follow Your Illustrious Lord's command,
then I would be an ordinary person.
How then would Your Illustrious Lord value me?"
Tàizǔ then stopped,
and transferred him to be an Assistant to the Chancellor for General Affairs.
Cuī Yǎn, as the Eastern Bureau Chief,
recorded a humble suggestion, saying:
"Assistant to the Chancellor Bǐng Yuán and Counsellor Zhāng Fàn
both possess pure and excellent virtue,
and their aspirations and conduct are loyal and upright.
Their purity and tranquility are sufficient to improve customs,
and their integrity and steadfastness are sufficient to handle affairs.
They are truly 'dragon's sinews and phoenix's wings,'
precious treasures of the state.
If they are promoted and employed,
the unrighteous will keep their distance."
He succeeded Liáng Mào as Chief Clerk to the General of the Five Garrisons,
kept his gates closed,
and did not go out except for public matters.
Tàizǔ campaigned against Wú,
and Yuán accompanied him,
and died.
After this, Zhāng Tàiy of Jùlù, Grand Minister of the Court, and Páng Dí of Fúfēng, Governor of Hénán, were known for their purity and wisdom;
Zhāng Gé of Dōngjùn, Grand Coachman of Yǒngníng, was known for his simplicity and integrity.
Guǎn Níng,
whose courtesy name was Yòu'ān, was a native of Zhūxū, Běihǎi.
At sixteen, he lost his father.
His relatives sympathized with his orphanhood and poverty,
and all together offered him condolences and burial gifts,
but he declined to accept them all,
and provided for the funeral according to his own means.
He was eight feet tall
and had fine eyebrows and beard.
He befriended Huá Xīn of Píngyuán and Bǐng Yuán, his fellow townsman,
and they all studied together in other regions,
and both highly respected Chén Zhònggōng.
When the world fell into great chaos,
he heard that Gōngsūn Dù's orders were effective overseas,
so he went to Liáodōng with Yuán and Wáng Liè of Píngyuán, among others.
Dù prepared a guest house for them.
After arriving and meeting Dù,
he built a hut in a mountain valley.
At that time, many refugees lived south of the commandery,
but Níng lived north,
showing no intention of moving.
Later, people gradually came to follow him.
Tàizǔ became Minister of Works
and invited Níng,
but Dù's son, Kāng, suppressed the order and did not announce it.
Wáng Liè,
whose courtesy name was Yànfāng,
was at that time more renowned than Yuán and Níng.
He resigned from being Gōngsūn Dù's Chief Clerk
and disgraced himself by engaging in commerce.
Tàizǔ appointed him as a Clerk for the Chancellor
and Assistant to the Chancellor for General Affairs,
but he died overseas
before arriving.
As China became stable,
all the guests returned,
only Guǎn Níng remained at peace, as if he were about to die.
In the fourth year of Huángchū,
an imperial edict ordered the dukes and ministers to recommend gentlemen of independent character.
Sītú Huá Xīn recommended Guǎn Níng.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he summoned Guǎn Níng.
Guǎn Níng then took his family and traveled by sea back to the commandery.
Gōngsūn Gōng saw him off at the southern suburbs,
and bestowed additional clothes and articles upon him.
From the time Guǎn Níng went east,
all the provisions and gifts Dù, Kāng, and Gōng had given him successively
he accepted and stored away.
Once he had crossed to the west,
he returned all of them.
An edict appointed Guǎn Níng as Tàizhōng Dàfū,
but he steadfastly declined it.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
Tàiwèi Huá Xīn yielded his position, offering it to Guǎn Níng.
An imperial edict was then issued, stating:
"Tàizhōng Dàfū Guǎn Níng
is deeply devoted to morality and virtue,
and embraces the Six Arts.
His purity and detachment are sufficient to match the ancients,
and his integrity and impartiality can serve the present age.
In the past, he encountered a decline and deficiency in the Way of Kings,
and fled by sea to live in seclusion.
When Great Wèi received the mandate,
he arrived, carrying his family.
This is indeed the way of the 应lóng (responding dragon) rising and descending,
and the principle of sages and worthies choosing to serve or withdraw.
However, since Huángchū,
summonses have been sent repeatedly,
yet each time he has cited illness
and refused to come.
Is it that the government of the court
has a different pursuit from his life?
Or does he simply enjoy the peace and happiness of the mountains and forests,
and having gone there, cannot return?
Even with the sageliness of Duke Jī,
if his virtue did not descend,
then the singing birds would not be heard.
Even with the worthiness of Duke Mù of Qín,
he still sought counsel from the yellow-haired elders.
How much more so for a man of meager virtue like Us,
how can We not wish to hear the Way from you, Sir?
We now appoint Guǎn Níng as Guānglù Xūn.
In rites, there is a great principle of human relations;
the way between ruler and minister
cannot be abolished.
We hope you will surely arrive quickly,
and fulfill Our wishes."
He further issued an edict to the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, saying:
"Guǎn Níng embraces the Way and holds fast to his integrity,
hiding himself in a corner of the sea.
Though summonses have been sent down repeatedly,
he has disobeyed the order and not come,
lingering contentedly in his dwelling,
holding his affairs in high esteem.
While he possesses the integrity of a reclusive gentleman with pure conduct,
he has lost the principle of piety and reverence like Kǎofù.
This has caused Us to hold an empty heart and stretch Our neck for years;
what can this mean?
If he merely wishes to live in peace,
and insists on pursuing his own will,
does he not consider that even the ancients also changed their principles and restored the people to greatness?
Days pass, months go by,
time has already passed.
To cleanse oneself and bathe in virtue,
what will it be for?
Zhòngní (Confucius) said: 'If I do not associate with the people of this world, with whom shall I associate?'
Therefore, order the Biéjià Cóngshì, Jùnchéng, and Yuàn
to respectfully convey the edict and dispatch Guǎn Níng with proper rites to the temporary imperial residence,
providing him with an ānchē (comfortable carriage), attendants, mats and bedding, and food along the way.
Report back first once he is on his journey."
Guǎn Níng, calling himself a subject from the wilds, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your humble servant, a solitary and insignificant person from the seashore,
is a retired farmer without companions.
My destiny has fortunately been bountiful.
I have undeservedly received Your Majesty's succession to the grand heritage,
Your virtue matching the Three August Ones.
Your transforming influence overflows even Táng.
For a long time, I have enjoyed Your abundant grace,
for twelve years,
yet I have been unable to repay Your Majesty's blessings of grace and nurture.
Suffering from a severe and chronic illness,
I have been confined to bed, lingering.
I have thus evaded the duties of a subject and reversed the proper order,
trembling in fear day and night,
having no place to put myself.
In the eleventh month of the first year, I received an order from the Gōngchē Sīmǎ Lìng, sent down to the province and commandery.
In the eighth month, on the day of Jiǎshēn, an imperial edict summoned me,
further granting me an ānchē, clothes, bedding,
and dispatching me with proper rites.
Honor and favor came together,
gracious orders arrived repeatedly.
I was startled and held my breath,
my heart saddened and my plans lost.
I wished to present my case,
to express my foolish sentiments,
but the clear edict restricted me,
not allowing me to even slightly revise a memorial.
Thus, I have been suppressed,
until today.
I truly thought that the heavenly canopy's
grace had a limit,
I did not expect the spiritual nourishment
to become even more grand and glorious.
I respectfully received the imperial edict of the twelfth month of the third year, issued by the province and commandery in the second month of this year, on the day of Xīnyǒu,
again granting an ānchē and clothes.
The Biéjià Cóngshì and the Jùn Gōngcáo were to dispatch me with proper rites.
Furthermore, I specifically received a sealed imperial letter,
appointing me as Guānglù Xūn,
personally holding the virtue of humility,
drawing analogies to Zhōu and Qín,
to benefit the lower ranks by diminishing the higher.
On the day I received the edict,
my spirit scattered,
with nowhere to throw myself to death.
Your humble servant repeatedly reflected and measured myself;
my virtue is not like Yuán or Qǐ, yet I receive the honor of an ānchē;
my merit is not like Dòu Róng, yet I receive the favor of a sealed imperial letter.
I am a mere prop or rafter, incompetent,
yet burdened with the responsibility of a ridgepole.
My life is on the verge of ending,
yet I am granted the position of a Jiǔjí.
I fear the calamity of Zhū Bó's omen.
Moreover, age and illness invade daily,
increasing without lessening.
I am unable to be carried and proceed on the road to fulfill this heavy responsibility.
I longingly gaze at the palace gates,
hesitating before the imperial court.
I respectfully submit this memorial to express my feelings,
begging for Your compassionate consideration,
to suppress Your grace and allow me to withdraw,
lest my bones fill the roadways."
From Huángchū to Qīnglóng,
summonses continued,
always granting cattle and wine in the eighth month.
An imperial edict asked Chéng Xǐ, the Inspector of Qīngzhōu:
"Is Guǎn Níng upholding his integrity as a recluse,
or is he truly old and infirm?"
Chéng Xǐ reported:
"Guǎn Gòng, a member of Guǎn Níng's clan, serves as a provincial official
and lives near Guǎn Níng.
Your humble servant often sends him to inquire about Guǎn Níng's situation.
Gòng said: 'Guǎn Níng always wears a black cap, cloth jacket and trousers, and a cloth skirt,
varying them according to the season.
He moves in and out of his house,
able to lean on a staff by himself,
without needing support.
For seasonal sacrifices,
he always exerts himself,
changes into more formal clothes,
and wears a padded turban.
He uses the white cloth plain garment he had in Liáodōng,
personally offering food and drink,
kneeling and bowing to complete the rites.
Guǎn Níng lost his mother young,
and does not remember her appearance,
but always specially adds a cup,
and sheds tears sorrowfully.
His residence is also seventy or eighty paces from the water.
In summer, he goes to the water to wash his hands and feet,
and observes his garden.'
Your humble servant believes Guǎn Níng's intentions in repeatedly declining were
that he himself felt he had grown up in reclusion,
and that his wisdom had declined with old age.
Therefore, he lingered,
always adhering to modesty and humility.
This is Guǎn Níng's strong desire to fully preserve his aspirations and conduct,
not merely to maintain an air of lofty reclusion."
In the second year of Zhèngshǐ,

Tàipú Táo Qiūyī, Yǒngníng Wèiwèi Mèng Guān, Shìzhōng Sūn Yōng, and Zhōngshū Shìláng Wáng Jī recommended Guǎn Níng, saying: "Your subjects have heard that dragons and phoenixes conceal their brilliance,
appearing in response to virtue,
and enlightened wise men withdraw,
moving when the time is right.
Thus, when the luán and zuò birds sang at Qí,
the Way of Zhōu greatly flourished,
and the Four Hoary Ones
assisted,
the Hàn emperor enjoyed peace.
We respectfully observe Tàizhōng Dàfū Guǎn Níng,
who embodies the harmony of the two cosmic forces,
and encompasses the pure virtues of the nine excellences.
He possesses inherent brilliance and pristine quality,
ice-like purity
and profound clarity.
Mysterious, detached, and indifferent,
he roams freely with the Dao;
he delights his mind with Huáng and Lǎo (Huang-Lao thought),
and devotes his will to the Six Arts,
entering their halls and inner chambers,
delving into their profound depths.
He keeps the past and present within his breast

At that time, Zhāng Jiàn
, courtesy name Zǐmíng
, from Jùlù, and Hú Zhāo
, courtesy name Kǒngmíng
, from Yǐngchuān, also cultivated their aspirations and did not take office.
Zhāng Jiàn in his youth traveled to the Imperial Academy
, studying both internal and external (teachings).
Later, he returned to his hometown.
Yuán Shào repeatedly offered him appointments
, but he did not accept them,
and moved to Shàngdǎng.
Gāo Gàn, the Provincial Governor of Bìngzhōu, memorialized to appoint him as Prefect of Lèpíng
, but he did not take the position,
moving instead to Xún in Chángshān.
His followers numbered several hundred,
and he then moved to Rèn County.
When Tàizǔ (Cáo Cāo) was Chancellor
, he summoned him
, but Zhāng Jiàn did not go.
During the Tàihé reign
, an imperial edict sought reclusive scholars capable of averting calamities and addressing anomalies.
The commandery repeatedly recommended Zhāng Jiàn
, and sent for him,
but he did not go due to old age and illness.
Lú Yù, the Grand Administrator of Guǎngpíng, arrived at his post, and on the third day
, his subordinates reported that, following previous practice, they should present an official visiting card to Zhāng Jiàn.
Lú Yù instructed them, saying:
"Mr. Zhāng is someone who 'above does not serve the Son of Heaven
, and below does not befriend feudal lords.'
How could an official visiting card embellish such a person! "
Instead, he sent his Chief Clerk to present a letter with a gift of sheep and wine.
In the fourth year of Qīnglóng, a Xīnhài edict stated:
"In Zhāngyè Commandery, the Xuánchuān River overflowed,
its surging waves stirring up and overflowing,
a precious stone bearing a diagram,
resembling a divine turtle,
settling on the west bank of the river,
majestically standing firm,
its green texture having plain patterns,
with Qílín, Fènghuáng, dragons, and horses
brilliantly formed,
and a text declaring a mandate,
shining clearly.
Gāo Tánglóng, the Grand Astrologer, reported: 'Ancient emperors and sagely rulers have never before received such (a sign).
This is truly an auspicious mandate for Wèi,
a generational treasure of the Eastern Order.' "
The matter was proclaimed throughout the empire.
Yú Chuò, the Prefect of Rèn, repeatedly brought this news to ask Zhāng Jiàn.
Zhāng Jiàn secretly told Yú Chuò:
"Spirit knows the future
, it does not pursue the past.
Auspicious signs appear first, and then decline or prosperity follows.
The Hàn has long perished,
Wèi has already obtained (the empire).
What past prosperity could an auspicious sign pursue?
This stone
is a current anomaly but a future auspicious omen."
In the first year of Zhèngshǐ
, a Hoopoe bird
nested in the shade of Zhāng Jiàn's gate.
Zhāng Jiàn told his household:
"The Hoopoe is a yang bird
, yet it nests in the shade of the gate.
This is an ominous sign."
Thereupon, he picked up his qín and sang,
composing two poems.
Ten days later, he passed away,
at the age of one hundred and five.
That year
, Wáng Sù, the Grand Administrator of Guǎngpíng, arrived at his post
, and instructed the counties under his jurisdiction:
"Previously, when in the capital
, I heard of Zhāng Zǐmíng.
I came to inquire about him
, but he had already passed away.
This causes me great sorrow and regret.
This gentleman was deeply learned and lived in seclusion
, not competing with his contemporaries
, finding joy in the Dao.
In the past, the elder of Jiàng County was mired in mud
, but Zhào Mèng elevated him
, and the feudal lords lived in harmony.
Feeling compassion for his diligent devotion to the Dao in his old age
, yet not receiving honor or favor,
upon receipt of this letter
, send an official to comfort his family
, prominently display a plaque on his gate
, and make every effort to accord him special distinction
, to console the deceased
and encourage those who come after."
Hú Zhāo initially sought refuge in Jìzhōu
, and also declined Yuán Shào's summons
, returning to his hometown.
When Tàizǔ (Cáo Cāo) was Sīkōng and Chancellor
, he repeatedly offered him courteous invitations.
Hú Zhāo went to accept the summons
, and upon arrival
, he stated that he was merely a recluse from the wild
, of no use to the military or the state
, and sincerely requested to leave.
Tàizǔ said:
"Each person has their own aspirations
, and their choices of engagement or withdrawal differ.
Strive to uphold your noble ideals,
it would be unrighteous to force you."
Hú Zhāo then moved to the Lùhún Mountains
, personally farming and finding joy in the Dao
, entertaining himself with classics and books.
The villagers respected and loved him.
In the twenty-third year of Jiàn'ān
, Zhāng Gù, the Prefect of Lùhún, received an order to mobilize male laborers
to be supplied to Hànzhōng.
The common people dreaded the distant service
and were all disturbed.
Mín Sūnláng and others consequently raised troops and killed the county chief clerk
, engaging in rebellion
, and the county was devastated.
Zhāng Gù led over ten officials and soldiers
, staying with Hú Zhāo
, rallying the remaining people
, and restoring stability to the community.
Sūnláng and his group then fled south to join Guān Yǔ.
Guān Yǔ granted them seals and provided them with troops
, and they returned as bandits
, reaching the Chánglè Pavilion south of Lùhún.
They made a mutual oath among themselves
, saying:
"Master Hú is a worthy man
, and no one shall violate his settlement."
The entire valley relied on Hú Zhāo
, and no one was startled or anxious.
When the empire was pacified
, he moved his residence to Yíyáng.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign
, Zhào Yǎn, the General of Agile Cavalry, Huáng Xiū and Guō Yí, Shangshū (Ministers), Xún Yǐ and Zhōng Yù, Sànqí Chángshì (Palace Attendants), Yǔ Ní, Grand Coachman
, Hé Zhēn, Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng, and others
successively recommended Hú Zhāo, saying:
"His natural purity is lofty and unsullied
, and he becomes even more steadfast in old age.
His profound emptiness and quiet simplicity
possess the integrity of Bó Yí and Shú Qí.
He should be summoned
to inspire the customs of the age."
In the second year of Jiāpíng
, a special summons was sent via public carriage
, but he passed away before it arrived
, at the age of eighty-nine.
His son, Hú Zuǎn, was appointed Lángzhōng.
Originally
, Hú Zhāo was skilled in clerical script,
and was famous alongside Zhōng Yáo, Hándān Chún, Wèi Jì, and Wéi Dàn.
His calligraphic works
were frequently seen as models.
Appraisal: Yuán Huàn, Bǐng Yuán, and Zhāng Fàn personally embodied purity and detachment
, advancing and retreating according to the Dao.
They were indeed comparable to Gòng Yǔ and the two Gōngs.
Liáng Mào and Guó Yuān were also next in order.
Zhāng Chéng's reputation and conduct were second only to Zhāng Fàn
, truly a capable younger brother.
Tián Chóu upheld his integrity
, Wáng Xiū was loyal and steadfast
, sufficient to rectify the customs;
Guǎn Níng was profound, elegant, and lofty
, resolute and unyielding;
Zhāng Jiàn and Hú Zhāo closed their doors and maintained tranquility
, not seeking to manage worldly affairs: therefore, they are all recorded here.
Biography of Cuī, Máo, Xú, Hé, Xíng, Bào, and Sīmǎ, Chapter Twelve.
Cuī Yǎn
, courtesy name Jìguī, was a native of Dōngwǔchéng, Qīnghé.
In his youth, he was simple and quiet, enjoyed swordsmanship,
and esteemed martial matters.
At twenty-three
, the village recommended him as a Zheng (village elder)
, and he began to feel inspired
, reading the Analects and the Han version of the Book of Songs.
By the age of twenty-nine
, he joined Gōngsūn Fāng and others to study under Zhèng Xuán.
Before a full year of study
, the Yellow Turban bandits of Xúzhōu attacked and broke through Běihǎi
, and Zhèng Xuán and his disciples went to Bùqí Mountain to seek refuge.
At that time, grain was scarce in the county
, and Zhèng Xuán dismissed his students.
Cuī Yǎn, having been sent away
, found the roads infested with bandits
, and the western route impassable.
Therefore, he traveled around the borders of Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, and Yù provinces
, went east to Shòuchūn
, and looked south towards the Jiāng and Hú (rivers/lakes).
After four years away from home, he finally returned
, entertaining himself with the qín and books.
Grand General Yuán Shào 聞 (heard of) and summoned him.
At that time, the soldiers were violent and unrestrained,
digging up graves and mounds.
Yán remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, Xún Qīng (Xúnzǐ) said: 'If soldiers are not instructed beforehand,
their weapons will be ineffective;
even Tāng and Wǔ could not achieve victory in battle.'
Now, exposed bones line the roads,
and the people have not yet seen your virtue.
It is fitting to instruct the commanderies and counties to cover the skeletons and bury the remains,
to show compassion and love,
and to emulate the benevolence of King Wén."
Shào appointed him Cavalry Commandant (Qí Dūwèi).
Later, Shào deployed his troops to Líyáng,
encamping at Yánjīn.
Yán again remonstrated, saying:
"The Son of Heaven is in Xǔ.
The people hope for assistance in maintaining order.
It is better to guard our borders and perform our duties,
to bring peace to the realm."
Shào did not listen,
and consequently was defeated at Guāndù.
When Shào died,
his two sons (Yuán Tán and Yuán Shàng) vied with each other,
both desiring to obtain Yán.
Yán pleaded illness and firmly declined,
and thereby incurred their displeasure,
being imprisoned in the jail.
Thanks to Yīn Kuí and Chén Lín's efforts, he was spared.
Grand Ancestor (Cáo Cāo) defeated the Yuán clan,
and took the post of Inspector (Mù) of Jìzhōu.
He appointed Yán as Aide-de-camp (Biéjià Cóngshì).
He said to Yán:
"Yesterday, I reviewed the household registers
and found that we can raise 300,000 men.
This is truly a large province!"
Yán replied:
"Today, the empire is fractured,
the nine provinces are torn apart.
The two Yuán brothers personally engaged in warfare,
and the populace of Jìzhōu lies exposed on the plains.
I have not yet heard of the King's army (Wáng Shī)'s benevolent reputation preceding them,
inquiring about local customs,
and rescuing them from their misery.
Instead, you count the soldiers and weapons,
prioritizing only this.
Is this what the gentlemen and ladies of this humble province expect from Your Excellency?"
Grand Ancestor's expression changed, and he apologized to him.
At that time, all the guests were astonished and lost color.
Grand Ancestor campaigned in Bìngzhōu,
leaving Yán to assist Prince Wén (Cáo Pī) in Yè.
The Heir Apparent (Cáo Pī) frequently went hunting,
changing his clothes and mounts,
with his mind set on chasing game.
Yán wrote a remonstrance, saying:
"I have heard that 'excessive hunting' (pán yú yóutián)
is cautioned against in the Shū (Book of Documents),
and 'Duke Yǐn of Lǔ observing fish'
is criticized in the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals).
These are the aphorisms of Zhōu and Kǒng (Confucius),
the clear meanings of the two Classics.
'The mirror of Yīn is not far from the Hòus (rulers) of Xià,'
as stated in the Shī (Book of Odes).
'Not enjoying oneself on zǐ (子) or mǎo (卯) days'
is considered a taboo in the Lǐ (Book of Rites).
These are the successes and failures of recent times,
which must be deeply examined.
The Yuán clan was wealthy and strong,
but their young lords were lenient and undisciplined.
Their excessive hunting led to extravagance,
and their reputation for righteousness was unheard of.
Wise men and gentlemen
soon developed the intention to leave;
brave men and warriors
indulged in plunder.
This is why, despite having a million followers
and occupying the region north of the Yellow River (Héshuò),
they found no place to stand.
Now, the state is exhausted,
and benevolent peace has not yet spread.
Gentlemen and ladies stand on tiptoe,
longing for virtue.
Moreover, since Your Excellency personally commands the army,
everyone above and below is toiling and distressed.
The Heir Apparent should follow the great path,
be cautious and act uprightly,
ponder the high strategies for governing the state,
inwardly reflect on recent warnings,
outwardly promote distant virtues,
deeply consider his role as heir,
and hold his person as precious.
Yet you recklessly wear the humble attire of a hunter (yú lǚ),
heedlessly rush and traverse dangerous terrain,
focusing on the petty pleasure of pheasants and rabbits,
forgetting the importance of the altars of soil and grain (shèjì).
This truly causes sadness in those who have insight.
I only wish that the Heir Apparent would discard his hunting gear (fán yì juān zhě),
to fulfill the hopes of the populace,
and not cause this old minister to incur the wrath of Heaven."
The Heir Apparent replied:
"Yesterday, I received your excellent command,
kindly showing me your elegant instructions.
You wished me to discard my hunting gear;
the 'yì' (hunting cloak) is already broken,
and the 'zhě' (hunting jacket) has also been removed.
If such a situation arises again,
I hope you will instruct me further."
When Grand Ancestor became Chancellor (Chéngxiàng),
Yán again served as an Aide (Yuánshǔ) in the Eastern and Western Bureaus, responsible for military affairs.
When he first appointed him to the Eastern Bureau,
he instructed him, saying:
"You possess the integrity of Bó Yí
and the uprightness of Shǐ Yú.
Greedy people, out of admiration for your reputation, become pure;
brave men, inspired by your example, become more rigorous.
Such a person can lead the times.
Therefore, I appoint you to the Eastern Bureau;
go and fulfill your duties."
When the State of Wèi was first established,
he was appointed Grand Secretary (Shàngshū).
At that time, a crown prince had not yet been established.
The Marquis of Línzī (Cáo Zhí) was talented and favored.
Grand Ancestor was hesitant
and secretly sought opinions from outside through sealed letters.
Only Yán openly replied in a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that according to the principle of the Chūnqiū,
the heir should be established based on seniority.
Moreover, the General of the Five Bureaus (Wǔguān Jiāng) is benevolent, filial, intelligent, and wise,
and is fit to inherit the legitimate succession.
Yán will defend this with his life."
Zhí was
Yán's elder brother's son-in-law.
Grand Ancestor valued his public-spiritedness and clarity,
sighed deeply,
and promoted him to Central Commandant (Zhōngwèi).
Yán's voice and demeanor were lofty and clear,
his eyebrows and eyes were open and bright,
and his beard was four feet long.
He possessed great dignity and authority.
Court officials looked up to him,
and Grand Ancestor also respected and feared him.
Yán once recommended Yáng Xùn of Jùlù.
Although his talent and character were not outstanding,
he was pure, upright, and adhered to the Dao.
Grand Ancestor immediately invited him to serve.
Later, when Grand Ancestor became King of Wèi,
Xùn submitted a memorial praising his achievements and campaigns,
extolling his great virtues.
At the time, some people mocked Xùn as a rare hypocrite,
saying that Yán had made a wrong recommendation.
Yán obtained the draft of Xùn's memorial to read,
and wrote to Xùn, saying:
"I have read your memorial.
The content is good!
What a time, what a time!
There will surely be a time of change."
Yán's original intention was to criticize those who liked to condemn others without considering the circumstances.
Someone reported Yán's letter as being arrogant and resentful towards the world.
Grand Ancestor angrily said:
"The proverb says 'just a daughter' (shēng nǚ ěr).
The word 'ěr' (耳)
is not a good word.
'There will surely be a time of change'
implies disrespect."
Thereupon, Yán was punished as a menial laborer (túlì),
and someone was sent to observe him.
His words and demeanor showed no yielding.
Grand Ancestor issued an order, saying:
"Although Yán is punished,
he still receives guests,
and his gate is like a marketplace.
When facing guests, he stares straight with his curly beard,
as if he is angry."
Consequently, Yán was granted death.
Initially, Cuī Yǎn and Sīmǎ Lǎng were good friends.
When Jìn Xuānwáng was in his prime,
Yǎn said to Lǎng:
“Your younger brother
is intelligent, wise, clear, and trustworthy,
resolute and eminent;
he is probably beyond your reach.”
Lǎng did not think so,
but Yǎn always held this opinion.
Yǎn’s cousin Lín
had little reputation in his youth;
even his in-laws and clan members often looked down on him,
but Yǎn often said:
“This is what is called a ‘great talent maturing late’;
he will certainly achieve great things in the end.”
When Sūn Lǐ of Zhuō Jùn and Lú Yù first entered the military administration,
Yǎn also named them, saying:
“Sūn is straightforward, clear, bold, and fervent,
resolute and capable of decisive action.
Lú is pure, alert, and clear-minded,
unyielding despite a hundred trials.
Both are talents for the state.”
Later, Lín, Lǐ, and Yù all reached the highest ministerial positions.
When Yǎn’s friends Gōngsūn Fāng and Sòng Jiē died prematurely,
Yǎn took care of their orphaned children,
showing kindness as if they were his own.
His discerning judgment and profound righteousness
were all of this kind.
At first,
Tàizǔ was jealous by nature;
those he could not tolerate,
such as Kǒng Róng of Lǔ Guó,
Xǔ Yōu of Nányáng,
and Lóu Guī,
were all executed for presuming on old acquaintance and showing disrespect.
However, Yǎn was the one most lamented by the world,
and people still feel injustice for him to this day.
Máo Jiè, courtesy name Xiàoxiān,
was a native of Píngqiū, Chénliú.
In his youth, he was a county official,
known for his integrity and impartiality.
He was about to escape the chaos to Jīng Zhōu,
but before arriving,
he heard that Liú Biǎo’s governance was unclear,
so he went to Lǔyáng.
When Tàizǔ was governing Yǎn Zhōu,
he appointed him as Zhìzhōng Cóngshì.
Jiè said to Tàizǔ:
“Today the empire is fractured,
the sovereign has relocated,
the people have abandoned their livelihoods,
and are suffering from famine and displacement.
The government has no provisions for more than a year,
and the people have no desire for stability and peace.
It is difficult to sustain this for long.
Currently, Yuán Shào and Liú Biǎo,
though they have many strong soldiers and people,
lack long-term foresight
and have not established a foundation.
Indeed, those who fight righteously win;
positions are maintained by resources.
It is advisable to uphold the Son of Heaven to command those who are disobedient,
cultivate agriculture,
and accumulate military supplies.
If this is done, the work of a hegemon-king can be achieved.”
Tàizǔ respectfully accepted his words
and transferred him to Mùfǔ Gōngcáo.
When Tàizǔ was Sīkōng Chéngxiàng,
Jiè once served as Dōngcáo Yuàn,
and oversaw elections alongside Cuī Yǎn.
Those he recommended and employed
were all upright and honest men;
even those who had great reputations at the time but whose conduct was not based on fundamental principles
could ultimately not be promoted.
He made it his business to lead people with frugality;
thus, all gentlemen in the empire were inspired to uphold integrity and节操,
and even favored high-ranking officials
dared not exceed proper limits in their carriages and attire.
Tàizǔ sighed and said:
“If people are employed like this,
and the people of the world govern themselves,
what more do I need to do!”
When Wéndì was Wǔguān Jiāng,
he personally visited Jiè
to recommend his relatives and associates.
Jiè replied:
“As an old minister, I am fortunate to have avoided blame by being able to uphold my duties.
The people you are recommending now are not in their proper order for promotion,
therefore I dare not obey your command.”
When the main army returned to Yè,
there was a discussion about merging and streamlining offices.
Jiè’s requests for audiences were not granted.
People at the time feared him
and all wanted to abolish Dōngcáo.
They jointly reported, saying:
“Formerly, Xīcáo was superior,
and Dōngcáo was secondary;
it is appropriate to abolish Dōngcáo.”
Tàizǔ understood their true intention
and issued an order, saying:
“The sun rises in the east,
the moon is brightest in the east,
and when people speak of directions,
they also mention east first.
Why abolish Dōngcáo?”
Consequently, he abolished Xīcáo.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ pacified Liǔchéng,
he distributed the captured artifacts,
and specifically gave a plain screen and a plain armrest to Jiè,
saying:
“You possess the style of ancient people,
therefore I bestow upon you the accouterments of ancient people.”
While holding a prominent position,
Jiè always wore plain clothes and ate simple food,
and raised his orphaned nephew with great care.
He used his rewards and gifts to assist impoverished relatives,
leaving nothing surplus in his home.
He was promoted to Yòujūn Shī.
When the state of Wèi was first established,
he became Shàngshū Púyè,
again overseeing elections.
At that time, the crown prince was not yet decided,
and Lord Zhí of Línzī was favored.
Jiè secretly remonstrated, saying:
“Recently, Yuán Shào, by failing to distinguish between嫡 and庶,
destroyed his clan and extinguished his state.
The great matter of deposition and establishment
is not something that should be heard of.”
Later, when the officials gathered,
Jiè stood up to change his clothes.
Tàizǔ gestured and said:
“This is what the ancients called the state’s Sīzhí,
my Zhōu Chāng.”
After Cuī Yǎn had died,
Jiè inwardly became displeased.
Later, someone informed against Jiè, saying:
"He saw a tattooed-face rebel
whose wife and children were confiscated to become official slaves and bondservants.
Jiè then said, 'It must be because of this that Heaven does not send rain!'"
Tài Zǔ was greatly enraged,
arrested Jiè, and committed him to prison.
Dà Lǐ Zhōng Yáo interrogated Jiè, saying:
"From ancient times, sagely emperors and enlightened kings
have extended punishment to wives and children.
The Shū states: 'If the left does not associate with the left,
and the right does not associate with the right,
then I will enslave and execute you.'
The duty of the Sī Kòu
was to consign males to penal servitude
and females to grinding grain.
The Hàn laws
confiscated the wives and children of criminals to become slaves and bondservants,
and tattooed their faces.
The tattooing punishment (qíngmò zhī xíng) practiced under Hàn law
is preserved in the ancient classics.
Now, if the ancestors of true slaves and bondservants committed a crime,
even after a hundred generations,
they still have their faces tattooed and serve the government.
Firstly, this is to spare the lives of good common people;
secondly, it is to mitigate the guilt of those implicated in crimes.
How can this contradict the will of the gods
and cause a drought?
According to the principles of governance,
when rule is strict, it is always cold;
when rule is lenient, it is always warm.
Excessive leniency leads to extreme yang,
which causes drought.
Were Jiè's words
intended to mean leniency
or strictness?
If strictness, it should lead to continuous overcast rain;
how could it cause drought instead?
During the sagely era of Chéng Tāng,
there was no grass growing in the fields.
During the reign of the able ruler Zhōu Xuān,
the drought demon (hàn bá) caused havoc.
Since the onset of the severe drought,
which has accumulated for thirty years,
do you attribute the blame to those with tattooed faces?
Is this a fitting connection?
When the Wèi people attacked Xíng,
the army set out and it rained.
If there is no evidence of evil deeds,
how can it be a response from Heaven?
Jiè's mocking and slanderous words
spread among the common people,
and his displeasure
reached the sacred ear of the emperor.
When Jiè uttered these words,
it is unlikely he spoke to himself.
How many people did he see
with tattooed faces at that time?
Did he recognize
these tattooed-face slaves and bondservants?
How did he come to see them,
and sigh with these words to them?
To whom did he speak at that time?
What was their reply?
On what date and month?
In what place?
The matter has been exposed;
you must not conceal or deceive.
State the full circumstances."
Jiè replied:
"I have heard that Xiāo Shēng was strangled to death,
oppressed by Shí Xiǎn;
Jiǎ Zǐ was exiled,
slandered by Jiàng and Guàn;
Bái Qǐ was granted a sword at Dù Yóu;
Cháo Cuò was executed at the Eastern Market;
Wǔ Yuán met his end in Wú Dū: these several individuals,
some were envied in their prime,
others harmed later in life.
From childhood, I, your servant, held the bamboo slips,
and by repeated diligence obtained official position.
My office is close to the seat of power,
and personal connections easily corrupt it.
People approach me with private matters,
and there is no influential person I do not dismiss;
they tell me of their grievances,
and there is no detail I do not investigate.
Human nature is greedy for profit,
which is forbidden by law.
Law forbids profit,
and power can cause harm.
Green flies (qīng yíng) appear from nowhere,
slandering your servant.
The people who slander your servant
must be no one else.
Formerly, Wáng Shú and Chén Shēng disputed right and wrong in the royal court,
and Xuān Zǐ arbitrated justly.
He ordered them to produce their contracts (qì),
and right and wrong were distinguished,
and guilt and innocence established.
The Spring and Autumn Annals commended this,
and thus recorded it.
I did not say these words;
there was no such time or person.
Whoever claims I said these words
must have compelling evidence.
I beg to be granted Xuān Zǐ's discernment,
and to seek Wáng Shú's counter-argument.
If your servant is found to be in the wrong,
then the day of my punishment
will be comparable to the gift given to Ān Sì;
the arrival of the bestowed sword
will be likened to the grace of a great reward.
I respectfully state the circumstances."
At that time, Huán Jiē and Hé Qià spoke up to save Jiè.
Jiè was consequently dismissed from office
and died at home.
Tài Zǔ bestowed a coffin, grave goods, money, and silk,
and appointed his son, Jī, as Láng Zhōng.
Xú Yì, whose courtesy name was Jì Cái,
was a native of Dōng Guǎn.
He fled the troubles to Jiāng Dōng,
and Sūn Cè formally invited him.
Yì changed his name,
and disguised himself to return to his home commandery.
When Tài Zǔ became Sī Kōng,
he was invited to be a Yuán Shǔ.
He followed the western campaign against Mǎ Chāo.
After Mǎ Chāo was defeated,
the army returned.
At that time, Guān Zhōng had newly submitted
and was not yet fully settled.
Yì was left as Céng Xiàng Cháng Shǐ
to pacify and administer the Western Capital.
The Western Capital praised his authority and trustworthiness.
He was transferred to be Yōng Zhōu Cì Shǐ,
then returned to be Dōng Cáo Shǔ.
Dīng Yí and others were favored at the time
and all resented him,
but Yì remained unmoved.
He was sent out to be Wèi Jùn Tài Shǒu.
When Tài Zǔ campaigned against Sūn Quán,
Yì was transferred to be Liú Fǔ Cháng Shǐ.
Tài Zǔ said to Yì:
"Your loyalty and integrity,
even the ancients could not surpass,
but you are a bit too strict.
Formerly, Xī Mén Bào wore a leather girdle to restrain himself.
I hope you can use gentleness to control strength.
I entrust you now to manage the affairs of the capital,
and I will no longer have worries about returning."
After the State of Wèi was established,
he became Shàng Shū,
again taking charge of selection.
He was promoted to Shàng Shū Lìng.
When Tài Zǔ campaigned in Hàn Zhōng,
Wèi Fèng and others plotted rebellion.
Zhōng Wèi Yáng Jùn was demoted.
Tài Zǔ sighed, saying:
"The reason Fèng dared to conceive rebellious thoughts
is because my 'claws and teeth' officials failed to curb treachery and prevent plots.
Where can I find someone like Zhū Gě Fēng
to replace Jùn?"
Huán Jiē said:
"Xú Yì is that person!"
Tài Zǔ then made Yì the Zhōng Wèi,
and issued a personal order which read:
"Formerly, Chǔ had Zǐ Yù,
and Wén Gōng sat on the edge of his mat for him;
Jí Àn was in court,
and Huái Nán altered his plans because of him.
The Shī says 'Director of Rectitude for the State'
— this refers to you!"
After several months in office,
he became seriously ill and requested to retire.
He was appointed Jiàn Yì Dà Fū,
and then died.
Hé Kuí, courtesy name Shúlóng,
was from Yángxià, Chén Jùn.
His great-grandfather, Xī,
served as Grand Marshal (chēqí jiāngjūn) during the reign of Emperor Ān of Hàn.
Kuí lost his father in his youth,
and lived with his mother and elder brother,
and was renowned for his filial piety and brotherly affection.
He was eight *chǐ* and three *cùn* tall,
and had a dignified and solemn appearance.
He took refuge from the chaos in Huáinán.
Later, Yuán Shù arrived in Shòuchūn
and invited him to join his staff,
but Kuí refused.
Nevertheless, he was detained by Shù.
After some time,
Shù, together with Qiáo Ruí, attacked and besieged Qíyáng.
Qíyáng was firmly defended by Tàizǔ.
Shù, knowing Kuí was from that commandery,
wanted to coerce him into persuading Qíyáng [to surrender].
Kuí said to Shù's strategist Lǐ Yè:
"In ancient times, Liǔxià Huì, hearing of a plan to attack a state, showed a worried expression,
and said, 'I have heard that attacking a state does not involve asking benevolent people;
why has this statement come to me?'"
He then fled and hid in the mountains.
Shù knew that Kuí would ultimately not serve him,
so he stopped [pursuing him].
Shù's cousin, the Administrator of Shānyáng, Yí Mǔ,
was Kuí's paternal aunt,
which is why, although Shù resented Kuí, he did not harm him.
In the second year of Jiàn'ān [197 CE],
Kuí intended to return to his hometown.
He anticipated that Shù would pursue him closely,
so he traveled secretly and managed to escape.
The following year, he arrived in his home commandery.
Soon after,
Tàizǔ appointed him as an aide (yuánshǔ) to the Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
At that time, there was a rumor that Yuán Shù's army was in chaos.
Tàizǔ asked Kuí:
"Do you think this is true?"
Kuí replied:
"What Heaven assists is compliance [with the Dao];
what men assist is trustworthiness.
Shù lacks the substance of trustworthiness and compliance,
yet he hopes for the assistance of Heaven and men.
This means he cannot achieve his ambitions in the world.
Indeed, for a lord who has lost the Dao,
his relatives will rebel against him,
let alone his close attendants!
In my view,
his chaos is inevitable."
Tàizǔ said:
"A state that loses worthy men perishes.
Since you were not used by Shù,
chaos [for him],
is it not fitting!"
Tàizǔ was strict by nature,
and his aides, for official matters,
were often flogged.
Kuí always kept poison,
vowing to die rather than suffer disgrace,
and thus he was never affected [by flogging].
He was sent out as Magistrate of Chéngfù.
He was promoted to Administrator of Chángguǎng.
The commandery bordered mountains and the sea,
the Yellow Turbans were not yet pacified,
and many local magnates revolted.
Yuán Tán further bestowed official titles upon them.
Guǎn Chéng, a man from Chángguǎng County,
with over three thousand households of followers,
caused banditry.
The counselors wanted to raise troops to attack him.
Kuí said:
"Chéng and his ilk are not born to enjoy chaos;
accustomed to disorder,
they cannot return [to order] on their own.
They have not yet received virtuous instruction,
so they do not know how to return to goodness.
If we press them hard with soldiers now,
they will fear annihilation [and]
will surely unite their strength to fight.
Attacking them will not be easy to subdue,
and even if we win,
it will surely harm officials and common people.
It is better to slowly persuade them with kindness and virtue,
allowing them to regret on their own,
then it can be pacified without troubling the army."
Thereupon, he sent the Commandery Assistant Huáng Zhēn,
who explained the consequences of success and failure,
and Chéng and his followers all requested submission.
Kuí sent the official Chéng Hóng to lead a commandant,
and the Chángguǎng County Assistant and others greeted them outside the city with offerings of beef and wine,
and proceeded to the commandery.
Yǐ Píng, another bandit with several thousand followers,
Kuí led the commandery troops and, together with Zhāng Liáo, suppressed and pacified him.
Wáng Yíng from Dōngmóu, with over three thousand households of followers,
threatened Chāngyáng County and caused rebellion.
Kuí sent officials Wáng Qīn and others,
gave them strategies,
and made them disperse the followers.
Within ten days to a month, all were pacified.
At this time, Tàizǔ had just established new laws to be implemented in the provinces and commanderies,
and also collected grain taxes and silk.
Kuí believed that since the commandery had only recently been established,
and had just emerged from the aftermath of war,
it could not be immediately bound by the law.
So he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since the great chaos began,
the people have lost their homes.
Although there is now a little peace,
their submission to instruction is shallow.
The new laws that have been issued
all clarify punishments and decree regulations,
aiming to unify and transform the whole.
The six counties under my administration
have only recently been pacified,
and furthermore, they have suffered from famine.
If all are uniformly bound by the new laws and prohibitions,
I fear there may be some who do not follow the teachings.
Those who do not follow the teachings cannot but be punished,
which would not accord with the intention of observing the people, setting up teachings, and adapting to the times.
The former kings distinguished the tributes of the nine regions (jiǔfú) to differentiate near and far,
and established the three codes of punishment (sāndiǎn) to govern peace and disorder.
I humbly believe that this commandery should follow the regulations for distant regions and newly established states.
For minor matters among the people,
let the chief officials (zhǎnglì) adapt to circumstances as appropriate,
so that they do not deviate from the correct laws above,
and comply with the wishes of the common people below.
After three years,
when the people are settled in their occupations,
then they can be brought under the law,
and there will be nothing that cannot be achieved."
Tàizǔ followed his advice.
He was recalled
and served as a military aide (cān chéngxiàng jūnshì) to the Chancellor.
The pirate Guō Zǔ plundered Luò'ān and Jìnán regions,
causing distress to the provinces and commanderies.
Tàizǔ, recalling Kuí's prestige and trustworthiness when he was in Chángguǎng,
appointed him Administrator of Luò'ān.
Within a few months of his arrival,
all the cities were pacified.
He entered service as a Clerk of the Eastern Bureau of the Chancellor (chéngxiàng dōngcáoyuán).
Kuí spoke to Grand Ancestor (tàizǔ), saying:
"Since the army arose,
systems and regulations have been hastily established.
The origins of the people employed have not been thoroughly investigated,
which has led to each drawing in their own kind,
at times forgetting virtue and morality.
I have heard that if positions are granted based on worthiness,
the people will be mindful of virtue;
if emoluments are determined by merit,
the people will strive for achievement.
I propose that from now on, all those to be employed
must first be verified in their local communities,
so that the elderly and young maintain their proper order,
without overstepping each other.
By making rewards for loyalty and rectitude manifest,
and making clear the recompense for public and true achievements,
then the distinction between the worthy and the unworthy
will become instantly clear.
Furthermore, regulations concerning false recommendations should be revised,
so that the responsible officials bear their own consequences.
Those ministers at court,
who sometimes receive instructions and are selected alongside those in the bureaus,
should each assume their responsibilities.
Upwards, this will observe the integrity of the court ministers,
downwards, it will curb the source of contention,
and will supervise the many subordinates,
and lead the myriad people.
If this is done, the empire will be greatly fortunate."
Grand Ancestor (tàizǔ) praised his words.
Once the state of Wèi (Wèiguó) was established,
he was appointed Senior Assistant to the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (shàngshū pūyè).
When Emperor Wén (Wéndì) was Crown Prince (tàizǐ),
Liáng Mào (Liáng Mào) was made Grand Tutor (tàifù),
and Kuí was made Junior Tutor (shǎofù).

It was specially ordered that the two Tutors, along with the Eastern Bureau of the Imperial Secretariat (shàngshū dōngcáo), should jointly select the officials for the Crown Prince (tàizǐ) and the lords.
When Mào died,
Kuí replaced Mào.
On the first day of each month,
the Grand Tutor (tàifù) would enter to see the Crown Prince (tàizǐ),
and the Crown Prince (tàizǐ) would don his ceremonial robes and pay his respects;
on other days, there was no such formal meeting.
Kuí was promoted to Grand Coachman (tàipú).
The Crown Prince (tàizǐ) wished to bid him farewell,
and prepared accommodations overnight.
Kuí had no intention of going;
so he sent a letter inviting him.
Kuí, citing the established regulations of the state,
still did not go.
Such was his adherence to rectitude.
However, in an era of frugality,
he was notably extravagant.
When Emperor Wén (Wéndì) ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chéngyáng Pavilion (Chéngyáng Tínghóu),
with an income of three hundred households.
When he fell ill,
he repeatedly requested to resign his position.
The imperial edict in reply said:
"To honor the worthy and cherish old friends
is a constant duty of emperors and kings.
As a friend, Your Lordship has the merit of aiding and assisting;
as a worthy man, Your Lordship possesses profound and solid excellence.
Indeed, those who possess hidden virtues will surely receive public rewards.
Although Your Lordship's illness has not yet recovered,
the divine spirits have heard it.
Your Lordship should thus find peace,
to comply with Our wishes."
Upon his death,
he was posthumously titled Marquis Jìng (Jìnghóu).
His son Zēng succeeded him,
and during the Xiánxī (Xiánxī) era, he served as Minister of Education (sītú).
Xíng Yóng (Xíng Yóng), courtesy name Zǐ'áng (Zǐ'áng),
was a native of Mò (Mò) in Héjiān (Héjiān).
He was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián),
and invited by the Minister of Education (sītú),
but he declined both.
He changed his surname and courtesy name,
and went to Yòuběipíng (Yòuběipíng),
where he associated with Tián Chóu (Tián Chóu).
After five years,
Grand Ancestor (tàizǔ) pacified Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu).
Yóng said to Chóu:
"For over twenty years since the Yellow Turban (Huángjīn) uprising,
the whole country has been in turmoil,
and the people have been displaced.
Now I hear that Lord Cáo's (Cáo Gōng) laws are strict.
The people are weary of chaos,
and extreme chaos leads to peace.
I ask to go first myself."
So he packed up and returned to his hometown.
Tián Chóu (Tián Chóu) said:
"Xíng Yóng (Xíng Yóng)
is a pioneer among the people."
He then met Grand Ancestor (tàizǔ),
and requested to serve as a local guide to conquer Liǔchéng (Liǔchéng).
Grand Ancestor (tàizǔ) appointed Yóng as an Attendant Officer of Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu cóngshì).
At that time, people praised him saying:
"Of imposing virtue and conduct, Xíng Zǐ'áng (Xíng Zǐ'áng)."
He was appointed Chief of Guǎngzōng (Guǎngzōng zhǎng).
Due to a former general's death, he abandoned his office.
The officials reported his transgression,
but Grand Ancestor (tàizǔ) said:
"Yóng is devoted to his former lord,
and shows singular integrity."
Do not question him.
He was again appointed Clerk to the Minister of Works (sīkōng yuàn),
and then Magistrate of Xíngtáng (Xíngtáng lìng).
He encouraged the people in agriculture and sericulture,
and his moral influence spread widely.
He entered service as Supervisor of the Chancellor's Gate (chéngxiàng ménxiàdū),
and was promoted to Administrator of Zuǒ Fēngyì (Zuǒ Fēngyì).
He fell ill,
and left office.
At this time,
Grand Ancestor's (tàizǔ) sons were selecting their officials,
and an order stated:
"The officials for the marquis' households
should be profound and principled, like Xíng Yóng (Xíng Yóng) and his ilk."
Thus, he was made Household Administrator for the Marquis of Píngyuán (Píngyuán Hóu) Zhí (Zhí).
Yóng maintained propriety with ritual,
and did not bend to pressure,
thus he was not in harmony with Zhí.
The secondary son Liú Zhēn (Liú Zhēn) wrote a letter advising Zhí (Zhí), saying:
"Household Administrator Xíng Yóng (Xíng Yóng),
is a talent of the northern lands,
who from a young age upheld high principles,
profoundly tranquil and detached,
speaking little but with much reason,
a truly elegant scholar.
I am truly unworthy to be counted alongside this man,
or to stand beside him.
Yet I receive especially generous treatment,
while Yóng is instead neglected.
I privately fear that observers will say that Your Lordship favors the unworthy,
and undervalues the worthy,
picking the spring blossoms of a secondary son,
and forgetting the autumn fruits of the Household Administrator.
Bringing slander upon Your Lordship is no small sin,
and this makes me uneasy."
Later, he participated in military affairs for the Chancellor (chéngxiàng),
and was transferred to Clerk of the Eastern Bureau (dōngcáoyuán).
Initially,
the Crown Prince (tàizǐ) had not yet been established,
and the Marquis of Línzī (Línzī Hóu) Zhí (Zhí) was favored.
Dīng Yí (Dīng Yí) and others all supported his excellence.
Grand Ancestor (tàizǔ) asked Yóng,
and Yóng replied:
"To replace the legitimate heir with a secondary son
is a warning from previous generations.
May Your Highness deeply and carefully consider this!"
Grand Ancestor (tàizǔ) understood his meaning,
and later made him Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ shàofù),
then promoted him to Grand Tutor (tàifù).
When Emperor Wén (Wéndì) ascended the throne,
he became Attendant (shìzhōng) and Senior Assistant to the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (shàngshū pūyè),
and was granted the title of Marquis of Guānnèi (Guānnèi Hóu).
He was sent out as Colonel Director of Retainers (sīlì xiàowèi),
and then moved to Grand Master of Ceremonies (tàicháng).
He died in the fourth year of Huángchū (Huángchū).
His son Yǒu succeeded him.
Bāo Xūn (Bāo Xūn), courtesy name Shúyè (Shúyè),
was a native of Píngyáng (Píngyáng) in Tàishān (Tàishān).
He was a ninth-generation descendant of Bāo Xuān (Bāo Xuān), Colonel Director of Retainers (sīlì xiàowèi) of the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty.
After Xuān's (Xuān) descendants, some moved from Shàngdǎng (Shàngdǎng) to Tàishān (Tàishān),
and settled there.
Xūn's father Xìn (Xìn),
served as Colonel of Cavalry (qídūwèi) during the reign of Emperor Líng (Língdì).
General-in-Chief Hé Jìn (Hé Jìn) sent him east to recruit soldiers.
Later, he became Chancellor of Jìběi (Jìběi xiàng),
and conspired with Grand Ancestor (tàizǔ),
and was himself killed.
His story is found in the Biography of Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó Zhuàn) and the Annals of Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì Jì).
In the seventeenth year of Jiàn'ān (Jiàn'ān),
Grand Ancestor (tàizǔ) posthumously recognized Xìn's (Xìn) merits,
and formally enfeoffed Xūn's (Xūn) elder brother Shào (Shào) as Marquis of Xīndū Pavilion (Xīndū Tínghóu).
He appointed Xūn (Xūn) as a Clerk to the Chancellor (chéngxiàng yuàn).
In the twenty-second year,
a crown prince was established,
and Xún was made Zhongshùzi.
He was transferred to be a Huángmén Shìláng,
then sent out as Wèijùn Xībù Dūwèi.
The younger brother of Crown Prince Guō Fūrén was a county official in Qǔzhōu,
and he was caught stealing government cloth.
According to the law, he was to be executed in the marketplace.
Tàizǔ was at Qiáo at the time,
and the Crown Prince remained in Yè.
He wrote numerous letters personally pleading for the man's pardon.
Xún dared not release him without authorization,
and he fully reported the matter to his superiors.
Xún had previously been in the Eastern Palace,
upholding righteousness without bending,
so the Crown Prince was already displeased with him.
When this incident occurred,
his resentment and frustration intensified greatly.
It happened that there was a delay in the cessation of hostilities in the county,
and the Crown Prince secretly ordered the Zhōngwèi to impeach Xún from his office.
After a long time,
he was appointed Shìyùshǐ.
In the first year of Yánkāng,
Tàizǔ passed away.
The Crown Prince ascended the throne as king,
and Xún was made Fùmǎ Dūwèi concurrently with Shìzhōng.
When Wéndì received the abdication,
Xún often stated,
"What is urgent now
lies only in military affairs and agriculture,
and in showing leniency and benevolence to the common people.
Terraces, pavilions, parks, and gardens
should be considered later."
When Wéndì was about to go hunting,
Xún stopped his carriage and submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that among the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
none failed to understand the root and establish teachings,
governing the world with filial piety.
Your Majesty is benevolent, sagacious, and compassionate,
emulating the ancient worthies.
Your servant hopes that you will follow in the footsteps of previous generations,
making yourself a model for ten thousand ages.
How can one engage in the act of galloping and hunting
while still in a period of mourning?
Your servant risks death to convey this,
and hopes Your Majesty will observe it."
The Emperor personally tore up the memorial and proceeded with the hunt.
Stopping halfway,
he asked his attendants,
"How does the pleasure of hunting
compare to the eight musical notes?"
The Shìzhōng Liú Yè replied,
"Hunting is superior to music."
Xún retorted with firm words, saying:
"Music,
upwards, connects with the divine;
downwards, it harmonizes human affairs.
It promotes order and brings about transformation,
causing all nations to be well-governed.
There is nothing better than music for changing customs and transforming practices.
How much more so hunting,
which exposes the imperial canopy to the wilderness,
harms the fundamental principle of life and growth,
and involves enduring wind and rain,
not to mention the impropriety of the timing?
In ancient times, Lǔ Yǐn's viewing of fishing at Táng
was criticized by the Chūnqiū.
Even if Your Majesty considers it a priority,
your foolish servant does not wish for it."
He then submitted,
"Liú Yè is sycophantic and disloyal,
flattering Your Majesty's excessive words about recreation.
In ancient times, Liáng Qiūjù sought favor at Chuántái;
Liú Yè is exactly like him.
I request the relevant officials to deliberate his punishment to purify the imperial temple."
The Emperor's face turned angry,
and upon returning,
he immediately removed Xún from office and made him Yòuzhōnglángjiàng.
In the fourth year of Huángchū,
Shàngshūlìng Chén Qún and Púyè Sīmǎ Xuánwáng both recommended Xún for Gōngzhèng.
Gōngzhèng was in fact Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
The Emperor had no choice but to employ him.
All officials respected and feared him,
and none were not solemn.
In the autumn of the sixth year,
the Emperor wanted to campaign against Wú.
The assembled officials held a great debate,
and Xún directly advised,
"The imperial army has campaigned repeatedly
but has yet to achieve victory because Wú and Shǔ are mutually dependent like lips and teeth,
relying on the barriers of mountains and rivers,
making them difficult to dislodge.
Last year, the dragon boat drifted away,
stranded on the south bank.
Your sacred person faced danger,
and your subjects were terrified.
At that time, the ancestral temple was almost overthrown;
this should serve as a warning for a hundred generations.
Now, to again exhaust our troops and attack a distant foe,
spending a thousand gold coins daily,
will deplete the Central Kingdom
and allow cunning barbarians to make light of our power.
Your servant secretly believes this is not permissible."
The Emperor became even more enraged
and demoted Xún to Zhìshū Zhífǎ.
When the Emperor returned from Shòuchūn,
he encamped at Chénliú Jùnjiè.
The administrator Sūn Yōng came to see him
and passed by Xún.
At that time, the camp's defenses were not yet complete,
only markers had been erected.
Yōng walked diagonally, not following the correct path.
The army camp's clerk, Liú Yào, wanted to reprimand him,
but Xún, seeing that the trenches and ramparts were incomplete,
stopped him and did not pursue the matter.
When the main army returned to Luòyáng,
Yào committed a crime.
Xún impeached and dismissed him.
Yào then secretly memorialized that Xún had privately let Sūn Yōng off the hook.
An imperial edict stated:
"Xún points to a deer and calls it a horse!
Arrest him and hand him over to the Tíngwèi!"
The Tíngwèi's legal council proposed,
"Imprisonment for five years."
The Sānguān refuted,
"According to the law, a fine of two jin of gold."
The Emperor was furious and said,
"Xún has no right to live,
and yet you dare to release him!
Arrest the Sānguān and those below them and hand them over to the Cìjiān.
Let ten rats be in the same hole!"
Tàiwèi Zhōng Yáo, Sītú Huá Xīn, Zhèn Jūn Dàjiàngjūn Chén Qún, Shìzhōng Xīn Pí, Shàngshū Wèi Zhēn, and Shǒu Tíngwèi Gāo Ròu, among others, jointly memorialized,
"Xún's father, Xìn, rendered meritorious service to Tàizǔ,"
and pleaded for Xún's pardon.
The Emperor did not allow it,
and subsequently executed Xún.
Xún's personal conduct was cultivated;
he was incorruptible yet capable of generosity.
On the day of his death,
his family had no surplus wealth.
Two decades later,
Wéndì also passed away,
and none did not sigh with regret for Xún.
Sīmǎ Zhī, courtesy name Zǐhuá,
was a native of Wēn, Hénèi.
In his youth, he was a scholar.
He fled the chaos to Jīngzhōu.
At Lǔyángshān, he encountered bandits.
His companions all abandoned the old and weak and fled,
but Zhī alone sat guarding his aged mother.
When the bandits arrived,
they held a blade to Zhī.
Zhī kowtowed and said,
"My mother is old;
her life depends entirely on you gentlemen!"
The bandits said,
"This is a filial son;
it would be unrighteous to kill him."
Thus, he escaped harm,
and pushed his mother in a deer cart.
He lived in the south for more than ten years,
personally farming and maintaining his integrity.
When Tàizǔ 平 Píng Jīngzhōu,
he appointed Zhī as the chief of Guǎnguǎn.
At that time, the world was just beginning to be established,
and many did not uphold the law.
The commander of the commandery, Liú Jié,
was from an old, influential family, and a powerful and chivalrous man.
He had over a thousand retainers,
who went out to become bandits
and interfered with official administration when they were inside.
After a short while,
Zhī ordered Jié's retainers, Wáng Tóng and others, to serve as soldiers.
The clerks reported:
"Jié's family has never before provided labor;
if they hide them at the appointed time,
it will certainly cause us arrears."
Zhī did not listen,
and wrote to Jié, saying:
"You are a great clan leader
and a key figure in the commandery,
yet your retainers have never participated in service.
This has caused widespread resentment
and may even reach the ears of the higher authorities.
Now that Tóng and others are being conscripted as soldiers,
please dispatch them promptly."
The soldiers had already assembled in the commandery,
but Jié hid Tóng and the others.
He then instructed the Inspector to use the pretext of military expenses to demand payment from the county.
The county clerks were in great distress
and begged to substitute for Tóng and the others.
Zhī then galloped with a proclamation to Jìnán,
thoroughly detailing Jié's crimes.
The Administrator Hǎo Guāng, who had always respected and trusted Zhī,
immediately had Jié substitute for Tóng and the others.
Qīngzhōu called Zhī
"the one who made the commandery commander into a soldier."
He was promoted to Magistrate of Guǎngpíng.
The General Who Conquers Barbarians, Liú Xūn,
was noble, favored, arrogant, and powerful.
Moreover, Zhī was his former commandery commander,
and his retainers and sons frequently broke the law in the jurisdiction.
Xūn wrote to Zhī,
without signing his name,
but entrusted many matters.
Zhī did not reply to his letter,
and handled all matters strictly according to the law.
Later, Xūn was executed for insubordination,
and all those involved with him were punished,
but Zhī was praised for it.
He was promoted to Grand Judge.
There was a case where someone stole official silk and placed it in the imperial privy.
The officials suspected a female artisan
and arrested her, handing her over to prison.
Zhī said:
"The errors in criminal justice
lie in harshness and cruelty.
Now the stolen goods were obtained first, and only then was her confession sought.
If she cannot endure the torture,
she might be forced into a false confession.
The circumstances of a false confession
cannot be used to decide a case.
Moreover, simplicity and ease of compliance
are the ways of a great person's transformation.
Not letting the guilty escape
is merely the governance of an ordinary age.
Now, to pardon those who are doubted,
in order to uphold the principle of ease of compliance,
would that not be acceptable?"
Tàizǔ followed his advice.
He successively served as Administrator of Gānlíng, Pèi, and Yángpíng,
achieving merits wherever he served.
During the Huángchū era,
he entered the capital as the Prefect of Hénán.
He suppressed the strong and supported the weak,
and private requests were not granted.
It so happened that an internal official wished to entrust a matter to Zhī
but dared not speak directly,
so he approached Dǒng Zhāo, Zhī's wife's maternal uncle.
Zhāo, however, feared Zhī
and did not facilitate the request.
Zhī issued an instruction to his subordinates, saying:
"A lord can establish teachings,
but cannot ensure that officials will never violate them.
Officials can violate teachings,
but cannot ensure that the lord will never hear of it.
If teachings are established but violated,
it is the lord's failing;
if teachings are violated and heard of,
it is the official's misfortune.
If the lord fails above,
and officials suffer misfortune below,
this is why governance is not well-ordered.
How can we not all strive to do our best?"
Thereupon, none of his subordinates failed to exert themselves.
A gate attendant, Xúnxíng, once suspected a gate guard, Gàn, of stealing hairpins.
Gàn's testimony was inconsistent,
and the judicial officer held him for trial.
Zhī instructed:
"For all things that are similar and difficult to distinguish,
unless one is Lílóu,
few can avoid being confused.
Even if it were truly so,
how could Xúnxíng bear to value a hairpin so highly
and lightly harm a colleague?
Let the matter be dropped and not questioned."
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
Zhī was granted the title of Marquis within the Pass.
Shortly thereafter,
Dāng, the wet nurse of the Grandee of Special Advance Cáo Hóng,
and a servant of Princess Línfén were imprisoned for jointly worshipping the spirit Wújiàn.
Empress Dowager Biàn sent a eunuch to the prefectural office to convey an order,
but Zhī did not admit him.
He immediately ordered the Luòyáng prison to investigate and conclude the case,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"All those who deserve capital punishment
must first be reported and await a reply.
The previous imperial decree prohibited lewd sacrifices to rectify customs.
Now, Dāng and others have committed a demonic crime,
and their confessions have just been finalized.
The eunuch Wú Dá came to me,
conveying the order of the Grand Empress Dowager.
Your subject dared not admit him,
fearing that there would be intervention.
I swiftly brought this to the sacred attention,
lest it be unavoidable
to grant a stay.
If the matter is not concluded promptly,
it is your subject's fault.
Therefore, I have ventured to violate the usual regulations,
immediately ordering the county to investigate and conclude the case,
and unauthorizedly carried out the execution.
I await your punishment."
The Emperor replied in his own hand:
"I have read your memorial,
which shows your lord's sincere heart,
wishing to uphold the imperial decree,
and acting with authority.
This is correct.
This is indeed your lord's intention to uphold the decree,
what is there to apologize for?
If a eunuch comes again in the future,
be sure not to admit him."
Zhī served as an official for eleven years,
frequently proposing reforms to inconvenient regulations.
Among the high officials,
he acted with integrity.
It happened that various kings came to court
and communicated with people in the capital,
for which he was dismissed.
Later, he became the Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng).
Previously, the various Directors of Agriculture (Diǎnnóng) organized officials and common people within their respective departments
to engage in commercial activities and generate income
to secure profits.
Sīmǎ Zhī memorialized, saying:
“The governance of a king
exalts the root and suppresses the branch,
prioritizing agriculture and valuing grain.
The Rites of Zhou (Wángzhì) state: ‘
Without three years’ worth of reserves, a state is not truly a state.’
Guǎnzi (Guǎnzi) also emphasized the urgency of accumulating grain.
Currently, with the two enemies (lǔ) not yet subdued
and military campaigns incessant,
the most crucial matters for the state
lie solely in grain and silk.
Emperor Wu (Wǔ Huángdì) specifically established the office of agricultural colonies (túntián zhī guān),
devoted entirely to farming and sericulture.
During the Jiàn’ān (Jiàn’ān) period,
the granaries throughout the land were full,
and the common people were prosperous and well-off.
Since the Huángchū (Huángchū) era,
allowing the various Directors of Agriculture to engage in commercial activities,
each planning for their subordinates,
is truly not in line with the overall system (dàtǐ) suitable for the state.
Indeed, a king considers the entire realm as his household;
thus, the tradition says: ‘
If the common people are not sufficient, with whom will the ruler be sufficient?’
The prosperity and sufficiency of the fields
depend on not missing the proper seasons and exhausting the land's potential.
Though the profits sought by merchants
may appear to be doubled,
in terms of the unified national plan,
there is already an immeasurable loss,
which is inferior to cultivating land and increasing the yield by even one *mǔ*.
As for the farmer’s work in the fields,
from the first month’s plowing and sowing,
weeding and hoeing, tending silkworms,
plowing, burning stubble, and sowing wheat,
to harvesting, reaping, and building threshing grounds,
it is not finished until the tenth month.
Building granaries and constructing bridges,
transporting rent and taxes,
clearing roads and repairing bridges,
plastering and painting houses—
thus, the entire year,
there is not a day without agricultural tasks.
Now, the various Directors of Agriculture
all say, ‘Those who remain act on behalf of those who are campaigning by tending their fields,
tasking their labor;
circumstances necessitate this.
If nothing is neglected,
then they must inherently have surplus labor.’
Your foolish servant believes it is not advisable to mix in commercial activities again;
instead, focus solely on farming and sericulture,
which would be beneficial for the state’s plans.”
Emperor Míng (Míngdì) adopted his suggestion.
Whenever a superior official summoned him for an inquiry,
he would always first meet with his subordinates (yuánshǐ),
preemptively clarify their intentions,
and instruct them on how to answer and respond,
all exactly as he had anticipated.
Sīmǎ Zhī’s nature was upright and candid,
without showing off his integrity or principles.
When discussing with guests,
if something was disagreeable,
he would directly point out their shortcomings to their face,
and there would be no different words behind their back.
He died in office,
leaving no surplus wealth in his home.
From Wèi (Wèi) until now, none of the Henan Governors (Hénán Yǐn) have surpassed Sīmǎ Zhī.
After Sīmǎ Zhī’s death,
his son Qí (Qí) succeeded him.
He transferred from Henan Aide (Hénán Chéng) to Court Judge (Tíngwèi Zhèng),
then was promoted to Administrator of Chénliú (Chénliú Xiàng).
In Jí Prefecture (Jí Jùn), there were prisoners,
many of whom were implicated, and their cases
remained unresolved for several years.
An imperial edict ordered the transfer of these prisoners to a county under Qí’s jurisdiction.
The county requested to prepare the prison facilities in advance.
Qí said:
“Currently, there are dozens of prisoners,
who are both cunning and difficult to reconcile with evidence,
and furthermore, they have already suffered torture,
so their true feelings are easy to discern.
Why should they remain long in prison?”
