When the prisoners were brought to his chamber
and questioned,
none dared to conceal their deceit,
and all cases were resolved in a single day.
Consequently, he was exceptionally promoted to Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi).
At this time, Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn) Cáozhào Guǎn (Cáozhào Guǎn) monopolized power,
and Grand Secretary (Shàngshū) Hé Yàn (Hé Yàn) and Dèng Yáng (Dèng Yáng) served as his supporters.
Guī Tài (Guī Tài) of Nányáng (Nányáng) once offended them with his words
and was interrogated and imprisoned by the Minister of Justice.
Dèng Yáng interrogated the prisoner
and intended to impose a severe sentence on Guī Tài.
Qí reprimanded Dèng Yáng, saying:
“Indeed, a pivotal minister,
an assistant to the imperial house,
cannot, on the one hand, aid in transforming and perfecting virtue
and match the excellence of the ancients,
while on the other hand, indulge his private resentment
and wrongly condemn the innocent.
Causing the common people to feel endangered—
where else does this come from?”
Dèng Yáng then retreated, ashamed and angry.
Qí eventually feared incurring blame for a long time
and left office due to illness.
He died at home within a year,
at the age of thirty-five.
His son Zhào (Zhào) succeeded him.
Commentary (Píng) says: Xú Yì (Xú Yì), Hé Kuí (Hé Kuí), and Xíng Yōng (Xíng Yōng) were esteemed for their strictness and severity,
becoming famous figures of their age.
Máo Jiè (Máo Jiè) was clear, impartial, and maintained his original principles.
Sīmǎ Zhī (Sīmǎ Zhī) was loyal and upright, never wavering,
almost reaching the point of not bending principle to expediency.
Cuī Yǎn (Cuī Yǎn) possessed the most excellent high character.
Bào Xūn (Bào Xūn) upheld righteousness without fault.
Yet none of them escaped personal misfortune;
what a pity!
The Greater Odes (Dàyǎ) values
“being both clear-sighted and wise.”
The Book of Yú (Yú Shū) praises
“being upright yet gentle.”
Unless one possesses both talents,
who can achieve them all?
Biography of Zhōng Yáo (Zhōng Yáo), Huá Xīn (Huá Xīn), and Wáng Lǎng (Wáng Lǎng), Chapter 13.
Zhōng Yáo (Zhōng Yáo), courtesy name Yuáncháng (Yuáncháng),
was a native of Chángshè (Chángshè), Yǐngchuān (Yǐngchuān).
He once went to Luòyáng (Luòyáng) with his paternal cousin Yú (Yú).
On the road, they encountered a physiognomist
who said:
“This child has a noble countenance,
but he will face a peril involving water.
Be very careful!”
They had not traveled ten *lǐ*
when, crossing a bridge,
the horse was startled,
and he fell into the water, almost dying.
Yú (Yú), realizing the physiognomist’s words were accurate,
valued Yáo (Yáo) even more,
and provided for his expenses,
allowing him to devote himself entirely to study.
He was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián), and appointed as Imperial Secretary (Shàngshū Láng) and Magistrate of Yánglíng (Yánglíng Lìng),
but left due to illness.
He was appointed by the Three Ducal Offices (sānfǔ),
and served as Court Judge (Tíngwèi Zhèng) and Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng).
At this time,
Emperor Hàn (Hàn Dì) was in the Western Capital (Xījīng),
and Lǐ Jué (Lǐ Jué), Guō Sì (Guō Sì) and others were creating chaos in Cháng’ān (Cháng’ān),
severing communication with Guāndōng (Guāndōng).
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ), who was the Governor of Yǎn Province (Yǎnzhōu Mù),
first sent an envoy to present a memorial.
Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì and others believed,
“Guāndōng (Guāndōng) intends to establish its own Son of Heaven.
Although Cáozhào Guǎn (Cáozhào Guǎn) now has an envoy,
it is not truly sincere,”
and debated detaining the Grand Ancestor’s envoy
and rejecting his intentions.
Zhōng Yáo (Zhōng Yáo) persuaded Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì and others, saying:
“Currently, heroes are rising everywhere,
each forging imperial decrees and acting independently.
Only Governor Cáo (Cáo Yǎnzhōu) truly devotes his heart to the imperial house,
yet to reject his loyal sincerity
is not the way to fulfill the hopes of the future.”
Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì and others accepted Zhōng Yáo’s advice
and replied generously.
Thus, the Grand Ancestor’s envoys were able to pass through.
The Grand Ancestor had often heard Xún Yù’s (Xún Yù) praise of Zhōng Yáo (Zhōng Yáo),
and now hearing his persuasion of Lǐ Jué and Guō Sì,
he became even more receptive.
Later, when Lǐ Jué (Lǐ Jué) threatened the Son of Heaven,
Zhōng Yáo (Zhōng Yáo) conspired with Imperial Secretary (Shàngshū Láng) Hán Bīn (Hán Bīn).
The Son of Heaven was able to escape Cháng’ān (Cháng’ān),
and Zhōng Yáo (Zhōng Yáo) played a vital role.

He was appointed Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), promoted to Palace Attendant and Minister of the Household (Shìzhōng Shàngshū Púyè), and simultaneously enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngwǔ Pavilion (Dōngwǔ Tíng Hóu) for his previous merits.
At that time, the various generals in Guānzhōng, Mǎ Téng, Hán Suí,
and others, each commanded strong armies and were contending with each other.
Tàizǔ was then occupied with affairs in Shāndōng,
and was concerned about Guānyòu.
So he memorialized to appoint Yáo as Attendant Secretary (Shìzhōng) and acting Colonel Director of Servants (Sīlì Xiàowèi),
holding the insignia of authority to supervise all armies in Guānzhōng.
He entrusted him with matters concerning the rear,
specifically allowing him not to be bound by regulations.
When Yáo arrived in Cháng'ān,
he sent letters to Téng, Suí,
and others, explaining the advantages and disadvantages.
Téng and Suí each sent their sons to serve at court.
When Tàizǔ was at Guāndù,
locked in a stalemate with Yuán Shào,
Yáo sent over two thousand horses to supply the army.
Tàizǔ wrote to Yáo, saying:
"The horses you sent
were greatly needed in this urgent situation.
With Guānyòu pacified,
the imperial court has no worries about the west,
which is your achievement.
In ancient times, Xiāo Hé guarded Guānzhōng,
supplying food and forming an army;
this is exactly the same."
Later, when the Xiongnú Chányú rebelled in Píngyáng,
Yáo led various armies to besiege him,
but had not yet captured him.
Meanwhile, Guō Yuán, whom Yuán Shàng had appointed as Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Hédōng, arrived in Hédōng,
with a very large force.
The generals discussed wanting to abandon the siege and leave.
Yáo said:
"The Yuán clan is currently strong,
and with Yuán's arrival,
Guānzhōng is secretly colluding with him.
The reason they haven't all rebelled yet
is simply out of regard for my prestige and reputation.
If we abandon them and leave,
showing weakness,
then among the people everywhere,
who would not become our enemy?
Even if we wanted to return,
would we be able to make it?
This would be to defeat ourselves before even fighting.
Furthermore, Yuán is stubborn and fond of winning,
and will surely underestimate our army.
If he crosses the Fén River to set up camp,
we should attack him before he finishes crossing;
we can achieve a great victory."
Zhāng Jì persuaded Mǎ Téng to join forces and attack Yuán.
Téng sent his son, Chāo, leading elite troops to meet him.
When Yuán arrived,
he indeed lightly crossed the Fén River.
His men tried to stop him,
but he did not listen.
When less than half had crossed the water,
they attacked
and greatly defeated him,
beheading Yuán
and forcing the Chányú to surrender.
The details are in Jì's biography.
Afterward, Wèi Gù of Hédōng rebelled,
joining with Zhāng Shèng, Zhāng Yǎn, and Gāo Gàn, among others, to become bandits.
Yáo again led various generals to suppress and defeat them.
Since the Son of Heaven moved west,
the population of Luòyáng had become completely depleted.
Yáo relocated people from Guānzhōng,
and also attracted and settled fugitives and rebels to fill it,
so that in a few years the number of households gradually became substantial.
When Tàizǔ campaigned in Guānzhōng,
he was able to use this as a resource,
and memorialized to appoint Yáo as Chief Military Advisor (Qián Jūnshī).
When the State of Wèi was first established,
he became Grand Judge (Dàlǐ),
then was promoted to Chancellor (Xiàngguó).
When Wén Dì was still the Heir Apparent (Dōnggōng),
he bestowed upon Yáo a five-compartment cauldron,
and inscribed it thus:
"Oh, how majestic is Wèi,
serving as a bulwark for Hàn.
Its Chancellor is Zhōng,
truly its heart and core.
Revering and diligent day and night,
not taking leisure or rest.
The hundred officials follow his example,
taking him as their model and standard."
Several years later,
due to his Western Bureau Head (Xīcáoyuàn) Wèi Fěng's plot to rebel,
he was dismissed from office and sent home.
When Wén Dì ascended to the throne,
he was reinstated as Grand Judge.
And when he formally ascended the imperial throne,
he changed his title to Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi),
and was advanced to the title of Marquis of Chónggāo Township (Chónggāo Xiānghóu).
He was promoted to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
and then transferred to the title of Marquis of Píngyáng Township (Píngyáng Xiānghóu).
At that time, Minister of the Masses (Sītú) Huà Xīn and Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Wáng Lǎng
were both famous ministers of previous generations.
When Wén Dì dismissed court,
he said to his attendants:
"These three dukes
are truly great men of their generation;
it will be difficult for later generations to match them!"
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he was advanced to the title of Marquis of Dìnglíng (Dìnglíng Hóu),
with an increase of five hundred households in his fief,
making a total of one thousand eight hundred households.
He was promoted to Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
Yáo had a knee ailment,
making bowing and rising inconvenient.
At that time, Huà Xīn also suffered from illness due to old age,
and when he attended court, he was always carried in a covered carriage,
with Tiger Warriors (Hǔbēn) carrying him up to the hall to his seat.
Thereafter, when any of the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng) were ill,
this became standard practice.
Initially,
Tàizǔ issued an order
to deliberate on whether those deserving capital punishment could be subjected to castration.
Yáo believed,
"The corporal punishments of antiquity,
having been reviewed by wise rulers throughout history,
should be restored
to replace capital punishment."
The debaters considered this not a way to please the people,
so it was put aside.
When Wéndì feasted with his officials,
he issued an edict saying,
"The Grand Judge wants to restore corporal punishment;
this is truly the law of sagely kings.
The high officials should discuss it thoroughly together."
The discussion was not concluded,
and there were military affairs,
so it was again put aside.
During the Tàihé reign,
Yáo submitted a memorial, saying:
"The Great Wèi received the mandate,
following the footsteps of Yú and Xià.
Emperor Xiàowén's reform of the law
did not align with ancient ways.
The former emperor's sagely virtue,
indeed granted by Heaven,
unified
the traditions of the Fén and Diǎn classics.
Therefore, throughout successive generations,
enlightened edicts were repeatedly issued,
desiring to restore ancient punishments
to be the law for a generation.
Repeated military affairs
prevented their implementation.
Your Majesty, far echoing the lingering intentions of the two ancestors,
regretting that a cut foot could prevent evil,
and lamenting the innocent who face death,
has commanded those skilled in laws and statutes
to deliberate with the officials.
For those who, by original judgment, should have their right foot amputated but face capital punishment,
this punishment should be reinstated.
The Shū Jīng says: 'The Emperor clearly inquired of the common people,
whether the few had complaints against Miáo.'
This means Yáo was about to abolish the punishments of Chīyóu and Yǒumiáo,
and first inquired thoroughly of those among the common people who had complaints.
If, during the current time of trying cases,
inquiry is made of the Sān Huái, Jiǔ Jí, the myriad officials, and the common people,
and if, like Emperor Xiàojǐng's decree,
those who are to be executed in the marketplace
are allowed to have their right foot amputated,
then for tattooing (qíng), nose-cutting (yí), left-foot amputation (zuǒzhǐ), and castration (gōngxíng),
following Emperor Xiàowén,
they should be replaced with shaving the head (kūn) and flogging (chī).
Those capable of committing crimes
are generally between twenty and forty or fifty years old;
even if their foot is cut off,
they can still procreate.
Today, the population of the empire is smaller than in Emperor Xiàowén's time.
At a conservative estimate, those spared
would be three thousand people annually.
When Zhāng Cāng abolished corporal punishment,
the number of those killed annually was in the tens of thousands.
I wish to restore corporal punishment,
and three thousand people will be spared annually.
Zǐgòng asked, 'Can one who saves the people be called benevolent?'
The Master replied, 'Why speak only of benevolence?
Must it not be sagely?
Even Yáo and Shùn would find it difficult!'
He also said, 'Is benevolence far away?
If I desire benevolence,
then benevolence arrives.'
If this is truly implemented,
the people will be eternally saved."
When the memorial was submitted,
an imperial edict said:
"The Grand Tutor's learning is excellent and his talent high;
he devotes his attention to government affairs
and his understanding of penal principles is profound.
This is a major matter;
the high officials and all magistrates should deliberate on it thoroughly."
Sītú Wáng Lǎng deliberated,
believing,
"Yáo wishes to lighten and reduce the articles of capital punishment
and increase the number of foot amputations (yuèxíng).
This is indeed raising the fallen and uprighting the inverted,
transforming a corpse into a person.
However, in my humble opinion,
there are still some minor points of disagreement.
The categories of the five punishments
are recorded in the statutes and laws,
and there is already a system for punishments one degree lighter than death;
not dying is already a reduction.
This has been in practice for a long time,
and there is no need to borrow the distant axe and chisel of corporal punishment
to establish a hierarchy of guilt.
Benevolent people of previous generations
could not bear the cruelty of corporal punishment,
which is why it was abolished and not used.
Since its disuse,
hundreds of years have passed.
If it is restored now,
I fear that the revised statutes may not yet be clear to the eyes of the common people,
while the news of corporal punishment has already reached the ears of our enemies,
which is not the way to attract distant people.
Currently, we can follow Yáo's desire to lighten death penalties
by reducing them to head-shaving (kūn) or foot-amputation (yuè).
If it is deemed too light,
the years of forced labor can be doubled.
Internally, there will be the immeasurable grace of exchanging life for death;
externally, there will be no alarming sound of exchanging foot-amputation for iron shackles (dài)."
Over a hundred debaters
agreed with Lǎng.
The Emperor, with Wú and Shǔ not yet pacified,
temporarily put it aside.
In the fourth year of Tàihé,
Yáo passed away.
The Emperor wore plain clothes to attend the condolence,
and he was posthumously granted the title Chéng Hóu.
His son Yù succeeded him.
Initially,
Wéndì divided Yù's households and fiefs,
and enfeoffed Yáo's brother Yǎn, and his son Shào, and grandson Yù as marquises.
Yù's courtesy name was Zhìshú.
At fourteen, he became a Sànqí Shìláng.
He was quick-witted in conversation and laughter,
possessing his father's style.
In the early Tàihé period,
the Shǔ Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng besieged Qíshān.
Míngdì wanted to lead a western expedition.
Yù submitted a memorial, saying:
"Indeed, strategy values victory in the ancestral temple,
and achievement is esteemed in the tent,
without descending from the hall,
yet deciding victory a thousand li away.
The imperial carriage should guard the central land,
serving as a formidable support for the four directions.
Now, a large army is marching west;
although its might is a hundredfold,
the expenses in Guānzhōng
will cause more than a single loss.
Moreover, campaigning in the height of summer,
which the poets value,
is truly not the time for the highest ruler to set out."
He was promoted to Huángmén Shìláng.
At that time, grand palaces were being built in Luòyáng,
and the imperial carriage conveniently went to Xǔchāng.
The whole empire was to assemble for court in Xǔchāng.
Xǔchāng was cramped,
so a felt hall was erected south of the city,
with elaborate fish, dragon, and meandering displays,
exhausting the people with labor.
Yù admonished,
believing
"that with untimely floods and droughts,
and empty treasuries,
all such matters
could await a year of abundance."
He further suggested,
"It is advisable to restore the cultivation of wasteland within the passes,
allowing the people to exert their strength in agriculture."
His suggestions were subsequently implemented.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign,
he served as Sànqí Chángshì.
The Grand General Cáo Shuǎng launched an army to attack Shǔ in mid-summer.
Shǔ resisted stubbornly,
and the army could not advance.
Shuǎng was about to send more troops,
when Yù wrote to him, saying:
"I humbly believe that the strategy for victory in the ancestral temple
does not involve facing arrows and stones;
the king's army
conquers without fighting.
Indeed, shields and axes can subdue Yǒumiáo,
and retreating three stages is enough to accept an enemy's surrender,
it is not necessarily to unleash Wú Hàn at Jiāngguān
or let Hán Xìn rush through Jǐngxíng.
Advancing when it is advantageous,
and retreating when it is difficult,
is truly the principle of governance since ancient times.
May your Grace consider this carefully!"
Shuǎng returned without achievement.
Later, having displeased Shuǎng,
he was transferred to Shìzhōng
and then sent out as Prefect of Wèijùn.
After Shuǎng was executed,
he was recalled as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, Shìzhōng, and Tíngwèi.
The allowance for subjects to defend the reputations of deceased rulers and fathers,
and for wives of men who became marquises
not to be remarried,
were Yù's innovations.
In the Zhèngyuán [era],
Wú Qín (毋丘儉) and Wén Qīn (文欽) rebelled.
Yù (毓) held a jié (節) and went to Yángzhōu (揚州) and Yùzhōu (豫州) to issue an amnesty,
announcing it to the soldiers and common people.
He returned to become a Shàngshū (尚書).
Zhūgě Dàn (諸葛誕) rebelled,
and Grand General Sīmǎ Wénwáng (司馬文王) discussed personally going to Shòuchūn (壽春) to suppress Dàn (誕).
It happened that Wú’s (吳) grand general Sūn Yī (孫壹) led his troops to surrender.
Some thought,
"Wú (吳) has just had internal strife;
they will certainly not be able to deploy troops again.
Our eastern forces are already numerous,
we can wait for further news."
Yù (毓) thought,
"In discussing matters and estimating the enemy,
one should measure others by oneself.
Now Dàn (誕) has offered the land of Huáinán (淮南) to the state of Wú (吳).
The force Sūn Yī (孫壹) led
was fewer than a thousand people,
and no more than three hundred soldiers.
What Wú (吳) has lost
is probably not much.
If the siege of Shòuchūn (壽春) is not lifted,
and the interior of Wú (吳) becomes more stable,
it cannot be certain that they will not send out troops."
The Grand General said,
"Good."
Thereupon, he took Yù (毓) with him.
After Huáinán (淮南) was pacified,
he became the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Qīngzhōu (青州),
and was promoted to Hòujiāngjūn (後將軍).
He was transferred to Dūdū Xúzhōu Zhūjūnshì (都督徐州諸軍事),
and granted a jié (節).
He was then transferred to Dūdū Jīngzhōu (都督荊州).
In Jǐngyuán (景元) 4, he passed away.
He was posthumously granted the title of Chējìjiāngjūn (車騎將軍)
and given the posthumous name Huìhóu (惠侯).
His son, Jùn (駿), succeeded him.
Yù's (毓) younger brother, Huì (會),
has his own biography.
Huá Xīn (華歆), courtesy name Zǐyú (子魚),
was from Gāotáng (高唐), Píngyuán (平原).
Gāotáng (高唐) was a famous city in Qí (齊),
and no gentry (衣冠) failed to roam its markets.
When Xīn (歆) was an official,
he would return home and close his gate when he had a rest day (休沐) from the yamen.
His discussions were fair,
and he never slandered others.
Táoqiū Hóng (陶丘洪) from the same commandery was also famous,
and considered himself more insightful than Xīn (歆).
At that time, Wáng Fēn (王芬) plotted with heroes to depose Emperor Líng (靈帝).
The account is in the Wǔjì (武紀).
Fēn (芬) secretly called Xīn (歆) and Hóng (洪) to conspire together.
Hóng (洪) wanted to go,
but Xīn (歆) stopped him, saying,
"The great matter of deposing and establishing [an emperor]
was difficult even for Yī (伊) and Huò (霍).
Fēn (芬) is reckless and not martial;
this will surely not succeed,
and disaster will befall your clan.
You must not go!"
Hóng (洪) followed Xīn's (歆) words and stopped.
Later, Fēn (芬) indeed failed,
and Hóng (洪) was then convinced.
He was nominated as a Xiàolián (孝廉)
and appointed Lángzhōng (郎中).
He fell ill
and resigned from office.
After Emperor Líng (靈帝) died,
Hé Jìn (何進) assisted in governance.
He summoned Zhèng Tài (鄭泰) from Hénán (河南), Xún Yōu (荀攸) from Yǐngchuān (潁川), and Xīn (歆), among others.
When Xīn (歆) arrived,
he became a Shàngshūláng (尚書郎).
When Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) moved the Son of Heaven to Cháng'ān (長安),
Xīn (歆) requested to be appointed Prefect of Xiàguī (下邽),
but due to illness, he did not go.
He then traveled from Lántián (藍田) to Nányáng (南陽).
At that time, Yuán Shù (袁術) was in Ráng (穰),
and detained Xīn (歆).
Xīn (歆) persuaded Shù (術) to advance his army and attack Zhuó (卓),
but Shù (術) could not use him.
Xīn (歆) wanted to leave,
when it happened that the Son of Heaven sent Grand Tutor Mǎ Rìdī (馬日磾) to pacify the Guāndōng (關東) region.
Rìdī (日磾) appointed Xīn (歆) as his Yuán (掾).
Going east to Xúzhōu (徐州),
an imperial edict immediately appointed Xīn (歆) as Prefect of Yùzhāng (豫章).
He governed with purity and simplicity,
and the officials and people were moved and loved him.
When Sūn Cè (孫策) was conquering territory in Jiāngdōng (江東),
Xīn (歆) knew that Cè (策) was skilled in using troops,
so he merely wore a simple headcloth and went to welcome him.
Cè (策), considering him an elder,
treated him with the courtesy due to a distinguished guest.
Later, Cè (策) died.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) was at Guāndù (官渡),
he submitted a memorial to the Son of Heaven summoning Xīn (歆).
Sūn Quán (孫權) wanted not to send him,
but Xīn (歆) said to Quán (權),
"General, you obey the king's command
and have just established friendly relations with Cáo Gōng (曹公).
Our shared righteousness is not yet firm.
If I could serve you with my whole heart,
would it not be beneficial?
To keep me here idly now
is to keep a useless object,
which is not a good plan for the General."
Quán (權) was pleased,
and thereupon sent Xīn (歆).
More than a thousand guests and old acquaintances saw him off,
and gave him hundreds of gold in gifts.
Xīn (歆) refused none of them,
but secretly marked each one.
When he was about to leave,
he gathered all the items
and said to his guests,
"I originally had no intention of refusing you all,
but what I have received has become numerous.
Considering that I am traveling far alone in a single carriage,
I fear that possessing such valuables will lead to trouble.
I ask my guests to advise me on this."
The crowd then each took back their gifts,
and admired his virtue.
Upon Xīn's (歆) arrival,
he was appointed Yìláng (議郎),
participated in the military affairs of the Sīkōng (司空),
entered as Shàngshū (尚書),
was transferred to Shìzhōng (侍中),
and replaced Xún Yù (荀彧) as Shàngshūlìng (尚書令).
When Tàizǔ (太祖) campaigned against Sūn Quán (孫權),
he appointed Xīn (歆) as Jūnshī (軍師).
After the state of Wèi (魏) was established,
he became Yùshǐdàfū (御史大夫).
When Emperor Wén (文帝) ascended the throne as king,
he was appointed Xiàngguó (相國)
and enfeoffed as Ānlèxiānghóu (安樂鄉侯).
When he ascended the imperial throne,
he was changed to Sītú (司徒).
Xīn (歆) had always been modest and poor;
his salary and grants were used to support relatives and old friends,
and his family had no stored grain (擔石之儲).
The Gōngqīng (公卿) were once all granted captured laborers,
but only Xīn (歆) released and married them off.
The Emperor sighed,
and issued an edict saying,
"The Sītú (司徒)
is an eminent elder of the state,
one who harmonizes yin and yang and manages various affairs.
Now the great officials have rich diets,
yet the Sītú (司徒) eats vegetables.
This is truly improper."
He specially bestowed imperial robes
and made clothes for his wife, children, and all male and female family members.
The Sānfǔ (三府) deliberated:
"The appointment of Xiàolián (孝廉)
is fundamentally based on virtue and conduct,
and should no longer be limited by examination of the classics."
Xīn (歆) believed,
"Since the time of chaos and destruction,
the Six Classics have fallen into disuse.
It is our duty to preserve and establish them
to uphold the kingly way.
Indeed, those who establish laws
do so to govern periods of prosperity and decline.
Now, to allow Xiàolián (孝廉) not to be tested on the classics,
I fear that scholarship will thereafter decline.
If there are outstanding individuals,
they can be specially summoned and employed.
The concern is not having such people;
why worry about not being able to obtain them?"
The Emperor followed his advice.
During the Huángchū period,
an imperial edict commanded the high officials to recommend gentlemen of unique conduct.
Xīn recommended Guǎn Níng,
and the emperor summoned him with an ānchē (comfortable carriage).
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he was promoted and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Bópíng,
with an additional five hundred households,
making a total of one thousand three hundred households.
He was then appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Xīn pleaded illness and asked to retire,
ceding his position to Níng.
The emperor did not permit it.
When a grand assembly was about to take place,
he dispatched the Attendant Counselor (Sànqí Chángshì) Miáo Xí to convey the imperial decree, saying:
"I have just assumed responsibility for all affairs,
with myriad tasks daily,
and I fear my judgments may not be clear.
I rely on virtuous officials
to assist me,
yet you have repeatedly resigned your post due to illness.
Indeed, assessing one's lord and choosing one's ruler,
not remaining in their court,
abandoning honor and discarding emoluments,
not staying to the end of one's tenure –
the ancients certainly did this.
However, I consider that the Duke of Zhōu and Yī Yǐn were not like that.
To keep one's person pure and sacrifice for one's principles
is what ordinary people do;
I do not expect it of you, my lord.
My lord, please exert yourself despite your illness and attend the assembly,
to bestow your favor upon me, the lonely one.
I will set up the seating and mats,
order all officials to organize themselves,
and await your arrival,
before I then take my seat."
He also commanded Xí:
"You must not return until Xīn definitely rises."
Xīn had no choice
but to rise.
In the Tàihé period,
when Cáo Zhēn was dispatched to attack Shǔ via the Zǐwǔ Road,
the imperial carriage journeyed east to Xǔchāng.
Xīn submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since the disturbances of war began,
more than two decennia have passed.
The Great Wèi has received the mandate from Heaven,
and Your Majesty, with your sagely virtue, is destined for the flourishing prosperity of Chéng and Kāng.
It is fitting to expand the governance of this generation
and continue the achievements of the Three Kings.
Although there are two bandits clinging to dangerous terrain, prolonging their lives,
if the sagely transformation progresses daily,
and distant peoples cherish your virtue,
they will come bearing their infants.
Indeed, weapons should only be used when there is no other option,
and thus they are sheathed and moved only at the appropriate time.
I sincerely wish that Your Majesty would first focus your mind on the path of governance,
and consider military campaigns as a secondary matter.
Furthermore, transporting provisions a thousand li
is not advantageous for military operations;
penetrating deep beyond dangerous terrain
will not lead to a solitary victory.
I hear that this year's conscription
has somewhat disrupted the work of agriculture and sericulture.
For a nation, the people are the foundation;
for the people, clothing and food are the root.
If the central plains are free from the worries of hunger and cold,
and the common people have no desire to leave their homes,
then the world will be greatly fortunate,
and the calamities of the two bandits
can be awaited while sitting.
I, your servant, hold the position of prime minister,
and my old age and illness are worsening daily.
The life of this dog or horse is nearing its end,
and I fear I may no longer have the honor of beholding the imperial carriage.
I dare not but exhaust the feelings of a loyal subject.
May Your Majesty decide and observe!"
The emperor replied:
"Your deep consideration for the national strategy
is greatly appreciated by me.
The bandits rely on mountains and rivers;
our two ancestors toiled in the previous age,
yet still could not pacify them.
How dare I be arrogant,
and presume to destroy them all?
My generals believe that unless we make an attempt,
there will be no way for them to exhaust themselves.
Therefore, we are observing their forces to find a weak point.
If the time is not yet right,
then King Wǔ of Zhōu's retreat
is a lesson from the past,
and I respectfully bear in mind the warning. "
At that time, there were heavy autumn rains,
and an edict ordered Zhēn to withdraw his army.
In the fifth year of Tàihé,
Xīn passed away,
and was posthumously named Jìng Hóu.
His son, Biǎo, succeeded him.
Initially,
Emperor Wén divided Xīn's households and fiefs,
and enfeoffed Xīn's younger brother, Jī, as a marquis (lièhóu).
Biǎo
was a Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū) during the Xiánxī period.
Wáng Láng, courtesy name Jǐngxīng,
was from Tán, Dōnghǎi (Commandery).
Having mastered the classics,
he was appointed Gentleman (Lángzhōng),
then made Magistrate of Zīqiū.
He was a student of the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Yáng Cì.
When Cì died,
he abandoned his office to observe mourning.
He was nominated as Xiàolián
and invited to the public office,
but did not accept.
Táo Qiān, the Inspector of Xú Province,
observed Láng's outstanding talent (màocái).
At that time, the Hàn emperor was in Cháng'ān,
and military uprisings occurred east of the passes.
Láng served as Qiān's Minister of Governance (Zhìzhōng),
and along with the Assistant Chief Clerk (Biéjià) Zhào Yù and others, persuaded Qiān, saying:
"According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
nothing is better for seeking the allegiance of regional lords than diligently serving the emperor.
Today, the Son of Heaven is far away in the Western Capital;
it is fitting to send an envoy to respectfully receive the imperial mandate."
Qiān then dispatched Yù to deliver a memorial to Cháng'ān.
The Son of Heaven commended his intention,
appointing Qiān General of the Pacified East (Āndōng Jiāngjūn).
Yù was made Administrator of Guǎnglín,
and Láng Administrator of Kuàijī.
Sūn Cè crossed the river and seized territory.
Láng's Chief Clerk (Gōngcáo), Yú Fān, believed that they lacked the strength to resist
and should instead avoid him.
Láng, however, considering himself a Hàn official,
believed he ought to defend the city,
and so he raised troops to fight Cè.
He suffered a defeat,
and fled by sea to Dōngyě.
Cè pursued him again
and inflicted a great defeat.
Láng then went to Cè.
Cè, considering Láng refined and cultured,
reprimanded him but did him no harm.
Although displaced and in dire straits,
not knowing where his next meal would come from,
he still cared for and relieved his relatives and old friends,
sharing what little he had.
His righteous conduct was very prominent.
Tài Zǔ memorialized to summon him.
Láng traveled from Qū'ā, wandering along rivers and seas,
and only arrived after many years.
He was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance (Jiànyì Dàfū)
and participated in the military affairs of the Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
When the state of Wèi was first established,
he was made Libationer of the Army (Jūnjìjiǔ) and concurrently Administrator of Wèijùn,
then promoted to Minor Court (Shàofǔ), Grand Master of Ceremonies (Fèngcháng), and Grand Judge (Dàlǐ).
His administration was characterized by leniency and forgiveness,
with doubtful cases of guilt treated lightly.
Zhōng Yáo, being clear-sighted and adhering strictly to the law,
and Láng were both praised for their administration of justice.
When Emperor Wén 文帝 ascended the throne,
he transferred the Grandee Remonstrant,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Ānlíng Tíng 安陵亭.
He submitted a memorial urging the nurturing of the people and reduction of punishments, saying:
"Since the wars began, more than thirty years have passed.
The four seas have been overturned,
and all states have been devastated and exhausted.
Relying on the former kings to clear away bandits,
and nurture the isolated and weak,
the Huáxià 華夏 was thus able to restore its order.
The countless people were gathered,
in this land of Wèi 魏.
Within the boundaries of the fiefs,
the crowing of cocks and barking of dogs
reached the four borders.
The populace rejoiced with delight,
happy to encounter an era of peace.
Now, the distant enemies have not yet submitted,
and military campaigns have not ceased.
If exemptions and remissions are sufficient to win over distant people,
and good ministers are sufficient to spread benevolent favor,
if the fields are all cultivated,
and the four classes of people are prosperous and thriving,
then it will surely surpass previous times and be richer than in peaceful days.
The Yì 易 says 'regulate the laws,'
and the Shū 書 records 'auspicious punishments.'
If one person has blessings,
the myriad people rely on it.
This refers to being cautious with laws and prisons.
In the past, Chancellor Cáo 曹 took the market and prisons as his charge.
Lù Wēnshū 路溫舒 criticized the officials who hastily administered justice.
If those who administer justice grasp the true circumstances,
then there will be no prisoners who die unjustly.
If able-bodied adults can fully exert their strength in the land,
then there will be no hungry people.
If the poor and elderly can depend on state granaries for food,
then there will be no starving corpses.
If marriages occur at the right time,
then men and women will have no regrets of being unmarried.
If pregnancy and rearing are fully protected,
then pregnant women will have no sorrow of self-harm.
If newborns are surely cared for,
then infants will have no burden of being unraised.
If service is only imposed upon adults,
then children will have no thoughts of leaving home.
If those with graying hair are not conscripted,
then the elderly will have no worries of being overthrown.
Medicine should be used to treat their illnesses,
lenient corvée to make them happy in their work,
punishments to restrain the strong,
grace and benevolence to help the weak,
and relief loans to provide for the needy.
After ten years,
girls who have reached marriageable age will surely fill the alleys.
After twenty years,
able-bodied soldiers will surely fill the fields."
When Emperor Wén 文帝 ascended the throne,
he was made Sīkōng 司空 and
advanced to Marquis of Lèpíng Xiāng 樂平鄉.
At that time, the emperor often went out hunting,
sometimes returning to the palace late at night.
Lǎng 朗 submitted a memorial saying:
"The residences of emperors and kings,
outwardly adorn the perimeter guards,
and inwardly have strict gates.
When preparing to travel, soldiers are arrayed before leaving the tent,
a warning is sounded before stepping onto the steps,
bows are drawn before ascending the carriage,
the path is cleared before escorting,
guards are arranged before turning the wheels,
and silence is made before resting the carriage.
All these are to show utmost尊 reverence,
to be diligent and cautious,
and to establish laws and teachings.
Recently, your carriage went out to hunt tigers.
You left in the afternoon
and returned at dusk,
violating the customary rules of warning and clearing the way.
This is not the utmost caution for the lord of ten thousand chariots."
The emperor replied:
"I have read your memorial.
Although Wèi Jiàng 魏絳 cited the 'Yú Zhēn 虞箴' to admonish Duke Dào of Jìn 晉悼,
and Xiàngrú 相如 presented 'Fierce Beasts' to warn Emperor Wǔ of Hàn 漢武,
they are not sufficient to compare with this.
At present, the two enemies have not been eradicated,
and generals are campaigning far away.
Therefore, I occasionally enter the wilderness to practice military preparedness.
As for the warning about returning at night,
I have already ordered the relevant officials to implement it."
Initially,
at the end of the Jiàn'ān 建安 era,
Sūn Quán 孫權 first sent envoys to declare allegiance,
but also engaged in battle with Liú Bèi 劉備.
An imperial decree sought counsel on
"whether to raise an army to join with Wú 吳 and take Shǔ 蜀."
Lǎng 朗 deliberated, saying:
"The army of the Son of Heaven
is more important than Mount Huá 華 and Mount Dài 岱.
It should truly sit and manifest heavenly majesty,
unmoving like a mountain.
Suppose Quán 權 personally engaged in a prolonged battle with the Shǔ 蜀 bandits,
fighting for many days,
with equal intelligence and strength, and the battle not quickly decided.
If it then required an army to be raised to turn the tide,
then it would be appropriate to select a general who is steadfast,
to seize the key points of the enemy,
to act only after observing the timing,
and to move only after selecting the terrain.
With one strike, there would be no further complications.
Now, Quán's 權 army has not yet moved,
so there is no reason for an auxiliary Wú 吳 army to advance first.
Furthermore, the rainy season is at its height,
which is not the time for military movement and mass deployment."
The emperor adopted his plan.
During the Huángchū 黃初 era,
pelicans gathered at the Língzhī Chí 靈芝池.
An imperial decree ordered the high officials to recommend virtuous gentlemen of independent conduct.
Lǎng 朗 recommended Grandee of Bright Favor Yáng Biāo 楊彪,
and also feigned illness,
yielding his position to Biāo 彪.
The emperor then appointed officials and soldiers for Biāo 彪,
placing his rank second only to the Three Ducal Ministers.
The imperial decree stated:
"I sought a worthy person from you but did not obtain one.
You, however, suddenly claimed illness.
Not only did I not gain a worthy person,
but you also opened a path to lose worthy people
and increased the tilting of the jade scale.
Could it be that residing in your chamber and speaking ill
caused you to be rejected by gentlemen?
You should not have any further excuses."
Lǎng 朗 then resumed his duties.
Sūn Quán 孫權 wanted to send his son Dēng 登 to serve at court,
but he did not arrive.
At this time, the imperial carriage moved to Xǔchāng 許昌,
and large-scale屯 tún fields were established.
The emperor wanted to lead a large army on an eastern expedition.
Lǎng 朗 submitted a memorial saying:
"In the past, the King of Nányuè 南越 maintained good relations,
and Yīng Qí 嬰齊 entered to serve at court,
eventually becoming the heir apparent
and returning to rule his country.
Kāngjū 康居 was arrogant and crafty,
their intentions not matching their words.
The Protector-General memorialized that it was appropriate to send a princely hostage
to curb their disrespect.
Moreover, the disaster of Wú Bì 吳濞
originated from his son entering service,
and the rebellion of Kuí Xiāo 隗囂
also disregarded his son.
Previously, I heard that Quán 權 spoke of sending his son but he has not arrived.
Now the six armies are on high alert.
I fear that the people in the chariots do not fully understand your sacred intentions,
and will think that the state is angered by Dēng's 登 delay,
and is therefore raising an army for this reason.
If the army marches and Dēng 登 then arrives,
what was moved was immense,
what was achieved was minuscule,
still not enough to be cause for celebration.
If he remains arrogant and stubborn,
with no intention of entering,
I fear that those who do not fully understand public opinion
will all harbor doubts and hesitations.
Your humble servant believes it would be appropriate to instruct the various generals on separate expeditions
to each clearly uphold imperial prohibitions,
and carefully guard their assigned territories.
Outwardly manifest fierce might,
and inwardly expand agriculture.
Make it tranquil like a mountain,
and calm like a deep pool,
whose power cannot be moved,
and whose plans cannot be fathomed."
At this time,
the emperor formed the army and proceeded.
Quán's 權 son did not arrive,
and the imperial carriage reached the river and returned.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he was promoted and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lánlíng,
with an increase of five hundred households to his邑 (fief),
making a total of one thousand two hundred households previously and currently.
He was sent on a mission to Yè to inspect the tomb of Wénzhāo Huánghòu,
where he saw that some of the common people were in want.
At this time, palaces were being built and renovated,
and Lǎng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
gracious edicts have been repeatedly issued,
and all the common people are overjoyed.
I recently served as an envoy on a northern journey,
and on the way there and back,
I heard that many of the labor services
could be remitted, abolished, or reduced.
I beg Your Majesty to give serious consideration even late in the day,
to devise strategies to counter the bandits.
In ancient times, when Dà Yǔ intended to alleviate the great suffering of the world,
he first humbled his palaces,
and economized on his clothing and food,
thereby being able to possess all of Jiǔzhōu,
and assist in the completion of the Five Zones.
Gōu Jiàn, desiring to expand the territory around his capital,
and to butcher Fūchā at Gūsū,
likewise restricted himself and extended it to his family,
and economized his family to benefit the state,
thereby being able to encompass the Five Lakes,
and sweep across the Three Rivers,
establishing his might in the Central Plains,
and confirming his hegemony over Huáxià.
Wén and Jǐng of Hàn also desired to expand their ancestral enterprise,
and elevate their grand legacy,
and thus they were able to relinquish the idea of a hundred-gold terrace,
and manifest frugality in their silk-and-coarse-silk garments.
Internally, they reduced the Grand Provisioner and accepted no tributes,
externally, they reduced corvée and taxes, and diligently promoted agriculture and sericulture,
thereby being able to be known as an era of peace and prosperity,
almost achieving a state where punishments were set aside.
The reason Xiàowǔ was able to display his military might
and expand his foreign borders
was truly due to the accumulated wealth of his ancestors, which was sufficient,
thus he was able to achieve great success.
Huò Qùbìng,
a general of average talent,
still, because the Xiōngnú were not yet vanquished,
did not build a grand mansion.
Those who clearly care for the distant neglect the near;
those who prioritize external matters simplify internal ones.
From the beginning of Hàn and throughout its restoration,
it was always after military conflicts had largely subsided
that the Fèngquè (Phoenix Gate) was grandly opened,
and the Déyáng (Virtuous Sun) palaces were built simultaneously.
Currently, the Jiànshǐ (Beginning of Establishment) palace is sufficient for court assemblies,
and the Chónghuá (Exalted Glory) palace is sufficient for arranging inner officials.
Huálín (Flowery Forest) and Tiānyuān (Heavenly Abyss) are sufficient for banquets and excursions.
If only the Xiàngwèi (ornamental gate) of Chānghé (Heavenly Gate) were completed first,
so it would be sufficient for foreign envoys to present tribute,
and the city walls were repaired,
so they would be sufficient to prevent trespassing,
forming a secure defense for the state,
all other matters
should await a year of abundance.
If we solely prioritize diligent farming
and preparing for war,
then there will be no resentment or idleness in the state,
the population will grow,
the people will be well-fed, and the army strong,
and if bandit-barbarians are not submissive,
and peace and prosperity are lacking,
such a thing has never happened."
He was transferred to become Sītú (Minister of Works).
At that time, the emperor frequently lost imperial sons,
and there were few concubines in the rear palace who were housed in separate residences for childbirth.
Lǎng submitted a memorial, saying:
"In ancient times, King Wén of Zhōu had King Wǔ at the age of fifteen,
and subsequently enjoyed the blessing of ten sons,
thereby expanding the lineage of the various Jī (royal surname).
King Wǔ, when already old, fathered King Chéng,
which is why King Chéng had few brothers.
These two kings
each established saintly virtues,
with no one surpassing the other;
but comparing the blessing of their descendants,
they are not alike.
Indeed, childbirth has its early and late times,
and what is produced has its many and few.
Your Majesty's virtuous blessings combine those of those two sages,
and your age is greater than when King Wén of Jī fathered King Wǔ;
yet sons have not yet been born in the inner chambers of the imperial palace,
and princely kings have not yet multiplied in the many rooms of the imperial harem.
Taking King Chéng as an example,
it is not yet too late;
taking Bóyì as an example,
it is not too early.
and scholars often say
that twelve is the limit.
By the end of the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
The 'Rites of Zhōu' specify one hundred and twenty inner officials for the six palaces,
However, even though they were numerous,
those who came at the auspicious time to the favorable residences were very few.
It is clear that the essence of 'may you have a hundred sons'
truly lies in singleness of purpose,
not merely in striving for multitude.
This old minister sincerely
wishes that the state's blessings might equal the 'five times five' of Xuānyuán,
but it has not yet reached the 'two times five' of King Wén of Zhōu,
which causes me distress.
Moreover, when young, one often suffers from overly warm bedding.
If it is too warm, one cannot comfortably adapt one's soft skin and weak body,
making it difficult to protect oneself,
and easy to become ill.
If children's quilted robes
are always kept from being too thick,
then they will surely all preserve their healthy nature,
and their lifespans will compare to that of Nánshān."
The Emperor replied:
"True loyalty is expressed in earnest words;
profound love is expressed in deep words.
You have labored with your thoughts,
and also penned your ideas in accordance with my wishes.
I have read your virtuous words three times,
and am immensely pleased.
I have not yet established an heir,
which causes you worry.
I respectfully accept your sincere words,
and wish to hear good counsel."
Lǎng authored commentaries on the Yì (Book of Changes), Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals), Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety), and Zhōuguān (Rites of Zhou),
and also wrote memorials and essays,
all of which have been passed down through the ages.
In the second year of Tàihé, he passed away
and was posthumously named Chénghóu (Accomplished Marquis).
His son, Sù, inherited his title.
Initially,
Emperor Wén divided Lǎng's household fief
and enfeoffed one of his sons as a列侯 (marquis).
Lǎng requested that his elder brother's son, Xiáng, be enfeoffed instead.
Sù’s courtesy name was Zǐyōng.
At eighteen,
he studied the *Tàixuán* under Sòng Zhōng,
and then created his own commentary on it.
During the Huángchū era,
he served as a Sànqí Huángmén Shìláng.
In the third year of Tàihé,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì.
In the fourth year,
when Dà Sīmǎ Cáo Zhēn was campaigning against Shǔ,
Sù submitted a memorial which stated:
“Previous records contain this:
‘When provisions are transported a thousand *lǐ*,
the soldiers have a hungry look.
When firewood is gathered and cooking is done afterward,
the army does not sleep full.’
This refers to marching on flat terrain.
How much more so when penetrating deep into treacherous terrain,
carving out roads to advance,
then the toil must be a hundredfold.
Now, heavy rain has been added,
making mountain slopes steep and slippery.
The multitudes are constrained and cannot spread out,
and provisions are distant and difficult to sustain.
This is truly a great taboo for campaigners.
I hear that Cáo Zhēn departed over a month ago, yet has only covered half the valley.
Road construction efforts
have engaged all the warriors.
This allows the enemy to rest while we toil,
which is what military strategists dread.
Speaking of previous generations,
when King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he went out of the pass and then returned.
Regarding recent events,
when Wǔ and Wén campaigned against Quán,
they reached the river but did not cross.
Are these not examples of what is called conforming to heaven’s will and knowing the opportune moment,
being adept at adapting to change!
The common people will know that Your Majesty, due to the difficulties of the rain,
has paused and rested the army.
When an opportunity arises in the future,
you can seize and exploit it.
Then, it will be a case of ‘delighting in facing hardship,’
and the people will forget their deaths.”
Thereupon, the campaign was indeed halted.
He also submitted a memorial:
“It is appropriate to follow old rites
and issue mourning announcements for high officials,
and offer fruits in the ancestral temple.”
All these matters were carried out.
He also submitted a memorial discussing the fundamentals of governance, stating:
“Eliminate unnecessary positions,
reduce salaries that are not urgent,
stop expenses incurred solely for sustenance,
and combine superfluous offices;
ensure that every official has a specific duty,
that duties are carried out by those appointed to them,
that for every task there is a corresponding salary,
and that salary replaces farming.
This was the constant practice of ancient times,
and is what is appropriate today.
If officials are few and salaries are generous,
then public expenses will be minimal,
and the ambition to advance in service will be encouraged.
Each will exert their talent and strength,
and none will rely on others.
Presenting memorials through words,
and testing them clearly with accomplishments,
whether one is capable or not,
is simply known to the emperor’s heart.
This is why during the times of Táng and Yú, positions were established and duties divided,
and commands were issued to the high ministers,
each according to their specific tasks.
Afterward, only Lóng served as the Nàyán,
similar to today’s Shàngshū,
solely for transmitting imperial commands.
The Xià and Yīn dynasties cannot be detailed.
The *Gān Shì* says, ‘people of the six tasks,’
making clear that the Six Ministers also managed affairs.
The offices of Zhōu are thoroughly documented:
the court met every five days,
with the high ministers and grand masters all advancing,
and the Sīshì distinguishing their positions.
Its record states: ‘
Those who sit and discuss the Way are called kings and dukes;
those who act and implement it are called scholars and grand masters.’
At the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
it imitated previous generations,
with high ministers all personally ascending to court for affairs.
Thus, Gāozǔ personally pursued Zhōu Chāng who had turned back,
and Emperor Wǔ approved from afar Jí Àn’s memorial presentation.
Emperor Xuān made high ministers attend court once every five days.
Emperor Chéng first established five Shàngshū.
From then on, things declined,
and court rites gradually became deficient.
The ritual of attending court every five days can be restored,
allowing high ministers and Shàngshū to advance according to their respective affairs.
Restoring neglected rites
and glorifying the sagely legacy
is truly what is called ‘beautiful in name and substantial in reality.’”
During the Qīnglóng era,
the Duke of Shānyáng died.
He was the former Hàn ruler.
Sù submitted a memorial, stating:
“In ancient times, Táng abdicated to Yú,
and Yú abdicated to Xià.
Both observed the three-year mourning period
before ascending to the尊 position of Son of Heaven.
Thus, the imperial title remained intact,
and the rites for a monarch were preserved.
Now, the Duke of Shānyáng accepted the Mandate of Heaven,
and truly responded to the people’s hopes,
abdicating to the Great Wèi,
and retiring to the position of an honored guest.
The Duke served Wèi
without daring to fail in his duty.
Wèi treated the Duke
with generosity and reverence, not as a subject.
Upon his death,
the regulations for his coffin and interment,
and the decorations for his procession,
were all made identical to those of a king.
Because of this, distant and near alike acclaimed his benevolence,
considering it a great and beautiful act.
Moreover, Hàn combined the titles of Emperor and Sovereign,
calling him Huángdì.
There is a separate title for Dì,
but not for Huáng,
so Huáng is the lesser of the two.
Therefore, in the time of Gāozǔ,
there were no two kings in the land,
and his father was still alive yet allowed to be called Huáng,
clearly indicating that it was not perceived as having two kings.
How much more so now,
when it is an posthumous honor,
he can be called Huáng to match his posthumous title.”
Emperor Míng did not follow the suggestion to call him Huáng,
but instead posthumously named him Hàn Xiàoxiàn Huángdì.
Later, Sù was appointed Secretary to the Imperial Household Grandee (Chángshì), overseeing the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān),
and concurrently Sacrificial Libationer of the Chongwen Pavilion (Chóngwén Guān Jìjiǔ).
During the Jǐngchū era,
palace construction flourished,
the people neglected agriculture,
trust and honesty were not upheld,
and executions were hasty.
Sù submitted a memorial saying:
"The Great Wèi inherits the ultimate authority of a hundred kings.
The common people are few,
and the implements of war have not ceased.
It is truly fitting to give the people a respite and benefit them with peace and quiet, in a time extending far and wide.
The effort to accumulate stores and give rest to the weary people
lies in reducing corvée labor and diligently pursuing agriculture.
Now, the palace construction is not yet finished,
the great projects are not yet complete,
transportation of supplies is being levied,
and transfers are constantly demanded.
Therefore, the able-bodied men are exhausted by labor,
farmers are leaving their fields,
those who sow grain are few,
and those who eat grain are many.
The old grain is depleted,
and no new grain is being replaced.
This is a great worry for the state,
and not a long-term strategy for preparation.
Currently, there are three or four tens of thousands of workers.
The Jiǔlóng Palace can secure Your Sacred Person,
and its interior is sufficient to accommodate the six imperial concubines (liùgōng).
The Xiǎnyáng Hall
is also nearing completion.
Only the Tàijí Palace and the areas before it
still require substantial effort.
It is now the height of winter,
and illnesses may arise.
I sincerely wish that Your Majesty would issue a virtuous decree,
and proclaim a clear edict,
deeply pitying the exhaustion of the laborers,
and generously sympathizing with the insufficiency of the myriad people.
Take the soldiers who receive regular rations from the granaries,
those who are not urgently needed,
select the strong and robust among them,
keep ten thousand men,
and rotate them after one period.
If all know that there is a day for rest and replacement,
then none will fail to cheerfully undertake their tasks,
laboring without resentment.
Calculating, one year requires 3,600,000 labor-days,
which is not a small number.
What is to be completed in one year,
allow it to take three years.
Dispatch the rest,
so that they all return to agriculture;
this is an endless plan.
When granaries overflow with grain,
and the people have surplus strength: using this to undertake projects,
what project will not be established?
Using this to implement transformation,
what transformation will not be achieved?
Indeed, trustworthiness towards the people
is the great treasure of the state.
Kǒng Ní said: 'From ancient times, all must die,
but without trust, the people cannot stand.'
That humble state of Jìn,
and the insignificant Chóng'ěr,
when wishing to utilize their people,
first showed them trustworthiness.
Therefore, even though Yuán was about to surrender,
it returned because of trust,
and thus was able to achieve hegemony in one battle,
still lauded to this day.
Previously, when the imperial chariot was about to visit Luòyáng,
the people were conscripted to build camps.
The officials ordered that upon completion of the camps, they would be dismissed.
Once completed,
the officials, however, valued their labor
and did not dismiss them in a timely manner.
The officials only sought their immediate benefit,
disregarding the principles of governing the state.
Your humble servant believes that from now on,
if the people are again conscripted,
the command should be clear,
ensuring it is fulfilled on schedule.
If there are further tasks,
it is better to issue another conscription
than to lose trust.
All the punishments Your Majesty administers on the spot
are for culpable officials
and those who deserve death.
However, the common people do not know this
and consider them hasty.
Therefore, I wish Your Majesty would hand them over to the proper officials and expose their crimes.
Even if they must die,
do not let it soil the imperial palace and cause suspicion among those near and far.
Moreover, human life is of utmost importance,
difficult to create and easy to destroy,
once the breath is cut off, it cannot be restored;
therefore, the sages valued it highly.
Mèng Kē said that to kill one innocent person to gain the empire,
a benevolent person would not do it.
In the Hàn dynasty, there was a person who violated the imperial prohibition (bì) and startled the emperor's carriage horses.
The Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi) Zhāng Shìzhī memorialized that he should be fined.
Emperor Wén was surprised by the lightness of the penalty,
but Shìzhī said: 'At that time,
if the emperor had ordered his execution, it would have been done.
Now he has been handed over to the Minister of Justice.
The Minister of Justice
is the standard of justice for the empire.
If it is once tilted,
then all laws throughout the empire will be applied with arbitrary severity and leniency,
and where will the people place their hands and feet?'
Your humble servant believes that this greatly misses the point of righteousness,
and is not what a loyal subject should present.
The Minister of Justice
is an official of the Son of Heaven;
if he cannot lose impartiality,
then how can the person of the Son of Heaven
himself be confused and mistaken?
This is valuing oneself overmuch,
and belittling one's lord,
an extreme of disloyalty.
The Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng) said: 'The Son of Heaven does not speak in jest;
when he speaks, the historians record it,
the musicians sing it,
and the scholars quote it.'
If words are not jested with,
how much less actions?
Therefore, Shìzhī's words must not be overlooked,
and Zhōu Gōng's admonition must be emulated."
He further stated:
"All useless birds and beasts,
which incur expenses for fodder, grain, and human labor,
can all be eliminated."
The Emperor once asked:
"During the reign of Emperor Huán of Hàn,
Lǐ Yún, the Magistrate of Báimǎ, memorialized: 'An emperor (dì)
is one who is discerning (dì).'
'This emperor wishes not to be discerning.'
Why did he not deserve to die?"
Sù replied:
"He merely spoke without regard for the proper order of directness and compliance.
Examining his original intention,
he wished to devote his whole heart,
mindful of preserving and supplementing the state.
Moreover, the majesty of an emperor
surpasses thunder and lightning.
Killing a common man
is no different from killing an ant.
To be lenient and pardon him
would demonstrate the capacity to accept frank counsel,
extending virtue throughout the world.
Therefore, your humble servant believes that killing him was not necessarily correct."
The Emperor then asked:
"Sīmǎ Qiān, due to having suffered punishment,
harbored hidden resentment,
and in writing the Shǐjì, he disparaged Emperor Wǔ,
causing people to gnash their teeth."
Sù replied:
"Sīmǎ Qiān, in recording events,
did not falsely praise,
nor conceal evil.
Liú Xiàng and Yáng Xióng admired his excellent work,
recognized his talent as a good historian,
and called it a 'true record'.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, hearing of his compilation of the Shǐjì,
took the imperial annals (běnjì) of Emperor Jǐng and himself to read them.
Thereupon, he became greatly enraged,
mutilated them and threw them away.
To this day, these two annals have records but no writings.
Later, he encountered the Lǐ Líng affair,
and then Sīmǎ Qiān was subjected to castration (cánshì).
This shows that the hidden resentment was directed at Emperor Wǔ,
and not originating from Sīmǎ Qiān."
In the first year of Zhèngshǐ [zhèng shǐ],
he was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Guǎngpíng [guǎng píng].
Recalled for official business,
he was appointed as an Attendant Officer (Yìláng [yì láng]).
After a short while,
he became a Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng [shì zhōng]),
then was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng [tài cháng]).
At that time, Grand Marshal Cáo Shuǎng [cáo shuǎng] held exclusive power,
employing Hé Yàn [hé yàn], Dèng Yáng [dèng yáng], and others.
Sù [sù], along with Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi [tài wèi]) Jiǎng Jì [jiǎng jì] and Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng [sī nóng]) Huán Fàn [huán fàn], discussed current politics.
Sù sternly said:
"This group is of the same ilk as Hóng Gōng [hóng gōng] and Shí Xiǎn [shí xiǎn];
are they to be listened to again!"
Shuǎng heard of this
and warned Hé Yàn and others, saying:
"We must all be careful!
The high officials have already compared you gentlemen to notorious people of previous generations."
He was dismissed due to an affair concerning the ancestral temple.
Later, he became Superintendent of the Palace Granaries (Guānglùxūn [guāng lù xūn]).
At that time, there were two fish, a foot long,
that gathered on the roof of the military arsenal (Wǔkù [wǔ kù]).
The officials in charge considered it an auspicious sign.
Sù said:
"Fish are born in the abyss but ascend to the roof;
scaled creatures have lost their proper place.
Will the frontier generals perhaps face a catastrophe of abandoning their armor?"
Afterward, there was indeed the defeat at Dōngguān [dōng guān].
He was transferred to become Governor of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn [hé nán yǐn]).
In the sixth year of Jiāpíng [jiā píng],
holding a staff of authority and concurrently Grand Master of Ceremonies,
he received the imperial carriage
to welcome the Duke of Gāoguì Township (Gāoguì Xiānggōng [gāo guì xiāng gōng]) in Yuánchéng [yuán chéng].
That year,
a white vapor spanned the sky.
Grand Marshal Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng [sī mǎ jǐng wáng] asked Sù its meaning.
Sù replied:
"This is the banner of Chīyóu [chī yóu];
will there be chaos in the southeast?
If you cultivate yourself to bring peace to the common people,
then those who enjoy peace in the world will return to your virtue,
and those who instigate chaos will perish first."
The next spring,
General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn [zhèn dōng jiāng jūn]) Wúqiū Jiǎn [wú qiū jiǎn] and Inspector of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Cìshǐ [yáng zhōu cì shǐ]) Wén Qīn [wén qīn] rebelled.
Jǐngwáng said to Sù:
"Huò Guāng [huò guāng] was influenced by Xiàhóu Shèng's [xià hóu shèng] words
and then began to value scholars;
there was indeed a reason for it.
How can one pacify the state and secure the ruler?"
Sù said:
"Formerly, Guān Yǔ [guān yǔ] led the forces of Jīngzhōu [jīng zhōu]
and made Yú Jìn [yú jìn] surrender by the Hàn River,
thus conceiving the ambition to contend for the empire by moving north.
Later, Sūn Quán [sūn quán] attacked and seized his officers' and soldiers' families,
and Yǔ's [yǔ] troops instantly disintegrated.
Now, the parents, wives, and children of the Huáinán [huái nán] generals and soldiers are all in the interior provinces.
If we just hurry to defend and prevent them from advancing,
there will surely be a situation like Guān Yǔ's [guān yǔ] collapse."
Jǐngwáng followed his advice,
and consequently defeated Jiǎn [jiǎn] and Qīn [qīn].
Later, he was promoted to Central Leader of the Army (Zhōnglǐngjūn [zhōng lǐng jūn]),
given the additional title of Cavalier Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì [sàn qí cháng shì]),
and his fief was increased by three hundred households,
making a total of two thousand two hundred households including the previous ones.
He died in the first year of Gānlù [gān lù],
with hundreds of disciples wearing mourning clothes.
He was posthumously granted the title of General of the Vanguard (Wèijiāngjūn [wèi jiāng jūn])
and given the posthumous name Jǐnghóu [jǐng hóu].
His son Yùn [yùn] succeeded him.
When Yùn [yùn] died,
he had no son,
and the peerage was abolished.
In the fourth year of Jǐngyuán [jǐng yuán],
Sù's son Xún [xún] was enfeoffed as Marquis of Lánlíng (Lánlíng Hóu [lán líng hóu]).
During Xiánxī [xián xī],
the Five Orders of Nobility were established,
and because Sù [sù] had made significant contributions in the previous dynasty,
Xún [xún] was re-enfeoffed as Viscount of Chéng (Chéngzǐ [chéng zǐ]).
Initially,
Sù [sù] excelled in the teachings of Jiǎ [jiǎ] and Mǎ [mǎ],
but disliked those of Zhèng Shì [zhèng shì].
He collected and synthesized similarities and differences,
writing commentaries on the Shàngshū [shàng shū], Shī [shī], Lúnyǔ [lún yǔ], Sānlǐ [sān lǐ], and Zuǒshì [zuǒ shì].
He also compiled and finalized his father Láng's [láng] commentaries on the Yìzhuàn [yì zhuàn],
all of which were listed in the imperial academy.
His discussions and refutations on court regulations,
suburban sacrifices, ancestral temples, mourning rites, and matters of importance,
totaled over a hundred chapters.
At that time, Sūn Shūrén [sūn shū rén] of Lè'ān [lè ān],
who studied under Zhèng Xuán [zhèng xuán],
was known as the Great Confucian of Dōngzhōu [dōng zhōu].
He was summoned to be Secretary of the Imperial Library (Mìshūjiān [mì shū jiān])
but did not accept.
Sù [sù] compiled the Shèngzhènglùn [shèng zhèng lùn] to criticize Xuán [xuán].
Shūrén [shū rén] refuted and clarified it,
and also wrote examples for the Zhōuyì [zhōu yì] and Chūnqiū [chūn qiū],
as well as commentaries on the Máoshī [máo shī], Lǐjì [lǐ jì], the three biographies of the Chūnqiū [chūn qiū], Guóyǔ [guó yǔ], and Éryǎ [ér yǎ],
and further commented on over ten chapters of other books.
Since the early Wèi [wèi] dynasty, the summoned scholar Zhōu Shēngliè [zhōu shēng liè] of Dūnhuáng [dūn huáng],
and during Emperor Míng's [míng] reign, Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng [dà sī nóng]) Dǒng Yù [dǒng yù] of Hóngnóng [hóng nóng] and others,
also successively annotated the Classics and commentaries,
which were widely circulated.
A commentary says: Zhōng Yáo [zhōng yáo] was open-minded and capable,
Huá Xīn [huá xīn] was pure and virtuous,
Wáng Láng [wáng láng] was learned and eloquent.
Indeed, they were all outstanding figures of their time.
When the Wèi [wèi] clan first received the mandate,
they ascended to the Three Ducal Ministers;
how glorious that was!
Wáng Sù [wáng sù] was upright and widely learned,
and capable of discernment!
Biographies of Chéng [chéng], Guō [guō], Dǒng [dǒng], Liú [liú], Jiǎng [jiǎng], Liú [liú], Chapter Fourteen.
Chéng Yù [chéng yù], courtesy name Zhòngdé [zhòng dé],
was a native of Dōng'ā [dōng ē], Dōngjùn [dōng jùn].
He was eight feet three inches tall
with a beautiful beard.
When the Yellow Turbans (Huángjīn [huáng jīn]) rose,
the county assistant Wáng Dù [wáng dù] responded to them
and burned the granaries.
The county magistrate fled over the city wall,
and the officials and people carried their elderly and young to the east, fleeing to Qúqiūshān [qú qiū shān].
Yù [yù] sent someone to scout Dù [dù].
Dù [dù] and his group, having obtained an empty city, could not hold it
and stopped to encamp five or six *lǐ* west of the city.
Yù [yù] said to the prominent local families, Xuē Fáng [xuē fáng] and others:
"Now Dù [dù] and his group have acquired the city but cannot inhabit it;
their situation is clear.
They merely want to plunder wealth
and do not have the intention of attacking and defending with strong armor and sharp weapons.
Why do we not lead the people back to the city and defend it?
Moreover, the city walls are high and thick,
and there is much grain.
If we now go back and seek the magistrate,
and together firmly defend,
Dù [dù] will surely not last long,
and we can defeat them by attacking."
Fáng [fáng] and others thought this was true.
The officials and common people refused to follow,
saying:
"The bandits are to the west;
there is only east to go."
Yù [yù] said to Fáng [fáng] and others:
"Ignorant people cannot be consulted on matters."
So he secretly sent several horsemen to raise banners on the eastern mountain,
making Fáng [fáng] and others see them.
They shouted loudly,
"The bandits have arrived!"
Then they descended the mountain toward the city,
and the officials and people rushed to follow them.
They found the county magistrate,
and together defended the city.
Dù [dù] and his group came to attack the city
but could not take it,
and intended to leave.
Yù [yù] led the officials and people to open the city gate and attacked them fiercely,
and Dù [dù] and his group were defeated and fled.
Dōng'ā [dōng ē] was thus preserved.
During the Chūpíng [chū píng] era,
Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ [yǎn zhōu cì shǐ]) Liú Dài [liú dài] invited Yù [yù],
but Yù [yù] did not respond.
At this time, Dài [dài] was in friendly relations with Yuán Shào [yuán shào] and Gōngsūn Zàn [gōng sūn zàn].
Shào [shào] had his wife and children reside with Dài [dài],
and Zàn [zàn] also sent his aide Fàn Fāng [fàn fāng] with cavalry to assist Dài [dài].
Later, Shào [shào] and Zàn [zàn] had a rift.
Zàn [zàn] defeated Shào's [shào] army
and then sent an envoy to Dài [dài],
ordering him to send back Shào's [shào] wife and children
and sever ties with Shào [shào].
He separately instructed Fàn Fāng [fàn fāng]:
"If Dài [dài] does not send back Shào's [shào] family,
return with your cavalry.
When I have settled with Shào [shào],
I will send troops against Dài [dài]."
Dài [dài] deliberated for several days without a decision.
His chief clerk (Biéjià [bié jià]) Wáng Yù [wáng yù] told Dài [dài]:
"Chéng Yù [chéng yù] is resourceful
and capable of deciding important matters."
Dài [dài] then summoned Yù [yù],
asked for his counsel,
and Yù [yù] said:
"If you abandon Shào's [shào] close support and seek Zàn's [zàn] distant aid,
this is like the saying of borrowing a man from Yuè [yuè] to save a drowning son.
Gōngsūn Zàn [gōng sūn zàn]
is not an match for Yuán Shào [yuán shào].
Although he has now defeated Shào's [shào] army,
he will ultimately be captured by Shào [shào].
If you pursue immediate advantage for a single day and do not consider long-term plans,
General, you will ultimately fail."
Dài [dài] followed his advice.
Fàn Fāng [fàn fāng] returned with his cavalry,
but before he arrived,
Zàn [zàn] was greatly defeated by Shào [shào].
Dài [dài] nominated Yù [yù] as Commandant of Cavalry (Qídūwèi [qí dū wèi]),
but Yù [yù] declined on account of illness.
Liú Dài 劉岱 was killed by the Huángjīn 黃巾.
Tài Zǔ 太祖 arrived in Yǎnzhōu 兗州,
and invited Yù 昱 to join him.
As Yù 昱 was about to leave,
his fellow villagers said to him,
"How can your present actions contradict your past ones!"
Yù 昱 smiled but did not respond.
Tài Zǔ 太祖 spoke with him,
was pleased by him,
and appointed Yù 昱 as the Prefect of Shòuzhāng 壽張.
When Tài Zǔ 太祖 campaigned in Xúzhōu 徐州,
he left Yù 昱 and Xún Yù 荀彧 to guard Juànchéng 鄄城.
Zhāng Miǎo 張邈 and others rebelled and welcomed Lǚ Bù 呂布;
the commanderies and counties all responded,
except for Juànchéng 鄄城, Fàn 范, and Dōng'ē 東阿, which remained steadfast.
Deserters from Lǚ Bù's 呂布 army
reported that Chén Gōng 陳宮 intended to lead troops to capture Dōng'ē 東阿,
and also sent Fàn Yì 氾嶷 to take Fàn 范.
The officials and common people were all terrified.
Yù 彧 said to Yù 昱,
"Now that Yǎnzhōu 兗州 has rebelled,
only these three cities remain.
Gōng 宮 and others are menacing them with heavy forces;
unless we can deeply win their hearts,
the three cities will certainly turn.
You,
sir, are the hope of the people;
go and persuade them,
and perhaps it can be done!"
Yù 昱 then returned home.
Passing through Fàn 范,
he persuaded its Prefect, Jìn Yǔn 靳允, saying,
"I hear that Lǚ Bù 呂布 has seized your mother, younger brother, wife, and children.
A filial son truly cannot bear such a thought!
Now the world is in great chaos,
heroes are rising everywhere,
and there must be someone destined
to calm the world's disorder.
This is what the wise meticulously consider.
Those who find the right lord prosper;
those who lose the right lord perish.
Chén Gōng 陳宮 rebelled and welcomed Lǚ Bù 呂布, and a hundred cities responded.
It seems he might accomplish something,
but from your perspective,
what kind of person is Bù 布?
Bù 布,
is coarse and lacks affection,
stubborn and without courtesy;
he is merely a hero among common men.
Gōng 宮 and others have allied with him out of temporary opportunism;
they cannot truly serve him as their lord.
Although his army is numerous,
he will ultimately achieve nothing.
Lord Cáo's 曹 wisdom and strategy are unparalleled in this era;
he is likely divinely appointed!
You must hold Fàn 范 firmly,
and I will guard Dōng'ē 東阿;
then the achievement of Tián Dān 田單 can be realized.
Which is better: to abandon loyalty and follow evil, and have both mother and son perish?"
Only you, sir, deliberate carefully!"
Yǔn 允 wept and said,
"I dare not harbor a second thought."
At that time, Fàn Yì 氾嶷 was already in the county.
Yǔn 允 then met Yì 嶷,
ambushed and assassinated him,
and returned to mobilize troops for defense.
Yù 昱 also dispatched a detachment of cavalry to cut off Cāngtíng Jīn 倉亭津.
When Chén Gōng 陳宮 arrived,
he could not cross.
When Yù 昱 reached Dōng'ē 東阿,
the Prefect of Dōng'ē 東阿, Zǎo Zhī 棗祗, had already rallied his officials and people,
and was firmly defending the city.
Moreover, Xuē Tì 薛悌, an aide in Yǎnzhōu 兗州, conspired with Yù 昱,
and together they successfully secured the three cities,
awaiting Tài Zǔ 太祖.
When Tài Zǔ 太祖 returned,
he held Yù's 昱 hand and said,
"Without your strength,
I would have nowhere to return to."
He then appointed Yù 昱 as the Administrator of Dōngpíng 東平,
stationing him in Fàn 范.
Tài Zǔ 太祖 battled Lǚ Bù 呂布 at Púyáng 濮陽,
and was repeatedly unsuccessful.
A locust plague broke out,
so both sides withdrew.
Thereupon, Yuán Shào 袁紹 sent someone to persuade Tài Zǔ 太祖 to form an alliance,
wishing to make Tài Zǔ 太祖 move his family to Yè 鄴.
Tài Zǔ 太祖 had recently lost Yǎnzhōu 兗州,
and his army's food supplies were exhausted,
so he was about to agree.
At this time, Yù 昱 returned from a mission;
he was granted an audience,
and then spoke, saying,
"I secretly heard that the General intends to send away his family
and form an alliance with Yuán Shào 袁紹.
Is this truly so?"
Tài Zǔ 太祖 said,
"Yes."
Yù 昱 said,
"It seems the General is perhaps afraid in the face of the matter,
otherwise why are your considerations not deeper?
Yuán Shào 袁紹 occupies the lands of Yān 燕 and Zhào 趙,
and has the ambition to conquer the world,
but his wisdom is insufficient to achieve it.
Does the General believe he can be subservient to him?
With the General's power like a dragon and tiger,
can he perform the deeds of Hán 韓 and Péng 彭?
Although Yǎnzhōu 兗州 is now ravaged,
there are still three cities.
The number of able fighting men
is no less than ten thousand.
With the General's divine martial prowess,
and with Wénruò 文若 and Yù 昱 and others,
to gather and employ them,
the enterprise of a hegemon king can be achieved.
I beg the General to reconsider!"
Tài Zǔ 太祖 then stopped.
The Son of Heaven made Xǔ his capital,
and appointed Yù as Shàngshū.
As Yǎnzhōu was not yet settled,
he was again appointed Yù as Dōng Zhōnglángjiàng,
concurrently Jìyīn Tàishǒu,
and Overseer of Yǎnzhōu's affairs.
Liú Bèi lost Xúzhōu,
and came to submit to Tàizǔ.
Yù persuaded Tàizǔ to kill Bèi,
but Tàizǔ did not listen.
This account is in the Wǔjì.
Later, he again sent Bèi to Xúzhōu to intercept and attack Yuán Shù.
Yù and Guō Jiā persuaded Tàizǔ, saying:
"My Lord, previously you did not plan for Bèi,
and we, Yù and others, were indeed not as insightful.
Now, if you lend him troops,
he will certainly harbor rebellious intentions."
Tàizǔ regretted it,
but could not catch him when he pursued.
At this time, Shù died of illness.
Bèi arrived at Xúzhōu,
and thereupon killed Chē Zhòu,
raising an army to rebel against Tàizǔ.
Shortly after,
Yù was promoted to Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn.
Yuán Shào was at Líyáng,
and was about to cross south.
At that time, Yù had seven hundred soldiers defending Juànchéng.
Tàizǔ heard of it,
and sent someone to tell Yù
that he wanted to add two thousand soldiers.
Yù refused,
saying:
"Yuán Shào commands a hundred thousand troops,
and considers himself unstoppable.
Now, seeing Yù's few troops,
he will certainly underestimate them and not come to attack.
If you add troops to Yù,
and they exceed a certain number, then he cannot but attack.
If he attacks, he will certainly conquer,
and both sides will merely lose strength.
I hope My Lord has no doubts!"
Tàizǔ followed his advice.
Shào heard Yù had few troops,
and indeed did not go.
Tàizǔ said to Jiǎ Xǔ:
"Chéng Yù's courage
surpasses that of Bēn and Yù."
Yù gathered exiles from the mountains and swamps,
obtaining several thousand elite soldiers.
He then led his army to meet Tàizǔ at Líyáng,
and attacked Yuán Tán and Yuán Shàng.
Tán and Shàng were defeated and fled.
Yù was appointed Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānguó Tíng.
Tàizǔ campaigned against Jīngzhōu,
and Liú Bèi fled to Wú.
Commentators thought that Sūn Quán would certainly kill Bèi.
Yù predicted this, saying:
"Sūn Quán is newly in power,
and is not yet feared by all under heaven.
Cáo Gōng is unrivaled in the world.
Upon his initial capture of Jīngzhōu,
his prestige shook the region south of the Yangtze River.
Though Quán has schemes,
he cannot stand alone against him.
Liú Bèi has a heroic reputation;
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi are both a match for ten thousand men.
Quán will certainly rely on him to resist us.
Once the difficulty is resolved and power divided,
Bèi will rely on this to establish himself,
and cannot then be killed."
Quán indeed generously gave Bèi troops
to resist Tàizǔ.
Afterwards, as the central plains were gradually pacified,
Tàizǔ patted Yù's back and said:
"During the Yǎnzhōu setback,
had I not heeded your words,
how could I have reached this point?"
His relatives offered oxen and wine for a great feast.
Yù said:
"Knowing contentment averts disgrace;
I can now retire."
He then memorialized to return his troops,
closed his gate, and did not go out.
Yù was stubborn and unyielding by nature,
and often clashed with people.
Someone accused Yù of plotting rebellion,
but Tàizǔ bestowed gifts and treated him even more generously.
After the Wèi State was established,
he became Wèiwèi.
He quarreled with Zhōngwèi Xíng Zhēn over decorum,
and was dismissed.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he again became Wèiwèi.
He was promoted in enfeoffment as Marquis of Ānxiāng,
and his fief was increased by three hundred households,
making a total of eight hundred households including his previous one.
His youngest son, Yán, and grandson, Xiǎo, were separately enfeoffed as Marquises.
He was just about to be appointed Duke,
when he passed away.
The Emperor shed tears for him,
and posthumously granted him the title Chēqí Jiāngjūn,
with the posthumous title Sù Hóu.
His son, Wǔ, succeeded him.
When Wǔ passed away,
his son, Kè, succeeded him.
When Kè passed away,
his son, Liáng, succeeded him.
Xiǎo,
during the Jiāpíng era, served as a Huángmén Shìláng.
