At that time, the Xiàoshì were acting presumptuously.
Xiǎo submitted a memorial, saying:
“The Zhōulǐ states: ‘Officials are established and duties are divided,
to serve as the standard for the people.’
The Chūnqiū Zhuàn says: ‘Heaven has ten suns,
humans have ten ranks.’
The foolish should not lord over the wise,
the lowly should not lord over the noble.
Thus, sagely and wise individuals were jointly established,
and their reputation was set forth.
Their achievements were clearly tested,
and their performance evaluated every nine years.
Each cultivated their own profession,
their thoughts not extending beyond their position.
Therefore, when Luán Shū wished to save the Jìn Hóu,
his son did not obey;
when dead bodies lay across the streets,
Bǐng Jí did not inquire.
Superiors did not demand achievements outside of one's designated duties,
and inferiors did not strive for rewards beyond their allotted share.
Officials had no power of dual oversight,
and the people were not subjected to dual service.
This is truly the essential principle for governing a state,
the means by which order is established and chaos averted.
Looking back at ancient records and treatises,
and observing the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
although official titles changed,
and their responsibilities differed,
the principle of honoring superiors and restraining inferiors,
and clearly defining distinctions and precedents,
remained consistent.
There were originally no Xiàoshì officials interfering in general governmental affairs.
In earlier times, when Emperor Wǔ was initiating his great enterprise,
many official positions were not yet fully established.
Moreover, the military was burdened with hardships,
and the people's hearts were uneasy.
Even small offenses,
could not go uninvestigated.
Therefore, Xiàoshì were appointed,
for their provisional utility only.
However, they were managed with proper methods,
and did not become reckless.
This was a pragmatic measure for an era of dominance,
not a regular institution for an emperor.
Later, they gradually gained trust,
and again became a problem.
They continued to perpetuate themselves,
with no one rectifying their fundamental issues.
Consequently, they were allowed to inspect the palace and ancestral temples above,
and oversee all departments below.
Officials had no fixed positions,
and duties had no defined limits.
They acted according to their whim and inclination,
whatever suited their fancy.
Laws were made at the stroke of a pen,
not in accordance with decrees and edicts;
judgments were made outside the courts,
without regard for review or cross-examination.
When selecting their subordinates,
they considered caution as sloppiness,
and recklessness as talent.
When handling affairs,
they regarded harshness as public impartiality,
and adherence to principle as timidity.
Externally, they invoked imperial authority to bolster their influence,
internally, they gathered a multitude of villains to be their confidantes.
High officials were ashamed to share power with them,
and endured in silence.
Lesser individuals feared their sharp edge,
and harbored grievances without recourse.
This even led Yǐn Mó to openly commit evil under their very eyes;
their crimes were manifest,
known to everyone on the road,
yet the smallest of their offenses
remained unheard of for years.
This is neither the intention of the Zhōulǐ in establishing officials,
nor the principle of the Chūnqiū's ten ranks.
Currently, externally there are Gōngqīng and Jiàngxiào who oversee all departments;
internally, there are Shìzhōng and Shàngshū who manage all affairs;
the Sīlì Jiàowèi supervises the capital;
the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng oversees the palaces.
All are highly selected virtuous talents to fill their positions,
and clear decrees and edicts are promulgated to monitor their transgressions.
If these virtuous individuals are still deemed insufficient,
then the minor officials of the Xiàoshì
are even less trustworthy.
If these virtuous individuals each strive to fulfill their loyalty,
the paltry Xiàoshì
will be of no further use.
If highly selected national talents were made Xiàoshì,
then it would simply be adding another official like the Zhōngchéng or Sīlì.
If they are chosen as before,
then the treachery of Yǐn Mó will recur.
Considering the options,
there is no use for them.
In the past, when Sāng Hóngyáng sought profit for the Hàn,
Bǔ Shì believed that only by cooking Hóngyáng alone
would Heaven send rain.
If the success or failure of governance must affect Heaven and Earth,
your minister fears that the disasters of floods and droughts
may not be unrelated to the Xiàoshì.
Cáo Gōnggōng kept worthy men at a distance
and befriended petty men,
and the Guófēng attributed this as a satire.
Wèi Xiàn Gōng dismissed his high officials
and plotted with petty ones,
which Dìng Jiāng deemed a crime.
Even if the Xiàoshì were beneficial to the state,
from the perspective of ritual and righteousness,
it would still wound the hearts of high officials.
How much more so now that their treachery is exposed,
and they are still not dismissed?
This is like not mending a gaping wound,
and being lost without returning.”
Thereupon, the Xiàoshì office was abolished.
Xiǎo was promoted to Rǔnán Tàishǒu,
and died at over forty years old.
Guō Jiā, courtesy name Fèngxiào,
was from Yǐngchuān Yángzhái.
Initially,
he met Yuán Shào in the north,
and said to Shào's strategists, Xīn Píng and Guō Tú:
“Indeed, a wise man carefully assesses his lord,
thus every action he takes is successful, and fame and achievement can be established.
Lord Yuán merely wishes to emulate the Duke of Zhōu in treating scholars with deference,
but he does not know the art of employing men.
He has many schemes but few essentials,
likes to deliberate but is indecisive.
To overcome the great difficulties of the world with him,
and establish a hegemonic empire,
would be difficult!”
Thereupon, he left him.
Earlier,
Xì Zhìcái from Yǐngchuān,
a man of strategy,
was highly esteemed by Tàizǔ.
He died young.
Tàizǔ wrote to Xún Yù, saying:
“Since Zhìcái's death,
there has been no one with whom I can plan affairs.
Rǔ and Yǐng certainly have many extraordinary individuals,
who can succeed him?”
Yù recommended Jiā.
He was summoned for an audience,
and discussed the affairs of the world.
Tàizǔ said:
“The one who will enable me to accomplish my great enterprise,
must be this man.”
When Jiā left,
he also happily said:
“He is truly my lord.”
He was appointed Sīkōng Jìjiǔ.
When attacking Lǚ Bù,
he defeated him in three battles.
Bù retreated and held a strong defense.
At that time, the soldiers were weary,
and Tàizǔ wanted to withdraw the army.
Jiā persuaded Tàizǔ to attack him urgently,
and thus Lǚ Bù was captured.
The details are in the biography of Xún Yōu.
Sūn Cè fought and traveled a thousand li,
and possessed all of Jiāngdōng.
He heard that Tàizǔ and Yuán Shào were locked in a stalemate at Guāndù,
and intended to cross the river north to attack Xǔ.
Everyone who heard this was afraid.
Jiā predicted:
“Cè has just annexed Jiāngdōng,
and those he executed were all brave and outstanding heroes,
men who could inspire others to fight to the death.
However, Cè is reckless and unprepared.
Even with a million troops,
it would be no different from him walking alone in the Central Plains.
If an assassin were to ambush him,
he would be but an enemy of one man.
In my opinion,
he will surely die at the hands of a common man.”
Cè was on the verge of crossing the river but had not yet done so,
when he was indeed killed by the retainers of Xǔ Gòng.
After defeating Yuán Shào,
and after Shào's death,
he again followed in attacking Tán and Shàng at Líyáng,
winning several consecutive battles.
The various generals wished to capitalize on their victory and attack them directly,
but Guō Jiā said:
"Yuán Shào loved these two sons,
so there is no one suitable to establish.
With Guō Tú and Féng Jì as their strategists,
they will surely fight among themselves
and then become separated.
If we press them, they will hold together;
if we relax, then a spirit of contention will arise.
It is better to turn south towards Jīngzhōu, as if to campaign against Liú Biǎo,
and await their change;
once the change occurs, then attack them,
and they can be settled in one stroke."
Tàizǔ said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he campaigned south.
When the army reached Xīpíng,
Tán and Shàng indeed contended for Jìzhōu.
Tán was defeated by Shàng's army,
and fled to secure Píngyuán,
sending Xīn Pí to beg for surrender.
Tàizǔ returned to rescue him,
and subsequently helped settle Yè.
He then followed in attacking Tán at Nánpí,
and Jìzhōu was pacified.
Guō Jiā was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wèiyáng Pavilion.
When Tàizǔ was about to campaign against Yuán Shàng and the Wūhuán of the Three Commanderies,
many of his subordinates feared that Liú Biǎo would send Liú Bèi to attack Xǔ and assault Tàizǔ.
Guō Jiā said:
"Although your might shakes the world,
the Hu, relying on their remoteness,
will surely not make preparations.
Taking advantage of their lack of preparation,
if we suddenly attack them,
they can be utterly destroyed.
Moreover, Yuán Shào had bestowed favors upon the common people and the barbarians,
and Shàng and his brothers are still alive.
Now the people of the four provinces,
though attached by might,
have not yet received benevolence.
If we abandon them and campaign south,
Shàng will use the resources of the Wūhuán,
recruit the retainers of his deceased lord,
and once the Hu people move,
the common people and barbarians will all respond,
giving rise to Tàdùn's ambition,
and realizing his scheme of covetousness.
I fear that Qīng and Jì will no longer be yours.
Liú Biǎo,
is merely a drawing-room orator;
he knows himself to be incapable of controlling Bèi,
and fears that if he gives him heavy responsibility, he will not be able to restrain him,
while if he gives him light responsibility, Bèi will not be used.
Therefore, even if you dispatch your entire nation on a distant campaign,
you need not worry."
Tàizǔ thereupon set out.
Upon reaching Yì,
Guō Jiā said:
"The essence of warfare is speed.
Now, to attack someone a thousand *lǐ* away,
with much baggage train,
it is difficult to move quickly.
Moreover, if they hear of it,
they will surely prepare.
It is better to leave the baggage train
and march light troops by double marches,
catching them unawares."
Tàizǔ then secretly exited through Lúlóng Sài,
heading straight for the Xīanrénchéng of the Chányú.
When the barbarians suddenly heard of Tàizǔ's arrival,
they fought in a state of terror.
They were greatly defeated,
and Tàdùn and the famous kings below him were beheaded.
Shàng and his brother Xī fled to Liáodōng.
Guō Jiā was profoundly discerning and possessed strategic foresight,
understanding the realities of affairs.
Tàizǔ said:
"Only Fèngxiào is able to understand my intentions."
At the age of thirty-eight,
returning from Liǔchéng,
he fell gravely ill,
and Tàizǔ's inquiries about his health were constant.
When he died,
Tàizǔ mourned him deeply at his funeral,
expressing profound sorrow,
and said to Xún Yōu and others:
"All you gentlemen are of my generation,
but only Fèngxiào was the youngest.
When the affairs of the world were settled,
I wished to entrust him with future matters,
but he died young in mid-life.
It is fate indeed!"
Thereupon, he memorialized, saying:
"Guō Jiā, Libationer of the Army,
has followed me on campaigns
for eleven years.
Whenever there was a major deliberation,
facing the enemy and adapting to changes,
when my plans were not yet decided,
Jiā would always complete them.
In pacifying the world,
his strategic contributions were supreme.
Unfortunately, he died young,
his work unfinished.
Recalling Jiā's achievements,
they are truly unforgettable.
His enfeoffment should be increased by 800 households,
making a total of 1000 households with the previous ones."
His posthumous title was Zhēnhóu.
His son, Yì, succeeded him.
Later, when Tàizǔ returned from campaigning in Jīngzhōu,
he encountered a plague at Bāqiū,
burned his boats,
and sighed:
"If Guō Fèngxiào were here,
he would not have let me come to this!"
Previously,
Chén Qún disapproved of Guō Jiā's lack of discipline in his conduct,
and repeatedly reported Guō Jiā to the court,
but Guō Jiā remained unperturbed.
Tàizǔ esteemed him even more,
yet also approved of Qún's ability to uphold righteousness.
Yì served as Gentleman of Literature to the Crown Prince,
and died early.
His son, Shēn, succeeded him.
After Shēn died,
his son, Liè, succeeded him.
Dǒng Zhāo, courtesy name Gōngrén,
was a native of Dìngtáo, Jìyīn.
He was recommended as *xiàolián*,
and appointed as Magistrate of Yǐngtáo and Prefect of Bǎirén.
Yuán Shào appointed him as Consultant in Military Affairs.
When Shào confronted Gōngsūn Zàn at Jièqiáo,
Lǐ Shào, the Administrator of Jùlù, and the local gentry
, seeing Zàn's army was strong,
all wished to side with Zàn.
Shào heard of this and
sent Dǒng Zhāo to take charge of Jùlù.
He asked:
"By what method will you control them?"
He replied:
"A single person, however insignificant,
cannot overcome the plans of the multitude.
I wish to entice their hearts
by pretending to agree with their discussions,
and once I understand their true feelings,
then I will exercise authority to control them.
The plan depends on the moment and cannot be spoken of in advance."
At that time, several tens of prominent local gentry, such as Sūn Kàng, exclusively served as planners,
alarming the officials and populace.
When Dǒng Zhāo arrived at the commandery,
he falsely created a proclamation from Shào to the commandery, saying:
"We have received a confession from the bandit scout Ānpíng Zhāng Jí,
stating that he intends to attack Jùlù,
and that the bandit former *xiàolián* Sūn Kàng and others are complicit.
Upon receipt of this proclamation, military law shall be immediately executed.
Only the guilty individual shall be punished;
their wives and children shall not be implicated."
Dǒng Zhāo, acting on this proclamation,
immediately executed them all.
The entire commandery was terrified,
whereupon he successively comforted them,
and thus all became peaceful and settled.
After the matter was concluded, he reported to Shào,
and Shào praised him.
Coincidentally, Lì Pān, the Administrator of Wèijùn, was harmed by soldiers,
and Shào appointed Dǒng Zhāo to take charge of Wèijùn.
At that time, the commandery's borders were in great chaos,
with tens of thousands of bandits,
who sent envoys back and forth,
engaging in trade.
Dǒng Zhāo treated them generously,
and then used them as spies,
striking them when they were unprepared,
always achieving great victories and breaking them.
Within two days, urgent dispatches arrived three times.
Zhāo's younger brother, Fǎng,
was in Zhāng Miǎo's army.
Miǎo and Shào had a rift,
and Shào, influenced by slander, intended to punish Zhāo.
Zhāo wanted to go to Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
but upon reaching Hénèi,
he was detained by Zhāng Yáng.
Through Yáng, he returned his official seal and ribbon,
and was appointed Jìdūwèi.
At that time, Tàizǔ governed Yǎnzhōu
and sent an envoy to Yáng,
wishing to borrow a path through his territory to reach Cháng'ān in the west.
Yáng did not agree.
Zhāo persuaded Yáng, saying:
"Though Yuán and Cáo are for now like one family,
their alliance will not last long.
Though Cáo is weak now,
he is truly a hero of the world;
you should cultivate a relationship with him.
Especially now, as there is an opportunity,
it is advisable to facilitate his submission of a memorial
and also recommend him.
If the matter succeeds,
it will establish a deep bond forever."
Yáng then facilitated Tàizǔ's submission of a memorial
and recommended Tàizǔ.
Zhāo wrote a letter for Tàizǔ to Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì, and other generals in Cháng'ān,
offering sincere regards according to their respective importance.
Yáng also sent an envoy to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ gave Yáng dogs, horses, gold, and silk,
and thus began communication with the west.
When the Son of Heaven was in Ānyì,
Zhāo went there from Hénèi,
and was appointed Yìláng by imperial edict.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān
Tàizǔ pacified the Yellow Turban rebels in Xǔ
and sent an envoy to Hédōng.
At that time, the Son of Heaven returned to Luòyáng,
and Hán Xiān, Yáng Fèng, Dǒng Chéng, and Yáng were all at odds and disagreed.
Zhāo, knowing that Fèng had the strongest army but few allies,
wrote a letter for Tàizǔ to Fèng, saying:
"I have long admired your name and integrity,
and now offer my sincere heart.
Today, General, you have rescued the sovereign from hardship,
returned him to the old capital.
Your achievement in assisting and protecting him
is unparalleled in this age.
How splendid it is!
At present, wicked factions plague Huáxià,
and the Four Seas are not yet peaceful.
The divine vessel (the throne) is of utmost importance,
and its stability depends on support.
It is essential to have many virtuous individuals to restore order to the royal court;
truly, this is not something one person can accomplish alone.
The heart and abdomen, and the four limbs,
truly rely on each other;
if one part is lacking,
then there is a defect.
General, you should be the inner pillar,
and I will be the outer support.
Now I have provisions,
and General has troops;
by sharing what we have,
we can help each other sufficiently.
In life and death, joy and sorrow,
we shall share it together."
Fèng was delighted upon receiving the letter
and told his generals:
"The troops of Yǎnzhōu are nearby in Xǔ;
they have soldiers and provisions,
and are whom the state should rely upon."
They then jointly memorialized to appoint Tàizǔ as Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn,
inheriting his father's peerage as Fèitíng Hóu.
Zhāo was promoted to Fújiélìng.
When Tàizǔ paid respects to the Son of Heaven in Luòyáng,
he invited Zhāo to sit with him
and asked:
"Now that I have come here,
what strategy should I employ?"
Zhāo replied:
"General, you raised a righteous army to punish the rebellious and chaotic,
entered the court to meet the Son of Heaven,
and assisted and protected the royal house.
This is an achievement worthy of the Five Hegemons.
However, among the generals here,
their intentions differ,
and they may not all obey.
To remain here to assist the court
is not strategically advantageous.
The only option is to move the imperial carriage to Xǔ.
However, the imperial court has been displaced,
and has only recently returned to the old capital;
people near and far are eagerly looking forward,
hoping for peace soon.
To move the carriage again now
will not satisfy the hearts of the multitude.
Yet, by undertaking extraordinary deeds,
one can achieve extraordinary merits.
I wish, General, that you would consider the greater advantage."
Tàizǔ said:
"This has been my original intention.
Yáng Fèng is nearby in Liáng.
I hear his troops are elite;
will he not cause trouble for me?"
Zhāo said:
"Fèng has few allies
and will have to pledge his allegiance alone.
The matters of Zhèndōng and Fèitíng
were all determined by Fèng;
moreover, the letter's explicit instructions
are enough to gain his trust.
You should immediately send an envoy with generous gifts to thank him,
to set his mind at ease.
Explain that 'there are no provisions in the capital,
and it is desired that the imperial carriage temporarily proceed to Lǔyáng.
Lǔyáng is near Xǔ,
making transport somewhat easier,
thus avoiding worries of shortage.'
Fèng is brave but lacks foresight;
he will certainly not suspect anything.
By the time the envoy comes and goes,
there will be enough time to finalize the plan.
How can Fèng cause trouble!"
Tàizǔ said:
"Excellent."
He immediately sent an envoy to Fèng.
The imperial carriage was moved to Xǔ.
Fèng was thereupon disappointed
and, with Hán Xiān and others, raided and plundered at Dìnglíng.
Tàizǔ did not respond,
but secretly attacked their camp at Liáng,
and quickly brought about their surrender and execution.
Fèng and Xiān lost their forces
and surrendered to Yuán Shù in the east.
In the third year,
Zhāo was promoted to Hénányǐn.
At that time, Zhāng Yáng was killed by his general Yáng Chǒu.
Yáng's Chángshǐ, Xuē Hóng, and Hénèi Tàishǒu, Miào Shàng, defended the city, awaiting rescue from Shào.
Tàizǔ ordered Zhāo to enter the city alone
to persuade Hóng and Shàng,
who immediately led their forces to surrender that very day.
Zhāo was appointed Jìzhōumù.
Tài-Zǔ ordered Liú Bèi to resist Yuán Shù.
Zhāo said:
"Bèi is brave and ambitious;
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi are his wings.
I fear Bèi's intentions are not to be fully ascertained!"
Tài-Zǔ said:
"I have already promised him."
Bèi arrived at Xiàpī,
killed Chē Zhòu, the Inspector of Xúzhōu,
and rebelled.
Tài-Zǔ personally campaigned against Bèi,
and transferred Zhāo to be the Administrator of Xúzhōu.
Yuán Shào dispatched his general Yán Liáng to attack Dōngjùn.
Zhāo was again transferred to be the Grand Administrator of Wèijùn,
and participated in the campaign against Liáng.
After Liáng's death,
the siege of Yèchéng was advanced.
Yuán Shào's clansman Chūnqīng was the Grand Administrator of Wèijùn,
located within the city.
His father, Yuánzhǎng, was in Yángzhōu.
Tài-Zǔ sent someone to welcome him.
Zhāo wrote to Chūnqīng, saying:
"It is said that a filial son does not betray his parent for gain,
a benevolent person does not forget his lord to pursue selfish interests,
a person of integrity does not exploit chaos for ill-gotten gains,
and a wise person does not resort to deceptive schemes to endanger himself.
Your esteemed father,
in the past, avoided domestic strife,
and traveled south to the hundred Yuè regions,
not because he estranged his flesh and blood,
but found joy in Wú and Huì.
A wise man deeply discerns,
and perhaps it was appropriate.
Duke Cáo, pitying his steadfast adherence to principles and uprightness,
alienated from his group and without peers,
therefore specially sent envoys to Jiāngdōng,
either to welcome or to escort him.
He is now about to arrive.
Even if you were in a peaceful and neutral place,
relying on a lord of virtue and righteousness,
having the solidity of Tài Shān as your abode,
and your person likened to the enduring pine and cypress,
morally speaking,
you should still turn away from them and towards us,
abandoning the people to seek your father.
Moreover, when the Marquis of Zhū first allied with Duke Yǐn,
the people of Lǔ praised him,
but his title was not recorded.
Thus, that which the king has not yet conferred,
a high noble title is not established;
this is the principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
How much more so is the country you rely on today a perilous and chaotic one,
and the command you have received a deceitful and false one?
If you do not strive to be with your kin,
and disregard your own father,
you cannot be called filial.
Forgetting the ancestral court where your ancestors resided,
and settling for an illegitimate and corrupt position,
it is difficult to call that loyal.
With loyalty and filial piety both neglected,
it is difficult to speak of wisdom.
Furthermore, you were formerly treated with respect and invited into service by Duke Cáo.
To be close to relatives but distant from one's own parent,
to harbor the locally residing while alienating the imperial house,
to covet ill-gotten gains and betray one's benefactor,
to distance oneself from blessings and good fortune while drawing near to peril and destruction,
to abandon clear righteousness and embrace great shame—
is this not regrettable!
If you can turn over a new leaf,
serve the Emperor and nourish your father,
entrust yourself to Duke Cáo,
your loyalty and filial piety will not falter,
and your glorious name will shine.
You should deeply ponder this plan,
and quickly make a good decision."
After Yè was pacified,
Zhāo was appointed remonstrance official (Jiànyì Dàfū).
Later, Yuán Shàng relied on the Wūhuán leader Tàdùn.
Tài-Zǔ was about to campaign against him.
Troubled by the difficulty of transporting military provisions,
he ordered the digging of two canals, Pínglǔ and Quánzhōu, connecting to the sea for transport.
This was Zhāo's suggestion.
Tài-Zǔ memorialized to enfeoff him as Marquis of Qiānqiū Tíng,
and he was subsequently appointed Wine-Sacrifice Libationer of the Minister of Works (Sīkōng Jìjiǔ).
Later, Zhāo suggested:
"It is fitting to restore the ancient system of enfeoffing five ranks."
Tài-Zǔ said:
"Establishing the five ranks
is the work of sages,
and not something that a minister should dictate.
How could I bear it?"
Zhāo said:
"Since ancient times,
no minister who aided the world
has achieved accomplishments like those of today.
No one with today's accomplishments
has long remained in the position of a mere minister.
Now, your Excellency is ashamed of having a deficit of virtue and not being perfectly good,
and delights in preserving your reputation and integrity without great reproach.
Your virtue and excellence surpass those of Yī and Zhōu;
this is the pinnacle of perfect virtue.
However, Tàijiǎ and King Chéng may not always be met.
Now, the people are difficult to transform,
even more so than in the times of Yīn and Zhōu.
To remain in the position of a great minister
and cause people to doubt one's intentions regarding great matters
is truly something that must be considered with great caution.
Although your Excellency has advanced your might and virtue,
and illuminated legal principles,
yet not establishing your foundation
for the sake of ten thousand generations
is still not perfect.
The root of establishing a foundation
lies in territory and people.
It is appropriate to gradually establish
them to protect yourself.
Your Excellency's loyalty and integrity are manifestly clear,
and the celestial awe is on your countenance.
The words of Gěng Yǎn by the bed,
and the ungrounded theories of Zhū Yīng,
should not be dismissed.
Zhāo has received extraordinary grace,
and dares not fail to present this."
Later, Tài-Zǔ consequently accepted the titles of Duke of Wèi and King of Wèi;
these were all initiated by Zhāo.
When Guān Yǔ besieged Cáo Rén at Fán,
Sūn Quán sent an envoy to state that
he was "sending troops westward,
intending to secretly seize Yǔ.
Jiānglíng and Gōng'ān are heavy with supplies.
If Yǔ loses these two cities,
he will surely flee on his own,
and the siege of Fán's army
will lift without intervention.
We beg that this be kept secret and not divulged,
so that Yǔ does not prepare."
Tài-Zǔ questioned his ministers,
and all the ministers said it should be kept secret.
Zhāo said:
"Military affairs prioritize expediency,
aiming for what is appropriate.
It is proper to respond to Quán with secrecy,
but reveal it internally.
If Yǔ hears of Quán's advance,
and returns to protect himself,
the siege will be swiftly lifted,
and we will gain the advantage.
We can cause the two enemies to confront each other and be entangled,
and wait for their exhaustion.
Keeping it secret and not revealing it,
allowing Quán to achieve his aim,
is not the best plan.
Moreover,
if the generals and officers within the siege
do not know help is coming, calculating provisions and being terrified,
if they happen to have other intentions,
the trouble will not be small.
Revealing it is convenient.
Furthermore, Yǔ is a strong and arrogant man,
who relies on the solidity of his two cities,
and will surely not retreat quickly."
Tài-Zǔ said:
"Excellent."
He immediately ordered the relief general Xú Huǎng to shoot Quán's letter into the besieged encampment and Yǔ's camp.
When those in the besieged encampment heard it,
their morale soared a hundredfold.
Yǔ indeed hesitated.
Quán's army arrived,
captured his two cities,
and Yǔ was then defeated.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne as king,
he appointed Zhāo as Grand Artisan.
When he later ascended the imperial throne,
Zhāo was promoted to Grand Messenger (Dà Hónglú),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yòuxiāng.
In the second year,
he allocated a hundred households from his fief
to bestow upon Zhāo's younger brother Fǎng the title of Marquis within the Passes (Guānnèi Hóu).
Zhāo was transferred to be Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng).
In the third year,
Cáo Xiū, the General Who Attacks the East (Zhēngdōng Dà Jiàngjūn), was on the Yangtze River at Dòngpǔkou.
He presented a memorial stating:
"I wish to lead elite troops, striding like a tiger into the lands south of the river,
to take resources from the enemy.
Success is certain.
If I am not present,
there is no need to worry."
The Emperor, fearing that Xiū would cross the river,
sent an urgent edict to stop him.
At that time, Zhāo was attending at his side
and then said:
"I perceive Your Majesty has a worried expression.
Is it solely because of Xiū crossing the river?
Now, crossing the river
is something difficult for human nature.
Even if Xiū has such an ambition,
he cannot act alone by force;
he must await other generals.
Zāng Bà and others are already rich and noble,
with no other aspirations,
they only wish to live out their natural years
and preserve their emoluments and prosperity.
How could they possibly risk danger and throw themselves into a place of death
in pursuit of a lucky chance?
If Bà and the others do not advance,
Xiū's resolve will naturally be thwarted.
I fear that even if Your Majesty issues an edict to cross,
they will still hesitate
and not immediately obey the command."
Not long after this,
a violent storm blew the enemy ships
all towards Xiū and the others' camp.
He beheaded many and captured others alive,
and the enemy then scattered.
An imperial edict ordered all armies to cross quickly.
Before the army could advance in time,
the enemy's relief fleet arrived.
The imperial carriage went to Wǎn.
Xiàhóu Shàng, the General Who Attacks the South (Zhēngnán Dà Jiàngjūn), and others attacked Jiānglíng,
but had not yet captured it.
At that time, the river was shallow and narrow.
Shàng wished to take ships carrying infantry and cavalry to set up camp on the islet,
build a pontoon bridge,
and move back and forth between north and south.
Many of the deliberators believed that the city could certainly be captured.
Zhāo presented a memorial stating:
"Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Huángdì), though surpassing others in wisdom and courage,
was cautious of the enemy when employing troops,
and dared not treat them lightly in this manner.
It is a constant principle of warfare that troops prefer to advance and dislike retreating.
Even on flat ground without natural barriers,
it is still difficult.
If one were to go deep into enemy territory,
the return path should be advantageous.
When troops advance and retreat,
it cannot always be as desired.
Now, to camp on the islet
is extremely deep (in enemy territory);
to cross by pontoon bridge
is extremely dangerous;
to advance by a single path
is extremely narrow: these three are what military strategists dread,
yet they are being undertaken now.
If the enemy frequently attacks the bridge
and there is an accidental mishap,
the elite forces on the islet
will no longer belong to Wèi,
but will transform and belong to Wú.
I am personally grieved by this,
forgetting sleep and food,
yet the deliberators are at ease and do not consider it a worry.
Is this not perplexing?
Furthermore, the river water is about to rise.
If it suddenly swells,
how can we defend against it?
Even if we do not defeat the enemy,
we should still preserve ourselves.
How can we venture into danger
without fear?
The matter is about to become perilous.
May Your Majesty please consider this!"
The Emperor understood Zhāo's words
and immediately issued an edict for Shàng and the others to withdraw quickly.
The enemy attacked from both ends,
and the government troops retreated along a single path,
unable to exit in time.
Generals Shí Jiàn and Gāo Qiān barely escaped with their lives.
Ten days after the army withdrew,
the river water suddenly rose.
The Emperor said:
"Your discussion of this matter,
how precise it is!
Even if Zhāng [Liáng] or Chén [Píng] were to handle it,
what more could they add?"
In the fifth year,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Chéngdūxiāng,
and appointed Grand Astrologer (Tàicháng).
That same year,
he was transferred to be Grand Master of Radiance (Guānglù Dàfū) and Palace Attendant (Jǐshìzhōng).
He followed the imperial carriage on the eastern campaign.
In the seventh year, he returned
and was appointed Grand Coachman (Tàipú).
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Marquis of Lèpíng,
with a thousand households in his fief,
and transferred to Colonel of the Guards (Wèiwèi).
A hundred households were allocated from his fief
to bestow upon one of his sons the title of Marquis within the Passes (Guānnèi Hóu).
In the fourth year of Tàihé,
he acted as Minister of Works (Sītú).
In the sixth year,
he was formally appointed.
Zhāo submitted a memorial detailing the弊 (bì, abuses) of the prevailing trends, stating:
"All who possess the realm
invariably value and esteem honest, simple, loyal, and trustworthy gentlemen,
and deeply detest those who are false and insincere,
because such people destroy teachings, disturb governance,
corrupt customs, and harm transformation.
Recently, Wèi Fěng was executed at the end of Jiàn'ān,
and Cáo Wěi was beheaded at the beginning of Huángchū.
I humbly reflect that the previous imperial edicts
deeply abhorred superficial falsehoods,
wishing to break up evil factions,
often speaking of it with gnashing teeth.
Yet, those who enforce the law all fear their power and influence,
and none are able to expose or rectify them,
thereby destroying customs
and increasing greed.
I secretly observe that the young people of today
no longer take scholarship as their foundation,
but exclusively make social connections their profession.
Gentlemen of the state do not prioritize filial piety, fraternal deference, or pure conduct,
but rather prioritize chasing power and seeking gain.
They form parties and gather groups,
mutually praising each other.
They use criticism as punishment
and partisan praise as rewards.
Those who attach themselves to them are praised profusely,
while those who do not are fabricated with flaws and faults.
They even say to each other, 'Why worry about not succeeding in this generation?
One only needs to diligently cultivate human connections
and cast a wide net;
why worry that others do not know oneself?
One only needs to swallow them with medicine and soften them.'
Furthermore, I hear that some use their servants or retainers, ostensibly as family members in official positions,
to brazenly enter and exit,
going to and from forbidden and secluded places,
exchanging letters,
and making inquiries.
All these matters
are not permitted by law
and are not pardoned by punishment.
Even the crimes of Fěng and Wěi
could not exceed these."
Thereupon, the Emperor issued a stern edict,
dismissing Zhūgě Dàn, Dèng Yáng, and others.
Zhāo passed away at the age of eighty-one
and was posthumously named Dìng Hóu.
His son Zhòu succeeded him.
Zhòu held positions as Commander (Jùnshǒu) and among the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng).
Liú Yè, courtesy name Zǐyáng,
was a native of Chéngdé, Huáinán.
(Dé is pronounced like dé.)
He was a descendant of Liú Yán, Prince Fúlíng, a son of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn.
His father was Pǔ,
his mother Xiū,
and they bore Huàn and Yè.
When Huàn was nine and
Yè was seven,
their mother fell gravely ill.
On her deathbed,
she admonished Huàn and Yè, saying:
"Pǔ's maidservants
have a treacherous and harmful nature.
After I die,
I fear they will surely bring chaos to the household.
If you grow up and can eliminate them,
then I will have no regrets."
When Yè was thirteen,
he said to his elder brother Huàn:
"Our deceased mother's words
can now be acted upon."
Huàn said:
"How can that be done!"
Yè immediately entered the room and killed the maidservant,
then went straight out to pay respects at the tomb.
There was great commotion in the house,
and Pǔ was informed.
Pǔ was enraged
and sent men to pursue Yè.
Yè returned and bowed in apology, saying:
"These were the dying instructions of our deceased mother;
I dare to accept punishment for acting without asking."
Pǔ found him extraordinary in his heart
and consequently did not blame him.
Xǔ Shào of Rǔnán, famed for his discerning eye for people,
took refuge in Yángzhōu
and declared Yè to possess talent fit to assist the world.
The gentry of Yángzhōu were mostly rash, chivalrous, cunning, and unruly.
There were those like Zhèng Bǎo, Zhāng Duō, and Xǔ Gān,
each commanding their own troops.
Bǎo was the most valorous and decisive,
with extraordinary talent and strength,
feared by the entire region.
He wished to plunder the populace and cross the Jiāngbiǎo (south of the Yangtze),
and because Yè was from a prominent clan and famous,
he wanted to forcibly compel Yè to lead and advocate this plan.
Yè was then in his twenties;
he was troubled internally
but had no opportunity.
Coincidentally, Tàizǔ (Cáo Cāo) sent an envoy to the province
to investigate some matters.
Yè went to see him,
discussed the situation,
and insisted on taking the envoy back with him,
detaining him for several days.
Bǎo, indeed, came with several hundred men carrying oxen and wine to visit the envoy.
Yè ordered his household retainers to seat Bǎo's followers outside the central gate
and provide them with wine and food;
he then entertained Bǎo inside.
He secretly ordered strong men
to strike Bǎo during the pouring of wine.
Bǎo disliked sweet wine and
was very observant,
so the cup-bearers dared not act.
Yè then personally drew his sword and killed Bǎo,
beheading him to command his army,
saying:
"Lord Cáo has given an order:
whoever dares to make a move
will suffer the same fate as Bǎo."
The multitude was all terrified
and fled back to their camp.
The camp had several thousand elite soldiers led by a commander.
Fearing they would cause trouble,
Yè immediately mounted Bǎo's horse,
took a few household retainers,
went to the gate of Bǎo's camp,
called out their leaders,
and explained the consequences of good and ill fortune.
They all kowtowed and opened the gate to let Yè in.
Yè comforted and appeased them;
they were all pleased and submitted,
endorsing Yè as their leader.
Yè observed that the Hàn dynasty was gradually weakening,
and as a collateral relative,
he did not wish to command troops.
He therefore handed over his troops to Liú Xūn, the Administrator of Lújiāng.
Xūn was puzzled by this,
and Yè said:
"Bǎo had no discipline,
and his troops have always profited from plunder.
I am naturally without resources,
and to try to bring them into order
would surely breed resentment and not last long,
hence I give them to you."
At that time, Xūn's army was strong between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
Sūn Cè disliked him
and sent an envoy with humble words and rich gifts,
writing to Xūn:
"The people of Shàngliáo
have repeatedly bullied our humble state,
and we have resented them for years.
To attack them directly,
the road is inconvenient;
we wish to rely on your great state to attack them.
Shàngliáo is very prosperous;
obtaining it can enrich the state.
Please send troops as an external reinforcement."
Xūn believed him,
and also received Cè's pearls, jewels, and woven fabrics,
making him joyful.
Everyone inside and outside congratulated him,
but Yè alone did not.
Xūn asked him why,
and he replied:
"Although Shàngliáo is small,
its city walls are strong and its moats deep;
it is difficult to attack and easy to defend,
so it cannot be taken in ten days.
Then your troops will be exhausted abroad,
while your state will be empty at home.
If Cè takes advantage of this emptiness to attack us,
then we cannot defend ourselves in the rear.
This means the general will be constrained by the enemy in advancing,
and have nowhere to return to in retreating.
If the army must go out,
disaster will strike today."
Xūn did not listen.
He raised an army to attack Shàngliáo,
and Cè indeed attacked his rear.
Xūn was cornered and distressed,
so he fled to Tàizǔ.
When Tàizǔ arrived at Shòuchūn,
there was a mountain bandit named Chén Cè in the Lújiāng region,
with tens of thousands of men,
holding strongholds in dangerous terrain.
Previously, a detached general had been sent to execute them,
but no one could capture or defeat them.
Tàizǔ asked his subordinates
whether they should attack or not.
They all said:
"The mountains are steep and high, and the valleys deep and narrow;
it is easy to defend and difficult to attack.
Moreover, not having them causes no harm,
and gaining them brings no benefit."
Yè said:
"Cè and his like are mere small-timers;
they took advantage of chaos to occupy dangerous terrain,
and thus relied on each other to become strong.
They have no official titles or prestige to make them submit to one another.
Previously, the detached general's authority was light,
and the central plains were not yet pacified,
so Cè dared to hold the strongholds and defend.
Today, the world is largely settled;
those who resist later will be executed first.
As for fearing death and seeking reward,
both fools and the wise share this sentiment.
Thus, Guǎngwǔ Jūn (Lǐ Zuǒjūn) strategized for Hán Xìn,
saying that his prestige and renown were enough to gain control through reputation before action, and make neighboring states submit.
How much more so with your sagacious virtue, Illustrious Lord?
Those in the east rebel, those in the west resent;
if you first issue rewards for surrender,
and a large army approaches them,
on the day the proclamation is made,
the camp gates will open and the bandits will rout themselves."
Tàizǔ laughed, saying:
"Your words are close to the truth!"
Thereupon, he sent fierce generals in the vanguard,
with the main army following.
Upon arrival, they defeated Cè,
just as Yè had predicted.
Tàizǔ returned
and appointed Yè as Registrar of the Granary of Sīkōng.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Zhāng Lǔ,
he transferred Yè to be chief clerk.
Upon reaching Hànzhōng,
the mountains were steep and difficult to climb,
and the army's provisions were quite scarce.
Tàizǔ said:
"This is merely a land of deceitful delusions.
How can it affect whether we have provisions or not?
Our army is short on food,
it would be better to return quickly."
He then personally led the return,
ordering Yè to oversee the rear armies
and have them withdraw in sequence.
Yè surmised that Lǔ could be defeated,
and considering that the supply lines were not secure,
even if they withdrew,
not all the troops would be preserved.
He rode quickly to inform Tàizǔ:
"It would be better to launch an attack."
So, the troops advanced,
discharging many crossbows to shoot into their camp.
Lǔ fled,
and Hànzhōng was thus pacified.
Yè then said:
"Your Lordship, with five thousand infantry,
you were able to execute Dǒng Zhuó,
defeat Yuán Shào in the north,
and campaign against Liú Biǎo in the south.
Of the nine provinces and a hundred commanderies,
you have annexed eight,
your might shakes the world,
and your influence overawes beyond the seas.
Now, having captured Hànzhōng,
the people of Shǔ are terrified at the mere rumor,
losing heart and abandoning their defenses.
Pushing forward from this,
Shǔ can be settled by merely sending a written declaration.
Liú Bèi
is a hero among men,
but though he has a sense of measure, he is slow.
He has only recently gained Shǔ,
and the people of Shǔ do not yet rely on him.
Now that Hànzhōng is defeated,
the people of Shǔ are terrified,
and their power will collapse on its own.
With your Lordship's divine sagacity,
taking advantage of their collapse to crush them,
there is nothing that cannot be conquered.
If you delay even slightly,
Zhūgě Liàng, who is skilled in governance, will become prime minister,
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi, whose bravery is unmatched by any army, will become generals.
Once the people of Shǔ are settled
and hold the strategic strongholds,
then they cannot be attacked.
If we do not take it now,
it will surely become a future sorrow."
Tàizǔ did not follow his advice,
and the great army consequently returned.
When Yè returned from Hànzhōng,
he was made Acting Chief Clerk of the Army
and concurrently Administrator of the Guards.
In the first year of Yánkāng,
the Shǔ general Méng Dá led his forces to surrender.
Dá had a dignified appearance and talent,
and Wén Dì greatly esteemed and loved him,
making Dá the Administrator of Xīnchéng
and adding the title of Attendant Censor.
Yè believed:
"Dá has a covetous heart,
and being reliant on his talent, he loves artifice,
so he will surely be unable to feel gratitude or uphold righteousness.
Xīnchéng borders Wú and Shǔ;
if there is any change,
it will create trouble for the state."
Wén Dì ultimately did not change his mind,
and later Dá indeed rebelled and was defeated.
In the first year of Huángchū,
Yè was made Court Attendant
and granted the title Marquis within the Pass.
An imperial edict asked the assembled officials to estimate whether Liú Bèi would retaliate against Wú on behalf of Guān Yǔ.
The general consensus was:
"Shǔ
is a small state.
Its only famous general was Yǔ.
With Yǔ dead and the army defeated,
the country is filled with worry and fear;
there is no reason for them to mobilize again."
Yè alone said:
"Although Shǔ is narrow and weak,
Bèi intends to strengthen himself with military might.
He will certainly use a large force to demonstrate his abundance.
Moreover, Guān Yǔ and Bèi,
though nominally lord and subject,
had an affection like father and son.
If Yǔ's death cannot prompt him to raise an army to avenge his enemy,
it would be a failure in the duty of their relationship from beginning to end."
Later, Bèi indeed sent troops to attack Wú.
Wú responded with its entire state
and sent envoys to declare vassalage.
All the court officials offered congratulations,
but Yè alone said:
"Wú has been isolated beyond the Jiāng and Hàn rivers
and has long harbored no sincere intention of being an internal subject.
Although Your Majesty's virtue rivals that of Yú,
the nature of these ugly barbarians
has not yet been moved.
Seeking submission out of difficulty
is certainly unreliable.
They must be outwardly pressed and inwardly distressed
before sending this envoy.
We can take advantage of their predicament,
attack and seize them.
Indeed, to let an enemy escape for a single day
is to invite trouble for generations.
This must not be overlooked."
Bèi's army was defeated and retreated,
and Wú's respectful gestures gradually ceased.
The Emperor wished to raise a large army to attack them,
but Yè believed:
"They have just achieved their ambition,
and their high and low are united.
Moreover, they are protected by the rivers and lakes,
so it will certainly be difficult to attack them hastily."
The Emperor did not listen.
In the fifth year,
he journeyed to Guǎnglíng Sìmén,
ordering the armies of Jīng and Yáng provinces to advance concurrently.
He assembled his officials
and asked:
"Will Quán come in person or not?"
All replied:
"When Your Majesty personally campaigns,
Quán will be terrified
and will certainly respond with his entire state.
Moreover, he would not dare to entrust a large army to his subordinates,
so he will surely lead them himself."
Yè said:
"He will believe that Your Majesty intends to use your weighty presence (of ten thousand chariots) to tie him down,
while the crossing of the rivers and lakes will be carried out by a separate general.
He will certainly keep his troops in readiness,
without advancing or retreating."
The imperial carriage remained halted for several days,
and Quán indeed did not arrive.
The Emperor then recalled his army.
He said:
"Your estimation is correct.
You should think about eliminating the two bandits for me;
you cannot merely know their intentions."
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
Jiǎng Yè’s title was advanced to Marquis of Dōngtíng,
with a fief of three hundred households.
An edict stated:
“Honoring one’s ancestors
is how filial piety and proper conduct are upheld;
tracing one’s origins and revering the beginning
is how teaching is strengthened and influence spreads.
This is why Chéng Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ,
who truly founded Shāng and Zhōu,
in the spirit of the Shī and Shū,
posthumously honored Jì and Qì,
and sang praises of the deeds of Yǒusōng and Jiāngyuán,
to illuminate the source and flow of their abundant virtue,
and the origin from which they received the Mandate.
Since our Wèi house received the heavenly succession,
its origins trace back to the High Emperor and Grand Emperor,
and its achievements were great under Emperor Wǔ and Emperor Wén.
As for the father of the High Emperor, the Scholar-in-Retirement Jūn,
he secretly cultivated virtue and humility,
and his actions were divinely illuminated.
He was indeed blessed and honored by heaven and earth,
the source from which our glorious spirit originates.
Yet his spirit is distant and profound,
and his title is unrecorded,
which is not what is meant by honoring filial piety and revering the source.
Let the dukes and ministers and those below them
convene to discuss a title and posthumous name.”
Jiǎng Yè deliberated, saying:
“The desire of a sagely emperor and filial grandson to honor his ancestors
is truly boundless.
However, the degrees of closeness and distance,
and the hierarchy of proximity,
are indeed governed by rites,
which serve to sever private emotions,
establish public law,
and serve as a model for ten thousand generations.
The reason King Zhōu honored Hòujì as an ancestor
was because he assisted Táng with merit,
and his name was in the sacrificial canon.
As for the early Hàn dynasty,
the custom of posthumous titles
did not extend beyond one’s father.
Comparing this upwards to the Zhōu house,
the Great Wèi’s origins begin with the High Emperor;
comparing this downwards to the Hàn house,
the rites of posthumous titles do not extend to one’s grandfather.
These are truly the established laws of past eras,
and the clear principles of the present.
Your Majesty’s filial thoughts, arising from within,
are indeed endless.
However, what the sovereign undertakes must be recorded,
which is why caution is exercised in matters of ritual.
I believe the custom of posthumous honor
should align with that of the High Emperor only.”
Shàngshū Wèi Zhēn agreed with Jiǎng Yè’s deliberation,
and the matter was consequently put into effect.
The Administrator of Liáodōng, Gōngsūn Yuān, usurped his uncle’s position,
declared himself independent,
and sent an envoy with a memorial.
Jiǎng Yè believed that the Gōngsūn clan, having been employed since the Hàn era,
had established a hereditary official position,
and was bordered by the sea on one side
and mountains on the other.
Thus, the foreign tribes were distant and difficult to control,
and their power had lasted for a long time.
If he were not executed now,
trouble would certainly arise later.
If he were allowed to harbor disloyalty and raise troops,
and then an execution were sought,
it would be difficult to accomplish.
It would be better, taking advantage of his recent establishment,
when he has factions and enemies,
to attack him unexpectedly
with troops,
and offer rewards to recruits.
This way, the situation could be settled without exhausting the army.
Later, Gōngsūn Yuān indeed rebelled.
When Jiǎng Yè was at court,
he hardly interacted with people of his time.
Someone asked him the reason,
and Jiǎng Yè replied:
“The Wèi house’s ascension to the throne is still new;
the wise understand fate,
but the common people may not yet be universally convinced.
I was a branch and leaf in Hàn,
and am a trusted confidant in Wèi.
Having few companions and disciples,
I have not failed in what is proper.”
In the sixth year of Tàihé,
due to illness, he was appointed Grand Master of the Household.
After a period,
he became Grand Minister of the Court,
resigned after two years in office,
and was again appointed Grand Master of the Household,
then passed away.
His posthumous title was Marquis Jǐng.
His son, Jiǎng Yǔ, succeeded him.
His younger son, Jiǎng Táo,
was also highly talented but of poor conduct,
and served as Administrator of Píngyuán.
Jiǎng Jì, courtesy name Zǐtōng,
was a native of Píng'ā, Chǔ State.
He served as a county clerk and provincial assistant inspector.
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
Sūn Quán led his forces to besiege Héféi.
At that time, the main army was campaigning in Jīng Province,
and encountered an epidemic.
Only General Zhāng Xǐ was sent with a single thousand cavalry,
to lead the Rǔnán troops to relieve the siege,
but they also suffered from the epidemic.
Jiǎng Jì secretly reported to the Inspector, feigning receipt of a letter from Zhāng Xǐ,
stating that forty thousand infantry and cavalry had already arrived at Yūlóu,
and sent a principal clerk to welcome Zhāng Xǐ.
Three messengers were sent with letters to the defending generals in the city;
one entered the city,
and two were captured by the enemy.
Sūn Quán believed it,
hastily burned the siege works and fled,
and the city was thus saved.
The next year, when Jiǎng Jì was on an envoy mission to Qiáo,
Grand Ancestor (Cáo Cāo) asked him:
“Previously, when I confronted Yuán Běnchū at Guāndù,
I moved the people of Yān and Báimǎ.
The people could not flee,
and the bandits also dared not plunder.
Now I wish to move the people of Huáinán.
What do you think?”
Jiǎng Jì replied:
“At that time, our army was weak and the bandits were strong;
if they were not moved, they would certainly be lost.
Since defeating Yuán Shào,
capturing Liǔchéng in the north,
and advancing south towards Jiāng and Hàn,
with Jīng Province joining us,
our prestige has shaken the world,
and the people have no other intentions.
However, the common people cherish their native land
and truly do not enjoy being moved.
I fear they will certainly not be at peace.”
Grand Ancestor did not heed him,
and over a hundred thousand people between Jiāng and Huái
were all startled and fled to Wú.
Later, when Jiǎng Jì went on an envoy mission to Yè,
Grand Ancestor met him, laughed heartily, and said:
“Originally, I only wanted them to avoid the bandits,
but instead, I drove them all away.”
Jiǎng Jì was appointed Administrator of Dānyáng.
When the main army returned from the southern campaign,
Wēn Huī was made Inspector of Yáng Province,
and Jiǎng Jì was made assistant inspector.
An order stated:
“With Jìzǐ as a minister,
Wú should have a lord.
Now that you are returning to the province,
I have no worries.”
There was a commoner who falsely accused Jiǎng Jì of leading a rebellion.
When Grand Ancestor heard this,
he pointed to the previous order and spoke to General of the Left Yú Jìn and Chancellor of Pèi Fēng Rén, saying:
“How could Jiǎng Jì have done such a thing!
If he had,
then I would be a poor judge of character.
This must be a foolish commoner who enjoys chaos
and implicates him baselessly.”
He promptly ordered his release.
He was appointed Chief Clerk of the Western Bureau to the Chancellor.
An order stated:
“Shùn appointed Gāo Táo,
and the inhumane kept their distance;
discerning right from wrong and achieving moderation
is expected of a worthy subordinate.”
Guān Yǔ besieged Fán and Xiāngyáng.
Grand Ancestor, considering that Emperor Hàn was in Xǔ,
close to the enemy, wanted to move the capital.
Sīmǎ Xuánwáng and Jiǎng Jì advised Grand Ancestor, saying:
“Yú Jìn and others were submerged by water,
which was not a loss in battle,
and thus not enough to harm the grand strategy of the state.
Liú Bèi and Sūn Quán
are outwardly親 but inwardly distant.
If Guān Yǔ achieves his ambition,
Sūn Quán will certainly not wish it.
You can send someone to persuade him to attack Guān Yǔ from behind,
promising to cede the south of the Jiāng River to Sūn Quán as a fief.
Then the siege of Fán will naturally be lifted.”
Grand Ancestor followed their advice.
When Sūn Quán heard this,
he immediately led his troops west to attack Gōng'ān and Jiānglíng.
Guān Yǔ was consequently captured.
When Emperor Wén 文帝 ascended to the throne as King,
he was transferred to serve as the Senior Clerk to the Chancellor.
When he later ascended the imperial throne,
he was sent out as the General of the Central East.
Jì 濟 requested to stay,
and an imperial edict stated:
"Emperor Gāozǔ 高祖 sang, 'How can I find brave warriors to guard the four directions?'
The world is not yet at peace;
we urgently need good ministers to pacify the borders.
If there are no troubles,
then you may return with your jade ornaments jingling,
and that would not be too late."
Jì 濟 submitted the Wànjī Lùn 萬機論 (Discourse on Ten Thousand Affairs),
and the Emperor approved of it.
He was brought in to serve as Palace Attendant.
At that time, an imperial edict
was issued to General Zhengnán 征南 (Pacifying the South) Xiàhóu Shàng 夏侯尚, saying:
"You are a trusted and important general,
and you are especially to be entrusted with tasks.
Your grace is enough to die for,
and your benevolence and love are to be cherished.
You may exercise authority and bestow blessings,
killing or saving lives."
Shàng 尚 showed this to Jì 濟.
When Jì 濟 arrived,
the Emperor asked:
"What have you seen and heard regarding the customs and teachings of the realm?"
Jì 濟 replied:
"I have not seen other good things,
but only heard words that lead to the ruin of a state."
The Emperor, indignant, changed color and asked for the reason.
Jì 濟 answered in detail,
and then said:
"Indeed, 'to exercise authority and bestow blessings'
is a clear admonition in the Shū 書 (Book of Documents).
'The Son of Heaven has no jesting words'
is what the ancients held in awe.
May Your Majesty observe this!"
Thereupon, the Emperor's anger subsided,
and he sent someone to retrieve the previous edict.
In the third year of Huángchū 黃初 (222 CE),
Jì 濟 joined Grand Marshal Cáo Rén 曹仁 in campaigning against Wú 吳.
Jì 濟 separately attacked Xiànxī 羨谿.
Rén 仁 wanted to attack Rúxū Zhōu 濡須洲中,
but Jì 濟 said:
"The enemy occupies the western bank,
and has arrayed their ships upstream.
For our troops to enter the island
is to throw ourselves into hell;
it is the path to danger and destruction."
Rén 仁 did not listen,
and indeed suffered a defeat.
When Rén 仁 died,
Jì 濟 was again appointed General of the Central East
and took command of his troops.
An imperial edict stated:
"You possess both civil and military talents,
and your ambition and integrity are fervent.
You always have the ambition to cross the rivers and lakes and swallow Wúhuì 吳會,
therefore I again entrust you with the duty of a commander."
After a short while,
he was summoned to be a Grand Minister.
When the imperial carriage visited Guǎnglíng 廣陵,
Jì 濟 submitted a memorial stating that the waterways were difficult to pass,
and also presented the Sānzhōu Lùn 三州論 (Discourse on the Three Provinces) to remonstrate with the Emperor.
The Emperor did not listen,
and consequently, thousands of warships became stranded and could not proceed.
Some deliberators wanted to leave the troops there to establish agricultural colonies,
but Jì 濟 believed that the east was close to the lake,
and the north bordered the Huái 淮 River.
If the water level rose,
the enemy could easily raid,
so it was not safe to station troops there.
The Emperor followed his advice,
and the imperial carriage immediately departed.
Upon returning to Jīnghú 精湖,
the water gradually receded completely,
and all the ships were left in Jì 濟's charge.
The ships were originally scattered over several hundred *lǐ* 里.
Jì 濟 newly dug four or five channels,
and pushed the ships to gather.
He had already built earth dikes to block the lake water,
and then pulled all the remaining ships,
opening the dikes at once to let them enter the Huái 淮 River.
When the Emperor returned to Luòyáng 洛陽,
he said to Jì 濟:
"One must not fail to understand matters.
My previous decision was to burn half the ships in the Shānyáng Chí 山陽池,
but you managed them afterward,
and nearly reached Qiáo 譙 at the same time as me.
Furthermore, everything you have presented
has truly aligned with my intentions.
From now on, for plans to subdue the bandits,
consider and discuss them well."
When Emperor Míng 明帝 ascended the throne,
Jì 濟 was granted the title Marquis within the Pass.
When Grand Marshal Cáo Xiū 曹休 led his army towards Wǎn 皖,
Jì 濟 submitted a memorial stating
"deeply entering enemy territory,
facing Qúan 權's elite troops,
while Zhū Rán 朱然 and others are upstream,
attacking Xiū 休's rear,
I do not see any advantage in this."
When the army reached Wǎn 皖,
Wú 吳 sent out troops to Ānlù 安陸.
Jì 濟 again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Now the enemy is showing their presence in the west,
they must intend to gather their forces to attack the east.
It is advisable to urgently order all armies to go and rescue them."
At that time, Xiū 休's army had already been defeated,
abandoning all weapons and baggage trains in their retreat.
Wú 吳 wanted to block Jiáshí 夾石,
but encountered relief troops,
which is why the imperial army was not annihilated.
He was promoted to Central Protector of the Army.
At that time, the Director and Chief of the Central Secretariat were said to be wielding exclusive power.
Jì 濟 submitted a memorial, saying:
"When powerful ministers are too influential, the state is in peril;
when those around the ruler are too intimate, the ruler's vision is obscured.
These are the gravest admonitions of the ancients.
In the past, when powerful ministers held sway,
both internal and external factions stirred up trouble.
Your Majesty, with extraordinary resolve, personally oversaw all affairs,
and everyone was reverent and submissive.
It is not that powerful ministers are disloyal,
but when power and authority are held below,
the hearts of the populace become disrespectful towards the superior;
this is the natural course of events.
Since Your Majesty has already perceived this in powerful ministers,
I hope you will not forget it regarding those around you.
Those around you, even if loyal, upright, and far-sighted,
may not necessarily be more virtuous than powerful ministers.
However, when it comes to being ingratiating and seeking favor,
they may be skilled at it.
Now, whatever is said externally
is always attributed to the Central Secretariat.
Even if they are respectful and cautious and dare not engage in external relations,
just having this reputation
still misleads the populace.
How much more so when they actually hold vital affairs,
daily before Your Majesty's eyes.
Should they, during a moment of weariness, make some arbitrary decision,
and the multitude of officials see that they can influence matters,
they will also adapt to the times and gravitate towards them.
Once such a situation arises,
they will then arrange for their own security internally,
and with these words among the populace,
privately recruit their associates,
making them internal supporters.
If this happens,
approvals and condemnations, praise and blame,
will certainly be initiated by them; rewards and punishments for merits and faults
will certainly be altered;
those who follow the righteous path and advance
may be obstructed,
while those who crookedly attach themselves to those around you
will instead succeed.
Entering subtly,
emerging through appearances,
they will be trusted and indulged,
no longer suspected or detected.
This is what a sagely and wise ruler should hear early,
and by observing it externally, the true situation will reveal itself.
Or perhaps court officials fear that their words will not be accepted and they will incur the resentment of those around you,
so none dare to report it.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty, quietly contemplating and reflecting,
listening publicly and observing broadly,
if affairs are not fully in line with reason, and things are not perfectly utilized,
will change what is wrong and adjust what is inappropriate,
competing in merit with the ancient sovereigns Huángdì 黃帝 and Táng 湯,
and closely emulating the achievements of King Wǔ 武 and King Wén 文.
How could it be merely about those close to you?
However, a monarch cannot personally understand all matters in the realm to suit his own clear perception;
there must be those to whom he delegates.
If the three official positions are entrusted to one minister,
unless he possesses the loyalty of Duke Zhōu Dàn 周公旦
or the impartiality of Guǎn Yíwú 管夷吾,
there will be the drawbacks of manipulating power and ruining official duties.
Although pillars of the state are few today,
those whose conduct is praised in a province,
whose wisdom is effective in an office,
who are loyal, trustworthy, and exhaust their lives,
each performing their duties,
can be jointly employed,
so that the enlightened court will not have the reputation of having monopolistic officials."
An imperial edict stated:
"A loyal and outspoken minister
is relied upon by the ruler.
Jì 濟 possesses both civil and military talents,
diligently serves and exhausts his integrity.
Whenever there are major military or state affairs,
he invariably submits memorials and discussions.
His loyalty and fervor are inspiring,
and I greatly admire him."
He was then promoted to Protector-General,
and granted the additional title of Palace Attendant.
During the Jǐngchū reign,
there were extensive external levies for military service
and internal construction of palaces.
Many people felt aggrieved and alienated,
and the harvests were poor.
Jì submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty should now be expanding upon the achievements of your predecessors
and glorifying their legacy.
Truly, this is not a time to rule by merely resting on your laurels.
Although there are now twelve provinces,
as for the number of commoners,
it is no more than a single large commandery in Hàn times.
The two bandits have not yet been vanquished,
and troops are stationed on the border regions,
both farming and fighting,
with grievances accumulating over years.
Ancestral temples and palaces,
a hundred undertakings, are just beginning.
Those engaged in agriculture and sericulture are few,
while those who consume food and clothing are many.
What is urgent now
is simply to let the common people rest and recuperate,
so that they do not become utterly exhausted.
If the people are exhausted,
should there be floods or droughts,
a million people
would not be available for the nation's use.
Generally, when employing the people, one must follow the agricultural seasons
and not usurp their time.
A ruler who wishes to undertake great endeavors
must first assess the strength of his people and allow them to rest and recuperate.
Gōujiàn nurtured the pregnant to prepare for their use,
and Zhāo Wáng sympathized with the sick to avenge his grievances.
Thus, the weak Yān was able to conquer the strong Qí,
and the frail Yuè destroyed the powerful Wú.
Now, if the two enemies are not attacked and destroyed,
if nothing is done, they will invade.
If they are not eliminated in one's lifetime,
it will be a responsibility for a hundred generations.
With Your Majesty's sagacious and divinely martial strategy,
setting aside the less urgent matters
and concentrating on subjugating the bandits,
your servant believes there will be no difficulty.
Furthermore, indulgence in pleasure
harms one's vitality;
when the spirit is overused, it becomes exhausted;
when the body is overworked, it becomes debilitated.
I wish for a grand selection of virtuous and excellent women,
sufficient to fulfill the prophecy of 'a hundred sons.'
Those who are redundant and not yet counted
should all be dismissed,
focusing on purity and tranquility."
The imperial edict stated:
"Without the Hùjūn,
I would not have heard these words."
When Qí Wáng ascended the throne,
Jì was transferred to be Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
advanced in rank to Chānglíng Tínghóu,
and then promoted to Tàiwèi.
Initially,
Shìzhōng Gāotáng Lóng debated the matters of suburban sacrifices,
considering Wèi to be descendants of Shùn,
and thus advocating for Shùn to be offered sacrifices alongside Heaven.
Jì believed that Shùn's original surname was Guī,
and his descendants were named Tián,
not ancestors of Cáo.
He wrote an essay to refute Lóng.
At this time,
Cáo Shuǎng monopolized power,
and Dīng Mì, Dèng Yáng, and others lightly altered laws and regulations.
There was then a solar eclipse,
and an imperial edict asked the officials about its implications.
Jì submitted a memorial, saying:
"In ancient times, when the great Shùn assisted in governance,
he warned against forming cliques;
when Zhōugōng assisted in administration,
he was cautious about his companions;
when Qí Hóu asked about disasters,
Yàn Yīng replied by advocating for benevolence;
when Lǔ Jūn asked about anomalies,
Zāng Sūn responded by suggesting the alleviation of corvée labor.
Responding to Heaven and averting calamities
is truly a matter of human affairs.
Now, the two bandits have not been eliminated,
and the generals and soldiers have been exposed to the elements for decades.
Men and women are resentful and alienated,
and the common people are impoverished and suffering.
Indeed, as for the laws and regulations of the state,
only those with generational great talent
can establish their frameworks to be passed down to later generations.
How can middle or lower-ranking officials be allowed to alter them?
Ultimately, this is of no benefit to governance,
but only harms the people.
It is hoped that civil and military officials will each guard their respective duties,
and lead with purity and tranquility,
then harmony and auspicious omens can be induced and achieved."
He followed Tàifù Sīmǎ Xuān Wáng to station at the floating bridge on the Luò Shuǐ,
where Cáo Shuǎng and others were executed.
He was advanced in rank to Dūxiāng Hóu,
with an estate of seven hundred households.
Jì submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant, though holding an honored position as a senior official,
did not prevent Shuǎng from harboring malicious intentions.
This is your servant's incompetence.
The Tàifù employed a decisive strategy,
and Your Majesty recognized his loyalty and integrity.
The guilty parties were punished,
which is a blessing for the altars of soil and grain.
However, conferring titles and bestowing rewards
must be given to those who have rendered meritorious service.
Now, concerning the plot, your servant did not know of it beforehand;
as for the battle, it was not led by your servant.
Yet, superiors lose their restraint,
and inferiors suffer the ill effects.
Your servant, being a high minister,
is looked up to by the people.
I truly fear that the gradual trend of usurping rewards will begin from this,
and the custom of humble deference will thus be abolished."
He firmly declined,
but it was not permitted.
He passed away that year
and was posthumously named Jǐng Hóu.
His son Xiù inherited the title.
When Xiù passed away,
his son Kǎi inherited it.
During the Xiánxī reign,
the Five Ranks were established.
Because Jì had outstanding achievements in the previous dynasty,
Kǎi was re-enfeoffed as Xiàcài Zǐ.
Liú Fàng, courtesy name Zǐqì,
was a native of Zhuójùn.
He was a descendant of Hóng,
Prince Shùn of Guǎngyáng and Marquis of Xīxiāng in the Hàn dynasty.
He successively served as an administrator in the commandery
and was nominated as Xiàolián.
He experienced great chaos in the world.
At that time, Wáng Sōng of Yúyáng occupied his territory,
and Fàng went to rely on him.
When Tàizǔ conquered Jìzhōu,
Fàng persuaded Sōng, saying:
"In the past, Dǒng Zhuó committed treason,
and heroes rose in unison,
obstructing military actions and acting on their own authority.
People established and cultivated themselves.
Only Cáo Gōng was able to rescue the endangered and chaotic situation,
uphold the Son of Heaven,
and carry out imperial decrees to punish the guilty.
He was victorious wherever he went.
Despite the strength of the two Yuán,
when they defended, Huáinán crumbled,
and when they fought, they suffered a great defeat at Guāndù.
Riding on his victories, he swept across the land
and was about to pacify Hèshuò.
With both might and punishment applied,
the general trend was evident.
Those who submit quickly will gradually receive blessings;
those who submit later will perish first.
This is the time to hasten without delay, not waiting until the end of the day.
In the past, Qíng Bù abandoned the honor of facing south as a ruler
and, sword in hand, returned to Hàn.
He truly understood the principles of rise and fall
and clearly discerned when to stay and when to leave.
General, you should commit yourself and your life
and form strong ties."
Sōng agreed with this.
When Tàizǔ attacked Yuán Tán at Nánpí,
he sent a letter inviting Sōng.
Sōng offered Yōngnú, Quánzhōu, and Āncì to surrender.
Fàng drafted Sōng's reply to Tàizǔ,
and its text was very elegant.
Tàizǔ not only praised it
but also heard of Fàng's persuasion,
and thus summoned Fàng.
In the tenth year of Jiàn'ān,
he arrived with Sōng.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased
and said to Fàng:
"In the past, Bān Biāo relied on Dòu Róng and achieved success in Héxī.
How similar this is today!"
He then appointed Fàng as a participant in the military affairs of Sīkōng,
successively serving as Zhǔbù and Jìshì,
and then as the magistrate of Héyáng and Duìxǔ.
(Duì is pronounced 'duō-huó fǎn.'
Xǔ is pronounced 'xǔ.')
After the state of Wèi was established,
Liú Fàng, together with Sūn Zī from Tàiyuán, both became secretaries (mìshū láng).
Before this,
Sūn Zī had also served as a county magistrate (xiàn lìng)
and participated in the Chancellor’s (chéngxiàng) military affairs.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī were transferred to be Left and Right Aides (zuǒyòu chéng).
After several months,
Liú Fàng was transferred to be a magistrate (lìng).
In the early days of Huángchū,
the Secretariat (mìshū) was changed to the Central Secretariat (zhōngshū),
with Liú Fàng as its Supervisor (jiān)
and Sūn Zī as its Director (lìng).
Each was additionally given the title of Attendant Official (gěishìzhōng).
Liú Fàng was bestowed the title of Marquis of the Interior Pass (Guānnèi Hóu),
and Sūn Zī that of Marquis of the Central Pass (Guānzhōng Hóu).
They subsequently took charge of confidential matters.
In the third year,
Liú Fàng's peerage was advanced to Marquis of Wèishòu Pavilion (Wèishòu Tínghóu),
and Sūn Zī's to Marquis of the Interior Pass (Guānnèi Hóu).
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
they were especially favored and trusted,
both being concurrently made Regular Mounted Attendants (sànqí chángshì).
Liú Fàng’s peerage was advanced to Marquis of Xīxiāng (Xīxiāng Hóu),
and Sūn Zī’s to Marquis of Lèyáng Pavilion (Lèyáng Tínghóu).
At the end of Tàihé,
Wú sent its general Zhōu Hè by sea to Liáodōng
to entice Gōngsūn Yuān.
The Emperor wished to intercept and attack them,
but most of the court debated against it.
Only Sūn Zī firmly advocated for the strategy,
which indeed led to a great victory.
His peerage was advanced to Marquis of Zuǒxiāng (Zuǒxiāng Hóu).
Liú Fàng was skilled at drafting proclamations (shūxí).
Many of the edicts and orders issued by the Three Ancestors for recruitment and persuasion
were drafted by Liú Fàng.
In the early Qīnglóng period,
Sūn Quán allied with Zhūgě Liàng,
intending to jointly launch an attack.
A border scout obtained Sūn Quán’s letter,
and Liú Fàng then altered its wording,
frequently replacing the original text and fabricating it,
sending it to the General Who Conquers the East (zhēngdōng jiāngjūn), Mǎn Chǒng,
as if it indicated a desire for submission.
Mǎn Chǒng sealed it and showed it to Zhūgě Liàng.
Zhūgě Liàng then sent it to the great Wú general Bù Zhì and others,
who in turn showed it to Sūn Quán.
Sūn Quán feared that Zhūgě Liàng would become suspicious,
and deeply explained himself.
In that year,
both were concurrently made Palace Attendant (shìzhōng) and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (guānglù dàfū).
In the second year of Jǐngchū,
after Liáodōng was pacified,
for their meritorious participation in the strategy,
both were advanced in peerage
and enfeoffed in their original counties.
Liú Fàng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Fāngchéng (Fāngchéng Hóu),
and Sūn Zī as Marquis of Zhōngdū (Zhōngdū Hóu).
In that year,
the Emperor fell gravely ill
and wished to appoint Yān Wáng Yǔ as Grand General (dàjiāngjūn),

along with the General of the Imperial Guard (lǐngjūn jiāngjūn) Xiàhóu Xiàn, General of the Martial Guard (wǔwèi jiāngjūn) Cáo Shuǎng, Colonel of the Mounted Troops (túnqí xiàowèi) Cáo Zhào, and General of the Agile Cavalry (xiāoqí jiāngjūn) Qín Lǎng, to jointly assist in governance.
Yān Wáng Yǔ was humble and virtuous by nature,
and sincerely and firmly declined.
The Emperor summoned Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī,
who entered his bedchamber,
and asked,
"Why is Yān Wáng acting like this?"
Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī replied,
"Yān Wáng indeed knows that he is not capable of such a great responsibility."
The Emperor said,
"Can Cáo Shuǎng replace Yǔ?"
Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī then approved of him.
They also earnestly urged for the swift summons of the Grand Commandant (tàiwèi) Sīmǎ Xuānwáng,
to stabilize the imperial house.
The Emperor accepted their words
and immediately handed a yellow paper to Liú Fàng to draft the edict.
After Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī exited,
the Emperor's mind changed again,
and he issued an edict to stop Xuānwáng from coming.
Soon after, he saw Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī again and said,
"I myself summoned the Grand Commandant,
but Cáo Zhào and others made me stop him,
almost ruining my affairs!"
He ordered another edict to be drafted.
The Emperor personally summoned only Cáo Shuǎng, along with Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī, to receive the edict,
and consequently dismissed Yǔ, Xiàn, Zhào, and Lǎng from their offices.
The Grand Commandant also arrived,
ascended the bed to receive the edict,
and then the Emperor passed away.
When Qí Wáng ascended the throne,
because Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī had made crucial decisions,
their fiefs were increased by three hundred households.
Liú Fàng's total became eleven hundred,
and Sūn Zī's one thousand households.
Their favorite sons were enfeoffed as Marquises of Pavilion (tínghóu),
their second sons as Commanders of Cavalry (qí dūwèi),
and their other sons all as Gentlemen (lángzhōng).
In the first year of Zhèngshǐ,
Liú Fàng was additionally made Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (zuǒ guānglù dàfū),
and Sūn Zī Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (yòu guānglù dàfū),
with golden seals and purple ribbons,
their ceremonial privileges equal to the Three Excellencies (sānsī).
In the sixth year,
Liú Fàng was transferred to General of Agile Cavalry (piàojì jiāngjūn),
and Sūn Zī to General of the Guard (wèijiāngjūn),
continuing to hold their posts as Supervisor and Director respectively.
In the seventh year,
one more son of each was enfeoffed as Marquis of Pavilion.
Both, due to old age, resigned their positions
and, as marquises, attended court on the first and fifteenth day of the month,
with the rank of Special Advance (tèjìn).
After Cáo Shuǎng was executed,
Sūn Zī was again made Palace Attendant (shìzhōng)
and concurrently Director of the Central Secretariat (zhōngshū lìng).
In the second year of Jiāpíng,
Liú Fàng died,
with the posthumous title Jìng Hóu.
His son Zhèng succeeded him.
Sūn Zī again resigned his position and returned to his residence,
where he was appointed General of Agile Cavalry (piàojì jiāngjūn),
and then transferred to Palace Attendant (shìzhōng),
with his rank of Special Advance (tèjìn) remaining as before.
In the third year, he died,
with the posthumous title Zhēn Hóu.
His son Hóng succeeded him.
Liú Fàng's talent and resourcefulness surpassed Sūn Zī's,
but his self-cultivation was inferior.
Both Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī were adept at following the emperor's wishes,
and never openly pointed out right or wrong.
They suppressed Xīn Pí and aided Wáng Sī,
for which they were criticized by their contemporaries.
However, at times, when officials offered remonstrances,
they would support their righteous arguments
and also secretly present advice on benefits and drawbacks,
not solely offering flattery, it is said.
During the Xiánxī period,
when the Five Ranks were established,
