because Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī had rendered distinguished service in the previous dynasty,
Zhèng was re-enfeoffed as Viscount of Fāngchéng (Fāngchéng Zǐ),
and Hóng as Viscount of Líshí (Líshí Zǐ).
The commentary states: Chéng Yù, Guō Jiā, Dǒng Zhāo, Liú Yè, and Jiǎng Jì, with their talents, strategies, and plans,
were extraordinary individuals of their time.
Although their governance and virtues
differed from those of Xún Yóu,
their strategic calculations and predictions
were comparable to his.
Liú Fàng's literary skill,
and Sūn Zī's diligence and prudence,
both managed the imperial secretariat and served as spokesmen.
Their authority was renowned at the time,
but their integrity was not in keeping with proper conduct.
Therefore, the criticisms and praises they received
often exceeded their true merit.
Biographies of Liú Fàng, Sīmǎ Zhī, Liáng Xí, Zhāng Wēn, and Jiǎ Xǔ, Chapter Fifteen.
Liú Fù, courtesy name Yuányǐng,
was a native of Péiguó.
He avoided the chaos by fleeing to Yángzhōu.
In the early Jiàn'ān period,
he persuaded Yuán Shù's generals Qī Jì and Qín Yì
to lead their troops with him to meet Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
The Grand Ancestor was pleased with him,
and the Minister of Works (sītú) invited him to be a clerk (yuàn).
Later, Lǐ Shù, the Administrator of Lújiāng appointed by Sūn Cè, attacked and killed the Inspector of Yángzhōu, Yán Xiàng.
Méi Gān, Léi Xù, Chén Lán, and others from Lújiāng gathered tens of thousands of people between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
and the commanderies and counties were ravaged.
The Grand Ancestor was then facing difficulties with Yuán Shào,
and deemed Liú Fù capable of handling affairs in the southeast.
He subsequently memorialized for him to be appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Upon receiving the appointment, Liú Fù
rode alone to the deserted city of Héféi,
established the provincial administration,
and pacified Léi Xù and others in the south,
all of whom he settled.
Tributes flowed continuously.
Within a few years, his benevolent influence was widespread,
the common people were happy with his governance,
and countless refugees crossed the rivers and mountains to return.
Thereupon, he gathered scholars (zhūshēng),
established schools,
expanded military colonies (túntián),
and undertook the construction of the Sháobēi, (Rú) [Jiā]bēi, Qīmén, and Wútáng dams to irrigate rice fields.
Both officials and commoners had provisions.
He also constructed high city walls
and stockpiled large quantities of wood and stone.
He had tens of millions of straw mats woven
and additionally stored several thousand *hú* of fish oil,
to prepare for defense in battle.
He died in the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān.
Sūn Quán led a hundred thousand troops to attack and besiege Héféi city for over a hundred days.
At that time, there were continuous rains,
and the city walls were on the verge of collapsing.
Therefore, they covered them with thatch and straw.
At night, they lit torches to illuminate outside the city,
observing what the bandits were doing to prepare for it,
and the bandits were defeated and fled.
The scholars and people of Yángzhōu increasingly cherished his memory,
believing that even Dǒng Ānyú's defense of Jìnyáng
could not surpass it.
As for the benefits of the reservoirs and ponds,
they are still in use today.
Fù's son, Jìng,
was promoted from Huángmén Shìláng to Lújiāng Tàishǒu during the Huángchū era.
An imperial edict stated:
"Your father was formerly the governor of that province,
and now you again hold this commandery.
You can be said to be one who has carried on the heavy responsibility."
He was then transferred to Hénèi,
promoted to Shàngshū,
granted the title Guānnèi Hóu,
and appointed Hénán Yǐn.
Sànqí Chángshì Yìng Qú wrote to Jìng, saying:
"You entered service as a speaker (Nàyán)
and went out to oversee the capital's responsibilities.
The art of enriching the people
grows daily and monthly.
The dikes and barriers are high and formidable,
cutting off any desire for trespassing or sneaking in.
The five types of crops are distinctly cultivated,
keeping away the disasters of flood and fire.
Agricultural tools are fully equipped,
with no lack of timely preparation.
Silkworms and wheat have the protection of thatch and coverings,
with no worries of rain or dampness.
Sealed tallies are issued with fixed dates,
so there are no procrastinating officials.
The poor, the widowed, the orphaned, and the solitary
receive the benefits of relief grain.
Adding to this is your clear elucidation of the obscure and subtle,
and your firm and unyielding adherence to the law;
subordinate officials carry out the king's commands,
and the hundred districts manage affairs by letting their arms hang down and looking up to you.
Even the governance of the former Zhào, Zhāng, and the Three Kings
is not sufficient to compare with yours."
Jìng's administration was largely like this.
Though it initially seemed meticulous,
it ultimately benefited the common people,
and he possessed Fù's inherited demeanor.
He resigned his office due to his mother's mourning.
Later, he served as Dàsīnóng Wèiwèi,
and was advanced to the title Guǎnglá Lú Tínghóu,
with an estate of three hundred households.
He submitted a memorial discussing the fundamentals of Confucian education, saying:
"Indeed, scholarship
is the standard for order and chaos,
and the great teaching of the sages.
Since the Huángchū era,
the Grand Academy has been established for over twenty years,
yet few have achieved success.
This is probably due to the light selection of erudites (bóshì),
the students avoiding service,
and the sons of noble families
feeling ashamed if they are not of their peers,
hence there are no scholars.
Though it has the name, it lacks the people;
though the teaching is established, it lacks achievement.
It is appropriate to highly select erudites,
choosing those whose conduct serves as a model for others,
and whose classical learning qualifies them as teachers,
to oversee the education of the imperial sons.
Following ancient laws,
the sons and grandsons of officials of two thousand dàns and above,
from the age of fifteen,
should all enter the Grand Academy.
Clearly establish paths for promotion, demotion, honor, and disgrace;
those whose classical learning is profound and conduct is upright
should be advanced to promote virtue;
those who abandon their studies and neglect their duties
should be demoted to punish evil;
by commending the good and teaching the less able, encouragement will thrive,
and superficial social climbing
will cease on its own.
This will propagate the great transformation,
thereby pacifying the unsubmissive;
the whole world will follow the trend,
and distant people will come to submit.
This is the teaching of the sages,
the fundamental way to achieve good governance."
Later, he was promoted to Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn,
and given authority over all military affairs north of the Yellow River with a staff of authority (jiǎjié).
Jìng believed that
"among the established great laws,
none is better than defending the borders,
making a distinction between the common people and the barbarians."
Thus, he expanded border defenses
and garrisoned strategic strongholds.
He also repaired and expanded the Lìlíngqú grand dam,
which irrigated areas north and south of Jì;
three crops of rice were planted,
benefiting the border residents.
He died in the sixth year of Jiāpíng,
and was posthumously granted the title Zhēng Běi Jiāngjūn,
advanced to the title Jiànchéng Xiānghóu,
and given the posthumous name Jǐng Hóu.
His son, Xī, inherited.
Sīmǎ Láng, courtesy name Bódá,
was a native of Wēn, Hénèi.
At nine years old,
someone mentioned his father's courtesy name,
and Láng said,
"He who disrespects another's parents
does not respect his own parents."
The guest apologized.
At twelve,
he was tested on the classics and became a tóngzǐláng.
The examiner, seeing his robust physique,
suspected Láng of concealing his age
and interrogated him.
Láng said,
"My ancestors, both paternal and maternal,
have for generations been tall and large.
Though I am young and weak,
I have no desire to appear older,
nor would I reduce my age to seek early success;
this is not what I intend to do."
The examiner was surprised by him.
Later, when the Guāndōng forces rose up,
Lǐ Shào, the former Inspector of Jìzhōu, was living at home in Yěwáng,
which was near mountains and dangerous terrain. He wished to move to Wēn.
Láng said to Shào,
"The analogy of lips and teeth
is not only for Yú and Guó;
Wēn and Yěwáng are exactly that.
Now to leave there and reside here
is to seek to avoid the moment of collapse.
Furthermore, you
are the hope of the people of the state.
If the bandits have not yet arrived and you move first,
the counties along the mountains will certainly be alarmed,
which would shake the hearts of the people and open the door to villainy
and treachery.
I secretly worry for the commandery."
Shào did not listen.
The people in the border mountains indeed rebelled,
moving inland,
and some became bandits and raiders.
At this time, Dǒng Zhuó moved the emperor's capital to Cháng'ān,
and Zhuó consequently remained in Luòyáng.
Láng's father, Fáng, was Zìshū Yùshǐ,
and was supposed to move west.
Because the four quarters were in turmoil,
he sent Láng to take his family back to their home county.
Someone accused Láng of wanting to flee,
so he was seized and brought before Zhuó.
Zhuó said to Láng,
"You are the same age as my deceased son;
you almost let me down greatly!"
Láng then said,
"Your Excellency, with your virtues surpassing the age,
encountered a time of great calamity.
You purged all evils
and widely promoted worthy scholars.
This truly shows an open mind and deep concern,
intending to bring about ultimate good governance.
Your prestige and virtue have risen,
and your accomplishments are evident.
Yet military difficulties arise daily,
and the provinces and commanderies are in turmoil.
Within the outskirts,
the people are not settled in their occupations,
abandoning their homes and property,
fleeing and hiding.
Even though the four passes are guarded and prohibited,
and severe punishments are inflicted,
this does not cease.
This is why I am grieved.
I hope Your Excellency will reflect on past events
and give it a little more thought;
then your glorious name will rival the sun and moon,
and Yī and Zhōu will not be enough to compare."
Zhuó said,
"I too realize this;
your words are insightful!"
Lǎng knew well that Zhúo would surely perish.
Fearing he would be detained,
he immediately distributed his wealth and property as bribes to those in Zhúo's service,
seeking to return to his hometown.
Upon arrival, he told the elders:
"Dǒng Zhuó is perverse and rebellious,
hated by all under Heaven.
This is the time for loyal ministers and righteous gentlemen to rise up.
Our commandery and the capital are contiguous,
east of Luòyáng there is Chénggāo,
and to the north lies the Yellow River.
If those who raise righteous armies in the world cannot advance,
their momentum will surely halt here.
This is a land of division, fragmentation, and warfare,
where it is difficult to secure oneself.
It is better, while the roads are still open,
to move our entire clan east to Líyáng.
Líyáng has encampment troops.
Zhào Wēisūn, a relative by marriage from our hometown,
serves as Inspector of the Encampment and Imperial Messenger,
commanding soldiers and horses,
which is enough to be our protector.
If there are changes later,
it will not be too late to observe the situation again."
The elders were nostalgic
and none followed him,
except Zhào Zī from the same county,
who took his family and went with Lǎng.
A few months later,
the various prefectures and commanderies east of the pass raised armies,
numbering hundreds of thousands,
all gathered at Xíngyáng and Hénèi.
The various generals could not unite,
and let their soldiers plunder,
causing nearly half of the people to die.
After a long time,
the Guāndōng forces dispersed.
Tàizǔ and Lǚ Bù were in a stalemate at Púyáng,
so Lǎng took his family back to Wēn.
At that time, there was a great famine,
and people cannibalized each other.
Lǎng took care of and provided for his clan,
and instructed his younger brothers,
not abandoning their studies due to the decadent era.
At the age of twenty-two,
Tàizǔ appointed him as a subordinate official of the Sīkōng.
He was then appointed Magistrate of Chénggāo,
but left due to illness.
He was again appointed Chief of Tángyáng.
His governance focused on leniency and benevolence,
without resorting to whips or canes,
yet the people did not violate prohibitions.
Previously,
some people had been resettled into the capital.
Later, when the county was tasked with building boats,
the resettled people feared they couldn't complete it,
so they voluntarily returned privately to help,
showing how much he was beloved.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Yuánchéng,
and then entered service as Chief Clerk to the Chancellor.
Lǎng believed that the crumbling state of the world
stemmed from Qín's abolition of the five ranks system,
and the lack of military training and readiness in the commanderies and states.
Although the five ranks could not be immediately restored now,
he suggested that prefectures and commanderies should all establish armies
to guard against the four barbarians externally
and deter rebels internally,
which would be a long-term strategy.
He also believed that the well-field system should be restored.
Previously, because people each had their hereditary land holdings
which were difficult to seize,
it had persisted until now.
Now, after a great chaos,
the people are scattered,
and land is without owners,
all becoming public land.
It is opportune to restore it at this time.
Although his proposals were not implemented,
the idea of prefectures and commanderies leading troops
was Lǎng's original intention.
He was promoted to Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
His administration and reforms were widely adopted,
and the common people praised him.
Even in military campaigns,
he always wore coarse clothes and ate poor food,
leading his subordinates with frugality.
He had a refined appreciation for human relations and classical texts.
When local people like Lǐ Dí gained great renown,
Lǎng often publicly belittled them.
Later, when Lǐ Dí and others failed,
people of the time admired Lǎng.
Zhōng Yáo and Wáng Càn wrote essays stating:
"Only a sage can bring about great peace."
Lǎng believed that
"even if people like Yī Yǐn and Yán Huí are not sages,
if they can succeed each other for several generations,
great peace can be achieved."
In the twenty-second year of Jiàn'ān [217 CE],
he campaigned against Wú with Xiàhóu Dūn, Zāng Bà, and others.
When they reached Jūcháo,
a great plague afflicted the soldiers.
Lǎng personally inspected them
and provided medicine.
He contracted the illness and died,
at the age of forty-seven.
His dying wish was to be dressed in plain cloth and a simple headscarf,
and buried in seasonal clothes.
The people of the prefecture mourned him.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Lǎng's son Yí as Marquis of Chāngwǔtíng,
with an estate of one hundred households.
Lǎng's younger brother Fú also allowed his son Wàng to succeed Lǎng.
After Yí died,
Wàng's son Hóng inherited.
Initially, Zhào Zī, who had moved with Lǎng,
rose to the rank of Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
and was well-regarded by his generation.
Liáng Xí, courtesy name Zǐyú,
was a native of Zhè in Chén Commandery.
He served as a principal officer of the commandery.
When Tàizǔ was Sīkōng,
he appointed him Magistrate of Zhāng.
He successively became Magistrate of Chéngshì, Hǎixī, and Xiàpī,
gaining a reputation for good governance wherever he served.
He returned as a clerk in the Western Section,
and was promoted to subordinate.
Since the Bīng Province had newly submitted,
Xí was appointed Separated Bureau Chief and concurrently Inspector of Bīng Province.
At that time, it was still recovering from Gāo Gàn's chaos.
The Hú and Dí tribes were on the border,
Zhāng Xióng was arrogant and tyrannical,
and officials and common people deserted
to join their tribes.
Soldiers gathered large numbers of followers,
committing acts of banditry,
inciting each other,
and often becoming powerful local strongmen.
Upon arriving at his post, Xí
lured, persuaded, and recruited them,
courteously summoning their powerful local magnates,
and gradually recommending them
to the Secretariat.
Once the powerful magnates were all gone,
he then successively conscripted able-bodied men as auxiliary troops.
Also, when large armies were sent on campaigns,
he requested some to serve as strong-men.
After the officials and soldiers had left,
he gradually moved their families
and sent them to Yè in successive batches,
totaling tens of thousands of people.
For those who disobeyed,
he raised armies to suppress them,
beheading thousands,
and those who surrendered numbered tens of thousands.
The Chányú became respectful and obedient,
the noble kings bowed their heads,
and the tribal units submitted and performed duties,
like registered households.
The frontier was pacified,
the people spread across the land,
diligently encouraged in agriculture and sericulture,
and orders were enforced.
He recommended famous scholars,
who all became prominent in the world,
as recorded in the biography of Cháng Lín.
Tàizǔ praised him,
bestowed upon him the title of Marquis of Guānnèi,
and reappointed him to his original post.
Elders praised him,
believing that among all the Inspectors they had known,
none could compare to Xí.
In the eighteenth year of Jiàn'ān [213 CE],
Bīng Province was merged into Jì Province.
He was then appointed Counselor-Gentleman and Grand Administrator of the Western Command,
governing the subordinate areas of Jì Province
and overseeing his former tribal units.
He was also sent to Shàngdǎng to obtain large timbers for the Yè palace.
Xí submitted a memorial to establish two Tuntian Commandants,
leading six hundred laborers,
to cultivate beans and grains along the roads
to supply the expenses of people and oxen.
Later, when the Chányú entered to serve the court,
the northwest was free from worry,
which was due to Xí's achievements.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
Bīng Province was reestablished,
and he was reinstated as Inspector,
further enfeoffed as Marquis of Shēnméntíng,
with an estate of one hundred households.
His governance was consistently the best in the realm.
In the second year of Tàihé [228 CE],
he was summoned to be appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Xí had been in the province for over twenty years,
yet his dwelling was poor,
without any exotic or precious items.
Emperor Míng found this unusual
and bestowed generous gifts upon him.
In the fourth year [230 CE],
he passed away.
His son Shī inherited.
Initially,
Jìyīn Wáng Sī and Xí both served as secretaries in the Western Bureau.
Once, Sī was on duty and submitted a report,
but he failed to grasp Tài-zǔ's intentions.
Tài-zǔ was greatly enraged,
and ordered the summoning of the official in charge,
intending to inflict severe punishment.
At that time, Sī had just stepped out,
and Xí went to respond in his place.
He had already been seized and taken into custody.
Sī then rushed back,
confessed his own crime,
which deserved death.
Tài-zǔ sighed at Xí's silence
and Sī's understanding of his duty,
saying,
"How is it that I have two righteous gentlemen in my army?"
Later, they were simultaneously promoted to Cìshǐ,
with Sī leading Yùzhōu.
Sī was also a capable official,
but he was overly meticulous and lacked a grand vision.
He rose to the position of a Jiǔqīng
and was enfeoffed as a Lièhóu.
Zhāng Jì, courtesy name Dé-róng,
was a native of Gāolíng, Fēngyì.
At sixteen,
he became a minor official in the commandery.
Later, he held several key positions,
was recommended as Xiàolián,
but did not take office.
When Tài-zǔ was Sīkōng,
he was invited to serve,
but before he arrived,
he was recommended as Màocái
and appointed as the magistrate of Xīnfēng.
His administration was the best among the Sānfǔ.
Yuán Shàng resisted Tài-zǔ at Líyáng
and sent Guō Yuán, the Administrator of Hédōng whom he had appointed, Gāo Gàn, the Cìshǐ of Bīngzhōu, and the Xiongnú Chányú to take Píngyáng,
and dispatched envoys to the west to form an alliance with the generals in Guānzhōng.
Sīlì Xiàowèi Zhōng Yáo sent Jì to persuade General Mǎ Téng and others.
Jì explained the advantages and disadvantages to them,
and Téng and the others agreed.
Téng sent his son Chāo with over ten thousand soldiers
to join Yáo in attacking Gàn and Yuán,
severely defeating them,
and beheading Yuán.
Gàn and the Chányú all surrendered.
Later, Gàn rebelled again in Bīngzhōu.
Zhāng Shèng of Hénèi had over ten thousand men with no allegiance,
and plundered the area between Xiáo and Miǎn.
Wèi Gù of Hédōng and Zhāng Yǎn of Hóngnóng each raised troops to respond to him.
Tài-zǔ appointed Jì as Yìláng
to participate in Yáo's military affairs,
and sent him to summon the western generals Mǎ Téng and others.
They all led their troops to attack Shèng and his allies,
defeating them.
Yǎn and Gù were beheaded,
and Gàn fled to Jīngzhōu.
Jì was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wǔshǐtíng.
When Tài-zǔ was about to campaign in Jīngzhōu,
Téng and others divided and occupied Guānzhōng.
Tài-zǔ again sent Jì to persuade Téng and others
to release their troops and return.
Téng had already agreed but then hesitated again.
Jì, fearing a change,
then moved to urge the various counties to prepare supplies
and for officials of two thousand *shí* to welcome them in the suburbs.
Téng had no choice
but to depart eastward.
Tài-zǔ memorialized Téng as Wèiwèi,
and his son Chāo as a general,
commanding his forces.
Later, Chāo rebelled,
and Jì followed Tài-zǔ to defeat Chāo at Huáyīn,
and pacified Guānyòu in the west.
Jì was appointed as Jīngzhàoyǐn,
where he attracted and appeased displaced people,
and revitalized counties and towns,
which the common people cherished.
After the state of Wèi was established,
he served as Shàngshū,
then went out as Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu.
Tài-zǔ said to Jì,
"Returning you to your home province
is like wearing embroidered clothes during the day."
He accompanied the campaign against Zhāng Lǔ,
and separately entered through Sànguān to attack the rebellious Dī,
collecting their wheat to supply the army.
When Lǔ surrendered,
Jì persuaded Tài-zǔ to relocate tens of thousands of households from Hánzhōng to populate Cháng'ān and the Sānfǔ.
Later, he and Cáo Hóng defeated Wú Lán at Xiàbiàn,
and also, with Xiàhóu Yuān, attacked Sòng Jiàn,
and separately attacked Líntáo and Dídao,
pacifying them.
At this time,
Tài-zǔ moved people to fill Héběi,
causing the people of Lǒngxī, Tiānshuǐ, and Nán'ān to become alarmed,
restless and uneasy.
Jì granted leave to those from the three commanderies serving as generals and officials,
and had them build houses and
construct water mills,
whereupon the people's hearts settled.
When Tài-zǔ was about to withdraw the garrison from Hánzhōng,
he feared that Liú Bèi would take the Dī of Wǔdū to threaten Guānzhōng,
and consulted Jì.
Jì said,
"One can persuade them to move north to gather grain to avoid the enemy.
Those who arrive first should be greatly rewarded and honored,
so that the first will know the benefit,
and the later will surely admire them."
Tài-zǔ followed his plan
and personally went to Hánzhōng to withdraw all the armies.
He ordered Jì to Wǔdū
to relocate over fifty thousand Dī households to reside in the border areas of Fúfēng and Tiānshuǐ.
At that time,
Yán Jùn of Wǔwēi, Hé Luán of Zhāngyè, Huáng Huá of Jiǔquán, Qū Yǎn of Xīpíng, and others all raised revolts in their commanderies,
proclaiming themselves generals,
and attacking each other.
Yán Jùn sent an envoy to bring his mother and son to the Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) as hostages,
seeking assistance.
Tàizǔ asked Jì,
and Jì said:
"Jùn and the others outwardly borrow the state's prestige,
but inwardly harbor arrogance and defiance.
Once their plans are settled and their power sufficient,
they will surely rebel.
Now, as we are in the midst of settling Shǔ,
it is best to allow both sides to exist and fight each other,
like Biàn Zhuāngzǐ stabbing a tiger,
and simply await their demise."
Tàizǔ said:
"Excellent."
After more than a year,
Hé Luán eventually killed Yán Jùn,
and Wǔwēi's Wáng Mì then killed Hé Luán.
At that time, Liángzhōu was not established.
From Sānfǔ to the Western Regions,
all were under Yōngzhōu.
When Emperor Wén (Wén Dì) ascended the throne,
Liángzhōu was first established,
with Zōu Qí, the Administrator of Āndìng, appointed as its Inspector (cìshǐ).
Zhāng Jìn of Zhāngyè seized the Administrator of the commandery and raised an army to resist Zōu Qí.
Huáng Huá and Qū Yǎn each drove out their former administrators,
raising armies to support Zhāng Jìn.
Jì advanced his troops to create momentum for the Protector of the Qiāng, Sū Zé,
thus enabling Sū Zé to achieve merit.
Jì was promoted in rank to Dūxiāng Hóu.
The Lúshuǐ Hú of Liángzhōu, Yījiàn Jìqiè and Zhì Yuánduō, rebelled,
causing great disturbance west of the Hé (Yellow River).
The Emperor (Dì) was concerned,
saying:
"No one but Jì can pacify Liángzhōu."
He then summoned Zōu Qí,
and replaced him with Jì.
An imperial edict stated:
"In the past, Jiǎ Fù requested to attack the Yǎn bandits,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ (Guāngwǔ Dì) smiled and said: 'If the Executive of the Guard (Zhíjīn Wú) attacks Yǎn,
what more do I have to worry about?'
Your strategies surpass others',
and now is the time.
Act according to expediency,
and do not seek prior approval."
He dispatched the Protector-General Xiàhóu Rú and General Fèi Yào and others to follow him.
When Jì arrived at Jīnchéng,
he wanted to cross the river.
The generals advised him, saying
"our troops are few and the path is dangerous,
we cannot advance deeply yet."
Jì said:
"Although the path is dangerous,
it is not as narrow as Jǐngxíng.
The barbarians are a disorderly mob,
with no strategy like Zuǒ Chē.
Wǔwēi is in critical danger,
and we should hasten to its aid."
So, he crossed the river.
More than seven thousand enemy cavalry met and resisted the army at Yīnkǒu.
Jì spread rumors that his army would pass through Zhānyīn,
but secretly went via Qiěcì and reached Wǔwēi.
The Hú thought it divine,
and withdrew to Xiǎnměi.
After Jì had already occupied Wǔwēi,
Fèi Yào then arrived,
but Xiàhóu Rú and the others had not yet reached.
Jì rewarded the officers and soldiers,
and wished to advance his army to attack the Hú.
All the generals said:
"The soldiers are tired,
and the enemy's morale is high,
it is difficult to contend with them."
Jì said:
"Currently, our army has no visible provisions;
we must rely on the enemy for supplies.
If the barbarians see our troops gathered,
they will retreat and rely on the deep mountains.
If we pursue them, the path will be dangerous and we will suffer hunger,
and if our troops return, they will go out and plunder.
If this continues,
our troops will not be able to disengage.
As the saying goes, 'One day of indulging the enemy,
and the trouble lasts for generations.'
Therefore,"
he advanced his army to Xiǎnměi.
Several thousand Hú cavalry, taking advantage of a strong wind, tried to set fire to the camp.
All the officers and soldiers were afraid.
That night, Jì secretly hid three thousand elite soldiers in an ambush,
and ordered his military advisor Chénggōng Yīng to lead over a thousand cavalry to challenge,
and commanded them to feign retreat.
The Hú indeed rushed to pursue them.
Jì then unleashed the ambush to cut off their rear,
and attacked them from front and back,
utterly defeating them,
slaying and capturing tens of thousands.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and issued an edict saying:
"You crossed rivers and traversed dangers,
attacking the rested with the weary,
and conquering the many with the few.
Your merits surpass Nán Zhòng,
and your diligence exceeds Jí Fǔ.
This achievement is not merely about defeating the Hú;
it will bring lasting peace to the region west of the Hé,
relieving me forever of the need to look westward with concern."
He was transferred and enfeoffed as Xīxiāng Hóu,
with an additional two hundred households,
totaling four hundred households with the previous ones.
Sū Héng of Jiǔquán rebelled,
and with the Qiāng chieftain Lín Dài and the Dīnglíng Hú,
over ten thousand cavalry attacked the border counties.
Jì and Xiàhóu Rú defeated them,
and Sū Héng, Lín Dài, and others all surrendered.
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial requesting to govern Zuǒchéng with Xiàhóu Rú,
build fortifications and barriers,
and establish beacon towers and granaries to guard against the Hú.
The Western Qiāng were afraid,
and over twenty thousand households surrendered.
Later, Qū Guāng of Xīpíng and others killed their Administrator.
The generals wanted to attack them,
but Jì said:
"Only Qū Guāng and his ilk have rebelled;
not all the people of the commandery necessarily agree.
If we immediately confront them with an army,
the officials, people, Qiāng, and Hú will surely think that the state does not distinguish right from wrong,
and it will cause them all to stand together,
which would be like 'giving wings to a tiger'.
Qū Guāng and others wish to rely on the Qiāng and Hú as aid.
Now, we should first send the Qiāng and Hú to raid and attack them,
offering generous rewards and bounties,
and giving all captured spoils to them.
This will externally deter their power,
and internally disrupt their alliances.
They will surely be settled without a battle."
Then he issued a proclamation to all the Qiāng,
pardoning those who were misled by Qū Guāng and his associates;
those who could decapitate and send the head of the rebel leader would be generously enfeoffed and rewarded.
Thereupon, Qū Guāng's faction decapitated and sent Qū Guāng's head,
and the rest of them settled down as before.
Jì governed two provinces for over ten years;
his benevolent administration was well-known.
Those he recommended and invited, such as Páng Yán of Fúfēng, Yáng Fù of Tiānshuǐ, Hú Zūn of Āndìng, Páng Yù of Jiǔquán, Zhāng Gōng of Dūnhuáng, Zhōu Shēngliè, and others,
all eventually achieved fame and position.
He died in the fourth year of Huángchū (223 CE).
An edict stated:
"In the past, Xún Huánzǐ performed meritorious deeds in the territory of the Dí,
and the Marquis of Jìn rewarded him with a city of a thousand households.
Féng Yì contributed his strength to the Hàn court,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ (Guāngwǔ Dì) enfeoffed his two sons.
The former Inspector of Liángzhōu, Zhāng Jì,
was able to be tolerant of the people and gather the masses,
causing the various Qiāng to return to their lands.
He can be called an excellent minister of the state.
It is unfortunate that he passed away;
I deeply grieve for him.
Therefore, his young son Wēngguī is granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu."
When Emperor Míng (Míng Dì) ascended the throne,
he was posthumously honored with the title Sù Hóu.
His son Jī succeeded him.
Jī, starting as a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng), gradually rose to become Administrator of Dōngguǎn.
In the Jiāpíng era (249-254 CE),
his daughter became empress,
and he was summoned and appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū),
with the special distinction of Extra Ordinaries (Tèjìn),
and his wife Xiàng was enfeoffed as Ānchéng Xiāngjūn.
Jī conspired with the Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Lìng) Lǐ Fēng,
and was executed.
The details are in the biography of Xiàhóu Xuán.
Wēn Huī, courtesy name Mànjī,
was a native of Qí, Tàiyuán.
His father, Shù,
served as the Administrator of Zhuōjùn
and died.
Huī was fifteen years old
when he escorted the funeral back to his hometown.
He had ample wealth within the family.
Huī said:
“The world is in turmoil;
why accumulate wealth?”
One morning he dispersed it all,
distributing it to his relatives.
The province and his locality esteemed him,
comparing him to Xún Yuè.
He was nominated as Xiàolián
and served as the Chief of Lǐnqīu,
Magistrate of Yānlíng and Guǎngchuān,
and Chancellor of Péngchéng and Lǔ.
Wherever he served, he was praised.
He entered the central government as the Chief Clerk of the Chancellor
and was later appointed as the Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Tàizǔ said:
“I very much wish to keep you close to me,
but I consider that the affairs of this province are of greater importance.
Thus the Classic says: ‘Good are the arms and legs!
All affairs are prosperous!’
Is it not appropriate to have Jiǎng Jì as the Administrator of this province?”
At that time, Jì was serving as the Administrator of Dānyáng,
so he was sent back to the province.
He also said to Zhāng Liáo, Lè Jìn, and others:
“The Inspector of Yángzhōu understands military affairs well;
consult with him on all movements.”
In the twenty-fourth year of Jiàn'ān
(219 CE), Sūn Quán attacked Héféi.
At this time, all provinces had garrisons stationed.
Huī said to Péi Qián, the Inspector of Yǎozhōu:
“Although there are bandits here,
there is no need to worry.
I fear that there will be changes in the south.
Now that the waters have risen, Zǐxiào’s army is isolated,
without distant preparations.
Guān Yǔ is fierce and brave,
and will advance with the advantage,
surely becoming a threat.”
Subsequently, the incident at Fánchéng occurred.
An imperial edict summoned Qián and Lǚ Gòng, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, among others.
Qián and the others were slow to respond.
Huī secretly told Qián:
“This must be an urgent situation in Xiāngyáng, and they wish to hasten to its aid.
The reason they do not call an urgent assembly
is to avoid alarming distant populations.
Within one or two days, there will surely be a secret letter urging you to advance,
and Zhāng Liáo and others will also be summoned.
Liáo and the others are well aware of the King’s intentions;
they will arrive before those summoned earlier,
and you will bear the blame!”
Qián accepted his words,
left his baggage,
and changed to light equipment for a rapid departure.
Indeed, he received the urgent order.
Liáo and the others were soon summoned,
just as Huī had predicted.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he appointed Huī as Shìzhōng,
then as the Administrator of Wèijùn.
After several years,
he was promoted to Inspector of Liángzhōu,
holding the imperial credential and overseeing the Protector of the Qiāng.
He died of illness on the road,
at the age of forty-five.
An imperial edict stated:
“Huī possessed the quality of a pillar and foundation.
He served the late emperor,
and his meritorious efforts were clearly outstanding.
And when he served me,
he was loyal to the royal house,
thus I entrusted him with a responsibility spanning ten thousand *lǐ*,
and tasked him with the affairs of a region.
How unfortunate that he did not succeed!
I deeply lament this!”
His son, Shēng, was granted the noble title of Guānnèihóu.
Shēng died young,
and the title became extinct.
After Huī's death,
Mèng Jiàn of Rǔnán became the Inspector of Liángzhōu,
gaining a reputation for good governance,
and his official position reached General Who Conquers the East.
Jiǎ Kuí, courtesy name Liángdào,
was a native of Xiānglíng, Hédōng.
From childhood,
his games often involved setting up military formations.
His grandfather found this unusual
and said:
“When you grow up, you will surely become a general.”
He orally taught him tens of thousands of words of military strategy.
Initially, he served as a county official,
then as the Chief of Jiàngyì.
When Guō Yuán attacked Hédōng,
all the cities and towns he passed fell.
Kuí held firm in his defense,
and Yuán attacked him without success.
He then summoned the Chányú to combine forces and vigorously attack.
When the city was about to fall,
the elders of Jiàng made an agreement with Yuán
not to harm Kuí.
After the people of Jiàng surrendered,
Yuán heard of Kuí’s reputation
and wanted to appoint him as a general.
He used soldiers to coerce him,
but Kuí remained unmoved.
His attendants led Kuí to kowtow,
but Kuí shouted at them, saying:
“How can a senior official of the state kowtow to a bandit!”
Yuán was enraged
and was about to execute him.
When the officials and people of Jiàng heard that Kuí was to be killed,
they all stood on the city walls and cried out:
“You violated your agreement to kill our worthy lord!
We would rather all die together!”
Those around felt righteous towards Kuí
and many pleaded on his behalf,
so he was spared.
Earlier,
when Kuí passed Píshì,
he said:
“In a territorial dispute, the one who occupies it first wins.”
When Jiàng was besieged,
knowing he could not escape,
he sent someone to secretly take his official seal and sash back to the commandery,
and also said,
“Urgently occupy Píshì.”
After Yuán incorporated the forces of Jiàng,
he was about to advance.
Kuí feared he would seize Píshì first,
so he used another plan to mislead Yuán’s advisor, Zhù Ào.
As a result, Yuán was delayed for seven days.
The commandery followed Kuí’s advice,
and thus avoided defeat.
Later, he was recommended as a Mào cái.
He was appointed as the Magistrate of Miǎnchí.
When Gāo Gàn rebelled,
Zhāng Yǎn intended to raise troops to support him.
Jiǎ Kuí, unaware of their plot,
went to see Zhāng Yǎn.
When he heard of the uprising,
he wanted to return,
but feared being captured.
So, he devised a plan for Zhāng Yǎn,
as if he were a co-conspirator,
and Zhāng Yǎn believed him.
At that time, the county administration was temporarily located in Líchéng,
and the city's defenses were not strong.
Jiǎ Kuí requested troops from Zhāng Yǎn to repair the city.
Those who intended to cause trouble did not conceal their plans,
so Jiǎ Kuí was able to execute them all.
He then repaired the city and resisted Zhāng Yǎn.
When Zhāng Yǎn was defeated,
Jiǎ Kuí resigned from office due to the mourning of his grandfather.
The Sītú appointed him as a Yuán,
and he participated in the military affairs of the Sīlì as a Yìláng.
Tài Zǔ campaigned against Mǎ Chāo,
and when he reached Hóngnóng,
he said,
"This is the vital pass to the western route,"
and appointed Jiǎ Kuí to govern Hóngnóng as its Tàishǒu.
He summoned him for a meeting to discuss affairs,
and was greatly pleased with him.
He said to his attendants,
"If all the Èrqiānshí in the world were like Jiǎ Kuí,
what worries would I have?"
Later, when troops were dispatched,
Jiǎ Kuí suspected that the Túntián Dūwèi was harboring fugitives.
The Dūwèi, considering himself not subordinate to the commandery,
spoke disrespectfully.
Jiǎ Kuí, enraged,
arrested him,
enumerated his crimes,
beat him and broke his leg,
and he was dismissed from office.
However, Tài Zǔ inwardly admired Jiǎ Kuí,
and appointed him as the Chéngxiàng Zhǔbù.
When Tài Zǔ campaigned against Liú Bèi,
he first sent Jiǎ Kuí to Xié Gǔ to observe the situation.
On the way, he encountered a Shuǐhéng [officer],
transporting dozens of carts of prisoners.
Jiǎ Kuí, considering the military situation urgent,
released all but one of the gravest offenders.
He released all the others.
Tài Zǔ approved of this,
appointed him as Jiànyì Dàfū,
and he, along with Xiàhóu Shàng, jointly managed military logistics.
When Tài Zǔ passed away in Luòyáng,
Jiǎ Kuí took charge of the funeral arrangements.
At that time, Yānlíng Hóu Zhāng, acting as Yuèqí Jiāngjūn,
came from Cháng'ān to attend.
He asked Jiǎ Kuí about the whereabouts of the late king's imperial seal and ribbons.
Jiǎ Kuí, with a stern expression, said,
"The crown prince is in Yè,
and the state has an heir apparent.
The late king's imperial seal and ribbons
are not something Your Lordship should inquire about."
He then escorted the coffin back to Yè.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne as king,
the tens of thousands of households in Yè County were under the capital,
and many were lawless.
So, he appointed Jiǎ Kuí as the Magistrate of Yè.
After more than a month,
he was promoted to Tàishǒu of Wèijùn.
When the grand army was dispatched for campaigns,
he was again appointed as Chéngxiàng Zhǔbù Jìjiǔ.
Jiǎ Kuí once interceded for someone who committed a crime.
The king said,
"Shūxiàng was still pardoned for ten generations;
how much more so Jiǎ Kuí, whose merits and virtues are personally manifest?"
He followed the emperor to Líyáng,
where those crossing the ferry were disorderly.
Jiǎ Kuí executed one,
and order was then restored.
Upon reaching Qiáo,
Jiǎ Kuí was appointed as the Cìshǐ of Yùzhōu.
At this time, the world was newly restored,
and many prefectures and commanderies were not well-governed.
Jiǎ Kuí said,
"Originally, the Zhöu [provinces] sent Yùshǐ to supervise the various commanderies,
and according to the six articles of the imperial edict, they inspected chief officials from the Èrqiānshí downwards.
Therefore, their reports all spoke of their strictness, ability, soaring ambition, and talent for supervision and inspection,
not of their peacefulness, leniency, benevolence, and virtue of kindness and harmony.
Now, chief officials disregard the law,
and bandits openly commit crimes.
If the Zhöu knows but does not rectify,
from where will the world find righteousness again?"
The Bīngcáo Cóngshì had received leave from the previous Cìshǐ.
Jiǎ Kuí arrived at his post, and several months later,
he returned;
he investigated and impeached those from Èrqiānshí downwards who were corrupt, indulgent, and did not act according to the law,
and had them all dismissed.
The emperor said,
"Jiǎ Kuí is truly a Cìshǐ!"
He announced to the world
that Yùzhōu should be taken as a model.
He was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
The southern part of the Zhöu bordered Wú.
Jiǎ Kuí established clear scouts,
repaired armor and weapons,
and made preparations for defense and battle,
so the enemy dared not invade.
Externally, he cultivated the military;
internally, he managed civil affairs.
He dammed the Yān and Rǔ rivers,
built new dikes,
and also diverted the long streams of mountain runoff,
creating the Xiǎo Yìyáng Pí.
He also dug a transport canal over two hundred *lǐ* long,
which was known as the Jiǎ Hóu Qú.
During the Huángchū era,
he campaigned against Wú with other generals,
defeating Lǚ Fàn at Dòngpǔ.
He was promoted and enfeoffed as Yánglǐ Tínghóu,
and given the additional title of Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
his fief was increased by two hundred households,
making a total of four hundred households.
At that time, Sūn Quán was in Dōngguān,
south of Yùzhōu,
about four hundred *lǐ* from the Jiāng [Yangtze River].
Whenever he dispatched troops to raid,
they would go west from Jiāngxià [Commandery]
or east from Lújiāng [Commandery].
When the state launched punitive expeditions,
it also went via Huái and Miǎn.
At this time, the Zhöu army was in Xiàng,
and the commanderies of Rǔnán and Yìyáng
were merely guarding their borders.
Sūn Quán had no worries from the north.
If there was an emergency in the east or west,
he would consolidate his forces to assist,
so he often suffered few defeats.
Jiǎ Kuí believed it was advisable to open a direct road to the river.
If Sūn Quán defended himself,
then the two sides would not receive aid;
if the two sides did not receive aid,
then Dōngguān could be captured.
So, he moved his garrison to Láokǒu,
and laid out a plan for attack and capture.
The emperor approved of it.
Wú general Zhāng Yīng and Wáng Chóng led their troops to surrender.
In the second year of Tàihé,
the Emperor ordered Kuí to supervise the four armies of former General Mǎn Chǒng and Dōngguǎn Administrator Hú Zhì,
to march straight from Xīyáng towards Dōngguān.
Cáo Xiū marched from Wǎn,
and Sīmǎ Xuānwáng from Jiānglíng.
When Kuí reached Wǔjiàngshān,
Xiū again submitted a memorial stating that some of the rebels wished to surrender,
and requested to penetrate deeper to respond to them.
An imperial edict ordered Xuānwáng to halt his army,
and Kuí to join Xiū in an eastward advance.
Kuí estimated that the rebels had no defenses at Dōngguān,
and would certainly concentrate their forces at Wǎn;
if Xiū advanced deep and fought the rebels,
he would surely be defeated.
So he deployed his generals,
advancing by both land and water.
After marching two hundred *lǐ*,
they captured a live rebel,
who reported that Xiū's army had been defeated,
and Sūn Quán had sent troops to cut off Jiāshí.
The generals did not know what to do,
some wanted to wait for the rear army.
Kuí said:
“Xiū's army is defeated outside,
its retreat cut off inside.
They cannot advance to fight,
nor retreat to return.
The critical moment of safety or danger
will not last the whole day.
The rebels believe our army has no rear support,
hence they have come to this point;
if we advance swiftly now,
taking them by surprise,
this is what is called pre-empting the enemy to seize their morale.
When the rebels see our troops, they will surely flee.
If we wait for the rear army,
the rebels will have already secured the dangerous passes.
Even if our troops are numerous, what good will it do!”
He then advanced his army at an accelerated pace,
setting up many flags and drums as a feint.
When the rebels saw Kuí's army,
they retreated.
Kuí occupied Jiāshí,
and provided troops and provisions to Xiū,
whereupon Xiū's army regained its spirits.
Previously,
Kuí and Xiū were not on good terms.
During the Huángchū era,
Emperor Wén wanted to grant Kuí a staff of authority,
but Xiū said:
“Kuí is by nature stubborn,
and has always looked down on other generals;
he should not be made a supervisor.”
The Emperor then desisted.
However, after the defeat at Jiāshí,
had it not been for Kuí,
Xiū's army would have been almost beyond rescue.
When he became critically ill,
he said to his attendants:
“I have received great kindness from the state.
I regret not having beheaded Sūn Quán to show to the late Emperor.
My funeral arrangements must not involve any elaborate preparations.”
He died,
and was posthumously named Sù Hóu.
His son Chōng inherited his title.
The officials and common people of Yùzhōu remembered him with gratitude,
and erected a stone monument and a shrine for him.
During the Qīnglóng era,
the Emperor went on an eastern campaign,
and rode in a palanquin into Kuí's shrine.
He issued an edict saying:
“Yesterday, passing by Xiàng,
I saw Jiǎ Kuí's stele and image,
and felt a pang of sadness recalling him.
The ancients had a saying:
one should worry about not establishing a name,
not about one's years not being long.
Kuí rendered loyal service in life,
and is remembered after death.
He can be said to have died yet remained immortal.
Let this be proclaimed throughout the empire,
to encourage future generations.”
Chōng,
served as Zhōnghùjūn during the Xiánxī era.
The commentary states: Since the end of the Hàn dynasty,
inspectors (cìshǐ) have governed all the commanderies,
administering policies externally,
not merely serving as overseers as in earlier times.
From Tàizǔ's founding of the base to the completion of the Wèi enterprise,
these are all those whose reputations and achievements are well-known.
They
were all adept at discerning opportunities,
and manifested both awe and kindness,
thus they were able to bring order to vast distances,
and are recounted by later generations.
Biographies of Rèn Sū Dù Zhèng Cāng, Chapter Sixteen
Rèn Jùn, courtesy name Bódá,
was a native of Zhōngmóu, Hénán.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, there was widespread chaos,
and the region east of the passes was all in turmoil.
Yáng Yuán, the magistrate of Zhōngmóu, was worried and fearful,
and wished to abandon his post and flee.
Jùn persuaded Yuán, saying:
“Dǒng Zhuó initiated the rebellion,
and everyone in the world is watching with apprehension.
However, no one has yet taken the initiative,
not because they lack the intention,
but because they don't yet dare.
If you, Your Excellency, can be the first to act,
there will surely be those who respond.”
Yuán said:
“What should I do?”
Jùn replied:
“Now there are more than ten counties east of the passes,
with no less than ten thousand able-bodied soldiers.
If you temporarily act as the Administrator of Hénán,
and mobilize them,
there is nothing that cannot be achieved.”
Yuán followed his plan,
and appointed Jùn as his Chief Clerk.
Jùn then petitioned on behalf of Yuán to act as Administrator,
ordered all counties to hold firm,
and then raised troops.
It happened that Tàizǔ rose in the east of the passes,
and entered the borders of Zhōngmóu.
The populace did not know whom to follow.
Jùn alone discussed with Zhāng Fèn of the same commandery,
and led the entire commandery to submit to Tàizǔ.
Jùn also separately gathered several hundred family troops from his clan and retainers,
and wished to follow Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased,
and appointed Jùn as Cavalry Commandant,
and married him to his younger female cousin,
showing him great trust and intimacy.
Whenever Tàizǔ went on campaigns,
Jùn always stayed behind to supply the army.
At that time, there was famine and drought,
and the army's provisions were insufficient.
Yǔlín Supervisor Zǎo Zhī of Yǐngchuān proposed establishing military agricultural colonies (túntián).
Tàizǔ appointed Jùn as Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiàng,
【recruiting common people to establish agricultural colonies in Xǔxià,
obtaining a million *hú* of grain.
Agricultural officials were then established in commanderies and states】 ,
and within a few years, grain was accumulated everywhere,
and granaries were all full.
During the Battle of Guāndù,
Tàizǔ made Jùn responsible for military equipment and grain transport.
As the rebels frequently raided and cut off supply routes,
he then organized a thousand carts into one unit,
marching in ten columns,
forming a fortified formation to protect them,
and the rebels dared not approach.
The prosperity of the army and state
began with Zǎo Zhī and was completed by Jùn.
Tàizǔ, seeing Jùn's great merits,
then memorialized to enfeoff him as Dūtíng Hóu,
with an estate of three hundred households,
and promoted him to Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi.
Jùn was broad-minded, principled, and understood affairs,
and Tàizǔ often approved of his proposals.
During times of famine,
he aided and comforted friends' orphans and widows,
and poor relatives both close and distant,
providing for those in need and supporting the lacking,
earning praise for his trustworthiness and integrity.
He died in the ninth year of Jiàn'ān,
and Tàizǔ wept for a long time.
His son Xiān inherited his title.
Xiān died,
leaving no son,
and the marquisate was abolished.
Emperor Wén, when reviewing the merits of his loyal officials,
posthumously named Jùn Chéng Hóu.
He also reinstated Jùn's second son Lǎn as Guānnèi Hóu.
Sū Zé
, whose courtesy name was Wénshī, was a native of Wǔgōng
in Fúfēng.
In his youth, he was known for his learning and conduct.
He was nominated as Xiàolián
and Màocái,
and was invited to the public administration,
but he did not accept any of these positions.
He started his career as the Administrator of Jiǔquán
and was then transferred to Āndìng
and Wǔdū.
Wherever he served, he earned a reputation for authority.
When Tàizǔ
campaigned against Zhāng Lǔ
and passed through Sū Zé's
commandery,
he was pleased to meet Sū Zé
and made him a military guide.
After Lǔ
was defeated,
Sū Zé
pacified and settled the various Dī tribes in Xiàbiàn,
opened the Hexi road,
and was transferred to become the Administrator of Jīnchéng.
At that time, after a period of chaos and war,
officials and common people were scattered,
starving,
and impoverished.
The household population had suffered great losses.
Sū Zé
managed and comforted them with great care.
Externally, he brought the Qiāng
and Hú
tribes to his side,
obtaining their cattle and sheep
to feed the poor and elderly.
He shared his food rations with the people.
Within a month,
all the displaced people returned,
amounting to several thousand families.
He then clearly established prohibitions,
immediately executing those who violated them,
and surely rewarding those who followed his instructions.
He personally taught the people to farm.
That year saw a great harvest,
and from then on, more people came to submit to him daily.
Lǐ Yuè
rebelled in Lǒngxī.
Sū Zé
led the Qiāng
and Hú
to besiege Yuè,
who immediately requested surrender.
When Tàizǔ
died,
Qū Yǎn
of Xīpíng
rebelled,
proclaiming himself Protector of the Qiāng.
Sū Zé
marshaled his troops to suppress him.
Yǎn
was afraid and begged for surrender.
Because of his achievements,
Wén Dì
appointed Sū Zé
as Protector of the Qiāng
and bestowed upon him the title of Marquis of Guānnèi.
Later, Yǎn
again allied with neighboring commanderies to create disturbances.
Zhāng Jìn
of Zhāngyè
seized Dù Tōng,
the Administrator.
Huáng Huá
of Jiǔquán
refused to accept Xīn Jī,
the Administrator.
Jìn
and Huá
both proclaimed themselves Administrators in response.
Moreover, three types of Hú
in Wǔwēi
plundered and raided,
cutting off the roads.
Wúqiū Xìng,
the Administrator of Wǔwēi,
urgently appealed to Sū Zé.
At that time, all the powerful families in Yōng
and Liáng
regions were marshaling Qiāng
and Hú
to join Jìn
and others.
The people of the commandery all believed that Jìn
was irresistible.
Furthermore, Generals Hǎo Zhāo
and Wèi Píng
had previously been stationed in Jīnchéng
and had received orders not to cross westward.
Sū Zé
then met with the high officials of the commandery, Zhāo
and others, and the Qiāng
tribal chiefs, and deliberated, saying:
"Although the rebels are strong now,
they are all newly assembled,
and some are coerced followers,
so they may not be of one mind.
If we strike them at this opportune moment,
the good and bad among them will surely separate.
When they separate and return to us,
we will grow stronger and they will weaken.
Having gained the substance of increased numbers,
and also possessing the momentum of doubled morale,
if we lead an attack,
we will surely defeat them.
If we wait for the main army,
it will be a protracted delay.
Good people will have nowhere to turn
and will inevitably join with the bad.
Once good and bad are united,
they will be difficult to separate suddenly.
Although there is an imperial edict,
it is permissible to disregard it and act expediently,
making an independent decision."
Thereupon, Zhāo
and others agreed with him.
So, he dispatched troops to rescue Wǔwēi,
compelled the three types of Hú
there to surrender,
and, with Xìng,
attacked Jìn
in Zhāngyè.
Yǎn
heard of this
and led three thousand cavalry and infantry to meet Sū Zé,
claiming to come to assist the army,
but actually intending to cause trouble.
Sū Zé
enticed him to a meeting
and then executed him,
displaying his head to the army.
His followers all scattered and fled.
Sū Zé
then, with the various armies, besieged Zhāngyè,
defeated it,
executed Jìn
and his confederates,
and everyone surrendered.
After Yǎn's
army was defeated,
Huá
became frightened,
released those he had captured,
and begged for surrender.
The Hexi region was pacified.
He then returned to Jīnchéng.
He was promoted to Marquis of Dūtíng
and given a fief of three hundred households.
He was summoned to serve as Imperial Household Grandee
and was a colleague of Dǒng Zhāo.
Zhāo
once rested his head on Sū Zé's
lap to sleep.
Sū Zé
pushed him off,
saying:
"Sū Zé's
lap is not for flattering people to rest upon."
Initially,
when Sū Zé
and Zhí,
the Marquis of Línzī,
heard that the Wèi
clan had supplanted the Hàn,
they both put on mourning clothes and wept in sorrow.
Wén Dì
heard that Zhí
had done so,
but did not hear about Sū Zé.
The Emperor,
while in Luòyáng,
once spoke casually, saying:
"I received the Mandate of Heaven and accepted the abdication,
yet I heard there were those who wept.
Why is that?"
Sū Zé
thought he was being questioned,
and his beard and whiskers bristled.
He wished to express his righteous views in response.
Imperial Household Grandee Fù Xùn
After Grand Ancestor [Tàizǔ] had pacified Héběi,
Gāo Gàn [Gāo Gàn] raised a rebellion in Bìngzhōu.
At that time, Wáng Yì [Wáng Yì], the Administrator of Hédōng, was summoned for an imperial appointment,
and the Hédōng people Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and Fàn Xiān [Fàn Xiān] ostensibly requested Wáng Yì's [Wáng Yì] return,
but inwardly were secretly in league with Gāo Gàn [Gāo Gàn].
Grand Ancestor [Tàizǔ] said to Xún Yù [Xún Yù]:
"The generals in Guānxī,
relying on the treacherous terrain and their horses,
will surely cause trouble if we campaign there.
Zhāng Shèng [Zhāng Shèng] is plundering the area between Xiáo [Xiáo] and Miǎn [Miǎn],
and communicating with Liú Biǎo [Liú Biǎo] to the south.
Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and others are taking advantage of this,
and I fear the harm they will cause will be profound.
Hédōng, with mountains to its back and a river as its belt,
and many volatile neighbors,
is a strategically vital location for the empire today.
For me, you should recommend a Xiāo Hé [Xiāo Hé] or Kòu Xún [Kòu Xún] to govern it."
Xún Yù [Xún Yù] replied:
"Dù Jī [Dù Jī] is that person."
Thereupon, Dù Jī [Dù Jī] was immediately appointed Administrator of Hédōng.
Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and others sent several thousand soldiers to block the Shǎn [Shǎn] ferry,
so Dù Jī [Dù Jī] could not cross.
Grand Ancestor [Tàizǔ] dispatched Xiàhóu Dūn [Xiàhóu Dūn] to suppress them,
but he had not yet arrived.
Someone said to Dù Jī [Dù Jī]:
"You should wait for the main army."
Dù Jī [Dù Jī] replied:
"Hédōng has thirty thousand households;
not all of them wish to rebel.
Now, if the army presses hard,
those who wish to do good will have no leader
and will inevitably fear and submit to Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù].
If Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and others gain full power,
they will surely fight to the death.
If we attack and do not win,
the neighbors will respond to them,
and the turmoil in the empire will not cease;
if we attack and win,
it will be at the cost of devastating the people of an entire commandery.
Moreover, Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and others have not openly defied imperial authority;
they outwardly use the pretext of inviting their former governor,
so they will certainly not harm the new governor.
I will go directly with a single carriage,
catching them by surprise.
Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] is a man of many schemes but indecisive,
so he will surely feign acceptance of me.
If I can reside in the commandery for a month,
and manipulate them with stratagems,
that will be enough."
So he took a circuitous route and crossed at the Dòu [Dòu] ferry.
(Dòu [Dòu] is pronounced 'dòu'.)
Fàn Xiān [Fàn Xiān] wanted to kill Dù Jī [Dù Jī] to assert authority over the masses.
And to observe Dù Jī's [Dù Jī] reaction,
he publicly executed over thirty people, from the Chief Clerk downwards, at the gate.
Dù Jī [Dù Jī] remained composed.
Thereupon, Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] said:
"Killing him will do no good,
only earn us a bad reputation;
moreover, we have him under our control."
So they accepted him.
Dù Jī [Dù Jī] said to Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and Fàn Xiān [Fàn Xiān]:
"Wèi [Wèi] and Fàn [Fàn],
you are the hope of Hédōng;
I merely follow your lead.
However, there is a defined relationship between ruler and minister,
and success or failure are linked.
Important matters should be deliberated together."
He appointed Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] as Chief Commander [Dūdū],
acting as Commissioner for Affairs [Chéngshì],
and concurrently Head of the Secretariat [Gōngcáo];
the three thousand odd officers and soldiers
were all placed under Fàn Xiān's [Fàn Xiān] command.
Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and others were pleased;
though they outwardly served Dù Jī [Dù Jī],
they did not take him seriously.
Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] wanted to raise a large army.
Dù Jī [Dù Jī] was concerned about this,
and persuaded Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù], saying:
"If one wishes to accomplish an extraordinary feat,
one must not disturb the hearts of the people.
If we now raise a large army,
the people will surely be agitated.
It is better to slowly recruit soldiers using wealth."
Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] thought this was correct,
and followed his advice,
thus making a financial levy for recruitment.
It took several tens of days to finalize,
and the various generals, being greedy, mostly accepted the levies but sent few soldiers.
Dù Jī [Dù Jī] then further explained to Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and others:
"People naturally care for their families.
The various generals' clerks and officials
can be sent home in shifts to rest;
it will not be difficult to summon them back urgently or gradually."
Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and others were loath to go against public sentiment,
so they again agreed.
Thus, good people were outside [the control of the rebels],
secretly serving as his [Dù Jī's] supporters;
while the bad people were dispersed,
each returning to their homes,
and the masses became disunited.
At that time, the Báiqí [Báiqí] attacked Dōngyuán [Dōngyuán],
Gāo Gàn [Gāo Gàn] entered Huòzé [Huòzé],
the various counties of Shàngdǎng [Shàngdǎng] killed their chief officials,
and Hóngnóng [Hóngnóng] seized its Administrator.
Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and others' secretly mobilized troops had not yet arrived.
Dù Jī [Dù Jī], knowing that the various counties were allied with him,
then went out,
leading only a few tens of cavalry,
and rushed to Zhāng Pì [Zhāng Pì] to defend it.
Many officials and commoners opened their cities to assist Dù Jī [Dù Jī].
Within several tens of days,
he had gathered over four thousand men.
Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and others, along with Gāo Gàn [Gāo Gàn] and Zhāng Shèng [Zhāng Shèng], jointly attacked Dù Jī [Dù Jī],
but could not take the position.
They then plundered the various counties,
but gained nothing.
Soon, the main army arrived.
Gāo Gàn [Gāo Gàn] and Zhāng Shèng [Zhāng Shèng] were defeated,
Wèi Gù [Wèi Gù] and others were executed,
and their remaining confederates were all pardoned
and allowed to return to their homes and occupations.
At this time, all the commanderies and counties in the empire were devastated and ruined,
but Hédōng was pacified first,
and suffered little loss.
Dù Jī [Dù Jī] governed it,
promoting leniency and kindness,
and allowing the people to live in peace.
When people had disputes or lawsuits,
and accused each other,
Dù Jī [Dù Jī] would personally meet them and expound upon moral principles,
sending them home to reflect carefully,
and if they felt anything was unclear,
they could return to the yamen.
The elders in the villages would rebuke each other, saying:
"With such a governor,
how can we not follow his teachings?"
From then on, there were few disputes.
He issued orders to the subordinate counties
to recommend filial sons, chaste women, and obedient grandsons,
exempting them from labor service,
and encouraging them from time to time.
He gradually instructed the people to raise breeding cattle and horses,
down to chickens, pigs, and dogs,
all with regulations.
The common people diligently farmed,
and every household became prosperous.
Dù Jī [Dù Jī] then said:
"The people are wealthy now;
they cannot be left uneducated."
So, in the winter months, he conducted military training and drills,
and also opened schools,
personally holding classics and teaching.
The commandery was transformed by his influence.
When Hán Suí [Hán Suí] and Mǎ Chāo [Mǎ Chāo] rebelled,
many counties and towns in Hóngnóng [Hóngnóng] and Féngyì [Féngyì] responded to them.
Although Hédōng bordered the rebels,
the people had no rebellious thoughts.
When Grand Ancestor [Tàizǔ] campaigned west to Púbǎn [Púbǎn],
and encamped with the rebels across the Wèi [Wèi] River,
the army's food supply depended entirely on Hédōng.
After the rebels were defeated,
there were still over two hundred thousand hú [hú] of grain remaining.
Grand Ancestor [Tàizǔ] issued an order saying:
"Dù Jī [Dù Jī], Administrator of Hédōng,
is what Confucius called 'Yǔ [Yǔ],
I find no fault in him.'
His rank is increased to Chief Minister of Two Thousand Piculs [Zhōng Èr Qiān Dàn]."
When Grand Ancestor [Tàizǔ] campaigned against Hànzhōng [Hànzhōng],
he sent five thousand men to transport supplies.
The transporters encouraged themselves, saying:
"A man has but one death;
we must not betray our Prefect [Fǔjūn]."
Not a single one deserted,
such was his popularity.
After the State of Wèi [Wèi] was established,
Dù Jī [Dù Jī] was made Shàngshū [Shàngshū].
After the matters were settled,
another order was issued, saying:
"In the past, Xiāo Hé [Xiāo Hé] pacified Guānzhōng [Guānzhōng],
and Kòu Xún [Kòu Xún] pacified Hénèi [Hénèi];
you have accomplished their deeds.
I had intended to appoint you to the position of Minister of Advice [Nàyán];
but considering Hédōng is my vital commandery,
a place of abundance [which could be filled with resources],
sufficient to control the empire,
I shall trouble you to continue governing it.
Dù Jī [Dù Jī] was in Hédōng for sixteen years,
and was always the best in the empire."
When Emperor Wén (Wén Dì) ascended the throne,
Dù Jī (Dù Jī) was granted the title of Marquis within the Passes (Guānnèi Hóu).
He was summoned to serve as an Imperial Secretary (Shàngshū).
When the emperor was enthroned,
Dù Jī was promoted and enfeoffed as Marquis of Fēnglè Tíng (Fēnglè Tíng Hóu).
He was given a stipend of a hundred households
and served as Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
When the emperor campaigned against Wú (Wú),
he appointed Dù Jī as Chief Imperial Secretary (Shàngshū Púyè)
to oversee affairs in the capital.
Later, when the emperor visited Xǔchāng (Xǔchāng),
Dù Jī again remained behind to guard the capital.
He received an imperial edict to construct imperial pleasure boats (yùlóuchuán).
While testing the boats on the Táo River (Táohé),
they encountered a storm and sank.
The emperor wept for him.
An edict stated:
"In ancient times, Míng (Míng) diligently served in his office and died in water,
and Jì (Jì) toiled over grains and died in the mountains.
Thus, the Chief Imperial Secretary, Dù Jī,
while testing boats at Mèngjīn (Mèngjīn),
met with an overturn and sank.
This was the utmost loyalty.
We are deeply saddened by this."
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Coachman (Tàipú)
and given the posthumous name Dài Hóu (Dài Hóu).
His son, Dù Shù (Dù Shù), inherited his title.
Dù Shù, whose courtesy name was Wùbó (Wùbó),
served as a Palace Attendant (Sànqí Huángmén Shìláng) during the Tàihé (Tàihé) era.
Dù Shù was sincere and unpretentious;
he did not bother with outward embellishment,
and had little reputation in his youth.
When he served at court,
he did not form alliances
and dedicated his heart to public service.
Whenever there were gains or losses in governance,
he always upheld principles to speak straightforwardly.
Thus, Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Xīn Pí (Xīn Pí) and others held him in high regard.
At that time, the high officials (gōngqīng) and others held a great debate on reforms.
Dù Shù believed that
"the Censors (Cìshǐ) of old
were entrusted to proclaim the Six Articles,
renowned for their purity and tranquility,
and distinguished by their awe-inspiring authority.
Now, they should not be allowed to command troops,
but rather concentrate on civil affairs."
Soon after, when General Who Guards the North (Zhènběi Jiāngjūn) Lǚ Zhāo (Lǚ Zhāo) also assumed command of Jì Province (Jì Zhōu),
Dù Shù submitted a memorial, saying: "Of the ways of emperors and kings,
none is more paramount than pacifying the people;
the art of pacifying the people
lies in enriching wealth.
To enrich wealth,
one must prioritize the root (agriculture) and be frugal in expenditure.
Currently, the two
enemies are not yet vanquished.
War chariots are frequently harnessed;
this is indeed the season for brave warriors to exert their strength.
However, scholars in official attire (jìnshēn zhī rú),
improperly coveting honor,
clench their fists and engage in spirited debate,
taking
Sūn (Sūn) and Wú (Wú) as their models.
The governors and administrators of commanderies and provinces (zhōu-jùn mùshǒu)
all neglect the art of caring for the people,
and instead pursue the affairs of generals and commanders.
The people engaged in agriculture and sericulture
are competing in the business of war.
This cannot be called
'prioritizing the root.'
The imperial treasury becomes emptier year by year, while expenses increase;
the people's strength declines year by year, while taxes and conscription rise.
This cannot be called 'frugal in expenditure.'
Now, the Great Wèi (Dà Wèi) possesses the territory of ten provinces,
yet it inherits the ills of prolonged chaos.
Its registered households are fewer than those of a single province in former times.
However, two regions are usurping power,
the northern barbarians are not yet subdued,
and difficulties beset the three borders,
encompassing nearly the entire land.
Thus, to use the people of one province
to govern the land of nine provinces,
the difficulty of this
is like urging a lean horse to travel a long distance.
How can we not
pay attention and cherish their strength?
Even with Emperor Wǔ's (Wǔ Huángdì) frugality,
which filled the imperial coffers,
he still could not maintain troops in ten provinces;
commandery armies were only about twenty.
Now, the border provinces of Jīng (Jīng),
Yáng (Yáng), Qīng (Qīng), Xú (Xú), Yōu (Yōu), Bīng (Bīng), Yōng (Yōng), and Liáng (Liáng) all have troops.
Those relied upon to fill the internal treasuries and control the four barbarians externally
are only Yǎn (Yǎn), Yù (Yù),
Sī (Sī), and Jì (Jì) provinces.
I previously stated that if provincial and commandery officials (zhōu-jùn) command troops,
they will focus solely on military achievements
and neglect civil affairs.
It would be more appropriate to appoint separate generals to guard
and ensure the full performance of administrative duties.
Yet, Your Majesty has again bestowed the prestigious position of Jì Province
upon Lǚ Zhāo.
Jì Province has the most households,
much cultivated land,
and an abundance of mulberries and dates.
It is a source of revenue for the state,
and truly should not again be tasked with military affairs.
If it is thought that the north requires defense,
a Grand General (dàjiàng) can certainly be specifically appointed to guard and pacify it.
The cost of appointing such officials and soldiers
would be no different
from combining offices.
However, Lǚ Zhāo, in terms of talent, is still relatively easy [to replace];
if the central court truly lacks capable people,
then those with combined talents are necessarily not abundant.
Inferring from this,
we know that
the state selects officials based on the individual,
not selects individuals for the office.
When the office finds its proper person,
then governance is equitable and disputes are settled.
When governance is equitable, the people prosper;
when disputes are settled, prisons
are empty.
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
the number of judicial cases in the realm was a hundred or so,
but it has increased year by year,
reaching over five hundred.
The population has not grown,
and the laws have not become
harsher.
Inferring from this,
is it not a clear sign that governance and education are declining,
and the governors and administrators are failing in their duties?
Last year, when oxen died,
on average, two out of ten throughout the land were lost;
the wheat
harvest was less than half,
and autumn planting was not completed.
If the two enemies roam along the borders,
transporting fodder and grain over a thousand miles
will not suffice.
The solution to this problem,
is it truly in strengthening the army?
The more brave warriors and elite soldiers,
the more troubles will arise.
Indeed, the realm is like a human body:
if the core is full and strong,
even if the limbs are ill,
there will ultimately be no great danger.
Now, Yǎn (Yǎn), Yù (Yù), Sī (Sī), and Jì (Jì) are also the core of the realm.
Therefore, this humble minister earnestly
wishes that the governors and administrators of these four provinces
would exclusively pursue the fundamental task
of prioritizing the root (agriculture),
thereby
bearing the heavy burden of the limbs.
However, a lone argument is hard to maintain,
offending desires is hard to accomplish,
accumulated popular resentment is hard to bear,
and ambiguity is hard to resolve.
Thus, for many years, my words have not been heeded by an enlightened ruler.
Those
who speak like this
are generally humble and lowly;
the words of the humble and lowly
are truly not easily heard.
If good strategies must come from the close and noble,
then the close and noble would certainly not defy the four difficulties
to seek loyalty and love.
This has been a common affliction throughout history.
At that time, there was also a great debate about the system of performance evaluation (kǎokè zhī zhì)
to assess all officials, internal and external.
Dù Shù believed that if people were not fully utilized for their talents,
even if talented, it would be useless.
What was maintained was not what was essential,
and what was essential was not what the world valued.
He submitted a memorial, saying: "The 'Book of Documents' (Shū) states,
'Clearly test by achievement,
and after three evaluations, promote or demote.'
This is indeed a grand system for emperors and kings.
It ensures that the capable hold their office
and the meritorious receive their emolument,
like
Wū Huò (Wū Huò) lifting a thousand catties,
or Liáng (Liáng) and Yuè (Yuè) selecting fleet-footed steeds.
Although six dynasties have passed, the method of evaluating performance (kǎojī zhī fǎ) has not been clearly established,
and it does not appear in the writings of the seven sages.
I truly believe that while its principles can be broadly followed,
its detailed implementation is difficult to fully
carry out.
The proverb says:
'There are people who cause disorder in the world, but no laws that cause disorder.'
If laws could be solely relied upon,
then Táng (Táng) and Yú (Yú) would not have needed the assistance of Jì (Jì) and Xiè (Xiè),
and Yīn (Yīn) and Zhōu (Zhōu) would not have valued the support of Yī (Yī) and Lǚ (Lǚ).
Now, those who propose performance evaluation
present the laws of Zhōu (Zhōu) and Hàn (Hàn) as the basis,
To collate the original principles of Jīng Fáng,
can be said to be essential for clearly assessing performance.
However, to use this to promote a culture of deference
and establish an orderly governance,
your servant believes it is not yet perfect.
The proposal that prefectures and commanderies evaluate candidates,
who must pass through the four categories,
all demonstrating practical achievements,
and only then be selected and recommended,
then tested by serving in a ducal office,
becoming an official close to the people,
and then promoted by merit to fill
the post of commandery administrator,
or even receive increased rank and titles—
this is the most urgent task for performance evaluation.
Your servant believes it would be fitting to elevate his status,
use his words,
and have him comprehensively formulate the laws for evaluating prefectures
and commanderies.
Once the laws are complete, they should be implemented,
establishing rewards that are absolutely trustworthy,
and imposing punishments that are absolutely enforced.
As for the grandees and the inner court ministers,
they too should all be evaluated based on their duties.
In ancient times, the Sān Gōng
sat and discussed the Way,
and the inner court ministers
received counsel and rectified deficiencies,
recording every good deed,
and reporting every fault.
Moreover, the world is immensely vast,
and the myriad
affairs are exceedingly numerous.
Indeed, no single discerning individual can illuminate them all.
Therefore, the ruler is the head,
and the ministers are the limbs,
making it clear that they rely on each other to complete the body.
This is why the ancients
said that the timber of the imperial court
does not rest on a single pillar;
and the enterprise of emperors and kings
does not depend on the strategy of a single scholar.
From this perspective,
how can ministers who merely guard their posts and differentiate in their evaluations
achieve peace and prosperity?
Even among commoners,
there are those who uphold their sworn promises and brave fire and water,
who are moved by a kindred spirit to lay bare their hearts,
and who pursue reputation and establish
integrity and righteousness.
How much more so for those who don official attire and stand in court,
attaining the ranks of grandees and prime ministers?
What they strive for is not merely the trust between commoners,
what moves them is not simply the kindness of a friend,
and what they pursue
how could it be merely reputation?
All who receive imperial favor and substantial salaries, and bear heavy responsibilities,
do not just wish to elevate the enlightened ruler above Táng and Yú;
they also wish to be counted among Jì and Qì.
Therefore,
the ancients were not concerned about a lack of earnest desire for good governance,
but rather about an insufficient sense of personal responsibility.
This is indeed how the ruler makes it so.
The rulers of Táng and Yú
entrusted
Jì, Qì, Kuí, and Lóng with responsibilities and demanded success.
And when they erred,
they punished Gǔn and banished the Four Fiends.
Now, if ministers personally receive enlightened edicts,
and serve directly under your majesty,
and there are those who
are diligent day and night in public service,
meticulous and uniquely upright,
who hold office without bending to influence,
who uphold fairness without favoritism,
and who speak and act boldly in court,
these are surely observed by the enlightened ruler.
Conversely, if one merely enjoys salary as a mark of eminence,
and silent acquiescence as wisdom;
if in office one merely seeks to avoid blame,
and in court never forgets to preserve one's own position;
if one maintains a facade of purity and speaks with humility while in
court,
these too are observed by the enlightened ruler.
Indeed, if one can preserve one's position without incurring the guilt of dismissal,
while those who fully dedicate themselves to public service
face the potential of suspicion,
then public justice
will not be cultivated, and private opinions will become common practice.
Even if Zhòngní were to plan,
he would not be able to fully utilize a single talent,
how much more so for ordinary people!
Scholars today
follow Shāng and Hán,
and extol legalism,
competing to dismiss Confucianism as impractical,
not suited for worldly use.
This is the greatest pitfall of current trends,
something the founders of enterprise must be extremely cautious about.
Later, the performance evaluations were not implemented.
Lián Zhāo of Lè'ān was promoted for his talent,
and was quite fond of speaking on affairs.
Shù then submitted a strongly remonstrating memorial, saying:
I humbly observe that Director of the Department of State Affairs Lián Zhāo has memorialized that Assistant Minister of the Left Cáo Fán was punished and detained for not complying with an edict.
He was then condemned and questioned.
He also said,
"Those who are to be condemned shall be separately memorialized."
The Minister of the Department of State Affairs Chén Jiǎo
personally memorialized, saying he dared not decline punishment,
nor dared to consider it humble to accept severe treatment.
His intention was deeply sincere.
Your servant secretly feels pity and cherishes him for the sake of the court!
A sage
does not choose an era to rise,
nor change the people to govern.
Yet, he is invariably assisted by wise and intelligent helpers,
presumably because he guides them with the Way,
and leads them with propriety.
The reason why ancient
emperors and kings were able to assist the world and lead the people
was that they invariably won the hearts of the distant populace,
and fully utilized the intelligence and strength of their close ministers.
Indeed, if all the ministers currently holding office
in court are the best selections in the realm,
yet cannot fully exert their strength,
it cannot be said that one knows how to employ people.
If they are not the best selections in the realm,
it cannot be said that one knows how to appoint officials.
Your Majesty labors exhaustively over myriad affairs,
even personally burning the midnight oil,
yet public affairs are not peaceful,
and prohibitions are daily relaxed.
