Is this not clear evidence of inadequate assistance from your ministers?
Tracing its origin,
it is not only that ministers do not fully dedicate themselves,
but also that the ruler is unable to employ them effectively.
Bǎi Lǐxī was foolish in Yú but wise in Qín.
Yù Ràng merely tolerated the Zhōngháng clan but showed his integrity
to Zhì Bó.
These are clear examples from the ancients.
Now, if your servant were to say that all ministers in court are disloyal,
that would be slandering the entire court.
However, the nature of these matters
can be inferred and understood.
Your Majesty is concerned about the insufficiency of the treasury,
and military affairs have not ceased,
even to the point of cutting off the seasonal allocations of clothing,
and reducing the private grain of the imperial storehouses.
These actions are guided by Your Majesty's sagely will,
and the entire
court praises their wisdom.
Among the ministers who participate in governmental affairs,
is there anyone who sincerely worries about this?
The unlawful actions of Cavalry Commandant Wáng Cái and the court musician Mèng Sī
shook the capital,
yet their crimes were exposed by minor officials,
and the grandees and ministers initially offered not
a single word.
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
have the Colonel Director of Retainers or the Imperial Censor-in-Chief ever upheld principles to investigate evildoers,
thereby making the court solemn and orderly?
If Your Majesty believes that there are no talented individuals in this era,
and the court lacks worthy assistants,
how can you hope to follow the distant footsteps of Jì and Qì,
and idly await the outstanding talents of future generations?
The so-called worthy ones of today
all hold high offices and enjoy generous salaries,
yet their dedication to Your Majesty has not been established,
and their hearts are not unified towards public service.
This is because the responsibility for appointing
is not specialized,
and popular customs are often fraught with taboos.
Your servant believes that loyal ministers are not necessarily close,
and close ministers are not necessarily loyal.
Why?
Because they serve in an uncontentious position, and their efforts
can be fully exerted.
Now, if a distant person slanders someone without substantiating the slander,
it will surely be said that they are privately retaliating against someone they dislike.
If they praise someone without substantiating the praise,
it will surely be said that they privately
favor their close acquaintance.
Those around them may then use this to introduce discussions of likes and dislikes.
This is not only true for praise and slander;
even in matters of political gain and loss,
there are always such suspicions.
Your Majesty should consider how to broaden the hearts of your court ministers,
and earnestly encourage those with integrity,
making them emulate the ancients,
and aspire to be recorded in history.
Instead, you allow people like Lián Zhāo to disrupt
Meanwhile,
your minister fears that the great ministers will then accommodate themselves and protect their positions,
sitting and observing what succeeds and what fails,
as a warning for future generations!
In the past, Zhōu Gōng cautioned the Marquis of Lǔ, saying,
"Do not let great ministers resent not being utilized,"
not speaking of their wisdom or foolishness,
making it clear that all should be employed in their generation.
Yáo counted Shùn's achievements,
praising the removal of the Four Evildoers,
not speaking of their significance,
meaning that those with crimes should be removed.
Now, court ministers do not consider themselves incapable;
instead, they consider Your Majesty unwilling to employ them.
They do not
consider themselves unintelligent;
instead, they consider Your Majesty unwilling to consult them.
Why does Your Majesty not follow the way Zhōu Gōng employed people,
and the way Dà Shùn removed people?
If the Shìzhōng and Shàng
shū sit with you in the imperial tent,
and follow your splendid carriage when you travel,
personally facing your imperial inquiries,
and whatever they present is surely conveyed,
then the conduct of all officials,
whether capable or not, can all be known.
If the loyal
and capable are advanced,
and the obscure and inferior are dismissed,
who would dare to be indecisive and not exert themselves?
With Your Majesty's sagely wisdom,
personally discussing government affairs with your officials,
so that every official
can exert themselves,
and each feels personally attended to,
and each thinks of how to repay you,
then whether they are wise or foolish, capable or not,
depends on Your Majesty's utilization.
If you manage affairs in this way,
what matter will not be accomplished?
If you establish merits in this way,
what merit will not be achieved?
Whenever there are military affairs,
the imperial edict often says:
"Who should worry about this?
I should worry about it myself."
A recent edict also
said:
"Those who worry about public matters and forget private ones will surely not be so;
but if one merely puts public matters before private, it will settle itself."
Humbly reading the clear edicts,
I realize that your sagely thoughts thoroughly grasp the feelings of your subjects;
however,
I also find it strange that Your Majesty does not address the root and worries about the branches.
Whether a person is capable or not
is truly a matter of their inherent nature,
and even your minister believes that court officials do not fully live up to their duties.
A discerning
ruler employs people
so that the capable dare not hold back their strength,
and the incapable do not occupy positions unfitting for them.
Electing the wrong person
is not necessarily a crime;
however,
when the entire court tolerates the wrong person,
that is indeed strange.
Your Majesty knows they do not exert themselves,
yet you worry about their duties on their behalf.
You know they are incapable,
yet
you teach them how to manage their affairs.
How can this merely lead to the ruler toiling while the subjects are at ease?
Even if sages and worthies lived in the same era,
they could ultimately not govern in this way.
Your Majesty also worries that the prohibitions of the táigé are not strict enough,
and that personal solicitations and recommendations never cease.
You listen to Yī Yǐn's proposal to establish regulations for guests entering and leaving,
and select Sìtú to appoint
stern officials to guard the monastery gates.
While deterrents may arise from this,
it has not truly grasped the root of the prohibition.
In the past, during the reign of Emperor Ān of Hàn,
the Shàofǔ Dòu Jiā cleared the name of the innocent nephew of the Tíngwèi Guō Gōng,
yet he was still impeached and reported,
with memorials of accusation arriving one after another.
Recently, the Sīlì Xiàowèi Kǒng Xiàn cleared the name of the unruly and arrogant younger brother of the Dàjiàngjūn,
yet the supervising officials remained silent,
looking
to the wind and observing hints,
even more so than receiving recommendations.
Not selecting based on merit
is the greatest of personal matters.
Dòu Jiā had the favor of his relatives,
and Guō Gōng was not a crucial minister of the state,
yet
it was
still like this.
Comparing the present to the past,
Your Majesty yourself does not enforce the necessary punishments to cut off the source of factions.
Yī Yǐn's regulations
and having stern officials guard the gates
are not tools for governing the world.
If my words receive a little consideration and acceptance,
why worry that evil will not be eliminated,
and that people like Zhāo will be nurtured?
Indeed, exposing cunning and wickedness
is a loyal act;
however, the world despises petty individuals who do it,
because they disregard principles and merely seek favor and advancement.
If Your
Majesty does not re-examine their beginning and end,
and insists on treating those who defy the public and offend the world as devoted to public service,
and those who secretly act to expose others as truly loyal,
how can there be great and accomplished individuals who cannot
do this?
They simply consider principles and refrain from doing so.
If everyone in the world abandons principles and rushes after profit,
then what the ruler most suffers from,
Your Majesty, what joy
will you find in it?
Why not cut off its source?
Those who anticipate your wishes and follow your instructions to gain favor
are generally shallow and unprincipled individuals in the world,
whose sole aim is to please the
ruler's heart,
not to govern the world and bring peace to the common people.
Why does Your Majesty not try to change your approach and show it to them?
How could they cling to their ways and defy the imperial will?
Indeed,
when officials gain the ruler's heart,
it is a secure profession.
To occupy a respected and prominent office
is an honorable matter.
To receive a salary of a thousand measures of grain
is substantial wealth.
Even if an official
is foolish,
none are unwilling to enjoy this and prefer to be disobedient;
they are compelled by principles,
forcing themselves.
Truly, I believe Your Majesty should pity and protect them,
and entrust them with
a little authority.
How can you instead accept the duplicitous intentions of people like Zhāo,
and disregard such individuals?
Currently, there are opportunistic invaders outside,
and impoverished and suffering people within.
Your Majesty
must extensively assess the gains and losses of the empire,
and the successes and failures of government.
Truly, you cannot be negligent.
Shù was in court for eight years,
and his discussions were direct and uncompromising,
all of this kind.
He was sent out as the Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng,
and after several years was transferred to the Chancellor of Zhào,
but left office due to illness.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Hédōng from his home,
and after more than a year,
was promoted to Dūdù Hùjūn of Huáiběi,
but again left due to illness.
Wherever Shù was,
he aimed to preserve the greater good,
and by establishing benevolence and love,
he further gained the affection of the common people,
but did not extend this to Jī.
Shortly after,
he was appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
When Shù was in the imperial court,
because he could not achieve harmony with the current climate,
he was repeatedly sent to outside postings.
He was again sent out as the Inspector of Yōuzhōu,
given the title of Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn,
granted a staff of authority,
and made Hù Wūwán Xiàowèi.
At that time, the Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn Chéng Xǐ was garrisoned at Jì.
Shàngshū Yuán Kǎn and others cautioned Shù, saying:
"Chéng Shēnbó lived in the time of the previous emperor,
and donated his private land to the state in Qīngzhōu.
You both now hold staffs of authority,
and are assigned to garrison the same city;
you should be very careful in how you treat him."
But Shù paid no heed.
Before a year had passed since his appointment,
a Xiānbēi chieftain's son
came directly to the province with several tens of horsemen,
without passing through the passes.
The province executed one of his followers, a young man,
without submitting a memorial to the emperor.
Chéng Xǐ then impeached Shù,
who was sent to the Tíngwèi
and sentenced to death.
Because his father Jī had diligently served and died by drowning,
he was spared from death but stripped of his commoner status,
and exiled to Zhāngwǔ Commandery.
This was the first year of Jiāpíng.
Shù was unrestrained and acted as he pleased,
but his thoughts did not prevent harm,
ultimately leading to this defeat.
Initially,
Shù returned from Zhào Jùn.
Ruǎn Wǔ of Chén Liú also came as a summoned official from Qīng Hé Tàishǒu,
and they both went to Bó Tíngwèi.
He said to Shù:
“Observing your talent and character, you can follow the public path and maintain it without severity;
your capacity can hold high office, yet seeking it is not smooth;
your talent and learning can narrate ancient and modern times, yet your ambition is not singular.
This is what is called having the talent but lacking its use.
Now that you have leisure,
you can try to ponder deeply
and form a school of thought.”
While in Zhāng Wǔ,
he then authored the eight sections of the Tǐlùn.
He also wrote an essay, Xìngxìnglùn,
which was probably inspired by self-cultivation.
In the fourth year,
he died at the place of banishment.
In the second year of Gānlù,
Lè Xiáng of Hé Dōng, over ninety years old,
submitted a memorial defending the posthumous achievements of Jī.
The imperial court was moved by it.
An edict bestowed upon Shù's son, Yù, the title of Fēnglè Tínghóu,
with an estate of a hundred households.
Shù's memorials, debates, and refutations are all worth reading;
the crucial matters of his era are collected in this chapter.
Zhèng Hún, courtesy name Wén Gōng,
was a native of Kāifēng, Hé Nán.
His great-great-grandfather Zhòng,
and Zhòng's father Xìng,
were all famous scholars.
Hún's elder brother, Tài,
conspired with Xún Yōu and others to assassinate Dǒng Zhuó,
served as Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and then died.
Hún took Tài's young son, Mào, to seek refuge in Huái Nán.
Yuán Shù treated them with great courtesy.
Hún knew that Shù would inevitably fail.
At that time, Huà Xīn was the Yùzhāng Tàishǒu,
and had always been on good terms with Tài.
Hún then crossed the river to join Xīn.
Tài Zǔ, hearing of his upright conduct,
summoned him as a clerk,
and later promoted him to Xiàcài Zhǎng and Shàolíng Lìng.
The world was not yet settled,
and the people were all restless and impulsive,
not bothering with production;
those who gave birth had no means to support their children,
and generally did not raise them.
Wherever Hún went, he confiscated their fishing and hunting tools,
assigned them to farming and sericulture,
and also opened rice paddies,
and heavily enforced the law against infanticide.
Initially, the people feared punishment,
but later, they gradually became prosperous and well-provided for,
and all raised and supported their children;
many of the children raised
were given Zhèng as their given name.
He was appointed as a minister's clerk,
and promoted to Zuǒ Fēngyì.
At that time, Liáng Xìng and others plundered five thousand households of officials and commoners, becoming bandits,
and the various counties could not defend against them;
all were terrified
and sought refuge in the commandery seat.
The debaters all thought it appropriate to move to a dangerous location for safety,
but Hún said:
“Xìng and his ilk are scattered
and hidden in the mountains.
Although some follow them,
they are mostly coerced.
Now we should widely open paths for surrender
and proclaim our grace and trustworthiness.
But to guard ourselves in dangerous places
shows weakness.”
Thereupon, he gathered officials and commoners,
repaired the city walls,
and prepared for defense.
He then dispatched the people to pursue the bandits,
clearly announced rewards and punishments,
and made a solemn oath,
stating that seven tenths of what was captured
would be given as reward.
The common people were greatly pleased
and all wished to capture bandits,
obtaining many women and valuables.
Those bandits who lost their wives and children
all returned to seek surrender.
Hún demanded that they first acquire other women
before their wives and children would be returned to them;
thus, they began to plunder each other,
and their factions dispersed.
He also dispatched trustworthy officials and commoners
to spread out in the valleys to proclaim and persuade,
and those who came out followed one after another.
He then ordered the chief officials of the various counties to return to their original seats to settle and pacify the people.
Xìng and others were afraid,
and gathered their remaining followers at Fū Chéng.
Tài Zǔ sent Xiàhóu Yuān to assist the commandery in attacking them.
Hún led his officials and commoners to ascend first,
and beheaded Xìng and his confederates.
Bandits like Jìn Fù and others
coerced the Xiàyáng Zhǎng and Shàolíng Lìng, along with their officials and commoners, into Wèi Shān.
Hún again attacked and defeated Fù and his group,
captured the two county chief officials,
and brought back those they had plundered.
And as for Zhào Qīnglóng,
who killed Zuǒ Nèishǐ Chéng Xiū,
when Hún heard of it,
he sent brave men to behead him.
Before and after, over four thousand households submitted,
and from this, all mountain bandits were pacified,
and the people settled down to their industries.
He was transferred to be Shàngdǎng Tàishǒu.
When Tài Zǔ campaigned in Hànzhōng,
he appointed Hún as Jīngzhào Yǐn.
Hún, seeing that the common people had recently settled,
established laws for relocating,
making those with ample resources and multiple family members associate with the single and less well-off,
and the warm and trustworthy with the isolated and elderly,
encouraging agriculture,
and clarifying prohibitions
to expose wrongdoers.
Because of this, the people were content with farming,
and banditry ceased.
When the large army entered Hànzhōng,
the transport of military provisions was paramount.
He also sent people to cultivate fields in Hànzhōng,
and there were no fugitives.
Tài Zǔ praised him even more
and again appointed him as a minister's clerk.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
he became Shìyùshǐ,
was given the additional title of Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and transferred to be Tàishǒu of Yángpíng and Pèi Jùn.
The commandery borders were low-lying and wet,
suffering from floods,
and the common people were hungry and destitute.
Hún, at the border between Xiāo and Xiàng counties,
constructed dikes and dams,
and opened rice paddies.
The people of the commandery all considered it inconvenient,
but Hún said:
“The terrain is low-lying,
suitable for irrigation,
and will eventually bring long-term benefits of fish and rice;
this is the foundation for enriching the people.”
So he personally led officials and commoners,
initiated the work,
and completed it all within one winter.
In successive years, there were great harvests,
the cultivated area increased annually,
and tax revenue doubled the usual amount.
The people benefited from it,
carved a stone inscription to praise him,
and called it Zhèng Bēi.
He was transferred to be Tàishǒu of Shānyáng and Wèi Jùn,
and his governance there was similar.
Also, as the people of the commandery
suffered from a lack of timber,
he assigned them to plant elm trees for fences,
and also to plant five kinds of fruit trees;
the elm trees all formed fences,
and the five fruit trees bore abundant fruit.
Upon entering the border of Wèi Jùn,
the villages were uniform and orderly,
and the people had ample wealth.
Míng Dì heard of this,
issued an edict praising him,
and proclaimed it throughout the realm,
promoting him to Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
Hún was pure and upright in public service,
and his wife and children were not exempt from hunger and cold.
When he died,
his son Chóng was made Lángzhōng.
Cāng Cí,
courtesy name Xiàorén, was a native of Huáinán.
He began as a commandery clerk.
During the Jiàn’ān period,
Tàizǔ established military agricultural colonies in Huáinán.
He appointed Cí as Suíjítūwèi.
Towards the end of the Huángchū period,
he became the Magistrate of Cháng’ān.
He was incorruptible and methodical,
and officials and commoners alike feared and loved him.
During the Tàihé period,
he was promoted to Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng.
The commandery was on the western frontier,
and due to turmoil and isolation,
it had been without a Grand Administrator for twenty years.
The great families had become powerful and oppressive,
and this had become the custom.
Previous Grand Administrators, such as Yǐn Fèng,
merely followed the old ways
and did nothing to rectify the situation.
When Cí arrived,
he suppressed the powerful,
and provided relief to the poor and weak,
handling matters very appropriately.
The old powerful families had an excess of land,
while the common people had not even enough land to stand an awl.
Cí assessed and allocated land based on family size,
gradually ensuring they received its original value.
Previously, lawsuits in the subordinate counties were numerous and complicated.
The counties could not resolve them,
so many cases accumulated in the prefectural seat.
Cí personally went to investigate and review them,
classifying their severity.
Unless it was a capital offense,
he would simply send them away after a flogging.
In one year, fewer than ten people were sentenced.
Moreover, Hú from the Western Regions often wished to come and pay tribute,
but many powerful families intercepted and cut them off.
When they did engage in trade,
there was much deceit and unfair dealing,
and they often could not clearly settle accounts.
The Hú frequently harbored resentment.
Cí, however, consoled them all.
For those wishing to travel to Luò,
he issued travel permits.
For those wishing to return from the commandery,
the government would purchase their goods fairly,
exchanging them for available government stores.
He also sent officials and commoners to escort them along the roads.
Because of this, both the people and the barbarians universally praised his virtue and benevolence.
After several years, he died in office.
Officials and commoners grieved as if they had lost a relative.
They drew his image
and thought of his likeness.
When the various Hú of the Western Regions heard of Cí’s death,
they all gathered at the headquarters of the Wùjǐ Jiàowèi and the chief officials to mourn.
Some even cut their faces with knives
to show their heartfelt sincerity.
They also established shrines
to worship him from afar.
From Tàizǔ until Xiánxī,

the Grand Administrator of Wèijùn, Wú Guàn of Chén Guó; the Grand Administrator of Qīnghé, Rèn Yù of Lè’ān; the Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào, Yán Fěi of Jìběi; the Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng, Línghú Shào of Tàiyuán; and the Chancellor of Jìnán, Kǒng Yì of Lǔ Guó—
some were compassionate and resolved legal cases,
some were sincere and benevolent,
some maintained personal integrity,
and some exposed treachery and hidden evils.
All were excellent two-thousand-dàn officials.
A commentary says: Rèn Jùn first raised righteous troops
and submitted to Tàizǔ.
He developed land and planted grains,
filling granaries to overflowing.
His meritorious achievements were truly great.
Sū Zé used his authority to quell disorder.
He was not only a skilled administrator,
but also remarkably upright and firm.
His integrity and reputation are worthy of praise.
Dù Jī combined leniency and strictness to achieve success,
and benefited the people with his benevolence.
Zhèng Hún and Cāng Cí
managed affairs methodically.
Are they not all renowned governors of the Wèi dynasty?
Shù frequently presented proposals on current policies
and discussed governance.
These are indeed noteworthy.
Chapter 17, Biographies of Zhāng Lè and Zhāng Xú
Zhāng Liáo,
courtesy name Wényuǎn, was a native of Mǎyì, Yànmén.
He was originally a descendant of Niè Yī,
but changed his surname to avoid enmity.
In his youth, he served as a commandery clerk.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
Dīng Yuán, the Inspector of Bīngzhōu, considered Liáo to possess extraordinary martial prowess
and summoned him as an Aide,
sending him to lead troops to the capital.
Hé Jìn dispatched him to Hébĕi to recruit soldiers,
and he obtained over a thousand men.
Upon his return,
Hé Jìn was defeated,
and Liáo's troops joined Dǒng Zhuó.
After Dǒng Zhuó's defeat,
his troops joined Lǚ Bù,
and he was promoted to Qídūwèi.
When Lǚ Bù was defeated by Lǐ Jué,
Liáo followed Bù eastward to Xúzhōu,
assuming the title of Chancellor of Lǔ.
He was then twenty-eight years old.
When Tàizǔ defeated Lǚ Bù at Xiàpī,
Liáo led his forces to surrender.
He was appointed Zhōnglángjiàng
and granted the title Guānnèihóu.
He repeatedly achieved military success and was promoted to Bíjiàngjūn.
After Yuán Shào's defeat,
Liáo was separately dispatched to pacify the various counties of Lǔ Guó.
He joined Xiàhóu Yuān in besieging Chāng Xī in Dōnghǎi.
After several months, their provisions ran out,
and they discussed withdrawing the army.
Liáo said to Yuān:
“For the past few days,
each time I patrol the various outposts,
Xī always fixes his gaze on Liáo.
Also, his arrows are becoming scarcer.
This must be because Xī is hesitating in his plans,
and therefore is not fighting with full strength.
I want to provoke him into conversation.
Perhaps I can induce him to surrender?”
He then sent someone to tell Xī:
“His Lord has a command
that Liáo is to convey to you.”
Xī indeed descended to speak with Liáo.
Liáo explained to him
that “Tàizǔ is divine and martial,
and intends to embrace the four quarters with his virtue.
Those who surrender first will receive great rewards.”
Xī then agreed to surrender.
Liáo thereupon went alone up Sāngōng Shān,
entered Xī’s house,
and paid respects to his wife and children.
Xī was delighted
and followed him to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ sent Xī back
and reprimanded Liáo, saying:
“This is not the proper conduct for a great general.”
Liáo apologized, saying:
“It is because Your Excellency’s prestige is renowned throughout the four seas,
and I, Liáo, was carrying out a sacred decree,
that Xī would certainly not dare to harm me.”
He followed in the campaign against Yuán Tán and Yuán Shàng at Líyáng.
Having achieved merit,
he was appointed Acting Zhōngjiān Jiāngjūn.
He followed in the attack on Shàng at Yè.
Shàng held firm and would not surrender.
Tàizǔ returned to Xǔ,
and sent Liáo and Lè Jìn to capture Yīn’ān,
and resettle its people in Hénán.
He again followed in the attack on Yè.
After Yè was captured,
Liáo separately campaigned in Zhàoguó and Chángshān,
recruiting and pacifying various mountain bandits and Sūn Qīng and others from Hēishān.
He followed in the attack on Yuán Tán.
After Tán was defeated,
he separately campaigned along the coast,
defeating the Liaódōng bandit Liǔ Yì and others.
Upon his return to Yè,
Tàizǔ personally went out to welcome Liáo,
invited him to ride in his carriage,
and appointed Liáo as Dàngkòu Jiāngjūn.
He again separately attacked Jīngzhōu,
pacifying the various counties of Jiāngxià.
He then returned and garrisoned at Línyǐng,
and was enfeoffed as Dūtínghóu.
He followed in the campaign against Yuán Shàng at Liǔchéng.
He unexpectedly encountered the enemy.
Liáo urged Tàizǔ to fight,
with great enthusiasm.
Tàizǔ was impressed by him
and personally handed his standard to Liáo.
He then attacked,
greatly defeating them,
and beheaded the Chányú Tàdùn.
At that time, Jīngzhōu was not yet settled.
Again, [Zhāng] Liáo was sent to garrison Chángshè.
As he was about to depart,
there were those in the army who plotted rebellion.
At night, a panic arose, chaos ensued, and fires broke out,
disturbing the entire army.
Liáo said to his attendants:
"Do not move.
It is not that the whole camp has rebelled;
there must be someone instigating the trouble,
simply wishing to stir up confusion among the people."
He then ordered the army
that those who were not rebelling should sit calmly.
Liáo led a few dozen personal guards
and stood in the midst of the formation.
After a moment, order was restored,
and the chief instigators were immediately apprehended and executed.
Chén Lán and Méi Chéng rebelled from Dǐliùxiàn.
Tàizǔ sent Yú Jìn, Zāng Bà, and others to suppress [Méi] Chéng,
while Liáo commanded Zhāng Hé, Niú Gài, and others to suppress [Chén] Lán.
[Méi] Chéng feigned surrender to [Yú] Jìn,
and [Yú] Jìn returned.
[Méi] Chéng then led his followers to join [Chén] Lán,
and they moved into the mountains.
Within these mountains was Tiānzhù Shān,
which was over twenty *lǐ* high and steep,
with treacherous and narrow paths.
The footpaths were barely passable,
and [Chén] Lán and his group fortified themselves on its summit.
Liáo wanted to advance,
but his generals said:
"Our troops are few and the path is perilous;
it is difficult to penetrate deeply."
Liáo said:
"This is what is called 'one against one,'
only the brave can advance."
He then advanced to the foot of the mountain, set up camp,
and attacked them.
He cut off the heads of [Chén] Lán and [Méi] Chéng,
and captured all their followers.
Tàizǔ discussed the merits of the generals,
saying:
"Ascending Tiān Shān,
traversing its steep and perilous terrain,
to capture [Chén] Lán and [Méi] Chéng,
is the achievement of suppressing bandits."
[Liáo's] fief was increased,
and he was granted the *jié*.
After Tàizǔ returned from campaigning against Sūn Quán,
he ordered Liáo, Yuè Jìn, Lǐ Diǎn, and others to lead over seven thousand men to garrison Héféi.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Zhāng Lǔ,
he gave instructions to the Protector of the Army, Xuē Tì,
with a note on the side of the letter saying:
"Open when the enemy arrives."
Soon after, [Sūn] Quán led a force of one hundred thousand to besiege Héféi.
They then jointly opened the instructions.
The instructions said:
"If Sūn Quán arrives,
Generals Zhāng [Liáo] and Lǐ [Diǎn] are to sally forth and fight;
General Yuè [Jìn] is to guard the Protector of the Army
and must not engage in battle."
All the generals were doubtful.
Liáo said:
"The Duke is away on a distant campaign;
by the time reinforcements arrive,
they will surely have defeated us.
Therefore, these instructions mean to strike them while they are still not fully formed,
to break their momentum,
and thereby settle the hearts of our troops,
after which we can defend the city.
The crucial moment for victory or defeat
lies in this one battle.
What do you gentlemen doubt?"
Lǐ Diǎn also agreed with Liáo.
Thereupon, Liáo recruited courageous volunteers that night,
gathered eight hundred men,
slaughtered cattle to feast the officers and soldiers,
and planned a great battle for the next day.
At dawn,
Liáo donned his armor and held his *jǐ*,
leading the charge to breach the enemy lines.
He killed several tens of men,
decapitated two generals,
shouted his own name aloud,
charged into the rampart,
and reached beneath [Sūn] Quán's banner.
[Sūn] Quán was greatly startled;
his men did not know what to do,
and fled, climbing a high mound,
defending himself with a long *jǐ*.
Liáo shouted at [Sūn] Quán to come down and fight.
[Sūn] Quán dared not move.
Seeing that Liáo had few men,
they gathered and surrounded Liáo several times over.
Liáo waved his weapon left and right through the encirclement,
striking fiercely straight ahead.
The encirclement broke open.
Liáo and a few dozen of his subordinates broke out,
but the remaining troops cried out:
"Has the general abandoned us?"
Liáo again returned and charged through the encirclement,
extricating the remaining troops.
[Sūn] Quán's men and horses all scattered and fell back,
none daring to oppose them.
They fought from dawn until midday.
The Wú Rén lost their morale.
[Liáo and his men] returned to strengthen their defenses,
and the morale of the troops was settled,
and all the generals were impressed.
[Sūn] Quán besieged Héféi for over ten days,
but the city could not be taken,
so he withdrew.
Liáo led all his forces in pursuit,
almost capturing [Sūn] Quán again.
Tàizǔ greatly admired Liáo,
and appointed him as Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn.
In the twenty-first year of Jiàn'ān (216 CE),
Tàizǔ again campaigned against Sūn Quán.
Upon reaching Héféi,
he inspected the place where Liáo had fought,
sighing for a long time.
He then increased Liáo's troops,
left many other armies behind,
and moved the garrison to Jūcháo.
Guān Yǔ besieged Cáo Rén at Fán,
at which time Quán declared himself a vassal,
and summoned Liáo and all the armies to return and relieve Rén.
Before Liáo arrived,
Xú Huǎng had already defeated Guān Yǔ,
and Rén's siege was lifted.
Liáo and Tài Zǔ met at Mópí.
When Liáo's army arrived,
Tài Zǔ rode out in a palanquin to greet them,
then returned to garrison at Chénjùn.
When Wén Dì ascended to the position of King,
Liáo was transferred to General of the Vanguard.
His elder brother Fàn and one son were enfeoffed as marquises.
Sūn Quán rebelled again,
and Liáo was sent back to garrison Héfèi,
and his noble rank was advanced to Dūxiāng Hóu.
Liáo's mother was provided with a carriage,
and soldiers and horses to escort Liáo's family to the garrison.
An order was given that when Liáo's mother arrived,
he should go out to meet her with an escort.
All the generals and officials under his command lined up and bowed by the roadside,
and those who witnessed it considered it an honor.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
Liáo was enfeoffed as Jìnyáng Hóu,
his stipend was increased by a thousand households,
making a total of two thousand six hundred households.
In the second year of Huángchū,
Liáo attended court at Luòyáng Palace.
Wén Dì invited Liáo to a meeting at the Jiànshǐ Palace,
and personally questioned him about the circumstances of his defeat of Wú.
The Emperor sighed and looked at his attendants, saying:
"This man is also a Zhàohǔ of old."
A residence was built for him,
and a special hall was also built for Liáo's mother.
The foot soldiers who had enlisted with Liáo in the defeat of Wú's army
were all made Hǔbēn.
Sūn Quán again declared himself a vassal.
Liáo returned to garrison Yōngqiū,
and fell ill.
The Emperor sent Imperial Attendant Liú Yè with imperial physicians to examine his illness,
and Hǔbēn officers inquired about his condition,
with a constant stream of them on the road.
As his illness had not yet healed,
the Emperor welcomed Liáo to his temporary imperial residence,
and personally visited in his imperial carriage,
holding his hand,
and bestowing upon him imperial robes.
The Grand Provisioner sent imperial meals daily.
When his illness slightly improved,
he returned to garrison.
Sūn Quán rebelled again,
and the Emperor sent Liáo by boat,
with Cáo Xiū, to Hǎilíng,
facing the river.
Quán greatly feared him,
and instructed his generals:
"Although Zhāng Liáo is ill,
he is not to be withstood.
Be cautious!"
That year,
Liáo and other generals defeated Quán's general Lǚ Fàn.
Liáo's illness became critical,
and he died at Jiāngdū.
The Emperor shed tears for him,
and he was posthumously granted the title Gāng Hóu.
His son Hǔ succeeded him.
In the sixth year,
the Emperor, recalling the merits of Liáo and Diǎn at Héfèi,
issued an edict saying:
"In the battle of Héfèi,
Liáo and Diǎn, with eight hundred foot soldiers,
defeated one hundred thousand bandits.
In all history of warfare,
such a feat has never occurred.
They caused the bandits to lose heart even to this day,
and can be called the nation's claws and teeth.
Therefore, divide one hundred households each from Liáo's and Diǎn's fiefs,
and bestow upon one of their sons the title Guānnèi Hóu."
Hǔ served as a General of the Household,
and then died.
His son Tǒng succeeded him.
Yuè Jìn, courtesy name Wénqiān,
was a native of Wèiguó, Yángpíng.
He was short in stature,
and joined Tài Zǔ with his courage and fierceness,
serving as an officer under his tent.
He was sent back to his home commandery to recruit soldiers,
and obtained over a thousand men.
He returned as a Provisional Major of the Army and Commander of Breaking Formations.
He followed in attacking Lǚ Bù at Púyáng,
Zhāng Chāo at Yōngqiū,
and Qiáo Ruí at Kǔ.
In all these, he was the first to scale the walls and achieved merit,
and was enfeoffed as Guǎngchāng Tínghóu.
He followed in campaigning against Zhāng Xiù at Ānzhòng,
besieged Lǚ Bù at Xiàpí,
defeated a separate general,
attacked Suī Gù at Shèquǎn,
and attacked Liú Bèi at Pèi.
He defeated all of them,
and was appointed Colonel Who Suppresses Bandits.
He crossed the river to attack Huòjiā,
then returned,
and followed in attacking Yuán Shào at Guāndù.
He fought bravely,
and beheaded Yuán Shào's general Chúnyú Qióng.
He followed in attacking Tán and Shàng at Líyáng,
beheaded their great general Yán Jìng,
and served as a Roving General.
Separately, he attacked the Yellow Turbans,
defeated them,
and pacified Lè'ān Commandery.
He followed in besieging Yè.
When Yè was pacified,
he followed in attacking Yuán Tán at Nánpí,
was the first to scale the walls,
and entered Tán's eastern gate.
When Tán was defeated,
he separately attacked Yōngnú,
and defeated it.
In the eleventh year of Jiàn'ān,
Tài Zǔ memorialized the Hàn Emperor,
praising Jìn, Yú Jìn, and Zhāng Liáo, saying:
"Their martial prowess is vast,
their strategies are thoroughly prepared,
their character is loyal and unified,
and they uphold righteousness and principle.
Whenever they face battle,
they always serve as commanders,
charging powerfully and breaking through strong defenses;
no stronghold is impregnable to them.
They personally beat the drums,
their hands never knowing fatigue.
Furthermore, when sent on separate campaigns,
they command and lead armies,
pacify the masses harmoniously,
obey orders without transgression,
make decisive judgments in the face of the enemy,
with no errors.
Considering their merits and contributions,
they should each be granted notable honors."
Thereupon, Yú Jìn was appointed General Who Manifests Awe;
Jìn,
General Who Breaks Assaults;
and Liáo,
General Who Eliminates Bandits.
Jìn separately campaigned against Gāo Gàn,
entering Shàngdǎng from the northern route,
and circling out behind him.
Gàn and others returned to defend Húguān,
and in successive battles, many were beheaded.
Gàn held firm and had not yet fallen,
when Tài Zǔ personally campaigned against him,
and then captured it.
Tài Zǔ campaigned against Guǎn Chéng,
and camped at Chúnyú.
He sent Jìn and Lǐ Diǎn to attack him.
Chéng was defeated and fled,
escaping to a sea island.
The coastal regions were pacified.
Jīngzhōu had not yet submitted,
so Jìn was sent to garrison Yángzhái.
Later, he followed in pacifying Jīngzhōu,
and was left to garrison Xiāngyáng.
He attacked Guān Yǔ, Sū Fēi, and others,
all of whom fled.
The Man and Yi people in the mountain valleys of Nánjùn and other commanderies came to Jìn and surrendered.
He also campaigned against Liú Bèi's Chief of Línjǔ, Dù Pǔ, and Chief of Jīngyáng, Liáng Dà,
and thoroughly defeated both of them.
Later, he followed in campaigning against Sūn Quán,
and Jìn was granted a provisional staff of authority.
When Tài Zǔ returned,
he left Jìn with Zhāng Liáo and Lǐ Diǎn to garrison Héfèi.
His stipend was increased by five hundred households,
making a total of one thousand two hundred households.
Because Jìn had repeatedly achieved merit,
five hundred households were separated from his fief,
and one of his sons was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Jìn was promoted to General of the Right.
He died in the twenty-third year of Jiàn'ān,
and was posthumously granted the title Wēi Hóu.
His son Lín succeeded him.
Lín was resolute and brave, with his father's demeanor,
and reached the office of Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Zhūgě Dàn rebelled,
surprised and killed Lín.
An imperial edict mourned and regretted his death,
posthumously appointing him Grand Commandant,
and granting him the posthumous title Mǐn Hóu.
His son Zhào succeeded him.
Yú Jìn, styled Wénzé,
was a native of Jùpíng in Tàishān.
When the Yellow Turbans rose,
Bào Xìn gathered followers.
Jìn joined him.
When Grand Progenitor [Cáo Cāo] took control of Yǎnzhōu,
Jìn and his comrades all went to him and were appointed Dūbó,
subordinate to General Wáng Lǎng.
Lǎng was impressed by him,
recommending Jìn as talented enough for a Grand General.
Grand Progenitor summoned and spoke with him,
then appointed him Jūnsīmǎ [military chief clerk],
and ordered him to lead troops to Xúzhōu
to attack Guǎngwēi.
He captured it,
and was appointed Xiànchén Dūwèi.
He followed in the campaign against Lǚ Bù at Púyáng,
and separately defeated two of Bù's camps south of the city.
He also separately led troops to defeat Gāo Yǎ at Xūchāng.
He followed in the attacks on Shòuzhāng, Dìngtáo, and Líhú,
and besieged Zhāng Chāo at Yōngqiū.
All were captured.
He followed in the campaigns against the Yellow Turbans Liú Pì, Huáng Shào and others.
They were encamped at Bǎnliáng.
Shào and others launched a night attack on Grand Progenitor's camp.
Jìn led his subordinates to defeat them,
beheaded Shào and others,
and compelled all their troops to surrender.
He was promoted to Pínglǔ Xiàowèi.
He followed in the siege of Qiáo Ruí at Kǔ,
and beheaded Ruí and three other generals.
He followed to Wǎn,
where Zhāng Xiù surrendered.
Xiù later rebelled.
Grand Progenitor fought an unfavorable battle,
suffered a military defeat,
and returned to Wǔyīn.
At this time, the army was in disarray,
each man secretly seeking Grand Progenitor.
Jìn alone disciplined the several hundred men he commanded,
fighting and retreating,
and despite casualties, they did not separate.
When the enemy's pursuit gradually slowed,
Jìn calmly reformed his ranks,
beat the drums, and returned.
Before reaching Grand Progenitor's location,
he saw more than ten men along the road, wounded and fleeing naked.
Jìn asked the reason,
and they said:
"We were robbed by the Qīngzhōu soldiers."
Initially,
when the Yellow Turbans surrendered,
they were called Qīngzhōu soldiers.
Grand Progenitor treated them leniently,
which is why they dared to take advantage and commit robberies.
Jìn was enraged,
and ordered his troops, saying:
"The Qīngzhōu soldiers belong to Lord Cáo,
yet they act as bandits!"
He then attacked them,
charging them with their crimes.
The Qīngzhōu soldiers quickly fled to Grand Progenitor to lodge a complaint.
When Jìn arrived,
he first established a camp,
and did not immediately pay his respects to Grand Progenitor.
Someone said to Jìn:
"The Qīngzhōu soldiers have already accused you;
you should hasten to the Lord to explain."
Jìn said:
"Now the enemy is behind us,
and their pursuit could come at any time.
If we don't first prepare,
how can we withstand the enemy?
Moreover, the Lord is intelligent;
how can slanders prevail!"
He then slowly dug trenches and set up camp.
Afterward, he entered to pay his respects,
and fully explained the situation.
Grand Progenitor was pleased,
and said to Jìn:
"During the disaster at Yùshuǐ,
I was in a dire situation.
The general was able to maintain order amidst chaos,
suppress violence, and fortify the camp.
You possess an unshakeable integrity.
Even the famous generals of antiquity,
how could they surpass this!"
Thereupon, he recorded Jìn's past and present merits,
and enfeoffed him as Yìshòu Tínghóu.
He again followed in the attack on Zhāng Xiù at Ráng,
captured Lǚ Bù at Xiàpī,
and separately, with Shǐ Huàn and Cáo Rén, attacked Suī Gù at Shèquǎn,
defeating and beheading him.
When Grand Progenitor first campaigned against Yuán Shào,
Shào's army was strong.
Jìn wished to be the vanguard.
Grand Progenitor admired him,
and dispatched two thousand infantry,
ordering Jìn to lead them,
to guard Yánjīn to resist Shào.
Grand Progenitor then led his main army back to Guāndù.
Liú Bèi rebelled from Xúzhōu.
Grand Progenitor campaigned east against him.
Shào attacked Jìn.
Jìn held his ground firmly,
and Shào could not capture it.
He again, with Lè Jìn and others, led five thousand infantry and cavalry,
to attack Shào's separate camps.
From southwest of Yánjīn, they advanced along the river to the two counties of Jí and Huòjiā,
burning more than thirty fortified strongholds,
beheading and capturing several thousand each,
and compelling the surrender of Shào's generals Hé Mào, Wáng Mó, and more than twenty others.
Grand Progenitor again ordered Jìn to separately lead troops to garrison Yuánwǔ,
and attack Shào's separate camp at Dùshìjīn,
defeating it.
He was promoted to Bì Jiāngjūn.
Later, he followed back to Guāndù.
Grand Progenitor and Shào established continuous camps,
erecting earthen mounds facing each other.
Shào fired arrows into the camp,
and many soldiers were killed and wounded.
There was fear in the army.
Jìn oversaw the defense of the earthen mound,
fighting vigorously,
his morale rising.
When Shào was defeated,
he was promoted to Piānjīangjūn.
Jìzhōu was pacified.
Chāng Xī rebelled again.
Jìn was sent to campaign against him.
Jìn advanced rapidly to attack Xī.
Xī had an old acquaintance with Jìn,
and went to Jìn to surrender.
All the generals thought that since Xī had surrendered,
he should be sent to Grand Progenitor.
Jìn said:
"Gentlemen, do you not know the Lord's standing order?
Those who surrender after being besieged are not pardoned.
To uphold the law and execute orders
is the principle of serving one's superior.
Though Xī is an old friend,
how can I lose my integrity!"
He personally oversaw Xī's execution,
shedding tears as he beheaded him.
At this time, Grand Progenitor was with the army at Chúnyú.
Hearing of this, he sighed, saying:
"Xī surrendered not to me but to Jìn.
Is this not fate!"
He valued Jìn even more.
When Dōnghǎi was pacified, Jìn was appointed Hǔwēi Jiāngjūn.
Later, he and Zāng Bà and others attacked Méi Chéng.
Zhāng Liáo, Zhāng Hé and others campaigned against Chén Lán.
When Jìn arrived,
Chéng led over three thousand men to surrender.
After surrendering, he rebelled again,
and his troops fled to Lán.
Liáo and others were at a stalemate with Lán,
and their military provisions were low.
Jìn's grain transport arrived in continuous succession,
and Liáo then beheaded Lán and Chéng.
His stipend was increased by two hundred households,
bringing the total to one thousand two hundred households.
At this time,
Jìn, along with Zhāng Liáo, Lè Jìn, Zhāng Hé, and Xú Huàng, were all famous generals.
Whenever Grand Progenitor launched a campaign,
they would alternately serve as the vanguard,
and upon return, as the rearguard.
Jìn, however, managed his army with strict discipline,
and did not secretly pocket any wealth or goods captured from the enemy.
Because of this, his rewards and gifts were exceptionally generous.
However, he governed his subordinates by law,
and did not win much of the hearts of his officers and soldiers.
Grand Progenitor often resented Zhū Líng,
and wanted to seize his camp.
Because Jìn possessed great authority and gravitas,
he dispatched Jìn with several tens of cavalry,
carrying an order,
to go directly to Líng's camp and seize his army.
Líng and his subordinates dared not make a move.
Líng was then appointed as Jìn's subordinate supervisor.
All were awestruck and submitted,
such was the fear he inspired.
He was promoted to Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
granted a ceremonial axe,
had five hundred households divided from his fief,
and one of his sons was enfeoffed as a Marquis.
In the 24th year of Jiàn'ān,
Tàizǔ was in Cháng'ān.
He sent Cáo Rén to attack Guān Yǔ at Fán,
and also dispatched Jìn to assist Rén.
In autumn,
there was a great continuous rain,
and the Hàn River overflowed.
The water on flat ground was several zhàng deep,
and Jìn's seven armies were all submerged.
Jìn and the other generals climbed to high ground and looked at the water;
there was no way to evade it.
Yǔ boarded large boats and attacked Jìn and the others.
Jìn consequently surrendered,
but only Páng Dé did not yield his integrity and died.
When Tàizǔ heard of this,
he sighed mournfully for a long time,
saying:
“I have known Jìn for thirty years.
How could he, when facing danger and difficulty,
be inferior to Páng Dé!”
Later, Sūn Quán captured Yǔ
and seized his troops,
and Jìn was again in Wú.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
Quán declared himself a vassal
and sent Jìn back.
The Emperor granted Jìn an audience.
His beard and hair were hoary white,
his appearance was gaunt and haggard,
and he wept, kowtowing repeatedly.
The Emperor comforted and admonished him with the stories of Xún Línfù and Mèng Míngshì,
and appointed him General Who Pacifies Afar (Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn).
He intended to send Jìn as an envoy to Wú,
but first ordered him to go north to Yè to visit the Gāolíng mausoleum.
The Emperor had paintings depicting Guān Yǔ's victory in battle, Páng Dé's righteous indignation, and Jìn's surrender placed in the mausoleum's hall.
When Jìn saw them,
he became ashamed and enraged, fell ill, and died.
His son, Guī, succeeded him, being enfeoffed as Marquis of Yìshòu Pavilion (Yìshòu Tínghóu).
Jìn was posthumously titled Marquis Lì.
Zhāng Hé, courtesy name Jùnyì,
was a man from Mò, Héjiān.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, he responded to the recruitment to suppress the Huángjīn (Yellow Turbans),
serving as a Major in the Army (Jūnsīmǎ),
subordinate to Hán Fù.
When Fù was defeated,
Hé returned with his troops to Yuán Shào.
Shào appointed Hé as a Colonel (Xiàowèi)
and sent him to resist Gōngsūn Zàn.
When Zàn was defeated,
Hé had great merit,
and was promoted to Commander of the Guards of Níngguó (Níngguó Zhōnglángjiāng).
When Tàizǔ and Yuán Shào were in a stalemate at Guāndù,
Shào sent General Chúnyú Qióng and others to supervise the transport of supplies and garrison Wūcháo.
Tàizǔ personally led a rapid attack against them.
Hé advised Shào, saying:
“Cáo Gōng’s troops are elite;
if they go, they will certainly defeat Qióng and the others.
If Qióng and the others are defeated,
then your Excellency’s affair will be lost.
It is advisable to quickly lead troops to rescue them.”
Guō Tú said:
“Hé’s plan is wrong.
It would be better to attack their main camp.
They will certainly return,
which means it will be resolved without needing rescue.”
Hé said:
“Cáo Gōng’s camp is strong;
attacking it will certainly not capture it.
If Qióng and the others are captured,
we will all become captives.”
Shào only sent light cavalry to rescue Qióng
but used heavy troops to attack Tàizǔ’s camp,
which they could not take.
Tàizǔ indeed defeated Qióng and the others,
and Shào’s army disintegrated.
Tú was ashamed
and slandered Hé again, saying:
“Hé was pleased by the army’s defeat
and spoke disrespectfully.”
Hé was afraid
and consequently submitted to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ was very pleased to get Hé
and said:
“In the past, Zǐxú did not realize early enough,
which caused his own danger.
How could he compare to Wēizǐ leaving Yīn or Hán Xìn returning to Hàn?”
He appointed Hé as General of the Household (Piānjiāngjūn)
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Dū Pavilion (Dūtínghóu).
He was entrusted with troops
and followed in the attack on Yè,
capturing it.
He also followed in the attack on Yuán Tán at Bóhǎi,
and as a separate general, besieged Yōngnú,
greatly defeating it.
He followed in the campaign against Liǔchéng,
and with Zhāng Liáo, served as the vanguard,
promoted to General Who Pacifies the Di (Píngdí Jiāngjūn) for his merits.
He separately campaigned in Dōnglái,
attacking Guǎn Chéng,
and also with Zhāng Liáo, attacked Chén Lán, Méi Chéng, and others,
defeating them.
He followed in the defeat of Mǎ Chāo and Hán Suì at Wèinán.
He besieged Āndìng
and secured the surrender of Yáng Qiū.
He and Xiàhóu Yuān attacked the bandits Liáng Xìng in Fū and the Dī people in Wǔdū.
He also defeated Mǎ Chāo
and pacified Sòng Jiàn.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Zhāng Lǔ,
he first sent Hé to supervise all armies in attacking Xìnghé and the Dī King Dòu Mào.
When Tàizǔ entered Hànzhōng from Sànguān,
he again first sent Hé to supervise five thousand infantry to clear the path ahead.
Upon reaching Yángpíng,
Lǔ surrendered.
When Tàizǔ returned,
he left Hé and Xiàhóu Yuān to defend Hànzhōng
and resist Liú Bèi.
Hé separately supervised all armies
and secured the surrender of the two commanderies of Bādōng and Bāxī,
moving their people to Hànzhōng.
He advanced his army to Dàngqú,
but was resisted by Bèi's general Zhāng Fēi,
and withdrew to Nánzhèng.
He was appointed General Who Smashes Bandits (Dàngkòu Jiāngjūn).
Liú Bèi was stationed at Yángpíng,
and Hé was stationed at Guǎngshí.
Bèi, with over ten thousand elite soldiers,
divided them into ten detachments,
and launched a rapid night attack on Hé.
Hé led his personal guards to fight,
and Bèi could not overcome them.
Later, Bèi burned the main camp at Zǒumǎ Gǔ,
and Yuān went to put out the fire,
meeting Bèi from another path.
They engaged in battle,
with short weapons clashing.
Yuān then perished,
and Hé returned to Yángpíng.
At this time,
the commander had just been lost,
and fearing that Bèi would take advantage,
all three armies turned pale.
Yuān's Major Guō Huái then ordered the troops, saying:
“General Zhāng
is a famous general of the state,
whom Liú Bèi fears.
Today's situation is urgent;
only General Zhāng can stabilize it.”
So they nominated Hé as the army commander.
Hé came out,
organized the troops and stabilized the formation.
All the generals received Hé's orders,
and the morale of the troops was then settled.
Tàizǔ was in Cháng'ān
and sent an envoy to confer the jié (insignia of authority) upon Hé.
Tàizǔ then personally came to Hànzhōng,
but Liú Bèi held the high mountains and dared not fight.
Tàizǔ then withdrew all the Hànzhōng armies,
and Hé returned to garrison Chéncāng.
When Emperor Wén (Wén Dì) ascended to the kingship,
he appointed Hé (Hé) as General of the Left,
and advanced his peerage to Marquis of Dūxiāng (Dūxiāng Hóu).
When he later ascended the imperial throne,
he was further enfeoffed as Marquis of Mò (Mò Hóu).
An imperial edict ordered Hé (Hé) and Cáo Zhēn (Cáo Zhēn) to suppress the Lúshuǐ Hú (Lúshuǐ Hú) and Eastern Qiāng (Dōng Qiāng) in Āndìng (Āndìng).
Hé (Hé) was summoned to court with Zhēn (Zhēn) at the Xǔ (Xǔ) Palace,
and then dispatched south with Xiàhóu Shàng (Xiàhóu Shàng) to attack Jiānglíng (Jiānglíng).
Hé (Hé) separately commanded his various armies to cross the river
and capture the fortified camps on the island.
When Emperor Míng (Míng Dì) ascended the throne,
Hé (Hé) was dispatched south to garrison Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu),
and, with Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (Sīmǎ Xuānwáng), attacked Sūn Quán's (Sūn Quán) separate general Liú Ā (Liú Ā) and others.
They pursued them to Qíkǒu (Qíkǒu),
engaged in battle,
and defeated them.
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) marched out from Qíshān (Qíshān).
Hé (Hé) was granted the position of Grandee Remonstrant (Tèjìn),
and dispatched to command various armies
to resist Liàng's (Liàng) general Mǎ Sù (Mǎ Sù) at Jiētíng (Jiētíng).
Sù (Sù) relied on the natural barriers of the southern mountains
and did not occupy a city.
Hé (Hé) cut off his water supply route,
attacked,
and heavily defeated him.
The commanderies of Nán'ān (Nán'ān), Tiānshuǐ (Tiānshuǐ), and Āndìng (Āndìng) had revolted in response to Liàng (Liàng);
Hé (Hé) defeated and pacified them all.
An imperial edict stated:
"The bandit Liàng (Liàng), with the forces of Bāshǔ (Bāshǔ),
stood against the army of fierce tigers.
General, you donned armor and wielded weapons,
conquering and pacifying wherever you went;
We greatly commend this.
We increase your fief by one thousand households,
making a total of four thousand three hundred households."
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (Sīmǎ Xuānwáng) was training a navy in Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu),
intending to sail down the Miǎn (Miǎn) into the Jiāng (Jiāng) to attack Wú (Wú).
An edict ordered Hé (Hé) to command the armies of Guānzhōng (Guānzhōng) to go and receive his orders.
When he arrived at Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu),
it happened that the winter waters were shallow,
and large ships could not navigate,
so he returned to garrison Fāngchéng (Fāngchéng).
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) again marched out
and urgently attacked Chéncāng (Chéncāng).
The Emperor dispatched post-horses to summon Hé (Hé) to the capital.
The Emperor himself went to Hénán Chéng (Hénán Chéng),
held a banquet to send Hé (Hé) off,
and dispatched thirty thousand northern and southern army soldiers, and also assigned soldiers from the Wǔwèi (Wǔwèi) and Hǔbēn (Hǔbēn) to escort Hé (Hé).
Then he asked Hé (Hé):
"General, if you are late in arriving,
will Liàng (Liàng) not have already taken Chéncāng (Chéncāng)?"
Hé (Hé) knew that Liàng's (Liàng) isolated army had no grain
and could not attack for long,
so he replied:
"Before your servant arrives,
Liàng (Liàng) will have already fled;
counting on my fingers, Liàng's (Liàng) provisions will not last ten days."
Hé (Hé) advanced day and night to Nánzhèng (Nánzhèng),
and Liàng (Liàng) retreated.
An edict ordered Hé (Hé) to return to the capital,
and he was appointed General of the Chariots and Cavalry Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Chējì Jiāngjūn).
Hé (Hé) understood changes and adaptations,
was skilled in deploying encampments,
and estimated battle situations and terrain;
nothing was contrary to his plans.
Even Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) feared him.
Although Hé (Hé) was a military general, he loved and enjoyed Confucian scholars.
He once recommended his fellow townsman, Bēi Zhàn (Bēi Zhàn), whose understanding of classics and conduct were excellent.
An imperial edict stated:
"In the past, Jì Zūn (Jì Zūn), as a general,
requested the establishment of Five Classics Grandees (Wǔjīng Dàfū),
who resided in the army
and, with the various scholars, elegantly sang and played投壺 (tóuhú).
Now, General, you exert yourself externally with military affairs
and internally hold the state in your heart.
We commend the General's intentions,
and now promote Zhàn (Zhàn) to Erudite (Bóshì)."
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) again marched out from Qíshān (Qíshān).
An edict ordered Hé (Hé) to command the various generals west to Lüèyáng (Lüèyáng).
Liàng (Liàng) returned to secure Qíshān (Qíshān).
Hé (Hé) pursued him to Mùmén (Mùmén),
and engaged Liàng's (Liàng) army in battle.
A flying arrow struck Hé (Hé) in the right knee,
and he died.
His posthumous title was Marquis Zhuàng (Zhuàng Hóu).
His son Xióng (Xióng) succeeded him.
Hé (Hé) had merits in his numerous campaigns and expeditions.
Emperor Míng (Míng Dì) divided Hé's (Hé) households
and enfeoffed Hé's (Hé) four sons as various marquises.
His youngest son was granted the peerage of Marquis of Guānnèi (Guānnèi Hóu).
Xú Huàng (Xú Huàng), courtesy name Gōngmíng (Gōngmíng),
was a native of Yáng (Yáng), Hédōng (Hédōng).
He served as a commandery official,
and, following the General of Chariots and Cavalry Yáng Fèng (Yáng Fèng) to suppress bandits, distinguished himself,
and was appointed Cavalry Commandant (Jì Dūwèi).
When Lǐ Jué (Lǐ Jué) and Guō Sì (Guō Sì) caused chaos in Cháng'ān (Cháng'ān),
Huàng (Huàng) persuaded Fèng (Fèng)
to return to Luòyáng (Luòyáng) with the Emperor.
Fèng (Fèng) followed his plan.
When the Emperor crossed the Hé (Hé) and reached Ānyì (Ānyì),
Huàng (Huàng) was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūting (Dūting Hóu).
Upon arriving in Luòyáng (Luòyáng),
Hán Xiān (Hán Xiān) and Dǒng Chéng (Dǒng Chéng) fought daily.
Huàng (Huàng) persuaded Fèng (Fèng) to return to Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ);
Fèng (Fèng) intended to follow,
but later regretted it.
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) attacked Fèng (Fèng) at Liáng (Liáng),
and Huàng (Huàng) then submitted to Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) gave Huàng (Huàng) troops,
and sent him to attack the bandits of Juǎn (Juǎn) (Juǎn (Juǎn) pronounced Xūquán Fǎn (Xūquán Fǎn))
and Yuánwǔ (Yuánwǔ).
He defeated them
and was appointed Assistant General (Bì Jiāngjūn).
He accompanied in the campaign against Lǚ Bù (Lǚ Bù),
and separately received the surrender of Bù's (Bù) generals Zhào Shù (Zhào Shù) and Lǐ Zōu (Lǐ Zōu) and others.
With Shǐ Huàn (Shǐ Huàn), he beheaded Suī Gù (Suī Gù) in Hénèi (Hénèi).
He accompanied in the defeat of Liú Bèi (Liú Bèi),
and again accompanied in the defeat of Yán Liáng (Yán Liáng),
capturing Báimǎ (Báimǎ).
He advanced to Yánjīn (Yánjīn),
defeated Wén Chǒu (Wén Chǒu),
and was appointed General of the Household (Piānjī Jiāngjūn).
With Cáo Hóng (Cáo Hóng), he attacked the powerful bandit Zhù Bì (Zhù Bì),
defeated him,
and again with Shǐ Huàn (Shǐ Huàn) attacked Yuán Shào's (Yuán Shào) transport carts at Gùshì (Gùshì).
He achieved the most merit,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūting (Dūting Hóu).
After Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) besieged Yè (Yè)
and defeated Hándān (Hándān),
the Prefect of Yìyáng (Yìyáng), Hán Fàn (Hán Fàn), feigned surrender with the city but resisted.
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) sent Huàng (Huàng) to attack him.
When Huàng (Huàng) arrived,
he shot arrows into the city
and explained the successes and failures of battle formations.
Fàn (Fàn) repented,
and Huàng (Huàng) immediately accepted his surrender.
Later, he spoke to Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ), saying:
"The two Yuáns (Yuáns) are not yet defeated,
and the cities not yet taken are listening intently.
If we destroy Yìyáng (Yìyáng today,
tomorrow all will fight to the death,
and I fear Hébĕi (Hébĕi) will never be settled.
I wish Your Grace would accept Yìyáng's (Yìyáng) surrender to show the other cities,
then none will fail to respond at the mere sight of your banner."
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) approved.
He separately attacked Máochéng (Máochéng),
set up ambushes,
and destroyed three camps.
He accompanied in the defeat of Yuán Tán (Yuán Tán) at Nánpí (Nánpí),
and suppressed the rebellious bandits of Píngyuán (Píngyuán),
capturing them.
He accompanied in the campaign against Tàdùn (Tàdùn),
and was appointed General Who Campaigns Across the Wilds (Héngyě Jiāngjūn).
He accompanied in the campaign against Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu),
and separately garrisoned Fán (Fán),
suppressing the bandits of Zhōnglú (Zhōnglú), Línjǔ (Línjǔ), and Yíchéng (Yíchéng).
He also, with Mǎn Chǒng (Mǎn Chǒng), attacked Guān Yǔ (Guān Yǔ) at Hànjīn (Hànjīn),
and with Cáo Rén (Cáo Rén), attacked Zhōu Yú (Zhōu Yú) at Jiānglíng (Jiānglíng).
In the fifteenth year,
he suppressed the rebels of Tàiyuán (Tàiyuán),
besieged Dàlíng (Dàlíng),
captured it,
and beheaded the bandit chief Shāng Yào (Shāng Yào).
When Hán Suì (Hán Suì), Mǎ Chāo (Mǎ Chāo) and others rebelled in Guān Yòu (Guān Yòu),
Huàng (Huàng) was dispatched to garrison Fényīn (Fényīn) to pacify Hédōng (Hédōng).
He was given cattle and wine
and allowed to visit his ancestors' graves.
When Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) arrived at Tóngguān (Tóngguān),
fearing he could not cross,
he summoned Huàng (Huàng) and questioned him.
Huàng (Huàng) said:
"Your Grace has a large army here,
yet the bandits have not separately guarded Púbǎn (Púbǎn);
this shows their lack of strategy.
Now, if you lend your servant elite troops
to cross at Púbǎn (Púbǎn) Ford,
to set up camp first for the army
and cut off their rear,
the bandits can be captured."
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) said:
"Excellent."
He sent Huàng (Huàng) with four thousand infantry and cavalry to cross the ford.
Before the trenches and palisades were completed,
the bandit Liáng Xìng (Liáng Xìng) led over five thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Huàng (Huàng) by night.
Huàng (Huàng) attacked and repelled him,
and Grand Ancestor's (Tàizǔ) army was able to cross.
Then they defeated Chāo (Chāo) and others.
Huàng (Huàng) was sent with Xiàhóu Yuān (Xiàhóu Yuān) to pacify the Dī (Dī) tribes of Yúmí (Yúmí) and Qiān (Qiān),
and then met Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) at Āndìng (Āndìng).
When Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) returned to Yè (Yè),
he sent Huàng (Huàng) with Xiàhóu Yuān (Xiàhóu Yuān) to pacify the remaining bandits in Fū (Fū) and Xiàyáng (Xiàyáng),
beheading Liáng Xìng (Liáng Xìng) and receiving the surrender of over three thousand households.
He accompanied in the campaign against Zhāng Lǔ (Zhāng Lǔ).
Huàng (Huàng) was separately dispatched to attack the Dī (Dī) tribes in the mountains of Gōngdú (Gōngdú) and Qiúyí (Qiúyí),
and they all surrendered.
He was promoted to General Who Pacifies Bandits (Píngkòu Jiāngjūn).
He lifted the siege on General Zhāng Shùn (Zhāng Shùn).
He attacked over thirty bandit camps of Chén Fú (Chén Fú) and others,
and defeated them all.
Tàizǔ returned to Yè,
leaving Huǎng with Xiàhóu Yuān to resist Liú Bèi at Yángpíng.
Bèi sent Chén Shì and over ten camps to cut off the Mǎmínggédào,
but Huǎng separately attacked and defeated them.
The bandits threw themselves into mountain valleys,
many dying.
Tàizǔ heard of this
and was greatly pleased.
He granted Huǎng an imperial staff,
and issued an order saying:
"This plank road
is the vital throat and strategic pass of Hànzhōng.
Liú Bèi wants to cut off communication inside and out
to seize Hànzhōng.
General, with a single action,
you have thwarted the bandits' plan;
this is the best of the best."
Tàizǔ then personally went to Yángpíng
and led out the various armies from Hànzhōng.
He again sent Huǎng to assist Cáo Rén in attacking Guān Yǔ,
stationing him at Wǎn.
At this time, the Hàn River suddenly flooded,
and Yú Jìn and others were lost.
Yǔ besieged Rén at Fán
and also besieged General Lǚ Cháng at Xiāngyáng.
Most of the soldiers Huǎng led were new recruits,
and considering that Yǔ was difficult to contend with head-on,
he advanced to Yánglíng Pí and encamped.
Tàizǔ returned again
and sent Generals Xú Shāng and Lǚ Jiàn to Huǎng,
ordering:
"Wait until the troops are fully assembled
before advancing together."
The bandits were encamped at Yǎncchéng.
When Huǎng arrived,
he deceptively dug a large trench,
feigning a desire to cut off their rear.
The bandits burned their camp and fled.
Huǎng seized Yǎncchéng,
set up continuous camps on two sides,
and gradually advanced,
stopping about thirty feet from the bandits' encirclement.
Before he attacked,
Tàizǔ successively sent Yīn Shǔ, Zhū Gài, and a total of twelve camps to Huǎng.
The bandits had a camp at Wéitóu
and another separate camp at Sìzǒng.
Huǎng loudly announced he would attack the Wéitóu camp
but secretly attacked Sìzǒng.
When Yǔ saw that Sìzǒng was about to fall,
he personally led five thousand infantry and cavalry out to battle.
Huǎng attacked them,
and they fled in retreat.
He then pursued, breaking through and entering the encirclement with them,
defeating them.
Some threw themselves into the Miǎn River and died.
Tàizǔ issued an order saying:
"The bandits' encirclement had ten layers of trenches and abatis.
General, you waged battle and achieved complete victory,
then broke through the bandits' encirclement,
beheading and capturing many.
I have been employing troops for over thirty years,
and among the ancient masters of warfare I have heard of,
none have driven straight into an enemy's encirclement.
Moreover, the siege of Fán and Xiāngyáng
surpassed those of Jǔ and Jìmò.
General, your achievement
exceeds Sūn Wǔ and Ráng Jū."
Huǎng triumphantly returned to Móbēi.
Tàizǔ met Huǎng seven *lǐ* out
and held a grand banquet.
Tàizǔ raised a wine cup to toast Huǎng,
and praised him, saying:
"Saving Fán and Xiāngyáng
is your achievement, General."
At that time, all the armies were assembled.
Tàizǔ inspected the various camps.
The soldiers all left their formations to watch,
but Huǎng's army camp was orderly,
with officers and soldiers standing firm without moving.
Tàizǔ sighed, saying:
"General Xú can be said to have the bearing of Zhōu Yàfū."
When Wén Dì ascended the throne as king,
he appointed Huǎng as Right General
and advanced his peerage to Marquis of Lùxiāng.
When he ascended to emperor,
he advanced his peerage to Marquis of Yáng.
Huǎng and Xiàhóu Shàng attacked Liú Bèi at Shàngyōng
and defeated him.
Huǎng was stationed at Yángpíng
and his peerage was transferred to Marquis of Yángpíng.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
Huǎng resisted the Wú general Zhūgě Jǐn at Xiāngyáng.
His fiefdom was increased by two hundred households,
making a total of three thousand one hundred households.
When he was gravely ill,
he left a will requesting to be clad in everyday clothes for burial.
He was by nature frugal, cautious, and circumspect.
As a general, he always sent out distant scouts,
first ensuring he could not be defeated,
then engaging in battle.
When pursuing a fleeing enemy to seize an advantage,
his soldiers had no time to eat.
He often sighed, saying:
"Ancient people worried about not encountering an enlightened ruler.
Now that I am fortunate to have met one,
I should always exert myself with merit.
What need is there for private reputation?"
He never cultivated extensive connections.
In the first year of Tàihé, he died,
receiving the posthumous title Marquis Zhuàng.
His son Gài succeeded him.
When Gài died,
his son Bà succeeded him.
Míng Dì divided Huǎng's households
and enfeoffed two of Huǎng's descendants as marquises.
Initially,
Zhū Líng of Qīnghé was a general under Yuán Shào.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Táo Qiān,
Shào sent Líng to command three camps to assist Tàizǔ,
and he performed meritorious service in battle.
When the various generals sent by Shào were all dismissed and returned home,
Líng said:
"I have observed many people,
but none are like Cáo Gōng.
This is truly an enlightened lord.
Now that I have met him,
where else should I go?"
So he stayed and did not leave.
His soldiers admired him
and all followed Líng to stay.
Líng later became a good general,
his fame second only to Huǎng and others,
reaching the rank of Posterior General
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāotáng Tíng.
Commentary says: Tàizǔ established these military achievements,
and among the excellent generals of his time,
the Five Generals were foremost.
Yú Jìn was most known for his steadfastness and gravity,
yet he did not end well.
Zhāng Hé was praised for his cunning and adaptability,
Lè Jìn distinguished himself with his bravery and ferocity,
but examining their actions,
they did not fully live up to what was heard.
Perhaps there are omissions in the records,
not as detailed as those of Zhāng Liáo and Xú Huǎng.
Biographies of the Two Lǐs, Zāng, Wén, Lǚ, Xǔ, Diǎn, the Two Pángs, and Yán, Chapter Eighteen
Lǐ Diǎn, courtesy name Mánchéng,
was a native of Jùyě, Shānyáng.
Diǎn's paternal uncle Gān was heroic
and gathered several thousand families of retainers in Chéngshì.
During the Chūpíng era,
he followed Tàizǔ with his multitude,
defeated the Yellow Turban rebels at Shòuzhāng,
and then followed him to attack Yuán Shù
and campaign in Xúzhōu.
During Lǚ Bù's rebellion,
Tàizǔ sent Gān back to Chéngshì
to console the various counties.
Lǚ Bù's *biéjià* Xuē Lán and *zhìzhōng* Lǐ Fēng invited Gān,
wanting to rebel together.
Gān refused to listen
and was consequently killed.
Tàizǔ ordered Gān's son Zhěng to lead Gān's troops
and attack Lán and Fēng with the other generals.
Lán and Fēng were defeated.
Zhěng then helped pacify the various counties of Yǎnzhōu and performed meritorious service,
gradually being promoted to Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
When Zhěng died,
Diǎn was transferred to be Magistrate of Yǐngyīn,
appointed as a Zhonglang Jiang,
leading Zhěng's army,
and promoted to Grand Administrator of Líhú.
At that time, Tài-Zǔ and Yuán Shào were locked in a standoff at Guān-Dù.
Diǎn led his clan and retainers to transport grain and silk to supply the army.
After Shào was defeated,
Diǎn was appointed General of the Household (Bì-Jiāngjūn)
and garrisoned at Ān-Mín.
Tài-Zǔ attacked Tán and Shàng at Lí-Yáng,
sending Diǎn and Chéng Yù to transport military provisions by boat.
Coincidentally, Shàng dispatched Gāo Fān, the Administrator of Wèi-Jùn, to lead troops and garrison the river,
cutting off the waterway.
Tài-Zǔ instructed Diǎn and Yù:
"If the boats cannot pass,
then proceed via the land route."
Diǎn discussed with the various generals, saying:
"Fān's army is lightly armored and relies on the water;
they have a negligent attitude,
so attacking them will surely lead to victory.
The army cannot be restricted by internal regulations;
if it benefits the state,
it is permissible to act independently,
so we should attack quickly."
Yù also agreed.
So, they crossed the river northwards,
attacked Fān,
defeated him,
and the waterway became open.
Liú Biǎo sent Liú Bèi to invade the north,
reaching Yè.
Tài-Zǔ sent Diǎn to resist him with Xiàhóu Dūn.
One day, Bèi burned his encampment and departed.
Dūn led the various armies in pursuit.
Diǎn said:
"The bandit has retreated without cause;
I suspect there must be an ambush.
The southern road is narrow,
and the vegetation is dense,
so we should not pursue."
Dūn did not listen,
and pursued with Yú Jìn.
Diǎn remained to guard.
Dūn and the others indeed entered the bandit's ambush,
and the battle went unfavorably.
Diǎn went to their rescue.
Bèi, seeing the rescue arrive,
dispersed and retreated.
He participated in the siege of Yè.
After Yè was settled,
he, with Lè Jìn, besieged Gāo Gàn at Hú-Guān,
and attacked Guǎn Chéng at Cháng-Guǎng,
defeating them all.
He was promoted to General Who Captures Enemies (Bǔlǔ-Jiāngjūn)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dū-Tíng.
Diǎn's clan and retainers, numbering over three thousand households,
resided in Chéng-Shì.
He personally requested to move to Wèi-Jùn.
Tài-Zǔ laughed and said:
"Do you wish to emulate Gěng Chún?"
Diǎn bowed and replied:
"Your servant is untalented and timid, with meager achievements,
yet my rank and favor are excessively generous.
It is truly proper for my entire clan to exert their strength.
Furthermore, with campaigns and expeditions not yet ceased,
it is advisable to strengthen the inner suburbs
to control the four directions.
I do not emulate Chún."
Thus, he moved his retainers and clan, over thirteen thousand individuals, to reside in Yè.
Tài-Zǔ commended him,
promoting him to General Who Breaks Enemies (Pòlǔ-Jiāngjūn).
He was garrisoned at Hé-Féi with Zhāng Liáo and Lè Jìn.
Sūn Quán led his forces to besiege it.
Liáo wanted to follow orders and sally out to battle.
Jìn, Diǎn, and Liáo had long been on unfriendly terms.
Liáo feared they would not comply.
Diǎn said with emotion:
"This is a great matter of the state.
It depends only on your plan.
How can I, for a private grudge, forget public righteousness!"
Thereupon, he led his troops with Liáo to defeat and rout Quán.
His enfeoffment was increased by one hundred households,
making a total of three hundred households.
Diǎn enjoyed learning,
valued refinement,
and did not contend for merit with the other generals.
He respected scholars and officials,
being humble as if feeling inferior,
and was called "the Elder" in the army.
He died at the age of thirty-six.
His son Zhēn inherited.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
remembering the merit at Hé-Féi,
he increased Zhēn's enfeoffment by one hundred households
and bestowed upon one of Diǎn's sons the title of Marquis of Guānnèi,
with an enfeoffment of one hundred households.
Diǎn was posthumously given the epithet Mǐn-Hóu.
Lǐ Tōng, courtesy name Wén-Dá,
was a native of Píng-Chūn, Jiāng-Xià.
He was known for his chivalry between the Jiāng and Rú rivers.
He raised an army with his fellow county-man Chén Gōng in Lǎng-Líng,
and many flocked to them.
At that time, there was Zhōu Zhí,
with over two thousand households, who was outwardly friendly but inwardly deceitful towards Gōng and Tōng.
Tōng wanted to plot to kill Zhí, but Gōng hesitated.
Tōng knew Gōng lacked resolve,
so he made the decision alone,
arranged a meeting with Zhí,
and killed Zhí when they were deep in their cups.
The multitude was greatly alarmed.
Tōng led Gōng to execute Zhí's faction leaders
and completely absorbed their encampment.
Later, Chén Hé, Gōng's wife's younger brother,
killed Gōng and seized his followers.
Tōng attacked and defeated Hé's army,
beheading Hé and offering his head as a sacrifice at Gōng's tomb.
He also captured alive Wú Bà, a great leader of the Yellow Turbans, and forced his subordinates to surrender.
During a year of great famine,
Tōng spent his entire family fortune on relief,
sharing dregs and husks with his soldiers,
and all eagerly served him,
which is why bandits dared not trespass.
Early in the Jiàn'ān [reign period],
Tōng led his entire host to Tàizǔ in Xǔ.
Tōng was appointed Zhènwēi Zhōnglángjiāng,
and garrisoned the western border of Rǔnán.
When Tàizǔ attacked Zhāng Xiù,
Liú Biǎo dispatched troops to assist Xiù,
and Tàizǔ's army was at a disadvantage.
Tōng led troops by night to Tàizǔ,
Tàizǔ was thus able to fight again,
Tōng was the first to ascend,
and greatly defeated Xiù's army.
He was appointed Bì Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Jiàngōng Hóu.
Two counties of Rǔnán were divided,
and Tōng was made Yáng'ān Dūwèi.
Tōng's wife's maternal uncle committed a crime,
and Zhào Yǎn, the Magistrate of Lánglíng, arrested and prosecuted him,
sentencing him to capital punishment.
At this time, the power of life and death
was decided by the Mùshǒu.
Tōng's wife and children wept and pleaded for his life.
Tōng said:
"I am currently exerting myself alongside Cáo Gōng;
it would be unrighteous to sacrifice public duty for private interests."
He admired Yǎn for upholding the law impartially,
and became close friends with him.
Tàizǔ and Yuán Shào confronted each other at Guāndù.
Shào sent an envoy to appoint Tōng as Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn,
Liú Biǎo also secretly tried to recruit him,
but Tōng rejected them all.
Tōng's relatives and subordinates wept and said:
"Now we are isolated and guarding alone,
having lost great support,
and demise can be expected immediately.
It is better to quickly follow Shào."
Tōng grasped his sword and rebuked them, saying:
"Cáo Gōng is wise and brilliant,
and will surely pacify the world.
Although Shào is strong and powerful,
he employs people without principle,
and will eventually become a captive.
I will not be disloyal even unto death."
He then executed Shào's envoy,
and sent the seal and ribbon to Tàizǔ.
He also attacked the bandit leaders Qú Gōng, Jiāng Gōng, Shěn Chéng, and others in the commandery,
breaking and scattering their forces,
and sending their heads.
Thus, the lands of Huái and Rǔ were pacified.
He was re-enfeoffed as Dūtíng Hóu,
and appointed Rǔnán Tàishǒu.
At that time, bandits like Zhāng Chì and over five thousand families gathered at Táo Shān,
and Tōng attacked and defeated them.
Liú Bèi and Zhōu Yú besieged Cáo Rén at Jiānglíng,
and separately dispatched Guān Yǔ to cut off the northern road.
Tōng led his forces to attack him,
dismounted, pulled out the deer antlers, and entered the encirclement,
fighting and advancing,
to meet Rén's army.
His bravery surpassed all other generals.
Tōng became ill and died on the road,
at the age of forty-two.
His fief was posthumously increased by two hundred households,
making a total of four hundred households.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he was given the posthumous title of Gāng Hóu.
An imperial edict stated:
"During the calamity of Yuán Shào,
from Xǔ and Cài southward,
people harbored disloyal intentions.
Tōng upheld righteousness without hesitation,
and caused those with wavering loyalties to submit;
We greatly commend him for this.
Unfortunately, he died early.
Although his son Jī has already inherited the peerage,
it is not enough to reward his meritorious service.
Jī's elder brother Xù
previously garrisoned Fánchéng,
and also had merits.
The family's efforts have been consistently diligent.
Therefore, let Jī be appointed Fèngyì Zhōnglángjiāng,
and Xù be Pínglǔ Zhōnglángjiāng,
to honor and distinguish them."
Zāng Bà, courtesy name Xuāngāo,
was a native of Huà in Tài-shān.
His father, Jiè,
was a prison clerk in the county.
He upheld the law and refused the Grand Administrator's wish to privately execute someone.
The Grand Administrator was furious,
and ordered Jiè to be arrested and brought to the prefecture.
At that time, there were more than a hundred escorts.
Bà, then eighteen years old,
led several dozen retainers directly to the Xī-shān mountains of Fèi to intercept and rescue him.
The escorts dared not move.
Consequently, he and his father fled to Dōng-hǎi,
and from then on, he became known for his bravery and strength.
When the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out,
Bà followed Táo Qiān and defeated them,
and was appointed Colonel of Cavalry (Qí Dūwèi).
He then gathered troops in Xú-zhōu,
and with Sūn Guān, Wú Dūn, Yǐn Lǐ, and others, assembled a large force.
Bà was their commander,
garrisoned at Kāi-yáng.
When Tài-zǔ (Cáo Cāo) was attacking Lǚ Bù,
Bà and the others led troops to assist Bù.
After Bù was captured,
Bà went into hiding.
Tài-zǔ sought him out and found him.
Upon seeing him, he was pleased,
and sent Bà to recruit Wú Dūn, Yǐn Lǐ, Sūn Guān, and Guān's elder brother Kāng, among others.
All of them went to Tài-zǔ.
Tài-zǔ appointed Bà as Grand Administrator of Láng-yá,
Dūn as Grand Administrator of Lì-chéng, Lǐ of Dōng-guǎn, Guān of Běi-hǎi, and Kāng of Chéng-yáng.
He divided Qīng and Xú provinces,
entrusting them to Bà.
When Tài-zǔ was in Yǎn-zhōu,
he had appointed Xú Xī and Má Hoé as generals.
When Yǎn-zhōu fell into chaos,
Xī and Hoé both rebelled.
Later, Yǎn-zhōu was pacified,
and Xī and Hoé fled to Bà.
Tài-zǔ spoke to Liú Bèi,
