asking him to tell Bà to send the heads of the two men.
Bà said to Bèi:
"The reason Bà has been able to establish himself
is precisely by not doing such things.
Bà has received the Duke's (Tài-zǔ's) grace of saving his life,
and dares not disobey orders.
However, a sovereign who practices hegemony (wáng-bà) can be reasoned with through righteousness.
I wish the General (Liú Bèi) would make a plea for them."
Bèi reported Bà's words to Tài-zǔ,
who sighed
and said to Bà:
"This is the deed of ancient men, and you are able to perform it.
This is my wish."
He then appointed both Xī and Hoé as commandery governors.
At that time, Tài-zǔ was resisting Yuán Shào,
and Bà repeatedly led elite troops into Qīng-zhōu,
thus Tài-zǔ was able to focus solely on Shào,
not needing to worry about the eastern region.
When Tài-zǔ defeated Yuán Tán at Nán-pí,
Bà and others gathered to congratulate him.
Bà then requested permission to send his sons, nephews, and the family members of his generals' fathers and elder brothers to Yè.
Tài-zǔ said:
"Your loyalty and filial piety,
how could it be merely in this!
In the past, Xiāo Hé sent his sons and nephews to serve,
and Gāo-zǔ did not refuse;
Gěng Chún burned his house and carried his coffin to follow,
and Guāng-wǔ did not oppose it.
What could I use to change this!"
When the eastern provinces were in turmoil,
Bà and others upheld righteousness and suppressed tyranny,
pacifying and settling the Hǎi and Dài regions.
Their achievements were immense,
and all were enfeoffed as marquises.
Bà was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dū-tíng,
and given the additional title of General Who Dominates Barbarians (Wēi-lǔ Jiāngjūn).
He also joined Yú Jìn in attacking Chāng Xī,
and Xiàhóu Yuān in attacking the remaining Yellow Turban bandits Xú Hé and others.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Inspector of Xú-zhōu (Xú-zhōu Cìshǐ).
Wǔ Zhōu of Pèi-guó (appointed (Duke)) served as Magistrate of Xià-pí.
Bà respected Zhōu extraordinarily,
and personally visited the magistrate's residence.
An aide in Bà's command, Zǒng Tǒng, acted unlawfully.
Zhōu discovered his crime,
immediately arrested and interrogated him to conclusion.
Bà increasingly admired Zhōu for this.
He followed in attacking Sūn Quán,
being the first to climb,
entering Cháo-hú twice,
attacking Jū-cháo,
and defeating it.
When Zhāng Liáo attacked Chén Lán,
Bà was separately dispatched to Wǎn,
to attack the Wú general Hán Dāng,
preventing Quán from rescuing Lán.
Dāng sent troops to intercept Bà.
Bà fought with them at Féng-lóng.
Dāng again sent troops to block Bà at Jiá-shí,
where Bà fought and defeated them,
then returned to garrison at Shū.
Quán sent tens of thousands of men by boat to garrison at the mouth of Shū,
dividing his troops to rescue Lán.
Upon hearing that Bà's army was at Shū,
he retreated.
Bà pursued them at night.
By dawn,
having traveled over a hundred *lǐ*,
he intercepted the bandits and attacked them from front and rear.
The bandits were in distress,
unable to board their boats,
and many jumped into the water.
Thus, the bandits could not rescue Lán,
and Liáo subsequently defeated him.
Bà followed in attacking Sūn Quán at Rú-xū-kǒu.
He and Zhāng Liáo were the vanguard.
As they marched, they encountered continuous rain.
The main army arrived first,
and the water level rose significantly.
The bandit boats gradually advanced,
and all the officers and soldiers were uneasy.
Liáo wanted to leave,
but Bà stopped him, saying:
"You (the Duke) are clear about advantages and disadvantages,
how could you abandon us?"
The next day, an order indeed arrived.
When Liáo arrived,
he told this to Tài-zǔ.
Tài-zǔ praised him,
and appointed him General Who Manifests Awe (Yáng-wēi Jiāngjūn),
and granted him the Staff of Authority (jiǎ-jié).
Later, Quán requested surrender,
and Tài-zǔ returned,
leaving Bà with Xiàhóu Dūn and others to garrison at Jū-cháo.
When Emperor Wén (Cáo Pī) ascended the throne as King,
Bà was promoted to General Who Guards the East (Zhèn-dōng Jiāngjūn),
advanced in peerage to Marquis of Wǔ'ān Rural District (Wǔ'ān Xiāng-hóu),
and Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Qīng-zhōu (Dū-dū Qīng-zhōu Zhū Jūnshì).
When he (Cáo Pī) ascended the imperial throne,
Bà was further enfeoffed as Marquis of Kāi-yáng,
then transferred to be Marquis of Liáng-chéng.
He joined Cáo Xiū in attacking the Wú bandits,
defeating Lǚ Fàn at Dòng-pǔ.
He was summoned to be Bearer of the Gilded Mace (Zhí-jīn-wú),
with the rank of Special Advanced Official (Tè-jìn).
Whenever there were military matters,
the Emperor (Cáo Pī) always consulted him.
When Emperor Míng (Cáo Ruì) ascended the throne,
his stipend was increased by five hundred households,
totaling three thousand five hundred households.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the title Marquis Wēi.
His son, Ài, succeeded him.
Ài reached the official positions of Inspector of Qīng-zhōu and Privy Treasurer (Shào-fǔ).
When Ài died,
he was posthumously granted the title Marquis Gōng.
His son, Quán, succeeded him.
Bà had merits both before and after,
and three of his sons were enfeoffed as marquises,
and one was granted the peerage of Marquis within the Passes (Guān-nèi Hóu).
Sūn Guān also reached the position of Inspector of Qīng-zhōu,
was granted the Staff of Authority,
and followed Tài-zǔ in attacking Sūn Quán.
He was wounded in battle
and died.
His son, Yù, succeeded him,
and also reached the position of Inspector of Qīng-zhōu.
Wén Pìn, courtesy name Zhòngyè,
was a native of Wǎn in Nányáng.
He was a great general under Liú Biǎo,
and was tasked with defending the northern frontier.
When Liú Biǎo died,
his son Cóng succeeded him.
When Tài Zǔ campaigned in Jīngzhōu,
Cóng surrendered the entire province.
He summoned Wén Pìn, intending to surrender together,
but Wén Pìn said:
"I, Pìn, could not preserve the province whole,
so I should await punishment instead."
When Tài Zǔ crossed the Hàn River,
Wén Pìn then went to meet him.
Tài Zǔ asked:
"Why are you so late?"
Wén Pìn replied:
"Previously, I could not assist Liú Jīngzhōu in serving the state.
Although Jīngzhōu has fallen,
I constantly wished to hold Hanchuan,
to preserve its territory,
so that alive I would not fail the vulnerable,
and dead I would have no shame underground.
But by force of circumstances,
it has come to this.
I truly feel sorrow and shame,
and had no face to see you earlier."
Thereupon, he sighed and wept.
Tài Zǔ, deeply moved, said:
"Zhòngyè,
you are truly a loyal minister!"
He treated him with great courtesy.
He assigned Wén Pìn troops
and sent him with Cáo Chún to pursue and attack Liú Bèi at Chángbǎn.
Tài Zǔ first pacified Jīngzhōu.
As Jiāngxià bordered Wú,
and the people were unsettled,
he appointed Wén Pìn as Administrator of Jiāngxià,
tasking him with commanding the northern troops,
and entrusted him with frontier affairs.
He was granted the title of Marquis within the Pass (Guānnèi Hóu).
He campaigned with Yuè Jìn against Guān Yǔ at Xúnkǒu,
achieving merit,
and was promoted to Marquis of Yánshòu Pavilion (Yánshòu Tínghóu),
and given the additional title of General Who Suppresses Rebels (Tǎonì Jiāngjūn).
He also attacked Guān Yǔ's baggage train at Hànjīn,
and burned his ships at Jīngchéng.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
Wén Pìn was advanced to Marquis of Cháng'ān Village (Cháng'ān Xiānghóu),
and granted a temporary credential (jiǎ jié).
He besieged Jiānglíng with Xiàhóu Shàng,
and Wén Pìn was ordered to set up a separate garrison at Miǎnkǒu,
stationing himself at Shífàn.
He commanded a contingent himself,
and for his merit in resisting the enemy,
he was promoted to General of the Rear (Hòu Jiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīnyě (Xīnyě Hóu).
Sūn Quán, with 50,000 men, personally besieged Wén Pìn at Shíyáng.
The situation was dire,
but Wén Pìn held his ground firmly.
Sūn Quán remained for more than twenty days before withdrawing.
Wén Pìn pursued and defeated him.
His household stipend was increased by 500 households,
making a total of 1900 households.
Wén Pìn was stationed in Jiāngxià for several decades,
possessing both authority and kindness.
His fame struck fear into enemy states,
and the bandits dared not invade.
A portion of Wén Pìn's households and fief was used to enfeoff Wén Pìn's son, Dài, as a 列侯 (liè hóu, marquis of a commandery or county).
Wén Pìn's cousin, Hòu, was also granted the title of Marquis within the Pass (Guānnèi Hóu).
When Wén Pìn died,
he was posthumously titled Zhuàng Hóu.
Dài had died earlier,
so Wén Pìn's adopted son, Xiū, inherited.
When Xiū died,
his son, Wǔ, inherited.
During the Jiāpíng era,
Huán Yú of Qiáojùn served as Administrator of Jiāngxià.
He was pure and frugal, possessing authority and kindness,
and his reputation was second only to Wén Pìn's.
Lǚ Qián, courtesy name Zǐkè,
was a native of Rènchéng.
When Tài Zǔ was in Yǎnzhōu,
hearing that Lǚ Qián possessed courage and strategy,
he appointed him as an aide (cóngshì),
and had him lead his personal troops to guard Húlù.
The people of 校尉 (xiàowèi) Dù Sōng's division, Jìng Mǔ and others, rebelled
and colluded with Chāng Xī.
Tài Zǔ appointed Lǚ Qián to replace Dù Sōng.
Upon arrival, Lǚ Qián
lured the leaders of Jìng Mǔ and several tens of their evil confederates,
and offered them wine and food.
He arranged for strong warriors to lie in ambush nearby.
When Lǚ Qián observed that Jìng Mǔ and the others were all drunk,
he ordered the hidden troops to kill them all.
He then pacified the remaining populace,
and the bandits were quelled.
Tài Zǔ appointed Lǚ Qián to govern Tàishān Commandery.
The commandery bordered mountains and the sea,
and due to the unrest of the age,
it was known that many commoners were hiding.
Guō Zǔ, Gōngsūn Dú and several tens of others, appointed as Colonels (Zhōnglángjiàng) by Yuán Shào,
occupied the mountains and became bandits,
causing suffering to the people.
Lǚ Qián led his personal troops to the commandery,
and extended grace and trust.
Guō Zǔ's and the others' followers all surrendered,
and all those who had fled and hidden in the mountains came out and settled down to their livelihoods.
He selected the strong among them to serve as warriors,
and Tàishān consequently acquired elite troops,
renowned throughout the provinces and commanderies.
The Yellow Turban rebels Xú Hé and others in Jìnán
robbed local officials wherever they went and
attacked cities and towns.
Lǚ Qián led his troops to join Xiàhóu Yuān in attacking them,
engaging in several tens of battles,
and slaying or capturing several thousand people.
Tài Zǔ made him supervise the troops of the various commanderies in Qīngzhōu to suppress the bandits Lǐ Tiáo and others in Dōnglái,
in which he was successful.
Tài Zǔ issued an order stating:
"Indeed, one who has the will
will certainly accomplish his task;
this is what true heroes pursue.
Since you took office in the commandery,
you have captured evildoers and suppressed the violent,
bringing peace to the common people.
You personally braved arrows and stones,
and whatever you campaigned against, you conquered.
Formerly, Kòu Xún established his name in Rǔ and Yǐng,
and Gěng Yǎn offered strategies in Qīng and Yǎn;
the past and present are one."
He was nominated as "Flourishing Talent" (Màocái),
given the additional title of Cavalry Commandant (Qí Dūwèi),
and continued to administer the commandery as before.
Lǚ Qián was in Tàishān for more than ten years,
and was greatly respected and benevolent.
When Wén Dì became king,
he was promoted to Assistant General (Bì Jiāngjūn),
enfeoffed as Marquis of Yìshòu Pavilion (Yìshòu Tínghóu),
and transferred to Inspector of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ),
with the additional title of General Who Intimidates Barbarians (Wēilǔ Jiāngjūn).
He invited Wáng Xiáng of Lángxié to be his chief aide (biéjià),
and entrusted all civil affairs to him.
People often praised his ability to employ the worthy.
He suppressed the rebel bandits in Lìchéng,
achieving merit through beheadings and captures.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Wànnián Pavilion (Wànnián Tínghóu),
his household stipend was increased by 200,
making a total of 600 households.
When Lǚ Qián died,
his son Fān inherited.
When Fān died,
his son Guì inherited.
Xǔ Chǔ, courtesy name Zhòngkāng,
was a native of Qiáo in Qiáoguó.
He was over eight chi tall,
with a waist ten spans in circumference,
a majestic and resolute appearance,
and strength surpassing others.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
he gathered several thousand families of youths and clansmen,
and together they fortified their stronghold to resist bandits.
At that time, over ten thousand bandits from Gé Pí in Rǔnán attacked Xǔ Chǔ's stronghold.
Xǔ Chǔ's forces were few and no match for them,
and after fighting fiercely, they were utterly exhausted.
Their arrows and weapons were depleted,
so he ordered the men and women in the stronghold
to gather and prepare stones the size of basins or buckets and place them at the four corners.
Xǔ Chǔ hurled the stones,
and whatever they hit was shattered.
The bandits dared not advance.
When provisions ran low,
he feigned a truce with the bandits,
offering a cow to exchange for food.
When the bandits came to take the cow,
the cow repeatedly bolted back.
Xǔ Chǔ then went out to the front of the formation,
and with one hand dragged the cow by its tail in the opposite direction,
moving it over a hundred paces.
The bandits were astonished,
and consequently dared not take the cow and fled.
From then on, throughout the area between the Huái, Rǔ, Chén, and Liáng rivers,
all who heard of him feared and dreaded him.
Tàizǔ campaigned through Huái and Rǔ.
Chǔ led his followers to join Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ saw him and was impressed, saying:
"This is my Fán Kuài!"
That very day, he appointed him Dūwèi
and brought him into the imperial guard.
All the swordsmen who followed Chǔ
were made tiger-warriors.
He accompanied on the campaign against Zhāng Xiù,
was the first to ascend,
beheaded tens of thousands,
and was promoted to Xiàowèi.
He accompanied the expedition against Yuán Shào at Guāndù.
At that time, Xú Tā and other constant attendants plotted rebellion.
Because Chǔ was always by the Emperor's side,
they feared him and dared not act.
They waited for a day when Chǔ was off duty.
Tā and the others entered with knives hidden.
When Chǔ reached his quarters, his heart stirred,
so he immediately returned to attendance.
Tā and the others did not know this
and entered the tent to see Chǔ,
whereupon they were greatly astonished.
Tā's expression changed,
Chǔ perceived this,
and immediately struck down Tā and the others.
Tàizǔ trusted him even more,
and they went in and out together,
never leaving each other's side.
He accompanied the siege of Yè,
fought bravely and gained merit,
and was bestowed the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
He accompanied the expedition against Hán Suì and Mǎ Chāo at Tóngguān.
Tàizǔ was about to cross north.
Upon reaching the Jì River,
he first sent the troops across,
and remained on the south bank with only Chǔ and over a hundred tiger-warriors to cover the rear.
Mǎ Chāo, leading over ten thousand infantry and cavalry,
came rushing towards Tàizǔ's army,
arrows falling like rain.
Chǔ told Tàizǔ,
"The enemy is numerous,
and our troops have all crossed.
We should leave."
Then he helped Tàizǔ onto a boat.
The enemy pressed hard,
the army scrambled to cross,
and the boat was heavy and about to sink.
Chǔ cut down those clinging to the boat,
and with his left hand held up a saddle to shield Tàizǔ.
The boatman was hit by a stray arrow and died.
Chǔ used his right hand to paddle the boat,
and barely managed to cross.
On that day,
had it not been for Chǔ, Tàizǔ would have been in great peril.
Afterwards, Tàizǔ met Hán Suì and Mǎ Chāo alone for talks,
allowing no attendants to follow,
except for Chǔ.
Mǎ Chāo, relying on his strength,
secretly intended to charge at Tàizǔ.
He had long heard of Chǔ's bravery,
and suspected that the attendant on horseback was Chǔ.
So he asked Tàizǔ:
"Where is your 'Tiger Marquis'?"
Tàizǔ looked and pointed at Chǔ,
and Chǔ glared at him with wide eyes.
Mǎ Chāo dared not move,
and they each withdrew.
A few days later, they met in battle,
and Mǎ Chāo and his forces were severely defeated.
Chǔ personally beheaded many,
and was promoted to Wǔwèi Zhōnglángjiàng.
The title of Wǔwèi
began from this time.
The army called Chǔ "Tiger Fool" because he was as strong as a tiger but somewhat slow-witted.
Therefore, he was called Hǔchī;
thus Mǎ Chāo asked about the Tiger Marquis,
and to this day people throughout the realm refer to him as such,
all believing it to be his name.
Chǔ's nature was cautious and law-abiding,
solid and taciturn.
Cáo Rén came from Jīngzhōu to pay respects at court.
As Tàizǔ had not yet come out,
he entered and met Chǔ outside the hall.
Rén called Chǔ to come in and sit down to talk.
Chǔ said:
"The King is about to come out."
Then he returned to the hall.
Rén was displeased.
Someone criticized Chǔ, saying:
"The Grand Marshal (Cáo Rén), a highly esteemed relative of the imperial clan,
humbled himself to call you.
Why did you refuse?"
Chǔ said:
"Although he is an esteemed relative,
he is an outer feudatory.
I am an inner minister.
Talking in public is sufficient.
Why speak privately in a room?"
Tàizǔ heard this
and loved and treated him even more,
promoting him to Zhōngjiān Jiāngjūn.
When Tàizǔ died,
Chǔ wailed and coughed up blood.
When Wéndì ascended the throne,
he was advanced to Wànsuìtíng Hóu,
promoted to Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn,
and made Dūdū of the Central Army's palace guard and forbidden troops.
He was very intimate with him.
Initially,
Chǔ's tiger-warriors who accompanied him on campaigns,
Tàizǔ considered them all brave warriors,
and appointed them all generals on the same day.
Afterwards, dozens of them were made generals and enfeoffed as marquises for their merits,
and over a hundred became Dūwèi and Xiàowèi.
All were swordsmen.
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
he was advanced to Mùxiāng Hóu,
with seven hundred households in his fief,
and one of his sons was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
When Chǔ died,
he was posthumously titled Zhuàng Hóu.
His son Yí succeeded him.
Chǔ's elder brother Dìng,
also for military merit, was appointed Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn,
and Dūdū of the border patrol's tiger-贲.
During the Tàihé era,
the Emperor, mindful of Chǔ's loyalty and filial piety,
issued an edict praising him,
and further granted two of Chǔ's descendants the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
Yí was killed by Zhōng Huì.
In the early Tàishǐ era,
his son Zōng succeeded him.
Diǎn Wěi,
was a man from Jǐwú in Chénliú.
He had a magnificent physique,
and his strength surpassed that of ordinary men.
He possessed a strong will, integrity, and a chivalrous spirit.
The Liú family of Xiāngyì was at odds with Lǐ Yǒng of Suīyáng,
and Wěi decided to avenge them.
Yǒng, a former Magistrate of Fùchūn,
maintained very strict security.
Wěi rode in a cart loaded with chickens and wine,
pretending to be a gate attendant.
When the gate opened,
he entered with a dagger hidden in his bosom and killed Yǒng,
and also killed his wife.
He then calmly exited,
took the saber and halberds from his cart,
and walked [went away].
Yǒng's residence was near the market,
and the entire market was alarmed.
Hundreds pursued him,
but none dared to approach.
After walking four or five Lǐ,
he met his companions,
and fighting his way, he managed to escape.
From then on, he became known to heroes.
During the Chūpíng era,
Zhāng Miǎo raised an army of righteousness.
Wěi joined as a soldier,
subordinate to the Sīmǎ Zhào Chǒng.
The flag of the yámén was very large,
and no one could manage it,
but Wěi erected it with one hand.
Chǒng was impressed by his talent and strength.
Later, he served under Xiàhóu Dūn,
and several times gained merit by beheading enemies,
whereupon he was appointed Sīmǎ.
Tàizǔ campaigned against Lǚ Bù at Púyáng.
Bù had a separate encampment forty to fifty Lǐ west of Púyáng.
Tàizǔ launched a night attack,
and by dawn, he had defeated them.
Before he could withdraw,
Bù's relief forces arrived,
and a battle ensued on three sides.
At that time, Bù personally engaged in battle.
From dawn until midday, there were dozens of engagements,
and the standoff was intense.
Tàizǔ recruited those who would break through the enemy lines.
Wěi was the first to volunteer,
leading dozens of recruits.
All were heavily clothed and wore two layers of armor,
discarding their shields,
and only carrying long spears and hooked halberds.
At that moment, the western front became critical.
Wěi advanced to confront them.
The rebels' bows and crossbows fired indiscriminately,
arrows falling like rain.
Wěi did not flinch,
and said to his men:
"Tell me when the enemy is ten paces away."
His men said:
"They are ten paces away!"
He then said:
"Tell me when they are five paces away."
His men, in fear,
quickly cried out,
"The enemy is here!"
Wěi, holding more than ten halberds,
let out a great roar and charged.
Wherever he struck, none failed to fall immediately.
Bù's forces retreated.
As it was getting dark,
Tàizǔ was able to withdraw.
Wěi was appointed Dūwèi,
and brought to Tàizǔ's side.
He commanded several hundred personal guards,
who constantly encircled the main tent.
Wěi was not only strong and brave,
but his subordinates were all elite soldiers.
In every battle,
he was always the first to climb the ramparts and break through enemy lines.
He was promoted to Xiàowèi.
He was inherently loyal, meticulous, and prudent.
He often stood guard throughout the day,
and slept by the tent at night,
rarely returning to his private quarters.
He loved wine and food;
he could drink and eat more than an ordinary person.
Whenever food was bestowed upon him in front of Tàizǔ,
he would drink copiously and slurp loudly,
with those on his left and right continuously serving him.
It took several men to keep him supplied,
and Tàizǔ admired his prowess.
Wěi liked to wield a pair of large halberds and long sabers.
The army had a saying about him:
"Among the valiant warriors under the tent, there is Lord Diǎn,
who carries a pair of halberds weighing eighty Jīn."
When Tàizǔ campaigned in Jīngzhōu,
he reached Wǎn,
where Zhāng Xiù surrendered.
Tàizǔ was very pleased,
and invited Xiù and his commanders
to a grand feast with wine.
As Tàizǔ walked around offering wine,
Wěi stood behind him, holding a large axe
with a blade a foot in diameter.
Wherever Tàizǔ went,
Wěi would raise his axe and glare at those present.
Throughout the feast,
Xiù and his commanders dared not look up.
More than ten days later,
Xiù rebelled,
attacking Tàizǔ's camp.
Tàizǔ's counterattack was unsuccessful,
and he withdrew with his light cavalry.
Wěi fought at the gate,
preventing the rebels from entering.
The soldiers then dispersed and entered through other gates.
At that time, Wěi's company still had more than ten men,
all fighting desperately,
each capable of holding off ten.
The rebels coming from front and rear gradually increased in number.
Wěi used his long halberd to strike left and right.
Each thrust
would shatter more than ten spears.
Almost all of his remaining men were dead or wounded.
Wěi suffered dozens of wounds.
Engaging in close combat with short weapons,
the rebels pressed in on him.
Wěi clasped two rebels under his arms and killed them.
The remaining rebels dared not advance.
Wěi again charged forward,
killing several more.
His severe wounds flared up,
and he died with glaring eyes and a great curse.
Only then did the rebels dare to advance,
take his head,
pass it around for all to see,
and then gather around to look at his body.
Tàizǔ retreated to Wǔyīn.
Upon hearing of Wěi's death,
he shed tears,
recruited men to retrieve his body in secret,
personally attended his mourning,
and sent his body back to Xiāngyì for burial.
He appointed Wěi's son, Mǎn, as Lángzhōng.
Whenever the imperial carriage passed by,
sacrifices of an "intermediate offering" were always made to him.
Tàizǔ missed Wěi,
so he appointed Mǎn as Sīmǎ
and kept him close.
When Emperor Wén ascended to the throne,
he made Mǎn a Dūwèi
and bestowed upon him the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
Páng Dé, courtesy name Lìngmíng,
was a man from Huándào, Nán'ān.
(Huán, pronunciation of 狟.)
In his youth, he served as a county official and a provincial subordinate.
During the Chūpíng era,
he followed Mǎ Téng in attacking rebellious Qiāng and Dī tribes.
He gained merit several times,
and was gradually promoted to Xiàowèi.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
Tàizǔ campaigned against Yuán Tán and Yuán Shàng at Líyáng.
Tán sent Guō Yuán and Gāo Gàn to seize Hédōng.
Tàizǔ ordered Zhōng Yáo to lead the generals of Guānzhōng to attack them.
Dé followed Mǎ Téng's son Chāo to resist Yuán and Gàn at Píngyáng.
Dé served as the vanguard of the army,
advancing to attack Yuán and Gàn.
He utterly defeated them,
and personally cut off Yuán's head.
He was appointed Zhōnglángjiàng
and ennobled as Dūtíng Hóu.
Later, Zhāng Báijì rebelled in Hóngnóng.
Dé again followed Téng to suppress him,
defeating Báijì in the area between the two Xiáo passes.
In every battle,
he always broke through enemy lines and repelled the foe,
his bravery surpassing that of Téng's entire army.
Later, Téng was summoned to serve as Wèiwèi,
and Dé remained subordinate to Chāo.
When Tàizǔ defeated Chāo at Wèinán,
Dé fled with Chāo into Hànyáng,
and defended Jìchéng.
Later, he again fled with Chāo to Hànzhōng,
serving under Zhāng Lǔ.
When Tàizǔ pacified Hànzhōng,
Dé surrendered with the others.
Tàizǔ had long heard of his valor,
appointed him Lìyì Jiāngjūn,
ennobled him as Guānmén Tíng Hóu,
and granted him an estate of three hundred households.
Hóu Yīn and Wèi Kāi rebelled with Wǎn.
Dé led his troops and attacked and captured Wǎn together with Cáo Rén,
beheading Yīn and Kāi.
Then they marched south to station at Fán,
to suppress Guān Yǔ.
The generals under Fán, knowing that Dé's elder brother was in Hànzhōng,
were quite suspicious of him.
Dé often said:
"I have received the nation's grace,
and my duty is to die in service.
I wish to personally attack Yǔ.
If I do not kill Yǔ this year,
Yǔ will surely kill me."
Later, he personally engaged Yǔ in battle,
shooting Yǔ in the forehead.
At that time, Dé often rode a white horse,
and Yǔ's army called him the 'White Horse General',
all fearing him.
Rén ordered Dé to encamp ten *lǐ* north of Fán.
Then, there was incessant rain for over ten days,
the Hàn River overflowed its banks,
and the flat ground below Fán was submerged five or six *zhàng* deep.
Dé and his generals took refuge on the levee.
Yǔ attacked them by boat,
using large boats to shoot arrows at the levee from all four sides.
Dé, armored and holding his bow,
did not waste a single arrow.
General Dǒng Héng and subordinate officer Dǒng Chāo and others wished to surrender.
Dé captured and executed them all.
From dawn, they fought fiercely until past noon.
Yǔ's attack became more urgent,
their arrows ran out,
and they engaged in close combat with short weapons.
Dé said to the supervising general Chéng Hé:
"I have heard that a good general does not fear death to escape it by chance,
and a brave warrior does not tarnish his integrity to seek survival.
Today
is my day to die."
His fighting grew fiercer,
his spirit more robust,
but the water continued to rise rapidly,
and all the officers and soldiers surrendered.
Dé, with one general under his command
and two *wǔ bó*,
drew their bows and nocked their arrows,
and tried to return to Rén's camp in a small boat.
The rising water capsized the boat,
he lost his bow and arrows,
and he alone clung to the overturned boat in the water.
He was captured by Yǔ,
standing rather than kneeling.
Yǔ said to him:
"Your elder brother is in Hànzhōng.
I intended to make you a general.
Why didn't you surrender earlier?"
Dé cursed Yǔ, saying:
"You mere boy!
What do you mean surrender?
King Wèi has a million armored soldiers,
and his might shakes the world.
You, Liú Bèi, are just a mediocre talent,
how could you be his equal?
I would rather be a ghost for the state
than a general for a rebel!"
He was then killed by Yǔ.
Tàizǔ heard of it and mourned him,
shedding tears for him,
and ennobled his two sons as marquises (*liè hóu*).
When Wéndì ascended to the throne as king,
he sent an envoy to Dé's tomb to bestow a posthumous title.
The proclamation read:
"In ancient times, Xiān Zhěn lost his head,
and Wáng Zhú cut off his own neck,
sacrificing their bodies for their principles,
which previous generations admired.
You, Marquis, brilliantly displayed courage and resolve,
faced danger and achieved fame,
your renown filled your time,
and your righteousness was lofty in antiquity.
We grieve for this,
and grant the posthumous title of Marquis Zhuàng."
He also granted his son Huì and four others the title of Marquis within the Pass (*Guānnèi Hóu*),
each with an estate of one hundred households.
Huì was brave and resolute, with his father's demeanor,
and rose to the official position of General of the Central Guard (*Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn*),
and was ennobled as a Marquis (*liè hóu*).
Páng Yù, courtesy name Zǐyì,
was a native of Biǎoshì, Jiǔquán.
Initially, as an aide (*cóngshì*) in Liángzhōu, he governed as the chief (*zhǎng*) of Pòqiāng.
At that time, Zhāng Měng, the Administrator (*Tàishǒu*) of Wǔwēi, rebelled,
killing the Inspector (*Cìshǐ*) Hándān Shāng.
Měng issued an order saying:
"Dare anyone attend Shāng's funeral,
and they shall die unpardoned."
Yù heard of this,
abandoned his office,
rushed day and night,
wept aloud at the funeral site,
then went to Měng's gate,
concealing a dagger,
intending to kill Měng during an audience.
Měng, knowing him to be a man of integrity,
ordered him to be sent away without killing him.
From then on, he was known for his loyalty and bravery.
Administrator Xú Yī invited him to be his Chief Clerk (*Zhǔbù*).
Later, a local man, Huáng Áng, rebelled,
besieging the city.
Yù abandoned his wife and children,
climbed over the city wall at night to exit the siege,
and reported the emergency to the two commanderies of Zhāngyè and Dùnhuáng.
Initially, they were hesitant to dispatch troops.
Yù wanted to fall on his sword.
The two commanderies were moved by his righteousness
and consequently raised an army.
Before the army arrived, the commandery city had already fallen,
and Yī had died.
Yù then collected Yī's corpse,
sent it back to his home commandery,
and observed mourning for three years before returning.
Tàizǔ heard of this and
summoned him to be an assistant officer (*yuán shǔ*).
When Wéndì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-law (*Fùmǎ Dūwèi*),
promoted to Administrator of Xīhǎi (*Xīhǎi Tàishǒu*),
and granted the title of Marquis within the Pass (*Guānnèi Hóu*).
Later, he was summoned and appointed Grand Master of the Household (*Zhōngsàn Dàfū*),
and died.
His son Zēng inherited.
Originally,
Yù's maternal grandfather, Zhào Ān, was killed by Lǐ Shòu of the same county.
Yù's three maternal uncles died simultaneously of illness,
which pleased Shòu's family.
Yù's mother, É, grieved that her father's revenge had not been taken.
So she veiled her carriage and hid a sword in her sleeve,
and stabbed Shòu in broad daylight in front of the capital pavilion.
Afterward,
she calmly went to the county office,
her expression unchanged,
and said:
"My father's revenge has been taken;
please execute me."
Yǐn Jiā, the Chief (*zhǎng*) of Lùfú, removed his seal and cord and released É.
É refused to leave,
so she was forcibly carried back home.
A general amnesty then granted her release.
The province and commandery admired her nobility
and erected a stone tablet to commemorate her at her village gate.
Yán Wēn, courtesy name Bójiǎn,
was a native of Xīchéng, Tiānshuǐ.
As an aide (*biéjià*) in Liángzhōu, he governed as the magistrate (*lìng*) of Shàngguī.
Mǎ Chāo fled to Shàngguī,
and local people like Rèn Yǎng gathered a crowd to welcome him.
Wēn tried to stop them,
but could not prevent it,
so he galloped back to the provincial capital.
Chāo then laid a very urgent siege to Jìchéng, where the provincial government was located.
The province then secretly dispatched Wēn
to report the emergency to Xiàhóu Yuān.
The rebel siege had several layers.
Wēn secretly slipped out through the water at night.
The next day,
the rebels discovered his tracks
and sent people to pursue and intercept him.
They caught Wēn at the border of Xiǎnqīn,
arrested him, and brought him before Chāo.
Chāo unbound him
and said:
"Now, success and failure are evident.
You requested aid for an isolated city and were captured by others.
Where is your righteousness to be applied?
If you follow my words
and tell the people in the city
that there is no aid from the east,
this is a plan to turn misfortune into fortune.
Otherwise,
you will be executed today."
Wēn pretended to agree,
so Chāo took Wēn to the foot of the city wall.
Wēn shouted towards the city:
"The main army will arrive in no more than three days!
Exert yourselves!"
Everyone in the city wept
and cried out "Long live!"
Chāo angrily rebuked him:
"Don't you care for your own life?"
Wēn did not respond.
At that time, Chāo had been attacking the city for a long time without success,
so he slowly tried to persuade Wēn,
hoping he would change his mind.
He said to Wēn again:
"Are there any old acquaintances in the city
who wish to join me?"
Wēn again did not respond.
Chāo then sternly pressed him,
and Wēn said:
"A subject serves his lord unto death, without wavering.
Yet you wish to make a man of integrity utter unrighteous words.
How could I be one who merely clings to life?"
Chāo then killed him.
Previously,
the area west of the Hé [Hé] was in turmoil,
and communications were cut off.
The Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng [Dūnhuáng], Mǎ Ài [Mǎ Ài], died in office,
and the administration had no assistant.
The Chief Clerk, Zhāng Gōng [Zhāng Gōng], was known for his learning and conduct.
The people of the commandery supported him to manage the affairs of the Chief Scribe.
His benevolence and trustworthiness were widely recognized,
so he sent his son, Jiù [Jiù], eastward to meet Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) [Tài Zǔ]
to request a Grand Administrator.
At that time, Huáng Huá [Huáng Huá] of Jiǔquán [Jiǔquán] and Zhāng Jìn [Zhāng Jìn] of Zhāngyè [Zhāngyè] each held their respective commanderies,
wishing to combine their forces with Gōng [Gōng].
When Jiù [Jiù] arrived at Jiǔquán [Jiǔquán],
he was seized by Huá [Huá]
and threatened with a drawn sword.
Jiù [Jiù] never wavered.
He secretly wrote a letter to Gōng [Gōng], saying:
"Your Excellency governs Dūnhuáng [Dūnhuáng],
and your loyalty and righteousness are clearly evident.
How could you abandon this because Jiù [Jiù] is in distress and danger?
In the past, Yuè Yáng [Yuè Yáng] ate his son,
and Lǐ Tōng [Lǐ Tōng] sacrificed his family.
A minister who manages the state,
how could he harbor affection for his wife and children?
Now, the main army will soon arrive;
you should merely hasten your troops to pin them down.
I beg you not to let your love for a humble person
cause Jiù [Jiù] to have regrets in the yellow earth."
Gōng [Gōng] immediately sent his younger cousin, Huá [Huá], to attack the two counties of Shātóu [Shātóu] and Gānqí [Gānqí] in Jiǔquán [Jiǔquán].
Gōng [Gōng] also joined his forces and followed immediately behind Huá [Huá],
to serve as mutual support.
He separately dispatched two hundred armored cavalry
to welcome the officials and their retinue,
traveling eastward along the northern border of Jiǔquán [Jiǔquán],
passing directly out through the Běihé [Běihé] river in Zhāngyè [Zhāngyè],
to meet Grand Administrator Yǐn Fèng [Yǐn Fèng].
Thereupon, Zhāng Jìn [Zhāng Jìn] sought help from Huáng Huá [Huáng Huá].
Huá [Huá] wanted to rescue Jìn [Jìn],
but looking westward at Gōng's [Gōng] forces,
he feared a swift attack on his rear.
So he went to Sū Zé [Sū Zé], the Grand Administrator of Jīnchéng [Jīnchéng], and surrendered.
Jiù [Jiù] eventually returned safely.
Fèng [Fèng] was able to take up his post.
In the second year of Huángchū [Huángchū] (221 CE),
an imperial edict commended him,
granting Gōng [Gōng] the title of Marquis within the Passes (Guānnèi Hóu) [Guānnèi Hóu]
and appointing him Commander of the Western Regions (Xīyù Wùjǐ Xiàowèi) [Xīyù Wùjǐ Xiàowèi].
Several years later, he was recalled.
He was about to be given the position of a court attendant,
but his son, Jiù [Jiù], took his place instead.
When Gōng [Gōng] arrived in Dūnhuáng [Dūnhuáng],
he firmly declined due to severe illness.
He died during the Tàihé [Tàihé] period (227-233 CE)
and was posthumously granted the title of Bearer of the Golden Mace (Zhí Jīnwǔ) [Zhí Jīnwǔ].
Jiù [Jiù] later became the Grand Administrator of Jīnchéng [Jīnchéng].
Father and son were renowned in Xīzhōu [Xīzhōu] (the Western Region).
Commentary: Lǐ Diǎn [Lǐ Diǎn] valued refinement and propriety;
his righteousness overcame personal enmities—
excellent indeed.
Lǐ Tōng [Lǐ Tōng], Zāng Bà [Zāng Bà], Wén Pìn [Wén Pìn], and Lǚ Qián [Lǚ Qián] guarded and protected the provinces and commanderies,
all demonstrating might and benevolence.
Xǔ Chǔ [Xǔ Chǔ] and Diǎn Wéi [Diǎn Wéi] bravely engaged the enemy on all sides;
they were truly the Fán Kuài [Fán Kuài] of Hàn [Hàn].
Páng Dé [Páng Dé], obeying orders, challenged the enemy,
possessing the integrity of Zhōu Kē [Zhōu Kē].
Páng Yù [Páng Yù] did not fear drawing his sword,
and his sincerity moved neighboring states.
Yán Wēn [Yán Wēn] cried out loudly towards the city,
matching the ferocity of Xiè [Xiè] and Lù [Lù].
Biography of the Prince Xiāo [Xiāo] of Rènchéng [Rènchéng], Chapter 19
Cáo Zhāng [Cáo Zhāng], the Prince Wēi [Wēi] of Rènchéng [Rènchéng],
courtesy name Zǐwén [Zǐwén].
From a young age, he excelled at archery and horsemanship,
possessing extraordinary physical strength.
He would personally fight fierce beasts
and never shied away from dangers.
He frequently participated in military campaigns,
full of spirit and ambition.
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) [Tài Zǔ] once restrained him, saying:
"You do not think of studying and aspiring to the path of the sages,
but instead enjoy riding swift horses and wielding swords.
This is the skill of a common man;
how can it be valued?"
He ordered Zhāng [Zhāng] to read the Odes and Documents.
Zhāng [Zhāng] said to his attendants:
"A true man should be like Wèi [Wèi] and Huò [Huò],
leading a hundred thousand cavalry to gallop across the desert,
driving away the Róng [Róng] and Dí [Dí],
and establishing merits and titles.
How can one become a scholar (bóshì) [bóshì]?"
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) [Tài Zǔ] once asked his sons about their preferences,
and had each state his ambition.
Zhāng [Zhāng] said:
"I like to be a general."
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) [Tài Zǔ] said:
"What does it mean to be a general?"
He replied:
"To wear strong armor and wield sharp weapons,
to disregard danger when facing difficulties,
and to lead the soldiers;
to always carry out rewards,
and to be trustworthy in punishments."
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) [Tài Zǔ] laughed heartily.
In the twenty-first year of Jiàn'ān [Jiàn'ān] (216 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yānlíng [Yānlíng].
In the twenty-third year (218 CE),
the Wūwán [Wūwán] of Dàijùn [Dàijùn] rebelled.
Zhāng [Zhāng] was appointed General of the Northern Gentlemen of the Household (Běi Zhōngláng Jiàng) [Běi Zhōngláng Jiàng]
and acting General of Agile Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn) [Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn].
Before his departure,
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) [Tài Zǔ] admonished Zhāng [Zhāng], saying:
"At home, you are father and son;
when undertaking duties, you are lord and minister.
Act according to the king's law in all matters.
You must be mindful of this!"
When Zhāng [Zhāng] campaigned north,
upon entering the border of Zhuōjùn [Zhuōjùn],
several thousand rebel Hú [Hú] cavalry suddenly arrived.
At that time, his troops had not yet assembled,
having only a thousand infantry
and several hundred cavalry.
Following Tián Yù's [Tián Yù] strategy,
he firmly defended the key passes,
and the barbarians then scattered and retreated.
Zhāng [Zhāng] pursued them,
personally engaging in combat.
He shot Hú [Hú] cavalry,
and those who fell at the twang of his bowstring were continuously numerous.
The battle lasted for more than half a day.
Zhāng's [Zhāng] armor was pierced by several arrows,
but his spirit grew even fiercer.
He pressed his advantage, chasing the retreating enemy
as far as Sānggān [Sānggān],
over two hundred *lǐ* from Dài [Dài].
His Chief Scribe and generals all believed that they had just traveled a long distance,
their soldiers and horses were exhausted,
and they were under orders
not to cross Dài [Dài].
They should not advance too far,
lest they violate orders and underestimate the enemy.
Zhāng [Zhāng] said:
"When leading an army,
one should only go where there is advantage.
What 'orders' are you talking about?
The Hú [Hú] have not fled far;
if we pursue them, we will surely defeat them.
To obey orders and let the enemy escape
is not the mark of a good general."
He then mounted his horse
and ordered his army:
"Whoever falls behind shall be executed!"
After a day and a night, he caught up with the barbarians,
attacked,
and utterly defeated them,
slaying and capturing thousands.
Zhāng [Zhāng] then distributed double the usual rewards to his generals and soldiers,
and everyone was delighted.
At that time, Kēbǐnéng [Kēbǐnéng], the chieftain of the Xiānbēi [Xiānbēi], was observing their strengths and weaknesses with tens of thousands of cavalry.
Seeing Zhāng [Zhāng] fight bravely
and defeat everything in his path,
he then requested submission.
The entire north was pacified.
At that time, Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) [Tài Zǔ] was in Cháng'ān [Cháng'ān]
and summoned Zhāng [Zhāng] to the provisional residence.
Zhāng [Zhāng] traveled from Dài [Dài] via Yè [Yè].
The crown prince told Zhāng [Zhāng]:
"You have recently achieved merit.
Now, when you see His Majesty in the west,
you should not boast about yourself.
Your replies should always appear as if you are lacking."
When Zhāng [Zhāng] arrived,
he followed the crown prince's advice
and attributed the achievements to his generals.
Grand Ancestor (Tài Zǔ) [Tài Zǔ] was pleased and,
stroking Zhāng's [Zhāng] beard, said:
"My yellow-bearded son is indeed extraordinary!"
Tài-zǔ returned to the east.
He made Zhāng the General of Agile Cavalry (Yuè-qí Jiāng-jūn)
and left him in Cháng'ān.
When Tài-zǔ reached Luòyáng,
he fell ill.
He urgently summoned Zhāng by courier,
but before Zhāng arrived,
Tài-zǔ passed away.
Wén-dì ascended the princely throne,
and Zhāng, along with the other marquises, went to their respective fiefs.
An edict stated:
"The way of the former king
was to honor meritorious deeds and cherish his kin,
establishing his younger brothers (by the same mother) as rulers,
founding states and inheriting households.
Thus, they could protect the main lineage
and repel invaders and quell difficulties.
Previously, Zhāng received orders to march north,
pacifying and settling the northern lands.
His accomplishments were significant.
His stipend was increased by five thousand households,
making a total of ten thousand households."
In the second year of Huáng-chū (221 CE),
he was promoted to the rank of duke.
In the third year (222 CE),
he was established as Rènchéng Wáng.
In the fourth year (223 CE),
he made a court visit to the capital.
He died of illness at his residence,
and was posthumously granted the title Wēi.
For his burial,
he was bestowed a royal carriage (luán-lù) and dragon banners (lóng-qí),
and a hundred tiger guards (hǔ-bēn),
following the precedent of the Hán Prince of Dōngpíng.
His son, Kǎi, succeeded him
and was moved to be enfeoffed in Zhōngmóu.
In the fifth year (224 CE),
he was re-enfeoffed as Rènchéng Xiàn.
In the sixth year of Tài-hé (232 CE),
he was again re-enfeoffed as Rènchéng Guó,
enjoying five counties and two thousand five hundred households.
In the third year of Qīnglóng (235 CE),
Kǎi was charged with privately sending his subordinates to the Imperial Workshop (Zhōng-shàng-fāng) to manufacture prohibited items,
and two thousand households of his stipend were cut.
In the seventh year of Zhèng-shǐ (246 CE),
he was moved to be enfeoffed in Jìnán,
with three thousand households.
In the early years of Zhèngyuán and Jǐngyuán,
his stipend was successively increased,
totaling four thousand four hundred households.
Chén-sī Wáng Zhí, courtesy name Zǐjiàn.
When he was over ten years old,
he could recite hundreds of thousands of words from the Shī (Book of Odes), Lún (Analects), and various rhapsodies (cífù),
and was skilled in writing essays.
Tài-zǔ once looked at his writings
and said to Zhí,
"Did you have someone else write this?"
Zhí knelt and replied,
"When I speak, it becomes a discourse;
when I put pen to paper, it becomes an essay.
I would gladly be tested in person,
how could I have someone else write it?"
At that time, the Copper Sparrow Terrace (Tóng-jué-tái) in Yè had just been completed.
Tài-zǔ took all his sons to ascend the terrace
and had each of them compose a rhapsody.
Zhí took up his brush and finished it immediately.
It was admirable,
and Tài-zǔ was greatly impressed.
His nature was simple and straightforward,
and he did not concern himself with solemn deportment.
His carriages, horses, clothing, and ornaments
were not adorned with extravagance.
Whenever he was summoned for an audience and questioned,
he would respond immediately,
and was especially favored.
In the sixteenth year of Jiàn'ān (211 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Píngyuán.
In the nineteenth year (214 CE),
he was moved to be enfeoffed as Marquis of Línzī.
When Tài-zǔ campaigned against Sūn Quán,
he left Zhí to guard Yè
and instructed him, saying:
"I was once Magistrate of Dùnqíu,
at the age of twenty-three.
Reflecting on what I did at that time,
I have no regrets today.
Now you are also twenty-three years old;
how can you not strive!"
Zhí, having already been singled out for his talent,
also had Dīng Yí, Dīng Yì, Yáng Xiū, and others as his supporters.
Tài-zǔ was uncertain
and several times nearly made him the crown prince.
However, Zhí acted according to his nature,
did not cultivate himself,
and drank intemperately.
Wén-dì managed him with cunning,
feigning sincerity and adorning himself.
The palace attendants and those around him
all spoke in his favor,
thus he was finally established as the heir.
In the twenty-second year (217 CE),
an additional five thousand households were granted,
making a total of ten thousand households.
Zhí once drove his carriage along the imperial road
and exited through the Sīmǎ Gate (Sīmǎ-mén).
Tài-zǔ was furious,
and the chief of the imperial carriage service (Gōng-chē-lìng) was executed.
From then on, the prohibitions on the marquises became stricter,
and Zhí's favor diminished daily.
Tài-zǔ, already concerned about potential changes in the succession,
considered Yáng Xiū to be quite talented and resourceful,
and also a maternal nephew of the Yuán clan.
Therefore, he executed Xiū for a crime.
Zhí felt even more insecure.
In the twenty-fourth year (219 CE),
Cáo Rén was besieged by Guān Yǔ.
Tài-zǔ appointed Zhí as General of the Central South (Nán-zhōng-láng-jiāng),
acting as General Who Conquers Barbarians (Zhēng-lǔ Jiāng-jūn).
He intended to send him to rescue Rén,
and called him to give instructions.
Zhí was too drunk to receive the orders,
so Tài-zǔ regretted it and dismissed the plan.
When Wén-dì ascended the princely throne,
he executed Dīng Yí and Dīng Yì, along with their male family members.
Zhí, along with the other marquises, went to his fief.
In the second year of Huáng-chū (221 CE),
Guàn Jūn, an imperial censor supervising the state, anticipating the emperor's wishes,
memorialized that
"Zhí was drunk and behaved outrageously and disrespectfully,
and coerced imperial envoys."
The authorities requested to punish him.
The emperor, for the sake of the Empress Dowager,
demoted him to Marquis of Ānxiāng.
In the same year, he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Juànchéng.
In the third year (222 CE),
he was established as Juànchéng Wáng,
with two thousand five hundred households.
In the fourth year (223 CE),
he was moved to be enfeoffed as Yōngqiú Wáng.
In that same year,
he paid court to the capital.
He submitted a memorial which stated: "Since I was involved in transgression and returned to my fief,
I have etched into my flesh and bone
the memory of my crimes,
eating only during the day
and sleeping only during the night.
Truly, the net of Heaven cannot be violated twice,
and the sagely grace is difficult to rely on again.
I secretly feel the meaning of the chapter 'Xiāng Shǔ' (Ode to the Rat),
that 'without propriety, one swiftly dies.'
My form and shadow console each other,
and my five emotions are ashamed and blushing.
To abandon life due to crime
would violate
the ancient sages'
exhortation to
'reform by evening.'
To endure life and barely survive
would incur the poet's
censure of
'what face do you have?'
I humbly believe Your Majesty's virtue is like Heaven and Earth,
and your grace is as profound as parents,
dispensed
like the spring breeze,
and nourishing like timely rain.
This is why those who do not distinguish thorns
benefit from the auspicious clouds;
the seven chicks equally nurtured
exemplify the benevolence of the cuckoo;
to pardon crimes
and demand merit
is the act of an enlightened ruler;
to pity the foolish and love the capable
is the grace of a loving father. It is for these reasons that your foolish subject wanders in your grace and cannot abandon himself.
Previously, by imperial edict,
your subjects were forbidden from court.
My heart was broken, my ambition severed,
and I resigned myself to having no hope of holding a jade tablet again.
I did not expect Your Sagely Majesty to condescend to summon me.
On the day
of my arrival,
my heart raced towards the imperial carriage.
Residing in the secluded western lodge,
not yet having paid respects at the imperial court,
my heart leaps with joy,
looking forward with restlessness.
I respectfully submit this memorial with two poems.
Their
verses say:
'How reverent was my illustrious father,
truly the Martial Emperor!
He received the mandate from Heaven,
pacifying and settling the four directions.
Wherever his vermilion banners waved,
the nine lands were swept clean,
his profound transforming influence flowed abundantly,
bringing order to the wild
submitted and came to pay homage.
It surpassed the Shāng and transcended the Zhōu,
standing shoulder to shoulder with the Táng.
Our August Emperor was born,
wise and sagacious through generations;
in military affairs, awe-inspiring and resolute;
in civil matters, timely and harmonious.
He received the abdication from the Yán Hàn,
ruling over myriad states.
Once the myriad states were transformed,
they generally followed the old rules;
he extensively appointed worthy relatives
to act as bulwarks for the kingdoms.
The Emperor said, "You, my noble lord,
govern this green land,
possessing the se
ashore,
on a par with Zhōu and Lǔ.
Your chariots and robes are splendid,
your banners and insignia are imposing;
many are the excellent and talented men
who assist and support me."
But I, this humble person,
presumed upon favor and became arrogant and overbearing;
my every action became entangled in
the nets of the time,
disturbing the nation's principles.
Serving as a bulwark and screen,
I abandoned the former path;
I was insolent to my imperial envoy,
and violated the court rituals.
The nation has its laws and penalties;
I was diminished and dismissed,
to be
placed under judgment,
with the prime offenders as my example.
Bright and sagacious is the Son of Heaven,
who deeply cherished those of his own kind;
he could not bear to inflict punishment on me,
or expose me in the public square.
He disregarded those who upheld the law,
pitying me, this humble person.
I was re-enfeoffed in Yǎn yì,
on the banks of the Hé;
my close advisors were not retained,
I had a lord but no ministers.
In this realm of wanton indulgence and neglect,
who will assist my person?
Lonely and helpless, this servant
resides in that Jì
region;
alas, I, this humble person,
have suffered this misfortune.
Majestic is the Son of Heaven,
whose grace leaves nothing untouched;
he crowned me with a dark ceremonial cap,
and girt me with a red sash.
The red sash shone brightly,
granting me
glory and splendor;
he granted me a tally and jade,
and bestowed upon me a princely title.
I looked up to the golden seal,
and bowed to receive the sacred edict;
the imperial grace was exceedingly profound,
I accepted it with awe and trepidation.
Alas, I, this humble person,
was entangled in
stubborn wickedness;
in death, I would be ashamed before the imperial tombs;
in life, I am ashamed before the court.
I dared not rely on my virtue,
but truly on this grace;
the awe-inspiring spiritual power has been reinstated,
sufficient for the rest of my life.
The vast heavens are boundless,
life and destiny are unpredictable;
I constantly fear downfall,
and bearing guilt into the yellow earth.
I wish to brave arrows and stones,
and raise banners at Dōngyuè,
hoping to achieve a tiny bit,
to atone for my minor transgressions.
To risk my life and
accept a command,
knowing contentment to avoid further offense;
I would gladly go to Jiāng and Xiāng,
and wield a halberd in Wú and Yuè.
Heaven revealed its will,
allowing me to meet in the capital region;
I long to attend upon the Sacred Countenance,
like one parched or starved.
My heart
yearns for it,
grieved and sorrowful;
Heaven is high but hears the lowly,
will His Majesty condescend to illuminate my insignificance!"
He also said:
"Solemnly receiving the clear edict,
to attend the imperial capital,
I harnessed my carriage at dawn,
fed
my horses and oiled my wheels.
I commanded my carriage drivers
to make my journey solemn;
I departed from Luántái in the morning,
and lodged at Lánzhǔ in the evening.
Vast were the plains and wetlands,
numerous were the men and women;
passing by the public fields,
they delighted in my millet and sorghum.
There were drooping trees,
their deep shade never ceased;
though I had dried provisions,
hunger left me no time to eat.
I looked at cities without stopping,
and passed towns without lingering;
my servants
urged on the horses,
following the straight road.
My dark team of four horses, luxuriant,
champed their bits, spurting foam;
the flowing wind assisted the crossbar,
light clouds supported the canopy.
I traversed the banks of the ravines,
and skirted the bends of the mountains;
I followed the river banks,
and ascended Huángbǎn.
Westward, I crossed Guāngǔ,
sometimes descending, sometimes ascending;
my outriders grew weary on the road,
resting and rising again and again.
About to appear before the Sacred Emperor,
I dared
not rest in peace;
I hastened my pace for a long journey,
setting a day for swift travel.
The vanguard lit torches,
the rear guard raised banners;
the wheels never stopped turning,
the phoenix bells never ceased sounding.
Upon reaching the Imperial Abode,
I halted by the western wall;
as no gracious edict was yet granted,
I could not attend court.
I gazed up at the city gate,
and thought down upon the court;
my long-held yearning and eternal admiration,
made my anxious heart feel like one drunken."
The Emperor praised his words and meaning,
and replied with a gracious edict of encouragement.
In the sixth year,
the Emperor campaigned eastward,
and on his return, passed through Yōngqiū.
He visited Zhí's palace,
and increased his household by five hundred.
In the first year of Tàihé,
he was re-enfeoffed at Jùnyí.
In the second year,
he returned to Yōngqiū.
Zhí often felt frustrated and resentful,
holding sharp weapons but having no place to use them.
He submitted a memorial requesting an opportunity to prove himself, saying: "Your servant has heard that a scholar, when born into the world,
at home serves his father,
and abroad serves his sovereign;
serving his father values glorifying his parents,
serving his sovereign values strengthening the nation.
Therefore, a loving father cannot
cherish a useless son,
nor can a benevolent ruler keep a useless minister.
Indeed, a ruler who assesses virtue and bestows office
is a successful ruler;
one who measures ability and accepts a title
is
a minister who devotes his life.
Thus, a ruler gives no empty appointments,
and a minister accepts no empty emoluments;
an empty appointment is called a mistaken choice,
an empty acceptance is called enjoying salary without service,
which is
why the poem
'eating without toil'
was composed.
In the past, the two Guó did not decline the responsibility of two states,
for their virtue was profound;
Dàn and Shì did not refuse the enfeoffments of Yān and Lǔ,
for their achievements were great.
Now, your servant
has received immense national grace,
for three generations up to the present.
Precisely at this time of Your Majesty's peaceful reign,
bathed in sacred favor,
and subtly nurtured by virtuous teachings,
it can be called exceedingly fortunate.
However, I secretly"
Occupying the position of an Eastern Vassal,
my rank is among the highest,
my body is clad in light, warm garments,
my mouth sated with a hundred flavors,
my eyes revel in splendor and luxury,
my ears weary of strings and flutes—
this is all due to my heavy rank and ample emoluments.
Reflecting on how those of old were granted ranks and emoluments,
it was different from this.
They all, through diligent efforts, benefited the state,
assisted their lord, and brought favor to the people.
Now, I have no virtue to speak of,
no accomplishments to record.
If I remain like this all year, useless to the imperial court,
I will incur the ridicule of the “Fēngrén”
‘Bǐ Qí’
stanza.
Therefore, I am ashamed before the dark ceremonial cap,
and embarrassed before the crimson ribbon.
Currently, the world is unified,
the nine provinces are at peace.
Yet, looking to the west, there is the disobedient Shǔ,
and to the east, the unsubmissive Wú.
This prevents the border garrisons from doffing their armor,
and strategists from resting easy,
for the sincere desire is to unite all within the universe to achieve great harmony.
Thus, when Qǐ destroyed Yǒuhù, Xià’s achievements shone;
when Chéng conquered Shāng and Yǎn, Zhōu’s
virtue became manifest.
Now, Your Majesty, with your sagely wisdom, rules the age,
intending to complete the accomplishments of Wén and Wǔ,
and continue the prosperity of Chéng and Kāng.
You select the worthy and appoint the capable,
using ministers like Fāngshū and Shàohǔ
to guard the four borders,
acting as the nation’s claws and teeth—
this may be called fitting.
However, the high bird is not yet caught by the light snare,
nor the deep fish yet hung by the hook and bait.
I fear that the arts of
angling and shooting may not yet be fully exploited.
In the past, Gěng Yǎn did not wait for Guāngwǔ,
but promptly attacked Zhāng Bù,
saying he would not leave the rebels to his lord and father.
Thus, the charioteer committed suicide by sword at the
clattering axle,
and Yōngmén slit his throat in Qí territory.
For such two gentlemen,
how could they despise life and prefer death?
It was truly their indignation at their lord’s negligence and contempt for their ruler.
Indeed, a lord
favors a minister
to eliminate calamities and promote benefits;
a minister serves his lord
by sacrificing his life to quell chaos,
thereby repaying his lord with accomplishments.
In the past, Jiǎ Yì, at a young age,
requested to be tested as a
vassal state official,
asking to tie the Xiongnú Chányú’s neck and control his destiny.
Zhōng Jūn, in his youth, was sent as an envoy to Yuè,
desiring to secure its king with a long rope,
and bring him shackled to the Northern Gate.
These two ministers,
how could they enjoy boasting to their lord and showing off to the world?
Their ambition was perhaps suppressed,
wishing to display their talent and strength,
and offer their abilities to an enlightened ruler.
In the past, Hàn Wǔdì had a mansion built for Huò Qùbìng,
who declined, saying:
“The Xiongnú are not yet vanquished;
I have no need for a home!”
(Indeed,) to worry about the state and forget one’s family,
to sacrifice one’s life to overcome difficulties—
this is the aspiration of a loyal minister.
Now, I reside in an outer province;
my treatment is not ungenerous,
yet I cannot rest peacefully at night,
nor enjoy my food,
for I humbly bear the concern that the two regions are not yet conquered.
I humbly observe that among the valiant ministers and veteran generals of the late Emperor Wǔdì,
some have grown old and passed away.
Although worthy men are not lacking in this world,
veteran generals and old soldiers
are still practiced in warfare.
I, presuming beyond my measure,
am resolved to offer my life,
hoping to achieve even a tiny accomplishment,
to repay the kindness I have received.
If Your Majesty would issue an unprecedented edict,
and allow me to be employed, even with the use of a small
knife or awl,
permitting me to serve the Grand General in the west,
commanding a single detachment,
or to serve the Grand Marshal in the east,
taking charge of a solitary boat,
I would surely brave dangers and risks,
drive my chariot and spur my
steeds,
charge into blades and meet spearheads,
leading the soldiers.
Although I may not be able to capture Quán and behead Liàng,
I shall likely capture their brave commanders,
annihilate their vile kind,
and surely achieve a momentary victory,
to dispel the shame of my whole life,
making my name recorded in historical writings,
and my deeds listed in court annals.
Even if my body is dismembered in Shǔ territory,
and my head hung at the Wú gate,
it would still be like living out my years.
If my humble talent
is not tried,
and I pass away unknown,
merely glorifying my body and fattening my physique,
living uselessly for affairs,
and dying without altering fate,
vainly enjoying a high position and shamefully receiving ample emoluments,
like a bird
resting and gazing,
until white-haired old age,
this would merely be livestock raised in a pen,
not what this minister aspires to.
I hear rumors that the Eastern army suffered a lapse in preparedness,
and its forces suffered a minor setback.
I stop eating
and abandon my meal,
flinging up my sleeves and hitching up my robes,
grasping my sword and looking eastward,
my heart already flying towards Wú and Huì.
In the past, I followed the late Emperor Wǔdì south to Chì’àn,
east to the vast sea,
west to Yùmén,
and north beyond Xuánsài.
I humbly observed the methods of troop deployment
and military strategy,
which could be called divine and marvelous.
Thus, military affairs cannot be predicted beforehand;
one must adapt to changes when facing difficulties.
I am resolved to dedicate myself to this enlightened age,
and achieve merit in this sagely era.
Whenever I read historical records,
and observe the loyal ministers and righteous gentlemen of antiquity,
who answered a single imperial decree
to brave national calamities,
their bodies, though dismembered,
had their accomplishments inscribed on tripods and bells,
and their names
handed down on bamboo and silk.
I have never failed to pat my heart and sigh with admiration.
I have heard that an enlightened ruler, when employing ministers,
does not discard those who have erred.
Thus, generals who fled in defeat or lost battles were used,
and Qín and Lǔ achieved their successes;
ministers who broke their cap-strings or stole horses were pardoned,
and Chǔ and Zhào overcame their difficulties.
I humbly feel that the late Emperor passed away early,
and Wēiwáng departed
this world.
Who am I,
to endure for long!
I constantly fear that I might perish like morning dew,
filling a ditch or gully,
my grave earth not yet dry,
while both my body and name are obliterated.
I have heard that if a fine steed
neighs loudly,
then Bólè recognizes its ability;
if a black dog howls mournfully,
then Hánguó knows its talent.
Therefore, they are put to the test on the roads of Qí and Chǔ,
to display their ability to travel a thousand *lǐ*;
they are tried against the swiftness of a cunning rabbit,
to prove their effectiveness in pursuit and attack.
Now, I, with the humble ambition of a dog or horse,
humbly reflect and estimate
that I shall never have the opportunity like Bólè or Hánguó.
Therefore, I feel distressed and secretly pain.
Indeed, when one is about to contend, one stands on tiptoe;
when one hears music, one secretly claps—
perhaps there are those who appreciate the sound and recognize the way.
In the past, Máo Suí,
a mere retainer of Zhào,
still used the analogy of the awl in a bag
to awaken his lord and establish merit.
How much more so in the illustrious court of the great Wèi, with its multitude of scholars,
should there not be ministers resolute to die for the state!
Indeed, self-promotion and self-advertisement
are ugly behaviors of
men and
women.
Seeking opportunities to advance
is a clear taboo for followers of the Dào.
Yet, I dare to present my words to Your Majesty,
because I truly share the nation's form and spirit,
and partake in its joys and sorrows.
I hope that my small contribution, like dust or mist, may augment mountains and seas;
and my dim candlelight may add luster to the sun and moon.
Therefore, I dare to disregard the impropriety and offer my
zhōng.
Three years later,
he was transferred and enfeoffed in Dōng'ā.
Five years later,
he again submitted a memorial, requesting to inquire about and visit his relatives,
thereby expressing his thoughts, saying: Your servant has heard that Heaven is called high
because there is nothing it does not cover;
Earth is called vast
because there is nothing it does not bear;
the sun and moon are called bright
because there is nothing they do not illuminate;
the rivers and seas are called great
because there is nothing they do not contain.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ said:
“How great was Yáo as a ruler!
Only Heaven is great,
and Yáo modeled himself upon it.”
Indeed, the
virtue of Heaven towards all things
can be called profound and vast.
Now, Yáo's teaching
prioritized kin over strangers,
and spread from near to far.
Its tradition says:
“He was able to make manifest his great virtue,
thereby
bringing harmony to the nine clans;
when the nine clans were harmonious,
he elucidated and distinguished the common people.”
And Wénwáng of Zhōu also exalted this transformation;
his poem says:
“He set an example for his wife,
then extended it to his
brothers,
so as to govern the state and the nation.”
Thus, there was harmony and reverence.
The poets sang of it.
In ancient times, Zhōugōng lamented the disharmony of Guǎn and Cài,
and broadly enfeoffed his noble kin to screen and protect
the royal house.
The tradition says:
“Among the alliances of the Zhōu clan,
those of different surnames were secondary.”
Truly, the affection between flesh and blood is never broken,
and the principle of cherishing kin is truly firm and solid.
There has never been
anyone who was righteous and yet put his ruler second,
or benevolent and yet abandoned his kin.
I humbly think that Your Majesty, endowed with the brilliant virtue of Dì Táng,
and embodying the meticulous benevolence of Wénwáng,
whose grace permeates the inner palace,
and whose favor illuminates the nine clans,
has all the princes and officials
taking
turns to rest and attend court,
with those in office not neglecting public affairs,
and those of lower rank able to express their feelings in private,
where the path for intimate relations is open,
and the feelings for celebrations and condolences are expressed.
This can truly be called exercising compassion to govern
others,
and extending kindness and bestowing favor.
As for your servant,
my human connections are severed,
imprisoned in these bright times;
I secretly lament this.
I dare not overly hope to associate with my peers,
to cultivate human affairs,
and human relations.
Recently, even marriages are not allowed,
and brothers are separated,
inquiries about auspicious and inauspicious events are blocked,
and rituals for celebrations and condolences are abandoned.
The violation of familial bonds
is worse than with
strangers,
and the estrangement and difference
is greater than between Hú and Yuè.
Now, with this uniform system,
your servant has no hope of ever having an audience,
yet my heart is focused on the imperial standard,
my feelings are tied to the purple
palace gate;
the gods know this.
However, Heaven truly caused this;
what can I say?
I withdraw and only wish that the kings always have that sorrowful and distressed heart.
I pray Your Majesty will generously issue
an edict,
allowing the various states to send congratulations and inquiries,
and to hold the four seasonal gatherings,
to maintain the joy and favor of flesh and blood,
and fully preserve the sincere righteousness of harmony.
The families of consorts,
the gifts of cosmetics and hair oil,
should
be allowed to be sent twice a year,
placing their righteousness on par with noble clans,
and their favors equal to all officials.
If this were so,
then what the ancients praised,
and what the Fēng and Yǎ sang of,
would be restored in this sacred age.
I humbly reflect on myself,
having no utility greater than a drill or a knife.
Yet, observing those whom Your Majesty promotes and appoints,
if I were considered an outsider,
I secretly estimate
I would not be inferior to
the court officials.
If I could decline the "Far Roaming" ode,
wear the martial cap,
untie the red sash,
and wear the green sash,
as Fùmǎ or Fèngchē,
just to gain one title,
and settle in the imperial capital,
holding the whip
and carrying the brush,
following the imperial carriage when going out,
and attending the emperor in the carriage when entering,
answering imperial questions,
and picking up forgotten words at Your Majesty's side,
that would be the ultimate wish of your servant's true heart,
never departing from my dreams.
From afar, I admire the "Lù Míng" feast of ruler and subject;
in the middle, I chant the "Cháng Dì" admonition against separation;
below, I ponder the "Fá Mù" righteousness of friends;
finally, I cherish the "Lǎo É" sorrow of boundless grief.
Every
time the four seasonal gatherings occur,
I sit alone, desolate.
Around me are only servants,
and facing me only my wife and children.
There is no one with whom to engage in lofty discussions,
no one with whom to express my noble ideas.
I never fail
to clasp my heart when hearing music,
or to sigh when facing a goblet.
Your servant humbly believes that if the sincerity of a dog or horse cannot move people,
how much less can the sincerity of a person move Heaven?
Collapsing cities,
falling frost—
I once believed these,
but judging by my own heart,
they are merely empty words.
Like the sunflower turning its leaves,
though the sun does not turn its light for it,
yet the sincerity of those
who turn towards it is real.
I secretly compare myself to a sunflower.
If a benevolence like that of Heaven and Earth were to descend,
or the brightness of the three luminaries were to be extended,
it would truly come from Your Majesty.
Your servant heard Wénzǐ say:
“Do not be the beginning of fortune,
nor be the first in calamity.”
Now, this separation and obstruction causes shared sorrow among friends.
And the reason your servant alone speaks out
is that I secretly do not
wish that in this sacred age there should be anything that does not receive benevolence.
If there is anything that does not receive benevolence,
there will surely be feelings of bitter resentment.
Therefore, "Bǎi Zhōu" has
the lament of "Heaven!"
and
"Gǔ
Fēng" has
the sigh of "abandoned by you."
Thus, Yī Yǐn was ashamed that his ruler was not like Yáo or Shùn,
and Mèngzǐ said:
“One who does not serve his ruler with the same devotion that Shùn served Yáo
is not
respectful to his ruler.”
Your servant's foolishness and ignorance
are certainly not like Yú or Yī.
As for wishing Your Majesty to uphold the beauty of glorious peace throughout the age,
and proclaim the virtues of bright harmony,
this
is your servant's sincere heart,
which I secretly cherish alone,
truly holding the aspiration of a crane standing on tiptoe.
I dare to present it again,
hoping that Your Majesty might perhaps open your heavenly ears and grant
divine audience.
The imperial rescript replied:
"Indeed, the means by which
civilizing influence is spread
each have their periods of flourishing and decline,
not all starting well and ending poorly;
circumstances make it so.
Thus, when loyalty and generosity reach the utmost for all beings,
the poem of 'Xíngwěi' is composed;
when grace and favor wane and become thin,
and kinship ties are not maintained,
the chapter of 'Juégōng' serves as a satire.
Now, if the brothers in the various states
are treated with indifference and neglect,
and the families of consorts and concubines
receive insufficient care and favor,
even if We cannot strengthen and harmonize these relations,
Your Highness has cited ancient examples and expounded on righteousness thoroughly.
How can it be said that sincerity is insufficient to inspire communication?
Indeed, distinguishing between noble and humble,
exalting kinship,
honoring the worthy,
and respecting elders and juniors,
these are the fundamental principles of the state.
Originally, there was no imperial edict prohibiting communication between the various states.
It is merely that in rectifying an error, the pendulum swung too far,
and subordinate officials, fearing censure,
have caused this situation.
We have already instructed the relevant authorities
to address the matters Your Highness has complained about."
Cáo Zhí again submitted a memorial, expounding on the principle of careful selection of officials,
saying: "Your servant has heard that when the qi of heaven and earth harmonize, all things are born;
when ruler and minister unite in virtue, all government affairs are accomplished.
The era of the Five Dì was not entirely wise,
nor were the latter days of the Three Jì entirely
foolish;
it was a matter of whether the capable were employed or not, and whether the wise were recognized or not.
Although there is a reputation for employing the worthy at times,
there is no reality of actually acquiring the worthy.
Instead, each invariably promotes those of their own kind.
The proverb
says:
'From the household of a Chancellor comes a Chancellor;
from the household of a General comes a General.'
Indeed, a Chancellor
is one whose civilian virtue is manifest;
a General
is one whose military achievements are outstanding.
When civilian virtue is manifest,
one can
rectify the imperial court,
and bring about an era of peace and prosperity,
like Jì, Xiè, Kuí, and Lóng.
When military achievements are outstanding,
one can conquer the disobedient,
and awe the four barbarians,
like Nán Zhòng and Fāng Shū.
In ancient times, Yī Yǐn was a slave accompanying a bride,
of the lowest status;
Lǚ Shàng dwelled among butchers and fishermen,
of the humblest origins.
Yet, when they were employed by Tāng and Wǔ, and Zhōu Wén,
it was truly because their Dao and aspirations aligned,
and their profound strategies were divinely efficacious.
How could they have relied on the recommendation of close attendants
or the mediation of those on the left and right?
The Shū Jīng says:
'When there is an unparalleled ruler,
they will certainly be able to employ unparalleled
ministers;
by employing unparalleled ministers,
they will certainly be able to achieve unparalleled accomplishments.'
The two kings of Yīn and Zhōu are examples of this.
As for those who are petty and confined to trivial matters,
who follow convention and cling to old ways,
how can they
be worthy of Your Majesty's attention?
Thus, if Yin and Yang are not harmonious,
the three luminaries do not shine brightly,
official posts are vacant,
and government affairs are not in order,
this is the responsibility of the Three Dàsī.
If the borders are in turmoil,
the surrounding regions are invaded,
armies are destroyed and lives are lost,
and warfare does not cease,
this is the concern of the frontier generals.
How can they idly enjoy state favors without fulfilling their duties?
Therefore,
the higher the office, the heavier the burden;
the more elevated the position, the deeper the responsibility.
The Shū Jīng says,
'Let no official post be vacant,'
and the Shī Jīng has the line,
'Let each attend to their duties with sorrow.'
This is the meaning.
Your Majesty embodies the true and pure sageliness of Heaven,
ascending to the divine throne to continue the lineage.
We hope to hear the song of 'Kāngzāi'
and witness the beauty of ending military campaigns and promoting civil governance.
However, in recent years,
droughts and floods have been untimely,
the people suffer from lack of food and clothing,
the dispatch of troops
increases levies year by year,
and furthermore, in the east there are defeated armies,
and in the west, generals who have perished.
This has even led to clams
floating and swimming in the Huái and Sì Rivers,
and martens and weasels clamoring in the forests.
Your servant, whenever I think of this,
have never failed to stop eating and flick away my food,
or grasp my wrist when raising a cup.
In ancient times, when Hàn Wén Dì set out from Dài,
he suspected a coup at court.
Sòng Chāng said:
'Internally, you have the close relatives of Zhūxū and Dōngmóu;
externally, there are Qí, Chǔ, Huáinán, and Lángxié.
These are your foundation, solid as a rock.
May Your Highness not doubt.'
Your servant respectfully considers Your Majesty's distant contemplation of the assistance of the two Guó for Jī Wén Wáng,
your mid-range consideration of the aid of Zhào and Bì for Zhōu Chéng Wáng,
and your close consideration of Sòng Chāng's assurance of a foundation as solid as a rock.
In ancient times, a fine steed on the slopes of Wú
could be said to be in distress.
But when Bólè identified it,
and Sūn Yóu drove it,
its body did not tire, yet it covered a thousand li effortlessly.
Indeed,
Bólè was skilled at driving horses;
a wise ruler is skilled at employing ministers.
Bólè could drive a thousand li;
a wise ruler brings about Great Peace.
This is truly the clear effect of employing the worthy and using the capable.
If the court officials
are all excellent,
and all affairs are managed internally,
and military generals lead their troops,
then difficulties can be overcome and pacified.
Your Majesty can then reside comfortably in the imperial city.
Why should you tire your imperial person,
and be exposed to the elements on the border?
Your servant has heard that a sheep with a tiger's skin
is pleased upon seeing grass,
but trembles upon seeing a jackal,
forgetting that its skin is that of a tiger.
The poor selection of generals today
is similar to this.
Therefore,
the saying goes:
'The trouble is that those who act do not know,
and those who know are not allowed to act.'
In ancient times, Yuè Yì fled to Zhào,
but his heart never forgot Yān.
Lián Pó was in Chǔ,
but longed to be a general for Zhào.
Your servant was born into chaos,
grew up among armies,
and frequently received instruction from Wǔ Huángdì.
I respectfully observe the essentials of leading armies and employing troops,
which, without necessarily following Sūn Wǔ or Wú Qǐ explicitly,
harmonize with them implicitly.
I privately gauge it in my heart,
and constantly wish to once attend a court audience,
pass through the golden gate,
tread on the jade steps,
be listed among the officials with duties,
and be granted a momentary interview,
so that your servant may
once express what I harbor,
and pour out my accumulated thoughts.
Then I would die without regret.
Having received the letter from the Hónglú instructing the dispatch of soldiers and a rest period,
the deadline is extremely urgent.
Moreover, I hear that the leopard-tail banners have already been erected,
and the war chariots are speeding forth.
Your Majesty will again tire your imperial person,
and disturb your divine thoughts.
Your servant is truly anxious,
