without a moment of peace.
I wish to mount my horse and grasp the whip,
to be the first to brave the dust and dew,
to gather the wonders of Fēng Hòu,
to adopt the essentials of Sūn Wǔ and Wú Qǐ,
to emulate Bǔ Shāng (Zǐ Xià) who could 'elicit understanding' at Your Majesty's side,
to offer my life as a vanguard,
and to dedicate my life to the chariot wheels.
Although it may be of no great benefit,
I hope it may be a small supplement.
However, Heaven is high and its hearing is distant,
and my feelings do not reach above."
通,
徒獨望青雲而拊心,
仰高天而歎息耳．
Qū Píng (屈平) said:
"If the state has a fine steed but does not know how to ride it,
why bother to eagerly
seek another!"
In the past, Guǎn (管) and Cài (蔡) were banished and executed,
while Zhōu (周) and Shào (召) served as pillars of support;
Shú Yú (叔魚) fell into punishment,
while Shú Xiàng (叔向) rectified the state.
In the calamity of the Three Overseers (三監),
a minister must shoulder the responsibility;
as for the
assistants from the 'Two Souths' (二南),
they should not be sought far away.
Among the illustrious clans and noble families,
and among the vassal princes,
there must be those who can respond to this call.
Therefore, the saying goes:
"Without the closeness of Zhōu Gōng (周公),
one cannot carry out the deeds
of Zhōu Gōng."
May Your Majesty only pay a little attention to this.
Recently, the Hàn (漢) dynasty widely established vassal princes;
the wealthy ones had dozens of connected cities,
while the modest ones merely enjoyed sacrificial offerings,
which was not like the state-founding of Jī Zhōu (姬周),
with its five ranks
and their regulated system.
If Fú Sū (扶蘇) remonstrated with Shǐ Huáng (始皇),
and Chúnyú Yuè (淳于越) challenged Zhōu Qīngchén (周青臣),
they could be said to have understood the changing times.
Indeed, the one who can make all under heaven incline their ears and fix their gaze
is
the one who holds power.
Thus, counsel can sway the sovereign,
and authority can awe subordinates.
The powerful and influential who govern
are not necessarily relatives;
where power resides,
even the distant will be respected,
and where influence departs,
even the close will be slighted.
Indeed, those who seized Qí (齊) were the Tián (田) clan,
not the Lǚ (呂) lineage.
Those who divided Jìn (晉) were Zhào (趙) and Wèi (魏),
not the Jī (姬) surname.
May Your Majesty observe
this.
If the auspicious monopolizes the position,
and the inauspicious avoids its troubles,
these are ministers of other surnames.
If one desires the stability of the state,
prays for the nobility of the family,
shares its glory in life,
and partakes in its
misfortunes in death,
these are ministers of the ducal clan.
Now, on the contrary, the ducal clan is estranged while those of other surnames are favored,
which Your Servant secretly finds perplexing.
Your Servant heard Mèngzǐ (孟子) say:
"A gentleman, when in straitened circumstances, cultivates his own virtue alone;
when successful, he extends his virtue to all under heaven."
Now, Your Servant and Your Majesty have trodden on ice and walked on coals,
climbed mountains
and floated across ravines,
sharing the cold and warmth, the dry and wet,
the highs and lows.
How could I leave Your Majesty?
Overwhelmed by indignation,
I bow and present this memorial to express my feelings.
If there is anything unsuitable,
I beg that it be temporarily stored in the
imperial archive,
and not be carelessly discarded.
After Your Servant's death,
the matter might perhaps be worth pondering.
If there is even a tiny bit that catches Your Sacred Intention,
I beg that it be brought forth to the court,
so that learned
scholars
may identify any parts of Your Servant's memorial that are not in accordance with righteousness.
If so,
Your Servant's wish will be fulfilled.
The Emperor (帝) immediately responded with a gracious reply.
In the winter of that year,
an edict summoned the vassal kings for the first month of the sixth year.
In the second month,
Zhí (植) was enfeoffed as Chén Wáng (陳王) with four counties of Chén (陳),
comprising three thousand five hundred households.
Zhí (植) constantly wished to have a private audience for discussion,
to deliberate on current affairs,
hoping for an opportunity to be employed,
but ultimately he could not achieve this.
After returning,
he was deeply disappointed and despairing.
At that time, the legal system
treated the vassal states with great severity;
their officials were all mere merchants and lowly talents,
and the soldiers allocated to them were the disabled and elderly,
numbering no more than two hundred in total.
Furthermore, due to Zhí's (植) previous offenses,
everything was further reduced by half.
In eleven years, he was relocated three times,
constantly anxious and unhappy,
and consequently fell ill and died,
at the age of forty-one.
His dying wish was for a simple burial.
He wanted to establish his young son Zhì (志),
as the master of the household,
wishing to enthrone him.
Originally,
Zhí (植) ascended Mount Yú (魚),
overlooking Dōng'ā (東阿),
and with a sigh, had the intention of ending his life there,
and thus began to construct his tomb.
His son Zhì (志) succeeded him,
and was moved to be enfeoffed as Jìběi Wáng (濟北王).
In the Jǐngchū (景初) reign, an edict stated:
"Although Chén Sī Wáng (陳思王) had faults in the past,
he managed to restrain himself and act cautiously,
making up for his former shortcomings.
Moreover, from a young age until his end,
books and writings never left his hands,
which is indeed a rare accomplishment.
Let all memorials submitted during the Huángchū (黃初) reign accusing Zhí (植) be collected,
and all discussions by the high officials and down to the Shàngshū (尚書), Mìshū (祕書), Zhōngshū (中書) three bureaus, and Dà Hónglú (大鴻臚) be deleted.
Compile and record all the odes, eulogies, poems, inscriptions, and miscellaneous treatises written by Zhí (植) before and after, totaling over one hundred pieces,
and store copies both internally and externally."
Zhì (志)'s enfeoffment was increased multiple times,
totaling two thousand seven hundred households including the previous ones.
Xiāo Huái Wáng Xióng (蕭懷王熊)
died young.
In the second year of Huángchū (黃初), he was posthumously granted the title of Xiāo Huái Gōng (蕭懷公).
In the third year of Tàihé (太和), he was again posthumously enfeoffed as a King.
In the second year of Qīnglóng (青龍), his son Āi Wáng Bǐng (哀王炳) succeeded him,
with an income of two thousand five hundred households.
He died in the sixth year,
having no son,
and the state was abolished.
A commentary states: Rènchéng Wǔ Wáng (任城武王) was brave and fierce,
possessing the spirit of a general.
Chén Sī Wáng (陳思王) was rich and brilliant in literary talent,
sufficient to make himself known to later generations.
However, he could not yield and act cautiously to prevent trouble from afar,
ultimately leading to estrangement and fissures.
The tradition says,
"Chǔ (楚) lost it.
But Qí (齊) did not necessarily gain it."
Is this what it refers to!
Biographies of the Martial and Literary Imperial Princes, Part 20
Emperor Wǔ (武皇帝) had twenty-five sons: Empress Biàn (卞皇后) gave birth to Emperor Wén (文皇帝), Rènchéng Wēi Wáng Zhāng (任城威王彰), Chén Sī Wáng Zhí (陳思王植), and Xiāo Huái Wáng Xióng (蕭懷王熊);
Consort Liú (劉夫人) gave birth to Fēng Mǐn Wáng Áng (豐愍王昂) and Xiàng Shāng Wáng Shuò (相殤王鑠);
Consort Huán (環夫人) gave birth to Dèng Āi Wáng Chōng (鄧哀王沖), Péngchéng Wáng Jù (彭城王據), and Yān Wáng Yǔ (燕王宇);
Consort Dù (杜夫人) gave birth to Pèi Mù Wáng Lín (沛穆王林) and Zhōngshān Gōng Wáng Gǔn (中山恭王袞);

Concubine Lǐ (李姬) gave birth to Gǔchéng Shāng Gōngzǐ Chéng (穀城殤公子乘), Méi Dài Gōngzǐ Zhěng (郿戴公子整), and Líng Shāng Gōngzǐ Jīng (靈殤公子京);
Concubine Zhōu (周姬) gave birth to Fán Ān Gōng Jūn (樊安公均);

Concubine Zhào (趙姬) gave birth to Lèlíng Wáng Mào (樂陵王茂).
Fēng Mǐn Wáng Áng (豐愍王昂), courtesy name Zǐxiū (子脩).
At the age of twenty, he was recommended as Xiàolián (孝廉).
He followed Tàizǔ (太祖) in the southern campaign,
and was killed by Zhāng Xiù (張繡).
He had no son.
In the second year of Huángchū (黃初), he was posthumously enfeoffed

In the third year,

and was enfeoffed as Zhōngdū Gōng (中都公).
In the same year, he was moved and enfeoffed as Chángzǐ Gōng (長子公).
In the fifth year,
Áng's (昂) title was additionally given the posthumous name Fēng Dào Wáng (豐悼王).
In the third year of Tàihé (太和), Áng's (昂) posthumous name was changed to Mǐn Wáng (愍王).
In the sixth year of Jiāpíng (嘉平), Wǎn (琬) succeeded Áng's (昂) peerage as Fēng Wáng (豐王).
During the Zhèngyuán (正元) and Jǐngyuán (景元) reigns,
his enfeoffment was increased multiple times,
totaling two thousand seven hundred households including the previous ones.
Wǎn (琬) died,
and was given the posthumous name Gōng Wáng (恭王).
His son Lián (廉) succeeded him.
Xiāng Shāngwáng Shuò (曹鑠),
died young,
and was posthumously enfeoffed and given a posthumous title in the 3rd year of Tàihé.
In the 1st year of Qīnglóng,
his son Mǐnwáng Qián (曹潛) succeeded,
but died in the same year.
In the 2nd year,
his son Huáiwáng Yǎn (曹偃) succeeded.
He held an estate of two thousand five hundred households,
and died in the 4th year.
He had no son,
so the state was abolished.
In the 2nd year of Zhèngyuán,
Sǒng (曹竦), the Duke of Yángdū Xiāng and son of Lèlíng Wáng Mào (曹茂), was made the successor to Shuò (曹鑠).
Dèng Āiwáng Chōng (曹沖), courtesy name Cāngshū.
When young, he was sagacious, observant, and exceptionally intelligent.
At five or six years old,
his understanding
was like that of an adult.
At that time, Sūn Quán (孫權) once presented a giant elephant.
Tàizǔ (曹操) wanted to know its weight,
and consulted his subordinates.
None could come up with a solution.
Chōng (曹沖) said:
"Place the elephant on a large boat,
mark the waterline it reaches,
then load objects onto the boat to weigh it,
and the weight can be calculated."
Tàizǔ (曹操) was greatly pleased,
and immediately put it into practice.
At that time, the military and state had many affairs,
and punishments were severe.
Tàizǔ's (曹操) horse saddle was in the storehouse,
and was gnawed by a rat.
The storehouse official feared certain death,
and discussed whether to bind himself and confess,
but still feared he would not escape.
Chōng (曹沖) said to him:
"Wait for three days,
then turn yourself in."
Chōng (曹沖) then used a knife to pierce his single garment,
making it look as if gnawed by a rat.
He feigned distress,
and appeared sorrowful.
Tàizǔ (曹操) asked him about it.
Chōng (曹沖) replied:
"The common saying is that if a rat gnaws one's clothes,
it portends misfortune for the owner.
Now my single garment has been gnawed,
and that is why I am troubled."
Tàizǔ (曹操) said:
"That is mere superstition,
do not be distressed by it."
Shortly after, the storehouse official reported the gnawed saddle.
Tàizǔ (曹操) laughed and said:
"My son's clothes are right beside him,
yet they are gnawed,
how much more so a saddle hanging on a pillar?"
He asked no questions at all.
Chōng's (曹沖) benevolence, kindness, and perceptiveness
were all of this kind.
All who deserved punishment and execution,
but were subtly reasoned for by Chōng (曹沖),
and thereby saved and pardoned,
numbered several tens over time.
Tàizǔ (曹操) often praised him to his officials,
and had the intention of making him his successor.
At the age of thirteen,
in the 13th year of Jiàn'ān, he fell ill.
Tàizǔ (曹操) personally prayed for his life.
When he died,
Tàizǔ (曹操) grieved greatly.
Wéndì (曹丕) tried to console Tàizǔ (曹操).
Tàizǔ (曹操) said:
"This is my misfortune,
but your good fortune."
As he spoke, tears flowed.
He arranged for a deceased daughter of the Zhēn (甄) clan to be married to Chōng (曹沖) and buried with him.
He was posthumously granted the seal and ribbon of a Qí Dūwèi.
He ordered Cóng (曹琮), the son of Wǎn Hóu Jù (曹據), to be the successor to Chōng (曹沖).
In the 22nd year,
Cóng (曹琮) was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dèng.
In the 2nd year of Huángchū,
Chōng (曹沖) was posthumously granted the title Dèng Āihóu,

In the 3rd year,

In the 4th year,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as the Duke of Jǐshì.
In the 5th year of Tàihé,
Chōng (曹沖)'s title was further elevated to Dèng Āiwáng.
In the 1st year of Jǐngchū,
Cóng (曹琮) was implicated in making forbidden items in the Central Imperial Workshop.
Three hundred households were cut from his estate,
and his rank was demoted to Marquis of Dūxiāng.
he was reinstated as Duke of Jǐshì.
In the 3rd year,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Duke of Píngyáng.
During Jǐngchū, Zhèngyuán, and Jǐngyuán periods,
his estate was repeatedly increased,
totaling one thousand nine hundred households, including the previous ones.
Péngchéng Wáng Jù (曹據),
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Fànyáng in the 16th year of Jiàn'ān.
In the 22nd year,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǎn.
In the 2nd year of Huángchū,
his rank was advanced to Duke.
In the 3rd year,
he became King of Zhānglíng.
In the same year, he was transferred and enfeoffed in Yìyáng.
Because Wéndì (曹丕) considered the south to be low and damp,
and also because his mother, Consort Huán Tàifēi, was from Péngchéng,
he was transferred and enfeoffed in Péngchéng.
Later he was transferred and enfeoffed in Jìyīn.
In the 5th year,
an edict stated:
"The former kings established states,

The Ancestor of Han (Liú Bāng 劉邦) increased the commanderies set up by Qin,

commanderies and counties were merged and reduced.
Compared to now,
it is even worse.
Therefore, all kings shall be re-enfeoffed
as county kings."
Jù (曹據) was re-enfeoffed in Dìngtáo County.
In the 6th year of Tàihé,
the enfeoffment of all kings was changed,

Jù (曹據) was again enfeoffed in Péngchéng.
In the 1st year of Jǐngchū,
Jù (曹據) was implicated in privately sending people to the Central Imperial Workshop to make forbidden items.
Two thousand households were cut from his county.
In the 3rd year,
the cut households were restored to his estate.
During Zhèngyuán and Jǐngyuán periods, his estate was repeatedly increased,
totaling four thousand six hundred households, including the previous ones.
Yān Wáng Yǔ (曹宇), courtesy name Péngzǔ.
In the 16th year of Jiàn'ān,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
In the 22nd year,
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Lǔyáng.

In the 6th year of Tàihé,
he was re-enfeoffed as King of Yān.
Míngdì (曹叡) had lived with Yǔ (曹宇) since childhood,
and always held him in special affection.
After ascending the throne,
his favor and grants to Yǔ (曹宇) surpassed those to other kings.
In the 3rd year of Qīnglóng,
he was summoned to court.
In the 1st year of Jǐngchū,
he returned to Yè (鄴).
In the summer of the 2nd year,
he was again summoned to the capital.
In the winter, 12th month,
Míngdì (曹叡) was gravely ill.
He appointed Yǔ (曹宇) as Grand General,
and entrusted him with his posthumous affairs.
He held the appointment for four days.
Yǔ (曹宇) firmly declined;
the Emperor's intention also changed,
and he thereupon relieved Yǔ (曹宇) of his office.
In the summer of the 3rd year,
he returned to Yè (鄴).
During Jǐngchū, Zhèngyuán, and Jǐngyuán periods,
his estate was repeatedly increased,
totaling five thousand five hundred households, including the previous ones.
Chángdào Xiāng Gōng Huàn (曹奐),
son of Yǔ (曹宇),
entered to succeed the main lineage.
Pèi Mùwáng Lín (曹林),

he was transferred and enfeoffed in Qiáo.

his rank was advanced to Duke.

he was re-enfeoffed in Pèi.
During Jǐngchū, Zhèngyuán, and Jǐngyuán periods,
his estate was repeatedly increased,
totaling four thousand seven hundred households, including the previous ones.
After Lín (曹林) died,
his son Wěi (曹緯) succeeded.
Zhōngshān Gōngwáng Gǔn,
in the 21st year of Jiàn'ān, was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Píngxiāng.
From a young age, he loved learning.
When he was a little over ten years old, he could compose essays.
Whenever he read,
his literary attendants and those around him often feared that he would fall ill from overexertion,
and frequently advised him to stop.
However, it was what he naturally enjoyed,
and he could not give it up.
In the 22nd year,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngxiāng.
In the same year, he was again re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zàn.
In the 2nd year of Huángchū,
his title was advanced to Duke.
All his officials and subordinates offered congratulations.
Gǔn said,
"Born in the depths of the palace,
unaware of the hardships of farming,
one is prone to the faults of pride and extravagance.
Since you, my worthy gentlemen, celebrate this good fortune,
you should also assist in correcting my shortcomings."
Whenever his brothers engaged in leisure activities,
Gǔn alone deeply pondered the classics.
His literary and advisory officials spoke among themselves, saying,
"We received an imperial edict to observe the Duke's conduct and actions.
If there are faults, we should report them.
If there are good deeds,
they should also be made known.
We must not conceal his virtues."
So they jointly submitted a memorial praising Gǔn's virtues.
When Gǔn heard of this,
he was greatly alarmed and frightened.
He reproached his literary attendants, saying,
"Cultivating oneself and maintaining integrity
are merely the actions of ordinary people.
For you gentlemen to report this to the Emperor
is precisely to increase my burden.
Moreover, if there are good deeds,
why worry that they won't be known?
To rush and do this together
is not to benefit me."
Such was his caution and circumspection.
In the 3rd year,
he became the Prince of Běihǎi.
In that same year,
a yellow dragon was seen in the Zhāng River west of Yè.
Gǔn submitted a memorial in praise.
An imperial edict bestowed upon him ten catties of gold.
The edict said,
"In ancient times, Tángshū returned the millet,
and Dōngpíng offered praise.
These were all praises from kinsmen,
demonstrating profound kinship.
The King has diligently studied the great classics,
and delights in savoring the true Dao.
His literary elegance is resplendent,
and We greatly commend him.
May the King be able to exercise caution and uphold bright virtue,
to ensure a good reputation till the end."
In the 4th year,
he was re-enfeoffed as the Prince of Zàn.
In the 7th year,
he was transferred and enfeoffed in Púyáng.
In the 2nd year of Tàihé, he proceeded to his domain.
He advocated frugality and simplicity,
instructing his concubines to spin and weave,
practicing domestic tasks.
In the winter of the 5th year,
he came to court.
In the 6th year,
he was re-enfeoffed in Zhōngshān.
Originally,
when Gǔn came to court,
he violated a prohibition in the capital.
In the 1st year of Qīnglóng,
the relevant officials impeached Gǔn.
An imperial edict stated,
"The King has always been respectful and cautious.
This happened by chance.
Let it be deliberated according to the principle of considering kinship."
The officials firmly insisted.
An imperial edict cut off two counties
and 750 households from his fief.
Gǔn was worried and fearful,
and he admonished his officials and subordinates with even greater strictness.
The Emperor praised his intention,
and in the 2nd year,
restored the counties that had been cut off.
In the autumn of the 3rd year,
Gǔn fell ill.
An imperial edict dispatched imperial physicians to attend to his illness.
Palace attendants and guards delivered imperial handwritten edicts and bestowed precious meals, one after another.
Furthermore, the Grand Consort and Pèiwáng Lín were also sent to visit and inquire about his illness.
When Gǔn's illness became critical,
he instructed his officials and subordinates, saying,
"I, with little virtue, have been unworthy of imperial favor,
and my great destiny is nearing its end.
Since I love frugality,
and the sacred court has instituted the system of posthumous edicts,
setting an example for all under Heaven,
on the day my breath ceases,
from the embalming to the burial,
you must diligently follow the imperial edicts.
In the past, Qú Yuàn, a grand master of Wèi, was buried in Púyáng.
I often look upon his tomb
and imagine his lingering customs.
I wish to rely on the spirit of that worthy to protect my remaining years.
When establishing my burial ground,
I must go and follow him.
According to ritual, a man does not die at the hands of women.
Quickly complete the East Hall in good time."
When the hall was completed,
he named it the Hall of Fulfilling Aspirations (Suìzhì zhī Táng),
and was carried there to reside in it due to his illness.
He further instructed his heir, saying,
"You are young,
and have not yet heard the principles of righteousness.
Becoming a ruler early,
you only know pleasure
but not hardship.
If you do not know hardship,
you will certainly fall into the errors of pride and extravagance.
When interacting with high officials,
always do so with courtesy.
Even if they are not high officials,
an elder should still be respectfully saluted in return.
Serve your elder brothers with respect,
and care for your younger brothers with kindness.
If your brothers engage in misconduct,
you should kneel and admonish them.
If they do not heed your admonition,
shed tears and persuade them.
If they still do not change after persuasion,
then inform your mother.
If they still do not reform,
you should report it to the Emperor,
and concurrently resign your domain.
Rather than clinging to favor and inviting disaster,
it is better to be poor and humble and preserve oneself whole.
This refers only to major offenses and evils.
For minor transgressions and petty matters,
you should conceal and cover them.
Alas, my young son,
diligently cultivate yourself,
serve the sacred court with loyalty and integrity,
and attend to the Grand Consort with filial piety and respect.
Within the women's quarters,
obey the commands of the Grand Consort.
Outside the threshold,
receive instruction from Pèiwáng.
Do not slacken your resolve,
so as to comfort my spirit."
He passed away that year.
An imperial edict ordered Pèiwáng Lín to stay until the burial.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (Dàhónglú) was sent with an imperial envoy's staff to oversee the funeral arrangements.
The Imperial Clan Court (Zōngzhèng) offered condolences and sacrifices,
and the funeral gifts were very generous.
In total, he authored over 20,000 words of writings.

Biographies of Wáng, Wèi, and the two Liú Fù, Chapter Twenty-One
Wáng Càn, courtesy name Zhòngxuān,
was a native of Gāopíng, Shānyáng.
His great-grandfather Gōng [Wáng Gōng]
and grandfather Chàng [Wáng Chàng]
both served as the Three Ducal Ministers of Hàn.
His father Qiān [Wáng Qiān]
was the Chief Clerk to Grand General Hé Jìn.
Hé Jìn, seeing that Qiān [Wáng Qiān] was the descendant of a ducal family,
wished to form a marriage alliance with him,
and upon seeing his two sons,
asked him to choose one.
Qiān [Wáng Qiān] refused.
He resigned due to illness
and died at home.
When Emperor Xiàn moved west,
Càn [Wáng Càn] moved to Cháng'ān.
Zuǒ Zhōngláng Jiàng Cài Yōng saw him and was struck by his talent.
At that time, Cài Yōng's talent and learning were renowned,
and he was highly respected at court.
His carriages and riders constantly filled the alleys,
and guests crowded his seats.
Hearing that Càn [Wáng Càn] was at the gate,
he rushed out to welcome him, putting on his shoes hastily.
When Càn [Wáng Càn] arrived,
he was still young and weak,
short in stature,
which astonished everyone present.
Cài Yōng said:
"This is the grandson of Wáng Gōng;
he possesses extraordinary talent,
I am not his equal.
All the books and writings in my home
should be given to him."
At seventeen,
he was summoned by the Sītú.
An imperial edict appointed him Huángmén Shìláng,
but due to the turmoil in Xījīng (the Western Capital),
he did not take up any of these posts.
Instead, he went to Jīngzhōu to depend on Liú Biǎo.
Liú Biǎo, seeing Càn's [Wáng Càn's] unattractive appearance and weak, casual demeanor,
did not think highly of him.
After Liú Biǎo died,
Càn [Wáng Càn] advised Liú Biǎo's son Cóng [Liú Cóng]
to surrender to Tàizǔ [Cáo Cāo].
Tàizǔ [Cáo Cāo] appointed him Chéngxiàng Yuàn [Aide to the Chancellor]
and bestowed upon him the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
Tàizǔ [Cáo Cāo] hosted a banquet on the banks of the Hàn River,
and Càn [Wáng Càn] offered a toast, saying:
"Currently, Yuán Shào has risen in Héběi,
relying on a large army,
with ambitions to conquer the world.
However, he admires the worthy but cannot employ them,
thus extraordinary men leave him.
Liú Biǎo remains in Jīngchǔ,
passively observing the changing times,
believing he can emulate Xībó [King Wén of Zhōu].
Those who fled to Jīngzhōu to escape the chaos
are all outstanding talents from across the land;
Liú Biǎo does not know how to employ them,
hence his state is in peril and without support.
When your sagacious self [Tàizǔ] pacified Jìzhōu,
upon arriving, you immediately repaired their armor and weapons,
gathered their heroes and employed them,
thereby sweeping across the land.
When you pacified Jiāng and Hàn,
you recruited their virtuous and eminent men and placed them in official positions,
causing the whole world to turn their hearts,
yearning for good governance at the mere mention of your name.
With both civil and military talents employed,
and all heroes dedicating their efforts,
this is an achievement worthy of the Three Kings."
Later, he was promoted to Jūnmóu Jìjiǔ.
After the state of Wèi was established,
he was appointed Shìzhōng.
He was widely learned and knowledgeable,
and there was no question he could not answer.
At that time, old rituals were abolished,
and new systems were being created,
Càn [Wáng Càn] always presided over this.
Initially,
Càn [Wáng Càn] was walking with someone
and read a stele by the roadside.
The person asked:
"Can you recite it from memory?"
He replied:
"Yes."
The person then made him turn his back and recite it,
and he did not miss a single character.
Once, observing people playing Go,
the board was disturbed,
and Càn [Wáng Càn] restored it.
The players did not believe him,
so they covered the board with a cloth
and asked him to recreate it on another board.
When compared,
he did not err by a single position.
His powerful memory and silent recollection were thus.
He was naturally good at calculation,
and in his work on arithmetic,
he explored its principles exhaustively.
He was skilled in composition,
drafting essays effortlessly without needing revisions.
People often thought he had composed them beforehand;
yet, even if he exerted deep thought and careful consideration,
he could not improve upon them.
He authored nearly sixty pieces of poetry, rhymed prose, treatises, and discussions.
In the twenty-first year of Jiàn'ān [216 CE],
he accompanied the campaign against Wú.
In the spring of the twenty-second year [217 CE],
he fell ill on the road and died,
at the age of forty-one.
Càn's [Wáng Càn's] two sons
were implicated by Wèi Fěng
and executed.
His line ended.

Càn [Wáng Càn], along with Xú Gàn, courtesy name Wěicháng, from Běihǎi; Chén Lín, courtesy name Kǒngzhāng, from Guǎnglín; Ruǎn Yǔ, courtesy name Yuányú, from Chénliú; Yìng Yáng, courtesy name Délǐan, from Rǔnán (Yáng

Xú Gàn served as Jūnmóu Jìjiǔ Yuànshǔ to Sīkōng and Wǔguān Jiāng Wénxué.
Lín formerly served as Hé Jìn's chief clerk (zhǔbù).
Jìn wished to execute all the eunuchs,
but the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) did not consent.
Jìn therefore summoned fierce generals from all four directions,
and made them lead their troops toward the capital (Jīngchéng),
intending to coerce and intimidate the Empress Dowager.
Lín remonstrated with Jìn, saying:
"The 'Yì' (Book of Changes) says: 'Hunting deer without a guide.'
There is a proverb: 'Covering one's eyes to catch a sparrow.'
Indeed, if even a tiny creature cannot be deceived to achieve one's goal,
how much more so for a great affair of the state?
How can it be achieved by deceit?
Now, general, you command the imperial authority,
hold the military essential;
with the dragon's soaring and tiger's stride,
victory or defeat is within your grasp.
To act in this manner
is no different from fanning a great furnace to burn away a hair.
You should only swiftly unleash thunder,
act with discretion and make a decisive break,
transgressing the classics but aligning with the Dao;
heaven and men will obey you.
But instead, you abandon your sharp weapon,
and seek it elsewhere.
When large armies gather,
the strong become supreme.
This is what is called 'holding one's shield and spear upside down,'
handing power to others.
Your endeavor will certainly fail,
and merely become a source of chaos."
Jìn did not heed his words,
and consequently met with disaster.
Lín fled the chaos to Jìzhōu,
where Yuán Shào employed him to manage documents and writings (diǎn wénzhāng).
When the Yuán clan was defeated,
Lín returned to Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
Grand Ancestor said to him:
"You formerly wrote that proclamation for Běnchū (Yuán Shào),
but you should have only condemned me for my faults,
and limited your hatred to my person.
Why did you extend it to my father and ancestors?"
Lín apologized,
and Grand Ancestor, admiring his talent, did not blame him.
Yǔ studied under Cài Yōng when he was young.
During the Jiàn'ān era, Commander of the Protectorate Cáo Hóng wanted him to serve as a secretary (zhǎng shūjì),
but Yǔ ultimately refused to yield.
Grand Ancestor appointed both Lín and Yǔ as Libationers of the Military Counsellors of the Minister of Works (Sīkōng Jūnmóu Jìjiǔ),
managing the secretarial office (jìshì).
Many of the military and state proclamations
were authored by Lín and Yǔ.
Lín was transferred to be the Palace Clerk (Ménxià Dū),
and Yǔ became the Senior Clerk of the Granary (Cāngcáo Yuánshǔ).
Yáng and Zhēn were each recruited by Grand Ancestor
to be Senior Clerks of the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng Yuánshǔ).
Yáng later became the Heir Apparent of the Marquis of Píngyuán (Píngyuán Hóu Shùzǐ),
and subsequently the Literary Advisor to the General of the Five Bureaus (Wǔguān Jiāng Wénxué).
Zhēn was punished for disrespect,
and after the punishment, he was appointed to office.
They all composed dozens of essays and rhapsodies (wénfù).
Yǔ died in the seventeenth year.
Gàn, Lín, Yáng, and Zhēn died in the twenty-second year.
Emperor Wén wrote to Wú Zhì, the Prefect of Yuánchéng, saying:
"In past years, there was a plague,
and many relatives and friends suffered from it.
Xú, Chén, Yīng, and Liú
all passed away at once.
Observing literary men throughout history,
they generally do not guard their minor conduct,
and few are able to establish themselves with their reputation and integrity.
But Wěicháng (Wáng Càn) alone possessed both literary talent and inner quality,
being tranquil, indifferent, and having few desires,
with the aspirations of Jīshān.
He can be called a refined gentleman.
He wrote 'Zhōng Lùn' (Discourses on the Mean) of more than twenty chapters,
the language and meaning of which are elegant and refined,
sufficient to be passed down to later generations.
Déluán (Xú Gàn) often showed an earnest intention to write,
and his talent and learning were sufficient to compose books,
but his noble aspirations were not realized,
which is truly regrettable and lamentable!
Kǒngzhāng's (Kǒng Róng) memorials and proclamations are particularly vigorous,
though slightly prolix.
Gōnggàn (Liú Zhēn) has an unrestrained spirit,
but is not yet robust enough.
Yuányú's (Ruan Yu) letters and records are elegant and free-flowing,
which is truly delightful.
Zhòngxuān (Wáng Càn) alone excels at rhapsodies and prose,
but it is a pity that his body was weak,
and could not fully embody his writing;
as for his strengths,
the ancients cannot greatly surpass him.
Formerly, Bóyá broke his zither strings for Zhōng Qī,
and Zhòngní (Confucius) overturned the minced meat for Zǐlù,
mourning the difficulty of meeting a kindred spirit,
and grieving that his disciples could not catch up.
These gentlemen, though not quite matching the ancients,
are nevertheless outstanding talents of their time."
Furthermore, Hándān Chún of Yǐngchuān,
Fán Qīn, (
Fán is pronounced Pó.)
Lù Cuì of Chénliú,
Dīng Yí and Dīng Yì of Pèiguó, Yáng Xiū of Hóngnóng, Gǒu Wěi of Hénèi, and others
also possessed literary talent,
but are not included in this group of seven.
Yáng's younger brother, Qú,
and Qú's son, Zhēn,
were both distinguished for their literary works.
Qú reached the office of Attendant Censor (Shìzhōng).
Zhēn participated in the military affairs of the Chancellor (Xiàngguó Jūnmìshì) during the Xiánxī era.
Yǔ's son, Jí,
had brilliant and unrestrained talent,
but was unconventional and uninhibited in his conduct,
having few desires,
taking Zhuāng Zhōu as his model.
He reached the office of Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
At that time, there was also Jī Kāng of Qiáojùn,
whose literary style was grand and beautiful,
who enjoyed discussing Lǎo and Zhuāng,
and valued eccentricity and chivalry.
He was executed for an offense during the Jǐngyuán era.
During the Jǐngchū era,
Huán Wēi of Xiàpí, who came from humble origins,
at the age of eighteen wrote the 'Húnyú Jīng' (Classic of the Cosmos),
expressing his ideas based on the Dao.
He served as a clerical assistant (shūzuǒ) under the gate of the state of Qí (Qíguó Ménxià), and as a clerk in the office of the Minister of Education (Sītú Shǔlì),
and later became the Prefect of Ānchéng.
Wú Zhì,
a man from Jìyīn,
was favored by Emperor Wén for his literary talent,
and reached the office of General Who Arouses Awe (Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn),
with authority to command all military affairs north of the Yellow River (Dūwěi Héběi Zhū Jūnmìshì),
and was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Wèi Jì
zì Bórú, was a native of Ānyì, Hédōng.
He matured early in his youth
and was known for his talent and learning.
Tàizǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Wèi) appointed him as a subordinate clerk in the Sīkōng office.
He was then made Magistrate of Màolíng and Shàngshū Láng.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Yuán Shào,
and Liú Biǎo supported Shào,
the various generals in Guānzhōng remained neutral.
The Governor of Yìzhōu, Liú Zhāng, had a rift with Liú Biǎo.
Wèi Jì, as Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ, was sent as an envoy to Yìzhōu,
to order Liú Zhāng to send troops to tie up Liú Biǎo's army.
When he reached Cháng'ān,
the roads were impassable,
and Wèi Jì could not proceed.
He therefore remained to guard Guānzhōng.
At that time, many people were returning from all directions.
The generals in Guānzhōng largely recruited them as their private retainers (bùqǔ).
Wèi Jì wrote to Xún Yù, saying:
"Guānzhōng is a fertile land,
but recently suffered from desolation and chaos.
More than 100,000 households flowed into Jīngzhōu.
Hearing that their homeland is peaceful,
they all eagerly wish to return.
However, those who return have no means to support themselves,
and the various generals compete to attract and pacify them,
making them their bùqǔ.
The commanderies and counties are poor and weak,
unable to contend with them,
so the military factions become strong.
Should there be any sudden change,
there will certainly be future troubles.
Now, salt
is a great treasure of the state.
Since the chaos, it has been dispersed and freely traded.
It should be managed as before, with envoys appointed to supervise its sale.
The revenue from this should be used to purchase plowing oxen for the markets.
If there are returning people,
these can be supplied to them.
Encourage diligent farming and accumulation of grain
to enrich and prosper Guānzhōng.
Distant people, hearing of this,
will surely return day and night.
Furthermore, send the Sīlì Xiàowèi to govern Guānzhōng as its master.
Then the power of the generals will diminish daily,
while that of the officials and common people will increase daily.
This is a strategy to strengthen the foundation and weaken the adversaries."
Xún Yù reported this to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ followed his advice
and first sent the Yèzhě Púyè to supervise the salt officials,
and the Sīlì Xiàowèi to govern Hóngnóng.
Once Guānzhōng submitted,
he requested Wèi Jì's return
and gradually promoted him to Shàngshū.
When the State of Wèi was established,
he was appointed Shìzhōng,
and jointly managed state institutions with Wáng Càn.
When Emperor Wén (Cáo Pī) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Shàngshū.
Soon after,
he returned to the Hàn court as Shìláng,
advocating and supporting the righteousness of abdication,
and drafting the proclamations for the imperial edicts.
When Emperor Wén assumed the imperial throne,
he was again made Shàngshū
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yángjí Tíng.
When Emperor Míng (Cáo Ruì) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Marquis of Wénxiāng,
with three hundred households.
(Wén is pronounced like 'wén'.)
Wèi Jì memorialized, saying:
"The Nine Chapters of Law,
transmitted since ancient times,
determine criminal offenses with subtle and profound meaning.
Magistrates of every county
should all understand the laws.
Criminal law
is what the state values highly,
yet it is despised in private discussions;
prison officials
are those upon whom the common people's lives depend,
yet they are considered low by those who select them.
The deterioration of royal governance
is perhaps not unrelated to this.
I request the establishment of Doctors of Law,
to teach each other in succession."
The matter was subsequently implemented.
At that time, the common people were impoverished and exhausted, yet corvée duties were heavy.
Wèi Jì submitted a memorial, saying:
"To change one's sentiments and alter one's nature
is beyond one's ability.
It is not easy for a subject to speak of it,
and it is difficult for a ruler to accept it.
Moreover, what people desire
is wealth, nobility, and renown,
and what they detest is poverty, lowliness, and death.
Yet these four things
are controlled by the ruler.
If the ruler loves them, they attain wealth, nobility, and renown;
if the ruler dislikes them, they suffer poverty, lowliness, and death.
Following the ruler's will leads to favor,
while going against the ruler's wishes leads to disfavor.
Therefore, all subjects compete to follow the ruler's will
and avoid going against it.
Unless one is willing to sacrifice one's family for the state,
and kill oneself to fulfill the ruler's ambition,
who can dare to offend the ruler's countenance,
touch upon taboos,
present a single word,
or open a single discussion?
If Your Majesty pays attention and observes this,
the true feelings of your subjects will be evident.
Currently, many counselors enjoy pleasing the ear.
When speaking of governance, they compare Your Majesty to Yáo and Shùn;
when speaking of campaigns, they compare the two enemies to raccoons and mice.
Your subject believes this is not so.
In the time of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
the feudal lords were powerful,
and Jiǎ Yì repeatedly sighed, considering it extremely perilous.
How much more so now, when within the four seas,
the realm is divided into three,
and scholars exert their strength, each serving their own lord.
Those who surrender
are not yet willing to abandon evil and turn to righteousness;
they all claim to be forced by desperation and urgency.
This is no different
from the division of the Six States.
At present, there are no cooking fires for a thousand li,
and the remaining people are suffering.
If Your Majesty does not pay careful attention,
the decline will continue and become irrecoverable.
According to the Rites,
the Emperor's utensils must have gold and jade ornaments,
and the food must include the eight delicacies.
However, in times of famine,
he must simplify his meals and change to plainer attire.
Thus, the balance of extravagance and frugality
must depend on the abundance or scarcity of the times.
During the time of Emperor Wǔ (Cáo Cāo),
the imperial concubines ate no more than one meat dish,
their clothes were not of brocade,
their bedding was without adornment,
and their utensils had no red lacquer.
With this, he was able to pacify the realm
and bequeath blessings to his descendants.
All of this Your Majesty personally witnessed.
The current priority
is for ruler and subjects, high and low,
to collectively use strategies
to calculate the state treasury
and regulate expenditures according to income.
Deeply contemplate Gōu Jiàn's method of nurturing the people,
lest it be too late.
Yet the objects of gold and silver created by the Shàngfāng bureau
are gradually increasing in scope,
the labor continues without cease,
extravagance daily escalates,
and the treasury daily depletes.
In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn sincerely sought the way of the immortals,
believing he could obtain dew from the clouds to consume jade powder.
Therefore, he erected the Immortal Palm to collect the high dew.
Your Majesty is enlightened
and often ridicules this.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn had a purpose for seeking the dew,
yet was still criticized.
Your Majesty has no purpose for the dew, yet idly sets it up;
it adds nothing to your virtue yet wastes effort and resources.
Truly, all these are things Your Majesty's sagacious consideration should curtail."
Wèi Jì served through both the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
often offering loyal advice like this.
He was commanded to oversee the compilation of writings,
and also compiled the Official Rites of Wèi,
totaling dozens of chapters.
He was skilled in ancient script, bird-and-seal script, and clerical and cursive scripts—
there was nothing he was not good at.
At the end of the Jiàn'ān era,
Pān Xù
of Hénán, the Shàngshū Yòuchéng;
and during the Huángchū era,
Wáng Xiàng
of Hénèi, the Sànqí Chángshì, also gained prominence for their literary compositions alongside Wèi Jì.
When Wèi Jì passed away,
he was posthumously titled Jìng Hóu.
His son Guàn succeeded him.
Wèi Guàn became Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn during the Xiánxī era.
Liú Yì, courtesy name Gōngsì,
was a man from Ānzhòng, Nányáng.
When he was ten years old,
he was playing in the lecture hall.
Sīmǎ Décāo of Yǐngchuān patted his head and said,
"Little one,
little one,
'the yellow center connects to reason,'
do you know this yourself or not?"
Yì's elder brother, Wàngzhī,
was famous in the world.
Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, appointed him as an aide.
However, two of his friends,
both due to slander,
were executed by Biǎo.
Wàngzhī, again because his upright remonstrances were not accepted,
threw away his credentials and requested to return home.
Yì said to Wàngzhī,
"Zhào killed Míng and Dú,
and Zhòngní turned his chariot around.
Now, since you, my brother, cannot emulate Liǔxià Huì by harmonizing with the times and blending in within,
then you should model Fàn Lǐ by adapting to change outwardly.
To sit idle and cut yourself off from the world
is likely unacceptable!"
Wàngzhī did not listen,
and soon after was again harmed.
Yì was afraid,
and fled to Yángzhōu,
eventually returning to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ appointed him as an aide in the Chancellor's office,
and then transferred him to the position of Literary Officer to the Prince of Wǔguān.
Wén Dì valued him [qì zhī],
and ordered Yì to write in cursive script.
Yì replied in a letter, saying:
"Initially, I considered that there is a distinction between superior and inferior,
which is the normal custom of ritual.
Therefore, I greedily maintained my humble integrity,
not daring to practice cursive writing.
If it must be as Your strict command dictates,
I sincerely understand that the essence of diligent humility
does not value uniqueness as highly as that,
but rather esteems the kindness of a 'plain dwelling' as this.
If Guō Kuí is not lightly regarded in Yān,
and Jiǔjiǔ is not overlooked in Qí,
then Yuè Yì will come on his own,
and the hegemonic enterprise will flourish.
To sacrifice the integrity of an ordinary man
to accomplish a magnificent beauty,
even if I am foolish and not clever,
how dare I refuse?"
When the state of Wèi was first established,
he served as a Palace Attendant.
When Tàizǔ was in Cháng'ān,
wishing to personally campaign against Shǔ,
Yì submitted a memorial, saying:
"A sage does not lightly regard common customs with his wisdom,
and a king does not disregard words on account of the person.
Therefore, one who can achieve success for a thousand years
must observe what is near to understand what is far,
and one whose wisdom encompasses independent judgment
is not ashamed to inquire of those below,
also wishing to broadly gather opinions to exhaust all possibilities.
Moreover, 'wéixián' are not things that can speak,
yet sages and worthies use them to rectify themselves.
My talent and wisdom are dark and shallow,
and I wish to compare myself to 'wéixián.'
In the past, Yuè Yì was able to defeat the great Qí with the weak Yān,
yet he could not conquer Jìmò with light forces.
This is because those who plan for themselves, though weak, will surely be firm;
those who wish to destroy themselves, though strong, will surely fail.
Since Your Highness raised an army,
for over thirty years,
no enemy has not been defeated,
no strong force has not been subdued.
Now, with the troops of the entire realm,
and the prestige of a hundred victories,
yet Sūn Quán relies on the dangers of Wú,
and Liú Bèi is not submissive in Shǔ.
The vassals of the barbarians [yí dí]
are not comparable to the soldiers of Jìzhōu,
and the registered population of Quán and Bèi
is not comparable to Yuán Shào's enterprise.
However, Běnchū perished,
yet the two bandits have not yet been overcome.
This is not because Your Highness is dark and weak now, but wise and martial in the past.
This is simply that those who plan for themselves are in a different situation from those who wish to destroy themselves.
Therefore, when Wén Wáng attacked Chóng,
he drove his chariot three times but did not dismount.
He returned and cultivated virtue,
and then Chóng submitted.
Qín, as a feudal lord,
subdued all it conquered.
But when it unified the world,
and faced east to proclaim itself emperor,
ordinary men raised a great cry and the altars of earth and grain were overthrown.
This was because its strength was exhausted externally,
and it did not care for the people internally.
I fear that the border bandits are not the equals of the Six States,
yet the world does not lack talent.
The potential for collapse [tǔ bēng zhī shì]
is something that must not be overlooked.
The world has major gains [zhòng dé]
and major losses [zhòng shī]. If a situation can be gained and I work hard for it,
this is a major gain.
If a situation cannot be gained and I work hard for it,
this is a major loss.
According to the current plan,
nothing is better than to assess the dangers of the four quarters,
select critical strategic points to defend,
choose the best armored soldiers in the realm,
and rotate them annually by direction.
Your Highness can recline peacefully in your grand hall,
and secretly ponder governing the state;
expand agriculture and sericulture,
practice economy,
cultivate this for ten years,
and then the state will be wealthy and the people secure."
Tàizǔ then stepped forward and replied to Yì, saying:
"Not only should a ruler know his ministers,
a minister should also know his ruler.
Now, to expect me to sit and practice the virtue of Xī Bó,
I fear I am not the right person for it."
When Wèi Fěng rebelled,
Yì's younger brother Wěi was implicated by Fěng,
and Yì was liable to be implicated and executed.
Tàizǔ issued an order, saying:
"Shūxiàng was not implicated by his younger brother Hǔ;
this is an ancient rule."
He specifically pardoned him and did not question him, transferring him to serve as a clerk in the Chancellor's Granary Office.
Yì submitted a memorial to express his gratitude, saying:
"My crime deserved the ruin of my clan,
my calamity deserved the overthrow of my family.
I encountered the spiritual essence of Heaven and Earth,
and met with a fortunate turn of destiny.
It was like pouring hot water to stop boiling,
preventing scorching and rotting;
raising smoke from cold ashes,
and causing flowers to bloom on withered wood.
Creatures do not repay the bounty of Heaven and Earth,
and children do not thank their parents for giving birth.
I can show my gratitude with my death,
but it is difficult to express it in writing."
Yì wrote dozens of essays,
and his discussions on criminal law and ritual with Dīng Yí
are all transmitted to the world.
When Wén Dì ascended to the throne,
Yì became a Palace Attendant,
and was granted the noble title of Marquis within the Pass.
He died in the second year of Huángchū (221 CE).
He had no sons.
The emperor ordered his nephew Fù to succeed him.
Liú Shào, courtesy name Kǒngcái,
was a man from Hándān, Guǎngpíng.
During the Jiàn'ān era (196-220 CE),
he served as an accounting officer,
and went to Xǔ.
The Grand Astrologer reported:
"There will be a solar eclipse on New Year's Day."
Shào was then at the residence of the Imperial Secretariat Director, Xún Yù.
Dozens of people present
either said that the court should be suspended,
or that the assembly should be canceled.
Shào said:
"Zǐshèn and Pí Zào,
excellent historians of antiquity,
still made mistakes when divining water and fire,
and erred in predicting celestial phenomena.
The Lǐjì states that among the four occasions when feudal lords meet the Son of Heaven and cannot complete the ritual upon reaching the gate,
a solar eclipse is one.
However, the sages established regulations
without pre-emptively suspending court rituals due to anomalies [yì] or changes.
This is either because the calamity dissipated and the anomaly subsided,
or because the calculations were erroneous."
Yù praised his words.
He ordered the court assembly to proceed as usual,
and the sun was not eclipsed.
The Grandee Secretary, Xī Lǜ, invited Shào,
but Lǜ was dismissed
before Shào could take up the post.
He was appointed Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince, then transferred to Secretary of the Imperial Library.
During the Huángchū period,
he served as Director of the Imperial Secretariat and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
He received an imperial edict to compile the Five Classics and various books,
categorizing them by type,
resulting in the work Huánglǎn.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Administrator of Chénliú.
He greatly promoted education and moral transformation,
and the common people praised him.
He was summoned back to court and appointed Commandant of Cavalry,
and together with Counselors Yú Nì and Xún Shēn, he established laws and ordinances,
creating the New Penal Code in eighteen chapters,
and also authored the Lǜlüèlùn.
He was promoted to Cavalier Regular Attendant.
At that time, it was heard that Gōngsūn Yuān had accepted the title of King of Yān from Sūn Quán.
Some counselors wished to detain Yuān's tribute envoys
and send troops to attack him.
Shào, however, argued:
"In the past, Yuán Shàng and his brother sought refuge with Yuān's father, Kāng,
and Kāng beheaded them and sent their heads to the court.
This was an act of loyalty by Yuān's ancestors.
Moreover, the veracity of what has been heard
cannot yet be definitively known.
In ancient times, when distant, wild regions had not yet submitted,
virtue was cultivated rather than punitive expeditions launched,
to avoid burdening the people.
It is appropriate to extend clemency and leniency,
allowing them an opportunity for self-renewal."
Later, Yuān indeed beheaded Sūn Quán's envoy Zhāng Mí and others, and sent their heads to the court.
Shào once composed the Zhàodūfù.
Emperor Míng admired it
and ordered Shào to compose the Xǔdūfù and Luòdūfù.
At that time, there were military campaigns abroad
and palace construction at home.
Shào's two rhapsodies
both subtly admonished the emperor.
During the Qīnglóng period,
Wú besieged Héfěi.
At that time, the eastern officers and soldiers were all on rotating leave.
The General Who Conquers the East, Mǎn Chǒng, memorialized requesting central army troops
and the recall of officers and soldiers on leave,
to gather and then attack.
Shào's deliberation was:
"The enemy forces have just arrived,
their morale is high and their spirits keen.
If Chǒng were to fight them with fewer men on his own territory,
advancing to attack immediately
would not necessarily secure victory.
Chǒng's request to await troops
does not entail any loss.
It is advisable to first dispatch five thousand infantry
and three thousand elite cavalry.
They should set out in advance,
making a show of their march,
to awe and display their strength.
When the cavalry reach Héfěi,
they should spread out their formations,
increase their banners and drums,
display their forces below the city,
and then move to the enemy's rear,
menacing their return route
and cutting off their supply lines.
When the enemy hears that a large army is coming,
and that cavalry are cutting off their rear,
they will surely be terrified and flee,
thus breaking the enemy without a battle."
The emperor followed this advice.
Before the troops even reached Héfěi,
the enemy indeed retreated.
At that time, an imperial edict broadly sought out talented individuals.
Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Xiàhóu Huì recommended Shào, saying:
"I humbly observe that Cavalier Regular Attendant Liú Shào
is deeply loyal and profoundly thoughtful,
his understanding is comprehensive in numerology,
and his comprehensive arrangements
have far-reaching origins and profound influence.
Therefore, all talents, great and small,
find common ground in his insights and draw upon them.
Hence, men of true character admire his fairness and righteousness;
men of purity and tranquility appreciate his profound and humble detachment;
men of letters commend his thorough and meticulous deductions;
men of law and reason clarify his precise calculations and comparisons;
men of deep thought recognize his profound and resolute understanding;
men of literary skill love his treatises and compositions;
men of institutional reform value his transformative strategies and key summaries;
men of policy and planning praise his clear thinking and subtle insight.
All these various assessments
are merely selecting what suits their own strengths and highlighting a branch thereof.
I have often listened to his insightful discussions
and perused his profound treatises,
being gradually immersed for years,
and have adhered to his principles for a long time.
He is truly a man whose remarkable caliber the court appreciates.
I believe that such a person
should assist in crucial state affairs,
offering counsel within the imperial curtained tent,
and that he will flourish together with the national Dao;
he is not one of the ordinary talents of this world.
I only hope that Your Majesty will listen with a leisurely mind,
allowing Shào to enjoy moments of quiet audience,
and to fully express himself before you,
then virtuous pronouncements will ascend,
and brilliance will be renewed daily."
During the Jǐngchū period,
he received an edict to formulate performance evaluations for officials.
Shào submitted a memorial, stating:
"The performance evaluations of all officials
are a major concern of royal governance,
yet successive generations have not made it a priority.
Thus, the principles of good governance are lacking and have not been supplemented,
and the capable and the incompetent are indistinguishable and obscure one another.
Your Majesty, with the vast strategies of a sagely emperor,
laments the decline and decay of the royal order.
Your divine thoughts illuminate from within,
and your clear edicts are issued externally.
Your servant, grateful for this favor, is emboldened
to offer his humble thoughts.
I have presumptuously composed seventy-two articles on performance evaluations for officials,
and also one chapter of explanatory summary.
Your servant's learning is meager and his understanding shallow;
he is truly insufficient to expound
the sagely will and establish definitive institutions."
He also believed that rituals and music should be established
to transform customs,
and authored fourteen chapters on the theory of music.
The work was completed but not yet presented.
At that time, Emperor Míng died,
and it was not implemented.
During the Zhèngshǐ period,
he held lectures on the classics
and was granted the title of Marquis within the Pass.
His selected writings, including the Fǎlùn and Rénwùzhì, amounted to over one hundred chapters.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously awarded the title Grand Master of Ceremonies.
His son, Lín, inherited his title.
At the same time as Shào, Miáo Xí of Dōnghǎi also possessed talent and learning,
and authored many works.
He rose to the offices of Director of the Imperial Secretariat and Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Xí's friend, Zhòngcháng Tǒng of Shānyáng,
served as Director of the Imperial Secretariat at the end of the Hàn dynasty
and died young.
He authored the Chāngyán,
whose prose is excellent and worth reviewing.
Cavalier Regular Attendant Sū Lín of Chénliú,
Grand Master of Radiance Wéi Dàn of Jīngzhào,
Administrator of Lè'ān Xiàhóu Huì of Qiáoguó,
Administrator of Chénjùn Sūn Gāi of Rènchéng, and Palace Attendant Dù Zhì of Hédōng, among others, also authored literary works and rhapsodies,
many of which were circulated in the world.
Fù Gǔ
with the courtesy name Lánshí, was a
native of Níyáng, Běidì, a descendant of
Fù Jièzi. His
uncle, Xùn, served as Shìzhōng Shàngshū
during the Huángchū era. Fù Gǔ gained fame in his
youth. Sīkōng Chén Qún appointed him as a Yuán.
At that time, Sànqí Chángshì Liú Shào drafted a system for evaluating officials' performance,
which was sent down to the Sānfǔ.
Fù Gǔ, challenging Liú Shào's proposal, said:
“I have heard that the imperial system is
profound and the sagely Way is abstruse.
If the talent is not present,
then the Way will not be effectively implemented.
To make it spiritual and enlightened
depends on the individual.
When royal strategies declined and eras passed without continuity,
subtle words vanished,
and the Six Classics were defiled.
Why?
Because the Way is grand and leads far, but no great talents emerge.
Upon reviewing Liú Shào's essay on performance evaluation,
although it seeks to trace the promotions and demotions of previous dynasties,
its institutional framework is largely incomplete or absent.
Among the surviving rituals,
only the Zhōu code exists.
Externally, marquises and earls were established
to form a screen for the Jiǔfú.
Internally, various offices were set up
to manage the Liùzhí.
The land had constant tributes,
and offices had fixed regulations.
All officials were in place,
and the four classes of people had distinct professions.
Thus, performance evaluation could be managed and promotions/demotions easily understood.
The Great Wèi followed the end of a hundred kings,
inheriting the ferocity of Qín and Hàn.
The flow of institutions
was not improved or adopted.
From Jiàn'ān
to Qīnglóng,
the divine martial power suppressed chaos,
founding the imperial sovereignty.
It swept away villains and rebels,
and eradicated remaining bandits.
Banners unfurled and furled;
there was no time to spare.
When it came to governing the state and managing military affairs,
expedient and legal methods were used simultaneously.
All officials and various departments
served both military and state affairs,
adapting to the circumstances of the time
to respond to the exigencies of government.
Applying ancient methods to the present,
matters are complex and principles distinct,
making it difficult to apply them universally.
The reason for this is that
institutions designed for long-term vision
may not be immediately applicable,
and laws suited for current affairs
may not be sufficient for later generations.
Establishing offices and distributing duties,
and bringing order to the people and things,
is what establishes the root;
following names to examine realities,
and correcting and encouraging established rules,
is what governs the branches.
If the root principles are not upheld and the branches not fully managed, yet a system is not yet presented,
and if national strategies are not esteemed but performance evaluation is prioritized,
I fear it will not suffice to distinguish between the wise and the foolish,
nor to refine the principles of the manifest and the subtle.
In ancient times, when the former kings selected talent,
they surely based it on conduct in the townships
and taught the Way in schools.
When conduct was complete, they called them worthy;
when the Way was cultivated, they called them capable.
Village elders presented the worthy and capable to the king.
The king humbly accepted them,
appointed the worthy ones
to be sent out as chiefs,
and selected the capable ones
to be brought in to govern.
This was the principle by which the former kings acquired talent.
At present, among the people of the Jiǔzhōu
and even in the capital city,
there is no system of selection by the liùxiāng.
The responsibility for selecting talent
rests solely with the Lìbù.
Relying on assessments and reports, actual talent may not necessarily be matched;
appointing based on superficial performance, moral conduct may not be considered.
Thus, the performance evaluations
do not fully exhaust all talents.
To comprehensively consolidate the royal measures
and explain national regulations
involves deep and broad principles,
making it difficult to detail.”
At the beginning of Zhèngshǐ,
he was appointed Shàngshū Láng,
then promoted to Huángmén Shìláng.
At that time, Cáo Shuǎng held power,
and Hé Yàn was Lìbù Shàngshū.
Fù Gǔ told Cáo Shuǎng’s younger brother, Xī,
“Hé Píngshú appears calm externally but is sharp and cunning internally.
He is greedy for profit
and does not focus on essential duties.
I fear he will surely first bewilder you and your brothers.
Benevolent people will be alienated,
and the court administration will fall into disuse.”
Hé Yàn and others thus became displeased with Fù Gǔ,
and using a minor issue, they dismissed him from office.
He was appointed Tàishǒu of Xíngyáng,
but did not take up the post.
Tàifù Sīmǎ Xuānwáng invited him to be Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
After Cáo Shuǎng was executed,
he became Hénán Yǐn,
then promoted to Shàngshū.
Fù Gǔ often believed that
“Qín Shǐ [Huáng] abolished marquises and established commanderies,
setting up offices and dividing duties,
which was not the same as antiquity.
Hàn and Wèi followed this practice
until now.
However, Confucian scholars
all wish to combine them with the rituals of the Three Dynasties.
The rituals are grand and far-reaching,
not suitable for current affairs.
Matters conflict with institutions,
and names and realities are not aligned.
Therefore, the reason why successive dynasties have not achieved good governance
is probably due to this.
I wish to greatly reform the official system
and rectify the root according to ancient ways,
but now the imperial house faces many difficulties
and cannot yet make changes.”
At the time, commentators discussed wanting to personally attack Wú,
but the three *Zhēng* (Generals) offered different strategies.
An imperial edict consulted Fù Gǔ,
who replied:
“In the past, Fū Chā overpowered Qí and defeated Jìn,
his prestige extending throughout the Central Plains,
but ultimately calamity befell Gūsū.
Qí Mǐn annexed territory and expanded his borders,
claiming a thousand *lǐ* of land,
yet he personally met with overthrow.
A good beginning does not necessarily guarantee a good end;
this is clearly demonstrated by ancient examples.
After Sūn Quán broke Guān Yǔ and annexed Jīngzhōu,
his ambition swelled and his desires were sated,
and his villainy reached its peak.
Therefore, Xuānwén Hóu deeply advocated a grand strategy of major action.
Now Quán is dead,
having entrusted his orphan to Zhūgě Kè.
If Kè rectifies Quán’s harsh tyranny
and abolishes his oppressive policies,
the people will be spared cruelty,
and will enjoy temporary peace from the new benevolence.
Both internal and external factions will be equally concerned,
feeling the dread of being in the same boat.
Even if they cannot ultimately preserve themselves completely,
it will still be enough to prolong their existence beyond the deep river.
However, some of the debaters wish to cross the river directly by boat
and traverse the lands south of the river;
others wish to advance simultaneously on four routes
and attack their strongholds;
still others wish to cultivate large tracts of land on the borders
and act when an opportunity arises. These are indeed common strategies for defeating the enemy.
However, since mobilizing the army,
three years have passed.
This is not a force for surprise attacks.
The enemy has been a bandit
for nearly sixty years;
lord and minister have falsely established themselves,
sharing fortune and misfortune.
Furthermore, they have lost their commander,
and those above and below are anxious and endangered.
Even if they arrange ships at key crossings
and hold strong cities and dangerous passes,
the strategy of traversing [the enemy territory]
will likely be difficult to achieve quickly.
Only advancing the army and undertaking large-scale cultivation
is the most complete and secure approach.
With troops deployed beyond the civilian population,
bandits and raiders will not encroach;
subsisting on accumulated grain,
there will be no need for arduous transport;
attacking when opportunity arises,
there will be no distant toil or expense: this is the urgent task for the army.
In the past, Fán Kuài wished to command a hundred thousand troops
to traverse the Xīongnú territory,
but Jì Bù openly criticized his flaw.
Now, to cross the long Jiāng [river]
and enter the enemy's court,
is also analogous to that time.
It is better to clarify laws and train soldiers,
to plan for a completely victorious position,
and to wield a long whip to guard against the enemy's lingering embers.
This is an inevitable outcome.”
Later, Wú’s great general Zhūgě Kè, having recently defeated the eastern passes,
rode on his victory, proclaiming his intention to move towards Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu.
The imperial court was preparing for this.
Gǔ argued that
“Huáihǎi is not a route the enemy would lightly take.
Furthermore, in the past, Sūn Quán sent troops by sea,
but they drifted and drowned,
with hardly any survivors.
How could Kè dare to exhaust his roots and foundations,
entrust his life to the vast currents,
to seek risky success?
Kè will do no more than dispatch a partial commander and minor general, skilled in naval warfare,
to go by sea and ascend the Huái [river],
to feign a movement towards Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu.
Kè himself will combine forces and come towards Huáinán.”
Later, Kè indeed planned to attack Xīnchéng,
but failed and returned.
Gǔ often discussed the similarities and differences in talents and temperaments.
Zhōng Huì compiled and discussed them.
At the end of Jiāpíng,
he was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
When Gāoguì Xiānggōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to the rank of Wǔqīng Tínghóu.
In the spring of Zhèngyuán two years,
Wúqiū Jiǎn and Wén Qīn rebelled.
Some believed that Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng should not personally lead the campaign,
and suggested sending Tàiwèi Fú.
Only Gǔ and Wáng Sù urged him to go.
Jǐngwáng then set out,
with Gǔ acting as Shàngshū Púyè,
and they traveled east together.
Jiǎn and Qīn were defeated,
and Gǔ had a hand in the strategy.
When Jǐngwáng died,
Gǔ and Sīmǎ Wénwáng immediately returned to Luòyáng.
Wénwáng then took on the role of regent.
The details are in the biography of Zhōng Huì.
Huì, from this, showed signs of conceit.
Gǔ warned him, saying:
“Your ambition exceeds your capacity,
and great achievements are difficult to accomplish.
How can you not be cautious!”
Gǔ, for his merits, was promoted to Yángxiāng Hóu,
with an increase of six hundred households in his fief,
totaling one thousand two hundred households.
He died that year
at the age of forty-seven,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng,
with the posthumous name Yuánhóu.
His son Zhī inherited.
During Xiánxī, when the five noble ranks were established,
because Gǔ had rendered outstanding service in the former court,
Zhī was re-enfeoffed as Jīngyuánzǐ.
Commentary says: In the past, Wéndì and Chénwáng, despite their noble status as sons of the emperor,
were fond of literary accomplishments,
responding to each other with common voices,
and talented scholars emerged en masse.
Among them, Càn and five others were most renowned.
Càn, in particular, held the office of Chángbó,
establishing a system for an era.
However, his humility and virtue
were not as pure as Xú Gàn’s.
Wèi Jǐ also, through his extensive knowledge of allusions,
assisted in establishing the style of the king.
Liú Shào thoroughly examined academic records,
his writing both refined and substantial.
Liú Yì was known for his clear judgment,
and Fù Gǔ became prominent through his talent.
Biography of Huán, Èr Chén, Xú, Wèi, Lú, Chapter Twenty-two
Huán Jiē, courtesy name Bóxù,
was a native of Línxiāng, Chángshā.
He served as Jùn Gōngcáo.
Tàishǒu Sūn Jiān recommended Jiē as Xiàolián,
and he was appointed Shàngshū Láng.
He returned to his hometown for his father’s mourning.
Coincidentally, Jiān attacked Liú Biǎo and died in battle.
Jiē braved danger to approach Biǎo and begged for Jiān’s corpse.
Biǎo, out of righteousness, granted it to him.
Later, Tàizǔ and Yuán Shào confronted each other at Guāndù.
Biǎo rallied his entire province to support Shào.
Jiē persuaded his Tàishǒu Zhāng Xiàn, saying:
“Indeed, those who undertake an endeavor without basing it on righteousness
have never failed to perish.
Thus, Qí Huán led the feudal lords to honor Zhōu,
and Jìn Wén drove out Shúdài to restore the king.
Now, the Yuán clan acts contrary to this,
and Governor Liú responds to them;
this is the path to disaster.
If Your Excellency truly wishes to achieve merit and uphold righteousness,
to secure good fortune and avoid calamity,
you should not align with them.”
Xiàn asked:
“Then towards whom should we turn?”
Jiē said:
“Although Cáo Gōng is weak,
he rose up on the basis of righteousness,
rescuing the imperial court from danger,
and carrying out the king’s mandate to punish the guilty.
Who would dare not submit?
If we now rally the four commanderies and hold the three rivers to await his arrival,
and act as his internal support,
would that not be acceptable!”
Xiàn said:
“Excellent.”
So he rallied Chángshā and the three neighboring commanderies to resist Biǎo,
and sent an envoy to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased.
At that time, Shào and Tàizǔ were locked in continuous battle,
and the army could not move south.
Meanwhile, Biǎo urgently attacked Xiàn,
who died of illness.
The city fell,
and Jiē then went into hiding.
After a long time,
Liú Biǎo invited him to be Cóngshì Jìjiǔ,
and wished to give him his wife’s sister, the Cài clan, in marriage.
Jiē stated that he was already married,
refused the offer,
and then resigned on grounds of illness.
Tài-Zǔ 定𠛼州,
heard that he had planned for Zhāng Xiàn,
and was impressed by him.
He was appointed as a Master of Records for the Chancellor's Assistant.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Zhào-Jùn.
When the State of Wèi was first established,
he served as a Colonel of the Tiger Guard and Attendant.
At that time, the Heir Apparent was not yet determined,
but the Marquis of Lín-Zī, Zhí, was favored.
Jiē repeatedly stated that Emperor Wén had superior virtue and was senior in age,
and should be the Heir.
He made public remonstrances and secret advice,
which were earnest throughout.
Also, Máo Jié and Xú Yì, being rigid and having few allies,
were disliked by Dīng Yí, the Head Clerk of the Western Bureau.
Yí frequently spoke ill of them,
but relied on Jiē's help to save themselves.
His acts of following the trend to rectify and save
were often of this kind.
He was promoted to Minister of Personnel,
in charge of selections.
Cáo Rén was besieged by Guān Yǔ.
Tài-Zǔ sent Xú Huàng to relieve him,
but it was not resolved.
Tài-Zǔ wanted to personally lead an expedition south,
and consulted his subordinates.
All the subordinates said:
"If Your Majesty does not go quickly,
we will be defeated now."
Jiē alone said:
"Does Your Majesty consider Rén and the others capable enough to assess the situation?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"Does Your Majesty fear that the two of them might not exert themselves fully?"
He replied:
"No."
"Then why do you wish to go yourself?"
He replied:
"I fear the enemy's multitude,
and that Huàng and the others are at a disadvantage."
Jiē said:
"Now, Rén and the others, being in a heavy siege and defending to the death without faltering,
are truly relying on Your Majesty to provide strategic support from afar.
One who is in a place of ten thousand deaths
must have the heart to fight to the death;
with the heart to fight to the death within,
and strong relief from without,
Your Majesty, by deploying the six armies to demonstrate your remaining strength,
why worry about defeat and wish to go yourself?"
Tài-Zǔ approved of his words
and stationed his army at Mó-Pí.
The bandits then retreated.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Minister of the Secretariat,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāo-Xiāng-Tíng,
and given the additional title of Attendant.
When Jiē fell ill,
the Emperor personally visited him,
and said:
"I am about to entrust a six-foot orphan
and the fate of the world to you, sir.
Exert yourself!"
He was transferred to be enfeoffed as Marquis of Ān-Lè-Xiāng,
with an income of six hundred households.
Jiē's three sons were also granted the title Marquis within the Passes.
Yòu, being a successor son, was not enfeoffed,
and died of illness.
He was posthumously granted the title Marquis within the Passes.
Later, when Jiē's illness became critical,
an envoy was sent to immediately appoint him Grand Master of Ceremonies.
He passed away,
and the Emperor wept for him,
bestowing the posthumous title Zhēn-Hóu.
His son Jiā succeeded him.
Jiē's younger brother, Zuǎn, was made Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary
and granted the title Marquis within the Passes.
Jiā married Princess Shēng-Qiān-Tíng.
During the Jiā-Píng period,
as Grand Administrator of Lè-Ān, he fought with Wú at Dōng-Guān,
his army was defeated,
and he perished.
He was posthumously titled Zhuàng-Hóu.
His son Yì succeeded him.
Chén Qún, courtesy name Cháng-Wén,
was from Xǔ-Chāng, Yǐng-Chuān.
His grandfather Shí,
father Jǐ,
and uncle Chén,
all had great reputations.
When Qún was a child,
Shí always found him extraordinary,
and said to his clansmen and elders:
"This child will surely make our clan prosper."
Kǒng Róng of Lǔ-Guó, being highly talented and arrogant,
was between Jǐ and Qún in age.
He first befriended Jǐ,
and later associated with Qún,
even bowing to Jǐ again because of Qún.
Through this, Qún gained prominence.
When Liú Bèi administered Yù-Zhōu,
he appointed Qún as Assistant to the Inspector.
At that time, Táo Qiān died of illness,
and Xú-Zhōu invited Bèi.
Bèi wanted to go,
but Qún advised Bèi, saying:
"Yuán Shù is still strong.
If you go east now,
you will surely contend with him.
If Lǚ Bù attacks you from behind,
even if you gain Xú-Zhōu,
nothing will be achieved."
Bèi then went east
and fought with Yuán Shù.
Bù indeed attacked Xià-Pí,
sent troops to aid Shù,
and utterly defeated Bèi's army.
Bèi regretted not taking Qún's advice.
He was recommended as a Mào-Cái
and appointed Magistrate of Zhè,
but he did not take office,
instead following Jǐ to seek refuge in Xú-Zhōu.
When Lǚ Bù was defeated,
Tài-Zǔ appointed Qún as a Subordinate in the Western Bureau of the Minister of Works.
At that time, someone recommended Wáng Mó of Lè-Ān and Zhōu Kuí of Xià-Pí.
Tài-Zǔ appointed them.
Qún returned the official document,
believing Mó and Kuí to be morally corrupt
and that they would eventually fail.
Tài-Zǔ did not listen.
Later, Mó and Kuí were both executed for corruption,
and Tài-Zǔ apologized to Qún.
Qún recommended Chén Jiǎo of Guǎng- Líng and Dài Gān of Dān-Yáng.
Tài-Zǔ employed both of them.
Later, the Wú people rebelled,
and Gān died a loyal and righteous death.
Jiǎo became a famous minister.
The world considered Qún to be a good judge of character.
He was appointed Magistrate of Xiāo, Zàn, and Cháng-Píng.
After his father died, he resigned from office.
Later, as a Sītú Clerk, he was recommended as a High Rank
and became Grandee Remonstrant and Censor.
He was transferred to participate in the military affairs of the Chancellor.
When the State of Wèi was established,
he was promoted to Imperial Censor.
At that time, Tài-Zǔ discussed restoring corporal punishment,
and issued an order saying:
"How can we find a gentleman who understands both ancient and modern times
to settle this matter?
Formerly, Chén Hóng-Lú believed that capital punishment could be mitigated by benevolence.
This is precisely what he meant.
Can the Imperial Censor elaborate on his father's argument?"
Qún replied:
"My father Jǐ believed that the Hàn abolished corporal punishment and increased flogging,
originally to promote compassion, but the number of deaths increased.
This is what is meant by 'light in name but heavy in reality.'
Light in name makes it easy to offend,
heavy in reality harms the people.
The Shū [Jīng] says: '
Reverently apply the five punishments
to perfect the three virtues.'
The Yì [Jīng] mentions the laws of cutting off the nose, severing the feet, and extinguishing the toes,
which are used to assist governance, help education,
deter evil, and stop killing.
Moreover, a murderer must pay with his life,
which conforms to ancient regulations.
As for injuring a person,
to mutilate their body or merely trim their hair is not reasonable.
If ancient punishments were used,
making the licentious enter the silkworm chamber,
and cutting off the feet of thieves,
then there would forever be no licentious transgressions or housebreaking.
Although the three thousand categories [of ancient punishments]
cannot all be restored,
if these few [types]
that are the troubles of the time
were applied first,
then for crimes punishable by death under Hàn law,
which mercy cannot reach,
the remaining offenses liable to death
could be replaced by corporal punishment.
In this way,
the number of those punished and those saved would be sufficient to compensate each other.
Now, to replace a non-lethal punishment with a lethal flogging
is to value a person's limbs but lightly treat a person's life."
At that time, Zhōng Yáo shared Qún's view,
but Wáng Lǎng and many other debaters thought it was not yet feasible.
Tài-Zǔ highly praised Yáo and Qún's words,
but because military affairs were not yet concluded
and he considered the majority opinion,
he temporarily deferred the matter.

Chén Qún [Chén Qún] submitted a memorial, stating:
"The Book of Odes (Shī [Shī]) says, 'Model yourself on King Wén [Wén Wáng],
and the myriad states will trust you';

The Way begins near at hand,

Since the chaos and disorder began,
the weapons of war have not ceased.
The common people do not understand the fundamentals of royal teachings,
and I fear their moral decline has already become severe.
Your Majesty, at the height of the prosperity of Wèi [Wèi],
carrying on the legacy of the two ancestors,
the world longs for perfect governance.
Only by promoting virtue and spreading transformation,
showing compassion and care for the common folk,
will the myriad people be truly fortunate.
The subordinates, echoing each other,
obscuring right and wrong,
is a great peril to the state.
If there is no harmony, then there will be factions;
if there are factions, then praise and blame will be baseless;
if praise and blame are baseless, then truth and falsehood will be confused.
One must not fail to guard deeply against this,
and cut off its source."
During the Tàihé [Tàihé] period,
Cáo Zhēn [Cáo Zhēn] submitted a memorial proposing multiple routes to invade Shǔ [Shǔ],
entering through Xié Gǔ [Xié Gǔ].
Chén Qún [Chén Qún] thought,
"Emperor Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] once went to Yángpíng [Yángpíng] to attack Zhāng Lǔ [Zhāng Lǔ],
and collected a great deal of soybeans and wheat to supplement army provisions,
but even before Zhāng Lǔ [Zhāng Lǔ] surrendered, food was still scarce.
Now, there is no such source to rely on,
and Xié Gǔ [Xié Gǔ] is rugged and dangerous,
making advance and retreat difficult.
Transport and supply lines will certainly be intercepted and plundered.
If many soldiers are left to guard critical points,
it will deplete the fighting force.
