This must be thoroughly considered."
The Emperor followed Chén Qún [Chén Qún]'s counsel.
Cáo Zhēn [Cáo Zhēn] again submitted a memorial proposing to enter through Zǐwǔ Dào [Zǐwǔ Dào].
Chén Qún [Chén Qún] again explained the disadvantages,
and also discussed the military expenditure plans.
An imperial edict conveyed Chén Qún [Chén Qún]'s advice to Cáo Zhēn [Cáo Zhēn],
who nevertheless proceeded based on his own plan.
It happened to rain continuously for days.
Chén Qún [Chén Qún] again suggested that an imperial edict should order Cáo Zhēn [Cáo Zhēn] to return.
The Emperor agreed.
Later, the imperial daughter Shú [Shú] died prematurely.
She was posthumously enfeoffed and given the posthumous title of Princess Yì of Píngyuán [Píngyuán Yì Gōngzhǔ].
Chén Qún [Chén Qún] submitted a memorial, stating:
"Life and death are decreed by fate,
existence and demise have their portions.
Therefore, the sages established rituals,
sometimes restraining, sometimes extending,
to seek the middle path.
There are the frugalities of unimproved tombs for those who die young, and the unreturning souls of Yíng [Yíng] and Bó [Bó] (referring to tragic deaths of children).
Indeed, great men's actions accord with heaven and earth,
extending infinitely;
moreover, great virtue does not overstep boundaries,
and their every action serves as a model.
An untimely death under eight years of age is not fully provided for by ritual.
How much more so for one who has not yet reached a month,
to be sent off with adult rites,
with additional mourning clothes prescribed,
the entire court in plain attire,
morning and evening lamentations?
From ancient times to the present,
there has been nothing comparable to this.
And now, Your Majesty even personally goes to view the tomb,
and personally oversees the ancestral offerings.
I wish Your Majesty would cut down on these unnecessary and harmful matters,
and simply allow your ministers to conduct the funeral.
I beg that the imperial carriage not proceed.
This is the earnest hope of all states.
I heard that the imperial carriage intends to go to Mópí [Mópí],
effectively moving to Xǔchāng [Xǔchāng].
The two palaces, high and low,
all moving eastward together,
the entire court, great and small,
none are not surprised and bewildered.
Some say it is to avoid misfortune,
some say it is to move the palace buildings to a more convenient location,
others do not know the reason.
I believe that good and ill fortune are decreed by fate,
and calamity and blessing come from human actions.
Moving to seek peace
is also fruitless.
If it is truly necessary to move and avoid,
then repair the Western Palace in Jīnyōng Chéng [Jīnyōng Chéng]
and the detached palace in Mèngjīn [Mèngjīn];
both can serve as temporary residences.
There is no need to move the entire palace to be exposed in the wilderness,
thereby neglecting the important seasonal farming and sericulture.
Moreover, if the enemy learns of this,
they will consider it a great decline.
In addition, the expenses incurred
are immeasurable.
Furthermore, virtuous gentlemen and wise men,
whether in prosperity or decline,
in safety or danger,
uphold the Way and believe in fate.
They do not move their homes to find peace.
The local communities follow their transforming influence,
without fear.
How much more so for the Emperor, the lord of all states?
When he is tranquil, the world is at peace;
when he moves, the world is disturbed.
How can his every movement and stillness
be treated lightly and carelessly?"
The Emperor did not heed him.
During the Qīnglóng reign,
palaces and chambers were constructed,
causing the common people to miss their farming season.
Qún submitted a memorial, saying:
"Yǔ, inheriting the prosperity of Táng and Yú,
still kept his palaces humble and disliked extravagant clothing.
How much more so now, after a period of chaos and war,
with very few people remaining?
Compared to the time of Hàn Wén and Jǐng,
our population is no more than that of a single large commandery.
Furthermore, there are affairs on the borders,
and the generals and soldiers are toiling hard.
If there were to be a disaster of flood or drought,
it would be a deep sorrow for the state.
Moreover, Wú and Shǔ are not yet eliminated,
and the altars of soil and grain are not secure.
It is advisable, before they make a move,
to train our military and encourage agriculture,
so as to be prepared for them.
Now, abandoning these urgent matters and prioritizing palaces,
your servant fears that the common people will be utterly exhausted.
With what then shall we confront the enemy?
In the past, Liú Bèi, from Chéngdū to Báishuǐ,
built many relay stations,
expending manpower and resources.
Tàizǔ knew that he was wearying his people.
Now, the common people of the Central Plains are toiling,
which is also what Wú and Shǔ desire.
This is a critical moment for safety or danger,
may Your Majesty consider it."
The Emperor replied:
"For a king, palaces
should also be established simultaneously.
After the bandits are eliminated,
we should merely dismiss the guards;
how can we resume construction projects?
This is the duty of a ruler,
the grand strategy of Xiāo Hé."
Qún further said:
"In the past, the founder of Hàn only contended with Xiàng Yǔ for天下 (the empire).
When Yǔ was already eliminated,
and the palaces were burned down,
Xiāo Hé then built armories and grand granaries.
All of these were urgent and essential,
yet they were still not magnificent.
Now, the two barbarian enemies are not yet pacified,
it is truly not appropriate to be the same as in ancient times.
Whatever a person desires,
there is always an excuse for it.
How much more so for the Heavenly King,
whom none dare defy?
Previously, when you wanted to destroy the armory,
you said it could not but be destroyed;
later, when you wanted to place it (elsewhere),
you said it could not but be placed.
If you are determined to build it,
it is certainly not something that your servant's words can dissuade;
if you could just spare a little thought,
and decisively change your mind,
that is also not something your servant can achieve.
Emperor Míng of Hàn wanted to build the Déyáng Hall.
Zhōnglí Yì remonstrated,
and his words were immediately adopted.
Later, it was built again;
when the hall was completed,
he said to his ministers: 'If Secretary Zhōnglí were here,
this hall could not have been completed.'
How could a king fear one minister?
It was for the sake of the common people.
Now, your servant cannot even slightly suspend Your Majesty's listening,
I am far inferior to Yì."
Thereupon, the Emperor made some reductions and economies.
Originally,
during Tàizǔ's time,
Liú Yì's younger brother was involved in a conspiracy to rebel with Wèi Fěng,
and was to be executed.
Qún spoke of it to Tàizǔ,
and Tàizǔ said:
"Yì
is a renowned minister;
I also wish to pardon him."
So he was reinstated.
Yì was deeply grateful to Qún.
Qún said:
"Deliberating on punishments is for the state,
not for private interests;
moreover, it was the enlightened ruler's own intention,
how could I have known?"
His magnanimity and lack of boasting
were all of this kind.
In the fourth year of Qīnglóng, he died,
with the posthumous title Jìng Hóu.
His son, Tài, inherited the title.
The Emperor, remembering Qún's merits and virtues,
divided Qún's household and fief,
enfeoffing one of his sons as a列侯 (Marquis of a Fief).
Tài's courtesy name was Xuánbó.
During the Qīnglóng reign,
he was appointed Sanjì Shìláng.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign,
he was transferred to the position of Yóujī Jiāngjūn,
then served as Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the added title Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn,
empowered with a staff of authority,
and as Hù Xióngnú Zhōnglángjiàng.
He pacified and reconciled the barbarian people,
gaining much prestige and favor.
Many nobles in the capital sent precious goods,
asking Tài to buy slaves for them.
Tài hung them all on the wall,
without opening their seals.
When he was summoned to serve as Shàngshū,
he returned them all.
In the beginning of Jiāpíng,
he replaced Guō Huái as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the added title Fènwēi Jiāngjūn.
The grand general of Shǔ, Jiāng Wéi, led his troops to establish two forts at Qūshān,
and sent his牙門將 (Lieutenant General) Gōu Ān and Lǐ Xīn to defend them.
He gathered the Qiāng and Hú and others, making them hostages, and encroached upon various commanderies.
The general who conquers the west, Guō Huái, consulted with Tài on how to defend against this.
Tài said:
"Although Qūchéng is fortified,
it is dangerously far from Shǔ,
and will require grain transport.
The Qiāng and Yí people are troubled by Wéi's labor demands,
and are probably not yet willing to submit.
If we besiege and take it,
we can capture its city without shedding blood;
even if they send relief,
the mountain roads are rugged and treacherous,
not suitable for troop movement."
Huái followed Tài's plan.
He sent Tài to lead the Tǎoshǔ Hùjūn Xú Zhì and the Nán'ān Tàishǒu Dèng Ài and others to advance and besiege it,
cutting off their supply route and the water flowing outside the city.
Ān and others challenged them to battle,
but they were not permitted.
The generals and soldiers became desperate,
dividing their rations and collecting snow to prolong their resistance for days and months.
Wéi indeed came to their rescue,
emerging from Niútóushān,
and confronted Tài.
Tài said:
"The art of war values subduing the enemy without fighting.
Now, if we cut off Niútóu,
Wéi will have no retreat route,
then he will be our captive."
He ordered all armies to strengthen their ramparts and not engage in battle,
and sent an envoy to inform Huái,
proposing to cross the Báishuǐ himself from the south,
follow the river eastward,
and have Huái advance towards Niútóu,
cutting off Wéi's return path.
Then Wéi could be captured together,
not just Ān and the others.
Huái approved of his strategy,
and advanced to station his armies at Táoshuǐ.
Wéi was fearful,
and fled.
Ān and others, isolated,
then all surrendered.
After Huái died,
Tài succeeded him as General of the Western Expedition,
granted a *jié* and given supervisory command over all armies in Yōng and Liáng provinces.
The following year,
Wáng Jīng, the Inspector of Yōng Province, reported to Tài,
saying that Jiāng Wéi and Xiàhóu Bà intended to advance along three routes towards Qíshān, Shíyíng, and Jīnchéng.
He requested to advance troops as a flank,
sending the Liáng Province army to Háo Hǎn
to attack the Shu Protector-General towards Qíshān.
Tài judged that the enemy's strength would ultimately not allow them to advance along three routes,
and that dividing forces was disadvantageous.
He also believed that the Liáng Province army should not cross the border prematurely.
He replied to Jīng:
"Wait until their intentions are certain,
and their direction of advance is known.
Only when the eastern and western forces are combined should we advance."
At that time, Wéi and others, with tens of thousands of men, reached Háo Hǎn
and headed for Dí Dào.
Tài ordered Jīng to advance and garrison Dí Dào,
and await the arrival of his army,
before planning to engage them.
Tài advanced his army to Chéncāng.
However, Jīng's forces were unsuccessful in battle against the enemy at Gùguān,
and Jīng thereupon crossed the Táo River.
Tài, thinking that Jīng had not firmly held Dí Dào,
believed that other complications were inevitable.
He dispatched five battalions ahead,
while Tài led the main army to follow.
Jīng had already fought Wéi,
suffered a great defeat,
and returned with over ten thousand men to hold Dí Dào city,
while the rest scattered.
Wéi, capitalizing on his victory, besieged Dí Dào.
Tài's army reached Shàngguī,
divided troops to guard critical points,
and advanced day and night.
Dèng Ài, Hú Fèn, and Wáng Mì also arrived.
Immediately, Tài divided his forces with Ài and Mì into three armies,
and advanced to Lǒngxī.
Ài and others believed:
"Wáng Jīng's elite troops were defeated in the west,
the enemy forces are greatly invigorated.
Their victorious army is irresistible,
and the General, with a hastily assembled force,
following a defeated army,
will find his officers and men disheartened,
and Lǒngyòu will be overwhelmed.
The ancients said: 'If a viper stings your hand,
a brave man will cut off his wrist.'
Sūnzǐ said:
'There are battles that should not be fought,
and territories that should not be defended.'
This is to say that by sacrificing a small part, the greater whole is preserved.
Now, the danger in Lǒngyòu is greater than a viper,
and the territory of Dí Dào is more than just 'not to be defended.'
Jiāng Wéi's army
is a sharp edge to be avoided.
It is better to secure strongholds and protect ourselves,
observe their weaknesses and wait for them to tire,
then advance to relieve the siege.
This is the optimal strategy."
Tài said:
"Jiāng Wéi has led light forces deep into our territory,
precisely intending to confront us in the open plains
and seek a decisive battle.
Wáng Jīng should have built high walls and deep moats
to blunt their vanguard.
Now, by engaging them in battle,
he has allowed the enemy to succeed,
defeated Wáng Jīng,
and trapped him in Dí Dào.
If Wéi, emboldened by his victory,
advances eastward,
seizes the accumulated grain at Lìyáng,
releases his troops to accept surrenders,
recruits Qiāng and Hú,
and competes for Guān and Lǒng in the east,
sending dispatches to the four commanderies,
this is what I dread.
But Wéi, with his victorious army,
is now stalled beneath a fortified city,
and his keen soldiers are exhausting their strength and risking their lives.
The dynamics of attack and defense are different;
the guest and the host are not the same.
The *Art of War* says: 'Mobile siege towers take
three months to build,
and earthen mounds take three months to complete.'
Indeed, this is not something that light forces, having advanced far,
or Wéi's cunning scheme, can achieve in a hurry.
With their army isolated and far from home,
and their grain supply cut off,
this is our moment to advance quickly and defeat the enemy,
like 'a swift thunderclap that leaves no time to cover the ears' —
a natural advantage.
The Táo River runs along its exterior,
Wéi and his forces are inside.
Now, if we occupy the high ground and seize the strategic advantage,
looming over their neck,
they will surely flee without a fight.
Bandits must not be allowed to escape,
and a siege must not be prolonged.
Why do you speak thus?"
So, he advanced his army across Gāochénglǐng,
moved stealthily,
and reached the high mountains southeast of Dí Dào at night.
They lit numerous signal fires
and sounded drums and horns.
The officers and soldiers inside Dí Dào city, seeing that reinforcements had arrived,
were all greatly invigorated.
Wéi initially thought that the government relief army would only move after assembling a large force,
but suddenly hearing of their arrival,
he believed there must be some unexpected maneuver or prearranged plan,
and both his superiors and subordinates were terrified.
Since his army had departed from Lǒngxī,
because the mountain roads were deep and treacherous,
the enemy would surely set ambushes.
Tài cunningly took the southern route,
and Wéi indeed set ambushes for three days.
The main army moved stealthily
and suddenly appeared to their south.
Wéi then advanced along the mountains to attack.
Tài engaged him in battle,
and Wéi retreated.
The Liáng Province army arrived at Wògānbǎn from south of Jīnchéng.
Tài and Jīng secretly agreed on a plan
to jointly intercept Wéi's return route.
Wéi and his forces, hearing of this,
then fled,
and the officers and soldiers in the city were able to escape.
Jīng sighed, saying:
"Our provisions would not have lasted ten days.
Had you not responded in time,
the entire city would have been slaughtered and shattered,
and the entire province would have been lost."
Tài comforted and rewarded his officers and soldiers,
sent them back in waves,
appointed new garrisons,
and also repaired the city walls and fortresses,
then returned to garrison Shàngguī.
Initially,
when Tài heard that Jīng was besieged,
he considered that the provincial army's officers and men had always been united,
and moreover, they could hold the city,
which Wéi would not be able to quickly overrun.
He reported his intention to advance his army day and night to arrive swiftly.
The general consensus was that Jīng had fled north,
and the city alone was not strong enough to defend itself.
If Wéi were to cut off the road to Liáng Province,
and gather the people and non-Han tribes of the four commanderies,
and occupy the strategic passes of Guān and Lǒng,
he could indeed wipe out Jīng's army and butcher Lǒngyòu.
It would be advisable to wait until large forces had gathered from all directions
before launching an attack.
Grand General Sīmǎ Wénwáng said:
"In the past, Zhūgě Liàng often had this ambition,
but ultimately could not achieve it.
Such a grand and far-reaching plan
is not within Wéi's capabilities.
Moreover, the city cannot be taken quickly,
but limited provisions are an urgent matter.
The General of the Western Expedition's swift rescue
is the best strategy."
Tài always, whenever there was an incident in one region,
would use false rumors to stir up the entire realm.
Therefore, he rarely made detailed reports to the emperor,
and his express letters never traveled more than six hundred *lǐ*.
Sīmǎ Wénwáng said to Xún Yǐ:
"Xuánbó is deeply courageous and decisive.
Bearing the heavy responsibility of a regional governor,
and rescuing a city about to fall,
yet not requesting additional troops,
and also rarely submitting detailed reports—
this means he is certainly capable of handling the enemy.
Should not a commander-in-chief
be like this!"
Later, Zhēng Tài was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púyè,
in charge of elections,
and given the additional titles of Shìzhōng and Guānglù Dàfū.
When Wú's great general Sūn Jùn ventured out into the Huái and Sì Rivers,
Tài was appointed Zhènqūn Jiāngjūn,
granted jié (imperial insignia) and made Dūdū of all military affairs north of the Huái River.
An imperial edict commanded that all military supervisors in Xúzhōu and below were to act under Tài's direction.
When Jùn retreated,
and the army returned,
he was transferred to be Zuǒ Púyè.
When Zhūgě Dàn rebelled in Shòuchūn,
Sīmǎ Wén Wáng led the six armies to garrison Qīutóu,
and Tài was in overall charge of the Xíngtái (traveling chancellery).
Sīmǎ Jǐng Wáng and Wén Wáng were both close friends with Tài,
and Wǔ Gāi of Pèiguó was also on good terms with Tài.
Wén Wáng asked Gāi,
"How does Xuánbó compare to his father, Sīkōng?"
Gāi replied,
"For being broadly elegant, expansive,
and taking the enlightenment and education of the realm as his personal responsibility,
he is not as good;
but for clear governance, simplicity leading to profundity,
and establishing accomplishments and deeds,
he surpasses him."
Tài, on various occasions, had his enfeoffment increased by 2,600 households for his merits,
and one of his sons or younger brothers was granted the title of Tínghóu,
and two others were granted Guānnèi Hóu.
In the first year of Jǐngyuán, he passed away,
and was posthumously granted Sīkōng.
His posthumous title was Mù Hóu.
His son Xún succeeded him.
When Xún passed away,
he had no heir.
His younger brother Wēn Shào was enfeoffed.
During the Xiánxī era, when the Five Orders of nobility were established,
because of Tài's distinguished service to the former dynasty,
Wēn was re-enfeoffed as Shènzǐ.
Chén Jiǎo, courtesy name Jìbì,
was a native of Dōngyáng, Guǎnglíng.
He fled the chaos to Jiāngdōng and Dōngchéng,
declined invitations from Sūn Cè and Yuán Shù,
and returned to his home commandery.
The Prefect Chén Dēng invited him to be Gōngcáo,
and sent Jiǎo to Xǔ,
saying,
"The discussions in Xǔ are not sufficient for me;
I ask that you observe on my behalf,
and return to enlighten me."
Upon his return, Jiǎo said,
"I have heard the discussions near and far,
which mostly say that your excellency is arrogant and self-important."
Dēng said,
"For harmony and solemnity within the family,
and possessing virtue and conduct,
I respect Chén Yuánfāng and his brothers;
for being profoundly clear and pure as jade,
and having propriety and order,
I respect Huà Zǐyú;
for being upright and abhorring evil,
and having discernment and righteousness,
I respect Zhào Yuándá;
for being widely learned and having a strong memory,
unconventional and outstanding,
I respect Kǒng Wénjǔ;
for having a heroic demeanor and outstanding talent,
and possessing the strategies of a king or hegemon,
I respect Liú Xuándé:
These are the ones I respect;
how can I be arrogant?
As for the other petty fellows,
they are not worth mentioning!"
Such was Dēng's refined sentiment,
yet he deeply respected and befriended Jiǎo.
When the commandery was besieged by Sūn Quán at Kuāngqí,
Dēng ordered Jiǎo to seek aid from Tàizǔ.
Jiǎo persuaded Tàizǔ, saying,
"Although our humble commandery is small,
it is a strategically convenient state.
If we receive aid,
and are made an outer bulwark,
then Wú's schemes will be frustrated,
Xúfāng will enjoy eternal peace,
your military prestige will shake afar,
your benevolence and love will flow profusely,
and states that have not yet submitted
will look upon you and join.
To uphold virtue and nurture might,
this is the work of a king!"
Tàizǔ was impressed by Jiǎo
and wished to keep him.
Jiǎo declined, saying,
"My home state is in dire straits;
I came running to report the emergency.
Even if I cannot achieve the effectiveness of Shēn Xū,
how can I forget the righteousness of Hóng Yǎn?"
Tàizǔ then dispatched troops to the rescue.
After the Wú army retreated,
Dēng set up many ambushes
and ordered his troops to pursue the fleeing enemy,
dealing them a great defeat.
Tàizǔ appointed Jiǎo as a staff officer to the Sīkōng,
then made him Xiàng Lìng,
Zhēngnán Zhǎngshǐ,
Prefect of Péngchéng and Lèlíng,
and Western District Commandant of Wèijùn.
A man in Qǔzhōu whose father was ill
sacrificed an ox to pray for him.
The county authorities determined it a capital offense punishable by public execution.
Jiǎo said,
"This is a filial son."
He memorialized for his pardon.
He was promoted to Prefect of Wèijùn.
At that time, there were thousands of prisoners,
some of whom had been held for years.
Jiǎo believed that the Zhōu dynasty had the system of the Three Ordinances,
and the Hàn dynasty had the law of the Three Chapters.
Now, to be meticulous about the severity or lightness of offenses
while neglecting the suffering of prolonged detention
could be called erroneous.
He personally reviewed all the criminal cases
and made decisions on them all at once.
When the main army campaigned eastward,
he was appointed Chéngxiàng Zhǎngshǐ.
When the army returned,
he was again made Prefect of Wèijùn,
then transferred to Xīcáo Shǔ.
He accompanied the campaign to Hànzhōng,
and upon return, became Shàngshū.
Before he could reach Yè,
Tàizǔ died in Luòyáng.
The assembled officials, bound by custom,
believed that the crown prince's ascension
must await an imperial edict.
Jiǎo said,
"The king has died abroad,
and the realm is in fear.
The crown prince should set aside his grief and immediately ascend the throne
to secure the hopes of those near and far.
Moreover, if a beloved son is at his side,
and changes occur between them,
then the state will be imperiled."
He immediately arranged for the official appointments and prepared the ceremonies,
completing everything in a single day.
The next morning,
by order of the queen,
the crown prince was enthroned,
and a great general amnesty was proclaimed.
Wén Dì said,
"Chén Jìbì, in a critical moment,
showed extraordinary foresight;
he truly is a hero of his time."
After the emperor ascended the throne,
Jiǎo was transferred to Lìbù,
enfeoffed as Gāolíng Tínghóu,
and promoted to Shàngshū Lìng.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
his peerage was advanced to Dōngxiāng Hóu,
with 600 households.
The emperor once arrived suddenly at the gate of the Shàngshū office.
Jiǎo knelt and asked the emperor,
"Where does Your Majesty wish to go?"
The emperor said,
"I wish to inspect the documents."
Jiǎo replied,
"This is my duty,
not something Your Majesty should personally attend to.
If I am not fit for my duty,
then please dismiss me.
Your Majesty should return."
The emperor was ashamed,
turned his carriage, and went back.
Such was his integrity and straightforwardness.
He was given the additional titles of Shìzhōng and Guānglù Dàfū,
and promoted to Sītú.
In the first year of Jǐngchū, he passed away,
and was posthumously titled Zhēn Hóu.
His son Běn succeeded him,
serving successively as commandery prefect and a Nine Minister.
Wherever he served, he maintained order
and focused on the broader principles,
enabling his subordinates to perform to their fullest.
He had talent for governance,
did not involve himself in trivial matters,
and, without studying law, earned the praise of a Tíngwèi.
He was superior to Sīmǎ Qí and others,
excelling in refining official documents.
He was promoted to Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn,
granted jié and made Dūdū of all military affairs north of the Hé River.
When he passed away,
his son Càn succeeded him.
Běn's younger brother Qiān
was Chēqí Jiāngjūn during the Xiánxī era.
Initially,
Chén Jiǎo served as the Gōngcáo of the commandery.
He was dispatched on a mission that took him past Tài-Shān.
Xuē Tì, the Grand Administrator of Tài-Shān and a native of Dōng-Jùn, thought highly of him,
and they formed a close friendship.
Xuē Tì playfully said to Chén Jiǎo,
"To, as a commandery official, befriend a two-thousand-shi official,
and for the ruler of a neighboring state to condescend to associate with a subordinate official—
is this not admirable!"
Later, Xuē Tì served as the Grand Administrator of Wèi-Jùn and as Shàngshū-Lìng,
both positions previously held by Chén Jiǎo.
Xú Xuān, courtesy name Bǎo-Jiān,
was a native of Hǎi-Xī, Guǎng-Líng.
He fled the chaos to Jiāng-Dōng,
and then declined Sūn Cè's summons,
returning to his home commandery.
He and Chén Jiǎo both served as Guāng-Jì.
The two were equally renowned but privately not harmonious.
Nevertheless, both were highly regarded by Grand Administrator Chén Dēng,
and together with Chén Dēng, they were wholeheartedly devoted to Tài-Zǔ.
When the people of Hǎi-Xī and Huái-Pǔ counties rebelled,
the Commandant Wèi Mí and the Magistrate Liáng Xí fled at night to Xú Xuān's house,
who secretly helped them escape.
Tài-Zǔ dispatched the Inspector-General Hù Zhì to suppress the rebels,
but he hesitated to advance due to insufficient troops.
Xú Xuān secretly reprimanded him,
showing him the situation,
whereupon Hù Zhì advanced and crushed the rebels.
Tài-Zǔ appointed him as a clerical official in the Sīkōng's office,
then made him Magistrate of Dōng-Mín and Fā-Gān,
and later promoted him to Grand Administrator of Qí-Jùn.
He entered the central government as Ménxià-Dū,
and followed Tài-Zǔ to Shòu-Chūn.
When Mǎ Chāo rebelled,
the main army campaigned westward.
Tài-Zǔ said to his officials,
"Now we are about to campaign far away,
but this region is not yet settled,
and I consider it a future worry.
We ought to get a virtuous and upright man to guard and oversee it."
He then made Xú Xuān the Zuǒ Hù-Jūn,
leaving him to command all the armies.
Upon his return,
he became Cìngxiàng Dōng Cáo-Yuàn,
and was then sent out as Grand Administrator of Wèi-Jùn.
When Tài-Zǔ died in Luò-Yáng,
the officials entered the palace hall to mourn.
Some suggested replacing the city defenders
with people from Qiáo and Pèi.
Xú Xuān sternly said,
"Currently, the distant and near are unified,
and everyone is loyal.
Why must it be people from Qiáo and Pèi,
and thereby discourage those who are already guarding the capital?"
Wén-Dì heard of this and said,
"This is what is called a minister of the state."
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
Xú Xuān became Yùshǐ Zhōng-Chéng,
and was granted the title Guānnèi-Hóu.
He was transferred to Chéngmén Xiàowèi,
and within a month, promoted to Sīlì Xiàowèi,
then transferred to Sànqí Chángshì.
He followed the Emperor to Guǎng-Líng.
When the Six Armies were on boats,
a sudden violent storm arose.
The Emperor's boat was spinning and capsizing.
Xú Xuān, who was ill and lagging behind,
rode the waves forward,
and no other official arrived before him.
The Emperor was impressed,
and promoted him to Shàngshū.
When Míng-Dì ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as the Tíng-Hóu of Jīn-Yáng,
with an estate of two hundred households.
Huán Fàn, the Zhōng Lǐng-Jūn, recommended Xú Xuān, saying,
"I have heard that when emperors use people,
they assess their abilities for the era.
In times of struggle for power,
strategy comes first;
after the realm is settled,
loyalty and righteousness are paramount.
Thus, Jìn Wén-Gōng employed the schemes of Jiù-Fàn but rewarded the words of Yōng-Jì,
and Gāo-Zǔ used the wisdom of Chén Píng but entrusted his successor to Zhōu Bó.
I humbly observe that Shàngshū Xú Xuān
embodies conduct of loyalty and integrity,
and possesses a character of straightforwardness and brilliance.
He is pure, refined, and stands out independently,
not constrained by worldly customs.
He is resolute and difficult to sway,
possessing the integrity of a pillar of the state.
He has served in various positions in provinces and commanderies,
and has been competent wherever he served.
Now, with the Púyè position vacant,
Xú Xuān is in charge of handling the affairs.
Given the heavy responsibility of a trusted minister,
no one is more suitable than Xú Xuān."
The Emperor then made Xú Xuān Zuǒ Púyè,
and later Shìzhōng and Guānglù Dàfū.
When the imperial carriage went to Xǔ-Chāng,
he oversaw the remaining affairs.
When the Emperor returned,
the officials in charge presented documents for inspection.
The imperial edict said,
"How is my review different from the Púyè's?"
And he did not look at them after all.
When the Shàngfāng-Lìng was summarily investigated and executed,
Xú Xuān submitted a memorial arguing that the punishment was excessive.
He also advised against constructing palaces and halls that exhausted the people's strength.
The Emperor personally issued edicts praising and accepting his advice.
Xú Xuān said,
"At seventy, there is the ceremony of hanging up one's carriage [in retirement].
Now I am sixty-eight,
I can leave."
He then repeatedly resigned due to illness, yielding his position.
The Emperor ultimately did not permit it.
He passed away in Qīng-Lóng fourth year.
His will stipulated plain clothes and a simple headscarf,
and burial in ordinary attire.
An imperial edict stated,
"Xú Xuān's conduct was utterly sincere,
straightforward internally and principled externally.
He served through three dynasties,
upright, brilliant, and principled.
He possessed the integrity to be entrusted with the orphan and given a vital mission,
and can be called a pillar of the state.
I always wished to rely on him as a grand minister,
but he did not reach that position.
Alas, his great life was not prolonged!
He is posthumously granted the title Chējì Jiāngjūn,
and his funeral shall be conducted according to the rites for a duke."
His posthumous title was Zhēn-Hóu.
His son Qīn succeeded him.
Wèi Zhēn, courtesy name Gōng-Zhèn,
was a native of Xiāng-Yì, Chén-Liú.
His father, Zī,
had great integrity
and did not respond to the summons of the Three Ducal Ministers.
When Tài-Zǔ first arrived in Chén-Liú,
Wèi Zī said,
"The one who will bring peace to the realm
must be this man."
Tài-Zǔ also thought highly of him,
and frequently visited Wèi Zī to discuss important matters.
He followed Tài-Zǔ in the campaign against Dǒng Zhuó,
and died in battle at Xíng-Yáng.
Whenever Tài-Zǔ passed through the commandery's territory,
he would send an envoy to offer sacrifices to him.
When Xiàhóu Dūn was Grand Administrator of Chén-Liú,
he recommended Wèi Zhēn as a Ji-Lì,
and ordered his wife to attend a banquet.
Wèi Zhēn considered it
"a custom of a degenerate age,
not in accordance with proper rites."
Xiàhóu Dūn was enraged
and had Wèi Zhēn arrested,
but later pardoned him.
Later, he became a Huángmén Shìláng of Hàn.
Zhū Yuè of Dōng-Jùn plotted rebellion
and implicated Wèi Zhēn.
Tài-Zǔ issued an order saying,
"I and your father jointly undertook affairs,
and I admire his good reputation.
When I first heard Zhū Yuè's words,
I naturally did not believe them.
Then I received a letter from Xún Lìng-Jūn,
which fully elucidated his loyalty and sincerity."
At that time, he was ordered to
engage a noble lady in Wèi,
and consequently he requested to retain Wèi Zhēn to participate in the Chancellor's military affairs.
In recognition of Wèi Zhēn's father's past merits,
he was granted the title Guānnèi-Hóu,
and transferred to Hù Cáo-Yuàn.
When Wén-Dì became King,
he was Sànqí Chángshì.
And when he ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as the Tíng-Hóu of Ān-Guó.
At that time, all the officials praised the virtue of Wèi,
often disparaging the previous dynasty.
Wèi Zhēn alone clarified the meaning of abdication
and lauded the virtues of Hàn.
The Emperor repeatedly gestured to Wèi Zhēn and said,
"The treasures of the world
should be shared with Shān-Yáng."
He was promoted to Shàngshū,
then transferred to Shìzhōng and Lìbù Shàngshū.
When the Emperor went to Guǎng-Líng,
Wèi Zhēn served as Xíng Zhōng Lǐng-Jūn
and accompanied him.
Cáo Xiū, the Zhēngjūn Dà Jiāngjūn, submitted a report citing the confession of a surrendered rebel,
stating that "Sūn Quán is already at Rúxū-Kǒu."
Wèi Zhēn said,
"Sūn Quán relies on the Cháng-Jiāng,
and would not dare to openly confront us yet.
This must be a false statement made out of fear."
Upon interrogation of the surrendered person,
it was indeed a fabrication by a defending general.
When Emperor Míng [Míng Dì] ascended the throne,
he was promoted and enfeoffed as Marquis of Kāngxiāng [Kāngxiāng Hóu].
Later, he was transferred to Right Grandee Secretary,
overseeing elections,
and was granted the additional title of Palace Attendant, as before.
Jiǎng Jì [Jiǎng Jì], Central Protector of the Army, sent a letter to Zhēn [Zhēn], saying:
"Emperor Gāo [Gāo Dì] of Hàn [Hàn] appointed a runaway slave as a supreme general;
King Wǔ [Wǔ Wáng] of Zhōu [Zhōu] elevated a fisherman to Grand Preceptor.
Men of common cloth, even servants,
can rise to be princes and dukes.
Why must we adhere to established rules,
testing before employing?"
Zhēn [Zhēn] replied:
"The ancients left behind wisdom and relied on broad-mindedness,
requiring performance evaluation before promotion or demotion.
Now you liken Mùyě [Mùyě] to Chéng [Chéng] and Kāng [Kāng],
and compare decisiveness to Wén [Wén] and Jǐng [Jǐng],
favoring unconventional actions
and opening the path for sudden advancements.
This will cause everyone in the world to rush forth."
When Zhūgě Liàng [Zhūgě Liàng] invaded Tiānshuǐ [Tiānshuǐ],
Zhēn [Zhēn] memorialized:
"It is advisable to send crack troops into Sànguān [Sànguān]
to cut off their supply lines."
Accordingly, Zhēn [Zhēn] was made General Who Conquers Shǔ [Shǔ],
granted a staff of authority, and oversaw all military affairs.
When he arrived at Cháng'ān [Cháng'ān],
Liàng [Liàng] retreated.
Upon his return,
he was restored to his post
and given the additional title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
At this time,
the emperor was greatly devoted to constructing palaces and halls,
and Zhēn [Zhēn] repeatedly remonstrated strongly.
When the Palace Supervisor, Fú [Fú], arrested a clerk from the Orchid Terrace,
Zhēn [Zhēn] memorialized to investigate him.
An imperial edict stated:
"The palaces and halls are not complete;
this is what I am focused on.
Why do you investigate this?"
Zhēn [Zhēn] submitted a memorial, saying:
"The ancient laws against overstepping one's authority
were not because they disliked diligent work,
but truly because the benefit gained was small,
while the harm caused was great.
I frequently observe the school officials;
they are all similar in this regard.
I fear that all officials will consequently overstep their duties,
leading to decline."
Liàng [Liàng] again emerged from Xié Gǔ [Xié Gǔ].
The General Who Conquers the South reported:
"Zhū Rán [Zhū Rán] and others' armies have already passed Jīngchéng [Jīngchéng]."
Zhēn [Zhēn] said:
"Rán [Rán]
is a brave general of Wú [Wú].
He will surely descend to follow Quán [Quán],
and this is merely a feint to tie down the General Who Conquers the South."
Quán [Quán] indeed recalled Rán [Rán] to Rújcháo [Rújcháo],
then advanced to attack Héféi [Héféi].
The emperor wanted to personally lead an eastern expedition,
but Zhēn [Zhēn] said:
"Quán [Quán] outwardly appears to be responding to Liàng [Liàng],
but inwardly he is actually observing and waiting.
Moreover, Héféi [Héféi] city is strong,
there is no cause for concern.
The imperial carriage need not personally go on campaign,
thereby saving the expenses of the six armies."
When the emperor arrived at Xúnyáng [Xúnyáng], Quán [Quán] indeed retreated.
The Inspector of Yōuzhōu [Yōuzhōu], Wúqiū Jiǎn [Wúqiū Jiǎn], submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
there has been nothing noteworthy.
Wú [Wú] and Shǔ [Shǔ] rely on their strategic advantages and cannot be quickly pacified.
We might as well use these idle men from this region to conquer Liáodōng [Liáodōng]."
Zhēn [Zhēn] said:
"What Jiǎn [Jiǎn] has presented are all petty tactics from the Warring States period,
not affairs for a king.
Wú [Wú] has repeatedly raised troops for years,
raiding and disturbing the borders,
yet we still keep our armor stored and nourish our soldiers,
not daring to quickly seek to punish them,
truly because the common people are weary.
Moreover, Yuān [Yuān] has grown up beyond the sea,
inheriting for three generations,
pacifying the barbarians externally
and cultivating warfare and archery internally.
Yet Jiǎn [Jiǎn] wishes to drive a partial army deep,
arriving in the morning and rolling it up by evening;
I know this is presumptuous."
Jiǎn's [Jiǎn] campaign subsequently met with unfavorable results.
Zhēn [Zhēn] was promoted to Minister of Works,
and then transferred to Minister of Education.
During the Zhèngshǐ [Zhèngshǐ] era,
he was advanced in peerage to Marquis of Chángyuán [Chángyuán],
with an income of one thousand households,
and one of his sons was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Earlier,
Grand Ancestor had long delayed in establishing an heir,
and instead favored and esteemed the Marquis of Línzī [Línzī].
Dīng Yí [Dīng Yí] and others acted as his supporters,
and encouraged Zhēn [Zhēn] to ally with him,
but Zhēn [Zhēn] refused them based on the greater righteousness.
When Emperor Wén [Wén Dì] ascended the throne,
Lín [Lín], Prince of Dōnghǎi [Dōnghǎi], was greatly favored.
The emperor asked Zhēn [Zhēn]:
"What about the Marquis of Píngyuán [Píngyuán]?"
Zhēn [Zhēn] praised his clear virtue and excellent qualities but ultimately said nothing.
When Cáo Shuǎng [Cáo Shuǎng] assisted in governance,
he had Xiàhóu Xuán [Xiàhóu Xuán] convey an imperial directive,
wanting to invite Zhēn [Zhēn] to take up the post of Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and also sought a marriage for his younger brother,
but Zhēn [Zhēn] refused both.
He steadfastly begged to relinquish his position.
An imperial edict stated:
"In the past, Gān Mù [Gān Mù] retired,
his righteousness suppressing mighty Qín [Qín];
Liú Hóu [Liú Hóu] preserved his spirit,
not forgetting the affairs of Chǔ [Chǔ].
Your upright words and excellent counsel
are hoped not to be withheld."
He was granted a residence,
given the rank of Special Advanced Official,
with emoluments equal to the Three Excellencies.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the title Grand Commandant,
and given the posthumous name Marquis Jìng [Jìng Hóu].
His son Liè [Liè] succeeded him.
During the Xiánxī [Xiánxī] era, he served as Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Lú Yù [Lú Yù], courtesy name Zǐjiā [Zǐjiā],
was a native of Zhuó [Zhuó] county, Zhuó [Zhuó] commandery.
His father Zhí [Zhí] [Zhí],
was famous in his time.
Yù [Yù] was orphaned at ten years old,
and encountered chaos in his home province,
with his two elder brothers dying in the disaster.
During the wars between Yuán Shào [Yuán Shào] and Gōngsūn Zàn [Gōngsūn Zàn],
Yōu [Yōu] and Jì [Jì] provinces suffered from famine.
He supported his widowed sister-in-law and his elder brother's orphaned son,
and was praised for his scholarship and conduct.
When Emperor Wén [Wén Dì] was General of the Five Official Ranks,
he summoned Yù [Yù] to be a clerk overseeing bandits in the household office.
Cuī Yǎn [Cuī Yǎn] recommended him to be Chief Clerk of Jìzhōu [Jìzhōu].
At that time, the empire was newly established,
and there were many fugitives.
Therefore, the law heavily punished those who fled,
with the crime extending to their wives and children.
The wife of a runaway, Bái [Bái],
had only married into her husband's family a few days prior,
and had not yet met her husband.
The Grand Judge memorialized to execute her in the marketplace.
Yù [Yù] refuted this, saying:
"The nature of a woman
is such that affection arises upon meeting,
and righteousness deepens upon becoming a wife.
Thus, the 'Odes' say, 'Before I saw my lord,
my heart was sorrowful;
Once I saw him,
my heart was at peace.'
Moreover, the 'Rites' state, 'If a woman dies before the temple ceremony,
she is buried with her mother's family,
because she has not yet become a wife.'
Now, Bái [Bái] and others experience the sorrow of not having met while alive,
and the pain of not being a wife in death.
Yet the officials deliberate to execute them with the great punishment.
If so, after sharing the same food and drinking from the same cup,
what additional punishment could be applied?
Furthermore, the 'Record' says, 'Follow the lighter,'
meaning that when a person is implicated in another's crime,
the lighter punishment is taken as a comparison.
Also, the 'Book' says, 'Rather than kill the innocent,
it is better to err on the side of not punishing,'
fearing that the punishment is too severe.
Even if Bái [Bái] and others accepted the betrothal gifts
and have entered the household,
to punish them is permissible,
but to kill them is too severe."
Grand Ancestor said:
"Yù's [Yù] [Yù] argument is correct.
Moreover, he cited classics with meaning,
which made me sigh."
From this, he became a clerk overseeing legal matters in the Chancellor's office,
and then transferred to a clerk overseeing western matters.
When the state of Wèi [Wèi] was established,
he served as the Director [Láng] of the Ministry of Personnel [Lìbù].
When Emperor Wén [Wén Dì] ascended the throne,
he was transferred to be a Palace Attendant [Huángmén Shìláng],
then sent out to be Administrator [Xiàng] of Jìyīn [Jìyīn],
and Grand Administrator [Tàishǒu] of the two commanderies of Liáng [Liáng] and Qiáo [Qiáo].
The Emperor [Dì] considered Qiáo [Qiáo] his old hometown,
and so he largely relocated people to fill it,
establishing military colonies [túntián] there.
However, the land in Qiáo [Qiáo] was barren and infertile,
and the common people were in distress.
Yù [Yù] pitied them,
and submitted a memorial requesting to relocate the people to Liángguó [Liángguó] where the land was fertile and abundant.
This displeased the Emperor [Dì].
Although he approved of Yù's [Yù] memorial,
he still resented it in his heart,
and so he demoted Yù [Yù],
making him the Colonel [Xiàowèi] in charge of agricultural colonies [diǎnnóng] at Suīyáng [Suīyáng] to lead the relocated people.
Yù [Yù]'s heart was set on benefiting the people,
and he personally oversaw the work,
selecting good land for their residences.
The common people relied on him.
He was then promoted to Grand Administrator [Tàishǒu] of Ānpíng [Ānpíng] and Guǎngpíng [Guǎngpíng],
and wherever he served, he brought benevolent reforms.
In the second year of Qīnglóng [Qīnglóng] (234 CE),
he entered the court as a Palace Attendant [Shìzhōng].
Before this,
the Regular Palace Attendant [Sànqí Chángshì] Liú Shào [Liú Shào] had been commissioned to codify the laws,
but had not yet completed it.
Yù [Yù] submitted a treatise discussing the essence of ancient and modern laws and codes,
believing that the law should be consistent and singular,
not have two extremes,
which would allow corrupt officials to manipulate it.
When the Palace Attendant [Shìzhōng] Gāotáng Lóng [Gāotáng Lóng] repeatedly and strongly remonstrated concerning matters of the palace buildings,
the Emperor [Dì] was displeased.
Yù [Yù] advanced and said:
"Your subject has heard that when the ruler is enlightened, his subjects are upright.
The ancient sage kings feared not hearing their faults,
and thus had a drum for those who dared to remonstrate.
That close officials exhaust their admonitions,
this is precisely why your subjects are inferior to Lóng [Lóng].
Lóng [Lóng] is a scholar,
known for being direct to the point of seeming mad.
Your Majesty [Bìxià] ought to tolerate him."
He served in this position for three years,
and frequently disputed and argued.
An imperial edict [zhào] stated:
"Appointing officials and ranking talents
is difficult even for sage emperors.
One must have good assistants [liángzuǒ]
to advance the worthy and replace the unworthy.
The Palace Attendant [Shìzhōng] Yù [Yù]'s nature is steadfast and firm,
his heart is fair and his conduct upright.
He can be called one who has shown merit in clear trials,
and who does not slacken in his position.
Let Yù [Yù] be appointed Minister of Personnel [Lìbù Shàngshū]."
The Emperor [Dì] told Yù [Yù] to select his own replacement,
saying:
"One must find someone like you to be acceptable."
Yù [Yù] recommended the Regular Palace Attendant [Chángshì] Zhèng Chōng [Zhèng Chōng].
The Emperor [Dì] said:
"Wénhé [Wénhé],
I know him myself.
Recommend someone else whom I have not yet heard of."
So he recommended Ruǎn Wǔ [Ruǎn Wǔ] and Sūn Yōng [Sūn Yōng].
The Emperor [Dì] then appointed Yōng [Yōng].
Before this, Zhūgě Dàn [Zhūgě Dàn] and Dèng Yáng [Dèng Yáng] had achieved great reputations,
and were accused of being "four [sōng] eight paths" (i.e., having a superficial reputation for talent but lacking substance),
and the Emperor [Dì] disliked this.
At that time, a Secretariat Gentleman [Zhōngshū Láng] was being selected.
An imperial edict [zhào] stated:
"Whether the right person is found or not
depends on Master Lú [Lú shēng].
In selection, do not choose those with a name;
a name is like drawing a cake on the ground,
it cannot be eaten."
Yù [Yù] replied:
"A name is not sufficient to attract extraordinary individuals,
but it can secure ordinary gentlemen.
Ordinary gentlemen fear instruction and admire goodness,
and then they acquire a name.
This is not something to be disliked.
Your foolish subject is neither able to recognize extraordinary individuals,
nor is it the duty of those in charge to do more than follow names and observe norms;
they should merely have means to verify their later conduct.
Thus, in ancient times, reports were presented verbally,
and merits were clearly tested by achievements.
Now, the method of evaluating performance has been abandoned,
and advancement or demotion is based on praise or blame,
thus genuineness and falsity are mixed,
and truth and falsehood obscure each other."
The Emperor [Dì] accepted his words,
and immediately issued an edict to create a law for performance evaluation.
When the position of Minister of Works [Sītú] became vacant,
Yù [Yù] recommended the recluse Guǎn Níng [Guǎn Níng].
The Emperor [Dì] could not use him.
He then asked for the next best.
Yù [Yù] replied:
"For earnestness and ultimate conduct,
there is the Grand Master of the Palace [Tàizhōng Dàfū] Hán Jì [Hán Jì];
for bright integrity and clear uprightness,
there is the Colonel Director of Retainers [Sīlì Xiàowèi] Cuī Lín [Cuī Lín];
for steadfastness and pure essence,
there is the Grand Master of Ceremonies [Tàicháng] Cháng Lín [Cháng Lín]."
The Emperor [Dì] then appointed Jì [Jì].
In his assessment of people and in elections,
Yù [Yù] first considered character and conduct,
and only then spoke of talent.
The Palace Attendant [Huángmén] Lǐ Fēng [Lǐ Fēng] once asked Yù [Yù] about this.
Yù [Yù] said:
"Talent is what enables goodness.
Therefore, great talent achieves great good,
and small talent achieves small good.
To say someone has talent yet cannot do good,
is to say that their talent does not match the vessel."
Fēng [Fēng] and others were convinced by his words.
When the King of Qí [Qí Wáng] ascended the throne,
he was granted the title Marquis within the Passes [Guānnèi Hóu].
At that time, Cáo Shuǎng [Cáo Shuǎng] held power,
and wishing to establish his faction,
he transferred Yù [Yù] to be Palace Assistant [Púshè],
replacing Yù [Yù] with the Palace Attendant [Shìzhōng] Hé Yàn [Hé Yàn].
Soon after,
he sent Yù [Yù] out to be Chief Justice [Tíngwèi].
The Colonel Director of Retainers [Sīlì] Bì Guǐ [Bì Guǐ] then wrongly impeached him, leading to his dismissal from office.
Many people spoke in his defense,
and so Yù [Yù] was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness [Guānglù Xūn].
When Shuǎng [Shuǎng] and others were arrested,
Grand Commandant [Tàifù] Sīmǎ Xuān Wáng [Sīmǎ Xuān Wáng] ordered Yù [Yù] to act as Colonel Director of Retainers [Sīlì Xiàowèi]
to handle their case.
He was again made Minister of Personnel [Lìbù Shàngshū],
given the additional title of Commandant of the Car of State [Fèngchē Dūwèi],
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāolè Tíng [Gāolè Tíng Hóu].
He was then transferred to be Palace Assistant [Púshè],
again in charge of elections,
and given the additional title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness [Guānglù Dàfū].
When the Duke of Gāoguì Xiāng [Gāoguì Xiāng Gōng] ascended the throne,
he was further enfeoffed as Marquis of Dàliáng Xiāng [Dàliáng Xiāng Hóu].
One of his sons was enfeoffed as Marquis of Tíng [Tíng Hóu].
When Wúqiū Jiǎn [Wúqiū Jiǎn] rebelled,
Grand General [Dà Jiāngjūn] Sīmǎ Jǐng Wáng [Sīmǎ Jǐng Wáng] led the expedition,
and Yù [Yù] took charge of the affairs behind the lines,
and was given the additional title of Palace Attendant [Shìzhōng].
In the third year of Zhèngyuán [Zhèngyuán] (256 CE),
he fell ill,
and resigned his position.
He was promoted to Minister of Works [Sīkōng],

but he firmly declined, recommending General of Agile Cavalry [Piàojì Jiāngjūn] Wáng Chǎng [Wáng Chǎng], Grand Master of Splendid Happiness [Guānglù Dàfū] Wáng Guān [Wáng Guān], and Colonel Director of Retainers [Sīlì Xiàowèi] Wáng Xiáng [Wáng Xiáng].
An imperial edict [zhào] ordered an envoy to immediately bestow upon him the seal and sash,
and he was advanced in peerage, enfeoffed as Marquis of Róngchéng [Róngchéng Hóu],
with two thousand three hundred households.
He died in the second year of Gānlù [Gānlù] (257 CE),
and was posthumously named Marquis Chéng [Chéng Hóu].
His grandson Fán [Fán] succeeded him.
Yù's [Yù] sons were Qīn [Qīn] and Tǐng [Tǐng].
During the Xiánxī [Xiánxī] era, Qīn [Qīn] served as Minister [Shàngshū],
and Tǐng [Tǐng] as Grand Administrator [Tàishǒu] of Tàishān [Tàishān].
A commentary states: Huán Jiē [Huán Jiē] was insightful regarding success and failure,
and his talent encompassed his era.
Chén Qún [Chén Qún] always upheld righteousness and principles,
and had the esteemed reputation of a pure stream;
Yù [Yù] was broad in his assistance and simple in his thoroughness,
truly capable of sustaining the structure.
During the Wèi [Wèi] dynasty, all affairs of government were handled by the imperial secretariat,
emphasizing the inner court and deemphasizing the outer provinces.
Thus, the eight Ministers [Bāzuò Shàngshū]
held the responsibilities of the ancient Six Ministers [Liù Qīng].
Chén [Chén], Xú [Xú], Wèi [Wèi], and Lú [Lú]
long held these positions.
Jiǎo [Jiǎo] and Xuān [Xuān] were resolute and principled,
Zhēn [Zhēn] and Yù [Yù] were clear in their discernment and management,
and all did not disgrace their offices.
Biographies of Hé Cháng Yáng Dù Zhào Péi [Hé Cháng Yáng Dù Zhào Péi Zhuàn] (Chapter 23)
Hé Qià, courtesy name Yángshì,
was a native of Xīpíng, Rǔnán.
He was recommended as Xiàolián
and invited by the Grand General,
but he declined both.
When Yuán Shào was in Jìzhōu,
he sent envoys to welcome the gentlemen of Rǔnán.
Only Qià thought,
"Jìzhōu's land is flat and its people strong,
which is advantageous for heroes and valiant individuals.
It is a land of four battles.
Běnchū (Yuán Shào), relying on his resources,
though he can become powerful,
yet as heroes are just rising,
success is not yet certain.
Liú Biǎo of Jīngzhōu has no great distant ambitions;
he loves people and is fond of scholars.
The land is rugged and perilous,
with mountain barbarians and weak people,
making it easy to rely on."
So he and his relatives and old friends went south to follow Biǎo,
who treated him as a distinguished guest.
Qià said,
"The reason I did not follow Běnchū
was to avoid contending for land.
The lord of a darkened age
should not be approached too closely,
for in time one becomes precarious,
and there will surely be slanderous and wicked individuals who sow discord."
So he went south across Wǔlíng.
When Tài Zǔ (Cáo Cāo) pacified Jīngzhōu,
he invited Qià to be an aide in the office of the Chancellor.
At that time, Máo Jiè and Cuī Yǎn, known for their loyalty, purity, and administrative ability,
prioritized frugality in their selections and appointments.
Qià said,
"The great task of the empire,
concerning those in positions of power and the people,
cannot be restricted by a single standard (of frugality).
Excessive simplicity and plainness,
while acceptable for oneself,
will lead to many losses if used as a standard to evaluate others.
Currently, the court's discussion holds that
officials who wear new clothes or ride fine carriages
are considered impure;
while chief officials who pass through camps,
whose appearance is unadorned
and clothes are tattered,
are considered incorruptible.
This has led gentlemen to intentionally soil their clothes
and hide their carriages and robes;
some high officials of the court
even carry their own food pot into the government office.
Now, establishing teachings and observing customs
values moderation,
as it is sustainable.
To now advocate a universally difficult conduct to judge diverse paths,
if forced upon people,
will inevitably lead to exhaustion.
The great teachings of antiquity
focused on understanding human nature alone.
All extravagant and peculiar behaviors
invite hypocrisy."
When the state of Wèi was established,
he became a Shìzhōng.
Later, someone reported that Máo Jiè slandered Tài Zǔ.
Tài Zǔ met with his close ministers,
greatly enraged.
Qià argued that Jiè's usual conduct had a basis,
and requested an investigation into the matter.
After the court session,
Tài Zǔ issued an order, saying,
"Those who speak now report that Jiè not only slandered me,
but also showed discontent for Cuī Yǎn.
This harms the affectionate relationship between lord and minister,
and falsely creates resentment and lamentations for a deceased friend.
This is almost intolerable.
In the past, Xiāo Hē and Cáo Shēn rose from humble beginnings with Gāo Zǔ (Liú Bāng),
achieving great merits and establishing achievements.
Whenever Gāo Zǔ was in difficulties,
the two chancellors were respectful and compliant,
thereby enhancing the way of a minister,
which is why their blessings extended to later generations.
Shìzhōng Hé wanted to verify this,
but I did not permit it because
I wanted to consult further."
Qià replied,
"If the accusers' words are true,
then Jiè's crimes are exceedingly grave,
such that neither heaven nor earth can contain him.
Your servant dares not twist the truth for Jiè to subvert the great principles;
but Jiè stood out among the multitude of officials,
was specially promoted,
prominently held a chief position,
enjoyed favor for years,
was upright, loyal, and public-spirited,
and feared by the masses.
He should not have done this.
However, human nature is difficult to guarantee,
so it is necessary to investigate and examine,
verifying the truth from both sides.
Now, Your Majesty's grace extends the benevolence of tolerance,
unwilling to submit him to justice,
which only leaves the distinction between right and wrong unclear,
and the suspicion begins with yourself."
Tài Zǔ said,
"The reason I did not investigate
was to protect both Jiè and his accusers."
Qià replied,
"If Jiè indeed spoke ill of his superior,
he should be publicly executed in the marketplace;
if Jiè did not do this,
then the accuser falsely accused a high official to mislead the emperor's judgment.
If neither of these is investigated,
your servant feels uneasy."
Tài Zǔ said,
"We have military matters pending;
how can we investigate based on someone's accusation right away?
Hú Shègū assassinated Yáng Chǔfù in court;
this is a warning for rulers."
When Tài Zǔ conquered Zhāng Lǔ,
Qià presented a practical proposal to timely withdraw troops and resettle the people,
which would save the cost of maintaining a garrison.
Tài Zǔ did not accept it initially,
but later indeed relocated the people and abandoned Hánzhōng.
He was appointed Lángzhōnglìng.
When Wén Dì (Cáo Pī) ascended the throne,
he was appointed Guānglùxūn
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānchéngtíng.
When Míng Dì (Cáo Ruì) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Marquis of Xīlíngxiāng,
with two hundred households.
During the Tàihé reign,
Sànqí Chángshì Gāotáng Lóng memorialized:
"The current customs are not proper,
and there is an atmosphere of decline and neglect.
This must be due to officials neglecting their duties and violating the natural order."
An imperial edict humbly admitted fault
and broadly sought differing opinions.
Qià believed that
"the people are few and cultivate little,
while there are many idlers.
The state takes the people as its foundation,
and the people take grain as their life.
Therefore, if agricultural labor is expended for a time,
the foundation for nurturing life is lost.
This is why the former kings diligently removed burdensome expenses
to focus solely on agriculture.
Since spring and summer,
the people have been exhausted by labor,
agriculture has been neglected,
and the common people are in turmoil.
The current customs being improper
may not be unrelated to this.
The greatest method for recovery and restoration
is frugality.
Tài Zǔ established a grand enterprise,
covering the expenses of teachers and disciples,
and supplying military rewards and expenditures.
Officials and soldiers were abundant in resources and food,
and granaries and treasuries overflowed with grain and silk,
due to not decorating useless palaces
and cutting off extravagant expenses.
The current priority
lies precisely in ceasing and reducing burdensome tasks,
eliminating other miscellaneous duties,
to serve as reserves for military campaigns.
The defense of the three borders
requires preparedness.
One should assess the enemy's strength and weakness,
accumulate soldiers and maintain the populace,
calculate strategies for victory in the ancestral temple,
clarify plans for attack and conquest,
and thoroughly consult the populace to seek the middle path.
If plans are not decided in advance,
and one lightly underestimates a small enemy,
military campaigns will be undertaken repeatedly,
but without merit.
This is what is called 'delighting in warfare without deterring,'
a warning from the ancients."
He was transferred to Tàicháng.
He was incorruptible and poor, adhering to simplicity,
even selling his fields and residence to support himself.
Míng Dì heard of this
and bestowed upon him additional grain and silk.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the title Marquis Jiǎn.
His son Lí succeeded him.
Lí's pronunciation is 'lí.'
Lí's younger brother Yōu
was talented, discerning, and capable of management.
He reached the official positions of Tíngwèi and Lìbù Shàngshū.
Xǔ Hùn, a man from Qià's commandery,
was the son of Xǔ Shào.
He was pure, refined, and possessed discernment.
During Míng Dì's reign, he served as Shàngshū.
Cháng Lín
was styled Bóhuái, and was a native of Wēn
in Hénèi.
At the age of seven,
a friend of his father’s
called at their gate and asked Lín,
“Is Bóxiān home? Why do you not bow?”
Lín replied,
“Although I should be a guest of lower standing,
I am but a child in the presence of my father’s friend.
What bowing is there to be done?”
Thereupon, everyone commended him.
The Grand Administrator Wáng Kuāng raised troops to attack Dǒng Zhuó,
and sent his students to various subordinate counties to secretly observe the offenses of officials and common people.
He would then arrest them,
interrogate them to exact money and grain as redemption for their crimes,
and if there was any delay, their entire clan would be exterminated,
to establish his prestige and authority.
Lín’s uncle struck a guest,
and this was reported by Wáng Kuāng’s students.
Kuāng, in a rage, had him arrested and tried.
The whole clan was terrified,
not knowing how much would be demanded,
and feared that those imprisoned could not be saved.
Lín went to see Húmǔ Biāo, who was from the same county as Kuāng, and said:
“Prefectural Lord Wáng, with your eminent military and literary talent,
you preside over our humble commandery.
Our humble commandery is bordered by mountains and rivers,
its land is vast, and its people are prosperous,
and it also has many wise and capable individuals,
whom you may choose and employ as you wish.
Currently, the Emperor is young and immature,
and treacherous officials hold sway like tigers,
causing the Central Plains to tremble with fear.
This is the season for heroic talents to rise and act.
If you wish to punish the rebels of the realm,
and support the weakening imperial house,
the wise will respond to your call like an echo,
and victory will be yours.
Success in restoring order lies in harmony;
what campaign could fail?
If, however, there is no benevolence or virtue,
and you appoint the wrong people,
overthrow and destruction will soon follow.
How then can you spare time to assist the court
and establish glorious achievements?
You should hide them!”
He then explained the reason for his uncle’s detention.
Biāo immediately wrote a letter rebuking Kuāng,
and Kuāng released Lín’s uncle.
Lín then fled to Shàngdǎng,
and farmed in the mountain valleys.
At that time, there was a drought and locusts,
but Lín alone had an abundant harvest.
He called all his neighbors
and distributed it to them by the sheng and dou.
He went to reside with Chén Yán, the former Grand Administrator of Héjiān.
The Chén and Féng clans
were old and prominent families.
Zhāng Yáng coveted their women
and desired their wealth.
Lín led his clan
in devising strategies for them.
After being besieged for over sixty days,
they successfully preserved the fortified village.
Gāo Gàn, the Inspector of Bìngzhōu, recommended him as a Cavalry Commandant,
but Lín declined the appointment.
Later, the Inspector Liáng Xí recommended the famous scholars of the province, Lín, as well as Yáng Jùn, Wáng Líng, Wáng Xiàng, and Xún Wěi.
Tàizǔ appointed all of them as county magistrates.
Lín governed Nánhé,
and his administration brought success,
leading to his swift promotion to Grand Administrator of Bólíng and Inspector of Yōuzhōu,
where he achieved merits wherever he served.
When Wén Dì was General of the Five Official Corps,
Lín served as Clerk of Merits.
When Tàizǔ marched west,
Tián Yín and Sū Bó rebelled,
causing agitation in Yōu and Jì.
Wén Dì wished to personally suppress them,
but Lín said:
“I once held the office of Bólíng
and also served in Yōuzhōu,
so the situation of the rebels
can be estimated.
The officials and common people of the north
prefer peace and dislike chaos.
They have long been accustomed to civilizing influence,
and many adhere to good conduct.
Yín and Bó are but a rabble of dogs and sheep,
small in wisdom but grand in ambition,
and incapable of causing great harm.
At present, the grand army is far away,
and there are strong enemies outside.
As General, you are the pillar of the realm,
so to move lightly and venture far
would not be martial, even if successful.”
Wén Dì followed his advice
and sent generals to attack,
who crushed the rebellion immediately.
He was sent out as Grand Administrator of Píngyuán and Commandant of the Eastern Commandery of Wèijùn,
then entered service as Registrar of the Eastern Section for the Chancellor.
After the state of Wèi was established,
he was appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Minister of the Imperial Household,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Lèyángtíng,
and then transferred to Grand Minister of Agriculture.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he was advanced in enfeoffment to Marquis of Gāoyángxiāng,
and transferred to Superintendent of the Imperial Household and Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
Jìn Xuān Wáng, regarding Lín as an elder of virtue from his native place,
would always bow to him.
Someone once said to Lín:
“Duke Sīmǎ is highly esteemed,
you ought to stop him.”
Lín replied:
“Duke Sīmǎ wishes to honor the aged
and set an example for those who come after him.
His eminence is not something I fear,
nor is his bowing something I can control.”
The speaker withdrew hesitantly.
At the time, public opinion considered Lín to be of pure and lofty integrity,
and wished to appoint him to a high ministerial post,
but Lín then claimed to be gravely ill.
He was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
At the age of eighty-three,
he passed away.
He was posthumously granted the title General of Agile Cavalry,
buried with the rites of a Duke,
and given the posthumous title Zhēn Hóu.
His son, Sì,
became Grand Administrator of Tàishān,
but was executed for a legal offense.
His younger brother, Jìng, inherited the enfeoffment.
Yáng Jùn
was styled Jìcái, and was a native of Huòjiā in Hénèi.
He studied under Biān Ràng of Chénliú,
who highly regarded him.
Jùn, seeing that military chaos was about to erupt,
and that Hénèi was situated at a crossroads,
which would inevitably become a battlefield,
then escorted the old and weak to the mountains between Jīng and Mì.
More than a hundred families accompanied him.
Jùn relieved the poor and destitute,
sharing what they had and had not.
There were six families of his clansmen and acquaintances who had been captured and made slaves,
and Jùn spent all his wealth to redeem them.
Sīmǎ Xuān Wáng, then sixteen or seventeen years old,
met Jùn,
and Jùn said:
“This is no ordinary man.”
Also, Sīmǎ Láng already had a reputation,
but his cousin Zhī
was not yet known to the public.
Only Jùn said:
“Although Zhī’s early reputation does not match Láng’s,
in actual ability, he is superior.”
Jùn then moved to take refuge in Bìngzhōu.
Wáng Xiàng of his home commandery
was orphaned young
and became a servant.
At seventeen or eighteen years old,
he was made to herd sheep but secretly read books,
for which he was then flogged.
Jùn admired his talent and character,
immediately redeemed Xiàng and brought him into his home,
arranged his marriage and built a house for him,
and then parted ways with him.
Tàizǔ appointed Jùn as the magistrate of Qǔliáng.
He entered as a clerk to the Chancellor,
was recommended as a *Màocái* (Flourishing Talent),
served as the magistrate of Ānlíng,
and was promoted to Administrator of Nányáng.
He propagated virtuous teachings,
established schools,
and was praised by officials and common people.
He was transferred to serve as the Army Advisor to the General who Attacks the South.
After the state of Wèi was established,
he was promoted to Central Commandant.
When Tàizǔ campaigned in Hànzhōng,
Wèi Fèng rebelled in Yè.
Jùn impeached himself and went to the imperial temporary residence.
Jùn, having narrowly escaped punishment himself,
wrote a memorial to resign from the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince was displeased
and said:
“Commander Yáng is leaving,
why such lofty detachment!”
Consequently, he received an imperial rescript demoting him to Administrator of Píngyuán.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he was again in Nányáng.
At that time, Wáng Xiàng, serving as a Cavalier Regular Attendant,
recommended Jùn, saying:
“I humbly observe Yáng Jùn, the Administrator of Nányáng,
possessing a pure and excellent character,
upholding loyal and respectful generosity.
His benevolence is sufficient to nurture the people,
and his sincerity is sufficient to move the masses.
He is able to guide the younger generation,
tirelessly imparting beneficial instruction.
He is outwardly lenient but inwardly upright,
benevolent yet decisive.
From the beginning of his career,
wherever he served, he brought about transformation.
Having twice governed Nányáng,
his kindness and virtue have become widely known,
attracting people from distant lands and different factions,
who arrive carrying their infants on their backs.
Now, his territory is peaceful and well-governed,
with no opportunity for him to fully display his wisdom and ability.
He ought to return to the imperial court
to exert his efforts in the capital,
and thus glorify the Emperor’s reign.”
From his youth to adulthood, Jùn
took it upon himself to uphold human ethics.
Shěn Gù and Wèi Xún of the same commandery, who both originally came from the military ranks,
were promoted and brought forward by Jùn,
and both became excellent gentlemen.
Later, Gù served successively as commandery administrator,
and Xún as censor and county magistrate.
His keen discernment and righteous conduct were evident in many such cases.
Initially,
the Marquis of Línzī was on good terms with Jùn.
When Tàizǔ’s successor had not yet been decided,
he secretly consulted his various officials.
Although Jùn discussed the respective strengths of Emperor Wén and the Marquis of Línzī,
he did not explicitly take a stand.
However, he praised the Marquis of Línzī more favorably,
which Emperor Wén always resented.
In the third year of Huángchū (222 CE),
the imperial carriage arrived at Wǎn.
Because the market was not prosperous and joyful,
the Emperor became angry and arrested Jùn.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Sīmǎ Xuān Wáng, and Attendants Wáng Xiàng and Xún Wěi pleaded for Jùn,
knocking their heads until they bled,
but the Emperor did not grant their request.
Jùn said:
“I know my crime.”
Then he committed suicide.
Everyone grieved and felt it was an injustice.
Dù Xí, courtesy name Zǐxù,
was a native of Dìnglíng in Yǐngchuān.
His great-grandfather Ān and
grandfather Gēn
were renowned in previous generations.
Xí sought refuge from the chaos in Jīngzhōu,
where Liú Biǎo treated him with the rites due to a guest.
Fán Qīn, of the same commandery, was often regarded as exceptional by Biǎo.
Xí admonished him, saying:
“The reason I came here with you
is simply to lie low like a coiling dragon in a secluded marsh,
waiting for the right time to soar like a phoenix.
How could I think that Pastor Liú is destined to be the lord who restores order,
and thus plan for a man of integrity to commit himself to him?
If you continue to display your abilities,
you are not one of my kind.
I shall cut ties with you!”
Qīn said with regret:
“I humbly accept your instruction.”
Xí then moved south to Chángshā.
In the early years of Jiàn'ān,
Tàizǔ welcomed the Son of Heaven to the capital, Xǔ.
Xí escaped and returned to his hometown.
Tàizǔ appointed him as the magistrate of Xī'è.
The county bordered the southern frontier,
where bandits were rampant.
At that time, all the chief magistrates gathered the people to guard the city walls,
and farming was neglected.
The fields were barren, the people were suffering,
and the granaries were empty.
Xí, knowing that he had earned the people's trust,
sent the old and weak to disperse and resume their farming,
while keeping the able-bodied men to defend.
Officials and common people were delighted.
Coincidentally, Jīngzhōu dispatched ten thousand infantry and cavalry to attack the city.
Xí then summoned all the county officials and common people, numbering more than fifty, who were suitable for defense,
and made a solemn pledge with them.
Those whose relatives were outside and wished to protect themselves
were freely allowed to leave;
they all kowtowed, willing to die.
Thereupon, he personally grasped arrows and stones,
leading them to exert their combined strength.
The officials and common people were grateful
and all served loyally.
In battle, several hundred heads were cut off,
while over thirty of Xí’s men died,
and the remaining eighteen were all wounded.
The enemy managed to enter the city.
Xí led the wounded officials and common people to break through the encirclement and escape.
Almost all were lost in death,
yet none turned their backs.
He then gathered the scattered people
and moved them to the Mópí camp.
Officials and common people admired him and followed him as if returning home.
The Minister over the Masses, Zhōng Yáo, memorialized for him to be appointed Consultant and Military Advisor.
Xún Yù also recommended Xí,
and Tàizǔ appointed him as Libationer of the Chancellor's Army.
After the state of Wèi was established,
he became a Palace Attendant,
serving alongside Wáng Càn and Hé Qià.
Càn had a strong memory and broad learning,
so Tàizǔ, when traveling or going out,
often had him ride in the same carriage,
yet the respect he received was less than Qià and Xí.
Xí once had a private audience
that lasted until midnight.
Càn, being impetuous and competitive,
rose and sat down, saying:
“I wonder what His Excellency discussed with Dù Xí?”
Qià laughed and replied:
“Are there no end to state affairs?
It is enough for you to serve during the day;
why be so anxious here,
wanting to take on everything?”
Later, Xí took charge as the Chancellor’s Chief Clerk,
following Tàizǔ to Hànzhōng to campaign against Zhāng Lǔ.
When Tàizǔ returned,
he appointed Xí as Equerry Commandant,
leaving him to oversee military affairs in Hànzhōng.
He pacified and guided the people,
and eighty thousand households
willingly relocated to Luò and Yè.
When Xiàhóu Yuān was captured by Liú Bèi,
the army lost its commander-in-chief,
and the officers and soldiers turned pale.
Xí, together with Zhāng Hé and Guō Huái, took charge of all military affairs,
temporarily appointing Hé as the commander-in-chief
to unify the army’s morale,
and the three armies were thus stabilized.
When Tàizǔ returned east,
he needed to select a Chief Clerk for the留府 (liu fu, retained administration)
to guard Cháng'ān.
Many of those chosen by the responsible officials were unsuitable.
Tàizǔ issued an order saying:
“To release a swift steed but not ride it,
why then frantically seek another?”
Consequently, Xí was appointed as Chief Clerk of the retained administration
and stationed in Guānzhōng.
At that time, General Xǔ Yōu 許攸 led his troops,
refusing to submit to Tài Zǔ 太祖 and speaking disdainfully.
Tài Zǔ 太祖 was greatly enraged,
and wished to attack him first.
Many officials remonstrated:
"We should try to win over Xǔ Yōu 許攸
and together attack the powerful enemy."
Tài Zǔ 太祖 rested his saber across his lap,
his face stern, and would not listen.
Xí 襲 entered, intending to remonstrate.
Tài Zǔ 太祖 anticipated him and said:
"My plan is settled.
You need not speak further."
Xí 襲 said:
"If Your Highness's plan is correct,
your subject will assist Your Highness in achieving it.
If Your Highness's plan is incorrect,
even if accomplished, it should be changed.
Your Highness obstructs your subject,
ordering him not to speak.
Why then do you expect those below not to hide their thoughts?"
Tài Zǔ 太祖 said:
"Xǔ Yōu 許攸 has insulted me.
How can I let it go?"
Xí 襲 said:
"Your Highness, what kind of person do you consider Xǔ Yōu 許攸 to be?"
Tài Zǔ 太祖 said:
"An ordinary person."
Xí 襲 said:
"Indeed, only the wise know the wise;
only the sagely know the sagely.
How can an ordinary person recognize an extraordinary one?
Currently, wolves are on the path, but we are prioritizing foxes.
People will say Your Highness is avoiding the strong and attacking the weak,
not courageous in advancing,
and not benevolent in retreating.
Your subject has heard that a crossbow of a thousand 100-catty weights is not triggered for a shrew,
nor is a bell of ten thousand 100-catty weights struck with a stalk to produce sound.
Now, how can the insignificant Xǔ Yōu 許攸
be worth troubling your divine martial spirit for?"
Tài Zǔ 太祖 said:
"Good."
Thereupon, he treated Xǔ Yōu 許攸 generously,
and Xǔ Yōu 許攸 immediately submitted.
At that time, Xiàhóu Shàng 夏侯尚 was intimate with the Crown Prince,
their affection exceedingly close.
Xí 襲 considered Shàng 尚 not a beneficial friend,
and not worthy of special treatment,
and reported this to Tài Zǔ 太祖.
Wén Dì 文帝 was initially very displeased,
but later remembered it with appreciation.
The account is in Shàng's 尚 biography.
His gentle yet unyielding nature
was always of this kind.
When Wén Dì 文帝 ascended to the princely throne,
he bestowed upon him the title of Guānnèi Hóu 關內侯.
When he ascended to the imperial throne,
he was made Dūjūnjūnliáng Yùshǐ 督軍糧御史,
enfeoffed as Wǔpíng Tínghóu 武平亭侯,
then changed to Dūjūnjūnliáng Zhífǎ 督軍糧執法,
and entered the court as Shàngshū 尚書.
When Míng Dì 明帝 ascended the throne,
he was promoted and enfeoffed as Píngyáng Xiānghóu 平陽鄉侯.
When Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮 emerged from Qín Chuān 秦川,
Grand General Cáo Zhēn 曹真 commanded the various armies to resist Liàng 亮.
Xí 襲 was transferred to become Grand General's Jūnshī 軍師,
and a hundred households from his fief were divided to bestow upon his elder brother Jī 基 the title of Guānnèi Hóu 關內侯.
After Zhēn 眞 died,
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng 司馬宣王 replaced him.
Xí 襲 again became Jūnshī 軍師,
and his fief was increased by three hundred households,
totaling five hundred and fifty households.
He was summoned back due to illness
and appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū 太中大夫.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the title Shàofǔ 少府,
and given the posthumous name Dìng Hóu 定侯.
His son Huì 會 succeeded him.
Zhào Yǎn 趙儼, courtesy name Bórán 伯然,
was a native of Yǐngchuān Yángzhái 潁川陽翟.
Fleeing the chaos to Jīngzhōu 荊州,
he shared wealth and plans with Dù Xí 杜襲 and Fán Qīn 繁欽,
forming a single household.
When Tài Zǔ 太祖 first welcomed Xiàn Dì 獻帝 to the capital of Xǔ 許,
Yǎn 儼 said to Qīn 欽:
"Cáo Zhèndōng 曹鎮東, in response to destiny, will certainly be able to rectify and save Huáxià 華夏.
I know where to pledge my allegiance."
In the second year of Jiàn'ān 建安 (197 CE),
at the age of twenty-seven,
he consequently supported the old and weak and went to Tài Zǔ 太祖.
Tài Zǔ 太祖 appointed Yǎn 儼 as Lánglíng Zhǎng 朗陵長.
The county had many powerful and cunning people,
who feared nothing.
Yǎn 儼 apprehended the most egregious among them,
bound them, investigated their cases,
and all were found guilty of capital crimes.
After Yǎn 儼 imprisoned them,
he then presented a memorial to the court to release them.
From then on, his authority and benevolence were both evident.
At that time, Yuán Shào 袁紹 raised an army to invade the south,
sending envoys to entice the various commanderies of Yùzhōu 豫州.
Most commanderies accepted his orders.
Only Yáng'ān Jùn 陽安郡 remained unmoved,
and its commandant, Lǐ Tōng 李通, urgently collected household levies.
Yǎn 儼 saw Tōng 通 and said:
"Currently, the world is not yet settled,
and the various commanderies are rebelling.
If we collect silk from those who have shown loyalty,
the common people, who enjoy chaos,
will surely harbor resentment!
Moreover, there are many dangers near and far;
one cannot but consider this carefully."
Tōng 通 said:
"Shào 紹 and the Grand General are in a very tense standoff.
Surrounding commanderies and counties have rebelled thus.
If the silk is not collected and sent,
observers will certainly think we are wavering
and awaiting something."
Yǎn 儼 said:
"Indeed, it is as you consider.
However, we must weigh the relative importance.
If you slightly delay the collection,
I will resolve this problem for you."
He then wrote to Xún Yù 荀彧, saying:
"Now Yáng'ān Jùn 陽安郡 must send silk,
but the roads are difficult and obstructed,
which will surely lead to banditry.
The common people are impoverished,
