neighboring cities are all rebelling,
and it is easy for the region to be overthrown.
This is a critical moment for the safety of a region.
Moreover, the people of this commandery uphold loyalty and integrity,
and do not waver in danger.
Minor good deeds must be rewarded,
so that those who act righteously are encouraged.
A good ruler
stores wealth among the people.
Therefore, I believe the state should offer comfort and solace,
and all the collected silk
should be returned to the people."
Yù 彧 replied:
"I shall immediately inform Cáo Gōng 曹公.
Cáo Gōng 曹公's official document will be sent down to the commandery,
and all the silk will be returned to the people."
Both high and low rejoiced,
and the commandery thereupon became stable.
He entered the court as Sīkōng Yuánshǔ Zhǔbù 司空掾屬主簿.
At that time, Yú Jìn 于禁 was stationed at Yǐngyīn 潁陰,
Lè Jìn 樂進 at Yángzhái 陽翟,
and Zhāng Liáo 張遼 at Chángshè 長社.
The various generals were opinionated
and often disagreed.
Yǎn 儼 was made to supervise and participate in the affairs of the three armies,
instructing and explaining in every matter,
and they subsequently became close and harmonious.
When Tài Zǔ 太祖 campaigned in Jīngzhōu 荊州,
he appointed Yǎn 儼 to lead as Zhānglíng Tàishǒu 章陵太守,
then transferred him to Dūdū Hùjūn 都督護軍,
overseeing the seven armies of Yú Jìn 于禁, Zhāng Liáo 張遼, Zhāng Hé 張郃, Zhū Líng 朱靈, Lǐ Diǎn 李典, Lù Zhāo 路招, and Féng Kǎi 馮楷.
He again served as Chéngxiàng Zhǔbù 丞相主簿,
then was promoted to Fúfēng Tàishǒu 扶風太守.
Tài Zǔ 太祖 relocated more than five thousand soldiers who were formerly under Hán Suì 韓遂, Mǎ Chāo 馬超, and others,
and appointed Píngnàn Jiāngjūn 平難將軍 Yīn Shǔ 殷署 and others to command them,
with Yǎn 儼 as Guānzhōng Hùjūn 關中護軍,
fully commanding all the armies.
The Qiāng 羌 barbarians frequently raided and caused harm.
Yǎn 儼 led Shǔ 署 and others to pursue them to Xīnpíng 新平,
where they inflicted a great defeat.
Lǚ Bìng 呂並, a tenant farmer, declared himself general,
gathered a party, and occupied Chéncāng 陳倉.
Yǎn 儼 again led Shǔ 署 and others to attack him,
and the bandits were immediately defeated and annihilated.
At that time, Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] was assigned to lead one thousand two hundred troops to assist the defender of Hànzhōng [漢中],
and was appointed supervisor for their dispatch.
The soldiers, upon parting from their families,
all looked sorrowful.
One day after Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] set out,
he worried there might be a mutiny,
so he personally rode to Xiégǔkǒu [斜谷口],
comforting and encouraging everyone,
and also sternly admonishing Zhào Yǎn [趙儼].
He returned to spend the night at the residence of Zhāng Jì [張既], the Inspector of Yōngzhōu [雍州].
Zhào Yǎn's [趙儼] troops advanced another forty *lǐ* [里],
and indeed the soldiers rebelled,
so Zhào Yǎn's [趙儼] safety was unknown.
But Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] himself was accompanied by one hundred and fifty cavalry and infantry,
all of whom belonged to the same unit as the rebels,
or were related by marriage.
Upon receiving this news,
they were all alarmed,
donned armor, and took up weapons,
no longer feeling secure.
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] wanted to return,
but Zhāng Jì [張既] and others said,
"Now the main camp's faction is already in disarray;
going there alone would be useless.
We should wait for definite news."
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] said,
"Although I suspect the main camp is conspiring with the rebels,
news of the travelers' mutiny must be heard
before they act on it.
And there are those who wish to do good but cannot make up their own minds.
It is best to seize their moment of hesitation
and promptly reassure and pacify them.
Moreover, as their commander,
if I cannot pacify them,
and suffer disaster myself,
it is fate."
So he departed.
He traveled thirty *lǐ* [里] and stopped,
letting the horses rest.
He summoned all his followers,
explaining success and failure,
comforting and encouraging them earnestly.
They all responded resolutely,
"In life or death, we will follow the Protector-General;
we dare not waver."
Upon reaching the various camps,
he summoned and screened out over eight hundred troublemakers and conspirators,
who were scattered across the plains.
He only punished the ringleaders who had instigated the plot,
ignoring all others.
Those whom the commanderies and counties had arrested and sent
were all released,
and then they immediately led each other back to surrender.
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] secretly reported:
"It is advisable to send generals to the main camp
to request the old troops to garrison Guānzhōng [關中]."
Tàizǔ [太祖] sent General Liú Zhù [劉柱] with two thousand men,
who were to be dispatched only upon arrival.
But the matter was exposed,
and the various camps were greatly alarmed,
and could not be appeased.
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] said to his generals,
"Since the old troops are few,
and the eastern troops have not yet arrived,
the various camps are planning wicked schemes.
If a mutiny were to occur,
the difficulty would be unpredictable.
While they are still wavering,
we must make them decide quickly."
So he declared that one thousand of the gentle and reliable new soldiers would be selected to garrison Guānzhōng [關中],
and all the rest would be sent east.
He then met the officials in charge,
brought in the rosters of the various camp's soldiers,
examined those with heavy burdens,
and immediately differentiated them.
Those who were to stay had their minds settled,
and were of one heart with Zhào Yǎn [趙儼].
Those who were to leave also dared not move.
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] dispatched them all on their way in one day,
and then had the thousand men who were left behind
distribute and watch over them.
The eastern troops soon arrived,
and then he again coaxed and persuaded them,
and also transferred the thousand men,
ordering them to join and travel east together,
thus saving a total of over twenty thousand people.
Guān Yǔ [關羽] besieged General of the South-Conquering Cáoyán [曹仁] at Fán [樊].
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼], as an Imperial Adviser, participated in Cáoyán's [曹仁] military affairs, traveling south,
and advanced together with General of the Pacifying Brigands Xú Huǎng [徐晃].
Upon arrival,
Guān Yǔ's [關羽] encirclement of Cáoyán [曹仁] was already strong,
and other relief troops had not yet arrived.
The troops Xú Huǎng [徐晃] commanded were insufficient to lift the siege,
but the generals urged and criticized Xú Huǎng [徐晃] to quickly relieve it.
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] said to the generals,
"The enemy's encirclement is currently firm,
and the floods are still severe.
Our soldiers are few and scattered,
and Cáoyán [曹仁] is cut off and cannot join forces with us.
This action would only exhaust both internal and external forces.
It would be better now to advance our army close to the siege,
send spies to communicate with Cáoyán [曹仁],
letting him know of outside relief,
to encourage his officers and men.
I estimate the northern army will arrive in no more than ten days,
which is still enough time to hold out.
Then, when both the inner and outer forces strike,
defeating the enemy will be certain.
If there is any punishment for slow relief,
I will bear it for all the armies."
All the generals were pleased,
and immediately dug tunnels,
shot arrows with letters to Cáoyán [曹仁],
and exchanged messages several times.
The northern army also arrived,
and combined forces for a great battle.
After Guān Yǔ's [關羽] army retreated,
his boats still occupied the Miǎnjìng [沔水],
and Xiāngyáng [襄陽] remained cut off.
However, Sūn Quán [孫權] attacked and seized Guān Yǔ's [關羽] baggage train.
When Guān Yǔ [關羽] heard of this,
he immediately fled south.
Cáoyán [曹仁] gathered his generals to deliberate,
and they all said,
"Now that Guān Yǔ [關羽] is in distress and fear,
he can surely be pursued and captured."
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] said,
"Sūn Quán [孫權] invited Guān Yǔ [關羽] to join forces in this difficulty,
wishing to surprise and control him from behind.
He is concerned that Guān Yǔ [關羽] might return to rescue,
fearing that we would take advantage of their mutual exhaustion.
Therefore, he offers flattering words to seek an advantage,
seizing the opportunity and changing circumstances,
to observe what is profitable and what is not.
Now Guān Yǔ [關羽] is isolated and fleeing.
It is better to preserve him as a harm to Sūn Quán [孫權].
If we pursue him deeply to the north,
Sūn Quán [孫權] will then shift his concern from them
and will cause trouble for us.
The King will certainly consider this deeply."
Cáoyán [曹仁] then lifted the state of alert.
Tàizǔ [太祖] heard that Guān Yǔ [關羽] had fled
and feared his generals would pursue him,
so he indeed quickly ordered Cáoyán [曹仁]
just as Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] had strategized.
When Emperor Wén [文] ascended the throne,
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] became a Court Attendant.
Soon after,
he was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law,
and concurrently Governor of Hédōng [河東] and
Colonel Director of Agriculture.
In the third year of Huángchū [黃初] (222 CE),
he was granted the title of Marquis within the Pass.
When Sūn Quán [孫權] encroached on the border,
General-in-Chief of the East-Conquering Cáo Xiū [曹休] commanded the armies of five provinces to resist him.
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] was summoned as Army Adviser.
Sūn Quán's [孫權] forces retreated,
and the army returned.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yítǔtíng [宜土亭],
then transferred to Colonel Director of Expenditure,
and promoted to Minister of the Palace.
He accompanied the campaign against Wú [吳],
reaching Guǎnglíng [廣陵],
where he was again left as Army Adviser for the Eastern Expedition.
When Emperor Míng [明] ascended the throne,
he was advanced in rank to Marquis of Dūxiāng [都鄉],
with an estate of six hundred households.
He was appointed Inspector of All Military Affairs in Jīngzhōu [荊州],
and granted the Imperial Credential.
He fell ill,
and did not take up the post.
He again served as Minister of the Palace,
then was dispatched to inspect all military affairs in Yùzhōu [豫州],
then transferred to Army Adviser for the Grand Marshal,
and entered government as Grand Minister of Agriculture.
When the King of Qí [齊] ascended the throne,
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼] was appointed Inspector of All Military Affairs in Yōng [雍] and Liáng [涼],
granted the Imperial Credential,
then transferred to General of the Shu-Conquering,
and further promoted to General of the West-Conquering,
and Grand Administrator of Yōng [雍] and Liáng [涼].
In the fourth year of Zhèngshǐ [正始] (243 CE),
due to old age and illness, he requested to return.
He was summoned to be General of Agile Cavalry,
and then promoted to Minister of Works.
He passed away
and was posthumously named Mùhóu [穆侯].
His son, Tíng [亭], inherited his title.
Originally,
Zhào Yǎn [趙儼], along with Xīn Pí [辛毗], Chén Qún [陳群], and Dù Xí [杜襲] from the same commandery, were all renowned,
and were known as "Xīn [辛], Chén [陳], Dù [杜], Zhào [趙]".
Péi Qián, zì Wénháng,
was a native of Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
Fleeing the chaos, he went to Jīngzhōu.
Liú Biǎo treated him with guest rites.
Péi Qián secretly said to his close friends Wáng Càn and Sīmǎ Zhī:
“Prefect Liú is not a talent for a hegemon or king.
He wishes to act as a Xībó,
and his defeat is imminent.”
So he went south to Chángshā.
When Tài Zǔ pacified Jīngzhōu,
he appointed Péi Qián as a Staff Officer for the Chancellor’s military affairs.
He served successively as magistrate of three counties,
then entered service as an Assistant in the Granary Department.
Tài Zǔ asked Péi Qián:
“You and Liú Bèi were both in Jīngzhōu previously.
What do you think of Liú Bèi’s talent and strategy?”
Péi Qián replied:
“If he were in the Central Plains,
he would be able to cause chaos among people but unable to govern.
However, if he seizes an opportunity and holds strategic strongholds,
he is sufficient to be a regional ruler.”
At that time, Dàijùn was in great disorder,
so Péi Qián was appointed Administrator of Dàijùn.
The Wūwán king and his tribal chiefs,
three in total,
each proclaimed themselves Chányú
and exclusively controlled the affairs of the commandery.
Previous administrators had been unable to bring order.
Tài Zǔ wished to grant Péi Qián elite troops to suppress them.
Péi Qián declined, saying:
“Dàijùn has a dense population,
and its soldiers and horses number
tens of thousands who can draw a bowstring.
The Chányú themselves know they have been unruly for a long time
and are internally uneasy.
If we bring many soldiers now,
they will certainly be frightened and resist at the border.
If we bring few soldiers, we will not be held in awe.
It is better to plan against them with strategy,
not to coerce them with military might.”
So he went to the commandery in a single carriage.
The Chányú were both surprised and pleased.
Péi Qián pacified them with tranquility.
The Chányú and their subordinates removed their caps and prostrated themselves,
returning all the women, tools, and valuables they had plundered before.
Péi Qián investigated and executed more than ten high-ranking officials in the commandery who had colluded with the Chányú, such as Hǎo Wēn and Guō Duān.
The northern border was greatly awed,
and the common people submitted their hearts.
After three years in Dài,
he returned to serve as Clerical Assistant in the Chancellor’s Department of Justice.
Tài Zǔ praised his achievements in governing Dài,
but Péi Qián said:
“While I was lenient with the common people,
I was stern with the various Hú tribes.
Now, those who evaluate me will certainly consider my governance excessively strict
and will subsequently apply more leniency;
those tribes are naturally proud and unrestrained,
and excessive leniency will surely make them lax.
Once lax, they will again need to be reined in by law,
which is how disputes arise.
Judging by the circumstances,
Dài will surely rebel again.”
Thereupon, Tài Zǔ deeply regretted recalling Péi Qián so quickly.
Dozens of days later,
news of the rebellion of the three Chányú arrived.
Then, Yānlíng Hóu Zhāng was dispatched as General of Agile Cavalry to campaign against them.
Péi Qián was appointed Chancellor of Pèiguó,
then promoted to Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
When Tài Zǔ stopped at Móbeī,
he praised the neatness of his army formations
and especially rewarded him.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
he entered service as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
He was appointed Commander of Agrarian Affairs for Wèijùn and Yǐngchuān,
and he memorialized to open up recommendations and selections,
making them equivalent to those in commanderies and states.
Because of this, the path for agrarian officials to advance in their careers became broad.
He was promoted to Inspector of Jīngzhōu
and granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he entered service as a Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was appointed Magistrate of Hénányǐn,
then transferred to Army Advisor to the Grand Commandant and Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and enfeoffed as Qīngyáng Tínghóu,
with a stipend of two hundred households.
He entered service as Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and memorialized to rectify functional divisions,
scrutinize names and realities,
and issued over one hundred and fifty directives to be decided by government offices.
After his father’s death, he resigned his office,
then was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
He passed away in the fifth year of Zhèngshǐ,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Astrologer,
with the posthumous epithet Zhēn Hóu.
His son Xiù succeeded him.
His will stipulated a simple burial,
with only one seat placed in the tomb,
and a few pottery vessels;
nothing else was provided.
Xiù,
during the Xiánxī period, served as Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
A commentary states: Hé Qià’s clear and harmonious administrative ability,
Cháng Lín’s pure and solid traditional conduct,
Yáng Jùn’s humane and righteous behavior,
Dù Xí’s gentle and profound understanding of governance,
Zhào Yǎn’s resolute and disciplined manner,
Péi Qián’s consistent and steadfast integrity,
all were fine gentlemen of their time.
As for Cháng Lín, he was able to not fix his mind on the Three Ducal Offices
and retired as Grand Master due to old age,
how admirable!
Biography 24: Hán, Cuī, Gāo, Sūn, Wáng
Hán Jì, zì Gōngzhì,
was a native of Dǔyáng, Nányáng.
A powerful local magnate, Chén Mào,
slandered Hán Jì’s father and elder brother,
nearly leading to their execution.
Hán Jì outwardly said nothing about it.
He worked as a laborer and accumulated wealth,
secretly gathering brave men.
Then he pursued, called out, and captured Chén Mào,
offering his head as a sacrifice at his father’s tomb.
From this, he became renowned.
He was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt,
and invited by the Minister of Works,
but he did not accept either.
Instead, he changed his name
and lived in seclusion to avoid chaos in the Lǔyáng Mountains.
The mountain people formed gangs,
intending to raid and plunder.
Hán Jì distributed his family wealth to provide cattle and wine,
invited their leaders,
and explained to them the dangers and benefits.
The mountain people were influenced by him
and ultimately did not cause harm.
Avoiding the summons from Yuán Shù,
he moved to the mountains of Shāndū.
Liú Biǎo, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, courteously invited him,
but he fled
and lived in the territory of Chánlíng.
Wherever he went, he was respected and loved,
but Liú Biǎo deeply resented him.
Hán Jì, fearing this,
accepted the summons
and was appointed Magistrate of Yíchéng.
When Tài Zǔ pacified Jīngzhōu,
he was appointed Staff Officer of the Chancellor’s Department of Military Personnel.
Later, he was selected as Administrator of Lèlíng,
then transferred to Inspector of Forges.
In old times at the forges,
they used horse-driven bellows
(pú bài反.
A bellows used to blow charcoal).
Each time a stone of ore was smelted, it required a hundred horses;
later, human-powered bellows were made,
which also expended much effort.
Hán Jì then adapted the flowing water to create water-powered bellows.
Calculating the benefits,
they were three times greater than before.
After seven years in office,
the tools and equipment were abundant.
An imperial decree praised him,
and he was promoted to Chief of Gold,
his rank second only to the Nine Ministers.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Yíchéng Tínghóu.
In the seventh year of Huángchū,
he was promoted to Grand Astrologer,
and further enfeoffed as Nánxiāng Tínghóu,
with a stipend of two hundred households.
At that time, the new capital, Luòyáng,
had not yet fully established its institutions and regulations,
and the spirit tablets and shrine chests (shí) of the ancestral temples
were all in Yèdū.
Then, a request was made to welcome the spirit tablets of the four ancestral temples from Yè,
establish a temple in Luòyáng,
and personally offer seasonal sacrifices.
He personally served the sacrificial grains.
He promoted proper rites,
abolished improper cults,
and corrected many things.
He served in office for eight years,
and then resigned due to illness.
In the spring of the second year of Jǐngchū [238 CE],
an imperial edict stated:
“Tàizhōng Dàfū Hán Jì
has cleansed his body and bathed in virtue,
his aspirations and integrity are lofty and pure.
Though over eighty years old,
he adheres ever more firmly to the Way.
He can be called truly sincere and earnest,
one who grows more vigorous with age.
Therefore, let Jì be Sītú.”
In the summer, fourth month, he passed away.
His dying wish was to be dressed in ordinary clothes for his burial
and interred in an earth mound.
His posthumous title was Gōnghóu.
His son Zhào succeeded him.
When Zhào passed away,
his son Bāng succeeded him.
Cuī Lín, courtesy name Dérú,
was a native of Dōngwǔchéng, Qīnghé.
When he was young, he matured late,
and his clan members did not recognize his abilities.
Only his cousin Yǎn regarded him as extraordinary.
When Tàizǔ settled Jìzhōu,
he was summoned and appointed as the Chief of Wū.
Being poor and without a carriage or horses,
he traveled to his office on foot.
When Tàizǔ campaigned at Húguān,
he asked which of the chief officials demonstrated the best virtue in their administration.
Zhāng Zhì, the Cìshǐ of Bìngzhōu, named Lín in response.
Thereupon, he was promoted to Jìzhōu Zhǔbù,
and then transferred to Bìejià and Chéngxiàng Yuánshǔ.
After the state of Wèi was established,
he gradually rose to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
When Wéndì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Shàngshū,
and then sent out as Cìshǐ of Yōuzhōu.
Wú Zhì, the Běi Zhōnglángjiàng, commanded the military affairs north of the Yellow River.
Wáng Xióng, the Tàishǒu of Zhuōjùn, said to Lín's Bìejià:
“Běi Zhōnglángjiàng Wú
is highly esteemed and trusted by His Majesty,
a noble official of the state.
He holds the credentials to command affairs,
and all prefectures and commanderies present memorials and show respect.
Yet Cūi Shǐjūn has never communicated with him.
If he were to execute you for neglecting border defenses,
could Shǐjūn protect you?”
The Bìejià reported this in detail to Lín,
who said:
“The Cìshǐ views leaving this prefecture as shedding a slipper;
how could it implicate me?
This prefecture borders the Hú barbarians;
it is appropriate to govern them with tranquility.
Disturbing them would stir their rebellious hearts,
specifically creating a northern concern for the state.
This is why I was entrusted with this post.”
After serving one term in office,
the banditry and incursions ceased.
Nevertheless, because he did not defer to his superiors,
he was demoted to Héxián Tàishǒu,
and many righteous commentators lamented for Lín.
He was later promoted to Dà Hónglú.
The King of Qiūcí sent a hostage prince to pay tribute.
The imperial court praised his long journey
and richly rewarded his king.
Other countries each sent their sons to pay tribute,
and messengers frequently arrived.
Lín feared that those sent might not be genuine,
perhaps merely distant relatives or traveling merchants,
who used this opportunity to establish diplomatic ties
and gain official seals and ribbons.
The expense of escorting them along the journey
was considerable.
This exhausted the common people
and funded a useless endeavor,
making them a laughingstock to the barbarians.
This was a problem in previous times.
So he issued a letter to Dūnhuáng explaining his intention,
and also recorded precedents of how previous dynasties had treated various states, whether generously or meagerly,
to establish a consistent standard.
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
he was granted the noble title Guānnèi Hóu,
and transferred to Guānglùxūn and Sīlì Xiàowèi.
All subordinate commanderies dismissed illegal and superfluous officials.
In his governance, Lín acted with sincerity
and adhered to broad principles.
Therefore, he was always remembered fondly after he left office.
Sànqí Chángshì Liú Shào compiled a treatise on performance evaluation,
which was circulated among all officials.
Lín's critique stated:
“Regarding the performance evaluations in the Zhōu Guān,
the texts are complete.
From King Kāng onwards,
they gradually declined.
This shows that the method of performance evaluation depends on the person implementing it.
As for the late Hàn dynasty,
was its failure truly due to the lack of strictness in the duties of assistant officials?
Currently, the military
is either sprawling or haphazard.
To prepare it with regulations,
to enforce them internally and externally,
with constant changes,
is indeed difficult to unify.
Moreover, one cannot stretch out ten thousand threads without grasping the main cord,
nor can one smooth out many hairs without shaking the collar.
Gāoyáo served Yú,
Yī Yǐn served Yīn,
and inhumane people kept their distance.
The Five Emperors and Three Kings were not necessarily uniform,
yet each achieved governance or chaos.
The Yì Jīng says: 'If it is easy and simple,
then the principles of the world will be obtained.'
Tàizǔ established his system according to circumstances,
passing it down to the present day.
There is no concern that it does not emulate antiquity.
I believe that the current system
is not lax.
The key lies only in maintaining unity and not losing it.
If court officials can bear the heavy responsibility of Zhòngshānfǔ,
and thereby set an example for all officials,
then who would dare not be reverent?”
In the first year of Jǐngchū [237 CE],
the positions of Sītú and Sīkōng were both vacant.
Sànqí Shìláng Mèng Kāng recommended Lín, saying:
“The prime minister
is someone whom the whole empire looks up to and emulates.
It is truly appropriate to choose a person who embodies loyalty, walks the path of righteousness, upholds virtue, and stands for justice,
one who can serve as a role model for all within the four seas.
I humbly observe that Sīlì Xiàowèi Cuī Lín
possesses a naturally upright character
and embodies a noble and magnanimous disposition.
Comparing his strengths to ancient figures,
in loyalty and integrity, he is a peer of Shǐ Yú;
in purity, frugality, and adherence to principles, he is a match for Jì Wén.
As a governor of prefectures and commanderies,
wherever he went, there was order.
When he served as an external official,
all within a thousand li were well-governed.
He is truly an excellent vessel for the three highest ministries,
a fine talent for the ducal offices.”
The following year, he was appointed Sīkōng,
ennobled as Ānyáng Tínghóu,
with an estate of six hundred households.
The ennoblement of the Three Dukes as Lièhóu
began with Lín.
Soon after,
he was further promoted to Ānyáng Xiānghóu.
The Chancellor of Lǔ
submitted a memorial, saying, "
The Hàn Dynasty traditionally established a temple to Kǒngzǐ,
where the Marquis Bāochéng offers sacrifices seasonally,
and in the Bìyōng, when rites are performed,
the先師 (First Teacher) must be sacrificed to.
The royal household provides grain for
spring and autumn sacrifices.
Now the Marquis Zōngshèng
has inherited the succession,
but there is no decree for sacrificial rites.
It is fitting to provide sacrificial animals,
for senior officials to offer sacrifices,
and to honor him as a noble deity."
An edict ordered the Sānfǔ to deliberate.
The Erudite Fù Zhī
stated that in the Chunqiū Zhuàn, it is said that "to establish means to be placed in the sacrificial canon,"
and Kǒngzǐ is such a one.
The Zōngshèng is merely sufficient to continue a lineage that would otherwise be extinguished
and to manifest great virtue.
As for conspicuously establishing his teachings
and promoting his luminous virtue,
it should be as the Chancellor of Lǔ proposed.
Lín
deliberated and thought,
"The Marquis Zōngshèng also offers sacrifices by royal decree;
it is not that there is no decree.
King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed the descendants of the Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn,
and established the Sānkè.
In the eras of Yǔ and Tāng,
they were not listed at that time,
nor were special officers commanded to sacrifice to them.
Now, from Duke Zhōu upwards,
reaching to the Sānhuáng,
if they are suddenly not sacrificed to,
yet their ritual classics preserve their words.
The sole reason Kǒngzǐ is sacrificed to now
is because his era is recent.
As a descendant of a Dàfū,
to specially receive boundless sacrifices,
a rite exceeding ancient emperors,
and a meaning surpassing Tāng and Wǔ,
can be called 'exalting and manifesting virtue in repayment.'
There is no need for repeated sacrifices to those not of his clan."
Emperor Míng also divided Lín Yì
and enfeoffed one son as a Marquis.
He died in the fifth year of Zhèngshǐ,
and was posthumously named Xiàohóu.
His son Shù succeeded.
Gāo Róu, courtesy name Wénhuì,
was a native of Yǔ, Chénliú.
His father, Jìng,
was the Commandery Commandant of Shǔjùn.
Róu remained in his hometown,
and said to the people of the district,
"Now heroes are rising in unison,
and Chénliú is a strategic battleground.
Although General Cáo occupies Yǎnzhōu,
he originally had plans for the four directions
and cannot sit still and guard it.
Moreover, Magistrate Zhāng has first gained control of Chénliú.
I fear that changes may occur when opportunity arises.
I wish to avoid this with you all."
Everyone thought that Zhāng Máo and Tàizǔ were on good terms,
and that Róu was young,
so they did not believe his words.
Róu's paternal cousin, Gàn,
was Yuán Shào's nephew.
He called Róu from north of the Yellow River,
and Róu led his entire clan to follow him.
It happened that Jìng died in Xīzhōu.
At that time, the roads were difficult,
and banditry was rampant.
Yet Róu braved the dangers to go to Shǔ to escort the coffin.
He endured bitter hardships and suffering,
tasting all difficulties,
and returned only after three years.
When Tàizǔ pacified the Yuán clan,
he appointed Róu as the Magistrate of Guǎn.
The county had long heard of his reputation.
Several corrupt officials
all resigned themselves.
Róu instructed them, saying,
"In the past, when Bǐng Jí governed,
there were times when officials erred,
yet he still tolerated them.
How much more so these officials,
who have not yet made any mistakes with me!
Summon them back."
They all returned,
all exerted themselves,
and all became good officials.
After Gāo Gàn surrendered,
he soon rebelled with Bīngzhōu.
Róu voluntarily returned to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ, intending to punish him for the incident,
appointed him as the Registrar for Detecting Transgressions.
He applied the law fairly and appropriately,
and there were no backlog of cases.
He was then promoted to Prefect of the Chancellor's Granary Bureau.
Tàizǔ wished to send Zhōng Yáo and others to attack Zhāng Lǔ.
Róu advised against it,
believing that if a large army were now rashly dispatched,
Hán Suì and Mǎ Chāo in the west
would think it was directed at them,
and would incite each other to rebel.
It would be better to first gather the Sānfǔ.
If the Sānfǔ were settled,
Hànzhōng could be pacified by a mere dispatch of a written summons.
When Yáo entered the pass,
Suì and Chāo indeed rebelled.
When the state of Wèi was first established,
he became a Secretary of the Department of State Affairs.
He was then appointed as Prefect of the Chancellor's Judicial Bureau.
An order stated,
"The governance of settled order
takes ritual as its foremost principle.
The administration for quelling chaos
takes punishment as its priority.
Thus, Shùn exiled the four wicked clans,
and Gāoyáo served as Minister of Justice.
Hàn Zǔ abolished Qín's harsh laws,
and Xiāo Hé established the legal code.
You, Prefect, have clear discernment and fairness,
and are enlightened in the constitutional laws.
Exert yourself diligently in this!"
The musicians Sòng Jīn and others
deserted at Héféi.
According to old law,
when soldiers deserted during a military campaign,
their wives and children were investigated and punished.
Tàizǔ, troubled that this did not stop desertions,
further increased the severity of the punishment.
Jīn had a mother, wife, and two younger brothers, all assigned to official service.
The responsible officials memorialized to have them all executed.
Róu memorialized, saying,
"Soldiers deserting the army is indeed detestable,
but I secretly hear that sometimes among them there are those who regret.
I foolishly suggest that it would be advisable to spare their wives and children.
Firstly, this can make the enemy ranks distrustful.
Secondly, it can entice them to return.
If the previous penalties are maintained,
their hopes are already completely extinguished.
And if they are rashly made even heavier,
I fear that from now on, soldiers in the army,
seeing one person desert,
and fearing punishment will reach them,
will also follow suit and flee,
and it will be impossible to kill them again.
This severe punishment is not for stopping desertion,
but for increasing flight."
Tàizǔ said,
"Good."
He immediately stopped the execution of Jīn's mother and brothers,
and many others were spared.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān,
then returned to serve as Prefect of the Judicial Bureau.
At that time, Inspectors Lú Hóng, Zhào Dá, and others were appointed
to observe all subordinates.
Róu advised against it, saying,
"Officials are established and duties divided,
each with their own responsibilities.
Now appointing Inspectors
is neither in line with the principle of superiors trusting subordinates.
Furthermore, Dá and others frequently exploit their likes and dislikes to arbitrarily wield power and influence.
They should be investigated and disciplined."
Tàizǔ said,
"You know Dá and others,
I fear, not as well as I do.
They are essential for detecting and exposing wrongdoing and managing many affairs.
If virtuous and upright gentlemen were to do it,
they would be incapable.
When Emperor Wén (Wéndì) ascended the throne,
he appointed Rán Rǒu (Rán Rǒu) as Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ (Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ).
He was granted the noble title Guānnèi Hóu (Guānnèi Hóu)
and was subsequently promoted to Zhìshū Zhífǎ (Zhìshū Zhífǎ).
There were frequently instances of slanderous and seditious remarks among the common people.
The Emperor detested this,
and whenever seditious remarks were made, he would execute the offender
and reward the accuser.
Rán Rǒu (Rán Rǒu) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Now, those who utter seditious remarks are certainly executed,
and those who report them are immediately rewarded.
This not only denies those who make mistakes a path to reform and goodness,
but it will also open the door to a gradual increase in malicious and cunning individuals falsely accusing and entrapping one another.
This is truly not the way to stop villainy and reduce lawsuits,
nor to illuminate the path of governance.
In ancient times, when Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng) composed his proclamations,
he mentioned the ancestors of Yīn (Yīn),
who all disregarded the grievances of the common people.
During the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty, Emperor Tàizōng (Tàizōng)
also abolished laws against seditious remarks and slander.
Your humble servant believes it is appropriate to abolish the law that rewards accusations of sedition and slander,
in order to uphold the benevolence of the Heavenly Father (Tiānfù) in nurturing all beings."
The Emperor did not immediately comply,
and false accusations became even more rampant.
The Emperor then issued an edict:
"Anyone who dares to accuse another of slander
shall be punished with the crime of the accused."
Thereupon, such practices ceased.
The investigating officials, such as Liú Cí (Liú Cí) and others,
from the early years of Huángchū (Huángchū) for several years,
had reported tens of thousands of official and civilian crimes.
Rán Rǒu (Rán Rǒu) requested that the truth of all these cases be ascertained and punished accordingly;
as for other minor legal infringements,
they were merely fined.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Tíngwèi (Tíngwèi).
In the early Wèi (Wèi) dynasty,
the Three Dukes (Sāngōng) had no significant duties
and rarely participated in court affairs.
Rán Rǒu (Rán Rǒu) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Heaven and Earth achieve their work through the four seasons;
the sovereign brings about good governance through his assistants.
King Chéng Tāng (Chéng Tāng) relied on the aid of Ā Héng (Ā Héng);
Kings Wén (Wén) and Wǔ (Wǔ) depended on the strength of Dàn (Dàn) and Wàng (Wàng).
Up to the early Hàn (Hàn) dynasty,
figures like Xiāo (Xiāo) and Cáo (Cáo) all served as the heart and backbone of the state based on their great achievements.
These are all examples of enlightened monarchs and sagely rulers employing ministers above,
and virtuous chancellors and good assistants acting as their limbs below.
Now, the officials of the Three Dukes (Sāngōng)
are all pillars of the nation,
looked up to by the people.
Yet, they are placed in these three positions
without being allowed to participate in government,
thus they all rest quietly, maintaining their high status,
with few offering advice.
This is truly not in keeping with the court's principle of valuing and employing high-ranking ministers,
nor is it consistent with the idea of ministers offering sound advice and rejecting the unsound.
In ancient times, whenever there was doubt about penal law or administration,
discussions were held beneath the huái (huái) and jí (jí) trees.
From now on,
whenever there are doubtful discussions in court, or major judicial cases,
it is advisable to frequently consult the Three Dukes (Sāngōng).
On the days of the new moon and full moon, when the Three Dukes (Sāngōng) attend court,
they should also be specially invited in
to discuss gains and losses,
and thoroughly express their opinions.
Perhaps this can contribute to the Emperor's understanding
and greatly benefit the grand transformation."
The Emperor greatly appreciated and accepted this.
Because of an old grudge, the Emperor
wanted to pervert the law and execute Zhìshū Zhífǎ (Zhìshū Zhífǎ) Bào Xūn (Bào Xūn),
but Rán Rǒu (Rán Rǒu) firmly refused to comply with the imperial decree.
The Emperor was furious.
He then summoned Rán Rǒu (Rán Rǒu) to the palace;
he sent an envoy to carry out his instructions to the Tíngwèi (Tíngwèi) to examine and condemn Bào Xūn (Bào Xūn).
Only after Bào Xūn (Bào Xūn) died did he allow Rán Rǒu (Rán Rǒu) to return to his office.
When Emperor Míng (Míngdì) ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Rán Rǒu (Rán Rǒu) as Yánshòu Tínghóu (Yánshòu Tínghóu).
At that time, the scholars (bóshì) were studying the classics.
Rán Rǒu (Rán Rǒu) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your humble servant has heard that following the Way and valuing learning
are profound teachings of the sages;
honoring culture and exalting Confucianism
are clear principles of emperors.
In the late Hàn (Hàn) dynasty, when things declined,
rites and music collapsed.
Heroes fought and tigers contended,
making military campaigns their primary concern.
This led to the scholars of the Confucian forest
being hidden and obscure.
When Emperor Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ) first rose,
he pitied this situation.
During the time of restoring order,
he also established educational officials in commanderies and counties.
When Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) ascended the throne,
he further developed this endeavor,
reviving the Pìyōng (Pìyōng) academy,
and establishing examinations in the provinces.
Consequently, scholars throughout the realm
once again heard the teachings of the xiángxù (xiángxù) schools
and personally observed the rites of zǔdòu (zǔdòu).
Your Majesty, in administering the government,
truly follows profound wisdom,
promulgating great principles,
and glorifying ancestral traditions.
Even the succession of Xià Qǐ (Xià Qǐ)
and the continuation of King Chéng of Zhōu (Zhōu Chéng)
could truly not surpass this.
However, the current scholars (bóshì) are all learned in the classics and cultivate virtuous conduct,
selected as the purest of the nation,
yet their promotions are limited and do not exceed that of a mere chief.
I fear this is not the way to honor and make manifest Confucian scholarship,
nor to encourage and stimulate the lazy.
Confucius said, 'To promote the good and educate the incapable encourages others.'
Therefore, when Chǔ (Chǔ) honored Shēn Gōng (Shēn Gōng),
scholars became keen;
when Hàn (Hàn) esteemed Zhuó Mào (Zhuó Mào),
officials vied to emulate him.
Your humble servant believes that the scholars (bóshì)
are the source of the Way, the venerated masters of the Six Arts (Liùyì).
They should be treated with extraordinary appointments
according to the excellence of their learning and conduct.
To profoundly honor the teachings of the Way
and thereby encourage learners
would be a grand benefit to transformation."
The Emperor accepted this.
Later, a large number of palaces were built,
and the common people suffered from forced labor;
many women were widely gathered,
filling the imperial harem;
the imperial princes in the harem repeatedly died young,
and no heir was yet nurtured.
Rán Rǒu (Rán Rǒu) submitted a memorial, saying:
"The two barbarian enemies are cunning
and secretly training,
planning to wage war;
they have not yet considered surrendering.
It is advisable to nurture generals and soldiers,
repair armor and weapons,
and await them at ease.
However, recently, palaces are being built,
causing labor and disturbance both high and low.
If Wú (Wú) and Shǔ (Shǔ) were to know our real situation,
conspire and combine forces,
and again come to their deaths together,
it would be very difficult indeed.
In ancient times, Emperor Wén of Hàn (Hàn Wéndì) valued the resources of ten families,
and did not engage in the pleasure of building small pavilions;
Qùbìng (Qùbìng) worried about the threat of the Xiōngnú (Xiōngnú),
and had no time for building residences.
How much more so now, when the loss is not merely the cost of a hundred gold pieces,
and the worry is not merely the threat of the northern barbarians?
It is acceptable to roughly complete what is currently under construction,
to serve the purpose of court banquets.
I beg that the workers be dismissed,
so they can return to farming.
After the two factions are pacified,
construction can slowly resume.
In ancient times, Xuānyuán (Xuānyuán) had twenty-five sons,
and his reign was passed down for a long time;
the Zhōu (Zhōu) house had forty Jī (Jī) states,
and its years lasted very long.
Your Majesty is intelligent and discerning,
thoroughly understanding principle and exhausting nature,
yet recently, the imperial princes have repeatedly died young,
and the auspicious sign of 'bears and grizzly bears' has not yet manifested.
The hearts of your subjects
are all troubled.
According to the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōu Lǐ),
the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ)'s empress and concubines numbered one hundred and twenty below;
the ritual of imperial consorts
was already grand.
I secretly hear that the number in the imperial harem
perhaps even exceeds this,
and the failure of the sacred heirs to prosper
can probably be attributed to this.
Your humble servant believes it is advisable to subtly select virtuous women
to fill the designated number of internal officials,
and send the rest home.
Furthermore, it is essential to nourish one's essence and spirit,
valuing tranquility as precious.
If this is done,
then the omen of the 'grasshoppers'
can be hoped for and achieved."
The Emperor replied:
"I know your loyalty and integrity,
and your devotion to the imperial house,
and that you are able to speak boldly.
I shall consider this again."
At that time, the hunting laws were extremely strict.
Liú Guī (劉龜), an agricultural superintendent in Yíyáng (宜陽), secretly shot a rabbit within the forbidden grounds.
His aide, Zhāng Jīng (張京), went to the investigating officials and reported him.
The Emperor concealed Jīng's name,
and had Guī arrested and imprisoned.
Róu (柔) submitted a memorial requesting the name of the accuser.
The Emperor was greatly angered and said:
"Liú Guī (劉龜) deserves death!
How dare he hunt in My forbidden territory!
Send Guī (龜) to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi),
and the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi) should immediately interrogate and torture him.
Why ask again for the name of the accuser?
Did I arrest Guī (龜) without reason?"
Róu (柔) replied:
"The Grand Judge (Tíngwèi)
is the standard of justice for the entire realm.
How can the law be violated based on the Supreme One's (Zhìzūn) pleasure or anger?"
He repeatedly submitted the same memorial,
with profound and urgent words.
The Emperor's mind was awakened,
and he then revealed Jīng's (京) name.
Upon immediate re-investigation,
each was found guilty of their respective crimes.
At that time, there was a regulation that
officials who suffered the loss of a close relative
were all to be given duties after one hundred days.
There was an official under the Minister of Works (Sītú), Jiě Hóng (解弘), who was mourning his father.
Later, there was a military matter,
and he received an order to set out,
but he used illness as an excuse.
The imperial edict angrily stated:
"You are neither Zēngshēn (曾參) nor Mǐn Sǔn (閔損)!
Why speak of being devastated by grief?"
He was immediately arrested, interrogated, and put to death.
Róu (柔) saw that Hóng (弘) was indeed extremely frail,
and submitted a memorial detailing his case,
suggesting that he should be treated with leniency.
The Emperor then issued an edict saying:
"What filial piety Hóng (弘) possesses!
Pardon him."
Initially,
Gōngsūn Yuān's (公孫淵) elder brother, Huǎng (晃),
served as an inner attendant due to his uncle, Gōng (恭).
Before Yuān (淵) rebelled,
Huǎng (晃) repeatedly reported on his impending treachery.
When Yuān (淵) plotted rebellion,
the Emperor could not bear to execute Huǎng (晃) publicly,
and wanted to have him killed in prison.
Róu (柔) submitted a memorial stating:
"The 'Shū Jīng' (書經) says: 'Use punishment to execute the wicked,
and use virtue to manifest the good.'
This is a clear standard of the royal system.
Huǎng (晃) and his wife and children are indeed of the rebel class,
and should be publicly displayed and exterminated,
leaving no descendants.
However, Your servant secretly heard that Huǎng (晃) had repeatedly reported himself earlier,
exposing Yuān's (淵) nascent plot.
Although he is from a treacherous clan,
his original intention can be forgiven.
Indeed, Zhòngní (仲尼) illuminated Sīmǎ Niú's (司馬牛) anxiety,
and Qí Xī (祁奚) made clear Shū Xiàng's (叔向) faults;
these were beautiful acts of righteousness in ancient times.
Your servant believes that if Huǎng (晃) truly made those statements,
he should be spared death;
but if he made no such statements,
then he should be publicly executed.
Now, to neither pardon his life
nor publicly reveal his crime,
but to keep him confined in prison
and make him take his own life,
will cause observers from all corners of the realm
to perhaps doubt this action."
The Emperor did not listen.
He ultimately sent an envoy to give Huǎng (晃) and his wife and children gold dust to drink,
bestowed coffins and clothing,
and buried them at their residence.
At this time,
those who killed deer in forbidden areas were put to death,
and their property was confiscated by the state.
Those who could expose such acts were greatly rewarded.
Róu (柔) submitted a memorial stating:
"When the sagely kings governed the world,
none did not make expanding agriculture their priority,
and frugal use their resource.
If agriculture is expanded, grain will accumulate;
if use is frugal, wealth will be stored.
Those who stored wealth and accumulated grain yet worried about calamities
have never existed.
In ancient times,
if one man did not farm,
someone might go hungry;
if one woman did not weave,
someone might suffer from cold.
From recent times onward,
the common people have supplied numerous labor services,
those who personally farm have decreased,
and additionally, there is now a hunting ban.
Herds of deer rampage and destroy,
consuming young shoots,
causing harm everywhere.
The damage is immeasurable.
Although the people erect barriers,
they are powerless to stop them.
For example, in the areas around Xíngyáng (滎陽),
extending for several hundred *lǐ*,
almost nothing is harvested each year.
The lives of the common people
are truly pitiable.
At present, those who produce wealth in the realm are very few,
while the damage from elk and deer is very great.
Should there suddenly be a military campaign
or a year of famine,
there will be nothing to rely on.
May Your Majesty heed the concerns of the ancient sages,
pity the hardship of farming,
relax the restrictions for the common people,
allow them to hunt deer,
and thereby abolish the ban.
Then the multitude of common people will be long relieved,
and none will be displeased."
After a while,
Dòu Lǐ (竇禮), a soldier in the Imperial Guard (Hùjūn) camp, went out and did not return.
The camp considered him a deserter,
reported it, and sought to apprehend him.
His wife Yíng (盈) and their children, male and female, were confiscated as government slaves.
Yíng (盈) was taken to the provincial and commandery offices,
where she pleaded her innocence,
but no one paid attention.
She then appealed to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
Róu (柔) asked:
"How do you know your husband did not desert?"
Yíng (盈) replied tearfully:
"My husband was an orphan from a young age,
and raised an old woman as his mother,
serving her with great reverence.
He also pitied his children,
nurturing and watching over them without separation.
He is not one who is frivolous and disregards his family."
Róu (柔) asked again:
"Did your husband have any grievances or enemies with anyone?"
She replied:
"My husband is good and kind,
and has no enemies with anyone."
He further asked:
"Did your husband have any financial dealings with anyone?"
She replied:
"He once lent money to Jiāo Zǐwén (焦子文), a fellow soldier in the camp,
but could not get it back."
At that time, Zǐwén (子文) happened to be imprisoned for a minor offense.
Róu (柔) then met Zǐwén (子文)
and asked about his offense.
In the course of conversation,
he said:
"Have you ever borrowed money from anyone?"
Zǐwén (子文) replied:
"As I am poor and solitary,
I have never dared to borrow money or goods from others."
Róu (柔) observed that Zǐwén's (子文) expression changed,
and then said:
"You borrowed Dòu Lǐ's (竇禮) money in the past,
why do you say no?"
Zǐwén (子文) was startled that the matter was exposed,
and responded incoherently.
Róu (柔) said:
"You have already killed Lǐ (禮),
it is best to confess early."
Zǐwén (子文) then kowtowed,
fully confessing the details of killing Lǐ (禮)
and the location where he buried him.
Róu (柔) then dispatched officers and soldiers,
who, following Zǐwén's (子文) confession, went and dug up Lǐ (禮),
and immediately found his corpse.
An imperial edict restored Yíng (盈) and her children to commoner status.
It was promulgated throughout the realm,
using Lǐ's (禮) case as a warning.
He served in office for twenty-three years,
and was transferred to Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
Ten days later, he was promoted to Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
and later moved to Minister over the Masses (Sītú).
Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (司馬宣王) memorialized for the dismissal of Cáo Shuǎng (曹爽).
The Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) issued an edict summoning Róu (柔), granting him the imperial credential (jiǎjié) and acting as Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn),
to take control of Shuǎng's (爽) camp.
The Grand Tutor (Tàifù) said to Róu (柔):
"You are Zhōu Bó (周勃)."
After Shuǎng (爽) was executed,
he was advanced in封 as Marquis of Wànsuì Township (Wànsuì Xiānghóu).
When the High and Noble Duke of Xiāng (Gāoguì Xiānggōng) ascended the throne,
he was advanced in封 as Marquis of Ānguó (Ānguó Hóu),
and transferred to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
When the Duke of Chángdào Township (Chángdào Xiānggōng) ascended the throne,
his fief was increased, totaling four thousand households including the previous grant.
His two sons were successively enfeoffed as Marquises of Pavilion (Tínghóu).
In the fourth year of Jǐngyuán (景元),
at the age of ninety, he passed away.
His posthumous title was Yuánhóu (元侯).
His grandson Hún (渾) succeeded him.
During the Xiánxī (咸熙) era,
the five ranks of nobility were established.
As Róu (柔) and others had rendered meritorious service in the previous dynasty,
Hún (渾) was re-enfeoffed as Viscount of Chānglù (Chānglù Zǐ).
Sūn Lǐ, courtesy name Dédá,
was a native of Róngchéng, Zhuōjùn.
When Tàizǔ pacified Yōuzhōu,
he was summoned to be an Attendant Officer for Military Counsel in the Sīkōng's office.
Initially, during the period of great chaos and loss,
Lǐ was separated from his mother.
Mǎ Tái, from the same commandery, found Lǐ's mother.
Lǐ then offered all his family wealth to Tái.
Later, Tái was condemned to death for a crime.
Lǐ secretly guided him to escape from prison and surrender himself.
After doing so, Tái said:
"Your servant has no intention of fleeing."
He went directly to Wēn Huī, the Chief Clerk of the Inspectorate.
Huī praised this act,
and reported it fully to Tàizǔ.
Both received a commutation of one degree from their death sentences.
Later, Lǐ was appointed Commander of Héjiān Commandery,
and gradually promoted to Commandant of Xíngyáng.
In Lǔshān, several hundred bandits
held fortified, dangerous positions,
causing harm to the people.
Therefore, Lǐ was transferred to become Chancellor of Lǔ.
Upon arriving at his post,
Lǐ distributed his official salary in grain,
mobilized officials and commoners,
offered rewards for enemy heads,
and welcomed those who surrendered,
using them as spies.
Immediately, peace and order were restored.
He successively served as Administrator of Shānyáng, Píngyuán, Píngchāng, and Lángyé.
He followed Grand Marshal Cái Xiū on an expedition against Wú at Jiáshí.
Lǐ advised against penetrating too deeply,
but his advice was not followed, and they suffered a defeat.
He was promoted to Administrator of Yángpíng,
and entered the court as Shàngshū.
When Emperor Míng was extensively constructing palaces,
and the seasonal qi was not harmonious,
the empire had little grain.
Lǐ strongly argued for
halting the labor.
An imperial edict stated:
"I respectfully accept your frank words;
dispatch the laborers promptly."
At that time, Lǐ Huì was supervising the work
and again requested to retain the laborers for another month
to complete some work.
Lǐ went directly to the construction site,
without again submitting a memorial,
and declared the imperial edict to dismiss the laborers.
The Emperor admired his determination and did not blame him.
When the Emperor was hunting in Dàshíshān,
a tiger rushed towards the imperial carriage.
Lǐ immediately threw down his whip and dismounted,
intending to brandish his sword and strike the tiger.
An edict ordered Lǐ to remount.
At the time of Emperor Míng's impending death,
he appointed Cáo Shuǎng as Grand General,
deeming it necessary to have capable assistants.
Lǐ received the imperial testament by the bedside
and was appointed Chief Clerk to the Grand General,
with the additional title of Sanqí Chángshì.
Lǐ was upright and unyielding,
which Shuǎng disliked.
He was made Inspector of Yángzhōu,
with the additional title of Fúbō Jiāngjūn,
and granted the noble title of Guānnèi Hóu.
When Wú's Grand General Quán Cóng led tens of thousands of troops to invade,
the provincial troops were on leave;
few were present.
Lǐ personally commanded the guard troops to resist them,
fighting at Shuòpí.
From dawn until dusk,
more than half of the officers and soldiers were killed or wounded.
Lǐ braved the gleaming blades,
his horse sustained several wounds,
he wielded the drumsticks with his hands,
and fought without regard for his own safety.
The enemy forces then retreated.
An imperial edict commended and comforted him,
bestowing seven hundred bolts of silk.
Lǐ set up sacrifices and wept for those who died in service,
his wails of grief coming from the heart.
He gave all the silk to the families of the deceased,
keeping none for himself.
He was summoned to be Grand Minister of the Privy Purse,
then sent out as Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
and promoted to Governor of Jìzhōu.
Grand Tutor Sīmǎ Xuánwáng said to Lǐ:
"Now Qīnghé and Píngyuán have been disputing their border for eight years,
and two Inspectors have come and gone,
none able to resolve it.
Yú and Ruì waited for King Wén to settle their dispute;
you should make the division clear and just."
Lǐ replied:
"The litigants rely on ancient tombs as evidence,
and the arbiters take the oldest elders' testimonies as correct.
However, elders cannot be subjected to torture,
and ancient tombs are sometimes moved to higher, open ground,
or relocated to avoid feuds.
From what I've heard now,
even Gāotáo would find it difficult.
If you wish to ensure there will be no lawsuits,
we should resolve it based on the map from when Emperor Lièzǔ first enfeoffed Píngyuán.
Why must we push back to ancient times and question old precedents
to only increase litigation?
In the past, King Chéng played a joke with a paulownia leaf and Shūyú,
and Duke of Zhōu immediately enfeoffed him.
Now the map is stored in the imperial archives,
so it can be decided right here,
why wait until I arrive at the province?"
Xuánwáng said:
"That is right.
We shall issue the map separately."
When Lǐ arrived,
he examined the map, which indicated the land belonged to Píngyuán.
However, Cáo Shuǎng believed the words of Qīnghé
and issued a decree saying:
"The map is not usable;
different accounts must be consulted."
Lǐ submitted a memorial stating:
"Guǎn Zhòng, an assistant to a hegemon,
though his character was somewhat petty,
was still able to take Biānyì from Bóshì,
ensuring no grievances for life.
Your servant, having received the responsibility of a governor,
has followed the clear map of the holy court,
and verified the boundaries marked on the ground.
The true boundary is marked by the Wángwēng Hé.
However, Yú relies on the Mǎdān Hòu as evidence,
falsely claiming the Míngdú Hé as the border.
They present false lawsuits,
misleading the imperial court.
I have heard that 'many mouths can melt gold,'
'float stones and sink wood,'
'three men make a tiger appear in the market,'
and 'a loving mother throws away her shuttle.'
Now, these two commanderies have been disputing their border for eight years.
The reason it can be decided in a single morning
is because there are explanatory documents and maps
that can be consulted, examined, and verified.
Píngyuán is between two rivers,
extending to the east.
Between them is the Jué Dī,
which is southwest of Gāotáng.
The disputed land is northwest of Gāotáng,
about twenty *lǐ* away.
It can be said that this causes deep sighs and tears.
Based on the explanation and map submitted, Yú does not accept the edict.
This indicates your servant is weak and unable to fulfill his duty.
How can your servant then hold office and receive emoluments for nothing?"
He immediately tied his belt and wore his shoes,
waiting in his carriage to be dismissed.
Shuǎng saw Lǐ's memorial and
was furious.
He impeached Lǐ for resentment and complaint,
sentencing him to five years of house arrest.
After a year at home,
many people spoke up for him,
and he was appointed Commander of the City Gates.
At that time, the multitude led by Hūnngnú King Liú Jìng was powerful,
and the Xiānbēi repeatedly raided the borders.
So, Sūn Lǐ was appointed Inspector of Bìngzhōu,
and given the additional title of General Who Shakes Awe,
entrusted with a staff of authority,
and made Colonel Protector of the Hūngnú.
He went to see Grand Tutor Sīmǎ Xuānwáng,
and wore an angry expression but said nothing.
Xuānwáng said:
"Have you obtained Bìngzhōu,
and it is too little?
Are you resentful that the boundaries were unfairly divided?
Now we are about to part for a long time,
why are you not joyful!"
Sūn Lǐ said:
"How could the Illustrious Lord speak such trivialities!
Though Lǐ is not virtuous,
how could I be concerned with official positions or past affairs?
I originally thought that the Illustrious Lord would emulate Yī [Yǐn] and Lǚ [Shàng],
assist the Wèi court,
above, repay the trust of the Illustrious Emperor,
and below, establish a legacy for ten thousand generations.
Now the altars of soil and grain are in peril,
the world is in turmoil;
this is why Lǐ is not pleased."
Thereupon, tears streamed down his face.
Xuānwáng said:
"Stop for now,
endure what is unbearable."
After Cáo Shuǎng was executed,
he entered the court as Colonel Director of Retainers,
and administered seven commanderies and five provinces in total,
everywhere commanding awe and trust.
He was promoted to Minister of Works,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dàlìtíng,
with a stipend of one hundred households.
Sūn Lǐ and Lú Yù were contemporaries from the same commandery,
but their relationship was not harmonious.
Though as individuals they both had strengths and weaknesses,
their fame and position were generally equal.
He died in the second year of Jiāpíng [250 CE],
and was given the posthumous title of Marquis Jǐng.
His grandson was Sūn Yuánsì.
Wáng Guān, courtesy name Wěitái,
was a native of Lǐnqīu, Dōngjùn.
Orphaned and poor in his youth, he was resolute.
Tàizǔ summoned him to be an assistant literary clerk to the Chancellor,
then he was sent out to be magistrate of Gāotáng, Yángquán, Cuó, and Rèn,
and everywhere he was praised for his governance.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne,
he entered the court as a Gentleman of the Secretariat and Supervisor of the Grand Judge,
then was sent out as Administrator of Nányáng and Zhuōjùn.
Zhuōjùn bordered the Xiānbēi to the north,
and there were frequent raids.
Wáng Guān ordered border residents, ten households or more,
to form garrisons
and build fortified watchtowers.
At times, some were unwilling,
so Wáng Guān temporarily dispatched court officials,
to return and assist their younger relatives,
without setting a deadline,
but simply ordering them to return once the task was complete.
Thereupon, officials and common people voluntarily led each other, without being supervised,
and within ten days,
all were completed at once.
Defenses were prepared,
and raiding and plundering ceased.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he issued an edict instructing commanderies and counties to categorize themselves as difficult, medium, or peaceful.
The official in charge wanted to report the commandery as medium or peaceful,
but Wáng Guān instructed him:
"This commandery is near the foreign barbarians,
and frequently suffers from raids;
how can it not be considered difficult?"
The official said:
"If the commandery is designated as difficult due to external factors,
I fear it may result in a personal imposition on Your Excellency."
Wáng Guān said:
"A lord [magistrate]
exists for the sake of the people.
Now, if the commandery is externally difficult,
then the labor service provisions should be reduced.
How can I prioritize the private interest of the administrator and betray the people of an entire commandery?"
Thus, he reported it as an externally difficult commandery,
and later sent his son to Yè to fulfill the conscription.
At that time, Wáng Guān had only one son, and he was also young and weak.
Such was his public spirit.
Wáng Guān himself lived frugally and simply,
and led his subordinates with thrift,
and his colleagues and subordinates followed his example,
all striving to better themselves.
When Míng Dì visited Xǔchāng,
he summoned Wáng Guān to be Imperial Clerk Managing Documents,
to oversee the prisons of the traveling court.
At that time, there were many sudden changes of mood,
but Wáng Guān did not flatter or comply with [the emperor's] wishes.
Grand Commandant Sīmǎ Xuānwáng invited Wáng Guān to be his Administrative Assistant,
then he was promoted to Palace Assistant,
then sent out as Prefect of Hénányǐn,
then transferred to Minister Steward.
General-in-Chief Cáo Shuǎng had his craftsmen Zhāng Dá cut timber for his personal residence,
as well as various other private uses.
Wáng Guān heard of this,
and confiscated it all for the government.
The Minister Steward oversaw the treasures of three Imperial Manufactories and the internal imperial storehouses for entertainment and play.
Cáo Shuǎng and others were extravagant and unrestrained,
and made many demands.
Fearing Wáng Guān's adherence to the law,
they transferred him to Grand Coachman.
When Sīmǎ Xuānwáng executed Cáo Shuǎng,
he sent Wáng Guān to act as Central Army Commander,
to take control of Cáo Xī's camp, Cáo Shuǎng's younger brother.
He was granted the title Marquis Within the Pass,
then made Palace Assistant again,
and given the additional title of Cavalry Commandant.
When the High Noble Duke of Xiāng ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Zhōngxiāngtíng.
Soon after,
he was given the additional title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
and then transferred to Right Director of the Palace.
When the Duke of Chángdàoxiāng ascended the throne,
he was advanced to Marquis of Yángxiāng,
with an increase of one thousand households,
making a total of two thousand five hundred households.
He was promoted to Minister of Works,
but firmly declined,
which was not permitted.
An envoy was dispatched to his residence to formally confer the appointment.
After holding the office for several days,
he submitted his seals and ribbons,
and simply drove his carriage back to his village home.
He died at home,
leaving instructions for his grave to be just large enough to fit his coffin,
with no burial treasures,
no mound, and no tree.
He was given the posthumous title of Marquis Sù.
His son Wáng Kuī succeeded him.
During the Xiánxī era,
when the five orders of nobility were established,
because Wáng Guān had rendered distinguished service to the previous dynasty,
Wáng Kuī was re-enfeoffed as Viscount of Jiāodōng.
Critique says: Hán Jì lived in quiet retirement to transform [people],
and went out to assume office and earn renown;
Cuī Lín was simple, plain, and discerning;
Gāo Ròu was clear in law and principle;
Sūn Lǐ was resolute, decisive, firm, and vigorous;
Wáng Guān was upright, strong, faithful, and pure: all were able to achieve the rank of public minister.
However, Hán Jì was over eighty when he began his career;
he started from humble origins and joined the ranks;
Gāo Ròu held office for twenty years, and as an elder statesman, finished his tenure. Compared to Xú Mò and Cháng Lín,
these were indeed shortcomings.
Biography of Xīn Pí, Yáng Fù, Gāotáng Lóng, Chapter 25
Xīn Pí
had the courtesy name Zuǒzhì and was a native of Yángzhái in Yǐngchuān.
His ancestors, in the Jiànwǔ era,
migrated east from Lǒngxī.
Pí followed his elder brother Píng and joined Yuán Shào.
When Tàizǔ was Sīkōng,
he invited Pí,
but Pí was unable to accept the summons.
Later, when Yuán Shàng attacked his elder brother Tán at Píngyuán,
Tán sent Pí to Tàizǔ to seek peace.
Tàizǔ was about to campaign in Jīngzhōu
and stopped at Xīpíng.
Pí met Tàizǔ and conveyed Tán’s intentions,
and Tàizǔ was greatly pleased.
A few days later,
he wanted to first pacify Jīngzhōu,
allowing Tán and Shàng to wear each other out.
Another day, during a banquet,
Pí observed Tàizǔ’s expression
and knew there was a change.
He told Guō Jiā.
Jiā informed Tàizǔ,
and Tàizǔ said to Pí:
“Can Tán be trusted?
Can Shàng certainly be defeated?”
Pí replied:
“Your Excellency, you need not ask whether they are trustworthy or deceitful;
you should simply consider their circumstances.
The Yuán clan originally fought among themselves,
not because others could sow discord,
but because they believed the world could be settled by themselves.
Now, all of a sudden, they seek rescue from Your Excellency;
this is understandable.
That Xiǎnfǔ (Yuán Shàng) saw Xiǎnsī (Yuán Tán) in distress but could not seize him
shows his strength is exhausted.
With military forces defeated externally
and strategists executed internally,
brothers backbiting and quarreling,
the state divided into two;
with years of continuous warfare,
and soldiers in armor infested with lice,
plus drought and locusts,
and famine arriving simultaneously,
the state has no granaries,
and travelers have no provisions;
heavenly disasters respond from above,
and human affairs are in distress below.
Regardless of whether people are foolish or wise,
they all know that the situation is collapsing like earth and tiles.
This is the time when Heaven is destroying Shàng.
Military strategy states that one who has stone cities and boiling moats and a million armored soldiers but no grain
cannot defend them.
If you now attack Yè,
and Shàng does not return to rescue,
then he cannot defend himself.
If he returns to rescue,
then Tán will follow closely behind him.
With Your Excellency’s might,
to face a desperate enemy
and strike a weary and exhausted foe
is no different from a swift wind shaking autumn leaves.
Heaven gives Yuán Shàng to Your Excellency,
but Your Excellency does not take him and instead attacks Jīngzhōu.
Jīngzhōu is prosperous and happy,
and the state has no weakness.
Zhòng Huǐ (Yi Yin) said: ‘Seize the chaotic, insult the fallen.’
Currently, the two Yuán brothers do not pursue distant strategies but plot against each other internally;
this can be called chaotic.
Those at home have no food,
and those traveling have no provisions;
this can be called fallen.
They do not plan for the morning,
and the people’s lives cannot continue.
If you do not pacify them now
and wish to wait for another year;
if another year brings a good harvest,
and they, knowing their demise, amend their virtues,
then you will lose the essence of employing military strategy.
Now, taking advantage of their request for rescue and pacifying them,
there is no greater benefit.
Moreover, among the bandits in the four directions,
none are greater than those in Héběi.
If Héběi is pacified,
then the Six Armies will flourish and the world will tremble.”
Tàizǔ said:
“Good.”
He then agreed to peace with Tán and
stationed his army at Líyáng.
The next year, he attacked Yè
and conquered it.
He then presented Pí as Yìláng.
After a long time,
Tàizǔ sent Dūhù Cáo Hóng to pacify Xiàbiàn,
and made Pí and Cáo Xiū participate in the plan,
giving the order:
“In the past, Gāozǔ was greedy for wealth and fond of women,
but Liáng and Píng rectified his faults.
Now, the worries of Zuǒzhì (Xīn Pí) and Wénliè (Cáo Xiū) are not light.”
When the army returned,
Pí became Chéngxiàng Zhǎngshǐ.
When Wéndì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng
and granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
At that time, there was discussion about reforming the calendar.
Pí believed that the Wèi clan followed the traditions of Shùn and Yǔ,
responding to Heaven and conforming to the people;
it was only with Tāng and Wǔ,
who settled the world through warfare,
that the calendar was reformed.
Confucius said,
“follow the times of Xià,”
and Zuǒshì Zhuàn said,
“the Xià number was considered to have obtained the true celestial alignment.”
Why must one necessarily aim for the opposite?
The Emperor approved and followed his advice.
The Emperor wished to move one hundred thousand households of scholar-families from Jìzhōu to settle in Hénán.
At that time, there were continuous locusts and famine among the people,
and all officials deemed it impermissible,
but the Emperor’s intention was very strong.
Pí and other court officials
all sought an audience.
The Emperor knew they wanted to remonstrate,
and showed his displeasure when he met them,
so no one dared to speak.
Pí said: “Your Majesty wishes to move the scholar-families;
what is the plan?”
The Emperor said:
“Do you think my moving them is wrong?”
Pí said:
“Indeed, I believe it is wrong.”
The Emperor said:
“I will not discuss this with you.”
Pí said:
“Your Majesty, though you do not consider me worthy,
you have placed me by your side,
and given me the position of an advisory official.
How can you not discuss it with me?
What I say is not for private gain,
but a concern for the state;
how can you be angry with me?”
The Emperor did not reply,
and rose to enter his chambers;
Pí followed and pulled his robe.
The Emperor then flung his garment and did not return.
After a long time, he came out
and said:
“Zuǒzhì,
why are you so insistent with me?”
Pí said:
“If you move them now,
you will both lose the people’s hearts
and have nothing to feed them with.”
The Emperor then moved half of them.
Once, he accompanied the Emperor to shoot pheasants.
The Emperor said:
“Shooting pheasants is delightful!”
Pí said:
“It is very delightful for Your Majesty,
but very difficult for your subordinates.”
The Emperor remained silent,
and thereafter rarely went out for such activities.
The Commander-in-chief, Dà Jiāngjūn Cáo Zhēn 征 Zhū Rán at Jiānglíng.
Pí served as military advisor.
Upon his return,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guǎngpíngtíng.
The Emperor wished to raise a large army to conquer Wú.
Pí remonstrated, saying:
"The people of Wú and Chǔ
are formidable and difficult to control.
Those on the superior path follow later,
while those on the inferior path rebel first.
This has been a problem since ancient times,
not merely now.
Now, Your Majesty's reign encompasses all within the seas.
How can those who refuse to submit
last long?
In the past, Wèi Tuó declared himself emperor,
and Zǐyáng usurped the title.
After only a few years,
some became subjects, others were executed.
Why?
Because the way of defiance cannot long endure complete,
and great virtue leaves none unsubdued.
At present, the world has just been pacified,
the land is vast, and the population sparse.
Even when military calculations are complete before an army is dispatched,
one still fears the actual event.
How much more so now, when military calculations are deficient, and you wish to employ them?
Your servant truly sees no benefit in it.
The Late Emperor repeatedly raised elite forces,
but turned back upon reaching the Jiāng.
Now the six armies are no stronger than before,
and yet you wish to follow that course again.
This is not easy.
The best plan for today
is to imitate Fàn Lǐ in nurturing the people,
to emulate Guǎn Zhòng in delegating governance,
to follow Chōngguó in establishing military agricultural colonies,
and to clarify Zhòngní's principle of winning over distant peoples.
Within ten years,
the strong will not yet be old,
the young will be capable of battle,
the myriad commoners will understand righteousness,
and the generals and soldiers will be eager to exert themselves.
Only then should you employ them;
thus, the campaign will not need to be raised again."
The Emperor said:
"According to your intention,
should I then bequeath these barbarians to my descendants?"
Pí replied:
"In the past, King Wén of Zhōu bequeathed Zhòu to King Wǔ,
simply because he knew the opportune time.
If the time is not yet right,
how can one possibly avoid it!"
The Emperor ultimately marched against Wú,
but returned upon reaching the Jiāng.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he was promoted and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǐngxīang,
with an estate of three hundred households.
At that time, the Central Secretariat Supervisors Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī were trusted by the ruler,
controlling and deciding the affairs of the time.
No great minister failed to curry favor with them,
but Pí did not associate with them.
Pí's son, Chǎng, remonstrated, saying:
"Now Liú and Sūn are in power,
and everyone else clings to them like shadows.
Father, you should show a little deference,
and 'harmonize your light, and become one with the dust.'
Otherwise, there will surely be slanderous remarks."
Pí sternly replied:
"Although the ruler above has not yet proven himself brilliant,
he is not utterly foolish.
My conduct
has its own principles.
Even if I am not on good terms with Liú and Sūn,
at most, it will only prevent me from becoming one of the Three Ducal Ministers.
What harm is there in that?
How can a true man, aspiring to become a Duke, destroy his noble integrity?"
The Palace Assistant and Cavalier Attendant Bì Guǐ submitted a memorial, stating:
"The Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Wáng Sī, is diligent and an old official,
but in loyalty, honesty, and strategic planning, he is inferior to Xīn Pí.
Pí should replace Sī."
The Emperor consulted Fàng and Zī about this.
Fàng and Zī replied:
"Your Majesty employs Sī
precisely because you desire his practical effectiveness,
not a hollow reputation.
Pí is indeed upright and suitable,
but his nature is unyielding and opinionated,
a point which Your Sacred Wisdom should deeply consider."
Consequently, he was not employed.
He was appointed as Wèi Wèi.
The Emperor was then constructing palaces and residences,
and the common people were burdened by labor.
Pí submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have secretly heard that Zhūgě Liàng is training troops and managing military affairs,
and Sūn Quán is buying horses in Liáodōng.
Estimating their intentions,
it seems they wish to support each other.
Preparing for the unexpected
is a good policy of the ancients.
Yet now, grand palace construction is underway,
in addition to consecutive years of poor grain and wheat harvests.
The Shī Jīng says: 'The people are also toiling.
May they at least have a little peace.
Grant favor to this central kingdom,
to pacify the four quarters.'
I only ask that Your Majesty consider the welfare of the state."
The Emperor replied:
"While the two barbarian enemies are not yet eliminated, I am building palaces and residences.
This is a time for honest remonstrators to make a name for themselves.
A king's capital
should be completed while the people are engaged in labor,
so that future generations have nothing more to add.
This was Xiāo Hé's strategic blueprint for the Hàn dynasty.
Now, as a senior minister of Wèi,
you too should understand this greater principle."
The Emperor also wanted to level Běimáng mountain,
and ordered the construction of a platform and observation tower on its summit,
from which Méngjīn could be seen.
Pí remonstrated, saying:
"It is the nature of heaven and earth
for the high to be high and the low to be low.
To act contrary to this now
is not only irrational;
moreover, it wastes human labor and resources,
and the people cannot endure the toil.
Furthermore, if the Jiǔhé rivers overflow
and floods cause disaster,
and the hills are all leveled,
how will we defend against them?"
The Emperor then stopped.
In the second year of Qīnglóng [234 CE],
Zhūgě Liàng led his forces out to Wèinán.
Previously,
the Grand Marshal, Sīmǎ Xuānwáng, repeatedly requested to engage Liàng in battle,
but Emperor Míng consistently refused.
In this year, fearing he could not restrain him,
he appointed Pí as Grand Marshal's Military Advisor,
granting him a credential.
All six armies were solemn,
following Pí's instructions and commands,
daring not to violate them.
After Liàng's death,
he returned to being Wèi Wèi.
He passed away
and was posthumously granted the title Sù Hóu.
His son Chǎng succeeded him,
and during the Xiánxī era, he served as Governor of Hénèi.
Yáng Fù, courtesy name Yìshān,
was a native of Jì county, Tiānshuǐ commandery.
As a provincial aide, he was sent by Governor Wéi Duān to Xǔ,
and was appointed as Administrator of Āndìng.
When Fù returned,
the various generals in Guānyòu asked who would prevail between Yuán and Cáo.
Fù said:
"Duke Yuán is lenient but indecisive,
fond of strategizing but lacking in resolution.
Indecision leads to no authority,
and lack of resolution causes one to miss opportunities.
Although he is strong now,
he will ultimately not accomplish great deeds.
Duke Cáo possesses heroic talent and far-reaching strategies,
decisive in making choices without hesitation.
His laws are unified and his troops elite.
He is able to employ extraordinary individuals,
and those he appoints all exert their full strength.
He is certain to accomplish great deeds."
As Administrator was not to his liking,
he resigned the office.
Wéi Duān was then summoned to serve as Grand Coachman (Tàipú),
and his son Kāng succeeded him as Inspector.
He invited Fù to be his Aide-de-camp (Biéjià).
He was then nominated as Xiaolian,
and invited to the Prime Minister's residence,
but the province memorialized to retain him as a Staff Officer (Cānjūnshì).
When Mǎ Chāo was defeated at Wèinán,
he fled to seek refuge with various Róng tribes.
Tàizǔ pursued him to Āndìng,
but Sū Bó rebelled in Héjiān,
so Tàizǔ planned to lead his army back east.
At that time, Jiāng Fù was on an imperial mission.
He spoke to Tàizǔ, saying:
"Mǎ Chāo has the courage of Xìn and Bù,
and has won the hearts of the Qiāng and Hú tribes,
so the western regions fear him.
If the grand army returns
without strict preparations,
the various commanderies of Lǒngshàng will no longer belong to the state."
Tàizǔ thought highly of this,
but the army returned hastily,
and preparations were inadequate.
Mǎ Chāo led the various Róng chieftains to attack the Lǒngshàng commanderies and counties.
All the Lǒngshàng commanderies and counties responded to him,
except Jìchéng, which upheld the loyalty of the province and commandery by holding firm.
Mǎ Chāo gathered all the forces east of Lǒng.
Moreover, Zhāng Lǔ dispatched his great general Yáng Áng to assist him,
with a total of over ten thousand men,
to attack the city.
Jiāng Fù led over a thousand capable soldiers from among the gentry and his clansmen and their sons,
and ordered his cousin Yuè to construct a crescent-moon camp on the city wall.
They engaged Mǎ Chāo in battle.
