From the first month to the eighth month, they held out, but no relief troops arrived.
The province sent the Biejia, Yán Wēn, to secretly go out by water to seek help,
but he was killed by Mǎ Chāo.
Thereupon, the Cishi and Tàishǒu lost color,
and for the first time considered surrendering to Mǎ Chāo.
Jiāng Fù wept and remonstrated, saying:
"We, your humble servants, leading our fathers, elder brothers, and sons, have encouraged each other with righteousness,
resolved to die rather than waver;
Tián Dān's defense was no firmer than this.
Tián Dān's defense
Do not abandon a nearly accomplished effort,
and fall into the infamy of unrighteousness.
I, your humble servant, will hold it to the death."
Then he wailed loudly.
The Cishi and Tàishǒu eventually sent men to request peace,
and opened the city gates to welcome Mǎ Chāo.
Mǎ Chāo entered,
detained Yuè in Jì,
and ordered Yáng Áng to kill the Cishi and Tàishǒu.
Jiāng Fù harbored a desire to avenge himself on Mǎ Chāo,
but had not found an opportunity.
After a while,
Jiāng Fù requested leave for his wife's funeral.
Jiāng Fù's maternal cousin, Jiāng Tún, was garrisoned in Lìchéng.
Jiāng Fù grew up in the family.
When he saw his mother,
he recounted the events in Jì,
and wept bitterly.
His mother said:
"Why has it come to this?"
Jiāng Fù replied:
"I could not complete the defense of the city,
and when my lord perished, I could not die for him.
What face do I have to live on in the world?
Mǎ Chāo betrayed his father and rebelled against his lord,
cruelly killing the provincial generals.
This is not only my concern and responsibility,
but the gentry of the entire province share in this shame.
You hold military power and absolute control, yet have no heart to punish the rebel.
This is why Zhào Dùn was recorded for regicide.
Mǎ Chāo is strong but unrighteous, full of flaws, and easy to plot against."
Mǎ Chāo is strong but unrighteous,
His mother assented with a sigh,
and ordered to follow Jiāng Fù's plan.
Once the plan was settled,
he conspired with local people Jiāng Yǐn, Zhào Áng, Yǐn Fèng, Yáo Qióng, Kǒng Xìn, and Lǐ Jùn and Wáng Líng from Wǔdū.
They set a date to attack Mǎ Chāo.
He sent his cousin Mó to Jì to inform Yuè,
and also to ally with Liáng Kuān from Āndìng, and Zhào Qú and Páng Gōng from Nán'ān, among others.
Once the oaths and alliances were clear,
in the ninth month of the seventeenth year,
they raised an army in Lǔchéng.
Mǎ Chāo heard that Jiāng Fù and others had raised troops,
and personally led his forces out.
Meanwhile, Qú and Kuān freed Yuè,
closed the gates of Jìchéng,
and attacked Mǎ Chāo's wife and children.
Mǎ Chāo attacked Lìchéng
and captured Jiāng Fù's mother.
His mother cursed him, saying:
"You are an unfilial son who betrayed his father,
a tyrannical bandit who killed his lord!
How can Heaven tolerate you for long?
Why do you not die sooner?
How dare you show your face to people!"
Mǎ Chāo was enraged
and killed her.
Jiāng Fù fought Mǎ Chāo,
sustaining five wounds himself.
Seven of his kinsmen and younger brothers died.
Mǎ Chāo then fled south to Zhāng Lǔ.
After Lǒngyòu was pacified,
Tàizǔ rewarded those who had contributed to the defeat of Mǎ Chāo.
Eleven people were enfeoffed as marquises,
and Jiāng Fù was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
Jiāng Fù declined, saying:
"When my lord was alive, I had no achievement in defending against difficulty.
When my lord perished, I showed no dedication to dying for principle.
According to righteousness, I should be demoted;
according to law, I should be executed.
Moreover, Mǎ Chāo is not dead.
It is inappropriate for me to presumptuously accept such a noble title and emolument."
Tàizǔ replied:
"You, along with the other virtuous men, have jointly established a great achievement,
which the people of the western lands praise as a fine story.
Zǐgòng declined a reward,
and Zhòngní called it 'stopping at goodness'.
You should open your heart and obey the national decree.
Jiāng Fù's mother
urged early action, her wisdom was truly great.
Her wisdom was truly great;
even Yáng Chǎng's wife could not surpass this.
How virtuous!
How virtuous!
Good historians will record this,
it will surely not be lost to the ground."
When Tàizǔ campaigned in Hànzhōng,
he appointed Jiāng Fù as Yìzhōu Cishi.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Jīnchéng Tàishǒu.
Before he could depart,
he was transferred to Wǔdū Tàishǒu.
The commandery bordered Shǔ Hàn.
Jiāng Fù requested to follow the precedent of Gōng Suì,
and simply pacify the region.
At that time, Liú Bèi sent Zhāng Fēi and Mǎ Chāo, among others, from Jǔdào to attack Xiàbiàn.
And the Dī tribes of Léi Dìng and others, numbering over ten thousand households from seven tribes, responded to them.
Tàizǔ sent Dūhù Cáo Hóng to resist Mǎ Chāo and the others.
Mǎ Chāo and the others retreated.
Cáo Hóng held a grand banquet,
ordering female entertainers to wear sheer gauze clothing,
and beat drums.
Everyone present laughed.
Jiāng Fù sternly rebuked Cáo Hóng, saying:
"The distinction between men and women
is a great principle of the state.
How can you expose the naked bodies of women in a large gathering?
Even during the chaos of Jié and Zhòu,
it was not worse than this."
Then he angrily shook out his clothes and left.
Cáo Hóng immediately dismissed the female musicians,
and invited Jiāng Fù to return to his seat,
respecting him with awe.
When Liú Bèi captured Hànzhōng and pressed towards Xiàbiàn,
Tàizǔ considered Wǔdū isolated and distant,
and wished to relocate its population,
fearing that the officials and common people would be reluctant to leave their homes.
Jiāng Fù's authority and trustworthiness were consistently prominent.
He subsequently relocated over ten thousand households of common people and Dī tribesmen,
settling them in the borders of Jīngzhào, Fúfēng, and Tiānshuǐ.
The commandery was moved to Xiǎohuáilǐ.
The common people carried their infants on their backs and followed him.
In governing, he merely grasped the main principles,
and those below him dared not deceive him.
Wén Dì asked the Shìzhōng, Liú Yè, and others:
"What kind of person is the Tàishǒu of Wǔdū?"
All praised Jiāng Fù as having the qualities of a ducal minister.
Before he could be employed,
the emperor passed away.
After serving in the commandery for over ten years,
he was summoned and appointed Chéngmén Xiàowèi.
Jiāng Fù once saw Míng Dì wearing an embroidered *xiù*
and a half-sleeved coat of green silk.
Jiāng Fù asked the emperor:
"According to ritual, what kind of ceremonial attire is this?"
The emperor remained silent and did not answer.
From then on, he did not wear non-ceremonial attire when seeing Jiāng Fù.
[Dùn] Fù was transferred to Grand Architect.
At that time, construction of palaces was just beginning,
and beautiful women were conscripted to fill the imperial harem.
The emperor frequently went out hunting.
In autumn,
there was heavy rain with thunder and lightning,
killing many birds and sparrows.
[Dùn] Fù submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your minister has heard that when an enlightened ruler is on the throne,
all subordinates fully express their views.
Yáo and Shùn, with their sagely virtue,
sought out criticism;
Great Yǔ, diligent in his accomplishments,
made his palaces humble;
Chéng Tāng, when he faced drought,
attributed the fault to himself;
King Wén of Zhōu set an example for his wife,
thereby governing his family and state;
Emperor Wén of Hàn personally practiced frugality,
even wearing coarse silk clothes himself. These are all examples of those who could illuminate a good reputation
and bequeath plans for their descendants.
I humbly consider that Your Majesty inherited the great enterprise of opening up territory from Emperor Wǔ,
and guards the grand legacy of Emperor Wén, who brought it to completion.
It is truly fitting to contemplate the good governance of ancient sages and worthies,
and to generally observe the depraved policies of later generations.
What is called good governance
is to prioritize frugality and value the people's strength;
what is called depraved policy
is to indulge one's desires
and act on every impulse.
I implore Your Majesty to examine why the early generations were so illustrious,
and why later generations declined to the point of extinction.
A recent look at the changes in the late Hàn dynasty
is enough to stir the heart and inspire fear.
Had Huán and Líng not abandoned the laws of Gāozǔ
and the reverence and frugality of Wén and Jǐng,
even if Grand Ancestor [Cáo Cāo] possessed divine martial prowess,
where could he have applied his abilities?
And how could Your Majesty then occupy this esteemed position?
Now, as Wú and Shǔ are not yet pacified,
and the army is abroad,
I wish Your Majesty would think thrice before acting,
deliberate before proceeding,
and exercise great caution in your outings,
using the past to learn about the future.
What I say may seem light,
but success or failure is of utmost importance.
Recently, there has been rain,
and also many sudden violent thunderstorms, which are unusual,
even killing birds and sparrows.
Heaven, Earth, and the divine spirits
regard the king as their son.
If governance is inappropriate,
then omens of disaster and condemnation appear.
Self-criticism is what the sages recorded.
I implore Your Majesty to consider dangers before they take shape,
and to be cautious at the very beginning of a slight manifestation.
Emulate Emperor Xiàowén of Hàn who sent away the beautiful women of Emperor Huì,
allowing them to marry themselves off.
The recently conscripted young women,
I hear from afar, are not compliant.
It would be appropriate to plan for their future.
All ongoing construction
should adhere to economy and moderation.
The Shū Jīng says:
'When the nine clans are harmonious,
the myriad states will be in accord.'
Consider what is appropriate in all matters,
follow the middle path,
plan with a focused mind,
and reduce expenses.
When Wú and Shǔ are pacified,
then the upper levels will be at ease, the lower levels joyful,
and the nine relatives will be harmonious.
If this continues,
your ancestors will be pleased,
and even Yáo and Shùn might find it difficult to surpass.
Now, it is fitting to open up great trust to all under Heaven,
to bring peace to the common people,
and to display this to distant peoples."
At that time, King Zhí of Yōngqiū resented not being treated as an equal,
and though he was a close relative in a vassal state,
the laws and prohibitions were very strict.
Therefore, [Dùn] Fù again presented the principle of the nine clans.
The imperial edict replied:
"Recently I received a secret memorial,
first presenting the enlightened kings and sagely rulers of antiquity,
thereby satirizing dark policies.
The words are earnest and direct,
sincerely and truthfully presented.
To reflect and rectify errors,
to comply and correct,
everything is thoroughly considered.
Upon reading these bitter words,
I greatly commend them."
Later, [Dùn] Fù was transferred to Minor Controller.
At this time, Grand Marshal Cáo Zhēn was campaigning against Shǔ,
but encountered rain and could not advance.
[Dùn] Fù submitted a memorial, saying:
"In ancient times, King Wén had the omen of a red crow,
yet he still did not have time to eat until sunset;
when King Wǔ saw a white fish enter his boat,
the monarch and his ministers changed color.
Even when obtaining auspicious omens,
they still worried and feared.
How much more so should one not tremble when there are unusual disasters?
Now, Wú and Shǔ are not yet pacified,
and Heaven has repeatedly sent down anomalies.
Your Majesty should deeply concentrate on responding
by sitting on the edge of your mat,
thinking of demonstrating virtue to distant peoples,
and pacifying nearby peoples with frugality.
Recently, the various armies began their advance,
but then encountered the trouble of heavenly rain,
causing delays and obstructions in the mountainous terrain,
for many days now.
The hardship of transport,
and the suffering of bearing burdens,
have already cost much.
If supplies cannot be maintained,
it will certainly deviate from the original plan.
The Zuo Zhuàn says:
'Advance when it is advantageous,
retreat when it is difficult: this is good military policy.'
Merely letting the six armies be trapped in the valleys,
unable to advance or achieve anything,
and unable to retreat,
is not the way of commanding troops.
King Wǔ withdrew his army,
and the Yīn dynasty consequently perished,
knowing the heavenly timing.
This year is calamitous, and the people are suffering from famine.
It is fitting to issue a clear edict to reduce meals and simplify clothing.
All objects of intricate craftsmanship and rare treasures
should be abolished.
In ancient times, Shào Xìnchén, as Minor Controller during a peaceful era,
proposed to abolish superfluous spending.
Now, military expenses are insufficient,
making it even more necessary to control spending."
The Emperor immediately ordered the various armies to return.
Later, an imperial edict called for a great discussion on political inconveniences for the people.
[Dùn] Fù argued, saying:
"Achieving good governance lies in employing the virtuous,
and building a strong nation lies in promoting agriculture.
If the virtuous are neglected and personal favorites are employed,
this is a great forgetting of governance.
Extensively opening palaces and halls,
building high towers and pavilions,
to interfere with the people's work,
this is a great harm to agriculture.
Craftsmen do not focus on their tools,
but compete to create exotic and clever items
to satisfy the emperor's desires,
this is a great injury to the fundamentals.
Confucius said: 'Harsh government is worse than a fierce tiger.'
Now, officials who cling to established customs and paperwork,
whose governance does not understand the principles of order,
and who merely enjoy being vexatious and harsh,
this is a great disturbance to the people.
The current urgency
is to eliminate these four great harms,
and concurrently issue an edict to the Dukes, Ministers, Commanderies, and States
to recommend virtuous, upright, honest, and simple scholars and select them for employment.
This is also a way to seek out the virtuous."
[Dùn] Fù also submitted a memorial desiring to reduce the number of palace women who were not favored.
He then summoned the Imperial Treasury official and asked about the number of women in the harem.
The official, adhering to old regulations,
replied:
"It is a secret,
and must not be divulged."
[Dùn] Fù was angered,
struck the official one hundred times with a staff,
and reprimanded him, saying:
"Does the state not keep secrets with the Nine Ministers,
but instead keeps secrets with a petty official?"
The Emperor heard of this and respected and feared [Dùn] Fù even more.
The Emperor loved his daughter, Shú,
who died before reaching her first year.
The Emperor grieved deeply,
posthumously enfeoffed her as Princess Píngyuán,
erected a temple for her in Luòyáng,
and buried her at Nánlíng.
The Emperor intended to personally attend the funeral.
[Dùn] Fù submitted a memorial, saying:
"When Emperor Wén and Empress Wǔxuān died,
Your Majesty did not attend their funerals,
out of concern for the altars of soil and grain and to guard against unforeseen circumstances.
How can one attend the funeral of a mere infant?"
The Emperor did not comply.
The Emperor had just built a new palace in Xǔgōng,
and was also constructing palaces, halls, pavilions, and towers in Luòyáng.
Fù shàng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Yáo still lived in a thatched hut, yet the myriad states were secure in their dwellings.
Yǔ had humble palaces, yet the empire rejoiced in its work.
By the time of Yīn and Zhōu,
some halls were but three *chǐ* high,
with a capacity for only nine banquets.
Among the sagely emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity,
none ever indulged in the extreme loftiness and splendor of palaces to exhaust the wealth and labor of the populace.
Jié built the Xuánshì and Xiàngláng,
Zhòu constructed the Qīnggōng and Lùtái,
thereby losing their altars of soil and grain.
Chǔlíng built Zhānghuá, and suffered misfortune because of it.
Qín Shǐhuáng built the Èfáng Palace, and disaster befell his son.
The empire rebelled against him,
and his dynasty perished in the second generation.
Indeed, those who fail to consider the strength of the myriad people,
in order to satisfy the desires of their eyes and ears,
have never failed to perish.
Your Majesty should take Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ as your models,
and Xià Jié, Yīn Zhòu, Chǔlíng, and Qín Huáng as grave warnings.
The August Heaven, high above,
truly observes the virtues of the sovereign.
Carefully guarding the heavenly mandate,
to uphold the legacy of your ancestors,
your grand and magnificent enterprise,
you should still fear losing it.
If you do not diligently respect and attend to affairs from dawn to dusk,
and sincerely compassionately care for the people,
but instead indulge in ease and idleness,
only focusing on the extravagance and adornment of palaces and towers,
there will surely be the calamity of overthrow, danger, and ruin.
The *Yì* says: 'If one enriches their house,
covers their family,
and spies on their door,
there will be no one left.'
Kings take the empire as their family,
meaning that the calamity of an enriched house
leads to the family being deserted.
Currently, the two barbarian groups have formed an alliance,
plotting to endanger the imperial ancestral temple.
One hundred thousand troops
are rushing to and fro, east and west.
The borders have not a single day of peace.
Farmers abandon their work,
and the people have hungry looks.
Your Majesty is not troubled by this,
but instead constructs palaces,
without cessation.
If the state were to perish and I, your minister, could alone survive,
then I would not speak.
But the sovereign is the head,
and ministers are the limbs.
Survival and destruction are one body,
gain and loss are shared.
The *Xiàojīng* says: 'If the Son of Heaven has seven remonstrating ministers,
even if he lacks the Way, he will not lose his empire.'
Though I am dull and timid,
how can I forget the duty of a remonstrating minister?
If my words are not sharp and direct,
they will be insufficient to move and awaken Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty does not heed my words,
I fear the legacy of your August Ancestors and Illustrious Forefathers
will fall to the ground.
If my death could remedy even one ten-thousandth of the situation,
then the day of my death
would be like the years of my life.
I respectfully knock on my coffin, bathe,
and await heavy punishment."
The memorial was presented to the Emperor.
The Son of Heaven was moved by his loyal words,
and personally penned an imperial rescript in reply.
Whenever there was a court conference,
Fù shàng always spoke with firm conviction, taking the affairs of the empire as his personal responsibility.
He frequently offered remonstrances and arguments,
but they were not always heeded.
He then repeatedly requested to relinquish his position,
but this was not granted.
He died shortly after,
with no surplus wealth in his home.
His grandson, Bào, inherited his position.
Gāotáng Lóng, courtesy name Shēngpíng,
was a native of Píngyáng, Tàishān,
and a descendant of the elder Gāotáng of Lǔ.
In his youth, he was a scholar.
Xuē Tì, the Administrator of Tàishān, appointed him as Supervising Clerk.
The Commander of the army in the commandery argued with Tì,
calling Tì by name and reprimanding him.
Lóng grasped his sword and rebuked the Commander, saying:
"In the past, when Lǔ Dìng Gōng was insulted,
Zhòngní ascended the steps. When
Zhào played the Qín zither,
Xiāngrú advanced with a *fǒu*.
To call a ruler by name in front of his minister
is an act that should be punished by righteousness."
The Commander's face turned pale.
Tì was startled and rose to stop him.
Later, Lóng left his post
and moved to Jǐnán to escape the turmoil.
In the eighteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
Tàizǔ summoned him to be an Advisor to the Chancellor's Army.
Later, he served as the literary tutor to Huī, the Marquis of Lìchéng,
and was then transferred to be his chancellor.
When Huī suffered the loss of Tàizǔ,
he did not show grief,
but instead indulged in hunting and racing.
Lóng righteously remonstrated with him,
and effectively guided him.
During the Huángchū era,
he became the Chief of Tángyáng,
and was then selected to be the Grand Tutor to the King of Píngyuán.
This King later ascended to the throne,
becoming Emperor Míng.
He appointed Lóng as Attendant Official, Erudite, and Equerry Commandant.
When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
some ministers suggested that a celebratory assembly should be held.
Lóng said:
"Táng and Yú observed mourning in seclusion,
Gāozōng contemplated in silence.
Thus, their supreme virtue was harmonious and flourishing,
radiating across the Four Seas."
He believed that a celebratory assembly was inappropriate,
and the Emperor respectfully accepted his counsel.
He was promoted to Administrator of Chénliú.
Dúmín Yǒumù,
over seventy years old,
possessed utmost integrity,
and was recommended for appointment as Controller of Accounts.
The Emperor commended him
and specifically appointed him as a Court Gentleman to honor him.
Lóng was summoned to be a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary
and was granted the noble rank of Marquis Within the Pass.
During the Qīnglóng era,
grand construction of palaces and dwellings was undertaken,
and a large bell was brought from Cháng'ān in the west.
Lóng submitted a memorial, saying:
"In the past, King Jǐng of Zhōu did not emulate the enlightened virtues of Wén and Wǔ,
and neglected the sagely institutions of Gōng Dàn.
He not only minted large coins
but also cast a large bell.
Dān Mùgōng remonstrated but was not heeded;
Líng Zhōujīu responded but was not followed.
Consequently, he became lost and did not return,
and the virtue of Zhōu declined.
Good historians recorded this
as an eternal warning.
Yet now, petty men
are fond of speaking of the extravagance and indulgence of Qín and Hàn to sway Your Sacred Heart,
seeking to acquire unmeasured artifacts of perished states,
causing toil and expenditure,
thereby harming virtuous governance.
This is not the way to foster the harmony of rites and music,
nor to preserve the auspiciousness of divine enlightenment."
On that day,
the Emperor visited the upper palace.
Lóng and Biàn Lán accompanied him.
The Emperor handed Lóng's memorial to Lán
and bade him challenge Lóng, saying:
"Rise and fall depend on governance;
what has music to do with it?
If transformation is not enlightened,
how can it be the fault of the bell?"
Lóng replied:
"Indeed, rites and music
are the great foundations of governance.
Therefore, when the *Xiāosháo* was played nine times,
the phoenixes came to display their forms.
When the thunder drums changed six times,
heavenly spirits descended.
Governance was thereby peaceful,
and punishments were thereby abolished;
this was the zenith of harmony.
When new sounds were emitted,
Shāng Xīn fell.
When the great bell was cast,
King Jǐng of Zhōu was brought to ruin.
The crucial moments of survival and destruction
consistently arise from such acts.
How can it be said that rise and fall are not caused by these steps?
Whatever the ruler undertakes must be recorded;
this is the ancient Way.
If actions are taken without following the law,
how can they be shown to later generations?
Sagely kings are pleased to hear of their shortcomings,
hence there is the Way of admonition and correction.
Loyal ministers wish to exhaust their integrity,
hence there is the principle of selfless devotion."
The Emperor praised him, saying it was good.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
still retaining the post of Tàishǐ Lìng.
When Chónghuá Diàn caught fire,
an imperial edict questioned Lóng:
"What calamity is this?
According to ritual,
is there any meaning in offering prayers and expiations for it?"
Lóng replied:
"The manifestations of calamities and strange events
are all for the purpose of clarifying instruction and warning.
Only by adhering to ritual and cultivating virtue
can one overcome them.
The Yìzhuàn says: 'If superiors are not frugal,
and inferiors are not restrained,
then destructive fire will burn their dwellings.'
It also says: 'If the ruler elevates his pavilions,
heavenly fire will be the calamity.'
This means that if a ruler thoughtlessly adorns his palaces
without considering the impoverishment of the common people,
Heaven therefore responds with drought,
and fire starts from the high pavilions.
The August Heaven looks down,
and therefore sends a warning to Your Majesty;
Your Majesty should greatly promote human morality
to respond to the will of Heaven.
In the past, when Tàiwù had mulberry and grain growing in his court,
and Wǔdìng had a crowing pheasant ascending to his tripod,
they all, upon hearing of the calamities, feared,
humbled themselves, and cultivated virtue.
Three years later,
distant barbarians came to pay tribute,
hence they were called Zhōngzōng and Gāozōng.
These are clear precedents from previous generations.
Now, according to ancient prognostication,
the outbreak of calamitous fires
all serve as warnings regarding pavilions, terraces, and palaces.
However, the reason why the current palaces are so excessively expanded
is truly due to the multitude of palace women.
It would be appropriate to select and keep only the virtuous and refined,
as in the system of Zhōu,
and dismiss the rest.
This is how Zǔjǐ instructed Gāozōng,
and how Gāozōng earned a lasting reputation."
The emperor questioned Lóng:
"I heard that during the reign of Hàn Wǔdì,
when Bǎiliáng caught fire,
he extensively built palaces to suppress the misfortune.
What is the meaning of that?"
Lóng replied:
"Your servant has heard that after the Bǎiliáng Palace in Xījīng was damaged by fire,
the Yuè shamans presented their methods,
and the Jiànzhāng Palace was constructed
to ward off the fire omen.
This was done by the shamans of the Yí and Yuè peoples,
not the clear instructions of sages and worthies.
The Wǔxíng Zhì says: 'After the Bǎiliáng fire,
there followed the affair of Jiāng Chōng and his witchcraft against Wèi Tàizǐ.'
As the Zhì says,
the construction of Jiànzhāng by the Yuè shamans was useless in warding off misfortune.
Kǒngzǐ said: 'Calamities respond to the actions of their kind,
and subtle influences interact,
to warn the ruler.'
Therefore, a sagely ruler, upon seeing a calamity, blames himself,
withdraws and cultivates virtue,
to avert and restore order.
Now, it is appropriate to dismiss the common laborers.
The construction of palaces
should be based on frugality and restraint,
internally sufficient to withstand wind and rain,
externally sufficient for the study of rites and ceremonies.
If the scorched area is cleaned,
and no construction is daringly undertaken there,
then rùpú and auspicious grains will surely grow in this place,
to reward Your Majesty's reverence and humility.
How can the people's strength be exhausted,
and the people's wealth depleted!
This is truly not the way to bring forth auspicious omens and attract distant peoples."
The emperor then rebuilt Chónghuá Diàn,
and at that time, nine dragons were seen in various commanderies and states,
so it was renamed Jiǔlóng Diàn.
When the Língxiāo Què was first built,
a magpie nested on top of it.
The emperor asked Lóng about it,
who replied:
"The Shī Jīng says, 'The magpie has a nest,
but the turtledove dwells in it.'
Now, when building palaces,
and erecting the Língxiāo Què,
if a magpie nests in it,
this is an omen that the palace, not yet completed, will not be inhabited by its builder.
The will of Heaven seems to say
that before the palace is finished,
another family will take control of it.
This is truly a warning from August Heaven.
The Way of Heaven shows no favoritism;
it only supports the good.
One must not fail to deeply guard against this,
and not fail to deeply consider it.
In the late Xià and Shāng dynasties,
the rulers, though inheriting the throne,
did not respectfully receive the clear mandate of August Heaven,
but only followed flatterers and sycophants,
abandoning virtue and indulging desires;
thus, their demise was sudden.
Tàiwù and Wǔdìng,
upon seeing calamities, were terrified and trembled,
and reverently accepted Heaven's warnings;
thus, their rise was vigorous.
Now, if all construction projects are suspended,
frugality is practiced to suffice for needs,
virtuous governance is greatly promoted,
and every action follows the imperial rules,
eliminating what troubles the entire world,
and promoting what benefits the myriad people,
then the Three Kings can become four,
and the Five Emperors can become six.
How could it be merely that the Yin Zōng turned misfortune into blessing!
Your servant holds a position of trust,
and if it can bring abundant blessings to Your Majesty's sacred person
and secure the existence of the state,
even if your servant's body were reduced to ashes and his clan destroyed,
it would still be like being alive.
How could I dread the disaster of offending Your Majesty
and let Your Majesty not hear the ultimate truth?"
Thereupon, the emperor's expression changed.
That year,
a comet appeared in Dàchén.
Lóng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Whenever emperors and kings move their capitals or establish cities,
they first determine the positions of Heaven, Earth, and the altars of the land and grain,
and reverently serve them.
When planning the construction of palaces,
the ancestral temple comes first,
stables and treasuries come next,
and living quarters come last.
Now, the Yuánqiū, Fāngzé, North and South Suburbs, Míngtáng, and altars of the land and grain—
the divine positions are not yet settled,
and the system of ancestral temples is not yet in accordance with ritual,
yet living quarters are being lavishly adorned,
and scholars and common people are losing their livelihoods.
Outsiders universally say that the expenses for palace women
and the costs of military campaigns and state affairs
are roughly equal.
The people cannot endure the burden,
and all harbor resentment and anger.
The Shū Jīng says: 'Heaven's hearing and sight come from my people's hearing and sight;
Heaven's clear might comes from my people's clear might.'
When the common people compose odes,
they are then given the Five Blessings;
when the common people sigh with anger,
they are then threatened with the Six Extremities.
This means that Heaven's rewards and punishments
follow the words of the people
and accord with the hearts of the people.
Therefore, in administering government, the priority must be to pacify the people,
and only then will ancient transformations
reach up and down.
From ancient times to the present,
it has never been otherwise.
Humble palaces with rafters of thorny wood [cǎi chuán bēi gōng]—this is how Táng, Yú, and Dàyǔ extended their imperial prestige;
Jade terraces and jasper chambers [yù tái qióng shì]—this is how Xià Guǐ and Shāng Xīn offended August Heaven.
The current palaces
are truly contrary to ritual standards,
and now the Jiǔlóng is being re-established,
its embellishments more extravagant than before.
The comet, glaring brightly,
first arose in Fángxīn,
transgressing the Emperor's Seat and violating Zǐwēi.
This is August Heaven, out of love for Your Majesty,
manifesting a sign of instruction and warning,
beginning and ending always at the venerable position,
earnestly and solemnly
wishing to awaken Your Majesty.
This is like the earnest instruction of a compassionate father;
it is appropriate to greatly promote the reverent and fearful rites of a filial son,
to lead those below,
and to clearly show future generations.
It should not be neglected,
lest Heaven's wrath be compounded."
At that time, the state was embroiled in many military and national affairs,
and the application of laws was severe.
Lóng submitted a memorial, saying:
“Indeed, to establish a grand legacy and found a lasting dynasty
requires a sagely and enlightened ruler;
to assist the world and correct its governance
also needs capable aides.
Only then can all undertakings be stabilized and all things enjoy peace and prosperity.
To change customs and transform habits,
to spread and clarify the Way’s teachings,
making all four quarters adopt the same customs,
turning their heads and facing inwards,
so that virtuous teachings shine brightly
and the nine regions long for righteousness—
this is certainly not something a common official can achieve.
Currently, the authorities are preoccupied with enforcing criminal laws
and do not base themselves on the Great Way.
This is why punishments are applied ceaselessly
and customs are decadent and not upright.
It is appropriate to elevate ritual and music,
to display the Míngtáng,
to restore the Sānyōng, the Great Archery ritual, and the Rearing of the Aged,
to construct the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
to honor Confucian scholars,
to promote reclusive talents,
to publicly commend institutions,
to rectify the calendar,
to change the color of vestments,
to disseminate benevolence and gentleness,
and to value frugality and simplicity.
Only then can the rites of Fēngshàn be fully performed,
attributing merit to Heaven and Earth,
so that the sounds of Yǎ and Sòng fill the six directions,
and the transformative influence of diligent brightness spreads universally to future generations.
This is indeed a beautiful achievement of ultimate governance,
a noble and imperishable undertaking.
Moreover, within the nine domains,
if one can govern through deferential yielding,
what is there to worry about!
Not correcting the root but saving the branches
is like entangled silk;
it is not proper governance.
It would be advisable to command the various dukes, ministers, and erudite scholars
to devise and prepare these matters
to serve as a standard and model.”
Lóng further believed that rectifying the calendar,
changing the color of vestments,
distinguishing emblems and symbols,
and differentiating tools and instruments,
were the means by which ancient emperors and kings manifested their divine governance
and changed the people’s perception.
Thus, the three springs are referred to as ‘kings,’
illustrating the three dynastic traditions.
Thereupon, he expounded upon the old regulations,
presented them, and had them changed.
The Emperor accepted his proposal,
changing the third month of spring in the fifth year of Qīnglóng to the fourth month of early summer in the first year of Jǐngchū.
The official color became yellow,
and white sacrificial animals were used,
following the Earth’s proper alignment.
He was promoted to Guānglùxūn.
The Emperor increasingly augmented and beautified palaces and halls,
carving and decorating pavilions and towers,
quarrying quartz from Tàiháng,
and collecting patterned stone from Gǔchéng.
He built Jǐngyángshān in Fānglín Yuán,
and constructed Zhāoyáng Diàn north of Tàijí.
He cast magnificent beasts like yellow dragons and phoenixes,
and adorned Jīnyōng, Língyúntái, and Língxiāo Què.
A hundred projects arose in rapid succession,
with tens of thousands of laborers.
From dukes and ministers down to students,
everyone exerted their strength,
and the Emperor even personally dug earth to lead them.
Meanwhile, Liáodōng did not pay tribute.
Empress Dào passed away.
Heaven sent incessant rains,
and Jìzhōu was flooded,
sweeping away people and property.
Lóng submitted a memorial, remonstrating sharply, saying:
“The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is to give birth;
the great treasure of the sage is his position.
How is one to maintain his position?
It is through benevolence.
How is one to gather people?
It is through wealth.”
Therefore,
the scholars and common people
are the foundation of the state;
grain and silk
are the lifeblood of the scholars and common people.
Grain and silk do not grow without creation,
nor are they perfected without human effort.
Therefore, the Emperor plows to encourage agriculture,
and the Empress raises silkworms to produce clothing,
thus demonstrating reverence for the Most High God,
showing piety, and repaying His bounty.
In the past, during the time of Yī and Táng,
the world encountered the disastrous period of Yángjiǔ,
when the mighty floodwaters surged to the heavens.
They tasked Gǔn with controlling it,
but his efforts were unsuccessful.
Then, they appointed Wénmìng,
who cleared forests and carved out mountains,
working for twenty-two years.
Never was there
a disaster
more severe than that,
nor an exertion of labor
more prolonged.
Yet, Yáo and Shùn, as ruler and minister,
merely sat facing south (governing).
Yǔ divided the Nine Provinces,
and all officials and commoners performed their merits,
each
with their respective ranks.
Gentlemen and commoners
had their designated attire.
Now, there is no such urgency as in that era,
yet dukes and ministers, along with common laborers, are made to participate in the same tasks.
If this is heard
by the four barbarians,
it is not a good reputation,
and if recorded in historical texts,
it is not a glorious name.
Therefore, those who govern a state or a family
look to themselves for immediate examples,
and to external things for distant ones,
nurturing and
raising their people.
Hence, it is said,
‘A benevolent and gentle gentleman
is the parent of the people.’
Currently, both high and low are toiling,
with sickness and severe famine.
Few are tilling the land,
and hunger and scarcity are recurring,
leaving no means to get through
the year.
It is appropriate to show compassion and relief
to alleviate their distress.
Your servant observes in the ancient books and records
that the interaction between Heaven and man
has never failed to elicit a response.
Therefore, the wise kings of antiquity,
fearing the clear mandate of August Heaven,
followed the course of
Yīn and Yáng,
acting with caution and diligence,
only fearing that they might transgress.
Then, the path of governance flourished,
and their virtue harmonized with the divine.
When calamities and anomalies appeared,
they feared and rectified their policies,
and none
failed to extend their reign and prosperity.
However, in later generations,
dark and dissolute rulers,
who did not uphold the excellent principles of the former kings
nor heed the upright words of righteous scholars,
but pursued their own desires
and ambitions,
negligently disregarding warnings of change,
none failed to swiftly encounter misfortune and disaster,
leading to their downfall.
Since the Way of Heaven is so clear,
allow me to discuss it in terms of the Way of Man.
The six emotions and five natures
are all present in man.
Desire, temperance, and integrity
each occupy a part.
When they are aroused,
they contend
within the heart.
If desire is strong and nature is weak,
then one indulges without restraint;
if sincerity and integrity are not controlled,
then one overflows without limit.
Wherever emotion resides,
it is either good or
beautiful.
But the aggregation of good and beautiful things
is not achieved without human effort,
nor established without grain and silk.
If emotion is without limit,
then people cannot bear their toil,
and things cannot satisfy their demands.
When toil and demands both increase,
it will lead to disaster and rebellion.
Therefore, if desires are not curbed,
there will be no way to provide for each other.
Zhòngní said:
‘If a man does not think far ahead,
trouble will be at hand.’
From this, we can see
it.
The regulations of ritual and righteousness
are not for the sake of mere restrictive adherence,
but rather to avert harm and promote good governance.
Now, the two brigands of Wú and Shǔ,
are not mere petty barbarians from barren lands or bandits from gathered villages.
Rather, they occupy strategic strongholds and ride the currents of events,
possessing territory and troops,
usurping imperial titles and claiming to be emperors,
wishing to contend for supremacy with
the Central Plain.
Now, if someone were to come and report that
Quán and Chán are both cultivating virtuous governance,
returning to frugality and simplicity,
lightening taxes and levies,
not indulging in lavish amusements,
in all actions
consulting with venerable elders,
and conducting affairs according to ritual standards—
when Your Majesty hears this,
would you not feel alarmed and displeased at such a state of affairs,
deeming them difficult to suppress and eliminate,
thus becoming a worry for the nation?
But if
the informant were to say that
those two brigands are both acting without principle,
indulging in excessive extravagance,
conscripting their soldiers and people,
heavily increasing their taxes,
with the common folk unable to endure their commands,
groaning and sighing daily—
when Your Majesty
hears this,
would you not be enraged at their oppressing our innocent people,
and wish to swiftly inflict punishment upon them?
Furthermore,
would you not then be fortunate that they are weakened and exhausted, making them easy to take
over?
If this is the case,
then you can easily change your heart and make an assessment,
and the principles of right conduct will not be far off.
Moreover, Qín Shǐhuáng did not lay the foundation of morality,
but built the Ēfáng Palace;
he did not worry about internal strife,
but carried out the construction of the Great Wall.
When his lord
and ministers devised these plans,
they also wished to establish an enterprise for ten thousand generations,
so that their descendants would forever possess the empire.
How could they have imagined that one day a common man would let out a great cry,
and the empire would be overturned?
Therefore, your servant believes that if the rulers of previous generations had known that their actions would inevitably lead to ruin,
they would not have done them.
This is why rulers of doomed states considered themselves not doomed,
and
then eventually perished;
while wise and sagely rulers considered themselves on the verge of ruin,
and then eventually did not perish.
In the past, Hàn Wéndì was praised as a wise ruler,
who personally practiced frugality and simplicity,
bestowing favor upon his subordinates
and nurturing the people.
Yet Jiǎ Yì compared him
to someone living in an upside-down world,
claiming there was one thing to weep bitterly over,
two things to shed tears over,
and three things to sigh deeply over.
How much more so now, when the world is ravaged and depleted,
the people have no savings of even a dān or shí of grain,
and the state has no reserves for a full year.
Externally, there are powerful enemies,
with six armies arrayed at the borders;
internally, earthworks are being initiated,
causing the commanderies and prefectures to be in turmoil
and unrest.
If there were an enemy alert,
your servant fears that the laborers building fortifications would not be able to offer their lives at the barbarian court.
Furthermore,
the stipends of generals and officials
are gradually being reduced;
compared to the past,
they now receive only one-fifth.
Moreover, those on leave have had their grain allowances cut off,
and those who were not obliged to contribute now
all contribute half. This means that the official revenue is more than before,
while the expenditure is commensurately less than in the past.
Yet the expenses of the Ministry of Finance
are always insufficient,
and small levies for beef
follow one after another.
Reflecting on this,
all these various expenses
must have a source.
Moreover, salaries, rewards, grain, and silk
are what the ruler uses to show kindness to and nourish his officials and people, and to be
their dispenser of life.
If these are now abolished,
it is equivalent to taking away their lives.
To obtain something and then lose it
is the source of resentment.
The Rítuals of Zhōu state:
The Grand
Treasurer is in charge of the wealth from the nine levies,
to provide for the needs of the nine regulations.
Revenue has its designated portion,
and expenditure has its designated purpose,
so they do not interfere with each other, and each use is sufficient.
After each use is sufficient,
the surplus from the regulated contributions
is used to supply the king's amusements.
Moreover, the ruler's expenditures
must be examined by the Auditor.
(Huì pronounced kuài.)
Now, those with whom Your Majesty sits
in the imperial halls to govern the empire,
whether the Three Ministers and Nine Dignitaries,
or close officials of the Palace Secretariat,
are all your confidants, privy to your inner thoughts,
and ought to speak without reservation.
If they see extravagance or reduction but dare not
report it,
merely following orders and diligently carrying them out,
fearing only that they might not succeed,
then these are merely compliant officials,
not upright counselors.
In the past, Lǐ Sī taught Qín Èrshì, saying:
"A ruler who does not indulge in his
desires
is said to be shackled by the world."
Èrshì adopted this,
and the Qín state was overthrown,
and Lǐ Sī himself was exterminated.
Therefore, Sī Qiān criticized him for not remonstrating properly,
and made it a warning
for later generations.
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor read it
and said to the Director and Superintendent of the Secretariat:
"Reading Lóng's memorial
truly makes me afraid!"
Lóng was gravely ill,
and dictated a memorial to the throne, saying: "Zēngzǐ was ill,
and Mèng Jìngzǐ inquired after him.
Zēngzǐ said:
'When a bird is about to die,
its cry is mournful;
when a man is about to die,
his words are good.'
Your servant is suffering from a lingering illness,
which only worsens,
and I constantly fear that I might suddenly pass away,
with my loyalty and sincerity unexpressed.
Your servant's fervent sincerity
is not merely like Zēngzǐ's;
I pray Your Majesty will give it a little consideration!
May you instantly correct the mistakes and errors of past affairs,
and vigorously initiate profound improvements in future affairs,
so that gods and men respond,
distant lands yearn for righteousness,
the Four Spiritual Animals show auspicious omens,
and the Jade Balancer shines brightly.
Then the achievements of the Three Kings can be surpassed,
and the Five Emperors can be exceeded,
not merely inheriting traditions and maintaining established patterns.
Your servant constantly laments that rulers of the world all desire to continue the governance of Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ,
yet tread the path of Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì.
They all mock the deluded and chaotic rulers of the later generations
who caused the downfall of their states,
yet fail to ascend and follow the tracks of Yú, Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu.
Alas!
With such actions,
to seek such results
is like climbing a tree to seek
fish,
or boiling water to make ice;
that it cannot be achieved
is clear.
Reflecting on how the Three Dynasties possessed the empire,
sages and worthy men succeeded each other,
lasting for hundreds of years.
Not a foot of land
was not theirs,
not a single person was not their subject.
All ten thousand states were at peace,
and the nine regions were well-ordered.
The gold of Lùtái
and the grain of Jùqiáo
were of no use;
they still faced south
as before.
Why was this so?
Yet those like Guǐ and Xīn,
relying on their strength,
knowing enough to resist remonstrance,
talented enough to gloss over their wrongs,
valuing flattery,
and building towers and pavilions.
崇 [Chóng]
honored licentious music,
delighted in singers and actors,
composed "Mǐmǐ" music,
and enjoyed the sounds of Púshàng.
Heaven did not forgive them;
it looked back with concern,
and the ancestral states became ruins.
The [lower classes] were enslaved,
Zhòu [Zhòu] hung white banners,
and Jié [Jié] was exiled to Míngtiáo.
The dignity of the Son of Heaven,
Tāng [Tāng] and Wǔ [Wǔ] possessed it.
Were they truly different individuals?
They were all descendants of enlightened kings.
Moreover,
during the time of the Six States,
the empire was turbulent.
After Qín [Qín] unified it,
it did not cultivate the sagely way.
Instead, it constructed the Èfáng [Èfáng] Palace,
built the defenses of the Great Wall,
boasted
to the Central Plain,
and subdued the hundred barbarian tribes by force.
The empire trembled in awe,
and people communicated by glances on the roads.
It considered its lineage to extend for a hundred generations,
forever spreading its great radiance.
How could it have foreseen its demise in the second generation,
and the collapse
of its altars of soil and grain?
More recently, Emperor Xiàowǔ [Xiàowǔ] of Hàn [Hàn], relying on the good fortune of Wén [Wén] and Jǐng [Jǐng],
repelled the barbarians externally
and built palaces internally.
In just over ten years,
the empire was in an uproar.
Then he believed in Yuè [Yuè]
shamans,
resented Heaven and transferred his anger,
and began building the Jiànzhāng [Jiànzhāng] Palace,
with a thousand gates and ten thousand households.
Ultimately, this led to the disaster of Jiāng Chōng's [Jiāng Chōng] sorcery,
resulting in the estrangement of the imperial household
and the mutual destruction of father and son.
The poison of that calamity
flowed for several generations.
Your servant observes that during the Huángchū [Huángchū] era,
Heaven showed its warning sign.
A bird of an unusual species
was raised in a swallow's nest,
with red beak, claws, and chest.
This was a great anomaly for the Wèi [Wèi] house.
It is advisable to guard
against "eagle-soaring" ministers within the inner court.
Princes should be selected
and allowed to govern their states and command troops,
stationed at various strategic points,
to guard and pacify the imperial domain
and assist the imperial house.
In the past, when Zhōu [Zhōu]
moved east,
it relied on Jìn [Jìn] and Zhèng [Zhèng].
During the chaos of Empress Lǚ [Lǚ] of Hàn,
it truly depended on Zhūxū [Zhūxū].
These are clear lessons from previous generations.
Heaven shows no favoritism;
it only aids the virtuous.
If the people praise virtuous governance,
then its duration will be extended beyond its allotted time.
If there are grievances and lamentations below,
it selects and bestows power upon the capable.
From this perspective,
the empire of the world
is not solely Your Majesty's empire.
Your servant is afflicted
by numerous illnesses,
and my strength is waning.
I will take my carriage and depart,
returning to my village home.
Should I sink into oblivion,
if my spirit has knowledge,
I will repay this kindness by tying grass.
An imperial edict stated:
"Shēng [Shēng] is incorruptible, like Bóyí [Bóyí];
his rectitude surpasses Shǐ Yú [Shǐ Yú].
His resolve is firm and pure,
and he speaks bluntly without regard for himself.
How can it be that his slight illness is not yet cured,
and he retreats to his village home?
In the past, Bǐng Jí [Bǐng Jí] recovered from illness and extended his life through hidden virtue.
Gòng Yǔ [Gòng Yǔ], by upholding his integrity,
recovered from a severe illness.
Shēng [Shēng] should strengthen himself by eating well and focusing his mind."
Lóng [Lóng] eventually died,
leaving instructions for a simple burial,
to be dressed in ordinary clothes.
Initially,
during the Tàihé [Tàihé] era,
the Central Protector of the Army, Jiǎng Jì [Jiǎng Jì], submitted a memorial stating:
"It is fitting to follow ancient custom and perform the Fēngshàn [Fēngshàn] sacrifice."
The emperor issued an edict saying:
"Hearing Ji's [Jì] words,
made sweat pour from my feet."
The matter was shelved for years.
Later, it was decided to proceed with it,
and Lóng [Lóng] was tasked with compiling the rituals.
When the emperor heard of Lóng's [Lóng] death,
he sighed:
"Heaven does not wish my undertaking to succeed.
Gāotáng Shēng [Gāotáng Shēng] has abandoned me and died."
His son Chēn [Chēn] inherited the peerage.
At first,
during the Jǐngchū [Jǐngchū] era,
the emperor, concerned that Sū Lín [Sū Lín] and Qín Jìng [Qín Jìng],
among others, were all old
and feared there would be no one to transmit their learning,
issued an edict stating:
"In ancient times, after the former sages passed away,
their teachings and remaining doctrines
were recorded in the Six Arts.
Among the texts of the Six Arts,
Ritual is the most urgent;
it cannot be abandoned even for a moment.
The latter generations have turned their backs on the fundamentals,
and this has been the case for a long time.
Therefore, Mǐn Zǐ [Mǐn Zǐ] criticized Yuán Bó [Yuán Bó] for his lack of learning,
and Xún Qīng [Xún Qīng] was disgusted by the Qín [Qín] era's burying of scholars alive.
If Confucian learning is abolished,
how can moral transformation flourish?
Currently, the veteran scholars and great Confucians
are all advanced in years.
Who will succeed them in the way of teaching?
In the past, when Fú Shēng [Fú Shēng] was growing old,
Emperor Wén [Wén] of Hàn [Hàn] appointed Cháo Cuò [Cháo Cuò] to succeed him.
When Gǔliáng [Gǔliáng] had few disciples,
Emperor Xuān [Xuān] followed with ten gentlemen.
Therefore, thirty high-ranking officials and talented scribes
who understood the meanings of the classics were selected
to study under Guānglù Xūn [Guānglù Xūn] Lóng [Lóng], Sànqí Chángshì [Sànqí Chángshì] Lín [Lín], and Bóshì [Bóshì] Jìng [Jìng],
to receive instruction in the Four Classics and Three Rituals.
The responsible officials shall devise methods for their examination and testing.
Xiàhóu Shèng [Xiàhóu Shèng] once said:
'A scholar's only ailment is not understanding the classical arts.
If the classical arts are thoroughly understood, obtaining high office will be as easy as picking up a blade of grass from the ground.'
Now, if any scholar can thoroughly investigate the way of the classics,
then titles, emoluments, glory, and honor
will arrive without being sought.
How can one not strive diligently?"
A few years later,
Lóng [Lóng] and the others all passed away,
and the scholarly pursuit was consequently abandoned.
Initially,
Zhàn Qián of Rènéng
served as a county magistrate in the era of Tàizǔ,
and once supervised the defense of Yèchéng.
At that time, Wéndì was Crown Prince,
and indulged in hunting,
leaving in the morning and returning at night.
Zhàn Qián remonstrated, saying:
“Kings and dukes establish defenses to secure their states;
the capital city’s guards
are used to prevent unforeseen calamities.
The Dàyǎ says: ‘The son of the宗 is the wall,
let it not be allowed to crumble.’
It also says: ‘Since it is not yet distant,
therefore I strongly remonstrate.’
If one indulges in hunting,
leaving in the morning and returning at dusk,
for the pleasure of a single day of hunting,
and forgets boundless dangers,
I am secretly puzzled by this.”
The Crown Prince was displeased,
but thereafter his excursions were somewhat curtailed.
During the Huángchū era,
Wéndì was about to establish Guō Guìpín as empress.
Zhàn Qián submitted a memorial of remonstrance,
the text of which is in the Biographies of Empresses and Consorts.
During the Míngdì era,
many public works projects were undertaken simultaneously,
and imperial relatives were alienated and dismissed.
Zhàn Qián submitted a memorial, saying:
“Heaven gives birth to the myriad people and establishes rulers over them,
in order to shelter and cover all living beings,
and to nurture the multitudes;
thus, ruling within the four seas is not for the Son of Heaven’s sake,
nor is dividing territories for the sake of the feudal lords.
From the Three Sovereigns
down to Táng and Yú,
all extended their great benevolence to the world,
and their pure virtue pervaded,
upon which the common people relied.
When the Three Kings declined,
and down to Hàn,
good governance became increasingly rare,
and chaos and disorder became abundant.
From that time onward,
none were able to govern well.
Tàizǔ was profound, wise, and divinely martial;
he cleared away tyranny and chaos,
restored the royal order,
and thus initiated the imperial enterprise.
Wéndì received the mandate of Heaven,
expanded the imperial foundation,
and for seven years on the throne,
he had no time for every matter.
Your Majesty, with your sagely virtue,
has inherited this grand undertaking;
it is fitting to cultivate peace and tranquility,
and allow the people to rest.
Yet the borders are not at peace,
conscripted soldiers are garrisoned far away,
there are affairs beyond the seas,
banners are flown ten thousand *lǐ* away,
the six armies are agitated,
supplies are transported by water and land,
the common people abandon their livelihoods,
and a thousand *jīn* are spent daily.
Grand palaces are being constructed,
with countless laborers;
pines from Cúlái
are felled from mountains and deep valleys;
strange rocks and fake jade
are floated down the Hé and Huái.
The entire area within the capital's confines
has become an imperial domain,
which ought to supply straw, grains, and millet for tribute,
but has become a park and hunting ground,
with luxuriant wild growth,
and abundant havens for deer and rabbits;
this harms agricultural work,
and the land is overgrown with thorns.
Disasters and epidemics are prevalent,
the people and things are greatly scattered,
above, the harmonious qi is diminished,
and auspicious grains do not grow.
I have heard that when Wénwáng built Fēng,
he began it without urgency,
and the people came like children,
completing it in a few days.
The Spiritual Pond and Spiritual Park
were shared with the people.
Now the palaces and observatories are grand and extravagant,
the carvings exquisitely marvelous;
you forget the three-year period of Yǒuyú,
and contemplate the jasper chamber of Yīn Xīn.
The forbidden land stretches a thousand *lǐ*,
one steps and falls into a net;
its beauty rivals Éfáng,
employing a hundred Qíxī.
I fear that the people's strength will be exhausted,
and those below will not be able to bear the command.
In the past, Qín occupied Xiáohán to control the six directions,
and considered its virtue to surpass the Three Sovereigns,
and its achievements to equal the Five Emperors,
wishing its reign title to last ten thousand generations,
yet in the second generation, it was overthrown,
and wished to be common people;
this was because its branches and trunk were already [扤],
and its roots and foundation were pulled out first.
Indeed, when a sagely king governs the world,
he is able to illuminate eminent virtues,
and reward meritorious relatives;
when outstanding talents are in office,
then achievements can flourish;
when relatives are prominently employed,
then they share concerns about safety and danger;
deep roots and solid foundations,
together forming trunk and wings,
even through periods of prosperity and decline,
will have internal and external support.
In the past, Chéngwáng was young,
and unable to govern,
Zhōu, Lǚ, Shào, and Bì
were all by his side.
Now there are no such monitors as the Marquis of Wèi and Kāngshú,
and those entrusted with divided territories
are also not Dàn and Shì.
The Eastern Palace has not been established,
and the empire has no successor.
May Your Majesty keep your mind on the passes and frontiers,
and forever preserve boundless prosperity;
then the people within the seas will be very fortunate.”
Later, he was appointed Commandant of Yān,
but declined due to illness,
and died.
The appraisal says: Xīn Pí and Yáng Fù were
resolute, upright, and impartial;
their remonstrances were righteous and selfless,
approaching Jí Àn’s lofty demeanor.
Gāotáng Lóng’s scholarship was profound and clear,
his ambition was to assist his ruler;
he offered warnings in response to changes,
speaking from sincerity;
truly loyal!
As for his insistence on correcting the calendar
and making Wèi follow Yú,
that is perhaps what is called ‘intention exceeding its understanding’!
Biographies of Mǎn Tián and Qiān Guō, Chapter 26
Mǎn Chǒng, courtesy name Bóníng,
was a native of Chāngyì, Shānyáng.
At eighteen,
he became a Commandery Inspector.
At that time, Lǐ Shuò and others within the commandery each commanded their own troops,
harming the common people.
The Grand Administrator ordered Mǎn Chǒng to investigate.
Lǐ Shuò and others pleaded guilty
and ceased their plundering.
He served as Magistrate of Gāopíng.
Zhāng Bāo of the county became a Commandery Inspector,
and was corrupt and took bribes,
interfering with official administration.
Mǎn Chǒng, finding him in a relay station,
led officials and soldiers to arrest him,
interrogated him about his offenses,
and concluded the case that same day.
He then resigned his office and returned home.
When Tàizǔ arrived in Yǎnzhōu,
he was appointed as an Aide.
When he (Tàizǔ) became Grand General,
he (Tàizǔ) appointed him (Chǒng) as an Assistant of the Western Bureau,
and as Magistrate of Xǔ.
At that time, Cáo Hóng, a close and noble member of the imperial clan,
had retainers within the jurisdiction,
who frequently broke the law.
Chǒng arrested and punished them.
Cáo Hóng wrote to Chǒng,
but Chǒng did not listen.
Cáo Hóng reported it to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ summoned the official in charge of Xǔ.
Chǒng knew that he intended to pardon them,
so he quickly executed them.
Tàizǔ said with pleasure:
「"Shouldn't one in charge of affairs act in just such a way?" 」
The former Grand Commandant, Yáng Biāo, was arrested and sent to the county prison.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Xún Yù, and the Minister of the Privy Purse, Kǒng Róng, among others, all instructed Chǒng:
「"You should merely take his statement,
and do not subject him to torture." 」
Chǒng did not respond at all,
and interrogated him according to the law.
After several days,
he requested an audience with Tàizǔ,
and said to him:
「"Yáng Biāo's interrogation has yielded no other testimony.
For those who deserve death, their crimes should first be clearly displayed;
this man is famous throughout the land.
If his crime is not clear,
it will surely greatly lose the people's trust,
and I humbly consider it a pity for Your Excellency." 」
Tàizǔ immediately pardoned and released Yáng Biāo that very day.
Initially,
Xún Yù and Kǒng Róng, upon hearing that Yáng Biāo was tortured,
were both angry.
But when the matter was resolved because of this,
they esteemed Chǒng even more.
At that time, Yuán Shào was powerful in Héshuò,
and Rǔnán was Yuán Shào's home commandery.
His disciples and retainers were spread across various counties,
holding troops and resisting.
Tàizǔ was worried about this,
and appointed Chǒng as Grand Administrator of Rǔnán.
Chǒng recruited five hundred men who submitted to him,
and led them to attack and capture more than twenty fortified camps.
He lured the chiefs who had not yet surrendered,
and killed more than ten of them at a meeting.
In one go, all was pacified.
He gained twenty thousand households,
and two thousand soldiers.
He ordered them to settle in agriculture.
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
he followed Tàizǔ on the campaign against Jīngzhōu.
When the main army returned,
Chǒng was left as Acting Fènwēi Jiāngjūn,
stationed at Dāngyáng.
Sūn Quán frequently disturbed the eastern frontier.
Chǒng was again recalled to serve as Rǔnán Tàishǒu,
and granted the noble title Guānnèi Hóu.
When Guān Yǔ besieged Xiāngyáng,
Chǒng assisted Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Cáo Rén in garrisoning Fánchéng to resist him.
However, the armies of Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Yú Jìn and others were submerged by Guān Yǔ due to continuous rain and rising waters.
Guān Yǔ urgently attacked Fánchéng.
Fánchéng was inundated,
and its walls collapsed in many places.
Everyone lost color.
Someone said to Rén:
“The danger today
cannot be withstood by force.
We should take advantage of the fact that Guān Yǔ’s encirclement is not yet complete,
and flee by light boat at night.
Although the city would be lost,
we could still save ourselves.”
Chǒng said:
“The mountain waters are swift;
I expect they will not last long.
I hear Guān Yǔ has dispatched a separate general who is already below Jiá,
and south of Xǔ,
the common people are agitated.
The reason Guān Yǔ dares not advance further
is that he fears our army will attack his rear.
If we flee now,
south of the Hónghé,
it will no longer belong to the state.
You should wait.”
Rén said:
“Good.”
Chǒng then submerged a white horse
and made a solemn oath with the soldiers.
Just then, Xú Huǎng and others arrived as reinforcements.
Chǒng fought valiantly and rendered meritorious service,
and Guān Yǔ subsequently retreated.
He was promoted and enfeoffed as Ānchāng Tínghóu.
When Wén Dì ascended the throne as king,
he was promoted to Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn.
For his meritorious service in defeating Wú at Jiānglíng,
he was re-appointed Fúbō Jiāngjūn,
and stationed at Xīnyě.
When the main army campaigned south,
reaching Jīnghú,
Chǒng led all the armies at the forefront,
facing the enemy across the water.
Chǒng ordered his generals, saying:
“Tonight the wind is very fierce;
the enemy will surely come to burn our camp.
We should prepare for them.”
All the armies were on alert.
At midnight,
the enemy indeed sent ten detachments to ambush and burn the camp.
Chǒng ambushed and defeated them,
and was promoted and enfeoffed as Nánxiāng Hóu.
In the third year of Huángchū,
Chǒng was granted a provisional staff of authority (Jiéyuè).
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Qián Jiāngjūn.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he was promoted and enfeoffed as Chāngyì Hóu.
In the second year of Tàihé,
he assumed the office of Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the spring of the third year,
a defector reported that Wú was making extensive preparations,
and spreading rumors of wanting to hunt north of the Jiāng;
Sūn Quán intended to personally lead the expedition.
Chǒng estimated that they would certainly attack Xīyáng and made preparations for it.
Quán, hearing of this,
retreated.
In the autumn,
Cáo Xiū was sent to advance south into Héféi from Lújiāng,
and Chǒng was ordered to head towards Xiàkǒu.
Chǒng submitted a memorial, saying:
“Although Cáo Xiū is intelligent and resolute, he rarely employs military tactics.
The path he is now taking,
with a lake behind and a river alongside,
is easy to advance on but difficult to retreat from.
This is a military trap (Wādì).
If they enter Wúqiáng Kǒu,
deep preparations should be made.”
Before Chǒng’s memorial was replied to,
Xiū had already advanced deep.
The enemy indeed cut off Jiáshí from Wúqiáng Kǒu,
blocking Xiū’s return path.
Xiū’s battle was unfavorable,
and he retreated.
Just then, Zhū Líng and others, coming from behind, blocked the road
and encountered the enemy.
The enemy fled in alarm,
and Xiū’s army was thus able to return.
In that year, Xiū died,
and Chǒng, as Qián Jiāngjūn, replaced him as Supreme Commander of all armies in Yángzhōu.
The soldiers and people of Rǔnán, missing and adoring him,
old and young, led each other,
rushing along the roads to follow him,
and could not be stopped.
The Hùjūn reported this to the emperor,
suggesting that the ringleaders be executed.
An imperial edict ordered Chǒng to bring a thousand of his personal guards with him,
and for the rest, no questions were to be asked.
In the fourth year,
Chǒng was appointed Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn.
That winter,
Sūn Quán spread rumors of intending to come to Héféi.
Chǒng submitted a memorial requesting the recall of all armies from Yǎn and Yù,
and they all assembled.
The enemy soon retreated,
and an edict was issued to disband the troops.
Chǒng believed that the enemy's grand advance and return
was not their original intention.
This must be a feigned retreat to disband our troops,
and then they would return to take advantage of our unpreparedness,
to launch a surprise attack.
He submitted a memorial requesting not to disband the troops.
More than ten days later,
Quán indeed returned,
reaching Héféi City,
but failed to capture it and returned.
The following year,
the Wú general Sūn Bù sent someone to Yángzhōu to request surrender,
stating:
“The road is long, and I cannot come myself.
I beg for troops to meet and escort me.”
The Cìshǐ Wáng Líng passed on Bù’s letter,
requesting troops and horses to meet him.
Chǒng believed it must be a trick,
did not provide troops,
and instead wrote a reply to Líng, saying:
“Knowing right from wrong,
and wishing to avoid disaster and submit to righteousness,
to leave tyranny and return to the Way,
is greatly commendable.
Now you wish to send troops to meet him,
but if the troops are too few, they will be insufficient for protection;
if many, the matter will surely become widely known.
Let us first secretly plan to accomplish this original intention,
and at the opportune moment, adjust according to circumstances.”
Chǒng was then summoned to court,
and instructed the Chief Clerk of his administration (Zhǎngshǐ) who remained:
“If Líng wishes to go and meet him,
do not give him troops.”
Later, Líng was unable to obtain troops,
so he sent a single commander with seven hundred infantry and cavalry to meet him.
Sūn Bù launched a night ambush,
the commander fled,
and more than half of his men were killed or wounded.
Initially,
Chǒng and Líng did not get along well in their shared duties.
Líng’s partisans slandered Chǒng, saying he was old and confused.
Therefore, Míng Dì summoned him.
Upon his arrival,
he was found to be hale and strong,
so the emperor saw him and sent him back.
Chǒng repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to remain.
The imperial edict replied:
“In ancient times, Lián Pō had a strong appetite,
and Mǎ Yuán sat firmly on his saddle.
Now you are not yet old but claim to be old.
How does this not go against the spirit of Lián and Mǎ?
You should think of stabilizing the frontier,
and benefit our central land.”
The next year,
Wú general Lù Xùn (陸遜) advanced towards Lújiāng (廬江).
Commentators believed it was advisable to quickly send aid to it.
Chǒng (寵) said:
“Although Lújiāng (廬江) is small,
its generals are strong and its soldiers are elite;
if they defend, it will take time.
Moreover, the bandits have come two hundred *lǐ* (里) from their ships,
leaving their rear empty and exposed.
We still want to lure them in.
Now, we should let them advance,
only fearing that they will flee and we cannot catch them.”
He marshaled his troops and hastened towards Yángyíkǒu (楊宜口).
When the bandits heard that a large army was advancing from the east,
they immediately fled that night.
At that time, Sūn Quán (孫權) made plans to attack every year.
In the first year of Qīnglóng (青龍) (233 CE),
Chǒng (寵) submitted a memorial, saying:
“Héféi (合肥) city faces the river and lake to the south,
and is far from Shòuchūn (壽春) to the north.
If the bandits attack and besiege it,
they can rely on the water for strategic advantage.
If government troops rescue it,
they must first defeat a large part of the bandits,
only then can the siege be lifted.
It is very easy for the bandits to go,
but very difficult for our troops to go and rescue.
It is advisable to move the troops from the city
thirty *lǐ* (里) to the west,
where there are treacherous and defensible positions.
A new city should be built there for strong defense.
This would be to draw the bandits to open ground and cut off their return route,
which would be more convenient strategically.”
The Protector of the Army, Jiǎng Jì (蔣濟), debated,
believing that:
“This would show weakness to the world,
and to destroy the city upon seeing the bandits' smoke and fire
would be to abandon it before being attacked.
Once it comes to this,
there will be unlimited plunder,
and they will surely establish a stronghold north of the Huái (淮) River.”
The Emperor did not agree.
Chǒng (寵) submitted another memorial, saying:
“Sūn Zǐ (孫子) said:
‘Warfare
is the Way of Deception.
Thus, though able, feign inability;
though effective, feign idleness;
though near, feign far; though far, feign near.’
This means that appearance and reality do not necessarily correspond.
He also said, ‘Those skilled in moving the enemy create formations.’
Now, to move the city further inland before the bandits arrive
is to create a formation and lure them.
To draw the bandits away from the water,
and act according to advantageous conditions,
if success is gained externally,
then blessings will arise internally.”
Shàngshū (尚書) Zhào Zī (趙咨) considered Chǒng's (寵) strategy superior,
and an imperial edict then approved it.
That year,
Sūn Quán (孫權) personally led an army,
intending to besiege the new city.
Because it was far from water,
he dared not disembark for twenty days.
Chǒng (寵) said to his generals:
“When Sūn Quán (孫權) learns of our city relocation,
he will surely boast among his troops.
Now he has launched a large expedition, hoping for a decisive victory.
Although he dares not reach the city,
he will certainly land and display his troops to show his strength.”
So he secretly dispatched six thousand infantry and cavalry,
who lay in ambush at a hidden spot in Féichéng (肥城) to await them.
Sūn Quán (孫權) indeed landed and displayed his troops.
Chǒng's (寵) hidden army suddenly rose and attacked them,
beheading several hundred,
and some drowned in the water.
The next year,
Sūn Quán (孫權) personally led an army, numbering a hundred thousand,
to the new city of Héféi (合肥).
Chǒng (寵) hurried to meet them,
recruited several dozen brave men,
broke pine branches for torches,
soaked them with hemp oil,
and set them on fire from upwind,
burning the bandits' siege equipment.
He also shot and killed Sūn Quán's (孫權) nephew, Sūn Tài (孫泰).
The bandits then retreated.
In the spring of the third year (235 CE),
Sūn Quán (孫權) sent several thousand households to cultivate land north of the Jiāng (江) River.
By August,
Chǒng (寵) believed that the fields were nearing harvest,
men and women were scattered across the countryside,
and their garrison troops were several hundred *lǐ* (里) away from the city.
They could be ambushed.
He dispatched his chief clerk to lead three armies down the Jiāng (江) River to the east,
destroying various encampments,
burning grain, and then returning.
An imperial edict praised him,
and all the spoils were given as rewards to the generals and soldiers.
In the second year of Jǐngchū (景初) (238 CE),
Chǒng (寵) was recalled due to old age
and promoted to Tàiwèi (太尉).
Chǒng (寵) did not manage property,
and his household had no surplus wealth.
An imperial edict said:
“You, sir, have commanded troops abroad,
devoting yourself to public concern,
possessing the style of Xíng Fǔ (行父) and Jì Zūn (祭遵).
I grant you ten *qǐng* (頃) of land,
five hundred *hú* (斛) of grain,
and two hundred thousand cash,
to illustrate your pure loyalty and frugal integrity.”
Chǒng (寵) had his fiefdom increased repeatedly,
totaling nine thousand six hundred households.
Two of his sons or grandsons were enfeoffed as Tínghóu (亭侯).
In the third year of Zhèngshǐ (正始) (242 CE), he died,
and was posthumously named Jǐnghóu (景侯).
His son Wěi (偉) inherited the title.
Wěi (偉) was known for his broad outlook,
and his official position reached Wèiwèi (衞尉).
Tián Yù (田豫), courtesy name Guóràng (國讓),
was a native of Yōngnú (雍奴) in Yúyáng (漁陽).
When Liú Bèi (劉備) sought refuge with Gōngsūn Zàn (公孫瓚),
Yù (豫) was young at the time,
and entrusted himself to Bèi (備).
Bèi (備) held him in high regard.
When Bèi (備) became the Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州),
Yù (豫) requested to return home because his mother was old.
Bèi (備) wept as he bade him farewell,
saying:
“I regret not being able to accomplish great things with you.”
Gōngsūn Zàn (公孫瓚) appointed Yù (豫) to govern Dōngzhōu (東州) as its magistrate.
Zàn's (瓚) general Wáng Mén (王門) rebelled against Zàn (瓚),
and came to attack with over ten thousand men as a general for Yuán Shào (袁紹).
The populace was afraid and wanted to surrender.
Yù (豫) ascended the city wall and said to Mén (門):
“You were highly favored by Gōngsūn (公孫) and then left,
perhaps with some unavoidable reason.
Now you return as a bandit,
which shows you are merely a troublemaker.
Even with the wisdom of merely carrying a bottle,
one defends without needing borrowed tools.
I have already accepted this responsibility.
Why do you not attack quickly?”
Mén (門) felt ashamed and retreated.
Although Zàn (瓚) knew Yù (豫) had strategic talent, he could not employ him.
After Zàn (瓚) was defeated, Xiānyú Fǔ (鮮于輔) was nominated by the local people
to act as Grand Administrator.
He had always been on good terms with Yù (豫),
and made him Chief Clerk.
At that time, heroes were rising everywhere,
and Fǔ (輔) did not know whom to follow.
Yù (豫) said to Fǔ (輔):
“The one who will ultimately unify the realm
must be the Cáo (曹) clan.
You should quickly pledge allegiance,
lest you face future calamity.”
Fǔ (輔) followed his advice,
and was thus enfeoffed and favored.
Tàizǔ (太祖) summoned Yù (豫) to be a military advisor to the Chancellor.
He was appointed magistrate of Yǐngyīn (潁陰) and Lánglíng (朗陵),
and then promoted to Grand Administrator of Yìyáng (弋陽).
Wherever he served, there was good governance.
When the Marquis of Yānlíng (鄢陵), Zhāng (彰), campaigned against Dàijùn (代郡),
he made Yù (豫) his chancellor.
When the army reached north of Yì (易),
the barbarians' hidden cavalry attacked them.
The soldiers were in disarray,
not knowing what to do.
Yù (豫), utilizing the terrain,
turned his chariots to form a circular array,
with bows and crossbows fully drawn within,
and diversionary troops blocking the gaps.
The Hú (胡) could not advance
and dispersed.
He pursued and attacked them,
greatly defeating them.
He then advanced and pacified Dài (代) commandery,
all thanks to Yù's (豫) strategies.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Nányáng (南陽).
Previously,
a local man Hóu Yīn (侯音) had rebelled,
with several thousand followers forming bandit groups in the mountains,
causing great trouble for the commandery.
The former Grand Administrator arrested over five hundred of his associates,
and memorialized that all should be executed.
Yù (豫) personally saw all the prisoners,
comforted and encouraged them,
and opened a path for their self-renewal,
breaking their shackles and releasing them all at once.
All the prisoners kowtowed,
wishing to serve him.
They immediately informed each other,
and the bandit groups disbanded overnight.
The commandery became peaceful.
He fully reported the situation,
and Tàizǔ (太祖) praised him.
Early in the reign of Emperor Wéndì,
the northern Dí were powerful and prosperous.
They encroached upon and harassed the border regions.
Therefore, Yù was dispatched with a staff of authority to serve as Hù Wūhuán Xiàowèi.
Qiān Zhāo and Xiè Jùn concurrently served as Hù Xiānbēi.
From Gāoliǔ to the east,
and Huìmò to the west,
there were dozens of Xiānbēi tribes.
Bǐnéng, Míjiā, and Sùlì divided the territory and held sway,
each having their own boundaries.
They then jointly swore an oath
that none of them would sell horses to Zhōngguó.
Yù believed that the Róng Dí forming a single entity
was not beneficial to Zhōngguó.
Therefore, he first sowed discord among them,
causing them to become enemies with each other
and attack one another.
Sùlì violated the alliance
and offered a thousand horses to the government.
He was then attacked by Bǐnéng
and sought help from Yù.
Yù feared that if they were allowed to conquer each other,
the harm would become more profound.
It was appropriate to rescue the good and punish the evil
to demonstrate trustworthiness to all the Dí.
He personally led elite troops
deep into the enemy territory.
The Hú people were numerous,
and they surrounded his army from front and rear,
cutting off his retreat route.
Yù then advanced his army
and established a camp ten-odd *lǐ* from the enemy.
He gathered a large quantity of ox and horse dung and set it ablaze,
then led his forces away via another route.
When the Hú saw the smoke and fire continuously,
they thought he was still there.
They left,
and only after traveling several dozen *lǐ* did they realize it.
They pursued Yù to Mǎchéng
and surrounded it ten layers deep.
Yù secretly prepared his forces,
ordering his Sīmǎ to raise banners,
beat drums and blow horns,
and lead infantry and cavalry out from the south gate.
The Hú people all focused their attention and rushed towards them.
Yù led his elite forces out from the north gate,
shouting and raising a clamor.
Both forces launched simultaneously,
catching the enemy by surprise.
The enemy troops scattered in confusion,
