abandoning their bows and horses and fleeing on foot.
They were pursued and attacked for over twenty *lǐ*,
their corpses covering the ground.
Furthermore, the Wūhuán King Gǔjìn was unruly and disobedient.
While Yù was inspecting beyond the frontier,
he personally led over a hundred cavalry from his command into Gǔjìn’s territory.
Gǔjìn came to greet him and bowed.
Yù then ordered his attendants to behead Gǔjìn,
displaying his crimes to instruct the masses.
All the people were terrified and dared not move.
He then appointed Gǔjìn’s brother to replace Gǔjìn.
From then on, the Hú people were disheartened
and awed throughout the desert.
The mountain bandit Gāo Ài,
with several thousand followers,
raided and plundered,
causing trouble for Yōu and Jì provinces.
Yù enticed the Xiānbēi Sùlì tribe to behead Gāo Ài,
and his head was sent to the capital.
Yù was enfeoffed as Chánglè Tínghóu.
He served as Xiàowèi for nine years.
In his governance of the Yídí,
he constantly suppressed and broke up alliances,
and scattered the strong and treacherous.
As for all those who absconded, engaged in illicit activities,
or conspired with the Hú to the detriment of the government,
Yù would sow discord and division among them,
preventing their wicked schemes from succeeding
and making their settlements unstable.
His work was not yet finished
when Wáng Xióng, the governor of Yōuzhōu, and his faction wanted Wáng Xióng to lead the Hù Wūhuán Xiàowèi.
They slandered Yù, claiming he was causing chaos on the frontier
and creating trouble for the state.
Consequently, Yù was transferred to serve as Rǔnán Tàishǒu,
with the added title of Tiǎnyí Jiāngjūn.
At the end of Tàihé,
Gōngsūn Yuān rebelled in Liáodōng.
The emperor wanted to conquer him but found it difficult to find the right person.
The Zhōnglǐngjūn Yáng Jì recommended Yù for the selection.
So Yù was dispatched with his original office to supervise all the armies of Qīngzhōu,
granted the staff of authority,
and sent to suppress the rebellion.
At that time, the Wú rebels sent envoys to ally with Gōngsūn Yuān.
The emperor, seeing the large number of rebels
and their crossing the sea,
issued an edict ordering Yù to withdraw his troops.
Yù estimated that the enemy ships were about to return,
and with the year-end winds being fierce,
they would certainly fear being adrift.
Going east without a shore,
they would have to head for Chéngshān.
As Chéngshān had no place to hide ships,
he immediately surveyed the coastal terrain
and various mountains and islands,
intercepting at strategic points
and deploying troops to garrison them.
He personally entered Chéngshān
and ascended the observation post of Emperor Hànwǔ.
When the rebels returned,
they indeed encountered a severe storm,
and all their ships struck the mountains and sank.
The waves swept them ashore,
leaving them nowhere to escape,
and all their troops were captured.
Initially,
all the generals laughed at the idea of waiting for the enemy on empty ground.
But when the enemy was defeated,
they vied to claim credit for the strategy,
and sought to enter the sea to salvage the wrecked ships.
Yù feared that the desperate enemy would fight to the death,
and did not allow any of them to go.
Initially,
Yù, as Tàishǒu, supervised Qīngzhōu,
but Chéng Xǐ, the governor of Qīngzhōu, secretly harbored resentment.
During military affairs,
they often disagreed and made mistakes.
Chéng Xǐ knew the emperor loved pearls,
so he secretly reported:
“Although Yù has military achievements, his regulations are lax.
He obtained many weapons, pearls, and gold,
which he disbursed without submitting them to the government.”
Because of this, his achievements were not acknowledged.
Later, Sūn Quán led a force of one hundred thousand to attack Xīnchéng.
The Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn Mǎn Chǒng wanted to lead the armies to rescue it.
Yù said:
“The enemy has deployed all their forces in a major offensive;
they are not merely aiming for small gains.
They wish to use Xīnchéng as bait to draw out our main army.
It is advisable to let them attack the city
to blunt their銳氣 edge,
and not to engage them directly.
If the city cannot be taken,
their troops will surely become exhausted;
once exhausted, then striking them
can lead to a great victory.
If the enemy sees through our plan,
they will certainly not attack the city,
and will naturally retreat.
If we advance our troops immediately,
we will play right into their hands.
Furthermore, when large armies face each other,
we should make our intentions hard to discern,
and not reveal our plans ourselves.”
Yù immediately submitted a memorial,
and the emperor followed his advice.
Soon after, the rebels fled.
Later, Wú attacked again.
Yù went to resist them,
and the rebels immediately retreated.
One night, the armies were alarmed,
saying:
“The rebels are coming again!”
Yù remained lying down and did not rise,
ordering his troops,
“Anyone who dares to move will be beheaded.”
After a short while,
there were indeed no rebels.
At the end of Jǐngchū,
his fief was increased by three hundred households,
making a total of five hundred households including the previous ones.
At the beginning of Zhèngshǐ,
he was promoted to Shǐchíjié Hù Xióngnú Zhōnglángjiàng,
with the added title of Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently served as Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ.
The foreign Hú heard of his formidable reputation
and came to offer tribute in droves.
The provincial border was peaceful and orderly,
and the common people cherished him.
He was summoned to serve as Wèiwèi.
He repeatedly requested to resign his position,
but the Tàifù Sīmǎ Xuānwáng believed Yù was still robust
and wrote to persuade him not to.
Yù wrote back saying:
“To remain in office after the age of seventy
is like a bell ringing and a clepsydra running out, yet one continues to travel at night—
this is a crime.”
He then steadfastly claimed severe illness.
He was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū,
enjoying the emoluments of a high official.
He died at the age of eighty-two.
His son, Péngzǔ, inherited his title.
Yù was always pure, frugal, and self-restrained.
All awards and gifts were distributed among his officers and soldiers.
Whenever the Hú and Dí privately offered him presents,
he would record them and store them in the official treasury,
never bringing them into his own home;
his household was constantly poor and lacking.
Though of different kinds,
all held Yù's integrity in high esteem.
In the sixth year of Jiāpíng,
an imperial edict was issued to commend him,
and his family was granted money and grain.
The account is in the biography of Xú Máo.
Qiān Zhāo, courtesy name Zǐjīng,
was a native of Guānjīn, Ānpíng.
When he was a little over ten years old,
he went to the same county's Lè Yǐn to study.
Later, Yǐn became the Chief Clerk for General of Chariots and Cavalry Hé Miáo,
and Zhāo followed him to complete his studies.
When the capital was in chaos,
and Miáo and Yǐn were harmed,
Zhāo and Yǐn's students, such as Shǐ Lù, fearlessly faced the blades,
and together they interred Yǐn's body,
then escorted the coffin back home.
On the way, they encountered bandits who plundered them,
and Lù and others all scattered and fled.
The bandits wanted to hack the coffin to take the nails,
but Zhāo, shedding tears, pleaded for them to be spared.
The bandits respected his righteousness,
so they released it and left.
He thus became famous.
Yuán Shào, the Governor of Jìzhōu, appointed him Supervisor of Military Affairs,
and concurrently put him in charge of the Wūhuán cavalry.
Shào's retainer violated an order,
and Zhāo first executed him then reported it.
Shào admired his spirit and did not punish him.
After Shào died,
he then served Shào's son, Shàng.
In the ninth year of Jiàn'ān,
Tàizǔ besieged Yè.
Shàng sent Zhāo to Shàngdǎng
to supervise the delivery of military provisions.
Before he returned,
Shàng was defeated and fled,
arriving in Zhōngshān.
At that time, Shàng's maternal cousin, Gāo Gàn, was the Inspector of Bìngzhōu.
Zhāo considered that Bìngzhōu had the danger of Héngshān to its left
and the security of the Great River to its right,
with fifty thousand armored soldiers,
and blocked the powerful Hú to the north.
He urged Gàn to welcome Shàng
and combine their strength to observe the changing situation.
Gàn was not only unable to do so,
but secretly wished to harm Zhāo.
Zhāo heard of this
and left secretly.
The road was cut off, preventing him from pursuing Shàng,
so he went east to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ, who governed Jìzhōu,
appointed him as an Attendant Official.
When Tàizǔ was about to attack Yuán Tán,
the Wūhuán of Liǔchéng wanted to send cavalry to assist Tán.
Tàizǔ, knowing Zhāo had once led the Wūhuán,
sent him to Liǔchéng.
Upon arrival,
he encountered Qiàowáng Yán,
who was about to send five thousand cavalry to Tán.
Also, Gōngsūn Kāng, the Grand Administrator of Liáodōng, had declared himself Governor of Píngzhōu,
and sent his envoy Hán Zhōng carrying the Xányú's seal and ribbon to grant it to Qiàowáng.
Qiàowáng convened a great meeting of the tribal chiefs,
and Zhōng was also present.
Qiàowáng asked Zhāo:
“In the past, Lord Yuán said he received the Son of Heaven's command
to grant me the title of Xányú;
now Lord Cáo again says he will report to the Son of Heaven
to grant me the true Xányú;
and Liáodōng also brings a seal and ribbon.
Given this,
who should be considered correct?”
Zhāo replied:
“In the past, Lord Yuán acted under imperial authority
and was able to bestow appointments.
But he made mistakes midway,
and the Son of Heaven commanded Lord Cáo to replace him,
saying he would report to the Son of Heaven
to grant the true Xányú,
which is correct.
Liáodōng is a subordinate commandery;
how can it presume to bestow appointments?”
Zhōng said:
“My Liáodōng is east of the Azure Sea,
possessing a million soldiers,
and also having the use of Fúyú and Huìmò;
in the current situation,
the strong are superior.
How can Cáo Cāo alone be correct?”
Zhāo sternly rebuked Zhōng, saying:
“Lord Cáo is sincere, respectful, wise, and discerning.
He supports the Son of Heaven,
punishes rebels and brings the submissive to peace,
calming the four seas.
You, your lord and ministers, are foolish and deceitful.
Now, relying on remote dangers,
you defy the King's command
and wish to presume to bestow appointments,
insulting the sacred instruments of power.
You are about to be slaughtered.
How dare you insult and denigrate a great man?”
He then seized Zhōng's head and slammed it,
drawing his knife to cut him down.
Qiàowáng was terrified,
barefoot he embraced Zhāo
to beg for Zhōng's life,
and those around them turned pale.
Zhāo then returned to his seat
and explained to Qiàowáng and the others the consequences of success and failure,
and where fortune and misfortune lay.
They all rose from their seats, knelt, and bowed,
reverently accepting his instructions.
They then dismissed the envoy from Liáodōng
and disbanded the cavalry that had been assembled.
After Tàizǔ defeated Tán at Nánpí,
he appointed Zhāo as an Army Advisor,
and he followed Tàizǔ in attacking the Wūhuán.
Arriving at Liǔchéng,
he was appointed Commandant Protector of the Wūhuán.
Upon returning to Yè,
Liáodōng sent Yuán Shàng's head,
which was displayed in the horse market.
Zhāo, seeing it, was overcome with grief,
and set up a sacrifice below the head.
Tàizǔ admired his righteousness
and recommended him as a Mào cái.
He followed Tàizǔ in pacifying Hánzhōng,
and when Tàizǔ returned,
Zhāo was left as Central Protector of the Army.
After this task,
he returned to Yè
and was appointed Commandant who Pacifies the Lǔ,
leading troops and overseeing all military affairs in Qīng and Xú Prefectures.
He attacked the bandits in Dōnglái,
beheaded their leader,
and the eastern region became peaceful.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he appointed Zhāo as Envoy with credentials, Commandant Protector of the Xiānbēi,
stationed at Chāngpíng.
At this time,
the border people were scattered in the mountains and marshes,
and there were also thousands of deserters and rebels among the Xiānbēi.
Zhāo widely disseminated kindness and trust,
and encouraged them to surrender and submit.
Gōngsūn Jí and others, the Internuncio who Established Righteousness,
led their detachments
and all pledged their allegiance;
they were allowed to return to their original commanderies.
He also attracted the Xiānbēi Suǒlì and Míjiā, among others, with over ten myriad households,
all of whom were brought to settle within the passes.
The grand army wished to campaign against Wú,
so Zhāo was summoned back.
Upon his arrival,
the army had already been disbanded.
He was appointed Right Zhongláng Jiàng.
He was then sent out to be the Grand Administrator of Yànmén.
The commandery was on the frontier,
and although there were watchtowers and defensive preparations,
raids and plunder were incessant.
Zhāo not only taught the people battle formations,
but also memorialized to restore the rent and taxes for over five hundred Wūhuán households,
enabling them to prepare saddles and horses,
and sending out scouts afar.
Whenever the barbarians violated the border,
he would mobilize troops to counterattack,
shattering them every time they came.
Consequently, the morale of the officials and people grew sharper by the day,
and the wilderness was safe.
He also sowed discord and dispersion,
causing the barbarians to suspect each other.
The Xiānbēi chieftains Bùdùgēn, Xièguīní, and others had a rift with Kēbǐnéng,
and brought over thirty thousand households from their tribes to the commandery, settling near the frontier.
Zhāo ordered them to attack Kēbǐnéng in return,
killing Kēbǐnéng's brother Jūluóhóu,
and the rebellious Wūhuán Guīyìhóu Wáng Tóng, Wáng Jì, and others,
thus forming a great enmity.
Therefore, Zhāo personally went out,
leading Guīní and others to attack Kēbǐnéng in the former commandery of Yúnzhōng,
severely defeating him.
Zhāo connected with Fùtóu and over ten thousand households of Xiānbēi west of the Hé,
repaired the old Shàngguǎn City north of Xíng,
and stationed garrisons to pacify both the interior and exterior.
All the barbarians, great and small,
submitted wholeheartedly.
Even relatives dared not conceal any rebels or fugitives,
but all captured and delivered them.
Consequently, those living in the wilderness could close their doors peacefully,
and banditry ceased.
Zhāo then selected those with talent and insight,
sending them to the Grand Academy for study,
and upon their return, they taught others.
Within a few years, schools flourished greatly.
The commandery seat, Guǎngwǔ,
had salty and bitter well water,
and the people all had to carry water from afar, fetching flowing water,
a round trip of seven *lǐ*.
Zhāo surveyed the terrain,
and taking advantage of the mountainous features,
dug through the plain and opened a canal,
bringing water into the city.
The people benefited from it.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he was granted the title of Guānnèihóu.
In the second year of Tàihé,
the Protector of Wūhuán, Tián Yù, went out of the frontier,
and was besieged by Kēbǐnéng in the old Máiyì City.
He sent a message to Zhāo requesting help.
Zhāo immediately organized his troops and horses,
intending to go to Yù's rescue.
Bìngzhōu, according to standard regulations, forbade Zhāo,
but Zhāo believed that a commanding general was under siege,
and he could not be constrained by bureaucratic deliberation.
He memorialized and proceeded without authorization.
He also swiftly dispatched urgent military dispatches,
stating the situation,
saying he would first attack the barbarians' homes in the northwest,
and then proceed east,
to meet and execute the barbarian leader himself.
When the dispatch arrived,
Yù's army was greatly encouraged.
He also sent one copy to the barbarians' critical path,
and the barbarians immediately became terrified,
their tribes scattering.
When his army arrived at the old Píngchéng,
they all dispersed and fled.
Kēbǐnéng then reassembled a large cavalry force,
reaching the area north of the old Píngzhōu pass.
Zhāo stealthily launched a surprise attack,
beheading a great many.
Zhāo believed that since the Shǔ barbarians' Zhūgě Liàng had repeatedly emerged,
and Kēbǐnéng was cunning,
they could communicate with each other, so he memorialized for defensive preparations.
The deliberators thought it was too far away
and did not believe it.
Coincidentally, Liàng was then at Qíshān,
and indeed sent envoys to ally with Kēbǐnéng.
Kēbǐnéng arrived at the old Běidì Shíchéng,
coordinating with him.
The Emperor then issued an edict to Zhāo,
ordering him to act as he saw fit to attack them.
At that time, Kēbǐnéng had already returned south of the desert.
Zhāo discussed with the Inspector Bì Guǐ, saying:
"The Hú barbarians migrate constantly.
If we exhaust our army in a distant pursuit,
then our speed will not match theirs.
If we wish to launch a stealthy attack,
then the mountains and valleys are difficult and dangerous,
and the transportation of provisions
will be hard to arrange secretly.
We can order the two commanders of Xīnxīng and Yànmén
to station troops north of Xíng,
outwardly for pacification,
and inwardly for military farming,
storing provisions.
When the horses are fat in autumn and winter,
and the troops of the prefecture and commanderies are assembled,
we can seize the opportunity to campaign,
and we are certain to achieve complete victory."
Before this could be implemented,
he fell ill and died.
Zhāo was in the commandery for twelve years,
and his reputation for awe-inspiring power spread far and wide.
His reputation for governing the frontier
was second only to Tián Yù,
and the common people missed him.
Fù Róng of Yúyáng was known for his achievements in Yànmén,
succeeding Zhāo,
and also had meritorious deeds in Liáodōng.
Zhāo's son Jiā inherited his title.
His second son Hóng
was also fierce and resolute, with Zhāo's demeanor.
As Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī, he accompanied Dèng Ài in conquering Shǔ, achieving merit.
During the Xiánxī era, he was Zhènwēi Hùjūn.
Jiā was the maternal half-brother of Jìn Sītú Lǐ Yìn,
and died young.
Guō Huái, courtesy name Bójì,
was from Yángqǔ, Tàiyuán.
During the Jiàn'ān era, he was nominated as Xiàolián,
and appointed Píngyuán Fǔchéng.
When Emperor Wén was Wǔguān Jiāng,
he summoned Huái to serve as Ménxià Zéicáo,
then transferred him to Chéngxiàng Bīngcáo Yìlìshǐ,
accompanying the campaign against Hànzhōng.
When Tàizǔ returned,
he left Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Xiàhóu Yuān to resist Liú Bèi,
appointing Huái as Yuān's Sīmǎ.
When Yuān battled Bèi,
Huái was ill and did not go out.
Yuān was killed,
and the army was in disarray.
Huái gathered the scattered soldiers,
and recommended Dàngkòu Jiāngjūn Zhāng Hé as the army commander,
whereupon the various camps stabilized.
The next day,
Bèi intended to cross the Hànshǔi to attack.
The generals discussed that their numbers were no match,
and Bèi, already victorious,
intended to form a formation near the water to resist him.
Huái said:
"This shows weakness and is insufficient to deter the enemy;
it is not a wise plan.
It is better to form a formation far from the water,
lure them forward,
and attack them when they are half-way across.
Bèi can then be defeated."
After the formation was set,
Bèi was suspicious and did not cross.
Huái then held his ground firmly,
showing no intention of retreating.
When this was reported,
Tàizǔ approved,
granted Hé a ceremonial axe,
and again appointed Huái as Sīmǎ.
When Emperor Wén ascended to the throne as King,
he was granted the title of Guānnèihóu,
and transferred to Zhènxī Zhǎngshǐ.
He also served as Xíng Zhēngqiāng Hùjūn,
protecting Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Zhāng Hé and Guànjūn Jiāngjūn Yáng Qiū in campaigning against the mountain bandits Zhèng Gān and the rebellious Hú of Lúshuǐ,
defeating and pacifying them all.
Guānzhōng was thus pacified,
and the people could live in peace.
In the first year of Huángchū,
he was dispatched as an envoy to congratulate Wéndì on his ascension to the throne.
However, he fell ill on the journey,
which caused a delay based on the distance.
When the officials gathered for celebrations,
the Emperor, with a stern expression, reproached him, saying:
“In ancient times, when Yǔ met with the feudal lords at Túshān,
Fángfēng arrived late
and was summarily executed.
Now, the whole realm celebrates together, yet you are the latest to arrive.
Why is this?”
Huái replied:
“Your servant has heard that the Five Emperors first taught the people with virtue,
and it was only when the government of the Xiàhou declined
that penal laws began to be used.
Now your servant lives in an age like that of Táng-Yú,
and therefore I know I am spared the execution of Fángfēng.”
The Emperor was pleased by this,
and promoted him to Governor of Yōngzhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Shèyángtíng.
After five years, this was made permanent.
When Pìtí, a great chief of the Qiāng in Āndìng, rebelled,
he attacked, defeated, and pacified him.
Whenever the Qiāng or Hú came to surrender,
Huái would always first send people to investigate their family situation,
the number of men and women,
and their ages.
And when he met them,
he would know their detailed circumstances at a glance.
His inquiries were so thorough
that all acclaimed him as divine.
In the second year of Tàihé,
Zhūgě Liàng, the Chancellor of Shǔ, marched out to Qíshān,
sending General Mǎ Sù to Jiētíng,
and Gāo Xiáng to encamp at Liǔchéng.
Zhāng Hé attacked Sù,
and Huái attacked Xiáng's camp.
Both were defeated.
He also defeated Tángtí, a renowned Qiāng from Lǒngxī, at Fúhǎn,
and was granted the title of Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn.
In the fifth year,
Shǔ troops marched out to Lǔchéng.
At this time,
there was no grain in Lǒngyòu,
and it was proposed that a large transport of grain be made from Guānzhōng.
Huái, through his authority and kindness, pacified the Qiāng and Hú,
and had each household contribute grain.
He made their contributions fair,
and the army's provisions were sufficient.
He was promoted to Zhuǎnyángwǔ Jiāngjūn.
In the second year of Qīnglóng,
Zhūgě Liàng marched out through Xié valley,
and also farmed in Lánkēng.
At this time, Sīmǎ Xuānwáng was stationed south of the Wèi River.
Huái predicted that Liàng would certainly contest Běiyuán,
and that it should be occupied first.
Many advisors disagreed.
Huái said:
“If Liàng crosses the Wèi River and occupies the plateau,
linking his forces with the northern mountains,
cutting off the Lǒng road,
and unsettling the people and barbarians,
this would not be beneficial to the state.”
Xuānwáng approved this,
and Huái then garrisoned Běiyuán.
Before the fortifications were complete,
a large Shǔ army arrived.
Huái met and repelled them.
A few days later,
Liàng moved a large force westward.
All the generals thought he intended to attack the western encirclement.
Huái alone believed that this was a feint to the west
to draw a heavy response from our army,
and that he would certainly attack Yángsuì.
That night, they indeed attacked Yángsuì,
but were unable to ascend due to the preparations.
In the first year of Zhèngshǐ,
the Shǔ general Jiāng Wéi marched out to Lǒngxī.
Huái advanced his army,
pursued him to Qiángzhōng,
and Wéi retreated.
He then attacked the Qiāng Mídāng and others,
and pacified over three thousand Dī households,
relocating them to populate Guānzhōng.
He was promoted to Zuǒ Jiāngjūn.
Liáng Yuánbì and others, Hú from Xiūtú in Liángzhōu,
led over two thousand households of their tribes to join Yōngzhōu.
Huái memorialized, requesting that they be settled in Gāopíng, Āndìng,
to serve as a defense for the people.
Later, a Xīzhōu Dūwèi was established there.
He was subsequently appointed Qián Jiāngjūn,
retaining his governorship as before.
In the fifth year,
Xiàhou Xuán attacked Shǔ,
and Huái commanded all the armies as the vanguard.
Huái judged the situation to be unfavorable,
and immediately withdrew his forces,
thus avoiding a major defeat.
Upon his return, Huái was granted a jǐe (credentials).
In the eighth year,
the Qiāng tribes of Lǒngxī, Nán'ān, Jīnchéng, and Xīpíng, including Èhé, Shāogē, Fátóng, and Ézhēsài, rebelled in concert,
attacking and besieging cities and towns.
They invited Shǔ forces from the south,
and Zhì Wúdài, a renowned Hú from Liángzhōu, also rebelled in response.
Xiàhou Bà, the Protector of the Army against Shǔ, commanded all armies and was stationed at Wéichì.
When Huái's army first arrived at Dídao,
advisors unanimously suggested that Fúhǎn should be subdued first,
to pacify the unruly Qiāng internally
and frustrate the enemy's plans externally.
Huái predicted that Wéi would certainly attack Bà,
so he entered Fèngzhōng
and moved south to meet Bà.
Wéi indeed attacked Wéichì,
but Huái's army arrived just in time,
and Wéi retreated.
He then advanced to attack the rebellious Qiāng,
beheading Èhé and Shāogē,
and over ten thousand households surrendered.
In the ninth year,
Zhēsài and others were stationed at Héguān and the old city of Báitǔ,
using the river to resist the army.
Huái observed their disposition upstream,
and secretly crossed troops downstream to occupy Báitǔ city.
He attacked
and heavily defeated them.
Zhì Wúdài besieged Wǔwēi,
leaving his family members in Xīhǎi.
Huái advanced his army towards Xīhǎi,
intending to surprise and capture his dependents.
However, Wúdài turned back,
and they fought north of Lóngyí,
defeating and routing him.
The wicked ruffians of Língjū were west of Shítou Shān,
blocking the main road
and cutting off royal envoys.
Huái attacked them on his return journey
and heavily defeated them.
Jiāng Wéi marched out from Shíyíng,
from Qiángchuān,
and went west to meet Zhì Wúdài.
He left Liáo Huà, the Administrator of Yīnpíng, to build a fort at Chéngzhòng Shān,
gathering defeated Qiāng and holding them as hostages.
Huái wanted to divide his forces to capture him.
The generals argued that Wéi's troops were linked with the strong Hú to the west,
and Huà was holding a strategic position.
Dividing the army into two to engage both
would weaken our military strength,
making it impossible to subdue Wéi by advancing
and impossible to dislodge Huà by retreating.
This was not a good plan.
It would be better to combine forces and go west together,
and before the Hú and Shǔ joined,
cut off their internal and external connections.
This would be a campaign to disrupt their alliances.
Huái said:
“If we now go to capture Huà,
it will be unexpected by the enemy,
and Wéi will certainly be apprehensive and turn back.
By the time Wéi arrives,
we will have sufficient time to subdue Huà,
and also make Wéi exhausted from rushing to and fro.
Our army will not have to go far west,
and the Hú alliance will naturally dissipate.
This is a strategy to achieve two objectives with one action.”
So he dispatched Xiàhou Bà and others to pursue Wéi at Tàzhōng,
while Huái himself led the various armies to attack Huà and his forces.
Wéi indeed rushed back to rescue Huà,
all as Huái had predicted.
He was further enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
In the first year of Jiāpíng
we were nearly overthrown.
Huái delivered us from danger and difficulty,
and his achievements are recorded in the imperial archives.
For over thirty years he has been in Guān Yòu,
campaigning against bandits and enemies externally,
and internally pacifying the people and barbarians.
In recent years,
he has crushed Liáo Huà,
captured Gōu Ān,
and his merits are manifest,
which I greatly commend.
I now appoint Huái as General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Ceremonial Commander (Yí Tóng Sān Sī),
retaining his credentials (chí jié) and oversight duties as before."
He was promoted to Marquis of Yángqǔ,
with a total of 2,780 households.
Three hundred households were allotted
to one of his sons, who was enfeoffed as a Marquis of a Pavilion.
He passed away in the second year of Zhèngyuán.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand General,
and his posthumous name was Zhēn Hóu.
His son Tǒng succeeded him.
Tǒng reached the official position of Inspector of Jīng Province,
then passed away.
His son Zhèng succeeded him.
In the Xiánxī period,
when the five ranks were established,
because Huái had performed distinguished service in the previous dynasty,
he was re-enfeoffed as Viscount of Fényáng.
The critique states: Mǎn Chǒng was resolute and unyielding,
courageous and resourceful.
Tián Yù conducted himself with integrity,
and his strategies were clear and well-practiced.
Qiān Zhāo upheld righteousness with heroic fervor,
and his prestige and achievements were manifest.
Guō Huái's strategies were precise and detailed,
and his reputation was known throughout Qín and Yōng.
However, Yù's rank stopped at a minor province,
and Zhāo ended his career as a commandery administrator,
their full potential not having been utilized.
Biography of Xú and Hú, Two Kings, Chapter 27
Xú Mò, courtesy name Jǐngshān,
was a native of Jì in Yān Commandery.
When Tài Zǔ pacified Héshuò,
he was summoned as an Aide-de-camp (jūnmóu yuàn) to the Chancellor,
provisionally appointed Magistrate of Fènggāo,
then entered service as a Clerk of the Department of Eastern Secretariat (dōng cǎo yì lì shǐ).
When the State of Wèi was first established,
he became a Director of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū láng).
At that time, a strict ban was placed on alcohol,
but Mò privately drank until he was heavily intoxicated.
The Imperial Investigator Zhào Dá questioned him about official matters,
and Mò replied:
"I am 'middle-sage' (zhōng shèngrén)."
Dá reported this to Tài Zǔ,
who was greatly angered.
General Who Crosses the Liao, Xiān Yú Fǔ, stepped forward and said:
"In daily life, intoxicated guests call clear wine 'sage' (shèngrén)
and turbid wine 'worthy' (xiánrén).
Mò is naturally cautious and prudent;
it was merely a drunken remark."
He was ultimately spared punishment.
Later he became Administrator of Lǒngxī,
then transferred to Nán'ān.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he successively served as Chancellor of Qiáo,
Administrator of Píngyáng and Ānpíng,
and Colonel-Director of Agriculture (diǎnnóng zhōnglángjiàng) of Yǐngchuān,
earning renown wherever he served,
and was granted the title of Marquis within the Pass.
When the imperial carriage visited Xǔchāng,
the Emperor asked Mò:
"Are you still often 'middle-sage'?"
Mò replied:
"Formerly, Zǐ Fǎn died at Gǔyáng,
and Yù Shū was punished for drinking.
My fondness is the same as these two men,
and I cannot restrain myself,
so I occasionally still get 'middle-sage'.
However, Sùliú was known for her ugliness,
and I am known for my drunkenness."
The Emperor laughed heartily,
and, looking at those around him, said:
"His reputation is not unfounded."
He was promoted to Military Advisor to the Grand General Who Soothes the Army.
Emperor Míng, considering Liáng Province to be remote and distant,
bordering the Shǔ invaders to the south,
appointed Mò as Inspector of Liáng Province,
with credentials (chí jié) and oversight as Colonel Protecting the Qiāng.
Upon arrival,
he found that Zhūgě Liàng had advanced to Qíshān, and the three commanderies west of Lǒng had rebelled.
Mò immediately dispatched his Staff Officer and the Administrator of Jīnchéng and others to attack the Nán'ān rebels,
defeating them.
The area west of the Yellow River often suffered from drought and scarcity of grain.
Mò memorialized to repair the salt ponds in Wǔwēi and Jiǔquán to collect grain from the barbarians,
and also greatly expanded irrigated fields,
recruiting poor people to cultivate them,
so that every household had ample provisions,
and storehouses overflowed.
He then used the surplus military funds within the province
to purchase gold, silk, dogs, and horses,
all for the expenses of the central government.
Gradually, he collected private weapons among the people
and stored them in the armories.
Then he led the people with benevolence and righteousness,
established schools and clarified teachings,
prohibited extravagant burials,
abolished irregular sacrifices,
promoted the good and censured the wicked,
and moral transformation spread widely,
winning the hearts of the people.
The Western Regions became accessible,
and the wild barbarians brought tribute,
all due to Mò's achievements.
For his meritorious service in suppressing the rebellious Qiāng leader Kē Wú,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of a Capital Pavilion,
with an income of three hundred households,
and additionally appointed General Who Establishes Awe.
When Mò dealt with the Qiāng and Hú,
he did not question minor transgressions;
but if they committed a major crime,
he would first inform their tribal chiefs,
ensuring they were aware,
and only then would he execute those who deserved death, as a warning.
Thus, they trusted him and feared his authority.
All rewards and grants were distributed among the generals and soldiers,
none entering his own household,
so his wife and children lacked sufficient clothing and food.
The Emperor heard of this and commended him,
providing for his family as needed.
He corrected evil and rectified wrong,
and the province became orderly and pure.
In the first year of Zhèngshǐ,
he was reinstated as Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng).
He was promoted to Inspector of the Capital Region (Sīlì Xiàowèi),
and all the officials held him in awe and dread.
He resigned from office due to official matters.
Later, he became Grand Master of Glorious Emolument (Guānglù Dàfū).
After several years, he was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Xú Miǎo sighed, saying:
"The Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng) are officials who discuss the Way.
If there is no suitable person, the position remains vacant.
How can I, old and sick, presume to hold it?"
He firmly declined and did not accept.
In the first year of Jiāpíng,
at the age of seventy-eight,
he passed away at home as a Grand Master (Dàfū).
He was buried with the rites befitting a Ducal Minister (Gōng).
His posthumous title was Mù Hóu.
His son Wǔ succeeded him.
In the sixth year,
the imperial court, recalling upright and pure-minded gentlemen,
issued an edict stating:
"Indeed, honoring the worthy and extolling virtue
is what sagely kings hold in high regard;
to promote goodness and educate
is what Zhòngní (Confucius) praised.
Therefore, the former Minister of Works Xú Miǎo, General Who Attacks the East (Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn) Hú Zhì, and Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi) Tián Yù all served in the former dynasty,
served four generations of emperors,
commanded armies on expeditions,
and assisted in various governmental affairs internally.
They were loyal and pure in public service,
concerned for the state and forgetful of private interests,
did not seek to accumulate property,
and after their deaths,
their families had no surplus wealth.
We greatly commend them.
Therefore, grant Xú Miǎo's family and others two thousand hū of grain
and three hundred thousand coins,
and proclaim this throughout the land."
Hán Guānmàn, from the same commandery as Xú Miǎo,
was insightful and capable,
and shared fame with Xú Miǎo.
He ranked ahead of Lǐ Lǐ and Lú Yù,
and served as Inspector of Yùzhōu.
He achieved great success in governance
and died in office.
Lú Qīn, in his writings,
praised Xú Miǎo, saying:
"Lord Xú's ambition was high and his conduct pure;
his talent was broad and his spirit fierce.
In his application,
he was lofty but not arrogant;
pure but not exclusive;
broad-minded but held to principles;
fierce but capable of leniency.
Sages considered purity difficult to achieve,
yet it was easy for Lord Xú."
Someone asked Lú Qīn:
"During the time of Emperor Wǔ,
people regarded Lord Xú as 'accommodating.'
But after he was in Liángzhōu and returned to the capital,
people regarded him as 'exclusive.'
Why is this?"
Lú Qīn replied:
"In the past, Máo Xiàoxiān, Cuī Jìguī, and others held power,
valuing pure and unadorned gentlemen.
At that time, everyone changed their carriages and clothes to seek high reputations,
but Lord Xú did not alter his usual ways,
hence people considered him 'accommodating.'
Recently, the world has become extravagant,
with people imitating each other,
but Lord Xú maintained his refined taste as before,
not conforming to the customs.
Therefore, what was 'accommodating' yesterday
is 'exclusive' today.
This shows the inconstancy of worldly people,
and the constancy of Lord Xú."
Hú Zhì, courtesy name Wéndé,
was a native of Shòuchūn in the state of Chǔ.
In his youth, he, along with Jiǎng Jì and Zhū Jì, were all renowned in the Jiāng and Huái region.
He served in the provincial and commandery administrations.
When Jiǎng Jì was Vice-Administrator (Biéjià), he was sent to see Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
Tàizǔ asked:
"Hú Tōngdá
was an elder.
Does he have any descendants?"
Jiǎng Jì replied:
"He has a son named Zhì.
His overall ambition and strategy do not match his father's,
but in meticulousness and comprehensive handling of affairs, he surpasses him."
Tàizǔ immediately summoned Hú Zhì to be the Magistrate of Dùnqiu.
A county resident, Guō Zhèng, had an illicit affair with his cousin
and killed her husband, Chéng Tā.
A commandery clerk, Féng Liàng, was imprisoned as a witness.
Guō Zhèng and his cousin endured torture and concealed their guilt,
while Féng Liàng, unable to bear the pain,
falsely accused himself,
and was about to have their crime reversed onto him.
When Hú Zhì arrived in office,
he observed their expressions
and thoroughly re-examined the matter,
and upon inspection, all confessed.
He entered officialdom as an Orderly of the Eastern Bureau (Dōngcáo Yìlì Shǐ) under the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng),
and the province requested him to be the Administrator of Justice (Zhìzhōng).
General Zhāng Liáo had a rift with his Protector of the Army (Hùjūn) Wǔ Zhōu.
Zhāng Liáo saw Inspector Wēn Huī and asked for Hú Zhì,
but Hú Zhì declined on grounds of illness.
Zhāng Liáo went out and said to Hú Zhì:
"I placed my trust in you,
why do you disappoint me so?"
Hú Zhì replied:
"The friendships of the ancients
were such that one knew their lack of greed by their wealth,
their lack of cowardice by their retreat,
and did not believe in rumors,
hence they could last.
Wǔ Bónán is a refined gentleman,
and in the past, the General praised him incessantly.
Now, due to a petty grudge,
a rift has formed.
(Yái,
pronounced Wǔ Mài Fǎn.
Zì,
pronounced Shì Mài Fǎn.)
Moreover, my talent is meager,
how can I maintain our friendship to the end?
That is why I do not wish to."
Zhāng Liáo was moved by his words
and reconciled with Wǔ Zhōu.
Tàizǔ appointed him as an aide to the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng Shǔ).
During the Huángchū era,
he was transferred to be a Bureau Director of Personnel (Lìbù Láng),
then became Governor of Chángshān,
and was later transferred to Dōngguǎn.
A scholar, Lú Xiǎn, was murdered by someone.
Hú Zhì said:
"This man had no enemies but had a young wife,
which is why he died!"
He interviewed all the young men living nearby.
When the clerk Lǐ Ruò was questioned, his expression changed.
Hú Zhì then pressed him thoroughly about the circumstances,
and Lǐ Ruò confessed immediately.
The criminal was thus apprehended.
Whenever he received rewards for military merits,
he would distribute them among the multitude,
none entering his own home.
He served in the commandery for nine years;
officials and common people lived in peace,
and soldiers and officers served with dedication.
He was promoted to Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
given the additional title of General Who Shakes Awe (Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed as an Attendant Marquis within the Pass (Guānnèi Hóu).
When the great Wu general Zhū Rán besieged Fánchéng,
Hú Zhì led a light force to its rescue.
Debaters all thought the enemy was too strong to approach,
but Hú Zhì said:
"Fánchéng is low-lying
and has few soldiers;
therefore, we must advance and provide external support;
otherwise,
it will be in danger."
He then led his troops to the siege,
and the city within was then secure.
He was promoted to General Who Attacks the East (Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn),
granted a battle-axe of authority (jiǎ jié), and made Area Commander of all armies in Qīng and Xú provinces.
He greatly increased agricultural production and stored grain,
having enough reserves for more than a year.
He established an Eastern Expedition Platform (Dōngzhēng Tái),
both cultivating and defending.
He also opened canals in various commanderies,
facilitating boat travel,
and strictly prepared defenses to await the enemy.
The coastal areas were peaceful.
He was deeply earnest and perceptive,
and did not use his own integrity to judge others.
He was remembered wherever he served.
He passed away in the second year of Jiāpíng.
His family had no surplus wealth,
only the bestowed clothes and a book satchel.
The army reported this to the emperor,
who posthumously advanced his enfeoffment to Marquis of Yánglíng Tíng (Yánglíng Tínghóu),
with an estate of one hundred households,
and gave him the posthumous title Zhēn Hóu.
His son Wēi succeeded him.
In the sixth year,
an imperial edict commended Hú Zhì's pure conduct
and bestowed money and grain upon his family.
The account is in the biography of Xú Miǎo.
Wēi,
during the Xiánxī era, rose to the position of Inspector of Xúzhōu,
achieved distinguished merits,
served as Governor of three commanderies,
and was renowned wherever he served.
He died in Āndìng.
Wáng Chǎng (王昶), courtesy name Wénshū (文舒),
was a man from Jìnyáng (晉陽), Tàiyuán (太原).
In his youth, he and Wáng Líng (王淩) from the same commandery were both well-known.
As Líng (淩) was older,
Chǎng (昶) treated him like an elder brother.
When Emperor Wén (文帝) was still crown prince,
Chǎng (昶) served as Palace Literary Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Wénxué),
then was promoted to Central Palace Secretary (Zhōngshùzǐ).
When Emperor Wén (文帝) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Shìláng),
and then became Administrator of Agriculture for Luòyáng (Luòyáng Diǎnnóng).
At that time, the capital region was covered in dense forests.
Chǎng (昶) cleared the wilderness,
diligently encouraged the populace,
and thus an exceptionally large amount of land was reclaimed.
He was promoted to Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ).
When Emperor Míng (明帝) ascended the throne,
he was given the additional title of General Yanglie (Yángliè Jiāngjūn),
and bestowed the title of Marquis within the Passes (Guānnèi Hóu).
Though Chǎng (昶) served in an outer post,
he always kept the imperial court in mind.
He believed that the Wèi (魏) dynasty inherited the failings of Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢),
with laws and regulations that were overly strict and fragmented.
Without making significant reforms to the national institutions to align with the ways of the ancient kings,
hoping for a revival of good governance and transformation
was impossible.
So he authored a treatise on governance, the Zhìlùn (治論),
consisting of over twenty chapters that roughly followed ancient systems but were adapted to contemporary affairs.
He also wrote over ten chapters of military treatises,
discussing the uses of orthodox and unorthodox strategies.
He submitted these during the Qīnglóng (青龍) era.
When naming his nephews and sons,
he always adhered to principles of humility and practicality,
to express his intentions.
Thus, his nephews Mò (默) and
Shěn (沈) were given the courtesy names Chùjìng (處靜) and Chùdào (處道) respectively.
His sons Hún (渾) and
Shēn (深) were given the courtesy names Xuánchōng (玄沖) and Dàochōng (道沖) respectively.
He then wrote an admonition saying: As for the way of a father towards his sons,
there is nothing greater than cherishing one's body and perfecting one's conduct,
in order to bring glory to one's parents.
People know these three things are good,
yet some endanger their lives and ruin their families,
falling
into the disaster of ruin and extinction.
Why is this?
It is because what they learn and practice is not the right way.
Filial piety, reverence, benevolence, and righteousness
are the foremost of all virtues.
Practicing them leads to establishment,
and they are the foundation
of one's being.
Through filial piety and reverence, one's clan feels secure.
Through benevolence and righteousness, one's community respects him.
These virtues are cultivated internally,
and their reputation becomes known externally.
If people are not earnest in their ultimate
conduct,
but abandon the root to pursue the branches,
thus falling into ostentation
or forming factions:
ostentation brings the burden of falsehood,
and factions bring the trouble of partisanship.
The warnings against these two
are clearly evident,
yet those who follow the overturned cart become increasingly numerous,
and those who pursue the branches become even more extreme.
This is all due to being deluded by contemporary praise
and being oblivious to immediate gain.
Wealth, nobility, fame, and reputation
are what human nature enjoys,
yet a superior man might obtain them but not dwell in them.
Why?
He dislikes obtaining them by improper means.
The problem is that people know how to advance but not
how to retreat,
know desire but not contentment.
Hence, there are burdens of distress and humiliation,
and regrets and lamentations.
A saying goes:
"If one does not know contentment,
then one loses what one desires."
Therefore, the contentment
of knowing contentment is always contentment.
Observing the successes and failures of past events,
and examining the good and ill fortune of the future,
there has never been anyone who sought fame and coveted gain,
desiring without satiation,
yet was able to preserve their generation and maintain
their family,
and eternally keep their blessings and emoluments.
I wish for you, my children, to establish yourselves and conduct yourselves,
to follow the teachings of the Confucians,
and tread the words of the Daoists.
Therefore, I have taken "profound silence" (xuánmò) and "empty tranquility" (chōngxū) as your
names,
desiring that you, my children, reflect on the meaning of your names
and dare not transgress them.
In ancient times, washbasins and tubs had inscriptions,
and armrests and staffs had admonitions.
One would observe them at every turn,
so their conduct was without
error.
How much more so for one's own name—
can one not be admonished by it!
Things that are quickly completed also perish quickly;
things that mature late come to a good end.
The morning glory grass
withers in the evening;
the flourishing pine and cypress
do not fade in deep winter.
For this reason, great gentlemen dislike quick success
and guard against partiality.
For example, when Fàn Gài (范匄) conversed with the Qin (秦) envoy and Wǔzǐ (武子) struck and broke
his hairpins,
he disliked his tendency to overshadow others.
Few people with good qualities do not boast,
and few capable people do not pride themselves.
Boasting leads to overshadowing others,
and pride leads to insulting
others.
Those who overshadow others will also be overshadowed by others,
and those who insult others will also be insulted by others.
Thus, the three Xì (郤) clans were executed in Jìn (晉),
and Wángshū (王叔) incurred guilt in Zhōu (周).
Was it not due to the fault of pride in one's goodness
and self-boasting, and a fondness for contention?
Therefore, a gentleman does not praise himself,
not out of deference to others,
but because he dislikes overshadowing others.
Indeed, those who can bend to extend,
yield to gain,
and be weak to become strong,
rarely fail to succeed.
Praise and blame
are the source of love and hate, and the pivot of disaster and fortune.
Therefore, the sages are cautious about them.
Confucius said:
"Among
people,
who do I blame, who do I praise?
If I praise someone,
it must be after testing them."
He also said:
"Zǐgòng (子貢) passes judgment on others.
Is Cì (賜) truly virtuous?
I do not
have the time."
Even with the virtue of a sage,
it was still like this.
How much more so for ordinary people to lightly engage in praise and blame?
In the past, General Fúbō (伏波將軍) Mǎ Yuán (馬援) admonished his nephews,
saying:
"When you hear of another's wrongdoing,
you should treat it as hearing the names of your parents.
Your ears may hear it,
but your mouth should not
speak of it."
This admonition is profound.
If someone blames you,
you should withdraw and seek the reason within yourself.
If you have actions that deserve blame,
then their words
are appropriate;
if you have no actions that deserve blame,
then their words are baseless.
If appropriate, then there is no resentment towards them;
if baseless, then there is no harm to yourself.
Why then respond in kind?
Moreover, those who become angry upon hearing others blame them
dislike ugly remarks being directed at them.
If one retaliates, the problem only worsens.
It is better to remain silent and cultivate oneself.
A proverb says:
"Nothing saves one from cold
like a heavy fur coat;
nothing stops slander like self-cultivation."
These words are true.
If one associates with contentious individuals
and treacherous people,
even proximity is undesirable,
how much more so to confront
and contend with them?
The harm is profound.
As for insincere people,
their words are not rooted in principles,
and their actions do not match their words.
Their superficiality is relatively easy to discern.
Yet people
are deluded,
and still do not examine them by their words and actions.
Recently, Wèi Fěng (魏諷) from Jìyīn (濟陰) and Cáo Wěi (曹偉) from Shānyáng (山陽) both failed and perished due to their crooked and perverse ways,
misleading their contemporaries
and harboring treachery.
driving later generations,
though punished with axes and hatchets,
take it as a great warning.
Yet, those corrupted
are already numerous.
How can one not be careful!
As for the recluses of the mountains and forests,
men like Bó Yí and Shū Qí,
who gladly endured long hunger at Shǒuyáng,
and willingly rushed into fire at Miánshān,
though they can inspire the greedy and motivate the common folk,
yet,
a sàint cannot be made from this,
and I do not wish for it either.
Now, your ancestors have for generations worn caps and robes of office,
taking benevolence and righteousness as their reputation,
and prudence and caution as their appellation.
They were filial and fraternal within their household,
and
diligently pursued learning with teachers and friends.
When I interacted with people of my time,
though our paths differed,
each had something commendable.
Guō Bóyì of Yǐngchuān,
his preferences were open and broad-minded,
and he was quick-witted
and intelligent.
As a person, he lacked grand magnanimity,
but had an excess of valuing the noble lightly.
If he favored someone, he esteemed them like a mountain;
if he did not favor someone, he disregarded them like grass.
Based on my understanding, I
was close and intimate with him,
but I do not wish for my son to be like him.
Xú Wěicháng of Běihǎi
did not seek high renown,
nor did he pursue ill-gotten gains.
He remained tranquil and self-possessed,
attending only to the Dao.
When he had opinions of right and wrong,
he would allude to the ancients to express his meaning,
without directly praising or criticizing at the time.
I respect and revere him,
and I wish for my son to emulate him.
Liú
Gōnggàn of Dōngpíng
was broadly learned and highly talented,
sincere in principle and grand in purpose.
However, his character was uneven,
and he was restrained by few inhibitions.
His strengths and weaknesses were sufficient to complement each other.
I love and respect him,
but I do not wish for my son to admire him.
Rèn Zhāoxiān of Lè'ān
was pure and simple, and he practiced the Dao.
He was inwardly astute and outwardly forgiving,
modest and yielding.
He did not shun lowly positions,
was timid yet righteously brave,
and forgot himself when serving at court.
I befriended him and praised his goodness,
and I wish for my son to follow him.
If you can draw lessons from these
and extend them by analogy,
you might just grasp one corner
of the whole.
As for his use of wealth, he prioritized his nine generations of relatives;
as for his charity, he made sure to relieve the urgent needs;
as for his comings and goings, he remembered old friends;
as for his discussions, he valued avoiding disparagement;
as for his advancement in office, he esteemed loyalty and integrity;
as for his selection of people, he aimed for practical conduct;
as for his conduct in the world, he guarded against arrogance and indulgence;
as for his poverty and low status, he was careful not to be sorrowful;
as for his advancement and retreat, he considered what was appropriate;
as for his actions, he applied the nine considerations.
If you do
this,
what more do I have to worry about?
In the fourth year of Qīnglóng,
an edict
stated, "We seek those with talent and literary skill,
with profound deliberation and foresight,
who can see the distant as if it were near,
perceive keenly even in dimness,
whose plans are never in vain,
whose strategies are never fruitlessly deployed,
who are upright and meticulous,
pure, refined, and serene,
diligently tireless,
and whose aspirations are for the public good.
Their age shall not be limited,
nor their social status restricted.
All officials from Qīng and Xiào upwards shall each recommend one person."
The Grand Commandant Sīmǎ Xuānwáng nominated Chǎng for selection.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign,
he was transferred to Xúzhōu,
ennobled as Marquis of Wǔguān Tíng,
and promoted to General Who Conquers the South,
granted the imperial credential (jié) and made Grand Supervisor of all military affairs in Jīngzhōu and Yùzhōu.
Chǎng believed that a state has a constant army,
but battles have no constant victor;
territory has constant strategic points,
but defense has no constant strength.
Currently, the troops are garrisoned at Wǎn,
over three hundred lǐ from Xiāngyáng,
the armies are scattered,
and the boats are at Xuānchí.
In an emergency, they would be unable to assist each other.
He therefore memorialized to move the administrative center to Xīnyě,
train the navy in the two prefectures,
expand agricultural cultivation,
and fill the granaries with grain.
In the early Jiāpíng reign,
after the Grand Tutor Sīmǎ Xuānwáng had executed Cáo Shuǎng,
he memorialized to broadly solicit opinions from senior ministers regarding gains and losses in governance.
Chǎng presented five strategic points for governance: First,
to uphold the Dao and earnestly promote learning,
suppressing ostentation and superficiality,
and making state sons enter the Grand Academy to cultivate their studies.
Second,
to implement examinations,
for examinations are like a carpenter's square and compass.
No one can abandon the square and compass and still judge straightness or crookedness by mere intention,
nor can one abolish promotion and demotion and idly discuss ability.
Third,
to ensure that officials remain in their posts for a long time,
and if they achieve good administrative results, they should be promoted and granted titles.
Fourth,
to streamline official positions and solidify salaries,
motivating officials with integrity and shame,
and preventing them from competing with the common people for profit.
Fifth,
to eliminate extravagance and waste,
diligently promote frugality,
ensure that clothing has regulations,
that there is a clear distinction between superior and inferior,
store grain and accumulate silk,
and restore the people to simplicity.
The imperial edict praised him.
Consequently, he was tasked with compiling a document on the evaluation of all officials.
Chǎng believed that although Táng and Yú had documents on promotion and demotion,
the method of evaluation was not passed down.
The system of the Duke Regent (Zhǒngzǎi) in the Zhōu dynasty
was to greatly assess the administration of all officials and then reward or punish,
but it also lacked a system for comparison.
From this, it can be said
that sagely rulers were clear in appointing the worthy,
briefly outlining the principles of promotion and demotion,
delegating this to the heads of high-ranking officials,
and supervising the overall governance.
Thus, ability could be known.
This was the general purport.
In the second year,
Chǎng memorialized:
“Sūn Quán has exiled worthy ministers,
and there is contention between his legitimate and illegitimate sons.
We can seize this opportunity to control Wú and Shǔ.
Between Báidì and Yílíng,
Qián, Wū, Zǐguī, and Fánglíng are all north of the Jiāng River.
Their people, both Hàn and non-Hàn, border Xīnchéng Commandery.
They can be taken by surprise attack.”
So Xīnchéng Administrator Zhōu Tài was dispatched to attack Wū, Zǐguī, and Fánglíng by surprise.
Jīngzhōu Inspector Wáng Jī proceeded to Yílíng,
and Chǎng went to Jiānglíng.
They stretched bamboo ropes across both banks to form a bridge,
crossed the water, and attacked.
The bandits fled to the south bank,
dug seven tunnels, and attacked simultaneously.
Thereupon, Chǎng ordered multiple crossbows to fire all at once.
The bandit general Shī Jì fled into Jiānglíng city by night.
They pursued and beheaded several hundred.
Chǎng wanted to draw them out to the open ground for a pitched battle.
So he first sent five armies to return along the main road,
allowing the bandits to see them and be pleased.
With the captured armor, horses, and enemy heads,
he galloped around the city to provoke them,
and set up ambush troops to await them.
Shī Jì indeed pursued the army,
engaged in battle,
and was defeated.
Shī Jì fled,
and his generals Zhōnglí Mào and Xǔ Mín were beheaded.
Their armor, heads, flags, drums, treasures, and weapons were seized.
The army returned triumphant.
Wáng Jī and Zhōu Tài both rendered meritorious service.
Thereupon, Chǎng was promoted to General-in-Chief Who Conquers the South, with the honors of the Three Ducal Ministers,
and advanced to the peerage of Jīnglíng Hóu.
When Wúqiū Jiǎn and Wén Qīn rebelled,
Chǎng led troops to resist Jiǎn and Qīn with merit,
and his two sons were enfeoffed as Tínghóu and Guānnèihóu.
Chǎng was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry.
When Zhūgě Dàn rebelled,
Chǎng occupied Jiáshí to press Jiānglíng,
preventing Shī Jì and Quán Xī from moving eastward.
After Dàn was executed,
an imperial edict stated:
“In ancient times, Sūn Bìn assisted Zhào,
directly advancing to Dàliáng.
The rapid advance of the western army
also contributed to the success of the eastern expedition.”
His enfeoffment was increased by one thousand households,
making a total of four thousand seven hundred households.
He was promoted to Minister of Works,
retaining his imperial staff and governorship as before.
He died in the fourth year of Gānlù,
and was posthumously named Mùhóu.
His son Hún succeeded him,
and during the Xiánxī era, served as Commandant of Yùqí Cavalry.
Wáng Jī, courtesy name Bóyú,
was a native of Qǔchéng, Dōnglái.
He was orphaned young,
and lived with his uncle Wēng.
Wēng nurtured him with great devotion,
and Jī was also known for his filial piety.
At seventeen,
the commandery summoned him to be an official,
but it was not to his liking,
so he left
and traveled to Lángyá Commandery to study.
During the Huángchū era,
he was identified as a filial and incorrupt official,
and appointed Lángzhōng.
At this time, Qīngzhōu had just been pacified.
Inspector Wáng Líng specially memorialized to request Jī as his Chief Clerk.
Later, he was summoned to be Secretary of the Secretariat,
but Líng again requested his return.
After a while,
Minister of Education Wáng Lǎng invited Jī to serve,
but Líng did not send him.
Lǎng wrote to impeach the province, saying:
“Generally, excellent household retainers
rise to public service, and excellent public servants
enter royal employ.
Therefore, in ancient times, marquises and earls had the rite of presenting scholars.
Now for a province to take a minister from the imperial guard
and retain an official from the imperial archives
is rarely heard of.”
Líng still did not send him.
Líng was renowned in Qīngzhōu,
which was likely due to Jī’s harmonious assistance.
The General-in-Chief Sīmǎ Xuānwáng invited Jī to serve,
but before he arrived,
he was promoted to Central Secretariat Attendant.
Emperor Míng vigorously constructed palaces,
causing the common people great hardship and exhaustion.
Jī submitted a memorial stating:
“I have heard that the ancients compared the people to water,
saying: ‘Water can carry a boat,
but also overturn it.’
Therefore, those above the people
must not fail to be cautious and fearful.
If the people are at ease, their thoughts are easily changed;
if they suffer, they contemplate difficulties.
Therefore, the former kings governed them with frugality
so that they would not generate trouble.
In the past, Yán Yuān said of Dōngyězǐ’s charioteering
that the horses' strength was exhausted, yet he demanded continued progress,
which is how he knew he would fail.
Now, service and labor are arduous and bitter;
men and women are separated and desolate.
I pray Your Majesty deeply consider the folly of Dōngyě
and heed the analogy of the boat and water.
Rest the galloping steeds before they are completely spent,
and moderate labor before the people are completely exhausted.
In ancient Hàn, when it possessed the empire,
by the time of Emperor Xiàowén, there were only feudal lords of the imperial clan,
yet Jiǎ Yì worried, saying:
‘To place fire beneath a stack of firewood and sleep upon it,
and then call it safe.’
Now, the bandits are not yet eliminated,
and fierce generals command troops.
To restrain them would mean no means to counter the enemy;
to prolong this would make it difficult to bequeath to posterity.
In this era of brilliant enlightenment,
if efforts are not made to eliminate dangers,
then if descendants are not strong,
it will be a sorrow for the altars of soil and grain.
If Jiǎ Yì were to rise again,
he would certainly be more deeply concerned than in his time.”
The Cavalry Regular Attendant Wáng Sù compiled commentaries on various classics and histories and revised court rituals,
changing Zhèng Xuán’s old interpretations.
However, Jī upheld Zhèng Xuán’s interpretations
and often contended with him.
He was promoted to Administrator of Ānpíng,
but lost his office due to public affairs.
General-in-Chief Cái Shuǎng invited him to be his Senior Clerk,
and he was later appointed Administrator of Ānfēng.
His commandery bordered the Wú bandits,
and his governance was pure and strict, with both authority and benevolence.
He established clear defenses,
and the enemy dared not invade.
He was given the additional title of General Who Suppresses Bandits.
Wú once raised a large army and gathered at Jiànyè,
claiming they intended to attack Yángzhōu.
Inspector Zhūgě Dàn asked Jī for a strategy.
Jī said:
“In the past, Sūn Quán twice went to Héfèi,
and once to Jiāngxià.
Later, Quán Cóng went out to Lújiāng,
and Zhū Rán attacked Xiāngyáng,
all returning without success.
Now, Lù Xùn and others are dead,
and Quán is old.
Internally, he has no worthy successor;
among his advisors, he has no strategists.
If Quán himself goes out, he fears internal strife might suddenly arise,
like an abscess bursting;
if he sends generals, his old generals are all gone,
and his new generals are not yet trusted.
This is merely an attempt to consolidate his factions
and protect himself.”
Afterward, Quán indeed could not go out.
At that time, Cái Shuǎng held exclusive power,
and moral customs declined.
Jī wrote 'Shíyàolùn' to criticize contemporary affairs.
He was recalled due to illness,
and appointed Hénán Yǐn without initial posting.
Before he was formally installed,
Cáo Shuǎng was executed.
Jī had served as Cáo Shuǎng’s subordinate official,
and was dismissed according to regulations.
That year, he served as a Shàngshū.
He was sent out as the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu,
and given the title of Yángliè Jiāngjūn.
He accompanied Zhēngnán Wáng Chǎng in attacking Wú.
Jī separately attacked Bù Xié at Yílíng.
Xié closed his gates and defended himself.
Jī feigned an attack,
but in reality, he divided his troops to capture Xióngfù’s storehouses,
collecting over 300,000 hú of rice,
capturing Ānběi Jiāngjūn Tán Zhèng,
and receiving the surrender of several thousand people.
Thereupon, he relocated these surrendered people
and established Yílíng Xiàn.
He was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
Jī also memorialized to fortify Shàng Chǎng,
moving its administration to Jiāngxià,
to press against Xiàkǒu.
Because of this, the rebels dared not lightly cross the river.
He clarified institutions,
reorganized the army and agriculture,
and concurrently reformed schools.
The South praised him.
At that time, the court deliberated on attacking Wú,
and an imperial edict ordered Jī to assess the suitability of an advance.
Jī replied:
“If an army moves without achieving success,
its prestige will be diminished externally,
and its resources exhausted internally.
Therefore, it must be fully prepared before being deployed.
If we do not provision for the preparations of water battles, connecting waterways, and accumulating grain,
then even if we amass troops within the Jiāng,
we will have no certainty of crossing.
Currently, Jiānglíng has the Jǔ and Zhāng rivers,
which irrigate thousands of fertile fields.
Around Ānlù,
there are vast, rich ponds.
If we farm both by land and water
to fill military provisions,
then lead troops to Jiānglíng and Yílíng,
divide to occupy Xiàkǒu,
and follow the Jǔ and Zhāng rivers,
transporting grain by water downstream.
When the rebels know that the imperial army has the potential for a prolonged campaign,
those resisting heavenly punishment will be dispirited,
and those inclining towards royal transformation will become more steadfast.
Then, we can gather the barbarians and Yi to attack them from within,
and use elite soldiers and strong troops to strike them from without.
Then, everything above Xiàkǒu will certainly be captured,
and the commanderies outside the Jiāng will not be held.
If this happens,
the connection between Wú and Shǔ will be severed.
With the connection severed, Wú will be captured.
Otherwise,
the advantage of deploying troops cannot be guaranteed.”
Thereupon, the plan was abandoned.
When Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng newly took charge of the government,
Jī wrote to warn him, saying:
“The world is vast,
and state affairs are exceedingly numerous.
One must truly be cautious and diligent,
not sitting idly awaiting dawn.
If one’s will is righteous, all evil will not arise.
If one’s mind is calm, all matters will not be agitated.
If thoughts and deliberations are careful and steady, decrees will not be numerous.
If loyal and good people are personally employed, those near and far will submit in harmony.
Thus, know that harmony in distant places lies in oneself,
and settling the masses lies in the mind.
Xǔ Yǔn, Fù Guǎ, Yuán Kǎn, and Cuī Zàn were all upright gentlemen of their time,
possessing honest character and no wavering mind.
They can be associated with in governing affairs.”
Jǐngwáng accepted his words.
When Gāoguì Xiānggōng ascended the throne,
Jī was promoted and enfeoffed as Chánglè Tínghóu.
When Wúqiū Jiǎn and Wén Qīn rebelled,
Jī was made Xíng Jiānjūn, given jiǎjié,
and commanded the Xǔchāng army.
He coincidentally met Jǐngwáng at Xǔchāng.
Jǐngwáng asked:
“What is your assessment of Jiǎn and his group?”
Jī replied:
“The rebellion in Huáinán
is not because the officials and people desire chaos,
but because Jiǎn and others have deceived, coerced, and intimidated them,
making them fear immediate execution.
That is why they are still gathered.
If a large army presses upon them,
they will certainly collapse like crumbling earth and shattered tiles.
The heads of Jiǎn and Qīn
will be hung at the army gate before the morning is over.”
Jǐngwáng said:
“Excellent.”
Then he ordered Jī to lead the vanguard.
The deliberators all believed that Jiǎn and Qīn were fierce and brave,
difficult to contend with.
An imperial edict ordered Jī to halt.
Jī thought:
“Jiǎn and his group have enough troops to penetrate deeply,
but their prolonged inaction shows that their deception has been exposed,
and the morale of their followers is doubtful and disheartened.
Now, if we do not display our might to meet the people’s expectations,
but halt our army and build high fortifications,
it will appear cowardly,
which is not the way to employ troops.
If they were to plunder the populace,
and if soldiers from prefectures and commanderies were captured by the rebels,
they would become disloyal.
Those coerced by Jiǎn and his group,
feeling their guilt is heavy,
would not dare to return.
This would be deploying troops ineffectively,
and fostering the source of traitors.
If the Wú bandits take advantage of this,
then Huáinán will no longer belong to the state,
and Qiáo, Pèi, Rǔ, and Yù will be in danger and unrest.
This is a major strategic error.
The army should quickly advance to occupy Nándùn.
Nándùn has large storehouses,
estimated to hold forty days’ rations for the troops.
Holding a strong city
and relying on accumulated grain,
to preemptively seize the enemy’s will,
this is the key to pacifying the rebels.”
Jī repeatedly requested,
and finally was permitted to advance and occupy Shuǐ.
Upon arrival,
he spoke again, saying:
“I have heard of clumsy speed in warfare,
but never of skillful prolonged delay.
Currently, there are strong invaders externally,
and rebellious ministers internally.
If we do not decide in a timely manner,
the depth of the situation cannot be measured.
Many deliberators wish for the general to act cautiously.
It is right for the general to act cautiously,
but halting the army and not advancing is wrong.
Acting cautiously does not mean not advancing;
it means advancing such that one cannot be attacked.
Now, to hold a strong city
and maintain fortifications,
while providing ample resources to the enemy,
and transporting military provisions over a distance,
is very ill-advised.”
Jǐngwáng wished to wait for all the armies to assemble,
and still did not grant permission.
Jī said:
“When a general is in the field,
there are orders from the sovereign that may not be followed.
If they get it, it’s advantageous for them;
if we get it, it’s advantageous for us.
This is called contesting a city,
and Nándùn is such a case.”
So, he immediately advanced and occupied Nándùn.
Jiǎn and his group, from Xiàng, also desired to go there,
but after advancing more than ten *lǐ*,
they heard that Jī had arrived first,
and returned to secure Xiàng.
At that time, Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Dèng Ài was stationed at Lèjiā.
Jiǎn sent Wén Qīn with troops to attack Ài.
Jī, knowing their forces were divided,
advanced his troops to press Xiàng,
and Jiǎn’s forces were consequently defeated.
After Qīn and others were pacified,
he was promoted to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn,
Dūdū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì,
and concurrently Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and further enfeoffed as Ānlè Xiānghóu.
He submitted a memorial requesting to divide 200 households
and grant his uncle’s son, Zǐqiáo, the title of Guānnèi Hóu,
to repay his uncle’s kindness of raising him.
An imperial edict specifically allowed this.
Zhūgě Dàn rebelled.
Jī, retaining his original office, acted as General Who Guards the East,
and Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yáng and Yù provinces.
At that time, the main army was in Xiàng.
Considering the enemy troops were elite,
an imperial edict ordered Jī to gather his troops and fortify the camp.
Jī repeatedly submitted petitions requesting to advance and attack.
Coincidentally, Wú sent Zhū Yì to rescue Dàn,
and he garrisoned at Ānchéng.
Jī then received an edict to lead all armies to relocate and occupy Běishān.
Jī said to his generals:
"Now our encircling fortifications are increasingly solid,
and our troops and horses are gathering.
We should simply meticulously prepare our defenses and await their overextension.
If we instead move our troops to guard strategic points,
allowing them to act freely,
even a wise person would not be able to handle the aftermath well."
So, acting on what was expedient, he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Now that we are facing the enemy,
we must remain as unmoving as a mountain.
If we move to rely on strategic positions,
people's hearts will waver,
which would greatly harm our advantage.
All armies are occupying deep trenches and high fortifications;
everyone's resolve is firm
and cannot be shaken.
This is the essence of deploying troops."
The memorial was presented,
and his request was granted.
The Grand General Sīmǎ Wénwáng advanced his camp to Qiūtóu,
dividing his forces to besiege and guard,
each having its own command.
Jī defended the twenty-six armies on the east and south sides of the city.
Wénwáng commanded his military officials not to send
even a single person into the southern command area.
Inside the city, food ran out,
and they attacked the fortifications day and night.
Jī repeatedly repelled and defeated them.
After Shòuchūn was captured,
Wénwáng wrote to Jī, saying:
"Initially, many people offered various opinions,
and many sought to relocate.
At the time, not having personally experienced it,
I also thought it seemed appropriate.
General, you deeply calculated the advantages and disadvantages,
and single-handedly held firm to your resolve,
disregarding imperial edicts above,
and resisting public opinion below.
Ultimately, you managed to control the enemy and capture the rebels.
Even what ancient people described
was not superior to this."
Wénwáng wanted to send generals with light troops deep into enemy territory,
to summon and welcome the sons and younger brothers of Táng Zī and others,
and thereby exploit the weakness to overthrow Wú.
Jī advised:
"In the past, Zhūgě Kè, taking advantage of the victory at Dōngguān,
exhausted the troops of the Jiāngbiǎo region
to besiege Xīnchéng.
The city was not captured,
and more than half of his troops died.
Jiāng Wéi, capitalizing on the advantage at Táoshàng,
advanced deep with light troops.
His supplies were insufficient,
and his army was defeated at Shàngguī.
Indeed, after a great victory,
superiors and subordinates alike become complacent regarding the enemy.
When one is complacent about the enemy, one does not deeply consider difficulties.
Now, the enemy has just suffered defeat externally,
and internal troubles have not yet been quelled.
This is the time for them to repair their defenses and make plans.
Furthermore, our troops have been deployed for over a year,
and people have a desire to return home.
Now, we have captured and beheaded a hundred thousand,
and the culprits have been apprehended.
Throughout the generations of campaigns and conquests,
there has never been such a grand achievement where an entire army was preserved and a unique victory achieved, as we have now.
Emperor Wǔ defeated Yuán Shào at Guāndù.
He considered what he had gained was already much,
and did not pursue the fleeing enemy,
fearing it would diminish his prestige."
Wénwáng then stopped.
As Huáinán had just been pacified,
Jī was transferred to be General Who Conquers the East,
Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yángzhōu,
and was promoted to Marquis of Dōngwǔ.
Jī submitted a memorial firmly declining,
attributing the merits to his assistants and staff.
As a result, seven people, including the Chief Clerk and Sīmǎ, all became marquises.
In this year,
Jī's mother passed away.
An edict ordered her death notice to be kept secret,
and Jī's father Bào's coffin was brought to be buried with her in Luòyáng.
Bào was posthumously granted the title of Grand Administrator of Běihǎi.
In Gānlù fourth year,
he was transferred to be General Who Conquers the South,
Supervisor of Military Affairs of Jīngzhōu.
When Chángdào Xiānggōng ascended the throne,
his fief was increased by a thousand households,
making a total of five thousand seven hundred households.
Previously and subsequently, two of his sons were enfeoffed as Marquis of a Pavilion and Marquis Within the Passes.
In Jǐngyuán second year,
the Grand Administrator of Xiāngyáng memorialized that Wú rebels Dèng Yóu and others wished to surrender and assimilate.
Jī received an edict that he should use this opportunity to shake the Jiāngbiǎo region.
Jī suspected it was a trick,
and immediately sent an urgent message to state the situation.
He also said:
"Since Jiāpíng,
there have been repeated internal difficulties.
The current priority
is to stabilize the state
and pacify the populace.
It is not appropriate to mobilize troops to seek external gains."
Wénwáng replied in a letter, saying:
"In handling affairs,
most people tend to readily comply and agree,
few are able to steadfastly exhaust the true principles.
I am truly moved by your loyalty and affection.
Every time I see your guidance,
I respectfully follow your instructions."
Later, Yóu and others indeed did not surrender.
In this year, Jī died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Sīkōng,
and his posthumous name was Jǐnghóu.
His son Huī succeeded him,
but died young.
During the Xiánxī period,
the five ranks were established.
Because Jī had established meritorious service in the previous dynasty,
his grandson Yì was re-enfeoffed,
and the remaining households of Dōngwǔ were bestowed upon one of his sons with the title of Marquis Within the Passes.
When the Jìn dynasty ascended the throne,
an imperial edict was issued, saying:
"The late Sīkōng Wáng Jī not only displayed virtue and established achievements,
but also conducted himself with purity and integrity,
and did not engage in accumulating property.
Despite holding important responsibilities for a long time,
his household had no private savings.
He can be said to have had a distinguished career even after his death,
and is worthy of inspiring the public.
Therefore, bestow two slaves upon his family."
A commentary states: Xú Máo was pure, noble, and broad-minded;
Hú Zhì was inherently upright and refined;
Wáng Chǎng was capable of initiating and assisting with discernment;
Wáng Jī's learning and conduct were firm and clear.
All held important responsibilities,
and left behind renowned achievements.
They can be called excellent ministers of the state
and outstanding scholars of their time.
Biography of Wáng, Wúqiū, Zhūgě, Dèng, and Zhōng, Chapter Twenty-Eight.
Wáng Líng, courtesy name Yàn Yún,
was a native of Qí in Tàiyuán.
His uncle Yǔn
served as Hàn Sītú and executed Dǒng Zhuó.
Zhuó's generals Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì, and others sought revenge for Zhuó,
entered Cháng'ān,
killed Yǔn,
and annihilated his entire family.
Líng and his elder brother Chén,
both young at the time,
escaped by climbing over the city walls
and fled back to their hometown.
Líng was recommended as Xiàolián,
became Magistrate of Fāgān,
and was gradually promoted to Grand Administrator of Zhōngshān.
Wherever he served, he governed well.
Tàizǔ invited him to be a subordinate of the Chancellor.
When Wén Dì 踐阼,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì.
He was then dispatched as Yǎnbóu Cìshǐ
and, with Zhāng Liáo and others, went to Guǎnglíng to attack Sūn Quán.
When they reached the river,
a great wind arose during the night.
The Wu general Lü Fàn and others' boats were blown to the north bank.
Líng and the generals counterattacked,
capturing and beheading many,
and seizing boats.
For his merits,
he was enfeoffed as Yí chéng Tínghóu,
given the additional title of Jiànwǔ Jiàngjūn,
and then transferred to Qīngzhōu.
At this time, after the chaos of mourning and war, the coastal areas
had not yet fully restored their laws and order.
Líng implemented policies and spread teachings,
rewarding good and punishing evil,
which created great discipline.
The common people praised him
without reservation.
Later, he followed Cáo Xiū on a campaign against Wu
and encountered the enemy at Jiáshí.
Xiū's army suffered a defeat,
but Líng fought bravely, breaking through the encirclement,
and Xiū was able to escape danger.
He was then transferred to be Yáng and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and he gained the affection of both the military and the populace.
Upon first arriving in Yùzhōu,
he honored the descendants of former worthies
and sought out undiscovered talents.
He issued various regulations and instructions,
the intent of which was excellent.
Initially,
