Líng was good friends with Sīmǎ Láng and Jiǎ Kuí.
When he oversaw Yǎn and Yù,
he continued their excellent legacy.
At the beginning of Zhèngshǐ era,
he was appointed Zhēngdōng Jiàngjūn,
granted the imperial credential (jié) and acted as Inspector-General of all military affairs in Yángzhōu.
In the second year,
the great Wu general Quán Cóng, with tens of thousands of troops, raided Sháopō.
Líng led his armies to counterattack,
contending with the enemy over the embankment.
After several days of fierce fighting,
the enemy retreated.
He was promoted and enfeoffed as Nánxiāng Hóu,
with an estate of 1,350 households,
and promoted to Chējì Jiàngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī.
At this time,
Líng's nephew, Lìnghú Yú, due to his talent, was appointed Yǎnbóu Cìshǐ
and stationed at Píng'ā.
Both uncle and nephew commanded troops,
wielding significant power in Huáinán.
Líng was then promoted to Sīkōng.
After Sīmǎ Xuānwáng executed Cáo Shuǎng,
he further promoted Líng to Tàiwèi,
granted him the jié [⿰金戊].
Líng and Yú secretly conspired,
believing that Qí Wáng was unfit for the throne
and that Chǔ Wáng Biāo was older and talented.
They wanted to welcome and establish Biāo as emperor, making Xǔchāng the capital.
In the ninth month of Jiāpíng first year,
Yú sent his general Zhāng Shì to Báimǎ
to communicate with Biāo.
Líng also sent his attendant Láo Jīng to Luòyáng
to speak with his son Guǎng.
Guǎng said:
"The matter of deposing and establishing an emperor is grave;
do not be the first to bring disaster."
In the eleventh month,
Yú again sent Shì to Biāo.
Before Shì returned,
Yú fell ill and died.
In the second year,
the planet Mars (Yínghuò) stayed in the Southern Dipper (Nándǒu).
Líng said:
"A star in the Dipper indicates an imminent rise of an unexpectedly noble person."
In the spring of the third year,
Wu bandits blocked the Tūshuǐ River.
Líng wanted to use this as an opportunity to launch his plan,
so he made extensive preparations for his armies,
memorializing the emperor to request an attack on the bandits;
the imperial edict replied, denying his request.
Líng's secret plot intensified.
He sent General Yáng Hóng to inform Yǎnbóu Cìshǐ Huáng Huá about the plan to depose and establish an emperor.
Huá and Hóng jointly reported this to Tàifù Sīmǎ Xuānwáng.
Xuānwáng led the central army by water to attack Líng,
first issuing an amnesty to pardon Líng's crimes.
He also took Shàngshū Guǎngdōng,
and had him write a letter to persuade Líng.
The main army swiftly arrived, pressing Líng at Bǎichǐ.
Líng, realizing his position was hopeless,
boarded a boat alone to meet Xuānwáng,
sending his clerk Wáng Yù to apologize,
and surrendering his seal, sash, and jié [⿰金戊].
When the army reached Qiūtóu,
Líng stood by the water, with his hands bound.
Xuānwáng, following the imperial edict, sent his chief clerk to untie him and restore his clothing.
He met Líng,
comforted him,
returned his seal, sash, and jié [⿰金戊],
and sent six hundred cavalry and infantry to escort him back to the capital.
When Líng reached Xiàng,
he drank poison and died.
Xuānwáng then proceeded to Shòuchūn.
Zhāng Shì and others all surrendered,
and then the matter was thoroughly investigated.
Biāo was granted death,
and all those implicated had their three familial clans exterminated.
The imperial court universally held that according to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Qí Cuī Zhù and Zhèng Guī Shēng were both posthumously punished,
their corpses exposed and their coffins hewn open,
and recorded in historical annals.
Líng and Yú's crimes deserved the same old punishment.
Thus, Líng and Yú's tombs were opened,
their coffins broken open,
and their corpses exposed in a nearby market for three days.
Their seals, sashes, and court robes were burned,
and their bodies were then buried in the earth.
Hóng and Huá were promoted to the rank of Xiānghóu.
Guǎng had noble aspirations and scholarly conduct;
he died at the age of over forty.
Wúqiū Jiǎn, courtesy name Zhònggōng,
was from Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
His father, Xīng,
was Wǔwēi Tàishǒu during the Huángchū era.
He attacked rebels and pacified the insubordinate,
opening up the Hexi Corridor,
his reputation ranking alongside that of Jīnchéng Tàishǒu Sū Zé.
He had achievements in suppressing the bandit Zhāng Jìn and in subduing rebellious Hú tribes,
and was enfeoffed as Gāoyáng Xiānghóu.
He entered the court as Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
Jiǎn inherited his father's noble title
and served as Píngyuán Hóu Wénxué.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he served as Shàngshū Láng,
and was promoted to Yǔlín Jiān.
Due to his former association with the Eastern Palace,
he was greatly trusted and favored.
He was dispatched as Luòyáng Diǎnnóng.
At that time, farmers were conscripted to build palaces.
Jiǎn submitted a memorial saying:
"Your humble servant believes that the two most urgent matters for the empire are to eliminate the two bandits,
and the most urgent necessity is clothing and food.
If the two bandits are not eliminated,
and the soldiers and common people are hungry and cold,
then even if magnificent palaces are erected,
it would still be of no benefit."
He was promoted to Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
During the Qīnglóng era,
the emperor planned to attack Liáodōng.
Because Jiǎn had strategic talent,
he was transferred to be Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ,
given the additional title of Dùliáo Jiàngjūn,
made to hold the imperial credential (jié),
and acted as Protector of the Wūhuán.
He led the Yōuzhōu armies to Xiāngpíng
and garrisoned at Liáosuì.
The Wūhuán Chányú Kòulóu Dūn of Yòuběipíng, and the Wūhuán Dūdū of Liáoxī, Shuàizhòng Wáng Hùliú and others,
who had previously followed Yuán Shàng in fleeing to Liáodōng,
led over five thousand people to surrender.
Kòulóu Dūn sent his brother Āluópán and others to the imperial court to pay tribute.
Over twenty of their chieftains were enfeoffed as Hóu and Wáng,
and given carriages, horses, silk, and brocade, each according to their rank.
Gōngsūn Yuān engaged Jiǎn in battle but
was unsuccessful and
withdrew.
The next year,
the emperor sent Tàiwèi Sīmǎ Xuānwáng to command the central army and Jiǎn's troops, numbering tens of thousands, to attack Yuān,
thereby pacifying Liáodōng.
For his merits, Jiǎn was further enfeoffed as Ānyì Hóu,
with an estate of 3,900 households.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign,
Jiǎn, because Gāogōulí repeatedly invaded and rebelled,
led an army of ten thousand infantry and cavalry out of Xuántú,
attacking them from various routes.
King Gōng of Gōulí led two myriad infantry and cavalry,
advanced his army to the Fèiliú River,
and fought a great battle at Liángkǒu.
(Liáng sounds like Kē.)
Gōng was repeatedly defeated and fled.
Jiǎn then tied up his horses and hung his chariots
to ascend Wándū.
He massacred the capital of Gōulí
and captured thousands of heads and captives.
Gōulí's Pèizhě named Délái
repeatedly admonished Gōng,
but Gōng did not follow his advice.
Délái sighed, saying:
"I will live to see this land overgrown with mugwort."
He then refused to eat and died,
and the whole country esteemed him.
Jiǎn ordered his armies not to damage Délái's tomb
or cut down his trees.
When his wife and children were captured,
all were released.
Gōng fled alone with his wife and children.
Jiǎn withdrew his army.
Six years later,
he again campaigned against him.
Gōng then fled to Mǎgōu.
Jiǎn sent Wáng Qí, the Administrator of Xuántú, to pursue him.
Wáng Qí traveled over a thousand li past Wòjū,
reached the southern border of the Sùshèn people,
carved a stone to record his achievements,
inscribed the mountain of Wándū,
and engraved the city of Bùnài.
The total number of people killed or captured was over eight thousand.
Rewards were distributed based on merit,
and over a hundred people were enfeoffed as marquises.
Mountains were pierced to provide irrigation,
and the people benefited from it.
He was promoted to General of the Left,
granted a tally of authority and made Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Yùzhōu,
and concurrently Inspector of Yùzhōu.
He was then transferred to General of the South.
When Zhūgě Dàn fought at Dōngguān
and suffered a defeat,
Dàn and Jiǎn were ordered to swap positions.
Dàn became General of the South
and Area Commander of Yùzhōu.
Jiǎn became General of the East
and Area Commander of Yángzhōu.
When Zhūgě Kè, Grand Tutor of Wú, besieged Xīnchéng in Héféi,
Jiǎn and Wén Qīn resisted him.
Sīmǎ Fú, Grand Commandant, led the central army eastward to relieve the siege,
and Kè retreated.
Initially,
Jiǎn was on good terms with Xiàhóu Xuán, Lǐ Fēng, and others.
Wén Qīn, Inspector of Yángzhōu and former General,
was a native of Cáo Shuǎng's district.
He was fierce and brave,
and had repeatedly achieved military successes.
He was fond of exaggerating his captures
to seek favor and rewards,
but often his claims were not accepted,
and his resentment grew daily.
Jiǎn treated Qīn generously through stratagem,
and their relationship became amicable and joyful.
Qīn was also grateful
and devoted himself without reservation.
In the first month of the second year of Zhèngyuán (255 CE),
a comet, dozens of zhàng long,
stretched across the sky in the northwest,
originating from the region of Wú and Chǔ.
Jiǎn and Qīn rejoiced,
believing it to be an auspicious sign for them.
They then forged an imperial edict from the Empress Dowager,
accusing Grand General Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng of crimes,
sent it to various commanderies and states,
and raised an army in rebellion.
They coerced and threatened the generals and administrators of Huáinán who were guarding various separate garrisons,
as well as officials and common people, young and old,
to all enter Shòuchūn city.
They built an altar west of the city,
drank blood and pledged allegiance, raising an army.
They assigned the old and weak to defend the city,
while Jiǎn and Qīn personally led fifty to sixty thousand troops across the Huái River,
advancing west to Xiàng.
Jiǎn held a strong defense,
while Qīn acted as a mobile force outside.
The Grand General commanded the central and outer armies to suppress them.
He separately sent Zhūgě Dàn to supervise the Yùzhōu armies from Ānfēngjīn to approach Shòuchūn.
Hú Zūn, General who Conquers the East, supervised the Qīng and Xú armies to emerge between Qiáo and Sòng,
cutting off their return route.
The Grand General encamped at Rǔyáng
and sent Wáng Jī, Supervisor of the Army, to lead the vanguard to hold Nándùn and await them.
All armies were ordered to fortify their positions and not engage in battle.
Jiǎn and Qīn could not advance to fight,
and feared that Shòuchūn would be attacked if they retreated,
preventing their return.
They were at their wit's end, not knowing what to do.
The generals and soldiers of Huáinán
all had their homes in the north,
and their morale was low and scattered.
Defectors came in succession;
only the recently attached peasants of Huáinán fought for them.
The Grand General sent Dèng Ài, Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, to lead over ten thousand troops from Tàishān to Lèjiā,
feigning weakness to lure them.
The Grand General then arrived from Zhū.
Qīn, unaware,
indeed came that night, intending to raid Ài and others.
At dawn,
seeing the great army's strength,
he retreated.
The Grand General unleashed his swift cavalry in pursuit,
utterly defeating him.
Qīn fled.
That day,
Jiǎn, hearing of Qīn's defeat,
fled in terror during the night,
and his forces disintegrated.
By the time he reached Shèn County,
his attendants and soldiers gradually abandoned Jiǎn and left.
Jiǎn alone, with his younger brother Xiù and grandson Zhòng, hid in the grass by the water.
Zhāng Shǔ, a local commander of Ānfēngjīn, found and shot Jiǎn dead,
sending his head to the capital.
Shǔ was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Xiù and Zhòng fled into Wú.
The generals and soldiers who had been coerced by Jiǎn and Qīn
all surrendered.
Jiǎn's son, Diàn, who was Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat,
had earlier learned of Jiǎn's impending rebellion,
and privately took his family and fled to Líng Mountain in Xīn'ān.
They were attacked and captured separately,
and Jiǎn's three clans were exterminated.
Qīn fled to Wú,
and Wú appointed Qīn as Protector, granted a tally of authority, General Who Guards the North, Governor of Yōuzhōu, and Marquis of Qiáo.
Zhūgě Dàn, courtesy name Gōngxiū,
was from Yángdū, Lángxié,
a descendant of Zhūgě Fēng.
Initially, as a Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat, he became Magistrate of Xíngyáng,
then entered as a Bureau Director in the Ministry of Personnel.
Whenever someone made a recommendation,
he would clearly state it and put it into use.
Later, if it was appropriate or not,
he would publicly discuss its merits and demerits to praise or criticize it.
From then on, none of his colleagues dared not to be cautious in their recommendations.
He was successively promoted to Imperial Censor and Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was on good terms with Xiàhóu Xuán, Dèng Yáng, and others,
gaining renown in court,
and was widely praised in the capital.
Those who spoke on current affairs said that Dàn, Yáng, and others cultivated superficiality,
accumulated false reputations,
and that this trend could not be allowed to grow.
Emperor Míng disliked this
and dismissed Dàn from office.
When the Emperor died,
at the beginning of the Zhèngshǐ reign,
Xuán and others were all in office.
Dàn was again made Imperial Censor and Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat,
and then sent out as Inspector of Yángzhōu,
with the additional title of General who Manifests Martial Prowess.
When Wáng Líng plotted his conspiracy,
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng, Grand Tutor, secretly led an army eastward.
He appointed Dàn as General Who Guards the East, granted him a tally of authority, and made him Area Commander of All Military Affairs in Yángzhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Shānyáng Pavilion.
When Zhūgě Kè started the campaign at Dōngguān,
Dàn was sent to lead the armies to suppress him.
He fought,
but was unsuccessful.
Upon his return,
he was transferred to General of the South.
Later, Wúqiū Jiǎn and Wén Qīn rebelled,
sending envoys to Zhūgě Dàn,
calling upon the gentry and common people of Yùzhōu.
Dàn executed their envoys
and made a public proclamation to the world
to let everyone know of Jiǎn and Qīn's heinous rebellion.
The Grand Marshal Sīmǎ Jǐng Wáng marched eastward,
ordering Dàn to supervise all the armies of Yùzhōu
and cross the Ānfēng Ford towards Shòuchūn.
When Jiǎn and Qīn were defeated,
Dàn arrived at Shòuchūn first.
The population of Shòuchūn, over one hundred thousand,
hearing of Jiǎn and Qīn's defeat,
feared execution,
so they all broke open the city gates and fled,
dispersing into the mountains and marshes,
or some fled into Wú.
Because Dàn had been in Huáinán for a long time,
he was again appointed Grand General of the Pacifying East, bearing the ceremonial insignia of the Three Ducal Ministers, and Supervisor of Yángzhōu.
The Grand Generals of Wú, Sūn Jùn, Lǚ Jù, Liú Zàn, and others, hearing of the chaos in Huáinán,
and coinciding with Wén Qīn's arrival,
led their forces and Qīn directly to Shòuchūn;
at that time, Dàn's armies had already arrived,
and the city could not be attacked,
so they fled.
Dàn sent General Jiǎng Bān to pursue and attack them,
executing Zàn,
sending his head,
and seizing his seal and credentials.
He was promoted to Marquis of Gāopíng,
with three thousand five hundred households as his fief,
and then transferred to General of the Conquering East.
Dàn was already very close to Xuán and Yáng,
and with Wáng Líng and Wúqiū Jiǎn having been exterminated one after another,
he feared for his own safety.
He emptied his treasury and distributed wealth to win over the hearts of the populace,
and generously supported his close associates and several thousand light-hearted swordsmen from Yángzhōu as elite fighters.
In the winter of the first year of Gānlù,
the Wú invaders wanted to advance towards Xúè.
Although it was calculated that the troops Dàn commanded were sufficient to resist them,
he still requested one hundred thousand men to guard Shòuchūn,
and also asked to build fortifications in Línhuái to guard against bandits,
secretly intending to secure Huáinán.
The court subtly perceived Dàn's self-doubting intentions,
but considering Dàn an old minister,
wished to bring him into the capital.
In the fifth month of the second year,
he was summoned to be Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Dàn received the imperial edict,
became even more fearful,
and consequently rebelled.
He summoned his generals
and personally led an attack on Lè Qín, the Inspector of Yángzhōu,
killing him.
He gathered over one hundred thousand official soldiers and settled households from Huáinán and the counties north of the Huái River,
and forty to fifty thousand newly surrendered able-bodied men from Yángzhōu.
He stockpiled enough grain for a year's provisions
and barricaded himself within the city.
He sent his Chief Clerk, Wú Gāng, with his young son Jìng to Wú to request aid.
The people of Wú were greatly pleased
and dispatched Generals Quán Yì, Quán Duān, Táng Zī, Wáng Zuò, and others,
leading thirty thousand men,
who secretly came with Wén Qīn to support Dàn.

They appointed Dàn as Left Protector-General, bearing the imperial credentials, Grand Minister of War (Dà Sītú), General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn), Governor of Qīngzhōu, and Marquis of Shòuchūn.
At this time, Wáng Jī, the General who Guards the South, had just arrived
and was supervising the various armies surrounding Shòuchūn,
but the encirclement was not yet complete.
Zī, Qīn, and others came from the northeast of the city,
taking advantage of the mountains and difficult terrain,
and managed to lead their troops to break into the city.
In the sixth month,
the imperial carriage marched eastward
to Xiàng.
The Grand Marshal Sīmǎ Wén Wáng supervised two hundred sixty thousand troops from both the inner and outer armies,
approaching the Huái River to suppress him.
The Grand Marshal encamped at Qiūtóu.
He ordered Jī and Chén Qiān, the General of the Pacifying East, and others to complete the encirclement from all four sides,
building two layers of defensive walls,
with very steep moats and ramparts.
He also sent Inspector-General Shí Bāo, Inspector of Yǎnzhōu Zhōu Tài, and others
to select elite troops as a mobile force
to guard against external invaders.
Qīn and others repeatedly sallied out to assault the encirclement,
but were repelled.
The Wú general Zhū Yì twice brought large forces to rescue Dàn and others,
crossing the Líjiāng River,
but Tài and others met them in battle,
always breaking their momentum.
Sūn Chěn, angered by Yì's failure to advance,
killed him.
Food in the city became increasingly scarce,
and no outside relief arrived,
leaving the populace with nothing to rely on.
Generals Jiǎng Bān and Jiāo Yí,
both Dàn's trusted advisors,
abandoned Dàn,
climbed over the city wall, and surrendered to the Grand Marshal.
The Grand Marshal then sent counter-agents
who used cunning stratagems to persuade Quán Yì and others,
and Yì and others, leading several thousand men, opened a gate and came out.
The city was shaken with fear,
not knowing what to do.
In the first month of the third year,
Dàn, Qīn, Zī, and others built a great many siege engines,
and for five or six days and nights attacked the southern encirclement,
intending to break through and escape.
The armies on the encirclement, from their high positions, used stone-throwing catapults and fire arrows to burn and destroy their siege engines,
while a rain of crossbow bolts and stones fell,
covering the ground with dead and wounded,
and blood flowing into the moats.
They returned to the city,
where food was becoming exhausted.
Tens of thousands surrendered and came out.
Qīn wanted to expel all the northerners
to conserve food
and hold the city with the Wú people,
but Dàn refused,
which led to a quarrel and resentment.
Qīn had always had a rift with Dàn,
and had only allied with him out of strategy;
as the situation became critical, their mutual suspicion deepened.
Qīn questioned Dàn's plans,
and Dàn then killed Qīn.
Qīn's sons Yāng and Hǔ, who commanded troops in the smaller city,
heard of Qīn's death
and ordered their troops to rush to his aid,
but the troops would not obey them.
Yāng and Hǔ fled alone,
climbed over the city wall,
and surrendered to the Grand Marshal.
The military officials requested their execution,
but the Grand Marshal issued an order saying:
"Qīn's crime deserved execution,
and his sons should indeed be killed.
However, Yāng and Hǔ have surrendered in desperation,
and since the city has not yet fallen,
killing them would only strengthen the resolve of those inside."
So he pardoned Yāng and Hǔ
and sent them with several hundred cavalry to ride around the city,
shouting to those inside:
"Even Wén Qīn's sons are not killed;
what else is there to fear?"
He appointed Yāng and Hǔ as generals
and each granted them the title of Marquis within the Pass.
Those in the city were joyful yet perturbed,
and also suffering daily from hunger.
Dàn, Zī, and others were at their wits' end.
The Grand Marshal then personally oversaw the encirclement,
advancing troops from all four sides,
simultaneously beating drums and shouting as they scaled the city walls.
No one inside the city dared to move.
Dàn, in despair,
rode a single horse and led his personal guard to burst out through a small city gate.
Sīmǎ Hú Fèn, a general under the Grand Marshal, intercepted and attacked them,
beheading Dàn,
sending his head,
and exterminating his three clans.
Several hundred of Dàn's personal guard,
who refused to surrender, were executed,
all saying:
"To die for Duke Zhūgě,
we have no regrets."
Such was his hold on people's hearts.
Táng Zī, Wáng Zuò, and other subordinate generals all surrendered with their hands bound,
and the Wú army of ten thousand men,
with their weapons and military supplies, were piled up like mountains.
When Shòuchūn was first surrounded,
many strategists wanted to attack it immediately.
But the Grand Marshal believed:
"The city is strong and its population large;
attacking it will certainly exhaust our forces.
If there is an external invader,
our defensive walls will be attacked on both sides,
which is a dangerous course.
Now, three rebels are gathered together in an isolated city;
perhaps Heaven intends for them to meet their doom together.
I should use a comprehensive strategy to ensnare them,
and then they can be controlled while sitting idle."
Dàn rebelled in the fifth month of the second year
and was defeated and exterminated in the second month of the third year.
The six armies kept their weapons sheathed,
dug deep trenches and built high ramparts,
while Dàn became trapped by his own actions,
and was conquered without the need for an assault.
When Shòuchūn was taken,
strategists again suggested that since Huáinán was repeatedly rebellious,
and the Wú soldiers had their families south of the Jiāng River,
they should not be released,
and all should be buried alive.
The Grand Marshal believed that in ancient warfare,
preserving the enemy's state was paramount,
and only the arch-criminals should be executed.
Even if the Wú soldiers managed to escape and return,
it would only serve to show the generosity of the Central Plains.
Not a single person was killed;
they were distributed among the nearby commanderies of the Three Rivers
and settled peacefully.
Táng Zī (唐咨) was originally from Lìchéng (利城).
In the middle of the Huángchū (黃初) reign,
Lìchéng (利城) Commandery rebelled,
killed the Administrator Xú Jī (徐箕),
and made Zī (咨) their leader.
Emperor Wén (文) dispatched various armies to suppress and defeat them.
Zī (咨) fled into the sea,
and eventually defected to Wú (吳).
He rose to the office of General of the Left,
was enfeoffed as a marquis, and held a tally of authority.
Dàn (誕) and Qīn (欽) were slaughtered,
and Zī (咨) was also captured alive.
All three rebels were apprehended,
and the whole empire rejoiced.
Zī (咨) was appointed General Who Pacifies Afar,
and the other subordinate generals were all granted titles and ranks.
The Wú (吳) populace was pleased and submitted.
The people of Jiāngdōng (江東) were touched by this,
and none of their families were executed.
As for the generals, officials, soldiers, and common people of Huáinán (淮南) who had been coerced or abducted by Dàn (誕),
only their principal leaders of the rebellion were executed;
the rest were all pardoned.
Yāng (鴦) and Hǔ (虎) were allowed to collect Qīn's (欽) corpse,
were provided with carts and oxen,
and were permitted to bury him in his old tomb.
Dèng Ài (鄧艾), courtesy name Shìzài (士載),
was from Jíyáng (棘陽) in Yìyáng (義陽).
He was orphaned young.
When Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ, 太祖) conquered Jīngzhōu (荊州),
Ài (艾) was relocated to Rǔnán (汝南),
where he worked as a farmer raising calves.
At the age of twelve,
he followed his mother to Yǐngchuān (潁川).
He read the inscription on the stele of Chén Shí (陳寔), the former Grand Administrator of Tàiqiū (太丘),
which stated,
"His writings served as a model for the world,
and his conduct as a standard for scholars."
Ài (艾) then named himself Fàn (範) and
styled himself Shìzé (士則).
Later, a relative happened to share the same name,
so he changed it.
He served as an academician of the Area Commander (Dūwèi, 都尉).
Because of his stutter,
he could not be made an assistant official.
He served as an officer guarding overgrown fields for rice paddies.
The father of a fellow commandery official pitied his poverty,
and provided him with generous assistance.
Ài (艾) never expressed gratitude initially.
Whenever he saw high mountains and vast marshes,
he would always measure, plan, and draw sketches of locations for military camps.
Many people at the time laughed at him.
Later, he became a supervisor of agricultural affairs,
and then a chief clerk for tribute.
On a mission, he had an audience with the Grand Commandant Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (司馬宣王).
Xuānwáng (宣王) found him extraordinary,
and appointed him as a clerk (yuán, 掾).
He was promoted to Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
At that time, there was a desire to expand cultivation and store grain
as resources for suppressing rebels.
Ài (艾) was sent to travel from Chén (陳) and Xiàng (項) eastward to Shòuchūn (壽春).
Ài (艾) believed that
"The land is fertile, but water is scarce,
insufficient to fully exploit the land's potential.
It would be advisable to dig canals
to divert water for irrigation,
greatly accumulate military provisions,
and also open up routes for transport by boat."
He then wrote the Jìhé Lùn (濟河論, 'Disquisition on Harnessing the River') to explain his ideas.
He also believed that
"In the past, when the Yellow Turbans were defeated,
agricultural garrisons (túntián, 屯田) were established,
and grain was accumulated in Xǔdū (許都) to control the four directions.
Now that three corners are settled,
the focus is on Huáinán (淮南).
Whenever a large army is raised for an expedition,
over half the soldiers are used for transport,
incurring enormous costs and effort,
which is a major burden.
Between Chén (陳) and Cài (蔡),
the land is low and fertile.
The rice paddies around Xǔchāng (許昌) could be reduced
and their water directed eastward.
Station 20,000 men north of the Huái (淮) and
30,000 men south of the Huái (淮),
with a twelve-part rotation,
constantly maintaining 40,000 men,
who would both farm and guard.
When water is abundant, the harvest would be three times that of the west.
Calculating all expenses removed,
five million hú (斛) could be saved annually as military provisions.
Within six or seven years,
thirty million hú (斛) could be accumulated along the Huái (淮) River.
This would be enough food for 100,000 men for five years.
Using this to attack Wú (吳),
there would be no expedition that would not succeed."
Xuānwáng (宣ānwáng) approved of this,
and all the measures were implemented.
In the second year of Zhèngshǐ (正始, 241 CE),
the transport canals were expanded.
Whenever there was an affair in the southeast,
and a large army was raised,
they would travel down by boat,
reaching the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) Rivers.
Resources and food were stored, and there were no water-related disasters.
This was all due to Ài's (艾) proposals.
He was dispatched to participate in military affairs of the General Who Conquers the West,
and later promoted to Administrator of Nán'ān (南安).
In the first year of Jiāpíng (嘉平, 249 CE),
he, along with the General Who Conquers the West, Guō Huái (郭淮), resisted Jiāng Wéi (姜維), a subordinate general from Shǔ (蜀).
Wéi (維) retreated,
and Huái (淮) then attacked the Qiāng (羌) westward.
Ài (艾) said:
"The enemy has not gone far;
they might return.
We should divide our forces to guard against the unexpected."
Thereupon, Ài (艾) was left to garrison north of Báishuǐ (白水).
Three days later,
Wéi (維) sent Liáo Huà (廖化) to set up camp opposite Ài (艾) south of Báishuǐ (白水).
Ài (艾) said to his generals:
"Wéi (維) has now suddenly returned.
Our forces are few.
By convention, he should cross over without building a bridge.
This is Wéi (維) using Huà (化) to hold us,
preventing us from returning.
Wéi (維) must personally attack and seize Táochéng (洮城) from the east."
Táochéng (洮城) was north of the river,
sixty *lǐ* (里) from Ài's (艾) garrison.
Ài (艾) immediately marched secretly that night directly to Táochéng (洮城).
Wéi (維) indeed came to cross the river,
but Ài (艾) had already arrived and secured the city,
thus avoiding defeat.
He was granted the noble title of Marquis within the Pass,
and additionally appointed General Who Suppresses Bandits.
Later, he was promoted to Administrator of Chéngyáng (城陽).
At this time, Liú Bào (劉豹), the Right Worthy King of Bìngzhōu (并州), united his tribes into one.
Ài (艾) submitted a memorial stating:
"The Róng (戎) and Dí (狄) have the hearts of beasts;
they are not bound by righteousness.
When strong, they invade and plunder;
when weak, they surrender.
Thus, King Xuān (宣) of Zhōu (周) faced the incursions of the Xiǎnyǔn (玁狁),
and Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) of Hàn (漢) suffered the siege at Píngchéng (平城).
Whenever the Xiōngnú (匈奴) grew strong,
they became a serious threat to previous dynasties.
Since the Chányú (單于) was kept outside,
no one could restrain Cháng Bēi (長卑).
By enticing him to come
and serve at court,
the Qiāng (羌) and Yí (夷) lost their unified command
and scattered without a leader.
With the Chányú (單于) within,
all within a myriad *lǐ* (里) followed the rules.
Now, the Chányú's (單于) prestige is diminishing daily,
and the power of the outer lands is gradually increasing.
Therefore, we must be deeply prepared against the Hú (胡) barbarians.
I hear that there are rebellious Hú (胡) in Liú Bào's (劉豹) tribe.
We could take advantage of this rebellion to divide them into two nations
to weaken their influence.
Qù Bēi (去卑) achieved distinction in the previous court,
but his son has not continued his legacy.
It would be advisable to grant his son a prominent title
and have him reside in Yànmén (鴈門).
Dividing nations, weakening enemies,
and recognizing old merits –
this is a long-term strategy for border defense."
He further suggested:
"As for the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) who live among our people,
they should gradually be moved out,
so that our residents can prominently uphold the teachings of integrity and modesty,
and block the path of villainy and deceit."
The Grand General Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng (司馬景王) had recently taken charge of governance,
and largely adopted his proposals.
Ài (艾) was promoted to Administrator of Rǔnán (汝nán).
Upon arrival, he immediately sought out the father of the official who had once been generous to him.
The man had long been dead,
so Ài (艾) sent an official to offer sacrifices to him,
generously presented gifts to his mother,
and nominated his son for the position of chief clerk.
Wherever Ài (艾) was stationed,
barren lands were cultivated,
and both military and civilian populations prospered.
Zhūgě Kè besieged Xīnchéng in Héféi,
but failed
and retreated.
Ài spoke to Jǐngwáng, saying:
"Sūn Quán is dead,
and the ministers are not yet attached.
The renowned clans and great families of Wú,
all have their own militias.
Relying on armed forces and their influence,
they are enough to establish their own commands.
Kè has newly assumed national governance,
but internally he has no master.
He does not think of comforting and nurturing the high and low to establish a foundation,
but competes in external affairs,
cruelly using his people.
He deployed the entire nation's army,
bogged down before a strong city.
Tens of thousands died,
and he returned with misfortune.
This is the day Kè will incur guilt.
In the past, Zǐxū, Wú Qǐ, Shāng Yāng, and Yuè Yì were all entrusted by their contemporary rulers;
when their lords died, they failed.
How much more so Kè, whose talent is not equal to these four sages,
yet he does not consider great perils?
His downfall is to be expected."
When Kè returned,
he was indeed executed.
Ài was promoted to Inspector of Yǎnzhōu and
additionally appointed General of Tremendous Awe.
He presented a memorial, saying:
"What the state urgently needs
are only agriculture and war.
If the state is rich, its army is strong;
if the army is strong, battles are won.
However, agriculture
is the foundation of victory.
Confucius said, 'sufficient food and sufficient military,'
food being before the military.
If the superiors do not offer encouragement with ranks,
then the subordinates will not exert themselves in accumulating wealth.
Now, if the rewards for performance
lie in accumulating grain and enriching the people,
then the path of social connections will be cut off,
and the source of superficiality will be blocked."
Gaoguì Xiānggōng ascended the throne,
and Ài was advanced to the title of Marquis of Fāngchéng Pavilion.
When Wúqiū Jiǎn rebelled,
he sent swift messengers carrying letters
to sow doubt among the populace.
Ài executed them,
advanced his army simultaneously along the roads,
and was the first to reach Lèjiā City,
where he built pontoon bridges.
When Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng arrived,
they then secured it.
Wén Qīn's main army was later defeated below the city,
and Ài pursued him to Qiūtou.
Qīn fled to Wú.
The Grand General Sūn Jùn of Wú and others, numbering 100,000,
were about to cross the river.
General of the East Zhūgě Dàn sent Ài to hold Féiyáng.
Ài, seeing that it was far from the enemy's position
and not a critical point,
promptly moved his garrison to Fùtíng.
He sent Grand Administrator of Tàishān Zhūgě Xù and others to resist at Líjiāng,
and consequently routed them.
In that year, he was summoned to be appointed Colonel of the Everlasting Waters.
For his achievements in defeating Qīn and others,
he was advanced to the title of Marquis of Fāngchéng Village,
and acted as General of the West-Pacifying Army.
He relieved the siege of Yǒngzhōu Inspector Wáng Jīng at Dídao.
Jiāng Wéi retreated and stationed himself at Zhōngtí.
Ài was then appointed General of the West-Pacifying Army,
granted the imperial staff, and made Commander of the Eastern Qiāng.
Many strategists believed that Wéi's strength was exhausted
and he could not sally forth again.
Ài said:
"The defeat at Táoxī was not a minor loss;
our army was broken, generals killed,
granaries empty,
and the people displaced,
almost leading to ruin.
Now, from a strategic perspective,
they have the momentum of victory,
while we are actually weak –
this is one point.
Their superiors and subordinates are accustomed to each other,
and their weapons are sharp;
our generals are new,
and our equipment has not yet recovered –
this is two points.
They travel by boat,
we by land;
the toil and ease are different –
this is three points.
Dídao, Lǒngxī, Nán'ān, and Qíshān
each must be defended;
they concentrate on one point,
we are divided into four –
this is four points.
From Nán'ān and Lǒngxī,
relying on the Qiāng's grain for sustenance,
if they head towards Qíshān,
a thousand acres of ripe wheat
will become their bait –
this is five points.
The enemy has cunning strategies,
their coming is certain."
Soon after,
Wéi indeed headed towards Qíshān.
Hearing that Ài was already prepared,
he turned back from Dǒngtíng and moved towards Nán'ān.
Ài occupied Wǔchéng Mountain to hold him off.
Wéi contended with Ài for strategic positions
but could not prevail.
That night,
he crossed the Wèi River eastward,
following the mountains towards Shàngguī.
Ài engaged him in battle at Duàngǔ
and severely defeated him.
In the first year of Gānlù, an imperial edict stated:
"The rebellious traitor Jiāng Wéi has been cunning for years,
causing unrest among the people and barbarians,
and making the western lands unsettled.
Ài's planning has been methodical,
and his loyalty and courage have shone forth.
He has cut down more than ten generals
and decapitated thousands of enemies;
the might of the state has shaken Bā and Shǔ,
and its martial prestige has resonated across Jiāng and Mín.
Now, Ài is appointed General Who Guards the West and Overall Commander of All Military Affairs in Lǒngyòu,
and advanced to the title of Marquis of Dèng.
Five hundred households are granted to his son Zhōng, who is enfeoffed as a Pavilion Marquis."
In the second year,
he resisted Jiāng Wéi at Chángchéng,
and Wéi retreated.
He was promoted to General Who Conquers the West,
and his total enfeoffed households, before and after, amounted to 6,600.
In the third year of Jǐngyuán,
he again defeated Wéi at Hóuhé,
and Wéi retreated to defend Dàzhōng.
In the autumn of the fourth year,
an imperial edict commanded all armies to conquer Shǔ.
Grand General Sīmǎ Wénwáng personally directed the strategy,
ordering Ài to keep Wéi engaged;
Yǒngzhōu Inspector Zhūgě Xù was to intercept Wéi
to prevent his return.
Ài sent Grand Administrator of Tiānshuǐ Wáng Qí and others to directly attack Wéi's camp,
Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī Qiān Hóng and others to intercept him from the front,
and Grand Administrator of Jīnchéng Yáng Xīn and others to advance to Gānsōng.
Wéi heard that Zhōng Huì's armies had already entered Hànzhōng
and withdrew to return.
Xīn and others pursued him at Qiángchuānkǒu,
engaging in a great battle,
and Wéi was defeated and fled.
Hearing that Yǒngzhōu had blocked the road and garrisoned Qiáotóu,
he entered the northern path through Kǒnghángǔ,
intending to come out behind Yǒngzhōu.
Zhūgě Xù heard of this
and retreated thirty *lǐ*.
Wéi entered the northern path for more than thirty *lǐ*.
Hearing that Xù's army had retreated,
he immediately turned back
and passed through Qiáotóu.
Xù rushed to intercept Wéi,
but missed him by just one day.
Wéi then moved eastward
and returned to defend Jiàngé.
Zhōng Huì attacked Wéi but could not overcome him.
Ài memorialized, saying:
"Now the enemy is shattered;
we should immediately press the advantage,
taking a devious path from Yīnpíng through Xiéjìng, passing Hándéyáng Tíng, and heading for Fú,
emerging a hundred *lǐ* west of Jiàngé,
and about three hundred *lǐ* from Chéngdū.
A surprise army will strike at their heart.
The defenders of Jiàngé will surely return to relieve Fú,
allowing Huì to advance unimpeded;
if the Jiàngé army does not return,
then the troops responding to Fú will be few.
The *Military Annals* say: 'Attack where they are unprepared,
appear where they do not expect.'
Now, we will strike at their emptiness,
and victory is certain."
In the tenth month of winter,
Dèng Ài traveled from Yīnpíng Road through uninhabited land for over seven hundred *lǐ*,
hewing mountains and opening paths,
constructing bridges and elevated walkways.
The mountains were high and the valleys deep,
reaching an extremely difficult and dangerous state.
Moreover, food supplies were nearly exhausted,
frequently nearing critical danger.
Dèng Ài wrapped himself in a felt blanket,
rolling himself down.
His officers and soldiers all clung to trees and climbed cliffs,
advancing in single file like fish.
The vanguard reached Jiāngyóu,
and the Shǔ commander Mǎ Miǎo surrendered.
Shǔ General of the Guards, Zhūgě Zhān, returned from Fú to Miánzhú,
and arrayed his forces to await Dèng Ài.
Dèng Ài dispatched his son, Huì Tángtínghóu Zhōng, and others to emerge on their right,
and Sīmǎ Shī Zuǎn and others to emerge on their left.
Zhōng and Zuǎn fought unsuccessfully,
and both retreated,
saying:
"The enemy cannot yet be attacked."
Dèng Ài angrily said:
"The distinction between survival and destruction
rests on this single action.
What is there that cannot be done?"
Thereupon he yelled at Zhōng and Zuǎn and the others,
and was about to execute them.
Zhōng and Zuǎn galloped back and fought again,
decisively defeating them,
beheading Zhān and the head of Shàngshū Zhāng Zūn and others.
They advanced their army to Luò.
Liú Shàn dispatched an envoy to present the Emperor's imperial seals and ribbons,
and sent a memorial to Dèng Ài requesting surrender.
When Dèng Ài arrived at Chéngdū,
Liú Shàn, leading the crown prince, various princes, and over sixty officials, with their hands bound and carrying a coffin, went to the army gate.
Dèng Ài, holding his staff, unbound their hands and burned the coffin,
accepting their surrender and pardoning them.
He kept his officers and soldiers in check,
preventing any plundering,
and pacified and accepted those who surrendered,
allowing them to return to their former occupations.
The people of Shǔ praised him for this.
He then, following the precedent of Dèng Yǔ,
acted by imperial authority to appoint Liú Shàn as acting General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn),
the crown prince as Attendant at the Chariot (Fèngchē), and the various princes as Cavalier Attendants-in-Ordinary (Fùmǎ Dūwèi).
The various Shǔ officials were appointed to Wang officials according to their rank,
or led Dèng Ài's subordinate officers.
He appointed Shī Zuǎn as Inspector of Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu Cìshǐ),
and Liú Xī Governor Qiān Hóng and others to govern the various commanderies in Shǔ.
He ordered a platform to be built at Miánzhú to serve as a 'capital mound' (Jīngguān),
to display his military achievements.
All soldiers who died in service
were buried together with the Shǔ soldiers.
Dèng Ài was deeply proud and boastful,
and said to the Shǔ gentry:
"Gentlemen, you rely on having met me,
and thus have today.
If you had met people like Wú Hàn,
you would have been annihilated."
He also said:
"Jiāng Wéi was a hero of his time,
but he met me,
and so he was brought to ruin."
Those with discernment laughed at him.
In the twelfth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"Dèng Ài displayed his might and wielded his military power,
penetrating deep into the enemy's territory,
beheading generals and seizing banners,
executing their great villains.
He caused the lord who usurped the title
to bow his head and offer his neck,
and the long-standing rebellion,
which had evaded punishment for generations, to be pacified in a single morning.
The army did not exceed its time,
the battle did not last a full day.
Like clouds dispersing and mats being swept away,
he pacified Bāshǔ.
Although Bái Qǐ broke the powerful Chǔ,
Hán Xìn conquered the strong Zhào,
Wú Hàn captured Zǐyáng,
and Yà Fū destroyed the Seven States,
when comparing achievements and judging merits,
none are sufficient to compare with his service.
Therefore, Dèng Ài is to be made Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
his enfeoffment increased by twenty thousand households,
and his two sons enfeoffed as Tínghóu,
each receiving a thousand households of revenue."
Dèng Ài spoke to Sīmǎ Wénwáng, saying:
"In warfare, there is the principle of a 'prelude' (xiānsheng) followed by 'reality' (hòushí).
Now, taking advantage of the momentum of pacifying Shǔ to attack Wú,
the people of Wú are terrified;
it is the time to sweep them away.
However, after a major campaign,
the officers and soldiers are weary
and cannot be immediately used.
So, let us proceed slowly for now.
Leave twenty thousand soldiers in Lǒngyòu
and twenty thousand Shǔ soldiers.
Boil salt and develop metallurgy
for essential military and agricultural use,
and also build boats and ships,
in preparation for affairs downstream.
Then, send envoys to inform Wú of the advantages and disadvantages.
Wú will surely submit;
it can be pacified without a campaign.
Currently, it is fitting to treat Liú Shàn generously to attract Sūn Xiū,
and to appease the populace to draw in distant people.
If Liú Shàn is immediately sent to the capital,
Wú will consider it an exile,
which will not encourage their inclination to submit.
It is advisable to temporarily keep him here
until autumn and winter next year,
by which time Wú will also be pacified.
I propose that Liú Shàn be enfeoffed as King of Fúfēng,
granted wealth and resources,
and provided with attendants.
There is Dǒng Zhuó's fort in the commandery;
make it his palace.
Enfeoff his sons as dukes and marquises,
to receive revenue from counties within the commandery,
to highlight the favor shown to those who surrender.
Open up Guǎnglíng and Chéngyáng to await the Wú people.
Then, they will fear our might and cherish our virtue,
and submit at first glance."
Sīmǎ Wénwáng sent Inspector-General Wèi Guàn to instruct Dèng Ài:
"Matters must be reported first;
it is not appropriate to act arbitrarily."
Dèng Ài reiterated, saying:
"I was commissioned to go on campaign,
and followed the instructed strategy.
The primary villain has submitted;
as for acting by imperial authority to appoint officials
to stabilize the newly surrendered,
I believe it is in line with expediency.
Now Shǔ has collectively submitted its mandate,
its territory extends to the South Sea,
and borders Wú and Kuàijī in the east.
It should be quickly stabilized.
If we wait for imperial commands,
the back-and-forth journey
will cause delays of months and days.
According to the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
when a high official is outside the borders,
if there is something that can stabilize the state
and benefit the nation,
they may act independently.
Now Wú has not yet submitted;
its situation is connected with Shǔ.
We cannot be constrained by routine and lose the opportune moment.
The Art of War states:
'Advance without seeking fame,
retreat without avoiding blame.'
Although I do not possess the integrity of the ancients,
I will ultimately not hesitate out of self-doubt and thus harm the state."
Zhōng Huì, Hú Liè, Shī Zuǎn, and others all reported Dèng Ài's rebellious actions,
and the seeds of conflict were sown.
An imperial edict ordered Dèng Ài to be brought back in a cage-cart.
After Dèng Ài and his son were imprisoned,
Zhōng Huì arrived at Chéngdū,
first sent Dèng Ài away,
and then rebelled.
After Zhōng Huì died,
Dèng Ài's original camp officers and soldiers pursued and released Dèng Ài from the cage-cart,
and welcomed him back.
Wèi Guàn dispatched Tián Xù and others to attack Dèng Ài,
encountered him west of Miánzhú,
and beheaded him.
His son Zhōng died with Dèng Ài.
His remaining sons in Luòyáng were all executed,
and Dèng Ài's wife and children and grandchildren were exiled to the Western Regions.
Initially,
when Dèng Ài was about to attack Shǔ,
he dreamed he was sitting on a mountain with flowing water,
and asked the Protector-General who Destroys Barbarians, Yuán Shào, about it.
Yuán Shào said:
"According to the *Yì Guà*,
a mountain with water above it is *Jiǎn* (Obstruction).
The *Jiǎn* hexagram states: 'Obstruction is beneficial to the southwest,
unfavorable to the northeast.'
Confucius said: 'Obstruction is beneficial to the southwest: there will be achievement in going.
Unfavorable to the northeast: its path is exhausted.'
You will surely conquer Shǔ by going,
but perhaps you will not return!"
Dèng Ài was disconsolate and unhappy.
In the first year of Tàishǐ (265 CE),
the Jìn dynasty ascended the throne.
An imperial edict stated:
“Formerly, Grand Commandant Wáng Líng plotted to depose the King of Qí,
but the King ultimately was not capable of holding his position.
General Who Attacks the West Dèng Ài,
prided himself on his achievements and lost his integrity,
and indeed deserved capital punishment.
However, on the day he received the decree,
he dismissed his troops,
and submitted to punishment with bound hands.
Compared to those who sought to preserve their lives and thus committed evil deeds,
he was indeed different.
Now, by great amnesty, he may return.
If he has no descendants, he is permitted to establish an heir,
so that his sacrifices may not cease.”
In the third year (267 CE),
Court Gentleman for Consultation Duàn Zhuó submitted a memorial in defense of Ài, stating:
“Ài, with utmost loyalty in his heart, bore the name of rebellion,
and having pacified Bāshǔ, received the punishment of extermination.
Your servant secretly mourns this.
Alas,
to speak of Ài’s rebellion!
Ài’s nature was stern and impetuous,
easily offending both refined and common folk,
and he could not cooperate with his peers;
thus, no one was willing to defend him.
Your servant dares to speak of the circumstances that prove Ài was not a rebel.
Formerly, Jiāng Wéi had the ambition to sever Lǒngyòu.
Ài repaired and maintained defenses,
accumulating grain and strengthening his forces.
When a year of severe drought occurred,
Ài personally tilled the fields,
wearing coarse clothes,
holding a spade and hoe in his hands,
to lead his officers and soldiers.
Both high and low were moved,
and none failed to exert their utmost effort.
Ài, holding his imperial credentials, guarded the frontier,
commanding tens of thousands of men,
yet he did not shy away from the toil of a servant
or the labor of a commoner.
Without steadfast loyalty and diligence,
who could have been like this?
Therefore, in the battles of Luòmén and Duàngǔ,
he struck many with few,
crushing powerful enemies.
The Late Emperor knew he was trustworthy
and entrusted Ài with strategic planning,
giving him long-term policies.
Ài, receiving his orders, forgot himself,
tied his horses and suspended his chariots,
and threw himself into deadly peril.
His courage pierced the clouds,
and his troops seized the momentum,
forcing Liú Shàn and his ministers to be bound face to face,
their hands clasped and knees bent.
Ài’s achievements and fame were complete;
they should have been written on bamboo and silk,
and passed down for ten thousand generations.
An old man of seventy,
what more could he possibly desire by rebelling?
Ài sincerely relied on the grace of his nurturing,
and had no self-doubt,
thus he acted under false imperial orders and assumed authority,
temporarily stabilizing the state.
Though he violated ordinary laws,
it conformed to ancient righteousness.
Judging his original intention to determine his crime,
it fundamentally warranted discussion.
Zhōng Huì envied Ài’s prestige
and fabricated the charges against him.
Loyal yet executed,
trustworthy yet suspected,
his head hung in the horse market,
his sons all beheaded.
Those who saw it wept,
and those who heard of it sighed.
Your Majesty, since your ascent to power,
has proclaimed great magnanimity,
releasing all suspicions and resentments.
Families of those executed
are not restricted from service.
Formerly, the people of Qín pitied Bái Qǐ’s innocence,
and the people of Wú mourned Zǐ Xū’s cruel injustice,
and both built shrines for them.
Today, the people of the world mourn Ài with aching hearts,
likewise.
Your servant believes that Ài’s body and head were separated,
discarded in the weeds and earth.
His corpse should be collected and buried,
and his fields and residences returned.
For his achievement in pacifying Shǔ,
his grandson should be enfeoffed,
so that his posthumous title may be settled upon closing the coffin,
leaving no lingering regret after death.
To pardon the wronged spirit in the underworld,
and uphold trust and righteousness for future generations:
bury one person, and the world will admire his conduct;
inter one soul, and the world will return to his righteousness.
What is done is little, but those who are pleased are many.”
In the ninth year (273 CE),
an imperial edict stated:
“Ài had great achievements,
and though he suffered punishment without escaping it,
his descendants became commoners.
I constantly pity this.
Let his eldest grandson Lǎng be made a Langzhong.”
When Ài was in the west,
he repaired and built barriers
and constructed walled forts.
During the Tàishǐ period,
the Qiāng barbarians rebelled greatly,
repeatedly killing regional governors,
and the road to Liángzhōu was cut off.
All officials and commoners who were safe
took refuge in the forts Ài had built.
Ài’s contemporary from his home region, Zhōu Tài of Nányáng,
also liked to establish achievements
and was skilled in warfare.
He rose to the rank of General Who Attacks the Captives, holding the imperial credentials and supervising all military affairs south of the Yangtze.
He died in the second year of Jǐngyuán (261 CE),
and was posthumously granted the title of General of the Guards,
with the posthumous name Zhuànghóu.
Zhōng Huì, courtesy name Shìjì,
was a native of Chángshè, Yǐngchuān,
and the youngest son of Grand Tutor Yáo.
From a young age, he was intelligent, astute, and mature.
The Central Protector of the Army, Jiǎng Jì, wrote an essay
stating,
“Observe his pupils,
and one can know a person.”
When Huì was five years old,
Yáo sent him to see Jì.
Jì was greatly surprised by him,
saying:
“This is no ordinary person.”
When he grew up,
he possessed many talents and skills,
and was widely learned, refined in philosophical discourse,
continuing his studies day and night,
thereby gaining a reputation.
During the Zhèngshǐ period (240-249 CE),
he was made Secretary to the Imperial Library,
then promoted to Palace Attendant and Imperial Secretariat.
When the Duke of Gāoguì Xiāng ascended the throne,
he was granted the title Marquis within the Pass.
When Wúqiū Jiǎn rebelled,
Grand General Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng led an eastern expedition.
Huì accompanied him,
managing confidential matters.
General of the Guards Sīmǎ Wénwáng followed as the rear guard of the main army.
When Jǐngwáng died in Xǔchāng,
Wénwáng took overall command of the six armies,
and Huì offered strategic counsel from within the tent.
At that time, an imperial edict instructed Grandee Secretary Fù Gǔ
that, as the southeast had just been pacified, to temporarily keep the General of the Guards garrisoned at Xǔchāng as internal and external support,
and ordered Gǔ to lead the various armies back.
Huì plotted with Gǔ,
and had Gǔ memorialize to the throne
that he would immediately depart with the General of the Guards
and return to encamp south of the Luò River.
Consequently, the court appointed Wénwáng as Grand General and regent,
and Huì was promoted to Yellow Gate Attendant,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngwǔ Pavilion,
with a stipend of three hundred households.
In the second year of Gānlù (257 CE),
Zhūgě Dàn was summoned to be Minister of Works.
At that time, Huì was at home observing mourning.
He predicted that Dàn would certainly not obey,
and galloped to inform Wénwáng.
Wénwáng, as the matter had already been enacted,
did not retract or change it.
When Dàn rebelled,
the imperial carriage stayed at Xiàng,
and Wénwáng went to Shòuchūn.
Huì again accompanied him.
Initially,
Wú’s grand general, Quán Cóng,
who was a marital relative and trusted high official of Sūn Quán,
had his sons Yì and Sūn Jìng, and his nephews Duān, Piān, and Jī,
all lead troops to relieve Zhūgě Dàn.
Yì’s nephews Huī and Yí remained in Jiànyè,
and quarreled with their family there.
They took their mother
and several dozen families of their troops across the river,
and surrendered to Wénwáng.
Zhōng Huì devised a plan,
secretly writing letters for Huī and Yí,
and had trusted confidants of Huī and Yí carry them into the city to inform Yì and the others,
stating that people in Wú were angry that Yì and the others could not capture Shòuchūn,
and intended to execute all their generals’ families,
which was why they had fled to surrender.
Yì and the others were terrified,
so they led their subordinates out through the East Gate and surrendered.
All were granted titles and favors,
and the city was thenceforth divided.
In the fall of Shòuchūn,
Zhōng Huì’s strategies accounted for the majority of the success,
and his favor and trust grew daily.
People at the time called him Zǐfáng.
When the army returned,
he was promoted to Tàipú,
but he firmly declined the post.
He served as a Mid-ranking Officer managing the Secretariat in the Grand General’s office,
a position of intimate trust.
For his achievements in suppressing Zhūgě Dàn,
he was advanced in noble rank to Chén Hóu,
but he repeatedly refused to accept it.
An imperial edict stated:
"Zhōng Huì has overseen military affairs,
participated in planning,
assessed the enemy, and secured victory,
possessing the merit of strategic counsel.
Yet he pushes away honor and firmly declines,
his words and reasons sincere and substantial.
Repeatedly, time and again,
his resolve cannot be swayed.
To achieve success yet not claim it
is something esteemed by the ancients.
Therefore, listen to what Zhōng Huì maintains,
to fulfill his virtue."
He was promoted to Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Although he was in an outer office,
he oversaw all current political matters regarding benefits and drawbacks,
and contemporary grants and retractions.
Jī Kāng and others were executed,
all as a result of Zhōng Huì’s schemes.
Wénwáng, seeing that Shǔ’s grand general Jiāng Wéi repeatedly harassed the borders,
and judging that Shǔ was a small state with exhausted people,
whose resources were depleted,
desired to launch a major campaign to conquer Shǔ.
Only Zhōng Huì also believed Shǔ could be taken,
and planned with him in advance, studying the terrain
and discussing the strategic situation.
In the winter of the third year of Jǐngyuán,
Zhōng Huì was made Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn, granted a provisional staff, and put in charge of all military affairs in Guānzhōng.
Wénwáng commanded the provinces of Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Jīng, and Yáng
to all build ships,
and also ordered Táng Zī to build large oceangoing ships,
outwardly as if preparing to attack Wú.
In the autumn of the fourth year,
an edict was issued ordering Dèng Ài and Zhūgě Xù to each command over 30,000 troops.
Dèng Ài was to advance on Gānsōng and Tàzhōng to pin down Jiāng Wéi,
and Zhūgě Xù was to advance on Wǔjiē and Qiáotóu to cut off Jiāng Wéi’s retreat.
Zhōng Huì commanded over 100,000 troops,
advancing separately through Xié Gǔ and Luò Gǔ.
He first ordered his Yámén General Xǔ Yí to clear the path ahead.
Zhōng Huì followed behind,
but a bridge collapsed,
and his horse’s hooves got stuck.
Thereupon, he executed Xǔ Yí.
Xǔ Yí was
the son of Xǔ Chǔ,
who had rendered service to the royal house,
yet he was not pardoned.
When the various armies heard of this,
none were not shocked and trembled.
Shǔ ordered all its garrisons not to engage in battle,
but to retreat and defend the two cities of Hàn and Lè.
Wèixīng Tàishǒu Liú Qīn advanced through Zǐwǔ Gǔ,
and the various armies marched in parallel along several routes,
reaching Hànzhōng.
Shǔ’s Supervisor of the Army, Wáng Hán, defended Lèchéng,
and Protector of the Army Jiǎng Bīn defended Hànchéng,
each with 5,000 troops.
Zhōng Huì sent Protector of the Army Xún Kǎi and Former General Lǐ Fǔ, each commanding 10,000 men.
Xún Kǎi besieged Hànchéng,
and Lǐ Fǔ besieged Lèchéng.
Zhōng Huì passed directly through,
exiting to the west via Yáng’ān Kǒu,
and sent someone to offer sacrifices at Zhūgě Liàng’s tomb.
He sent Protector of the Army Hú Liè and others ahead,
who attacked and broke through the pass,
obtaining stored provisions from the armory.
Jiāng Wéi returned from Tàzhōng,
reaching Yīnpíng,
where he gathered his officers and troops,
intending to rush to the pass.
Before arriving,
he heard it had already been broken,
so he retreated to Báishuǐ,
and joined Shǔ generals Zhāng Yì and Liáo Huà to hold Jiàngé against Zhōng Huì.
Zhōng Huì issued a proclamation to Shǔ officers, officials, and common people, saying: "In the past, when the Hàn dynasty’s fate declined,
the entire land was fragmented and scattered,
and the lives of the people
were almost extinguished.
Tàizǔ Wǔ Huángdì, with divine martial prowess and sagely wisdom,
rectified disorder and restored
order,
saving what was about to fall,
and established our central realm.
Gāozǔ Wén Huángdì, responding to Heaven and aligning with the people,
received the mandate and ascended the throne.
Lièzǔ Míng Huángdì, in successive generations, restored glory,
and expanded
our grand enterprise.
However, beyond the rivers and mountains,
there were different governments and diverse customs;
the people across the land had not yet received the king’s transforming influence.
This was the lingering regret of the Three Ancestors.
Now the present ruler
possesses sagely virtue, reverent and brilliant,
continuing and enhancing the previous legacy.
His chief ministers are loyal, solemn, clear-sighted, and just,
toiling for the royal house.
They spread governance and bestow benevolence, bringing harmony to all states,
and extend virtue to all barbarians, resulting in
tribute from the Sùshèn.
We lament those of Bāshǔ,
who alone remain disloyal subjects,
and pity these common people,
whose labors and hardships are endless.
Therefore, we have commanded the Six Armies,
to enact Heaven’s punishment in unison.
The Zhēng
Xī, Yōngzhōu, and Zhèn Xī armies
are advancing along five routes simultaneously.
Ancient military campaigns
were founded on benevolence,
and governed by righteousness.
The king’s army
conquers without
fighting.
Thus, Yú Shùn danced with shields and axes to subdue the Yǒumiáo,
and Zhōu Wǔ demonstrated the virtues of distributing wealth, opening granaries, and honoring the righteous.
Now the Zhèn Xī, receiving the imperial command,
takes charge of this great
military responsibility.
He hopes to promote the instruction of a civilized proclamation,
to save the lives of the common people,
not to exhaust military might and wage extreme war
to satisfy a moment’s political ambition.
Therefore, I briefly lay out the essentials of security and danger;
please
listen carefully to my words.
Yìzhōu’s former ruler, an eminent talent of his age,
raised an army in the north,
was troubled and thwarted in the suburbs of Jì and Xú,
and his fate was controlled by Shào and Bù.
Tàizǔ rescued and saved
him,
and they formed a great friendship.
Later, he turned against us,
abandoning common cause for difference.
Zhūgě Kǒngmíng repeatedly sought to control Qínchuān,
and Jiāng Bóyuē frequently ventured out into Lǒngyòu,
disturbing our border
regions,
and invading and harassing our Dī and Qiāng peoples.
As the state was preoccupied with many affairs,
we did not have time to undertake the Nine Punishments.
Now the border regions are peaceful and clear,
and there are no internal troubles.
We have accumulated strength and waited
for the opportune moment,
concentrating our forces in one direction.
The forces of Bāshǔ, a single province,
are dispersed in defense,
making it difficult to resist the army of all under Heaven.
The disheartened morale from Duàn Gǔ and Hóu Hé
makes it difficult
to face a grand formation.
In recent years,
there has been no year of peace;
the conscripted soldiers are weary and exhausted,
making it difficult to contend with people who come willingly.
All of this, gentlemen, you have personally witnessed.
Shǔ’s minister Zhuàng was captured by Qín,
and Gōngsūn Shù was beheaded by Hàn.
The strategic strongholds of the Nine Provinces
do not belong to a single family.
All of this, gentlemen, you have fully heard.
Thus..."
Shìzhě (wise men) see danger in its nascent form,
zhìzhě (intelligent men) prevent calamity before it sprouts.
This is why Wēizǐ (微子) left the Shāng (商) dynasty
and forever became a guest of Zhōu (周);
Chén Píng (陳平) turned his back on Xiàng Yǔ (項羽)
and established meritorious service for Hàn (漢).
How could they have been
content with comfort, like those who drink poisoned wine,
clinging to their emoluments and unwilling to change?
Now, the imperial court extends a heaven-covering benevolence,
and the prime ministers promote a virtue of broad magnanimity.
They offer kindness first, then punish;
they love life and abhor killing.
In the past, Wú (吳) general Sūn Yī (孫壹) led his troops to surrender and join us,
and he was granted the position of a high official,
with extraordinary favor and rank.
Wén Qīn (文欽) and Táng Zī (唐咨), who were great scourges to the state,
rebelled against their lord and sided with the enemy,
still becoming
leaders of the barbarians.
Zī (咨) was cornered and captured,
and Qīn's (欽) two sons returned and surrendered;
all were made generals and enfeoffed as marquises.
Zī (咨) was even allowed to participate in state affairs.
If even those like Yī (壹) who were in dire straits and surrendered their lives
were still granted great
favor,
how much more so for the sagacious and discerning people of Bāshǔ (巴蜀) who act on their opportunities!
If they can truly deeply discern success and failure,
and bravely step forward,
following in the footsteps of Wēizǐ (微子),
and aligning themselves with the path of Chén Píng (陳平),
then their blessings will be like those of the ancients,
and their good fortune will flow to future generations.
The common people and officials
will reside peacefully in their old professions,
farmers will not change their fields,
merchants will not close their shops.
They will abandon the danger of stacked eggs
and embrace
the blessing of eternal peace.
How beautiful would that not be!
But if they cling to temporary comfort,
deluded and unwilling to turn back,
once the great army is unleashed,
both jade and stone will be shattered.
Even if they wish to regret it,
it will be too late.
Therefore,
they should carefully weigh the advantages and disadvantages,
and seek abundant blessings for themselves.
Let this be announced to all,
so everyone may hear and know.
Dèng Ài (鄧艾) pursued Jiāng Wéi (姜維) to Yīnpíng (陰平).
He selected elite troops,
intending to enter Jiāngyóu (江由) from Hàndéyáng (漢德陽) along the Zuǒdān (左儋) path to Yì Miánzhú (詣緜竹),
and hasten to Chéngdū (成都),
marching together with Zhūgě Xù (諸葛緒).
Xù (緒),
however, had been originally ordered to intercept Jiāng Wéi (姜維),
and moving west was not part of his original imperial edict.
So, he advanced his army towards Báishuǐ (白水)
to meet up.
Zhōng Huì (鍾會) dispatched General Tián Zhāng (田章) and others from Jiàngé (劍閣) to the west,
directly out through Jiāngyóu (江由).
Before reaching a hundred lǐ,
Zhāng (章) first broke three Shuǐ (蜀) ambushes.
Ài (艾) made Zhāng (章) lead the vanguard.
They then drove straight forward.
Huì (會) and Xù’s (緒) armies marched towards Jiàngé (劍閣).
Huì (會) wished to command the army exclusively,
so he secretly reported that Xù (緒) was timid and unwilling to advance,
and had him brought back in a prisoner cart.
The entire army was thus placed under Huì’s (會) command.
He then attacked Jiàngé (劍閣),
but failed.
He withdrew,
as the Shǔ (蜀) army held the strategic pass and defended it.
Ài (艾) then reached Miánzhú (緜竹),
fought a great battle,
and killed Zhūgě Zhān (諸葛瞻).
Wéi (維) and others heard that Zhān (瞻) had been defeated,
and led their forces east into Bā (巴).
Huì (會) then advanced his army to Fú (涪),
and dispatched Hú Liè (胡烈), Tián Xù (田續), Páng Huì (龐會) and others to pursue Wéi (維).
Ài (艾) advanced his army towards Chéngdū (成都).
Liú Shàn (劉禪) went to Ài (艾) and surrendered,
sending envoys to order Wéi (維) and others to surrender to Huì (會).
Wéi (維) reached Guǎnghàn Qī Xiàn (廣漢郪縣),
ordered his soldiers to lay down all their weapons,
sent his official seal and tally to Hú Liè (胡烈),
and then proceeded along the eastern road to surrender to Huì (會).
Huì (會) then submitted a memorial, stating:
“The rebels Jiāng Wéi (姜維), Zhāng Yì (張翼), Liáo Huà (廖化), Dǒng Jué (董厥) and others fled for their lives,
intending to head towards Chéngdū (成都).
Your servant immediately dispatched Sīmǎ Xiàhóu Xián (司馬夏侯咸) and Hùjūn Hú Liè (護軍胡烈) and others,
via Jiàngé (劍閣),
to come out through Xīndū (新都) and Dàdù (大渡) to intercept them from the front.
Cānjūn Yuán (參軍爰) and General Gōu Ān (句安) and others pursued them from the rear.
Cānjūn Huángfǔ Kǎi (參軍皇甫闓) and General Wáng Mǎi (王買) and others came out from south of Fú (涪) to attack their flank.
Your servant held Fú Xiàn (涪縣) as a strategic point to support both east and west.
Wéi (維) and his subordinates commanded forty to fifty thousand infantry and cavalry.
Clad in armor and with sharpened weapons,
they filled rivers and valleys,
with their forces stretching for hundreds of lǐ, head to tail.
Relying on their numbers,
they marched abreast to the west.
Your servant ordered Xián (咸), Kǎi (闓), and others to divide their forces to occupy strategic positions,
spreading a wide net.
To the south, they blocked the path to Wú (吳);
to the west, they blocked the road to Chéngdū (成都);
to the north, they cut off the escape routes.
They gathered from all four sides,
advancing from both front and rear.
The paths were cut off,
leaving no place to flee or hide.
Your servant also personally wrote an explanation,
showing them a path to survival.
The bandit groups, trapped and pressed,
knew their fate was sealed and their time was up.
They laid down their armor and threw away their spears,
bound their hands and surrendered their allegiance.
Their seals and ribbons numbered in the tens of thousands,
their equipment piled up like mountains.
In ancient times, Shùn (舜) danced with shields and axes,
and the Miáo (苗) tribes submitted themselves.
At the Battle of Mùyě (牧野),
the Shāng (商) warriors turned their spears: there was conquest without battle,
the ultimate achievement of an emperor.
To preserve a state whole is best,
to break a state is secondary;
to preserve an army whole is best,
to break an army is secondary: these are the excellent principles of military strategy.
Your Majesty's (Bìxià's 陛下的) sacred virtue
rivals that of previous generations.
Your loyal and wise advisors
follow in the footsteps of Gōng Dàn (公旦).
You nurture all living beings with benevolence,
and righteously punish the disobedient.
Foreign customs turn to transformation,
none think not to submit.
The army does not exceed its time,
and weapons are not stained with blood.
For ten thousand lǐ, there is a common ethos,
and the nine provinces are united.
Your servant then respectfully proclaimed Your Majesty's (Zàomìng's 詔命) edict,
propagating Your benevolent transformation.
We restored their ancestral altars,
pacified their villages,
remitted their taxes and levies,
eased their conscriptions and labor.
We instructed them in virtue and etiquette to change their customs,
and showed them proper conduct to transform their ways.
The people are joyful and contented,
each enjoying peace and leisure.
Later generations will surely recover.
There is no greater righteousness than this.”
Huì (會) then strictly ordered his officers and soldiers not to plunder,
humbly welcomed and accepted
the officials of Shǔ (蜀),
and developed a very cordial relationship with Wéi (維).
In the twelfth month, an imperial edict stated:
“Wherever Huì (會) advanced, he crushed and destroyed;
there were no strong enemies before him.
He secured numerous cities,
and netted all those who fled.
The valiant chiefs of Shǔ (蜀)
bound their hands and surrendered their lives.
His plans left no strategy unused,
and every action yielded success.
All who surrendered or were executed
numbered in the tens of thousands.
He achieved complete victory and singular conquest,
conquering without battle.
He pacified the western regions,
and the borders are now peaceful and tranquil.
Therefore, Huì (會) is appointed Sītú (司徒),
further enfeoffed as a xiànhóu (縣侯),
with an additional ten thousand households.
Two of his sons are enfeoffed as tínghóu (亭侯),
each with a thousand households.”
Zhōng Huì, however, harbored different intentions within himself.
Because Dèng Ài acted on his own authority and was solely in charge of affairs,
Zhōng Huì secretly reported that Dèng Ài showed signs of rebellion.
Thereupon, an imperial edict summoned Dèng Ài in a cage-cart.
Sīmǎ Wénwáng feared that Dèng Ài might not obey the order,
so he ordered Zhōng Huì to advance with his army to Chéngdū.
The supervisor of the army, Wèi Guàn, proceeded ahead of Zhōng Huì,
carrying a handwritten decree from Wénwáng to announce to Dèng Ài's army.
Dèng Ài's soldiers all laid down their weapons,
and he was then captured and placed in a cage-cart.
The only person Zhōng Huì had feared was Dèng Ài.
Once Dèng Ài was captured, Zhōng Huì soon arrived,
taking sole command of the large army,
and his might shook the western lands.
He considered his achievements and fame to surpass the age,
and felt he could no longer serve beneath others.
Moreover, with fierce generals and elite soldiers all under his command,
he then plotted rebellion.
He intended to have Jiāng Wéi and others lead the Shǔ forces out through Xié Gǔ,
while Zhōng Huì himself would lead the main army following behind them.
Once they reached Cháng'ān,
he would order the cavalry to take the land route,
and the infantry to take the water route, floating down the Wèi River into the Yellow River,
believing they could reach Mèngjīn in five days
and rendezvous with the cavalry in Luòyáng.
In a single day, the empire could be pacified.
Zhōng Huì received a letter from Wénwáng saying:
"I fear that Dèng Ài might not comply with the summons.
I am now sending the Central Protector of the Army, Jiǎ Chōng, with ten thousand infantry and cavalry directly into Xié Gǔ
to garrison Lèchéng.
I myself will lead one hundred thousand troops to Cháng'ān.
We shall meet soon."
Upon receiving the letter, Zhōng Huì
exclaimed in surprise to his close associates, saying:
"I merely captured Dèng Ài,
and the Prime Minister knew I could handle it alone;
now he comes with such a large force,
he must suspect my ulterior motives.
I must act quickly.
If I succeed,
I can win the empire;
if I fail,
I can retreat and hold Shǔ-Hàn,
still being no less than Liú Bèi.
Since Huáinán,
I have not made a single false move in my plans,
which is known to all under heaven.
With this reputation, where can I return?"
On the fifteenth day of the first month of the fifth year, Zhōng Huì arrived.
The next day,
he invited all the Protectors of the Army, Prefects, Commanders of the Guards, and former officials of Shǔ,
to mourn the Empress Dowager in the Shǔ imperial court.
He forged the Empress Dowager's dying edict,
ordering Zhōng Huì to raise an army to depose Wénwáng.
He distributed this to all present,
instructing them to discuss it.
After their deliberation, they signed the tablets,
and he had his trusted confidants replace and lead the various armies.
All the invited officials
were locked in the various offices of Yìzhōu,
and the city gates and palace gates were all closed,
with heavily armed guards surrounding them.
A supervisor in Zhōng Huì's command, Qiū Jiàn, originally belonged to Hú Liè.
Hú Liè had recommended him to Wénwáng,
and Zhōng Huì requested him to follow him,
greatly favoring him.
Qiū Jiàn pitied Hú Liè, who was confined alone,
and appealed to Zhōng Huì
to allow one of Hú Liè's close soldiers to go out for food and drink.
The other commanders of guards each sent in one person as well, following the example.
Hú Liè deceived his close soldier and sent a message to his son saying:
"Qiū Jiàn secretly told me that Zhōng Huì has dug a large pit,
and prepared thousands of white clubs.
He intends to summon all the external troops inside,
give each man a white club,
appoint them as scattered generals,
and then kill them one by one in the pit with the clubs."
(Bàng is the same as bàng.)
(Kǔ qià fǎn.)
The close soldiers of the various commanders also all repeated this story,
and it spread throughout the night,
reaching everyone.
Someone suggested to Zhōng Huì:
"You should kill all the commanders of guards and above."
Zhōng Huì hesitated and could not decide.
On the eighteenth day, at midday,
Hú Liè's soldiers and Hú Liè's son sounded drums and charged out of the gate.
The soldiers of all the armies, without prior arrangement, also rushed out with shouts and drumbeats,
without anyone needing to urge them on,
and they vied to be first to reach the city.
At that time, Zhōng Huì was giving armor and weapons to Jiāng Wéi.
They heard a clamor outside,
like a fire had broken out.
After a moment,
they heard soldiers rushing towards the city.
Zhōng Huì was alarmed,
and said to Jiāng Wéi:
"The soldiers seem to be intending mischief,
what should we do?"
Jiāng Wéi said:
"We should simply attack them."
Zhōng Huì sent soldiers to kill all the confined commanders and prefects.
Those inside lifted tables to barricade the gates.
The soldiers chopped at the gates,
but could not break them.
Soon,
those outside propped ladders against the city and climbed over,
or set fire to the city roofs.
They swarmed forward like ants in a chaotic advance,
arrows fell like rain.
The commanders and prefects climbed out from the roofs,
and joined their own soldiers.
Jiāng Wéi led Zhōng Huì's personal guards in battle,
personally killing five or six men.
The crowd then hacked and killed Jiāng Wéi,
and rushed to kill Zhōng Huì.
Zhōng Huì was forty years old at the time,
and several hundred officers and soldiers died.
Initially,
Dèng Ài was Grand Commandant,
and Zhōng Huì was Minister of Works,
both holding imperial credentials and commanding all armies as before.
They both died before receiving their full appointments.
Zhōng Huì's elder brother, Zhōng Yù,
had died in the winter of the fourth year.
Zhōng Huì never knew about this.
Zhōng Huì's nephew, Zhōng Yōng,
followed Zhōng Huì and died with him.
Zhōng Huì's adopted nephews, Zhōng Yì, Zhōng Jùn, and Zhōng Chán,
(Chì lián fǎn.)
were imprisoned
and slated for execution.
Sīmǎ Wénwáng memorialized the Emperor, who issued an edict saying:
"Zhōng Jùn and others' grandfather, Zhōng Yóu,
during the reigns of the Three Ancestors,
reached the highest positions of the Three Ducal Ministers,
assisting the dynasty and establishing merits,
and his spirit was honored in the ancestral temple.
His father, Zhōng Yù,
served in various posts, internal and external,
performing his duties with achievement.
In the past, Chǔ, recalling Zǐwén's governance,
did not extinguish the sacrifices of the Dòu clan.
Jìn, recognizing Chéng Xuān's loyalty,
preserved the descendants of the Zhào clan.
Should the crimes of Zhōng Huì and Zhōng Yōng
lead to the extermination of Zhōng Yóu and Zhōng Yù's lineage,
I would feel pity!
Zhōng Jùn and Zhōng Chán, the brothers, are specifically pardoned;
those with official titles shall retain them.
Only Zhōng Yì and Zhōng Yōng's son shall suffer the prescribed punishment."
Some say
that Zhōng Yù had secretly memorialized Sīmǎ Wénwáng,
saying that Zhōng Huì, with his cunning, was unreliable
and should not be fully entrusted,
which is why Zhōng Jùn and others were pardoned.
Initially,
Wén Wáng欲遣Zhōng Huì伐Shǔ,
the Xī Cáo Shǔ, Shào Tì, sought an audience and said:
“Now you are sending Zhōng Huì to lead over ten myriad troops to attack Shǔ.
I foolishly believe that Huì, being single and without heavy responsibilities,
should not be the one to go. It would be better to send someone else.”
Wén Wáng smiled and said:
“Do I not know this myself?
Shǔ has been a menace to the world,
preventing the people from living in peace.
I can conquer it now as easily as turning my hand.
However, everyone else says Shǔ cannot be conquered.
When people are pre-emptively timid, their wisdom and courage are both exhausted.
If their wisdom and courage are exhausted and you force them to act,
they will simply become prey for the enemy.
Only Zhōng Huì shares my intention.
Now, if I send Huì to attack Shǔ,
it will surely be conquered.
After Shǔ is conquered,
even if it turns out as you fear,
what could he possibly achieve alone?
A general of a defeated army cannot be spoken of for courage,
and a grand master of a lost state cannot be plotted with for survival;
their spirit and courage are already broken.
If Shǔ is conquered,
its surviving people will be terrified
