and not suitable for plotting with.
The officers and soldiers from the Central Plains will all think of returning home
and will not be willing to act with him.
If he commits evil,
he will only bring about the destruction of his own clan.
You need not worry about this;
be careful not to let anyone hear this.”
When Huì later reported Dèng Ài’s insubordination,
Wén Wáng was about to go west.
Tì again said:
“Zhōng Huì’s forces
are five or six times those of Dèng Ài.
You only need to order Huì to capture Ài;
there is no need for you to go in person.”
Wén Wáng said:
“Have you forgotten what you said before,
and now you say there’s no need to go?
Even so,
these words must not be spread.
I must treat people with trustworthiness and integrity,
but people should not betray me.
How could I first harbor suspicions about others?
Recently, Jiǎ Hùjūn asked me,
saying: ‘Do you harbor any doubts about Zhōng Huì?’
I replied: ‘If I were to send you now,
would I still doubt you?’
Jiǎ also had no way to counter my words.
When I arrive at Cháng'ān,
it will become clear.”
When the army reached Cháng'ān,
Huì had indeed already died.
Everything was as predicted.
Huì once discussed the absence of ‘mutual bodies’ in the Yì and the similarity and difference of talent and nature.
After Huì’s death,
twenty chapters of a book were found in his home,
titled Dào Lùn,
but it was actually from the Xíng Míng school,
and its writing style resembled Huì’s.
Initially,
Huì, in his youth, and Shānyáng Wáng Bì were equally renowned.
Bì was fond of discussing Confucianism and Daoism,
with extraordinary eloquence.
He annotated the Yì and Lǎozi,
served as Shàngshū Láng,
and died at over twenty years old.
He jokingly said:
“Indeed, one’s clarity is sufficient to trace the profound and subtle,
yet one cannot depart from one’s inherent nature.
Yán Zǐ’s capacity,
though anticipated by Kǒng Fù,
still meant that when he met with joy, he could not be without it,
and when he suffered loss, he could not be without
grief.
Moreover, I used to disdain such people,
thinking that they were unable to let their emotions follow reason,
but now I know that natural inclination cannot be changed.
Your capacity,
though already settled within your breast,
yet after more than a decade or
a month,
how is it that your longing is so great?
Therefore, I know that Ní Fù’s feelings for Yán Zǐ
can be understood as not having great fault.”
Bì's annotation of Lǎozi,
for which he provided an outline,
achieved a coherent structure.
His work Dào Lǜe Lùn,
and his commentary on the Yì,
often contained profound words.
Tàiyuán Wáng Jì was fond of discourse,
and was critical of Lǎo and Zhuāng.
He often said:
“After seeing Bì’s Yì commentary,
I understood much more.”
However, Bì was shallow as a person and did not understand human emotions.
Initially, he was close to Wáng Lí and Xún
Róng.
Lí took his post as Huángmén Láng,
which caused Bì to resent Lí,
and his relationship with Róng also did not last.
In the tenth year of Zhèngshǐ,
Cáo Shuǎng was deposed,
and he was dismissed due to official matters.
That autumn, he succumbed to a plague and died,
at the age of twenty-four,
without sons,
thus ending his line.
When Bì died,
Jìn Jǐng Wáng heard of it
and sighed for several days,
showing how much he was cherished by those of high discernment.
Sūn Shèng said: The book of Yì,
exhausts the divine and comprehends transformations.
If not for the utmost essence in the world,
who could partake in this?
The commentaries of the world
are mostly baseless.
How much more so Bì, who with his sophistical arguments sought to generalize
profound principles?
Thus, his superficial explanations are full of ornate phrases,
but when it comes to creating yin and yang, no subtle profoundness is heard.
As for the transformations of the six hexagram lines,
the effects of various phenomena,
the hours, days, months, years,
and the interactions of the five phases,
Bì rejected
and ignored them,
not touching upon many things.
Although there are things in it worth observing,
I fear it will lead one astray from the Great Dao.
The Bó Wù Jì says: Initially,
Wáng Càn and his clan elder brother Kǎi both sought refuge in Jīngzhōu.
Liú Biǎo wanted to marry his daughter to Càn,
but found him ugly in appearance and rude in conduct.
Seeing Kǎi had a good demeanor,
he married her to Kǎi instead.
Kǎi begot
Yè,
and Yè was thus Liú Biǎo’s maternal grandson.
Cài Yōng had nearly ten thousand scrolls of books.
In his later years, he loaded several carts with them and gave them to Càn.
After Càn’s death,
Xiàngguó Yuàn Wèi Fèng plotted rebellion,
and Càn’s son was involved.
After they were executed,
all the books Cài Yōng had given
were passed to Yè.
Yè, courtesy name Chángxù,
reached the position of Yèzhě Púyè.
His son, Hóng, courtesy name Zhèngzōng,
was Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Hóng was
Bì’s elder brother.
The Wèi Shì Chūnqiū says: After Wén Dì executed Càn’s two sons,
he made Yè inherit Càn’s legacy.
A critique says: Wáng Líng’s moral integrity and aspirations were lofty,
Wúqiū Jiǎn’s talent and discernment were outstanding,
Zhūgě Dàn was stern, resolute, and imposing,
Zhōng Huì was refined in strategy and calculation.
All achieved prominent reputations
and attained glorious appointments.
Yet, they were all ambitious and misguided in their aims,
failing to foresee disaster and difficulty.
When trouble arose, it was as sudden as a triggered mechanism,
and their clans were wiped out.
Were they not confused and deluded?
Dèng Ài was exceptionally robust
and accomplished great deeds,
yet he was dim-witted in guarding against danger,
and his downfall quickly ensued.
How could he foresee Zhūgě Kè at a distance yet not perceive himself up close?
This is what the ancients called ‘seeing with the eyes’ (superficial observation).
Biographies of Technicians, Twenty-Ninth
Huà Tuó
had the courtesy name Yuánhuà. He was from Qiáo in Pèiguó.
His other name was Fū.
He studied in Xútǔ,
and was well-versed in several classics.
Chén Guī, the Chancellor of Pèi, recommended him as Xiàolián,
and Grand Commandant Huáng Wǎn invited him,
but he did not accept either.
He understood the art of nurturing life,
and people at the time believed he was almost a hundred years old yet had the appearance of a young man.
He was also skilled in medicine and remedies.
When he treated illnesses,
the decoction he prepared involved no more than a few ingredients.
He intuitively understood the dosages
and did not need to weigh them.
Once cooked, the patient would drink it immediately,
and after he explained the regimen,
the patient would leave and recover.
If moxibustion was needed,
it would be applied to no more than one or two spots,
and each spot received no more than seven or eight applications,
and the illness would also be cured.
If acupuncture was needed,
it would also be applied to no more than one or two spots.
He would insert the needle and say,
"It should be withdrawn after a certain sensation.
When it reaches that point,
tell me."
The patient would say,
"It has arrived,"
and he would then withdraw the needle,
and the illness would quickly improve.
If an illness was deeply rooted inside,
beyond the reach of needles or medicine,
requiring incision and excision,
he would administer his màfèisǎn.
In a moment, the patient would be as if drunk or dead, unconscious,
and he would then cut open and remove the affected part.
If the illness was in the intestines,
he would cut and wash the intestines,
suture the abdomen, and apply ointment.
After four or five days, the patient would recover,
feel no pain,
and not even realize what had happened.
Within a month,
they would be completely restored to health.
For example, the wife of the Chancellor of Gānlíng was six months pregnant,
suffering from abdominal pain and discomfort.
Huà Tuó felt her pulse
and said,
"The fetus is already dead."
He had someone feel for its location with their hand.
If on the left, it was male;
if on the right, it was female.
The person said,
"It's on the left."
So, he gave her a decoction to expel it.
Indeed, a male fetus was expelled,
and she recovered immediately.
The county official Yǐn Shì suffered from severe discomfort in all four limbs,
a dry mouth,
a dislike of hearing human voices,
and difficulty with urination.
Huà Tuó said,
"Try eating hot food.
If you sweat, you will recover;
if not,
you will die in three days."
Yǐn Shì ate hot food but did not sweat.
Huà Tuó said,
"The vital energy of the organs has already ceased internally;
he will die crying."
It happened exactly as Huà Tuó had said.
The prefectural officials Ér Xún and Lǐ Yán stayed together,
both suffering from headaches and fever,
their symptoms exactly the same.
Huà Tuó said,
"Xún should be purged,
and Yán should be made to sweat."
Someone questioned the difference in treatment.
Huà Tuó said,
"Xún's condition is externally replete,
while Yán's is internally replete,
so the treatment should differ."
He gave them each medicine,
and the next morning, both were up and well.
Yán Xīn of Yándú, along with several others, went to visit Huà Tuó.
Just as they arrived,
Huà Tuó said to Xīn,
"How is your body?"
Xīn replied,
"As usual."
Huà Tuó said,
"You have a serious illness visible on your face.
Do not drink too much wine."
After the visit, Xīn returned.
After traveling a few *lǐ*,
Xīn suddenly became dizzy and fell from his carriage.
People helped him back
to his home,
and he died overnight.
The former Supervising Secretary Dùn Zǐxiàn had recovered from an illness.
He went to Huà Tuó to have his pulse checked.
Huà Tuó said,
"You are still weak and not yet fully recovered.
Do not engage in strenuous activity.
If you have intercourse, you will die.
When you die,
your tongue will protrude several inches."
His wife, hearing of his recovery,
traveled over a hundred *lǐ* to visit him.
They stayed together and had intercourse.
After three days, he fell ill,
exactly as Huà Tuó had predicted.
Supervising Secretary Xú Yì fell ill,
and Huà Tuó went to visit him.
Yì said to Huà Tuó,
"Yesterday, Medical Officer Liú Zū needled my *wèiguǎn*,
and since then I've suffered from coughing
and restlessness when trying to lie down."
Huà Tuó said,
"He did not pierce the *wèiguǎn*;
he mistakenly hit the liver.
Your food intake will decrease daily,
and you will not survive five days."
It happened exactly as Huà Tuó had said.
Chén Shúshān of Dōngyáng had a two-year-old son who suffered from diarrhea,
always crying before having a bowel movement,
and becoming weaker by the day.
He consulted Huà Tuó.
Huà Tuó said,
"When his mother was pregnant,
her Yang energy was used to nourish the fetus,
leaving her breasts cold and deficient.
The child contracted cold from his mother,
which is why he is not recovering."
Huà Tuó gave her the Sīwù Nǚwǎn Wán (Four-Ingredient Women's Decoction Pills),
and in ten days the illness was gone.
Lady of Péngchéng went to the latrine at night
and was stung on the hand by a scorpion.
She groaned and cried uncontrollably.
Huà Tuó instructed her to place her hand
in warm, almost hot water.
She was suddenly able to sleep,
but those beside her had to repeatedly change the water
to keep it warm.
By the next morning, she was cured.
The military officer Méi Píng fell ill
and was discharged to return home.
His home was in Guǎnglín.
Less than two hundred *lǐ* from his destination,
he stopped at a relative's house.
After a short while,
Huà Tuó happened to arrive at the host's place.
The host asked Huà Tuó to examine Píng.
Huà Tuó said to Píng,
"If you had seen me earlier,
you would not have reached this point.
Now your illness is already deeply rooted.
If you leave quickly, you might still see your family.
You will die in five days."
Píng returned immediately,
and died on the exact day Huà Tuó had predicted.
While traveling on the road,
Huà Tuó saw a man suffering from a blocked throat,
who craved food but could not swallow it.
His family was taking him by cart to see a doctor.
Huà Tuó heard his groans,
stopped his carriage, went to examine him,
and said to him,
"Just now, by the roadside, there was a bakery selling very sour garlic biscuits.
Get three *shēng* of the juice and drink it.
The illness will naturally leave."
The man followed Huà Tuó's instructions immediately,
and promptly vomited a single object,
which he hung on the side of his cart.
He intended to go to Huà Tuó's house.
Huà Tuó had not yet returned.
Children playing in front of his gate
saw the object first
and said to each other,
"It looks like he met our master;
the thing on the cart is proof."
The sick man then entered and sat down.
He saw about ten such objects hanging on Huà Tuó's north wall.
There was also a commandery governor who was ill.
Huà Tuó believed that if the man became extremely angry, he would recover.
So he accepted a large sum of money from him but did not treat him.
After a short while, he left,
leaving a letter insulting the governor.
The governor indeed became enraged
and ordered men to pursue and kill Huà Tuó.
The governor's son, knowing the situation,
urged them not to pursue.
As the governor's fury intensified,
he vomited several *shēng* of black blood and recovered.
There was also a high official who was ill and distressed.
Huà Tuó said:
“Your illness is severe.
It requires opening your abdomen to remove the affliction.
However, your lifespan will not exceed ten years,
and this illness cannot kill you.
Endure the illness for ten years,
and your lifespan will naturally come to an end together with it.
There is no need to deliberately cut yourself open.”
The high official could not bear the pain and discomfort,
and insisted on having it removed.
Huà Tuó then proceeded with the operation.
The ailment was soon cured,
and ten years later, he died as predicted.
Chén Dēng, the Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng, fell ill,
suffering from chest discomfort and irritation,
a flushed face, and inability to eat.
Huà Tuó took his pulse and said:
“Your Excellency has several sheng of worms in your stomach,
which are about to form an internal ulcer.
This is caused by eating raw and tainted foods.”
He immediately prepared two sheng of decoction.
Chén Dēng first drank one sheng,
and after a short while, he drank the rest.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
he vomited out about three sheng of worms.
Their red heads were all wriggling,
and half of their bodies were like raw fish sashimi.
His suffering immediately ceased.
Huà Tuó said:
“This illness will recur after three periods.
Only if you encounter a good physician will you be saved.”
At the appointed time, the illness indeed flared up.
At that time, Huà Tuó was not present,
and Chén Dēng died as predicted.
Tài Zǔ heard of this and summoned Huà Tuó,
who then often remained by his side.
Tài Zǔ suffered from severe headaches (tóu fēng).
Whenever they flared up,
he became disoriented and dizzy.
Huà Tuó would needle the diaphragm,
and the symptoms would subside immediately.
General Lǐ’s wife was gravely ill.
Huà Tuó was called to examine her pulse,
and he said:
“She suffered a miscarriage, but the fetus has not been expelled.”
The general said:
“I heard she indeed had a miscarriage,
and the fetus has already been expelled.”
Huà Tuó said:
“According to the pulse,
the fetus has not yet been expelled.”
The general did not believe him.
Huà Tuó left,
and the woman's condition improved slightly.
After more than a hundred days, the symptoms recurred.
They called Huà Tuó again,
who said:
“This pulse still indicates the presence of a fetus.
Previously, she was supposed to give birth to two children.
One child came out first,
with a great deal of blood loss,
and the second child could not be delivered in time.
The mother did not realize it,
nor did those around her.
They did not try to deliver the second child,
so it could not be born.
The fetus died,
and the blood vessels did not return to normal,
so it dried up and adhered to the mother's spine,
causing her severe back pain.
Now I shall give her a decoction
and needle a specific point.
This dead fetus will surely be expelled.”
After the decoction and acupuncture were administered,
the woman experienced severe pain as if about to give birth.
Huà Tuó said:
“This dead fetus has been dry for a long time
and cannot be expelled on its own.
Someone should extract it.”
Indeed, a dead male fetus was found,
with complete limbs,
black in color,
and about one chi long.
Such were Huà Tuó’s extraordinary skills,
and all of this type.
However, he was originally a scholar,
and seeing medicine as his profession,
he often regretted it.
Later, when Tài Zǔ personally managed affairs
and fell critically ill,
he ordered Huà Tuó to attend to him exclusively.
Huà Tuó said:
“This condition is difficult to cure quickly.
Constant treatment
can prolong your life for years.”
Huà Tuó, having been away from home for a long time, yearned to return.
He then said:
“I have received a letter from home,
and I wish to return temporarily.”
Upon arriving home,
he used his wife’s illness as an excuse,
repeatedly requesting extensions and not returning.
Tài Zǔ repeatedly wrote to him,
and also ordered the commanderies and counties to send him back.
Huà Tuó, relying on his skills, was contemptuous of the situation
and still did not set out.
Tài Zǔ was greatly enraged
and sent someone to investigate.
If his wife was genuinely ill,
he was to be granted forty hu of black beans
and an extension of his leave;
if it was a fabrication,
he was to be arrested and sent back.
Consequently, he was handed over to the Xǔ prison,
where he was interrogated and confessed.
Xún Yù pleaded:
“Huà Tuó’s medical skills are truly excellent,
and human lives depend on them.
He ought to be pardoned.”
Tài Zǔ said:
“Do not worry,
will there be no such scoundrel in the world?”
And so, Huà Tuó was executed after interrogation.
Before his death, Huà Tuó
handed a scroll of books to the prison official,
saying:
“This can save lives.”
The official, fearing the law, did not accept it.
Huà Tuó did not insist
and asked for fire to burn it.
After Huà Tuó’s death,
Tài Zǔ’s headaches remained uncured.
Tài Zǔ said:
“Huà Tuó could cure this.
That petty man nurtured my illness,
wishing to make himself indispensable.
However, even if I hadn't killed this fellow,
he would still ultimately not cut out the root cause for me.”
Later, when his beloved son Cāng Shū fell ill,
Tài Zǔ sighed, saying:
“I regret having killed Huà Tuó,
causing this child to die so tragically.”
Initially,
the military officer Lǐ Chéng suffered from a severe cough,
unable to sleep day and night,
and occasionally spitting out pus and blood.
He consulted Huà Tuó.
Huà Tuó said:
“Your illness is an intestinal abscess,
and what you cough up
does not come from your lungs.
I will give you two qián of powder.
After you spit out more than two sheng of pus and blood,
take good care of yourself.
In a month, you can slightly recover,
and if you cherish yourself well,
in a year, you will be healthy.
At eighteen years old, you will have a minor relapse.
Take this powder,
and you will recover again.
If you do not get this medicine,
you will surely die.”
He then gave him two qián of powder.
Lǐ Chéng took the medicine and left.
Five or six years later,
a relative of his suffered from an illness similar to Lǐ Chéng’s.
He said to Lǐ Chéng:
“You are now strong and healthy,
while I am about to die.
How can you bear not to quickly give me the medicine,
waiting for misfortune?
Lend it to me first,
and when I recover,
I will ask Huà Tuó for more for you.”
Lǐ Chéng gave it to him.
He then happened to go to Qiáo,
just as Huà Tuó was being arrested.
In his haste, he could not bear to ask for more.
Eighteen years later,
Lǐ Chéng’s illness indeed flared up,
and with no medicine available,
he consequently died.
Wú Pǔ of Guǎnglíng and Fán Ā of Péngchéng both learned from Huà Tuó.
Pǔ followed Huà Tuó's methods in his treatments,
and saved many lives.
Huà Tuó said to Pǔ:
"The human body desires to move and work,
but it should not be overworked.
Movement allows the grain qi to be digested,
blood vessels to flow,
and illness not to arise.
This is like a door hinge that never rots.
Therefore, the immortals of antiquity practiced 'guiding and pulling' exercises,
such as 'bear-neck and owl-gaze,'
pulling and stretching the waist and body,
and moving all joints,
to seek a long life.
I have a technique
called the 'Frolics of the Five Animals.'
First is the tiger,
second is the deer,
third is the bear,
fourth is the ape,
fifth is the bird.
It also eliminates ailments
and benefits the feet and legs,
serving as 'guiding and pulling.'
When one feels unwell,
one performs the frolic of one animal,
until one is drenched and sweating,
then applies powder.
The body becomes light and agile,
and one desires food in the stomach."
Pǔ practiced this,
and at over ninety years old,
his hearing and sight were keen,
and his teeth were complete and strong.
Ā was skilled in acupuncture.
All doctors said that one should not rashly needle between the back and the chest cavity,
and that a needle should not go deeper than four fen.
However, Ā inserted needles into the back by one or two cùn,
and into the Jùquē point in the chest cavity by five or six cùn.
Yet, all patients invariably recovered.
Ā asked Huà Tuó for something edible that would benefit people.
Huà Tuó gave him Qīyè Qīngnián Sǎn (Lacquer Leaf and Green Mistletoe Powder).
Lacquer leaf powder one shēng,
green mistletoe powder fourteen liǎng.
Using this as the ratio,
he said that long-term use would eliminate the "three worms,"
benefit the five zàng organs,
lighten the body,
and prevent one's hair from turning white.
Ā followed his words
and lived to be over a hundred years old.
Lacquer leaves grow everywhere,
while green mistletoe grows in Fēng, Pèi, Péngchéng, and Cháogē.
Dù Kuí, courtesy name Gōngliáng,
was a native of Hénán.
Known for his musical knowledge, he became an Yǎyuèláng (officer for court music).
In the fifth year of Zhōngpíng (188 CE),
he left his post due to illness.
The provincial and commandery officials and Sītú invited him,
but due to the chaotic times, he fled to Jīngzhōu.
Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, ordered him to collaborate with Mèng Yào to compose court music for the Han emperor.
When the music was ready,
Liú Biǎo wanted to view it in his courtyard.
Dù Kuí admonished him, saying:
"Now the General is said to be composing music for the Son of Heaven,
but to perform it in the courtyard,
would this not be improper!"
Liú Biǎo accepted his words and stopped.
Later, Liú Biǎo's son Cóng surrendered to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ appointed Dù Kuí as Jūnmóu Jìjiǔ (Libationer of Military Strategy)
and involved him in grand music affairs,
then ordered him to create new court music.
Dù Kuí was skilled in bells and pitch pipes,
with intelligence surpassing others.
He mastered string and wind instruments and all eight sounds,
leaving nothing he could not do.
Only singing and dancing were not his strengths.
At that time, Sǎnláng Dèng Jìng and Yǐn Qí were skilled in chanting court music;
the singer Yǐn Hú could sing the songs for ancestral temples and suburban sacrifices;
the dancers Féng Sù and Fú Yǎng understood the dances of previous generations.
Dù Kuí oversaw and meticulously researched,
consulting ancient classics from afar,
and collecting past practices nearby.
He taught, practiced, and rehearsed,
prepared musical instruments,
and restored the ancient music of previous generations.
All this began with Dù Kuí.
During the Huángchū era,
he served as Tàiyuèlìng (Director of the Grand Music Bureau) and Xiélǜ Dūwèi (Colonel-Protector of Pitch Regulation).
Chái Yù, a Han bell-casting artisan, was ingenious and creative.
He made many innovations in the forms of instruments,
and was also recognized by the nobles of the time.
Dù Kuí ordered Chái Yù to cast bronze bells.
Their pitches, both clear and dull, often did not conform to the standards.
He repeatedly had them destroyed and recast.
Chái Yù was very annoyed,
thinking Dù Kuí's standards for clear and dull pitches were arbitrary,
and somewhat resisted Dù Kuí.
Dù Kuí and Chái Yù reported each other to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ took the cast bells,
mixed and tested them repeatedly.
Then he realized Dù Kuí was meticulous and Chái Yù was deceptive.
Thereupon, Chái Yù and his sons were punished
and all became horse grooms.
Wéndì, who favored and treated Chái Yù well,
once also ordered Dù Kuí to play the shèng and qín among the guests,
along with Zuǒ Xiàn and others.
Dù Kuí showed a difficult expression,
which displeased the Emperor.
Later, Dù Kuí was imprisoned for another matter,
and Xiàn and others were sent to learn from him.
Dù Kuí considered what he practiced to be refined,
and that holding office was fundamental.
He remained dissatisfied,
and was eventually dismissed from office, dying thereafter.
His disciples, Shào Dēng, Zhāng Tài, and Sāng Fù from Hénán,
each reached the position of Tàiyuèchéng (Assistant Director of the Grand Music Bureau).
Chén Háng of Xiàpī became Sīlǜ Zhōnglángjiàng (Colonel-Protector in Charge of Pitch Regulation).
Although Zuǒ Yánnián and others were skilled in music,
they were all good at Zhèng music.
None matched Dù Kuí in their love for antiquity and preservation of correctness.
Zhū Jiànpíng,
a native of Pèiguó,
was skilled in physiognomy.
In the villages and alleys,
his predictions were proven true on more than one occasion.
When Tàizǔ became Wèigōng,
he heard of him
and summoned him to be a Láng (gentleman-in-waiting).
When Wéndì was Wǔguānjiāng,
he hosted over thirty guests at a banquet.
Wéndì asked about his own lifespan
and then had him examine all the guests.
Zhū Jiànpíng said:
"The General will live to eighty,
but at forty, you will encounter a minor tribulation.
Please guard against it carefully."
He said to Xiàhóu Wēi:
"At forty-nine, you will become a Zhōumù (Provincial Governor),
but you will face a tribulation.
If you overcome it,
you can live to seventy
and attain the position of a Gōngfǔ (Grand Minister)."
He said to Yīng Qú:
"At sixty-two, you will become a Chángbó (Chief Minister),
but you will face a tribulation.
A year before this,
you will see a white dog alone,
but others will not see it."
He said to Cáo Biāo:
"You will hold a vassal state,
but at fifty-seven, you will face a military tribulation.
You should guard against it well."
Initially,
Xún Yōu of Yǐngchuān and Zhōng Yáo were close friends.
Xún Yōu died first,
leaving a young son.
Zhōng Yáo managed his household
and intended to marry off Xún Yōu's concubine.
He wrote in a letter:
"Gōngdá and I once went together for Zhū Jiànpíng to read our fortunes.
Jiànpíng said: 'Although Lord Xún is young,
he will entrust his future affairs to Lord Zhōng.'
I joked at the time, saying: 'I will only marry off your concubine Āwù.'
How could I have imagined that this son would perish so early,
and my jest would come true!
Now I wish to marry off Āwù
so she can find a good home.
Recalling Jiànpíng's marvels,
even Táng Jǔ and Xǔ Fù could not surpass him!"
In the seventh year of the Huángchū era of [Wén Dì],
at the age of forty,
he fell seriously ill.
He said to his attendants:
"What [Jiànpíng] said about eighty
refers to day and night.
I will certainly die now."
A moment later,
he indeed passed away.
When Xiàhóu Wēi was the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
at the age of forty-nine,
he contracted an illness in the first ten days of the twelfth month.
Recalling [Jiànpíng]'s words,
he concluded that he would surely die,
and prepared his last will and arrangements for his funeral,
ensuring everything was ready in advance.
Towards the last ten days of the month, he began to recover,
nearly reaching full recuperation.
On the thirtieth day, at sunset,
he invited the principal officials (jìgāng dàlì) to a banquet,
saying:
"My suffering is gradually subsiding.
Tomorrow, at cockcrow,
I will turn fifty.
[Jiànpíng]'s warning
will truly be surpassed."
After [Wēi] dismissed his guests,
his illness suddenly flared up again as he closed his eyes,
and he died in the middle of the night.
When Qú was sixty-one and serving as Attendant Counselor (shìzhōng),
on duty in the inner palace,
he suddenly saw a white dog.
When he asked others about it,
none of them had seen it.
Thereupon, he frequently attended gatherings
and eagerly indulged in sightseeing and excursions to the countryside,
drinking and feasting to amuse himself.
A year after the predicted time,
he died at sixty-three.
Cáo Biāo, who was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chǔ,
at the age of fifty-seven,
was implicated in colluding with Wáng Líng
and was granted death.
In general, all these individuals
fulfilled the predictions.
I cannot detail every case,
so I have merely recorded a few incidents.

Only Chancellor (xiàng) Sīkōng Wáng Chǎng, General Who Conquers the North (zhēngběi jiāngjūn) Chéng Xǐ, and Central Army Commander (zhōnglǐngjūn) Wáng Sù are said to have deviated from the predictions.
[Sù] was sixty-two years old
and critically ill.
All doctors thought he would not recover.
Madame [Sù] asked him to make his last wishes.
[Sù] said:
"[Jiànpíng] predicted that I would live beyond seventy
and reach the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers (sāngōng).
Neither of these has happened yet,
so what is there to worry about?"
Yet [Sù] eventually died.
[Jiànpíng] was also good at physiognomizing horses.
When [Wén Dì] was about to go out,
a horse was led in from outside.
[Jiànpíng] encountered it on the road
and said:
"According to the physiognomy of this horse,
it will die today."
When the emperor was about to mount the horse,
the horse disliked the scent of his robes
and, startled, bit [Wén Dì]'s knee.
The emperor was furious
and immediately had it killed.
[Jiànpíng] died during the Huángchū era.
Zhōu Xuān, courtesy name Kǒnghé,
was a native of Lè'ān.
He served as a commandery official.
The Administrator (tàishǒu) Yáng Pèi dreamt that someone said:
"On the first day of the eighth month, Duke Cáo will arrive,
and he will surely give you a staff
and make you drink medicated wine."
He ordered [Xuān] to interpret it.
At that time, the Yellow Turban Rebellion (Huángjīn Zéi) had erupted.
[Xuān] replied:
"A staff supports the weak,
and medicine cures illness.
On the first day of the eighth month,
the rebels will surely be eliminated."
On the appointed day,
the rebels were indeed defeated.
Later, Liú Zhēn of Dōngpíng dreamt of having four feet
and living in a hole in his doorway.
He had [Xuān] interpret it.
[Xuān] said:
"This is a dream for the state,
not for your family.
Female rebels will be killed."
A short while later,
the female bandits Zhèng and Jiāng were indeed annihilated.
This was because it was an omen for women,
as feet were not suitable for the door.
[Wén Dì] asked [Xuān]:
"I dreamt that two tiles from the palace roof fell to the ground
and transformed into a pair of mandarin ducks.
What does this mean?"
[Xuān] replied:
"Someone in the imperial harem will die violently."
The emperor said:
"I was only teasing you!"
[Xuān] replied:
"Dreams are merely thoughts;
if one expresses them in form,
they will predict fortune or misfortune."
Before he finished speaking,
the Prefect of the Yellow Gates (huángmén lìng) reported that palace women had killed each other.
Not long after,
the emperor again asked:
"Last night, I dreamt of a green qi extending from the earth to the sky."
[Xuān] replied:
"A noble woman in the realm will die unjustly."
At that time,
the emperor had already dispatched an envoy with an imperial rescript to grant death to Empress Zhēn.
Hearing [Xuān]'s words, he regretted it
and sent someone to chase the envoy, but it was too late.
The emperor asked again:
"I dreamt of rubbing the inscription on a coin,
wanting to erase it, but it became clearer instead.
What does this mean?"
[Xuān] looked distressed and did not reply.
The emperor asked him again,
and [Xuān] replied:
"This is a family matter for Your Majesty.
Although you [intend] to do so, the Empress Dowager does not permit it.
Thus, the inscription wanted to fade but became clearer."
At that time, the emperor wanted to punish his brother Zhí,
but pressured by the Empress Dowager,
he merely demoted him.
[Xuān] was made a Gentleman of the Palace (zhōngláng)
and attached to the Grand Astrologer (tàishǐ).
Someone once asked [Xuān]:
"Last night I dreamt of a straw dog.
What is its interpretation?"
[Xuān] replied:
"You will get good food!"
A moment later,
he went out
and indeed encountered a bountiful meal.
Later, he again asked [Xuān]:
"Last night I dreamt of a straw dog again.
What does it mean?"
[Xuān] said:
"You will fall from a carriage and break your leg.
You should be cautious."
A short while later,
it happened as [Xuān] had said.
Later, he again asked [Xuān]:
"Last night I dreamt of a straw dog again.
What does it mean?"
[Xuān] said:
"Your house will catch fire.
You should guard it well."
Soon after, a fire broke out.
He said to [Xuān]:
"The three times before,
I did not dream.
I was just testing you.
Why were they all accurate?"
[Xuān] replied:
"This was a divine spirit moving you to speak,
thus it was no different from a true dream."
He also asked [Xuān]:
"You dreamt of a straw dog three times, but the interpretations were different.
Why is that?"
[Xuān] said:
"A straw dog
is an object for sacrificing to the gods.
Therefore, when you first dreamt,
you were to receive leftover food.
After the sacrifice is completed,
the straw dog is run over by a carriage,
thus in the second dream, you were to fall from a carriage and break your leg.
After the straw dog has been run over by a carriage,
it must be carried away as firewood,
thus in the last dream, you were worried about a fire."
Such were [Xuān]'s dreams.
Eight or nine out of ten were accurate.
The world compared him to [Jiànpíng]'s physiognomy.
The other effective cases are not listed in order.
He died at the end of [Míng Dì]'s reign.
Guǎn Lù, courtesy name Gōngmíng,
was a native of Píngyuán.
His appearance was rough and ugly,
he lacked dignity but was addicted to alcohol.
In eating, drinking, speaking, and playing,
he did not choose companions,
so people generally liked him but did not respect him.
My father was the Lìcáo,
and three brothers of the Lìcáo people, named Guō Ēn,
all suffered from a crippling disease.
They asked Guǎn Luò to divine the cause.
Guǎn Luò said:
“In the hexagram, there is a tomb of your clan's root.
Within the tomb, there is a female ghost.
If not your paternal aunt (bómǔ),
then she must be your paternal uncle’s wife (shūmǔ).
In a past era of famine,
she must have coveted a few *shēng* of rice,
pushed someone into a well,
where they made gurgling sounds,
then pushed a large stone
down, breaking their head.
The lone spirit suffered grievously,
and appealed to Heaven.”
Thereupon, Guō Ēn wept and confessed his guilt.
In Guǎngpíng, Liú Fènglín’s wife was gravely ill,
and a coffin had already been purchased.
It was the first month,
and they asked Guǎn Luò to divine.
He said:
“Her life will end in the eighth month, on the *Xīnmǎo* day, at noon.”
Liú Fènglín thought it could not possibly be so,
but his wife gradually recovered.
When autumn arrived, her illness recurred,
exactly as Guǎn Luò had said.
Guǎn Luò went to see Wáng Jī, the Grand Administrator of Ānpíng.
Wáng Jī asked him to cast a hexagram.
Guǎn Luò said:
“There will be a low-born woman
who gives birth to a boy,
who immediately after falling to the ground will run into the stove and die.
Also, on the bed, there will be a large, bit-holding object,
which everyone, big and small, will look at,
and then it will disappear shortly.
Furthermore, a crow will enter the room,
fight with a swallow,
the swallow will die,
and the crow will leave.
There will be these three strange occurrences.”
Wáng Jī was greatly alarmed
and asked about their auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
Guǎn Luò said:
“It’s merely that your guest-house has been standing for a long time,
and the *chīmèi wǎngliǎng* are causing mischief.
The child running immediately upon birth,
it is not that he can run on his own,
it is simply the demon of Sòng Wújì leading him into the stove.
The large, bit-holding object
is just an old clerk (shūzuǒ).
The crow fighting with the swallow
is just an old subordinate (língxià).
Now, the hexagram shows the phenomena but not their harm,
so I know these are not omens of misfortune or calamity;
you have no need to worry.”
Afterward, there was indeed no trouble.
At that time, the women in the household of the Magistrate of Xìndū were frightened
and fell ill one after another.
They asked Guǎn Luò to divine for them.
Guǎn Luò said:
“At the western end of your north hall,
there are two dead men.
One man holds a spear,
the other holds a bow and arrows.
Their heads are inside the wall,
and their feet are outside the wall.
The one holding the spear causes stabbing pains in the head,
which is why your heads ache severely and cannot be lifted.
The one holding the bow and arrows causes shooting pains in the chest and abdomen,
which is why your hearts feel suspended in pain and you cannot eat or drink.
By day they float around,
by night they come to the sick,
which is why they cause fright.”
Thereupon, they dug up and moved the bones,
and everyone in the family recovered.
Wáng Jīng of Qīnghé, having resigned from office and returned home,
met Guǎn Luò.
Wáng Jīng said:
“Recently, there was a strange occurrence,
which greatly displeased me.
I wish to trouble you to cast a hexagram.”
When the hexagram was cast,
Guǎn Luò said:
“The *yáo* are auspicious,
so it is not a strange omen.
Last night, as you were in front of the hall door,
a stream of light, like a sparrow,
flew into your bosom,
making a rumbling sound.
Your inner spirit was uneasy,
you took off your clothes and paced about,
calling to your wife,
seeking the remaining light.”
Wáng Jīng laughed heartily and said:
“It is exactly as you say.”
Guǎn Luò said:
“It is auspicious,
a sign of promotion in office,
and its fulfillment is imminent.”
Shortly thereafter,
Wáng Jīng became the Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià.
Guǎn Luò again visited Guō Ēn’s house.
A flying dove came and perched on the beam,
its cries very mournful.
Guǎn Luò said:
“An old man will arrive from the east,
carrying a piglet
and a pot of wine.
Although the host will be pleased,
there will be a minor mishap.”
The next day, a guest indeed arrived,
as predicted.
Guō Ēn instructed the guest to drink sparingly, refrain from meat, and be careful with fire.
But they shot a chicken for food,
and an arrow, deflected from among the trees, struck the hand of a several-year-old girl,
causing blood to flow and great fright.
Guǎn Luò went to the house of Liú Chángrén, Magistrate of Āndé.
A magpie came and chirped on the roof of the inner chambers,
its cry very urgent.
Guǎn Luò said:
“The magpie says that to the northeast, a woman killed her husband yesterday,
and is implicating a man from the west, a Li Lóu.
The matter will be revealed no later than when the sun sets in Yúyuān.
The informant will arrive.”
At the appointed time,
an informer from the same village to the northeast indeed arrived,
reporting that a neighboring woman had personally killed her husband,
and falsely claimed that a westerner had a grudge against her husband
and came to kill her husband.
Guǎn Luò went to the residence of Wáng Hóngzhí, the Diǎnnóng of Lièrén.
A whirlwind, over three *chǐ* high,
came from the direction of Shēn,
swirling and revolving in the courtyard,
stopping and then starting again,
and only ceased after a long time.
Wáng Hóngzhí asked Guǎn Luò about it.
Guǎn Luò said:
“A cavalry officer will arrive from the east;
I fear a father will mourn his son,
how tragic!”
The next day, an officer from Jiāodōng arrived,
and Wáng Hóngzhí’s son indeed died.
Wáng Hóngzhí asked the reason.
Guǎn Luò said:
“That day was *Yǐmǎo*,
which is the sign of the eldest son.
Wood falls in Shēn,
the Dipper points to Shēn,
Shēn clashes with Yín,
these are signs of death and mourning.
The sun reaches Wǔ when the wind rises,
which is the sign of a horse.
*Lí* represents literature,
which is the sign of an officer.
Shēn and Wèi represent the tiger,
and the tiger represents a great man,
which is the sign of the father.”
A male pheasant flew in
and perched on the inner bell-pillar of Wáng Hóngzhí’s house.
Wáng Hóngzhí was greatly uneasy
and asked Guǎn Luò to cast a hexagram.
Guǎn Luò said:
“By the fifth month, you will certainly be promoted.”
It was the third month then.
At the appointed time,
Wáng Hóngzhí was indeed appointed Grand Administrator of Bóhǎi.
Zhūgě Yuán, Magistrate of Guǎntáo, was promoted to Grand Administrator of Xīnxīng.
Guǎn Luò went to bid him farewell,
and many guests gathered.
Zhūgě Yuán himself stood up and placed a swallow’s egg, a wasp’s nest, and a spider
into a container and asked for a divination without seeing the objects.
When the hexagram was cast,
Guǎn Luò said:
“The first object,
containing nascent life that must transform,
clinging to the eaves and hall,
male and female in form,
wings spread wide—
this is a swallow’s egg.
The second object,
its home hangs upside down,
with many entrances,
concealing essence and nurturing venom,
transforming in autumn—
this is a wasp’s nest.
The third object,
trembling, with long legs,
spinning silk to form a web,
seeking food through its net,
active in the twilight—
this is a spider.”
Everyone present was astonished and delighted.
Guǎn Lù's paternal cousin, Xiàoguó,
lived in Chìqiū.
Lù went to visit him,
and met two guests.
After the guests left,
Lù said to Xiàoguó:
"These two men have an aura of misfortune on their foreheads, and between their mouths and ears.
When strange changes arise,
their twin souls will have no home;
their wandering souls will float in the sea,
and their bones will return to their homes.
In a short while, they will both die."
A few tens of days later,
the two men got drunk while drinking.
That night, they were riding in a cart together.
The ox was startled and ran off the road into the Zhāng Hé.
They both drowned immediately.
At this time,
among Lù's neighbors,
outer doors were not closed,
and there were no thieves.
Huá Biǎo, the Grand Administrator of Qīnghé,
summoned Lù to serve as a Literary Aide (Wénxué Yuàn).
Zhào Kǒngyào of Ānpíng recommended Lù to Péi Huī, the Inspector of Jìzhōu, saying:
"Lù's nature is broad and magnanimous,
unconstrained by the world.
When observing astronomy, he rivals Gān Gōng and Shí Shēn in subtlety;
when examining the Zhōu Yì, he matches Jìzhǔ in insight.
Now, your enlightened Lord is extending your divine presence to the deep valleys,
and focusing your essence on the nine marshes.
Lù should receive the corresponding peaceful harmony
and seize the opportune moment to spread his wings."
Huī thereupon appointed him Literary Attendant Official (Wénxué Cóngshì),
invited him for an audience,
and befriended him greatly.
He was transferred to Jùlù Commandery,
and promoted to Assistant Administrator (Zhìzhōng Biéjià).
When first responding to the provincial summons,
he rode with his younger brother, Jìrú.
Upon reaching the west of Wǔchéng,
he divined the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness himself
and told Rú:
"You will see three civets in the old city,
and then you will become prominent."
Proceeding to the corner of the old city west of the river,
they indeed saw three civets sitting together by the city wall.
Both brothers rejoiced.
In the ninth year of Zhèngshǐ (248 CE), he was recommended as Xiùcái.
On the 28th day of the twelfth month,
Hé Yàn, the Minister of Personnel, invited him.
Dèng Yáng was with Yàn.
Yàn said to Lù:
"I hear that your hexagram interpretations are divinely subtle.
Please try to cast a hexagram for me
to know if my position will reach that of the Three Excellencies?"
He also asked:
"I have repeatedly dreamt of dozens of green flies
coming to my nose,
and when I drive them away, they refuse to leave.
What does this mean?"
Lù replied:
"An owl
is a lowly bird in the world,
but when it is in the forest eating mulberries,
it harbors good tidings for me.
How much more so for Lù, whose heart is not of grass or wood;
how dare I not be utterly loyal?
In ancient times, Yuán and Kǎi assisted Chónghuá,
spreading kindness and harmony.
The Duke of Zhōu supported King Chéng,
sitting and waiting until dawn.
Thus, they were able to spread their glory across the six directions,
and all nations enjoyed peace.
This is the auspicious response of following the Way.
It is not something that divination can reveal.
Now, your Lordship's position is as heavy as mountains,
and your power like thunder and lightning.
Yet, those who cherish virtue are few,
while those who fear your might are many.
This is perhaps not the benevolence of 'being cautious and wary, receiving much good fortune.'
Furthermore, the nose is Gèn (the trigram of the mountain),
the central mountain of the heavens,
high but not perilous,
which is why one can long maintain nobility.
Now, green flies, which are foul and evil,
gather upon it.
Those who are highly placed may stumble,
and those who are arrogant may perish.
One must contemplate the principle of avoiding excess,
and the cycle of prosperity and decline.
Therefore, 'Mountain in the Earth' is Humility (Qiān),
and 'Thunder in the Heaven' is Vigor (Zhuàng).
Humility means 'to decrease the many and increase the few,'
while Vigor means 'not to tread where it is not proper.'
Never has one diminished oneself and not become glorious and great,
nor acted improperly and not suffered damage and ruin.
May your Lordship aspire to the meaning of King Wén's six hexagram lines,
and ponder the interpretations of our Master (Confucius) on the 'image' and 'judgment.'
Only then can the Three Excellencies be decided,
and the green flies driven away."
Dèng Yáng said:
"This is just common talk from an old scholar."
Lù replied:
"An old scholar (Lǎoshēng) sees what is not born (bùshēng); common talk (chángtán) sees what is not talked about (bùtán)."
Yàn said:
"We shall meet again after the New Year."
Lù returned to his residence
and recounted these words to his maternal uncle.
His uncle reprimanded Lù for speaking too sharply and bluntly.
Lù said:
"Speaking to dead men,
what is there to fear?"
His uncle was greatly angered
and called Lù insane and rebellious.
On New Year's Day,
there was a strong northwest wind,
and dust obscured the sky.
After more than ten days,
he heard that Yàn and Yáng had both been executed.
Only then did his uncle submit.
Earlier, when Lù visited Zhōng Yù, the Grand Administrator of Wèijùn,
they discussed the meaning of the Yì.
Lù then said:
"Divination can reveal the day of your birth and death."
Yù made him divine the month and day of his birth,
and it was exactly as Lù said, without error.
Yù was greatly astonished
and said:
"You are to be feared!
Death is entrusted to Heaven,
not to you."
Thereupon, he never sought divination again.
Yù asked Lù:
"Will there be peace in the world?"
Lù replied:
"Currently, the 'four nines' are flying in the sky,
it is opportune to see great men.
Divine might is rising and establishing,
and the Kingly Way is enlightened and civilized.
Why worry about lack of peace?"
Yù did not understand Lù's words.
Not long after,
Cáo Shuǎng and others were executed,
and then he awoke to the meaning.
Liú Bīn, the Grand Administrator of Píngyuán, took an impression bag and a mountain pheasant feather, put them into a container,
and asked Lù to divine.
Lù said:
"Square inside and round outside,
with five colors forming patterns,
containing treasures and upholding trust,
when displayed, it has its regulations—
this is an impression bag.
The towering mountains are majestic,
there is a bird with a red body,
its wings are black and yellow,
its call does not miss the morning—
this is a mountain pheasant feather."
Bīn said:
"The official residences in this commandery
have repeatedly experienced strange phenomena,
causing people to be terrified.
What is the reason for this?"
Lù replied:
"Perhaps due to the chaos at the end of the Hàn dynasty,
with soldiers and horses disrupting everything,
and the corpses of soldiers shedding blood,
polluting the hills and mountains.
Therefore, in the dim evening,
there are often strange apparitions.
Your Lordship's virtue is lofty and profound;
Heaven itself assists you.
May you enjoy all blessings,
to illuminate your auspicious favor."
Xú Jìlóng, the Magistrate of Qīnghé, sent someone out hunting,
and asked Lù to divine what would be caught.
Lù said:
"You will catch a small beast,
not a fowl for eating.
Though it has claws and teeth,
they are small and not strong.
Though it has patterns,
they are dense but not bright.
It is neither a tiger nor a pheasant;
its name is civet."
The hunter returned in the evening,
and it was indeed as Lù had said.
Jìlóng took thirteen different items,
put them in a large basket,
and asked Lù to guess them.
He said:
"There are indeed thirteen items in the container."
First, he named a chicken egg,
then a silkworm pupa,
and so he named each one,
only calling a comb a 'bì' (fine-toothed comb).
Guǎn Lù followed the army west,
passing by Múqiū Jiǎn’s tomb.
He leaned against a tree and sighed mournfully,
his spirits low.
When people asked him why,
Guǎn Lù said:
“Though the trees are lush,
there is no enduring form;
though the stele and eulogy are fine,
there are no descendants to guard them.
The Xuánwǔ hides its head,
the Cānglóng has no feet,
the Báihǔ holds a corpse in its mouth,
and the Zhūquè weeps sorrowfully.
With these four dangers present,
it is destined for the clan to be exterminated.
In no more than two years,
its manifestation will arrive.”
It turned out exactly as he had said.
Later, having a break,
he visited Ní, the Grand Administrator of Qīnghé.
At the time, there was a drought,
and Ní asked Guǎn Lù when it would rain.
Guǎn Lù replied:
“It will rain this evening.”
That day was sunny and dry,
with no sign of rain during the day.
The Commandant of the prefecture and the county magistrate were present,
and all believed it to be impossible.
When the drum struck once at night,
the stars and moon vanished,
wind and clouds arose together,
and a heavy rain ensued.
Thereupon, Ní lavishly observed the host’s rites,
and they rejoiced together.
In the second year of Zhèngyuán,
his younger brother Chén said to Guǎn Lù:
“The Grand General treats you with great kindness;
do you hope for wealth and high position?”
Guǎn Lù sighed deeply, saying:
“I know I have a certain destiny,
but Heaven gave me talent and intelligence,
not longevity.
I fear that between forty-seven and forty-eight,
I will not see my daughter marry or my son take a wife.
If I could escape this,
I would wish to be the Magistrate of Luòyáng,
so that people would not pick up lost items from the road,
and drums would not sound [for punishment].
But I only fear that I am destined to govern ghosts at Tài Shān,
and not living people.
What can I do?”
Chén asked him why,
and Guǎn Lù said:
“I have no bone of life on my forehead,
no spirit of preservation in my eyes,
no bridge pillar for my nose,
no heavenly root for my feet,
no three shells on my back,
and no three 'Rén' on my belly.
These are all signs of short life.
Furthermore, my natal year is Yín,
and I was born on the night of a lunar eclipse.
Heaven has a fixed number [for life],
which cannot be evaded,
but people simply do not know it.
More than a hundred people whose deaths I have predicted before and since
have never been wrong.”
In the eighth month of that year,
he became the Commandant-Assistant of the Privy Treasury.
He died in the second month of the following year,
aged forty-eight.
Commentary says: Huà Tuó’s medical diagnosis,
Dù Kuí’s music,
Zhū Jiànpíng’s physiognomy,
Zhōu Xuān’s dream interpretation,
and Guǎn Lù’s divination
were indeed all profound and mysterious and exceptional skills,
extraordinary and unique arts.
Formerly, Sǐmǎ Qiān recorded the biographies of Biǎn Què, Cāng Gōng, and the Rìzhě [diviners],
in order to expand on unusual accounts and highlight strange occurrences.
Therefore, these are recorded here.
Biography of the Wūhuán, Xiānbēi, and Eastern Yí, Chapter 30.
The *Shū* records,
“The Mányí disturb the Huá Xià,”
and the *Shī* states,
“The Xiǎnyǔn are greatly rampant.”
Long have they been a scourge to the Central States.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
the Xiōngnú had long been a border menace.
Though Emperor Xiàowǔ externally engaged the Four Barbarians,
pacifying the two Yuè and Cháoxiǎn in the east,
and attacking Èrshī and Dàyuān in the west,
and opening routes to Qióngzā and Yèláng,
all these were beyond the regions of loose suzerainty,
and could not significantly affect the Central States.
However, the Xiōngnú were the most pressing threat to the various Xià states;
when Hú cavalry invaded from the south, the three borders were endangered.
Therefore, generals such as Wèi and Huò were repeatedly dispatched
to deep northern expeditions,
pursuing the Chányú relentlessly,
and seizing their fertile lands.
Later, they protected the frontier and submitted as vassals,
becoming weaker generation after generation.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
Hūchúquán, the Southern Chányú, came to court,
and was subsequently detained for internal service,
while the Right Worthy King was sent to govern his state.
Thus, the Xiōngnú submitted,
more so than in former Hàn times.
However, the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi gradually grew stronger,
also taking advantage of the chaos at the end of the Hàn dynasty,
when the Central States had many internal affairs
and no time for foreign campaigns.
Thus, they were able to dominate the lands south of the Mò,
raiding cities and towns,
killing and abducting people.
The northern border continued to suffer from them.
At that time, Yuán Shào annexed Héběi,
and then brought the Wūhuán of the three commanderies under his control,
favoring their famous kings and recruiting their elite cavalry.
Thereafter, Shàng and Xī fled to Tàdùn.
Tàdùn was also valorous and skilled in warfare;
the elders of the border regions all compared him to Mòdú.
Relying on his remote and difficult-to-reach territory,
he dared to harbor fugitives,
thereby dominating the hundred barbarians.
Tài Zǔ secretly led an army on a northern expedition,
catching them by surprise,
and settled them in one battle.
The Yí and Dí submitted in awe,
and his prestige shook the northern lands.
He then led the Wūhuán forces to serve in his campaigns,
and the border people were able to live in peace.
Later, Kēbǐnéng, a great leader of the Xiānbēi, again controlled the various Dí tribes,
reclaiming all the former Xiōngnú territories.
From Yúnzhōng and Wǔyuán eastward to the Liáo River,
all became Xiānbēi territory.
They frequently violated the frontier and raided the border,
causing suffering in Yōu and Bìng provinces.
Tián Yù experienced the siege of Mǎchéng,
and Bì Guǐ suffered defeat north of the Xíng Pass.
During the Qīnglóng era,
the Emperor then listened to Wáng Xióng,
and sent an assassin to kill him.
After that, the tribes dispersed,
fighting each other.
The strong ones fled afar,
and the weak ones sought submission.
Consequently, the border regions were relatively peaceful,
and there were few incidents south of the Mò.
Although there were occasional raids and thefts,
they could no longer incite each other.
The Wūhuán and Xiānbēi are what were called the Dōnghú in ancient times.
Their customs and past events
have already been recorded and written down by the compilers of the Hàn records.
Therefore, only events from the late Hàn and early Wèi periods are cited
to supplement the changes among the Four Barbarians.
In the late Hàn dynasty,
Qiūlìjū, a great leader of the Wūhuán in Liáoxī,
had more than five thousand settlements.
Nánlóu, a great leader of the Wūhuán in Shànggǔ,
had more than nine thousand settlements.
Each claimed the title of king.
Sūpúyán, a great leader of the Wūhuán of the tributary state of Liáodōng,
had more than one thousand settlements,
and called himself King Qiào.
Wūyán, a great leader of the Wūhuán in Yòuběipíng,
had more than eight hundred settlements,
and called himself King Hánlǔ.
All of them were resourceful, brave, and strong.
Zhāng Chún, the Grand Administrator of Zhōngshān, rebelled and joined Qiūlìjū’s forces.
He styled himself King Mítiān Āndìng,
and became the commander-in-chief of the Wūhuán of the three commanderies.
He plundered the four provinces of Qīng, Xú, Yōu, and Jì,
killing and abducting officials and common people.
At the end of Emperor Líng’s reign,
Liú Yú was made Provincial Governor,
and he recruited Hú people to behead Zhāng Chún.
Then the northern provinces were pacified.
Later, Qiūlìjū died.
His son, Lóubān, was young,
so his nephew, Tàdùn, who possessed military strategy,
succeeded him,
taking overall command of the divisions of the three kings.
All the tribes followed his commands and orders.
Yuán Shào and Gōngsūn Zàn fought many indecisive battles.
Tàdùn sent envoys to Yuán Shào to seek peaceful relations,
and helped Shào attack Gōngsūn Zàn,
defeating him.
Yuán Shào falsely issued an imperial decree bestowing seals and ribbons upon Tàdùn, King Qiào, and King Hánlǔ,
appointing all of them as Chányú.
Later, Lóu Bān became powerful.
Qiào Wáng led his followers to enthrone Lóu Bān as Chányú,
and Tà Dùn as king.
However, Tà Dùn was more resourceful in devising strategies.
Yán Róu of Guǎngyáng,
as a youth, had been lost among the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi,
and was trusted by their tribes.
Róu then, relying on the Xiānbēi masses,
killed the Wūhuán Colonel Xíng Jǔ and took his place.
Shào subsequently favored and consoled him to pacify the northern frontier.
Later, Yuán Shàng was defeated and fled to Tà Dùn,
relying on his power,
to again plan for Jìzhōu.
Coincidentally, Tàizǔ pacified Héběi,
and Róu led the Xiānbēi and Wūhuán to submit.
Consequently, Róu was appointed colonel,
still holding the Han envoy's credentials,
governing Guǎngníng as before.
In the eleventh year of Jiàn'ān,
Tàizǔ personally campaigned against Tà Dùn at Liǔchéng.
With a stealthy army and deceptive routes,
when they were still over a hundred *lǐ* away,
the enemy finally became aware.
Shàng and Tà Dùn led their forces to meet them in battle at Fánchéng,
with a very strong army.
Tàizǔ ascended a height to survey the enemy's formation,
[抑] his army did not advance,
observed their slight movements,
then attacked and routed their forces,
personally beheading Tà Dùn on the battlefield,
with casualties covering the fields.
Sùfùwán, Lóu Bān, Wū Yán, and others fled to Liáodōng.
Liáodōng had them all beheaded
and sent their heads.
The remaining scattered remnants all surrendered.
The Wūhuán, numbering over ten thousand households, under Róu's jurisdiction in Yōuzhōu and Bìngzhōu,
all had their clans moved to live in Zhōngguó,
with their marquises, kings, and great chiefs leading their tribes to participate in campaigns.
From this, the Wūhuán of the three commanderies became renowned cavalry throughout the realm.
The Xiānbēi
Bùdùgēn, after he was established,
saw his forces gradually weaken.
His elder brother Fúluóhán also separately commanded tens of thousands of followers as a great chief.
During Jiàn'ān,
Tàizǔ pacified Yōuzhōu,
and Bùdùgēn, Kēbǐnéng, and others offered tribute through Wūhuán Colonel Yán Róu.
Later, the Wūhuán Néngchén Dī and others of Dàijùn rebelled,
seeking allegiance with Fúluóhán.
Fúluóhán led over ten thousand cavalry to welcome them.
Upon reaching Sānggān,
Dī and others discussed,
believing that Fúluóhán's tribe had lax discipline,
and feared they would not be assisted.
They then sent someone to summon Kēbǐnéng.
Kēbǐnéng immediately arrived with over ten thousand cavalry,
intending to form an alliance.
Kēbǐnéng then killed Fúluóhán at the meeting.
Fúluóhán's son Xièguīní and his followers all joined Kēbǐnéng.
Kēbǐnéng, considering he had killed Guīní's father,
treated him exceptionally well.
Bùdùgēn consequently resented Kēbǐnéng.
When Wéndì ascended the throne,
Tián Yù was appointed Wūhuán Colonel,
holding credentials and also overseeing the Xiānbēi,
garrisoned at Chāngpíng.
Bùdùgēn sent envoys to offer horses,
and the Emperor appointed him king.
Later, he frequently engaged in attacks with Kēbǐnéng,
and Bùdùgēn's forces gradually dwindled.
He led his over ten thousand households to seek refuge in Tàiyuán and Yànmén Commandery.
Bùdùgēn then sent someone to call out to Xièguīní, saying:
"Your father was killed by Kēbǐnéng,
yet you do not think of revenge,
but rather join your enemy.
Although he treats you well now,
this is a plot to kill you.
It is better to return to me.
You and I are blood relatives,
how can we be compared to an enemy?"
Consequently, Guīní led his tribe to escape back to Bùdùgēn,
and Kēbǐnéng pursued but could not catch him.
In the fifth year of Huángchū,
Bùdùgēn went to the court to offer tribute,
and was generously rewarded.
Thereafter, he single-mindedly guarded the frontier,
not causing banditry,
while Kēbǐnéng's forces became increasingly powerful.
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
he was intent on pacifying the barbarians,
to end military campaigns,
merely maintaining loose control over the two tribes.
In the first year of Qīnglóng,
Kēbǐnéng enticed Bùdùgēn to form a deep and peaceful alliance.
Thereupon, Bùdùgēn, along with Xièguīní and his followers, all joined Kēbǐnéng,
raiding Bìngzhōu,
and killing and abducting officials and common people.
The Emperor sent General of Galloping Cavalry Qín Lǎng to campaign against them.
Guīní rebelled against Kēbǐnéng,
and led his forces to surrender,
was appointed King of Guīyì,
bestowed with banners, a curved canopy, and drum music,
and resided in Bìngzhōu as before.
Bùdùgēn was killed by Kēbǐnéng.
Kēbǐnéng was originally from a small Xiānbēi tribe.
Due to his bravery and strength,
fair and just enforcement of laws,
and lack of greed for wealth,
the people acclaimed him as a great chief.
His tribe was close to the frontier.
Ever since Yuán Shào occupied Héběi,
many people from Zhōngguó defected to him,
teaching them to make weapons, armor, and shields,
and somewhat learning to read and write.
Therefore, when he commanded his tribesmen,
he imitated Zhōngguó,
establishing banners and pennants when going out hunting,
using drumbeats to signal advance and retreat.
In Jiàn'ān,
he offered tribute through Yán Róu.
When Tàizǔ campaigned west against Guānzhōng,
Tián Yín rebelled in Héjiān.
Kēbǐnéng led over three thousand cavalry to follow Róu and defeat Yín.
Later, the Wūhuán of Dàijùn rebelled,
and Kēbǐnéng again assisted in their depredations.
Tàizǔ appointed Marquis of Yānlíng Zhāng as General of Galloping Cavalry,
who campaigned north,
and severely defeated them.
Kēbǐnéng fled beyond the frontier,
and later resumed offering tribute.
In early Yánkāng,
Kēbǐnéng sent envoys to offer horses,
and Wéndì also appointed Kēbǐnéng as King of Fùyì.
In the second year of Huángchū,
Kēbǐnéng moved over five hundred households of Wei people who were among the Xiānbēi,
back to live in Dàijùn.
The following year,
Kēbǐnéng led his tribal great chiefs and minor chiefs, along with the Dàijùn Wūhuán Xiūwǔlú and others, over three thousand cavalry,
herding over seventy thousand cattle and horses to trade,
and sent over one thousand Wei people to live in Shànggǔ.
Later, he fought with Sùlì, the great chief of the Eastern Xiānbēi, and Bùdùgēn's three tribes,
attacking each other.
Tián Yù mediated a peace,
preventing them from invading each other.
In the fifth year,
Kēbǐnéng again attacked Sùlì.
Yù led light cavalry to advance directly and harass his rear.
Kēbǐnéng sent his subordinate petty chief Suǒnú to resist Yù.
Yù advanced to attack,
defeated and routed him,
causing Kēbǐnéng to harbor resentment.
He then wrote to General of the Guards Xiānyú Fǔ, saying:
"Barbarians do not understand written characters,
therefore Colonel Yán Róu vouched for me to the Son of Heaven.
I am an enemy of Sùlì.
Last year I attacked him,
but Colonel Tián assisted Sùlì.
I sent Suǒnú from the battle line,
and upon hearing of your excellency's arrival,
he immediately withdrew his army.
Bùdùgēn frequently raided and plundered,
and also killed my younger brother,
yet falsely accused me of raiding.
Although we barbarians do not know propriety and righteousness,
my brothers and descendants have received the Son of Heaven's seals and ribbons.
Even cattle and horses know good water and grass,
how much more so do I have a human heart!
General, you should vouch for me to the Son of Heaven."
Fǔ received the letter and reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor again sent Yù to recruit and appease them.
Kēbǐnéng's forces grew increasingly powerful,
numbering over one hundred thousand archers.
Whenever he raided and obtained wealth,
he distributed it fairly and equally,
resolving matters immediately,
never hoarding anything for himself.
Thus, he gained the unwavering loyalty of his followers.
The great chiefs of other tribes all respected and feared him,
yet he still could not compare to Tánshíhuái.
In the second year of Tàihé,
Yù secretly dispatched the interpreter Xià Shè to the tribe of Bǐnéng's son-in-law, Yùzhújiān.
Shè was killed by Yùzhújiān.
That autumn,
Yù led the western Xiānbēi chieftains Pútóu and Xièguīní out of the frontier to attack Yùzhújiān,
and decisively defeated them.
Upon returning to Mǎchéng,
Bǐnéng himself led thirty thousand cavalry to besiege Yù for seven days.
The Administrator of Shànggǔ Commandery, Yán Zhì,
who was the younger brother of Yán Róu,
had always been trusted by the Xiānbēi.
Zhì went to mediate,
and the siege was immediately lifted.
Later, Wáng Xióng, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, concurrently held the position of Commander of the Colonel-Protector,
and pacified them with kindness and trust.
Bǐnéng frequently offered allegiance at the frontier
and went to the provincial capital to pay tribute.
By the first year of Qīnglóng,
Bǐnéng enticed and absorbed Bùdùgēn,
causing him to rebel against Bìngzhōu,
and established a peaceful alliance with him.
He personally led ten thousand cavalry to welcome their baggage train north of Xíng.
The Inspector of Bìngzhōu, Bì Guǐ, dispatched Generals Sū Shàng and Dǒng Bì and others to attack them.
Bǐnéng sent his son to lead cavalry to meet Sū Shàng and the others in battle at Lóufán,
and Sū Shàng and Dǒng Bì were harmed in the field.
By the middle of the third year,
Wáng Xióng sent the brave warrior Hán Lóng to assassinate Bǐnéng,
and installed his younger brother in his place.
Sùlì, Míjiā, and Juéjī were all chieftains,
located outside the frontier of Liáoxī, Yòuběipíng, and Yúyáng.
Due to their distant location, they initially posed no border threat,
yet their tribes were more numerous than Bǐnéng's.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
through Yán Róu, they presented tribute
and traded.
Tàizǔ honored them by enfeoffing them all as kings.
When Juéjī died,
his son Shāmòhàn was also made King Qīnhàn.
In the early Yánkāng era,
they again each sent envoys to offer horses.
Emperor Wén enfeoffed Sùlì and Míjiā as Kings Guīyì.
Sùlì and Bǐnéng often attacked each other.
In the second year of Tàihé,
Sùlì died.
His son was young,
so his younger brother Chénglǜguī was made king
to temporarily govern his people.
The text states,
"Eastward it reaches the sea,
westward it covers the quicksands."
The system of its nine domains
can thus be spoken of.
However, beyond the desolate regions,
where double interpreters are needed to arrive,
and which is beyond the reach of footsteps and carriage tracks,
no one has yet understood the peculiar customs and different ways of those countries.
From the Yú to the Zhōu dynasties,
the Western Róng presented white jade rings,
and the Eastern Yí offered tribute from Sùshèn.
Both arrived after many generations,
such was their remoteness.
When the Hàn dynasty sent Zhāng Qiān as an envoy to the Western Regions,
he traced the source of the Yellow River
and traveled through various countries.
Subsequently, a Protector-General was established to oversee them all,
and only then were the affairs of the Western Regions fully recorded.
Hence, the official historians could detail them.
When Wèi arose,
although not all of the Western Regions could reach them,
the major states such as Qiūcí, Yúzhèn, Kāngjū, Wūsūn, Shūlè, Yuèzhī, Shànshàn, and Chēshī,
without fail, paid annual tribute to the court,
largely following the Hàn dynasty's old practices.
However, Gōngsūn Yuān, whose father and grandfather had held Liáodōng for three generations,
was, by the Son of Heaven, due to its remote location,
entrusted with the affairs of the overseas regions.
He then cut off the Eastern Yí,
preventing them from communicating with Zhūxià.
In the Jǐngchū era,
a large army was dispatched
to execute Yuān.
A hidden force was also sent across the sea
to recover the commanderies of Lèlàng and Dàifāng.
After this, the regions beyond the sea were peaceful,
and the Eastern Yí submitted.
Later, Gāogōulí rebelled,
and a detached force was again dispatched to punish them.
They pursued them to the furthest extremes,
crossing Wūwán and Gǔdū,
passing through Wòjǔ,
treading upon the territory of Sùshèn,
and reaching the Eastern Sea.
Elders spoke of people with different faces,
who emerged from nearby.
Thus, they thoroughly observed various countries,
collecting their laws and customs.
Distinctions were made between large and small,
each having its own name,
which can be recorded in detail.
Although they were barbarian lands,
the symbols of ritual vessels (zǔdòu) existed.
When Zhōngguó lost its rites,
it sought them among the four barbarian tribes,
which was still credible.
Therefore, these countries are compiled and arranged,
listing their similarities and differences,
to supplement what was incomplete in previous histories.
Fúyú is north of the Great Wall,
a thousand *lǐ* from Xuántú.
To its south it borders Gāogōulí,
to its east Yìlóu,
and to its west Xiānbēi.
To its north is the Ruòshuǐ,
and its area is about two thousand *lǐ* across.
It has eighty thousand households,
and its people are settled,
with palaces, granaries, and prisons.
There are many mountains and hills, and vast marshes,
but it is the most level and open in the Eastern Yí region.
The land is suitable for the five grains,
but does not grow the five fruits.
Its people are large and sturdy,
naturally strong, brave, cautious, and upright,
and do not raid or plunder.
The country has a king,
and all officials are named after six domestic animals:
Mǎjiā, Niújiā, Zhūjiā, Gǒujiā, Dàshǐ, Dàshǐzhě, and Shǐzhě.
In the settlements, there are powerful commoners,
and those called "lower households" are all their slaves.
The various *jiā* separately govern the four directions.
The greater ones rule several thousand households,
the smaller ones several hundred.
For eating and drinking, they all use *zǔdòu*.
At gatherings, they bow and offer cups, cleanse cups,
and engage in respectful bows ascending and descending.
In the first month of the Yīn calendar, they sacrifice to Heaven.
There is a grand national assembly,
with continuous eating, drinking, singing, and dancing for days,
named "Welcoming the Drum."
At this time, criminal punishments are suspended
and prisoners are released.
In the country, they wear white,
large-sleeved robes of white cloth,
trousers,
and leather boots.
When leaving the country, they favor silk embroidery and brocade rugs.
High-ranking individuals add furs of fox, raccoon-dog, and black marten,
and adorn their hats with gold and silver.
Interpreters, when conveying messages,
all kneel,
place their hands on the ground, and speak softly.
Punishments are severe and strict.
Those who kill are put to death,
and their family members are enslaved.
For theft, one is made to pay twelve times the amount stolen.
If men and women commit adultery,
or if women are jealous,
they are all killed.
Jealousy is especially detested.
After killing,
the corpse is placed on a southern mountain in the country
until it rots away.
If the woman's family wishes to retrieve it,
they must pay with oxen and horses before it is given to them.
When an elder brother dies, his younger brother marries his widow,
a custom shared with the Xiōngnú.
Their country is good at raising livestock,
and produces famous horses, red jade, marten and raccoon-dog furs, and beautiful pearls.
The largest pearls are the size of sour dates.
They use bows, arrows, swords, and spears as weapons,
and every family has its own armor and weapons.
The elders of the country themselves say they are descendants of ancient refugees.
Their city walls and fences are all circular,
resembling prisons.
When traveling, day and night, regardless of age, everyone sings,
with voices continuously heard throughout the day.
When there is a military campaign, they also sacrifice to Heaven,
killing an ox and examining its hooves to divine auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
If the hooves split, it is inauspicious;
if they remain joined, it is auspicious.
When there is an enemy,
the various *jiā* fight themselves,
while the lower households all carry provisions and food for them.
When they die,
ice is used in summer.
Human sacrifices are made for burial,
sometimes numbering a hundred or more.
Burials are elaborate,
with an outer coffin but no inner coffin.
Fúyú originally belonged to Xuántú Commandery.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
Gōngsūn Dù rose to prominence east of the sea,
subjugating foreign barbarians.
Wèiqíu Tái, the King of Fúyú, then submitted to Liáodōng.
At that time, Gōulí and Xiānbēi were powerful.
Dù, considering Fúyú to be between these two barbarian tribes,
gave a daughter of his clan in marriage to Wèiqíu Tái.
After Wèiqíu Tái died,
Jiǎnwèijū was enthroned.
He had no legitimate son,
but had a concubine's son, Máyú.
When Wèijū died,
the various jiā jointly enthroned Máyú.
Niújiā's nephew, also named Wèijū,
served as Grand Envoy (dàshǐ).
He was generous with wealth and benevolent in giving,
and the people of the state were attached to him.
Annually, he sent envoys to the capital to offer tribute.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign,
Wúqiū Jiǎn, the Inspector (cìshǐ) of Yōuzhōu, launched a punitive expedition against Gōulí.
He sent Wáng Qí, the Administrator (tàishǒu) of Xuántú, to Fúyú.
Wèijū sent the Grand Jia (dàjiā) to welcome him on the outskirts,
and supplied military provisions.
His paternal uncle, Niújiā, had a change of heart.
Wèijū killed the uncle and his son,
confiscated their property,
and sent an envoy to register and deliver it to the officials.
According to the old customs of Fúyú,
if there were unseasonal floods or droughts,
and the five grains did not ripen,
they would always blame the king,
some saying he should be replaced,
others saying he should be killed.
After Máyú died,
his son Yīlǜ, then six years old,
was enthroned as king.
In Hàn times,
Fúyú kings were buried using jade caskets.
These were usually entrusted beforehand to Xuántú Commandery,
and when a king died, they would be retrieved for burial.
When Gōngsūn Yuān was executed,
the Xuántú treasury still held one jade casket.
Now, the Fúyú treasury possesses jade bi discs, guī scepters, and zàn libation cups from several generations,
passed down as treasures.
The elders say these were gifts from previous generations.
The inscription on their seal says
"Seal of the King of Huì."
The state has an old city named Huìchéng.
This was probably originally Huì Mò territory,
and the King of Fúyú resided there,
calling himself
"a displaced person."
This is certainly [thus].
Gāogōulí is a thousand li east of Liáodōng,
bordering Cháoxiǎn and Huì Mò to the south,
Wòjǔ to the east,
and Fúyú to the north.
Its capital is below Wándū,
an area about two thousand li square,
with thirty thousand households.
There are many high mountains and deep valleys,
with no plains or wetlands.
They live along the mountains and valleys,
drinking stream water.
There is no good farmland;
even with diligent farming,
it is not enough to feed their mouths.
Their custom is to eat sparingly.
They are fond of building palaces and houses.
To the left and right of their dwellings, they erect large houses
for sacrificing to ghosts and spirits,
and also worship Língxīng and the altars of the soil and grain.
Their nature is fierce and impetuous,
and they are skilled at raiding and plundering.
Their state has a king.
Their officials include Xiàngjiā, Duìlú, Pèizhě, Gǔchújiā, Zhǔbù, Yōutáichéng, Shǐzhě, and Zàoyīxiānrén.
There are distinct ranks of noble and humble.
The old sayings of the Eastern Yi consider them a separate branch of Fúyú.
Their language and many customs
are similar to Fúyú,
but their temperament and clothing are different.
Originally, there were five clans:
the Juānnu tribe, the Juénú tribe, the Shùnnú tribe, the Guànnu tribe, and the Guìlóu tribe.
Originally, the Juānnu tribe provided the kings,
but they gradually weakened.
Now the Guìlóu tribe has replaced them.
In Hàn times, they were granted drums, horns, and entertainers.
They regularly received court attire and headbands from Xuántú Commandery.
Gāogōulí officials were tasked with managing their registers.
Later, they gradually became arrogant and willful,
no longer going to the commandery.
They built a small city on their eastern border,
placed the court attire and headbands there,
and came to retrieve them annually.
Today, the barbarians still call this city Zégoūlóu.
Goūlóu
is the Gōulí word for city.
Regarding their official appointments,
if there is a Duìlú, there is no Pèizhě;
if there is a Pèizhě, there is no Duìlú.
The great jiā of the king's clan are all called Gǔchújiā.
The former rulers of the Juānnu tribe,
although not kings now,
are the hereditary leaders of adults (dàrén),
and are allowed to be called Gǔchújiā.
They are also allowed to establish ancestral temples
and sacrifice to Língxīng and the altars of soil and grain.
The Juénú tribe intermarries with the royal family for generations
and is granted the title Gǔchú.
All the great jiā also appoint their own Shǐzhě and Zàoyīxiānrén.
Their names are all reported to the king,
similar to the household retainers of ministers and grand masters.
When they meet and sit together,
they are not allowed to be in the same rank as the king's Shǐzhě and Zàoyīxiānrén.
In their state, the great households do not farm;
those who live off others number over ten thousand mouths.
The lower households carry rice, grain, fish, and salt from afar to supply them.
Their people enjoy singing and dancing.
In the cities and villages of the state,
men and women gather in groups at night,
singing and playing together.
They have no large granaries;
each family has its own small granary,
which they call Fújīng.
Their people are clean and self-satisfied,
and fond of storing fermented drinks.
When kneeling and bowing, they extend one leg,
which differs from Fúyú.
All their walking is done by running.
In the tenth month, they sacrifice to Heaven.
There is a great assembly throughout the state,
called Dōngméng.
In their public assemblies,
everyone adorns themselves with brocade, embroidery, gold, and silver.
The Dàjiā and Zhǔbù wear headbands (cè)
that are like cè but without flaps.
The Xiǎojiā wear zhéfēng,
which are shaped like biàn caps.
To the east of their state, there is a large cave
called the Suì Cave.
In the great state assembly of the tenth month,
they welcome the Suì spirit back to the eastern part of the state and sacrifice to it,
placing a wooden suì in the spirit's seat.
They have no prisons.
If someone commits a crime, the various jiā deliberate and judge.
They then kill the person,
and confiscate their wife and children as slaves.
Regarding their marriage customs,
once the betrothal is settled,
the girl's family builds a small house behind the main house,
called the "son-in-law's house."
The son-in-law arrives at the girl's family's doorstep in the evening,
announces himself, bows and kneels,
and begs to be allowed to stay with the girl.
After doing this two or three times,
the girl's parents finally allow him to stay in the small house.
He places money and silk beside him.
