Not until a child is born and has grown up
does he take his wife home.
Their custom is licentious.
Once men and women are married,
they gradually begin to make their burial clothes.
They practice elaborate burials.
Gold, silver, and valuables
are all used for the funeral.
Stones are piled up to form a mound,
and pine and cypress trees are planted in rows.
Their horses are all small
and adept at climbing mountains.
The people of the state are strong and spirited,
skilled in combat.
Wòjǔ and Dōnghuì are all subordinate to them.
There is also Xiǎoshuǐ Mò.
Gōulí established its state
by a great river.
North of Xī'ānpíng County, there is a small river
that flows south into the sea.
A separate branch of Gōulí established a state by this small river,
and thus it was named Xiǎoshuǐ Mò.
They produce good bows,
which are known as Mò bows.
Wáng Mǎng 王莽 initially conscripted soldiers from Gāogōulì 高句麗 to attack the Hú 胡.
They were unwilling to go,
but were forcefully dispatched.
They all fled outside the frontier to become bandits.
Liáoxī Dà Yǐn 遼西大尹 Tián Tán 田譚 pursued and attacked them,
but was killed by them.
The prefectures, commanderies, and counties blamed the Gōulì Hóu 句麗侯 Táo 騊.
Yán Yōu 嚴尤 memorialized, saying:
“The Mò 貊 people violated the law,
but the fault does not originate with Táo 騊.
It would be better to pacify them.
Now, if they are groundlessly accused of a great crime,
I fear they may rebel.”
Mǎng 王莽 did not listen,
and instead ordered Yōu 嚴尤 to attack them.
Yōu 嚴尤 enticed Gōulì Hóu 句麗侯 Táo 騊 to come and then beheaded him,
sending his head to Cháng'ān 長安.
Mǎng 王莽 was greatly pleased,
announced it to the world,
and renamed Gāogōulì 高句麗 to Xiàgōulì 下句麗.
At this time, it was a marquisate.
In the eighth year of Hàn Guāngwǔ Dì 漢光武帝,
the King of Gāogōulì 高句麗 sent envoys to pay tribute,
and was first referred to as King.
Between the reigns of Shāng 殤 and Ān 安,
Gōulì Wáng Gōng 句麗王宮 frequently raided Liáodōng 遼東,
and was subsequently subordinated to Xuántú 玄菟.
Liáodōng Tàishǒu 遼東太守 Cài Fēng 蔡風 and Xuántú Tàishǒu 玄菟太守 Yáo Guāng 姚光 considered Gōng 宮 a menace to both commanderies,
and raised an army to attack him.
Gōng 宮 feigned surrender and requested peace,
and the two commanderies did not advance.
Gōng 宮 secretly dispatched troops to attack Xuántú 玄菟,
burned down the outpost cities,
entered Liáosuì 遼隧,
and killed officials and common people.
Later, Gōng 宮 again invaded Liáodōng 遼東.
Cài Fēng 蔡風 lightly led officials and soldiers to pursue and suppress him,
but his army was defeated and lost.
Gōng 宮 died,
and his son Bó Gù 伯固 was enthroned.
Between the reigns of Shùn 順 and Huán 桓,
they again invaded Liáodōng 遼東,
raiding Xīn'ān 新安 and Jūxiāng 居鄉,
and also attacked Xī'ānpíng 西安平.
On the road, they killed the Dàifāng Lìng 帶方令
and captured the wife and children of the Lèlàng Tàishǒu 樂浪太守.
In the second year of Líng Dì 建寧 靈帝,
Xuántú Tàishǒu 玄菟太守 Gěng Lín 耿臨 attacked them,
beheading and capturing several hundred individuals.
Bó Gù 伯固 surrendered
and was subordinated to Liáodōng 遼東.
During the Xīpíng 熹平 period,
Bó Gù 伯固 requested to be subordinated to Xuántú 玄菟.
When Gōngsūn Dù 公孫度 dominated the area east of the sea,
Bó Gù 伯固 sent Dàjiā Yōujú 大加優居 and Zhǔbù Rán Rén 主簿然人 to assist Dù 度 in attacking the Fùshān Zéi 富山賊,
and they defeated them.
Bó Gù 伯固 died,
having two sons:
the elder son Bá Qí 拔奇,
and the younger son Yīyímó 伊夷模.
Bá Qí 拔奇 was unworthy,
so the people of the state jointly enthroned Yīyímó 伊夷模 as king.
From Bó Gù's 伯固 time,
they frequently raided Liáodōng 遼東,
and also received over five hundred refugee Hú 胡 families.
During the Jiàn'ān 建安 period,
Gōngsūn Kāng 公孫康 led an army to attack them,
defeating their state
and burning their settlements.
Bá Qí 拔奇 resented being the elder brother yet not being enthroned,
and with Juān nú jiā 涓奴加, each leading over thirty thousand households, surrendered to Kāng 康,
and resettled at Fèiliú Shuǐ 沸流水.
The surrendered Hú 胡 also rebelled against Yīyímó 伊夷模.
Yīyímó 伊夷模 then established a new state,
which is the current location.
Bá Qí 拔奇 then went to Liáodōng 遼東.
He had a son who remained in the Gōulì Guó 句麗國,
who is the current Gǔchújiā Bó Wèijū 古雛加駮位居.
Later, they again attacked Xuántú 玄菟.
Xuántú 玄菟 and Liáodōng 遼東 jointly attacked,
and greatly defeated them.
Yīyímó 伊夷模 had no sons,
and committed adultery with the Guànnú Bù 灌奴部,
begetting a son named Wèigōng 位宮.
When Yīyímó 伊夷模 died,
he was enthroned as king,
who is the current Gōulì Wáng Gōng 句麗王宮.
His great-grandfather was named Gōng 宮.
When he was born, he could open his eyes and see.
His countrymen disliked this,
and when he grew up,
he indeed became ferocious and cruel,
frequently raiding and plundering,
and the state was devastated.
The present king, when he fell to the ground at birth,
could also open his eyes and look at people.
Gōulì 句麗 calls similarity "wèi 位".
He resembled his grandfather,
hence he was named Wèigōng 位宮.
Wèigōng 位宮 was strong and courageous,
skilled in riding and horsemanship,
and good at hunting and archery.
In the second year of Jǐngchū 景初,
Tàiwèi Sīmǎ Wáng 太尉司馬王 led troops to suppress Gōngsūn Yuān 公孫淵.
Gōng 宮 sent his Zhǔbù Dàjiā 主簿大加 with several thousand men to assist the army.
In the third year of Zhèngshǐ 正始,
Gōng 宮 raided Xī'ānpíng 西安平.
In its fifth year,
he was defeated by Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ Wúqiū Jiǎn 幽州刺吏毋丘儉.
The account is in Jiǎn's 儉 biography.
Dōng Wòjū 東沃沮 is located east of the Gāogōulì Gàimǎ Dàshān 高句麗蓋馬大山,
dwelling by the great sea.
Its terrain is narrow in the northeast
and long in the southwest,
about a thousand *lǐ* (li) long.
To the north, it borders Yìlóu 挹婁 and Fúyú 夫餘.
To the south, it borders Huì Mò 濊貊.
It has five thousand households.
There is no great monarch;
for generations, the settlements
each have their own chiefs.
Their language is largely similar to Gōulì 句麗,
with occasional minor differences.
In the early Hàn 漢,
the Yān 燕 refugee Wèi Mǎn 衞滿 became King of Cháoxiǎn 朝鮮.
At that time, all of Wòjū 沃沮 was subject to him.
In the second year of Yuánfēng 元封 of Hàn Wǔ Dì 漢武帝,
he attacked Cháoxiǎn 朝鮮,
killed Mǎn's 滿 grandson Yòu Qú 右渠,
and divided his territory into four commanderies,
making Wòjū Chéng 沃沮城 the Xuántú Jùn 玄菟郡.
Later, due to invasions by the Yí Mò 夷貊,
the commandery was relocated to the northwest of Gōulì 句麗,
which is what is now called the former seat of Xuántú 玄菟.
Wòjū 沃沮 then became subject to Lèlàng 樂浪.
Because the Hàn 漢 considered the territory vast and distant,
east of the Dāndān Dàlǐng 單單大領,
they established a Dōngbù Dūwèi 東部都尉,
governing from Bùnài Chéng 不耐城,
separately overseeing the seven eastern counties.
At that time, Wòjū 沃沮 was also entirely comprised of counties.
In the sixth year of Jiànwǔ 建武 of Hàn 漢,
the border commanderies were abolished,
and the Dūwèi 都尉 office was consequently dissolved.
Thereafter, the chiefs within their counties were all made county marquises.
Bùnài 不耐, Huálì 華麗, Wòjū 沃沮, and other counties all became marquisates.
The Yí Dí 夷狄 attacked each other,
but only the Bùnài Huì Hóu 不耐濊侯 still retained the offices of Gōngcáo 功曹, Zhǔbù 主簿, and other officials,
all of whom were appointed from the Huì 濊 people.
The chiefs of the Wòjū 沃沮 settlements
all called themselves Sānlǎo 三老,
which was the system of the former county-states.
The state was small,
pressed between larger states,
and thus became a vassal of Gōulì 句麗.
Gōulì 句麗 then appointed its prominent individuals as envoys within Wòjū 沃沮,
making them overseers,
and also sent Dàjiā 大加 to collect their taxes and tributes:
Mòbù 貊布 (Mò cloth), fish, salt, and seafood.
They were carried a thousand *lǐ* (li) to be presented.
They also sent their beautiful women as slave-concubines,
treating them like servants.
Their land was fertile and beautiful,
backed by mountains and facing the sea,
suitable for five grains,
and good for farming.
The people were naturally honest, strong, and brave,
with few cattle and horses,
skilled in fighting on foot with spears.
Their food, drink, dwellings,
clothing, and customs
were similar to Gōulì 句麗.
For burial, they made large wooden coffins,
over ten *zhàng* (zhang) long,
with one end opened to serve as a door.
The newly deceased were all temporarily buried,
just enough to cover their form.
When the flesh had completely decayed,
the bones were taken and placed in the coffin.
The entire family shared one coffin,
and wooden figures carved to resemble the living
were placed according to the number of the deceased.
There were also earthenware jars,
with rice placed inside,
hung near the coffin door.
Wúqiū Jiǎn (毋丘儉) attacked Gōulí (句麗).
King Gōng (宮) of Gōulí (句麗) fled to Wòjū (沃沮).
(Wúqiū Jiǎn) then advanced his army to strike him.
All the towns and settlements of Wòjū (沃沮) were destroyed.
Over three thousand heads and captives were taken.
Gōng (宮) fled to Northern Wòjū (沃沮).
Northern Wòjū (沃沮) is also called Zhìgōulóu (置溝婁).
It is over eight hundred *lǐ* (里) from Southern Wòjū (沃沮).
Its customs are the same in both north and south.
It borders Yìlóu (挹婁).
The Yìlóu (挹婁) are fond of sailing boats to raid and plunder.
Northern Wòjū (沃沮) fears them.
In summer, (they) always take refuge in deep caves among the mountain cliffs for defense.
In winter, when the ice freezes,
and boat routes are impassable,
they descend to live in villages.
Wáng Qí (王頎) separately dispatched (an army) to pursue and attack Gōng (宮),
reaching the full extent of its eastern territory.
(He) asked their elders,
"Are there still people to the east of the sea?"
The elders said that their countrymen once sailed boats to fish,
were caught in a storm and blown for several tens of days,
and found an island to the east.
There were people on it,
but their languages were not mutually intelligible.
Their custom was to drown virgin girls in the sea every seventh month.
(They) also said there was another country also in the sea,
composed entirely of women with no men.
(They) also spoke of obtaining a piece of cloth clothing
that floated out of the sea.
Its body was like the clothes of Zhong (國) [zhōngguó] (中（(國)）) people,
but its two sleeves were three *zhàng* (丈) long.
(They) also found a broken boat
that drifted ashore with the waves.
There was a man whose neck had another face.
(He) was captured alive.
They could not communicate with him.
He died without eating.
All these domains are in the great sea east of Wòjū (沃沮).
Yìlóu (挹婁) is over a thousand *lǐ* (里) northeast of Fúyú (夫餘),
bordering the great sea.
To the south, it borders Northern Wòjū (沃沮).
Its northern extent is unknown.
Its land is mostly mountainous and treacherous.
Its people resemble the Fúyú (夫餘) in appearance.
Their language is not the same as Fúyú (夫餘) or Gōulí (句麗).
They have five grains, cattle, horses, and linen cloth.
Many people are brave and strong.
They have no great ruler or chief.
Each settlement has its own elder.
Living among mountains and forests,
they often dwell in caves.
Large houses are nine steps deep,
considering greater depth to be better.
The climate is cold,
more severe than Fúyú (夫餘).
Their custom is to raise pigs,
eat their meat,
and wear their skins.
In winter, they smear their bodies with pig fat,
several *fēn* (分) thick,
to protect against wind and cold.
In summer, they are naked,
covering their front and back with a *chǐ* (尺) of cloth
to conceal their bodies.
Their people are not clean.
They build their latrines in the center (of their dwelling),
with people living in a circle around it.
Their bows are four *chǐ* (尺) long,
with the force of a crossbow.
Arrows are made of *hú* (楛) wood,
one *chǐ* (尺) eight *cùn* (寸) long,
with arrowheads of green stone.
This is the country of the ancient Sùshèn (肅慎) clan.
They are skilled archers;
arrows shot at people all hit the eye (目).
Arrows are coated with poison;
anyone hit by them dies.
They produce red jade
and fine sables,
which are what are now called Yìlóu (挹婁) sables.
Since the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
they have been vassals of Fúyú (夫餘).
Fúyú (夫餘) demanded heavy taxes and tributes from them.
In the middle of the Huángchū (黃初) era, they rebelled against it.
Fúyú (夫餘) attacked them repeatedly.
Although their population was small,
the mountains and treacherous terrain where they lived
made neighboring countries fear their bows and arrows,
and they were ultimately unable to subdue them.
This country is adept at sailing boats to raid and plunder,
which troubles neighboring countries.
The Dōngyí (東夷) peoples generally use *zǔ dòu* (俎豆) for eating,
but Yìlóu (挹婁) does not.
Their laws and customs are the most devoid of order.
The Huì (濊) borders Chénhán (辰韓) to the south,
and Gāogōulí (高句麗) and Wòjū (沃沮) to the north.
To the east, it reaches the great sea.
All the land east of modern Cháoxiǎn (朝鮮) is their territory.
There are twenty thousand households.
In the past, Jīzǐ (箕子), having gone to Cháoxiǎn (朝鮮),
established eight articles of teaching to instruct them.
There were no locked doors, and the people did not commit theft.
Forty-some generations later,
Lord Huì (準) [Zhǔn] (（(淮)）【準】) of Cháoxiǎn (朝鮮) usurped the title and called himself king.
When Chén Shèng (陳勝) and others rose up,
the world rebelled against Qín (秦),
and tens of thousands of people from Yān (燕), Qí (齊), and Zhào (趙) fled to Cháoxiǎn (朝鮮).
Wèi Mǎn (衞滿) from Yān (燕),
with a topknot and dressed in foreign clothes,
came again to rule as king.
Emperor Wǔ (武) of Hàn (漢) attacked and destroyed Cháoxiǎn (朝鮮),
dividing its territory into four commanderies.
From then on,
the Hú (胡) and Hàn (漢) gradually became distinct.
(The Huì) had no great ruler or chief.
Since the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
their officials included the Marquis of the邑君 (*yìjūn*), and the Sanlǎo (三老),
who governed the lower households.
Their elders historically claimed to be of the same stock as Gōulí (句麗).
Their people are sincere and simple,
with few desires,
possess integrity and shame,
and do not beg (匄).
Their language, laws, and customs are largely similar to Gōulí (句麗),
but their clothing is different.
Men and women both wear garments with curved collars.
Men wear silver flowers several *cùn* (寸) wide as ornaments.
The area west of the Dāndān Dàshānlǐng (單單大山領) belonged to Lèlàng (樂浪).
The seven counties east of the range
were governed by a Commandant,
all using the Huì (濊) as their populace.
Later, the Commandant was abolished,
and their chieftains were enfeoffed as Marquises.
Today's Bùnài Huì (不耐濊) are all of their kind.
In the late Hàn (漢) dynasty, they again belonged to Gōulí (句麗).
Their custom is to revere mountains and rivers.
Mountains and rivers each have their own sections,
and one may not trespass into them.
People of the same surname do not marry.
They have many taboos.
When illness or death occurs, they immediately abandon the old dwelling
and build a new one.
They have linen cloth.
They raise silkworms and make silk floss.
They are skilled at observing the stars and constellations
to predict the abundance or scarcity of the harvest year.
They do not value pearls or jade as treasures.
They usually hold a heavenly sacrifice in the tenth month,
drinking, singing, and dancing day and night.
This is called "Dance to Heaven."
They also worship the tiger as a god.
When their settlements trespass against each other,
they punish each other by demanding human captives, cattle, or horses.
This is called "demanding recompense for misfortune."
Those who kill are punished with death.
There are few bandits.
They make spears three *zhàng* (丈) long.
Sometimes several people hold one together.
They are capable of fighting on foot.
Lèlàng (樂浪)檀弓 (Tán Gōng) originates from their land.
Their sea produces striped fish skin.
The land abounds with clouded leopards.
They also produce *guǒ xià mǎ* (果下馬) (ponies),
which were offered as tribute during the reign of Emperor Huán (桓) of Hàn (漢).
In the sixth year of Zhèngshǐ (正始) (245 CE),
Liú Mào (劉茂), the Administrator of Lèlàng (樂浪), and Gōng Zūn (弓遵), the Administrator of Dàifāng (帶方), attacked the eastern Huì (濊), who were under Gōulí (句麗),
launching an army against them.
The Marquis of Bùnài (不耐) and others surrendered with their settlements.
In its eighth year (247 CE),
(they) went to the imperial court to offer tribute.
An imperial edict re-appointed the King of Bùnài Huì (不耐濊).
(They) live interspersed among the common people.
Four times a year, (they) go to the commandery for an audience.
When the two commanderies have military levies or conscriptions,
(they) are supplied for service,
treated like ordinary citizens.
Hán is to the south of Dàifāng,
bordered by the sea to the east and west,
and adjoins Wō to the south.
It is approximately four thousand *lǐ* across.
There are three kinds [of Hán people]:
The first is Mǎhán,
the second is Chénhán,
and the third is Biànhán.
Chénhán
is the ancient Chén Guó.
Mǎhán is in the west.
Its people are settled,
cultivate crops,
know how to raise silkworms,
and make cotton cloth.
Each has its own chiefs.
The larger ones call themselves Chénzhì,
while the next in rank are Yìjiè.
They are scattered among the mountains and seas,
and have no walled cities.

There are Yuánxiāng Guó, Móushuǐ Guó, Sāngwài Guó, Xiǎoshísuǒ Guó, Dàshísuǒ Guó, Yōuxiūmóuzhuó Guó, Chénfēngū Guó, Bójì Guó, Sùlúbùsī Guó, Rìhuá Guó, Gǔdànzhě Guó, Gǔlí Guó, Nùlán Guó, Yuèzhī Guó, Zīlímóulú Guó, Sùwèigān Guó, Gǔyuán Guó, Mòlú Guó, Bēilí Guó, Zhànlíbēi Guó, Chénxìn Guó, Zhīqīn Guó, Gǒulú Guó, Bēimí Guó, Jiānxībēilí Guó, Gǔpú Guó, Zhìlíjú Guó, Rǎnlù Guó, Érlín Guó, Sìlú Guó, Nèibēilí Guó, Gǎnxī Guó, Wànlú Guó, Pìbēilí Guó, Jiùsīwūdàn Guó, Yīlí Guó, Bùmí Guó, Zhībàn Guó, Gǒusù Guó, Jiélú Guó, Móulúbēilí Guó, Chénsūtú Guó, Mòlú Guó, Gǔlà Guó, Línsùbàn Guó, Chényúnxīn Guó, Rúláibēilí Guó, Chǔshāntúbēilí Guó, Yīnán Guó, Gǒuxī Guó, Bùyún Guó, Bùsīfénxié Guó, Yuánchí Guó, Gānmǎ Guó, Chǔlí Guó,
in total more than fifty states.
The large states have over ten thousand households,
the small states several thousand households,
totaling more than one hundred thousand households.
The king of Chén governs Yuèzhī Guó.
The Chénzhì sometimes add the titles Yōuhūchényúnqiǎnzhībàoānxiécùzhīfénchénlíérbùlìgūxiáqínzhīlián.
Their officials include Wèilǜshàn, Yìjūn, Guīyìhóu, Zhōnglángjiàng, Dūwèi, and Bócháng.
Hóu Zhǔn, having usurped the title of king,
was attacked and overthrown by Wèi Mǎn, a refugee from Yān.
He took his attendants and palace women and fled into the sea,
settling in Hán territory,
and styled himself King of Hán.
His line later died out,
but even now, there are still Hán people who offer sacrifices to him.
During the Hàn dynasty, Hán was subordinate to Lèlàng Jùn,
and paid tribute seasonally.
Towards the end of the Huán and Líng reigns,
Hán and Huì grew strong,
and the commanderies and counties could not control them.
Many people flowed into the Hán states.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
Gōngsūn Kāng divided the desolate land south of Túnyǒu Xiàn to form Dàifāng Jùn,
and sent Gōngsūn Mó and Zhāng Chǎng to gather the remaining people.
He raised an army to attack Hán and Huì,
and the old residents gradually emerged.
After this, Wō and Hán became subordinate to Dàifāng.
During the Jǐngchū era,
Emperor Míng secretly sent Dàifāng Tàishǒu Liú Xīn and Lèlàng Tàishǒu Xiānyú Sì across the sea to pacify the two commanderies.
The Chénzhì of the various Hán states were additionally bestowed with the seals and ribbons of Yìjūn,
and the next in rank with those of Yìzhǎng.
It was their custom to favor clothing and turbans.
When commoners went to the commandery for an audience,
they were all lent clothing and turbans.
More than a thousand people wore their own seals, ribbons, clothing, and turbans.
Bù Cóngshì Wú Lín, considering that Lèlàng originally governed Hán,
divided off eight Chénhán states and gave them to Lèlàng.
The officials and interpreters had different opinions,
and the Chénzhì incited the Hán people's anger,
attacking the Qílí Camp of Dàifāng Jùn.
At that time, Tàishǒu Gōng Zūn and Lèlàng Tàishǒu Liú Mào raised an army to attack them.
Gōng Zūn died in battle,
and the two commanderies then subjugated Hán.
Their customs lack strict order.
Although the states and settlements have chiefs,
the villages are mixed together
and cannot control each other well.
There is no bowing or kneeling礼.
They live in grass huts and earth chambers,
shaped like tombs.
Their doors are at the top,
and the family lives together inside,
without distinction between old and young, male and female.
For burials, they have an outer coffin but no inner coffin.
They do not know how to ride oxen or horses;
all oxen and horses are used for funerals.
They value precious beads as wealth,
sometimes using them to adorn clothes,
or hanging them around their necks and from their ears.
They do not consider gold, silver, brocade, or embroidery to be treasures.
Their nature is strong and brave.
They tie their hair in a topknot and leave it exposed,
like men in armor.
They wear cloth robes
and leather sandals on their feet.
When there is work to be done in their state, or when the officials make them build walled cities,
all the young and brave men
pierce their back skin,
thread a large rope through it,
and then insert a wooden pole about a *zhàng* long.
They exert themselves and shout all day long,
feeling no pain,
both to encourage work
and to show their strength.
They usually plant seeds in the fifth month,
then sacrifice to ghosts and spirits.
They gather in groups to sing and dance,
drinking wine day and night without rest.
In their dance,
dozens of people rise together and follow each other,
stomping the ground, moving up and down,
with hands and feet moving in unison.
The rhythm resembles the *duó* dance.
In the tenth month, when agricultural work is finished,
they do the same.
They believe in ghosts and spirits.
Each state and settlement appoints one person to preside over sacrifices to the heavenly spirits,
naming him Tiānjūn.
Moreover, each state has its own separate settlements,
called Sūtú.
They erect large wooden poles
and hang bells and drums,
serving ghosts and spirits.
All who flee and reach these places
are not returned.
They are fond of banditry.
The meaning of establishing Sūtú
is somewhat similar to Fútú (Buddhism),
but their actions, whether good or evil, differ.
The states in the north, closer to the commanderies, are somewhat familiar with etiquette and customs.
Those in remote areas are just like prisoners and slaves gathered together.
They have no other precious treasures.
Their birds, beasts, plants, and trees are generally the same as in Zhōngguó.
They produce large chestnuts,
as big as pears.
They also produce fine-tailed chickens,
whose tails are all more than five *chǐ* long.
Their men sometimes have tattoos.
There is also Zhōuhú on a large island in the sea west of Mǎhán.
Their people are somewhat short,
and their language is not the same as Hán.
They all shave their heads like the Xiānbēi,
but wear only leather,
and are fond of raising oxen and pigs.
Their clothing covers the upper body but not the lower,
roughly like nudity.
They travel by boat
to trade in Hán.
Chénhán is to the east of Mǎhán.
Their elders have passed down through generations
that they are ancient refugees who fled from Qín's labor service and came to settle in Hán territory.
Mǎhán ceded its eastern borderland to them.
They have walled settlements.
Their language is not the same as Mǎhán.
They call a state a *bāng*,
a bow an *hú*,
a bandit a *kòu*,
and serving wine serving *shāng*.
They all call each other *tú*,
which resembles the Qín people,
not merely the terms of Yān and Qí.
They call the Lèlàng people *Ācán*;
the people of the east call us *Ā*,
meaning the Lèlàng people are their remnants.
Some now call them Qínhán.
Initially, there were six states,
which gradually divided into twelve states.
Biànchén also had twelve states,
and furthermore, several small separate settlements,
each with its own chieftain.
The major ones were called Chénzhì,
the next XiǎnCè,
then FánHuì,
then Shā Xī,
and then YìJiè.

There were the states of YǐZhī, BùSī, Biànchén Mílímǐdòng, Biànchén Jiētú, QínQí, NánMílímǐdòng, Biànchén Gǔzīmǐdòng, Biànchén Gǔchúnshì, Rǎnxī, Biànchén Bànlù, Biàn LèNún, Jūnmí (also Biàn Jūnmí), Biànchén Mǐwūyé Mǎ, Rúzhàn, Biànchén Gānlù, Hùlù, Zhōuxiān (also Mǎyán), Biànchén Gǒuyá, Biànchén Zǒucáomǎ, Biànchén Ānxié (also Mǎyán), Biànchén Dúlú, Sīlú, and Yōuyóu.
Biàn and Chénhán combined had twenty-four states.
The large states had four or five thousand families,
the small states six or seven hundred families,
totaling forty to fifty thousand households.
Among these, twelve states belonged to the Chén King.
The Chén King was usually chosen from Mǎhán people,
succeeding from generation to generation.
The Chén King was not allowed to establish himself as king.
The land was fertile and beautiful,
suitable for growing five grains and rice.
They understood sericulture,
and made fine silk and cloth.
They rode cattle and horses.
In marriage customs,
there was a distinction between males and females.
They used large bird feathers to send off the dead,
their intention being to enable the deceased to fly up.
The country produced iron,
and Hán, Huì, and Wō all obtained it from there.
Iron was used in all markets for trade,
just as China used coins.
It was also supplied to the two commanderies.
The custom was to enjoy singing, dancing, and drinking.
They had a *sè*,
whose shape resembled a *zhú*,
and playing it also produced musical tunes.
When a child was born,
they would press its head with a stone,
desiring it to be flat.
Today, Chénhán people all have flat heads.
Men and women are close to the Wō,
and also tattoo their bodies.
They are good at infantry combat,
and their weapons are the same as Mǎhán.
According to their customs,
when travelers met,
they would all stop and yield the way.
Biànchén and Chénhán lived mixed together,
and also had walled cities.
Their clothing and dwellings were the same as Chénhán.
Their language and legal customs were similar,
but their sacrifices to spirits and gods were different.
Their hearths were all built on the west side of the dwelling.
Their Dúlú State bordered Wō.
The twelve states also had kings,
and their people were all large in stature.
Their clothing was pure and clean,
and they had long hair.
They also made wide, fine cloth.
Their laws and customs were especially strict.
The Wō people are in the great sea southeast of Dàifāng,
forming states and settlements on mountainous islands.
Formerly there were over a hundred states.
During the Hàn dynasty, there were those who came to court.
Today, through envoys and interpreters, thirty states are known.
From the commandery to Wō,
traveling by water along the coast,
passing through Hánguó,
sometimes south, sometimes east,
one reaches the Gǒuyá Hánguó on its northern shore,
over seven thousand *lǐ*.
Then one crosses a sea,
over a thousand *lǐ*, to Duìmǎguó.
Its chief official is called Bēigǒu,
the deputy Bēinúmólí.
They reside on an isolated island,
about four hundred *lǐ* in circumference.
The land is mountainous and rugged,
with many deep forests.
The roads are like paths for birds and deer.
There are over a thousand households,
no good fields,
they live by eating seafood.
They travel by boat north and south to buy and sell grain.
Further south, crossing a sea over a thousand *lǐ*,
named Hànhǎi,
one reaches a large state.
Its official is also called Bēigǒu,
the deputy Bēinúmólí.
It is about three hundred *lǐ* in circumference,
with many bamboo and wooded thickets.
There are about three thousand families.
It has some arable land,
but cultivating the land is still not enough for food.
They also buy and sell grain north and south.
Then crossing another sea,
over a thousand *lǐ*, one reaches Mòlúguó.
It has over four thousand households,
residing near mountains and the sea.
Plants and trees are lush and dense,
one cannot see the person ahead when walking.
They are fond of catching fish and abalone.
Regardless of water depth,
they all dive to retrieve them.
Traveling five hundred *lǐ* southeast by land,
one reaches Yīdūguó.
Its official is called Erzhī,
the deputies Xièmógū and Bǐngqúgū.
It has over a thousand households.
It has had kings for generations,
all subject to the Queen's State.
It is the usual stopping place for commandery envoys traveling to and from.
Southeast to Núguó is one hundred *lǐ*.
Its official is called SìMǎgū,
the deputy Bēinúmólí.
It has over twenty thousand households.
Traveling east to Bùmíguó is one hundred *lǐ*.
Its official is called Duōmó,
the deputy Bēinúmólí.
It has over a thousand families.
South to Tóumǎguó,
ten days by water travel.
Its official is called Mímí,
the deputy Mímínàlí.
It has about fifty thousand households.
South to Yámǎyīguó,
the capital of the Queen.
Ten days by water travel,
one month by land travel.
Its officials include Yīzhīmǎ,
next Mǐmǎshēng,
next Mǐmǎhuòzhī,
next Nújiāchǐ.
It has about seventy thousand households.
North from the Queen's State,
the number of households and distances can be briefly recorded.
The other surrounding states are far and remote,
and cannot be detailed.
Next is Sīmǎguó,
next Yǐbǎizhīguó,
next Yīxiéguó,
next Dūzhīguó,
next Mǐnúguó,
next Hǎogǔdūguó,
next Bùhūguó,
next Jiěnńúguó,
next Duìsūguó,
next Sūnúguó,
next Hūyìguó,
next Huánúsūnúguó,
next Guǐguó,
next Wéiwúguó,
next Guǐnúguó,
next Xiémǎguó,
next Gōngchénguó,
next Bālìguó,
next Zhīwéiguó,
next Wūnńúguó,
next Núguó.
This is the extent of the Queen's territory.
To its south is Gǒunúguó,
whose king is a man.
Its official is Gǒugǔzhìbēigǒu.
It does not belong to the Queen.
From the commandery to the Queen's State is over twelve thousand *lǐ*.
Both men, regardless of age, had their faces tattooed and bodies adorned.
Since ancient times,
when their envoys went to Zhōngguó,
they all called themselves Dàfū.
The son of Xià Hòu Shàokāng was enfeoffed in Kuàijī,
cutting his hair and tattooing his body to avoid harm from jiaolóng.
Now, the Wō people of the waters like to dive and catch fish and clams.
Body tattooing also serves to ward off large fish and aquatic birds,
and later gradually became an adornment.
The tattoos of various states differ;
some are on the left, some on the right,
some large, some small,
indicating distinctions in status.
Estimating their distance,
they should be to the east of Kuàijī and Dōngyě.
Their customs are not licentious.
Men all wear their hair in uncovered chignons,
using cotton cloth to wrap their heads.
Their clothes are made of horizontal panels,
merely tied and joined together,
with almost no seams.
Women wear their hair loose and tied in a bent chignon.
They make clothes like a single quilt,
piercing its center
to put their head through and wear it.
They grow rice and ramie,
raise silkworms and weave,
producing fine ramie and silk floss.
Their land has no cattle, horses, tigers, leopards, sheep, or magpies.
Their weapons are spears, shields, and wooden bows.
The wooden bows are short at the bottom and long at the top.
Bamboo arrows have either iron or bone tips.
All they possess is not different from Dān'ěr and Zhūyá.
The Wō land is warm;
in winter and summer, they eat raw vegetables
and all go barefoot.
They have houses.
Parents and siblings sleep in separate places.
They smear their bodies with cinnabar and red pigment,
like Zhōngguó uses powder.
They eat and drink using biāndòu,
eating with their hands.
When they die,
there is a coffin but no outer coffin,
and earth is piled up to form a tomb.
Immediately after death, the body is kept for more than ten days.
During this time, they do not eat meat.
The chief mourner cries and weeps,
while others sing, dance, and drink alcohol.
After burial,
the entire family goes to the water to bathe,
as if purifying themselves.
When they travel by crossing the sea to Zhōngguó,
they always send one person
who does not comb his hair,
does not remove lice or nits,
wears dirty clothes,
does not eat meat,
and does not approach women,
like a mourner.
He is called Zhíchuī.
If the travelers have good fortune,
they share the wealth of his life and property.
If there is illness
or they suffer violence,
they immediately want to kill him,
saying that his Zhíchuī was not diligent.
They produce pearls and green jade.
Their mountains have cinnabar.
Their trees include nán, zhù, yùzhāng, róulì, tóujiāng, wūháo, and fēngxiāng.
Their bamboos are xiāogǎn and táozhī.
They have ginger, oranges, pepper, and xiānghé,
but do not know how to use them for flavor.
They have monkeys and black pheasants.
It is their custom that when undertaking matters or traveling,
whatever they do,
they immediately scorch bones to divine,
to predict good or ill fortune.
They first state what is to be divined.
The words are like the methods for consulting tortoises.
They observe the cracks made by fire to interpret the omen.
When they gather and sit or rise,
there is no distinction between father and son, or male and female.
Their nature is fond of alcohol.
When they see an adult whom they respect,
they merely clasp their hands instead of kneeling and bowing.
These people are long-lived,
some a hundred years,
some eighty or ninety years.
According to their customs,
the adults of the state all have four or five wives,
while common households have two or three wives.
Women are not licentious
and are not jealous.
They do not steal
and have few disputes.
If they break the law,
for minor offenses, their wives and children are confiscated;
for serious offenses, their household is exterminated.
Among their clans, the respected and the humble
each have their differences in rank,
and are capable of submission to each other.
They collect taxes.
There are states with warehouses.
Each state has a market,
where goods are exchanged.
A great Wō supervises it.
North of the Queen's State,
a Dàshuài is specially appointed
to inspect all the states.
The states fear and dread him.
He always governs Yīdū Guó,
acting like a Cìshǐ within the state.
When the king sends envoys to Jīngdū, Dàifāng Jùn, and the various Hánguó,
and when the commander of the commandery sends envoys to Wō Guó,
they all examine them thoroughly at the ford,
transmitting documents and gifts to the queen,
without any errors.
When commoners meet adults on the road,
they respectfully step aside into the grass.
When conveying messages or discussing matters,
they either squat or kneel,
placing both hands on the ground,
showing respect.
They respond with the sound "yī,"
similar to saying "yes" or "no."
Originally, their state also had a man as king.
He ruled for seventy or eighty years.
Wō Guó fell into chaos,
with mutual attacks lasting for years.
Then they jointly enthroned a woman as king,
named Bīmǐhū.
She served the way of ghosts
and could enchant the populace.
She was already advanced in age,
had no husband,
and had a younger brother to assist her in governing the state.
Since becoming queen,
few people had seen her.
She had a thousand maids to attend her.
Only one man served her food and drink,
and transmitted messages in and out.
Her residence was a palace with towers and watchtowers,
and city walls were strictly erected,
with people constantly holding weapons and guarding.
East of the Queen's State, crossing the sea for over a thousand lǐ,
there are other states,
all of Wō ethnicity.
Further south is the Zhūrú Guó,
where people are three or four chǐ tall,
over four thousand lǐ from the Queen.
Further to its southeast are the Luǒ Guó and Hēichǐ Guó,
which can be reached by a year of sailing.
Enquiring about the Wō land,
it is entirely situated on islands and islets in the sea,
some separated, some connected,
with a circumference of over five thousand lǐ.
In the sixth month of Jǐngchū second year (238 CE),
the Wō Queen sent Dàfū Nánshēngmǐ and others to the commandery,
requesting an audience with the Son of Heaven to present tribute.
The Grand Administrator Liú Xià sent an official to escort them to Jīngdū.
In the twelfth month of that year,
an imperial edict was sent to the Wō Queen, stating:

"An imperial edict to Pīnwèi Wō Wáng Bīmǐhū: Dàifāng Grand Administrator Liú Xià sent an envoy to deliver your Dàfū Nánshēngmǐ and secondary envoy Dūshì Niúlì, who presented your tribute of four male slaves
and six female slaves, and two bolts and two zhàng of patterned cloth.
They have arrived.
Your land is exceedingly distant,
yet you sent an envoy to present tribute.
This shows your loyalty and filial piety.
I deeply appreciate you.
Now I appoint you as Pīnwèi Wō Wáng,
granting you a golden seal and purple ribbon.
It is sealed and entrusted to the Dàifāng Grand Administrator to bestow upon you.
You are to pacify and comfort your people,
and strive for filial reverence.
Your envoys Nánshēngmǐ and Niúlì traveled a great distance,
enduring hardship on the road.
Now I appoint Nánshēngmǐ as Shuàishàn Zhōnglángjiàng,
and Niúlì as Shuàishàn Xiàowèi,
granting them silver seals and green ribbons.
They are granted an audience, rewarded for their efforts, and sent back.
Now I give you five bolts of crimson ground dragon-patterned brocade,
ten pieces of crimson ground pleated wool felt, fifty bolts of scarlet silk, and fifty bolts of dark blue silk,
in return for the value of your tribute.

Additionally, I specially bestow upon you three bolts of dark blue ground patterned brocade, five pieces of fine patterned wool felt, fifty bolts of white silk, eight liǎng of gold, two five-chǐ swords, one hundred bronze mirrors, fifty jīn of pearls, and fifty jīn of lead white respectively.
All are sealed and entrusted to Nánshēngmǐ and Niúlì to receive upon their return.
You may show all of these to the people of your state,
so that they may know that the state cherishes you,
and thus solemnly bestows these fine items upon you."
In the first year of Zhèngzhì,
the Grand Administrator Gōng Zūn dispatched Jiànzhōng Xiàowèi Tī Jùn and others to Wōguó, bearing an imperial edict, seal, and ribbon,
to appoint the King of Wō.
They also carried an edict bestowing gold, silk, brocade, swords, mirrors, and various colorful objects.
The King of Wō thereupon sent an envoy to present a memorial of thanks for the imperial grace.
In its fourth year,
the King of Wō again dispatched envoys, Dàfū Yīshēngqí and Yèxiégǒu, with eight others,
to present living captives, Wō brocade, scarlet and green plain silk, padded clothing, plain silk fabric, cinnabar wood, and short bows and arrows.
Yèxiégǒu and others were appointed as Shuàishàn Zhōnglángjiàng and given a seal and ribbon.
In its sixth year,
an imperial edict bestowed a yellow banner upon Wō Nánshēngmǐ,
to be conferred by the commandery.
In its eighth year,
Grand Administrator Wáng Qí arrived in office.
The Queen of Wō, Bēimíhū, and the King of Gǒunúguó, Bēimí Gōnghū, had long been at odds.
She sent Wō Zàisī and Wūyuè to the commandery to report on the mutual attacks.
Zhāng Zhèng, the Sāicáo Yuánshǐ, was dispatched with an imperial edict and a yellow banner,
to appoint Nánshēngmǐ as a bearer of a proclamation to admonish them.
When Bēimíhū died,
a large tomb was built,
over a hundred paces in diameter,
and over a hundred male and female slaves were immolated.
A male king was then enthroned,
but the people of the country did not submit,
and they slaughtered each other,
with over a thousand people killed at that time.
A relative of Bēimíhū, Yīyǔ, was again enthroned,
at the age of thirteen, as king.
The country then became settled.
Zhèng and others presented the proclamation to Yīyǔ.
Yīyǔ dispatched Wō Dàfū and Shuàishàn Zhōnglángjiàng Yèxiégǒu, with twenty others, to escort Zhèng and others back.
They then proceeded to the court,
and presented thirty male and female living captives,
contributed five thousand white pearls,
two large blue curved pearls with holes,
and twenty rolls of patterned brocade.
Commentary says: The Shǐ Jì and Hàn Shū documented Cháoxiǎn and Liǎngyuè;
the Dōngjīng recorded the Xīqiāng.
In the Wèi era, the Xiongnú finally declined,
and there were further Wūwán and Xiānbēi.
Extending to the Eastern Barbarians,
envoys and interpreters frequently traveled.
The records followed events as they happened;
how could they be constant?
Liú Yān, courtesy name Jūnláng,
was from Jìnglǐng, Jiāngxià.
He was a descendant of Hù Lǔ Gōngwáng.
During the Yuánhé reign of Emperor Zhāng, his branch was relocated and enfeoffed in Jìnglǐng,
where his collateral family resided.
Yān served in the provincial and commandery governments in his youth.
As a member of the imperial clan, he was appointed Zhōngláng.
Later, he resigned from office due to the mourning for his teacher, Zhùgōng.
He resided on Yángchéng Shān,
accumulating knowledge and teaching.
He was recommended as Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng,
and was appointed to the Sītú’s office.
He successively served as Luòyáng Lìng, Jìzhōu Cìshǐ, Nányáng Tàishǒu, Zōngzhèng, and Tàicháng.
Yān observed the declining and deficient governance of Emperor Líng,
and the frequent troubles of the imperial house.
He then proposed, saying:
"The Cìshǐ and Tàishǒu,
who obtained office through bribery,
oppress the common people,
leading to defection and rebellion.
One should select officials of high repute and integrity to be Mùbó,
to pacify and secure the regions."
Yān secretly sought the position of Jiāozhǐ Mù,
wishing to avoid the troubles of the world.
While the proposal had not yet been implemented,
Shìzhōng Dǒng Fú of Guǎnghàn privately told Yān:
"The capital is about to fall into chaos,
and Yìzhōu, in its astrological division, shows the aura of an Son of Heaven."
When Yān heard Fú's words,
his intention shifted to Yìzhōu.
It happened that Qì Jiǎn, the Cìshǐ of Yìzhōu, was excessively taxing and troublesome,
and rumors spread far and wide.
Moreover, Bìngzhōu killed Cìshǐ Zhāng Yī,
and Liángzhōu killed Cìshǐ Gěng Bǐ.
Yān's plan was thus able to be carried out.
He was dispatched as Jiānjūn Shǐzhě,
and concurrently held the position of Yìzhōu Mù,
enfeoffed as Yángchéng Hóu,
responsible for arresting Jiǎn and punishing him.
Fú also sought to be Shǔjùn Xībù Shǔguó Dūwèi.
And Tàicāng Lìng Zhào Wěi of Bāxī resigned from office.
Both accompanied Yān.
At this time, the rebel leaders Mǎ Xiāng and Zhào Zhī and others in Yìzhōu declared themselves "Yellow Turbans" in Miánzhú Xiàn,
gathering exhausted and conscripted people.
Within a day or two, they gained several thousand men.
They first killed Lǐ Shēng, the magistrate of Miánzhú,
and officials and common people flocked to them,
totaling over ten thousand.
They then advanced and captured Luò Xiàn,
attacked Yìzhōu and killed Jiǎn.
They further reached Shǔjùn and Qiánwéi.
Within a month,
they destroyed three commanderies.
Xiāng declared himself Son of Heaven,
and his followers numbered in the tens of thousands.
Jiǎ Lóng, a staff officer of the province, who commanded several hundred family troops in the eastern border of Qiánwéi,
gathered officials and common people,
obtaining over a thousand men.
He attacked Xiāng and others,
defeating them in a few days,
and the provincial borders became peaceful.
Lóng then selected officials and soldiers to welcome Yān.
Yān relocated his administration to Miánzhú,
soothing and accepting defectors and rebels.
He diligently implemented leniency and kindness,
secretly planning other schemes.
Zhāng Lǔ's mother had initially practiced Daoist sorcery,
and also had a youthful appearance.
She frequently visited Yān's household.
Therefore, Yān sent Lǔ as Dūyì Sīmǎ,
to reside in Hànzhōng,
block the Gǔ Pass,
and kill Han envoys.
Yān submitted a memorial stating that the rice bandits had blocked the roads,
making communication impossible.
He also used other pretexts to kill over ten prominent figures in the province, such as Wáng Xián and Lǐ Quán,
to establish his authority and penalties.
Rèn Qí, the Tàishǒu of Qiánwéi, and Jiǎ Lóng, thereupon rebelled and attacked Yān.
Yān attacked and killed Qí and Lóng.
Yān's ambitions gradually grew.
He commissioned the manufacture of over a thousand imperial carriages and equipment.
Liú Biǎo, the Mù of Jīngzhōu, memorialized that Yān's words resembled Zǐxià's doubts about the sage in Xīhé.
At that time, Yān's son Fàn was Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng,
Dàn was Zhìshū Yùshǐ,
and Zhāng was Fèngchē Dūwèi.
All were with Emperor Xiàn in Cháng'ān.
Only his younger son, Biébù Sīmǎ Mào, always followed Yān.
Emperor Xiàn sent Zhāng to admonish Yān,
but Yān detained Zhāng and did not send him back.
At that time, Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Mǎ Téng was stationed in Méi and rebelled.
Yān and Fàn colluded with Téng,
leading troops to attack Cháng'ān.
Fàn's plot was discovered,
and he fled to Huáilǐ.
Téng was defeated
and retreated to Liángzhōu.
Fàn was killed at that time,
and thereupon Dàn was arrested and executed.
Páng Xī of Hénán, a Yìláng, had family ties with Yān,
and he recruited soldiers to escort Yān's grandsons into Shǔ.
At this time, Yān's city was burned by a heavenly fire,
and all the carriage equipment was destroyed,
the fire spreading to common people's homes.
Yān relocated his administration to Chéngdū.
Grieving for his son
and affected by the ominous disaster,
in the first year of Xīngpíng,
he died from a carbuncle on his back.
Zhào Wěi and other high officials of the province, coveting Zhāng's gentle and kind nature,
jointly recommended Zhāng as Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
An imperial edict then appointed him as Jiānjūn Shǐzhě
and concurrently Yìzhōu Mù.
Wěi was appointed Zhēngdōng Zhōnglángjiàng,
leading troops to attack Liú Biǎo.
Zhāng,
whose courtesy name was Jìyù,
after succeeding to his position,
Zhāng Lǔ gradually became arrogant and willful,
and did not obey Zhāng.
Zhāng killed Lǔ's mother and younger brother,
thus becoming his enemy.
Zhāng repeatedly dispatched Páng Xī and others to attack Lǔ,
but they were frequently defeated.
Many of Lǔ's soldiers were in Bāxī,
so Xī was appointed Administrator of Bāxī,
leading troops to defend against Lǔ.
Later, Xī and Zhāng became estranged,
and Zhào Wěi raised an army and turned inward.
Their forces scattered and were killed,
all because Zhāng lacked decisive judgment and listened to outside talk.
Zhāng heard that Cáo Gōng was campaigning in Jīngzhōu
and had already pacified Hànzhōng,
so he sent Yīn Pǔ from Hénèi to pay respects to Cáo Gōng.
Zhāng was appointed General Who Manifests Awe,
and his elder brother Mào was appointed General Who Pacifies Bandits.
Mào died of a severe illness.
Zhāng again sent the Special Aide and Commandant Zhāng Sù from Shǔjùn to deliver three hundred elderly soldiers and various imperial items to Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng appointed Sù as Administrator of Guǎnghàn.
Zhāng again sent the Special Aide Zhāng Sōng to Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng had at that time already pacified Jīngzhōu
and driven away the Former Lord,
so he no longer paid attention to Sōng,
and Sōng resented this.
It happened that Cáo Gōng's army suffered a setback at Chìbì,
and also many died of plague.
When Sōng returned,
he disparaged Cáo Gōng
and advised Zhāng to break off relations,
then said to Zhāng:
"Liú Yùzhōu
is like a close relative to you,
you can establish communication with him."
Zhāng agreed with all of this,
and sent Fǎ Zhèng to establish good relations with the Former Lord.
Soon after, he again ordered Zhèng and Mèng Dá to send several thousand soldiers to assist the Former Lord in defense.
Zhèng then returned.
Later, Sōng again said to Zhāng:
"Now all the generals in the province, such as Páng Xī and Lǐ Yì, are arrogant and powerful due to their achievements,
and harbor ulterior motives.
If we do not have Yùzhōu,
then the enemy will attack from outside,
and the people will attack from within,
which is a sure path to defeat."
Zhāng again followed his advice,
and sent Fǎ Zhèng to invite the Former Lord.
Zhāng's Chief Clerk Huáng Quán presented the advantages and disadvantages,
and the Commandant of Guǎnghàn, Wáng Lěi, hanged himself upside down at the provincial gate to remonstrate.
Zhāng accepted none of it,
and ordered his subordinates to provide for the Former Lord,
so the Former Lord entered the territory as if returning home.
The Former Lord reached the north of Jiāngzhōu,
and from Diànjiāng waterway (Diàn pronounced as dú-xié fǎn)
went to Fú,
(pronounced fú)
three hundred sixty *lǐ* from Chéngdū.
This was the sixteenth year of Jiàn'ān.
Zhāng led over thirty thousand infantry and cavalry,
with carriages and tents,
their brilliance shining on the sun,
and went to meet with him;
the officers and soldiers brought by the Former Lord
mingled with each other,
drinking joyfully for over a hundred days.
Zhāng provided supplies to the Former Lord,
so he could attack Zhāng Lǔ,
and then they separated.
The next year,
the Former Lord reached Jiāmáng,
turned his troops south,
conquering all places.
In the nineteenth year,
he advanced and besieged Chéngdū for several tens of days.
There were still thirty thousand elite soldiers in the city,
and enough grain and silk to last for a year.
The officials and people all wished to fight to the death.
Zhāng said:
"My father and I have been in the province for over twenty years,
but have bestowed no kindness upon the common people.
The common people have fought for three years,
their bodies coating the wilds,
because of me.
How can I feel at ease!"
Thereupon, he opened the city and surrendered,
and all his subordinates shed tears.
The Former Lord relocated Zhāng to Gōng'ān in Nánjùn,
and returned all his property and the seal and ribbon of his former title, General Who Manifests Awe.
Sūn Quán killed Guān Yǔ
and seized Jīngzhōu,
then appointed Zhāng as Governor of Yìzhōu,
stationed at Zǐguī.
After Zhāng died,
the local strongman Yōng Kǎi from Nánzhōng occupied Yìjùn and rebelled,
allying with Wú.
Quán again appointed Zhāng's son Chǎn as Inspector of Yìzhōu,
situated at the border of Jiāo and Yì.
When Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng pacified the southern territories,
Chǎn returned to Wú
and became Palace Assistant Imperial Censor.
Originally,
Zhāng's eldest son Xún's wife
was Páng Xī's daughter.
When the Former Lord pacified Shǔ,
Xī was General of the Left and Commandant.
Zhāng at that time, through Xī's petition, requested Xún to stay,
and the Former Lord appointed him Commandant of Chariots.
Thus, the descendants of Zhāng's two sons
were divided between Wú and Shǔ.
The commentary says: In the past, Wèi Bào, hearing Xǔ Fù's words, took Bó Jī into his household.
Liú Xīn, seeing the texts of prognostication and prophecy, changed his name.
Ultimately, they could not escape their fate,
yet blessings fell upon two lords.
This shows that divine guidance cannot be idly sought,
and heavenly mandates cannot be wished for presumptuously;
it is a verification of inevitability.
However, Liú Yān, hearing Dǒng Fú's words, harbored ambitions for the land of Yì;
listening to the words of a physiognomist, he sought marriage with the Wú clan;
he hastily prepared carriages and robes,
scheming to usurp the divine implements of power;
his delusion was extreme.
Zhāng's talent was not that of a hero,
yet he occupied territory in a chaotic era.
Riding on a carriage and bringing about an enemy,
it was a natural principle
that he would be seized;
it was not misfortune.
Biography of the Former Lord, Part Two
The Former Lord's surname was Liú,
his given name Bèi,
and his courtesy name Xuándé.
He was from Zhuōxiàn, Zhuōjùn,
a descendant of Liú Shèng, the Prince Jìng of Zhōngshān, son of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn.
Shèng's son Zhēn
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Lùchéngtíng, Zhuōxiàn, in the sixth year of Yuánshòu.
Due to the *zhòu* gold incident, he lost his marquisate,
and subsequently settled there.
The Former Lord's grandfather was Xióng,
and his father Hóng;
generations of their family served in commanderies and counties.
Xióng was nominated as *xiàolián* [filial and incorruptible],
and served as Magistrate of Fàn in Dōngjùn.
The Former Lord was orphaned young,
and he and his mother made a living by selling shoes and weaving mats.
At the southeastern corner of their house, on the fence, a mulberry tree grew over five *zhàng* tall,
appearing from a distance to be luxuriant like a small carriage canopy.
Passersby all marvelled that this tree was extraordinary,
some saying that a noble person would emerge from there.
When the Former Lord was young,
he played with the other young children of his clan under the tree,
saying:
"I shall certainly ride in such a feathered-canopy carriage."
His uncle Zǐjìng said to him:
"Do not speak wildly; you will destroy our family!"
At the age of fifteen,
his mother sent him to study,
and he, along with his kinsman Liú Dérán and Gōngsūn Zàn from Liáoxī,
together served Lú Zhí, the former Administrator of Jiǔjiāng from the same commandery.
Dérán's father Yuánqǐ often provided financial assistance to the Former Lord,
treating him like Dérán and others.
Yuánqǐ's wife said:
"Each has their own family;
how can this continue forever!"
Yuánqǐ said:
"Among our clan, there is this child;
he is no ordinary person."
And Zàn was deeply friendly with the Former Lord.
Zàn was older,
and the Former Lord treated him as an elder brother.
The Former Lord was not very fond of reading,
but enjoyed dogs, horses, music, and fine clothes.
He was seven *chǐ* five *cùn* tall,
his hands hung down below his knees,
and he could see his own ears when he looked back.
He spoke little,
was good at treating others with humility,
and did not show his joy or anger in his expression.
He liked to associate with heroes and chivalrous men,
and young people eagerly attached themselves to him.
The great merchants Zhāng Shìpíng and Sū Shuāng from Zhōngshān, whose wealth amounted to thousands of gold,
travelled to and from Zhuōjùn selling horses,
saw him and found him extraordinary.
They then gave him a large amount of gold and property.
The Former Lord was thus able to gather followers.
Late in the reign of Emperor Líng,
the Yellow Turbans rose.
The commanderies and states each raised righteous armies.
The Former Lord, leading his subordinates, followed Commandant Zōu Jìng to suppress the Yellow Turban bandits, and for his accomplishments,
he was appointed Magistrate of Ānxǐ.
When the Inspector-Supervisor arrived at the county on official business,
the Former Lord requested an audience,
but was refused.
He went straight in, bound the Inspector-Supervisor,
gave him two hundred strokes with a staff,

removed his official sash and tied it around the Inspector-Supervisor's neck, fastening him to a horse (the character 馬 here is read 'mǎ' but means 'horse' in the sense of a whipping post or a punishment tool),
(meaning to bind something firmly like a five-pronged fork),
abandoned his post, and fled.
Shortly thereafter,
Grand General Hé Jìn dispatched Commandant Wúqiū Yì to Dānyáng to recruit soldiers.
The Former Lord accompanied him.
Upon reaching Xiàpī, they encountered bandits,
fought bravely and achieved merit.
He was then appointed Assistant Magistrate of Xiàmì.
He again left office.
Later, he became Magistrate of Gāotáng,
and was promoted to Prefect.
When his commandery was destroyed by bandits,
he went to seek refuge with Colonel Gōngsūn Zàn.
Gōngsūn Zàn memorialized the throne to appoint him as a Divisional Major,
and sent him with the Governor of Qīngzhōu, Tián Kǎi, to resist the Pastor of Jìzhōu, Yuán Shào.
He achieved numerous military successes,
was provisionally appointed Prefect of Píngyuán,
and later became Chancellor of Píngyuán.
A commoner of the commandery, Liú Píng, who had always looked down on the Former Lord
and was ashamed to be under him,
sent an assassin to kill him.
The assassin could not bring himself to do it,
told him about the plot, and left.
Such was the way he won people's hearts.
When Yuán Shào attacked Gōngsūn Zàn,
the Former Lord and Tián Kǎi camped east in Qí.
When Cáo Gōng campaigned against Xúzhōu,
the Pastor of Xúzhōu, Táo Qiān, sent an envoy to Tián Kǎi to report the urgency of the situation.
Tián Kǎi and the Former Lord together went to his aid.
At this time, the Former Lord had over a thousand of his own soldiers and cavalry of the Wūhuán and various Hú tribes from Yōuzhōu,
and had also gathered several thousand famine refugees.
Upon their arrival,
Táo Qiān added four thousand Dānyáng soldiers to the Former Lord's forces.
The Former Lord then left Tián Kǎi and returned to Táo Qiān.
Táo Qiān memorialized the throne to appoint the Former Lord as Governor of Yùzhōu,
stationed in Xiǎopèi.
When Táo Qiān became critically ill,
he said to his Separate-Cavalry Commandant, Mí Zhú:
“No one but Liú Bèi can stabilize this state.”
After Táo Qiān's death,
Mí Zhú led the people of the state to welcome the Former Lord.
The Former Lord did not dare to accept immediately.
Chén Dēng of Xiàpī said to the Former Lord:
“Now the Hàn dynasty is in decline,
and the realm is in upheaval.
The opportunity to achieve great deeds
is today.
This state is rich and prosperous,
with a million households.
We wish to humbly ask Your Excellency to assume command of the state's affairs.”
The Former Lord said:
“Yuán Gōnglù is nearby in Shòuchūn.
This gentleman's family has held high office for four generations and five times produced dukes.
He is the one to whom the realm looks up.
You may give the state to him.”
Chén Dēng said:
“Yuán Gōnglù is arrogant and tyrannical;
he is not a lord who can govern in times of chaos.
Now I wish to gather a hundred thousand infantry and cavalry for Your Excellency.
Above, you can uphold the sovereign and save the people,
achieving the accomplishments of the Five Hegemons.
Below, you can divide land and guard borders,
and have your achievements recorded on bamboo and silk.
If Your Excellency does not agree to this,
I, Dēng, also dare not listen to Your Excellency.”
Kǒng Róng, the Chancellor of Běihǎi, said to the Former Lord:
“How can Yuán Gōnglù be concerned with the state and forget his family?
He is but a dry bone in a tomb,
not worth minding.
In today's matters,
the common people are capable and Heaven bestows.
If you do not take what Heaven gives,
regrets will be unavailing.”
The Former Lord then took charge of Xúzhōu.
Yuán Shù came to attack the Former Lord.
The Former Lord resisted him at Xūyí and Huáiyīn.
Cáo Gōng memorialized the throne to appoint the Former Lord as General Who Stabilizes the East
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yíchéng Pavilion.
This year was the first year of Jiàn'ān.
The Former Lord and Yuán Shù were locked in a standoff for over a month.
Lǚ Bù took advantage of the vulnerability and attacked Xiàpī.
The defending general of Xiàpī, Cáo Bào, rebelled,
and secretly welcomed Lǚ Bù.
Lǚ Bù captured the Former Lord's wife and children.
The Former Lord moved his army to Hǎixī.
Yáng Fèng and Hán Xiān raided the area between Xú and Yáng.
The Former Lord ambushed and attacked them,
killing them all.
The Former Lord sought peace with Lǚ Bù.
Lǚ Bù returned his wife and children.
The Former Lord sent Guān Yǔ to guard Xiàpī.
The Former Lord returned to Xiǎopèi,
and reassembled his army, gaining over ten thousand men.
Lǚ Bù resented this
and personally led troops to attack the Former Lord.
The Former Lord was defeated and fled to Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng treated him generously,
appointing him Pastor of Yùzhōu.
He was sent to Pèi to gather scattered soldiers,
supplied with military provisions,
and given additional troops to attack Lǚ Bù in the east.
Lǚ Bù sent Gāo Shùn to attack him.
Cáo Gōng sent Xiàhóu Dūn,
but he could not rescue them.
He was defeated by Gāo Shùn,
who again captured the Former Lord's wife and children and sent them to Lǚ Bù.
Cáo Gōng personally led an eastern campaign,
assisting the Former Lord in besieging Lǚ Bù at Xiàpī,
and capturing Lǚ Bù alive.
The Former Lord recovered his wife and children,
and returned with Cáo Gōng to Xǔ.
Cáo Gōng memorialized the throne to appoint the Former Lord as General of the Left,
treating him with even greater respect.
When they went out, they shared a carriage;
when they sat, they shared a mat.
Yuán Shù wished to pass through Xúzhōu north to join Yuán Shào.
Cáo Gōng sent the Former Lord, overseeing Zhū Líng and Lù Zhāo, to intercept Yuán Shù.
Before they arrived,
Yuán Shù died of illness.
Before the Former Lord departed,
Dǒng Chéng, the Emperor Xiàn's maternal uncle and General of Chariots and Cavalry,
received a secret imperial edict in an imperial sash,
ordering the execution of Cáo Gōng.
The Former Lord had not yet acted.
At this time, Cáo Gōng casually said to the Former Lord:
“Today, the heroes of the realm
are only Your Excellency and Cáo.
As for those like Běnchū,
they are not worth mentioning.”
The Former Lord was eating and
dropped his spoon and chopsticks.
He then conspired with Dǒng Chéng, Colonel of Chángshuǐ Zhǒng Jí, General Wú Zǐlán, Wáng Zǐfú, and others.
However, an envoy arrived,
and they did not act.
When the plot was discovered,
Dǒng Chéng and the others were all executed.
The Former Lord seized Xiàpī.
When Zhū Líng and others returned,
the Former Lord then killed the Governor of Xúzhōu, Chē Zhòu,
left Guān Yǔ to guard Xiàpī,
and personally returned to Xiǎopèi.
Chāng Bà of Dōnghǎi rebelled.
Many commanderies and counties betrayed Cáo Gōng for the Former Lord,
totaling tens of thousands of people.
He sent Sūn Gān to establish an alliance with Yuán Shào.
Cáo Gōng sent Liú Dài and Wáng Zhōng to attack him,
but they were unsuccessful.
In the fifth year [of Jiàn'ān],
Cáo Gōng led an eastern campaign against the Former Lord.
The Former Lord was defeated.
Cáo Gōng seized all his troops,
captured the Former Lord's wife and children,
and also captured Guān Yǔ, returning with them.
The Former Lord fled to Qīngzhōu.
The Governor of Qīngzhōu, Yuán Tán,
who was a former *Máocái* (Filial and Incorrupt) recommended by the Former Lord,
led infantry and cavalry to welcome the Former Lord.
The Former Lord followed Yuán Tán to Píngyuán.
Yuán Tán quickly sent an envoy to inform Yuán Shào.
Yuán Shào sent generals along the road to welcome him.
He personally traveled two hundred *lǐ* from Yè,
and met the Former Lord.
After staying for over a month,
the lost and scattered soldiers gradually gathered.
Cáo Gōng and Yuán Shào were in a standoff at Guāndù.
Liú Pì and other Yellow Turbans of Rǔnán rebelled against Cáo Gōng and sided with Yuán Shào.
Yuán Shào sent the Former Lord to lead troops with Liú Pì and others to raid the area around Xǔ.
Guān Yǔ escaped and returned to the Former Lord.
Cáo Gōng sent Cáo Rén to lead troops to attack the Former Lord.
The Former Lord returned to Yuán Shào's army.
Secretly wishing to leave Yuán Shào,
he persuaded Yuán Shào to ally south with the Pastor of Jīngzhōu, Liú Biǎo.
Yuán Shào sent the Former Lord with his original troops back to Rǔnán,
where he joined with the bandit Gōng Dū and others,
totaling several thousand men.
Cáo Gōng sent Cài Yáng to attack them,
but Cài Yáng was killed by the Former Lord.
Cáo Gōng 既破 Shào,
自南擊先主．
先主遣 Mí Zhú, Sūn Gān 與 Liú Biǎo 相聞，
Biǎo 自郊迎，
以上賓禮待之，
益其兵，
使屯 Xīnyě．
Jīngzhōu 豪傑歸先主者日益多，
Biǎo 疑其心，
陰禦之．
使拒 Xiàhóu Dūn, Yú Jìn 等於 Bówàng．
久之，
先主設伏兵，
一旦自燒屯偽遁，
Dūn 等追之，
為伏兵所破．
十二年，
Cáo Gōng 北征 Wūhuán，
先主說 Biǎo 襲 Xǔ，
Biǎo 不能用．
Cáo Gōng 南征 Biǎo，
會 Biǎo 卒，
子 Cóng 代立，
遣使請降．
先主屯 Fán，
不知 Cáo Gōng 卒至，
至 Wǎn 乃聞之，
遂將其衆去．
過 Xiāngyáng，
Zhūgě Liàng 說先主攻 Cóng，
Jīngzhōu 可有．
先主曰：
「吾不忍也．」
乃駐馬呼 Cóng，
Cóng 懼不能起．
Cóng 左右及 Jīngzhōu 人多歸先主．
比到 Dāngyáng，
衆十餘萬，
輜重數千兩，
日行十餘里，
別遣 Guān Yǔ 乘船數百艘，
使會 Jiānglíng．
或謂先主曰：
「宜速行保 Jiānglíng，
今雖擁大衆，
被甲者少，
若 Cáo Gōng 兵至，
何以拒之？ 」
先主曰：
「夫濟大事必以人為本，
今人歸吾，
吾何忍棄去！ 」
Cáo Gōng 以 Jiānglíng 有軍實，
恐先主據之，
乃釋輜重，
輕軍到 Xiāngyáng．
聞先主已過，
Cáo Gōng 將精騎五千急追之，
一日一夜行三百餘里，
及於 Dāngyáng 之 Chángbǎn．
先主棄妻子，
與 Zhūgě Liàng, Zhāng Fēi, Zhào Yún 等數十騎走，
Cáo Gōng 大獲其人衆輜重．
先主斜趨 Hànjīn，
適與 Yǔ 船會，
得濟 Miǎn，
遇 Biǎo 長子 Jiāngxià Tàishǒu Qí 衆萬餘人，
與俱到 Xiàkǒu．
先主遣 Zhūgě Liàng 自結於 Sūn Quán，
Quán 遣 Zhōu Yú, Chéng Pǔ 等水軍數萬，
與先主并力，
與 Cáo Gōng 戰於 Chìbì，
大破之，
焚其舟船．
先主與 Wú 軍水陸並進，
追到 Nánjùn，
時又疾疫，
北軍多死，
Cáo Gōng 引歸．
先主表 Qí 為 Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ，
又南征四郡．
Wǔlíng Tàishǒu Jīn Xuán, Chángshā Tàishǒu Hán Xuán, Guìyáng Tàishǒu Zhào Fàn, Línglíng Tàishǒu Liú Dù 皆降．
Lújiāng Léi Xù 率部曲數萬口稽顙．
Qí 病死，
羣下推先主為 Jīngzhōu Mù，
治 Gōng'ān．
Quán 稍畏之，
進妹固好．
先主至 Jīng 見 Quán，
綢繆恩紀．
Quán 遣使云欲共取 Shǔ，
或以為宜報聽許，
Wú 終不能越 Jīng 有 Shǔ，
Shǔ 地可為己有．
Jīngzhōu Zhǔbù Yīn Guān 進曰：
「若為 Wú 先驅，
進未能克 Shǔ，
退為 Wú 所乘，
即事去矣．
今但可然贊其伐 Shǔ，
而自說新據諸郡，
未可興動，
Wú 必不敢越我而獨取 Shǔ．
如此進退之計，
可以收 Wú, Shǔ 之利． 」
先主從之，
Quán 果輟計．
遷 Guān 為 Biéjià Cóngshì．
十六年，
Yìzhōu Mù Liú Zhāng 遙聞 Cáo Gōng 將遣 Zhōng Yáo 等向 Hànzhōng 討 Zhāng Lǔ，
內懷恐懼．
Biéjià Cóngshì Shǔjùn Zhāng Sōng 說 Zhāng 曰：
「Cáo Gōng 兵彊無敵於天下，
若因 Zhāng Lǔ 之資以取 Shǔ 土，
誰能禦之者乎？ 」
Zhāng 曰：
「吾固憂之而未有計． 」
Sōng 曰：
「Liú Yùzhōu，
使君之宗室而 Cáo Gōng 之深讎也，
善用兵，
若使之討 Lǔ，
Lǔ 必破．
Lǔ 破，
則 Yìzhōu 彊，
Cáo Gōng 雖來，
無能為也． 」
Zhāng 然之，
遣 Fǎ Zhèng 將四千人迎先主，
前後賂遺以巨億計．
Zhèng 因陳 Yìzhōu 可取之策．
先主留 Zhūgě Liàng, Guān Yǔ 等據 Jīngzhōu，
將步卒數萬人入 Yìzhōu．
至 Fú，
Zhāng 自出迎，
相見甚歡．
Zhāng Sōng 令 Fǎ Zhèng 白先主，
及謀臣 Páng Tǒng 進說，
便可於會所襲 Zhāng．
先主曰：
「此大事也，
不可倉卒． 」
Zhāng 推先主行 Dàsīmǎ，
領 Sīlì Xiàowèi；
先主亦推 Zhāng 行 Zhèn Xī Dàjiàngjūn，
領 Yìzhōu Mù．
Zhāng 增先主兵，
使擊 Zhāng Lǔ，
又令督 Báishuǐ jūn．
先主并軍三萬餘人，
車甲器械資貨甚盛．
是歲，
Zhāng 還 Chéngdū．
先主北到 Jiāmēng，
未即討 Lǔ，
厚樹恩德，
以收衆心．
The next year,
Cáo Gōng征 Sūn Quán,
Quán called upon the Former Lord to defend himself.
The Former Lord sent an envoy to inform Zhāng, saying:
"Cáo Gōng is campaigning against Wú,
and Wú is in grave danger.
The Sūn clan and I are fundamentally like lips and teeth;
moreover, Lè Jìn is engaged in a standoff with Guān Yǔ at Qīngní.
If I do not go to rescue Yǔ now,
Jìn will surely achieve a great victory,
then encroach upon the provincial borders.
That worry is far greater than the worry of Lǔ.
Lǔ is a self-preserving bandit,
not worth worrying about."
Thereupon, he requested from Zhāng ten thousand soldiers and provisions (treasures),
intending to travel east.
Zhāng only promised four thousand soldiers,
and supplied only half of everything else.
Zhāng Sōng wrote to the Former Lord and Fǎ Zhèng, saying:
"A great enterprise is now on the verge of being established;
why abandon this and leave?"
Sōng’s elder brother, Sù, the Grand Administrator of Guǎnghàn,
fearing disaster would befall himself,
reported Sōng’s plan to Zhāng.
Thereupon, Zhāng arrested and executed Sōng,
and the rift began to form.
Zhāng ordered the generals guarding the passes not to communicate with the Former Lord again.
The Former Lord was greatly enraged.
He summoned Yáng Huái, Zhāng’s supervisor of the Báishuǐ army,
reproached him for rudeness,
and executed him.
Then he sent Huáng Zhōng and Zhuó Yīng to lead troops against Zhāng.
The Former Lord proceeded directly to Guānzhōng,
held the wives and children of the generals and soldiers as hostages,
and led his army with Zhōng and Yīng forward to Fú,
where they occupied the city.
Zhāng sent Liú Guì, Lěng Bāo, Zhāng Rèn, Dèng Xián, and others to resist the Former Lord at Fú,
but they were all defeated,
and retreated to defend Miánzhú.
Zhāng again sent Lǐ Yán to supervise the armies at Miánzhú,
but Yán led his troops to surrender to the Former Lord.
The Former Lord’s army grew stronger.
He dispatched various generals to pacify the subordinate counties.
Zhūgě Liàng, Zhāng Fēi, Zhào Yún, and others led troops upstream to secure Báidì, Jiāngzhōu, and Jiāngyáng,
while only Guān Yǔ remained to guard Jīngzhōu.
The Former Lord advanced and besieged Luò;
at that time, Zhāng’s son Xún defended the city,
which was attacked for nearly a year.
In the summer of the nineteenth year,
Luò Chéng fell.
He then besieged Chéngdū for several tens of days,
and Zhāng surrendered.
Shǔ was prosperous and joyful.
The Former Lord hosted a grand feast for his officers and soldiers,
took gold and silver from the city of Shǔ and distributed it to his generals and soldiers,
and returned their grain and silk.
The Former Lord again assumed the office of Governor of Yìzhōu.
Zhūgě Liàng served as his chief aide,
Fǎ Zhèng as his chief strategist,
Guān Yǔ, Zhāng Fēi, and Mǎ Chāo as his trusted warriors,
and Xǔ Jìng, Mí Zhú, and Jiǎn Yōng as his honored friends.
Dǒng Hé, Huáng Quán, Lǐ Yán, and others who were originally appointed by Zhāng,
Wú Yī, Fèi Guān, and others who were Zhāng’s relatives by marriage,
Péng Yàng, who was marginalized by Zhāng,
and Liú Bā, who was feared and hated from long ago—
all were placed in prominent positions,
and their talents were fully utilized.
Ambitious individuals
all competed eagerly.
In the twentieth year,
Sūn Quán, knowing that the Former Lord had already obtained Yìzhōu,
sent an envoy to report his desire to obtain Jīngzhōu.
The Former Lord said:
"Once I obtain Liángzhōu,
I will hand Jīngzhōu over to you."
Quán was incensed,
and thereupon sent Lǚ Méng to seize Chángshā, Línglíng, and Guìyáng commanderies.
The Former Lord led fifty thousand troops downstream to Gōng'ān,
and ordered Guān Yǔ to enter Yìyáng.
That year,
Cáo Gōng pacified Hànzhōng,
and Zhāng Lǔ fled to Bāxī.
Hearing this, the Former Lord
allied with Quán,
dividing Jīngzhōu: Jiāngxià, Chángshā, and Guìyáng belonged to the east (Wú),
while Nánjùn, Línglíng, and Wǔlíng belonged to the west (Shǔ-Hàn).
He then led his army back to Jiāngzhōu.
He sent Huáng Quán to lead troops to meet Zhāng Lǔ,
but Zhāng Lǔ had already surrendered to Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng sent Xiàhóu Yuān and Zhāng Hé to garrison Hànzhōng,
and they frequently encroached upon the Bā region.
The Former Lord ordered Zhāng Fēi to advance his troops to Dàngqú,
where he fought with Hé and others at Wǎkǒu.
He defeated Hé and others,
and Hé gathered his troops and returned to Nánzhèng.
The Former Lord also returned to Chéngdū.
In the twenty-third year,
the Former Lord led his generals to advance troops into Hànzhōng.
He dispatched Generals Wú Lán and Léi Tóng and others into Wǔdū,
but they were all captured by Cáo Gōng’s army.
The Former Lord encamped at Yángpíngguān,
and was engaged in a standoff with Yuān and Hé and others.
In the spring of the twenty-fourth year,
he crossed the Miǎnshuǐ River south from Yángpíng,
advanced gradually along the mountains,
and established a fortified camp on Dìngjūnshān.
Yuān led troops to contest the land.
The Former Lord ordered Huáng Zhōng to ascend to a high position, beat drums, and shout to attack them.
He heavily defeated Yuān’s army,
and executed Yuān and Zhào Yóng, whom Cáo Gōng had appointed as the Inspector of Yìzhōu, and others.
Cáo Gōng himself led a large army south from Cháng'ān.
The Former Lord remarked from afar:
"Although Cáo Gōng comes,
he can do nothing;
I will surely have Hànchuān."
When Cáo Gōng arrived,
the Former Lord consolidated his troops to defend strategic points,
consistently avoiding direct engagement.
After months without success,
Cáo Gōng’s casualties increased daily.
In the summer,
Cáo Gōng indeed withdrew his army,
and the Former Lord thus gained Hànzhōng.
He sent Liú Fēng, Méng Dá, Lǐ Píng, and others to attack Shēn Dān at Shàngyōng.
In autumn,
the various officials petitioned the Former Lord to be King of Hànzhōng,
and submitted a memorial to the Hàn Emperor which said:

“The General Who Pacifies the West, Marquis of Dūtíng, your servant Mǎ Chāo; the Left General, Chief Clerk of the Military (who also holds the position of) General Who Guards the Army, your servant Xǔ Jìng; the Commander of the Camp, your servant Páng Xī; the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Bureau of Deliberations, General Who Deliberates on Military Affairs, your servant Shè Yuán;

the General of the Military Advisor, your servant Zhūgě Liàng; the General Who Suppresses Bandits, Marquis of Hànshòu Village, your servant Guān Yǔ; the General Who Conquers Barbarians, Marquis of Xīntíng, your servant Zhāng Fēi; the General Who Conquers the West, your servant Huáng Zhōng; the General Who Guards the Faraway, your servant Lài Gōng; the General Who Spreads Martial Might, your servant Fǎ Zhèng; the General Who Initiates Enterprise, your servant Lǐ Yán, and one hundred and twenty other individuals, submit the following: In the past, Yáo of Táng was a supreme sage, yet the Four Fiends were in his court;
Chéng of Zhōu was benevolent and wise, yet the Four States created difficulties;
Empress Gāo ruled as regent, yet the various Lǚ clans usurped authority;
and Emperor Xiàozhāo was young and immature, yet Shàngguān planned rebellion.
All of them relied on worldly favor,
grasped state power,
and committed extreme evil and chaos,
bringing the altars of soil and grain to near peril.
If not for the likes of Dà Shùn, Duke of Zhōu, Zhūxū, and Bólù,
they could not have been banished, captured, or punished,
nor could stability have been restored and danger averted.
We humbly observe that Your Majesty, endowed with sagely virtue,
governs all nations,
but has encountered the hardships of an inauspicious fate.
Dǒng Zhuó initiated the rebellion,
overthrowing the capital region;
Cáo Cāo escalated the calamity,
usurping control of the state;
the Empress and Crown Prince
were poisoned and murdered;
the empire was plundered and disordered,
and the people and their livelihoods were ruined.
For a long time, Your Majesty has suffered indignity and distress,
residing in a desolate city.
With neither gods nor humans as their masters,
they have cut off the imperial commands,
obscured the imperial order,
and sought to steal the divine instruments of power.
The Left General, who also holds the positions of Colonel Director of Retainers and Governor of the three provinces of Yù, Jīng, and Yì, Marquis of Yíchéng Village, Bèi,
having received imperial titles and ranks,
is committed to exerting his strength
to serve the nation in its peril.
Seeing the opportune moment,
he boldly rose up in anger,
and conspired with the General of Chariots and Cavalry Dǒng Chéng to execute Cáo Cāo,
to secure the state
and pacify the old capital.
However, Dǒng Chéng's plot was not kept secret,
allowing Cáo Cāo's evil spirit to continue its malicious ways,
destroying and ruining the realm.
We, your servants, constantly fear that the royal house might suffer a disaster like Yán Lè,
or a lesser calamity like Dìng'ān,
and are anxious day and night,
trembling with every breath.
In ancient times, the Yú Book
emphasized the ranking of the nine clans;
Zhōu observed the two preceding dynasties
and enfeoffed those of the same surname,
an principle elaborated in the Odes,
which lasted for a long time.
At the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
territory was divided,
and the imperial princes and brothers were honored;
it was thus that the calamity of the various Lǚ clans was eventually broken,
and the foundation of Emperor Tàizōng was established.
We, your servants, believe that Bèi, as a close relative and collateral branch,
a scion of the imperial clan and a bulwark,
has the state in his heart
and is intent on quelling the chaos.
Since Cáo Cāo's defeat in Hànzhōng,
heroes throughout the realm have flocked to him like ants,
yet his noble title is not prominent,
nor have the Nine Bestowals been conferred.
This is not how to guard the altars of soil and grain
and illuminate all generations.
Receiving orders from afar,
ritual commands are cut off.
In the past, when the Grand Administrator of Héxī, Liáng Tǒng, and others lived through the Hàn restoration,
they were separated by mountains and rivers,
their positions equal and authority similar,
unable to lead one another.
They all acclaimed Dòu Róng as their supreme commander,
and he ultimately achieved great deeds,
crushing Wěi Xiāo.
Now, the peril to the altars of soil and grain
is more urgent than that in Lǒng and Shǔ.
Cáo Cāo outwardly devours the empire,
and inwardly slaughters the various officials;
the imperial court faces danger within its own walls,
yet a defender against aggression has not been established.
This is truly heartbreaking.
We, your servants, therefore, in accordance with old precedents,
enfeoff Bèi as King of Hànzhōng,
appoint him Grand Marshal,
and grant him command over the six armies,
to rally the allies
and sweep away the rebellious villains.
We propose that Hànzhōng, Bā, Shǔ, Guǎnghàn, and Jiànwéi constitute his kingdom,
and that the appointments made therein follow the old precedents of the feudal kings in the early Hàn dynasty.
As for expedient measures,
if they benefit the altars of soil and grain,
it is permissible to act independently.
Then, when success is achieved and the task completed,
we, your servants, will retreat and submit to the charge of usurpation;
even if we die, we will have no regrets.”
Thereupon, a platform was erected in Miànyáng,
troops were arrayed and the populace assembled,
the various officials attended in their positions,
and after the memorial was read,
the imperial crown was placed on the Former Lord.
The Former Lord reported to the Han Emperor, saying:
"I, your subject, with the talent of a mere subject,
bear the responsibility of a high general,
overseeing the three armies,
and fulfilling my duties outside the capital.
Yet I have been unable to sweep away the bandit troubles,
stabilize the imperial house,
and have long caused Your Majesty's sagely teachings to decline,
so that within the six directions,
misfortune prevails and prosperity has not arrived.
I am only anxious and restless,
troubled as if with a severe headache.
In the past, Dǒng Zhuó initiated the rebellion,
and since then,
numerous villains ran rampant,
ravaging the land.
Relying on Your Majesty's sagely virtue and awesome power,
with both men and gods responding,
some loyal and righteous ones valiantly fought,
or Heaven sent down punishment,
the tyrannical rebels were all exterminated,
gradually melting away like ice.
Only Cáo Cāo,
has long remained unpunished,
usurping national authority,
and indulging in extreme chaos.
I formerly conspired with Chēqí Jiāngjūn Dǒng Chéng to eliminate Cáo,
but the plan was not kept secret,
and Chéng was entrapped and harmed.
I fled and lost my base,
and my loyal and righteous endeavor failed.
Thus, Cáo was able to reach the peak of wickedness and rebellion,
slaying empresses and imperial consorts,
and poisoning imperial princes.
Although I gathered allies,
intending to exert myself,
my weakness and lack of military prowess
have yielded no results over the years.
I constantly fear that I might perish,
failing the nation's grace,
sighing endlessly awake or asleep,
cautious day and night as if facing a grave illness.
Now, my officials believe that in ancient times, the *Yú Shū* emphasized strengthening the nine clans,
and that numerous wise men would assist,
and that the Five Emperors made adjustments,
but this principle was not abandoned.
The Zhōu dynasty observed the two previous dynasties,
and concurrently established many Jī,
truly relying on the aid and support of Jìn and Zhèng for their good fortune.
Gāozǔ rose with dragon-like might,
honored the imperial princes and younger brothers,
greatly established nine kingdoms,
and ultimately executed the various Lǚ,
to secure the great imperial lineage.
Now, Cáo abhors the upright and despises the righteous,
indeed having many followers (of evil),
harboring treacherous intentions,
his usurpation is already evident.
Since the imperial clan is weak,
and the imperial relatives hold no positions,
considering ancient precedents,
and acting expediently,
they recommend me, your subject, to be Dà Sīmǎ and Hànzhōng Wáng.
I humbly reflect upon myself,
having received the nation's immense grace,
bearing responsibility for one region,
yet my efforts have not yielded results,
what I have gained is already excessive,
it is inappropriate for me to again disgrace a high position and incur greater blame.
However, my officials pressed me,
urging me with righteousness.
I retreated to consider that the bandits are not yet exterminated,
the national crisis is not over,
the ancestral temples are in peril,
and the altars of soil and grain (the state) are about to fall,
creating for me the burden of worrying and being responsible unto death.
If I am to adapt to circumstances and respond to changes,
to bring peace and stability to the sagely court,
even if it means plunging into fire and water,
I cannot refuse.
How dare I consider what is usually appropriate,
to avoid future regret.
Therefore, I complied with the public consensus,
accepted the seal,
to enhance the nation's prestige.
