Looking up at this noble title,
the position is high and the favor is immense,
looking down, I consider my duty to repay,
my worries are profound and my responsibilities heavy,
I am startled and panting repeatedly,
as if standing on the edge of a chasm.
I shall exert all my strength and sincerity,
encourage the six armies,
unite all righteous forces,
respond to Heaven and follow the times,
strike down the wicked rebels,
to stabilize the state,
and repay a ten thousandth (of the grace).
I respectfully submit this memorial and by messenger return the seals and cords of Zuǒ Jiāngjūn and Yíchéng Tínghóu that I had temporarily held."
Thereupon, he returned to govern in Chéngdū.
He promoted Wèi Yán to Dūdū,
to guard Hànzhōng.
At that time, Guān Yǔ attacked Cáo Gōng's general Cáo Rén,
capturing Yú Jìn at Fán.
Soon after, Sūn Quán ambushed and killed Yǔ,
and seized Jīngzhōu.
In the 25th year,
Wèi Wéndì proclaimed himself emperor,
and changed the era name to Huángchū.
Some heard that the Han Emperor had been harmed,
so the Former Lord held a funeral and wore mourning clothes,
posthumously conferring the title Xiàomǐn Huángdì.
After this, everywhere people reported numerous auspicious omens,
with sun and moon appearing together.

Therefore, Yìláng Yángquán Hóu Liú Bào, Qīngyī Hóu Xiàng Jǔ, Piān Jiāngjūn Zhāng Yì, Huáng Quán, Dà Sīmǎ shǔ Yīn Chún, Yìzhōu Biéjià Cóngshì Zhào Zuò, Zhìzhōng Cóngshì Yáng Hóng, Cóngshì Jìjiǔ Hé Zōng, Yìcáo Cóngshì Dù Qióng, Quànxué Cóngshì Zhāng Shuǎng, Yǐn Mò, Qiáo Zhōu and others submitted a memorial:
"We, your subjects, have heard that the *Hétú* and *Luòshū*,
and the *chèn* and *wěi* commentaries to the Five Classics,
were verified by Kǒngzǐ,
and their predictions have been confirmed from ancient times.
We respectfully note that the *Luòshū Zhēnyàodù* says: 'The red three suns, virtue flourishes,
in the ninth generation, Bèi will meet,
converging to become the Imperial Era.'
The *Luòshū Bǎohàomìng* says: 'Heaven's measure, the Imperial Way, Bèi is called emperor,
holding the covenant of rule,
a hundred successes without failure.'
The *Luòshū Lùyùnqī* says: 'Nine marquises and seven heroes contend for the mandate, the people cook bones,
the roads are strewn with human skulls,
who will be the master, the 'Xuán' is about to arrive.'
The *Xiàojīng Gōumìngjuélù* says: 'The emperor builds three and meets nine Bèi.'
When my late father, Qún, was still alive,
he said there were often yellow mists in the southwest,
standing upright several *zhàng*,
observed for many years,
and from time to time auspicious clouds and propitious winds,
descended from the *xuánjī* to respond to it,
this was an extraordinary omen.
Also, in the 22nd year,
there were often vapors like flags,
moving from west to east,
traveling across the sky,
the *tú* and *shū* say 'an Son of Heaven will certainly emerge from that direction.'
Moreover, in that year, Tàibái, Yínghuò, and Tiánxīng,
constantly chased after Suìxīng.
When Hàn first arose,
the five planets followed Suìxīng in deliberation;
Suìxīng signifies righteousness,
the position of Hàn is in the west,
which is above righteousness,
thus, Hàn law always used Suìxīng to observe the ruler.
A sage ruler should arise in this province,
to bring about a restoration.
At that time, Xǔ Dì was still alive,
so the officials dared not reveal these words.
Recently, Yínghuò again chased Suìxīng,
appearing in Wèi, Mǎo, and Bì constellations;
Mǎo and Bì form the Celestial Net,
the classics say 'where the Emperor Star resides,
all evils perish.'
The sagely omens were foreseen,
and upon calculating the expected verifications,
numerous confirmations appeared,
and this was not the only instance.
We have heard that a sage king precedes Heaven, and Heaven does not oppose him,
follows Heaven and respects the celestial seasons,
therefore, he is born to respond to the juncture,
and unite with the divine covenant.
We wish that Your Great King will respond to Heaven and comply with the people,
and quickly undertake this grand endeavor,
to pacify the land."

Grand Tutor Xǔ Jìng, General Who Pacifies Han Mí Zhú, General of the Military Adviser Zhūgě Liàng, Grand Minister of Ceremonies Lài Gōng, Minister of the Imperial Clan (Huáng Quán) [Huáng Zhù], Minister of the Privy Purse Wáng Móu, and others made a petition saying:
“Cáo Pī usurped and murdered,
extinguishing the Hàn imperial house.
He seized the sacred implements,
coerced loyal and good people,
and acted cruelly and without principle.
Gods and men alike are enraged and resentful,
all thinking of the Liú clan.
Now there is no Son of Heaven above;
the whole realm is in a state of fear and agitation,
with nowhere to look up to or emulate.
More than eight hundred officials from various ranks have successively submitted memorials,
all speaking of auspicious signs and omens,
and the clear verifications in diagrams and prophecies.
Recently, a yellow dragon was seen in the Chìshuǐ River of Wǔyáng,
remaining for nine days before departing.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshén Qì says, ‘When virtue reaches the depths of springs, a yellow dragon appears.’
A dragon
is the symbol of the ruler.
The Yì Jīng, Qián Hexagram, ninth line in the fifth place says, ‘Flying dragon in the sky.’
Your Majesty should ascend like a dragon
and ascend the imperial throne.
Also, previously, when Guān Yǔ besieged Fán and Xiāngyáng,
two men from Xiāngyáng, Zhāng Jiā and Wáng Xiū, presented an imperial seal.
The seal had been submerged in the Hànshǔi River,
hidden in a deep spring,
its brilliant light shining brightly,
its spiritual radiance piercing the sky.
Now, Hàn
is the dynastic title that Gāozǔ originally established to pacify the world.
Your Majesty follows the path of the Former Emperor,
and also rose from Hànzhōng.
Today, the divine light of the Son of Heaven’s imperial seal appeared first;
the seal emerged from Xiāngyáng,
at the lower reaches of the Hànshǔi River,
clearly indicating that Your Majesty is to inherit its downstream,
and that the position of Son of Heaven is bestowed upon Your Majesty.
These auspicious signs and prophecies
are not achievable by human effort.
In ancient times, Zhōu had the auspicious omen of the black fish,
and all said it was a blessing.
When the Two Ancestors received the Mandate,
diagrams and books were already present,
serving as verifications.
Now, Heaven announces auspiciousness,
and numerous scholars and outstanding talents
have brought forth the Hé and Luò writings,
as well as the prophecies and records of Kǒngzǐ,
all complete and arrived.
We humbly consider that Your Majesty descends from Emperor Xiàojǐng through the Prince Jìng of Zhōngshān,
a branch that has continued for a hundred generations.
Heaven and Earth bestow fortune,
Your sacred demeanor is grand and abundant,
divine martial power is embodied in you,
benevolence covers all and accumulates virtue,
you love people and cherish worthy men.
This is why the four quarters return their hearts to you.
Examining the spiritual diagrams
and opening the prophecies and weft texts,
the divine manifestations
and your name are clearly evident.
It is fitting that you immediately ascend the imperial throne,
to succeed the Two Ancestors,
and continue the ancestral line.
The world would be exceedingly fortunate.”
“We, your servants, along with Doctor Xǔ Cí and Gentleman-Consultant Mèng Guāng,
have respectfully established the rituals,
selected an auspicious date,
and are prepared to offer the尊号 (Zūn Hào, august title).”
He was enthroned as emperor south of Wǔdān in Chéngdū.
The proclamation read:
“On the day Pǐngwǔ in the fourth month of the twenty-sixth year of Jiàn’ān,
I, Emperor Bèi, dare to use a dark bull
to respectfully announce to August Heaven, the Supreme Emperor, and the Empress of Earth, the Gods of Earth: The Hàn possessed the realm;
its Mandate was boundless.
Previously, Wáng Mǎng usurped and stole;
Emperor Guāngwǔ, in righteous fury, punished him to death,
and the state was restored.
Now, Cáo Cāo relied on military strength and acted with callous cruelty,
murdering the empress and lord,
his evil reaching to the heavens and extinguishing the realm of Huáxià,
disregarding the manifest will of Heaven.
Cáo’s son, Pī,
carried on his heinous rebellion
and usurped the sacred implements.
All the officials and generals believed that the state had fallen into ruin,
and that I, Bèi, should restore it,
succeeding the Two Ancestors
and reverently carrying out Heaven’s punishment.
I, Bèi, considering my meager virtue,
feared shaming the imperial throne.
Consulting the common people,
and even the chieftains of the barbarians,
they all said, ‘The mandate of Heaven cannot be refused,
the ancestral enterprise cannot be long abandoned,
the four seas cannot be without a ruler.’
The whole land looks up
to me, Bèi, alone.
I, Bèi, fearing the clear mandate of Heaven,
and also fearing that the Hàn throne would perish on earth,
respectfully chose an auspicious day,
and with all the officials ascended the altar
to receive the imperial seal and ribbon.
I performed the burning and burial sacrifices,
making a classified announcement to the gods of Heaven.
May the gods accept the offerings and bestow fortune upon the Hàn house,
forever pacifying the four seas!”
In the summer, fourth month of the first year of Zhāngwǔ,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign title was changed.
Zhūgě Liàng was appointed Chancellor,
and Xǔ Jìng was appointed Minister of Education.
All officials were appointed,
ancestral temples were established,
and joint sacrifices were offered to Emperor Gāo and his descendants.
In the fifth month,
Empress Wú was established,
and his son Chán was made Crown Prince.
In the sixth month,
his son Yǒng was made Prince of Lǔ,
and Lǐ was made Prince of Liáng.
General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhāng Fēi was killed by his subordinates.
Initially,
the Former Lord was enraged by Sūn Quán’s attack on Guān Yǔ,
and was preparing to launch an eastern expedition.
In the autumn, seventh month,
he then led all his armies to attack Wú.
Sūn Quán sent a letter proposing peace,
but the Former Lord, in great anger, refused.
Wú generals Lù Yì, Lǐ Yì, Liú Ā and others were stationed at Wū and Zǐguī;
Generals Wú Bān and Féng Xí attacked and defeated Lǐ Yì and others from Wū.
The army then proceeded to Zǐguī,
and the Five Streams barbarians of Wǔlíng sent envoys to request troops.
In the spring, first month of the second year,
the Former Lord’s army returned to Zǐguī.
Generals Wú Bān and Chén Shì stationed their navy at Yílíng,
on both the east and west banks of the river.
In the second month,
the Former Lord led his generals from Zǐguī to advance,
traversing mountains and cutting across ridges,
stationing his camp at Xiāotíng in Yídào (Xiāo,
pronounced xiāo).
From Hèngshān (Hèng,
pronounced héng)
he opened a path to Wǔlíng,
sending Imperial Attendant Mǎ Liáng to comfort the Five Streams barbarians,
who all rallied and responded.
General Who Guards the North Huáng Quán commanded all the armies north of the river,
and resisted the Wú army along the Yílíng Road.
In the summer, sixth month,
a yellow vapor appeared about ten li from Zǐguī,
several tens of zhàng wide.
About ten days later,
Lù Yì heavily defeated the Former Lord’s army at Xiāotíng.
Generals Féng Xí, Zhāng Nán, and others were all lost.
The Former Lord returned from Xiāotíng to Zǐguī,
gathering the scattered soldiers.
He then abandoned his boats
and returned to Yúfù via a foot path,
renaming Yúfù County to Yǒng’ān.
Wú sent generals Lǐ Yì, Liú Ā and others to pursue the Former Lord’s army,
stationing them at Nánshān.
In the autumn, eighth month,
they withdrew their troops and returned to Wū.
Minister of Education Xǔ Jìng died.
In the winter, tenth month,
an imperial edict ordered Chancellor Liàng to build the northern and southern suburbs in Chéngdū.
Sūn Quán heard that the Former Lord was staying at Báidì,
was very fearful,
and sent an envoy to request peace.
The Former Lord agreed,
and sent Grand Master of Remonstrance Zōng Wěi to respond.
In the winter, twelfth month,
Administrator of Hànjiā Huáng Yuán heard that the Former Lord was gravely ill,
and raised an army to resist.
In the spring, second month of the third year,
Chancellor Liàng arrived at Yǒng’ān from Chéngdū.
In the third month,
Huáng Yuán advanced his troops and attacked Línqióng County.
General Chén Hù (Hù,
pronounced hù) was sent to suppress Yuán.
Yuán’s army was defeated,
and he drifted downriver.
He was bound by his own close soldiers
and delivered alive to Chéngdū,
where he was executed.
The Former Lord’s illness became critical,
and he entrusted his orphan son to Chancellor Liàng,
with Director of the Imperial Secretariat Lǐ Yán as his deputy.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day Guǐsì,
the Former Lord passed away at Yǒng’ān Palace,
at the age of sixty-three.
Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) reported to the Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ) saying:
"I humbly reflect that the late Emperor (Dàháng Huángdì) cultivated benevolence and established virtue,
covering all with boundless grace.
Heaven (Hàotiān) did not bless him,
and he suffered from a lingering illness.
On the twenty-fourth day of this month, he suddenly ascended to the heavens.
Your subjects wailed and cried,
as if losing a parent.
I then examined the imperial will,
which states that matters concern the great ancestral rites (dàzōng),
and any actions should be carefully considered to avoid harm.
All officials should express their grief,
remove their mourning clothes after three days,
and resume ceremonial rites at the time of the funeral.
As for the grand administrators (tàishǒu), chancellors (xiàng), commandants (dūwèi), and magistrates (lìngzhǎng) of the commanderies and states,
they shall remove their mourning clothes after three days.
I, Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮), personally received these imperial instructions and commands,
and I tremble with awe before the divine spirits,
not daring to violate them.
I request that these be proclaimed and implemented."
In the fifth month,
the coffin (zǐgōng) returned from Yǒng'ān (永安) to Chéngdū (成都),
and he was posthumously given the title Emperor Zhāoliè (Zhāoliè Huángdì).
In autumn,
the eighth month,
he was buried at Huìlíng (惠陵).
The appraisal says: The Former Lord (Xiānzhǔ) was resolute and magnanimous,
understanding people and treating scholars well.
He possessed the demeanor of Gāozǔ (高祖),
and the character of a hero.
When he entrusted the entire state to Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮),
his heart and mind were unwavering.
This was indeed the utmost fairness between a ruler and his minister,
and a splendid example throughout history.
In strategy and military capability,
he did not equal Wèi Wǔ (魏武),
which is why his foundation was also limited.
However, he bent without breaking,
and ultimately never submitted to others.
This was perhaps because he knew that their measure would certainly not tolerate him,
and it was not merely to contend for profit,
but also to avoid harm.
Biography of the Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ Chuán) Chapter Three.
The Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ)'s given name was Chán (禪),
and his courtesy name was Gōngsì (公嗣).
He was the son of the Former Lord (Xiānzhǔ).
In the twenty-fourth year of Jiàn'ān (建安) [219 CE],
when the Former Lord (Xiānzhǔ) became King of Hànzhōng (Hànzhōng Wáng),
Chán (禪) was established as the Crown Prince (Wáng Tàizǐ).
When he assumed the imperial title,
the decree stated:
"On the *xīnsì* day of the fifth month in the first year of Zhāngwǔ (Zhāngwǔ) [221 CE],
the Emperor (Huángdì) speaks thus: Crown Prince Chán (Tàizǐ Chán),
I encountered the hardships of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
when treacherous ministers usurped power.
The altars of soil and grain (shèjì) had no master.
Upstanding people and the populace,
by Heaven's clear mandate,
caused me to succeed to the great lineage.
Now I establish Chán (禪) as the Imperial Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ),
to inherit the ancestral temples,
and respectfully govern the altars of soil and grain (shèjì).
I have sent the bearer of the imperial credential, Chancellor (chéngxiàng) Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng), to confer upon him the seal and sash.
Respectfully listen to your tutors.
If you act in one matter, three good results will all be obtained.
How can you not strive for this!"
In the summer, fourth month, of the third year [223 CE],
the Former Lord (Xiānzhǔ) passed away at Yǒng'ān Gōng (永安宮).
In the fifth month,
the Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ) ascended the throne in Chéngdū (成都),
at the age of seventeen.
He honored the Empress (Huánghòu) as the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu).
A general amnesty was declared,
and the reign era was changed.
That year was the fourth year of Huángchū (Huángchū) of Wèi (魏).
In the summer of the first year of Jiànxīng (Jiànxīng) [223 CE],
Zhū Bāo (朱褒), the Grand Administrator (tàishǒu) of Zāngkē (牂牁), rebelled with his commandery.
Before this,
in Yìzhōu Jùn (益州郡), the powerful clan leader Yōng Kǎi (雍闓) had rebelled,
sending Grand Administrator Zhāng Yì (張裔) to Wú (吳),
occupying the commandery and refusing allegiance.
Gāo Dìng (高定), the Yi (Yí) king of Yuèsuì (越嶲), also rebelled.
That year,
the principal Empress (zhǔ huánghòu) was Lady Zhāng (Zhāng Shì).
Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎) Dèng Zhī (鄧芝) was sent to secure good relations with Wú (吳).
Sūn Quán (孫權), the King of Wú (Wú Wáng), sought alliance and peace with Shǔ (蜀) through envoys.
Good relations were established that year.
In the spring of the second year [224 CE],
agriculture was promoted and grain cultivated,
borders were closed, and the people rested.
In the spring, third month, of the third year [225 CE],
Chancellor (chéngxiàng) Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) marched south and pacified the four commanderies;
all four commanderies were pacified.
Yìzhōu Jùn (益州郡) was renamed Jiànníng Jùn (建寧郡).
Jiànníng (建寧) and Yǒngchāng Jùn (永昌郡) were divided to form Yúnnán Jùn (雲南郡).
Jiànníng (建寧) and Zāngkē (牂牁) were also divided to form Xīnggǔ Jùn (興古郡).
In the twelfth month,
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) returned to Chéngdū (成都).
In the spring of the fourth year [226 CE],
Dūhù (都護) Lǐ Yán (李嚴) returned from Yǒng'ān (永安) to reside in Jiāngzhōu (江州),
where he built a large city.
In the spring of the fifth year [227 CE],
Chancellor (chéngxiàng) Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) marched out to garrison Hànzhōng (漢中),
establishing camps at Mǐanběi Yángpíng Shímǎ (沔北陽平石馬).
In the spring of the sixth year [228 CE],
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) marched out to attack Qíshān (祁山),
but was unsuccessful.
In winter,
he again marched out from Sànguān (散關),
besieged Chéncāng (陳倉),
but retreated when his supplies ran out.
Wèi (魏) general Wáng Shuāng (王雙) led his army to pursue Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng).
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) engaged him in battle,
defeated him,
beheaded Wáng Shuāng (王雙),
and returned to Hànzhōng (漢中).
In the spring of the seventh year [229 CE],
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) sent Chén Shì (陳式) to attack Wǔdū (武都) and Yīnpíng (陰平),
and successfully pacified the two commanderies.
In winter,
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) moved his headquarters and camps to the plateau beneath Nánshān (南山),
and built the two cities of Hàn (漢) and Lè (樂).
That year,
Sūn Quán (孫權) declared himself Emperor (Dì),
and made an alliance with Shǔ (蜀),
agreeing to divide the world between them.
In the autumn of the eighth year [230 CE],
Wèi (魏) sent Sīmǎ Yì (司馬懿) via Xīchéng (西城),
Zhāng Hé (張郃) via Zǐwǔ (子午),
and Cáo Zhēn (曹真) via Xié Gǔ (斜谷),
(Xié (斜) is pronounced *yú shē*.)
intending to attack Hànzhōng (漢zhōng).
Chancellor (chéngxiàng) Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) awaited them at Chénggù (城固) and Chìbǎn (赤阪).
Heavy rains cut off the roads,
and Cáo Zhēn (Cáo Zhēn) and the others all returned.
That year,
Wèi Yán (魏延) defeated Guō Huái (郭淮), the Inspector (cìshǐ) of Yōngzhōu (雍州) of Wèi (魏), at Yángxī (陽谿).
King Yǒng (Yǒng Wáng), the King of Lǔ (Lǔ Wáng), was moved to become King of Gānlíng (Gānlíng Wáng).
King Lǐ (Lǐ Wáng), the King of Liáng (Liáng Wáng), was moved to become King of Ānpíng (Ānpíng Wáng).
This was because Lǔ (魯) and Liáng (梁) were within Wú (吳)'s sphere of influence.
In the spring, second month, of the ninth year [231 CE],
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) again led his army to besiege Qíshān (祁山),
and for the first time used wooden oxen (mùniú) for transport.
Sīmǎ Yì (司馬懿) and Zhāng Hé (張郃) of Wèi (魏) came to the aid of Qíshān (祁shān).
In the summer, sixth month,
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng)'s supplies ran out, and he withdrew his army.
Zhāng Hé (張郃) pursued him to Qīngfēng (青封),
engaged Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) in battle,
and was struck by an arrow and died.
In the autumn, eighth month,
Dūhù (都護) Lǐ Píng (李平) was deposed and exiled to Zǐtóng Jùn (梓潼郡).
In the tenth year [232 CE],
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) rested his troops and encouraged agriculture at Huángshā (黃沙),
completed the construction of the 'flowing horse' (liúmǎ) and 'wooden ox' (mùniú),
and trained his soldiers in martial arts.
In the winter of the eleventh year [233 CE],
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) ordered all armies to transport rice,
collecting it at Xié Gǔ Kǒu (斜谷口),
and built supply depots in Xié Gǔ (斜谷).
That year,
Liú Zhòu (劉冑) of the Southern Yi (nán Yí) rebelled.
General Mǎ Zhōng (馬忠) defeated and pacified him.
In the spring, second month, of the twelfth year [234 CE],
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) marched out via Xié Gǔ (斜谷),
using the 'flowing horse' (liúmǎ) for transport for the first time.
In the autumn, eighth month,
Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) died by the Wèi (渭) River.
Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn (征西大將軍) Wèi Yán (魏延) and Chancellor (chéngxiàng)'s Chief Clerk (chángshǐ) Yáng Yí (楊儀) contended for power and were at odds.
They raised troops against each other.
Wèi Yán (魏延) was defeated and fled.
Wèi Yán (魏延)'s head was cut off,
and Yáng Yí (楊儀) led all armies back to Chéngdū (成都).
A general amnesty was declared.
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍) Wú Yī (吳壹) was made Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍),
provisionally holding the *jié* (節) and overseeing Hànzhōng (漢zhōng).
Jiǎng Wǎn (蔣琬), the Chief Clerk (chángshǐ) of the Chancellor (chéngxiàng)'s Residence, was made Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令),
taking overall charge of state affairs.
In the spring, first month, of the thirteenth year [235 CE],
Zhōngjūnshī (中軍師) Yáng Yí (楊儀) was deposed and exiled to Hànjiā Jùn (漢嘉郡).
In the summer, fourth month,
Jiǎng Wǎn (蔣琬) was promoted to the position of Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍).
In the summer, fourth month, of the fourteenth year [236 CE],
the Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ) arrived at Jiān (湔),
ascended Guānbǎn (觀阪),
and observed the flow of the Wènshuǐ (汶水).
After ten days, he returned to Chéngdū (成都).
Fú Jiàn (苻健), the Di (Dī) King of Wǔdū (武都), and over four hundred Di (Dī) households were moved to Guǎngdū (廣都).
In the summer, sixth month, of the fifteenth year [237 CE],
Empress (huánghòu) Lady Zhāng (Zhāng Shì) passed away.
In the spring, first month, of the first year of Yánxī (Yánxī) [238 CE],
Empress (huánghòu) Lady Zhāng (Zhāng Shì) was enthroned.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the reign era was changed.
His son Xuán (璿) was made Crown Prince (tàizǐ),
and his son Yáo (瑤) was made King of Āndìng (Āndìng Wáng).
In the winter, eleventh month,
Dàjiāngjūn (大將jūn) Jiǎng Wǎn (蔣琬) moved to garrison Hànzhōng (漢zhōng).
In the second year, in the third month of spring,
Jiǎng Wǎn’s position was advanced to Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ).
In the third year, in spring,
Yuexī Administrator (Tàishǒu) Zhāng Ní was sent to pacify Yuexī Commandery (Yuèxī Jùn).
In the fourth year, in the tenth month of winter,
Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng) Fèi Yī arrived in Hànzhōng,
and consulted with Jiǎng Wǎn on state affairs and strategies.
He returned at the end of the year.
In the fifth year, in the first month of spring,
Superintendent of the Army (Jiānjūn) Jiāng Wéi led a detached force,
returning from Hànzhōng to garrison Fú County (Fú Xiàn).
In the sixth year, in the tenth month of winter,
Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) Jiǎng Wǎn returned from Hànzhōng,
and resided in Fú.
In the eleventh month,
a general amnesty was issued.
Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng) Fèi Yī was appointed General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn).
In the seventh year, in the intercalary month,
Wèi General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Cáo Shuǎng, Xiàhóu Xuán and others advanced towards Hànzhōng.
General Who Guards the North (Zhèn Běi Dà Jiāngjūn) Wáng Píng resisted at Xīngshì Encampment.
General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Fèi Yī led various armies to go to their relief,
and the Wèi army retreated.
In the summer, in the fourth month,
Ánpíng Prince Lǐ passed away.
In the autumn, in the ninth month,
Fèi Yī returned to Chéngdū.
In the eighth year, in the eighth month of autumn,
the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) passed away.
In the twelfth month,
General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Fèi Yī arrived in Hànzhōng,
and supervised the perimeter defenses.
In the ninth year, in the sixth month of summer,
Fèi Yī returned to Chéngdū.
In autumn,
a general amnesty was issued.
In the winter, in the eleventh month,
Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) Jiǎng Wǎn passed away.
In the tenth year,
the Hú kings of Liáng Province (Liángzhōu), Báihǔ Wén and Zhìwúdài, led their people to surrender.
General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn) Jiāng Wéi welcomed and appeased them,
settling them in Fán County (Fán Xiàn).
In this year,
the Píngkāng Yí of Wènshān rebelled.
Jiāng Wéi went to suppress them,
defeating and pacifying them.
In the eleventh year, in the fifth month of summer,
General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Fèi Yī went out to garrison Hànzhōng.
In autumn,
the common people and Yí of Fúlíng Commandery (Fúlíng Jùn) rebelled.
General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn) Dèng Zhī went to suppress them,
and defeated and pacified them all.
In the twelfth year, in the first month of spring,
Wèi executed General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Cáo Shuǎng and others,
and General of the Right (Yòu Jiāngjūn) Xiàhóu Bà came to surrender.
In the summer, in the fourth month,
a general amnesty was issued.
In autumn,
General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn) Jiāng Wéi went out to attack Yōng Province (Yōngzhōu),
but did not succeed and returned.
Generals Jù Ān and Lǐ Sháo surrendered to Wèi.
In the thirteenth year,
Jiāng Wéi again went out to Xīpíng,
but did not succeed and returned.
In the fourteenth year, in summer,
General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Fèi Yī returned to Chéngdū.
In winter,
he again stationed north at Hànshòu.
A general amnesty was issued.
In the fifteenth year,
King Sūn Quán of Wú passed away.
His son Cóng was established as King of Xīhé (Xīhé Wáng).
In the sixteenth year, in the first month of spring,
General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Fèi Yī was killed in Hànshòu by the Wèi defector Guō Xún.
In the summer, in the fourth month,
General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn) Jiāng Wéi again led his troops to besiege Nán'ān,
but did not succeed and returned.
In the seventeenth year, in the first month of spring,
Jiāng Wéi returned to Chéngdū.
A general amnesty was issued.
In the summer, in the sixth month,
Jiāng Wéi again led his troops out to Lǒngxī.
In winter,
he evacuated the people from the three counties of Dí Dào, Héguān, and Líntáo,
settling them in Miánzhú and Fán County (Fán Xiàn).
In the eighteenth year, in spring,
Jiāng Wéi returned to Chéngdū.
In summer,
he again led various armies out to Dí Dào,
and fought with Wèi Yōng Province (Yōngzhōu) Inspector (Cìshǐ) Wáng Jīng at Táoxī,
greatly defeating him.
Wáng Jīng retreated to defend Dí Dào city,
and Jiāng Wéi withdrew and resided at Zhōngtí.
In the nineteenth year, in spring,
Jiāng Wéi's position was advanced to General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn),
supervising the military.
He arranged to meet General Who Guards the West (Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn) Hú Jì at Shàngguī,
but Hú Jì broke his promise and did not arrive.
In the autumn, in the eighth month,
Jiāng Wéi was defeated at Shàngguī by Wèi General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Dèng Ài.
Jiāng Wéi withdrew his army and returned to Chéngdū.
In this year,
his son Zàn was established as King of Xīnpíng (Xīnpíng Wáng).
A general amnesty was issued.
In the twentieth year,
upon hearing that Wèi General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Zhūgě Dàn had rebelled at Shòuchūn,
Jiāng Wéi again led his troops out through Luò Valley (Luò Gǔ),
reaching Máng River (Máng Shuǐ).
In this year, a general amnesty was issued.
In the first year of Jǐngyào,
Jiāng Wéi returned to Chéngdū.
Historians reported that a auspicious star (jǐng xīng) was seen,
whereupon a general amnesty was issued,
and the era name was changed.
The eunuch Huáng Hào began to wield sole power.
Wú General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Sūn Chén deposed their lord Liàng,
and established Liángyá Prince Xiū.
In the second year, in the sixth month of summer,
his son Chén was established as King of Běidì (Běidì Wáng),
Xún as King of Xīnxīng (Xīnxīng Wáng),
and Qián as King of Shàngdǎng (Shàngdǎng Wáng).
In the third year, in the ninth month of autumn,
the late Generals Guān Yǔ, Zhāng Fēi, Mǎ Chāo, Páng Tǒng, and Huáng Zhōng were posthumously enfeoffed.
In the fourth year, in the third month of spring,
the late General Zhào Yún was posthumously enfeoffed.
In the winter, in the tenth month,
a general amnesty was issued.
In the fifth year, in the first month of spring,
King of Xīhé (Xīhé Wáng) Cóng passed away.
In this year,
Jiāng Wéi again led his troops out to Hóuhé,
was defeated by Dèng Ài,
and returned to reside at Tàzhōng.
In the sixth year, summer,
**Wèi** greatly mobilized its forces,
ordering the **Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn** **Dèng Ài**, **Zhènxī Jiāngjūn** **Zhōng Huì**, and **Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ** **Zhūgě Xù** to attack simultaneously along several routes.
Thereupon, [**Shǔ**] dispatched the **Zuǒyòu Chējì Jiāngjūn** **Zhāng Yì**, **Liáo Huà**, and **Fǔguó Dà Jiāngjūn** **Dǒng Jué**, among others, to resist them.
A general amnesty was declared.
The era name was changed to **Yánxīng**.
In winter,
**Dèng Ài** defeated **Wèi Jiāngjūn** **Zhūgě Zhān** at **Miánzhú**.
Following the counsel of **Guānglù Dàfū** **Qiáo Zhōu**,
[the Latter Lord] surrendered to **Ài**,
and presented a letter, saying:
“Bounded by the **Jiāng** and the **Hàn**,
our separation has been profound and long.
Taking advantage of the land of **Shǔ**,
[we] have defiantly occupied a corner.
Interfering with the course of destiny, we have recklessly presumed,
and gradually, over many years,
have been separated from the imperial capital by ten thousand *lǐ*.
I recall that during the **Huángchū** period,
Emperor **Wén** ordered **Hǔyá Jiāngjūn** **Xiānyú Fǔ**,
to proclaim a gentle and secret edict,
extending the grace of 'three excellences,'
opening a path,
with great righteousness shining forth.
But my meager virtue and dim weakness,
secretly clung to the remnant legacy.
Bowing and rising for many years,
[I] have not followed the great instruction.
Now that heavenly might has shaken [us],
people and spirits alike reckon [with its] power.
Terrified by the royal army,
where divine might arrives,
how dare [we] not change our ways,
and submit to the command!
I have already ordered the various commanders to cast down their spears and remove their armor.
Public offices and stores shall be left utterly intact.
The common people are spread across the fields,
surplus grain rests in the fields,
awaiting the kindness of those who come later,
to preserve the lives of the multitude.
I humbly consider that Great **Wèi** spreads virtue and enacts transformation.
Its chief ministers are like **Yī** and **Zhōu**,
enveloping and concealing flaws.
I respectfully send my privately appointed **Shìzhōng** **Zhāng Shào**, **Guānglù Dàfū** **Qiáo Zhōu**, and **Fùmǎ Dūwèi** **Dèng Liáng**, to present the seals and tallies,
to request commands and declare sincerity,
respectfully conveying our loyalty.
Regarding our survival or destruction, or any imperial grant,
it is solely for [Your Majesty] to decide.
My coffin is near [me],
I will not elaborate further."
On that day,
**Běidì Wáng Chén**, grieving the fall of the state,
first killed his wife and children,
then committed suicide.
**Shào** and **Liáng** met **Ài** in **Luòxiàn**.
When **Ài** received the letter,
he was greatly pleased.
He immediately sent a reply letter,
and dispatched **Shào** and **Liáng** to return first.
When **Ài** arrived north of the city,
the **Hòuzhǔ**, carrying a coffin and binding himself,
went to the gate of the army camp.
**Ài** untied his bonds and burned the coffin,
and invited him to meet.
Thereupon, acting on imperial authority, he appointed the **Hòuzhǔ** as **Piàojì Jiāngjūn**.
All those defending garrisons received the **Hòuzhǔ**'s command,
and then surrendered.
**Ài** had the **Hòuzhǔ** reside in his former palace,
and personally went to visit him.
Before the imperial convoy could depart,
in the first month of spring of the following year,
**Ài** was arrested.
**Zhōng Huì**, coming from **Fú**, instigated a rebellion in **Chéngdū**.
After **Huì** died,
the troops in **Shǔ** plundered,
with numerous deaths and casualties scattered about.
It was several days before order was restored.
The **Hòuzhǔ** moved his entire family eastward.
Upon arriving in **Luòyáng**,
an imperial edict was issued, stating:
“On the *dīnghài* day of the third month of the fifth year of **Jǐngyuán**.
The Emperor, presiding from the carriage-portico,
ordered the **Tàicháng** to formally appoint **Liú Chán** as **Ānlè Xiàngōng**.
Alas!
Advance and heed Our command!
Indeed, to govern the heavens and sustain all things,
harmony and peace are paramount.
To brightly inhabit the world,
timely accord is most splendid.
Therefore, that which nurtures all living beings,
is the way of a ruler of men.
And that which complies with Heaven,
is the meaning of *kūnyuán*.
When high and low intermingle smoothly,
then all things achieve harmony,
and all beings prosper.
In times past, the **Hàn** clan lost its control,
and the six directions were shaken and disturbed.
Our **Tàizǔ**, receiving Heaven's mandate, rose like a dragon,
and spread aid to the eight extremities [of the world].
Thus, in response to Heaven and in accord with the people,
[He] pacified and possessed all of **Qūxià**.
At that time, [your] late father, due to the fierce contention of many heroes,
and the unrest within the nine zones [of the realm],
seized an opportunity to occupy a distant, difficult-to-reach area,
securing and holding **Yōng** and **Shǔ**.
Thus making the western corner a separate domain,
blocked and isolated from beyond its borders.
Since then,
weapons of war have not been sheathed.
The common people,
could not live out their lives in peace,
for almost five *jì*.
We forever ponder the last wishes of Our ancestors,
and desire to pacify and unite the Four Seas,
making all lands under Heaven follow the same track.
Therefore, We mobilized the six armies,
displaying Our might in **Liáng** and **Yì**.
You, Duke, grandly cultivated your virtue and disposition,
deeply held great righteousness.
Did not shrink from humbling yourself and surrendering your person,
esteeming the love of the people and the preservation of the state as paramount.
Lowering your heart and changing your thoughts,
swiftly transforming in response to the moment,
acting on your words and thinking of submission.
So as to enjoy boundless blessings from both sides.
Is this not far-reaching!
We are pleased that you, Duke, shall long enjoy distinguished emoluments.
By examining previous precedents,
[We] establish a state and grant territory,
following the old statutes.
Bestowing these dark oxen,
bundled with white *máo* grass,
to forever be a vassal and supporter of **Wèi**.
Go, and be respectful!
You, Duke, shall reverently obey Our command,
and be able to broaden your virtuous heart,
to complete your illustrious achievements."
He was granted a fief of ten thousand households,
bestowed ten thousand bolts of silk,
a hundred servants,
and other items commensurate with this.
More than fifty of his descendants became **Dūwèi** or were enfeoffed as **Lièhóu**.
The **Shàngshū Lìng** **Fán Jiàn**, **Shìzhōng** **Zhāng Shào**, **Guānglù Dàfū** **Qiáo Zhōu**, **Mìshū Lìng** **Xì Zhèng**, and **Diànzhōng Dū** **Zhāng Tōng**, were all enfeoffed as **Lièhóu**.
The Duke died in **Luòyáng** in the seventh year of **Tàishǐ**.
Commentary says: When the **Hòuzhǔ** employed worthy ministers, he was a ruler who followed principles.
When he was misled by eunuchs, he became a benighted and weak ruler.
The *Zhuàn* says:
“Plain silk has no constancy;
it is only what it is dyed.”
This is truly credible!
According to rites,
when a ruler succeeds to the throne,
the era name is changed after a year has passed.
But in the third year of **Zhāngwǔ**,
it was changed to **Jiànxīng**.
Examining ancient principles,
the underlying principle was violated.
Moreover, the state did not establish official historians,
and there were no officials for keeping records.
Thus, many events were omitted,
and calamities and anomalies were not recorded.
Although **Zhūgě Liàng** excelled in governance,
things like these
were still not fully addressed.
However, for twelve periods, the era name was not changed,
and though military campaigns were frequently launched, amnesties were not idly granted.
Was this not admirable!
After **Liàng**'s death,
these systems gradually deteriorated.
The superiority and inferiority are evident.
Biography of the Two Consorts and Children, Chapter Four
First Emperor Xiānzhǔ’s Gān Hòuhòu (Empress Gān)
was from Pèi.
When Xiānzhǔ was in Yùzhōu
and residing in Xiǎopèi,
he took her as a concubine.
Xiānzhǔ repeatedly lost his principal wives,
so she often managed internal affairs.
She followed Xiānzhǔ to Jīngzhōu
and gave birth to the Later Emperor.
When Cáo Gōng’s army arrived
and pursued Xiānzhǔ at Dāngyáng Chángbǎn,
he was in dire straits at that time,
and abandoned the Empress and the Later Emperor.
Thanks to Zhào Yún’s protection,
they escaped the calamity.
The Empress died
and was buried in Nánjùn.
In the second year of Zhāngwǔ,
she was posthumously honored as Huángsī Fūrén (Lady Huángsī),
and her burial was moved to Shǔ.
Before she arrived, Xiānzhǔ passed away.
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng submitted a memorial, stating:
“Huángsī Fūrén’s conduct was refined and benevolent,
and she was modest and careful in her person.
When the Great Deceased Emperor was formerly an Upper General,
the嫔妃 (pínfēi) formed a union,
and nurtured the Sagely Body.
The great mandate was not yet fulfilled.
During the Great Deceased Emperor’s lifetime,
he showed profound righteousness and bestowed grace.
He thought of Huángsī Fūrén’s spirit coffin, which was far away and adrift,
and specially sent an envoy to welcome it.
The Great Deceased Emperor then died.
Now Huángsī Fūrén’s spirit coffin has arrived,
and the Emperor’s coffin is also on its way.
The imperial mausoleum will soon be completed,
and the reburial date is set.
Your servant, along with Grand Minister of Ceremonies Lài Gōng and others, discussed this. The Lǐjì (Book of Rites) says: ‘Establishing love begins with one’s parents,
teaching the people filial piety;
establishing respect begins with one’s elders,
teaching the people obedience.’
Not forgetting one’s parents
is the origin.
According to the principles of the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals),
a mother is honored through her son.
In the past, Emperor Gāozǔ posthumously honored Tàishàng Zhāolíng Fūrén as Zhāolíng Hòuhòu (Empress Zhāolíng).
Emperor Xiàohé reburied his mother, Liáng Guìrén (Noble Lady Liáng),
and conferred the honored title of Gōnghuái Hòuhòu (Empress Gōnghuái).
Emperor Xiàomǐn also reburied his mother, Wáng Fūrén (Lady Wáng),
and conferred the honored title of Línghuái Hòuhòu (Empress Línghuái).
Now Huángsī Fūrén should have an honored title
to comfort the yearning for the departed.
Your servant, along with Lài Gōng and others, consulted the regulations for posthumous titles,
and it is fitting to call her Zhāoliè Hòuhòu (Empress Zhāoliè).
The Shījīng (Classic of Poetry) says: ‘Though alive in different rooms,
in death they share the same tomb.’
Therefore, Zhāoliè Hòuhòu should be buried together with the Great Deceased Emperor.
Your servant requests that the Grand Commandant inform the ancestral temple,
make it known throughout the realm,
and submit a separate report on the complete rites and ceremonies.”
An imperial edict approved it.
First Emperor Xiānzhǔ’s Mù Hòuhòu (Empress Mù)
was from Chénliú.
Her elder brother, Wú Yī,
was orphaned young.
Wú Yī’s father had an old acquaintance with Liú Yān,
so the whole family followed Liú Yān into Shǔ.
Liú Yān had other ambitions
and heard that a good physiognomist predicted the Empress would become greatly honored.
Liú Yān, who then had his son Mào with him,
arranged for Mào to marry the Empress.
After Mào died,
the Empress became a widow.
After Xiānzhǔ pacified Yìzhōu,
and Sūn Fūrén (Lady Sūn) returned to Wú,
his subordinates advised Xiānzhǔ to marry the Empress.
Xiānzhǔ hesitated because she was of the same clan as Mào.
Fǎ Zhèng (法正) stepped forward and said:
“In terms of closeness or distance,
how does this compare to Jìn Wén’s (Duke Wén of Jìn) relationship with Zǐyǔ?”
Thus, he married the Empress and made her a Fūrén (Lady).
In the twenty-fourth year of Jiàn'ān,
she was established as the Queen of Hànzhōng.
In the fifth month of summer in the first year of Zhāngwǔ,
the imperial edict stated:
“I receive the mandate of Heaven,
serve the Supreme Being,
and rule over all nations.
Now I establish this Lady as Empress.
I send an envoy, the Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng, holding the imperial credential, to bestow the imperial seal and ribbon,
to preside over the ancestral temple,
and to be the mother of the realm.
Empress, respect this!”
In the fifth month of the first year of Jiànxīng,
the Later Emperor ascended the throne
and honored the Empress as Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager),
residing in Chánglè Gōng (Chánglè Palace).
Wú Yī (her brother) reached the rank of Chēqí Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry)
and was enfeoffed as a county marquis.
In the eighth year of Yánxī,
the Empress passed away
and was buried together in Huìlíng (Huì Mausoleum).
Later Emperor’s Jìng'āi Hòuhòu (Empress Jìng'āi)
was the eldest daughter of Chēqí Jiāngjūn Zhāng Fēi.
In the first year of Zhāngwǔ,
she was taken as the Crown Prince’s consort.
In the first year of Jiànxīng,
she was established as Empress.
She passed away in the fifteenth year
and was buried in Nánlíng.
Later Emperor’s Zhāng Hòuhòu (Empress Zhāng)
was the younger sister of the former Empress Jìng'āi.
In the fifteenth year of Jiànxīng,
she entered the palace as a Guìrén (Noble Lady).
In the first month of spring in the first year of Yánxī,
the imperial edict stated:
“I inherit the great enterprise,
rule over all under Heaven,
and preside over the suburban altars, ancestral temples, and altars of soil and grain.
Now I establish this Guìrén (Noble Lady) as Empress.
I dispatch Xiàng Lǎng (向朗), Acting Chancellor and Left General, holding the imperial credential, to bestow the imperial seal and ribbon.
Diligently manage the inner household,
solemnly and respectfully perform the sacrifices.
Empress, respect this!”
In the first year of Xiánxī,
she followed the Later Emperor in his relocation to Luòyáng.
Liú Yǒng, courtesy name Gōngshòu,
was Xiānzhǔ’s son
and the Later Emperor’s half-brother.
In the sixth month of the first year of Zhāngwǔ,
the Grand Minister of Works, Jìng (靖), was sent to establish Liú Yǒng as the King of Lǔ.
The imperial edict stated:
“My young son Yǒng,
receives this green earth.
I follow the heavenly order,
succeed to the great enterprise,
and diligently follow ancient precedents.
I establish your state,
enfeoff you in the eastern land,
possessing Guīméng,
to be a bulwark for generations.
Alas!
Obey my edict!
That state of Lǔ,
once transformed, will follow the Dao,
and its customs and reforms will endure.
People will love virtue,
and this splendid beauty will be passed down through generations.
May the King hold to his heart, follow the rites,
and bring peace to your officers and people.
May this be enjoyed and proper.
Be warned!”
In the eighth year of Jiànxīng,
he was re-enfeoffed as the King of Gānlíng.
Originally,
Liú Yǒng hated the eunuch Huáng Hào.
After Huáng Hào gained trust and influence,
he slandered Liú Yǒng to the Later Emperor.
The Later Emperor gradually estranged Liú Yǒng,
to the point that he was not permitted to attend court for over ten years.
In the first year of Xiánxī,
Liú Yǒng moved eastward to Luòyáng,
was appointed Fèngchē Dūwèi (Colonel of the Imperial Carriages),
and enfeoffed as a xiāng hóu (Marquis of a Township).
Liú Lǐ, courtesy name Fèngxiào,
was also the Lattered Lord’s illegitimate younger brother,
born of a different mother than Yǒng.
In the sixth month of the first year of Zhāngwǔ,
the Grand Minister Sìtú Jìng was dispatched to install Lǐ as the Prince of Liáng.
The imperial edict read:
“My young son Lǐ,
I have succeeded to the Hàn lineage,
reverently obeying the mandate of Heaven,
following and cultivating the traditional order.
I establish you in the east,
to be a bulwark for Hàn.
That land of Liáng,
a region within the imperial domain,
whose people are accustomed to civilizing influences,
is easily guided by ritual.
Go forth and devote your heart
to cherishing and protecting the common people,
thereby perpetuating your state.
O King, treat this with reverence!”
In the eighth year of Jiànxīng,
Lǐ was re-enfeoffed as the Prince of Ānpíng.
He died in the seventh year of Yánxī,
and was posthumously named Prince Dào.
His son, Prince Āi Yìn, succeeded him,
and died in the nineteenth year.
His son, Prince Shāng Chéng, succeeded him,
and died in the twentieth year.
An imperial edict in the fourth year of Jǐngyào stated:
“The Prince of Ānpíng
was appointed by the Former Emperor.
Three generations died young,
and the succession to the state is broken.
I am deeply saddened by this.
Let Jí, the Marquis of Wǔyì, succeed to the princely title.”
Jí
was Lǐ’s son.
In the first year of Xiánxī,
he moved east to Luòyáng,
was appointed Fèngchē Dūwèi,
and enfeoffed as a Xiang Hóu.
The Latter Lord’s crown prince, Xuán,
courtesy name Wénhéng,
his mother was Consort Wáng,
originally a handmaiden of Empress Jìng'āi Zhāng.
In the first month of the first year of Yánxī, an edict stated:
“In ancient times, emperors and kings,
in succeeding to the throne and establishing an heir,
to be a secondary ruler of the national lineage,
this has been the constant way from antiquity to the present.
Now, Xuán is made the Crown Prince,
to manifest the awe of the ancestors.
I command the acting Chancellor and General of the Left, Lǎng, to take the insignia and seal and bestow them.
Strive to cultivate noble qualities,
reverently and diligently adhere to the Dao and righteousness,
consult the classics and rituals,
respect and befriend your teachers,
weigh and adopt all good counsel,
to assist in perfecting your virtue.
How can you not exert yourself in cultivation and encourage yourself?”
He was fifteen years old at the time.
In the winter of the sixth year of Jǐngyào,
Shǔ fell.
In the first month of the first year of Xiánxī,
Zhōng Huì rebelled in Chéngdū,
and Xuán was killed by the rebel soldiers.
The commentary states: The Yì Jīng says, “When there are husband and wife, then there are father and son.”
Indeed, among human relationships,
the flourishing of kindness and order,
none surpasses this.
Therefore, this record is made
to fully detail the structure of a state.
Biography of Zhūgě Liàng, Fifth
Zhūgě Liàng, courtesy name Kǒngmíng,
was a native of Yángdū, Lángyá.
He was a descendant of Zhūgě Fēng, the Grandee Secretary Sìlì Xiàowèi of Hàn.
His father, Guī,
courtesy name Jūngòng,
was a Táishān Commandery Assistant in the late Hàn period.
Liàng was orphaned early.
His uncle, Xuán, was appointed Governor of Yùzhāng by Yuán Shù.
Xuán took Liàng and Liàng’s younger brother Jūn to his post.
It happened that the Hàn court later selected Zhū Hào to replace Xuán.
Xuán had long-standing ties with Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and went to rely on him.
After Xuán’s death,
Liàng personally tilled the fields,
and enjoyed reciting “Liángfǔ Yín”.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
and often compared himself to Guǎn Zhòng and Yuè Yì.
No one at the time agreed with him,
except for Cuī Zhōupíng of Bólíng and Xú Shù Yuánzhí of Yǐngchuān, who were good friends with Liàng
and believed it to be truly so.
At that time, the Former Lord was stationed at Xīnyě.
Xú Shù met the Former Lord,
and the Former Lord valued him.
He said to the Former Lord:
“Zhūgě Kǒngmíng
is a Sleeping Dragon.
Does the General wish to see him?”
The Former Lord said:
“You may bring him along.”
Shù replied:
“This man must be visited;
he cannot be summoned.
The General should condescend to visit him.”
Thereupon, the Former Lord went to see Liàng,
making three visits in all
before finally meeting him.
He then dismissed his attendants and said:
“The Hàn house has declined,
treacherous ministers have usurped authority,
and the sovereign is in distress.
I, not judging my virtue or weighing my strength,
wished to uphold great righteousness in the world,
but my wisdom and tactics are shallow and inadequate,
and thus I acted recklessly,
reaching this point today.
However, my ambition is not yet extinguished.
What strategy do you think should be adopted?”
Liàng replied:
“Since Dǒng Zhuó’s time,
heroes have risen everywhere,
those who span across provinces and link commanderies are innumerable.
When Cáol Cāo is compared to Yuán Shào,
his reputation was obscure and his forces few,
yet Cāo was able to defeat Shào,
turning weakness into strength.
This was not only due to opportune timing,
but also human strategy.
Now Cāo already commands a million troops,
holding the Son of Heaven hostage to command the feudal lords.
This is truly not to be contended with.
Sūn Quán holds Jiāngdōng,
which he has occupied for three generations.
His state is strategically formidable and his people are loyal,
and worthy and capable men are employed by him.
This can be an ally but not an object of conquest.
Jīngzhōu is located north of the Hàn and Miǎn rivers,
its prosperity extends south to the Nánhǎi,
it connects east to Wú and Kuàijī,
and communicates west to Bā and Shǔ.
This is a land for military action,
yet its ruler cannot defend it.
This is perhaps what Heaven provides to the General;
does the General have any interest in it?
Yìzhōu is rugged and secluded,
with a fertile plain stretching a thousand *lǐ*,
a land of heavenly abundance.
Gāozǔ relied on it to establish his imperial enterprise.
Liú Zhāng is dim-witted and weak,
Zhāng Lǔ is to the north.
The people are prosperous and the state is rich, yet he does not know how to cherish and care for them.
Men of wisdom and ability long for an enlightened ruler.
Since the General is a scion of the imperial house,
whose trustworthiness and righteousness are known throughout the four seas,
who gathers heroes and
longs for the wise as if parched,
if you could occupy Jīng and Yì,
secure their strategic defenses,
form alliances with the various Róng in the west,
pacify the Yí and Yuè in the south,
forge good relations with Sūn Quán externally,
and cultivate good governance internally;
then, should there be a change in the world,
you could command a grand general to lead the Jīngzhōu army towards Wǎn and Luò,
while the General personally leads the Yìzhōu forces out into the Qínchuan.
Which of the common people would not come with baskets of food and pots of drink to welcome the General?
If this truly comes to pass,
then the hegemon’s enterprise can be achieved,
and the Hàn house can be restored.”
The Former Lord said:
“Excellent!”
From then on, his relationship with Liàng grew increasingly close.
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi were displeased,
but the Former Lord explained to them:
“My having Kǒngmíng
is like a fish having water.
I beg all of you not to speak of it again.”
Yǔ and Fēi then desisted.
Liú Biǎo’s eldest son, Qí,
also had deep sagacity and brilliance.
Biǎo, swayed by his second wife’s words,
loved his younger son, Cóng,
and was displeased with Qí.
Qí often wanted to consult with Liàng about a method for his own security,
but Liàng always refused and blocked him,
not planning anything with him.
So Qí took Liàng to tour the back garden,
and together they ascended a tall building.
During their drinking and feasting,
he ordered someone to remove the ladder,
then said to Liàng:
“Today, above, we do not reach heaven;
below, we do not reach earth.
Words come out of your mouth,
and enter my ears.
Can we speak now?”
Liàng replied:
“Have you not seen Shēn Shēng was endangered while within the state,
whereas Chóng Ěr was safe while outside?”
Qí's mind was enlightened and moved,
and he secretly devised a plan to go out.
It so happened that Huáng Zǔ died,
and he was able to leave,
thus becoming the Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià.
Soon after, Biǎo passed away.
Cóng, hearing that Cáo Gōng was coming to conquer,
sent an envoy to surrender.
The Former Lord, in Fán, heard of this,
and led his troops southward.
Liàng and Xú Shù followed him,
but were pursued and defeated by Cáo Gōng,
who captured Xú Shù’s mother.
Xú Shù bid farewell to the Former Lord and pointed to his heart, saying:
“Originally, I wanted to conspire with the General to achieve a royal and hegemonic enterprise,
with this small plot of land (my heart).
Now I have lost my old mother,
my heart is in turmoil,
and I am of no benefit to the cause.
I beg to part ways here.”
He then went to Cáo Gōng.
When the Former Lord arrived at Xiàkǒu,
Liàng said:
“The situation is urgent.
Please permit me to seek aid from General Sūn.”
At that time, Quán had his army in Cháisāng,
observing the outcome of events.
Liàng persuaded Quán, saying:
“There is great chaos within the seas.
The General raised an army and occupies Jiāngdōng,
and Liú Yùzhōu also gathered his forces south of the Hàn River,
contending with Cáo Cāo for the world.
Now Cāo has swept away great difficulties
and has largely pacified the realm.
He then defeated Jīngzhōu,
and his might shakes the four seas.
Heroes have nowhere to display their prowess,
which is why Yùzhōu fled here.
General, weigh your strength and decide: if you can, with the forces of Wú and Yuè, contend against the Central Plains,
it would be better to break ties with him early.
If you cannot withstand him,
why not put aside your weapons and armor,
and turn north to serve him!
Now, General, you outwardly claim submission,
but inwardly harbor hesitant plans.
If you do not decide in this urgent situation,
disaster will arrive in no time!”
Quán said:
“If it is as you say,
why does Liú Yùzhōu not simply serve him?”
Liàng said:
“Tián Héng was merely
a brave man of Qí,
yet he upheld righteousness and would not be disgraced.
How much more so Liú Yùzhōu, a descendant of the royal house,
whose heroic talent surpasses the age,
and whom all gentlemen admire and look up to,
like water returning to the sea.
If the enterprise is not successful,
this is fate,
how can he again submit to another!”
Quán indignantly said:
“I cannot, with the entirety of the Wú territory
and an army of 100,000,
be controlled by others.
My decision is made!
No one but Liú Yùzhōu can withstand Cáo Cāo.
However, Yùzhōu has just suffered a defeat;
how can he resist this difficulty?”
Liàng said:
“Although Yùzhōu’s army was defeated at Chángbǎn,
the returning warriors and Guān Yǔ’s elite naval forces now number 10,000,
and Liú Qí’s combined Jiāngxià warriors are also no less than 10,000.
Cáo Cāo’s forces,
having come from afar, are exhausted.
Hearing that Yùzhōu was being pursued,
his light cavalry traveled over 300 *lǐ* in a day and a night.
This is what is called ‘the end of a strong crossbow’s shot,
whose force cannot pierce even Lǔ silk.’
Therefore, military strategy forbids this,
saying ‘it will certainly cause the collapse of the supreme general.’
Moreover, the people of the north
are not accustomed to naval warfare;
and the people of Jīngzhōu who have submitted to Cāo
are merely coerced by military might,
not genuinely convinced.
Now, if the General can truly order a fierce general to lead several tens of thousands of troops,
and cooperate with Yùzhōu with a unified plan and strength,
Cāo’s army will certainly be defeated.
Once Cāo’s army is defeated,
he will certainly return north.
In this way, the power of Jīng and Wú will be strong,
and the formation of a tripod (three-way division of power) will be achieved.
The critical moment for success or failure
is today.”
Quán was greatly pleased,
and immediately dispatched Zhōu Yú, Chéng Pǔ, Lǔ Sù, and others with a naval force of 30,000,
to follow Liàng to the Former Lord,
and jointly resist Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng was defeated at Chìbì,
and withdrew his army back to Yè.
The Former Lord then recovered Jiāngnán,
appointed Liàng as Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs and Colonel of the Central Division (Jūnshī Zhōngláng Jiāng),
and assigned him to oversee the three commanderies of Línglíng, Guìyáng, and Chángshā,
to regulate their taxes and tribute,
to replenish military resources.
In the sixteenth year of Jiàn'ān (211 CE),
Liú Zhāng, the Governor of Yìzhōu,
sent Fǎ Zhèng to welcome the Former Lord
to attack Zhāng Lǔ.
Liàng and Guān Yǔ garrisoned Jīngzhōu.
The Former Lord returned from Jiāmáng to attack Zhāng,
and Liàng, with Zhāng Fēi, Zhào Yún, and others, led their forces up the river,
subduing commanderies and counties one by one,
and joined the Former Lord in besieging Chéngdū.
When Chéngdū was pacified,
Liàng was appointed General of the Military Affairs (Jūnshī Jiāngjūn),
and oversaw the affairs of the General of the Left’s (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn) office.
When the Former Lord was away,
Liàng always garrisoned Chéngdū,
ensuring ample food and troops.
In the twenty-sixth year (221 CE),
his subordinates urged the Former Lord to assume the imperial title,
but the Former Lord had not yet agreed.
Liàng persuaded him, saying:
“In the past, Wú Hàn, Gěng Yǎn, and others first urged Emperor Shìzǔ to ascend the throne,
and Shìzǔ declined
four times both before and after.
Gěng Chún then advised: ‘The heroes of the world are eagerly waiting,
hoping for something.
If you do not follow their counsel,
the literati and officials will each return to seek their own lord,
and will not serve Your Grace.’
Shìzǔ was deeply moved by Chún’s sincere words,
and then agreed.
Now, the Cáo clan has usurped the Hàn,
and the world is without a master.
Your Royal Highness, being a descendant of the Liú lineage,
has arisen to continue the dynastic line.
It is therefore fitting
that you now ascend the imperial throne.
The literati and officials who have long toiled and suffered with Your Royal Highness
also desire a small measure of merit, just as Chún said.”
The Former Lord then ascended the imperial throne,
and appointed Liàng as Chancellor with the following edict:
“I have encountered misfortune in my family,
and have taken on the great succession.
With trepidation and diligence,
I dare not seek ease.
I desire to bring peace to the common people,
but fear I cannot pacify them.
Alas!
Chancellor Liàng, understand my intentions,
and do not fail to assist me in my shortcomings,
help proclaim the brilliant light (of virtue),
to illuminate the world.
You must strive diligently!”
Liàng, as Chancellor, supervised the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū Shì)
and was granted the imperial insignia (jiǎ jié).
After Zhāng Fēi’s death,
he took charge of the affairs of the Colonel-Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
In the spring of the third year of Zhāngwǔ,
the Former Emperor fell gravely ill at Yǒng'ān.
He summoned Zhūgě Liàng to Chéngdū,
entrusting him with affairs after his death,
and said to Liàng:
"Your talent is ten times that of Cáo Pī;
you will surely be able to pacify the nation
and ultimately accomplish the great task.
If the heir apparent can be assisted,
then assist him;
if he is untalented,
then you may take the throne yourself."
Liàng wept and said:
"I dare to exert all my strength,
to demonstrate my loyalty and integrity,
and to follow it with death!"
The Former Emperor then issued an edict to the Latter Emperor, saying:
"You are to work with the Chancellor
and serve him as a father."
In the first year of Jiànxīng,
Zhūgě Liàng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔxiāng
and granted permission to establish an administration.
Soon after,
he was also appointed Governor of Yìzhōu.
All governmental matters, great or small,
were decided by Zhūgě Liàng.
The various commanderies of Nánzhōng
had all rebelled.
Zhūgě Liàng, having just suffered a great loss,
did not immediately deploy troops.
Instead, he sent envoys to Wú
to forge a peace alliance,
thus becoming an allied state.
In the spring of the third year,
Zhūgě Liàng led his troops on a southern expedition.
By that autumn, all was pacified.
With military resources abundantly available,
the state became prosperous.
He then trained his army and practiced martial arts,
in preparation for a major campaign.
In the fifth year,
he led all the armies north to station in Hànzhōng.
Before departing,
he submitted a memorial saying: The Former Emperor started his great enterprise but halfway through collapsed and died.
Now the world is divided into three,
and Yìzhōu is exhausted and weak.
This is truly a critical autumn for survival or destruction.
However, the attendant
officials are unflagging within the palace,
and the loyal and dedicated warriors forget themselves outside,
because they remember the Former Emperor's exceptional treatment
and wish to repay it to Your Majesty.
It is truly advisable to broaden your sagely
listening,
to glorify the Former Emperor's enduring virtue,
and to amplify the morale of loyal men.
You should not belittle yourself arbitrarily,
or make inappropriate analogies,
thereby obstructing the path of loyal counsel.
The palace and the administration are one entity;
promotions, demotions, rewards, and punishments
should not differ.
If there are those who commit wickedness and violations, or who are loyal and good,
they should be handed over to the proper authorities to decide their punishment
or reward,
to demonstrate Your Majesty's fair and impartial governance.
There should be no favoritism,
causing different laws for inside and outside.
The Palace Attendants and Palace Gentlemen Guō Yōuzhī, Fèi Yī, Dǒng Yǔn, etc.,
these are all good and honest men,
whose thoughts and intentions are loyal and pure.
This is why the Former Emperor selected them to entrust to Your Majesty.
I humbly believe that in palace affairs,
regardless of their magnitude,
you should consult with them fully,
and then implement,
which will surely help to amend deficiencies and omissions,
and bring broader benefits.
General Xiàng Chǒng
is of virtuous and balanced character,
and is thoroughly knowledgeable in military affairs.
He was tested in the past,
and the Former
Emperor praised his ability.
Therefore, the general consensus was to appoint Chǒng as commander.
I humbly believe that in affairs of the camp,
you should consult with him fully,
which will surely make the ranks harmonious
and ensure that both superior and inferior
find their proper place.
To be close to worthy ministers and
keep distant from petty men—
this is how the Former Hàn flourished;
to be close to petty men and
keep distant from worthy ministers—
this is how the Latter Hàn declined.
When the Former
Emperor was alive,
whenever he discussed this matter with me,
he never failed to sigh and deeply regret the reigns of Huán and Líng.
The Palace Attendants, Masters of Writing, Chief Clerks, and Army Advisors,
these are all loyal
and principled ministers who would die for their integrity.
I wish Your Majesty to be close to them and trust them;
then the prosperity of the Hàn dynasty
can be awaited day by day.
I was originally a commoner,
tilling the fields in Nányáng,
seeking merely to preserve my life in a chaotic world,
not striving for fame or recognition from the feudal lords.
The Former Emperor did not consider me lowly,
but condescended
to humble himself,
visiting me thrice in my humble thatched cottage,
consulting me on the affairs of the time.
Because of this, I was moved and grateful,
and thus promised to serve the Former Emperor.
Later, during a time of collapse
and overthrow,
I was appointed to a post amidst a defeated army,
and received orders during a time of peril and difficulty.
Twenty-one years have passed since then.
The Former Emperor knew my prudence,
and so at his death
entrusted me with this great task.
Since receiving this charge,
I have worried and sighed day and night,
fearing that my entrusted duty might not be effective,
thereby harming the Former Emperor's discernment.
Therefore, in the fifth month, I crossed the Lú River,
penetrating deep into
the barbarian lands.
Now that the south is settled,
and arms and armor are sufficient,
it is time to encourage and lead the three armies
north to pacify the Central Plains,
hoping to exert my humble and limited abilities,
to eliminate the treacherous and wicked,
to revive the Hàn
dynasty,
and return to the old capital.
This is how I shall repay the Former Emperor
and fulfill my duty to Your Majesty.
As for weighing gains and losses
and offering full and loyal counsel,
that is the responsibility of Yōuzhī, Yī, and Yǔn.
I ask Your Majesty to entrust me with the task of suppressing the rebels and restoring the dynasty;
if I am ineffective,
then punish my crime
to report to the spirit of the Former Emperor.
【If there are no words to advance virtue,
then】 blame the negligence of Yōuzhī, Yī, Yǔn, and others,
to expose their
faults.
Your Majesty should also deliberate for yourself,
consulting good ways,
observing and accepting excellent advice,
and deeply following the Former Emperor's dying wishes.
I am overwhelmed with gratitude for the kindness I have received.
Now I must
depart afar,
and as I face this memorial, tears stream down,
I know not what to say.
He then departed
and garrisoned at Miǎnyáng.
In the spring of the sixth year [of Jiànxīng],
Yáng Shēng marched from the Xié Valley Road to Qí.
Zhào Yún and Dèng Zhī were dispatched as a diversionary force,
stationed at Jīgǔ.
The Grand General of Wèi, Cáo Zhēn, led his army to resist them.
Zhūgě Liàng personally led the various armies to attack Qíshān.
His military formations were orderly and well-arranged;
rewards and punishments were strict, and commands were clear.
The three commanderies of Nán'ān, Tiānshuǐ, and Āndìng rebelled against Wèi and sided with Zhūgě Liàng,
and Guānzhōng was shaken.
Wèi Emperor Míng Di stationed himself in Cháng'ān in the west [to oversee the defense],
and ordered Zhāng Hé to resist Zhūgě Liàng.
Zhūgě Liàng sent Mǎ Sù to command the vanguard forces,
and they engaged Zhāng Hé at Jiētíng.
Mǎ Sù disregarded Zhūgě Liàng's strategy,
and his actions were inappropriate,
leading to a crushing defeat by Zhāng Hé.
Zhūgě Liàng relocated over a thousand households from Xī Xiàn [to Hànzhōng]
and returned to Hànzhōng.
He executed Mǎ Sù to apologize to the masses.
He submitted a memorial, saying:
"I, with my meager talent,
usurped a position I did not deserve.
Personally holding the mao-yuè (general's axe) to inspire the three armies,
I failed to instruct and clarify the laws,
and became fearful in the face of affairs,
leading to the error of disobeying orders at Jiētíng,
and the oversight of being unwary at Jīgǔ.
The fault for all of this lies with my improper selection of appointees.
I am clearly ignorant of people,
and often dim-witted in managing affairs.
According to the Spring and Autumn Annals tradition of holding the commander responsible,
this duty falls upon me.
I request to be demoted three ranks
to underscore my fault."
Thereupon, Zhūgě Liàng was made Right General,
acting as Chancellor,
with his overall command remaining as before.
In winter,
Zhūgě Liàng again marched out from Sànguān,
and besieged Chéncāng.
Cáo Zhēn resisted him,
and Zhūgě Liàng, running out of provisions, returned.
The Wèi general Wáng Shuāng led cavalry to pursue Zhūgě Liàng.
Zhūgě Liàng engaged him in battle,
defeated him,
and beheaded Wáng Shuāng.
In the seventh year [of Jiànxīng],
Zhūgě Liàng sent Chén Shì to attack Wǔdū and Yīnpíng.
Guō Huái, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu of Wèi, led his forces, intending to strike Chén Shì.
Zhūgě Liàng personally advanced to Jiànwēi,
whereupon Guō Huái retreated,
and thus the two commanderies were pacified.
An imperial edict to Zhūgě Liàng stated:
"In the campaign of Jiētíng,
the fault lay with Mǎ Sù,
yet you took the blame,
deeply humbling yourself.
Reluctant to go against your wishes,
we complied with what you upheld.
Two years ago, your army was brilliant,
capturing and beheading Wáng Shuāng;
this year, you again campaigned,
and Guō Huái fled;
you brought down and settled the Dī and Qiāng tribes,
and restored the two commanderies.
Your awesome power suppresses the violent,
and your merits are clear.
At this time, the world is in turmoil,
and the primary evil has not been eliminated.
You bear a great responsibility,
the crucial burden of the state,
yet you have long diminished yourself,
which is not how to glorify your vast achievements.
We now restore you as Chancellor;
you should not decline."
In the ninth year [of Jiànxīng],
Zhūgě Liàng again marched out to Qíshān,
transporting provisions with 'wooden oxen.'
Running out of supplies, the army retreated,
and engaged the Wèi general Zhāng Hé in battle,
shooting and killing Zhāng Hé.
In the spring of the twelfth year [of Jiànxīng],
Zhūgě Liàng led his entire army out through the Xié Valley,
transporting provisions with 'gliding horses.'
He occupied Wǔgōng Wǔzhàng Yuán,
facing Sīmǎ Xuānwáng across the Wèi River.
Zhūgě Liàng constantly worried about insufficient provisions,
which prevented him from achieving his ambitions.
Therefore, he divided his troops for屯田 (military agricultural colonies)
as a basis for long-term stationing.
The cultivators were interspersed among the residents along the Wèi River,
and the common people were peaceful,
with no private dealings in the army.
They were stalemated for over a hundred days.
In August of that year,
Zhūgě Liàng fell ill,
and died in the army [camp],
at the age of fifty-four.
When the army retreated,
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng inspected the location of his camps and fortifications,
and said:
"He was truly a remarkable talent under heaven!"
Zhūgě Liàng's dying wish was to be buried on Dìngjūn Shān in Hànzhōng,
with the mountain serving as the mound,
the tomb just large enough for a coffin,
and dressed in everyday clothes,
requiring no valuable artifacts.
An imperial edict stated:
"Only you, with your natural disposition for both civil and military arts,
your sagacity and utmost sincerity,
received the dying entrustment and the orphaned child,
assisting Our person,
continuing what was broken and reviving what was weak,
with the ambition to pacify the chaos.
You marshaled the six armies,
campaigning every year,
with divine might manifest,
intimidating the eight directions,
about to establish extraordinary achievements for Jì Hàn,
rivalling the great merits of Yī [Yǐn] and [Duke of] Zhōu.
How lamentable that you were not blessed by fortune!
With success almost achieved,
you encountered illness and perished!
We are heartbroken by this loss,
Our liver and heart are as if rent asunder.
Indeed, to exalt virtue and order merit,
to record deeds and bestow posthumous titles,
is to brilliantly illuminate the future,
and engrave them for immortality.
Now, We dispatch the Imperial Envoy, Left Palace Commandant Dù Qióng,
to posthumously bestow upon you the Chancellor and Marquis of Wǔxiāng seal and ribbon,
and to grant you the posthumous title of Zhōngwǔ Hóu.
If your soul has spirit,
may you rejoice in this honor.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Alas, how sorrowful!"
Previously,
Zhūgě Liàng had presented a memorial to the Latter Lord, saying:
"In Chéngdū, there are eight hundred mulberry trees,
and fifteen qīng of barren land.
For my sons and younger brothers, food and clothing [from this]
is more than sufficient.
As for myself, when serving away from home,
I have no separate arrangements;
my personal food and clothing
all depend on the government;
I do not separately manage a livelihood
to increase my possessions by an inch.
Should the day of my death arrive,
there should be no surplus silk within [my home],
nor any excess wealth outside,
so as not to fail Your Majesty."
When he died,
it was as he had said.
Zhūgě Liàng was by nature skilled in ingenious devices.
The improved repeating crossbows,
the 'wooden oxen' and 'gliding horses,'
all originated from his ideas;
he expounded on military strategy,
and created the Eight Battle Array Diagrams,
all of which reportedly grasped the essentials.
Many of Zhūgě Liàng's oral teachings and written memorials are worth seeing,
and have been compiled into a collection.
In the spring of the sixth year of Jǐngyào,
an imperial edict ordered the erection of a temple for Zhūgě Liàng in Miǎnyáng.
In autumn,
Zhōng Huì, the Wèi General Who Guards the West, campaigned against Shǔ.
Upon reaching Hànchuān,
he offered sacrifices at Zhūgě Liàng's temple,
and forbade his soldiers from grazing animals or gathering firewood near Zhūgě Liàng's tomb.
Zhūgě Liàng's younger brother, Zhūgě Jūn,
reached the official position of Commandant of Chángshuǐ.
Zhūgě Liàng's son, Zhūgě Zhàn,
inherited his title.

The above twenty-four chapters,
totaling one hundred and four thousand one hundred and twelve characters.
Your minister Chén Shòu and others state: Formerly, when I was an Archivist,

Sūn Xù, the Attendant Censor and concurrently Director of the Imperial Secretariat and Marquis of Jìběi, and Hé Jiào, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat and Marquis within the Pass, submitted a memorial,
instructing me to compile the anecdotes of the late Shǔ Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng.
Zhūgě Liàng assisted a precarious state,
and, entrenched in strongholds, was not submissive.
However, to preserve and record his words,
ashamed to leave out any good,
is truly
the enlightened and utmost virtue of the great Jìn dynasty,
whose benevolence reaches boundless limits,
something that, since ancient times,
has had no equal.
Therefore, I have deleted repetitions,
and grouped them by category,
making in total twenty
four chapters.
The titles are as follows.
Zhūgě Liàng, when young, possessed extraordinary talent,
and the spirit of a heroic霸.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
with a remarkably impressive appearance,
and people of his time considered him exceptional.
During the chaos at the end of the Hàn dynasty,
he followed his uncle
Xuán to take refuge in Jīngzhōu.
He tilled the land himself in the wilderness,
seeking no fame or advancement.
At that time, the Left General Liú Bèi, recognizing Liàng's unusual qualities,
paid three visits to Liàng at his thatched cottage.
Zhōng;
Liàng deeply admired Bèi's heroic and outstanding demeanor,
and so, he unburdened himself and spoke sincerely,
forming a deep bond with him.
When Wèi Wǔdì marched south to Jīngzhōu,
Liú Cóng surrendered the entire province,
and Bèi, outnumbered and without power,
had no place to stand.
Liàng, then twenty-seven years old,
devised an ingenious strategy,
personally acting as envoy to Sūn Quán,
seeking aid from Wúhuì.
Quán had long
admired Bèi,
and also saw Liàng's exceptional elegance,
respecting him greatly.
He immediately dispatched thirty thousand troops to assist Bèi.
With this, Bèi was able to engage Wǔdì in battle,
utterly defeating his army.
Capitalizing on their victory, they conquered
and pacified the entire Jiāngnán region.
Later, Bèi also marched west to take Yìzhōu.
After Yìzhōu was pacified,
Liàng was appointed Army Advisor General.
When Bèi claimed the imperial title,
he appointed
Liàng as Chancellor,
and concurrently Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
After Bèi passed away,
his successor was young and weak,
and Liàng took sole charge of all matters,
big or small.
Thus, externally he allied with Dōngwú,
and internally
pacified the Nányuè.
He established laws and regulations,
reorganized the military,
perfected engineering and craftsmanship,
pushing everything to its extreme.
His laws and teachings were clear and strict,
rewards and punishments were always trustworthy,
no evil went unpunished,
and no
good went unacknowledged.
As a result, officials dared not commit corruption,
people were inspired to improve themselves,
lost items were not picked up on the roads,
the strong did not bully the weak,
and public morality was solemn.
At this time,
Liàng's long-held ambition
was to advance, soaring like a dragon and glaring like a tiger,
encompassing the Four Seas;
or, if retreating, to command the borders,
and shake the entire realm.
He also
believed that without his presence,
there would be no one capable of crossing into the Central Plains and rivaling the great states.
Therefore, he did not cease military campaigns,
repeatedly displaying his might.
However, Liàng's talent
was stronger in military administration and weaker in ingenious strategies.
His ability to govern the people
surpassed his military tactics.
Yet,
those he faced as enemies
were sometimes exceptional individuals,
and moreover, the numbers were unequal,
and the methods of attack
and defense differed.
Hence, although he mobilized forces for successive years,
he was unable to achieve victory.
In the past, Xiāo Hé recommended Hán Xìn,
and Guǎn Zhòng promoted Wángzǐ Chéngfù;
both calculated their own strengths,
and were unable
to possess all talents themselves.
Liàng's capacity for governance
was also comparable to Guǎn and Xiāo.
But the renowned generals of his time were not Chéngfù or Hán Xìn.
Did this cause his achievements
to decline,
and the great cause to falter?
Perhaps it was due to the decree of Heaven,
which cannot be contended with by wisdom and strength.
In the spring of the second year of Qīnglóng,
Liàng led his forces out to Wǔgōng,
and divided his troops to establish agricultural garrisons,
laying the foundation for a long-term encampment.
In the autumn of that year, he fell ill and died.
The common people remembered him with longing,
and it became
a subject of conversation.
Even today, the people of Liáng and Yì
who speak of Liàng,
their words are still fresh in one's ears.
Even the praises of Zhào Gōng in the "Gāntáng" ode
or the people of Zhèng singing of Zǐchǎn,
cannot compare
to him.
Mèng Kē said:
"If one governs the people with an easy way,
though they toil, they will not resent;
if one kills people with a way that nurtures life,
though they die, they will not be angry."
Indeed!
Some commentators
find it strange that Liàng's writings lack embellishment
and are excessively detailed and thorough.
Your humble servant believes that Gāoyáo was a great worthy,
and Duke of Zhōu a sage.
Examining the *Shàngshū*,
Gāoyáo's
counsels are concise and elegant,
while the Duke of Zhōu's pronouncements are verbose and exhaustive.
Why is this?
Gāoyáo discussed with Shùn and Yǔ,
while the Duke of Zhōu made solemn declarations to his subordinates.
Liàng's
conversations were all with common people and ordinary officials,
hence the scope of his writings could not be far-reaching.
However, his teachings and posthumous words
all encompassed practical matters and integrated various objects,
and his public-spirited and sincere heart
was evident in his writings,
sufficient to understand his character and reasoning,
and beneficial to the present age.
I humbly submit that Your Majesty follows the footsteps of ancient sages,
being open and unrestrained.
Therefore, even the slanders of enemy states
are freely expressed without suppression or concealment,
thus illuminating
the path of great openness.
I have respectfully transcribed and submitted this to the Directorate of Historiography.
Your humble servant Shòu, trembling with fear and dread,
bows his head repeatedly,
deserving of death, deserving of death.
On the *Guǐsì* day of the second month,
the first day of the second month,
in the tenth year of Tàishǐ,
Your humble servant Chén Shòu, Minister of Píngyánghóu, submits this.
Qiáo, courtesy name Bósōng,
