was the second son of Liàng's elder brother Jǐn.
His original courtesy name was Zhòngshèn.
He and his elder brother Yuánsùn were both famous at the time,
commentators believed that Qiáo's talent was inferior to his brother's,
but his character and conduct surpassed him.
Initially,
Liàng had no son,
and sought Qiáo to be his heir.
Jǐn petitioned Sūn Quán to send Qiáo to the west,
and Liàng adopted Qiáo as his legitimate son,
thus changing his courtesy name.
He was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law,
and followed Liàng to Hànzhōng.
At the age of twenty-five,
he died in the sixth year of Jiànxīng.
His son, Pān,
rose to the office of Acting Protector of the Army and General Who Assists the Martial,
but also died young.
After Zhūgě Kè was executed in Wú,
all his descendants perished,
but since Liàng had his own lineage,
Pān was returned to become Jǐn's heir.
Zhān's courtesy name was Sīyuǎn.
In the twelfth year of Jiànxīng,
Zhūgě Liàng went out to Wǔgōng.
He wrote a letter to his elder brother Jǐn, saying:
"Zhān is now eight years old,
intelligent and lovable.
I worry that he is developing too early,
and fear he may not become a truly great talent."
At the age of seventeen,
he married a princess,
and was appointed Colonel of Cavalry (Qí dūwèi).
The following year, he became Commander of the Feathered Forest (Yǔlín zhōnglángjiāng),
and was repeatedly promoted to Colonel of Archers (Shèshēng xiàowèi), Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), and Assistant to the Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū púshè),
and was given the additional title of General of the Military Adviser (Jūnshī jiāngjūn).
Zhān was skilled in calligraphy and painting,
and had an excellent memory.
The people of Shǔ, recalling Zhūgě Liàng,
all admired Zhān's talent and quick wit.
Whenever there was a good policy or a fine achievement in court,
even if it was not initiated by Zhān,
the common people would spread the word among themselves, saying:
"This is the work of Marquis Gě."
Thus, his good reputation and praise
exceeded the reality.
In the fourth year of Jǐngyào,
he was appointed Acting Protector-General and Grand General of the Guard (Xíng dūhù wèijiāngjūn),
and along with Grand General of Auxiliary State and Marquis of Nánxiāng, Dǒng Jué, he jointly managed affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
In the winter of the sixth year,
Dèng Ài, General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī jiāngjūn) of Wèi, invaded Shǔ.
He entered from Yīnpíng through the Jǐnggǔ Pass.
Zhān led all the armies to Fú and halted,
but his vanguard was defeated,
and he retreated
and stopped at Miánzhú.
Dèng Ài sent a letter to lure Zhān, saying:
"If you surrender, you will surely be enfeoffed as King of Lángxié."
Zhān was enraged
and executed Dèng Ài's envoy.
Thereupon, they fought,
and suffered a great defeat.
Zhān died in battle,
at the age of thirty-seven.
The troops all scattered,
and Dèng Ài advanced rapidly to Chéngdū.
Zhān's eldest son, Shàng,
died with Zhān.
His second son, Jīng, and Pān's son, Xiǎn, and others,
were moved to Hédōng in the first year of Xiánxī.
Dǒng Jué was
a clerk in the Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng's office.
Zhūgě Liàng praised him, saying:
"Clerk Dǒng
is an excellent man.
Whenever I speak with him,
I find his thoughts prudent and appropriate."
He was then promoted to Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù).
After Zhūgě Liàng's death,
he gradually rose to Assistant to the Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū púshè),
replaced Chén Zhī as Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū lìng),
and was promoted to Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
managing the affairs of the court.
Fán Jiàn of Yìyáng then succeeded him.
In the fourteenth year of Yánxī,
he was sent as a Colonel (Xiàowèi) on a mission to Wú.
It happened that Sūn Quán was gravely ill
and did not personally see Fán Jiàn.
Sūn Quán asked Zhūgě Kè:
"How does Fán Jiàn compare to Zōng Yù?"
Zhūgě Kè replied:
"In talent and discernment, he is not as good as Zōng Yù,
but in elegant disposition, he surpasses him."
Later, he became Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
and then concurrently Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū lìng).
From the time Zhān, Jué, and Jiàn jointly managed affairs,
Jiāng Wéi was constantly away on military campaigns,
and the eunuch Huáng Hào secretly seized control of power.
Though they all jointly guarded against him,
none could correct or stop him.
However, Jiàn specifically did not associate with Huáng Hào in a friendly manner.
In the spring of the year after Shǔ's fall,
Jué and Jiàn both went to the capital,
and both served as Consultant to the Prime Minister (Xiàngguó cānjūn).
That autumn, they both additionally held the position of Attendant Counselor (Sànqí chángshì),
and were sent to Shǔ to offer comfort and recognition.
A commentary states: When Zhūgě Liàng was Chancellor (Xiàngguó),
he comforted the people,
established norms and regulations,
simplified official duties,
adapted to circumstances,
opened his heart with sincerity,
and applied public justice;
those who were loyal and beneficial to the times, even if enemies, were surely rewarded;
those who violated laws and were negligent, even if relatives, were surely punished;
those who confessed their crimes and showed remorse, even if their offenses were serious, were surely released;
those who used evasive words and clever deceptions, even if their offenses were light, were surely executed;
no good deed, however small, went unrewarded;
no evil, however minute, went unpunished;
all affairs were meticulously handled,
the root principles of things were explored,
names were checked against realities,
and hypocrisy was not tolerated;
finally, within the borders of the state,
all feared and loved him.
Although his laws and administration were strict, there were no complaints,
because his intentions were fair and his admonitions clear.
He can be called a wise talent in governance,
a peer of Guǎn Zhòng and Xiāo Hé.
However, he mobilized armies for many years
without achieving success.
Perhaps adapting to changes and military strategy
were not his strengths!
Biography of Guān Yǔ, Zhāng Fēi, Mǎ Chāo, Huáng Zhōng, Zhào Yún, Chapter Six.
Guān Yǔ, courtesy name Yúncháng,
originally named Chángshēng, was a man from Xiè in Hédōng.
He fled due to a crime and went to Zhuōjùn.
The Former Lord gathered followers in his hometown,
and Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi served as his protectors.
When the Former Lord became Prefect of Píngyuán,
he made Yǔ and Fēi Commanders of Separate Divisions (Biébù sīmǎ),
assigning them to command various units.
The Former Lord shared a bed with the two of them,
their affection like brothers.
Yet in large gatherings and public assemblies,
they would stand attending all day,
following the Former Lord everywhere,
without avoiding hardship or danger.
When the Former Lord ambushed and killed Chē Zhòu, the Inspector of Xúzhōu,
he ordered Yǔ to guard Xiàpī city,
acting as Administrator (Tàishǒu),
while he himself returned to Xiǎopèi.
In the fifth year of Jiàn'ān,
Cáo Cāo launched an eastern campaign.
The Former Lord fled to Yuán Shào.
Cáo Cāo captured Yǔ and brought him back,
appointed him General of the Household (Piānjiāngjūn),
and treated him with great generosity.
Yuán Shào sent his grand general Yán Liáng to attack Liú Yán, the Administrator of Dōngjùn, at Báimǎ.
Cáo Cāo sent Zhāng Liáo and Yǔ as vanguards to attack him.
Yǔ spotted Yán Liáng's parasol,
spurred his horse, and stabbed Yán Liáng amidst ten thousand men,
returning with his head.
None of Yuán Shào's generals could stand against him,
and the siege of Báimǎ was thus lifted.
Cáo Cāo immediately memorialized to enfeoff Yǔ as Marquis of Hànshòu Village (Hànshòu tínghóu).
At first,
Cáo Cāo admired Yǔ's character,
but noticed that he had no intention of staying long.
He said to Zhāng Liáo:
"Try to ask him about his feelings."
Zhāng Liáo then asked Yǔ.
Yǔ sighed and said:
"I fully know that Lord Cáo treats me generously,
but I have received great kindness from General Liú,
and swore to die together with him;
I cannot betray him.
I will not stay forever;
I must render service to repay Lord Cáo before I leave."
Zhāng Liáo reported Yǔ's words to Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo respected his integrity.
When Yǔ killed Yán Liáng,
Cáo Cāo knew he would surely leave,
and gave him even more rewards.
Yǔ sealed up all the gifts he had received,
wrote a letter of farewell,
and fled to the Former Lord in Yuán Shào's army.
His subordinates wanted to pursue him,
but Cáo Cāo said:
"Each serves his own lord;
do not pursue him."
Following Xiānzhǔ, Guān Yǔ went to Liú Biǎo.
When Liú Biǎo died,
Cáo Gōng pacified Jīngzhōu.
Xiānzhǔ, from Fánchéng, intended to cross the river southward.
He separately dispatched Guān Yǔ with several hundred boats to meet at Jiānglíng.
Cáo Gōng pursued them to Dāngyáng Chángbǎn.
Xiānzhǔ obliquely headed for Hànjīn,
where he happened to meet Guān Yǔ's boats.
Together, they reached Xiàkǒu.
Sūn Quán sent troops to assist Xiānzhǔ in resisting Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng withdrew his army and returned.
Xiānzhǔ took control of the various commanderies south of the Yangtze River.
He then conferred titles upon his meritorious officers.
Guān Yǔ was appointed Prefect of Xiāngyáng and General Who Sweeps Away Bandits,
stationed north of the river.
When Xiānzhǔ conquered Yìzhōu to the west,
he appointed Guān Yǔ to supervise the affairs of Jīngzhōu.
When Guān Yǔ heard that Mǎ Chāo had surrendered,
since Mǎ Chāo was not an old acquaintance,
Guān Yǔ wrote to Zhūgě Liàng,
asking whose talent Mǎ Chāo could be compared to.
Zhūgě Liàng, knowing Guān Yǔ was protective of his reputation,
replied to him, saying:
"Mèngqǐ possesses both civil and military talents,
his heroism and ferocity surpass others.
He is an outstanding figure of his generation,
on par with Qíng Bù and Péng Yuè.
He should contend for supremacy with Yìdé,
but he is still not as peerless and exceptional as the Bearded One."
Guān Yǔ had a beautiful beard,
thus Zhūgě Liàng called him the Bearded One.
Guān Yǔ was greatly pleased upon reading the letter
and showed it to his guests.
Guān Yǔ was once struck by a stray arrow,
which pierced his left arm.
Although the wound later healed,
whenever it was cloudy and rainy,
the bone would often ache.
A physician said:
"The arrowhead has poison,
and the poison has entered the bone.
The arm must be cut open to create a wound,
and the bone scraped to remove the poison.
Only then can this ailment be cured."
Guān Yǔ then extended his arm and allowed the physician to cut it open.
At that time, Guān Yǔ had just invited several generals to dine opposite him.
Blood flowed from his arm,
filling the basin,
yet Guān Yǔ continued to cut and eat roasted meat, drink wine,
and converse and laugh as if nothing were amiss.
In the twenty-fourth year [24 CH 219 CE],
Xiānzhǔ became King of Hànzhōng,
and appointed Guān Yǔ as General of the Vanguard,
granting him an imperial staff and axe.
In this year,
Guān Yǔ led his troops to attack Cáo Rén at Fánchéng.
Cáo Gōng sent Yú Jìn to assist Cáo Rén.
In autumn,
there was heavy continuous rain,
and the Hàn River overflowed.
All seven armies under Yú Jìn's command were submerged.
Yú Jìn surrendered to Guān Yǔ.
Guān Yǔ also beheaded General Páng Dé.
Bandits from Liángjiá and Lùhún sometimes received seals and titles from Guān Yǔ from afar,
becoming his allies.
Guān Yǔ's prestige shook Huáxià.
Cáo Gōng considered moving Xǔdū to avoid his might.
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng [Sīmǎ Yì] and Jiǎng Jì believed that if Guān Yǔ succeeded,
Sūn Quán would surely not be pleased.
They suggested sending someone to persuade Sūn Quán to attack Guān Yǔ from behind,
promising to cede the regions south of the Yangtze River to Sūn Quán as his fief.
Then the siege of Fánchéng would naturally be lifted.
Cáo Gōng agreed.
Before this,
Sūn Quán had sent an envoy to request Guān Yǔ's daughter for his son.
Guān Yǔ insulted the envoy,
refusing the marriage.
Sūn Quán was greatly angered.
Moreover, Mí Fāng, the Prefect of Nánjùn, was in Jiānglíng,
and General Shì Rén was stationed in Gōng'ān.
They both had always resented Guān Yǔ for looking down on them.
When Guān Yǔ's army set out, Mí Fāng and Shì Rén were supposed to supply military provisions,
but they did not fully assist.
Guān Yǔ said,
"When I return, I will deal with them."
Mí Fāng and Shì Rén were both afraid and uneasy.
Thereupon, Sūn Quán secretly enticed Mí Fāng and Shì Rén.
Mí Fāng and Shì Rén sent people to welcome Sūn Quán.
Meanwhile, Cáo Gōng sent Xú Huǎng to rescue Cáo Rén.
Guān Yǔ could not prevail
and withdrew his army.
Sūn Quán had already occupied Jiānglíng
and captured all of Guān Yǔ's officers, soldiers, wives, and children.
Guān Yǔ's army then dispersed.
Sūn Quán sent a general to intercept and attack Guān Yǔ,
beheading Guān Yǔ and his son Píng at Línjǔ.
He was posthumously granted the title of Zhuàngmiù Hóu.
His son, Xīng, inherited his title.
Xīng, courtesy name Ānguó,
had a good reputation in his youth.
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng deeply valued his exceptional talent.
At the age of twenty, he became an Imperial Household Grandee and Central Army Supervisor.
He died a few years later.
His son, Tǒng, inherited his title,
married a princess,
and served as Colonel of the Tiger Swift Guards.
He died
without a son,
so Xīng's illegitimate son, Yí, succeeded to the fief.
Zhāng Fēi, courtesy name Yìdé,
was from Zhuōjùn.
In his youth, he and Guān Yǔ both served Xiānzhǔ.
Guān Yǔ was several years older,
and Zhāng Fēi treated him as an elder brother.
When Xiānzhǔ, together with Cáo Gōng, defeated Lǚ Bù,
he returned with him to Xǔdū.
Cáo Gōng appointed Zhāng Fēi as Colonel.
Xiānzhǔ defied Cáo Gōng and sought refuge with Yuán Shào and Liú Biǎo.
When Liú Biǎo died,
Cáo Gōng entered Jīngzhōu.
Xiānzhǔ fled to the south of the Yangtze River.
Cáo Gōng pursued him,
and after one day and one night,
caught up with him at Chángbǎn in Dāngyáng.
Xiānzhǔ, hearing that Cáo Gōng had arrived suddenly,
abandoned his wife and children and fled,
sending Zhāng Fēi with twenty riders to guard the rear.
Zhāng Fēi stood by the bridge, breaking it,
glared with wide eyes, held his spear horizontally, and said:
"I am Zhāng Yìdé! Come, let us fight to the death!"
None of the enemies dared to approach,
so he was able to escape.
After Xiānzhǔ had pacified the region south of the Yangtze River,
he appointed Zhāng Fēi as Prefect of Yídū and General Who Conquers Barbarians,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Xīntíng.
Later, he was transferred to Nánjùn.
When Xiānzhǔ entered Yìzhōu
and attacked Liú Zhāng,
Zhāng Fēi, along with Zhūgě Liàng and others, went upstream
and conquered various commanderies and counties.
Upon reaching Jiāngzhōu,
he defeated Yán Yán, Liú Zhāng's general and Prefect of Bāyùn,
and captured Yán Yán alive.
Zhāng Fēi scolded Yán Yán, saying:
"Our great army has arrived;
why do you not surrender and dare to resist?"
Yán Yán replied:
"You are all unprincipled,
invading and seizing my province.
My province has only generals who will lose their heads,
not generals who will surrender."
Zhāng Fēi was enraged
and ordered his attendants to drag him away and behead him.
Yán Yán's expression did not change,
and he said:
"If I am to be beheaded, then behead me!
Why be angry?"
Zhāng Fēi admired his bravery and released him,
treating him as an honored guest.
Zhāng Fēi won every battle he fought
and met Xiānzhǔ in Chéngdū.
After Yìzhōu was pacified,
Zhūgě Liàng, Fǎ Zhèng, Zhāng Fēi, and Guān Yǔ were each rewarded with five hundred *jīn* of gold,
one thousand *jīn* of silver,
fifty million *qián* (coins),
and one thousand bolts of brocade.
Other awards varied.
Zhāng Fēi was appointed Prefect of Bāxī.
Cáo Gōng broke Zhāng Lǔ,
and left Xiàhóu Yuān and Zhāng Hé to guard Hànchuān.
Hé, separately commanding all the armies, went down to Bāxī,
intending to relocate its people to Hànzhōng.
He advanced his army to Dàngqú, Méngtóu, and Dàngshí,
and confronted Fēi for over fifty days.
Fēi led more than ten thousand elite soldiers,
and from another path intercepted Hé's army to engage in battle.
The mountain path was narrow,
so those in front and behind could not aid each other.
Fēi then decisively defeated Hé.
Hé abandoned his horse and climbed the mountain,
retreating alone with over ten of his subordinates through a hidden path.
He led his army back to Nánzhèng,
and the land of Bā was pacified.
The Former Lord became King of Hànzhōng,
and appointed Fēi as Right General of the Army and granted him the Staff of Authority.
In the first year of Zhāngwǔ,
he was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and concurrently held the office of Minister of the Household and Commandant of the Capital District,
and was further enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīxiāng.
The imperial edict said:
succeeding to the grand enterprise by the heavenly order,
eliminating the wicked and pacifying the chaos,
have not yet fully illuminated the principles of governance.
Now the bandits and enemies cause harm,
and the people suffer bitterly.
Those who long for Hàn
stretch their necks, hoping like cranes.
I am therefore deeply distressed,
unable to sit still,
and food has no taste.
I have prepared the army and issued a solemn oath,
and am about to carry out the Mandate of Heaven.
Considering your loyalty and steadfastness,
emulating Zhào and Hǔ,
your fame spreads far and wide.
Therefore, I specially grant this conspicuous appointment,
elevating your rank,
and entrusting you with jurisdiction over the capital district.
May you grandly wield heavenly might,
subdue with virtue,
and punish rebels with law,
thus fulfilling my intentions.
Does not the Odes say,
'Without sickness, without distress,
the royal domain comes to its utmost.
Promptly accomplishing military feats,
thereby are you granted blessings'?
How can you not exert yourself!"
Originally,
Fēi was valiant and fierce,
second only to Guān Yǔ.
Wèi's strategists such as Chéng Yù all praised Yǔ and Fēi as adversaries of ten thousand men.
Yǔ treated his soldiers well but was arrogant towards scholar-officials;
Fēi respected gentlemen but showed no concern for commoners.
The Former Lord often cautioned him, saying:
"You are already excessive in your punishments and killings,
and you daily whip brave warriors,
yet keep them by your side.
This is a path to disaster."
Fēi still did not reform.
When the Former Lord campaigned against Wú,
Fēi was to lead ten thousand soldiers
from Lángzhōng to meet at Jiāngzhōu.
On the eve of his departure,
his subordinate generals Zhāng Dá and Fàn Qiáng assassinated Fēi,
took his head,
and fled downstream to Sūn Quán.
The camp commander of Fēi reported this to the Former Lord.
When the Former Lord heard that Fēi's commander had a report,
he said:
"Alas!
Fēi is dead."
He posthumously honored Fēi as Marquis Huán.
His eldest son, Bāo,
died young.
His second son, Shào, succeeded him,
and served as Attendant and Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Bāo's son, Zūn, became a Director of the Department of State Affairs.
He followed Zhūgě Zhān at Miánzhú,
fought against Dèng Ài,
and died.
Mǎ Chāo, courtesy name Mèngqǐ,
was a native of Màolíng, Fúfēng.
His father, Téng,
along with Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì, rose in rebellion in Xīzhōu at the end of Emperor Líng's reign.
In the third year of Chūpíng,
Suì and Téng led their forces to Cháng'ān.
The Hàn court appointed Suì as General Who Guards the West,
and sent him back to Jīnchéng;
Téng was appointed General Who Conquers the West,
and sent to garrison Méi.
Later, Téng attacked Cháng'ān,
was defeated,
and retreated to Liángzhōu.
Zhōng Yáo, the Commandant of the Capital District, who guarded Guānzhōng,
sent a letter to Suì and Téng,
explaining the consequences of good and bad fortune.
Téng sent Chāo to follow Yáo in attacking Guō Yuán and Gāo Gàn at Píngyáng.
Chāo's general, Páng Dé, personally beheaded Yuán.
Later, Téng and Hán Suì fell out,
and Téng requested to return to the capital region.
Thereupon, he was summoned to be Minister of the Guards,
and Chāo was appointed General of the Household,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng,
and took command of Téng's former troops.
Once Chāo took command,
he allied with Hán Suì,
and also formed a bond with Yáng Qiū, Lǐ Kān, Chéng Yí, and others,
advancing their army to Tóngguān.
Cáo Gōng met with Suì and Chāo on horseback for a discussion.
Chāo, relying on his great strength,
secretly intended to rush forward and seize Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng's attendant general, Xǔ Chǔ, glared at him with wide eyes,
and Chāo then dared not move.
Cáo Gōng used Jiǎ Xǔ's strategy
to sow discord between Chāo and Suì,
causing them to suspect each other,
and their army was utterly defeated.
Chāo fled and took refuge among the various Róng tribes.
Cáo Gōng pursued him to Āndìng,
but as there were troubles in the north,
he led his army back east.
Yáng Fù advised Cáo Gōng, saying:
"Chāo has the courage of Xìn and Bù,
and is very popular with the Qiāng and Hú.
If the main army returns
without strict preparations,
the commanderies in Lǒngshàng will no longer belong to the state."
Indeed, Chāo led the various Róng tribes to attack the commanderies and counties in Lǒngshàng.
All the commanderies and counties in Lǒngshàng responded to him.
He killed Wéi Kāng, the Inspector of Liángzhōu,
occupied Jìchéng,
and possessed its population.
Chāo proclaimed himself General Who Conquers the West,
and concurrently held the office of Inspector of Bìngzhōu,
supervising military affairs in Liángzhōu.
Wéi Kāng's former officials and people, Yáng Fù, Jiāng Xù, Liáng Kuān, Zhào Qú, and others,
conspired to attack Chāo.
Yáng Fù and Jiāng Xù rose up in Lǔchéng.
Chāo attacked them,
but could not overcome them.
Liáng Kuān and Zhào Qú closed the gates of Jìchéng,
preventing Chāo from entering.
Caught in a desperate situation,
he then fled to Hànzhōng to rely on Zhāng Lǔ.
Zhāng Lǔ was not competent to plan affairs with,
so Chāo harbored discontent internally.
Hearing that the Former Lord was besieging Liú Zhāng in Chéngdū,
he secretly wrote a letter to surrender.
Xiānzhǔ sent someone to welcome Mǎ Chāo.
Mǎ Chāo led his troops directly to the city walls.
The city was struck with terror.
Liú Zhāng immediately bowed his head,
appointing Mǎ Chāo as Píngxī Jiāngjūn,
and superintendent of Línjǔ.
He was then made Qián Dūtíng Hóu.
When Xiānzhǔ became Hànzhōng Wáng,
he appointed Mǎ Chāo as Zuǒ Jiāngjūn
and granted him imperial authority.
In the first year of Zhāngwǔ (221 CE),
he was promoted to Piàojí Jiāngjūn,
took charge as Liángzhōu Mù,
and was enfeoffed as Tái Xiāng Hóu.
The imperial edict read:
"I, though unworthy,
have succeeded to the position of the Exalted One,
and inherited the ancestral temple.
Cáo Cāo and his son
have accumulated crimes generation after generation.
I am deeply distressed by this,
as if suffering from a painful illness.
The people within the Four Seas are resentful and indignant,
seeking righteousness and returning to their origins.
Even the Dī and Qiāng have submitted,
and the Xūnzhú yearn for righteousness.
Since your trustworthiness is well-known in the northern lands,
and your martial prowess equally shines,
I entrust this responsibility to you,
to confront and defeat the fierce tigers,
and to govern over ten thousand *lǐ*,
seeking to relieve the suffering of the people.
You should clearly proclaim the imperial transformation,
cherish and protect those near and far,
and be solemn and careful in rewards and punishments,
to solidify the blessings of Hàn,
and to respond to the expectations of all under Heaven."
In the second year (222 CE), he died,
aged forty-seven.
Before his death, he submitted a memorial which said:
"My clan, over two hundred mouths,
was almost entirely exterminated by Mèngdé.
Only my cousin Dài remains,
who should continue the lineage and sacrificial offerings for my humble clan.
I deeply entrust him to Your Majesty.
I have no further words."
He was posthumously granted the title Wēi Hóu.
His son, Chéng, succeeded him.
Dài rose to the position of Píngběi Jiāngjūn,
and was enfeoffed as Chéncāng Hóu.
Mǎ Chāo's daughter was married to Ānpíng Wáng Lǐ.
Huáng Zhōng, courtesy name Hànshēng,
was a native of Nányáng.
Liú Biǎo, the Jīngzhōu Mù, appointed him Zhōnglángjiàng,
and he jointly defended Chángshā Yōuxiàn with Liú Biǎo's cousin Pán.
When Cáo Gōng conquered Jīngzhōu,
he was temporarily granted the title of Bì Jiāngjūn,
and remained in his former post,
subordinate to Hán Xuán, the Administrator of Chángshā.
When Xiānzhǔ pacified the southern commanderies,
Huáng Zhōng pledged his allegiance,
and followed him into Shǔ.
From Jiāmáng, he was given responsibility,
and returned to attack Liú Zhāng.
Huáng Zhōng always took the lead and broke enemy formations,
his courage and resolve surpassed the three armies.
After Yìzhōu was pacified,
he was appointed Tǎolú Jiāngjūn.
In the twenty-fourth year of Jiàn'ān (219 CE),
he attacked Xiàhóu Yuān at Dìngjūn Shān in Hànzhōng.
Xiàhóu Yuān's troops were very elite,
but Huáng Zhōng pushed forward resolutely,
encouraging and leading his soldiers.
With gongs and drums shaking the heavens
and shouts of joy echoing through the valleys,
he killed Xiàhóu Yuān in a single battle.
Xiàhóu Yuān's army was utterly defeated.
He was promoted to Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn.
That year,
when Xiānzhǔ became Hànzhōng Wáng,
he intended to appoint Huáng Zhōng as Hòujiāngjūn.
Zhūgě Liàng advised Xiānzhǔ, saying:
"Huáng Zhōng's reputation
has never been on par with Guān [Yǔ] or Mǎ [Chāo].
If he is now placed on the same rank,
Mǎ [Chāo] and Zhāng [Fēi], being nearby and
personally witnessing his achievements,
can still be reasoned with;
but Guān [Yǔ], hearing of it from afar,
will surely be displeased.
Is this not inadvisable?"
Xiānzhǔ said:
"I will personally explain it to him."
So, he was ranked equally with Guān Yǔ and others,
and granted the title Guānnèi Hóu.
The following year, he died,
and was posthumously granted the title Gāng Hóu.
His son
died young
without issue.
Zhào Yún, courtesy name Zǐlóng,
was a native of Zhēndìng, Chángshān.
Originally, he belonged to Gōngsūn Zàn.
When Gōngsūn Zàn sent Xiānzhǔ to resist Yuán Shào on behalf of Tián Kǎi,
Zhào Yún followed him,
becoming Xiānzhǔ's chief cavalry officer.
When Xiānzhǔ was pursued by Cáo Gōng at Dāngyáng Chángbǎn,
he abandoned his wife and children and fled south.
Zhào Yún personally carried the infant son,
who later became Hòuzhǔ,
and protected Gān Fūrén,
who later became Hòuzhǔ's mother.
All escaped harm.
He was promoted to Yámén Jiāngjūn.
When Xiānzhǔ entered Shǔ,
Zhào Yún remained in Jīngzhōu.
When Xiānzhǔ returned from Jiāmáng to attack Liú Zhāng,
he summoned Zhūgě Liàng.
Zhūgě Liàng led Zhào Yún and Zhāng Fēi up the river west,
pacifying commanderies and counties.
Upon reaching Jiāngzhōu,
he dispatched Zhào Yún to ascend the Jiāng River via the outer waterways to Jiāngyáng,
to meet Zhūgě Liàng in Chéngdū.
After Chéngdū was pacified,
Zhào Yún was appointed Yìjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Jiànxīng (223 CE),
he was made Zhōnghùjūn and Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed as Yǒngchāng Tínghóu,
and then promoted to Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn.
In the fifth year (227 CE),
he followed Zhūgě Liàng to station in Hànzhōng.
The following year (228 CE),
Zhūgě Liàng marched out his army,
feigning a move through the Xié Gǔ Dào.
Cáo Zhēn sent a large force to counter it.
Zhūgě Liàng ordered Zhào Yún and Dèng Zhī to resist them,
while he personally attacked Qíshān.
Zhào Yún and Dèng Zhī's forces were weak and the enemy strong,
resulting in a defeat at Jīgǔ.
However, they rallied their troops and held their ground,
avoiding a complete rout.
Upon the army's retreat,
he was demoted to Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn.
He died in the seventh year (229 CE),
and was posthumously granted the title Shùnpíng Hóu.
Initially,
during Xiānzhǔ's time,
only Fǎ Zhèng received a posthumous title.
During Hòuzhǔ's time,
Zhūgě Liàng's accomplishments and virtues overshadowed the world,
and Jiǎng Wǎn and Fèi Yī bore the heavy responsibilities of the state,
so they also received posthumous titles.
Chén Zhī, due to imperial favor,
received special commendation.
Xiàhóu Bà, having come from afar to return to the state,
also received a posthumous title.
Thus, Guān Yǔ, Zhāng Fēi, Mǎ Chāo, Páng Tǒng, Huáng Zhōng, and Zhào Yún were subsequently granted posthumous titles.
Contemporary opinion regarded this as an honor.
Zhào Yún's son, Tǒng, succeeded him.
He rose to the position of Hǔbēn Zhōngláng,
supervising the acting Commander of the Army.
His second son, Guǎng,
was a Yámén Jiāng.
He followed Jiāng Wéi to Tàzhōng
and died in battle on the front line.
Commentary says: Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi were both called enemies of ten thousand men,
and were renowned fierce warriors of their time.
Guān Yǔ repaid Cáo Gōng for his kindness,
and Zhāng Fēi righteously released Yán Yán.
Both possessed the demeanor of national heroes.
However, Guān Yǔ was rigid and arrogant,
and Zhāng Fēi was violent and ungrateful.
Their shortcomings led to their defeats,
which is a natural consequence.
Mǎ Chāo, relying on his martial prowess and courage,
caused the downfall of his entire clan.
What a pity!
Would it not have been better
to achieve prosperity through adversity?
Huáng Zhōng and Zhào Yún were strong, tenacious, and fierce,
both serving as crucial enforcers.
Were they not like Guàn Yīng and Téng Yìn?
Biography of Páng Tǒng and Fǎ Zhèng, Chapter Seven
Páng Tǒng, courtesy name Shìyuán,
was a native of Xiāngyáng.
In his youth, he was plain and dull,
and no one recognized his talent.
Sīmǎ Huī of Yǐngchuān, who was refined and discerning in recognizing people,
met Páng Tǒng when the latter was in his prime.
Sīmǎ Huī was picking mulberries from a tree,
and had Páng Tǒng sit beneath it.
They conversed from noon until night.
Sīmǎ Huī was greatly impressed by him,
and declared that Páng Tǒng would be the finest scholar in the southern provinces.
From then on, Páng Tǒng gradually became known.
Later, the commandery appointed him as Registrar (Gōngcáo).
He had a fondness for human relationships
and was diligent in nurturing them.
Whenever he praised someone,
he often exaggerated their abilities.
People at the time found this strange and asked him about it.
Páng Tǒng replied:
"The world is now in great chaos,
and the refined way is in decline.
Good people are few, and bad people are many.
If we wish to revive customs
and promote morality,
without embellishing their reputation, their fame will not be sufficient to inspire admiration and emulation.
If there is nothing to admire and emulate, fewer people will strive to do good.
If I praise ten and am wrong about five,
I still get half right,
and this can elevate worldly instruction
and encourage the ambitious to exert themselves.
Is this not acceptable?"
When the Wú general Zhōu Yú helped the Former Lord (Liú Bèi) capture Jīngzhōu,
he was subsequently appointed Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Nánjùn.
When Zhōu Yú died,
Páng Tǒng escorted the funeral cortege to Wú.
Many people in Wú had heard of his reputation.
When he was about to return west,
everyone gathered at Chāngmén.
Lù Jì, Gù Shào, and Quán Cóng all came.
Páng Tǒng said,
"Lù Zǐ can be called a 'nag with the strength of a swift horse,'
and Gù Zǐ can be called a 'dull ox that can carry heavy loads and travel far.'"
He said to Quán Cóng,
"You are fond of charity and desirous of fame,
much like Fán Zǐzhāo of Rǔnán.
Although your wisdom and strength are not abundant,
you are still a fine talent of your time."
Lù Jì and Gù Shào said to Páng Tǒng,
"If the world were at peace,
we would analyze the talents of the four seas together with you."
They formed a deep bond with Páng Tǒng before returning.
When the Former Lord governed Jīngzhōu,
Páng Tǒng was appointed Magistrate of Léiyáng as an Assistant (Cóngshì).
He neglected his duties in the county
and was dismissed from office.
The Wú general Lǔ Sù wrote a letter to the Former Lord, saying:
"Páng Shìyuán is not a talent for a mere county of a hundred *lǐ*.
If he were placed in the positions of Administrator of Affairs (Zhìzhōng) or Aide-de-camp (Biéjià),
only then would he be able to fully display his outstanding abilities."
Zhūgě Liàng also spoke of this to the Former Lord.
The Former Lord, upon meeting him and conversing well,
esteemed him greatly
and appointed him Administrator of Affairs (Zhìzhōng Cóngshì).
He was treated with affection and respect, second only to Zhūgě Liàng,
and subsequently served alongside Zhūgě Liàng as Army Adviser and Colonel (Jūnshī Zhōnglángjiàng).
Zhūgě Liàng remained to guard Jīngzhōu.
Páng Tǒng accompanied the Former Lord into Shǔ (Yìzhōu).
When Liú Zhāng, the Inspector (Mù) of Yìzhōu, met the Former Lord at Fú,
Páng Tǒng proposed a strategy:
"Now, taking advantage of this meeting,
you can seize him.
Then the General will not have the toil of warfare and can peacefully secure a province."
The Former Lord said,
"Having just entered another's territory,
our benevolence and trustworthiness are not yet established.
This is not permissible."
After Liú Zhāng returned to Chéngdū,
the Former Lord was to campaign north for Liú Zhāng against Hànzhōng.
Páng Tǒng again advised:
"Secretly select elite troops,
travel day and night,
and directly attack Chéngdū.
Liú Zhāng is not martial,
and has always been unprepared.
If a large army arrives suddenly,
it can be settled in one stroke.
This is the best plan.
Yáng Huái and Gāo Pèi
are Liú Zhāng's renowned generals,
each relying on strong troops,
guarding the passes.
We hear they have repeatedly submitted memorials and admonitions to Liú Zhāng,
urging him to send the General back to Jīngzhōu.
Before the General arrives,
send a message to them,
saying that Jīngzhōu is in urgent danger
and you wish to return to rescue it,
and also order preparations,
outwardly making it appear as if you are returning.
These two men, being convinced by the General's renowned valor
and delighted by the General's departure,
will surely come to meet you on light cavalry.
The General can then seize them,
take their troops,
and then march towards Chéngdū.
This is the middle plan.
To retreat to Báidì,
link up with Jīngzhōu,
and then slowly plot to conquer it,
this is the inferior plan.
If you hesitate and do not leave,
it will lead to great trouble,
and you cannot delay much longer."
The Former Lord approved of the middle plan,
and immediately executed Yáng Huái and Gāo Pèi,
then turned towards Chéngdū,
conquering every place he passed.
At a grand gathering in Fú,
wine was served and music played.
The Former Lord said to Páng Tǒng,
"Today's gathering
can be called joyful."
Páng Tǒng replied,
"To attack another's country and find joy in it
is not the act of a benevolent army."
The Former Lord, being drunk,
angrily said,
"King Wǔ attacked King Zhòu,
with singing before and dancing after.
Was he not benevolent?
Your words are inappropriate;
you should quickly get up and leave!"
Thereupon, Páng Tǒng slowly withdrew.
The Former Lord soon regretted it
and asked him to return.
Páng Tǒng resumed his former seat,
without any hint of apology or gratitude,
eating and drinking as usual.
The Former Lord said to him,
"Regarding the discussion just now,
who was at fault?"
Páng Tǒng replied,
"Both ruler and minister were at fault."
The Former Lord laughed heartily,
and the feast continued as before.
Advancing to besiege Luòxiàn,
Páng Tǒng led his troops to attack the city.
He was struck by a stray arrow
and died
at the age of thirty-six.
The Former Lord grieved deeply,
weeping whenever he spoke of him.
He appointed Páng Tǒng's father as Gentleman Consultant (Yìláng)
and later promoted him to Grand Master of Remonstrance (Jiànyì Dàfū).
Zhūgě Liàng personally performed the ceremonial bow for him.
Páng Tǒng was posthumously granted the title Marquis within the Passes (Guānnèi Hóu)
and given the posthumous name Jìng Hóu.
Páng Tǒng's son, Hóng,
courtesy name Jùshī,
was upright and discerning in judging others.
He treated Chén Zhī, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng), with arrogance
and was suppressed by Chén Zhī.
He died while serving as Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Fúlíng.
Páng Tǒng's younger brother, Lín,
as Administrator of Affairs (Zhìzhōng Cóngshì) in Yǐzhōu, joined General Who Guards the North (Zhènběi Jiāngjūn) Huáng Quán in the campaign against Wú.
When the army was defeated,
he followed Huáng Quán into Wèi.
Wèi enfeoffed him as a Marquis (Lièhóu)
and he reached the position of Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Jùlù.
Fǎ Zhèng, courtesy name Xiàozhí,
((Right) ) was a man from Méi
His grandfather, Zhēn,
was known for his integrity and high reputation.
In the early Jiàn'ān period,
the empire suffered from famine.
Zhèng, along with Mèng Dá from the same commandery, went to Shǔ to seek refuge with Liú Zhāng.
After a long time, he became the Magistrate of Xīndū,
and was later summoned to serve as Aide-de-Camp for Military Affairs.
As he was not given important positions,
and was slandered by other sojourners in the province and district for his immoral conduct,
his ambitions remained unfulfilled.
Zhāng Sōng, an assistant of Yìzhōu, was on good terms with Zhèng.
He felt that Liú Zhāng was not capable of achieving great things
and often secretly sighed.
When Zhāng Sōng returned from seeing Cáo Gōng in Jīngzhōu,
he advised Liú Zhāng to break ties with Cáo Gōng and ally himself with the Former Lord.
Liú Zhāng asked,
"Who can be sent as an envoy?"
Zhāng Sōng then recommended Zhèng.
Zhèng declined,
but was compelled to go.
Upon his return,
Zhèng praised the Former Lord to Zhāng Sōng, saying he possessed great strategic talent.
They secretly conspired and agreed
to jointly support him,
but lacked an opportunity.
Later, when Liú Zhāng heard that Cáo Gōng intended to send a general to conquer Zhāng Lǔ and became fearful,
Zhāng Sōng then persuaded Liú Zhāng that he should invite the Former Lord
to campaign against Zhāng Lǔ.
Zhèng was again ordered to carry the message.
After Zhèng conveyed the instructions,
he secretly presented a plan to the Former Lord, saying:
"With your brilliant general's exceptional talent,
and taking advantage of Governor Liú's weakness;
Zhāng Sōng,
the province's trusted aide,
will respond from within;
then, relying on the wealth of Yìzhōu
and the natural defenses of the Heavenly Storehouse,
to accomplish this great task
is as easy as turning one's hand."
The Former Lord agreed.
He sailed upstream and west,
and met Liú Zhāng at Fú.
He went north to Jiāmèng,
then returned south to take Liú Zhāng.
Zhèng Dù said to Zhāng:
"The Left General's army is isolated, attacking us;
his troops number less than ten thousand,
his soldiers and masses have not yet submitted,
he relies on wild grains,
and his army lacks baggage trains.
His best plan would be to drive all the people of Bāxī and Zītóng west of the Fúshuǐ river,
burning all their granaries and wild grains,
without exception.
Then, we should build high ramparts and deep moats,
and calmly await them.
When they arrive
and request battle,
do not agree.
After a long time without resources,
in no more than a hundred days,
they will certainly flee on their own.
If we then strike them as they flee,
we will surely capture them."
The Former Lord heard of this and disliked it,
asking Zhèng about it.
Zhèng said:
"He will ultimately not use it;
there is nothing to worry about."
Zhāng indeed acted as Zhèng had said,
telling his subordinates:
"I have heard of repelling enemies to bring peace to the people,
but I have never heard of moving the people to avoid enemies."
Thereupon, he dismissed Dù
and did not use his plan.
When the army had surrounded Luòchéng,
Zhèng sent a letter to Zhāng, saying:
"I, Zhèng, am by nature without stratagems,
and our allied relationship has been damaged.
I fear that those around you do not understand the beginning and end of the matter,
and will certainly attribute all blame to me,
causing me shame and ruin,
and bringing disgrace upon your subordinates.
This is why I have withdrawn myself externally,
not daring to report back.
I fear that your sagacious hearing would be defiled by my voice,
and thus I have not sent letters of respect in the interim.
Reflecting on our past encounters,
I gaze with deep regret.
However, considering how I repeatedly revealed my innermost thoughts before,
from the very beginning to the end,
I truly concealed no feelings
and left nothing unsaid.
It is only that my foolishness and shallow strategy
and my sincerity failed to move you,
leading to this outcome.
Now, the affairs of the state are in peril,
and disaster is imminent.
Though cast aside and external,
my words may still be hateful,
yet I am greedy to express my full thoughts
to exhaust my remaining loyalty.
Your original intentions, enlightened General,
are known to me, Zhèng.
You truly wished not to displease the Left General,
and yet it ultimately came to this.
Those around you do not understand the ways of heroes in their undertakings,
deeming it permissible to violate trust and defile oaths,
and to deal with matters based on whims and emotions.
As days and months pass,
they seek to please your ears and eyes,
conforming and assenting to your wishes,
failing to plan far ahead and consider deep strategies for the state.
Once the situation had changed,
they again failed to assess the balance of strength and weakness,
believing the Left General's army to be isolated and distant,
without stored provisions,
and hoping to use superior numbers to defeat fewer,
prolonging the confrontation.
But from the pass to this point,
every place they passed through has been broken.
Our detached palaces and separate garrisons
are falling apart daily.
Though Luòchéng has ten thousand soldiers,
they are all troops from broken formations,
and generals from defeated armies.
If you wish to contend in a battle of a single day,
then the strength of your soldiers and generals
is truly incomparable.
If each side wishes to plan for a long period and calculate provisions,
then this camp's defenses are already solid,
and grains have been stockpiled.
But your territory, enlightened General, is shrinking daily,
your people are increasingly distressed,
your enemies are growing numerous,
and the areas you supply are vast and distant.
In my humble opinion,
I believe you will surely be exhausted first,
and will not be able to sustain a long duration.
Even just holding out pointlessly,
you cannot endure.
Now, Zhāng Yìdé's tens of thousands of troops
have already secured Bādōng,
entered the borders of Jiānwéi,
and are dividing and pacifying Zīzhōng and Déyáng.
With three paths of invasion,
how will you defend against them?
Those who initially advised you, enlightened General,
must have believed this army to be isolated and distant without provisions,
with inadequate supply lines,
and few troops without reinforcements.
Now, the path from Jīngzhōu is open,
with forces tens of times greater.
Moreover, Sūn Chējì has sent his younger brother and Lǐ Yì, Gān Níng, and others as their reinforcements.
If you contend over the relative strength of host and guest,
seeking victory through territory,
then they now fully possess Bādōng,
and over half of Guǎnghàn and Jiānwéi
is already secured.
The single commandery of Bāxī
is also no longer yours, enlightened General.
Considering that Yìzhōu relies solely on Shǔ,
Shǔ itself is also broken;
two-thirds are lost,
officials and people are exhausted and distressed,
and eight out of ten households desire rebellion.
If the enemy is distant, the common people cannot bear the levies;
if the enemy is near, they will change allegiance overnight.
The various counties of Guǎnghàn
are a clear example.
Furthermore, Yúfù and Guāntóu are truly the gates of fortune and misfortune for Yìzhōu.
Now both gates are entirely open,
strong cities have all fallen,
all armies are broken,
and soldiers and generals are utterly depleted.
Yet the enemy forces are advancing on several paths simultaneously,
already having entered your vital regions.
Sitting idly guarding Dū and Luò,
the prospects of survival or destruction
are clearly visible.
These are but broad outlines,
merely external comparisons;
the remaining intricate details
are difficult to express fully in words.
Even I, Zhèng, with my humble foolishness,
know that this matter cannot be salvaged.
How much more so the enlightened and resourceful strategists around you, enlightened General?
How could they not see these facts?
They merely seek temporary good fortune morning and evening,
aiming for acceptance and flattery,
without considering long-term plans,
none willing to offer their wholehearted good counsel.
If the situation becomes desperate and forces are exhausted,
they will each seek their own survival,
to save their households,
turning and shifting allegiances,
differing from their present calculations,
and will not die for you, enlightened General.
Yet your esteemed household will still have to bear the sorrow.
Although I, Zhèng, incur the slander of disloyalty,
my heart tells me that I have not betrayed your sagacious virtue.
Reflecting on our shared principles,
I truly feel a secret pang of sorrow.
The Left General, from the very beginning of his campaign,
has held an enduring affection,
truly without ill intent.
I humbly believe a change can be planned
to protect your esteemed household."
In the nineteenth year,
he advanced and besieged Chéngdū.
Liú Zhāng's Shǔjùn Administrator Xǔ Jìng intended to scale the wall and surrender,
but the matter was discovered
and did not succeed.
Liú Zhāng, sensing that ruin was near,
therefore did not execute Xǔ Jìng.
After Liú Zhāng submitted,
the Former Lord, because of this, lightly regarded Xǔ Jìng and did not employ him.
Fǎ Zhèng said:
“There are those in the world who acquire an empty reputation without the substance,
and Xǔ Jìng is one such person.
However, our Lord is now beginning a great enterprise,
and it is impossible to explain to every person in the world.
Xǔ Jìng's undeserved fame
has spread throughout the four seas.
If he is not treated with courtesy,
people in the world will on this account say that our Lord belittles worthy men.
It is appropriate to treat him with respect
to dazzle those near and far,
recalling how King Yān treated Guō Kuí.”
Thereupon, the Former Lord treated Xǔ Jìng generously.
He appointed Fǎ Zhèng as Shǔjùn Administrator and General Wielding Military Might (Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn),
to command the capital region externally
and be the chief strategist internally.
Any kindness he received,
or even the slightest grudge,
was always repaid.
He arbitrarily killed and injured several people who had offended him.
Someone said to Zhūgě Liàng:
“Fǎ Zhèng acts too wildly in Shǔjùn.
General, you should inform the Lord
to curb his power and influence.”
Zhūgě Liàng replied:
“When the Lord was in Gōng'ān,
he feared the strength of Cáo Gōng to the north,
and dreaded Sūn Quán's pressure to the east.
Closer still, he feared Lady Sūn causing trouble right under his nose.
At that time,
he was like a wolf stumbling forward and backward.
Fǎ Xiàozhí (Fǎ Zhèng) served as his wings,
allowing him to soar freely
and become unrestrainable.
How can we stop Fǎ Zhèng from acting as he wishes!”
Originally,
Sūn Quán had given his sister in marriage to the Former Lord.
The sister was quick-witted and fierce,
possessing the character of her brothers.
Her maids, numbering over a hundred,
all personally held swords and stood by her.
Whenever the Former Lord entered,
his heart was always filled with apprehension.
Zhūgě Liàng also knew that the Former Lord genuinely loved and trusted Fǎ Zhèng,
hence he spoke in this manner.
In the twenty-second year,
Fǎ Zhèng advised the Former Lord, saying:
“Cáo Cāo, with one move, brought down Zhāng Lǔ
and secured Hànzhōng.
Yet he did not leverage this momentum to conquer Bā and Shǔ,
but instead left Xiàhóu Yuān and Zhāng Hé to garrison it,
and hastily returned north himself.
This is not because his intelligence was lacking or his strength insufficient;
he must have had internal worries forcing him to do so.
Now, considering the talents and strategies of Xiàhóu Yuān and Zhāng Hé,
they are no match for our nation's generals.
If we gather our forces and attack them,
we will surely be able to defeat them.
On the day we defeat them,
we can expand agriculture and accumulate grain,
observing vulnerabilities and waiting for opportunities.
At best, we can overthrow the enemy
and honor the imperial house.
In the middle, we can gradually annex Yōng and Liáng,
expanding our territory.
At worst, we can hold vital strongholds
and prepare for a protracted war.
This is truly heaven granting us this opportunity,
and the time must not be lost.”
The Former Lord approved of his plan,
and so he led his generals to advance troops into Hànzhōng.
Fǎ Zhèng also accompanied him.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the Former Lord crossed the Miǎnhuǐ south from Yángpíng,
advancing gradually along the mountains,
and established camps at Dìngjūn and Xìngshì.
Xiàhóu Yuān led troops to contest the ground.
Fǎ Zhèng said:
“We can strike now.”
The Former Lord ordered Huáng Zhōng to take the high ground, beat drums, and attack him.
Xiàhóu Yuān's army was greatly defeated,
and Xiàhóu Yuān and others were beheaded.
Cáo Gōng campaigned in the west,
and upon hearing Fǎ Zhèng's strategy,
said:
“I knew Xuándé (Liú Bèi) could not have come up with this himself;
he must have been taught by someone.”
The Former Lord was established as King of Hànzhōng,
and appointed Fǎ Zhèng as Minister of the Imperial Household (Shàngshūlìng) and General Protecting the Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
The following year, he died,
at the age of forty-five.
The Former Lord wept for him for several days.
He was posthumously titled Yìhóu.
His son, Fǎ Miǎo, was granted the title Marquis within the Pass (Guānnèihóu)
and served as Commandant of Chariots (Fèngchē Dūwèi) and Administrator of Hànyáng.
Although Zhūgě Liàng and Fǎ Zhèng
had different tastes and preferences,
they valued each other for their public service.
Zhūgě Liàng always admired Fǎ Zhèng's wisdom and stratagems.
After the Former Lord assumed the imperial title,
he intended to campaign east against Sūn Quán to avenge the disgrace of Guān Yǔ.
Many of his officials remonstrated,
but he did not listen.
In the second year of Zhāngwǔ,
the great army was defeated,
and returned to reside at Báidì.
Zhūgě Liàng sighed, saying:
“If Fǎ Xiàozhí (Fǎ Zhèng) were still alive,
he would have been able to restrain the Lord
and prevent him from going east.
Even if he had gone east,
he certainly would not have suffered such a catastrophic defeat.”
The commentary says: Páng Tǒng had a refined appreciation for people,
and was learned in scholarship and strategic thought.
At that time, people in Jīng and Chǔ called him a man of outstanding talent.
Fǎ Zhèng had keen insight into success and failure,
and possessed extraordinary plans and calculations,
but he was not known for his moral integrity.
If we compare them to officials of Wèi,
Páng Tǒng might be likened to Xún Yù's equal,
and Fǎ Zhèng to the likes of Chéng Yù and Guō Jiā?
Biography of Xǔ, Mí, Sūn, Jiǎn, Yī, Qín, Chapter Eight
Xǔ Jìng, courtesy name Wénxiū,
was a native of Píngyú, Rǔnán.
In his youth, he and his cousin Shào were both renowned,
and both had a reputation for judging human character,
but their private relationship was not harmonious.
Shào, as the Commandery's Supervisor of Merit (Jùn Gōngcáo),
excluded Xǔ Jìng, preventing him from being ranked and employed,
so he supported himself by grinding grain for horses.
Liú Yì of Yǐngchuān, who was Rǔnán Administrator,
then nominated Xǔ Jìng as an administrative clerk,
and he was examined as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate (Xiàolián).
He was appointed as a Gentleman of the Imperial Household (Shàngshū Láng)
and was in charge of selection.
When Emperor Líng died,
Dǒng Zhuó held power,
and appointed Zhōu Bì of Hànyáng as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
He and Xǔ Jìng jointly deliberated
on the advancement and demotion of scholars throughout the realm,
sifting out the corrupt
and promoting the obscure.
They promoted and employed Xún Shuǎng, Hán Róng, Chén Jì, and others from Yǐngchuān as Grandees, Ministers, and Commandery Administrators.
Hán Fù, a Minister of the Imperial Household, was appointed Governor of Jìzhōu.
Liú Dài, an Attendant Official, was appointed Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
Zhāng Zī of Yǐngchuān was appointed Administrator of Nányáng.
Kǒng Zhòu of Chénliú was appointed Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Zhāng Miǎo of Dōngjùn was appointed Administrator of Chénliú.
Xǔ Jìng was transferred to be Administrator of Bājùn,
but did not take the post,
and was appointed Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
When Hán Fù and the others arrived at their posts,
each raised an army and turned back towards the capital,
intending to execute Dǒng Zhuó.
Dǒng Zhuó angrily said to Zhōu Bì:
“You gentlemen said that I should promote worthy men.
I followed your advice,
not wishing to go against the hearts of the people in the world.
But the people you employed,
on the day they arrived at their posts,
turned around and plotted against me.
How have I let you down!”
He yelled at Zhōu Bì to leave
and had him executed outside.
Xǔ Jìng's cousin, Chén Liáng, the Chancellor of Chén,
also conspired with Kǒng Zhòu.
Xǔ Jìng, fearing execution,
fled to Kǒng Zhòu.
After Kǒng Zhòu's death,
he relied on Chén Yī, the Inspector of Yángzhōu.
After Chén Yī died,
Xǔ Gòng, the Commandant of Wújùn, and Wáng Láng, the Administrator of Kuàijī, had long been friends with Xǔ Jìng,
so he went to seek refuge with them.
Xǔ Jìng gathered and cared for his relatives,
managing their affairs and providing for them generously,
out of benevolence and kindness.
When Sūn Cè crossed the river eastward,
everyone fled to Jiāozhōu to escape the chaos.
Jìng sat by the riverbank himself,
first loading his dependants,
and all his distant relatives,
before leaving afterwards.
Those who witnessed it at the time could not help but sigh in admiration.
Upon reaching Jiāozhǐ,
the Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, Shì Xiè, treated him with great respect.
Yuán Huī of Chénguó resided temporarily in Jiāozhōu.
Huī wrote a letter to the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Xún Yù, saying:
"Xǔ Wénxiū is a man of outstanding talent and great distinction,
whose wisdom and strategy are sufficient to manage affairs.
Since his exile and wandering,
he has accompanied scholars,
and whenever there was trouble or urgency,
he always put others before himself,
sharing hunger and cold with his extended relatives, both close and distant.
His management of his peers,
his benevolence, forgiveness, and compassion,
all demonstrate effective actions;
it is impossible to enumerate them one or two at a time."
Zhāng Xiáng of Jùlù
was dispatched to Jiāobù on royal command.
He took the opportunity to recruit Jìng,
wishing to make a solemn pact with him,
but Jìng refused.
Jìng wrote a letter to Cáo Gōng, saying: "The world's paths are beset by war and strife,
calamities and disorder have converged.
Faint-hearted and timid, I stole away to live,
hiding myself among the barbarians.
Ten years have passed,
and the rituals of joy and sorrow have been abandoned.
Formerly, in Kuàijī,
I received your
letter,
its words and sentiments were sincere and intimate,
an enduring promise not forgotten.
Pressured by Yuán Shù, who defied commands and ruined his clan,
inciting numerous rebels,
all routes were blocked.
Although my heart longed for the north wind,
I wished
to go but had no means.
Zhènglǐ's army retreated,
Shù's forces advanced,
Kuàijī was overthrown,
Jǐngxīng lost his position,
and the Three Rivers and Five Lakes
all became the territory of the invaders.
At that time, I was in dire straits,
with no one to turn to.
So I, along with Yuán Pèi, Dèng Zǐxiào, and others, drifted across the vast sea,
south to Jiāozhōu.
We passed through the lands of Dōng'ōu, Mǐn, and Yuè,
travelling for tens of thousands of
lǐ,
without seeing Hàn territory.
Tossed about by wind and waves,
we ran out of food and ate grass.
Starving corpses piled up,
more than half of us died.
After reaching Nánhǎi,
I met with the administrator's son Xiàodé,
and learned
that you, sir, had risen with loyalty and righteousness,
marshalled your grand army,
welcomed the Emperor's chariot westward,
and inspected Zhōngyuè.
Hearing this good news,
I was both sad and joyful.
Immediately, with Yuán Pèi
and Xú Yuánxián, I once again made preparations,
intending to go north to Jīngzhōu.
However, the Yí and Yuè tribes in various counties of Cāngwú suddenly rose in revolt,
the provincial administration was overthrown,
and the roads were blocked.
Yuánxián
was killed,
and the old and weak were all slaughtered.
Jìng then followed the riverbanks for over five thousand lǐ,
and again encountered a plague.
My aunt perished,
as did many of my relatives,
and among my own wives and children,
almost all
were lost at once.
Again supporting each other,
we arrived at this commandery.
By my reckoning, of those who died from warfare or illness,
only one or two out of ten survived.
The hardships of life,
the extent of the suffering,
how
can it be fully expressed!
Fearing ultimate downfall,
and forever becoming captives,
I was consumed by anxiety and sorrow,
forgetting sleep and food.
I wished to attach myself to an envoy bringing tribute to the court,
and if I could secure passage,
to return to the imperial court and die there.
But the land and water routes in Jīngzhōu were impassable,
and the postal service in Jiāobù was cut off.
I wished to go up to Yìzhōu,
but there were also strict defenses,
and former officials and magistrates
were not
allowed entry.
The former Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, Shì Wēiyàn,
had entrusted me deeply to his brothers in Yìzhōu,
and Jìng also wrote a letter himself,
with painstaking earnestness,
but it remained
unanswered,
with no response yet.
Though I look up to your radiant light,
stretching my neck and standing on tiptoe,
how can I sprout wings and reach you myself?
I know that the sagely lord is truly wise,
and has clearly bestowed upon you, sir, the charge of exclusive military command.
All those who rebel,
most have been punished and suppressed.
I imagine those who contend with you are now of one mind,
and those who submit share
your aims.
Furthermore, Zhāng Zǐyún, formerly in the capital,
was dedicated to upholding the royal house.
Although he is now in a desolate region,
unable to participate in the central government,
he is also a bulwark of the state,
and your
external support.
If Jīng and Chǔ are pacified,
and the king's beneficence reaches south,
and you, sir, should suddenly send a message to Zǐyún,
diligently asking him to secure my safety and connect with me,
allowing me to borrow a route
to exit via Jīngzhōu,
otherwise,
you should introduce me to your brothers in Yìzhōu,
so they may receive me.
If Heaven grants me more years,
and people delay my misfortune,
and I can return to
the state to die,
releasing me from the burden of being a fugitive,
and my body can mingle with the Nine Springs,
what more regrets could I have!
But if times are perilous or easy,
affairs are advantageous or difficult,
human life is impermanent,
and I perish without
achieving this,
then I will forever bear the guilt and responsibility,
entering the distant lands.
Formerly, Yíngqiū assisted the Zhōu dynasty,
wielding the battle-axe with sole authority.
Bólù assisted the Hàn dynasty,
with Hǔbēn guards clearing the way.
Today, you, sir, support the endangered and uphold the tottering,
serving as a pillar of the state,
bearing the responsibility of Shī Wàng,
and combining the gravitas of Huò Guāng.
The Five Marquises and Nine Earls
are controlled by your hand.
From ancient times to the present,
no minister has been as honored as you, sir.
Indeed, those with high rank have deep worries,
and those with abundant stipends bear heavy responsibilities.
You, sir, occupy a position of high rank,
and hold a place of heavy responsibility.
Words spoken from your mouth
immediately become rewards and punishments;
the thoughts
you harbor
become fortune and misfortune.
If your actions accord with the Way,
then the state will be at peace;
if your actions deviate from the Way,
then the four quarters will be scattered in chaos.
The safety or danger of the state
rests upon
you, sir;
the lives of the common people
depend on your administration.
From China to the barbarians,
all look to you with expectation.
As you, sir, undertake this responsibility,
how can you not extensively review historical records for the causes of rise and fall,
and
the mechanisms of honor and disgrace,
abandon old animosities,
be broad-minded and harmonious with all officials,
carefully assess all talents,
and select people for office?
If you find the right person,
even if he is an enemy, you must promote him;
if
If he is not the right person,
even if closely related, he should not be entrusted.
To bring peace to the state and its altars,
and to save the common people,
when the task is accomplished and the功gōng achieved,
then let his name be recorded in music,
and his deeds carved in metal and stone.
I wish you, my lord,
to strive for this!
Cherish yourself for the sake of the country,
and love yourself for the sake of the people.”
Fēi Xiáng 費翔 regretted that Yǐng Jìng 尹靖 did not accept his offer,
so he searched for the letters Yǐng Jìng 尹靖 had sent to him
and threw them all into the water.
Later, Liú Zhāng 劉璋 sent an envoy to invite Yǐng Jìng 尹靖,
and Yǐng Jìng 尹靖 came to enter Shǔ 蜀.
Liú Zhāng 劉璋 appointed Yǐng Jìng 尹靖 as the Administrator of Bā Jùn 巴郡 and Guǎnghàn 廣漢.
Sòng Zhòngzǐ 宋仲子 of Nányáng 南陽 wrote to Wáng Shāng 王商, the Administrator of Shǔ Jùn 蜀郡, from Jīng Zhōu 荊州, saying:
“Wénxiū 文休 is unrestrained and outstanding,
possessing abilities fit for his generation;
you should take him as your guide.”
In the sixteenth year of Jiàn'ān 建安 (211 CE),
he was transferred to Shǔ Jùn 蜀郡.
In the nineteenth year (214 CE),
the Former Lord conquered Shǔ 蜀,
and appointed Yǐng Jìng 尹靖 as Chief Clerk to the General of the Left.
When the Former Lord became King of Hànzhōng 漢中,
Yǐng Jìng 尹靖 was appointed Grand Tutor.
When the Former Lord assumed the imperial title,
he issued an edict to Yǐng Jìng 尹靖, saying:
“I have been fortunate to receive this great enterprise,
and to rule over all the states.
Day and night I am fearful,
dreading that I cannot bring peace.
The hundred surnames are not harmonious,
the five ranks are not humble.
You shall be the Minister of Education;
reverently propagate the five teachings,
and be broad-minded.
My lord, strive diligently!
Uphold virtue without slackness,
and thus fulfill my intentions.”
Although Yǐng Jìng 尹靖 was over seventy years old,
he loved and delighted in people,
and encouraged and admitted rising talents,
never tiring of insightful discussions.
Even Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮 would bow to him.
He died in the second year of Zhāngwǔ 章武 (222 CE).
His son, Qīn 欽,
died young before Yǐng Jìng 尹靖.
Qīn's 欽 son, Yóu 游,
was a Master of Writing during the Jǐngyào 景耀 reign (258-263 CE).
Initially, Yǐng Jìng 尹靖 treated Chén Jì 陳紀 of Yǐngchuān 潁川 as an elder brother,
and was close to Yuán Huàn 袁渙 of Chén Jùn 陳郡, Huà Xīn 華歆 of Píngyuán 平原, Wáng Lǎng 王朗 of Dōnghǎi 東海, and others.
Huà Xīn 華歆, Wáng Lǎng 王朗, and Chén Jì's 陳紀 son Qún 群,
who became high officials and grand tutors in the early Wèi 魏 dynasty,
all wrote letters to Yǐng Jìng 尹靖,
expressing their enduring friendship.
The sentiments were sincere and heartfelt,
but the writings are numerous and therefore not recorded here.
Mí Zhú 麋竺, courtesy name Zǐzhòng 子仲,
was a native of Qú 朐 in Dōnghǎi 東海.
His ancestors were merchants for generations,
with tens of thousands of retainers and servants,
and wealth amounting to hundreds of millions.
Later, Táo Qiān 陶謙, the Governor of Xú Zhōu 徐州, appointed him as Senior Clerk.
When Táo Qiān 陶謙 died,
Mí Zhú 麋竺, following Táo Qiān's 陶謙 dying wish,
welcomed the Former Lord at Xiǎopèi 小沛.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān 建安 (196 CE),
Lǚ Bù 呂布, taking advantage of the Former Lord's absence to repel Yuán Shù 袁術,
attacked Xiàpèi 下邳,
and captured the Former Lord's wife and children.
The Former Lord moved his army to Hǎixī 海西 in Guǎnglíng 廣陵.
Mí Zhú 麋竺 then offered his younger sister to the Former Lord as his wife,
and provided two thousand servants and retainers,
and gold, silver, and currency to assist the military funds;
at that time of dire need,
the army was revived thanks to this.
Later, Cáo Gōng 曹公 recommended Mí Zhú 麋竺 to oversee Yíng Jùn 嬴郡 as its Administrator,
and Mí Zhú's 麋竺 younger brother Fāng 芳 as Chancellor of Péngchéng 彭城.
Both resigned their offices
and followed the Former Lord in his wanderings.
When the Former Lord was about to go to Jīng Zhōu 荊州,
he sent Mí Zhú 麋竺 ahead to communicate with Liú Biǎo 劉表,
and appointed Mí Zhú 麋竺 as Aide to the General of the Left.
After Yì Zhōu 益州 was pacified,
he was appointed General who Pacifies Hàn,
his rank being above that of the General of the Army Adviser.
Mí Zhú 麋竺 was graceful and dignified,
but organizational talent was not his strength.
Therefore, he was treated with the courtesy due to a distinguished guest,
and never given command.
However, his rewards and favors were exceptional,
with no one comparable to him.
Fāng 芳 was appointed Administrator of Nán Jùn 南郡.
He worked with Guān Yǔ 關羽,
but privately harbored disloyalty
and defected to welcome Sūn Quán 孫權,
leading to Guān Yǔ's 關羽 defeat.
Mí Zhú 麋竺 bound himself and requested punishment.
The Former Lord comforted and admonished him, saying that a brother's crime does not implicate others,
and continued to treat him as before.
Mí Zhú 麋竺, ashamed and resentful, fell ill
and died about a year later.
His son, Wēi 威,
rose to the office of Commandant of Tiger Bannermen.
Wēi's 威 son, Zhào 照,
was Inspector of Tiger Cavalry.
From Mí Zhú 麋竺 to Zhào 照,
all were skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and adept at shooting and driving chariots, it is said.
Sūn Gān 孫乾, courtesy name Gōngyòu 公祐,
was a native of Běihǎi 北海.
When the Former Lord governed Xú Zhōu 徐州,
he appointed Sūn Gān 孫乾 as Aide,
who later followed him in his travels.
When the Former Lord turned against Cáo Gōng 曹公,
he sent Sūn Gān 孫乾 to establish ties with Yuán Shào 袁紹.
When he was about to go to Jīng Zhōu 荊州,
Sūn Gān 孫乾, along with Mí Zhú 麋竺, again served as envoys to Liú Biǎo 劉表,
and all matters were handled as desired.
Later, Liú Biǎo 劉表 wrote to Yuán Shàng 袁尚,
describing the disputes and divisions between his brothers,
saying:
“Whenever I discussed this matter with General Liú 劉 and Sūn Gōngyòu 孫公祐,
I never failed to feel heartbroken to the core,
and grieved for them.”
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
When the Former Lord pacified Yì Zhōu 益州,
Sūn Gān 孫乾 was promoted from Aide to General of Upholding Loyalty,
treated with less formality than Mí Zhú 麋竺,
and on par with Jiǎn Yōng 簡雍.
After a short while,
he died.
Jiǎn Yōng 簡雍, courtesy name Xiànhé 憲和,
was a native of Zhuō Jùn 涿郡.
He had known the Former Lord since childhood
and followed him in his travels.
When the Former Lord arrived in Jīng Zhōu 荊州,
Jiǎn Yōng 簡雍, along with Mí Zhú 麋竺 and Sūn Gān 孫乾, all served as Aides,
often acting as a debater
and traveling on missions.
When the Former Lord entered Yì Zhōu 益州,
Liú Zhāng 劉璋 met Jiǎn Yōng 簡雍
and liked him very much.
Later, when the Former Lord besieged Chéngdū 成都,
he sent Jiǎn Yōng 簡雍 to persuade Liú Zhāng 劉璋.
Liú Zhāng 劉璋 then rode in the same carriage with Jiǎn Yōng 簡雍
and surrendered outside the city.
The Former Lord appointed Jiǎn Yōng 簡雍 as General who Illuminates Virtue.
He was easy-going and eloquent in discussions,
with a character that was simple, arrogant, and unconventional.
Even when seated with the Former Lord,
he would sit with his legs spread out and lean back,
without proper decorum,
indulging himself;
below Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮, he alone would occupy a whole mat,
pillowing his head and speaking while lying down,
never showing deference.
At that time, due to drought, alcohol was prohibited,
and brewers were punished.
An official found brewing equipment in someone's home,
and some argued that the owner should be punished the same as a brewer.
Jiǎn Yōng 簡雍 was with the Former Lord on an outing,
and saw a man and woman walking on the road.
He said to the Former Lord:
“Those people want to commit adultery,
why aren't they bound?”
The Former Lord said:
“How do you know that?”
Jiǎn Yōng 簡雍 replied:
“They have the equipment for it,
just like those who want to brew.”
The Former Lord laughed heartily,
and pardoned the would-be brewers.
Jiǎn Yōng's 簡雍 humor
was all of this type.
Yī Jí, courtesy name Jībó,
was a native of Shānyáng.
In his youth, he relied on his fellow townsman, General of the Guard of the South Liú Biǎo.
When the Former Lord was in Jīngzhōu,
Jí often went to and from him, entrusting himself to him.
After Biǎo died,
he then followed the Former Lord south across the river,
and accompanied him into Yìzhōu.
Once Yìzhōu was pacified,
Jí was appointed Attendant Official for the General of the Left,
and was treated only slightly less favorably than Jiǎn Yǒng, Sūn Gān, and others.
He was dispatched east on a mission to Wú,
and Sūn Quán, hearing of his talent for debate,
wished to verbally humble him.
As Jí entered and bowed,
Quán said:
"Are you not weary serving a lord who lacks the Way?"
Jí immediately replied:
"One bow and one rise
are hardly enough to cause weariness."
Jí's quick wit
was always like this,
and Quán was greatly surprised by him.
Later, he was promoted to General of the Illustrious Civil Service,
and along with Zhūgě Liàng, Fǎ Zhèng, Liú Bā, and Lǐ Yán, he jointly drafted the Shǔ Code;
the formulation of the Shǔ Code
was due to these five men.
Qín Mì, courtesy name Zǐchì,
was a native of Miánzhú, Guǎnghàn.
From a young age, he possessed talent and learning.
When the prefecture and commandery offered him appointments,
he always claimed illness and did not go.
He submitted a memorial to the Provincial Governor Liú Yān,
recommending the scholar Rèn Dìngzǔ, saying:
"In the past, Bǎilǐ and Jiǎn Shú, though elderly, settled strategies,
and Gānlúo and Zǐqí, though young, established achievements.
Therefore, the Book of Documents praises the aged,
and the Classic of Changes commends Yán Yuān.
Thus, it is clear
that in selecting officials, ability is used
without regard for age.
However, since then,
throughout the empire, when talents are recommended and examined,
the majority are rising stars who overlook the old and established.
Public opinion is divided,
with agreements and disagreements equally split.
This is a leisurely pace for times of peace,
not an urgent matter for times of chaos.
Indeed, if one wishes to rescue the imperiled and pacify the chaotic,
cultivate oneself to bring peace to others,
then one should be outstanding and transcend the ordinary,
having different aims from the times,
astonishing neighboring states,
and startling the four directions,
conforming above to the will of Heaven
and below to the will of men.
When Heaven and man are in harmony,
and one examines oneself without fault,
even if one encounters misfortune and chaos,
what is there to worry about or fear?
In the past, Duke Yè of Chǔ loved dragons,
and when a divine dragon descended,
his feigned love was pierced through to Heaven;
how much more so should it be for genuine love?
Now, the recluse Rèn Ān possesses
benevolence, righteousness, and a straightforward path,
his fame spreading far and wide.
If he were to be examined and recognized,
then the entire province would submit.
In ancient times, Tāng elevated Yī Yǐn,
and the unbenevolent kept their distance;
Hé Wǔ recommended the two Gōngs,
and their double fame was recorded in bamboo and silk.
Thus, to covet the common high ground and neglect the ten-thousand-ren Mount Sōng,
to delight in immediate adornment and forget the praise of the world,
this is truly what the ancients valued and were cautious about.
If one is about to chisel stone to seek jade,
and dissect a clam to find pearls,
and now Suí and Hé gems are already brilliantly clear
like the bright sun,
what more is there to doubt?
Although I know one does not carry a torch in daylight,
as the sun provides ample light,
my foolish heart is merely
eager to present what it has seen."
During Liú Zhāng's time,
Wáng Shāng of the same commandery as Mì was an Administrator,
and he wrote to Mì, saying:
"Poverty and hardship,
when can they possibly end for a lifetime?
Biàn Hé flaunted his jade to illuminate the world;
you should come once
to meet with the honorable governor."
Mì replied in a letter, saying:
"In the past, Yáo honored Xǔ Yóu,
not that he wasn't magnanimous,
but Xǔ Yóu washed his ears.
Chǔ invited Zhuāng Zhōu,
not that they weren't expansive,
but he held his fishing rod and did not look back.
The Classic of Changes says, 'Firm indeed, it cannot be uprooted,'
so what is there to flaunt?
Moreover, with the lord's sagacity
and your being an excellent aide,
not to put forth the strategies of Xiāo and Zhāng at this time
is not enough to be considered wise.
I am able to bask my back in the fields,
recite Yán Shì's bamboo basket and gourd,
sing of Yuán Xiàn's humble dwelling,
and sometimes roam in the forests and marshes,
among the likes of Jú and Nì,
listening to the mournful cries of black apes,
observing cranes calling in the nine marshes.
To be at peace is joy,
to have no worries is blessing.
To occupy a name of emptiness,
to dwell as a tortoise without spiritual efficacy,
few know me,
then I am noble.
This is the autumn when I achieve my aspirations,
what sorrow of hardship is there?"
Later, Shāng established a shrine for Yán Jūn-píng and Lǐ Hóng.
Mì wrote to him, saying:
"Though ill and in reclusion,
I just learned that you are establishing shrines for Yán and Lǐ.
This can be called being generous to one's associates and diligent towards one's kind.
Observing Yán's writings,
they are unsurpassed in the world.
His noble conduct, like Yóu and Yí,
is as unmoving as mountains and peaks.
Even if Yáng Zǐ did not praise him,
he would naturally be illustrious.
If Lǐ Zhòngyuán had not encountered Fǎ Yán,
his renowned name would surely have fallen into oblivion,
because he lacked the writings of a tiger or leopard.
He can be said to have climbed the dragon and attached himself to the phoenix.
As for Yáng Zǐyún, he immersed himself in writing,
benefiting the world.
Mud-bound yet unsoiled,
his conduct rivaled the sages and teachers.
To this day, throughout the empire,
his words are spoken and praised.
When a state has such a person
to illuminate the four directions,
I find it strange that you neglect him
and do not establish a shrine.
Shǔ originally had no scholars.
Wén Wēng sent Xiàngrú east to receive the Seven Classics,
and on his return, he taught the officials and people.
Thus, Shǔ's scholarship rivaled Qí and Lǔ.
Therefore, the Geography Treatise says:
'Wén Wēng initiated its teaching,
and Xiàngrú was its master.'
The Han Dynasty acquired scholars
who flourished in their generation.
Those like Zhòngshū did not comprehend the fengshan sacrifices,
but Xiàngrú composed their rites.
Indeed, to be able to establish rites and create music,
to change customs and transform traditions,
is this not something beneficial to the world, regulated by rites?
Although there were the burdens of the royal grandson,
it is still like Confucius greatly admiring Duke Huán of Qí's hegemony,
and Gōngyáng deeming Shúshù's resignation admirable.
I too appreciate Chángqīng's transformative influence.
A shrine should be established for him,
and its inscription quickly finalized."
Previously,
Lǐ Quán (李權) borrowed the Zhàn Guó Cè (戰國策) from Mì (宓).
Mì (宓) said:
“The Warring States saw shifting alliances and power plays;
what good is it to use that?”
Quán (權) replied:
“Zhòngní (仲尼) and Yán Píng (嚴平)
assembled many books
to complete the Chūn Qiū (春秋) and Zhǐ Guī (指歸) writings.
Therefore, the sea is great because it gathers all streams,
and a _jūnzǐ_ (君子) is broad-minded because of his extensive knowledge.”
Mì (宓) retorted:
“If a book is not like the Shǐ Jì (史記) or Zhōu Tú (周圖),
Zhòngní (仲尼) would not collect it.
If a Dao is not void, tranquil, and natural,
Yán Píng (嚴平) would not expound it.
The sea, though it receives silt,
is cleansed once a year.
A _jūnzǐ_ (君子), despite extensive knowledge,
will not look upon what is contrary to _lǐ_ (禮).
Now, the Warring States is about the repeated strategies of Yí (儀) and Qín (秦),
killing others to preserve oneself,
and ruining others to sustain oneself—
this is what the classics condemn.
Therefore, Kǒng Fūzǐ (孔夫子), in his indignation, compiled the Chūn Qiū (春秋),
greatly emphasizing uprightness,
and re-edited the Xiào Jīng (孝經),
extensively presenting virtuous conduct.
Preventing trouble when it is nascent,
and suppressing it in advance,
this is why Lǎo Zǐ (老子) eliminates calamity before it even sprouts.
Is this not to be trusted!
Chéng Tāng (成湯), a great sage,
saw fish in the wilderness and felt the fault of excessive hunting.
Dìng Gōng (定公), a worthy ruler,
saw female musicians and abandoned court affairs.
Such examples
cannot be fully enumerated.
The Daoist school states: ‘Do not see what you desire,
to keep your heart undisturbed.’
Therefore, heaven and earth are upright and stable,
the sun and moon are upright and bright.
Their straightness is like an arrow;
this is what a _jūnzǐ_ (君子) follows.
The Hóng Fàn (洪範) records calamities
as arising from speech and appearance.
Why then the cunning power plays of the Warring States!”
Someone said to Mì (宓):
“You wish to compare yourself to Cháo Fù (巢父), Xǔ Yóu (許由), and the Four Hào (四皓).
Why then do you display literary elegance and rare brilliance?”
Mì (宓) replied:
“My writing cannot fully express my words,
and my words cannot fully express my thoughts.
How can there be any literary elegance to display!
In the past, Kǒng Fūzǐ (孔夫子) met Ái Gōng (哀公) three times,
and his words became seven volumes.
There are indeed matters that cannot be kept silent.
Jiē Yú (接輿) walked and sang,
and scholars honored him in their writings.
The Fisherman (漁父) sang of the Canglang (滄浪),
and the worthy acclaimed him in chapters.
These two individuals
had no desire for worldly fame.
A tiger is born with brilliant markings,
a phoenix is born with five colors.
Do they adorn themselves with five colors?
It is their natural disposition.
Indeed, the Hé Tú (河圖) and Luò Shū (洛書) arose from patterns,
the Six Classics arose from writings.
A _jūnzǐ_ (君子) admires literary virtue.
What harm is there in collecting literary embellishments!
With my foolishness,
I still feel shame at rectifying Zǐ Chéng's (子成) errors,
how much more so for those wiser than myself!”
After the Former Lord (先主) had settled Yìzhōu (益州),
Xiàhóu Zuǎn (夏侯纂), the Grand Administrator of Guǎnghàn (廣漢), invited Mì (宓) to be his mentor and Master of Rites (祭酒),
and to lead the Officer of the Five Bureaus (五官掾),
calling him "Zhòngfù" (仲父).
Mì (宓) claimed illness,
and lay in his chamber.
Zuǎn (纂) brought the Commandant of Merit (功曹) Gǔ Pǔ (古朴) and the Chief Clerk (主簿) Wáng Pǔ (王普),
and held a banquet with provisions at Mì's (宓) residence,
but Mì (宓) remained lying down as before.
Zuǎn (纂) asked Pǔ (朴):
“As for the means of livelihood in your noble province,
they truly surpass those of other provinces.
I wonder how the scholars compare to those of other provinces?”
Pǔ (朴) replied:
“Indeed, since the Former Hàn (漢) dynasty,
those holding peerage or official positions might not have been as numerous as in other provinces,
but as for their writings serving as models for the world,
they are not inferior to other provinces.
Yán Jūnpíng (嚴君平) saw the Huáng Lǎo (黃老) and wrote Zhǐ Guī (指歸).
Yáng Xióng (揚雄) saw the Yì (易) and wrote Tài Xuán (太玄);
he saw the Lùn Yǔ (論語) and wrote Fǎ Yán (法言).
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú (司馬相如) composed the Fēng Shàn (封禪) writings for Emperor Wǔ (武帝).
These are now known throughout the world.”
Zuǎn (纂) said:
“How about Zhòngfù (仲父)?”
Mì (宓) struck his cheek with a book,
and said:
