“May your Excellency not use the words of Zhòngfù (仲父) to refer to a lowly person.
I beg to present to your Excellency its fundamental records.
Shǔ (蜀) has the Wèn Fù (汶阜) mountains,
from whose heart the Jiāng (江) river flows.
The Emperor relies on it for prosperity,
and the spirits for blessings.
Thus, it can water a thousand _lǐ_ (里) of fertile land.
Among the four great rivers (淮､濟四瀆),
the Jiāng (江) is the foremost.
This is the first reason.
Yǔ (禹) was born in Shí Niǔ (石紐),
which is now Wènshān Jùn (汶山郡).
In ancient times, Yáo (堯) encountered great floods,
which Gǔn (鯀) failed to control.
Yǔ (禹) dredged the Jiāng (江) and channeled the Hé (河),
making them flow eastward into the sea,
thus removing harm for the people.
Since the birth of mankind, no achievement has been greater than this.
This is the second reason.
The Celestial Emperor governs from Fáng Xīn (房心),
and decides policies from Cān Fá (參伐).
Cān Fá (參伐) is the astrological domain of Yìzhōu (益州).
The Three Sovereigns (三皇) rode a divine chariot out of Gǔ Kǒu (谷口),
which is now Xié Gǔ (斜谷).
These are the fields and paths of my humble province.
How does your Excellency, with your refined perception, judge it compared to the rest of the world?”
At this, Zuǎn (纂) hesitated and had no further reply.
Yìzhōu invited Mì to be Jìjiǔ, an attendant.
After the Former Lord (Xiānzhǔ) assumed the imperial title,
he intended to campaign eastward against Wú.
Mì argued that the timing was certainly not advantageous.
He was consequently imprisoned and confined,
but later released.
In the second year of Jiànxīng (224 CE),
Chancellor Liàng, serving as Yìzhōu Mù,
selected Mì and welcomed him as Biéjià.
Soon after, he was appointed Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng and Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi.
Wú sent an envoy, Zhāng Wēn, to establish relations.
All the officials went to bid him farewell.
Everyone had gathered except for Mì.
Liàng repeatedly sent messengers to urge him to come.
Wēn asked:
"Who is that person?"
Liàng replied:
"He is a scholar from Yìzhōu."
When Mì arrived,
Wēn asked:
"Sir, do you study?"
Mì replied:
"Even five-foot tall children study, why would a humble person like me not?"
Wēn then asked:
"Does heaven have a head?"
Mì replied:
"It does."
Wēn asked:
"Where is it located?"
Mì replied:
"In the west.
The *Shī* (Odes) says: 'He then looked back to the west.'
From this, we can infer
that its head is in the west."
Wēn asked:
"Does heaven have ears?"
Mì replied:
"Heaven is high but hears the humble.
The *Shī* (Odes) says: 'The crane cries in the nine marshes,
its sound is heard in heaven.'
If it had no ears,
how could it hear?"
Wēn asked:
"Does heaven have feet?"
Mì replied:
"It does.
The *Shī* (Odes) says: 'Heaven's steps are difficult and dangerous,
this son does not follow.'
If it had no feet,
how could it walk?"
Wēn asked:
"Does heaven have a surname?"
Mì replied:
"It does."
Wēn asked:
"What surname?"
Mì replied:
"It is Liú."
Wēn asked:
"How do you know that?"
Mì answered:
"The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) is surnamed Liú,
thus I know it."
Wēn asked:
"Does the sun rise in the east?"
Mì replied:
"Although it rises in the east, it sets in the west."
His answers to questions were like an echo,
coming forth instantly.
Thereupon, Wēn greatly admired and submitted to him.
Mì's literary arguments
were all of this kind.
He was promoted to Dà Sīnóng
and died in the fourth year (226 CE).
Initially, when Mì saw the texts on the Imperial Lineage (Dìxì),
which stated that the Five Emperors (Wǔdì) were all from the same clan,
Mì argued against the basis of this claim.
He also discussed the theory of the Emperors (Huángdì), Kings (Wáng), and Hegemons (Bà) "rearing dragons" (*huànlóng*),
which was very insightful.
Qiáo Yǔnnán, when he was young, frequently visited him for consultation,
recording his words in the *Chūnqiū Ránfǒu Lùn*.
The text is extensive, so it is not included here.
A comment says: Xǔ Jìng had an early reputation,
known for his integrity and generosity,
and also for his discernment of talent.
Although his actions and conduct
were not always perfectly appropriate,
Jiǎng Jì considered him
"largely an instrument for the imperial court."
Mí Zhú, Sūn Gān, Jiǎn Yǒng, Yī Jí
were all distinguished by their dignified demeanor and eloquence,
and were respected by their contemporaries.
Qín Mì at first admired the loftiness of retreat,
but lacked the reality of feigning ignorance.
However, he was more than capable in diplomatic exchanges,
and his literary expression was grand and beautiful.
He can be called a talent of his time.
The Biography of Dǒng, Liú, Mǎ, Chén, Dǒng, Lǚ, Chapter Nine.
Dǒng Hé, courtesy name Yòuzǎi,
was a native of Zhījiāng, Nánjùn.
His ancestors were originally from Jiāngzhōu, Bājùn.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
Hé led his clan westward.
The Yìzhōu Mù, Liú Zhāng, appointed him as the Chief of Niúyǎ,
Jiāngyuán, and Magistrate of Chéngdū.
The land of Shǔ was rich and abundant,
and the customs of the time were luxurious.
Families engaged in commerce
wore noble attire and ate lavish food.
Marriages and funerals
exhausted families' wealth.
Hé personally set an example of frugality,
wearing simple clothes and eating plain food,
preventing extravagance and excess,
and establishing regulations.
Wherever he went, customs changed for the better,
and people feared him and did not transgress.
However, the powerful local magnates feared Hé's strict laws
and persuaded Zhāng to transfer Hé to the position of Bādōng Shǔguó Dūwèi.
Several thousand old and young officials and common people clung to each other, begging for Hé to remain.
Zhāng allowed him to stay for two years.
Afterwards, he was transferred to be Yìzhōu Tàishǒu.
His integrity and simplicity remained as before.
In his dealings with the tribal peoples (Mányí),
he strove to show sincerity.
The southern lands loved and trusted him.
When the Former Lord (Xiānzhǔ) pacified Shǔ,
he summoned Hé to be Zhǎngjūn Zhōnglángjiàng,
and he jointly managed affairs with the Army Advisor General (Jūnshī Jiāngjūn), Zhūgě Liàng, in the office of the Left General (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn) and Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ).
They proposed what was acceptable and rejected what was not,
enjoying a harmonious relationship.
From the time Hé held office and received salary,
externally governing distant regions
and internally managing crucial affairs,
for over twenty years,
on the day of his death, his household had no accumulated wealth.
Liàng later became Chancellor (Chéngxiàng),
and instructed his subordinates, saying:
"Those who participate in discussions
gather collective thoughts and broaden loyal benefits.
If one shuns minor disagreements,
making it difficult to openly oppose,
then opportunities will be lost.
If one opposes and hits the mark,
it is like discarding worn sandals and obtaining pearls and jade.
However, human hearts unfortunately cannot fully achieve this.
Only Xú Yuánzhí was not perplexed in this regard.
Furthermore, Dǒng Yòuzǎi, who participated in discussions for seven years,
if there was something not right,
would come and inform me
up to ten times.
If you can emulate even one-tenth of Yuánzhí's spirit,
or Yòuzǎi's diligence,
being loyal to the state,
then Liàng will have fewer faults."
He also said:
"In the past, when I first befriended Zhōu Píng,
I often heard about gains and losses.
Later, when I befriended Yuánzhí,
he frequently offered advice.
Previously, when I served with Yòuzǎi,
he always spoke his mind.
Afterwards, when I served with Wěidù,
he repeatedly offered remonstrance and stopped me.
Although my disposition is humble and dull,
and I could not accept everything,
yet I maintained a good relationship with these four individuals from beginning to end.
This is enough to show that I did not doubt frank words."
His remembrance of Hé was thus.
Liú Bā, courtesy name Zǐchū,
was a native of Zhēngyáng, Línglíng.
He was famous in his youth.
The Jīngzhōu Mù, Liú Biǎo, repeatedly invited him,
and also nominated him as Màocái,
but he never accepted.
When Biǎo died,
Cáo Gōng campaigned against Jīngzhōu.
The Former Lord (Xiānzhǔ) fled south of the Yangtze.
Many scholars from Jīng and Chǔ followed him like clouds,
but Bā went north to Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng appointed him as a Yuàn
and sent him to recruit Chángshā, Línglíng, and Guìyáng.
Coincidentally, the Former Lord (Xiānzhǔ) conquered the three commanderies.
Bā could not return from his mission
and thus traveled far to Jiāozhǐ.
The Former Lord (Xiānzhǔ) deeply regretted this.
Bá Fù returned from Jiāozhǐ to Shǔ.
Soon after, the Former Lord established Yìzhōu,
and Bá apologized for his past transgressions.
The Former Lord did not blame him.
Zhūgě Kǒngmíng repeatedly praised and recommended him,
so the Former Lord appointed him as Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Xī Cáo Yuàn.
In the 24th year of Jiàn'ān,
the Former Lord became Hànzhōng Wáng,
and Bá became a Shàngshū.
Later, he replaced Fǎ Zhèng as Shàngshū Lìng.
He lived a life of integrity and frugality,
not managing any private property.
Furthermore, he considered his allegiance not to be long-standing,
feared being suspected and resented,
and thus remained humble and silent,
having no private social interactions in retirement.
He would not speak unless it was about public affairs.
When the Former Lord assumed the imperial title,
proclaiming it to the August Heaven, the Supreme Emperor, and the Earth Deities,
all the proclamations, edicts, and investiture documents
were written by Bá.
He died in the second year of Zhāngwǔ.
After his death,
Wèi Shàngshū Púyè Chén Qún wrote to Chéngxiàng Zhūgě Liàng,
asking about Bá's news,
referring to him as "Lord Liú Zǐchū,"
showing great respect for him.
Mǎ Liáng, whose courtesy name was Jìcháng,
was a native of Xiāngyáng Yíchéng.
His five brothers
all had talent and reputation.
The local people had a proverb about them:
"Among the five Cháng of the Mǎ family,
the white-browed one is the best."
Liáng had white hairs among his eyebrows,
hence the saying.
When the Former Lord took control of Jīngzhōu,
he appointed him as a Cóngshì.
When the Former Lord entered Shǔ,
Zhūgě Liàng also followed later.
Liáng remained in Jīngzhōu
and wrote to Liàng, saying:
"I hear that Luòchéng has been taken;
this is a blessing from Heaven.
My esteemed elder brother should respond to the times and assist the world,
glorifying the state with your achievements;
the omens are apparent.
Truly, in adapting to change with refined wisdom
and discerning what is valuable with clear insight,
in selecting talent,
one should suit the moment.
If one can temper one's brilliance and please those far away,
surpassing others in virtue between Heaven and Earth,
causing the times to be at peace in listening,
and the world to submit to the Way,
harmonizing the highest and most exquisite sounds,
correcting the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
benefiting all matters
without any contention for superiority,
this is the ultimate of string and wind instruments,
the harmony of Yá and Kuàng.
Although I am not Zhōng Qī,
how can I not applaud!"
The Former Lord appointed Liáng as Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Yuàn.
Later, when he was dispatched as an envoy to Wú,
Liáng said to Liàng:
"Now I carry the state's mandate
to foster harmony between our two houses.
I hope you will introduce me to General Sūn."
Liàng replied:
"You may try to write the message yourself."
Liáng immediately drafted it, saying:
"My humble lord sends his Yuàn Mǎ Liáng to establish friendly relations
and continue the merits of Kūnwú and Shǐwéi.
This man is a virtuous gentleman,
a model of Jīngchǔ,
seldom given to superficiality in speech,
but possessing the virtue of seeing things through to the end.
I wish for you to graciously receive him
to soothe the envoy's mission."
Quán treated him with respect.
When the Former Lord assumed the imperial title,
he appointed Liáng as Shìzhōng.
When he launched the eastern campaign against Wú,
he sent Liáng into Wǔlíng to recruit and pacify the Five Streams Man and Yi,
and their chieftains all received seals and titles,
acting entirely as he wished.
It happened that the Former Lord suffered a defeat at Yílíng,
and Liáng was also killed.
The Former Lord appointed Liáng's son, Bǐng, as Qí Dūwèi.
Liáng's younger brother, Sù,
whose courtesy name was Yòucháng,
followed the Former Lord into Shǔ as a Jīngzhōu Cóngshì.
He was appointed Miánzhú Chéngdū Lìng and Yuèxī Tàishǒu.
His talent and capacity surpassed others,
and he was fond of discussing military strategies.
Chéngxiàng Zhūgě Liàng greatly admired his unusual abilities.
Before his death, the Former Lord said to Liàng:
"Mǎ Sù exaggerates his abilities beyond reality;
he cannot be entrusted with great responsibility.
You should carefully observe him!"
Liàng still thought otherwise
and appointed Sù as Cānjūn.
He would often summon him for discussions
that lasted from day to night.
In the sixth year of Jiànxīng,
Liàng marched his army towards Qíshān.
At that time, there were seasoned generals such as Wèi Yán and Wú Yī,
and commentators all said they should be made the vanguard.
However, Liàng went against the consensus and promoted Sù,
placing him in command of the main army in front.
He fought against Wèi General Zhāng Hé at Jiētíng,
and was defeated by Hé.
The soldiers scattered.
Liàng had no basis to advance,
so he retreated to Hànzhōng.
Sù died in prison,
and Liàng wept for him.
Liáng was thirty-six years old when he died,
and Sù was thirty-nine.
Chén Zhèn, whose courtesy name was Xiàoqǐ,
was a native of Nányáng.
When the Former Lord served as Jīngzhōu Mù,
he appointed Zhèn as Cóngshì,
overseeing various commanderies,
and followed the Former Lord into Shǔ.
After Shǔ was pacified,
he became Shǔjùn Běibù Dūwèi.
The commandery name was then changed,
and he became Wénshān Tàishǒu,
then transferred to Jiānwéi.
In the third year of Jiànxīng,
he was appointed Shàngshū,
then promoted to Shàngshū Lìng,
and was ordered to be an envoy to Wú.
In the seventh year,
Sūn Quán assumed the imperial title,
and Zhèn was appointed Wèiwèi
to congratulate Quán on his ascension.
Zhūgě Liàng wrote to his elder brother Jǐn, saying:
"Xiàoqǐ's loyal and pure nature
grows stronger with age.
His praises for the East and West,
and his joyful and harmonious disposition,
are truly admirable."
When Zhèn entered the borders of Wú,
he sent a dispatch to the border guards, saying:
"Between the East and the West,
imperial envoys come and go,
their caps and carriages constantly in sight,
renewing their alliance and initial goodwill,
refreshing their affairs daily.
The revered lord of the East should preserve his sacred throne,
proclaim to Heaven, receive the omens,
and divide the land.
The world echoes in response,
each finding its allegiance.
At this time,
if we unite our hearts to eliminate the bandits,
what enemy cannot be vanquished!
The rulers and ministers of the Western court
eagerly look forward to this with joy and reliance.
Although Zhèn is untalented,
he is honored to serve as a humble envoy,
dispatched to foster goodwill.
Upon crossing the border, I am overjoyed,
entering as if returning home.
When Xiàn Zǐ went to Lǔ,
he transgressed its mountain taboo,
for which the Spring and Autumn Annals criticized him.
I hope you will certainly inform me
to ensure the envoy's harmony.
On this day, I display my banner and proclaim to the multitude,
each making their own oath.
Flowing swiftly downstream,
the state's regulations differ,
and I fear there might be violations.
I earnestly request your guidance
to show what is appropriate."
When Zhèn arrived at Wǔchāng,
Sūn Quán and Zhèn ascended the altar to swear an oath,
dividing the world: Xú, Yù, Yōu, and Qīng belonged to Wú;
Bīng, Liáng, Jì, and Yǎn belonged to Shǔ.
As for the land of Sīzhōu,
Hàgǔguān was to be the boundary.
Upon Zhèn's return,
he was enfeoffed as Chéngyáng Tínghóu.
In the ninth year,
Dūhù Lǐ Píng was dismissed for fraud and deception.
Zhūgě Liàng wrote to Chángshǐ Jiǎng Wǎn and Shìzhōng Dǒng Yǔn, saying:
"Xiàoqǐ, before he arrived in Wú,
told me that Zhèngfāng had 'scales in his belly,'
and that the locals considered him unapproachable.
I thought that these 'scales' merely meant one should not provoke him,
but I did not expect another incident like Sū and Zhāng to occur unexpectedly.
You can let Xiàoqǐ know about this."
In the thirteenth year,
Zhèn died.
His son Jì succeeded him.
Dǒng Yǔn, courtesy name Xiūzhāo,
was the son of Zhǎngjūn Zhōnglángjiàng Hé.
When the Former Emperor established the Crown Prince,
Yǔn was selected to be a shèrén,
and later transferred to xǐmǎ.
When the Later Emperor succeeded to the throne,
he was promoted to Huángmén Shìláng.
When Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng was about to embark on a northern campaign,
stationed in Hànzhōng,
he was concerned that the Later Emperor was young in years,
and might not be able to distinguish between good and bad.
Because Yǔn was of upright and honest character,
Zhūgě Liàng wished to entrust him with affairs of the palace.
He submitted a memorial, saying:
"Shìzhōng Guō Yōuzhī, Fèi Yī, Shìláng Dǒng Yǔn and others
were selected by the late emperor and bequeathed to Your Majesty.
As for deliberation on what is beneficial and corrective,
and presenting loyal counsel,
that is their duty.
I humbly believe that regarding matters in the palace,
no matter how big or small,
they should all be consulted.
They will surely be able to supplement deficiencies and correct oversights,
and bring about extensive benefits.
If there are no words to promote virtue,
then Dǒng Yǔn and others should be punished to highlight their negligence."
Zhūgě Liàng soon after requested Fèi Yī to be a cānjūn,
and Dǒng Yǔn was promoted to Shìzhōng,
also holding the title of Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng,
commanding the imperial guards and personal troops.
Guō Yōuzhī was naturally gentle and compliant,
merely fulfilling his post.
The responsibility of offering advice
was entirely monopolized by Dǒng Yǔn.
Dǒng Yǔn managed affairs by setting strict regulations,
and fully exercised the principles of rectifying and assisting.
The Later Emperor often wished to select women to fill the imperial harem,
but Dǒng Yǔn believed that in ancient times, the number of empresses and consorts of the Son of Heaven did not exceed twelve.
Since the concubines were already sufficient,
it was not proper to increase their number.
He firmly insisted and would not permit it.
The Later Emperor thus became more respectful and wary of him.
Shàngshū Lìng Jiǎng Wǎn, who also held the post of Yìzhōu Cìshǐ,
submitted a memorial to yield his position to Fèi Yī and Dǒng Yǔn,
and also memorialized,
"Dǒng Yǔn has served in the inner court for years,
assisting and supporting the royal house,
and should be granted a noble title and territory to commend his meritorious service."
Dǒng Yǔn firmly declined and did not accept.
As the Later Emperor gradually grew older,
he became fond of the eunuch Huáng Hào.
Huáng Hào was cunning, flattering, and intelligent,
and wished to ingratiate himself.
Dǒng Yǔn would always sternly admonish the emperor above,
and frequently reprimand Huáng Hào below.
Huáng Hào feared Dǒng Yǔn,
and dared not commit wrongdoing.
Throughout Dǒng Yǔn's lifetime,
Huáng Hào's position did not exceed Huángménchéng.
Dǒng Yǔn once planned to go on an excursion and banquet with Shàngshū Lìng Fèi Yī, Zhōngdiǎnjūn Hú Jì, and others.
The carriages were already prepared,
when Lángzhōng Dǒng Huī of Xiāngyáng came to pay his respects to Dǒng Yǔn.
Dǒng Huī was young and held a minor official position.
Seeing that Dǒng Yǔn had stopped his departure,
he hesitated and sought to leave.
Dǒng Yǔn did not permit it,
saying:
"The reason I was originally going out
was to converse and tour with like-minded friends.
Now that you have humbled yourself by coming,
and I am about to unburden my accumulated thoughts,
to abandon this conversation
and go to that banquet
is not what is right."
Thereupon, he ordered the harnesses to be unhitched,
and Fèi Yī and the others dismissed their carriages and did not go.
His adherence to righteousness and humility towards scholars
was always like this.
In the sixth year of Yánxī (243 CE),
he was granted the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
In the seventh year (244 CE),
he served as Shàngshū Lìng while remaining Shìzhōng,
and became the deputy to Dàjiāngjūn Fèi Yī.
In the ninth year (246 CE),
he died.
Chén Zhī succeeded Dǒng Yǔn as Shìzhōng,
and he and Huáng Hào mutually supported each other,
and Huáng Hào began to involve himself in state affairs.
After Chén Zhī's death,
Huáng Hào was promoted from Huángmén Lìng to Zhōngchángshì and Fèngchē Dūwèi,
manipulating power and authority,
ultimately leading to the collapse of the state.
No one in Shǔ failed to remember Dǒng Yǔn with sorrow.
When Dèng Ài reached Shǔ,
hearing of Huáng Hào's treachery,
he arrested and imprisoned him,
intending to kill him.
However, Huáng Hào heavily bribed Dèng Ài's attendants,
and thus escaped death.
Chén Zhī, courtesy name Fèngzōng,
was a native of Rǔnán,
and the grandnephew of Xǔ Jìng's elder brother.
He was orphaned young
and grew up in Xǔ Jìng's household.
He became famous in his youth,
and gradually rose to Xuǎncáo Láng.
He was dignified and had an imposing manner.
He possessed many skills
and was adept at various arts.
Fèi Yī greatly admired him,
and thus he was exceptionally chosen to succeed Dǒng Yǔn in the inner court.
When Lǚ Yì died,
Chén Zhī again served as Shàngshū Lìng while remaining Shìzhōng,
and was granted the title of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn.
Although Dàjiāngjūn Jiāng Wéi outranked Chén Zhī,
he was often leading troops outside,
and rarely involved himself in court politics.
Chén Zhī, receiving instructions from the emperor above,
and associating with the eunuchs below,
was deeply trusted and loved,
and his power surpassed Jiāng Wéi's.
He died in the first year of Jǐngyào (258 CE).
The Later Emperor grieved deeply,
speaking with tears flowing.
He then issued an imperial edict which stated:
"Chén Zhī held office for twelve years.
He was gentle and virtuous as a model,
efficient and orderly in his duties,
harmonious and righteous, benefiting all things.
All his achievements were clearly illuminated.
His life was not long-lasting,
and I mourn him for this.
Indeed, if one has a good reputation while alive,
then after death, a beautiful posthumous title should be bestowed.
Let him be posthumously titled Zhōnghóu."
His son Càn was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu,
and his second son Yù was promoted to Huángmén Shìláng.
From the time Chén Zhī gained favor,
the Later Emperor's resentment towards Dǒng Yǔn deepened daily.
He considered Dǒng Yǔn to have belittled himself,
because Chén Zhī flattered this one person,
and Huáng Hào sowed discord and spread rumors.
Dǒng Yǔn's grandson Hóng was Jìn Bāxī Tàishǒu.
Lǚ Yì, courtesy name Jìyáng,
was a native of Nányáng.
His father, Cháng,
accompanied the former General Liú Yān into Shǔ.
When the royal road was cut off and blocked,
he was unable to return.
Yì was orphaned young,
and fond of reading and playing the qín.
Initially,
when the Former Lord pacified Yìzhōu,
he established a Salt Official (Yánfǔ Xiàowèi),
to manage the profits from salt and iron.
Later, the official Wáng Lián invited Yì, along with Dù Qí of Nányáng and Liú Gàn of Nánxiāng, to all serve as Duty Officers (Diǎncáo Dūwèi).
Yì was promoted to magistrate of Xīndū and Miánzhú.
He sincerely cared for the distressed,
and the common people praised him,
making him the foremost among the various city officials in the province.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Bāxī.
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng launched military campaigns for several years,
dispatching troops from various commanderies,
many of whom were unwilling to assist.
Yì recruited five thousand soldiers and went to see Liàng,
comforting and restraining them,
so that none fled.
He was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Hànzhōng,
also overseeing agriculture (Dū nóng),
providing military provisions.
After Liàng’s death,
he was successively promoted to Grand Administrator of Guǎnghàn and Shǔjùn.
Shǔjùn was the capital and meeting place,
with a large population.
Moreover, after Liàng’s death,
soldiers fled,
repeatedly concealing their identities or re-enlisting.
There were countless cunning deceptions.
When Yì arrived in office,
he established preventative measures,
enlightened and guided them.
Within a few years,
over ten thousand households who had evaded registration came forward voluntarily.
Later, he entered the central government as a Minister (Shàngshū),
succeeding Dǒng Yǔn as Director of the Chancellery (Shàngshū Lìng).
No affairs were left unattended,
and no guests lingered at his gate.
Yì served in various internal and external positions.
He lived frugally,
was humble, quiet, and spoke little.
His governance was simple and not bothersome,
and he was known as pure and capable.
However, he applied the law with severity,
and was fond of employing literate but common officials.
Therefore, while holding high office,
his reputation suffered in the commanderies and counties.
He died in the fourteenth year of Yánxī.
His son, Chén,
was Magistrate of Chéngdū during the Jǐngyào era.
Chén's younger brother, Yǎ,
was an Usher (Yèzhě).
Yǎ was pure, strict, and had literary talent,
authoring fifteen chapters of Grids and Arguments (Gélùn).
Dù Qí successively held positions as Grand Administrator, Supervisor of the Army, and Chief Clerk to the General-in-Chief.
Liú Gàn's highest office was Grand Administrator of Bāxī.
All were close to Yì,
and also had a good reputation at the time,
but in their frugality and adherence to the law,
they did not equal Yì.
The commentary states:
Dǒng Hé followed the simplicity of a lamb,
Liú Bā observed the principles of purity and integrity,
Mǎ Liáng was upright and honest,
called an excellent scholar,
Chén Zhèn was loyal and diligent,
growing more steadfast with age,
Dǒng Yǔn assisted his lord,
his righteousness evident in his expression.
All were good officials of Shǔ.
Lǚ Yì earned praise when governing commanderies,
but suffered damage to his reputation when in court.
He was also of the same ilk as Huáng and Xuē.
Biography Ten: Liú, Péng, Liáo, Lǐ, Liú, Wèi, Yáng.
Liú Fēng,
originally the son of the Kòu clan of Luóhóu,
and the nephew of the Liú clan of Chángshā.
When the Former Lord arrived in Jīngzhōu,
as he had no successor,
he adopted Fēng as his son.
When the Former Lord entered Shǔ,
returning from Jiāmáng to attack Liú Zhāng,
Fēng was then over twenty years old,
possessed martial skills,
and extraordinary strength.
Leading troops, he ascended west along the river with Zhūgě Liàng, Zhāng Fēi, and others,
winning every battle.
Once Yìzhōu was pacified,
Fēng was made Vice Colonel of the Army (Fùjūn Zhōnglángjiàng).
Initially,
Liú Zhāng dispatched Mèng Dá of Fúfēng as deputy to Fǎ Zhèng,
each leading two thousand soldiers,
to welcome the Former Lord.
The Former Lord then ordered Dá to take overall command of their forces,
and remain stationed in Jiānglíng.
After Shǔ was pacified,
Dá was made Grand Administrator of Yídū.
In the twenty-fourth year of Jiàn'ān,
Dá was ordered to advance north from Zǐguī to attack Fánglíng.
Kuǎi Qí, the Grand Administrator of Fánglíng, was killed by Dá's troops.
As Dá was about to attack Shàngyōng,
the Former Lord secretly feared Dá might not be able to handle it alone,
so he dispatched Fēng from Hànzhōng to descend the Miǎn River and take command of Dá's army,
meeting Dá at Shàngyōng.
Shēn Dān, the Grand Administrator of Shàngyōng, led his people to surrender,
sending his wife, children, and clan members to Chéngdū.
The Former Lord appointed Dān General Who Attacks the North (Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn),
retaining his positions as Grand Administrator of Shàngyōng and Marquis of Yuánxiāng as before.
Dān's younger brother, Yí, was made General Who Builds Trust (Jiànxìn Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator of Xīchéng.
Fēng was promoted to Vice General of the Army (Fùjūn Jiāngjūn).
When Guān Yǔ besieged Fánchéng and Xiāngyáng,
he repeatedly called upon Fēng and Dá,
ordering them to send troops to assist him.
Fēng and Dá refused, citing that the mountain commanderies had only recently submitted
and should not be disturbed,
thus not complying with Yǔ's order.
When Yǔ was subsequently defeated,
the Former Lord resented this.
Furthermore, Fēng and Dá had a quarrel and were not in harmony,
and Fēng soon took away Dá's military band.
Dá, fearing punishment
and resenting Fēng,
then memorialized the Former Lord with his resignation,
and led his subordinates to surrender to Wèi.
Emperor Wén of Wèi admired Dá's talent and appearance,
making him Attendant Officer of the Cavalier (Sànqí Chángshì) and General Who Builds Martial Prowess (Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn),
and enfeoffing him as Marquis of Píngyángtíng.
He combined the three commanderies of Fánglíng, Shàngyōng, and Xīchéng [to form Xīnchéng Commandery,
and appointed] Dá as Grand Administrator of Xīnchéng.
He dispatched General Who Attacks the South Xiàhóu Shàng and General of the Right Xú Huàng to attack Fēng together with Dá.
Dá wrote to Fēng, saying: "The ancients said: 'The distant should not interfere with the close,
and the new should not be preferred over the old.'
This means that when the superior is clear-sighted and the inferior is upright,
slander and wickedness do not prevail.
But if the ruler is authoritarian and deceitful,
or the father wise and the mother kind,
there are still loyal ministers who perform meritorious deeds and suffer calamity,
and filial sons who embrace benevolence and fall into hardship.
Zhǒng, Shāng, Bái Qǐ, Xiàojǐ, Bóqí,
are all examples of this.
The reason for this
is not that blood relatives like to separate, or that kin enjoy suffering.
Rather, it is sometimes because affection changes and love shifts,
or because slander comes between them,
so that even a loyal minister cannot
sway his lord,
nor a filial son change his father.
When power and profit are involved, intimacy is changed into enmity,
let alone when there is no blood relationship!
Therefore, Shēn Shēng,
Wèi Jí, Yù Kòu, Chǔ Jiàn, who received their form and spirit,
and were destined to succeed legitimately,
still met such fates.
Now, Your Excellency and the King of Hànzhōng
are merely people encountered on the road;
you are not blood relatives yet hold positions of power,
and your relationship is not one of ruler and minister, yet you occupy a high position.
When campaigning, you have the awe of an independent command,
and when at court, you hold the title of Vice General of the Army.
This is heard far and wide.
Ever since Ādǒu was established as Crown Prince,
all discerning people have felt a chill in their hearts.
If Shēn Shēng had followed Zǐ Yú's words,
he would surely have been like Tàibó;
if Wèi
Jí had listened to his brother's counsel,
he would not have earned the criticism of 'making his father manifest.'
Moreover, Xiǎo Bái fled,
but returned and became a hegemon;
Chóng Ěr scaled a wall,
and eventually succeeded in restoration.
This has been so since ancient times,
not just today.
Indeed, wisdom values avoiding misfortune,
and insight values early discernment.
I reckon that the King of Hànzhōng's deliberations are settled internally,
but doubts arise externally.
If deliberations are settled, the mind is firm;
if doubts arise,
the mind is afraid.
The rise of chaos and disaster
has never failed to stem from matters of deposition and establishment.
Private grievances and human nature
cannot but be seen.
I fear that there will certainly be those on the left and right who will cause estrangement between you and Hàn
became the central king.
If that is the case, suspicion breeds resentment,
and its eruption is like stepping on a tripwire.
Now, your excellency is far away,
and can still breathe for a while;
but if the great army advances,
and your excellency loses your stronghold and returns,
I secretly worry for your danger.
In the past, Wēi Zǐ left Yīn,
Zhì Guǒ separated from his clan,
fleeing difficulties and avoiding disaster,
and they all did just that.
Now, your excellency
abandons your parents to become someone else's successor,
which is against propriety;
knowing disaster is coming and staying put,
is not wisdom;
seeing the right path but not following it and doubting it,
is not righteousness.
Claiming
to be a man of integrity,
yet doing these three things,
what is there to value?
With your excellency's talent,
abandoning yourself to come east,
continuing the lineage of Luó Hóu,
would not be betraying your relatives;
facing
north to serve your lord,
and rectifying the discipline,
would not be abandoning old ties;
controlling anger to prevent chaos,
and thereby avoiding danger and destruction,
would not be acting fruitlessly.
Moreover, His Majesty has recently received the
mandate,
is open-minded and eager to welcome,
embracing distant lands with virtue.
If your excellency were to suddenly turn inward,
not only would you be my peer,
receive a fief of three hundred households,
and continue the lineage of Luó kingdom,
but
you would moreover be granted a large state with a tally,
as a founding prince.
His Majesty's great army,
with gongs and drums resounding,
will relocate its capital to Wǎn and Dèng;
if the two enemies are not pacified,
the army
will have no return date.
Your excellency should take this opportunity to decide on a good plan early.
The Yì (Book of Changes) says, 'It is beneficial to see a great man,'
and the Shī (Book of Odes) says, 'Seek much fortune for yourself.'
Go forth!
Now, your excellency,
strive hard,
and do not be like Hú Tū who closed his door and did not come out.
Fēng did not follow Dà's advice.
Shēn Yí betrayed Fēng,
and Fēng was defeated and fled back to Chéngdū.
Shēn Dān surrendered to Wèi,
Wèi granted Dān the title of Huáijí Jiāngjūn,
relocating him to Nányáng.
Yí became Wèixīng Tàishǒu,
Fēng (Zhēnxīang Hóu) [Yuánxiāng Hóu],
garrisoned at Xúnkǒu.
Once Fēng arrived,
Xiānzhǔ reprimanded Fēng for encroaching upon Dà,
and also for not rescuing Yǔ.
Zhūgě Liàng feared Fēng's fierce and violent nature,
believing he would eventually be difficult to control after a change of era,
and advised Xiānzhǔ to eliminate him on this account.
Thereupon, Fēng was granted death,
and ordered to commit suicide.
Fēng sighed, saying:
"I regret not having heeded Mèng Zǐdù's words!"
Xiānzhǔ wept for him.
Dà's original courtesy name was Zǐjìng,
but to avoid the courtesy name of Xiānzhǔ's uncle, Jìng,
it was changed.
Péng Yàng, courtesy name Yǒngnián,
was a native of Guǎnghàn.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
with a very imposing appearance.
His nature was arrogant,
and he often slighted others,
only respecting Qín Zǐchì, a fellow native of his commandery,
whom he recommended to the Administrator Xǔ Jìng, saying:
"In ancient times, Gāo Zōng dreamed of Fù Yuè,
King Wén of Zhōu sought Lǚ Shàng,
and down to Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
who received Shí Qí, a commoner.
This is how emperors initiated their enterprises, established their lineage,
and brilliantly achieved their merits.
Now, your excellency studies the imperial principles of antiquity,
sincerely upholds spiritual wisdom,
embodies the virtue of Gōng Liú,
and practices the kindness of 'Do not cut down.'
The construction of the pure temple thus begins,
and the principles of praise and censure thus arise.
However, the six wings are not yet fully equipped.
I humbly observe the recluse Qín Mì from Miánzhú,
who possesses the virtue of Shān Fǔ,
walks the upright path of Jùn Shēng,
rests on rocks and sips from streams,
recites poetry in coarse robes,
finds peace in the path of benevolence and righteousness,
and finds tranquility in the realm of vast spiritual energy.
His noble character and integrity
preserve truth without blemish;
even ancient recluses
cannot surpass him.
If your excellency can recruit this man,
you will surely gain the reputation of being loyal and upright,
achieve abundant merits and great benefits,
and establish your achievements and contributions.
Then, your achievements will be recorded in the royal court,
and your fame will spread to future generations.
Would this not be wonderful!"
Yàng served the province,
but was no more than a clerical assistant.
Later, he was slandered and disparaged by many people to the Provincial Governor Liú Zhāng,
who shaved Yàng's head and shackled him as a convict laborer.
At that time, Xiānzhǔ entered Shǔ
and traveled upstream north.
Yàng wished to offer advice to Xiānzhǔ,
so he went to see Páng Tǒng.
Tǒng and Yàng were not old acquaintances,
and there were guests present.
Yàng directly went onto Tǒng's bed and lay down,
saying to Tǒng:
"When the guests leave, I will have a good talk with you."
After Tǒng's guests left,
he went to sit with Yàng.
Yàng first demanded food from Tǒng,
and only then did they talk.
Consequently, he stayed for two nights,
and even for several days.
Tǒng greatly approved of him,
and Fǎ Zhèng had long known Yàng,
so they jointly recommended him to Xiānzhǔ.
Xiānzhǔ also found him extraordinary,
and often ordered Yàng to convey military orders,
and give instructions to the various generals.
He carried out his missions satisfactorily,
and his recognition and treatment increased daily.
After Chéngdū was settled,
Xiānzhǔ assumed the post of Yìzhōu Mù,
and promoted Yàng to Zhìzhōng Cóngshì.
Yàng rose from a commoner,
and in one morning was above all the people in the province.
His demeanor was boisterous,
and he boasted excessively of his good fortune.
Although Zhūgě Liàng outwardly received Yàng,
inwardly he was not favorably disposed.
He repeatedly secretly told Xiānzhǔ that
Yàng was ambitious and aspiring,
and difficult to keep safe.
Since Xiānzhǔ respected and trusted Liàng,
and moreover observed Yàng's conduct,
his attitude gradually cooled,
and he demoted Yàng to Jiāngyáng Tàishǒu.
Yàng heard that he was to be sent far away,
and was privately displeased.
He went to visit Mǎ Chāo.
Chāo asked Yàng:
"Your talent is outstanding and exceptional,
and the lord treats you with great importance.
He expects you to stand shoulder to shoulder with Kǒngmíng, Xiàozhí, and others,
so how can he assign you to an outer, small commandery,
disappointing people's original expectations?"
Yàng said:
"That old rascal is absurd and perverse,
what more can be said!"
He then said to Chāo:
"You be his outside,
and I be his inside,
and the world will not be difficult to settle."
Chāo, having returned to the state as a sojourner,
always felt precarious and apprehensive.
Hearing Yàng's words, he was greatly startled,
and remained silent.
After Yàng left,
Chāo fully reported Yàng's words,
whereupon Yàng was arrested and handed over to the authorities.
Yáng [Yǒng] wrote a letter to Zhūgě Liàng [Zhūgě Liàng] from prison, saying:
"In the past, I served the various feudal lords,
believing Cáo Cāo [Cáo Cāo] to be tyrannical,
Sūn Quán [Sūn Quán] to be unprincipled,
and the Grand General Zhenwei [Zhènwēi] to be obscure and weak.
Only the Lord [zhǔgōng] possessed the qualities of a hegemon and king,
capable of establishing a great enterprise and bringing order to the world.
Therefore, I suddenly had the ambition to make a lighthearted move.
When you came west,
I, through Fǎ Xiàozhí [Fǎ Xiàozhí], promoted and offered myself,
and Páng Tǒng [Páng Tǒng] deliberated in between.
Thus, I was able to meet you at Jiāmáng [Jiāmáng],
where we spoke freely,
discussed the affairs of governing the world,
expounded the righteousness of a hegemon and king,
and proposed the strategy for taking Yìzhōu [Yìzhōu].
You, too, had long considered and clearly decided,
immediately agreed and praised it,
and thus embarked on the endeavor.
I, in my former province, could not escape being ordinary and mediocre,
worried by the net of crime,
yet I encountered a time of wind and clouds, like arrows flying.
I sought a lord and found one,
my ambition fulfilled and my name made famous.
From among commoners, I was promoted to a national scholar,
surreptitiously acquiring the title of 'Maocai' [Mào Cái].
Who could surpass [Your] generosity [fēnzi zhī hòu] like this?
Who could surpass this?
If I, Yáng [Yáng], in one morning became mad and perverse,
seeking my own mincemeat,
would I become a ghost of disloyalty and unrighteousness!
The ancients had a saying:
'To hold the map of the world in the left hand,
and with the right hand to slit one's own throat,'
even a fool would not do it.
How much less would I, who can distinguish beans from wheat!
The reason I harbored resentful thoughts
was that I did not measure myself.
I merely believed that since I was the first to initiate the enterprise,
and there was the discussion of throwing [my ideas] into Jiāngyáng [Jiāngyáng],
I did not understand Your intention.
My emotions were greatly stirred,
and perhaps, being somewhat intoxicated,
I inadvertently let slip the word 'old'.
This was due to my utter foolishness and shallow considerations.
This was caused by my utter foolishness and shallow considerations.
Your Lordship is indeed not old.
Moreover, establishing an enterprise,
how can it depend on age?
Xī Bó [Xī Bó] was ninety,
yet he had no declining ambition.
To fail my benevolent father [fù],
my crime deserves a hundred deaths.
As for internal and external discussions,
it was to enable Mèngqǐ [Mèngqǐ] to achieve merits in the northern province,
and with combined effort, together with Your Lordship,
to attack Cáo Cāo [Cáo Cāo];
how could I dare to have other ambitions?
Mèngqǐ [Mèngqǐ]'s suggestion was correct,
but not distinguishing between them,
it hurt people's feelings.
In the past, Páng Tǒng [Páng Tǒng] and I often swore an oath together,
hoping to follow in your footsteps,
and dedicate our hearts to Your Lordship's enterprise,
to achieve fame like the ancients,
and have our merits recorded in bamboo and silk.
Tǒng [Tǒng] unfortunately died,
and I failed and incurred disaster.
Since I brought it upon myself,
whom else should I blame!
You,
are the Yī [Yī] and Lǚ [Lǚ] of this era.
You should plan affairs well with Your Lordship,
and complete his great strategy.
Heaven is clear and Earth observes,
the spirits are efficacious,
what more is there to say!
I only wish that you would understand my original intention.
Go and strive,
take care of yourself,
take care of yourself!"
Yáng [Yáng] was eventually executed;
he was thirty-seven at the time.
Liáo Lì [Liáo Lì] (Liáo [Liáo] pronounced like 'lǐ jiù fǎn' [lǐ jiù fǎn])
whose courtesy name was Gōngyuān [Gōngyuān],
was a native of Línyuán [Línyuán], Wǔlíng [Wǔlíng].
The Former Lord [Xiānzhǔ] was made Governor of Jīngzhōu [Jīngzhōu],
and appointed him as an aide.
Before he was thirty,
he was promoted to Grand Administrator of Chángshā [Chángshā].
When the Former Lord [Xiānzhǔ] entered Shǔ [Shǔ],
Zhūgě Liàng [Zhūgě Liàng] was garrisoned in Jīng [Jīng] territory.
Sūn Quán [Sūn Quán] sent an envoy to foster good relations with Liàng [Liàng],
and incidentally asked which scholars were capable of governing.
Liàng [Liàng] replied:
"Páng Tǒng [Páng Tǒng] and Liáo Lì [Liáo Lì] are excellent talents of Chǔ [Chǔ],
and are capable of assisting in establishing an enterprise."
In the twentieth year of Jiàn'ān [Jiàn'ān] (215 CE),
Quán [Quán] sent Lǚ Méng [Lǚ Méng] to suddenly attack the three southern commanderies.
Lì [Lì] escaped and fled,
returning to the Former Lord [Xiānzhǔ].
The Former Lord [Xiānzhǔ], who had always known and valued him,
did not blame him severely,
and made him Grand Administrator of Bājùn [Bājùn].
In the twenty-fourth year (219 CE),
the Former Lord [Xiānzhǔ] became King of Hànzhōng [Hànzhōng],
and summoned Lì [Lì] to be Attendant Official.
When the Later Lord [Hòuzhǔ] succeeded to the throne,
he was transferred to Commander of Changshui [Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi].
Lì [Lì]'s original intention
was that his talent and fame were worthy of being Zhūgě Liàng [Zhūgě Liàng]'s second-in-command,
but instead he was idly placed beneath Lǐ Yán [Lǐ Yán] and others,
constantly harboring discontent.
Later, when the Chancellor's aides (Lǐ Hé [Lǐ Hé]) [Lǐ Shào [Lǐ Shào]] and Jiǎng Wǎn [Jiǎng Wǎn] arrived,
Lì [Lì] remarked:
"The army is about to embark on a distant expedition.
You gentlemen should carefully examine this matter.
In the past, the Former (Lord) [Emperor] [Xiāndì] did not take Hànzhōng [Hànzhōng],
but instead rushed to contend with the Wú [Wú] people over the three southern commanderies,
ultimately giving the three commanderies to the Wú [Wú] people.
The officials and soldiers were toiled in vain,
returning without benefit.
Having lost Hànzhōng [Hànzhōng], Xiàhóu Yuān [Xiàhóu Yuān] and Zhāng Hé [Zhāng Hé] were allowed to penetrate deep into Bā [Bā],
nearly losing an entire province.
Later, when Hànzhōng [Hànzhōng] was reached, Guān Hóu [Guān Hóu] was caused to die without a single descendant,
and Shàngyōng [Shàngyōng] was defeated,
losing a whole region in vain.
This was because Yǔ [Yǔ] relied on his brave reputation,
conducting military affairs without discipline,
merely acting on impulse,
hence suffering numerous losses of troops both before and after.
As for Xiàng Lǎng [Xiàng Lǎng] and Wén Gōng [Wén Gōng],
they are merely common folk.
Gōng [Gōng] served as Zìzhōng [Zìzhōng] without proper principles;
Lǎng [Lǎng] formerly supported Mǎ Liáng [Mǎ Liáng] and his brothers,
calling them sages,
and now serves as Chief Clerk,
yet he always acts in accordance with the Way.
Commander Guō Yǎnzhǎng [Guō Yǎnzhǎng] is merely a follower of others,
not capable of handling important affairs,
yet he serves as Attendant Official.
This is a weak era,
and it is not right to rely on these three people.
Wáng Lián [Wáng Lián] is a common opportunist,
who merely acts as an extortionist,
causing the common people to be weary and destitute,
leading to the present situation."
(Hé [Hé]) [Shào [Shào]] and Wǎn [Wǎn] fully reported his words to Zhūgě Liàng [Zhūgě Liàng].
Liàng [Liàng] impeached Lì [Lì], saying:
"Changshui Commander Liáo Lì [Liáo Lì],
due to his own inflated self-importance,
criticized all the scholars,
publicly stating that the state does not employ the virtuous and talented but rather corrupt officials,
and also saying that all those who lead ten thousand men are mere youngsters;
slandering the Former Emperor [Xiāndì] and disparaging all the ministers.
When someone said that the state's troops were well-trained and disciplined,
Lì [Lì] raised his head, looked at the roof,
and angrily exclaimed with a changed expression, 'What's there to talk about!'
Such instances are countless.
If sheep can disturb the flock,
they can still cause harm,
how much more so Lì [Lì], who holds a high position,
can people of middling or lower intelligence discern the truth from falsehood?"
Thereupon, Lì [Lì] was dismissed from office and reduced to a commoner,
and exiled to Wènshān Commandery [Wènshān Jùn].
Lì [Lì] personally led his wife and children to cultivate the land and maintain themselves.
When he heard that Zhūgě Liàng [Zhūgě Liàng] had died,
he wept and sighed, saying:
"I shall ultimately wear the robes of a barbarian!"
Later, Supervisor of the Army Jiāng Wéi [Jiāng Wéi] led a detached army through Wènshān [Wènshān] and visited Lì [Lì],
saying that Lì [Lì]'s spirit was undiminished
and his discourse was as usual.
Lì [Lì] then died in his place of exile.
His wife and children returned to Shǔ [Shǔ].
Lǐ Yán, courtesy name Zhèngfāng,
was a native of Nányáng.
In his youth, he served as a subordinate official in the commandery
and was renowned for his talent and capability.
Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, made him serve in various commanderies and counties.
When Cáo Gōng entered Jīngzhōu,
Yán was the magistrate of Zǐguī.
He then traveled west to Shǔ,
where Liú Zhāng appointed him as the magistrate of Chéngdū,
and he again gained a reputation for competence.
In the eighteenth year of Jiàn'ān (213 CE),
Yán was appointed Hùjūn,
to resist the Former Lord at Miánzhú.
Yán led his troops to surrender to the Former Lord,
and the Former Lord appointed Yán as Píjiāngjūn.
After Chéngdū was pacified,
he became the Administrator of Jiànwéi and Xīngyè Jiāngjūn.
In the twenty-third year (218 CE),
the bandits Mǎ Qín and Gāo Shèng and others rebelled in Shē
(pronounced Qī).
They gathered tens of thousands of followers
and reached Zīzhōng County.
At that time, the Former Lord was in Hànzhōng,
but Yán did not dispatch additional troops;
he merely led five thousand commandery soldiers to suppress them,
beheading Qín and Shèng and others.
Their factions scattered,
and all were returned to civilian registration.
Furthermore, Gāo Dìng, the leader of the Yuèxī barbarians, sent troops to besiege Xīndào County.
Yán rushed to its rescue,
and all the bandits were defeated and fled.
He was promoted to Fǔhàn Jiāngjūn,
retaining his commandery position as before.
In the second year of Zhāngwǔ (222 CE),
the Former Lord summoned Yán to Yǒng'ān Palace
and appointed him Shàngshūlìng.
In the third year (223 CE),
the Former Lord fell ill.
Yán and Zhūgě Liàng jointly received the deathbed edict to assist the Young Lord.
Yán was appointed Zhōngdūhù,
in charge of all military affairs, both internal and external,
and was left to garrison Yǒng'ān.
In the first year of Jiànxīng (223 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dūxiāng,
granted a jié (credentials),
and additionally appointed Guānglùxūn.
In the fourth year (226 CE),
he was transferred to the position of Qiánjiāngjūn.
As Zhūgě Liàng wished to send an army to Hànzhōng,
Yán was to oversee affairs in the rear.
He moved his garrison to Jiāngzhōu,
leaving Hùjūn Chén Dào to station at Yǒng'ān,
both under Yán's overall command.
Yán wrote to Mèng Dá, saying:
"Kǒngmíng and I have both been entrusted with grave responsibilities,
our worries are deep and our duties heavy.
We desire good companions."
Liàng also wrote to Dá, saying:
"His dispositions are like flowing water,
his advancing and retreating unobstructed—
this is Zhèngfāng's nature."
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
In the eighth year (230 CE),
he was promoted to Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
As Cáo Zhēn intended to advance on Hànchuān by three routes,
Liàng ordered Yán to lead twenty thousand men to Hànzhōng.
Liàng memorialized to have Yán's son Fēng appointed Jiāngzhōu Dūdū Dūjūn,
to oversee Yán's affairs in the rear.
As Liàng intended to send out an army the following year,
he ordered Yán, as Zhōngdūhù, to oversee the affairs of the chancellery.
Yán changed his name to Píng.
In the spring of the ninth year (231 CE),
Liàng's army was at Qíshān,
and Píng was pressing for transport affairs.
Between autumn and summer,
there was continuous heavy rain,
and the grain supply was not sustained.
Píng sent his Cānjūn Hú Zhōng and Dūjūn Chéng Fān to convey his intention,
summoning Liàng to return.
Liàng complied and withdrew the army.
When Píng heard the army had withdrawn,
he feigned surprise
and said,
"The army's provisions were abundant,
why did they return so quickly?!"
He wished to absolve himself of the responsibility for his inadequacy,
and to highlight Liàng's fault in not advancing.
He also memorialized to the Latter Lord,
saying,
"The army feigned retreat,
intending to lure the enemy into battle."
Liàng then fully presented Píng's written memorials and letters, both before and after,
showing Píng's transgressions to be evident.
Píng, having exhausted his arguments and his pretense,
confessed and apologized for his wrongdoing.
Thereupon, Liàng memorialized regarding Píng, saying:
"Since the demise of the Former Lord,
Píng's management of his household
has been marked by petty favors,
seeking personal comfort and reputation,
with no concern for the nation.
When I was about to march north,
I wished to use Píng's troops to garrison Hànzhōng,
but Píng made difficulties and objections,
showing no willingness to come,
and instead requested five commanderies to be the Inspector of Bāzhōu.
Last year, when I intended to campaign west,
I wished to let Píng oversee Hànzhōng,
but Píng spoke of Sīmǎ Yì and others establishing offices and making invitations.
I knew Píng's base intentions,
that he wished to take advantage of the campaign to coerce me for profit.
Therefore, I memorialized to make Píng's son Fēng the Dūjūn overseeing Jiāngzhōu,
exalting his treatment,
to accomplish a temporary task.
On the day Píng arrived,
all matters were entrusted to him.
All officials, high and low, were surprised at how generously I treated Píng.
This was precisely because the great task was not yet settled,
and the Han house was in peril.
To punish Píng's shortcomings
was less advisable than to praise him.
However, I believed Píng's motivation lay only in glory and profit;
I did not expect Píng's heart to be so utterly perverse.
If matters are delayed,
it will lead to disaster and defeat.
This is my lack of astuteness,
and my words only increase my faults."
Thereupon, Píng was deposed to commoner status
and exiled to Zǐtóng Commandery.
In the twelfth year (234 CE),
when Píng heard of Liàng's death,
he fell ill and died.
Píng had always hoped Liàng would eventually reinstate him,
calculating that no one else would be able to do so,
hence his intense indignation.
Fēng's official rank reached Zhūtí Tàishǒu.
Liú Yǎn, courtesy name Wēishuò,
was a native of Lǔguó.
When the Former Lord was in Yùzhōu,
he appointed him as Cóngshì.
Because he was of the imperial clan,
had a refined demeanor,
and was skilled in discourse,
the Former Lord treated him with great warmth and intimacy.
He consequently followed and traveled with him,
always serving as a guest.
When the Former Lord pacified Yìzhōu,
he appointed Yǎn as Gùlíng Tàishǒu.
When the Latter Lord ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dūxiāng.
His rank was always second only to Lǐ Yán.
He served as Wèiwèi Zhōngjūnshī Hòujiāngjūn,
and was promoted to Chēqí Jiāngjūn.
However, he did not participate in national governance,
only leading a thousand or so soldiers,
following Chancellor Liàng to offer criticisms and suggestions.
His carriages, clothes, food, and drink
were called extravagant and luxurious.
He had dozens of maidservants,
all of whom could perform music and singing,
and were also taught to recite the "Fù on the Lǔ Língguāng Palace."
In the tenth year of Jiànxīng (232 CE),
he was at odds with Qiánjūnshī Wèi Yán,
and his words were boastful and fantastical.
Liàng reprimanded him.
Yǎn wrote a memorial of apology to Liàng, saying:
"Yǎn's inherent nature is empty and superficial,
his conduct fundamentally weak.
Moreover, he suffers from the illness of excessive drinking.
Since the time of the Former Lord,
the various controversies
almost led to his downfall.
Fortunately, I have received the Public Lord's (Liàng's) understanding, who considered my single-minded devotion to the state,
pardoned the filth within me,
supported and saved me,
and granted me emoluments and rank,
thus reaching today.
Recently, confused and drunk,
my words contained errors.
Your benevolent grace tolerated and endured it,
not bringing me to justice,
allowing me to remain whole
and preserving my life.
Although I must certainly restrain myself and blame myself,
correct my mistakes and dedicate myself to death
to swear before the spirits,
if I have no purpose for my life,
then I have nowhere to put my face."
Thereupon, Liàng sent Yǎn back to Chéngdū,
his official rank remaining as before.
Yǎn lost his composure and was distraught.
In the first month of the twelfth year [234 CE],
Yǎn’s wife, Hú Shì, entered the palace to offer congratulations to the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager ordered Hú Shì to be detained there specially,
and she was only released after a month.
Hú Shì was beautiful.
Yǎn suspected she had an affair with the Later Lord,
so he called his attendants to give Hú five hundred lashes,
even beating her face with a shoe,
and then he divorced her and sent her away.
Hú Shì reported everything about Yǎn to the authorities.
Yǎn was imprisoned.
The officials debated, saying:
“Attendants are not people to lash one’s wife;
the face is not a place to receive a shoe.”
Yǎn was ultimately executed in the marketplace.
From then on, the morning felicitations of ministers' wives and mothers ceased.
Wèi Yán, courtesy name Wéncháng,
was a native of Yìyáng.
He followed the Former Lord into Shǔ as a commander of a contingent,
achieving numerous military merits,
and was promoted to Yámén Jiāngjūn.
When the Former Lord became Hánzhōng Wáng [King of Hánzhōng],
and moved his administration to Chéngdū,
he needed a senior general to garrison Hánchuān.
Public opinion believed it must be Zhāng Fēi,
and Fēi himself also expected it.
The Former Lord then promoted Wèi Yán to be Dū Hánzhōng Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn [General Who Guards the Distant for Hánzhōng],
and concurrently the Grand Administrator of Hánzhōng.
The entire army was astonished.
The Former Lord held a grand assembly of his ministers
and asked Wèi Yán:
“Now I entrust you with a grave responsibility.
What do you intend to do with it?”
Wèi Yán replied:
“If Cáo Cāo comes with all the forces of the empire,
I ask to repel him for Your Majesty;
if a subordinate general arrives with ten myriad troops,
I ask to swallow him for Your Majesty.”
The Former Lord praised him,
and all the assembled officials admired his words.
When the Former Lord ascended to the imperial throne,
Wèi Yán was further appointed Zhènběi Jiāngjūn [General Who Guards the North].
In the first year of Jiànxīng [223 CE],
he was enfeoffed as Dūtíng Hóu.
In the fifth year [227 CE],
Zhūgě Liàng was stationed in Hánzhōng,
and Wèi Yán was again appointed Dū Qiánbù [Supervisor of the Vanguard],
concurrently serving as Chéngxiàng Sīmǎ and Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu.
In the eighth year [230 CE],
Wèi Yán was sent west into Qiāngzhōng.
Wèi’s Later General Fèi Yáo and Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu Guō Huái engaged Wèi Yán in battle at Yángxī.
Wèi Yán thoroughly defeated Guō Huái and his forces,
and was promoted to Qiánjūnshī Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn [Commander of the Vanguard, Grand General Who Conquers the West],
granted the imperial staff of authority,
and further enfeoffed as Nánzhèng Hóu.
Whenever Wèi Yán accompanied Zhūgě Liàng on expeditions,
he invariably asked for ten thousand troops
to meet Liàng at Tóngguān by different routes,
following the precedent of Hán Xìn.
Liàng restrained him and did not permit it.
Wèi Yán often called Liàng timid,
and lamented that his talents were not fully utilized.
Wèi Yán was good at nurturing his soldiers,
and his bravery surpassed others.
He was also naturally arrogant,
and everyone at the time yielded to him.
Only Yáng Yí did not make concessions to Wèi Yán,
which made Wèi Yán extremely indignant,
and they were like fire and water.
In the twelfth year [234 CE],
Liàng advanced out of Běigǔ Kǒu,
with Wèi Yán as the vanguard.
Ten *lǐ* out from Liàng’s camp,
Wèi Yán dreamed that horns grew on his head.
He asked the dream interpreter Zhào Zhí about it.
Zhào Zhí deceived Wèi Yán, saying:
“The Qílín has horns but does not use them.
This is a sign that the enemy will defeat themselves without battle.”
He then retreated and told others:
“The character for 'horn' (角 *jiǎo*)
means 'use' (用 *yòng*) under 'knife' (刀 *dāo*);
a knife used on the head
portends extreme misfortune.”
In autumn,
Liàng became critically ill.
He secretly made arrangements for the army’s retreat after his death with Chángshǐ Yáng Yí, Sīmǎ Fèi Yī, Hùjūn Jiāng Wéi, and others,
ordering Wèi Yán to be the rearguard,
with Jiāng Wéi second;
if Wèi Yán should disobey,
the army should depart on its own.
When Liàng died,
his death was kept secret.
Yáng Yí ordered Fèi Yī to ascertain Wèi Yán’s intentions.
Wèi Yán said:
“Although the Chancellor is dead,
I am still here.
The Chancellor’s close relatives and staff can take his coffin back for burial,
but I myself shall lead all the armies to attack the enemy.
How can the affairs of the empire be abandoned just because one person has died?
Furthermore, who is Wèi Yán,
to be commanded by Yáng Yí
and act as a rearguard general!”
He then conferred with Fèi Yī to formulate plans for action and stay,
asking Fèi Yī to write it down by hand and sign their names together,
to be announced to all generals.
Fèi Yī deceived Wèi Yán, saying:
“I will return to explain to Chángshǐ Yáng on your behalf.
Chángshǐ is a civil official,
rarely handles military affairs,
and will surely not defy your orders.”
Fèi Yī left the gate and rode off on his horse.
Wèi Yán soon regretted it
and pursued him but could not catch him.
Wèi Yán sent someone to spy on Yáng Yí and his group,
and they were indeed proceeding according to Liàng’s established plans,
with all the camps successively withdrawing their armies.
Wèi Yán was furious.
Before Yáng Yí had departed,
Wèi Yán led his subordinates directly back south,
burning and destroying the gallery roads as he passed.
Wèi Yán and Yáng Yí each submitted memorials accusing the other of rebellion.
Within a single day,
urgent military dispatches arrived one after another.
The Later Lord consulted Shìzhōng Dǒng Yǔn and Liúfǔ Chángshǐ Jiǎng Wǎn.
Jiǎng Wǎn and Dǒng Yǔn both vouched for Yáng Yí and suspected Wèi Yán.
Yáng Yí and his group cleared mountains and opened paths,
traveling day and night,
also following behind Wèi Yán.
Wèi Yán arrived first
and occupied Nángǔ Kǒu,
sending troops to attack Yáng Yí and his group.
Yáng Yí and his group ordered Hé Píng to advance and resist Wèi Yán.
Hé Píng shouted at Wèi Yán’s vanguard:
“The lord is dead,
his body is not yet cold,
how dare you act like this!”
Wèi Yán’s officers and soldiers knew that the fault lay with Wèi Yán,
and none were willing to fight for him;
his army dispersed.
Wèi Yán fled alone with a few of his sons,
escaping to Hánzhōng.
Yáng Yí sent Mǎ Dài to pursue and kill him,
and his head was brought to Yáng Yí.
Yáng Yí got up and stomped on it himself,
saying:
“You common slave!
Can you still cause trouble?”
Then he exterminated Wèi Yán’s three generations of relatives.
Originally,
Jiǎng Wǎn led the palace guards and various camps north to address the crisis.
After traveling several tens of *lǐ*,
the news of Wèi Yán’s death arrived,
so he turned back.
Wèi Yán’s intention was not to surrender to Wèi in the north but to return south,
merely wishing to eliminate Yáng Yí and his group.
He believed that the generals were usually not his equal,
and hoped that public opinion at the time would certainly appoint him to succeed Zhūgě Liàng.
This was his original intention,
not to betray.
Yáng Yí, courtesy name Wēigōng,
was a native of Xiāngyáng.
During the Jiàn’ān period,
he served as the Chief Clerk to Fù Qún, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
He abandoned Qún and went to see Guān Yǔ, the Administrator of Xiāngyáng.
Yǔ appointed him as Gongcáo,
and sent him as an envoy west to see the Former Lord.
The Former Lord discussed with him military and state strategies,
and the successes and failures of governance,
and was greatly pleased with him.
He was then invited to be the Registrar of the Left General's Military Office.
When the Former Lord became King of Hànzhōng,
he promoted Yí to Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
When the Former Lord assumed the imperial title
and launched an eastern campaign against Wú,
Yí was at odds with Liú Bā, the Imperial Secretary,
and was demoted and remotely appointed as Administrator of Hóngnóng.
In the third year of Jiànxīng,
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng appointed him as Aide-de-camp,
to manage the affairs of the chancellery
before setting out for the south.
In the fifth year,
he followed Liàng to Hànzhōng.
In the eighth year,
he was promoted to Chief Clerk,
and given the additional title of General Who Pacifies the Army.
Liàng frequently launched military campaigns,
and Yí always planned and divided the tasks,
and estimated the grain provisions.
He did not hesitate in his thoughts,
and finished in a moment.
Military regulations and arrangements
were all handled by Yí.
Liàng deeply cherished Yí's talent and ability,
and relied on Wèi Yán's valor and courage.
He often regretted that the two men were not on good terms,
and could not bear to favor one over the other.
In the twelfth year,
he followed Liàng to garrison at Gǔkǒu.
Liàng died on the battlefield.
Yí then led the army back,
and also suppressed and executed Yán.
He believed that his achievements were immense,
and that he should succeed Liàng in administering the government.
He summoned Commandant Zhào Zhèng to divine with the *Zhōuyì*,
and the hexagram obtained was Jiārén.
He remained silent and displeased.
However, Liàng's secret intention throughout his life
was that Yí's nature was narrow and irritable,
and his preference was for Jiǎng Wǎn.
Wǎn thus became Imperial Secretary and Inspector of Yìzhōu.
When Yí arrived,
he was appointed as Central Army Strategist,
without any command,
merely enjoying a leisurely life.
Initially,
when Yí was the Former Lord's Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
Wǎn was an Imperial Secretariat Gentleman.
Later, although both became Aide-de-camp and Chief Clerk to the Chancellor,
Yí always accompanied him on campaigns,
bearing the hardships and difficulties.
He considered that his seniority in age and official rank preceded Wǎn's,
and his talent surpassed his.
Thus, his resentment and indignation showed in his voice and expression,
and sighs of lamentation came from his heart.
At that time, people feared his unrestrained speech,
and no one dared to approach him.
Only Fèi Yī, the Chief Strategist of the Rear Army, went to comfort him.
Yí expressed his resentment and disappointment to Yī,
uttering many things,
and also said to Yī:
"When the Chancellor died,
if I had led the army to surrender to the Wèi state,
would my life now be so fallen!
It makes me regret it endlessly."
Yī secretly reported his words.
In the thirteenth year,
Yí was dismissed as a commoner
and exiled to Hànjiā Commandery.
Upon arriving at the place of exile,
Yí again submitted a memorial slandering others,
with sharp and vehement language.
Consequently, the commandery was ordered to arrest Yí.
Yí committed suicide,
and his wife and children were returned to Shǔ.
Commentary states: Liú Fēng was in a situation of suspicion,
and his defensive foresight was insufficient to protect himself.
Péng Yàng and Liáo Lì advanced through their talents,
Lǐ Yán achieved through his ability and competence,
Wèi Yán was appointed through his bravery and strategy,
Yáng Yí became prominent through his official duties,
Liú Yǎn was an old official.
All were highly esteemed.
Examining their actions,
and tracing their conduct,
they brought disaster and blame upon themselves,
without exception.
Biography 11: Huò, Wáng, Xiàng, Zhāng, Yáng, Fèi
Huò Jùn, courtesy name Zhòngmiáo,
was a native of Zhījiāng in Nánjùn.
His elder brother, Dú,
gathered several hundred troops in his hometown.
When Dú died,
Liú Biǎo, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, ordered Jùn to take command of his forces.
When Biǎo died,
Jùn led his troops to submit to the Former Lord.
The Former Lord appointed Jùn as Commandant.
When the Former Lord returned south from Jiāméng to attack Liú Zhāng,
he left Jùn to guard Jiāméng City.
Zhāng Lǔ sent his general Yáng Bó to entice Jùn,
asking to jointly guard the city.
Jùn said:
"My head can be taken,
but the city cannot be taken."
Bó then retreated.
Later, Zhāng's generals Fú Jìn and Xiàng Cún, leading over ten thousand men, ascended the Lángshuǐ River
and attacked and besieged Jùn.
After nearly a year,
they could not capture it.
Jùn, with only a few hundred soldiers in the city,
watched for their moment of laxity,
selected elites to launch an attack,
and greatly defeated them,
immediately beheading Cún.
When the Former Lord pacified Shǔ,
he commended Jùn's achievements.
He divided Guǎnghàn into Zītóng Commandery,
appointing Jùn as Administrator of Zītóng and General of the Household.
He served for three years,
and died at the age of forty.
He was buried back in Chéngdū.
The Former Lord deeply mourned him,
and issued an edict to Zhūgě Liàng, saying:
"Jùn was an excellent man,
and moreover rendered service to the state.
I wish to perform
Therefore, he personally led his officials to attend the condolence and sacrifice,
and stayed overnight at the grave,
which was considered a great honor at the time.
His son, Yì,
courtesy name Shàoxiān,
was a Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince in the Former Lord's later years.
When the Latter Lord ascended the throne,
he was appointed Herald.
When Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng was stationed north in Hànzhōng,
he requested Yì to be his Secretary,
and had him associate and reside with his son, Qíao.
When Liàng died,
he became a Yellow Gate Attendant.
When the Latter Lord established Crown Prince Xuán,
he appointed Yì as his Grand Tutor.
Xuán was fond of riding and archery,
and had no moderation in his comings and goings.
Yì cited ancient principles
and fully remonstrated,
which was considered excellent and principled advice.
Later, he became Aide-de-camp, Deputy Commandant of the Làijiàng Garrison,
and then transferred to Protector of the Army,
managing affairs as before.
At that time, the Yí and Láo barbarians of Yǒngchāng Commandery, relying on the rugged terrain, were disobedient
and frequently committed raids.
Thus, Yì was appointed Administrator of Yǒngchāng,
and led a detachment to suppress them.
He then beheaded their chieftains,
destroyed their settlements,
and the commandery border became peaceful.
He was promoted to Supervisor of the Army and General Who Assists the Army,
and concurrently Administrator of Jiànníng,
and returned to manage the affairs of Nánjùn.
In the sixth year of Jǐngyào,
he was advanced to the title of General Who Pacifies the South.
In that year,
Shǔ was annexed by Wèi.
Yì and Luó Xiàn of Xiāngyáng, the Commander of Bādōng, each preserved a region,
and surrendered them to the central government.
Both were retained in their former positions,
and received increased favor and treatment.
Wáng Lián, courtesy name Wényí,
was a native of Nányáng.
During Liú Zhāng's time, he entered Shǔ
and served as the magistrate of Zītóng.
When the Former Lord (Liú Bèi) launched his campaign from Jiāmēng
and advanced south,
Lián closed the city gates and refused to surrender.
The Former Lord respected his integrity
and did not force him.
When Chéngdū was pacified,
Lián was appointed magistrate of Shífāng,
then transferred to Guǎngdū,
where he achieved merits in his posts.
He was promoted to Supervisor of Salt (Sīyán Xiàowèi),
managing the profits from salt and iron.
The revenues were substantial,
greatly benefiting the state's finances.
Consequently, he selected talented individuals to serve as his subordinates,
such as Lǚ Yì, Dù Qí, and Liú Gàn,
who all eventually reached high offices,
having been promoted by Lián himself.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Shǔjùn and General Who Develops Enterprise (Xīngyè Jiāngjūn),
continuing to oversee the Salt Office as before.
In the first year of Jiànxīng (223 CE),
he was appointed Commandant of Cavalry (Túnqí Xiàowèi)
and concurrently Chief Clerk to the Imperial Chancellor (Chéngxiàng Zhǎngshǐ),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Píngyáng Tíng.
At that time, the southern commanderies were not compliant,
and Zhūgě Liàng was preparing to personally lead a campaign against them.
Lián advised him, saying,
"This is barren land,
a region of plague and disease.
It is not fitting for a person of the state's high esteem
to undertake such a dangerous journey."
Liàng, considering that no other general matched his capabilities,
was determined to go.
However, Lián's words were always sincere and urgent,
which caused Liàng to delay his departure for a long time.
Soon after, Lián passed away.
His son, Shān, succeeded him
and rose to the office of Grand Administrator of Jiāngyáng.
Xiàng Lǎng, courtesy name Jùdá,
was a native of Yíchéng, Xiāngyáng.
Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, appointed him Magistrate of Línjǔ.
After Biǎo's death,
he returned to the Former Lord.
When the Former Lord pacified Jiāngnán,
he sent Lǎng to supervise military and civilian affairs in the four counties of Zǐguī, Yídào, Wūshān, and Yílíng.
After Shǔ was pacified,
Lǎng was appointed Grand Administrator of Bāxī,
and shortly thereafter transferred to Zāngkē,
then moved to Fánglíng.
When the Latter Lord ascended the throne,
he became Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi)
and succeeded Wáng Lián as Chief Clerk to the Imperial Chancellor.
When Imperial Chancellor Liàng marched south,
Lǎng remained to oversee affairs in the rear.
In the fifth year (227 CE),
he accompanied Liàng to Hànzhōng.
Lǎng had always been on good terms with Mǎ Sù.
When Sù fled,
Lǎng, knowing the situation, did not report him.
Liàng resented this
and dismissed him from office, sending him back to Chéngdū.
Several years later,
he was made Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglùxūn).
After Liàng's death, he was transferred to General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn).
In recognition of his past achievements,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiǎnmíng Tíng
and granted the status of Minister Who Has the Honor of the First Rank (Tèjìn).
Initially,
though Lǎng had dabbled in literature in his youth,
he did not adhere to plain conduct,
and was praised for his administrative abilities.
After he was dismissed from the Chief Clerk position,
he enjoyed leisurely inactivity for nearly thirty years,
and then immersed himself in classical texts,
working diligently and tirelessly.
Even past eighty years old,
he still personally proofread books,
corrected errors,
and accumulated a large collection of writings,
the most at that time.
He opened his doors to guests
and encouraged junior scholars,
discussing only ancient principles
and not interfering in contemporary affairs,
for which he was highly regarded.
From high-ranking officials
to young children,
all respected him.
He died in the tenth year of Yánxī (247 CE).
His son, Tiáo, succeeded him
and became Imperial Household Grandee (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) during the Jǐngyào era.
Lǎng's nephew, Chǒng,
served as a Tooth-Gate General (Yámén Jiāng) during the Former Lord's time.
In the defeat at Zǐguī,
Chǒng's camp remained particularly intact.
In the first year of Jiànxīng, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng,
and later became Central Supervisor (Zhōngbù Dū),
commanding the palace guards.
When Zhūgě Liàng was about to march north,
he memorialized to the Latter Lord, saying:
"General Xiàng Chǒng
is of excellent and balanced character,
and well-versed in military affairs.
He was tested in the past,
and the late emperor (Former Lord) praised him as capable.
Therefore, public opinion nominated Chǒng as supervisor.
Your foolish servant believes that matters within the camp
should all be consulted with him.
He will surely be able to ensure harmony in the ranks
and proper placement for both the able and the less able."
He was promoted to Central Leader of the Army (Zhōng Língjūn).
In the third year of Yánxī (240 CE),
while campaigning against the Mán-Yí in Hànjiā,
he was killed.
Chǒng's younger brother, Chōng,
successively served as Commandant of Archery (Shèshēng Xiàowèi) and Minister (Shàngshū).
Zhāng Yì, courtesy name Jūnsì,
was a native of Chéngdū, Shǔjùn.
He studied the Gōngyáng Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals
and extensively read historical records and the Hàn histories.
When Xǔ Wénxiū of Rǔnán entered Shǔ,
he remarked that Yì was quick and capable in administration,
comparable to Zhōng Yuáncháng of Zhōngxià (the Central Plains).
During Liú Zhāng's time,
he was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián)
and became Magistrate of Yúfù.
He returned to the provincial office to serve as Attendant Official (Cóngshì),
and concurrently held the post of Horseman Under the Tent (Zhàngxià Sīmǎ).
When Zhāng Fēi advanced from Jīngzhōu via Diànjiāng,
Zhāng granted Yì troops
to resist Zhāng Fēi at Déyáng Mòxià.
His army was defeated,
and he returned to Chéngdū.
He was sent by Zhāng as an envoy to the Former Lord.
The Former Lord promised to treat his lord with courtesy and bring peace to his people.
When Yì returned,
the city gates were opened.
The Former Lord appointed Yì Grand Administrator of Bājùn,
and later, he returned to serve as Central Gentleman of Gold (Sījīn Zhōnglángjiāng),
overseeing the production of agricultural and military implements.
Previously,
in Yìzhōujùn, the Grand Administrator Zhèng Áng had been murdered.
The chieftain Yōng Kǎi enjoyed widespread trust and influence in the southern region
and engaged in frequent diplomatic exchanges,
even establishing communication with Sūn Quán.
Thus, Yì was appointed Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu
and proceeded directly to the commandery.
Kǎi, however, hesitated and refused to submit.
He pretended to receive a divine message, saying,
"Grand Administrator Zhāng is like a gourd,
smooth on the outside but rough within.
There is no need to kill him.
Just tie him up and send him to Wú."
So, he sent Yì to Quán.
At this time, the Former Lord passed away.
Zhūgě Liàng dispatched Dèng Zhī as an envoy to Wú.
Liàng instructed Zhī to subtly request Yì from Quán during their conversation.
Yì had been in Wú for several years,
wandering and hiding,
and Quán was unaware of his presence.
Thus, Quán agreed to Zhī's request to send Yì back.
Just before Yì's departure,
Quán summoned him for an audience
and asked Yì,
"The widowed daughter of the Zhuó clan in Shǔ
ran off with Sīmǎ Xiāngrú.
Why are the customs of your land like that?"
Yì replied,
"Your foolish servant believes that the widowed daughter of the Zhuó clan
was still more virtuous than Mǎi Chén's wife."
Quán then said to Yì,
"When you return,
you will surely be employed in the western court,
and will certainly not remain a farmer in your village.
How will you repay me?"
Yì replied,
"Your servant returns guilty,
and will commit his life to the proper authorities.
If I am fortunate enough to keep my head,
the years before I was fifty-eight belong to my parents;
all years thereafter are the generous gift of Your Majesty."
Quán spoke and laughed with pleasure,
showing admiration for Yì's character.
After Yì left the palace,
he deeply regretted not feigning foolishness,
and immediately boarded a boat,
traveling day and night at double speed.
Quán indeed sent pursuers,
but Yì had already entered the borders of Yǒng'ān by several tens of *lǐ*,
and the pursuers could not catch him.
Upon arriving in Shǔ,
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng appointed him as Aide-de-camp (cānjūn),
and put him in charge of the affairs of the chancellery.
He also held the post of Chief Administrator (zhìzhōng cóngshì) of Yìzhōu.
When Liàng went out to station himself at Hànzhōng,
Yì, as Archer-General (shèshēng xiàowèi), took charge of the Chief Clerks (liúfǔ zhǎnglì) of the chancellery.
He often remarked:
"The Duke’s rewards do not overlook the distant,
his punishments do not favor the close.
Nobility cannot be obtained without merit,
and punishment cannot be evaded by status or power.
This is why both the wise and the foolish forget themselves."
The following year,
he went north to meet Liàng to consult on matters.
Hundreds of people escorted him,
and carriages filled the road.
Upon his return, Yì wrote a letter to his intimates saying:
"Recently, while on the road,
I received guests day and night,
unable to rest peacefully.
People pay their respects to the Chancellor’s Chief Clerk himself,
and also to Lord Zhāng Jūnsì.
I am tired to death."
His discussions and rapid speech
were all of this kind.
When young, he was on good terms with Yáng Gōng of Jiànwéi.
Gōng died early,
leaving young orphans not yet a few years old.
Yì took them in,
shared a house with them,
and served Gōng’s mother as his own.
When Gōng’s children grew up,
he found wives for them,
bought them fields, houses, and property,
and enabled them to establish their own households.
He cared for old friends,
and provided for declining clans,
showing great benevolence.
He was promoted to General Who Assists the Hàn (fǔhàn jiāngjūn),
and remained Chief Clerk (zhǎnglì) as before.
He died in Jiànxīng year 8 [230 CE].
His son Mù succeeded him.
(Mù is pronounced as 'máng jiǎo fǎn',
as seen in the Zìlín,
which says,
"Mù
means 'contemplative appearance'." )
