He successively served as Administrator of three commanderies and Supervisor of the Army.
Mù’s younger brother, Dū,
was a Gentleman-in-Waiting to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ zhōngshùzǐ).
Yáng Hóng, courtesy name Jìxiū,
was a native of Wǔyáng, Jiànwéi.
During the time of Liú Zhāng, he successively served in various commanderies.
When the Former Sovereign (Xiānzhǔ) pacified Shǔ,
Prefect Lǐ Yán appointed him as Registrar (gōngcáo).
Yán wanted to move the commandery’s seat of government.
Hóng steadfastly remonstrated against it, but was not heeded,
so he resigned as Registrar
and requested to retire.
Yán wanted to recommend Hóng to the province
to serve as an Administrator (cóngshì) of the Shǔ Department.
When the Former Sovereign contended for Hànzhōng,
urgent dispatches were sent to mobilize troops.
Military Advisor General (jūnshī jiāngjūn) Zhūgě Liàng consulted Hóng,
who said:
"Hànzhōng is the throat of Yìzhōu,
a critical juncture for survival or destruction.
Without Hànzhōng, there will be no Shǔ.
This is a disaster for our very household.
In the current situation,
men should fight,
and women should transport supplies.
Why hesitate to dispatch troops?"
At that time, Fǎ Zhèng, the Administrator of Shǔ Commandery, had gone north with the Former Sovereign.
Liàng then memorialized to appoint Hóng as acting Administrator of Shǔ Commandery.
All affairs were managed,
and he was then made the actual Administrator.
A short while later,
he was transferred to be Chief Administrator (zhìzhōng cóngshì) of Yìzhōu.
After the Former Sovereign proclaimed himself emperor,
his campaign against Wú was unsuccessful,
and he returned to reside in Yǒng’ān.
Huáng Yuánsù, the Administrator of Hànjiā, who was disliked by Zhūgě Liàng,
hearing that the Former Sovereign was seriously ill,
feared future repercussions,
and raised a rebellion in his commandery,
burning the city of Línqióng.
At that time, Liàng had traveled east to visit the sick,
and Chéngdū was left weakly guarded,
which is why Yuán felt no apprehension.
Hóng immediately reported to the Crown Prince,
dispatched his personal guard,
and sent Generals Chén Hū and Zhèng Chuò to suppress Yuán.
The general consensus was that if Yuán could not besiege Chéngdū,
he would surely go via Yuèxī to hold Nánzhōng.
Hóng said:
"Yuánsù’s nature is fierce and violent,
without any other grace or trust.
How could he accomplish this?
He will merely travel east downriver,
hoping the Emperor is safe,
to surrender himself for execution;
if there is any other intention,
he will flee to Wú to seek survival.
Just instruct Hū and Chuò to intercept him at Nán’ān Gorge, and they will surely get him."
Hū and Chuò followed Hóng’s words,
and indeed captured Yuán alive.
In Jiànxīng year 1 [223 CE], Hóng was granted the title of Marquis of the Interior (guānnèihóu).
He was again appointed Administrator of Shǔ Commandery and General of Integrity (zhōngjié jiāngjūn).
Later, he became Colonel of the Elite Cavalry (yuèqí xiàowèi),
continuing to lead the commandery as before.
In year 5 [227 CE],
Chancellor Liàng stationed himself in Hànzhōng,
and wanted to appoint Zhāng Yì as Chief Clerk of the Chancellery in his absence.
He asked Hóng for his opinion.
Hóng replied:
"Yì is naturally perceptive,
and skilled at managing complex affairs.
His talent is truly equal to the task.
However, his nature is not entirely impartial,
and I fear he cannot be solely relied upon.
It would be better to keep Xiàng Lǎng.
Lǎng’s character is less prone to artifice.
Yì could follow you personally,
to demonstrate his abilities,
which would be good for both matters."
Initially,
Yì and Hóng were good friends in their youth.
When Yì was exiled to Wú,
Hóng oversaw Yì’s commandery.
Yì’s son, Yù, served as a clerk in the commandery government.
For a minor transgression, he was punished
and not specially pardoned from leave.
When Yì later returned and heard of this,
he deeply resented it,
and his affection for Hóng was diminished.
When Hóng saw Liàng come out [of the chancellery],
he went to Yì’s residence
and fully recounted what he had said.
Yì replied to Hóng:
"You have completely kept me here.
My lord (Zhūgě Liàng) cannot stop me."
At the time, some suspected that Hóng himself wanted to be Chief Clerk.
Others suspected that Hóng knew Yì was self-conscious
and did not wish Yì to hold such an important position
and manage the affairs behind the Chancellor.
Later, Yì was at odds with Cén Shù, the Colonel of Salt Affairs,
to the point of deep resentment.
Liàng wrote to Yì saying:
"When you were previously in Bòxià
and your camp was destroyed,
my heart was so troubled I could not taste my food.
Later, when you were exiled to Nánhǎi,
I grieved and sighed for you,
unable to rest in my bed.
Upon your return,
I entrusted you with great responsibilities,
to jointly aid the imperial house.
I considered myself and you to be ancient 'rock-friends'.
The way of 'rock-friends' is
to point out enemies to benefit each other,
and to cut flesh and bone to clarify matters for each other,
without offering apologies.
How much more so now that
I merely entrusted my thoughts to Yuánjiǎn (Hóng’s courtesy name),
and you cannot tolerate it?"
Commentators from this understood that Hóng was selfless.
Hóng was not fond of scholarship in his youth,
but he was loyal, upright, and sincere,
worrying about public affairs as if they were his own family’s,
and served his stepmother with utmost filial piety.
He died in office in year 6 [228 CE].
When Hóng first served as Lǐ Yán’s Registrar,
Yán had not yet gone to Jiànwéi, but Hóng was already Administrator of Shǔ Commandery.
Hóng welcomed Hé Zhī, a clerk under his administration,
who possessed talent, strategy, and administrative skill.
He was promoted to a commandery official,
and after several years became Administrator of Guǎnghàn.
At that time, Hóng was still in Shǔ Commandery.
Therefore, the people of the Western Lands all admired Zhūgě Liàng’s ability to fully utilize the talents of his contemporaries.
Fèi Shī, courtesy name Gōngjǔ,
was a man from Nán'ān, Jiānwéi.
During Liú Zhāng's time, he served as the Magistrate of Miánzhú.
When the Former Lord attacked Miánzhú,
Shī was the first to surrender the city.
After Chéngdū was pacified,
the Former Lord assumed the governorship of Yìzhōu,
appointing Shī as Dūjūn Cóngshì.
He was sent out to serve as the Administrator of Zānggē,
and upon his return, became Zhōu Qiánbù Sīmǎ.
When the Former Lord became the King of Hànzhōng,
he dispatched Shī to confer upon Guān Yǔ the title of Qián Jiāngjūn.
When Yǔ heard that Huáng Zhōng had been appointed Hòu Jiāngjūn,
Yǔ angrily declared:
"A great man will never be ranked alongside an old soldier!"
He refused to accept the appointment.
Shī said to Yǔ:
"Indeed, those who establish royal enterprises
employ various kinds of people.
In the past, Xiāo and Cáo were close friends of Gāozǔ from youth,
while Chén and Hán, having been fugitives, arrived later.
When their ranks were discussed,
Hán was placed highest,
yet we have never heard of Xiāo and Cáo resenting this.
Now, the King of Hàn, based on a temporary achievement,
has greatly honored Hànshēng.
However, the weight of his intentions
can hardly be compared to that for you, Junhóu!
Moreover, the King and you, Junhóu,
are like one body,
sharing joy and sorrow equally,
sharing both misfortune and good fortune.
As your humble servant,
I believe it is not proper for you to be concerned with the hierarchy of official titles,
nor the amount of emoluments and stipends.
I am but a lowly envoy,
bearing a command.
If you, Junhóu, do not accept the appointment,
I shall simply return.
However, I feel sorry for this action of yours,
fearing you might regret it later!"
Yǔ was greatly moved and enlightened,
and immediately accepted the appointment.
Later, when the officials deliberated on urging the King of Hànzhōng to assume the imperial title,
Shī submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your Highness, because Cáo Cāo and his son usurped the throne by coercing the sovereign,
you therefore traveled ten thousand *lǐ*
and gathered an army
to punish the rebels.
Now, the great enemy is not yet defeated,
yet you would first establish yourself.
This might cause doubt in people's hearts.
In ancient times, Gāozǔ made a pact with Chǔ,
that whoever first broke Qín would become king.
Even after he captured Xiányáng
and apprehended Zǐyīng,
he still harbored thoughts of declining the position.
How much more so now, when Your Highness has not even left your courtyard,
do you wish to establish yourself!
Your humble servant genuinely believes this is not beneficial for Your Highness."
Because of this, he offended the ruler,
and was demoted to Bù Yǒngchāng Cóngshì.
In the third year of Jiànxīng,
he accompanied Zhūgě Liàng on his southern expedition.
Upon returning to Hànyáng County,
the surrendered man Lǐ Hóng came to meet Liàng.
When Liàng met Hóng,
Jiǎng Wǎn and Shī were also present.
Hóng said:
"I recently passed through Méng Dá's place,
and just saw Wáng Chōng coming from the south.
He said that in the past, regarding Dá's departure,
you, Mínggōng, gnashed your teeth
and wanted to execute Dá's wife and children,
but fortunately, the Former Lord did not permit it.
Dá said: 'Zhūgě Liàng has shown me consideration with a full understanding of the situation,
he would never do that.'
He completely disbelieved Chōng's words,
and trusted and relied on you, Mínggōng,
without any wavering."
Liàng said to Wǎn and Shī:
"When we return to the capital, I shall send a letter to Zǐdù to convey my greetings."
Shī interjected:
"Méng Dá is but a petty fellow.
In the past, he was disloyal to Zhènwēi,
and later betrayed the Former Lord.
He is a fickle person;
why bother corresponding with him?"
Liàng remained silent and did not reply.
Liàng wished to entice Dá to serve as an external ally,
and ultimately sent Dá a letter stating:
"Last year, on the southern campaign,
I returned only at the end of the year.
I happened to meet Lǐ Hóng in Hànyáng,
and learned of the news.
I sighed deeply with emotion,
remembering your past aspirations.
How could it be merely an empty pursuit of fame and honor,
leading to separation?
Alas, Méngzǐ,
it was truly Liú Fēng's encroachment upon you
that harmed the Former Lord's principle of treating gentlemen.
Moreover, Hóng relayed that Wáng Chōng fabricated false stories,
saying that you understood my heart
and were not swayed by Chōng's words.
Seeking out the truth of this statement,
and recalling our lifelong friendship,
I look eastward with longing,
and thus send this letter."
Upon receiving Liàng's letter, Dá
exchanged messages with him several times,
expressing his desire to betray Wèi.
Wèi sent Sīmǎ Xuānwáng to suppress him,
and Dá was immediately executed.
Liàng also believed that Dá lacked sincerity,
and therefore did not aid him.
When Jiǎng Wǎn held power,
Shī was appointed Jiànyì Dàfū,
and he died at home.
Wáng Chōng
was a man from Guǎnghàn.
He served as a Yámén Jiàng,
under the command of Lǐ Yán, the Dū of Jiāngzhōu.
He was disliked by Yán,
and fearing punishment, surrendered to Wèi.
Wèi appointed Chōng as the Administrator of Lèlíng.
The commentary states: Huò Jùn's isolated city did not fall,
Wáng Lián's firm integrity did not waver,
Xiàng Lǎng was tirelessly fond of learning,
Zhāng Yì was quick and responsive,
Yáng Hóng was loyal and impartial in his heart,
Fèi Shī spoke his mind.
All are worthy of record.
Given the Former Lord's broad benevolence
and Zhūgě's adherence to standards,
Shī, who spoke frankly,
was still treated with indifference.
How much more so under an ordinary ruler!
Biographies of Dù Zhōu, Dù Xǔ, Méng Lái, Yǐn Lǐ, Qiáo Xí – Chapter Twelve
Dù Wēi, courtesy name Guófǔ,
was a man from Fú in Zītóng.
In his youth, he studied under Rèn Ān of Guǎnghàn.
Liú Zhāng appointed him as an Attendant Officer,
but he left office due to illness.
When the Former Sovereign (Xiānzhǔ) pacified Shǔ,
Wēi always pretended to be deaf
and remained secluded at home.
In the second year of Jiànxīng (224 CE),
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng, acting as the Governor of Yìzhōu,
carefully selected and invited worthy old men.
He appointed Qín Mì as Assistant Officer,
Wǔ Liáng as Superintendent of Merit,
and Wēi as Chief Clerk.
Wēi firmly declined,
but was brought to office in a carriage.
Once he arrived,
Liàng granted Wēi an audience,
and Wēi personally offered his apologies.
Considering that Wēi could not hear others speak,
Liàng wrote him a letter at the meeting, saying:
“I have long heard of your virtuous conduct,
and have thirsted for it for a long time.
As pure and turbid waters flow separately,
I have had no opportunity to consult with you.
Wáng Yuántài, Lǐ Bórén, Wáng Wényí, Yáng Jìxiū, Dīng Jūngàn, Lǐ Yǒngnán and his brothers, Wén Zhòngbǎo, and others,
have often sighed in admiration of your noble aspirations,
and have not seen your like since ancient times.
I am merely empty and unworthy,
yet I govern your esteemed province.
My virtue is meager, but my responsibility is heavy,
filling me with deep anxiety.
The court (Our Lord) is only eighteen this year,
with a benevolent and intelligent natural disposition,
and a fondness for virtuous and humble scholars.
The people of the world yearn for the Hàn dynasty,
and I wish to unite with you, in accordance with heaven and the people,
to assist this enlightened ruler,
to bring about the success of the revival of the dynasty,
and to engrave his achievements on bamboo and silk.
I thought that the wise and the foolish do not conspire together,
hence I cut myself off
and simply kept to my toil,
not planning to humble myself.”
Wēi then begged to return home, citing old age and illness.
Liàng again wrote a letter in reply, saying:
“Cáo Pī usurped and assassinated,
and enthroned himself as emperor.
This is like a clay dragon or a straw dog – it has a name but no substance.
I wish to unite with all worthy gentlemen, using their wickedness and falsehood,
to destroy them with the righteous path.
It is strange that you have not offered any advice,
and instead wish to return to the mountains and wilderness.
Pī is also launching great labor projects
to move against Wú and Chǔ.
Now, taking advantage of Pī’s numerous engagements,
we should close our borders and diligently farm,
nurture the people and their livelihood,
and at the same time prepare our weapons,
to await his defeat,
and then attack him.
This way, we can pacify the world without our soldiers fighting or our people toiling.
You only need to assist the times with your virtue;
I do not demand military affairs from you.
Why are you so eager to leave?”
Such was his respect for Wēi.
He was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance,
in accordance with his wishes.
Wǔ Liáng,
courtesy name Déshān,
was a man from Nán'ān in Jiānwéi.
He was renowned for his scholarship and integrity.
He was promoted from Consultant to Grand Master of Remonstrance and Commander of the Five Bureaus.
Zhōu Qún, courtesy name Zhòngzhí,
was a man from Lángzhōng in Bāxī.
His father, Shū,
courtesy name Shūbù,
studied scholarship in his youth under Yáng Hòu of Guǎnghàn,
and his fame was second only to Dǒng Fú and Rèn Ān.
He was repeatedly summoned,
but never went.
At the time, someone asked:
“The Spring and Autumn prognostications say that ‘he who replaces the Hàn shall be Gāo on the Dāngtú (road),’
what does this mean?”
Shū replied:
“Gāo on the Dāngtú means Wèi.”
Scholars in his hometown privately spread his words.
Qún studied under Shū in his youth,
and dedicated himself to observing omens.
He built a small tower in his courtyard,
and being wealthy with many slaves,
he always ordered his slaves to take turns on the tower to observe celestial phenomena.
As soon as they saw a new atmospheric omen,
they would immediately report it to Qún,
who would then go up the tower himself to observe it,
regardless of morning or night.
Thus, whenever there was a climate phenomenon,
he never failed to see it,
which is why his predictions were often accurate.
The Provincial Governor Liú Zhāng
appointed him as an advisor and attendant officer.
When the Former Sovereign pacified Shǔ,
he appointed him Scholarly Officer of the Imperial Forest.
When the Former Sovereign wanted to contend with Cáo Gōng for Hánzhōng,
he asked Qún.
Qún replied:
“You will gain the land,
but not the people.
If you send out a detached army,
it will certainly be unfavorable.
You must be cautious!”
At that time, Zhāng Yù of Shǔjùn, the Rear Major of the province, also understood prognostication,
and his natural talent surpassed Qún’s.
He remonstrated with the Former Sovereign, saying:
“You cannot contend for Hánzhōng;
the army will certainly be at a disadvantage.”
The Former Sovereign ultimately did not heed Yù’s words,
and indeed gained the land but not the people.
He sent Generals Wú Lán and Léi Tóng into Wǔdū,
and they were all lost and did not return,
exactly as Qún had predicted.
Thereupon, Qún was promoted as a “Flourishing Talent.”
Yù also privately told people:
“In the year Gēngzǐ,
the world will change dynasties,
and the mandate of the Liú clan will end.
The Lord obtained Yìzhōu,
but nine years later,
between the years Yín and Mǎo,
he will lose it.”
Someone secretly reported his words.
Initially,
when the Former Sovereign met Liú Zhāng at Fú,
Yù was Zhāng’s attendant officer
and was present at the sitting.
Yù had a thick beard,
and the Former Sovereign joked with him, saying:
“In the past, when I lived in Zhuōxiàn,
there were many people with the surname Máo (毛, hair).
East, west, north, and south were all the various Máos.
The Magistrate of Zhuō exclaimed, ‘Are the many Máos surrounding Zhuō?’”
Yù immediately replied:
“In the past, there was someone who served as the Chief of Lù in Shàngdǎng,
and was promoted to Magistrate of Zhuō.
When he left office and returned home,
people wrote letters to him.
If they addressed him as Lù, they would lose Zhuō;
if they addressed him as Zhuō, they would lose Lù.
So they addressed him as ‘Lord Lùzhuō’.”
The Former Sovereign had no beard,
so Yù used this to allude to him.
The Former Sovereign always held a grudge against his impertinence,
and was further angered by his leaked words.
He then openly declared Yù’s remonstrance against contending for Hánzhōng to be unproven,
imprisoned him,
and was about to execute him.
Zhūgě Liàng memorialized to plead for his crime.
The Former Sovereign replied:
“If a fragrant orchid grows at the gate,
one cannot but weed it out.”
Yù was then executed in the marketplace.
Later, the establishment of the Wèi dynasty
and the death of the Former Sovereign
all happened exactly as Yù had predicted.
He also understood physiognomy.
Whenever he held a mirror to his face,
he knew he would die by execution,
and never failed to smash it to the ground.
Qún died,
and his son Jù largely inherited his techniques.
Dù Qióng
with the courtesy name Bóyú, was a native of Chéngdū, Shǔ Jùn.
In his youth, he studied under Rèn Ān,
and thoroughly mastered Ān's techniques.
During Liú Zhāng's time, he was appointed as a Cóngshì.
When the Former Emperor pacified Yì Zhōu,
and became the Governor,
he made Qióng the Yìcáo Cóngshì.
When the Later Emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Jiànyì Dàfū,
and later promoted to Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng, Dàhónglú, and Tàicháng.
He was a quiet and reticent person,
keeping to himself behind closed doors,
and not engaging in worldly affairs.
Jiǎng Wǎn, Fèi Yī, and others all held him in high regard.
Although he had profound scholarly knowledge,
he never observed celestial phenomena or made pronouncements about them.
A later accomplished scholar, Qiáo Zhōu, often asked him about his reasons,
to which Qióng replied:
"To fully understand this art is very difficult.
One must personally observe
and recognize its forms and colors;
one cannot rely on others.
It involves arduous effort day and night,
only then can one comprehend it.
Moreover, I worry about leakage (of secrets),
so it is better not to know.
That is why I no longer observe it."
Zhōu then asked:
"In the past, the recluse Zhōu thought that the 'high one on the road' referred to Wèi.
What is the meaning of this?"
Qióng replied:
"Wèi
is the name of a palace gate.
To be 'high on the road' (dāngtú ér gāo) is a similarity taken by the sage to express his meaning."
He then asked Zhōu:
"Do you still have any other strange thoughts?"
Zhōu replied:
"I have not yet understood."
Qióng then said:
"In ancient times, official titles did not include 'cáo' (曹).
Since the Hàn dynasty,
all official titles include 'cáo,'
such as 'shǐyán shǔcáo' (使言屬曹) and
'zúyán shìcáo' (卒言侍曹).
This is probably Heaven's will."
Qióng died at over eighty years of age
in the thirteenth year of Yánxī (250 CE).
He authored over a hundred thousand words of commentary on the Hán Shī Zhāngjù,
but he did not teach his sons,
so his inner learning had no successor.
Zhōu, based on Qióng's words,
then elaborated on them by analogy, saying:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals records that Jìn Mùhóu named his crown prince Chóu,
and his younger brother Chéngshī.
Shīfú said: 'How strange is Your Lordship's naming of your sons!
A good match is called fēi (妃, consort),
a resentful match is called chóu (仇, enemy).
Now Your Lordship names the crown prince Chóu,
and your younger brother Chéngshī (成師, become a master).
This is the beginning of disorder;
will the elder brother be replaced?'
Later, it indeed happened as Shīfú had said.
When Emperor Líng of Hàn named his two sons Shǐhóu and Dǒnghóu,
after one was established as emperor,
both were later demoted to marquises.
This is similar to Shīfú's words.
The Former Emperor's given name was Bèi (備),
which means 'to prepare' or 'to complete'.
The Later Emperor's given name was Chán (禪),
which means 'to cede' or 'to bestow'.
It is as if to say, 'Liú has completed its course,
and should be ceded to others.'
Perhaps this is even more significant than Mùhóu's and Língdì's naming of their sons."
Later, the eunuch Huáng Hào wielded power in the palace.
In the fifth year of Jǐngyào (262 CE),
a large tree in the palace courtyard inexplicably broke by itself.
Zhōu was deeply worried,
and having no one to speak to,
he wrote on a pillar:
"Numerous and great,
the time of gathering,
complete and ceded,
how can it be restored?"
He meant that 'cáo' (曹) implies numerous,
and 'wèi' (魏) implies great.
Numerous and great,
the world will indeed converge.
Complete and ceded,
how can there still be anyone to establish (a new rule)?
After Shǔ fell,
everyone considered Zhōu's words to be prophetic.
Zhōu said:
"Although this was my own deduction,
it was based on something;
I merely expanded upon Dù Jūn's words,
there was nothing extraordinarily divine or uniquely profound about it."
Xǔ Cí
with the courtesy name Rénzú, was a native of Nányáng.
He studied under Liú Xī,
was skilled in Zhèng's scholarship,
and specialized in the Yì, Shàngshū, Sān Lǐ, Máoshī, and Lúnyǔ.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
he, along with Xǔ Jìng and others, entered Shǔ from Jiāozhōu.
At that time, there was also Hú Qián
from Wèi Jùn, with the courtesy name Gōngxìng;
the reason for his presence in Yì territory is unknown.
Although Qián's scholarship was not extensive,
he was outstanding and had a powerful memory.
Regarding the rituals and institutions of ancestors,
and the details of mourning rites and the five degrees of mourning,
he could explain them as clearly as pointing to his palm or drawing on the ground,
easily demonstrable.
When the Former Emperor pacified Shǔ,
following periods of chaos and disorder,
scholarship had declined.
Therefore, he assembled ancient texts,
and filtered various schools of thought.
Cí and Qián were both appointed as Xúeshì,
and along with Méng Guāng, Lái Mǐn, and others, they were in charge of ancient texts.
At a time when everything was being established from scratch,
and many matters were subject to doubt and debate,
Cí and Qián constantly clashed with each other,
exchanging slanders, complaints, and fierce arguments,
which were evident in their voices and expressions.
Regarding books, whether available or not,
they would not lend them to each other.
Sometimes they would resort to physical threats,
to intimidate each other.
(Xuān,
Xūwǎn fan).
Their self-pride and jealousy towards others
reached such an extent.
The Former Emperor, pitying their state,
convened a large gathering of officials,
and had entertainers impersonate the two men.
They mimicked their arguments,
and as the wine flowed and music played,
this was presented as entertainment.
Initially, they challenged each other with words and meanings,
and eventually resorted to using swords and staffs to subdue each other,
to give them a poignant lesson.
Qián died first.
Cí was gradually promoted to Dàchángqiū during the Later Emperor's reign,
and then died.
His son, Xūn, carried on his profession,
and also became a Bóshì.
Mèng Guāng, courtesy name Xiàoyù,
was a native of Luòyáng in Hénán.
He was a member of the clan of Mèng Yù, Grand Commandant of the Hàn dynasty.
At the end of the Língdì's reign, he served as an officer in the lecture department (jiǎngbù lì).
When Xiàndì moved the capital to Cháng'ān,
he fled to Shǔ,
where Liú Yān and his son treated him with the courtesy due to a guest.
He was learned and well-versed in ancient lore,
having read every book,
and he particularly applied himself to the Three Histories (Sān Shǐ).
He was expert in the old institutions of the Hàn house.
He favored the Gōngyáng Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals and criticized the Zuǒ Commentary,
often debating these two points with Lái Mǐn.
Mèng Guāng was always clamorous and boisterous in these arguments.
(The sound of náo is nuó jiāo fǎn.
The sound of huān is xiū yuán fǎn.
The sound of zè is cú gé fǎn.)
When the Former Sovereign (Xiānzhǔ) pacified Yìzhōu,
he was appointed Counselor (Yìláng)
and, together with Xǔ Cí and others, was in charge of institutions and regulations (zhìdù).
When the Latter Sovereign (Hòuzhǔ) ascended the throne,
he served as Prefect of the Seal Office (Fújié Lìng), Colonel of Cavalry (Túnqí Xiàowèi), and Lesser Prefect of Chánglè (Chánglè Shàofǔ),
before being promoted to Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng).
In the ninth year of Yánxī (246 CE), in autumn,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
Mèng Guāng publicly rebuked Grand General Fèi Yī, saying:
“A general amnesty
is a partial and flawed thing,
unsuitable for an enlightened age.
Only when one is in a state of extreme decline and exhaustion,
and has no other recourse,
can one expediently implement it.
Now, the sovereign is benevolent and wise,
and all officials perform their duties well.
What imminent danger
or urgent crisis, like being hung upside down, do we face
that we repeatedly grant extraordinary favors
to benefit the wicked and treacherous?
Moreover, for a hawk to begin its attack
and then to pardon the guilty
violates the proper timing of Heaven above
and goes against human reason below.
This old man, decrepit with age,
does not comprehend the principles of governance,
but I privately believe this law is difficult to maintain in the long run.
How can it be considered a lofty and admirable display of comprehensive foresight,
which we would expect from an enlightened ruler?”
Fèi Yī merely looked at him, bowed, and shuffled his feet in apology.
Mèng Guāng's criticisms, which hit at the vital points,
were often of this kind.
Therefore, the governing high officials
were not pleased with him in their hearts,
and his rank did not advance.
He always spoke bluntly without evasion,
which made him disliked by his contemporaries.
This is why Tán Chéng of Guǎnghàn, Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng),
Péi Jùn of Hédōng, Grand Master of Guanglu (Guānglùxūn), and others,
whose seniority and experience were all less than Mèng Guāng's,
were promoted to higher positions,
placing them to Mèng Guāng's right.
Later, the newly advanced scholar-official Xí Zhèng, Secretary of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Láng), frequently consulted Mèng Guāng.
Mèng Guāng asked Xí Zhèng about the crown prince's studies and his disposition and preferences.
Xí Zhèng replied:
“He is reverent and respectful towards his parents,
diligent day and night without slackening,
possessing the demeanor of an ancient crown prince.
In his dealings with officials,
his actions are characterized by benevolence and forbearance.”
Mèng Guāng said:
“What you have described
are qualities found in every household.
What I ask now
is to know his strategies and wisdom; how are they?”
Xí Zhèng replied:
“The way of a crown prince
lies in carrying out his father's will and striving to please him.
He is neither allowed to act presumptuously,
nor can his wisdom and disposition be displayed.
His strategies emerge when the time is right.
How can their presence or absence
be predetermined?”
Mèng Guāng understood that Xí Zhèng was being cautious and appropriate,
not engaging in reckless talk,
and so he said:
“I like to speak frankly
without evasion,
and I often criticize flaws and defects,
which makes me ridiculed and disliked by people.
(I suspect) you do not much approve of my words either,
but there is a sequence to speech.
Today, the world is not yet settled,
and wisdom and intention come first.
Although wisdom and intention can be natural,
they can also be cultivated through effort.
When the heir apparent studies,
should he strive to be extensively learned to await questions, like us,
or like a scholar-official (fùshì) seeking office by demonstrating knowledge in lectures and examinations?
He should attend to what is urgent.”
Xí Zhèng deeply considered Mèng Guāng's words to be correct.
Later, Mèng Guāng was dismissed from office due to an incident
and died at over ninety years of age.
Lái Mǐn, courtesy name Jìngdá,
was a native of Xīnyě in Yìyáng,
a descendant of Lái Xī.
His father, Yàn,
was Grand Minister of Works (Sīkōng) of the Hàn dynasty.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, when there was great chaos,
Lái Mǐn followed his elder sister (and her husband) to Jīngzhōu.
His sister's husband, Huáng Wǎn, was Liú Zhāng's grandmother's nephew.
Therefore, Liú Zhāng sent for Huáng Wǎn's wife,
and Lái Mǐn accompanied his sister into Shǔ.
He was always treated as a guest by Liú Zhāng.
He had extensively read books,
was skilled in the Zuǒ Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and particularly excelled in the commentary and exegesis of Cāngjié and Ěryǎ,
liking to correct characters.
When the Former Sovereign pacified Yìzhōu,
he appointed Lái Mǐn as Colonel overseeing schools (Diǎnxué Xiàowèi).
When the crown prince was established,
he was made Steward of the Heir Apparent (Jiālìng).
When the Latter Sovereign ascended the throne,
he became Commander of the Tiger Guards (Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng).
When Chancellor Zhūgé Liàng resided in Hànzhōng,
he invited Lái Mǐn to be Libationer of the Army (Jūnjìjiǔ) and General Assisting the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn),
but he was dismissed from office due to an incident.
After Zhūgé Liàng's death,
he returned to Chéngdū and became Grand Chamberlain (Dàchángqiú),
but was again dismissed.
Later, he was repeatedly promoted to Grand Master of Guanglu (Guānglù Dàfū),
but again dismissed due to misconduct.
He was repeatedly demoted and stripped of office,
all because his words were unrestrained
and his actions went against the norm.
At that time, Mèng Guāng was also indiscreet in his key pronouncements
and commented on current affairs,
but he was still better than Lái Mǐn.
Both were revered by their contemporaries as venerable scholars.
However, Lái Mǐn, being from a prominent family in Jīngchǔ
and a former official of the Eastern Palace,
received special preferential treatment,
which is why he was dismissed and then reinstated.
Later, Lái Mǐn was made General for Upholding Caution (Zhíshèn Jiāngjūn),
intending that he should be self-vigilant because of his high office.
He died in the Jǐngyào era
at the age of ninety-seven.
His son, Zhōng,
also extensively studied the Classics,
and had Lái Mǐn's disposition.
He, along with Xiàng Chōng, Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū), and others, were able to assist Grand General Jiāng Wéi.
Jiāng Wéi favored him
and appointed him as Military Counselor (Cānjūn).
Yǐn Mò, courtesy name Sīqián,
was a native of Fú in Zītóng.
The region of Yìzhōu favored the New Text tradition (jīnwén) but did not emphasize textual analysis,
and Yǐn Mò, knowing its lack of breadth,
traveled far to Jīngzhōu
to study ancient learning (gǔxué) with Sīmǎ Décāo, Sòng Zhòngzǐ, and others.
He was conversant with all the Classics and Histories,
and specialized in the Zuǒ Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals.
From Liú Xīn's classifications
to the commentaries of Zhèng Zhòng, Jiǎ Kuí and his son, Chén Yuán, and Fú Qián,
he had memorized and recited them all,
no longer needing to consult the original texts.
When the Former Sovereign pacified Yìzhōu
and assumed the governorship,
he appointed Yǐn Mò as Administrator for Promoting Learning (Quànxué Cóngshì).
When the crown prince was established,
Yǐn Mò was made his Tutor (Pú),
and instructed the Latter Sovereign in the Zuǒ Commentary.
When the Latter Sovereign ascended the throne,
he was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance (Jiànyì Dàfū).
When Chancellor Zhūgé Liàng resided in Hànzhōng,
he invited Yǐn Mò to be Libationer of the Army.
After Zhūgé Liàng's death,
he returned to Chéngdū
and was appointed Grand Master of the Center (Tàizhōng Dàfū).
He died.
His son, Zōng, inherited his scholarship
and became an Erudite (Bóshì).
Lǐ Zhuàn, courtesy name Qīnzhòng,
was a native of Fú, Zìtóng.
His father, Rén,
courtesy name Déxián,
traveled with Yǐn Mò from the same county to Jīngzhōu,
where they studied under Sīmǎ Huī, Sòng Zhōng, and others.
Zhuàn fully inherited their scholarship,
and also discussed principles and meanings with Mò.
There was nothing among the Five Classics and various philosophers
that he did not extensively read.
Additionally, he was fond of various arts and crafts;
he applied his thoughts to arithmetic, divination, medicine, archery, and the ingenuity of machinery.
He applied his thoughts to all of these.
Initially, he served as a Registrar of the prefecture and a Clerk in the Department of the Imperial Secretariat.
In the first year of Yánxī (238 CE),
the Later Lord established a crown prince,
and appointed Zhuàn as a Tutor to the Crown Prince.
He was promoted to Aide to the Crown Prince.
He was subsequently transferred to Central Grand Master for Scattered Cavalry and Right Commandant of the Gentlemen-at-Arms,
still attending the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince loved him for his extensive knowledge
and was very pleased with him.
However, he was light-hearted and frivolous,
and fond of joking and ridiculing,
which prevented him from being highly regarded by his contemporaries.
He authored *Gǔwén Yì*, *Shàngshū*, *Máoshī*, *Sānlǐ*, *Zuǒshì Zhuàn*, and *Tàixuán Zhǐguī*,
all of which followed the standards of Jiǎ [Kuì] and Mǎ [Róng],
differing from Zhèng Xuán.
Though completely separate from the Wáng clan,
he had never seen their writings,
yet many of his intentions aligned with theirs.
He died during the Jǐngyào period (258–263 CE).
At that time, there was also Chén Shù from Hànzhōng,
courtesy name Shēnbó,
who was also broadly learned and well-informed.
He authored *Shì Wèn* in seven chapters and *Yìbù Qíjiù Zhuàn jí Zhì*.
He successively held positions as Grand Administrator of three commanderies.
Qiáo Zhōu, courtesy name Yǔnnán,
was a native of Xīchōngguó, Bāxī.
His father, [Hóng],
courtesy name Róngshǐ,
studied the *Shàngshū*,
and was also conversant with various classics, diagrams, and apocrypha.
The prefecture and commandery invited him,
but he did not respond to any of them.
The prefecture then provisionally appointed him as an Advisor from the Teacher-Friend Bureau.
Zhōu was orphaned young
and lived with his mother and elder brother.
When he grew up,
he was devoted to ancient studies and diligent in learning.
Despite being poor, he never concerned himself with property,
but happily read and recited classics,
often laughing to himself,
forgetting food and sleep.
He deeply researched the Six Classics,
and was especially skilled in writing.
He had some understanding of astronomy,
but did not pay much attention to it;
as for the writings of the various philosophers, if they were not what he cared for,
he would not read them all.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
his appearance was plain and unadorned,
and his nature was sincere and unpretentious.
He lacked the talent for impromptu debate,
but his latent understanding was keen.
During the Jiànxīng period (223–237 CE),
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng, acting as Inspector of Yìzhōu,
appointed Zhōu as Admonishing Officer for Scholarship.
When Liàng died on the battlefield,
Zhōu heard the news at home
and immediately rushed to the scene.
Soon after, an imperial edict forbade such travel,
but Zhōu, by his swift action, managed to arrive.
When Grand General Jiǎng Wǎn became Inspector,
he transferred Zhōu to Officer in Charge of Scholarship,
overseeing all scholars in the prefecture.
Later, when the Later Lord established a crown prince,
Zhōu was appointed Aide to the Crown Prince,
and then transferred to Household Manager.
At that time, the Later Lord often went out to sightsee
and expanded the scale of music and entertainment.
Zhōu submitted a memorial, advising:
"In the past, when Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
heroes rose in unison,
claiming prefectures and commanderies,
desiring to manipulate the divine instruments of power.
At that time, virtuous talents and wise men looked for a ruler to follow,
not necessarily judging by the extent of their power,
but solely by the depth or shallowness of their virtue.
Therefore, at that time, Gēngshǐ, Gōngsūn Shù, and many others with large followings had already achieved great scale,
yet all indulged their desires and inclinations,
were remiss in doing good, indulged in hunting and feasting,
and disregarded the people and their welfare.
When Emperor Shìzǔ (Guāngwǔ) first entered Héběi,
Féng Yì and others advised him:
'You should do what others cannot.'
Thus, he diligently attended to redressing wrongful lawsuits,
was frugal in food and drink,
and in every action followed the laws and regulations.
Consequently, the northern prefectures sang his praises,
and his fame spread far and wide.
Thereupon, Dèng Yǔ pursued him from Nányáng,
and Wú Hàn and Kòu Xún, though they had not yet met Emperor Shìzǔ,
hearing of his virtue from afar,
then used strategy to lead the cavalry from Yúyáng and Shànggǔ to welcome him at Guǎng'ā.
As for others who admired his virtue from afar, such as Pī Róng, Gěng Chún, and Liú Zhí,
even those who brought their sick and coffins,
or came carrying infants,
were innumerable.
Thus, he was able to turn weakness into strength,
slaughter Wáng Láng,
swallow the Bronze Horses,
defeat the Red Eyebrows, and establish his imperial enterprise.
When he was in Luòyáng,
he once wanted to take a short outing.
His carriage was already harnessed,
when Diāo Qī advised him: 'The world is not yet peaceful;
I sincerely do not wish for Your Majesty to make frequent small outings.'
He immediately turned back the carriage.
When he was campaigning against Wěi Xiāo,
bandits rose in Yǐngchuān.
Emperor Shìzǔ returned to Luòyáng,
but only sent Kòu Xún.
Xún said: 'Yǐngchuān, seeing Your Majesty on a distant campaign,
has allowed villains to rise in rebellion.
They do not know Your Majesty has returned,
and I fear they will not surrender in time;
if Your Majesty personally goes,
the Yǐngchuān bandits will immediately surrender.'
He then went to Yǐngchuān,
and it turned out just as Xún said.
Thus, for non-urgent matters, he dared not make small outings,
and for urgent matters,
he would not seek personal comfort.
Such was the emperor's desire for virtue!
Thus, it is said, 'The common people do not attach themselves idly,'
truly because virtue leads them.
Now, Hàn faces calamity,
the world is divided into three,
and this is a time when heroic and brilliant individuals look for a ruler.
Your Majesty's natural disposition is of utmost filial piety;
your mourning exceeded three years,
and speaking of it still brings tears to your eyes,
surpassing even Zēng [Shēn] and Mǐn [Zǐqiān].
You respect the virtuous and appoint the talented,
allowing them to exert their full abilities,
surpassing Chéng [Wáng] and Kāng [Wáng].
Therefore, the country is harmonious and unified,
and all, great and small, exert themselves in concert;
this is something your servant cannot fully express.
However, your servant cannot overcome his great wish;
I wish you would further cultivate what others cannot.
Indeed, for one who pulls a heavy load,
his effort is not considered great;
for one who overcomes great difficulties,
his skill is not considered extensive.
Moreover, those who serve in the ancestral temple
do not merely seek blessings and good fortune;
it is how they lead the people to respect superiors.
Yet, for the seasonal sacrifices,
Your Majesty sometimes does not attend,
while for viewing the ponds and gardens,
you sometimes still go out.
Your servant, in his dullness,
privately feels uneasy.
Indeed, one who bears the burden of worry and responsibility
does not have time for complete enjoyment.
The ambition of the late emperor,
whose grand edifice is not yet complete,
is truly not a time for complete enjoyment.
I wish you would reduce and curtail the additions made to the music officials and the imperial harem,
and simply uphold what the late emperor established,
setting an example of frugality for your descendants below."
He was transferred to Central Grand Master for Scattered Cavalry,
still attending the Crown Prince.
At that time, military expeditions were frequent,
and the common people were exhausted.
Zhōu and Shàngshūlìng Chén Zhī discussed their advantages and disadvantages,
then Zhōu retired and wrote it down,
calling it the Qiúguólùn.
Its text reads:
"The state of Yīnyú is small,
while the state of Zhàojiàn is large.
They contend in the world and are enemies.
In the state of Yīnyú, there was a high minister named Gāo Xiánqīng,
who asked Fú Yúzi, saying: 'Now the state's affairs are unsettled,
and those above and below are anxious.
In ancient times,
how did those who used the weak to overcome the strong
achieve their methods?'
Fú Yúzi said: 'I have heard that
those who are great and without worry are often complacent,
while those who are small and anxious often think of what is good;
complacency leads to disorder,
and thinking of what is good leads to order.
This is the constant principle.
Thus, King Wén of Zhōu nurtured his people
to gain much with little,
and Gōujiàn cared for his populace
to defeat the strong with the weak.
These are their methods.'
Xiánqīng said: 'In the past, Xiàng was strong and Hàn was weak;
they were at war,
with no day of peace.
However, Xiàng Yǔ and Hàn agreed to divide Hónggōu as their border,
each wanting to return and rest their people.
Zhāng Liáng thought that once the people's will was settled,
it would be difficult to stir them.
He then led his troops to pursue Yǔ,
eventually defeating the Xiàng clan.
How could it necessarily follow the affairs of King Wén?
The state of Zhàojiàn now has an ailment.
We should seize this opportunity,
invade its borders,
hoping to worsen its illness and defeat it.'
Fú Yúzi said: 'During the time of Yīn and Zhōu,
kings and marquises were honored for generations,
and the bond between ruler and minister was long solidified;
the people were accustomed to what was established.
Those with deep roots are hard to pull up,
and those firmly established are hard to move.
At such a time,
even Hàn Zǔ, how could he wield his sword and whip his horse to conquer the world?
After Qín abolished the feudal lords and set up commanderies,
the people were exhausted by Qín's labor,
and the empire crumbled.
Some changed rulers annually,
others monthly.
Like startled birds and frightened beasts,
no one knew whom to follow.
At that time, powerful heroes contended,
tearing apart like tigers and dividing like wolves.
Those who acted swiftly gained much,
while those who lagged were swallowed.
Now, both we and Zhàojiàn have passed through generations and changed eras.
This is neither the tumultuous time of the late Qín,
but truly a situation where six states stand in contention.
Therefore, one can be like King Wén,
but it is difficult to be like Hàn Zǔ.
When the people are weary, signs of unrest arise.
When the superiors are complacent and the inferiors are oppressive, the form of disintegration emerges.
The proverb says:
'Frequent reckless attempts
are not as good as a careful shot.'
Therefore, the wise do not shift their gaze for small gains,
nor change their steps for a mere resemblance of an idea.
They act only when the time is right,
and move only when the odds are favorable.
Thus, the armies of Tāng and Wǔ conquered without a second battle,
truly valuing the people's toil and carefully assessing the times.
If one continues to exert military might and wage constant wars,
a situation of collapse will arise.
Should misfortune strike,
even the wisest will be unable to strategize.
As for strange and unpredictable changes,
moving in and out without hindrance,
breaking through waves and cutting across tracks,
leaping over valleys and crossing mountains,
and reaching Méngjīn without boats or oars –
I am but a foolish man,
truly incapable of such things.' "
Later, Zhōu was promoted to Guānglùdàfū,
his rank second only to the Jiǔliè.
Although Zhōu did not participate in political affairs,
he was treated with respect for his Confucian conduct.
When major issues were discussed, he was often consulted,
and he would always respond based on the classics.
Later generations and those who loved learning also consulted him on their doubts.
In the winter of Jǐngyào sixth year (263 CE),
Wèi's Grand General Dèng Ài conquered Jiāngyóu
and advanced rapidly.
Shǔ had originally believed that the enemy would not easily reach them
and had not prepared city defenses or dispositions.
When news came that Ài had already entered Yīnpíng,
the common people were in turmoil,
all fleeing to the mountains and wilderness,
beyond control.
The Latter Ruler ordered his ministers to convene a meeting,
but they could not come up with a plan.
Some thought that Shǔ and Wú
were originally allied states,
and it would be advisable to flee to Wú;
others thought that the seven commanderies of Nánzhōng
were rugged and isolated,
easy to defend,
and it would be advisable to flee south.
Only Zhōu believed:
"Since ancient times,
there has been no Son of Heaven who has relied on another state.
If we now enter Wú,
we will surely have to become its subject.
Moreover, if governance is not different,
then the large can swallow the small.
This is the natural order of things.
From this, it is clear that
Wèi can incorporate Wú,
but Wú cannot incorporate Wèi.
If we are to be subjects to a small state,
how does it compare to being subjects to a great state?
The shame of a second humiliation,
how does it compare to a single humiliation?
Furthermore, if you wish to flee south,
you should have planned for it early,
and then it could have succeeded.
Now, the great enemy is close,
disaster is imminent,
and the hearts of the common people
cannot be trusted.
I fear that on the day we set out,
unpredictable changes will occur.
How could we even reach the south!"
Some ministers challenged Zhōu, saying:
"Now Ài is not far away,
I fear he will not accept surrender.
What then?"
Zhōu replied:
"Currently, Dōngwú has not yet submitted,
so circumstances dictate that he must accept
(it). After
accepting it, he must treat us with courtesy.
If Your Majesty surrenders to Wèi,
and Wèi does not divide its territory to enfeoff Your Majesty,
I, Zhōu, will personally go to the capital
and argue for it based on ancient righteousness."
No one could refute Zhōu's reasoning.
The Latter Lord (Hòuzhǔ) was still hesitant about entering the South.
Zhōu submitted a memorial, saying:
"Some tell Your Majesty that the northern armies have penetrated deeply
and suggest a plan to head south.
Your humble servant foolishly believes this to be unsafe.
Why?
The South is a land of distant barbarians.
Normally, they provide nothing,
yet they have repeatedly rebelled.
Ever since Prime Minister Zhūgé Liàng (Zhūgé Liàng) campaigned in the South,
his military might pressured them,
and only out of desperation did they reluctantly submit.
Afterwards, they supplied official taxes
which were taken to support the army,
causing resentment.
These are people who cause trouble for the state.
Now, if out of extreme duress,
we wish to rely on them,
I fear they will certainly rebel again.
This is the first reason.
The coming of the northern armies
is not merely to seize Shǔ.
If we flee to the South,
they will surely take advantage of our weakened state
and pursue us in time.
This is the second reason.
If we reach the South,
we will face external enemies,
and internally we will have to provide for imperial needs.
Expenses will greatly increase,
with nowhere else to obtain resources.
The depletion of the various barbarians will be severe;
if severe, they will quickly rebel.
This is the third reason.
In the past, Wáng Láng (Wáng Láng) proclaimed himself emperor in Hándān (Hándān).
At that time, Emperor Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ) was in Xìndū (Xìndū),
and, fearing pressure from Wáng Láng,
wished to abandon it and return to Guānzhōng (Guānzhōng).
Pī Róng (Pī Róng) advised, 'If Your Lordship returns west,
the citizens of Hándān will not be willing to abandon their parents
and their city lord
to escort you for a thousand *lǐ*;
their desertion and rebellion are certain.'
Emperor Shìzǔ followed his advice
and subsequently defeated Hándān.
Now that the northern armies have arrived,
if Your Majesty travels south,
I sincerely fear that Pī Róng's words will again prove true today.
This is the fourth reason.
I implore Your Majesty to make plans early,
and you may secure titles and territory.
If you insist on going south,
and submit only when driven to extremity,
the disaster will certainly be profound.
The *Yì Jīng* (Yì Jīng) says: 'The meaning of 'Kàng' (亢)
is knowing gain but not loss,
knowing existence but not destruction;
is it not the sage who knows gain and loss, existence and destruction, yet never deviates from the right path?'
This means a sage knows fate but does not act rashly.
Thus, Yáo (Yáo) and Shùn (Shùn), seeing their sons were unworthy,
knew Heaven had a mandate
and sought to bestow it upon others.
Even though their sons were unworthy,
and disaster had not yet arisen,
they proactively transferred the mandate to others;
how much more so when disaster has already arrived!
Thus, Wēizǐ (Wēizǐ), a kinsman of the Yīn (Yīn) king,
returned to King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) with his hands tied and a jade disk in his mouth.
Was this what he desired?
He had no choice.
Thereupon, he followed Zhōu's (Zhōu) counsel.
The Liú (Liú) clan was spared calamity,
and the whole state benefited;
this was Zhōu's (Zhōu) strategy.
At that time, Jìn Wén Wáng (Jìn Wén Wáng) was the Chancellor of Wèi (Wèi),
and because Zhōu (Zhōu) had the merit of preserving the entire state,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángchéng Tíng (Yángchéng Tíng).
An imperial edict was also issued to summon Zhōu (Zhōu).
Zhōu (Zhōu) set out, but upon reaching Hànzhōng (Hànzhōng),
he fell ill and could not proceed.
In the summer of the second year of Xiánxī (Xiánxī) [265 CE],
Wén Lì (Wén Lì) of Bājùn (Bājùn) returned to Shǔ (Shǔ) from Luòyáng (Luòyáng),
and visited Zhōu (Zhōu) on the way.
During their conversation,
Zhōu (Zhōu) wrote on a wooden tablet and showed it to Wén Lì (Wén Lì), saying:
"Diǎnwǔ (Diǎnwǔ) suddenly;
Yuèyǒu (Yuèyǒu) sets."
"Diǎnwǔ" (Diǎnwǔ) refers to Sīmǎ (Sīmǎ);
"Yuèyǒu" (Yuèyǒu) refers to the eighth month.
By the eighth month, Jìn Wén Wáng (Jìn Wén Wáng) indeed died.
When the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty was established,
successive imperial edicts were issued to send for Zhōu (Zhōu) from his locality.
Zhōu (Zhōu) then traveled by litter while ill to Luòyáng (Luòyáng),
arriving in the third year of Tàishǐ (Tàishǐ) [267 CE].
Due to his illness, he could not rise,
so he was appointed Cavalry Commandant (Qí Dūwèi) from his bed.
Zhōu (Zhōu) then pleaded that he had no merit yet was enfeoffed,
requesting the return of his title and territory,
but none of these requests were granted.
In the fifth year [269 CE],
I once served as the Central Investigator (Zhōngzhèng) for my home commandery.
After settling the matters of purity and stability,
I requested leave to return home,
and went to bid farewell to Zhōu (Zhōu).
Zhōu (Zhōu) said to me:
"In the past, Kǒngzǐ (Kǒngzǐ) died at seventy-two, Liú Xiàng (Liú Xiàng) and Yáng Xióng (Yáng Xióng) at seventy-one.
Now I am over seventy.
I hope to emulate the remaining virtues of Kǒngzǐ (Kǒngzǐ)
and follow the same path as Liú (Liú) and Yáng (Yáng).
I fear I will not live past next year,
and will certainly pass away forever,
never to see you again."
I suspect Zhōu (Zhōu) knew this through some art,
and merely used this as an excuse to speak.
In the autumn of the sixth year [270 CE],
he was made a Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì),
but was too ill to accept the appointment,
and died in the winter.
All his writings, compilations, and treatises, such as *Fǎ Xùn* (Fǎ Xùn), *Wǔ Jīng Lùn* (Wǔ Jīng Lùn), and *Gǔ Shǐ Kǎo* (Gǔ Shǐ Kǎo), totaled over a hundred *piān*.
Zhōu (Zhōu) had three sons:
Xī (Xī), Xián (Xián), and Tóng (Tóng).
His youngest son, Tóng (Tóng), was quite fond of Zhōu's (Zhōu) pursuits,
and also distinguished himself by his loyalty, sincerity, and simplicity.
He was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián),
and appointed Magistrate of Xī (Xī) and Groom of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng Xǐmǎ),
but he declined the summons.
Xì Zhèng (Xì Zhèng), courtesy name Lìngxiān (Lìngxiān),
was a native of Yǎnshī (Yǎnshī) in Hénán (Hénán).
His grandfather, Jiǎn (Jiǎn),
served as Inspector of Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu) at the end of Emperor Líng (Líng Dì)'s reign,
and was killed by bandits.
At the time of great chaos in the realm,
Xì Zhèng's (Xì Zhèng) father, Yī (Yī), consequently remained in Shǔ (Shǔ).
Yī (Yī) served as Chief Commandant (Dūdū) for General Méng Dá (Méng Dá),
followed Méng Dá (Méng Dá) in surrendering to Wèi (Wèi),
and became a clerk in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìshǐ).
Xì Zhèng's (Xì Zhèng) original name was Zuǎn (Zuǎn).
As a youth, his father died and his mother remarried,
leaving him orphaned and alone.
However, he was content in poverty and fond of learning,
extensively reading ancient texts.
By the time he was twenty, he could compose literature.
He entered service as a clerk in the Imperial Library (Mìshū Lì),
was transferred to a clerkship (Lìshǐ),
promoted to Gentleman (Láng),
and then to Prefect (Lìng).
He was indifferent to fame and profit,
but particularly devoted to literary works.
From the surviving prose and *fù* of the likes of Sīmǎ (Sīmǎ), Wáng (Wáng), Yáng (Yáng), Bān (Bān), Fù (Fù), Zhāng (Zhāng), and Cài (Cài),
as well as the beautiful writings and excellent treatises of his own time,
if there were any in Yìbù (Yìbù),
he would diligently seek them out and study them,
having perused almost all of them.
While serving in internal positions,
he lived next door to the eunuch Huáng Hào (Huáng Hào) for thirty years.
Huáng Hào (Huáng Hào) rose from obscurity to nobility,
manipulating power and authority.
Xì Zhèng (Xì Zhèng) was neither loved
nor hated by Huáng Hào (Huáng Hào),
and thus his official rank never exceeded six hundred *shí*,
but he was spared from worry and misfortune.
Following earlier Confucians,
he used writing to convey his meaning,
titling it *Shì Jī* (Shì Jī),
and its style followed Cuī Yǐn's (Cuī Yǐn) *Dá Zhǐ* (Dá Zhǐ).
Its text reads:
Someone criticized me, saying:
"I have heard from earlier records that
affairs advance with the times,
and reputation accompanies achievement.
Thus, reputation and achievement
were the urgent tasks of the ancient sages.
Therefore, innovations and creations
could not be established without the right time;
widespread acclaim and enduring fame
could not be recorded without achievement.
Fame must rely on achievement to become manifest,
and affairs also await the right time to proceed
or cease.
To die without one's name surviving
is what a gentleman considers shameful.
Therefore, enlightened individuals investigate the Way,
exploring the profound and seeking the subtle,
observing the signs of Heaven's movement
and examining the rise and fall of human affairs.
The eloquent rush to speak,
the wise respond to opportunities,
strategists devise plans,
and warriors display their might.
They gather like clouds and mists,
fly like wind and lightning.
They assess the times and weigh what is appropriate,
using this to gain worldly resources.
Small
Qū Dàshēn
said, "When public duty outweighs private interest,
though there may be a moment of deviation,
truth will ultimately prevail and shine forth.
Currently, three powers stand like tripods,
the land is not yet unified,
and the vast
seas
are fraught with disaster and ruin.
Alas, the way of righteousness is obstructed,
and the common people suffer hardship.
This is truly the autumn for sages to save the world,
and the occasion for heroes to achieve great deeds.
My
son, with your lofty and clear talent,
and your noble and pure character,
you have read widely and deeply,
dedicating your mind to the Dao and its methods.
There is nothing distant you cannot reach,
nothing obscure you do not comprehend.
You bravely commit yourself,
mastering these
profound secrets.
You stand hesitant at the purple gates of the palace,
holding the position of a spokesman.
Nine examinations cannot sway you,
once in, there is no turning back.
You investigate the true and false of ancient and modern times,
and weigh the gains and losses of current affairs.
Though
you may occasionally offer a plan,
or sometimes present a word,
releasing them from official censure,
and comforting their long-held hopes,
you have surely not yet fully expressed your loyalty,
nor poured out your whole heart and liver,
to remove evil and establish rectitude,
and bestow
benevolence upon the common people,
so that we humble folk might also hear of it.
Why not rein in your horses and ease the reins,
change your course and alter your path,
make your carriage stable and expand your journey,
thinking of the horses as they travel?
Deliberately
prepare to wade across and aid in crossing,
seeking the glorious splendor of the smooth and level path,
spreading the fragrance of autumn orchids to the world,
fulfilling the blueprint of us common folk?
Would this not be magnificent!"
I heard this and sighed, saying:
"Alas,
does it speak like this?
The hearts of men are not alike,
truly like their faces.
Though your words are brilliant and beautiful,
both exquisite and eloquent,
you view things through a tube and measure with a basket,
guarding only what you have seen.
It is not possible to speak of the shapes and limits of the entire world,
nor to believe in the essence and refinement of all things."
Someone abruptly,
while suppressing my words, said with raised voice, "What kind of talk is this!
What kind of talk is this!"
I replied to him, "Emperor Yú took outward agreement as a warning,
and Confucius took pleasing oneself as a fault.
Your words,
are indeed what I have been thinking.
I will explain
and elaborate them for you.
In ancient times, in the primordial wilderness,
when obscurity first began,
the Three Sovereigns responded to the omens,
and the Five Emperors received the symbols.
Then came the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
whose earlier records are written down.
When the Jī dynasty declined and the Dao
was lacking,
the hegemons rose to support it.
The Yíng clan was cruel and oppressive,
devouring the eight regions.
Thus, vertical and horizontal alliances sprang up like clouds,
and stratagems and deceptions were as numerous as stars.
Strange and perverse schemes
stirred, and clever tricks emerged.
Some embellished truth to attack falsehood,
some harbored evil to seek glory,
some used devious ways to gain favor with superiors,
some peddled their skills to boast of themselves.
They turned their backs on uprightness and revered depravity,
abandoned integrity and embraced flattery.
Loyalty had no fixed standard,
and righteousness had no constant principle.
Thus, Shāng Yāng's laws led to wickedness,
Lǐ Sī's righteousness failed and treachery succeeded,
Lǚ Bùwèi's power grew but his clan was exterminated,
and Hán Fēi's debates were established but he was punished with death.
Why was this?
Profit turned their hearts,
and favor dazzled their eyes.
The brilliant dragon robes,
the gleaming chariots and attire,
they sought undeserved gain and temporary good fortune,
like being overturned or listing.
They were steeped in depravity,
delusion,
and unrestrained indulgence.
Before the bridle bells were adjusted, their bodies were already beside the shaft;
before they had trod the palace courtyard, the ridgepole broke and the rafters collapsed.
Heaven withdrew its essence,
Earth diminished its bounty,
men
mourned their persons,
and spirits cut them down.
At first, they ascended high peaks,
but in the end, they plunged into deep ravines.
In the morning, they were moist with glory,
in the evening, they became withered souls.
Therefore, wise men and noble persons,
plan deeply
and think far ahead,
fearing retribution and blame,
they rise above it all.
They would rather drag their tails in the mud,
and defile the praise of a corrupt world.
How could they despise their lord and neglect the people,
and disregard current
affairs?
It is because the Book of Changes speaks of the warning of action and inaction,
and the Book of Odes has the lament of peace and reverence.
It is the spirits hearing this and the Dao causing it to be so.
Since our great Hàn dynasty,
responding to Heaven and following the people,
the flourishing of governance
is like the clear spring sun.
They look down to emulate the Earth's principles,
and look up to model themselves on Heaven's patterns.
They spread imperial benevolence to gladden the world,
and propagate profound and pure transformative influence.
Rulers and ministers abide by the rules,
each guarding their true nature.
The emperor extends great magnanimity in seeking advice,
and those below have the responsibility to correct and save.
Scholars have no empty or superficial favors,
and the people have a path of consistent conduct.
Splendidly and diligently,
they uphold this loyalty and benefit.
However, the Dao has its ups and downs,
things have their rise and fall,
there is sound and silence,
there is light and shadow.
The sun is obscured in autumn,
the dark yin is suppressed in early spring.
Xīhé departs and Wàngshū is bound,
the cosmic energy hides and the shining spirit (sun) is arrayed.
Chōng and Zhì were not long-lived,
Huán and Líng
fell into ruin.
Heroes spread like clouds,
and exceptional talents covered the world.
Each family held divergent views,
and every person harbored different schemes.
Thus, the advocates of vertical and horizontal alliances suddenly revealed their hearts,
and the schemers temporarily unfurled their tongues.
Today, the net of Heaven has been mended,
and the tree of virtue stands in the western neighborhood.
The grand plans of our illustrious ancestors are greatly manifested,
and good official positions are offered to scholars.
The five teachings are promoted to instruct customs,
and the nine virtues are enriched to
benefit the people.
Solemn and clear sacrifices are offered to the gods,
approaching the imperial Dao to assist the true.
Though the tripods are not yet unified,
and the false are not yet distinguished,
the sages have left a warning,
that fairness should preclude greed.
Therefore,
rulers and ministers together create beauty in the court,
and the common people rejoice in supporting them in the countryside.
In action, they are like stacked compasses;
in stillness, they are like layered squares.
The numerous great talents
are of the same caliber as Yuán Kǎi;
if they have faults, they will
surely know them,
possessing the benevolence of Yán Zǐ.
The frank and upright administration of public affairs
is like the governance of Rǎn and Jì.
Soaring like eagles and fierce birds of prey,
these are the deeds of Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng.
They encompass the superior strategies of all outstanding individuals,
and contain
Xuē Shì's three strategies,
the secret plans of Fū Zhāng and Chén,
were for the sake of exerting oneself in campaigning to relieve the world,
and assisting the brilliant and distinguished without rest.
How could there be leisure to cultivate withered bamboo shoots in the wilderness!
However, I am untalented.
I have been in court for many years,
entrusting myself to Heaven,
and my heart relies on this.
I delight in the vastness and depth of the blue sea,
and sigh at the towering majesty of Sōngyuè.
I heard Mèng
Ní praise Shāng,
and felt inspired by the village schools' benefit to myself.
That Píng Zhòng's seasoning of the soup
also distinguished what was acceptable from what was not.
Therefore, I have ignorantly offered my foolish opinions,
occasionally presenting suggestions,
like a
tax collector gathering from markets and alleys,
or a wandering child reciting poems by the roadside.
I hope to thereby increase great blessings and auspiciousness,
and contribute my efforts in remonstrance.
If they align,
then I, in my obscurity,
will assist the enlightened,
and my advancement will accord with auspicious omens.
If they deviate,
it is my usual lot,
and I will retreat and guard my foolishness.
Advancing and retreating are subject to fate;
I do not feign or deceive.
Following my nature and delighting in Heaven,
what
is there to regret?
This is why I, having entered, do not depart,
and, possessing, am as if without.
I find Qu Qū Shì's constant sobriety too narrow,
and the Fisherman's inevitable drunkenness too muddy.
I consider Liǔ Jì's
humiliation mixed,
and Yí Shú's lofty resentment too narrow-minded.
Alignment does not bring gain,
deviation does not bring loss.
Gain does not allow me to be constrained,
loss does not make me tremble in sorrow.
I do not rejoice in the front to look after the carriage,
nor rely on the rear to consider its lightness.
I do not sell my reputation to seek favors,
nor decline errors to avoid being dismissed.
What blame is released?
What sorrow is worried over?
What method is repelled?
What
honesty enters?
Nine examinations do not sway me;
this is my steadfast adherence.
At present, court officials are piled up like mountains,
and talents form groups,
like fish and scale-covered creatures latent in the vast sea,
or birds with feathers gathered in Dènglín.
Wandering birds leaving do not make it
sparse;
swimming bream arriving do not make it dense.
Moreover, the solar spirit was obscured in the age of Táng Yè,
and the lunar essence responded in the time of Shāng.
When Yáng Xū prayed, the great flood ceased;
when Sānglín prayed, sweet
rain increased.
Movement and stillness have their Dao,
opening and closing have their time.
My teacher's遗训 (yíxùn - posthumous instructions) teach
not to resent or blame,
but to resign oneself to fate and be respectful.
What more can I say?
Words exhausted, the road
solitary,
I will return to my initial resolve,
surveying the lingering fragrance of ancient classics,
seeking the remaining arts of Kǒng Shì.
I will string together humble words to preserve the Dao,
model the former paths, and submit my regulations.
I praise Shú Xī's
leisurely freedom,
and admire Shū Shì's distant departure.
I will stop at sufficiency to speak of returning,
and drift freely and serenely.
I will delight in my humble dwelling with tranquil joy,
and avoid blame and regret in this world.
Considering
that this heart is not yet at peace,
and fearing being stuck in the quagmire of the final path,
I still seek to be roused and increase my indignation,
and thus declare my inner feelings with an oath.
Formerly, Jiǔ Fāng investigated essence in the supremely noble,
and Qín Yá
meditated deeply on unique forms.
Xuē Zhú discerned treasures and gained renown,
Hú Liáng relied on strings to spread his fame.
The Qi servant slapped his thigh to compose literature,
the Chu
guest secretly invaded to protect Jīng.
Yōng Mén plucked his zither and argued,
Hán Āi held the reins and galloped to fame.
Lú Áo soared in the dark palace,
and Ruò
Shì lifted himself into the clear clouds.
〔一０〕I am truly unable to match the skills of these several gentlemen,
therefore I calmly maintain myself and find peace. '
In the sixth year of Jǐngyào (263 CE),
the Latter Lord followed Qiáo Zhōu's plan,
sending an envoy to request surrender from Dèng Ài.
The letter
was precisely what Zhèng had drafted.
In the first month of the following year (264 CE),
Zhōng Huì rebelled in Chéngdū.
The Latter Lord moved east to Luòyáng.
At that time, in the chaos and urgency,
none of Shǔ's high officials escorted him,
only Zhèng and Diànzhōng Dū Zhāng Tōng of Rǔnán,
who left their wives and children and accompanied him alone.
The Latter Lord relied on Zhèng to guide him appropriately,
and his actions were without fault.
He then sighed with emotion,
regretting that he had known Zhèng so late.
Public opinion praised him at the time.
He was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
During the Tàishǐ era,
he was appointed Ānyáng Lìng,
and then promoted to Bāxī Tàishǒu.
An imperial edict in the eighth year of Tàishǐ (272 CE) stated:
"Zhèng, formerly in Chéngdū,
persevered in righteousness through hardship,
and did not violate loyalty and integrity.
When he was employed,
he devoted his heart to his duties,
and achieved administrative merits.
Therefore, let Zhèng be Bāxī Tàishǒu."
He died in the fourth year of Xiánníng (278 CE).
All his writings, including poems, essays, and rhapsodies,
numbered nearly a hundred pieces.
Commentary says: Dù Wēi cultivated himself in reclusion and tranquility,
not serving the current age,
almost akin to Yí and Hào.
Zhōu Qún's observations of Heaven were verifiable,
Dù Qióng was silent and cautious,
pure scholars indeed.
Xǔ, Mèng, Lái, and Lǐ
were extensively learned and widely informed.
Yǐn Mò was skilled in Zuǒ Shì.
Although they were not praised for their virtue and accomplishments,
they were truly scholars of their time.
Qiáo Zhōu's rhetoric and reasoning were profound and far-reaching,
making him a great scholar of his age,
with the demeanor of Dǒng and Yáng.
Xì Zhèng's prose was brilliant,
with the style of Zhāng and Cài.
Adding his conduct,
a gentleman would take him as an example.
These two men served the Jìn dynasty little,
but served Shǔ much,
hence they are recorded in this chapter.
Biography of Huáng, Lǐ, Lǚ, Mǎ, Wáng, Zhāng, Chapter Thirteen
Huáng Quán 字 Gōnghéng,
a native of Làngzhōng, Bāxī Commandery.
In his youth, he served as a commandery clerk.
The Provincial Governor, Liú Zhāng, summoned him to be Registrar.
At that time, the Aide-de-camp, Zhāng Sōng, suggested
that it would be advisable to invite the Former Lord (Liú Bèi)
to attack Zhāng Lǔ.
Quán remonstrated, saying:
"The General of the Left (Liú Bèi) has a name for bravery.
If we invite him here now,
and wish to treat him as a subordinate,
his heart will not be content.
If we wish to treat him with the courtesy due to a guest,
then one country cannot accommodate two lords.
If the guest has the stability of Mount Tài,
then the host will face the danger of piled eggs.
It is better to simply close the borders
and wait for the Yellow River to run clear."
Zhāng did not listen,
and indeed sent an envoy to welcome the Former Lord.
He sent Quán out as the Prefect of Guǎnghàn.
When the Former Lord attacked and seized Yìzhōu,
generals and commanders were dispatched to the various commanderies and counties.
The commanderies and counties submitted at the mere sight of his approach.
Quán, however, closed his city and held out firmly,
waiting for Liú Zhāng to submit.
Only then did he go and surrender to the Former Lord.
The Former Lord provisionally appointed Quán as a Partial General.
When Cáo Gōng defeated Zhāng Lǔ,
Lǔ fled into Bāzhōng.
Quán advised:
"If Hànzhōng is lost,
then the three Bā commanderies will be unstable.
This is like cutting off the arms and legs of Shǔ."
Thereupon, the Former Lord appointed Quán as Protector of the Army,
leading various generals to intercept Lǔ.
Lǔ had already returned to Nánzhèng
and surrendered to Cáo Gōng in the north.
Nevertheless, they eventually defeated Dù Huò and Pú Hú,
killed Xiàhóu Yuān,
and occupied Hànzhōng.
These were all due to Quán's original plan.
When the Former Lord became King of Hànzhōng,
still holding the post of Provincial Governor of Yìzhōu,
he appointed Quán as Chief Clerk.
When he assumed the imperial title,
he intended to launch an eastern expedition against Wú.
Quán remonstrated, saying:
"The Wú people are fierce in battle,
and their navy moves with the current.
Advancing is easy, retreating is difficult.
I request to serve as the vanguard to test the enemy;
Your Majesty should serve as the rearguard."
The Former Lord did not comply.
He appointed Quán as General Who Guards the North,
to oversee the army north of the river to defend against the Wèi forces;
the Former Lord himself was south of the river.
When the Wú general Lù Yì took advantage of the current to cut off the encirclement,
the southern army suffered a defeat,
and the Former Lord retreated.
However, the path was cut off,
and Quán could not return.
Therefore, he led his troops and surrendered to Wèi.
The officials in charge of justice
reported that Quán's wife and children should be arrested.
The Former Lord said:
"I have failed Huáng Quán;
Quán has not failed me."
He treated them as before.
Emperor Wén of Wèi said to Quán:
"You abandoned rebellion and chose loyalty.
Do you wish to emulate Chén Píng and Hán Xìn?"
Quán replied:
"I received extraordinary favor from Lord Liú.
To surrender to Wú was impossible,
and there was no path back to Shǔ.
Therefore, I surrendered my life.
Moreover, a general of a defeated army,
it is fortunate to escape death.
How can one aspire to the ancients?"
Emperor Wén praised him,
appointed him General Who Guards the South,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yùyáng,
added the title of Attendant,
and made him a companion in his carriage.
Some Shǔ defectors reported that Quán's wife and children had been executed.
Quán knew this was false,
and did not immediately mourn.
Later, when he received definite news,
it was indeed as he had believed.
When the news of the Former Lord's death arrived,
the Wèi ministers all congratulated, but Quán alone did not.
Emperor Wén observed that Quán had a broad and steady character,
and wished to test and startle him.
He sent his attendants to summon Quán.
Before they arrived,
repeated urgent summons followed one after another.
Messengers on horseback raced past,
crossing paths on the road.
His subordinate officials and attendants were all terrified,
but Quán's demeanor and expression remained composed.
Later, he was appointed Governor of Yìzhōu,
and moved to settle in Hénán.
The Grand General Sīmǎ Xuānwáng greatly admired him.
He asked Quán:
"How many people like you are there in Shǔ?"
Quán smiled and replied:
"I did not expect such high regard from your enlightened lord!"
Xuānwáng wrote to Zhūgě Liàng, saying:
"Huáng Gōnghéng
is a fine gentleman.
Whenever he sits or stands, he sighs and speaks of you,
never ceasing to praise you."
In the third year of Jǐngchū (239 CE),
which was the second year of Yánxī in Shǔ,
Quán was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry and granted the same prerogatives as the Three Ducal Ministers.
The following year, he died,
and was posthumously named Jǐng Hóu.
His son Yōng succeeded him.
Yōng had no son,
and so the line ended.
Quán's son who remained in Shǔ, Chóng,
served as a Bureau Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He followed the General Who Guards the Army, Zhūgě Zhān, to resist Dèng Ài.
Upon reaching Fúxiàn,
Zhān hesitated and did not advance.
Chóng repeatedly urged Zhān to quickly move and occupy strategic passes,
to prevent the enemy from entering the open plains.
Zhān still deliberated and did not accept.
Chóng even wept.
Soon, Ài advanced rapidly.
Zhān fought defensively, retreating to Miánzhú.
Chóng encouraged the troops,
determined to die,
and was killed in battle.
Lǐ Huī 字 Dé'áng,
a native of Yúyuán, Jiànníng Commandery.
He served as a Commandery Supervisor.
His maternal uncle's husband, Cuàn Xí, was the Prefect of Jiànlíng
and committed violations.
Huī was dismissed from office due to Xí.
The Administrator Dǒng Hé, considering Xí a prominent local magnate,
suppressed the matter and did not permit it.
Later, Huī was recommended to the province.
Before he arrived on the journey,
he heard that the Former Lord had returned from Jiāmáng to attack Liú Zhāng.
Huī knew that Zhāng was destined to fail
and the Former Lord was destined to succeed.
So, he feigned a mission from the commandery
and went north to meet the Former Lord,
encountering him at Miánzhú.
The Former Lord praised him,
and Huī accompanied him to Luòchéng.
He then dispatched Huī to Hànzhōng to foster good relations with Mǎ Chāo.
Mǎ Chāo then complied.
After Chéngdū was settled,
the Former Lord became Provincial Governor of Yìzhōu,
and appointed Huī as Secretary and Registrar to the Chief Clerk.
Later, he was falsely accused by a captured fugitive,
who implicated Huī in plotting rebellion.
The authorities arrested and delivered him.
The Former Lord recognized his innocence
and instead promoted Huī to Aide-de-camp.
In the first year of Zhāngwǔ (221 CE),
the Grand Administrator of Lāijiàng, Dèng Fāng, died.
The Former Lord asked Huī:
"Who can replace him?"
Huī replied:
"The talents of people
each have their strengths and weaknesses.
Hence Confucius said, 'When employing people, use them according to their capacity.'
Moreover, when an enlightened lord is above,
his ministers will fully express their thoughts.
Thus, in the campaign against the Xiānlíng,
Zhào Chōngguó said, 'No one is better than this old minister.'
I secretly do not overestimate myself,
but I ask Your Majesty to consider me."
The Former Lord smiled and said:
"My original intention
was also already with you."
Thereupon, he appointed Huī as Grand Administrator of Lāijiàng,
entrusting him with a marshal's staff and the provisional title of Governor of Jiāozhōu,
stationed at Píngyí County.
After the Former Sovereign died,
Gāo Dìng rampaged in Yuèsuī,
Yōng Kǎi was arrogant in Jiànníng,
and Zhū Bāo rebelled in Zānggē.
Chancellor Liàng launched a southern expedition.
He first went through Yuèsuī,
while Huī followed the route towards Jiànníng.
Many counties gathered together
and besieged Huī's army in Kūnmíng.
At that time, Huī's forces were few, outnumbered,
and he had not yet received news from Liàng.
He deceptively told the Southerners:
"The government army's provisions are exhausted,
and we intend to retreat.
I have been away from my hometown for a long time,
and now that I can return,
I cannot go back north again.
I wish to return and plan with you all,
so I am telling you this in sincerity."
The Southerners believed him,
and thus their siege became lax.
Thereupon, Huī launched an attack
and greatly defeated them.
He pursued the fleeing and routed,
reaching Pánjiāng to the south
and connecting with Zānggē to the east,
linking his momentum with Liàng's.
With the southern lands pacified,
Huī's military merits were many.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Hànxīng Tíng,
and appointed General of Ānhàn.
Later, when the army returned,
the Southern Yi rebelled again,
killing the defending commanders.
Huī personally went to suppress them,
eliminating all evil elements.
He relocated their powerful chieftains to Chéngdū
and levied oxen, buffalo, warhorses, gold, silver, and rhinoceros hide from the Sōu and Pú peoples,
