using them to replenish military supplies,
so that there was no shortage of expenses at that time.
In the seventh year of Jiànxīng [229 CE],
as Jiāozhōu belonged to Wú,
Huī was relieved of his post as Inspector.
He was then appointed Grand Administrator of Jiànníng,
returning to reside in his home commandery.
He later moved to Hànzhōng
and died in the ninth year [231 CE].
His son Yí inherited his title.
Huī's nephew Qiú
was the Right Department Commander of the Imperial Guards.
He followed Zhūgě Zhān to resist Dèng Ài,
died in battle,
and was killed at Miánzhú.
Lǚ Kǎi, courtesy name Jìpíng, was a native of Bùwéi, Yǒngchāng Commandery.
He served as Chief Clerk and Meritorious Officer in the commandery.
At that time, Yōng Kǎi and others, hearing that the Former Sovereign had died at Yǒng'ān,
became increasingly arrogant and cunning.
Governor Lǐ Yán wrote Kǎi a six-page letter,
explaining the advantages and disadvantages.
Kǎi only replied with one page, saying:
"I have heard that there cannot be two suns in the sky
nor two kings on earth.
Now the world stands divided among three powers,
and there are three calendars.
Thus, people from afar are confused
and do not know where to pledge their allegiance."
His arrogance and insolence were like this.
Kǎi also submitted to Wú.
Wú remotely appointed Kǎi as Grand Administrator of Yǒngchāng.
As Yǒngchāng was to the west of Yìzhōu Commandery,
the roads were blocked
and it was cut off from Shǔ.
When the commandery Grand Administrator was replaced,
Kǎi, together with the Administrator's Assistant, Wáng Kàng of Shǔ Commandery, led the officials and people
to close the borders and resist Kǎi.
Kǎi repeatedly issued proclamations to Yǒngchāng,
making various statements.
Kǎi replied with a proclamation, saying:
"Heaven sent down chaos and turmoil,
and treacherous heroes seized the opportunity.
The whole world gnashed its teeth,
and all nations grieved.
From ministers to servants, great and small,
none did not desire to exhaust their strength,
their brains smeared on the ground,
to eliminate the national calamity.
I humbly believe that Your Excellency's family has for generations received the favor of Hàn,
and thus you ought to personally gather followers
and take the lead,
so as to repay the state above
and not disappoint your ancestors below,
recording your deeds on bamboo and silk
and leaving a name for a thousand years.
How could you possibly serve Wú and Yuè
and abandon the root for the branch?
In ancient times, Shùn worked diligently for his people
and died in Cāngwú.
Books praise him,
and his fame is boundless.
To die by the Jiāngpǔ,
what is there to be sad about?
Wén and Wǔ received the mandate,
and King Chéng then brought peace.
When the Former Emperor rose,
the realm looked up to him,
and his wise ministers,
as if from heaven, brought prosperity.
Yet Your Excellency does not see the laws of rise and fall,
nor the omens of success and failure.
This is like a prairie fire on the plain,
or treading on river ice.
When the fire is extinguished and the ice melts,
what will you rely on?
In the past, Your Excellency's late father, Marquis Yōng,
created enmity yet was enfeoffed.
Dòu Róng knew of the rise,
and pledged his allegiance to Emperor Shìzǔ.
Both left names for future generations,
and their virtues are sung throughout the ages.
Now, Chancellor Zhūgě is exceptionally talented,
perceiving what has not yet manifested.
He received the dying entrustment and the orphaned child,
assisting and supporting Jìxīng,
openly with the populace,
recording merits and forgetting faults.
If Your Excellency can suddenly change your plans,
alter your path and step,
it is not difficult to surpass the ancients.
What is this contemptible land worth ruling?
I have heard that when the state of Chǔ was disrespectful,
Qí Huán criticized it.
When Fūchā usurped the title,
the Jìn people did not tolerate it.
How much less so when a minister serves a non-rightful lord,
who would be willing to submit to him?
I humbly consider the ancient principle that
ministers have no cross-border dealings.
Therefore, there have been messages from you before, but none from me.
Upon receiving your further notification,
I was so enraged I forgot to eat.
Therefore, I briefly state my thoughts,
and hope Your Excellency will consider them."
Kǎi's prestige and benevolence were evident internally,
and he was trusted by the commandery,
thus he was able to maintain his integrity.
When Chancellor Liàng launched his southern expedition against Kǎi,
he had already set out.
Kǎi had already been killed by Gāo Dìng's forces.
When Liàng arrived in the south,
he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Yǒngchāng Commandery official Lǚ Kǎi, Administrator's Assistant Wáng Kàng, and others
upheld their loyalty in a remote region for
more than ten years.
Yōng Kǎi and Gāo Dìng pressed them from the northeast,
but Kǎi and the others upheld righteousness and did not associate with them.
I did not expect the customs of Yǒngchāng to be so honest and upright!"
Kǎi was appointed Grand Administrator of Yúnnán
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángqiān Tíng.
He was unfortunately killed by rebellious Yi.
His son Xiáng inherited his title.
Wáng Kàng was also enfeoffed as a Marquis of Tíng
and served as Grand Administrator of Yǒngchāng.
Mǎ Zhōng, courtesy name Déxìn,
was a native of Lángzhōng, Bāxī Commandery.
In his youth, he was raised by his maternal family,
who had the surname Hú
and the given name Dǔ.
Later, he reverted to his original surname
and changed his name to Zhōng.
He served as a commandery clerk.
At the end of Jiàn'ān, he was recommended as xiàolián
and appointed as the Prefect of Hànchāng.
When the Former Sovereign campaigned eastward,
he suffered a defeat at Xiāotíng.
Yán Zhī, the Grand Administrator of Bāxī, dispatched five thousand soldiers from various counties to fill the depleted ranks,
sending Zhōng to deliver them.
The Former Sovereign had already returned to Yǒng'ān.
Seeing Zhōng and speaking with him,
he said to the Imperial Secretary Liú Bā:
"Though we have lost Huáng Quán,
we have again gained Hú Dǔ.
This shows that the world is never without worthy men."
In the first year of Jiànxīng,
Chancellor Liàng established his headquarters,
appointing Zhōng as Menxià Dū (Supervisor of the Household).
In the third year,
when Liàng marched south,
Zhōng was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Zāngkē.
The Commandery Assistant, Zhū Bāo, rebelled.
After the rebellion,
Zhōng fostered and managed the people,
earning great prestige and benevolence.
In the eighth year,
he was summoned to serve as Aide-de-camp to the Chancellor,
and, as deputy to Chief Clerk Jiǎng Wǎn, oversaw affairs at the Chancellor's Residence.
He also served as Zhìzhōng Cóngshì for the province.
The following year,
when Liàng marched out to Qíshān,
Zhōng went to Liàng's headquarters
to manage military affairs.
When the army returned,
he oversaw General Zhāng Ní and others in suppressing the rebellious Qiāng in Wénshān Commandery.
In the eleventh year,
Liú Zhòu, a chieftain of the southern Yi, rebelled,
disrupting various commanderies.
The Jīxiáng Dūdū (Inspector of the Jīxiáng Region), Zhāng Yì, was recalled,
and Zhōng was appointed to replace Yì.
Zhōng subsequently executed Zhòu
and pacified the southern lands.
Zhōng was granted the additional title of Jiānjūn Fènwēi Jiāngjūn (Supervisor of the Army and General Who Displays Awe),
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Bóyángtíng.
Initially,
in Jiànníng Commandery, the Grand Administrator Zhèng Áng was killed,
and the Grand Administrator Zhāng Yì was bound and sent to Wú.
Therefore, the Dūdū (Inspector) had always been stationed in Píngyí County.
When Zhōng took office,
he moved the administrative seat to Wèi County,
situating it between the Han Chinese and the Yi.
Furthermore, Yuèxī Commandery had long lost its territory.
Zhōng led Grand Administrator Zhāng Ní to reclaim the old commandery.
Because of this, he was promoted to Ānnán Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the South)
and further enfeoffed as the Marquis of Péngxiāngtíng.
In the fifth year of Yánxī, he returned to the court.
He then went to Hànzhōng,
met with Grand Marshal Jiǎng Wǎn,
and conveyed imperial edicts.
He was further appointed Zhènnán Dàjiāngjūn (General-in-Chief Who Guards the South).
In the spring of the seventh year,
Grand General Fèi Yī marched north to resist the Wei enemy.
Zhōng remained in Chéngdū
to manage the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
When Yī returned,
Zhōng then returned to the south.
He died in the twelfth year,
and his son Xiū succeeded him.
Zhōng was a man of broad-mindedness, self-restraint, and magnanimity.
Although he was known for jovial laughter,
he never showed anger on his face.
However, he was decisive in handling affairs,
and his authority and benevolence were equally established.
Therefore, the barbarians feared and loved him.
When he died,
none failed to come to his funeral,
shedding tears and expressing their deepest sorrow.
They erected a temple to sacrifice to him,
which remains to this day.
Zhāng Biǎo,
a renowned scholar of the time,
had a reputation for integrity that surpassed Zhōng's.
Yán Yǔ,
who had long been meritorious and capable,
was diligent and meticulous in his duties.
Following in Zhōng's footsteps,
their prestige and achievements
nevertheless fell short of Zhōng's.
Wáng Píng, courtesy name Zǐjūn,
was a native of Dàngqú, Bāxī Commandery.
He was originally raised by his maternal family, the Hé clan,
but later reverted to the surname Wáng.
He followed Dù Huò and Pú Hú to Luòyáng.
He was provisionally appointed Xiàowèi (Commander).
He accompanied Cáo Gōng on the campaign to Hànzhōng
and then surrendered to the Former Sovereign.
He was appointed Yámén Jiāng (General of the Gate Guard) and Píjiāngjūn (Auxiliary General).
In the sixth year of Jiànxīng,
he was subordinate to Aide-de-camp Mǎ Sù as a vanguard.
Sù abandoned the water source and occupied a mountain,
his actions being chaotic and troublesome.
Píng repeatedly advised Sù,
but Sù would not listen,
resulting in a great defeat at Jiētíng.
The troops scattered entirely.
Only the thousand men led by Píng
beat their drums and held their ground.
The Wei general Zhāng Hé suspected an ambush,
and did not press forward.
Thereupon, Píng slowly gathered the remaining scattered soldiers from the various camps
and returned with his officers and men.
After Chancellor Liàng executed Mǎ Sù and Generals Zhāng Xiū and Lǐ Shèng,
and stripped Generals Huáng Xí and others of their troops,
Píng was uniquely honored and promoted.
He was further appointed Aide-de-camp,
commanded five divisions, and concurrently managed camp affairs.
He was promoted to Tǎokòu Jiāngjūn (General Who Suppresses Bandits)
and enfeoffed as a Marquis of a Ting.
In the ninth year,
when Liàng besieged Qíshān,
Píng separately guarded the southern perimeter.
When the Wei Grand General Sīmǎ Xuānwáng attacked Liàng,
Zhāng Hé attacked Píng.
Píng held firm and did not move;
Hé could not overcome him.
In the twelfth year,
Liàng died at Wǔgōng.
When the army retreated,
Wèi Yán caused unrest,
but was defeated in one battle.
This was due to Píng's efforts.
He was subsequently promoted to Diǎnjūn (Commander of the Army) and Ānhàn Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies Han),
and, as deputy to General of Chariots and Cavalry Wú Yī, resided in Hànzhōng.
He also served as the Grand Administrator of Hànzhōng.
In the fifteenth year,
he was further enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānhàn
and replaced Yī as the Inspector of Hànzhōng.
In the first year of Yánxī,
Grand General Jiǎng Wǎn resided in Miányáng,
and Píng was further appointed Qiánhùjūn (Front Protector of the Army),
overseeing affairs at Wǎn's residence.
In the sixth year,
Wǎn returned to Fú,
and Píng was appointed Qiánjiānjūn (Front Supervisor of the Army) and Zhènběi Dàjiāngjūn (General-in-Chief Who Guards the North),
commanding Hànzhōng.
In the spring of the seventh year,
the Wei Grand General Cáo Shuǎng led over one hundred thousand infantry and cavalry towards Hànchuān.
Their vanguard had already reached Luògǔ.
At that time, the defending forces in Hànzhōng numbered less than thirty thousand.
The generals were greatly alarmed.
Some said:
"Our current strength is insufficient to resist the enemy.
We should firmly defend the two cities of Hàn and Lè.
Let the enemy enter;
by then,
the Fú army will be able to rescue the passes."
Píng said:
"That is not right.
Hànzhōng is nearly a thousand li from Fú.
If the enemy seizes the passes,
it will be a disaster.
We should first dispatch Protector of the Army Liú and Aide-de-camp Dù to hold Xīngshì,
with me as the rear guard.
If the enemy divides and heads towards Huángjīn,
I will lead a thousand men to confront them.
By then,
the Fú army will have arrived.
This is the best plan."
Only Protector of the Army Liú Mǐn agreed with Píng's idea,
and it was immediately implemented.
The Fú armies and Grand General Fèi Yī arrived successively from Chéngdū.
The Wei army retreated,
just as Píng had originally planned.
At this time,
Dèng Zhī was in the east,
Mǎ Zhōng in the south,
and Píng in the northern border region,
all achieving renown.
Throughout his life, he was often on military campaigns.
He could not write with his own hand;
what he recognized did not exceed ten characters.
Yet, when he dictated and composed documents,
they all contained meaning and reason.
He would have people read records and biographies from the *Shǐ* and *Hàn* histories,
and listening to them,
he thoroughly understood their main points,
often discussing them without losing their essence.
He adhered to laws and regulations,
spoke no jests,
and from morning until evening,
sat upright all day long.
He lacked the demeanor of a military general.
However, his nature was narrow-minded and prone to suspicion,
and he held himself in low esteem,
which was his drawback.
He died in the eleventh year,
and his son, Xùn, succeeded him.
Initially,
Gōu Fú (Gōu, ancient pronunciation of Hóu) from Hanchāng in Píng's commandery, was loyal, brave, generous, and upright.
He achieved several military successes.
His merit, fame, and noble rank were second only to Píng.
He rose to the office of General of the Left [Zuǒ Jiāngjūn]
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dàngqú.
Zhāng Ní, courtesy name Bóqí,
was a native of Nánchōngguó, Bājùn.
At the age of twenty (upon capping), he served as a merit official [gōngcáo] in the county.
When the Former Lord [Xiānzhǔ] conquered Shǔ,
mountain bandits attacked the county.
The county magistrate abandoned his family and fled.
Ní braved drawn swords,
carrying and protecting the magistrate's wife,
who thus escaped harm.
From this, he gained renown,
and the province summoned him to serve as an assistant [cóngshì].
At that time, Gōng Lù and Yáo Zhóu, gentlemen from within the commandery, held positions worth two thousand *shí* of grain,
and had significant reputations in their era.
They were all good friends with Ní.
In the fifth year of Jiànxīng,
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng moved his base north to Hànzhōng.
Mountain bandits like Zhāng Mù from Guǎnghàn and Miánzhú plundered military supplies [jūnzī]
and robbed officials and commoners.
Ní, as commandant [dūwèi], led troops to suppress them.
Ní judged that they would scatter like birds,
making it difficult to capture them in battle.
So he feigned a peace agreement,
setting a date to hold a feast.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Ní personally led his retinue,
and consequently slew more than fifty heads of Mù and others.
Their chieftains were all annihilated.
He then sought out the remaining elements,
and within ten days, peace and stability were restored.
Later, he fell gravely ill.
His family was habitually poor and destitute.
Hé Zhī of Shǔjùn, the Administrator of Guǎnghàn,
was known for his generosity and integrity.
Ní had previously been estranged from him.
So, he personally traveled by litter to see Zhī,
entrusting himself to him for medical treatment.
Zhī spent his wealth on medical care,
and after several years, Ní recovered.
His integrity and trustworthiness among his peers were all of this kind.
He was appointed Gate General [yámén jiàng],
and assigned to Mǎ Zhōng.
He campaigned north to suppress the rebellious Qiāng of Wénshān,
and pacified the southern Mán and Yí of the Four Commanderies,
always achieving strategic planning and battle victories.
In the fourteenth year,
the Dī king Fú Jiàn of Wǔdū requested to surrender.
General Zhāng Wèi was dispatched to welcome him.
He was overdue and had not arrived,
causing Great General [Dà Jiāngjūn] Jiǎng Wǎn deep concern.
Ní calmly said:
“Fú Jiàn's request to submit is sincere,
there will certainly be no other change.
I have long heard that Jiàn's younger brother is cunning and sly,
and moreover, the barbarians cannot share a common endeavor.
There will likely be discord,
which is why he is delayed.”
A few days later,
an inquiry arrived,
and indeed, Jiàn's younger brother had taken four hundred households to Wèi,
while only Jiàn came to submit.
Initially,
after Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng's campaign against Gāo Dìng, the Yí of Yuèsuì Commandery [Yuèsuì Jùn] had repeatedly rebelled,
killing the administrators Gōng Lù and Jiāo Huáng.
Thereafter, the administrators dared not go to the commandery seat,
but stayed only in Ānshàng County,
more than eight hundred *lǐ* from the commandery seat.
The commandery existed in name only.
At the time, public opinion wished to restore the old commandery.
Ní was appointed Administrator of Yuèsuì.
Ní led his subordinates to the commandery seat,
enticing them with benevolence and trustworthiness.
The Mán and Yí all submitted,
many coming to surrender and attach themselves.
The Zhuōmǎ of the northern border were the most fierce and powerful,
and did not follow regulations.
Ní then went to suppress them,
capturing their chieftain Wèi Láng alive.
He then released him and instructed him to recruit and appease the remaining groups.
He memorialized to have Láng appointed Yì Hóu,
and over three thousand households of his tribe were settled and served their duties.
When the various tribes heard of this,
many gradually surrendered.
Ní was granted the title of Marquis within the Passes [Guānnèi Hóu] for his merits.
Dōng Féng, the chieftain of Sūqí, and Féng's younger brother Wěi Qú, etc.,
who had surrendered, rebelled again.
Ní executed Féng.
Féng's wife,
the daughter of the Máo Niú King,
was spared by Ní's stratagem.
Qú, however, fled into the western border.
Qú was fierce, brave, swift, and valiant,
and deeply feared and respected by the various tribes.
He sent two trusted men to feign surrender to Ní,
actually to gather intelligence.
Ní detected this,
promised them lavish rewards,
and had them act as double agents.
The two then conspired and killed Qú.
With Qú dead,
all the tribes were pacified.
Furthermore, Lǐ Qiúchéng, the elder chieftain of Sīdū,
who had personally killed Gōng Lù in the past,
was sought out and captured by Ní's bounty.
Ní recounted his past evils and executed him.
Initially, Ní found the commandery walls and buildings dilapidated,
so he built a smaller stockade.
After three years in office,
he moved back to the old commandery seat,
repairing the city walls and fortifications.
Men and women of the Yí tribes all exerted their efforts.
The three counties of Dìngzuò, Táidēng, and Bēishuǐ, located over three hundred *lǐ* from the commandery seat,
traditionally produced salt, iron, and lacquer.
However, the Yí on the border had long monopolized these resources.
Ní led his forces to seize them,
and appointed chief officials there.
When Ní arrived in Dìngzuò,
Láng Cén, the chieftain of Dìngzuò,
and the uncle of Pánmù King,
was highly trusted by the Mán and Yí.
He resented Ní's encroachment
and did not come to pay respects himself.
Ní sent several dozen strong men directly to arrest him,
flogged him, and killed him.
He brought the corpse back to the tribe,
lavishly rewarded them,
and explained the wickedness of Láng Cén.
He also said:
“Do not make any rash moves;
if you move, you will be annihilated!”
The tribes all tied their hands and apologized for their transgressions.
Ní slaughtered oxen for a feast,
reiterating his benevolence and trustworthiness,
and thus secured salt and iron,
providing ample supplies for daily use.
In Hànjiā Commandery, there were over four thousand households of the Máo Niú Yí.
Their chieftain, Láng Lù,
wished to avenge his cousin's husband, Dōng Féng.
He sent his uncle, Lí, to lead Féng's followers to assess the situation.
Ní preemptively sent trusted associates with cattle and wine to bestow gifts,
and also ordered Lí's (sister) to go to Féng's wife and clearly convey his intentions.
After Lí received the gifts and met his sister,
the siblings were joyful.
They all led their followers to Ní,
who treated them generously and sent them back.
From then on, the Máo Niú ceased to be a problem.
There was an old road in the commandery
that passed through the Máo Niú territory to Chéngdū;
it was both peaceful and short.
The Máo Niú had cut off this road
for over a hundred years,
forcing people to use the path via Ānshàng,
which was both perilous and long.
Ní sent his attendants with currency and gifts to Lù,
and again ordered Lù's paternal aunt to convey his intentions.
Lù then led his brothers and wives and children to Ní.
Ní made a sworn alliance with him,
reopened the old road,
clearing a thousand *lǐ* of territory,
and restored the ancient post stations.
He memorialized to enfeoff Lù as Pí Wáng of Máo Niú,
and sent an envoy to bring Lù to pay tribute to the court.
The Later Lord [Hòuzhǔ] thereupon added the title General Who Cherishes the Barbarians [Wǔróng Jiāngjūn] to Ní,
who continued to administer the commandery as before.
Zhāng Yí (張嶷) first saw Fèi Yī (費禕) as grand general.
He indulged his nature in widespread affection,
and was overly trusting of newcomers.
Zhāng Yí (張嶷) wrote to admonish him, saying:
“In the past, Cén Péng (岑彭) led an army,
and Láixī (來歙) held a staff of authority.
Both were harmed by assassins.
Now, esteemed general, your position is exalted and your power great.
You should reflect on these past events
and take them as a small warning.”
Later, Fèi Yī (費禕) was indeed killed by Guō Xiū (郭脩), a surrendered soldier from Wèi (魏).
Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪), grand tutor of Wú (吳), having just defeated the Wèi (魏) army,
raised a large force to plan an attack and capture.
Zhūgě Zhān (諸葛瞻), attendant,
son of Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮),
was a cousin of Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪).
Zhāng Yí (張嶷) wrote to him, saying:
“The Eastern Lord (Sūn Quán 孫權) has just died,
and the Emperor (Sūn Liàng 孫亮) is indeed young and weak.
The Grand Tutor (Zhūgě Kè 諸葛恪) has received a heavy trust –
how can he take it lightly!
Zhōu Gōng (周公) himself, with his talent,
still faced the slanderous rumors of Guǎn (管) and Cài (蔡).
Huò Guāng (霍光) received his appointment,
and also faced the treacherous plots of Yān (燕), Gài (蓋), and Shàngguān (上官).
It was thanks to the clarity of Chéng (成) and Zhāo (昭)
that they escaped these difficulties.
In the past, I often heard that the Eastern Lord (Sūn Quán 孫權) handled matters of life and death, rewards and punishments,
without entrusting them to subordinates.
And now, with his life nearing its end,
he suddenly summoned the Grand Tutor (Zhūgě Kè 諸葛恪)
and entrusted him with future affairs.
This is truly cause for concern.
Moreover, Wú (吳) and Chǔ (楚) are known for their impetuosity,
as recorded in the past.
For the Grand Tutor (Zhūgě Kè 諸葛恪) to leave the young lord
and venture into enemy territory,
I fear this is not a good strategy or a long-term plan.
Although it is said that the governance of the Eastern household (Wú 吳) is orderly
and its superiors and subordinates are harmonious,
one mistake in a hundred
is surely not what an enlightened person would consider?
What is learned from the ancients applies to the present;
what applies to the present applies to the ancients.
If it is not you, my lord, who offers loyal words to the Grand Tutor (Zhūgě Kè 諸葛恪),
who else will speak fully?
Recall the army, expand agriculture,
and strive to implement kindness and benevolence.
Within a few years,
both east and west can be attacked simultaneously.
This would indeed not be too late.
I hope you will deeply consider this.”
Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪) was eventually exterminated along with his clan because of this.
Such instances of Zhāng Yí's (張嶷) insight were numerous.
He served in the commandery for fifteen years,
and the region was peaceful and stable.
He repeatedly begged to return,
and was finally summoned to Chéngdū (成都).
The local Yi (夷) people
loved and admired him, supporting his carriage and weeping.
When he passed Máo Niú (旄牛) county,
the county magistrate carried his infant on his back to greet him.
They pursued him all the way to the border of Shǔjùn (蜀郡),
and over a hundred of their leaders followed Zhāng Yí (張嶷) to pay tribute.
When Zhāng Yí (張嶷) arrived,
he was appointed General Pacifying Rebels (Dàngkòu Jiāngjūn 盪寇將軍).
He was bold and valiant,
and scholars mostly esteemed him.
However, he was uninhibited and lacked etiquette,
and people also criticized him for this.
This was the seventeenth year of Yánxī (延熙) (254 CE).
Lǐ Jiǎn (李簡), the chief of Dídào (狄道) in Wèi (魏), secretly wrote to request surrender.
Wèi (衛) General Jiāng Wéi (姜維) led Zhāng Yí (張嶷) and others, using Lǐ Jiǎn’s (李簡) resources to march into Lǒngxī (隴西).
Upon reaching Dídào (狄道),
Lǐ Jiǎn (李簡) led all the officials and common people of the city to welcome the army.
The army then engaged in battle with the Wèi (魏) general Xú Zhì (徐質).
Zhāng Yí (張嶷) died in battle,
but the enemy he killed and wounded was more than double his own casualties.
After his death,
his eldest son Yīng (瑛) was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīxiāng (西鄉侯),
and his second son Hùxióng (護雄) inherited the title.
When the Yi (夷) people of Yuèsuì (越嶲) in the south heard of Zhāng Yí's (張嶷) death,
none did not weep in sorrow.
They erected a temple for Zhāng Yí (張嶷),
and offered sacrifices to him during droughts and floods in all four seasons.
A commentary says: Huáng Quán (黃權) was broad-minded and thoughtful;
Lǐ Huī (李恢) was public-spirited and resolute in his endeavors;
Lǚ Kǎi (呂凱) upheld his integrity without wavering;
Mǎ Zhōng (馬忠) was diligent and persevering;
Wáng Píng (王平) was loyal, brave, and disciplined;
Zhāng Yí (張嶷) possessed clear judgment and resolve.
All, by their respective strengths,
achieved fame and made their mark,
seizing their opportune time.
Biography of Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬), Fèi Yī (費禕), Jiāng Wéi (姜維), Chapter 14.
Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬), courtesy name Gōngyǎn (公琰), was from Xiāngxiāng (湘鄉), Línglíng (零陵).
At the age of twenty, he and his maternal cousin Liú Mǐn (劉敏) of Quánlíng (泉陵) were both famous.
Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬), as a provincial clerk, followed the Former Lord (Liú Bèi 劉備) into Shǔ (蜀),
and was appointed Magistrate of Guǎngdū (廣都).
The Former Lord (Liú Bèi 劉備) once, during an excursion, unexpectedly arrived at Guǎngdū (廣都),
and saw that Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) was neglecting many affairs
and was also deeply intoxicated at the time.
The Former Lord (Liú Bèi 劉備) was greatly enraged
and intended to punish him with death.
Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮), General of the Military Advisor, pleaded, saying:
“Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬)
is a vessel for the state,
not a talent for mere administrative districts.
His governance takes the peace of the people as its foundation,
not elaborate embellishment as its priority.
I hope Your Lordship will re-examine him.”
The Former Lord (Liú Bèi 劉備) deeply respected Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮),
and thus did not inflict punishment,
but merely dismissed him from office in haste.
After Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) was recommended,
he dreamt at night of a ox head at his gate,
with blood profusely flowing.
He felt very ill about it,
and called to consult Zhào Zhí (趙直), a dream interpreter.
Zhào Zhí (趙直) said:
“Indeed, seeing blood
means affairs will be clear.
The ox horns and nose
resemble the character 'Gōng' (公).
Your position will surely reach that of a Duke (Gōng 公).
This is a sign of great auspiciousness.”
Shortly after,
he became the Magistrate of Shífāng (什邡).
When the Former Lord (Liú Bèi 劉備) became King of Hànzhōng (漢中),
Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) entered as a Secretariat Director (Shàngshū Láng 尚書郎).
In the first year of Jiànxīng (建興) (223 CE),
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) established his administration,
and appointed Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) as Eastern Clerk (Dōngcáo Yuàn 東曹掾).
He was nominated as a “Flourishing Talent” (Màocái 茂才).
Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) firmly declined in favor of Liú Yōng (劉邕), Yīn Huà (陰化), Páng Yán (龐延), and Liáo Chún (廖淳).
Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) instructed him to reply, saying:
“Considering how abandoning one's kin and casting aside virtue
would bring ruin upon the common people,
if people do not feel it in their hearts,
it would also cause those near and far not to understand its meaning.
Therefore, you should display your merit and nomination
to clarify the purity and importance of this selection.”
He was promoted to Army Advisor (Cānjūn 參軍).
In the fifth year (227 CE),
Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) resided in Hànzhōng (漢中),
and Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) and Chief Clerk Zhāng Yì (張裔) oversaw the affairs of the remaining office.
In the eighth year (230 CE),
he succeeded Zhāng Yì (張裔) as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ 長史),
and was additionally appointed General Pacifying the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn 撫軍將軍).
Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) often went on expeditions,
and Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) always provided ample food and troops to supply him.
Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) often said:
“Gōngyǎn (公琰) is loyal and elegant in his aspirations,
and should assist me in establishing the royal enterprise.”
He secretly reported to the Later Lord (Liú Chán 劉禪), saying:
“If I should be so unfortunate as to die,
my successor should be entrusted to Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬).”
After Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮)'s death,
Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) was made Director of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令).
Soon after, he was additionally appointed Acting Protector-General (Xíng Dūhù 行都護),
granted the ceremonial staff (jiǎjié 假節),
and concurrently held the post of Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州 Cìshǐ 刺史).
He was promoted to Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn 大將軍),
oversaw the affairs of the Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū Shì 錄尚書事),
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānyáng Tíng (安陽亭侯).
At that time, with the recent loss of the commander-in-chief,
everyone near and far was anxious and frightened.
Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) stood out from the crowd,
placing him above all other officials.
He showed neither sorrow
nor joy,
maintaining his composure and demeanor
as if it were an ordinary day.
Because of this, public confidence gradually settled.
In the first year of Yánxī (延熙) (238 CE),
an imperial edict to Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) said:
“The rebellion and difficulties are not yet quelled.
Cáo Ruì (曹叡) is arrogant and cruel.
The three commanderies of Liáodōng (遼東) suffered under his tyranny,
and so they formed alliances
and separated from him.
Cáo Ruì (曹叡) raised large forces
and attacked them in return.
When Qín (秦) perished in the past,
Chén Shèng (陳勝) and Wú Guǎng (吳廣) were the first to revolt.
Now there is this change,
which is indeed a timely opportunity.
You should prepare your forces,
lead all armies to garrison in Hànzhōng (漢中),
and wait for Wú's (吳) actions,
to form a pincer attack from east and west
and seize the opportune moment.”
He also ordered Jiāng Wǎn (蔣琬) to establish an administration,
and the following year, he was further promoted to Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ 大司馬).
Dōngcáo Yuàn
Yáng Xì
was by nature simple and unpretentious.
Jiǎng Wǎn
spoke with him,
but
Xì
sometimes did not respond.
Someone wanted to slander
Xì
to
Wǎn, saying:
“When you speak with
Xì,
he doesn’t respond.
Isn’t
Xì’s
disrespect towards his superior excessive?”
Wǎn
said:
“People’s hearts are different,
just as their faces are.
To agree in person and speak ill behind one’s back
is what the ancients warned against.
If
Xì
were to praise my rightness,
it would not be his true feeling.
If he were to contradict my words,
it would expose my faults.
Therefore, he remained silent.
This is
Xì’s
quickness of mind.”
Furthermore,
Dūnóng
Yáng Mǐn
once criticized
Wǎn, saying:
“His actions are muddled,
he is truly not as good as his predecessors.”
Someone reported this to
Wǎn.
The official in charge requested to investigate and punish
Mǐn.
Wǎn
said:
“I am indeed not as good as my predecessors,
there is nothing to investigate.”
The official insisted on following the instruction not to investigate,
but then requested to ask about the nature of his muddled actions.
Wǎn
said:
“If one is truly not as good,
then things are not handled properly.
If things are not handled properly,
then they are muddled.
Why ask further?”
Later,
Mǐn
was imprisoned for a crime.
Everyone feared that he would surely die.
Wǎn
bore no personal favor or dislike,
and
Mǐn
was spared from a heavy sentence.
His likes and dislikes were based on principle;
all such cases were of this type.
Wǎn
believed that in the past,
Zhūgě Liàng
had repeatedly attempted to invade
Qínchuān.
The roads were treacherous and transport difficult,
and he ultimately failed to conquer it.
It would be better to descend eastward by water.
So he had many boats built,
intending to attack
Wèixīng
and
Shàngyōng
via the
Hàn
and
Miǎn
rivers.
However, his old illness flared up repeatedly,
and he could not set out at the planned time.
And the general opinion was that if they did not achieve victory,
the return journey would be extremely difficult,
and it was not a good strategy.
Thereupon, he sent
Shàngshū Lìng
Fèi Yī
and
Zhōngjiānjūn
Jiāng Wéi
and others to convey his intentions.
Wǎn,
following the imperial decree, submitted a memorial, saying:
“To eliminate corruption and quell difficulties is my duty.
Since I was ordered to
Hànzhōng,
six years have already passed.
I am both ignorant and weak,
and afflicted by illness.
My plans have come to nothing,
and I grieve day and night.
Now
Wèi
spans nine provinces,
its roots and branches spread wide,
and it is not easy to completely clear them away.
If we combine our forces from east and west,
attacking from front and rear,
although we may not quickly achieve our desires,
we should at least divide and gradually consume them,
first destroying their supporting factions.
However,
Wú’s
commitment is inconsistent,
and it has repeatedly failed to achieve its objectives.
I contemplate the difficulties and truly forget sleep and food.
I have discussed with
Fèi Yī
and others that
Liángzhōu
is a strategic frontier for the
Hú
barbarians,
offering advantages for advance and retreat,
and is valued by the enemy.
Moreover, the
Qiāng
and
Hú
long for
Hàn
as if thirsty.
Also, when a detached force entered
Qiāng
in the past,
Guō Huái
was defeated and fled.
Considering their strengths and weaknesses,
we believe the priority
should be to appoint
Jiāng Wéi
as the Governor of
Liángzhōu.
If
Wéi
campaigns and holds the territory west of the river,
I will lead my army to support him.
Now,
Fú’s
land and water routes connect in all directions,
ready to respond to any emergency.
If there is trouble in the northeast,
it will not be difficult to go there.”
Consequently,
Wǎn
then returned to reside in
Fú.
His illness worsened,
and he died in the ninth year.
His posthumous title was
Gōng.
His son
Bīn
succeeded him,
and became
Suīwǔ Jiāngjūn
and
Hànchéng Hùjūn.
When
Wèi
Grand General
Zhōng Huì
arrived at
Hànchéng,
he wrote to
Bīn,
The Former Emperor (Liú Bèi 劉備) established the crown prince.
Fèi Yī 費禕 and Yǔn 允 were both palace attendants,
and then promoted to庶子 (shùzǐ, household administrator for a prince).
When the Later Emperor (Liú Chán 劉禪) ascended the throne,
Fèi Yī was made a Palace Gentleman (huángmén shìláng 黃門侍郎).
When Prime Minister Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮 returned from his southern campaign,
many officials went tens of li to meet him.
Many of them were older and held higher ranks than Fèi Yī,
but Zhūgě Liàng specifically ordered Fèi Yī to ride in the same carriage as him.
Because of this, everyone was astonished.
Since Zhūgě Liàng had just returned from the south,
he appointed Fèi Yī as Zhāoxìn Xiàowèi (昭信校尉, Commandant who Manifests Trust) and sent him to Wú 吳.
Sūn Quán 孫權 was naturally jovial
and often mocked others without restraint.
Zhūgě Kè 諸葛恪, Yáng Dào 羊衜, and others were learned and eloquent,
their arguments and challenges came in a torrent.
Fèi Yī's words were agreeable and his principles sound;
he responded based on reason,
and ultimately could not be intimidated.
Sūn Quán greatly esteemed him,
and said to Fèi Yī:
"Sir, you possess excellent virtue in the realm;
you will surely be a pillar of the Shǔ (蜀) court.
I fear you will not be able to visit frequently."
Upon his return,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng (侍中, Palace Attendant).
Zhūgě Liàng resided in Hànzhōng 漢中
and invited Fèi Yī to be a Cānjūn (參軍, Administrator).
Because his diplomatic missions consistently pleased,
he frequently traveled to Wú.
In the eighth year of Jiànxīng (建興) [229 CE],
he was transferred to Zhōnghùjūn (中護軍, Central Protector of the Army),
and later also became Sīmǎ (司馬, Cavalry Commander).
At that time, Jūnshī (軍師, Army Advisor) Wèi Yán 魏延 and Chángshǐ (長史, Chief Clerk) Yáng Yí 楊儀 intensely disliked each other.
Whenever they sat together, they would argue.
Wèi Yán would sometimes raise a blade to Yáng Yí,
and Yáng Yí would weep profusely.
Fèi Yī often went between them,
mediating and explaining,
and throughout Zhūgě Liàng's lifetime,
both Wèi Yán and Yáng Yí were able to fully utilize their talents.
This was due to Fèi Yī's harmonizing and salvaging efforts.
After Zhūgě Liàng's death,
Fèi Yī became Hòujūnshī (後軍師, Rear Army Advisor).
Shortly thereafter,
he replaced Jiǎng Wǎn 蔣琬 as Shàngshūlìng (尚書令, Director of the Imperial Secretariat).
When Jiǎng Wǎn returned from Hànzhōng to Fú 涪,
Fèi Yī was promoted to Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍, Grand General)
and Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事, concurrently in charge of the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat).
In the seventh year of Yánxī (延熙) [244 CE],
the Wèi 魏 army advanced to Xīngshì 興勢.
Fèi Yī was granted a marshal's staff (jié 節),
and led his troops to repel them.
Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫, Grand Master of Guanglu) Lái Mǐn 來敏 came to bid farewell to Fèi Yī
and asked to play a game of encirclement chess (wéiqí 圍棋) with him.
At that time, urgent dispatches flew back and forth.
Soldiers and horses were already armored,
and carriages were ready.
Yet, Fèi Yī and Lái Mǐn intently played chess,
showing no sign of fatigue.
Lái Mǐn said:
"I was just trying to test you!
You are indeed a remarkable man,
and will surely be able to defeat the enemy."
When Fèi Yī arrived,
the enemy withdrew.
He was enfeoffed as Chéngxiāng Hóu (成鄉侯, Marquis of Chéngxiāng).
Jiǎng Wǎn firmly declined his provincial post,
so Fèi Yī again took charge as Yìzhōu Cìshǐ (益州刺史, Inspector of Yìzhōu).
Fèi Yī's accomplishments in governance
were roughly comparable to Jiǎng Wǎn's.
In the eleventh year [248 CE],
he moved out to reside in Hànzhōng.
From Jiǎng Wǎn to Fèi Yī,
even though they were personally away from the capital,
all rewards, punishments, and displays of authority
were first consulted upon and decided from afar,
and only then carried out.
Such was the trust placed in them.
In the summer of the fourteenth year [251 CE],
he returned to Chéngdū 成都.
A diviner in Chéngdū observed the qi and said there was no prime ministerial aura in the capital.
Therefore, in winter, he again garrisoned north at Hànshòu 漢壽.
In the fifteenth year of Yánxī [252 CE],
Fèi Yī was ordered to establish his own government (kāifǔ 開府).
In the first day of the sixteenth year [253 CE], at a grand assembly,
a Wèi defector named Guō Xún 郭循 was present.
Fèi Yī drank joyfully and became heavily intoxicated,
and was killed by Guō Xún with a blade in hand.
He was posthumously given the title Jìng Hóu (敬侯).
His son, Fèi Chéng 費承, succeeded him
and became Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎, Palace Gentleman).
Chéng's younger brother, Fèi Gōng 費恭,
married a princess.
Fèi Yī's eldest daughter married Crown Prince Xuán 璿 as his consort.
Jiāng Wéi 姜維, courtesy name Bóyuē 伯約,
was a native of Jì 冀, Tiānshuǐ 天水.
He was orphaned young
and lived with his mother.
He was fond of the scholarship of the Zhèng 鄭 clan.
He served as a Jìyuán (計掾, Accountant) in the commandery,
and was appointed Cóngshì (從事, Assistant) by the province.
Because his father Jiāng Jiǒng 姜冏 had formerly been a Gōngcáo (功曹, Chief Clerk) in the commandery
and, at the time of the Qiāng 羌 and Róng 戎 rebellion,
protected the commandery administrator,
dying on the battlefield,
Jiāng Wéi was granted the official post of Zhōngláng (中郎, Gentleman of the Household)
and participated in military affairs of his native commandery.
In the sixth year of Jiànxīng (建興) [228 CE],
Prime Minister Zhūgě Liàng's army advanced towards Qíshān 祁山.
At that time, the Administrator of Tiānshuǐ happened to be out on an inspection tour,
and Jiāng Wéi, along with Gōngcáo Liáng Xù 梁緒, Zhǔbù (主簿, Registrar) Yǐn Shǎng 尹賞, Zhǔjì (主記, Recorder) Liáng Qián 梁虔, and others, were accompanying him.
The Administrator heard that the Shǔ army was approaching,
and that various counties were responding to them.
He suspected that Jiāng Wéi and the others harbored disloyal intentions.
So, that night, he fled to defend Shàngguī 上邽.
Jiāng Wéi and the others realized the Administrator had left,
but their pursuit was delayed.
When they reached the city gate,
the city gate was already closed
and they were not admitted.
Jiāng Wéi and the others then went together to Jì,
but Jì also would not admit Jiāng Wéi.
Jiāng Wéi and the others then all went to Zhūgě Liàng.
Coincidentally, Mǎ Sù 馬謖 was defeated at Jiētíng 街亭,
so Zhūgě Liàng evacuated over a thousand households from Xīxiàn 西縣, along with Jiāng Wéi and the others, and returned.
Thus, Jiāng Wéi was separated from his mother.
Zhūgě Liàng appointed Jiāng Wéi as Cāngcáo Yuàn (倉曹掾, Registrar of Granaries),
additionally giving him the title Fèngyì Jiāngjūn (奉義將軍, General who Upholds Righteousness),
and enfeoffed him as Dāngyáng Tínghóu (當陽亭侯, Marquis of Dāngyáng Pavilion).
He was twenty-seven years old at the time.
Zhūgě Liàng wrote to Zhāng Yì 張裔, the Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk) who remained in the capital, and Cānjūn (Administrator) Jiǎng Wǎn, saying:
"Jiāng Bóyuē is loyal and diligent in current affairs,
and his thoughts are precise and subtle.
Examining his abilities,
people like Yǒngnán 永南 and Jìcháng 季常 are not his equal.
This man
is a superior scholar from Liángzhōu 涼州."
He also said:
"It is necessary to first train five or six thousand of the central tiger infantry.
Jiāng Bóyuē is very keen in military affairs,
possessing both courage and righteousness,
and deeply understands military strategy.
This man's heart is devoted to the Hàn 漢 dynasty,
and his talent surpasses others.
Once he has thoroughly learned military matters,
he should be sent to the palace
to meet the Emperor."
Later, he was promoted to Zhōngjiānjūn Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (中監軍征西將軍, Central Supervisor of the Army and General who Conquers the West).
In the twelfth year [234 CE],
Zhūgě Liàng died.
Jiāng Wéi returned to Chéngdū
and became Yòujiānjūn Fǔhàn Jiāngjūn (右監軍輔漢將軍, Right Supervisor of the Army and General who Assists Hàn),
commanding all armies,
and was advanced in enfeoffment to Píngxiāng Hóu (平襄侯).
In the first year of Yánxī [238 CE],
he accompanied Grand General Jiǎng Wǎn to reside in Hànzhōng.
When Jiǎng Wǎn was promoted to Dàsīmǎ (大司馬, Grand Minister of War),
he made Jiāng Wéi a Sīmǎ (Cavalry Commander),
who frequently led detached forces westward.
In the sixth year [243 CE],
he was promoted to Zhènxī Dàjiāngjūn (鎮西大將軍, Grand General who Guards the West)
and concurrently held the post of Liángzhōu Cìshǐ (涼州刺史, Inspector of Liángzhōu).
In the tenth year [247 CE],
he was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍, General of the Guards)
and concurrently recorded the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat with Grand General Fèi Yī.
That year,
the Yí 夷 people of Píngkāng 平康 in Wénshān 汶山 rebelled.
Jiāng Wéi led his troops to suppress and pacify them.
He also went out into the territories of Lǒngxī 隴西, Nán'ān 南安, and Jīnchéng 金城,
and fought Wèi Grand General Guō Huái 郭淮 and Xiàhóu Bà 夏侯霸 at Táoxī 洮西.
Hú 胡 King Zhìwúdài 治無戴 and others surrendered their tribes.
Jiāng Wéi led them back and settled them.
In the twelfth year [249 CE],
Jiāng Wéi was granted a marshal's staff
and again went out to Xīpíng 西平,
but returned without success.
Jiāng Wéi, believing he was familiar with the customs of the western regions
and confident in his talent and martial prowess,
wished to entice the various Qiāng and Hú peoples to be his wings,
thinking that the area west of Lǒng could be seized and held.
Whenever he wanted to launch a large-scale military campaign,
Fèi Yī always restrained him and did not comply,
limiting his troops to no more than ten thousand men.
In the sixteenth year, in spring,
Fèi Yī died.
In summer,
Jiāng Wéi led several tens of thousands of men out of Shíyíng,
passing through Dǒngtíng,
and besieged Nán'ān.
Chén Tài, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu of Wèi, relieved the siege and reached Luòmén.
Jiāng Wéi, with his provisions exhausted, retreated.
The following year,
he was appointed Supervisor of the Armies of the Interior and Exterior.
He again sallied forth into Lǒngxī.
Lǐ Jiǎn, the Magistrate of Dídào, surrendered the city.
He advanced to besiege Xiāngwǔ,
and engaged in battle with the Wèi general Xú Zhì.
He beheaded and defeated the enemy,
and the Wèi army was routed and retreated.
Jiāng Wéi, taking advantage of his victory, brought many to submission,
relocating the people of the three counties of Hégūan, Dídào, and Líntáo.
Eighteen years later,
he again went out from Dídào with the General of Chariots and Cavalry Xiàhóu Bà and others,
and thoroughly defeated Wáng Jīng, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu of Wèi, at Táoxī.
Tens of thousands of Wáng Jīng's troops were killed.
Wáng Jīng retreated and defended Dídào city,
which Jiāng Wéi then besieged.
Chén Tài, the General Who Attacks the West of Wèi, advanced his troops to relieve the siege.
Jiāng Wéi withdrew and stationed himself at Zhōngtí.
In the nineteenth year, in spring,
Jiāng Wéi was promoted to Grand General.
He reorganized his army,
and arranged to rendezvous with Hú Jì, the Grand General Who Guards the West, at Shàngguī.
Hú Jì broke his promise and did not arrive,
thus Jiāng Wéi was defeated by Dèng Ài, the Grand General of Wèi, at Duàngǔ.
His forces scattered and wandered away,
and very many died.
The common people consequently resented and cursed him,
and the region west of Lǒng was also restless and uneasy.
Jiāng Wéi apologized for his fault and admitted his failures,
requesting to be demoted.
He became General of the Rear,
acting as Grand General.
In the twentieth year,
Zhūgě Dàn, the Grand General Who Attacks the East of Wèi, rebelled in Huáinán,
and a portion of the Guānzhōng army moved eastward.
Jiāng Wéi wanted to take advantage of this vulnerability to advance towards Qínchuān,
and again led several tens of thousands of men out of Luògǔ,
directly reaching Shěnlǐng.
At that time, the granaries at Chángchéng held much grain, but the defending troops were few.
Hearing that Jiāng Wéi was approaching,
all were fearful.
Sīmǎ Wàng, the Grand General of Wèi, resisted him,
and Dèng Ài also came from Lǒngyòu.
Both encamped at Chángchéng.
Jiāng Wéi advanced to Mángshuǐ,
all making camps against the mountains.
Sīmǎ Wàng and Dèng Ài formed a strong encirclement along the Wèi River.
Jiāng Wéi repeatedly issued challenges,
but Sīmǎ Wàng and Dèng Ài did not respond.
In the first year of Jǐngyào,
Jiāng Wéi heard that Zhūgě Dàn had been defeated,
and so returned to Chéngdū.
He was again appointed Grand General.
Originally,
the Former Lord (Liú Bèi) had stationed Wèi Yán to guard Hànzhōng,
filling all the defensive positions with actual troops to guard against external enemies,
so that if the enemy came to attack,
they would not be able to enter.
During the campaign of Xìngshì,
Wáng Píng resisted Cáo Shuǎng,
all following this system.
Jiāng Wéi suggested,
thinking that scattering troops to defend various outposts,
though in line with the Yìjīng's
"heavy gates"
principle,
was only suitable for defense and did not achieve great advantage.
It would be better, he argued,
upon hearing of the enemy's approach,
for all the outposts to withdraw their troops and gather their grain,
and retreat to the two cities of Hànchéng and Lèchéng,
preventing the enemy from easily entering the plains,
and instead reinforcing the passes for defense.
On the day of an incident,
mobile forces would advance in unison to seek out the enemy's weaknesses.
If the enemy attacked the passes unsuccessfully,
and found no scattered grain in the fields,
and had to transport provisions over a thousand *lǐ*,
they would naturally become fatigued.
When they began to retreat,
then all the cities would sally forth simultaneously,
and combine forces with the mobile army to strike them.
This was the strategy to eliminate the enemy.
Thus, he ordered Hú Jì, the Supervisor of Hànzhōng, to withdraw and station himself at Hànshòu,
Wáng Hán, the Military Supervisor, to guard Lèchéng,
and Jiǎng Bīn, the Protector of the Army, to guard Hànchéng.
He also established defensive outposts at Xī'ān, Jiànwēi, Wǔwèi, Shímén, Wǔchéng, Jiànchāng, and Línyuǎn.
In the fifth year,
Jiāng Wéi led his forces out of Hànchéng and Hóuhé,
was defeated by Dèng Ài,
and returned to station himself at Tàzhōng.
Jiāng Wéi was originally a sojourner who had placed his trust in the state.
For many years he had engaged in attacks and battles,
but his achievements were not established.
Meanwhile, the eunuch Huáng Hào and others wielded power internally.
Yán Yǔ, the Grand General of the Right, conspired with Huáng Hào,
and Huáng Hào secretly wished to depose Jiāng Wéi and install Yán Yǔ.
Jiāng Wéi also suspected this.
Therefore, feeling insecure and fearful,
he no longer returned to Chéngdū.
In the sixth year,
Jiāng Wéi memorialized the Latter Lord (Liú Chán):
"I hear that Zhōng Huì is training troops in Guānzhōng,
intending to advance and take territory.
It is advisable to dispatch Zhāng Yì and Liáo Huà to supervise the various armies and guard the Yang'an Pass and Yīnpíng Bridgehead respectively, to prevent unforeseen events."
Huáng Hào trusted omens and sorcerers,
believing that the enemy would ultimately not reach them,
and persuaded the Latter Lord to put the matter aside,
which the ministers did not know.
When Zhōng Huì was about to advance towards Luògǔ,
and Dèng Ài was about to enter Tàzhōng,
only then was Liáo Huà, General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Right, dispatched to Tàzhōng to reinforce Jiāng Wéi.
Zhāng Yì, General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Left, Dǒng Jué, Grand General Who Supports the State, and others were sent to the Yáng'ān Pass to assist the various outposts.
By the time they reached Yīnpíng,
they heard that Zhūgě Xù, a Wèi general, was heading towards Jiànwēi,
so they halted to await him.
More than a month later,
Jiāng Wéi was defeated by Dèng Ài,
and returned to station himself at Yīnpíng.
Zhōng Huì besieged the two cities of Hànchéng and Lèchéng,
and sent a separate general to attack the pass.
Jiǎng Shū opened the city gates and surrendered,
while Fù Qiān fought to the death.
Zhōng Huì attacked Lèchéng
but could not conquer it.
Hearing that the pass had fallen,
he advanced rapidly.
Zhāng Yì and Dǒng Jué had just arrived at Hànshòu,
and Jiāng Wéi and Liáo Huà also abandoned Yīnpíng and retreated,
coincidentally joining with Zhāng Yì and Dǒng Jué.
They all retreated to defend Jiàngé against Zhōng Huì.
Zhōng Huì wrote a letter to Jiāng Wéi, saying:
"Your Excellency, with your civil and military virtues,
and your strategic talent surpassing your era,
your achievements have aided Bā and Hàn,
and your fame resonates throughout Huáxià.
Those near and far alike attribute renown to you.
I often recall the past,
when we shared the same great civilization.
Wú Zhá and Zhèng Qiáo
could understand such friendship."
Jiāng Wéi did not reply,
but arrayed his camps and defended the strategic points.
Zhōng Huì could not overcome him,
and his grain supplies were far away.
He was about to discuss returning.
Meanwhile, Dèng Ài entered from Yīnpíng via the Jǐnggǔ Road,
and subsequently defeated Zhūgě Zhān at Miánzhú.
The Latter Lord requested to surrender to Dèng Ài,
and Dèng Ài then occupied Chéngdū.
When Jiāng Wéi and others first heard of Zhūgě Zhān's defeat,
some heard that the Latter Lord intended to strongly defend Chéngdū,
some heard he wanted to go east into Wú,
and some heard he wanted to go south into Jiànníng.
So they led their army via Guǎnghàn and Qī Road to ascertain the situation.
Soon after, they received an imperial edict from the Latter Lord,
whereupon they cast aside their spears and armor,
and went to meet Zhōng Huì at his army camp in Fú.
The officers and soldiers were all enraged,
drawing their swords and hacking at stones.
Zhōng Huì treated Jiāng Wéi and others generously,
temporarily returning their seals, titles, and ceremonial umbrellas.
Zhōng Huì and Jiāng Wéi rode in the same carriage when they went out,
and sat at the same table when they sat down.
He said to his Chief Clerk Dù Yù:
"Comparing Bóyuē (Jiāng Wéi) to the famous scholars of the central plains,
Gōngxiū (Zhōng Huì's own courtesy name) and Tàichū (Dèng Ài's courtesy name) cannot surpass him."
After Zhōng Huì framed Dèng Ài,
and Dèng Ài was transported in a cage-cart,
he then took Jiāng Wéi and others to Chéngdū,
declared himself Governor of Yìzhōu, and rebelled.
He wanted to give Jiāng Wéi fifty thousand troops,
to serve as his vanguard.
The Wèi officers and soldiers were furious,
and killed Zhōng Huì and Jiāng Wéi.
Jiāng Wéi's wife and children were all executed.
Xì Zhèng著 Lùn Lún Wéi said:
"Jiāng Bóyuē held the heavy responsibility of a senior general,
and occupied a position above all other officials.
His residence was dilapidated,
he had no surplus wealth,
his private chambers had no concubines to serve him,
and his rear garden had no musical entertainment.
He obtained clothes as needed,
carriages and horses were provided as required.
His food and drink were disciplined,
neither extravagant nor overly frugal.
Official expenses were provided,
and spent as they came to hand.
Investigating the reason for this,
it was not to provoke the greedy and shame the corrupt,
nor to suppress desires and restrict himself,
but simply because he considered this sufficient,
and did not seek more.
People's discussions
always praise success and condemn failure,
exalting the high and suppressing the low.
All consider that Jiāng Wéi had no place to rest his head,
died, and his clan was exterminated,
and on account of this, they disparage and diminish him,
without further examination or discrimination.
This is contrary to the meaning of praise and blame in the Chūnqiū.
Such a person as Jiāng Wéi, who delighted in learning without tiring,
was pure and simple, and self-controlled and frugal,
was truly a model for his time."
Among those who formerly came to Shǔ with Wéi,
Liáng Xù's official position reached Dàhónglú,
Yǐn Shǎng was Zhí Jīnwú,
and Liáng Qián was Dàchángqiū;
all died before Shǔ perished.
The commentary states: Jiǎng Wǎn was upright and had gravitas;
Fèi Yī was broad-minded, helpful, and benevolent.
Both followed Zhūgě Liàng's established regulations,
adhering to them without change.
Thus, the borders were free from worry,
and the state was harmonious and unified.
However, they did not fully apply the appropriate methods for governing a small state,
nor the principles of maintaining tranquility.
Jiāng Wéi was somewhat accomplished in both civil and military arts,
and was determined to achieve fame and merit,
but he trifled with the masses and defiled the army,
and his judgments were not comprehensive,
ultimately leading to his downfall.
Lǎozǐ said:
"Governing a large state is like cooking a small fish."
How much more so for a small, insignificant state;
how could it be frequently disturbed?
The Biography of Dèng, Zhāng, Zōng, and Yáng, Chapter 15.
Dèng Zhī, courtesy name Bómiáo,
was a native of Xīnyě, Yìyáng,
and a descendant of Hòu Sītú Yǔ.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, he entered Shǔ,
but was not yet recognized or valued.
At that time, Zhāng Yù, a clerk in Yìzhōu, was skilled in physiognomy.
Zhī went to him,
and Yù said to Zhī:
"When you are over seventy,
your position will reach that of Dàjiàngjūn,
and you will be enfeoffed as a Marquis."
Zhī heard that Páng Xī, the Administrator of Bāxī, esteemed worthy men,
and went to rely on him.
When the Former Sovereign established Yìzhōu,
Zhī served as Pídǐ Gédū.
When the Former Sovereign went to Pí,
he conversed with Zhī,
and was greatly impressed,
promoting him to Pí Lìng,
then transferring him to Guǎnghàn Tàishǒu.
Wherever he served, he was clear and strict, with good administrative achievements,
and entered the court as Shàngshū.
The Former Sovereign died at Yǒng'ān.
Before this,
Sūn Quán, the King of Wú, sought peace,
and the Former Sovereign repeatedly sent Sòng Wěi, Fèi Yī, and others to return messages.
Prime Minister Zhūgě Liàng deeply worried that Quán, upon hearing of the Former Sovereign's death,
might entertain different plans,
and did not know what to do.
Zhī saw Liàng and said:
"Now the current ruler is young and weak,
and has just ascended the throne.
It is appropriate to send a grand envoy to reaffirm the good relations with Wú."
Liàng replied:
"I have been thinking about this for a long time,
but have not found the right person until now.
Today I have found him."
Zhī asked who this person was.
Liàng said:
"It is you."
So he sent Zhī to establish good relations with Quán.
Quán was indeed hesitant and suspicious,
and did not immediately grant an audience to Zhī.
Zhī then formally requested an audience with Quán, saying:
"I have come now also for Wú,
not just for Shǔ."
Quán then met him,
and said to Zhī:
"I sincerely wish to make peace and kinship with Shǔ,
but I fear that the Shǔ ruler is young and weak,
the state is small and its power constrained,
and it will be exploited by Wèi,
unable to preserve itself.
Because of this, I hesitate."
Zhī replied:
"The two states of Wú and Shǔ possess four prefectures of land.
Your Majesty is a hero born of your age,
and Zhūgě Liàng is also a hero of his time.
Shǔ has the security of great dangers,
and Wú has the obstacles of the Three Rivers.
Combining these two strengths,
they form a relationship like lips and teeth.
Advancing, they can conquer the whole world;
retreating, they can stand in a tripartite balance.
This is the natural course of things.
If Your Majesty now pledges allegiance to Wèi,
Wèi will certainly expect Your Majesty to attend court,
and demand your Crown Prince to serve internally.
If you do not obey,
they will declare war on the rebels.
Shǔ will surely follow the current, seize the opportunity, and advance.
In such a case,
the lands south of the river will no longer belong to Your Majesty."
Quán was silent for a long time, then said:
"Your words are correct."
He then severed ties with Wèi
and allied with Shǔ,
sending Zhāng Wēn to return the courtesy visit to Shǔ.
Shǔ again ordered Zhī to go,
and Quán said to Zhī:
"If the world achieves great peace,
and the two rulers govern separately,
would that not be delightful!"
Zhī replied:
"Indeed, there cannot be two suns in the sky,
nor two kings on the earth.
If, after conquering Wèi,
Your Majesty does not deeply understand the mandate of Heaven,
and each ruler asserts his virtue,
and each minister exhausts his loyalty,
then, taking up drums and drumsticks,
warfare will only just begin."
Quán laughed heartily and said:
"Your sincerity
is truly like this!"
Quán wrote to Liàng, saying:
"The brilliant display of Dīng Fàn's talents
does not exhaust the hidden transformative power;
for uniting the two states,
there is only Dèng Zhī."
When Liàng went north to reside in Hànzhōng,
he made Zhī Zhōng Jiānjūn and Yángwǔ Jiàngjūn.
When Liàng died,
he was promoted to Qián Jūnshī Qián Jiàngjūn,
leading the Inspectorate of Gǔnzhōu,
and was enfeoffed as Yángwǔ Tíng Hóu.
Soon after, he became Dū Jiāngzhōu.
Quán frequently sent messages to Zhī,
and generously sent gifts.
In the sixth year of Yánxī,
he was promoted to Chējì Jiàngjūn,
and later granted a ceremonial staff.
In the eleventh year,
the people of Fúlíng Commandery killed their Commandant and rebelled.
Zhī led an army to suppress them,
immediately beheading their leader,
and the common people settled down.
He died in the fourteenth year.
Zhī served as a general for over twenty years.
His rewards and punishments were clear and decisive,
and he was good at caring for his soldiers.
His personal clothing and food depended on official provisions;
he was not overly simple or frugal,
but he never accumulated private property.
His wife and children could not escape hunger and cold,
and on the day of his death, his household had no surplus wealth.
His nature was stern and straightforward,
not given to pretentious displays of emotion,
and thus he did not get along well with all types of scholars.
At that time, few people were highly esteemed by him;
he only admired Jiāng Wéi.
His son Liáng
inherited his title.
During the Jǐngyào era, he served as Shàngshū Zuǒxuǎnláng,
and in the Jìn dynasty, as Guǎnghàn Tàishǒu.
Zhāng Yì, courtesy name Bógōng,
was a native of Wǔyáng, Jiānwéi Commandery.
His great-great-grandfather was Sīkōng Hào,
and his great-grandfather was Guǎnglín Grand Administrator Gāng;
both were famous.
When the Former Lord settled Yìzhōu,
and became governor,
Yì served as a clerical assistant.
At the end of Jiàn'ān,
he was recommended as xiàolián,
and became the chief of Jiāngyáng.
He was transferred to be the magistrate of Fúlíng,
then promoted to Grand Administrator of Zǐtóng,
and successively promoted to Grand Administrator of Guǎnghàn and Shǔjùn.
In the ninth year of Jiànxīng (231 CE),
he became the Dūjiàng Dūdū and Suī Nánzhōng Zhōnglángjiàng.
Yì was by nature strict in enforcing laws,
and failed to win the favor of the various indigenous peoples.
The local chieftain Liú Zhòu rebelled and caused unrest.
Yì led troops to attack Zhòu.
Before Zhòu was defeated,
Yì was summoned back to court.
His subordinates all thought it best to immediately ride back and report his crime.
Yì said:
"No.
I am returning because the barbarians are stirring up trouble,
and I am not performing my duty well.
However, my replacement has not yet arrived,
and I am currently at the battlefield.
I must transport provisions and store grain
as resources for defeating the rebels.
How can I abandon the state's affairs just because of my demotion and recall?"
Thereupon, he continued to manage affairs without slackening,
and only departed when his replacement arrived.
Mǎ Zhōng then used the foundations Yì had laid to utterly defeat Zhòu.
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng heard of this and praised him.
When Liàng marched out to Wǔgōng,
he made Yì the Qiánjūn Dūdū
and concurrently the Grand Administrator of Fúfēng.
After Liàng's death,
Yì was appointed Qián Lǐngjūn.
His merit in suppressing Liú Zhòu was posthumously recognized,
and he was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
In the first year of Yánxī (238 CE),
he entered the court as Shàngshū.
He was gradually promoted to Dū Jiànwēi,
granted a 'false-axe' (jǐajié),
advanced to be enfeoffed as Dūtíng Hóu,
and became Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn.
In the eighteenth year (255 CE),
he returned to Chéngdū with General of the Guards Jiāng Wéi.
Wéi proposed another military expedition.
Only Yì argued strongly against it at court,
believing that the state was small and the people weary,
and it was not appropriate to engage in excessive warfare.
Wéi did not listen,
and led Yì and others on the expedition.
Yì was promoted to Zhènnán Dàjiāngjūn.
Wéi reached Dí Dào
and inflicted a great defeat on Wèi's Grand Inspector of Yōngzhōu, Wáng Jīng.
Tens of thousands of Jīng's troops died in the Táo River.
Yì said:
"We should stop now;
it is not advisable to advance further.
Advancing might ruin this great achievement."
Wéi was greatly angered.
He said:
"This is like drawing feet on a snake!"
Wéi then besieged Jīng at Dí Dào,
but could not take the city.
From the time Yì voiced his differing opinion,
Wéi held ill will towards Yì.
Nevertheless, Wéi often compelled Yì to accompany him,
and Yì had no choice but to go.
In the second year of Jǐngyào (259 CE),
Yì was promoted to Zuǒ Chējì Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently held the post of Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the sixth year (263 CE),
Yì and Wéi were both at Jiàngé,
and together they went to Fú to surrender to Zhōng Huì.
In the first month of the following year (264 CE),
he followed Huì to Chéngdū,
where he was killed by mutinying soldiers.
Zōng Yù, courtesy name Déyàn,
was a native of Ānzhòng, Nányáng.
In the Jiàn'ān period (196-220 CE),
he accompanied Zhāng Fēi into Shǔ.
At the beginning of Jiànxīng (223 CE),
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng made him his chief clerk (zhǔbù),
and he was promoted to Cānjūn Yòu Zhōnglángjiàng.
When Liàng died,
Wú feared that Wèi might take advantage of the weakness to seize Shǔ,
so they increased the garrison at Bāqiū by ten thousand men.
One reason was for mutual aid,
the second was to cause a division of forces.
Shǔ, upon hearing this,
also increased the garrison at Yǒng'ān
to guard against unforeseen events.
Yù was dispatched on a mission to Wú.
Sūn Quán asked Yù:
"The East and the West,
are like one family.
Yet I hear the West has increased the garrison at Báidì.
Why is this?"
Yù replied:
"Your servant believes that the East increasing its garrison at Bāqiū,
and the West increasing its garrison at Báidì,
are both appropriate due to circumstances and strategic necessity.
Neither should be questioned by the other."
Quán laughed heartily,
praised his straightforwardness and integrity,
and treated him with great affection and respect,
holding him in esteem only slightly less than Dèng Zhī and Fèi Yī.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
then transferred to Shàngshū.
In the tenth year of Yánxī (247 CE),
he became Túnjí Xiàowèi.
At that time, General of Chariots and Cavalry Dèng Zhī returned from Jiāngzhōu
to attend court,
and said to Yù:
"According to the Rites,
a man of sixty does not bear arms.
Yet you have just accepted a military post.
Why is this?"
Yù replied:
"You, sir, do not relinquish your military command at seventy,
so why should I, at sixty, not accept one?"
Zhī was arrogant by nature,
and even Grand General Fèi Yī and others deferred to him,
but Yù alone refused to yield.
Yù later went on another mission to Wú.
Sūn Quán clasped Yù's hand,
and with tears in his eyes, bade farewell, saying:
"You have always carried out your mission to forge good relations between our two states.
Now you are old,
and I, too, am aging.
I fear we may not meet again!"
He presented Yù with a hu of large pearls
before Yù returned.
He was promoted to Hòujiāngjūn,
overseeing Yǒng'ān,
and was then appointed Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn,
and granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
In the first year of Jǐngyào (258 CE),
he was recalled to Chéngdū due to illness.
Later, he became Zhènjūn Dàjiāngjūn,
concurrently holding the post of Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
At that time, Protector-General Zhūgě Zhān was beginning to manage court affairs.
Liáo Huà visited Yù,
wanting to go with Yù to visit Zhān.
Yù said:
"We are both over seventy.
We have already overstayed our welcome.
All that remains is one death.
Why should we bother to visit those younger men?"
So he did not go.
Liáo Huà, courtesy name Yuánjiǎn,
originally named Chún,
was from Xiāngyáng.
He served as the chief clerk for Former General Guān Yǔ.
When Yǔ was defeated,
he belonged to Wú.
Longing to return to the Former Lord,
he feigned death.
People at the time believed it to be true.
He then took his old mother and traveled west day and night.
At that time, the Former Lord was campaigning eastward,
and they met at Zǐguī.
The Former Lord was greatly pleased
and appointed Huà as Grand Administrator of Yídū.
After the Former Lord died,
he became Chancellor's Cānjūn,
then Dū Guǎngwǔ.
He was gradually promoted to Yòu Chējì Jiāngjūn,
granted a 'false-axe' (jǐajié),
concurrently held the post of Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and was enfeoffed as Zhōngxiāng Hóu.
He was known for his bravery and fierce determination.
His official rank was equal to Zhāng Yì's,
and above Zōng Yù's.
In the spring of the first year of Xiánxī (264 CE),
Huà and Yù were both moved eastward to Luòyáng,
and died of illness on the way.
Yáng Xì (楊戲), courtesy name Wénrán (文然),
was a native of Wǔyáng (武陽) in Jiànwéi (犍為).

In his youth, he was as renowned as Chéng Qí (程祁), courtesy name Gōnghóng (公弘), from Bāxī (巴西), Yáng Tài (楊汰), courtesy name Jìrú (季儒), from Bājùn (巴郡), and Zhāng Biǎo (張表), courtesy name Bódá (伯達), from Shǔjùn (蜀郡).
Xì (戲) always regarded Qí (祁) as the foremost,
and Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) deeply appreciated this.
When Xì (戲) was just over twenty,
he went from a secretariat clerk in the province to an Inspector of the Army,
in charge of legal and penal affairs.
His judgments on laws and resolutions of doubts
were praised as fair and just.
He was then appointed by the chancellery as a subordinate Chief Clerk.
After Liàng (亮) passed away,
he served as the Director of the Right Selection Department in the Secretariat.
The Inspector Jiǎng Wǎn (蔣琬) invited him to be an Administrator and Attendant Official.
When Wǎn (琬) established his office as Grand General,
he again appointed Xì (戲) as Supervisor of the Eastern Office.
He was then promoted to Military Advisor to the Central Cavalier General for the South,
serving as deputy to the Grand Administrator of Láijiàng (庲降),
and concurrently holding the position of Administrator of Jiànníng (建寧).
Due to illness, he was recalled to Chéngdū (成都),
appointed as Protector of the Army and Inspector of the Army,
then sent out to concurrently serve as Administrator of Zǐtóng (梓潼),
and later returned to the capital as General of the Archers.
Wherever he served, he was known for being clean, frugal, and undemanding.
In the twentieth year of Yánxī (延熙),
he accompanied Grand General Jiāng Wéi (姜維) on a military expedition to Mángshuǐ (芒水).
Xì (戲) had always secretly resented Wéi (維).
When he drank and joked,
he often spoke in an arrogant and mocking tone.
Wéi (維) was outwardly generous but inwardly resentful,
and could not tolerate this.
When the army returned,
the officials, following Wéi's (維) implicit command, impeached Xì (戲),
and he was dismissed to become a commoner.
He later died in the fourth year of Jǐngyào (景耀).
Although Xì's (戲) nature was simple, lazy, and concise,
he never flattered others with sweet words,
nor did he excessively engage with people.
When writing official documents or pointing out matters,
he rarely filled a whole sheet of paper.
However, he was deeply loyal to old acquaintances
and truly sincere and benevolent.
He was intimately close with Hán Yǎn (韓儼) and Lí Tāo (黎韜) from Bāxī (巴西) since childhood.
Later, Yǎn (儼) became disabled by a chronic illness,
and Tāo (韜) was abandoned due to his misconduct.
Xì (戲) managed their affairs and provided relief,
his kindness and affection remaining as before.
Moreover, contemporaries regarded Qiáo Zhōu (譙周) as lacking talent for the times,
and few paid him respect;
only Xì (戲) held him in high esteem,
once remarking,
"We of a later generation
will ultimately not surpass this elder."
Those with discernment valued Xì (戲) for this.
Zhāng Biǎo (張表) possessed a dignified and impressive demeanor.
Initially, his rank and position were equal to Xì's (戲),
but he later rose to be a Secretariat Director
and Grand General of the Rear Army in charge of Láijiàng (庲降),
dying before Xì (戲).
Qí (祁) and Tài (汰) both died young.
In the fourth year of Yánxī (延熙), Xì (戲) composed the "Eulogies for the Aiding Ministers of Jìhàn" (季漢輔臣贊).
Many of those he praised
are now recorded in the "Records of Shu" (蜀書),
which is why they are noted to the left.
Those who died after this
were not granted posthumous titles,
hence there are some who ought to be mentioned but are not included in this chapter.
As for those praised by Xì (戲) for whom no biography is now written,
I have appended a brief explanation of their origins and outcomes below their eulogies,
so that one can roughly understand their situation.
In ancient times, King Wén (文王) sang of virtue,
and King Wǔ (武王) sang of prosperity.
A destined ruler
establishes himself and practices the Dao,
not only for his own time,
but also by laying the foundation and establishing the lineage,
shining upon future generations.
Since the end of our Central Hàn (漢) dynasty,
the royal authority was abandoned,
heroes rose in multitudes,
wars raged endlessly,
and the people suffered greatly.
Thereupon, the Lord of the Age was moved by this and pondered it.
Beginning in Yān (燕) and Dài (代), his benevolent reputation spread widely;
proceeding through Qí (齊) and Lǔ (魯), his heroic influence flowed afar;
establishing his enterprise in Jīng (荊) and Yǐng (郢), ministers and subjects gave him their hearts;
turning to assist Wú (吳) and Yuè (越), both wise and foolish relied on his influence;
displaying his might in Bā (巴) and Shǔ (蜀), tremors were felt across ten thousand li;
marching his army into Yōng (庸) and Hàn (漢), the primary enemies retreated.
Thus, he was able to inherit the initial auspicious signs of Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖)
and restore the ancestral sacrifices of the Imperial Hàn (漢).
Yet, the treacherous and dangerous were resentful,
and divine retribution had not yet been fully applied,
like the gathered army at Mèngjīn (孟津),
still needing to fight at Míngtiáo (鳴條).
The heavenly bounty had its end,
and suddenly he fell ill.
Although unification was eventually achieved,
and the myriad states converged and allied,
it was due to the eminent talents of the time who supported and uplifted him,
and the embracing power of his enlightened virtue.
Indeed, it was a magnificent sight to behold.
So I shall now describe his glorious deeds,
to be heard by later generations.
The eulogy reads:
The Emperor's descendant,
flourished in all directions.
Separated from Zhōngshān (中山),
the divine essence gathered.
Born at the opportune time,
he rose heroically like a soaring dragon.
Starting in Yān (燕) and Dài (代),
he pacified and ruled Jīng (荊).
Wú (吳) and Yuè (越) relied upon him,
seeking alliance at his prestige.
He held Bā (巴) and straddled Shǔ (蜀),
bringing Yōng (庸) and Hàn (漢) under his sway.
Heaven and Earth were restored to order,
the ancestral sacrifices were peaceful.
Following the foundation and treading the path,
he spread virtue and a fragrant name.
Huáxià (華夏) yearned for his excellence,
like the sound of the Western Earl.
Opening blessings for future generations,
his reign brought prosperity for ages.
Eulogy for Emperor Zhāoliè (昭烈皇帝).
Loyal, martial, brave, and noble,
he offered strategies on the riverbank.
Clinging to Wú (吳) and uniting with Shǔ (蜀),
he held the true authority for our generation.
Entrusted by the regent,
he rectified military and civil affairs.
He expounded virtuous teachings,
governed the people, and transformed customs.
Wise and foolish vied with each other,
all forgetting their own lives.
He brought peace to the realm,
and the four barbarians were appeased.
Repeatedly facing the enemy,
he truly displayed his might.
He deeply studied the great states,
regretting that they were not yet pacified.
Eulogy for Chancellor Zhūgě (諸葛).
The Minister of Works, pure and lofty,
was consulted and praised.
He recognized and loved humanity,
his words resounded like Kǒngzǐ (孔子).
Eulogy for Minister Sī Tú (司徒) Xǔ (許).
Guān (關) and Zhāng (張) were valiant and fierce,
coming forth to save the world.
They supported and assisted their lord,
brave and fierce like tigers.
They shielded his left and right,
moving swiftly like lightning.
They delivered him from hardship,
assisting their lord in his grand enterprise.
Their achievements matched Hán (韓) and Gěng (耿),
their reputations equally virtuous.
Yet, their interactions lacked courtesy,
leading to treachery.
Alas for their rashness,
they sacrificed their lives for the state.
Eulogy for Guān Yúncháng (關雲長) and Zhāng Yìdé (張益德).
The General of Agile Cavalry rose up,
forming alliances.
He initiated affairs in Sān Qín (三秦),
and secured Hé (河) and Tóng (潼).
His plans at court,
were sometimes different, sometimes similar.
The enemy took advantage of the weakness,
his family was broken and his army destroyed.
He deviated from the Dao and turned against virtue,
attaching himself to the phoenix and climbing the dragon.
Eulogy for Mǎ Mèngqǐ (馬孟起).
The Marquis of Yì (翼侯) had excellent strategies,
foreseeing the rise and fall of the world.
He pledged himself to his lord,
giving counsel and advice.
He quickly pondered calculations,
observing events and knowing opportunities.
Eulogy for Fǎ Xiàozhí (法孝直).
The Military Advisor was splendid,
his refined spirit shining brightly.
He dedicated his life to his enlightened lord,
his loyal feelings coming from his heart.
This paragon of righteousness,
sacrificed his life to repay kindness.
Eulogy for Páng Shìyuán (龐士元).
The General was robust,
overcoming peaks and ascending difficulties.
He achieved merits and accomplishments,
a pillar of his time.
Eulogy for Huáng Hànshēng (黃漢升).
The Army Commander was pure and upright,
always firm and constant.
He was in charge of just words,
the people thought of his principles.
Eulogy for Dǒng Yòuzǎi (董幼宰).
Ānyuǎn’s resolve was strong;
he was truly excellent and glorious.
He disregarded wealth and was resolute and robust,
never bewildered when facing difficulties.
He commanded the few to control the many,
securing his enterprise in distant lands.
A eulogy for Dèng Kǒngshān. Kǒngshān’s given name was Fāng,
and he was a man from Nánjùn.
He followed the Former Lord into Shǔ as an official from Jīngzhōu.
After Shǔ was settled,
he became the Grand Administrator of Jiànwéi Commandery’s Dependency,
and consequently, the name of the commandery was changed
to Zhūtí, where he served as Grand Administrator.
He was then selected as General Who Pacifies the Distant (Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn) and Grand Superintendent of Láijiàng Commandery (Láijiàng Dūdū),
residing in Nánchāng County.
He died in the second year of Zhāngwǔ (222 CE).
His deeds are lost,
hence no biography is written for him.
Yángwēi was talented and capable,
sighing over literary and martial arts.
When in office, he managed his duties,
speaking cheerfully and persuasively.
He planned to accumulate and distribute wealth,
possessing both righteousness and wisdom.
A eulogy for Fèi Bīnbó. Bīnbó’s given name was Guàn,
and he was a man from Méng, Jiāngxià.
Liú Zhāng’s mother
was Guàn’s paternal aunt (zúgū).
Zhāng also gave his daughter in marriage to Guàn.
In the eighteenth year of Jiàn’ān (213 CE), Guàn joined Lǐ Yán’s army,
resisting the Former Lord at Miánzhú.
He surrendered along with Yán.
After the Former Lord settled Yìzhōu,
he was appointed Vice-General (Bì Jiāngjūn),
later becoming Grand Administrator of Bājùn and Superintendent of Jiāngzhōu.
In the first year of Jiànxīng (223 CE), he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng,
and additionally appointed General Who Spreads Awe (Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn).
Guàn was skilled in making connections.
The Protector-General (Dūhù) Lǐ Yán was naturally proud and arrogant.
The Military Protector (Hùjūn) Fǔ Kuāng and others were similar to Yán in age and rank,
but Yán did not associate closely with them.
Guàn was more than twenty years younger than Yán,
yet he conversed and associated with Yán as if they were peers, it is said.
He died at the age of thirty-seven.
His deeds are lost,
hence no biography is written for him.
Túnqí’s lord was steadfast,
firm in his principles and unwavering.
Having accepted his initial appointment,
he devoted his heart to the world’s regulations.
The military provisions he relied upon
were clarified and augmented.
A eulogy for Wáng Wényí.
The Minister (Shàngshū) was pure and upright,
regulating his conduct and disciplining himself.
