He upheld his resolve and cherished righteousness,
relishing the study of classics and literature.
Leaning on his noble character,
he desired to emulate the ancients.
A eulogy for Liú Zǐchū.
Ānhàn was serene and composed,
whether at weddings or as a guest.
He was respected at the time,
and was called a dutiful minister.
A eulogy for Mí Zǐzhòng.
The Privy Treasurer (Shàofǔ) was meticulous and cautious,
the Grand Herald (Hónglú) was discerning and true.
The Remonstrance Official (Jiànyì) acted discreetly,
a Confucian scholar of celestial patterns.
They proclaimed the great transformation,
some as leaders, some as a forest.
A eulogy for Wáng Yuántài, Hé Yànyīng, Dù Fǔguó, Zhōu Zhòngzhí. Wáng Yuántài’s given name was Móu,
and he was a man from Hànjiā.
He had a dignified demeanor and upright conduct.
During Liú Zhāng’s time,
he served as Grand Administrator of Bājùn,
then returned to serve as Administrator of the Provincial Government (Zhìzhōng Cóngshì).
When the Former Lord settled Yìzhōu
and assumed the governorship,
he appointed him as Chief Clerk (Biéjià).
When the Former Lord became King of Hànzhōng,
he employed seasoned scholars from Jīngchǔ: Lài Gōng from Línglíng as Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng),
Huáng Zhù from Nányáng as Grand Master of Palace Leisure (Guānglùxūn),
and Móu as Privy Treasurer (Shàofǔ).
In the early Jiànxīng period,
he was granted the title Marquis Within the Pass (Guānnèi Hóu).
Later, he succeeded Lài Gōng as Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
Gōng, Zhù, and Móu all lost their deeds,
hence no biographies are written for them.
Gōng’s son, Kǎ,
served as Chief Clerk of the Western Bureau (Xīcáo Lìngshǐ) to the Chancellor,
and accompanied Zhūgé Liàng to Hànzhōng.
He died young,
and Liàng deeply regretted it.
He wrote to Zhāng Yì and Jiǎng Wǎn, Chief Clerks and Military Advisors in the Left-Behind Office, saying:
“The Clerk Lài Kǎ is lost,
and the Attendant Officer Yáng Yǒng is dead.
This is a great loss and gain for the court.”
Yǒng was also a man from Jīngzhōu.
Later, the Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn) Jiǎng Wǎn asked Zhāng Xiū:
“Among the elders of Hànjiā, there was Wáng Yuántài.
Who succeeds him now?”
Xiū replied:
“As for Yuántài,
there is no successor in the province,
let alone in my humble commandery!”
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
The Chariot and Cavalry General was vigorous,
indeed, he possessed universal love.
He controlled the strong with the weak,
not falling into danger or ruin.
A eulogy for Wú Zǐyuǎn. Zǐyuǎn’s given name was Yī,
and he was a man from Chénliú.
He followed Liú Yān into Shǔ.
During Liú Zhāng’s time,
he served as General of the Household (Zhōnglángjiāng),
leading troops to resist the Former Lord at Fú,
but later surrendered.
After the Former Lord settled Yìzhōu,
he appointed Yī as Protector-General, General Who Attacks Rebels (Hùjūn Tǎonì Jiāngjūn),
and took Yī’s sister as his Lady (fūrén).
In the first year of Zhāngwǔ (221 CE),
he became Superintendent of Guānzhōng.
In the eighth year of Jiànxīng (230 CE),
he and Wèi Yán entered the Nán’ān border,
defeating the Wèi general Fèi Yáo.
He was transferred to a marquisate (tínghóu),
advanced to Marquis of Gāoyáng Township,
and promoted to General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn).
In the twelfth year (234 CE),
after Chancellor Zhūgé Liàng died,
Yī was appointed Superintendent of Hànzhōng,
General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn),
granted imperial credentials (jiǎjié),
concurrently Governor of Yōngzhōu (Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ),
and advanced to Marquis of Jìyáng.
He died in the fifteenth year (237 CE).
His deeds are lost,
hence no biography is written for him.
Yī’s paternal younger cousin (zúdì) Bān,
courtesy name Yuánxióng,
was the son of Wú Kuāng, an official under Grand General Hé Jìn.
He was known for his heroism and chivalry,
and his official rank was often similar to Yī’s.
During the Former Lord’s time,
he served as Commander of the Guards (Lǐngjūn).
In the Latter Lord’s reign,
he was gradually promoted to General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojí Jiāngjūn),
granted imperial credentials (jiǎjié),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Miánzhú.
The magistrate of Ānhàn in the south,
he valiantly attacked his old homeland.
He eradicated the corrupt and unclean,
maintaining justice through punishment.
He widely resettled the Mán and Pú people,
making the state’s resources ever stronger.
A eulogy for Lǐ Dé’áng.
He assisted Hàn with great intelligence,
being both sagacious and benevolent.
From his words, one could infer distant thoughts;
his pointed questions elicited immediate replies.
He praised the excellence of his time,
harmonizing with the world’s endeavors.
A eulogy for Zhāng Jūnsì.
The General Who Guards the North (Zhènběi Jiāngjūn) was keen-witted;
his strategies were well-devised.
He guided and purified,
accomplishing tasks to completion.
He was entrusted with the eastern flank,
but his final fate was inauspicious.
Grieving for his original aspirations,
he was banished to a distant frontier.
A eulogy for Huáng Gōnghéng.
The General of Agile Cavalry (Yuèqí Jiāngjūn) was truly loyal,
striving to be respectful.
He dedicated himself to internal and external affairs,
remembering public duty and forgetting personal interests.
A eulogy for Yáng Jìxiū.
The General Who Attacks the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn) was dignified and steady;
the General Who Attacks the West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn) was loyal and resolute.
He commanded and selected soldiers,
displaying the valor of a fierce general.
A eulogy for Zhào Zǐlóng and Chén Shúzhì. Shúzhì’s given name was Dào,
and he was a man from Rǔnán.
He followed the Former Lord from Yùzhōu,
his reputation and rank always second to Zhào Yún.
Both were praised for their loyalty and courage.
In the early Jiànxīng period,
his highest office was Superintendent of Yǒng’ān (Yǒng’ān Dūdū) and General Who Attacks the West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn),
and he was enfeoffed as a Marquis (tínghóu).
Zhèn-Nán was rough and strong,
Jiān-Jūn was still earnest,
both participated in military duties,
their responsibilities extending from the borders.
In praise of Yuán-Bì Liú Nán and Fǔ Yuán-Bì, whose given name was Kuāng,
was a man from Xiāngyáng.
He followed the Former Lord into Shǔ.
After Yìzhōu was settled,
he became the Administrator of Bājùn.
During the Jiànxīng era,
he was transferred to Zhèn-Nán,
becoming Right General,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhōngxiāng.
Liú Nán and whose given name was Yōng,
was a man from Yìyáng.
He followed the Former Lord into Shǔ.
After Yìzhōu was settled,
he became the Administrator of Jiāngyáng.
During the Jiànxīng era,
he gradually rose to Jiān-Jūn Rear General,
was granted the title Marquis of Guānnèi,
and died.
His son, Shì, inherited.
His younger son, Wǔ,
was cultured,
and was as famous as Fán Jiàn,
his official post also reaching Shàngshū.
Sī-Nóng's nature was talented,
his words were clear and proper,
his rhetoric was elegant and refined,
splendidly luminous.
In praise of Qín Zǐ-Chì:
Zhèng-Fāng received his dying wishes,
heard of the later plans,
neither presented nor gathered opinions,
creating this unusual doctrine,
being expelled at the time,
and losing his post by his actions.
In praise of Lǐ Zhèng-Fāng:
Wén-Cháng was bold and rough,
receiving orders in times of difficulty,
repelling enemies and defending externally,
protecting the nation's borders.
Inharmonious and uncooperative,
forgetting propriety and speaking disorder,
quickly ending what began with care,
this was truly his nature.
In praise of Wèi Wén-Cháng:
Wēi-Gōng was narrow-minded and irritable,
differing from the multitude;
at leisure, he would follow reason,
when pressed, he would cause harm,
abandoning conformity and entering calamity,
as the Great Changes say.
In praise of Yáng Wēi-Gōng:
Jì-Cháng was good and honest,
Wén-Jīng was diligent and orderly,
Shì-Yuán spoke with foresight,
Chǔ-Rén was known for his strategies,
Kǒng-Xiū and Wén-Xiáng,
some talented, some virtuous,
all expressing their aspirations,
like the orchids of Chǔ.
In praise of Mǎ Jì-Cháng, Wèi Wén-Jīng, Hán Shì-Yuán, Zhāng Chǔ-Rén, Yīn Kǒng-Lín, Xí Wén-Xiáng. Wén-Jīng and Shì-Yuán,
both lost their names, actions, and administrative divisions.
Chǔ-Rén's original name was Cún,
and he was a man from Nányáng.
He followed the Former Lord into Shǔ as an assistant from Jīngzhōu.
When he arrived in Luò from the south,
he was appointed Administrator of Guǎnghàn.
Cún had always disliked Páng Tǒng.
When Tǒng died from an arrow,
the Former Lord spoke words of praise and lament.
Cún said:
"Although Tǒng died loyal, it is regrettable,
yet he violated the meaning of the Great Propriety."
The Former Lord angrily said:
"Tǒng sacrificed himself for benevolence,
is this considered wrong?"
He dismissed Cún from office.
Soon after,
Cún died of illness.
His deeds are lost,
hence no biography is made for him.
Kǒng-Xiū's given name was Guān,
he was the Registrar and Chief Clerk of Jīngzhōu,
mentioned in the biography of the Former Lord.
His administrative division is lost.
Wén-Xiáng's given name was Zhēn,
and he was a man from Xiāngyáng.
He followed the Former Lord into Shǔ,
serving as Magistrate of Luò and Pí,
(and) Administrator of Guǎnghàn.
His deeds are lost.
His son, Zhōng,
rose to the post of Shàngshū Láng.
Guó-Shān's noble manner,
Yǒng-Nán's deep contemplation;
Shèng-Héng and Chéng-Bó,
some concealing words, some speaking timely;
Sūn-Dé's keen sharpness,
Wěi-Nán's unwavering constancy;
Dé-Xù and Yì-Qiáng,
with strong aspirations and firm spirit.
Numerous and cultivating aspirations,
the fragrance of Shǔ.
In praise of Wáng Guó-Shān, Lǐ Yǒng-Nán, Mǎ Shèng-Héng, Mǎ Chéng-Bó, Lǐ Sūn-Dé, Lǐ Wěi-Nán,
Gōng Dé-Xù, Wáng Yì-Qiáng. Guó-Shān's given name was Fǔ,
a man from Qī, Guǎnghàn.
He enjoyed discussing people's words.
During Liú Zhāng's time,
he was a provincial clerk.
After the Former Lord settled Shǔ,
he became Magistrate of Miánzhú,
then returned as an advisor to Jīngzhōu.
He followed the Former Lord in the campaign against Wú,
and the army was defeated at Zǐguī,
where he was killed.
His son, Yòu,
had his father's style,
and rose to Shàngshū Yòuxuǎnláng.
Yǒng-Nán's given name was Shào,
a man from Qī, Guǎnghàn.
After the Former Lord settled Shǔ,
he was a provincial clerk and departmental assistant.
In the first year of Jiànxīng,
Chancellor Liàng appointed him as Western Clerk.
When Liàng campaigned in the south,
he left Shào as Chief Assistant,
and he died that year.
Xiū-Yuán lightly regarded the enemy,
harming himself and causing disaster,
Wén-Jìn exerted himself,
and suffered the same downfall,
trouble arising from one person,
leading to widespread disaster.
In praise of Féng Xiū-Yuán, Zhāng Wén-Jìn. Xiū-Yuán's given name was Xí,
a man from Nánjùn.
He followed the Former Lord into Shǔ.
When the Former Lord campaigned against Wú in the east,
Xí was the Commander of the Army,
leading all the armies,
and suffered a great defeat at Xiāotíng.
Wén-Jìn's given name was Nán,
also followed the Former Lord into Shǔ from Jīngzhōu,
commanded troops following the Former Lord in the campaign against Wú,
and died along with Xí.
At that time, there was also Fù Róng from Yìyáng.
When the Former Lord's army retreated,
he covered the rear and resisted the enemy.
All his soldiers died,
and a Wú general told Róng to surrender.
Róng cursed, saying:
"Wú dogs!
How can a Hàn general surrender?"
He then fought to the death.
His son, Qiān, was appointed Left Central Cavalier,
later becoming Commander of Guānzhōng.
In the sixth year of Jǐngyào,
he again received orders in a time of crisis.
Commentators praised the father and son for their loyalty and righteousness through generations.
Jiāngyáng was firm and resolute,
establishing his integrity before an enlightened ruler.
His army met with bandits,
but he would not bend his will.
A lone man, a single soldier,
he died in battle.
A eulogy for Chéng Jìrán. Jìrán's given name was Jī.
He was from Làngzhōng, Bāxī.
During Liú Zhāng's time, he was the Magistrate of Hànchāng.
The county had the Cóng people,
whose tribes were fierce and brave.
Emperor Gāozǔ had formerly used them to pacify Guānzhōng.
Páng Xī, the Administrator of Bāxī, considering the world to be in chaos,
thought the commandery needed military protection,
and so he recruited troops and retainers.
Someone slandered him to Zhāng,
saying Xī intended to rebel.
Zhāng secretly doubted this.
When Xī heard of it,
he was very afraid,
and planned to defend himself.
He sent Jī's son, Yù, to convey his message,
asking for troops to help himself.
Jī replied,
"The commandery's recruitment of retainers
was originally not for rebellion.
Although there might be suspicion,
the crucial thing is to be utterly sincere.
If, out of fear,
one develops rebellious intentions,
that is not what Jī has heard of."
He also instructed Yù, saying,
"I have received the province's grace
and should dedicate myself to the provincial governor.
As a commandery official,
you should exert yourself for the Administrator.
Do not have different intentions on my account."
Xī sent someone to tell Jī,
"Your son is in the commandery,
and if he does not obey the Administrator,
your family will suffer disaster!"
Jī said,
"Formerly, when Yuè Yáng was a general,
he drank his son's soup.
It was not that father and son had no affection,
but that the great principle required it.
Even if I were to eat my son's soup again today,
I would surely drink it."
Xī knew that Jī would certainly not act for him,
so he profusely apologized to Zhāng, thereby avoiding trouble.
When Zhāng heard of this,
he promoted Jī to Administrator of Jiāngyáng.
Later, the Former Sovereign became the Governor of Yìzhōu
and appointed him as Attending Official of Libations.
Later, he followed the Former Sovereign on the campaign against Wú.
When the great army suffered a crushing defeat,
he returned upstream along the river.
Someone told him,
"The pursuers have already arrived.
Untie your boat and leave quickly,
then you can escape."
Jī said,
"While in the army, I have never fled from an enemy,
much less when accompanying the Son of Heaven and facing danger!"
The pursuers then reached Jī's boat.
Jī personally wielded a halberd and fought,
and some enemy boats capsized.
A great many more arrived
and attacked him together.
He then died.
Gōnghóng was born later,
outstanding and remarkably brilliant.
His life was cut short at twenty.
Alas, his talents remained unshown.
A eulogy for Chéng Gōnghóng. Gōnghóng's
given name was Qí.
He was Jìrán's son.
In ancient times, fleeing ministers,
if they had been forced by rites,
their resentment arose from the official,
disregarding great virtue.
Without correction or rescue,
they doubled down on their flight,
cutting themselves off from others,
becoming a laughingstock for two states.
A eulogy for Mí Fāng, Shì Rén, Hǎo Pǔ, Pān Jùn.
Mí Fāng, courtesy name Zǐfāng,
was from Dōnghǎi.
He was the Administrator of Nánjùn.
Shì Rén, courtesy name Jūnyì,
was from Guǎngyáng.
He was a general
stationed in Gōng'ān,
subordinate to Guān Yǔ.
He had a rift with Yǔ
and defected, welcoming Sūn Quán.
Hǎo Pǔ, courtesy name Zǐtài,
was from Yìyáng.
When the Former Sovereign entered Shǔ from Jīngzhōu,
he appointed Pǔ as Administrator of Línglíng.
He was deceived by the Wú general Lǚ Méng
and opened the city gates to surrender to Méng.
Pān Jùn, courtesy name Chéngmíng,
was from Wǔlíng.
When the Former Sovereign entered Shǔ,
he appointed him as Administrator of Jīngzhōu,
entrusting him with provincial affairs.
He also was not on good terms with Guān Yǔ.
When Sūn Quán attacked Yǔ,
he then entered Wú.
Pǔ rose to Minister of the Court of Justice,
Jùn to Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
and was enfeoffed as a marquis.
A critique says: Dèng Zhī was steadfast and clear-minded,
forgetting his family in office.
Zhāng Yì countered Jiāng Wéi's sharpness.
Zōng Yù resisted Sūn Quán's severity.
All are worthy of praise.
Yáng Xì's deliberations
aimed at being unique.
However, he was lacking in wisdom and foresight,
and thus almost suffered from the world's difficulties.
Biography of Sūn, the Subduer of Savages and Punisher of Rebels, Volume One
Sūn Jiān, courtesy name Wéntái,
was from Fùchūn, Wújùn.
He was a descendant of Sūn Wǔ.
In his youth, he was a county official.
At seventeen,
he and his father were traveling by boat to Qiántáng.
They happened to encounter pirates led by Hú Yù and others, who had come ashore from Páolǐ to plunder merchants' goods,
and were dividing them on the bank.
All travelers stopped,
their boats daring not to proceed.
Jiān said to his father,
"These bandits can be attacked.
Please let me suppress them."
His father said,
"This is not something you can plan."
Jiān walked ashore, wielding a knife,
and gestured east and west with his hands,
as if deploying troops to encircle the bandits.
The bandits, seeing this from afar,
thought it was government troops capturing them.
They immediately abandoned their goods and scattered.
Jiān pursued,
cut off one head, and returned;
his father was greatly surprised.
Because of this, he became renowned,
and the prefecture summoned him to be appointed Acting Commandant.
At that time, the demon bandit Xǔ Chāng of Kuàijī rose up in Gōuzhāng,
calling himself the Yangming Emperor.
He and his son Zhào incited various counties,
their followers numbering in the tens of thousands.
Jiān, as the Commandery Chief Clerk, recruited brave and elite soldiers,
obtaining over a thousand men,
and jointly attacked and defeated them with the province and commandery.
That year was
the first year of Xīpíng.
The Inspector Zāng Mín reported his meritorious service,
and an imperial edict appointed Jiān as Salt Creek Chief.
A few years later, he was transferred to Xūyí Chief,
and then again to Xiàpī Chief.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng,
the Yellow Turban bandit leader Zhāng Jiǎo rose up in Wèijùn.
Claiming to possess divine powers,
he sent eight envoys to teach the Way throughout the world,
while secretly linking up with each other,
calling themselves "Yellow Heaven Great Peace."
On the *jiǎzǐ* day of the third month,
thirty-six (myriads) [sides] launched simultaneously,
and the whole empire responded,
burning down commanderies and counties,
and killing chief officials.
The Hàn court dispatched the General of Cavalry and Chariots, Huángfǔ Sōng, and the Colonel, Zhū Jùn, to lead troops and attack them.
Jùn memorialized to request Jiān as his Assistant Military Sima.
Young men from his hometown who were with him in Xiàpī all wished to follow.
Jiān also recruited merchants and elite soldiers from Huái and Sì,
totaling about a thousand men,
and joined forces with Jùn to fight fiercely,
sweeping away all opposition.
The bandits of Rǔ and Yǐng were cornered and pressed,
and fled to defend Wǎnchéng.
Jiān personally took charge of one section,
climbed the city wall, and was the first to enter.
His troops then swarmed after him like ants,
and they utterly defeated the bandits.
Jùn reported the situation in detail to the emperor,
and Jiān was appointed Separate Division Sima.
Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì rebelled in Liángzhōu.
Colonel Dǒng Zhuó was ordered to suppress them but achieved nothing.
In the third year of Chúnpíng [186 CE],
Sīkōng Zhāng Wēn was sent to act as Chējì Jiāngjūn,
to suppress Zhāng and the others in the west.
Wēn memorialized the throne, requesting Sūn Jiān to be his参軍事 (cānjūnshì),
and garrison at Cháng'ān.
Wēn summoned Dǒng Zhuó by imperial edict.
Zhuó took a long time to arrive before Wēn.
Wēn reprimanded Zhuó,
but Zhuó's replies were defiant.
Jiān was present at the time.
He leaned forward and whispered to Wēn, saying:
“Dǒng Zhuó, fearing no punishment, is arrogant and speaks loudly.
He should be executed according to military law
for arriving late when summoned.”
Wēn replied:
“Dǒng Zhuó has always been known for his prestige between Lǒng [Xī] and Shǔ.
If we kill him today,
we will have no one to rely on for the western campaign.”
Jiān said:
“Your Excellency personally leads the imperial army,
whose might shakes the world.
Why rely on Dǒng Zhuó?
Judging by Dǒng Zhuó’s words,
he doesn't even acknowledge Your Excellency,
showing disrespect to his superiors.
This is his first crime.
Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì have been rampant for years,
and should be suppressed promptly.
Yet Dǒng Zhuó says it is not yet advisable,
disheartening the army and creating doubt among the troops.
This is his second crime.
Dǒng Zhuó was given an important task but achieved nothing,
and when summoned, he delayed.
Yet he acts haughtily and considers himself superior.
This is his third crime.
Among famous generals of old,
who wielded the battle-axe and commanded armies,
none failed to execute offenders to assert their authority.
Thus, Ráng Jū executed Zhuāng Jiǎ,
and Wèi Jiàng slew Yáng Gān.
Now, if Your Excellency shows leniency to Dǒng Zhuó,
and does not punish him immediately,
it will diminish your authority and disciplinary power.
This is precisely what will happen.”
Wēn could not bring himself to act,
and said:
“Please return for now.
Dǒng Zhuó will suspect something.”
Jiān then rose and left.
Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì heard that a large army was approaching,
their followers scattered,
and they all begged for surrender.
When the army returned,
some discussed that since the army had not yet engaged the enemy,
it was not appropriate to bestow merits and rewards.
However, upon hearing that Jiān had enumerated Dǒng Zhuó's three crimes
and urged Wēn to execute him,
all sighed in admiration.
Jiān was appointed Yìláng.
At this time, a bandit named Ōu Xīng in Chángshā declared himself a general,
with over ten thousand men,
attacking and besieging cities and towns.
Jiān was then appointed Grand Administrator of Chángshā.
Upon arriving in the commandery, he personally led his officers and soldiers,
implementing strategies.
Within ten days or a month,
he defeated Ōu Xīng and his followers.
Zhōu Cháo and Guō Shí also led their followers in rebellion in Líng and Guì,
acting in concert with Ōu Xīng.
Jiān then crossed the borders to seek and suppress them,
and all three commanderies were pacified.
The Hàn court, acknowledging his past and present achievements,
enfeoffed Jiān as Wūchéng Hóu.
When Emperor Líng died,
Dǒng Zhuó usurped control of the court,
acting arbitrarily in the capital.
All the provincial and commandery administrations raised righteous armies,
intending to suppress Dǒng Zhuó.
Jiān also raised an army.
Wáng Ruì, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, had always treated Jiān disrespectfully,
so Jiān killed him on his way.
By the time he reached Nányáng,
his army numbered several tens of thousands.
Zhāng Zī, the Grand Administrator of Nányáng, heard of the army's arrival,
but remained calm and unconcerned.
Jiān offered Zī cattle and wine as a courtesy.
Zī reciprocated by visiting Jiān the next day.
During the drinking party,
the Chángshā Registrar entered and reported to Jiān:
“We previously notified Nányáng,
but the roads were not maintained,
and military provisions were not prepared.
I request to arrest the Registrar [of Nányáng] and interrogate him about his intentions.”
Zī, greatly alarmed, tried to leave,
but was surrounded by soldiers and could not exit.
After a short while,
the Registrar re-entered and reported to Jiān:
“The Grand Administrator of Nányáng delayed the righteous army,
preventing the swift suppression of the bandits.
I request to arrest him and proceed according to military law.”
Thereupon, Zī was dragged to the army gate and executed.
The commandery was struck with terror,
and all requests were granted.
Earlier, he had arrived at Lǔyáng [and]
met Yuán Shù.
Shù memorialized the throne to appoint Jiān as acting Pòlǔ Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Jiān then trained his troops in Lǔyáng city.
When it was time to advance and suppress Dǒng Zhuó,
he sent his Chief Clerk Gōngqiú Chēng with troops to return to the province to oversee and urge the supply of military provisions.
He set up tents and canopies outside the east gate of the city,
held a farewell ceremony for Chēng,
and all his officials attended.
Dǒng Zhuó sent tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry to intercept Jiān,
with several tens of light cavalry arriving first.
Jiān was still drinking and conversing cheerfully,
but ordered his troops to arrange their formations
and not to make any rash moves.
Later, more cavalry arrived.
Jiān slowly adjourned the gathering,
and led his men into the city.
He then said to his attendants:
“The reason I didn't immediately rise just now
was that I feared the soldiers would trample each other,
and you gentlemen would not be able to enter.”
Dǒng Zhuó's troops, seeing Jiān's forces so orderly,
did not dare to attack the city,
and so withdrew.
Jiān moved his camp to Liángdōng,
where he was heavily attacked by Dǒng Zhuó's army.
Jiān, with several tens of cavalry, broke through the encirclement and escaped.
Jiān usually wore a red wool turban.
He took off his turban and ordered his trusted general Zǔ Mào to wear it.
Dǒng Zhuó's cavalry fiercely pursued Zǔ Mào,
which allowed Jiān to escape through a side path.
Zǔ Mào, cornered,
dismounted,
placed the turban on a burnt pillar among graves,
and then hid in the grass.
Dǒng Zhuó's cavalry saw it,
surrounded it several layers deep.
When they approached and realized it was a pillar,
they left.
Jiān regrouped his troops
and engaged in battle at Yángrén,
severely defeating Dǒng Zhuó's army,
and beheading its commander Huà Xióng and others.
At this time,
someone slandered Jiān to Yuán Shù.
Shù grew suspicious
and stopped transporting military provisions.
Yángrén was over a hundred *lǐ* from Lǔyáng.
Jiān rode quickly by night to see Shù,
drew on the ground to make calculations,
and said:
“The reason I put my life on the line and disregarded personal safety
is primarily to suppress bandits for the state,
and secondarily to avenge the private grievances of your general's family.
I have no deep-seated enmity with Dǒng Zhuó.
Yet you listen to slanderous words
and now suspect me!”
Shù was abashed
and immediately dispatched military provisions.
Jiān returned to his camp.
Dǒng Zhuó, fearing Jiān's ferocity and bravery,
sent his generals Lǐ Què and others to seek peace and alliance,
proposing that Jiān list his sons and younger brothers who could serve as Inspectors and Grand Administrators,
and promising to memorialize for their appointment.
Jiān said:
“Dǒng Zhuó defies Heaven and is without principle,
overthrowing the imperial house.
If I do not exterminate your three clans
and display your heads to the world,
I will not rest in peace even after death.
How could I possibly form an alliance with you?”
He then advanced his army to Dàgǔ,
ninety *lǐ* from Luòyáng.
Dǒng Zhuó then moved the capital westward into the pass,
and burned Luòyáng.
Jiān then advanced into Luòyáng,
repaired the imperial tombs,
and filled the graves Dǒng Zhuó had dug up.
After completing this,
he led his army back
and stayed at Lǔyáng.
In the third year of Chūpíng [192 CE],
Yuán Shù sent Jiān to campaign in Jīngzhōu,
attacking Liú Biǎo.
Liú Biǎo sent Huáng Zǔ to intercept him between Fán and Dèng.
Jiān defeated him,
pursued him across the Hàn River,
and then besieged Xiāngyáng.
While riding alone on Xiànshān,
he was shot and killed by Huáng Zǔ's soldiers.
His elder brother's son, Sūn Bēn,
led his officers and troops to Yuán Shù.
Shù again memorialized the throne to appoint Sūn Bēn as Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Sūn Jiān had four sons: Cè, Quán, Yì, and Kuāng.
When Sūn Quán eventually assumed the imperial title,
he posthumously honored Sūn Jiān as Emperor Wǔliè.
Sūn Cè's courtesy name was Bófú.
When Sūn Jiān first raised his righteous army,
Sūn Cè moved his mother to Shū,
where he befriended Zhōu Yú.
He gathered scholars and officials,
and people between the Jiāng and Huái Rivers all gravitated towards him.
When Sūn Jiān died,
Sūn Cè returned to Qū'ē to bury him.
Afterwards, he crossed the Jiāng River and resided in Jiāngdū.
Táo Qiān, the Governor of Xúzhōu, deeply feared Sūn Cè.
Sūn Cè's maternal uncle, Wú Jǐng,
was then the Administrator of Dānyáng Commandery.
Sūn Cè therefore took his mother and moved to Qū'ē,
and together with Lǚ Fàn and Sūn Hé, went to join Wú Jǐng.
Through their connections, they managed to recruit several hundred men.
In the first year of Xīngpíng (194 CE),
he followed Yuán Shù.
Yuán Shù thought highly of him,
and returned Sūn Jiān's troops to Sūn Cè.
Grand Tutor Mǎ Rìdī, holding the imperial staff, was pacifying and settling Guāndōng.
While in Shòuchūn, he courteously invited Sūn Cè,
and memorialized to appoint him as Colonel of Huáiyì.
Yuán Shù's top generals, Qiáo Ruì and Zhāng Xūn, all respected him wholeheartedly.
Yuán Shù often sighed and said:
"If I had a son like 'Sun-láng,'
what regret would I have even if I were to die!"
A cavalryman under Sūn Cè committed a crime,
and fled into Yuán Shù's camp,
hiding in the inner stables.
Sūn Cè ordered men to go and execute him there.
After it was done,
he went to Yuán Shù to apologize.
Yuán Shù said:
"Soldiers are prone to rebellion;
we should collectively detest them.
Why apologize?"
From then on, the army respected and feared him even more.
Yuán Shù had initially promised to make Sūn Cè the Administrator of Jiǔjiāng,
but later appointed Chén Jì of Dānyáng instead.
Later, Yuán Shù wished to attack Xúzhōu,
and requested thirty thousand hu of rice from Lù Kāng, the Administrator of Lújiāng.
Lù Kāng did not provide it,
and Yuán Shù was greatly enraged.
Sūn Cè had once visited Lù Kāng,
but Lù Kāng did not receive him,
instead sending his Chief Clerk to meet him.
Sūn Cè had long harbored resentment.
Yuán Shù dispatched Sūn Cè to attack Lù Kāng,
saying:
"Previously, I made a mistake using Chén Jì,
and I always regret that my original intention was not fulfilled.
If you now get Lù Kāng,
Lújiāng will truly be yours."
Sūn Cè attacked Lù Kāng,
captured the commandery,
but Yuán Shù again appointed Lú Kāng's former subordinate Liú Xūn as Administrator.
Sūn Cè became even more disappointed.
Earlier,
Liú Yáo was the Inspector of Yángzhōu;
the provincial capital was formerly Shòuchūn.
Shòuchūn
had already been occupied by Yuán Shù,
so Liú Yáo crossed the Jiāng River and made Qū'ē his seat.
At that time, Wú Jǐng was still in Dānyáng,
and Sūn Cè's cousin Sūn Bēn was also the Commander of Dānyáng.
When Liú Yáo arrived,
he forced them both out.
Wú Jǐng and Sūn Bēn retreated to Líyáng.
Liú Yáo sent Fán Néng and Yú Mí to
encamp at Héngjiāngjīn and Zhāng Yīng to encamp at Dānglìkǒu,
to resist Yuán Shù.
Yuán Shù, on his own authority, appointed his former subordinate Huì Qú of Lángxié as Inspector of Yángzhōu,
and further appointed Wú Jǐng as Colonel Who Supervises the Army.
Wú Jǐng and Sūn Bēn together led troops to attack Zhāng Yīng and others,
but failed for consecutive years.
Sūn Cè then persuaded Yuán Shù,
asking to assist Wú Jǐng and others in pacifying Jiāngdōng.
Yuán Shù memorialized Sūn Cè as Colonel Who Breaks the Ranks,
acting as General Who Destroys Bandits.
He had only a little over a thousand soldiers,
several dozen cavalry horses,
and several hundred retainers who wished to follow him.
By the time they reached Líyáng,
his force numbered five or six thousand.
Sūn Cè's mother had earlier moved from Qū'ē to Líyáng.
Sūn Cè then moved his mother to Fùlíng,
crossed the Jiāng River, and fought his way through.
Wherever he went, he was victorious;
no one dared to stand against his vanguard.
His military discipline was strict and orderly,
and the common people cherished him.
Sūn Cè as a person
had a handsome appearance,
enjoyed laughter and conversation,
was open-minded and receptive to advice,
and was skilled at employing people.
Thus, all the officers and common people who met him
gave their full dedication,
and were willing to die for him.
Liú Yáo abandoned his army and fled.
All the commandery administrators abandoned their cities and fled.
Yán Báihǔ and others among the Wú people, each with more than ten thousand men,
camped in various places.
Wú Jǐng and others wanted to first defeat Yán Báihǔ and his ilk,
and then proceed to Kuàijī.
Sūn Cè said:
"Yán Báihǔ and his ilk are mere bandits,
with no great ambitions.
They are like trapped animals."
He then led his troops across the Zhèjiāng River,
occupied Kuàijī,
sacked Dōngyě,
and then attacked and defeated Yán Báihǔ and his ilk.
He replaced all the chief officials.
Sūn Cè personally took the post of Administrator of Kuàijī.
He again appointed Wú Jǐng as Administrator of Dānyáng,
and Sūn Bēn as Administrator of Yùzhāng.
He divided Yùzhāng to form Lúlíng Commandery,
appointing Sūn Bēn's younger brother Sūn Fǔ as Administrator of Lúlíng.
Zhū Zhì of Dānyáng was made Administrator of Wújùn.
Zhāng Zhāo of Péngchéng, Zhāng Hóng of Guǎnglíng, Qín Sōng, Chén Duān, and others became his strategists.
At that time, Yuán Shù usurped the imperial title.
Sūn Cè wrote a letter condemning him and severed ties.
Cáo Gōng memorialized Sūn Cè as General Who Attacks Rebels,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Wú.
Later, Yuán Shù died.
His Chief Clerk Yáng Hóng and Grand General Zhāng Xūn, among others, were leading their troops to join Sūn Cè.
Liú Xūn, the Administrator of Lújiāng, ambushed them,
captured all of them,
and seized their treasures to take back.
When Sūn Cè heard this,
he feigned friendship and allied with Liú Xūn.
Liú Xūn had newly acquired Yuán Shù's troops.
At that time, more than ten thousand households of the Zōng clan of Shàngliáo in Yùzhāng were in Jiāngdōng.
Sūn Cè persuaded Liú Xūn to attack and seize them.
Once Liú Xūn had departed,
Sūn Cè, with a light force, raided and captured Lújiāng day and night.
Liú Xūn's troops all surrendered.
Liú Xūn, with only a few hundred men under his command, went to surrender to Cáo Gōng.
At this time, Yuán Shào was strong,
and Sūn Cè had annexed Jiāngdōng.
Cáo Gōng's strength was not yet sufficient to contend with him,
and he also wished to pacify him.
He therefore married his younger sister's daughter to Sūn Cè's youngest brother Sūn Kuāng,
and also took Sūn Bēn's daughter for his son Cáo Zhāng.
He also courteously invited Sūn Cè's brothers Sūn Quán and Sūn Yì,
and furthermore ordered Yán Xiàng, the Inspector of Yángzhōu, to recommend Sūn Quán as Màocái (Flourishing Talent).
In the fifth year of Jiàn'ān (200 CE),
Cáo Gōng and Yuán Shào were stalemated at Guāndù.
Sūn Cè secretly intended to attack Xǔ,
welcome the Han Emperor,
secretly prepare his army,
and deploy his generals.
Before he could depart,
he was unfortunately killed by retainers of Xǔ Gòng, the former Administrator of Wújùn.
Earlier,
Sūn Cè had killed Xǔ Gòng.
Xǔ Gòng's young son and retainers had fled and hidden by the Jiāng River.
Sūn Cè went out alone on horseback,
and suddenly encountered the retainers.
The retainers wounded Sūn Cè.
His wounds were severe.
He called Zhāng Zhāo and others and said:
"The Central Plains are in chaos.
With the multitude of Wú and Yuè,
and the strongholds of the Three Jiāngs,
it is enough to observe success or failure.
All of you, take good care of my younger brother!"
He called Sūn Quán and gave him the seal and ribbon of office,
saying:
"In leading the armies of Jiāngdōng,
making swift decisions between two battle lines,
and contending for supremacy with all under Heaven,
you are not as good as I.
But in raising the worthy, appointing the capable,
allowing each to do their utmost,
and thus preserving Jiāngdōng,
I am not as good as you."
He died that night,
at the age of twenty-six.
When Sūn Quán assumed the imperial title,
he posthumously honored Sūn Cè as King Huán of Chángshā,
and enfeoffed his son Sūn Shào as Marquis of Wú.
Later, he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Shàngyú.
When Sūn Shào died,
his son Sūn Fèng succeeded him.
During the time of Sūn Hào,
a rumor spread that Sūn Fèng was to be made emperor,
and he was executed.
A commentary states: Sūn Jiān
was brave, resolute, and unwavering. From humble origins,
he led the campaign against Wēn and killed Zhuó,
and when mountains and passes were blocked,
he displayed the spirit of a loyal and valorous hero.
Sūn Cè was heroic, outstanding, and resourceful,
with a ferocity that surpassed his contemporaries.
He sought out the remarkable and embraced the extraordinary,
with an ambition to dominate all of China.
However, both were impetuous and irritable,
leading to their deaths and defeats.
Moreover, the establishment of the territory in Jiāngdōng
was Sūn Cè's foundation,
yet Sūn Quán's veneration for him was insufficient;
Sūn Cè's son was only granted a marquisate.
This was a deficiency in righteousness.
Biography of the Lord of Wú II
Sūn Quán, courtesy name Zhòngmóu.
When his elder brother, Sūn Cè, had already pacified several commanderies,
Sūn Quán, then fifteen years old,
was appointed Prefect of Yángxiàn.
The commandery nominated him as a filial and incorruptible candidate,
and the province recommended him as an outstanding talent.
He served as Colonel of Righteousness.
The Hàn court, observing Sūn Cè’s distant fulfillment of tribute duties,
dispatched an envoy, Liú Wǎn, to confer imperial honors.
Liú Wǎn said to others:
"I observe that although the Sūn brothers are each talented, brilliant, and perceptive,
their good fortune will not last until the end.
Only the middle brother, the filial and incorruptible one,
has an extraordinary and imposing physique,
with an uncommon bone structure,
displaying the characteristics of great nobility,
and he will also live the longest.
You should take note of this."
In the fourth year of Jiàn'ān
(199 CE), he followed Sūn Cè to campaign against Liú Xūn, the Administrator of Lújiāng.
After Xūn was defeated,
they advanced to attack Huáng Zǔ at Shāxiàn.
In the fifth year
(200 CE), Sūn Cè died,
entrusting affairs to Sūn Quán.
Sūn Quán was still weeping and had not yet ceased.
Sūn Cè's Chief Clerk, Zhāng Zhāo, said to Sūn Quán:
"My lord,
is this a time for weeping?
Moreover, the Duke of Zhōu established laws, but Bóqín did not follow them.
This was not a violation of his father's wishes,
but rather because the times did not permit it.
How much more so now, when villains compete fiercely,
and jackals and wolves fill the roads?
To wish to mourn relatives
and adhere to rituals
is like opening the door to invite bandits.
This cannot be considered benevolence."
Thereupon, he changed Sūn Quán's clothes,
helped him mount his horse,
and sent him out to inspect the army.
At this time, only Kuàijī, Wújùn, Dānyáng, Yùzhāng, and Lúlíng commanderies were secured,
yet the deeply treacherous areas were not yet fully subdued,
and heroes and outstanding men throughout the realm were scattered across provinces and commanderies.
Visiting scholars and sojourners considered their safety and where they would go,
and there was no firm bond between ruler and minister.
Zhāng Zhāo, Zhōu Yú, and others believed Sūn Quán could accomplish great deeds with them,
and thus wholeheartedly served him.
Cáo Gōng memorialized Sūn Quán as General Who Attacks the Barbarians,
Administrator of Kuàijī,
stationed at Wú,
and sent a clerk to the commandery to handle administrative matters.
He treated Zhāng Zhāo with the courtesy due a mentor,
and Zhōu Yú, Chéng Pǔ, Lǚ Fàn, and others became his generals.
He recruited outstanding talents
and sought out famous scholars.
Lǔ Sù and Zhūgě Jǐn, among others, began as his retainers.
He divided his generals into various commands,
to pacify the mountain Yue people
and suppress those who disobeyed.
In the seventh year
(202 CE), Sūn Quán's mother, Lady Wú, died.
In the eighth year
(203 CE), Sūn Quán campaigned west against Huáng Zǔ,
defeating his navy.
Only the city was not yet taken,
and the mountain bandits became active again.
Returning, he passed through Yùzhāng,
and sent Lǚ Fàn to pacify Póyáng,
Chéng Pǔ to attack Lè'ān,
Tài Shǐcí to command Hǎicūn,
and Hán Dāng, Zhōu Tài, Lǚ Méng, and others to serve as prefects and magistrates of key counties.
In the ninth year
(204 CE), Sūn Quán's younger brother Sūn Yì, the Administrator of Dānyáng, was harmed by his attendants.
His cousin Sūn Yú was appointed to replace Sūn Yì.
In the tenth year
(205 CE), Sūn Quán sent Hè Qí to attack Shàngráo,
which was then divided to form Jiànpíng county.
In the twelfth year
(207 CE), he campaigned west against Huáng Zǔ,
capturing his people and returning.
In the spring of the thirteenth year
(208 CE), Sūn Quán again campaigned against Huáng Zǔ.
Huáng Zǔ first sent naval forces to resist the army.
Commander Lǚ Méng broke their vanguard,
while Líng Tǒng, Dǒng Xí, and others attacked with full force,
and thus annihilated his city.
Huáng Zǔ escaped on his own,
but the cavalryman Féng Zé pursued and decapitated him,
capturing tens of thousands of men and women.
That year,
he sent Hè Qí to attack Yī and Shè.
(Yī pronounced yī.
Shè pronounced shè.)
Shè was divided into Shǐxīn, Xīndìng,
Líyáng, and Xiūyáng counties,
and these six counties were established as the Xīndū Commandery.
Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, died.
Lǔ Sù requested to be dispatched to offer condolences to Liú Biǎo's two sons,
and also to observe the developing situation.
Before Lǔ Sù arrived,
Cáo Gōng had already approached the border,
and Liú Biǎo's son, Liú Cóng, surrendered with his entire host.
Liú Bèi intended to cross the river south.
Lǔ Sù met him,
conveying Sūn Quán's intentions,
and explaining the likelihood of success or failure.
Liú Bèi advanced to Xiàkǒu,
and sent Zhūgě Liàng to meet Sūn Quán.
Sūn Quán dispatched Zhōu Yú, Chéng Pǔ, and others to proceed.
At this time, Cáo Gōng had newly acquired Liú Biǎo's forces,
and his military strength was extremely formidable.
All the advisors were intimidated by the prevailing atmosphere
and mostly urged Sūn Quán to welcome him.
Only Zhōu Yú and Lǔ Sù insisted on resistance,
and their intention aligned with Sūn Quán's.
Zhōu Yú and Chéng Pǔ were appointed Left and Right Commanders respectively,
each leading ten thousand men.
They advanced together with Liú Bèi,
met Cáo Gōng at Chìbì,
and greatly defeated his army.
Cáo Gōng burned his remaining ships and retreated.
His soldiers suffered from hunger and disease,
and more than half died.
Liú Bèi, Zhōu Yú, and others pursued them to Nánjùn.
Cáo Gōng then returned north,
leaving Cáo Rén and Xú Huǎng at Jiānglíng,
and ordering Yuè Jìn to guard Xiāngyáng.
At that time, Gān Níng was at Yílíng
and was surrounded by Cáo Rén's faction.
Following Lǚ Méng's plan,
Líng Tǒng was left to resist Cáo Rén,
and half of the forces were sent to rescue Gān Níng.
The army returned victorious.
Sūn Quán personally led his forces to besiege Héféi,
and sent Zhāng Zhāo to attack Dāngtú in Jiǔjiāng.
Zhāng Zhāo's troops were unsuccessful,
and Sūn Quán attacked the city for over a month without taking it.
Cáo Gōng returned from Jīngzhōu
and sent Zhāng Xǐ to lead cavalry to Héféi.
Before he arrived,
Sūn Quán retreated.
In the fourteenth year
(209 CE), Zhōu Yú and Cáo Rén held out against each other for over a year,
with many killed and wounded.
Cáo Rén abandoned the city and fled.
Sūn Quán appointed Zhōu Yú as Administrator of Nánjùn.
Liú Bèi memorialized Sūn Quán as acting General of Agile Cavalry
and Governor of Xúzhōu.
Liú Bèi himself was appointed Governor of Jīngzhōu
and stationed at Gōng'ān.
In the fifteenth year
(210 CE), Yùzhāng was divided to form Póyáng Commandery;
Chángshā was divided to form Hànchāng Commandery,
with Lǔ Sù as Administrator,
stationed at Lùkǒu.
In the sixteenth year
(211 CE), Sūn Quán moved his capital to Mòlíng.
The following year,
he fortified Shítou
and renamed Mòlíng to Jiànyè.
Hearing that Cáo Gōng was coming to invade,
he built the Rúxū Docks.
In the first month of the eighteenth year
(213 CE), Cáo Gōng attacked Rúxū.
Sūn Quán resisted him for over a month.
Cáo Gōng observed Sūn Quán's army,
admiring its order and solemnity,
and then retreated.
Initially,
Cáo Gōng, fearing that the commanderies and counties along the riverbank would be seized by Sūn Quán,
ordered their populations to relocate inland.
The people became alarmed,
and over one hundred thousand households from Lújiāng, Jiǔjiāng, Qíchūn, and Guǎnglíng all crossed the Jiāng river eastward.
The area west of the Jiāng river was thus emptied,
and south of Héféi, only Wǎncchéng remained.
In the fifth month of the nineteenth year,
Sūn Quán campaigned against Wǎnchéng.
In the intercalary month,
he conquered it,
capturing Zhū Guāng, the Administrator of Lújiāng, and Dǒng Hé, an aide,
along with tens of thousands of men and women.
In this year, Liú Bèi pacified Shǔ.
Sūn Quán, considering that Liú Bèi had already obtained Yìzhōu,
ordered Zhūgě Jǐn to request the various commanderies of Jīngzhōu from him.
Liú Bèi refused,
saying:
"I am currently planning to conquer Liángzhōu.
When Liángzhōu is pacified,
then I will surrender all of Jīngzhōu to Wú."
Sūn Quán said:
"This is a loan that is not returned,
and he wishes to stall for time with empty words."
Thereupon, he appointed chief officials for the three southern commanderies,
but Guān Yǔ completely expelled them.
Sūn Quán was greatly enraged,
and so he dispatched Lǚ Méng to lead a force of twenty thousand soldiers under Xiān Yú Dān, Xú Zhōng, Sūn Guī, and others, to seize the three commanderies of Chángshā, Línglíng, and Guìyáng.
He sent Lǔ Sù with ten thousand men to garrison Bāqiū
to resist Guān Yǔ.
Sūn Quán stayed at Lùkǒu
to direct all the armies.
When Lǚ Méng arrived,
two commanderies submitted,
but only Hǎo Pǔ, the Administrator of Línglíng, had not yet surrendered.
At this time, Liú Bèi arrived at Gōng'ān
and sent Guān Yǔ with thirty thousand troops to Yìyáng.
Sūn Quán then recalled Lǚ Méng and others to assist Lǔ Sù.
Lǚ Méng sent someone to entice Hǎo Pǔ,
and Hǎo Pǔ surrendered.
After completely securing the generals and garrisons of the three commanderies,
Lǚ Méng then led his army back
and advanced alongside Sūn Jiǎo, Pān Zhāng, and Lǔ Sù's armies,
resisting Guān Yǔ at Yìyáng.
Before battle,
Cáo Cāo entered Hànzhōng,
and Liú Bèi feared losing Yìzhōu.
He sent an envoy to seek peace.
Sūn Quán ordered Zhūgě Jǐn to respond,
renewing their alliance and good relations.
Consequently, Jīngzhōu was divided: Chángshā, Jiāngxià, and Guìyáng, east of the divide, belonged to Sūn Quán;
Nánjùn, Línglíng, and Wǔlíng, west of the divide, belonged to Liú Bèi.
When Liú Bèi returned,
Cáo Cāo had already withdrawn.
Sūn Quán returned from Lùkǒu
and then campaigned against Héféi.
Before Héféi could be taken,
he withdrew his army and returned.
As all the soldiers were on their way,
Sūn Quán, along with Líng Tǒng, Gān Níng, and others, was attacked on the north bank of the ford by the Wèi general Zhāng Liáo.
Líng Tǒng and others defended Sūn Quán to the death,
and Sūn Quán escaped by riding a swift horse and leaping over the ford bridge.
In the winter of the twenty-first year,
Cáo Cāo encamped at Jūcháo
and then attacked Rúxū.
In the spring of the twenty-second year,
Sūn Quán ordered Commandant Xú Xiáng to go to Cáo Cāo to request surrender.
Cáo Cāo sent a messenger back to improve relations
and swore to renew their marital alliance.
In the tenth month of the twenty-third year,
Sūn Quán was about to go to Wú.
He personally rode a horse to hunt a tiger at Chū Tíng.
(Chū is pronounced like 'chū' in chūlíng.)
The horse was wounded by the tiger,
and Sūn Quán threw a pair of halberds at it.
The tiger stumbled backward,
and Zhāng Shì, his constant attendant, struck it with a dagger-axe,
capturing it.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Guān Yǔ besieged Cáo Rén at Xiāngyáng.
Cáo Cāo dispatched General of the Left Yú Jìn to relieve him.
The Hàn River suddenly rose,
and Guān Yǔ used his naval forces to capture Yú Jìn's and others' thirty thousand infantry and cavalry, sending them to Jiānglíng.
Only the city had not yet been taken.
Sūn Quán, internally apprehensive of Guān Yǔ
but externally wishing to claim this feat as his own,
sent a memorial to Cáo Cāo
offering to personally lead an expedition against Guān Yǔ.
Cáo Cāo, intending to pit Guān Yǔ and Sūn Quán against each other in battle,
sent Sūn Quán's letter by relay
and had Cáo Rén shoot it with crossbows to show Guān Yǔ.
Guān Yǔ hesitated and could not depart.
In the intercalary month,
Sūn Quán campaigned against Guān Yǔ.
He first sent Lǚ Méng to raid Gōng'ān,
capturing General Shì Rén.
When Lǚ Méng arrived at Nánjùn,
Mí Fāng, the Administrator of Nánjùn, surrendered the city.
Lǚ Méng occupied Jiānglíng,
comforted the old and weak,
and released Yú Jìn's prisoners.
Lù Xùn separately took Yídū,
capturing Zǐguī, Zhījiāng, and Yídào.
He then returned to garrison Yílíng,
guarding Xiákǒu to defend against Shǔ.
Guān Yǔ returned to Dāngyáng
and took refuge in Màichéng.
Sūn Quán sent people to entice him.
Guān Yǔ feigned surrender,
setting up banners and effigies on the city walls.
He then fled,
his troops all dispersed,
leaving only a dozen or so cavalry.
Sūn Quán had previously sent Zhū Rán and Pān Zhāng to cut off his escape routes.
In the twelfth month,
Mǎ Zhōng, a Sīmǎ under Pān Zhāng, captured Guān Yǔ, his son Píng, and Commander Zhào Lèi, among others, at Zhāngxiāng.
Thus, Jīngzhōu was pacified.
In this year, there was a great plague,
and all land taxes in Jīngzhōu were abolished for the people.
Cáo Cāo memorialized Sūn Quán as General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn),
granted him the ceremonial axe and the title of Governor of Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu Mù),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Nánchāng.
Sūn Quán sent Commandant Liáng Yù to present tribute to Hàn,
and also ordered Wáng Dūn to purchase horses,
and sent Zhū Guāng and others back.
In the spring, the first month of the twenty-fifth year,
Cáo Gōng passed away.
Prince Pī succeeded him as Chancellor and King of Wèi.
The year name was changed to Yánkāng.
In autumn,
Wèi General Méi Fū sent Zhāng Jiǎn to seek an audience and offer submission.
Five thousand families from the five counties of Nányáng, Yīn, Cuó, Zhúyáng (Zhú pronounced as zhú),
Shāndū, and Zhōnglú came to surrender.
In winter,
the successor King of Wèi claimed the imperial title,
and changed the era name to Huángchū.
In the fourth month of the second year,
Liú Bèi claimed the title of Emperor in Shǔ.
Quán moved his capital from Gōng'ān to È,
renaming it Wǔchāng,
and made Wǔchāng, Xiàzhì, Xúnyáng, Yángxīn, Cháisāng, and Shāxiàn six counties into Wǔchāng Commandery.
In the fifth month,
Jiànyè reported the descent of sweet dew.
In the eighth month,
Wǔchāng was fortified with walls,
and an order was issued to the generals:
"Indeed, while existing, not forgetting ruin;
while at peace, always contemplating danger:
this is the excellent teaching of antiquity.
In the past, Jùn Bùyí, a famous minister of Hàn,
in times of peace and stability, never let swords and knives leave his person.
This shows that a gentleman's military preparedness
cannot be neglected.
How much more so now, when we are on the borderlands,
with jackals and wolves all around,
can we afford to be negligent and not consider the possibility of change and difficulty?
Recently, I have heard that when generals go out and return,
they all practice modesty and simplicity,
not taking many soldiers with them.
This is certainly not what is meant by preparing for danger and cherishing one's life.
To preserve oneself and leave a good name,
thereby bringing peace to one's lord and parents,
how does that compare to danger and disgrace?
You should be deeply vigilant,
strive to uphold what is grand,
and fulfill my intention."
Since Wèi Wéndì ascended the throne,
Quán sent envoys to declare himself a vassal,
and also sent Yú Jìn and others back.
In the eleventh month,
an edict was issued to Quán, saying:
"Indeed, the laws of the sagely kings
establish ranks based on virtue,
and determine emoluments based on merit.
Those with great labor receive generous emoluments;
those with abundant virtue receive rich ceremonies.
Therefore, Shū Dàn had the achievement of assisting and supporting,
and Tài Gōng had the merit of soaring like an eagle.
Both opened up territories
and received abundant provisions,
thus to manifest their foundational achievements
and distinguish the worthy and wise.
Recently, at the beginning of Hàn Gāozǔ's receiving the Mandate,
he divided fertile lands to enfeoff eight surnames.
This is an excellent deed of former generations
and a prime example for future kings.
I, though unworthy,
have received the Mandate and started a new dynasty,
ruling over myriad states,
grasping the heavenly mechanism,
and aspire to emulate the predecessors,
sitting and awaiting dawn.
You, my lord, are naturally loyal and upright,
born to assist the world,
deeply discerning the heavenly cycles,
and clearly understanding rise and fall.
You sent distant envoys,
floating on the Qián-Hàn rivers.
Responding to the wind, you attached yourself to us,
presenting memorials and declaring yourself a vassal,
and moreover offering the thin silk, a tribute from the South.
You broadly sent back all the generals to this imperial court.
Your loyalty and solemnity emerged from within,
and your sincere devotion was manifested externally.
Your trustworthiness is as firm as metal and stone,
and your righteousness covers mountains and rivers.
I greatly commend this.
Now I enfeoff you as King of Wú.
I send my envoy, Zhēn, Grand Minister of Ceremonies and Marquis of Gāopíng, bearing the imperial credentials,
to bestow upon you the seal and sash, the edict, the gold tiger tally (numbers one to five), and the left bamboo tally (numbers one to ten).
You are made Grand General, Imperial Commissioner, overseeing Jiāozhōu,
and concurrently acting as Governor of Jīngzhōu.
I grant you the soil of the east,
wrapped in white rushes,
to solemnly announce my decree
and govern the eastern Xia.
Your former seal, sash, tally, and edict as General of Agile Cavalry and Marquis of Nánchāng are to be returned.
Now, I also bestow upon you the Nine Bestowals.
Please respectfully heed the subsequent commands.
Because you have pacified the southeast
and governed the regions beyond the Jiāng,
the people and the Yi barbarians are settled in their livelihoods,
with no wavering or disloyalty,
I therefore bestow upon you one grand chariot and one military chariot,
each drawn by two black stallions.
You have diligently managed resources and encouraged agriculture,
so that granaries and storehouses are full,
I therefore bestow upon you the imperial ceremonial robes
and a pair of red slippers.
You have transformed the people with virtue
and promoted rites and education,
I therefore bestow upon you court music with suspended bells.
You have propagated good customs
and brought the Baiyuè into submission,
I therefore bestow upon you vermilion doors for your residence.
You have exercised your talent and strategy,
appointing officials justly and employing the worthy,
I therefore bestow upon you a covered stairway for ascent.
Your loyalty and courage are equally fervent,
clearing away wickedness and evil,
I therefore bestow upon you one hundred guards of the tiger-and-wolf banner.
You have displayed awe-inspiring might and advanced triumphantly,
exerting your strength in Jīngnán,
slaughtering and exterminating wicked villains,
so that criminals are apprehended,
I therefore bestow upon you one axe and one battle-axe.
You are cultivated and harmonious internally,
and militarily trustworthy externally,
I therefore bestow upon you one red bow, one hundred red arrows, ten black bows, and one thousand black arrows.
You take loyalty and solemnity as your foundation,
and reverence and frugality as your virtue,
I therefore bestow upon you one jar of black millet wine,
with a jade libation cup.
Respect this!
Reverently implement these instructions and principles,
to obey my command,
and to exert yourself in assisting our state,
thereby perpetually completing your glorious achievements."
That year,
Liú Bèi led his army to attack,
reaching Wūshān and Zǐguī.
He sent envoys to induce the Mán-Yí of Wǔlíng,
granting them seals and tallies,
and promising them enfeoffment and rewards.
Thereupon, all the counties and the people of Wǔxī rebelled for Shǔ.
Quán appointed Lù Xùn as commander,
to oversee Zhū Rán, Pān Zhāng, and others to resist them.
He sent Commandant Zhào Zī as envoy to Wèi.
The Wèi Emperor asked:
"What kind of ruler is the King of Wú?"
Zī replied:
"He is an intelligent, benevolent, and wise ruler,
a sovereign of heroic strategy."
The Emperor asked for his characteristics.
Zī said:
"Accepting Lǔ Sù from a common background,
this is his intelligence;
elevating Lǚ Méng from the ranks,
this is his insight;
capturing Yú Jìn but not harming him,
this is his benevolence;
taking Jīngzhōu without bloodshed,
this is his wisdom;
holding three provinces and eyeing the world like a tiger,
this is his heroism;
humbling himself before Your Majesty,
this is his strategy."
The Emperor wished to enfeoff Quán's son Dēng,
but Quán, citing Dēng's youth,
submitted a memorial declining the enfeoffment.
He again sent Western Cáo Aide Shěn Héng to express thanks,
and also presented local products.
Dēng was established as the Crown Prince.
In the spring, the first month of Huángwǔ Year One,
Lù Xùn's subordinate generals Sòng Qiān and others attacked five Shǔ garrisons,
and all were defeated,
their generals beheaded.
In the third month,
Póyáng reported the sighting of a yellow dragon.
The Shǔ army was divided, occupying strategic points,
with over fifty camps, front and rear.
Xùn responded to their varying strengths with troops,
from the first month to the intercalary month,
he inflicted a great defeat,
slaying tens of thousands in battle and capturing countless surrendering soldiers.
Liú Bèi fled,
barely escaping with his life.
Initially, Quán outwardly submitted to Wèi,
but his sincerity was not forthcoming.
Wèi then sent Palace Attendant Xīn Pí and Grand Secretary Huán Jiē to make an oath with him,
and requested a son to be held as a hostage.
Quán declined and did not accept.
In autumn, the ninth month,
Wèi then ordered Cáo Xiū, Zhāng Liáo, and Zāng Bà to march out to Dòngkǒu,
Cáo Rén to march out to Rúxū,
and Cáo Zhēn, Xiàhóu Shàng, Zhāng Hé, and Xú Huàng to besiege Nánjùn.
Quán sent Lǚ Fàn and others to command five armies,
using a naval force to resist Xiū and his group,
Zhūgě Jǐn, Pān Zhāng, and Yáng Càn to relieve Nánjùn,
and Zhū Huán, as supervisor of Rúxū, to resist Rén.
At that time, many of the Yáng and Yuè barbarian tribes had not yet been pacified or gathered,
and internal troubles had not ceased.
Therefore, Quán humbly submitted a memorial,
seeking to reform himself,
saying, "If my crimes are difficult to absolve,
and I must not be spared,
I will respectfully return the land and its people,
and beg to be allowed to live in Jiāozhōu,
to live out my remaining years."
Emperor Wén replied:
"You were born in a tumultuous era,
and originally had the ambition to maneuver vertically and horizontally.
You lowered yourself and served the state,
to enjoy this prosperity.
Since you first pledged your allegiance,
your contributions have filled the roads.
Your achievement in attacking Bèi,
the imperial court praises and relies upon.
To bury and then dig up (a matter),
is what ancient people regarded as shameful.
Between Us and you,
the great righteousness has already been settled.
How could We enjoy exhausting Our armies to reach Jiānghàn from afar?
The discussions in the court,
cannot be monopolized by the sovereign.
When the Three Dukes reported your transgressions,
they all had their origins and conclusions.
We, being unenlightened,
though We had the doubt of Zēng Mǔ throwing the shuttle,
still hoped that the accusers were not credible,
and considered it a fortune for the state.
Therefore, We first sent envoys to offer rewards,
and then sent the Grand Secretary and Palace Attendant to confirm Our previous words,
to settle the matter of the hostage son.
You then made excuses,
not wishing for him to come forward,
which the deliberators found strange.
Moreover, former Commandant Hào Zhōu urged you to send a son;
this was actually a coordinated scheme by Our court officials,
to divine your intentions through this.
You indeed had excuses,
outwardly citing Wěi Xiāo, whose sending of a son did not lead to a good end,
and inwardly alluding to Dòu Róng, who merely maintained his loyalty.
Times have changed, circumstances are different,
and each person has their own mind.
When Hào Zhōu returned,
he verbally reported his observations and instructions,
further causing the deliberators to voice their numerous suspicions.
The root of the beginning and end (of this matter),
had no basis for reliance.
Therefore, We finally bowed to the will of Our officials and followed their deliberations.
Now, having reviewed your memorial,
your sincerity is profound and utmost,
and Our heart is deeply moved,
filled with sorrow, and Our expression changes.
On this very day, We issue an edict,
commanding all armies merely to dig deep trenches and build high ramparts,
and not to advance recklessly.
If you are truly determined to demonstrate loyalty and integrity,
to resolve the doubts and discussions,
if you present yourself at court in the morning,
by evening We shall recall Our troops.
The sincerity of these words,
is as immense as the Great River!"
Quán then changed his reign title,
and defended himself by the river.
In winter, the eleventh month,
a great wind struck,
and several thousand of Fàn's troops drowned,
the remaining forces returned to Jiāngnán.
Cáo Xiū ordered Zāng Bà, with five hundred light boats and ten thousand dare-to-die soldiers, to attack Xú Líng,
burning siege engines,
and killing or capturing several thousand people.
Generals Quán Cóng and Xú Shèng pursued and beheaded Wèi general Yǐn Lú,
killing and capturing several hundred.
In the twelfth month,
Quán sent Grand Master Zhèng Quán to invite Liú Bèi at Báidì,
and they began to communicate again.
However, he still maintained contact with Wèi Emperor Wén,
only severing ties the year after next.
In this year, Yílíng was renamed Xīlíng.
In the second year, spring, the first month,
Cáo Zhēn divided his forces to occupy the central island of Jiānglíng.
In this month,
they fortified the mountains of Jiāngxià.
The "Sìfēn" calendar was changed,
and the "Qiánxiàng" calendar was adopted.
In the third month,
Cáo Rén sent General Cháng Diāo and others,
with five thousand soldiers,
on oil-coated boats,
to cross to the central island of Rúxū at dawn.
Rén's son, Tài, then led his army to urgently attack Zhū Huán.
Huán's troops resisted them,
and sent General Yán Guī and others to defeat Diāo and his group.
In this month,
all Wèi armies retreated.
In summer, the fourth month,
Quán's officials urged him to immediately assume the imperial title,
but Quán refused.
Liú Bèi died at Báidì.
In the fifth month,
it was reported in Qū'ā that sweet dew had fallen.
Earlier, Jìn Zōng, the defending general of Xìkǒu, killed General Wáng Zhí,
and with his troops defected to Wèi.
Wèi appointed him Grand Administrator of Qíchūn,
and he repeatedly violated the border.
In the sixth month,
Quán ordered General Hè Qí to supervise Mí Fāng, Liú Shào, and others in attacking Qíchūn.
Shào and his group captured Zōng alive.
In winter, the eleventh month,
Shǔ sent Middle Commandant Dèng Zhī to make an alliance.
In the third year, summer,
(Quán) sent Auxiliary Righteous Middle Commandant Zhāng Wēn to make an alliance with Shǔ.
In autumn, the eighth month,
(he) pardoned capital crimes.
In the ninth month,
Wèi Emperor Wén went to Guǎnglíng,
looked at the Great River (Yangtze),
and said,
"There are men there,
they cannot be easily plotted against,"
and then returned.
In the fourth year, summer, the fifth month,
Chancellor Sūn Shào died.
In the sixth month,
Grand Herald Gù Yōng was made Chancellor.
At Wǎnkǒu, it was reported that trees had grown with interlocked branches.
In winter, the twelfth month,
Póyáng bandit Péng Qǐ proclaimed himself general,
attacked and captured several counties,
with tens of thousands of followers.
In this year, the ground continuously trembled (earthquakes).
In the fifth year, in spring,
an order was issued, saying:
"The army has been mobilized for a long time,
the people have left their farms,
fathers and sons, husbands and wives,
are not allowed to help each other.
I am deeply saddened by this.
Now the northern barbarians have retreated and fled,
and there is peace beyond the borders,
so let the prefectures and commanderies below
have some respite and relief."
At this time, Lù Xùn (陸遜), seeing that grain was scarce in various places,
submitted a memorial ordering the generals to expand the cultivated land.
Quán (權) replied, saying:
"This is excellent.
Now I and my sons will personally cultivate the fields,
with eight oxen in a carriage forming four pairs.
Although this does not match the ancients,
I also wish to share the labor equally with the multitude."
In autumn, in the seventh month,
Quán (權) heard that Emperor Wén (文帝) of Wèi (魏) had died.
He campaigned against Jiāngxià (江夏),
besieged Shíyáng (石陽),
but failed to conquer it and returned.
Cāngwú (蒼梧) reported that a phoenix was seen.
Ten counties of inhospitable land from three commanderies were separated to establish Dōng'ān Jùn (東安郡),
with Quán Cóng (全琮) as its Grand Administrator,
to pacify and suppress the Shānyuè (山越).
In winter, in the tenth month,
Lù Xùn (陸遜) presented a memorial on what was expedient,
advising to extend benevolence and lighten punishments,
and to broaden levies and cease conscription.
He also said:
"Words of loyalty and uprightness
cannot be fully expressed.
I seek to be tolerated as a humble subject,
and frequently report on matters of benefit."
Quán (權) replied, saying:
"The establishment of laws and regulations
is intended to curb evil and prevent wickedness,
and to warn against what has not yet happened.
How can there be no punishments to awe the ignoble?
This is to decree first and punish later,
not wishing for anyone to commit offenses.
If you think it is too severe,
how do I benefit from it being so?
It is only that I have no choice but to do so.
Now, upon receiving your intentions,
I shall consult extensively
to ensure what is feasible.
Moreover, close officials have advice that fully sets out their counsel,
and relatives have admonitions that supplement and observe,
which serves to rectify the ruler, correct the lord, and clarify loyalty and trustworthiness.
The Book says, 'If I am wrong, you should correct me;
do not comply merely to my face.'
How can I not be pleased with loyal words to help and supplement myself?
Yet you say,
'I dare not express them fully.'
How can this be considered loyal and upright?
If among the humble subjects,
there are those whose words can be accepted and used,
how could I reject their words because of the person and not adopt them?
But as for flattery and seeking favor,
even the ignorant can clearly discern it.
As for the raising of levies,
it is simply because the world is not yet settled,
and affairs are accomplished with the multitude.
If we merely guard Jiāngdōng (江東)
and cultivate lenient policies,
the troops would be sufficient,
why use so many more?
It is only the sitting idly by and guarding oneself that is deplorable.
If we do not prepare levies in advance,
I fear that when the time comes, they may not be immediately usable.
Furthermore, the bond between you and me is especially unique;
we truly share honor and sorrow.
Your memorial says you dare not follow the multitude to preserve yourself and avoid trouble.
This is indeed what I earnestly hope for from you."
Thereupon, he ordered the officials in charge to fully transcribe the regulations
and sent the Palace Gentleman Chǔ Féng (褚逢) to take them to Xùn (遜) and Zhūgě Jǐn (諸葛瑾),
so that they could add or subtract
whatever they deemed inappropriate.
In this year,
Jiāozhōu (交州) was divided to establish Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
but it was soon restored to its former state.
In the sixth year, in spring, in the first month,
the generals captured Péng Qǐ (彭綺).
In the intercalary month,
Hán Dāng's (韓當) son, Zōng (綜), surrendered to Wèi (魏) with his troops.
In the seventh year, in spring, in the third month,
his son, Lǜ (慮), was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiànchāng (建昌侯).
Dōng'ān Jùn (東安郡) was abolished.
In summer, in the fifth month,
Zhōu Fáng (周魴), the Grand Administrator of Póyáng (鄱陽), feigned rebellion
to lure the Wèi (魏) general Cáo Xiū (曹休).
In autumn, in the eighth month,
Quán (權) arrived at Wǎnkǒu (皖口)
and sent General Lù Xùn (陸遜) to supervise the generals, who severely defeated Xiū (休) at Shítíng (石亭).
Grand Marshal Lǚ Fàn (呂範) died.
In this year,
Hépǔ (合浦) was renamed Zhūguān Jùn (珠官郡).
In the spring of the first year of Huánglóng,
all the Gōngqīng and officials urged Quán to assume the imperial title.
In the fourth month of summer,
reports came from Xiàkǒu and Wǔchāng that yellow dragons and phoenixes had been seen.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
he ascended the imperial throne in the southern suburbs.
On that day, there was a great amnesty,
and the year name was changed.
His father, the General Who Breaks the Enemy, Jiān, was posthumously honored as Wǔliè Huángdì.
His mother, Lady Wú, was honored as Wǔliè Huánghòu.
His elder brother, the General Who Quells the Rebels, Cè, was honored as Chángshā Huán Wáng.
Sūn Dēng, the Crown Prince of Wú Wáng, became the Imperial Crown Prince.
All generals and officials were promoted in rank and awarded.
Initially,
during the Xīngpíng reign,
a children's rhyme in Wúzhōng said:
"A golden carriage,
with striped ears,
opens the Chāngmén gate,
and out comes the Son of Heaven."
In the fifth month,
he sent Colonel Zhāng Gāng and Guǎn Dǔ to Liáodōng.
In the sixth month,
Shǔ sent Wèiwèi Chén Zhèn to congratulate Quán on his ascension.
Quán then divided the empire into three parts:
Yù, Qīng, Xú, and Yōu belonged to Wú;
Yǎn, Jì, Bìng, and Liáng belonged to Shǔ.
As for the territory of Sīzhōu,
Hángǔguān was to be the boundary.
An alliance was made, stating:
"Heaven sent down chaos and disorder,
the imperial order lost its sequence.
Rebellious ministers seized the opportunity,
usurping the reins of the state,
beginning with Dǒng Zhuó,
and ending with Cáo Cāo,
who committed extreme wickedness,
overthrowing all under heaven,
leading to the fragmentation of the Nine Provinces,
and the entire world without a ruler.
Both men and gods feel pain and resentment,
with no place to settle.
And Cāo's son, Pī,
a treacherous and vile remnant,
repeatedly committed evil,
stealing the heavenly throne.
And Ruì, that insignificant fellow,
followed Pī's wicked footsteps,
using his army to plunder territory,
and has not yet been punished.
In the past, when Gònggōng brought chaos to the cosmos, Gāoxīn marched his army.
When the Sānmiáo tribe violated the norms, Yúshùn campaigned against them.
Today, to eliminate Ruì,
and capture his followers,
if not Hàn and Wú,
who else can take on this responsibility?
Indeed, in punishing evil and suppressing violence,
their crimes must be proclaimed.
It is appropriate to first divide and regulate,
taking away their lands,
so that the hearts of the soldiers and common people
each know where to belong.
Therefore, in the Spring and Autumn period, when Jìn Hóu attacked Wèi,
he first divided its fields to give to the people of Sòng.
This is its righteousness.
Moreover, the ancients, when undertaking great matters,
must first make oaths.
Hence, the Zhōu Lǐ has the official of the Sīméng,
and the Shàngshū has the text of 'Gàoshì'.
Though the mutual trust between Hàn and Wú comes from within,
yet the division of lands and splitting of territories
should have an alliance pact.
Chéngxiàng Zhūgě's virtue and prestige are renowned far and wide.
He assists and supports his native state,
commands the army externally.
His sincerity influences Yin and Yang,
and moves Heaven and Earth.
Let us repeatedly form an alliance,
and widely declare this sincere oath,
so that the people of the east and west may all hear and know it.
Thus, we erect an altar and slay sacrifices,
to clearly announce to the gods.
We thrice taste the blood and add it to the written covenant,
depositing it in the heavenly archives.
Heaven is high and hears below,
its divine power assists and verifies.
Sīshèn and Sīméng,
all gods and all sacrifices,
none do not oversee this.
From today, after Hàn and Wú have formed this alliance,
they shall exert their strength with one heart,
jointly attack the Wèi rebels,
rescue the endangered and relieve the distressed,
share in calamities and rejoice together.
Their likes and dislikes shall be the same,
without any defection or disloyalty.
If there is harm to Hàn,
Wú shall attack it.
If there is harm to Wú,
Hàn shall attack it.
Each shall guard their allotted territory,
and not invade each other.
This shall be passed down to future generations,
to be maintained from beginning to end.
All hundred clauses of this pact
are as written in this document.
True words are not boastful,
sincerity resides in goodwill.
Should anyone violate this alliance,
initiate disaster and first cause chaos,
act contrary or disloyal,
or be arrogant and scornful of Heaven's command,
the bright gods and the Supreme Lord shall punish and oversee them.
The mountains, rivers, and all hundred gods shall correct and exterminate them,
causing their armies to fall,
and preventing them from establishing a state.
Oh, you great spirits,
may you clearly scrutinize this!"
In the ninth month of autumn,
Quán moved the capital to Jiànyè.
He did not change his residence in the old palace.
He summoned Grand General Lù Xùn to assist Crown Prince Dēng,
and to manage the affairs left behind in Wǔchāng.
In the first month of spring of the second year,
Wèi built a new city in Héfèi.
An edict was issued to establish the Dūjiǎng Jìjiǔ,
to teach the imperial princes.
He sent Generals Wèi Wēn and Zhūgě Zhí with ten thousand armored soldiers to sail the sea in search of Yízhōu and Dànzhōu.
Dànzhōu is in the middle of the sea.
Elders transmitted stories that Qín Shǐhuángdì sent the fangshi Xú Fú with several thousand boys and girls into the sea,
to seek the divine mountain Pénglái and the elixir of immortality,
and that they stopped at this island and never returned.
Generations have passed, and there are tens of thousands of families there.
The people on it
sometimes came to Kuàijī to trade cloth.
People from the eastern counties of Kuàijī who sailed the sea
also sometimes drifted to Dànzhōu due to storms.
Its location was extremely remote,
and they could not reach it in the end.
They only returned with several thousand people from Yízhōu.
In the second month of spring of the third year,
he sent Tàicháng Pān Jùn to lead fifty thousand troops to suppress the barbarian tribes of Wǔlíng.
Wèi Wēn and Zhūgě Zhí were both imprisoned and executed for disobeying orders and having no achievements.
In summer,
wild silkworms formed cocoons
as large as eggs.
Wild rice grew naturally in Yóuquán,
which was then renamed Héxīng County.
Zhōnglángjiàng Sūn Bù feigned surrender to lure Wèi General Wáng Líng.
Líng came with his army to meet Bù.
In the tenth month of winter,
Quán lay in ambush with a large army in Fùlíng, waiting for him.
Líng realized it and fled.
Nánshǐpíng in Kuàijī reported the growth of auspicious grain (jiāhé).
On the day Dīngmǎo in the twelfth month,
a great amnesty was proclaimed,
and the next year's era name was changed.
In the first month of spring of the first year of Jiāhé,
Jiànchāng Hóu Lǜ died.
In the third month,
he sent General Zhōu Hè and Colonel Péi Qián by sea to Liáodōng.
In the ninth month of autumn,
Wèi General Tián Yù intercepted and attacked them,
beheading Hè at Chéngshān.
In the tenth month of winter,
Gōngsūn Yuān, the Administrator of Liáodōng for Wèi, sent Colonel Sù Shū and Lángzhōng Lìng Sūn Zōng to declare vassalage to Quán,
and also offered marten furs and horses.
Quán was greatly pleased
and granted Yuān a noble title.
In the second year, in spring, the first month,
an edict stated:
"I, being without virtue,
first received the grand mandate.
Morning and night I have been vigilant,
without leisure to lay down and rest.
I think of pacifying the world's troubles
and saving the common people,
thereby responding to the gods above
and comforting the hopes of the people below.
It is for this reason that I am ever mindful,
diligently seeking out heroes
to join forces with me
to together pacify the realm.
If only we are of one mind,
I will grow old with them.
Now, the Imperial Envoy, Inspector of Yōuzhōu, Administrator of Qīngzhōu, Grand Administrator of Liáodōng, the King of Yān,
has long been coerced by the bandits,
separated in one region.
Although his heart is for the state,
the path to communication was non-existent.
Now, in accordance with Heaven's will,
he has sent two envoys from afar.
His sincere intentions are clearly revealed,
his memorials are earnest.
That I have gained this,
what joy is comparable to it!
Though Tāng met Yīyǐn,
and Zhōu acquired Lǚwàng,
and Shìzǔ, before pacifying the realm, obtained Héyòu,
when compared to today,
how could that ever surpass this?
The unification of all under Heaven
is hereby settled.
Does the *Shūjīng* not say,
'When one man has cause for rejoicing,
the myriad people rely upon him'?
Therefore, grant a great amnesty to all under Heaven,
and let them start anew.
Let this be clearly proclaimed throughout the commanderies and counties,
so that all may hear and know.
Specifically, send this to the state of Yān
to proclaim and spread the imperial grace,
so that all within the four seas may fully hear of this felicity."
In the third month,
Shū and Zōng were sent back.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies Zhāng Mí, the Commandant of Escorting Cavalry Xǔ Yàn, General Hè Dá and others led ten thousand soldiers,
gold, jewels, precious goods,
and the full set of Nine Bestowals,
to cross the sea to give them to Yuān.
All the high officials of the court,
from Chancellor Yōng downwards, all remonstrated,
believing that Yuān was not yet trustworthy,
and that the favor and treatment were too generous.
It would be better to merely send a few hundred officers and soldiers to escort Shū and Zōng.
Quán ultimately did not listen.
Yuān indeed beheaded Mí and the others,
sent their heads to Wèi,
and confiscated their soldiers and supplies.
Quán was greatly enraged,
and wished to personally lead an expedition against Yuān.
Only after Grandee Secretary Xuē Zōng and others earnestly remonstrated did he stop.
In this year,
Quán advanced towards the New City of Héféi.
He sent General Quán Cóng to attack Liù'ān,
but both failed to conquer and returned.
In the third year, in spring, the first month,
an edict stated:
"War has not ceased for a long time,
the people are distressed by service,
and harvests sometimes fail.
Therefore, ease all arrears,
and do not press for their collection again."
In summer, the fifth month,
Quán sent Lù Xùn, Zhūgě Jǐn, and others to garrison Jiāngxià and Miǎnkǒu.
Sūn Sháo, Zhāng Chéng, and others advanced towards Guǎnglíng and Huáiyáng.
Quán personally led a large army to besiege the New City of Héféi.
At this time, the Chancellor of Shǔ, Zhūgě Liàng, had advanced to Wǔgōng.
Quán thought that Emperor Míng of Wèi would not be able to travel far,
but the Emperor sent troops to assist Sīmǎ Xuánwáng in resisting Liàng,
and personally led a naval force on an eastern campaign.
Before reaching Shòuchūn,
Quán retreated and returned.
Sūn Sháo also withdrew.
In autumn, the eighth month,
Zhūgě Kè was appointed Grand Administrator of Dānyáng
to suppress the Shānyuè.
On the first day of the ninth month,
frost fell and damaged the crops.
In winter, the eleventh month,
Grand Master of Ceremonies Pān Jùn pacified the Mányí of Wǔlíng.
After the matter was concluded,
he returned to Wǔchāng.
An edict renamed Qǔ'ā to Yúnyáng,
and Dāntú to Wǔjìn.
The bandits Lǐ Huán and Luó Lì from Lúlíng caused unrest.
In the fourth year, in summer,
Lǚ Dài was sent to suppress Huán and others.
In autumn, the seventh month,
there was hail.
