The Wèi envoys sought to trade horses for pearls, kingfisher feathers, and tortoise shells.
Quán said:
"These are all things I do not use,
and I can obtain horses;
why should I not allow the exchange?"
In the fifth year, in spring,
large coins were minted,
one worth five hundred.
An edict instructed officials and common people to surrender copper,
and they were paid based on the amount of copper.
Regulations against counterfeiting were established.
In the second month,
it was reported from Wǔchāng that sweet dew had fallen on the Lǐbīn Hall.
General Who Assists Wú, Zhāng Zhāo, died.
Commandant of the Central Army Wú Càn captured Lǐ Huán.
General Táng Zī captured Luó Lì and others.
From October, there was no rain
until summer.
In winter, the tenth month,
a comet was seen in the east.
The Pōyáng bandits Péng Dàn and others caused unrest.
In the spring, the first month of the sixth year,
an edict stated:
"The three-year mourning period
is a universal custom throughout the realm,
and the utmost expression of human sorrow.
The virtuous suppress their grief to follow the rites;
the unworthy strive to achieve it.
When the world is at peace and the Way prospers,
and there is no trouble for those above or below,
a gentleman does not hinder human emotions.
Therefore, for three years, he does not enter the gate of a filial son.
However, when there are affairs to attend to,
the rites are curtailed to suit expediency,
and one wears mourning clothes while attending to business.
Thus, when the sages established laws,
if there were rites but no opportune time, they would not be implemented.
Not rushing to a funeral in times of mourning is not ancient practice;
rather, it is to follow what is appropriate for the time,
and to cut off personal affection based on righteousness.
Previously, regulations were established
that if a senior official was in office,
they should await a replacement.
But those who deliberately violated this,
though punished immediately,
had already caused dereliction of duty.
At a time when affairs are pressing,
and the state faces many difficulties,
all those in official positions
should exert their utmost loyalty,
prioritizing public interest over private.
To not respectfully comply
is utterly unacceptable.
All officials, both within and outside the court,
should deliberate further,
ensuring a balanced solution,
and detail the regulations."
Gù Tán ɡuān debated,
believing
"establishing regulations for rushing to funerals,
if too lenient, will be insufficient to restrain the emotions of filial sons;
if too severe, it is fundamentally not a crime punishable by death.
Even if stricter penalties are imposed,
violations and deprivations will still be few.
If perchance someone does violate it,
to increase their punishment would be unbearable in terms of human compassion,
while to reduce it would render the law廢 nugatory.
My humble opinion is that if a senior official is far away,
and is not informed,
they cannot possibly know.
During the interval of selection and replacement,
if anyone transmits the news (to encourage them to return),
they must be sentenced to capital punishment.
Then the senior official will not bear the blame of abandoning their post,
and the filial son will not incur a severe penalty."
General Hú Zōnɡ debated,
believing
"though the rites of mourning
have canonical regulations,
if the time is not opportune,
they cannot be implemented.
Currently, military affairs and national defense present different circumstances.
If a senior official encounters mourning,
knowing there are prohibitive regulations,
and openly dares to transgress,
merely mindful of the shame of hearing of sorrow but not rushing home,
without considering the crime of a subject violating prohibitions,
this is caused by the inherent leniency of the regulations.
Loyalty and integrity belong to the state,
filial piety establishes the family.
Having dedicated oneself as a subject,
how can one achieve both?
Therefore, one who is a loyal subject cannot be a filial son.
The legal text should be settled,
indicating capital punishment.
If one deliberately violates it,
they are guilty without pardon.
By using execution to stop executions,
if applied to one person,
such occurrences will surely cease thereafter."
Chancellor Yōnɡ memorialized to adopt capital punishment.
Thereafter, Méng Zōnɡ, the magistrate of Wú, rushed home upon his mother's death.
Afterward, he voluntarily confined himself in Wǔchāng to await punishment.
Lù Xùn detailed his usual conduct
and pleaded for him.
Quán then reduced Zōnɡ's sentence by one degree,
stating that this should not be taken as a precedent thereafter.
Consequently, such acts ceased.
In the second month,
Lù Xùn attacked Pénɡ Dàn and others.
That year,
he defeated them all.
In the tenth month of winter,
General of the Guards Quán Cónɡ was dispatched to raid Lù'ān,
but did not succeed.
After Zhūɡě Kè finished pacifying the Shānyuè,
he was stationed in Lújiānɡ.
In the spring of the first year of Chìwū (238 CE),
large "thousand-cash" coins were minted.
In the summer,
Lǚ Dài attacked the bandits of Lúlín.
After completing this,
he returned to Lùkǒu.
In the eighth month of autumn,
a Qílín was reported to have been seen in Wǔchāng.
The officials in charge submitted a memorial stating that the Qílín was an omen of great peace,
and that the era name should be changed.
An imperial edict stated:
"Recently, a red crow (chìwū) gathered in front of the palace;
I saw it myself.
If the divine spirits consider this a propitious sign,
then the era name should be changed to Chìwū."
The assembled officials submitted a memorial stating:
"In antiquity, when King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
there was the auspicious omen of the red crow.
When ruler and ministers observed it,
they subsequently gained control of All Under Heaven.
The reason why the sages' writings record and narrate this in the greatest detail
is because it was a recent and auspicious event,
and it was clearly seen personally."
Thereupon, the era name was changed.
Empress Bù died,
and was posthumously granted the title of Empress.
Initially,
Quán trusted Lǚ Yī, a director of investigations.
Yī was by nature harsh and cruel,
and his application of the law was severe.
Crown Prince Dēng repeatedly remonstrated,
but Quán did not accept it.
Consequently, no high minister dared to speak.
Later, Yī's crimes and illicit activities were exposed, and he was executed.
Quán blamed himself and took responsibility,
and then sent Middle Scribe Yuán Lǐ to offer apologies to the various great generals,
and to inquire about current affairs that needed to be improved or abolished.
When Lǐ returned,
another edict was issued, reproaching Zhūgě Jǐn, Bù Zhì, Zhū Rán, Lǚ Dài, and others, saying:
"Yuán Lǐ has returned,
and says he met with Zǐyú, Zǐshān, Yìfēng, and Dìnggōng.
They all believed that certain priorities should be set for current affairs,
but each claimed not to be in charge of civil matters,
and were unwilling to immediately present anything.
They all deferred to Bóyán and Chéngmíng.
When Bóyán and Chéngmíng met Lǐ,
they wept with sincere emotion,
and their words were full of distress and hardship,
even to the point of harboring fear and danger,
and having a sense of unease.
Hearing this, I was disheartened
and deeply blamed myself.
Why?
Indeed, only a sage can be without faults,
and only an enlightened person can see their own.
How can a person's every action
always be correct?
It must be that I stubbornly insisted on my own views, thereby harming and rejecting the opinions of the multitude,
and failed to realize it myself.
Hence, you gentlemen have felt difficulty and apprehension;
otherwise,
how could it have reached this point?
For fifty years since I raised an army,
all the levies and taxes have come from the people.
The world is not yet settled,
and rebellious elements still exist.
The hard work and suffering of the soldiers and people
are truly known to me.
However, burdening the populace
is a matter of necessity.
Working with you gentlemen,
from youth to old age,
my hair has become two-colored.
I believed that my sincerity was clearly evident,
and that the distinction between public and private accounts
was sufficient to ensure mutual trust.
Speaking frankly and offering direct remonstrance is what I expect from you gentlemen;
remedying omissions and making up for deficiencies
is also what I expect.
In the past, Duke Wǔ of Wèi, though advanced in years, was strong in ambition,
diligently sought out advisors and assistants,
and often sighed and reproached himself in private.
Moreover, even commoners with coarse clothes and belts,
when forming friendships
and sharing in good times and bad,
do not differ in their lack of pretense.
Today, you gentlemen are working with me;
although the bond of ruler and minister exists,
I still consider us to be like flesh and blood, so this situation should not occur again.
We share in glory and fortune, joy and sorrow.
The loyal do not conceal their feelings,
and the wise do not withhold their strategies.
Regarding the right and wrong of governing affairs,
how can you gentlemen simply remain composed?
If we are in the same boat crossing water,
who else will I rely on?
Duke Huán of Qí was merely a hegemon among the feudal lords,
yet he never failed to praise Guǎn Zǐ when he did well,
and never failed to remonstrate when he made a mistake.
If his remonstrance was not accepted,
he would not stop remonstrating until it was.
Now, I examine myself and find I lack the virtue of Duke Huán,
yet your gentlemen's remonstrances have not left your mouths,
and you still harbor apprehension and difficulty.
Judging by this,
I am far superior to Duke Huán of Qí
— I wonder how you gentlemen compare to Guǎn Zǐ?
It has been a long time since we last met;
I must laugh at this situation.
Who else will help me
to achieve this great enterprise
and bring order to All Under Heaven?
For all important matters that need to be improved or abolished,
I welcome differing opinions
to rectify my shortcomings."
In the third month of the
spring of the second year (239 CE),
envoys Yáng Dào and Zhèng Zhòu,
and General Sūn Yí, were dispatched to Liáodōng
to attack the Wei defending generals Zhāng Chí and Gāo Lǜ, etc.,
and captured men and women.
Línglíng reported the descent of sweet dew.
In the fifth month of summer,
Shāxiàn was fortified.
In the tenth month of winter,
General Jiǎng Mì attacked the Yi barbarians to the south.
Liao Shì, the commander under Mì, killed the Administrator of Línghè, Yán Gāng, and others,
proclaimed himself General Who Pacifies the South,
and with his brother Qián, jointly attacked Línglíng and Guìyáng,
and agitated the various commanderies of Jiāozhōu, Cāngwú, and Yùlín.
Their forces numbered several tens of thousands.
Generals Lǚ Dài and Táng Zī were dispatched to suppress them,
and after more than a year, they were all defeated.
In the first month of the spring of the third year (240 CE),
an imperial edict stated:
"Indeed, a ruler cannot be established without the people,
and the people cannot live without grain.
Recently,
the people have been frequently conscripted for labor,
and the year has also seen floods and droughts,
resulting in damage to the year's harvest.
Moreover, some officials are not good,
encroaching upon the people's time,
leading to hunger and distress.
From now on,
military governors and commandery administrators
shall carefully investigate unlawful acts.
If, during the farming and sericulture seasons,
people are disturbed by labor conscription,
they shall report and rectify the matter."
In the fourth month of summer,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
An imperial edict ordered all commanderies and counties to repair their city walls,
erect watchtowers,
dig moats, and excavate canals,
to guard against bandits.
In the eleventh month of winter,
the people were suffering from famine.
An imperial edict ordered granaries to be opened
to relieve the poor.
In the first month of the spring of the fourth year (241 CE),
there was heavy snow,
three *chi* deep on level ground,
and more than half of the birds and beasts died.
In the fourth month of summer,
Guardian General Quán Cóng attacked Huáinán,
breached the Quèpí reservoir,
burned the supply depots in Ānchéng,
and captured its people.
General Who Awe the North, Zhūgě Kè, attacked Liù'ān.
Cóng fought the Wei general Wáng Líng at Quèpí,
and more than ten officers, including Colonel Qín Huǎng, died in battle.
General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhū Rán besieged Fán,
and Grand General Zhūgě Jǐn captured Zābù.
In the fifth month,
Crown Prince Dēng died.
In this month,
the Wei Grand Tutor Sīmǎ Xuānwáng relieved Fán.
In the sixth month,
the army returned.
In the intercalary month,
Grand General Jǐn died.
In the eighth month of autumn,
Lù Xùn fortified Zhū.
In the spring, the first month of the fifth year,
Zǐ Hé was established as Crown Prince.
There was a general amnesty,
and Héxīng was renamed Jiāxīng.
The hundred officials memorialized to establish an empress and four kings.
An imperial edict stated:
"Today, the world is not yet settled.
The people and resources are weary and exhausted.
Moreover, those who have rendered meritorious service have perhaps not yet been rewarded,
and those who suffer from hunger and cold have not yet received relief.
To arbitrarily carve out territory to enrich one's children
and elevate ranks to favor concubines
is something I strongly disapprove of.
Dismiss this deliberation."
In the third month,
Hǎiyán County reported the sighting of a yellow dragon.
In the summer, the fourth month,
gifts for the emperor were prohibited,
and the provisions for the Grand Steward were reduced.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
General Niè Yǒu and Commandant Lù Kǎi were dispatched with thirty thousand troops to attack Zhūyá and Dān'ěr.
This year, there was a great plague.
The relevant officials again memorialized to establish an empress and various kings.
In the eighth month,
Zǐ Bà was established as the King of Lǔ.
In the spring, the first month of the sixth year,
Xīndū reported the sighting of a white tiger.
Zhūgě Kè attacked Liù'ān,
defeated the camp of the Wèi general Xiè Shùn,
and captured its people.
In the winter, the eleventh month,
Chancellor Gù Yōng passed away.
In the twelfth month,
Fúnán King Fàn Zhān sent envoys to offer musicians and local products.
This year,
Sīmǎ Xuān Wáng led an army into Shū.
Zhūgě Kè moved from Wǎn to Cháisāng.
In the spring, the first month of the seventh year,
Grand General Lù Xùn was appointed Chancellor.
In the autumn,
Wǎnlíng reported the growth of auspicious grain.
This year,
Bù Zhì, Zhū Rán, and others separately submitted memorials, stating:
"Those who returned from Shǔ
all say that [Shǔ] intends to break the alliance and communicate with Wèi,
building many boats and ships and repairing cities and fortifications.
Furthermore, Jiǎng Wǎn, guarding Hànzhōng,
upon hearing that Sīmǎ Yì was moving south,
did not send troops to take advantage of the emptiness to support from both sides,
but instead abandoned Hànzhōng
and returned close to Chéngdū.
The matter is already clear and manifest,
leaving no room for doubt.
Preparations should be made."
Quán considered it unlikely
and said:
"My treatment of Shǔ has not been meager.
With invitations, tributes, alliances, and oaths,
I owe them nothing.
Why would this happen?
Moreover, Sīmǎ Yì previously entered Shū
and retreated within ten days.
Shǔ is ten thousand *lǐ* away.
How could they know the urgency and immediately send troops?
In the past, when Wèi wanted to enter Hànchuān,
this region only then became vigilant
and had not yet taken action.
They halted upon hearing that Wèi had returned.
How can Shǔ possibly be doubted again for this?
Furthermore, when people govern a state,
how can they not maintain
boats, ships, cities, and fortifications?
Now, when this region mobilizes its army,
is it again with the intent to defend against Shǔ?
People's words are truly not to be trusted.
I, the Emperor, will vouch for them with my family."
Shǔ indeed had no such plans,
just as Quán had anticipated.
In the spring, the second month of the eighth year,
Chancellor Lù Xùn passed away.
In the summer,
thunder and lightning struck the palace gate pillars
and also hit the main pillars of the Nánjīn Great Bridge.
The Hóngshǔi River in Chálíng County overflowed,
sweeping away over two hundred households.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
General Mǎ Mào and others plotted rebellion
and were exterminated with their three clans.
In the eighth month,
there was a general amnesty.
Commandant Chén Xūn was dispatched with thirty thousand *túntián* colonists and laborers to dig the central road of Jùróng,
from Xiǎoqí to Yúnyáng Xīchéng,
to connect markets
and build storehouses.
In the spring, the second month of the ninth year,
Chariot and Cavalry General Zhū Rán campaigned against Wèi Zǔzhōng,
beheading and capturing over a thousand.
In the summer, the fourth month,
Wǔchāng reported the descent of sweet dew.
In the autumn, the ninth month,
Galloping Cavalry General Bù Zhì was appointed Chancellor,
Chariot and Cavalry General Zhū Rán was appointed Left Grand Marshal,
Guard General Quán Cóng was appointed Right Grand Marshal,
General Who Guards the South Lǚ Dài was appointed Grand General,
and General Who Commands the North Zhūgě Kè was appointed General.
In the spring, the first month of the tenth year,
Right Grand Marshal Quán Cóng passed away.
In the second month,
Quán visited the Southern Palace.
In the third month,
the Tàichū Palace was rebuilt.
All generals and officials of the commanderies and provinces contributed labor.
In the summer, the fifth month,
Chancellor Bù Zhì passed away.
In the winter, the tenth month,
capital offenses were pardoned.
In the spring, the first month of the eleventh year,
Zhū Rán fortified Jiānglíng.
In the second month,
there was another earthquake.
In the third month,
the palace was completed.
In the summer, the fourth month,
there was a hailstorm.
Yúnyáng reported the sighting of a yellow dragon.
In the fifth month,
Póyáng reported the manifestation of a white tiger.
An imperial edict stated:
"In ancient times, the sagely kings accumulated good deeds
and cultivated themselves and practiced the Dao
to possess the world.
Therefore, auspicious omens responded to them,
thereby manifesting their virtue.
How can I, being unenlightened,
achieve this?
The *Shū* says, 'Though in rest, do not rest.'
Let the ducal ministers and all officials
diligently perform their duties
to rectify my deficiencies."
In the spring, the third month of the twelfth year,
Left Grand Marshal Zhū Rán passed away.
In the fourth month,
two crows were seen carrying a magpie, which fell at Dōngguǎn.
On *bǐngyín* day,
Galloping Cavalry General Zhū Jù was appointed Acting Chancellor,
and offered the magpie as a sacrifice by burning it.
In the summer, the fifth month of the thirteenth year,
on the solstice,
Huǒxīng entered Nándǒu.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
it encroached upon the second star of Kuí and moved eastward.
In the eighth month,
the mountains in Dānyáng, Jùróng, Gùzhāng, and Níngguó collapsed,
and the Hóngshǔi River overflowed.
An imperial edict remitted outstanding debts
and provided loans of seeds and food.
Crown Prince Hé was deposed
and resided in Gùzhāng.
King Bà of Lǔ was granted death.
In the winter, the tenth month,
Wèi general Wén Qīn feigned defection to lure Zhū Yì.
Quán dispatched Lǚ Jù to join Yì to welcome Qīn.
Yì and others were cautious,
and Qīn dared not advance.
In the eleventh month,
Zǐ Liàng was established as Crown Prince.
An army of one hundred thousand was dispatched
to build Tángyì Tútáng to inundate the northern road.
In the twelfth month,
Wèi Grand General Wáng Chǎng besieged Nánjùn.
Jīngzhōu Inspector Wáng Jī attacked Xīlíng.
Generals Dài Liè and Lù Kǎi were dispatched to resist them,
and both Wáng Chǎng and Wáng Jī withdrew.
This year,
a divine being imparted a text,
announcing a change of reign year and the establishment of an empress.
In the summer, fifth month of the first year of Tài-Yuán,
Empress Pān Shì was enthroned.
There was a general amnesty,
and the reign title was changed.
Previously, in Luó-Yáng County, Lín-Hǎi Commandery, there was a spirit
that called itself Wáng Biǎo.
It moved among the common people;
its speech and diet
were no different from a human's,
yet its form was never seen.
It also had a maid,
named Fǎng-Jì.
In this month,
Zhōng-Shū Láng Lǐ Chóng was sent with the seal and ribbon of Fǔ-Guó Jiāng-Jūn, King of Luó-Yáng, to welcome Biǎo.
Biǎo accompanied Chóng out,
and conversed with Chóng and the local commandery administrators and prefects.
Chóng and the others found no fault in him.
Whenever they passed mountains and rivers,
he would send his maid to communicate with their spirits.
In autumn, seventh month,
Chóng and Biǎo arrived.
Sūn Quán temporarily built a residence for him outside the Cāng-Lóng Gate
and repeatedly sent close ministers with food and drink.
Biǎo spoke of minor matters like droughts and floods,
which often proved true.
On the first day of autumn, eighth month,
there was a great wind.
The rivers and sea surged and overflowed,
the flat ground was eight *chǐ* deep.
The pines and cypresses of Wú Gāo-Líng were uprooted,
and the south gate of the commandery city flew off.
In winter, eleventh month,
there was a general amnesty.
Sūn Quán returned after sacrificing at the southern suburb
and fell ill.
In twelfth month,
Dà-Jiāng-Jūn Zhū-Gě Kè was summoned by urgent dispatch
and appointed Tài-Zǐ Tài-Fù.
An edict ordered the reduction of corvée labor
and taxes,
and the removal of hardships suffered by the people.
In spring, first month of the second year,
the former Crown Prince Hé was made King of Nán-Yáng,
residing in Cháng-Shā;
his son Fèn was made King of Qí,
residing in Wǔ-Chāng;
and his son Xiū was made King of Láng-Yé,
residing in Hǔ-Lín.
In second month,
there was a general amnesty,
and the reign title was changed to Shén-Fèng.
Empress Pān Shì passed away.
Various generals and officials frequently visited Wáng Biǎo to ask for blessings,
but Biǎo disappeared.
In summer, fourth month,
Sūn Quán passed away,
at the age of seventy-one.
His posthumous title was Dà Huáng-Dì.
In autumn, seventh month,
he was buried at Jiāng-Líng.
The assessment states: Sūn Quán humbled himself and endured humiliation,
relied on talent and valued strategy.
He possessed the extraordinary heroism of Gōu Jiàn,
truly a hero among men.
Thus, he was able to control the region south of the Yangtze
and establish the enterprise of a tripartite division.
However, his nature was prone to suspicion and jealousy,
and he was resolute in killing.
As he reached his later years,
this tendency became increasingly severe.
Even slanders caused actions to be extinguished,
and his heirs were deposed and perished.
How can this be called planning for his descendants to bring peace and assist his sons?
His later generations declined,
eventually leading to the downfall of the state.
This may not be unrelated to these factors.
The Third Account of the Three Successor Rulers
Sūn Liàng, courtesy name Zǐ-Míng,
was Sūn Quán's youngest son.
Sūn Quán was advanced in years,
and Liàng was the youngest,
so he paid him particular attention.
His elder sister, Princess Quán, had once slandered Crown Prince Hé and his mother,
and felt uneasy in her heart.
Thus, relying on Sūn Quán's intentions,
she wanted to secure her own position beforehand.
She frequently praised the daughter of Quán Shàng
and urged that she be taken as Liàng's consort.
In the thirteenth year of Chì-Wū,
Hé was deposed,
and Sūn Quán then established Liàng as Crown Prince,
taking the Quán clan woman as his consort.
In the summer of the first year of Tài-Yuán,
Liàng's mother, Pān Shì, was established as Empress.
In winter,
Sūn Quán fell ill.
He summoned Dà-Jiāng-Jūn Zhū-Gě Kè to be Tài-Zǐ Tài-Fù,
and Huì-Jī Tài-Shǒu Téng Yìn to be Tài-Cháng,
both receiving edicts to assist the Crown Prince.
In the fourth month of the following year,
Sūn Quán passed away.
The Crown Prince ascended the throne,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the reign title.
This year
was the fourth year of Jiā-Píng of Wèi.
[Jiàn-Xīng First Year] In the intercalary month,
Kè was appointed Dì Tài-Fù,
Yìn was appointed Wèi Jiāng-Jūn and concurrently held the position of Shàng-Shū Shì.
Shàng-Dà-Jiāng-Jūn Lǚ Dài was made Dà Sī-Mǎ.
All civil and military officials in office were promoted in rank and awarded.
Superfluous officials were also upgraded.
In winter, tenth month,
Tài-Fù Kè led an army to blockade Cháo-Hú,
(Cháo pronunciation is *zǔ liǎo* inverse)
and built a city at Dōng-Xīng,
ordering Jiāng-Jūn Quán Duān to guard the west city,
and Dū-Wèi Liú Lüè to guard the east city.
On the *bǐng-shēn* day, the first day of twelfth month,
there was a great wind, thunder, and lightning.
Wèi sent Jiāng-Jūn Zhū-Gě Dàn, Hú Zūn, and others with seventy thousand infantry and cavalry to besiege Dōng-Xīng.
Jiāng-Jūn Wáng Chǎng attacked Nán-Jùn,
and Wú-Qiū Jiǎn advanced towards Wǔ-Chāng.
On the *jiǎ-yín* day,
Kè marched with a large army to meet the enemy.
On the *wù-wǔ* day,
the army reached Dōng-Xīng and engaged in battle,
severely defeating the Wèi army,
killing Jiāng-Jūn Hán Zōng, Huán Jiā, and others.
In this month,
there was thunder and rain.
Heaven inflicted disaster on the Duān-Mén of Wǔ-Chāng;
the Duān-Mén was rebuilt,
and then disaster again struck the inner palace.
In spring, first month, *bǐng-yín* day of the second year,
Empress Quán Shì was enthroned,
and there was a general amnesty.
On the *gēng-wǔ* day,
Wáng Chǎng and others all retreated.
In second month,
the army returned from Dōng-Xīng,
and great rewards and enfeoffments were bestowed.
In third month,
Kè led an army to attack Wèi.
In summer, fourth month,
he besieged Xīn-Chéng,
where a great plague occurred,
killing more than half of the soldiers.
In autumn, eighth month,
Kè withdrew his army and returned.
In winter, tenth month,
a grand banquet was held.
Wǔ-Wèi Jiāng-Jūn Sūn Jùn ambushed and killed Kè in the palace hall.
There was a general amnesty.
Jùn was appointed Chéng-Xiàng
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Fù-Chūn.
In eleventh month,
five large birds were seen at Chūn-Shēn.
(The following year the reign title was changed) The reign title was changed the following year.
In the summer of the first year of Wǔ-Fèng,
there was a great flood.
In autumn,
Wú-Hóu Yīng plotted to kill Jùn,
but was discovered,
and Yīng committed suicide.
In winter, eleventh month,
a star obscured Dǒu and Niú.
In the second year, in spring, the first month,
Wèi’s General Who Guards the East, Wúqiū Jiǎn, and Former General Wén Qīn, with the forces from Huáinán, advanced westward,
and fought at Lèjiā.
In the intercalary month, on the day Rénchén,
Jùn, along with Cavalry General Lǚ Jù and Left General Liú Zàn, led troops to attack Shòuchūn.
Their army reached Dōngxīng
and heard that Qīn and others had been defeated.
On the day Rén’yín,
the army advanced to Tuógāo.
Qīn went to Jùn and surrendered,
and tens of thousands of the remaining people from Huáinán came to defect.
Wèi’s Zhūgě Dàn entered Shòuchūn,
and Jùn withdrew his army.
In the second month,
Jùn met with Wèi General Cáo Zhēn at Gāotíng,
engaged in battle,
and Zhēn suffered a crushing defeat.
Liú Zàn was defeated at Gūpī by Jiǎng Bān, a detached general under Dàn,
and Zàn, along with Generals Sūn Léng and Jiǎng Xiū, were all killed.
In the third month,
General Who Guards the South, Zhū Yì, was sent to attack Ānfēng,
but did not succeed.
In autumn, the seventh month,
Generals Sūn Yí, Zhāng Yí, Lín Xún, and others plotted to assassinate Jùn.
The plot was discovered,
Yí committed suicide,
and Xún and others were executed.
At Lílǐ Shān in Yángxiàn, a large rock stood up on its own.
Court Grandee of the Guards Féng Cháo was sent to fortify Guǎnglíng,
and General Wú Ráng was appointed Administrator of Guǎnglíng,
and Liú Lüè was appointed Administrator of Dōnghǎi.
This year there was a great drought.
In the twelfth month,
the Grand Ancestral Temple was constructed.
Féng Cháo was made Inspector-Envoy,
supervising military affairs in Xúzhōu.
The people suffered from famine,
and the soldiers resented and rebelled.
In the first year of Tàipíng, in spring,
on the first day of the second month,
Jiànyè caught fire.
Jùn adopted the plan of General Who Conquers the North Wén Qīn
to lead a campaign against Wèi.
In the eighth month,

Qīn, along with Cavalry General Lǚ Jù, Chariot and Cavalry General Liú Zuǎn, General Who Guards the South Zhū Yì, and Former General Táng Zī, were first dispatched with their armies to enter the Huái and Sì Rivers from Jiāngdū.
In the ninth month, on the day Dīnghài,
Jùn died.
His younger cousin, the Partial General Lín, was made Attendant at the Palace and General of the Martial Guard,
and given command of all military affairs inside and outside the court.
Jù and others were recalled.
When [Jù] heard that Lín had replaced Jùn,
he was greatly enraged.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Grand Marshal Lǚ Dài died.
On the day Rénchén,
Tàibái (Venus) encroached upon the Southern Dipper.
Jù, Qīn, Zī, and others submitted a memorial recommending General of the Guards Téng Yìn as Chancellor,
but Lín did not approve.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Yìn was instead made Grand Marshal,
replacing Lǚ Dài and stationed at Wǔchāng.
Jù led his troops back,
intending to punish Lín.
Lín sent envoys with imperial edicts to inform and instruct Qīn, Zī, and others,
ordering them to apprehend Jù.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Dīngwèi,
Sūn Xiàn, along with Dīng Fèng and Shī Kuān, were sent with a naval force to intercept Jù at Jiāngdū.
General Liú Chéng was sent to supervise infantry and cavalry to attack Yìn.
Yìn’s army was defeated and annihilated.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the era name was changed.
On the day Xīnhài,
Lǚ Jù was captured at Xīnzhōu.
In the eleventh month,
Lín was made Grand General and granted the authority of Jiǎjié,
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yǒngníng.
Sūn Xiàn and General Wáng Dūn plotted to assassinate Lín.
When the plot was discovered,
Lín killed Dūn,
and forced Xiàn to commit suicide.
In the twelfth month,
Diāo Xuán, the Gentleman of the Household of the Five Offices, was sent to report the unrest to Shǔ.
In the second year, in spring, the second month, on the day Jiǎyín,
there was heavy rain,
thunder, and lightning.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
it snowed,
and it was extremely cold.
The eastern part of Chángshā was made Xiāngdōng Commandery,
the western part Hēngyáng Commandery.
The eastern part of Kuàijī was made Línhǎi Commandery,
and the eastern part of Yùzhāng was made Línchuān Commandery.
In summer, the fourth month,
Liàng presided over the main hall,
granted a general amnesty,
and began to personally handle government affairs.
Many of the memorials submitted by Lín
were met with difficulties and questions.
Furthermore, he conscripted sons and younger brothers of soldiers aged eighteen and below, but fifteen and above,
obtaining over three thousand men,
and selected young, brave, and strong sons of great generals to be their commanders.
Liàng said:
“I established this army
desiring to grow together with them.”
He drilled them daily in the imperial park.
In the fifth month,
Wèi’s General Who Conquers the East Zhūgě Dàn, with the forces of Huáinán, held the city of Shòuchūn,
and sent General Zhū Chéng to declare allegiance and submit a memorial,
and also sent his son Jìng, Chief Clerk Wú Gāng, and other sons and younger brothers of Tooth-gate officers as hostages.
In the sixth month,
Wén Qīn, Táng Zī, Quán Duān, and others were sent with thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to relieve Dàn.
Zhū Yì, from Húlín, led his forces to attack Xiàkǒu,
and Sūn Yī, the Inspector of Xiàkǒu, fled to Wèi.
In autumn, the seventh month,
Lín led his forces to relieve Shòuchūn,
and encamped at Huòlǐ.
Zhū Yì arrived from Xiàkǒu.
Lín made Yì the Front Commander,
and with Dīng Fèng and others, led fifty thousand armored soldiers to lift the siege.
In the eighth month,
the southern part of Kuàijī rebelled,
killing the commandant.
People from Póyáng and Xīndū caused disturbances.
Grand Judge Dīng Mì, Infantry Commandant Zhèng Zhòu, and General Zhōnglí Mù led armies to suppress them.
Zhū Yì, whose soldiers lacked food, withdrew.
Lín was greatly enraged.
On the first day of the ninth month, Jǐsì,
Yì was killed at Huòlǐ.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Lín returned from Huòlǐ to Jiànyè.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
In the eleventh month,
Quán Xù’s sons Yī and Yí fled to Wèi with their mother.
In the twelfth month,
Quán Duān, Yì, and others went from the city of Shòuchūn to Grand Marshal Sīmǎ Wénwáng.
In the third year, in spring, the first month,
Zhūgě Dàn killed Wén Qīn.
In the third month,
Grand Marshal Sīmǎ Wénwáng captured Shòuchūn.
Dàn and his retinue fought to the death,
and his generals, officials, and subordinates all surrendered.
In autumn, the seventh month,
the former King of Qí, Fèn, was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhāng’ān.
An imperial edict ordered commanderies and prefectures to fell timber for palace construction.
From the eighth month, it was overcast without rain for over forty days.
Liàng, seeing Lín’s arrogance and arbitrary rule,
conspired with Grand Herald Quán Shàng
and General Liú Chéng to execute Lín.
In the ninth month, on the day Wùwǔ,
Lín used his troops to seize Shàng.
He sent his younger brother Ēn to attack and kill Chéng outside the Cānglóng Gate.
He summoned the high officials to gather at the palace gate,
deposed Liàng as the King of Kuàijī.
At the time, he was sixteen years old.
Sūn Xiū, courtesy name Zǐliè,
was the sixth son of Quán.
At thirteen,
he studied under the Palace Writers Shè Cí and Shèng Chōng.
In the first month of the second year of Tàiyuán,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lángxié,
residing in Hǔlín.
In the fourth month,
Quán died,
and Xiū's younger brother, Liàng, succeeded to the throne.
Zhūgě Kè held political power
and did not wish for the princes to be in areas with military forces bordering the river.
So, Xiū was moved to Dānyáng Commandery.
The Administrator, Lǐ Héng, repeatedly encroached upon Xiū's affairs,
so Xiū submitted a petition requesting to be moved to another commandery.
An imperial edict ordered him moved to Kuàijī.
After residing there for several years,
he dreamt of riding a dragon to heaven,
and looking back, he could not see its tail.
Upon waking, he found it unusual.
When Sūn Liàng was deposed,
on the day Jǐwèi,
Sūn Chěn sent the Imperial Clan Director Sūn Kǎi and Palace Writer Dǒng Cháo to welcome Xiū.
When Xiū first heard the news,
he was suspicious.
Kǎi and Cháo fully explained Chěn's original intention for the welcome.
After staying for one day and two nights,
he departed.
On the day Wùyín in the tenth month,
as he traveled to Qū'ā,
an old man bowed to Xiū and said:
"Delay will cause change;
the world is anxiously awaiting.
May Your Majesty proceed quickly!"
Xiū approved of this,
and on that day, he advanced to the Bùsài Pavilion.
Wǔwèi General Ēn, acting as Chancellor,
led the hundred officials with the imperial carriage and ceremonial escort to welcome him at Yǒngchāng Pavilion.
A palace was built,
using a military tent as the temporary hall,
and the imperial seat was arranged.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Xiū arrived.
He stopped upon seeing the temporary hall
and sent Sūn Kǎi to see Ēn first.
When Kǎi returned,
Xiū advanced in his palanquin,
and the assembled officials bowed twice, declaring themselves his subjects.
Xiū ascended to the temporary hall,
humbly not immediately taking the imperial seat,
but staying in the east wing.
The Minister of Household Registrations stepped forward to the foot of the stairs to present his commendation,
and the Chancellor offered the imperial seal and tally.
Xiū declined three times,
and the assembled officials requested three times.
Xiū said:
"Since the generals, ministers, and marquises all recommend this humble person,
how dare I not accept the imperial seal and tally?"
The assembled officials then successively led the way,
and Xiū took the imperial carriage.
The hundred officials accompanied him in their positions.
Chěn, with a thousand soldiers, welcomed him in the middle of the fields,
bowing by the roadside.
Xiū descended from his carriage and returned the bow.
On the same day,
he entered the main hall,
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
This year
was the third year of Gānlù of Wèi.
In the tenth month, on the day Rénwǔ, of the first year of Yǒng'ān,
an imperial edict stated:
"To praise virtue and reward merit
is a universal principle of ancient and modern times.
Therefore, Grand General Chěn is appointed Chancellor and Governor of Jīngzhōu,
with an increase of five counties to his emolument.
Wǔwèi General Ēn is appointed Grandee Secretary, General of the Guard, and Central Army Commander,
enfeoffed as a county marquis.
Wēiyuǎn General Jù is appointed Right General and a county marquis.
Piān General Gàn is appointed a miscellaneous general and a pavilion marquis.
Chángshuǐ Commandant Zhāng Bù, for his diligent assistance and guidance,
is appointed Fǔyì General,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngkāng.
Dǒng Cháo, for personally welcoming the emperor,
is enfeoffed as a township marquis."
Another imperial edict stated:
"Dānyáng Administrator Lǐ Héng,
due to the suspicion of past events,
has surrendered himself to the authorities.
Indeed, like Shè Gōu and Zhǎn Qū,
when the ruler is ruler,
Lǐ Héng is to be sent back to his commandery;
he should not be allowed to doubt himself."
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Sūn Hào was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wūchéng,
Hào's younger brother Dé as the Marquis of Qiántáng,
and Qiān as the Marquis of Yǒng'ān.
In the eleventh month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the wind changed direction four or five times,
and dense fog lasted for several days.
All five marquises of Chěn's family controlled the imperial guards,
wielding power that overshadowed the sovereign.
Whatever they proposed,
it was respectfully obeyed without dissent,
which made them even more arrogant.
Xiū feared they might cause trouble,
so he repeatedly bestowed rewards upon them.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Grand General, with his loyal and sincere heart,
first proposed the great plan to secure the state.
All civil and military officials, inside and outside the court,
supported his proposal,
and all contributed meritorious service.
In the past, when Huò Guāng made his decision,
all the officials were of one mind;
there was no greater precedent than this.
Immediately investigate the names of those who were consulted and finalized the plan and reported it to the ancestral temple previously.
For those who, according to precedent, should be granted titles and ranks,
promptly carry out the implementation."
On the day Wùxū,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Grand General commands all military affairs, internal and external.
His responsibilities are numerous and burdensome.
Therefore, General of the Guard and Grandee Secretary Ēn is to assist,
sharing and reducing the various duties with the Grand General."
On the day Rénzǐ,
an imperial edict stated:
"For officials whose families have five or three members serving concurrently,
with fathers and elder brothers in the capital while sons and younger brothers serve as commandery or county officials,
who both pay the limited grain and are conscripted for military expeditions,
such that there is no one to manage family affairs,
I am deeply sympathetic to this.
For those who have five or three members serving,
allow their fathers and elder brothers to choose who to keep.
Keep one person,
exempt them from the grain limit,
and they shall not be conscripted for military expeditions."
It also said:
"All generals and officials who welcomed and accompanied the emperor at Yǒngchāng Pavilion
shall all have their rank increased by one grade."
Not long after,
Xiū heard of Chěn's treacherous plot
and secretly conspired with Zhāng Bù.
On the day Wùchén in the twelfth month, during the winter sacrifice,
when all officials offered their New Year's greetings,
and the high officials ascended the hall,
an imperial edict commanded warriors to bind Chěn.
On the same day, he was executed.
On the day Jǐsì,
an imperial edict appointed Left General Zhāng Bù to suppress the treacherous minister.
Bù was promoted to Central Army Commander,
his younger brother Dùn was enfeoffed as Dū Tínghóu
and given three hundred soldiers,
and Dùn's younger brother Xún was appointed Commandant.
An imperial edict stated:
"In ancient times, when establishing a state,
education was prioritized,
to guide the world and refine character,
and to nurture talent for the times.
Since Jiànxīng,
events have been numerous,
and officials and common people have somewhat pursued immediate trends,
abandoning fundamentals for trivialities,
not following ancient ways.
If what is valued is not substantial,
then it harms culture and corrupts customs.
Therefore, establish educational officials according to ancient customs,
appoint Five Classics Scholars,
rigorously select suitable candidates,
grant them favor and emoluments,
and instruct existing officials and the sons and younger brothers of generals and officials who possess aspirations and good character
to each pursue their studies.
After one year, assess them through examinations,
differentiate their grades,
and grant them positions and rewards.
This will make those who see it delight in its glory,
and those who hear of it envy its reputation,
thereby strengthening royal transformation
and promoting customs."
In the second year, in spring, the first month,
there was thunder and lightning.
In the third month,
the offices of the Nine Ministers were established.
An imperial edict stated:
“I, being without virtue,
am entrusted above the kings and dukes.
From dawn to dusk, I am filled with trepidation,
forgetting sleep and food.
Now I wish to cease military activities and cultivate literary arts,
to promote great civilization.
Following this principle,
it is necessary for the common people to be self-sufficient,
which absolutely requires agriculture and sericulture.
Guǎn Zǐ has said: ‘When granaries are full,
people know propriety;
when clothing and food are abundant,
people know honor and shame.’
If one man does not farm,
someone suffers hunger;
if one woman does not weave,
someone suffers cold.
That hunger and cold arrive together and the people do not commit wrongdoing,
this has never happened.
Since recent years,
many officials and common people in the commanderies and counties, as well as soldiers in various camps,
have neglected this occupation.
They all float boats on the Long Jiāng,
engaging in trade up and down,
good fields are gradually abandoned,
and the visible grain decreases daily.
How can we achieve great stability
under such circumstances?
Perhaps it is also because the tax burden is too heavy,
and the farmers’ profits are meager,
which causes this!
Now I wish to greatly expand agricultural enterprises,
lighten their taxes,
classify levies based on strength and weakness,
and assess their fields and acres,
making sure they are fair and equitable,
so that both public and private interests are well-served,
and every household is self-sufficient,
able to support each other.
Then they will cherish their lives and value their existence,
not violating laws and regulations.
Only then will punishments be unnecessary,
and customs can be rectified.
With the loyalty and virtue of my assembled officials,
if they devote themselves wholeheartedly to the times,
even the flourishing civilization of high antiquity,
though not achievable overnight,
and the peaceful prosperity of Hàn Wén Dì,
may perhaps be approached.
If we approach it, then both ruler and ministers will be honored;
if we do not, then there will be damage, diminution, and humiliation.
How can we remain complacent and simply go along?
All you ministers and Imperial Secretaries,
you should consult and deliberate together,
striving for what is convenient and good.
It is already time for farming and sericulture;
we cannot delay.
Once the matter is settled and implemented,
it will conform to my intention.”
In the third year, in spring, the third month,
Xīlíng reported the sighting of a red crow.
In autumn,
following the proposal of Commandant Yán Mì,
Pǔlǐ Táng was constructed.
In Kuàijī Commandery, there was a rumor that Wáng Liàng would return and become emperor.
Then Wáng Liàng’s palace women reported that Wáng Liàng had witches perform rituals and sacrifices,
with evil pronouncements.
The relevant authorities reported this.
He was demoted to Hóu of Hòuguān,
and dispatched to his fief.
He committed suicide on the way,
and his escorts were punished.
The southern part of Kuàijī was established as Jiàn'ān Commandery,
and Jiànpíng Commandery was established by partitioning Yídū.
In the fourth year, in summer, the fifth month,
there was heavy rain,
and springs overflowed.
In autumn, the eighth month,
Guānglù Dàfū Zhōu Yì and Shí Wěi were sent to inspect local customs,
observe the integrity of generals and officials,
and the hardships of the people,
for an edict of promotion and demotion.
In the ninth month,
Bùshān reported the sighting of a white dragon.
In this year,
Chén Jiāo, a commoner from Ānwú, died.
He was buried,
but six days later he revived,
emerging from beneath the earth.
In the fifth year, in spring, the second month,
the northern tower of Báihǔ Mén caught fire.
In autumn, the seventh month,
Shǐxīn reported the sighting of a yellow dragon.
On the day Rénwǔ in the eighth month,
there was heavy rain with thunder and lightning,
and springs overflowed.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
Empress Zhū Shì was established.
On the day Wùzǐ,
the son was established as Crown Prince,
and a general amnesty was granted.
In winter, the tenth month,
Wèi Jiāngjūn Púyáng Xìng was appointed Chancellor,
while Tíngwèi Dīng Mì and Guānglù Xūn Mèng Zōng were appointed Left and Right Imperial Censors.
Xiū, relying on Chancellor Xìng and Left General Zhāng Bù due to their old favor,
entrusted them with affairs.
Zhāng Bù managed the palace,
while Púyáng Xìng oversaw military and state matters.
Xiū was earnestly dedicated to classics,
wishing to thoroughly read all schools of thought.
He especially enjoyed pheasant hunting,
and often went out in the morning and returned at night during spring and summer,
only at these times setting aside his books.
Xiū wished to discuss principles and arts with Bóshì Jìjiǔ Wéi Yào and Bóshì Shèng Chōng.
Wéi Yào and Shèng Chōng were both known for their directness and integrity.
Zhāng Bù feared their admission
would expose his hidden transgressions,
preventing him from exercising exclusive control.
Thus, he fabricated excuses to obstruct them.
Xiū replied:
“When I delved into learning,
I have generally perused all books;
what I have seen is not little.
The affairs of wise rulers and ignorant kings,
treacherous ministers and rebellious sons,
the successes and failures of the worthy and the foolish, ancient and modern,
I have not failed to examine.
Now, Wéi Yào and the others are coming in
simply because I wish to discuss books with them;
it is not that I will begin to learn anew from Wéi Yào and the others.
Even if it were so,
what harm would there be?
You merely suppose that Wéi Yào and the others might reveal the treachery of your subordinates,
and that is why you do not want them to enter.
As for such matters,
I am already prepared for them myself;
I do not need Wéi Yào and the others to explain them to me.
This poses no harm at all;
your intention is simply due to some apprehension.”
Zhāng Bù received the edict, offered apologies,
and repeatedly explained himself,
also stating that he feared it would hinder state affairs.
Xiū replied:
“Regarding books,
the problem is when people do not like them;
liking them causes no harm.
There is nothing wrong with this,
yet you consider it improper,
which is why I have gone so far as to mention it.
State affairs and academic pursuits,
their currents are different;
they do not interfere with each other.
I did not expect that you, being in charge today,
would act in this manner towards me;
it is truly something I do not approve of.”
Zhāng Bù bowed, presenting his memorial, and kowtowed.
Xiū replied:
“I merely intended to enlighten you;
why go so far as to kowtow!
Your loyalty and sincerity,
are known far and wide.
What moved me in the past
is your eminence today.
The Shī Jīng says: ‘None lacks a beginning,
but few are able to persevere to the end.’
Persevering to the end is truly difficult;
you must persevere to the end.”
Initially, when Xiū was a king,
Zhāng Bù was the Left and Right Grand Overseer,
and was always trusted and loved.
Upon his ascension,
he greatly favored and treated him well.
Zhāng Bù usurped state power,
and committed many improprieties.
He himself was conscious of his flaws and shortcomings,
and feared that Wéi Yào and Shèng Chōng would speak of them,
hence his particular apprehension and jealousy.
Although Xiū understood this intention,
his heart was not pleased.
Fearing his suspicion and apprehension even more,
he ultimately yielded to Zhāng Bù’s wishes,
abandoned his lectures,
and no longer allowed Shèng Chōng and the others to enter.
In this year, he sent observers to Jiāozhǐ to procure peacocks and large pigs.
In the sixth year, summer, fourth month,
Quánlíng reported that a yellow dragon was seen.
Fifth month,
the officials Lǚ Xīng and others of Jiāozhǐ Commandery rebelled,
killing the Grand Administrator Sūn Xǔ.
Earlier, Sūn Xǔ had conscripted over a thousand artisans from the commandery and sent them to Jiànyè.
When a military inspection arrived,
fearing they would be taken again,
Lǚ Xīng and others used this to instigate soldiers and commoners,
and recruit various barbarian tribes.
Winter, tenth month,
Shǔ reported that Wèi was attacking them.
On Guǐwèi day,
a fire broke out in the small city of Shítóu in Jiànyè,
burning one hundred and eighty zhàng in the southwest.
On Jiǎshēn day,
Dīng Fèng, the Grand General, was sent to lead all the armies towards Wèi’s Shòuchūn.
General Líu Píng went separately to Shī Jì in Nánjùn
to discuss the direction of the military campaign.
Generals Dīng Fēng and Sūn Yì went to Miǎnzhōng,
all to rescue Shǔ.
When news arrived that Liú Chán, the lord of Shǔ, had surrendered to Wèi,
they then withdrew.
After Lǚ Xīng killed Sūn Xǔ,
he sent envoys to Wèi,
requesting a Grand Administrator and troops.
Prime Minister Púyáng Xīng raised ten thousand men from the Túntián (agricultural colonies) to form an army.
Wǔlíng was divided to establish Tiānmén Commandery.
In the seventh year, spring, first month,
there was a general amnesty.
Second month,
Lù Kàng, General Who Guards the Army, Bù Xié, General Who Protects the Army, Líu Píng, General Who Attacks the West, and Shèng Màn, Grand Administrator of Jiànpíng,
led their troops to besiege Luó Xiàn, the defending general of Bādōng in Shǔ.
Summer, fourth month,
Wáng Zhì, the Wèi general and Newly Attached Supervisor, entered Gōuzhāng by sea,
plundering the officials' [wealth] and over two hundred men and women.
General Sūn Yuè intercepted a boat
and captured thirty people.
Autumn, seventh month,
sea pirates plundered Hǎiyán,
killing Luò Xiù, the Salt Commissioner.
Liú Chuān, the Central Secretariat Gentleman, was sent to raise troops in Lúlíng.
Zhāng Jié and others, commoners from Yùzhāng, caused unrest,
with over ten thousand people.
Wèi sent General Hú Lì to invade Xīlíng with twenty thousand cavalry and infantry
to rescue Luó Xiàn.
Lù Kàng and the others withdrew their armies.
Jiāozhōu was again divided to establish Guǎngzhōu.
On Rénwǔ day,
there was a general amnesty.
On Guǐwèi day,
Xiū died,
aged thirty at the time,
and was posthumously named Emperor Jǐng.
Sūn Hào, courtesy name Yuánzōng,
was a grandson of Quán,
and son of Hé.
He was also known as Péngzǔ,
and courtesy name Hàozōng.
When Sūn Xiū ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Hào as Marquis of Wūchéng,
and sent him to his domain.
Jǐng Yǎng, a commoner from Xīhú, divined that Hào would become greatly noble.
Hào was secretly pleased but dared not reveal it.
When Xiū died,
Shǔ had just fallen,
and Jiāozhǐ had defected.
The country was shaken with fear,
desiring a grown ruler.
Wàn Yù, the Left Supervisor of the Army, had previously been Magistrate of Wūchéng,
and was on good terms with Hào.
He praised Hào's talent, insight, and decisive judgment,
saying he was a peer of Huán Wáng of Chángshā,
and moreover, fond of learning,
and respectful of laws and regulations.
He repeatedly spoke of this to Prime Minister Púyáng Xīng and Left General Zhāng Bù.
Púyáng Xīng and Zhāng Bù persuaded Empress Dowager Zhū, Xiū's empress,
to make Hào the successor.
Empress Zhū said:
"I am a widow,
how can I know the concerns of the state?
As long as Wú is not harmed,
and the ancestral temple has support, that is sufficient."
Thereupon, Hào was welcomed and enthroned,
aged twenty-three at the time.
The era name was changed,
and a general amnesty was declared.
This year
was the first year of Xiánxī in Wèi.
In the first year of Yuánxīng, eighth month,
Shī Jì, the Grand General Above, and Dīng Fèng, the Grand General, were made Grand Marshals of the Left and Right,
Zhāng Bù was made General of Agile Cavalry,
and granted the additional title of Palace Attendant.
All promotions in rank and rewards
were carried out as before.
Ninth month,
the Empress Dowager was demoted to Empress Jǐng.
His father Hé was posthumously named Emperor Wén.
His mother Hé was honored as Empress Dowager.
Tenth month,
Xiū's eldest son was enfeoffed as Prince of Yùzhāng,
the second son as Prince of Rǔnán,
the third son as Prince of Liáng,
the fourth son as Prince of Chén.
Empress Téng was enthroned.
Once Hào achieved his ambition,
he became crude, violent, arrogant, and excessive.
He was full of suspicions and taboos,
and fond of wine and women.
Both great and small lost hope.
Púyáng Xīng and Zhāng Bù secretly regretted it.
Someone slandered Hào,
and in the eleventh month,
Púyáng Xīng and Zhāng Bù were executed.
Twelfth month,
Sūn Xiū was buried in Dìnglíng.
Téng Mù, the father of the empress, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāomì.
His maternal uncle Hé Hóng and three others were all made marquises.
This year,
Wèi established the commandery of Jiāozhǐ with a Grand Administrator.
Jìn Wén Dì, as Chancellor of Wèi,
sent Xú Shào and Sūn Yù, former Wú generals who had surrendered from Shòuchūn city, bearing imperial orders and letters,
explaining the situation's advantages and disadvantages
to enlighten Hào.
In the first year of Gānlù, third month,
Hào sent envoys with Xú Shào and Sūn Yù to reply in a letter, saying:
"I know that with your exceptional talent,
you hold the position of Prime Minister.
Your efforts in gradual guidance
have been most diligent.
I, being unworthy,
have inherited the succession.
I desire to govern the world with the worthy and virtuous,
but due to separation, I have had no means of connection.
Your kind intentions are truly evident,
and I feel deeply attached.
Now I send Jì Zhì, Grand Master of Guanglu, and Hóng Qiú, Central Commandant of the Five Offices, to convey my utmost feelings."
Xú Shào traveled to Rúxū,
was recalled and killed.
His family was moved to Jiàn'ān.
This was because Xú Shào had earlier praised the beauty of the Central Plains.
Summer, fourth month,
Jiánglíng reported the descent of sweet dew.
Thereupon, the era name was changed and a general amnesty declared.
Autumn, seventh month,
Hào forced Empress Dowager Zhū to commit suicide.
She was not in the main palace hall when she died,
and her funeral was held in a small hut in the imperial garden.
Everyone knew it was not a natural illness,
and none were not deeply pained.
He also sent Xiū's four sons to Wúxiǎochéng,
and soon after recalled and killed the two elder ones.
Ninth month,
following the memorial of Bù Chǎn, Commander of Xīlíng,
the capital was moved to Wǔchāng.
Dīng Gù, Grandee Secretary, and Zhūgě Jìng, General of the Right, guarded Jiànyè.
Jì Zhì and Hóng Qiú arrived in Luòyáng,
and encountered the death of Jìn Wén Dì.
Eleventh month,
they were sent back.
When Hào arrived in Wǔchāng,
he again declared a general amnesty.
The southern part of Línglíng was made Shǐ'ān Commandery,
and the southern part of Guìyáng was made Shǐxīng Commandery.
Twelfth month,
Jìn received the abdication.
In the first month of the first year of Baodǐng,
Grand Herald Zhāng Yǎn and Gentleman of the Five Bureaus Dīng Zhōng were dispatched to mourn and offer sacrifices to Emperor Wén of Jìn.
When they returned,
Zhāng Yǎn died of illness on the way.
Dīng Zhōng told Hào:
"The North has not prepared its defensive and offensive equipment;
Yìyáng can be attacked and taken."
Hào consulted his officials, and
Grand General Guarding the West Lù Kǎi said:
"Warfare is used only when there is no other option.
Moreover, since the Three Kingdoms were established,
they have continuously invaded each other,
with no year of peace.
Now, a strong enemy has newly unified Bāshǔ,
possessing the reality of combined territory.
Yet they sent envoys to seek kinship,
wishing to cease military actions.
It cannot be said that they are seeking aid from us.
Currently, the enemy's strength is formidable,
and to seek victory by chance
does not appear to be advantageous."
General of Cavalry Liú Zuǎn said:
"Heaven created the five talents;
who can abandon weapons?
Deception and mutual competition
have existed from time immemorial.
If there is an opportunity,
how can it be abandoned?
It is advisable to send spies
to observe their situation."
Hào secretly adopted Liú Zuǎn's advice,
and also because Shǔ had just been pacified,
he did not proceed,
but nevertheless broke off relations.
In the eighth month,
reports came from various places of a great tripod being discovered.
Thereupon, the reign year was changed,
and a great amnesty was granted.
Lù Kǎi was made Left Chancellor,
and Palace Attendant Wàn Yù was made Right Chancellor.
In the tenth month of winter,
the Yong'ān mountain bandits Shī Dàn and others gathered several thousand people.
In the spring of the second year,
a great amnesty was granted.
Right Chancellor Wàn Yù went to garrison Bāqiū.
In the sixth month of summer,
Xiǎnmíng Palace was built.
In the twelfth month of winter,
Hào moved in.
In this year, Yùzhāng, Lúlíng, and Chángshā were divided to form Ānchéng Commandery.
In the second month of spring of the third year,
Left and Right Censors-in-chief Dīng Gù and Méng Rén were made Grand Minister of Agriculture (Sītú) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
In the ninth month of autumn,
Hào set out for Dōngguān,
and Dīng Fèng reached Héfèi.
In this year,
Liú Jùn, Governor of Jiāozhōu, and Xiū Zé, Front Army Supervisor, were dispatched to attack Jiāozhǐ.
They were defeated by Jìn generals Máo Jiǒng and others,
all died,
and their scattered troops returned to Hépǔ.
In the first month of spring of the first year of Jiànhéng,
his son Jǐn was appointed Crown Prince,
as well as the Princes of Huáiyáng and Dōngpíng.
In the tenth month of winter,
the reign year was changed,
and a great amnesty was granted.
In the eleventh month,
Left Chancellor Lù Kǎi passed away.
Inspector of the Army Yú Sì, General Awe-the-South Xuē Xǔ, and Administrator of Cāngwú Táo Huáng were sent via Jīngzhōu,
while Inspector of the Army Lǐ Xù and Army Supervisor Xú Cún went via the Jiàn'ān sea route,
all to converge on Hépǔ to attack Jiāozhǐ.
In the spring of the second year,
Wàn Yù returned to Jiànyè.
Lǐ Xù, finding the Jiàn'ān route impassable,
killed guide general Féng Fěi,
and led his army back.
In the third month,
a heavenly fire burned over ten thousand homes,
killing seven hundred people.
In the fourth month of summer,
Left Grand Marshal Shī Jì passed away.
Palace Commander Hé Dìng said:
"Privy Treasurer Lǐ Xù wrongly killed Féng Fěi
and arbitrarily withdrew his army."
Lǐ Xù and Xú Cún's families were all executed.
In the ninth month of autumn,
Hé Dìng led five thousand troops to hunt at Xiàkǒu.
Area Commander Sūn Xiù fled to Jìn.
A great amnesty was granted this year.
On the last day of the first month of spring of the third year,
Hào led a large army out of Huálǐ.
Hào's mother and consorts also traveled.
Palace Secretary Huá Hé and others strongly remonstrated,
and he then returned.
In this year,
Yú Sì and Táo Huáng defeated Jiāozhǐ,
captured and killed the Jìn-appointed commandant,
and Jiǔzhēn and Rìnán both returned to allegiance.
A great amnesty was granted,
and Jiāozhǐ was divided to form Xīnchāng Commandery.
The generals defeated Fúyán,
and established Wǔpíng Commandery.
Fàn Shèn, Supervisor of Wǔchāng, was made Grand Commandant.
Right Grand Marshal Dīng Fèng and Minister of Works Méng Rén passed away.
The Western Park reported that phoenixes had gathered,
so the next year's era name was changed.
In the eighth month of autumn of the first year of Fènghuáng,
Bù Chǎn, Supervisor of Xīlíng, was summoned.
Bù Chǎn did not respond,
but held the city and surrendered to Jìn.
Lù Kàng, Area Commander of Yuèxiāng, was sent to besiege and capture Bù Chǎn,
and all of Bù Chǎn's forces surrendered.
Bù Chǎn and dozens of others involved in the plot had their three clans exterminated.
A great amnesty was granted.
In this year, Right Chancellor Wàn Yù was reproached and died of grief;
his sons and younger brothers were exiled to Lúlíng.
Hé Dìng's depraved acts were discovered,
and he was executed.
Hào, considering his wickedness similar to Zhāng Bù's,
posthumously changed Hé Dìng's name to Bù.
In the third month of spring of the second year,
Lù Kàng was made Grand Marshal.
Grand Minister of Agriculture Dīng Gù passed away.
In the ninth month of autumn,
Huáiyáng was re-enfeoffed as Lǔ,
Dōngpíng as Qí,
and nine other princes including Chénliú and Zhānglíng were enfeoffed,
totaling eleven princes,
each prince was granted three thousand soldiers.
A great amnesty was granted.
One of Hào's beloved concubines sent people to the market to rob and plunder people's property.
Market Superintendent Chén Shēng,
who was usually favored by Hào,
presuming on Hào's favor,
enforced the law against her.
The concubine complained to Hào,
and Hào was furious.
On a pretext, he had Chén Shēng's head sawn off
and his body thrown down from the Sìwàng tower.
In this year,
Grand Commandant Fàn Shèn passed away.
In the third year,
a prophetic rumor in Kuàijī claimed that the Marquis of Zhāng'ān, Fèn, would become the Son of Heaven.
Administrator of Línhǎi, Xī Xī, wrote a letter to Administrator of Kuàijī, Guō Dàn,
criticizing national policies.
Guō Dàn only reported Xī Xī's letter
but not the prophetic rumor,
and was sent to Jiàn'ān to build ships.
Hé Zhí, Supervisor of the Three Commanderies, was sent to arrest Xī Xī.
Xī Xī raised troops to defend himself
and cut off the sea route.
Xī Xī's subordinates killed Xī Xī,
sent his head to Jiànyè,
and his three clans were exterminated.
In the seventh month of autumn,
twenty-five envoys were dispatched to various prefectures and commanderies
to investigate and apprehend fugitives.
Grand Marshal Lù Kàng passed away.
From the change of reign year until this year,
there was a continuous great plague.
Yùlín was divided to form Guìlín Commandery.
In the first year of Tiāncè,
Wú Commandery reported digging up silver,
one foot long,
three fen wide,
with year and month characters engraved on it.
Thereupon, a great amnesty was granted,
and the reign year was changed.
In the first year of Tiānxǐ,
Wújùn reported that Língpíng Hú, which had been choked with weeds since the end of the Hàn dynasty,
was now open again.
Elders passed down the saying,
"When this lake is blocked,
the world is in chaos.
When this lake opens,
the world is at peace."
Also, by the lake, a stone casket was found.
Inside it was a small stone,
bluish-white,
four cùn long,
more than two cùn wide,
with the character "Huángdì" (Emperor) carved on it.
Thereupon, the regnal year was changed,
and a general amnesty was issued.
The Grand Administrator of Kuàijī, Chē Jùn, and the Grand Administrator of Xiāngdōng, Zhāng Yǒng, did not pay the poll tax.
They were executed on the spot,
their heads displayed in all the commanderies.
In the eighth month of autumn,
the Capital Commandant, Sūn Kǎi, surrendered to the Jìn.
Póyáng reported that the stone patterns on Lìyáng Shān formed characters,
twenty in all,
saying:
"Chǔ is the islet of the Nine Provinces,
Wú is the capital of the Nine Provinces.
A scholar from Yángzhōu
will become Son of Heaven,
ruling for four generations,
and then great peace will begin."
Also, on Yángxiàn Shān in Wúxīng, there was a hollow stone,
more than ten zhàng long,
named Shíshì (Stone Chamber).
It was reported as a great auspicious omen from the locality.
Then, Jiān Sītú Dǒng Cháo and Jiān Tàicháng Zhōu Chǔ were sent to Yángxiàn Xiàn
to perform the fēngshàn sacrifices on Guó Shān.
(The next year was changed) [Changed to the next year] The first year,
a general amnesty was granted
to accord with the stone inscription.
In the summer of the first year of Tiānjì,
the Commandant of Xiàkǒu, Sūn Shèn, attacked Jiāngxià and Rǔnán,
burning and plundering the inhabitants.
Previously,
the palace attendant Zhāng Chù had slandered many,
and was successively promoted to Sīzhí Zhōnglángjiàng,
enfeoffed as a marquis,
and greatly favored.
In this year, his wicked deeds came to light,
and he was executed.
In the seventh month of autumn of the second year,
eleven kings were enfeoffed, including Chéngjì and Xuānwēi.
Each king was given three thousand soldiers,
and a general amnesty was issued.
In the summer of the third year,
Guō Mǎ rebelled.
Mǎ was originally a military supervisor under Xiū Yǔn, the Grand Administrator of Hépǔ.
When Yǔn was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Guìlín,
he fell ill
and stayed in Guǎngzhōu,
first sending Mǎ with five hundred soldiers to the commandery to pacify the various barbarians.
After Yǔn died,
the soldiers were to be redistributed.
Mǎ and his troops, who had been an old army for generations,
were unwilling to be separated.
At that time, Hào also ordered a census of households in Guǎngzhōu.
Mǎ, along with his military commanders Hé Diǎn, Wáng Zú, Wú Shù, and Yīn Xīng, used this to incite fear among the soldiers and civilians,
gathered a large crowd,
and attacked and killed the Guǎngzhōu Commandant, Yú Shòu.
Mǎ proclaimed himself Overall Supervisor of Military Affairs of Jiāo and Guǎng Two Provinces and General Who Pacifies the South;
Xīng became the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu;
Shù became the Grand Administrator of Nánhǎi.
Diǎn attacked Cāngwú,
and Zú attacked Shǐxīng.
In the eighth month,
the Army Advisor, Zhāng Tì, was appointed Chancellor,
and the Commandant of Niúzhǔ, Hé Zhí, was appointed Minister of Works.
The Commander of the Palace Guard, Téng Xún, was appointed Grand Guardian.
Before he was invested,
he was transferred to General Who Guards the South,
given the staff of authority, and appointed Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
He led ten thousand men from the eastern route to attack Mǎ,
and encountered Zú at Shǐxīng,
but was unable to advance.
Mǎ killed Liú Lüè, the Grand Administrator of Nánhǎi,
and drove away Xú Qí, the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
Hào also sent Xú Líng to oversee Táo Jùn, who led seven thousand men from the western route,
and ordered Táo Huáng, the Governor of Jiāozhōu, to marshal his forces and the troops from Hépǔ and Yùlín commanderies,
to jointly attack Mǎ with the eastern and western armies.
A "ghost-eye vegetable" grew in the house of a worker, Huáng Jiā.
It wound around a date tree,
was more than a zhàng long,
its stem four cùn wide,
and three fēn thick.
Another "buy vegetable" grew in the house of a worker, Wú Píng.
It was four chǐ high,
three fēn thick,
shaped like a loquat,
one chǐ eight cùn wide at the top,
and five cùn wide at the stem below,
with green leaves growing on both sides.
The Eastern Bureau examined the illustrations,
naming the "ghost-eye" as zhīzhǎo (auspicious fungus),
and the "buy vegetable" as pínglǜzhǎo (calm-thought fungus).
Consequently, [Huáng Jiā] was appointed Shìzhī Láng (Gentleman Attendant to the Auspicious Fungus),
and [Wú Píng] Pínglǜ Láng (Gentleman of Calm Thought),
both with silver seals and green ribbons.
In winter,
the Jìn Emperor ordered the General Who Guards the East, Sīmǎ Zhòu, to advance towards Túzhōng;
the General Who Pacifies the East, Wáng Hún, and the Inspector of Yángzhōu, Zhōu Jùn, to advance towards Niúzhǔ;
the General Who Establishes Might, Wáng Róng, to advance towards Wǔchāng;
the General Who Pacifies the South, Hú Fèn, to advance towards Xiàkǒu;
the General Who Guards the South, Dù Yù, to advance towards Jiānglíng;
the General Who Soars Like a Dragon, Wáng Jùn, and the General of Broad Might, Táng Bīn, to sail down the Jiāng River to the east.
The Grand Commandant, Jiǎ Chōng, was appointed Grand Chief Controller,
to assess circumstances and position key forces,
commanding the entire military might.
Táo Jùn arrived at Wǔchāng,
and hearing of the large-scale advance of the northern army,
stopped and did not proceed.
Originally,
whenever Hào hosted a banquet for his ministers,
he would make sure everyone got completely drunk.
He appointed ten Palace Attendants,
specifically forbidding them alcohol,
to stand by all day,
serving as officials to record faults.
After the banquet,
each would report shortcomings,
offenses of inappropriate gazing,
and errors of misguided speech,
leaving nothing unreported.
Serious offenses immediately incurred severe penalties;
minor ones were also considered crimes.
His rear palace had thousands of women,
and yet he never stopped selecting more.
He also diverted water into the palace,
and if any palace woman displeased him,
he would kill and float her away.
Sometimes he would peel off people's faces,
or gouge out people's eyes.
Cén Hūn, being treacherous and obsequious, gained favor and high position,
reaching the rank of the Nine Dignitaries.
He was fond of initiating construction projects,
which caused widespread suffering.
Because of this, both high and low were disaffected,
and no one exerted themselves fully for Hào.
It was truly because his accumulated evil had reached its extreme,
and he could no longer endure his fate.
In the spring of the fourth year,
eleven kings were enfeoffed, including Zhōngshān and Dài.
A general amnesty was issued.
Wherever Jùn and Bīn went,
there was collapse and disintegration,
with no one able to resist them.
Dù Yù also beheaded Wǔ Yán, the Commandant of Jiānglíng,
and Wáng Hún further beheaded the Chancellor, Zhāng Tì, and Shěn Yíng, the Grand Administrator of Dānyáng, and others,
winning battles everywhere.
On the day Bingyin in the third month,
several hundred close attendants from the palace prostrated themselves, requesting Hào to kill Cén Hūn.
Hào, bewildered, agreed.
On the day Wuchen,
Táo Jùn returned from Wǔchāng.
He was immediately granted an audience,
and asked about the news of the naval forces.
He replied:
"The Shu boats are all small.
Now if we get twenty thousand soldiers,
and fight with large ships,
it will be enough to defeat them."
Thereupon, the troops were assembled,
and Jùn was granted the staff and axe of authority.
He was to depart the next day,
but that night, all the troops fled.
Meanwhile, Wáng Jùn was sailing downstream and about to arrive.
Sīmǎ Zhòu and Wáng Hún were both close to the border.
Hào followed the advice of the Minister of Ceremonies, Xuē Yíng, and the Central Secretariat Director, Hú Chōng, and others,
and dispatched envoys with letters to Jùn, Zhòu, and Hún, saying:
"Formerly, the Hàn imperial house lost control,
and the Nine Provinces were all fractured.
Our ancestors, seizing the opportunity,
briefly possessed Jiāngnán,
and thus divided by mountains and rivers,
separated from Wèi.
Now the great Jìn has risen like a dragon,
its virtue covering the four seas.
Being dull and inferior, and clinging to temporary peace,
we have not yet understood the mandate of Heaven.
Now,
to our great vexation, your six armies
are arrayed along our roads,
advancing far to the river islets,
causing the whole nation to tremble with fear,
barely drawing breath.
Presuming upon the vast benevolence of the Heavenly Court,
we respectfully send our privately appointed Grand Commandant, Zhāng Kuí, and others, to present their seals and ribbons,
offering ourselves as subjects and requesting mercy.
We humbly hope you will accept us in good faith,
to save the common people."
On the *rénshēn* day,
Wáng Jùn arrived first.
Thus, he accepted Hào’s surrender,
untied his bonds, burned his coffin,
and invited him to meet.
Zhòu, having received the imperial seals from Hào,
sent an envoy to escort Hào.
Hào’s entire family moved westward,
and on the *dīnghài* day of the fifth month of the first year of Tàikāng, they arrived in the capital.
On the *jiǎshēn* day of the fourth month,
an imperial edict stated:
“Sūn Hào, being in dire straits, has surrendered.
A previous edict promised him that he would not be put to death.
Now that Hào is about to arrive,
Our intention is still to commiserate with him.
Therefore, he shall be granted the title of Guīmìng Hóu.
He shall be provided with clothing, carriages,
thirty *qǐng* of land,
an annual stipend of five thousand *hú* of grain,
five hundred thousand coins,
five hundred bolts of silk,
and five hundred *jīn* of floss.”
Hào’s heir apparent, Jǐn, was appointed Middle-ranking Officer.
His sons who had been enfeoffed as kings
were appointed Gentlemen of the Palace.
In the fifth year,
Hào died in Luòyáng.
The commentary says: Sūn Liàng was a mere child and lacked worthy assistants,
so his deposition and failure to reign to the end
was an inevitable outcome.
Xiū, relying on old affections and past favors,
appointed Xīng and Bù,
but was unable to promote talented individuals
or change his ways.
Although he was earnest and fond of learning,
how could that help save a chaotic situation?
Moreover, he did not allow the deposed Liàng to die a natural death,
which shows a lack of fraternal righteousness.
As for Hào’s excessive and cruel punishments,
the number of those who were executed, banished, or exiled
is countless.
Because of this, all his subordinates were gripped by fear,
and each day they hoped
that the morning would not be followed by evening.
His reliance on omens and shamanistic rituals,
which constantly produced auspicious signs,
was considered of utmost urgency.
In ancient times, Shùn and Yǔ personally tilled the fields,
and with their most sagely virtues,
they still swore oaths to their ministers,
saying, “If I err, you shall assist me,”
or bowed to frank remonstrations,
always acting as if they were insufficient.
How much more so Hào, who was brutal and stubborn,
and indulged in cruelty and violence,
executing loyal remonstrators and
promoting flatterers,
tyrannizing his people,
and exhausting himself in debauchery and extravagance!
He deserved to be decapitated and quartered
to apologize to the common people.
Yet, he received an edict granting him immunity from death,
and was further favored with the title of Guīmìng.
Was this not a vast and generous favor,
an overly lavish grace indeed!
Biography of Liú Yáo, Tàishǐ Cí, Shì Xiè, Chapter 4
Liú Yáo, courtesy name Zhènglǐ,
was a native of Móupíng in Dōnglái.
A younger son of Qí Xiào Wáng was enfeoffed as Móupíng Hóu,
and his descendants settled there.
Yáo’s paternal uncle Chǒng
served as Grand Commandant of Hàn.
Yáo’s elder brother Dài,
courtesy name Gōngshān,
successively held the positions of Palace Attendant
and Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
When Yáo was nineteen,
his paternal cousin Wěi was kidnapped and held hostage by bandits.
Yáo seized him back and returned,
thus gaining fame.
He was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt,
served as a Palace Attendant,
and was appointed Magistrate of Xiàyì.
At that time, the Prefect of the commandery was a relative of the imperial clan and relied on his connections,
so Yáo resigned his office and left.
The province invited him to supervise Jìnán.
The Chancellor of Jìnán was the son of a Regular Palace Attendant,
and was corrupt and undisciplined.
Yáo impeached him and had him dismissed.
Táo Qiūhóng of Píngyuán recommended Yáo,
wishing to nominate him as a Flourishing Talent.
The Inspector said:
“Last year we nominated Gōngshān,
how can we nominate Zhènglǐ again?”
Hóng replied:
“If the wise Lord Inspector employed Gōngshān before,
and promoted Zhènglǐ afterward,
it would be like harnessing two dragons to a long chariot,
and driving swift steeds for a thousand *lǐ*.
Would that not be splendid!”
He was then invited to serve as an assistant in the Ministry of Works,
and was appointed Censor,
but he did not accept.
He fled the chaos to Huáipǔ,
and an imperial edict appointed him Inspector of Yángzhōu.
At that time, Yuán Shù was in Huáinán,
and Yáo feared and dreaded him,
not daring to proceed to the province.
He wished to cross south of the Jiāng (Yangzi River),
and Wú Jǐng and Sūn Bēn welcomed and settled him in Qǔ'ē.
Shù planned to usurp the throne,
and attacked and seized various commanderies and counties.
Yáo sent Fán Néng and Zhāng Yīng to garrison the riverbank to resist him.
Considering that Jǐng and Bēn were appointed by Shù,
he pressured and expelled them.
Thereupon, Shù appointed himself Inspector of Yángzhōu,
and together with Jǐng and Bēn, they attacked Yīng and Néng.
For over a year, they failed to conquer them.
The Hàn court commanded Yáo to be promoted to Governor,
and General of Military Might,
with several tens of thousands of troops.
Sūn Cè crossed eastward,
and defeated Yīng and Néng.
Yáo fled to Dāntú,
then ascended the Jiāng (river) to secure Yùzhāng,
stationing in Péngzé.
Zé Róng had arrived earlier,
(The character 笮 is pronounced *zhuàng lì*.)
killed the Grand Administrator Zhū Hào,
and occupied the commandery.
Yáo advanced to attack Róng,
but was defeated by Róng.
He then reassembled forces from neighboring counties,
and defeated Róng.
Róng fled into the mountains
and was killed by the local people.
Soon after, Yáo fell ill and died,
at the age of forty-two.
As for Zé Róng,
he was a native of Dānyáng.
Initially, he gathered several hundred followers
and went to rely on Táo Qiān, the Inspector of Xúzhōu.
Qiān put him in charge of supervising the transport of grain from Guǎnglíng and Péngchéng.
He then indulged in arbitrary killings
and appropriated the tribute from the three commanderies for himself.
He then erected a large Buddhist temple,
made a bronze statue of a man,
gilded its body with gold,
dressed it in brocade,
and hung nine tiers of bronze plates.
Below, he built multi-storied pavilions and walkways,
which could accommodate over three thousand people.
He had everyone recite Buddhist scriptures,
and allowed those in the region and neighboring commanderies who loved Buddhism to listen to the teachings,
exempting them from other labor to attract them.
Because of this, over five thousand households from near and far, from past and present, came.
Each time a Buddha bathing ceremony was held,
much wine and food were provided,
and mats were spread along the roads
for dozens of *lǐ*.
The people who came to watch and eat numbered nearly ten thousand,
and the expenditure was estimated in the hundreds of millions.
When Cáo Gōng attacked Táo Qiān,
the land of Xú was in turmoil.
Róng, with ten thousand men, women,
and three thousand horses,
fled to Guǎnglíng.
Zhào Yù, the Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng, treated him with courtesy as a guest.
Before this,
Xuē Lǐ, the Chancellor of Péngchéng, had been pressed by Táo Qiān
and garrisoned Mòlíng.
Róng, coveting the population of Guǎnglíng,
killed Yù while drunk,
let his soldiers plunder widely,
and then loaded his spoils and departed.
He then passed by and killed Lǐ,
and afterward killed Hào.
Later, Cè campaigned westward to Jiāngxià.
