On his return, he passed through Yùzhāng,
collected Yáo's remains,
and treated his family well.
Wáng Lǎng sent a letter to Cè, saying:
"Liú Zhènglǐ, when he first became governor of the province,
was unable to establish himself;
he truly relied on your esteemed family for support,
which enabled him to cross the Jiāng and establish order,
and settle affairs.
The etiquette of entering his territory,
the feeling of gratitude and mutual understanding,
was present from beginning to end.
Later, due to his suspicion of the Yuán clan,
things gradually became estranged.
Then, as allies,
we became enemies.
If one considers his original intention,
it was truly not what he desired.
After peace was restored,
I always wished for reconciliation and renewed friendship,
to revive our old good relations.
This sudden separation,
with heartfelt intentions unclarified,
and his abrupt demise,
is truly regrettable!
I know that you treat the generous with generosity and
repay grievances with virtue,
collecting bones and raising orphans,
mourning the dead and pitying the living.
You cast aside past suspicions
and safeguard the trust given to a child;
this is truly deep kindness and great distinction,
a beautiful reputation and substantial deed.
In the past, though the people of Lǔ harbored resentment against Qí,
they did not neglect funeral rites.
The Chūnqiū praised them for this,
calling it 'observing the rites.'
This is indeed what good historians should record,
and what village schools should admire and speak of.
Zhènglǐ's eldest son,
has indeed a strong character;
I imagine he must possess something extraordinary.
With your might manifest and punishments enforced,
to bestow favor upon him,
is this not excellent! "
Yáo's eldest son, Jī,
whose courtesy name was Jìngyú,
was fourteen years old.
He observed Yáo's mourning rites with full propriety,
and received no provisions from former officials.
His appearance was beautiful,
and Sūn Quán loved and respected him.
When Quán was General of Agile Cavalry,
he appointed Jī as Chief Clerk of the Eastern Bureau,
and made him Commandant of the Auxiliary Righteousness and Zhonglang General of Loyal Construction.
When Quán became King of Wú,
he promoted Jī to Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Quán once held a banquet,
during which Cavalry Commandant Yú Fān, being drunk, offended him.
Quán wanted to kill him,
his rage was exceedingly great.
Jī intervened and argued,
and Fān was thus spared.
During a great heat, Quán
once held a banquet on a boat.
While on the upper deck, a thunderstorm broke out.
Quán covered himself with a canopy,
and also ordered one to cover Jī.
No other person received this.
This was the extent of his favorable treatment.
He was moved to Minister of the Palace Guard.
When Quán assumed the title of Emperor,
he changed Jī's position to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
and shared the duties of the Imperial Secretariat.
He died at the age of forty-nine.
Later, Quán arranged for his son, Bà, to marry Jī's daughter,
granted them a mansion,
and bestowed favors upon them throughout the four seasons,
comparable to those given to the Quán and Zhāng families.
Jī had two younger brothers,
Shuò and Shàng,
both of whom were Cavalry Commandants.
Tàishǐ Cí, courtesy name Zǐyì,
was a man from Huáng in Dōnglái.
In his youth, he loved learning
and served as a Chief Clerk in the commandery's record office.
At that time, there was a dispute between the commandery and the province;
the right and wrong had not been determined,
and whoever reported first would be considered in the right.
At that moment, the province's memorial had already been dispatched,
and the commandery governor feared being too late,
so he sought a suitable messenger.
Cí, at twenty-one years old,
was chosen to go.
He traveled day and night,
arrived in Luòyáng,
and went to the Gōngchē gate.
He saw a provincial official who was just about to request an audience.
Cí asked,
"Are you going to submit a memorial?"
The official replied,
"Indeed."
Cí asked,
"Where is the memorial?"
He replied,
"In the carriage."
Cí said,
"Are you sure there's no error in the title or signature of the memorial?
Bring it here, let me see it."
The official did not realize at all that Cí was from Dōnglái,
and so he brought the memorial.
Cí had already concealed a knife;
he immediately cut it up and ruined it.
The official jumped up and cried loudly,
saying,
"Someone has ruined my memorial!"
Cí led him aside to the carriage
and said to him,
"If you hadn't given me the memorial just now,
I wouldn't have been able to ruin it.
This is a matter of fortune and misfortune, equally shared.
I alone will not bear this crime.
Wouldn't it be better if we both left quietly,
so that the living can escape death,
and neither of us would be punished?"
The official said,
"You ruined my memorial for your commandery;
you've already gotten what you wanted.
Why do you want to run away now?"
Cí replied,
"When I first received the commandery's orders,
I was only to come and see if the memorial had been submitted or not.
I was too zealous,
and ended up ruining your memorial.
Now if I return,
I also fear being reprimanded and angered for this,
so I want us both to leave."
The official found Cí's words reasonable,
and that very day they both left.
After Cí had led him out of the city,
he then returned and submitted his commandery's memorial.
When the provincial authorities heard of this,
they sent another official to submit their memorial.
However, the authorities in charge refused to handle it due to the previous obstruction,
and the province suffered the disadvantage.
Because of this, Cí became famous,
but was resented by the provincial authorities.
Fearing repercussions,
he fled to Liáodōng.
Kǒng Róng, the Chancellor of Běihǎi, heard of this and was greatly impressed.
He repeatedly sent people to inquire after [Tài] Cí’s mother,
and sent her provisions and gifts.
At this time, Róng, due to the Yellow Turban bandits' violence,
had moved his garrison to Dūchāng,
where he was besieged by the bandit Guǎn Hài.
Cí returned from Liáodōng,
and his mother said to Cí:
“You and Kǒng Běihǎi have never met,
yet since you departed,
he has provided for and cared for me with such diligence,
more than old acquaintances.
Now he is besieged by bandits,
you should go to his aid.”
Cí stayed for three days,
then walked alone directly to Dūchāng.
At that time, the siege was not yet tight.
At night, he watched for a gap
and managed to enter to see Róng,
then asked for soldiers to sally out and attack the bandits.
Róng did not agree,
wishing to wait for external relief.
None had arrived,
and the siege tightened daily.
Róng wished to send an urgent message to Liú Bèi, the Chancellor of Píngyuán,
but no one in the city could get out.
Cí personally requested to go.
Róng said:
“Now the bandit siege is very tight;
everyone says it is impossible.
Though your intention is bold,
is it not truly difficult?”
Cí replied:
“Previously, the Prefect focused his kindness on my aged mother.
My aged mother, grateful for the encounter,
sent me to attend to the Prefect's emergency,
certainly because she believed I had something commendable
and that my arrival would surely be beneficial.
Now everyone says it is impossible,
and if I too say it is impossible,
how would that match the Prefect’s benevolent care,
and my aged mother’s intention in sending me?
The situation is already urgent;
I beg the Prefect not to hesitate.”
Róng then agreed.
Thereupon, [Cí] prepared his journey and ate by the roadside.
At dawn,
he put on his quiver, took his bow, mounted his horse,
and, taking two cavalrymen with him,
each carrying a target,
opened the gate and rode straight out.
The surrounding besiegers on both sides were all startled and panicked,
and their troops and horses moved to intercept him.
Cí led his horse to the moat below the city wall,
stuck the targets he held, one each,
and shot at them.
After shooting,
he rode straight back through the gate.
The next morning, he did the same.
Among the besiegers, some were standing, some were lying down.
Cí again stuck his targets,
and after shooting,
returned through the gate.
The next morning, he again rode out and did the same,
but no one stood up again.
Thereupon, [Cí] lashed his horse and galloped straight through the besieging lines.
By the time the bandits realized,
Cí had already passed.
He also shot and killed several people,
all falling at the sound of the bowstring.
Thus, no one dared to pursue him.
He then arrived at Píngyuán
and persuaded Bèi, saying:
“Cí
is a rustic from Dōnglái.
He is not related by blood to Kǒng Běihǎi,
nor is he from the same village.
It is only due to their shared aspirations that they became friends,
and there is a bond to share disaster and endure hardship.
Now Guǎn Hài is rampaging violently,
Běihǎi is besieged,
isolated and without aid,
in peril at any moment.
Because you have a reputation for benevolence and righteousness,
and are able to rescue those in distress,
Běihǎi humbly,
with neck outstretched, relies upon you,
and sent Cí to brave sharp blades,
and break through multiple sieges,
entrusting himself to you from amidst a myriad of deaths.
I only ask how you might preserve him.”
Bèi composed himself and replied:
“Does Kǒng Běihǎi truly know that there is a Liú Bèi in the world?!”
Immediately, he dispatched three thousand elite soldiers with Cí.
When the bandits heard the troops were approaching,
they lifted the siege and fled.
Having been saved, Róng
esteemed Cí even more,
saying:
“You are my young friend.”
When the matter was concluded,
he returned to report to his mother,
who said:
“I am glad you had a way to repay Kǒng Běihǎi.”
Liú Yáo, the Inspector of Yángzhōu, was from the same commandery as Cí.
When Cí returned from Liáodōng,
he had not yet met him.
He briefly crossed the river to Qū'ā to see Yáo,
but before he left,
Sūn Cè arrived.
Someone advised Yáo that he could make Cí a Grand General.
Yáo said:
“If I were to use Zǐyì,
would Xǔ Zǐjiāng not laugh at me?”
But he only had Cí scout the situation.
At that time, [Cí] encountered Cè alone with a single cavalryman.
Cè had thirteen cavalrymen with him,
all of the likes of Hán Dāng, Sòng Qiān, and Huáng Gài.
Cí immediately went forward to fight,
directly facing Cè.
Cè stabbed Cí’s horse
and snatched the *shǒují* from Cí’s neck,
while Cí also got Cè’s helmet.
Just then, soldiers and cavalry from both sides came to join the fray,
so they broke off.
Cí should have fled with Yáo to Yùzhāng,
but he escaped to Wúhú,
fleeing into the mountains,
and proclaimed himself Administrator of Dānyáng.
At this time,
Cè had already pacified the area east of Xuānchéng,
but the six counties west of Jīng were still unsubdued.
Cí then moved into Jīng County,
established a garrison headquarters,
and was largely joined by the Shānyuè.
Cè personally led an attack,
and [Cí] was captured and imprisoned.
Cè immediately untied him
and held his hand, saying:
“Do you remember the time at Shéntíng?
If you had gotten me then, what would you have done?”
Cí said:
“It could not have been predicted.”
Cè laughed heartily and said:
“Today’s matters
I shall share with you.”
He immediately appointed him Household Supervisor,
and upon returning to Wú, gave him troops,
and promoted him to Colonel of the Campaigning Cavalry.
Later, when Liú Yáo died in Yùzhāng,
his more than ten thousand soldiers had not yet pledged allegiance to anyone.
Cè ordered Cí to go and pacify them.
All his aides said:
“Cí will surely go north and not return.”
Cè said:
“If Zǐyì abandons me,
who else can I rely on?”
He saw him off at Chāngmén,
grasping his wrist and parting with him, saying:
“When can you return?”
He replied:
“No more than sixty days.”
He indeed returned as scheduled.
Liú Biǎo’s nephew Pán,
was brave and fierce,
and repeatedly raided the various counties of Ài and Xī'ān.
Cè therefore divided the six counties around Hǎixūn and Jiànchāng,
appointed Cí as Commandant of Jiànchāng,
governing Hǎixūn,
and commanded all the generals to resist Pán.
Pán ceased his activities and no longer committed raids.
Cí was seven feet seven inches tall,
with a handsome beard,
an ape-like arm, skilled in archery,
his arrows never missed.
Once, he followed Cè to attack the Má Bǎo bandits.
A bandit on a watchtower along the rampart was shouting insults,
holding a rafter in his hand.
Cí drew his bow and shot him;
the arrow pierced his hand and stuck in the rafter.
Ten thousand people outside the siege all acclaimed his skill.
His mastery was thus.
Cáo Gōng heard of his name
and sent Cí a letter,
sealed in a casket.
When opened, it contained no words,
but only *dāngguī*.
When Sūn Quán took control of affairs,
seeing Cí’s ability to restrain Pán,
he entrusted him with affairs in the south.
He died at the age of forty-one
in the eleventh year of Jiàn'ān.
His son, Xiǎng,
rose to the office of Colonel of the Yue Cavalry.
Shì Xiè
had the courtesy name Wēi Yàn. He was a native of Guǎngxìn, Cāngwú.
His ancestors were originally from Wènyáng in the state of Lǔ.
During the chaos of Wáng Mǎng,
they sought refuge in Jiāozhōu.
Six generations later, his father, Shì Cì,
served as the Administrator of Rìnán during Emperor Huán's reign.
When Shì Xiè was young, he traveled to the capital for study,
serving Liú Zǐqí of Yǐngchuān,
and specialized in the Zuǒ Shì Chūn Qiū.
He was nominated as Xiàolián
and appointed as Shàngshū Láng,
but was dismissed from office due to official matters.
After the mourning period for his father Shì Cì was over,
he was nominated as Màocái
and appointed as Magistrate of Wū.
Later, he was promoted to Administrator of Jiāozhǐ.
His younger brother, Yī,
was initially a Dūyóu of the commandery.
When the Inspector Dīng Gōng was summoned back to the capital,
Yī diligently accompanied him.
Dīng Gōng was touched by this
and said to him at their parting:
"If this Inspector should be charged with the duties of the Three Excellencies,
I shall certainly recommend you."
Later, Dīng Gōng became the Sītú
and recommended Yī.
By the time Yī arrived,
Dīng Gōng had already been dismissed,
and Huáng Wǎn had replaced him as Sītú.
Huáng Wǎn treated Yī with great respect.
When Dǒng Zhuó caused turmoil,
Yī fled back to his hometown.
The Inspector of Jiāozhōu, Zhū Fú, was killed by barbarians,
and the province and commanderies fell into disorder.
Shì Xiè then memorialized to have Yī appointed Administrator of Hépǔ,
his next younger brother, Xúwén Líng, appointed Administrator of Jiǔzhēn,
(pronounced 'yú bǐ' according to
Zìlín)
and his youngest brother, Wǔ,
appointed Administrator of Nánhǎi.
Shì Xiè was broad-minded and generous,
humble and respectful to scholars.
Hundreds of scholars from the Central Plains sought refuge with him.
He indulged in the study of the Chūn Qiū
and wrote commentaries for it.
Yuán Huī of Chén Guó wrote a letter to the Minister of the Secretariat, Xún Yù, saying:
"Lord Shì, the Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, possesses extensive and profound scholarship,
and is also adept at governance.
Amidst great chaos,
he has preserved a commandery,
with no border incidents for over twenty years.
The people have not lost their livelihoods,
and travelers
have all benefited from his blessings.
Even if Dòu Róng protected Héxī,
how could he surpass this?
When official duties allow a brief respite,
he invariably enjoys studying classic texts.
His analysis of the Zuǒ Shì Chūn Qiū is particularly clear and precise.
I have frequently consulted him about various ambiguities in the commentaries,
and he always has explanations based on the teachings of masters,
with very thorough reasoning.
Furthermore, he is conversant with both ancient and modern versions of the Shàngshū,
and its profound principles are comprehensively detailed.
I hear that in the capital, the ancient and modern schools
are fiercely disputing right and wrong.
I now wish to itemize the extensive principles of the Zuǒ Shì and Shàngshū and submit them."
This is how he was praised.
Shì Xiè and his brothers all held positions in various commanderies,
dominating an entire province.
Being ten thousand *lǐ* away,
their authority was supreme and unrivaled.
When they went out, bells and chimes rang,
all ceremonial instruments were arrayed,
and pipes, flutes, drums, and trumpets sounded.
Their chariots and cavalry filled the roads,
and dozens of "Hu" people constantly flanked their carriages, burning incense.
Their wives and concubines rode in closed carriages,
and their sons and younger brothers were accompanied by armed riders.
At that time, they were held in high esteem,
awe-inspiring to all the various barbarians.
Wèi Tuó could not surpass them.
Wǔ died young from illness.
After Zhū Fú's death,
the Hàn sent Zhāng Jīn as Inspector of Jiāozhōu.
Zhāng Jīn was later killed by his own general, Ōu Jǐng.
Then, Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, sent Lài Gōng of Línglíng to replace Zhāng Jīn.
At this time, the Administrator of Cāngwú, Shǐ Huáng, died,
so Liú Biǎo also sent Wú Jù to replace him.
Both arrived with Lài Gōng.
When the Hàn court heard of Zhāng Jīn's death,
it sent Shì Xiè a sealed letter saying:
"Jiāozhōu is a remote region,
bounded to the south by rivers and seas.
The grace of the emperor is not proclaimed,
and the loyalty of the people below is obstructed.
We know that the rebel Liú Biǎo has again sent Lài Gōng to spy on the southern lands.
Therefore, We appoint Shì Xiè as the General of the Household Who Pacifies the South,
to oversee the seven commanderies,
and to retain his position as Administrator of Jiāozhǐ as before."
Later, Shì Xiè sent his official Zhāng Mín to bring tribute to the capital.
At that time, the empire was in chaos,
and roads were cut off.
However, Shì Xiè did not neglect his duty of tribute.
A special edict was issued, appointing him General Who Pacifies the Distant,
and enfeoffing him as Marquis of Lóngdù Tíng.
Later, Wú Jù and Lài Gōng fell out,
and Wú Jù raised troops to pursue Lài Gōng.
Lài Gōng fled back to Línglíng.
In the fifteenth year of Jiàn'ān [210 CE],
Sūn Quán sent Bù Zhì as Inspector of Jiāozhōu.
When Bù Zhì arrived,
Shì Xiè and his brothers submitted to his authority.
Wú Jù, however, harbored disloyal intentions,
so Bù Zhì executed him.
Sūn Quán added the title General of the Left to Shì Xiè.
At the end of the Jiàn'ān era,
Shì Xiè sent his son Xīn as a hostage.
Sūn Quán appointed Xīn as Administrator of Wǔchāng.
All of Shì Xiè's and Yī's sons who remained in the south
were appointed Generals of the Household.
Shì Xiè also persuaded the influential families of Yìzhōu, such as Yōng Kǎi,
to lead the people of their commanderies to remotely align with the east.
Sūn Quán was even more pleased with him,
promoting him to General Who Protects the Army
and enfeoffing him as Marquis of Lóngbiān.
His brother Yī was appointed General of the Household
and Marquis of Dūxiāng.
Whenever Shì Xiè sent envoys to Sūn Quán,
he would present various spices and fine gé cloth,
often by the thousands.
Bright pearls, large cowries, glazes, kingfisher feathers, tortoise shell, rhinoceros horn, and elephant ivory,
rare objects and exotic fruits,
such as plantains, shá fruit, and longan,
arrived every year.
At one point, he contributed several hundred horses.
Sūn Quán would always write letters
and bestow lavish gifts
in return, to comfort him.
Shì Xiè served in the commandery for over forty years.
In the fifth year of Huángwǔ [226 CE],
he died at the age of ninety.
Quán, deeming Jiāozhǐ to be a distant county,
therefore divided the region north of Hépǔ to form Guǎngzhōu,
with Lǚ Dài as the Cìshǐ;
the region south of Jiāozhǐ became Jiāozhōu,
with Dài Liáng as the Cìshǐ.
He also dispatched Chén Shí to replace Shì Xiè as the Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ.
Dài remained in Nánhǎi.
Liáng and Shí advanced together to Hépǔ,
but Xiè's son, Shì Huī, appointed himself Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ
and mobilized his clan's troops to resist Liáng.
Liáng remained in Hépǔ.
In Jiāozhǐ, Huán Lín,
an official appointed by Xiè,
叩tended to entreat Huī to welcome Liáng,
but Huī was enraged
and had Lín beaten to death.
Lín's elder brother, Huán Zhìzǐ Fā, then also gathered his clan's troops to attack Huī.
Huī closed his gates and defended the city.
Zhì and others attacked for several months but could not overcome him.
They then agreed to a peaceful settlement
and each withdrew their troops.
However, Lǚ Dài received an imperial edict to execute Huī,
and, leading troops from Guǎngzhōu, he sped day and night,
passing Hépǔ,
and advanced together with Liáng.
Shì Yī's son, the Commandant-General Shì Kuāng, had a long-standing friendship with Dài.
Dài appointed Kuāng as a Shīyǒu Cóngshì,
and first sent a letter to Jiāozhǐ,
explaining the consequences of both good and bad fortune.
He also sent Kuāng to see Huī
to persuade him to admit his guilt,
assuring him that although he would lose his governorship,
he would be free from other worries.
Dài followed closely after Kuāng's departure.
Huī's elder brother, Shì Zhī,
and younger brothers Gàn and Sòng, along with six others, bared their torsos in welcome.
Dài asked them to resume their clothes
and then proceeded to the commandery seat.
The next morning, tents were set up early,
and Huī and his brothers were invited in sequentially.
Guests filled the seats.
Dài rose,
held his ceremonial staff, and read the imperial edict,
enumerating their crimes and transgressions.
His attendants then bound them and led them out.
They were all immediately executed,
and their heads sent to Wǔchāng.
Shì Yī, Gàn, and Kuāng were released later.
Quán pardoned their crimes,
as well as Xiè's hostage son Shì Xīn,
and they were all reduced to commoners.
Several years later,
Shì Yī and Gàn were executed for violating the law.
Xīn died of illness,
without a son.
His wife remained a widow,
and an edict ordered that she be given a monthly stipend of grain from her locality
and awarded four hundred thousand cash.
Commentary says: Liú Yáo adorned his reputation and conduct,
and valued rectitude and censure.
However, in times of turmoil,
to hold a territory of ten thousand *lǐ*
was not his strength.
Tài Shǐcí was faithful, righteous, and resolute,
possessing the qualities of ancient men.
Shì Xiè governed Nányuè,
living a life of ease until his old age.
His sons, however, were not careful,
and brought disaster upon themselves.
This was likely due to mediocre talents indulging in wealth and status
and relying on natural barriers, which caused such an outcome.
Biographies of Empresses and Concubines, Chapter 5
Sūn Pòlǔ Wú Fūrén,
the mother of Wú Lord Quán.
She was originally from Wú,
later moved to Qiántáng,
lost her parents early,
and lived with her younger brother Jǐng.
Sūn Jiān heard of her talent and beauty
and wished to marry her.
Wú's relatives disliked Jiān's recklessness and cunning
and intended to refuse him.
Jiān was greatly ashamed and resentful.
The lady said to her relatives:
"Why begrudge one daughter and bring disaster?
If there is an unfortunate outcome,
it is fate."
Thus, they agreed to the marriage,
and she bore four sons and one daughter.
Jǐng often followed Jiān on campaigns and rendered meritorious service,
and was appointed Qí Dūwèi.
Yuán Shù recommended Jǐng to be Grand Administrator of Dānyáng
to suppress the former Grand Administrator Zhōu Xīn,
and he subsequently seized the commandery.
Sūn Cè, with Sūn Hū, and Lǚ Fàn, relied on Jǐng,
and together they gathered troops to attack the mountain bandit Zǔ Láng in Jīngxiàn.
Láng was defeated and fled.
At the time, they were pressured by Liú Yáo,
and Jǐng again sought refuge with Shù to the north.
Shù appointed him Dūjūn Zhōnglángjiàng,
and with Sūn Bēn, they attacked Fán Néng and Yú Mí at Héngjiāng,
and also attacked Zé Róng and Xuē Lǐ at Mòlíng.
At that time, Cè was wounded at Niúzhǔ,
and the surrendered rebels revolted again.
Jǐng attacked and suppressed them,
capturing them all.
He followed in the campaign against Liú Yáo,
who fled to Yùzhāng.
Cè sent Jǐng and Bēn to Shòuchūn to report to Shù.
Shù was then contending with Liú Bèi for Xúzhōu,
and appointed Jǐng as Grand Administrator of Guǎnglín.
Later, Shù usurped the imperial title.
Cè sent a letter to admonish Shù,
but Shù did not accept it.
Cè then cut off the river crossing
and ceased communication with him,
sending someone to inform Jǐng.
Jǐng immediately abandoned his commandery and returned east.
Cè again appointed Jǐng as Grand Administrator of Dānyáng.
The Han court dispatched Yìláng Wáng Pǔ (pronounced Pǔ)
with an imperial commission to travel south,
and he memorialized for Jǐng to be appointed Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn,
retaining his commandery as before.
When Quán, in his youth, took over the family enterprise,
the Lady assisted in managing military and state affairs,
rendering great benefit.
In the seventh year of Jiàn'ān [202 CE],
before her death,
she summoned Zhāng Zhāo and others,
entrusting them with her final wishes.
She was interred together in Gāolíng.
In the eighth year [203 CE],
Jǐng died in office.
His son Fèn was given troops and became a general,
and was enfeoffed as Xīntíng Hóu.
He died.
His son Ān succeeded.
Ān was implicated in the faction of Prince Lǔ Bā and died.
Fèn's younger brother Qí succeeded,
was enfeoffed as Dūtíng Hóu,
and died.
His son Zuǎn succeeded.
Zuǎn's wife was the daughter of Téng Yìn.
When Yìn was executed,
she also met with harm.
Wú Lord Quán's Xiè Fūrén was
from Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
Her father Xiè Yú
was a Han Shàngshū Láng and Xú Lìng.
Quán's mother, Wú,
arranged for Quán to marry her as his concubine.
She was loved and favored.
Later, Quán took his maternal aunt's daughter, Xú Shì,
and wanted Xiè to yield to her,
but Xiè refused.
Because of this, she lost favor
and died young.
More than ten years later,
her younger brother Xiè Chéng was appointed Wǔguān Lángzhōng,
gradually rising to Chángshā Dōngbù Dūwèi and Grand Administrator of Wǔlíng.
He compiled over one hundred chapters of the *Hòuhànshū*.
Wú Lord Quán's Xú Fūrén was
from Fùchūn, Wújùn.
Her grandfather, Xú Zhēn,
was close to Quán's father, Sūn Jiān.
Jiān gave his sister in marriage to Zhēn,
who begot Xú Kūn.
Kūn served in the province and commandery in his youth.
During the turmoil at the end of the Han dynasty,
he resigned his post
and followed Jiān on campaigns, rendering meritorious service.
He was appointed Piān Jiāngjūn.
When Jiān died,
he followed Sūn Cè to attack Fán Néng and Yú Mí at Héngjiāng,
and attacked Zhāng Yīng at Dānglìkǒu.
As his boats were few,
he intended to station the army and seek more.
Kūn's mother, who was then with the army,
said to Kūn:
"I fear the provincial government may send many naval forces to intercept us,
which would be disadvantageous.
How can we encamp here?
We should cut reeds to make rafts
to assist the boats in crossing the army."
Kūn reported this fully to Cè,
and Cè immediately acted upon it.
All the troops successfully crossed,
and they subsequently defeated Yīng,
and routed Zé Róng and Liú Yáo,
thereby establishing their enterprise.
Cè memorialized for Kūn to be Grand Administrator of Dānyáng.
When Wú Jǐng abandoned Guǎnglín and came east,
he again became the Grand Administrator of Dānyáng.
Kūn, as Dūjūn Zhōnglángjiàng, led troops
and followed in the defeat of Lújiāng Grand Administrator Lǐ Shù.
He was enfeoffed as Guǎngdé Hóu
and promoted to Pínglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Later, while campaigning against Huáng Zǔ,
he was struck by a stray arrow and died.
Kūn's wife
first married Lù Shàng of the same commandery.
After Shàng died,
Quán, then General Who Attacks the Barbarians, was in Wú.
He took her as his consort,
and had her raise his son, Dēng.
Later, when Quán moved,
because the夫人 was jealous,
he deposed her and placed her in Wú.
After more than ten years,
when Quán became King of Wú and then assumed the imperial title,
and Dēng was made Crown Prince,
the officials requested that the夫人 be made empress.
Quán's intention was to make Bù Shì empress,
and he ultimately did not permit it.
She later died of illness.
Her elder brother, Jiǎo,
inherited their father Kūn's title of marquis.
He pacified the Shānyuè,
and was appointed General of the Household.
He died before the夫人,
and had no sons.
Her younger brother, Zuò, inherited the封,
and also, by virtue of military achievements, rose to Wúhú Dū and General Who Pacifies Wèi.
Empress Bù, wife of Wú Lord Quán,
was a native of Huái'yīn, Línchuái.
She was of the same clan as Prime Minister Zhì.
In the late Hàn period,
her mother took her and moved to Lújiāng.
Lújiāng was conquered by Sūn Cè,
and they all crossed the Jiāng River eastward.
Because of her beauty, she gained Quán's favor,
and her charm was unsurpassed in the inner palace.
She bore two daughters:
the elder was Lǔbān,
styled Dàhǔ,
who first married Zhōu Yú's son Xún,
and later married Quán Cóng;
the younger was Lǔyù,
styled Xiǎohǔ,
who first married Zhū Jù,
and later married Liú Zuǎn.
The夫人 was not jealous by nature,
and greatly promoted others,
thus she was loved and favored for a long time.
When Quán became king and then emperor,
he intended to make her empress,
but the officials' discussions focused on Xú Shì.
Quán hesitated for more than ten years.
However, within the palace, everyone referred to her as empress,
and her relatives, in memorials, referred to her as the central palace.
When she died,
the officials, following Quán's intention,
requested that her title be formally posthumously confirmed.
Thereupon, an imperial seal and ribbon were bestowed,
and the proclamation stated:
"On the Wùzǐ day of the intercalary month in the first year of Chìwū,
the Emperor says: Alas, Empress!
You assisted in the founding of the dynasty,
together upholding Heaven and Earth.
Reverent and diligent day and night,
you shared the toil with me.
Your inner teachings were cultivated and orderly,
and your ritual and righteousness were without fault.
Generous and benevolent,
you possessed virtues of goodness and grace.
Officials and common people looked up to you,
and hearts from far and near turned to you.
I, considering that the difficulties of the age had not yet been pacified,
and the grand unification had not yet been achieved,
followed your noble aspiration,
and always harbored humility and self-effacement.
Therefore, at that time, I did not confer the formal title,
also certainly believing that you would live for many years,
forever with me, responding to and manifesting Heaven's favor.
Unexpectedly, in a sudden instant,
your great destiny drew near its end.
I regret that my original intention was not manifested earlier,
grieved by your demise,
not to fulfill the heavenly bounty.
The depth of my sorrow,
pains my heart.
Now, I send the Acting Imperial Envoy and Prime Minister Yōng,
to respectfully present this proclamation and confer the title,
to be enshrined and offered sacrifices alongside the preceding empresses.
If your soul has awareness,
appreciate this honor and glory.
Alas, how sorrowful!"
She was buried at Jiǎnglín.
Empress Wáng, wife of Wú Lord Quán,
was a native of Lángyá.
The夫人 was selected to enter the palace,
and gained favor during the Huángwǔ era.
She gave birth to Hé,
and her favor was second only to Bù Shì.
After Bù Shì died,
and Hé was made Crown Prince,
Quán was about to establish the夫人 as empress,
but Princess Quán had always hated the夫人,
and gradually slandered her.
When Quán fell ill,
she showed signs of happiness,
and because of this, Quán deeply blamed and angered her,
and she died of worry.
When Hé's son Hào ascended the throne,
he posthumously honored the夫人 as Empress Dàyì,
and enfeoffed her three younger brothers as marquises.
Empress Wáng, wife of Wú Lord Quán,
was a native of Nányáng.
She was selected to enter the palace,
and gained favor during the Jiāhé era.
She gave birth to Xiū.
When Hé was made Crown Prince,
Hé's mother was highly esteemed,
and all other concubines who had gained favor
were sent to live outside the palace.
The夫人 moved to Gōng'ān,
and when she died,
she was buried there.
When Xiū ascended the throne,
he sent an envoy to posthumously honor her as Empress Jìnghuái,
and reburied her at Jìnglín.
The Wáng clan had no successor,
so her full younger brother Wén Yōng was enfeoffed as a Tínghóu.
Empress Pān, wife of Wú Lord Quán,
was a native of Jùzhāng, Kuàijī.
Her father was an official who
died under the law.
The夫人 and her elder sister were both sent to the weaving workshop.
Quán saw her and was struck by her beauty,
so he summoned her to fill the inner palace.
She gained favor and became pregnant.
She dreamt that someone gave her a dragon's head,
and she received it with her knee-cover.
She then gave birth to Liàng.
In the thirteenth year of Chìwū,
Liàng was made Crown Prince.
She requested to have her elder sister married off,
and Quán permitted it.
The following year,
the夫人 was established as empress.
Her nature was cunning, jealous, and charming,
and from beginning to end,
she slandered and harmed Yúan夫人 and many others.
When Quán was unwell,
the夫人 sent to inquire of the Chief Imperial Scribe Sūn Hóng about Empress Lǚ's exclusive control of state affairs.
Exhausted from attending to his illness,
and thus weakened by sickness,
the palace women, watching for her to fall into a昏睡,
together strangled her to death,
falsely claiming she had been struck by an evil influence.
Later, the matter was exposed,
and six or seven people were executed.
Quán died soon after,
and they were buried together at Jiǎnglín.
When Sūn Liàng ascended the throne,
he made the夫人's brother-in-law Tán Shào a Cavalry Commandant,
and gave him troops.
When Liàng was deposed,
Shào and his family were sent to their native commandery, Lúlíng.
Empress Quán, wife of Sūn Liàng,
was the daughter of Quán Shàng.
Her paternal grand-aunt, the princess, loved her,
and always brought her along when she went to visit.
When Empress Pān and her son gained favor,
Princess Quán, considering her rift with Sūn Hé's mother,
persuaded Quán to take the夫人 as a consort for Pān Shì's son Liàng,
and Liàng subsequently became the heir.
The夫人 was established as empress,
and Shàng was made Commandant of the City Gates,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng,
replacing Téng Yìn as Grand Minister of Ceremonies and General Who Guards the Army,
advanced to Marquis of Yǒngpíng,
and recorded matters of the Imperial Secretariat.
At that time, there were five marquises of the Quán clan,
all commanding troops and horses;
the rest were Attendants and Cavalry Commandants,
guarding the palace.
Since Wúxīng,
no imperial in-laws were as noble and prosperous.
When Zhūgě Dàn, a great general of Wèi, defected with Shòuchūn,
Quán Yì, Quán Duān, Quán Yī, and Quán Yí, among others, consequently surrendered to Wèi during this occasion.
Quán Xī's plot was exposed and he was killed,
and thus the Quán clan declined.
Sūn Chěn then deposed Liàng as King of Kuàijī,
and later demoted him to Marquis of Hòuguān.
The夫人 accompanied him to his fief,
residing in Hòuguān.
Shàng moved his family to Línglíng,
and was later killed.
Sūn Xiū's Zhū Fūren [Lady Zhū]
was the daughter of Zhū Jù,
born to Sūn Xiū's elder sister, the Princess.
At the end of the Chìwū era,
Sūn Quán betrothed her to Sūn Xiū as his consort.
When Sūn Xiū was enfeoffed as the King of Lángxié,
she accompanied him to reside in Dānyáng.
During the Jiànxīng era,
Sūn Jùn held absolute power,
and all the imperial clan members were troubled by him.
Quán Shàng's wife was Sūn Jùn's elder sister,
so only Princess Quán offered him protection.
Initially,
when Sūn Hé was the crown prince,
Princess Quán slandered and harmed Lady Wáng,
wishing to depose the crown prince
and install the King of Lǔ.
Lady Zhū did not consent,
which created a rift between them.
During the Wǔfèng era,
Sūn Yí conspired to assassinate Sūn Jùn,
but the plot was discovered, and he was executed.
Princess Quán thereupon claimed that Lady Zhū was involved in Sūn Yí's conspiracy,
and Sūn Jùn unjustly executed Lady Zhū.
Sūn Xiū, in fear,
sent his lady back to Jiànyè,
holding her hand and weeping at their farewell.
Upon her arrival,
Sūn Jùn sent her back to Sūn Xiū.
During the Tàipíng era,
Sūn Liàng learned that Lady Zhū had been harmed by Princess Quán,
and asked about the circumstances of Lady Zhū's death.
Princess Quán, in fear, said:
"I truly didn't know;
it was all reported by Jù's two sons, Xióng and Sǔn."
Sūn Liàng then executed Xióng and Sǔn.
Sǔn's wife was Sūn Jùn's younger sister,
which made Sūn Chén even more wary of Sūn Liàng.
Consequently, Sūn Chén deposed Sūn Liàng
and installed Sūn Xiū.
In the fifth year of Yǒng'ān,
Lady Zhū was established as empress.
After Sūn Xiū died,
the officials honored her as Empress Dowager.
A little over a month after Sūn Hào ascended the throne,
she was demoted to Empress Jǐng
and resided in Āndìng Gōng.
In the seventh month of the first year of Gānlù,
she was forced to die,
and was buried together in Dìnglíng.
Sūn Hé's Hé Jī [Concubine Hé]
was a native of Gòuróng, Dānyáng.
Her father, Suí,
was originally a cavalryman.
Sūn Quán once toured various camps,
and Hé Jī was watching along the road.
Sūn Quán saw her from afar and was struck by her unusual beauty,
so he ordered a eunuch to summon her
and bestowed her upon his son, Sūn Hé.
She bore a son,
and Sūn Quán was delighted,
naming him Péngzǔ,
who was later Sūn Hào.
After Crown Prince Sūn Hé was deposed,
he later became the King of Nányáng and resided in Chángshā.
When Sūn Liàng ascended the throne,
Sūn Jùn assisted in governing.
Sūn Jùn had always flattered Princess Quán,
and Princess Quán had a rift with Sūn Hé's mother.
So she persuaded Sūn Jùn to move Sūn Hé to Xīndū,
and sent an envoy to grant him death.
His primary consort, Zhāng Shì, also committed suicide.
Hé Jī said:
"If we all follow him in death,
who will raise the orphans?"
Thereupon, she fostered and raised Sūn Hào
and his three younger brothers.
When Sūn Hào ascended the throne,
he honored Sūn Hé as Emperor Zhāoxiàn,
and Hé Jī as Empress Zhāoxiàn,
residing in Shēngpíng Gōng.
A little over a month later,
she was promoted to Empress Dowager.
Her younger brothers Hóng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yǒngpíng,
Jiǎng as the Marquis of Lìyáng,
and Zhí as the Marquis of Xuānchéng.
After Hóng died,
his son Miǎo inherited the title
and served as the Supervising General of Wǔlíng,
where he was killed by Jìn forces.
Zhí's official position reached Grand Minister of Works.
In the late Wú period, there was great confusion and disorder,
and the Hé clan became arrogant and presumptuous,
with its members acting unrestrainedly,
causing distress among the common people.
Thus, the people spread a false rumor,
saying:
"Sūn Hào died long ago,
and the one enthroned is a son of the Hé clan."
Sūn Hào's Téng Fūren [Lady Téng]
was a distant kinswoman of the late Grand Chamberlain, Yìn.
When Yìn's clan was annihilated,
Lady Téng's father, Mù,
was exiled to a border commandery due to their distant relationship.
When Sūn Xiū ascended the throne,
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
allowing Mù to return.
Mù was then appointed Wǔguān Zhōngláng.
After Sūn Hào was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wūchéng,
he took Mù's daughter as his consort.
When Sūn Hào ascended the throne,
she was established as empress,
and Mù was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Gāomì,
appointed General-in-Chief,
and Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat.
Later, court officials, recognizing Mù's honorable status as a relative,
often encouraged him to offer remonstrance.
However, the empress's favor gradually declined,
and Sūn Hào became increasingly displeased.
Sūn Hào's mother, Hé, constantly sided with her.
Moreover, the Grand Astrologer stated
that according to the cycles of fate,
the empress could not be replaced.
Sūn Hào believed in shamans and spirit mediums,
and thus she was not deposed,
but continued to be provided for in Shēngpíng Gōng.
Mù was sent to reside in Cāngwú Commandery;
although his rank and title were not removed,
he was effectively exiled,
and died of sorrow on the journey.
The officials of the Chángqiū Palace
merely filled their posts,
but still received morning greetings and memorials as before.
However, Sūn Hào brought many favored concubines into the palace,
and many of them wore the imperial empress's seals and ribbons.
In the fourth year of Tiānjì,
she accompanied Sūn Hào in his relocation to Luòyáng.
Commentary: The *Yì* states,
"When the family is set in order, the world is settled."
The *Shī* says:
"Be a model to your wife,
and then to your brothers,
and so govern the family and the state."
Indeed,
these words are true!
Looking back at Duke Huán of Qí,
and observing Sūn Quán in recent times,
both possessed the discernment of enlightened scholars
and the ambition of exceptional individuals,
yet they failed to distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate heirs,
and their inner courts were in disarray,
leaving a legacy of ridicule for all time
and calamity flowing down to their descendants.
From this perspective,
only those who take morality and righteousness as their guiding principle,
and unity as their main concern,
can then escape such burdens!
Biographies of the Imperial Clan, Chapter Six
Sūn Jìng
was the youngest brother of Jiān.
When Jiān first raised an army,
Jìng gathered five or six hundred people from his hometown and clan to form a defense force,
and the masses all attached themselves to him.
When Cè defeated Liú Yáo,
settled various counties,
and advanced to attack Kuàijī,
he sent someone to invite Jìng.
Jìng brought his family and met Cè in Qiántáng.
At that time, the Grand Administrator Wáng Láng resisted Cè at Gùlíng.
Cè engaged in several naval battles
but could not overcome him.
Jìng advised Cè, saying:
"Láng is relying on the natural barriers and defending the city;
it will be difficult to capture him quickly.
Zhādú is several tens of *lǐ* to the south of here,
(Zhā has the pronunciation of *zǔ jiā fǎn*.)
and it is a crucial route.
It would be best to approach from there and secure its interior.
This is what is called attacking where they are unprepared and appearing where they are unexpected.
I will personally lead the troops as the vanguard;
we are sure to defeat them."
Cè said:
"Excellent."
Then he falsely announced to the army:
"Recently, continuous rain has made the water muddy,
and many soldiers who drank it have suffered stomachaches.
Hastily prepare several hundred jars and pots to clarify the water."
When it was dusk,
he set up fires to deceive Láng,
then divided the army and marched secretly by night along the Zhādú route,
launching a surprise attack on Gāoxiān Tún.
Láng was greatly alarmed
and dispatched the former Dānyáng Grand Administrator Zhōu Xīn and others to lead troops to battle.
Cè defeated Xīn and others,
beheaded them,
and thus stabilized Kuàijī.
He memorialized to appoint Jìng as Fènwǔ Xiàowèi.
He wanted to entrust him with important responsibilities,
but Jìng was fond of his ancestral tombs and clan,
and was not happy to serve in office,
requesting to remain to guard the locale.
Cè assented to this.
When Quán took charge of affairs,
Jìng was promoted to Zhāoyì Zhōnglángjiàng,
and died at home.
He had five sons:
Gǎo, Yú, Jiǎo, Huàn, and Qiān.
Gǎo had three sons: Chuò, Chāo, and Gōng.
Chāo became Piān Jiāngjūn.
Gōng gave birth to Jùn.
Chuò gave birth to Lín.
Yú, courtesy name Zhòngyì,
began leading troops as Gōngyì Xiàowèi.
At that time, many guests and generals were from east of the river.
Yú was humble and appeased them,
earning their goodwill.
In the ninth year of Jiàn'ān [2004 CE],
he took office as Dānyáng Grand Administrator,
and was supported by the masses,
reaching over ten thousand people.
He was additionally appointed Suīyuǎn Jiāngjūn.
In the eleventh year [2006 CE],
he and Zhōu Yú jointly attacked the two strongholds of Má and Bǎo
and defeated them.
Later, he followed Quán to resist Cáo Gōng at Rúxū.
Quán wanted to engage in battle,
but Yú advised Quán to remain cautious.
Quán did not comply,
and the army indeed achieved nothing.
He was promoted to Fènwēi Jiāngjūn,
retained his commandery as before,
and moved his garrison from Lìyáng to Niúzhǔ.
Yú appointed Ráo Zhù from Yǒng'ān as the Magistrate of Xiāng'ān,
and Yán Lián from Wúxī as the Magistrate of Jūcháo,
sending them to recruit from the two commanderies of Lújiāng,
and each secured their surrender and allegiance.
Mǎ Pǔ from Jìyīn was a diligent scholar who loved antiquity.
Yú treated him with great respect
and had several hundred sons of his two prefectures' generals and officials attend his lectures.
He then established a school
where he would regularly host feasts and give lessons.
At that time, all the generals focused on military affairs,
but Yú loved the ancient classics.
Even during military campaigns,
his chanting of texts never ceased.
At the age of thirty-nine,
he died in the twentieth year of Jiàn'ān [2015 CE].
Yú had five sons: Mí, Xī, Yào, Màn, and Hóng.
Màn rose to the rank of general
and was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Sūn Jiǎo, courtesy name Shúlǎng,
was initially appointed Hùjūn Xiàowèi (Protector of the Army, Commandant),
commanding over two thousand troops.
At that time, Cáo Gōng frequently attacked Rúxū.
Jiǎo went to repel him every time,
renowned for his elite forces.
He was promoted to Dūhù Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (Area Commander, General who Attacks the Barbarians),
replacing Chéng Pǔ in commanding Xiàkǒu.
When Huáng Gài and his elder brother Yú died,
he also took over their armies.
He was granted Shāxiàn, Yúndù, Nánxīnshì, and Jìnglíng as his fiefs,
where he appointed his own chief officials.
He was generous with wealth and capable of bestowing favors,
skilled in forging connections.
He was extremely close to Zhūgé Jǐn.
He entrusted Liú Jìng of Lújiāng with matters of success and failure,
Lǐ Yǔn of Jiāngxià with public affairs,
and Wú Shuò of Guǎnglíng and Zhāng Liáng of Hénán with military matters.
He wholeheartedly treated them with intimacy and respect,
and none failed to devote themselves entirely.
Jiǎo once sent troops who captured beautiful women from the border generals and officials of Wèi and presented them to Jiǎo.
Jiǎo changed their clothes and sent them back,
issuing an order which stated:
"The one we are now executing is the Cáo clan.
What crime have their common people committed?
From now on,
do not attack their old and weak."
Because of this, many people in the Jiāng-Huái region submitted to him.
He once had a furious argument with Gān Níng over a minor issue.
Someone admonished Níng,
who said:
"As subjects, we are all equal.
Although the General who Attacks the Barbarians is a son of the Lord,
how can he arbitrarily insult others?
I serve an enlightened ruler,
and should only exert my strength and risk my life
to repay my sovereign.
I truly cannot follow the common custom of bending to others."
Quán heard of this,
and wrote a letter rebuking Jiǎo, saying:
"Since I became an enemy of the North,
ten years have passed in between.
At first, when we confronted each other, you were young.
Now you are almost thirty.
Confucius said 'At thirty, I stood firm,'
not merely referring to the Five Classics.
I have entrusted you with elite troops,
and delegated a great responsibility to you.
You command all generals as Area Commander from a thousand *lǐ* away.
I wish for you to be like Chǔ's Rèn Zhāoxīxù (Chancellor Zhāoxīxù of Chǔ),
displaying your might in the northern border,
not merely to allow you to indulge your private desires.
Recently I heard that you drank with Gān Xīngbà,
and due to the alcohol,
you affronted him.
He sought to be transferred to Lǚ Méng's command.
Although this man is coarse and unrefined,
and sometimes does not meet expectations,
he is nevertheless a truly courageous man.
My closeness to him
is not due to personal favoritism.
I cherish and love him,
while you alienate and hate him.
Your actions always go against my wishes;
how can this last?
To be respectful in bearing and simple in conduct
allows one to govern the people;
to love people and be tolerant
allows one to win the masses.
If you cannot even understand these two things,
how can you supervise from afar,
repel invaders, and overcome difficulties?
You are a man of mature conduct,
specially entrusted with heavy responsibilities.
Above, there are distant gazes looking upon you;
below, there are subordinates who work with you day and night.
How can you indulge in arbitrary and excessive anger?
Who among men is without fault?
The valuable thing is to be able to reform.
You should reflect on your past transgressions
and deeply blame yourself.
Therefore, I now trouble Zhūgé Zǐyú to reiterate my intentions.
As I write this letter, I am saddened and distressed,
my heart grieves, and tears fall."
Upon receiving the letter, Jiǎo
submitted a memorial expressing his apologies,
and subsequently forged a strong bond with Níng.
Later, when Lǚ Méng was to attack Nánjùn,
Quán wanted Jiǎo and Méng to serve as grand commanders of the left and right divisions.
Méng advised Quán, saying:
"If Your Highness believes the General who Attacks the Barbarians is capable,
then employ him.
If you believe I am capable,
then employ me.
In the past, Zhōu Yú and Chéng Pǔ were commanders of the left and right divisions,
jointly attacking Jiānglíng.
Although the decision rested with Yú,
Pǔ relied on his long service as a general
and on being an equal commander,
so they became disunited,
nearly ruining the national enterprise.
This is a warning before our very eyes."
Quán understood,
and apologized to Méng, saying:
"I shall make you the grand commander,
and order Jiǎo to be your successor."
When Guān Yǔ was captured
and Jīngzhōu pacified,
Jiǎo contributed significantly.
He died in the twenty-fourth year of Jiàn'ān.
Quán posthumously recognized his achievements,
ennobling his son Yìn as Dānyáng Hóu (Marquis of Dānyáng).
Yìn died
without a son.
His younger brother Xī succeeded,
commanded troops,
committed a crime and committed suicide,
and the marquisate was abolished.
His younger brothers Zī, Mí, and Yí were all generals
and ennobled as marquises.
Zī was the commander of the Yǔlín (Feathered Forest imperial guards),
Yí the commander of the Wúnán (Fearless imperial guards).
Zī was killed by Téng Yìn,
and Yí was harmed by Sūn Jùn.
Sūn Huàn, courtesy name Jìmíng.
After his elder brother Jiǎo died,
he took over command of his troops,
and served as Yángwǔ Zhōnglángjiàng (Gentleman of the Household, Who Displays Martial Might) and administrator of Jiāngxià commandery.
He served for one year,
following Jiǎo's former practices,
treating Liú Jìng, Lǐ Yǔn, Wú Shuò, Zhāng Liáng, and Lǘ Jǔ of Jiāngxià with respect,
and accepting all their good advice.
Huàn was slow-witted in spontaneous situations but diligent in his official duties;
the military and civilians praised him.
In the fifth year of Huángwǔ,
Quán attacked Shíyáng.
Huàn, being the local commander,
ordered his subordinate general Xiānyú Dān to lead five thousand men to first cut off the Huái River route.
He himself, leading Wú Shuò and Zhāng Liáng with five thousand men, served as the army's vanguard,
capturing Gāochéng
and taking three generals.
When the main army returned,
Quán issued an edict for him to precede the main force.
As his carriage passed Huàn's army,
Quán saw that Huàn's formation was orderly.
Quán sighed, saying:
"Initially, I worried about his slowness and dullness.
Now, in managing the army,
few generals can match him.
I have no worries anymore."
He was appointed Yángwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Displays Might)
and enfeoffed as Shāxiàn Hóu (Marquis of Shāxiàn).
Wú Shuò and Zhāng Liáng were both Píjiāngjūn (Minor Generals),
and granted the noble title Guānnèihóu (Marquis within the Pass).
Huàn also loved and enjoyed scholars,
again ordering his subordinates' sons and younger brothers to pursue studies.
Later, dozens of them served in the imperial court.
At the age of forty,
he died in the third year of Jiāhé.
His son Chéng succeeded him,
and as Zhāowǔ Zhōnglángjiàng (Gentleman of the Household, Who Manifests Martial Might), took over command of the troops
and administered the commandery.
He died in the sixth year of Chìwū
without a son.
His distant younger brother Yī was enfeoffed to continue Huàn's line,
inheriting the position and serving as a general.
When Sūn Jùn executed Zhūgé Kè,
Yī, along with Quán Xī and Shī Jì, attacked Kè's younger brother Róng, the commander of Gōng'ān.
Róng committed suicide.
Yī was promoted from Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the South) to Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Suppresses the Army),
given *jiǎjié* (staff of authority) and commanded Xiàkǒu.
When Sūn Lín executed Téng Yìn and Lǚ Jù,
Jù and Yìn were both Yī's brothers-in-law.
Yī's younger brother Fēng also knew of Yìn and Jù's plot
and committed suicide.
Lín sent Zhū Yì to secretly attack Yī.
When Yì reached Wǔchāng,
Yī knew he was being attacked.
He led over a thousand of his subordinates, taking Yìn's wife, and fled to Wèi.
Wèi appointed Yī as Chējì Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry), Yítóng Sānsī (Equal in Rank to the Three Excellencies),
and enfeoffed him as Wú Hóu (Marquis of Wú),
giving him Lady Xíng, a noble consort of the late Emperor Fāng, as his wife.
Xíng was beautiful but jealous,
and her subordinates could not endure her demands,
so they jointly killed Yī and Lady Xíng.
Yī died three years after entering Wèi (during the Huángchū era).
Sūn Bēn, courtesy name Bóyáng.
His father, Qiāng, courtesy name Shèngtái,
was Sūn Jiān's full brother.
Bēn lost both parents early.
His younger brother, Fǔ, was an infant,
so Bēn personally raised and cared for him.
Their fraternal affection was very deep.
He served as a Dūyóu Shǒuzhǎng for the commandery.
When Sūn Jiān raised an army of righteousness in Chángshā,
Bēn left his post to join the campaign.
When Sūn Jiān died,
Bēn temporarily took command of the remaining troops
and escorted the coffin.
Later, Yuán Shù moved to Shòuchūn,
and Bēn again became dependent on him.
Yuán Shù’s cousin, Yuán Shào, appointed Zhōu Áng of Kuàijī as the Administrator of Jiǔjiāng.
As Shào and Shù were not on good terms,
Shù sent Bēn to attack and defeat Áng at Yīnlíng.
Shù memorialized Bēn as Governor of Yùzhōu,
then transferred him to Dānyáng Commandant,
acting as General Who Conquers Barbarians,
to suppress and pacify the Shānyuè.
He was then expelled by Liú Yáo, the Inspector of Yángzhōu,
and consequently led his troops and followers back to reside in Lìyáng.
After a short while,
Shù again sent Bēn and Wú Jǐng to jointly attack Fán Néng, Zhāng Yīng, and others,
but they were unable to capture them.
When Sūn Cè crossed the river eastward,
he assisted Bēn and Jǐng in defeating Yīng, Néng, and others,
and then advanced to attack Liú Yáo.
Yáo fled to Yùzhāng.
Sūn Cè sent Bēn and Jǐng back to Shòuchūn to report to Shù.
It was at this time that Shù usurped the imperial title,
appointed all officials,
and made Bēn Administrator of Jiǔjiāng.
Bēn did not accept the post,
abandoning his wife and children to return to Jiangnán.
By then, Sūn Cè had already pacified the two commanderies of Wú and Kuàijī.
Bēn joined Sūn Cè in campaigns against Liú Xūn, the Administrator of Lújiāng, and Huáng Zǔ, the Administrator of Jiāngxià.
When the army returned,
they heard that Yáo had died of illness.
They passed through and pacified Yùzhāng.
Sūn Cè appointed Bēn as Administrator,
and later he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng.
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn’ān (208 CE),
the envoy Liú Yǐn, acting on an imperial edict, appointed Bēn as General Who Conquers Barbarians,
retaining his commandery as before.
He died after eleven years in office.
His son Lín succeeded him.
Lín, at the age of nine,
took over the administration of Yùzhāng,
and was advanced to Marquis of Dūxiāng.
He served in the commandery for nearly twenty years,
suppressing rebellious bandits,
and his achievements were well-managed.
He was recalled to Wǔchāng
to serve as Ràozhàng Dū.
At that time, Pān Jùn, the Grand Minister of the Court, was in charge of affairs in Jīngzhōu.
Shū Xiè of Chénliú, the Prefect of Zhòng’ān, was imprisoned for a crime.
Pān Jùn had once overlooked Shū Xiè
and now wished to apply the law to him.
Many argued on his behalf,
but Pān Jùn remained unyielding.
Lín said to Pān Jùn:
“Shū Bóyīng and his brother competed to die for each other,
which was considered righteous throughout the land,
and became a beautiful tale.
Moreover, Zhòngyīng (Shū Xiè) still harbors old intentions of serving the state.
If you kill his son (or junior kinsman) today,
and if the empire were to be unified,
and the blue canopy (imperial carriage) were to tour northward,
the gentry of the central plains would surely ask about Zhòngyīng's successor.
If the answer is that Pān Chéngmíng (Pān Jùn) killed Xiè,
how would that be for the matter?”
Pān Jùn's intentions immediately softened,
and Shū Xiè was thus spared.
Lín was promoted to Xiàkǒu Miánzhōng Dū and General Who Manifests Awe,
serving diligently wherever he was stationed.
He died in the twelfth year of Chìwū (249 CE).
His son Miáo succeeded him.
Miáo's younger brother Lǚ, and his uncles Ān, Xī, and Jī,
all held prominent positions.
Sūn Fǔ, courtesy name Guóyí,
was Bēn's younger brother.
As Yangwǔ Commandant, he assisted Sūn Cè in pacifying the three commanderies.
When Sūn Cè campaigned against the seven counties of Dānyáng,
he sent Fǔ to garrison Lìyáng in the west to resist Yuán Shù,
and also to recruit and attract remaining inhabitants,
gathering the scattered populace.
He also accompanied Sūn Cè in campaigning against Língyáng,
capturing Zǔ Láng and others alive.
When Sūn Cè launched a surprise attack westward against Liú Xūn, the Administrator of Lújiāng,
Fǔ followed,
leading his soldiers into battle,
and distinguished himself.
Sūn Cè established Fǔ as Administrator of Lúlín,
where he pacified the subordinate cities
and appointed chief officials.
He was promoted to General Who Pacifies the South
and was granted the imperial insignia and appointed Inspector of Jiāozhōu.
He sent an envoy to communicate with Cáo Gōng (Cáo Cāo).
When the matter was discovered,
Sūn Quán imprisoned him.
He died several years later.
His sons Xīng, Zhāo, Wěi, and Xīn
all held prominent positions.
Sūn Yì, courtesy name Shúbì,
was Sūn Quán's younger brother.
He was valiant and resolute,
with the demeanor of his elder brother, Sūn Cè.
Zhū Zhì, the Administrator, recommended him as Xiàolián,
and the Minister of Works invited him to serve.
In the eighth year of Jiàn’ān (203 CE),
he was appointed General of the Household and Administrator of Dānyáng,
at the age of twenty.
Later, he was killed by his attendants Biān Hóng and others.
Hóng was also immediately executed.
His son Sōng served as Commander of Shooters and Marquis of Dūxiāng.
He died in the third year of Huánglóng (231 CE).
Zhūgě Liàng, the Chancellor of Shǔ, wrote to his elder brother Jǐn, saying:
“Having received such kind treatment from the Eastern Court (Wú),
I am deeply attached to your sons and nephews.
Furthermore, Zǐqiáo (Sūn Sōng) was an excellent vessel,
and I feel profound sorrow for him.
Seeing the items he gave to me, Liàng,
I am moved to tears.”
This is how he mourned Sōng,
because Liàng's adopted son, Zhūgě Qiáo, related it.
Sūn Kuāng, courtesy name Jìzuǒ,
was Yì's younger brother.
He was recommended as Xiàolián and Máocái,
but died before being appointed to office,
at the age of just over twenty.
His son Tài
was a nephew of the Cáo clan,
and served as Commandant of Chángshuǐ.
In the third year of Jiāhé (234 CE),
he accompanied Sūn Quán in besieging Xīnchéng,
and died from a stray arrow.
Tài's son Xiù served as General of the Van and Commander of Xiàkǒu.
Xiù was a close relative of the imperial house
and held military power outside the capital,
which Hào (Sūn Hào) found unsettling.
In the second year of Jiànhéng (270 CE),
Hào sent Hé Dìng with five thousand men to Xiàkǒu for a hunt.
Previously,
there were widespread rumors among the people that Xiù was to be targeted.
When Hé Dìng was far away hunting, Xiù became alarmed,
and that night, he fled to Jìn with his wife, children, and several hundred personal guards.
Jìn appointed Xiù as General of Agile Cavalry and Minister (Yí Tóng Sānsī),
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Kuàijī.
Sūn Sháo, courtesy name Gōnglǐ.
His paternal uncle, Hé,
courtesy name Bóhǎi,
originally had the surname Yú,
and was also a native of Wú.
Sūn Cè loved him,
bestowed upon him the surname Sūn,
and included him in the family registry.
Later, he became a general
and was stationed at Jīngchéng.
Originally,
Sūn Quán killed Shèng Xiàn, the Administrator of Wú Commandery.
Shèng Xiàn's former Xiàolián, Guī Lǎn and Dài Yuán, fled and hid in the mountains.
When Sūn Yì became Administrator of Dānyáng,
he treated them both with respect and brought them into his service.
Guī Lǎn became Grand Commander overseeing the troops,
and Dài Yuán became Commandery Assistant.
When Yì was murdered,
Hé rushed to Wǎnlíng
and angrily reprimanded Lǎn and Yuán,
for not being able to protect Sūn Quán,
allowing the treacherous conspirators to succeed.
The two men deliberated, saying:
“Bóhǎi (Sūn Hé) is distantly related to the General (Sūn Quán),
yet he reprimands us so severely.
If Tǎolǔ (Sūn Quán) comes,
none of us will be spared.”
So, they killed Hé,
and sent messengers north to welcome Liú Fù, the Inspector of Yángzhōu,
asking him to reside in Lìyáng,
and offering Dānyáng in support.
At that time, Xú Yuán, Sūn Gāo, Fù Yīng, and others from Yì's personal guard killed Lǎn and Yuán.
Sūn Sháo was seventeen.
He gathered the remaining troops from Hé,
repaired and governed the capital city,
erected towers and battlements,
and prepared equipment to defend against enemies.
Sūn Quán heard of the chaos,
returned from Jiāoqū,
passed Dānyáng to pacify it,
and led his army back to Wú.
He arrived outside the capital city and set up camp at night.
He attempted a feigned attack to startle them.
The soldiers all manned the city walls, circulated messages to prepare for an alert,
and their clamor shook the earth.
They shot at some outsiders,
and Sūn Quán had them informed and only then did they stop.
The next day, he met Sūn Sháo
and greatly admired him.
He immediately appointed him as Chéngliè Xiàowèi,
to command the Hé部曲 (bùqū),
and granted him the revenue of the two counties of Qū'ā and Dāntú.
He was allowed to appoint his own chief officials,
all as Sūn Hé had done previously.
Later, he became the Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng and a Piān Jiāngjūn.
When Sūn Quán became King of Wú,
he was promoted to Yángwēi Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Jiàndé Hóu.
When Sūn Quán assumed the imperial title,
he was made Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn.
Sūn Sháo served as a frontier general for several decades,
excelling at caring for his soldiers,
who gave their lives for him.
He always made it his duty to guard the borders and keep distant patrols,
foreknowing movements and preparing for them.
Therefore, he rarely suffered defeats.
Many people from Qīng, Xú, Rǔ, and Pèi came to pledge allegiance.
The garrisons and outposts along the Huáinán riverbanks all withdrew their troops and moved far away,
leaving the lands of Xú, Sì, Jiāng, and Huái
unoccupied for several hundred li.
After Sūn Quán launched his western expedition
and returned to the capital at Wǔchāng,
Sūn Sháo did not have an audience for more than ten years.
When Sūn Quán returned to Jiànyè,
he was then able to have an audience.
Sūn Quán asked about the strategic points of the various garrisons in Qīng and Xú,
the numbers of men and horses, both near and far,
and the names of the Wèi generals.
Sūn Sháo knew them all thoroughly
and answered every question.
He was eight *chi* tall
and had a dignified and elegant appearance.
Sūn Quán was delighted and said,
"I haven't seen Gōnglǐ for a long time,
and I didn't expect him to have improved so much!"
He was additionally made Inspector of Yōuzhōu and granted *jiǎjié*.
He died in the fourth year of Chìwū.
His son, Sūn Yuè, succeeded him,
reaching the rank of Yòu Jiāngjūn.
Sūn Yuè's elder brother, Sūn Kǎi, was Wǔwèi Dà Jiāngjūn and Língchéng Hóu.
He replaced Sūn Yuè as Jīngxià Dū.
Sūn Kǎi's younger brother, Sūn Yì, became Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn;
Sūn Yì, Zōngzhèng Qīng;
and Sūn Huī, Wǔlíng Tàishǒu.
In the first year of Tiānxǐ,
Sūn Kǎi was summoned to be Gōngxià Zhèn Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
Initially, the Yong'an bandits Shī Dàn and others kidnapped Hào's younger brother, Sūn Qiān,
and attacked Jiànyè.
Someone reported that Sūn Kǎi was ambivalent and did not immediately go to suppress them.
Hào repeatedly sent messengers to question Sūn Kǎi.
Sūn Kǎi was constantly terrified,
and when he was finally summoned,
he took his wife, children, and several hundred personal guards and defected to Jìn.
Jìn appointed him Chēqí Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed him as Dānyáng Hóu.
Sūn Huán, courtesy name Shúwǔ,
was a son of Sūn Hé.
At twenty-five,
he was appointed Āndōng Zhōnglángjiàng,
and together with Lù Xùn, he resisted Liú Bèi.
Liú Bèi's army was very strong,
filling the mountains and valleys.
Sūn Huán threw his knife and fought for his life,
working together with Lù Xùn.
Liú Bèi was subsequently defeated and fled.
Sūn Huán cut off the road at Shàngkuí
and blocked its strategic pass.
Liú Bèi climbed mountains and traversed dangerous terrain,
barely escaping.
In anger and frustration, he sighed,
"When I first arrived in Jīngchéng,
Huán was still a little child,
yet now he has pressed me to this extent!"
For his achievements, Sūn Huán was appointed Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Dāntú Hóu.
He was assigned to oversee Niúzhǔ,
where he built a floating fort across the river.
He soon died.
The commentary states: Indeed, the kindness and righteousness of kinship
are constant throughout ancient and modern times.
That imperial clansmen serve as a protective screen
is praised by poets.
How much more so these various Sūns,
some of whom aided in establishing the initial foundation,
others who guarded the frontiers,
proving themselves capable of their responsibilities
and not disgracing their honor!
Therefore, they are extensively recorded here.
Biography of Zhāng, Gù, Zhūgě, and Bù, Chapter Seven
Zhāng Zhāo, courtesy name Zǐbù,
was a native of Péngchéng.
In his youth, he loved learning
and was skilled in *lìshū*.
He studied the *Zuǒshì Chūnqiū* under Bái Hóu Zǐ'ān.
He extensively read many books
and gained renown and befriended Zhào Yù of Lángyá and Wáng Lǎng of Dōnghǎi.
At the age of twenty, he was nominated as *xiàolián*,
but did not accept.
He and Wáng Lǎng discussed the naming taboos of former rulers,
and talented gentlemen from the province, such as Chén Lín, all praised their excellence.
The Inspector Táo Qiān nominated him as *màocái*,
but he did not respond.
Táo Qiān thought he was slighting him
and consequently had him arrested.
Zhào Yù risked his own life to rescue him,
and only then was he able to escape.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, there was great chaos,
and many scholars and commoners from Xú province fled to Yáng province.
Zhāng Zhāo all crossed the Jiāng (Yangtze River) southwards.
When Sūn Cè began his enterprise,
he appointed Zhāng Zhāo as Chángshǐ and Fǔjūn Zhōnglángjiàng.
He ascended the hall to pay respects to Zhāng Zhāo's mother,
treating them as old equals.
Matters of both civil and military affairs
were entirely entrusted to Zhāng Zhāo.
Whenever Zhāng Zhāo received letters from northern literati and officials,
they invariably attributed all merits to Zhāng Zhāo.
Zhāng Zhāo wanted to keep silent and not announce them, fearing it would appear he had private motives;
but to announce them, he feared, would be inappropriate.
He was uneasy in his dilemma.
Sūn Cè heard of this
and laughed joyfully, saying,
"In ancient times, Guǎn Zhòng was Chancellor of Qí.
Firstly 'Zhòngfù',
secondly 'Zhòngfù',
and yet Duke Huán became the hegemon's patriarch.
Now Zǐbù is virtuous,
and I am able to employ him.
Will his achievements and fame not still be mine alone?"
When [Sūn] Cè was dying,
he entrusted his younger brother, [Sūn] Quán, to [Zhāng] Zhāo.
Zhāo, leading all the officials, enthroned and assisted him.
He submitted a memorial to the Hàn court,
and issued orders to the subordinate cities.
He instructed all the generals and officers, both within and outside the capital,
to each attend to their duties.
Quán, overcome with grief, had not yet attended to affairs.
Zhāo said to Quán:
"Indeed, one who succeeds to a position [of leadership]
should be able to bear the burden of the precedents set by their predecessors
and brilliantly continue their established work,
thereby achieving great merit and enterprise.
Currently, the world is in turmoil,
with bandits filling the mountains.
How can the Filial and Incorruptible [i.e., you] immerse yourself in sorrow
and indulge in the sentiments of a common man?"
Then, he personally helped Quán onto his horse,
displayed the troops, and rode out.
Only then did the hearts of the multitude know where to turn.
Zhāo again became Quán's Chief Clerk,
and was given responsibilities as before.
Later, Liú Bèi appointed Quán as acting General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and Zhāo was made Army Advisor.
Whenever Quán went hunting,
he would often ride a horse and shoot tigers.
The tigers would often charge forward and cling to the horse's saddle.
Zhāo's expression changed, and he stepped forward saying:
"General, why must you act like this?
Indeed, one who is a ruler
is expected to control heroes
and employ the wise.
How can one be said to be chasing across the plains
and competing in bravery with fierce beasts?
If a mishap were to occur someday,
what would the world's laughter mean?"
Quán apologized to Zhāo, saying:
"Being young, I do not consider things far enough.
For this, I am ashamed before you."
However, he still could not stop.
So, he built a tiger-shooting chariot,
which had square openings,
but no cover in between.
One person drove it,
while he shot from inside.
At times, there would be exceptionally powerful beasts
that would charge the chariot again,
and Quán would personally strike them, finding it enjoyable.
Although Zhāo remonstrated,
Quán often laughed and did not reply.
In the second year of Huángchū of Wèi (221 CE),
an envoy, Xíng Zhēn, was sent to enfeoff Quán as King of Wú.
When Zhēn entered the gate,
he did not dismount from his carriage.
Zhāo said to Zhēn:
"Indeed, there is no rite without reverence,
and thus no law that is not observed.
Yet you dare to act with such arrogance.
Is it because you think Jiāngnán is weak and small,
and has no inch of a blade?"
Zhēn immediately dismounted from his carriage.
Zhāo was appointed General Who Pacifies the Distant,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yóuquán.
When Quán was in Wǔchāng,
he sat on a fishing platform,
drinking wine until he was greatly intoxicated.
Quán had someone sprinkle water on the assembled officials, saying:
"Today we drink to our hearts' content;
only when one gets so drunk as to fall into the platform
will we stop."
Zhāo looked stern and said nothing,
but went outside and sat in his carriage.
Quán sent someone to call Zhāo back,
and said:
"We are just having fun together,
why are you angry, sir?"
Zhāo replied:
"In the past, Zhòu indulged in long nights of drinking amidst mounds of dregs and ponds of wine.
At the time, he also considered it enjoyable,
not evil."
Quán fell silent,
looking ashamed,
and thereupon stopped the drinking.
Initially,
when Quán was about to appoint a Chancellor,
the general consensus pointed to Zhāo.
Quán said:
"At present, there are many affairs;
the responsibilities of the chief administrator are heavy.
This is not a way to show him favor."
Later, Sūn Shào died,
and all the officials again nominated Zhāo.
Quán said:
"Am I, the lonely one, sparing Zǐbù [Zhāng Zhāo] due to personal preference?
The affairs of the Chancellor are troublesome,
and this gentleman's nature is rigid.
If his words are not followed,
resentment and blame will arise,
which is not a way to benefit him."
So, he appointed Gù Yōng instead.
After Quán adopted the imperial title,
Zhāo, due to old age and illness,
requested to resign his official position and the commands he held.
He was re-appointed General Who Assists Wú,
his rank equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers,
and his enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Lóu,
with an income from ten thousand households.
Residing at home with nothing to do,
he then authored commentaries on the Chunqiu Zuoshi Zhuan and Lunyu.
Quán once asked Wei尉 Yán Jùn:
"Do you still remember the books you memorized when you were young?"
Jùn then recited from the Xiaojing,
"Zhòngní resided..."
Zhāo said:
"Yán Jùn is a boorish scholar;
I beg to recite it for Your Majesty."
Then he recited
"The gentleman's service to his superior..."
Everyone agreed that Zhāo knew what to recite.
Whenever Zhāo had an audience at court,
his words and demeanor were resolute and awe-inspiring,
and his righteousness was evident in his expression.
He once spoke frankly in defiance of the imperial will,
and was not granted an audience for some time.
Later, an envoy from Shǔ arrived,
extolling the virtues of Shǔ.
None of the officials could refute him,
and Quán sighed, saying:
"If Zhāng-gōng were here,
he would either silence him or render him useless.
How could he boast like this?"
The next day,
he sent a palace envoy to convey his regards and inquire after Zhāo,
and then invited Zhāo for an audience.
Zhāo moved from his mat to bow in thanks,
and Quán knelt to stop him.
After Zhāo was seated,
he looked up and said:
"In the past, the Empress Dowager and King Huán [Sūn Cè] did not entrust this old minister to Your Majesty,
but rather entrusted Your Majesty to this old minister.
Therefore, I sought to exhaust my duty as a minister
to repay their profound kindness,
so that after my demise,
there might be something commendable to speak of.
However, my thoughts and considerations were shallow and short-sighted,
and I went against Your August Will,
thus resigning myself to obscurity
and being permanently discarded in a ditch.
I had not expected to again be granted an audience
and serve within the imperial court.
However, the intention of this foolish minister in serving the country
is to be loyal and beneficial,
until death.
As for changing my mind and thoughts
to seek glory and ingratiate myself,
this is something this minister cannot do."
Quán offered his apologies.
Quán, based on Gōngsūn Yuān's claiming vassalage,
sent Zhāng Mí and Xǔ Yàn to Liáodōng to appoint Yuān as King of Yān.
Zhāo remonstrated, saying:
“Yuān defected from Wèi and fears punishment,
coming from afar to seek aid.
This is not his original intention.
If Yuān changes his mind
and wishes to make himself clear to Wèi,
and the two envoys do not return,
would this not be a laughingstock to the world?”
Quán and Zhāo argued back and forth,
Zhāo's resolve becoming even firmer.
Quán could not bear it,
gripped his sword and angrily said:
“The gentlemen of Wú Kingdom, when they enter the palace, bow to me;
when they leave the palace, they bow to you.
My respect for you
is also extreme,
yet you repeatedly oppose me in front of the crowd,
I often fear I might make a miscalculation.”
Zhāo stared intently at Quán and said:
“Although I know my words might not be heeded,
the reason I always exhaust my foolish loyalty
is truly because when the Empress Dowager was on her deathbed,
she called this old minister to her bedside,
and her testamentary edict and dying instructions still remain.”
Then, tears streamed down his face.
Quán threw his sword to the ground
and wept with Zhāo.
However, he ultimately sent Mí and Yàn.
Zhāo was indignant that his words were not used
and claimed illness, refusing to attend court.
Quán resented this,
and had dirt block his gate.
Zhāo then blocked it from within with dirt.
Yuān indeed killed Mí and Yàn.
Quán repeatedly offered comfort and apologies to Zhāo,
but Zhāo firmly refused to rise.
Quán then went past his gate and called out to Zhāo.
Zhāo pleaded that his illness was severe.
Quán burned his gate,
wishing to frighten him,
but Zhāo merely closed his door tighter.
Quán had someone extinguish the fire,
and stood at the gate for a long time.
Zhāo's sons together helped Zhāo rise,
and Quán carried him back to the palace,
deeply reproaching himself.
Zhāo, having no choice,
then attended court meetings.
Zhāo's appearance was dignified and solemn,
possessing an imposing demeanor.
Quán often said:
“When I speak with Master Zhāng,
I dare not speak rashly.”
The entire state feared him.
At the age of eighty-one,
he died in the fifth year of Jiāhé.
His will instructed a simple cloth headscarf and plain coffin,
and to be clothed in everyday attire for burial.
Quán wore plain clothes to mourn and offer condolences,
and posthumously named him Wén Hóu.
His eldest son Chéng had already been enfeoffed as a marquis,
and his younger son Xiū inherited the title.
Zhāo's nephew Fèn, at twenty years old,
invented a large siege vehicle for attacking cities.
He was recommended by Bù Zhì.
Zhāo disapproved, saying:
“You are still young,
why do you entrust yourself to the military?”
Fèn replied:
“In the past, Tóng Wāng died in distress,
and Zǐ Qí governed Ā.
Fèn is truly untalented,
but as for age, I am not young.”
So he led troops as a general,
achieving repeated successes,
reaching the position of Dūdū of Bànzhōu,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Lèxiāngtíng.
Chéng, courtesy name Zhòngsì,
was known for his talent and learning in his youth,
and was good friends with Zhūgě Jǐn, Bù Zhì, and Yán Jùn.
When Quán was General of Agile Cavalry,
he appointed Chéng as his Xīcáocuàn,
then he was sent out as Administrator of Chángshā Xībù.
He suppressed and pacified the mountain bandits,
obtaining fifteen thousand elite soldiers.
Later, he served as Dūdū of Núxū and Fènwēi Jiāngjūn,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng,
and commanded five thousand retainers.
Chéng was brave, resolute, loyal, and outspoken,
able to discern and identify individuals.
He promoted Cài Kuǎn of Péngchéng and Xiè Jǐng of Nányáng from obscurity in their youth,
who later both became national scholars.
Kuǎn reached Wèiwèi,
and Jǐng became Administrator of Yùzhāng.
Also, when Zhūgě Kè was young,
everyone marveled at his outstanding talent,
but Chéng said that it would be Yuánsùn who would ultimately ruin the Zhūgě clan.
He was diligent in making progress,
and devoted to his peers.
All those who showed promise
would visit his gate.
At the age of sixty-seven,
he died in the seventh year of Chìwū,
and was posthumously named Dìng Hóu.
His son Zhèn inherited the title.
Initially,
after Chéng lost his wife,
Zhāo wanted to find him Zhūgě Jǐn's daughter.
Chéng found it difficult because they were good friends.
Quán heard about it and encouraged it,
so he became Zhūgě Jǐn's son-in-law.
They had a daughter,
whom Quán arranged for his son Hé to marry.
Quán often instructed Hé to show respect to Chéng,
observing the rites of a son-in-law.
Zhèn also died when Zhūgě Kè was executed.
Xiū, courtesy name Shúsì,
in his youth, along with Zhūgě Kè and Gù Tán,
was a colleague and friend of Crown Prince Dēng,
teaching Dēng the Hàn Shū.
He was transferred from Zhōngshùzǐ to Yòubì Dūwèi.
Quán often went hunting,
returning only in the evening.
Xiū submitted a memorial advising caution,
Quán greatly approved of it
and showed it to Zhāo.
After Dēng's death,
he became Shìzhōng,
appointed Yǔlín Dūdū,
and pacified the affairs of the three Diǎnjūn.
He was promoted to Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn.
He was slandered by the faction of King Lǔ, Bà.
Along with Gù Tán and Chéng, he was involved in discussing merits at Quèpí.
Xiū and Chéng colluded with Diǎnjūn Chén Xún,
falsely increasing their achievements,
and were all exiled to Jiāozhōu.
Zhōngshūlìng Sūn Hóng was treacherous, deceitful, and crooked.
Xiū had always resented him.
Hóng used this to slander him,
and an imperial edict was issued granting Xiū death.
He was forty-one years old at the time.
Gù Yōng, courtesy name Yuántàn,
was a native of Wú County, Wú.
Cài Bójiē, upon returning from Shuòfāng,
once sought refuge in Wú to avoid enmity.
