Yōng learned to play the qín and read books from him.
He was recommended by the province and commandery,
and in his youth, became the Magistrate of Héfèi.
Later, he was transferred to Lóu, Qǔ'ā, and Shàngyú,
all places where he had good administrative records.
When Sūn Quán took the post of Administrator of Kuàijī,
but did not go to the commandery,
he appointed Yōng as his Aide,
to act as Administrator.
Yōng suppressed the bandits,
and the commandery became peaceful.
Officials and common people submitted to him.
After several years,
he entered the court as Zuǒsīmǎ.
When Quán became King of Wú,
Yōng was successively promoted to Dàlǐ Fèngcháng,
and concurrently served as Shàngshūlìng.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángsuìxiāng.
Upon returning home after being appointed marquis,
his family did not know,
and were only surprised upon hearing it later.
In the fourth year of Huángwǔ,
he welcomed his mother from Wú.
Upon her arrival,
Sūn Quán personally went to congratulate her,
and bowed to her mother in the courtyard.
All the high officials and ministers were present.
Later, the crown prince also went to offer congratulations.
Gù Yōng was not a drinker;
he spoke little,
and his actions were always appropriate.
Sūn Quán once sighed, saying:
"Lord Gù does not speak,
but when he does, his words always hit the mark."
During banquets and festive occasions,
those around him feared making a drunken mistake that Gù Yōng would surely witness,
and thus did not dare to indulge their feelings.
Sūn Quán also said:
"With Lord Gù present,
it makes people unhappy."
Such was the extent to which he was feared.
That year,
he was changed to Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng),
promoted to be enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lǐlíng,
and replaced Sūn Shào as Chancellor (Chéngxiàng),
supervising matters of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū).
The civil and military officers he selected and employed were each appointed according to their abilities,
without favoritism or prejudice in his heart.
Whenever he inquired about conditions among the common people
or matters suitable for government administration,
he would secretly report them.
If his suggestions were adopted,
he would attribute them to the sovereign;
if not adopted,
he would never divulge them.
Sūn Quán esteemed him for this.
However, when he had something to present in court,
though his words and demeanor were compliant, what he upheld was righteous.
Sūn Quán once consulted him about gains and losses,
and Zhāng Zhāo then presented a report on what he had heard and observed,
stating that laws were too numerous
and punishments slightly too severe,
and that some should be abolished or reduced.
Sūn Quán remained silent,
then turned to Gù Yōng and asked:
"What do you think, sir?"
Gù Yōng replied:
"What I have heard
is also as Zhāng Zhāo has stated."
Thereupon, Sūn Quán discussed reducing the severity of punishments.
After a long time,
Lǚ Yī and Qín Bó became Clerks of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū),
in charge of reviewing documents from various government offices and prefectures.
Lǚ Yī and his colleagues gradually used this to wield power,
and subsequently created the profitable monopolies of salt and iron (quekū zhàngguǎn).
They exposed crimes and denounced wrongdoing,
reporting even the smallest details.
Moreover, they deeply investigated and maliciously slandered,
defaming high officials
and framing the innocent.
Gù Yōng and others were all accused
and consequently reprimanded.
Later, Lǚ Yī's corruption was exposed,
and he was arrested and imprisoned in the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi).
When Gù Yōng went to judge the case,
Lǚ Yī appeared before him as a prisoner.
Gù Yōng spoke kindly,
asking about his confession and circumstances.
Before leaving,
he also said to Lǚ Yī:
"Do you have anything you wish to say?"
Lǚ Yī kowtowed silently.
At that time, Shàngshūláng Huái Xù cursed and insulted Lǚ Yī to his face.
Gù Yōng reproached Huái Xù, saying:
"The state has its proper laws;
why resort to this!"
Gù Yōng served as Chancellor for nineteen years.
He died in the sixth year of Chìwū
at the age of seventy-six.
When his illness first became minor,
Sūn Quán ordered the physician Zhào Quán to examine him,
and appointed his youngest son, Jì, as Cavalry Commandant (Jì Dūwèi).
When Gù Yōng heard this,
he sadly said:
"Zhào Quán is skilled at discerning life and death;
I will surely not recover.
Therefore, the sovereign wishes for me to see Jì appointed before I die."
Sūn Quán wore plain clothes to mourn him
and gave him the posthumous title of Sù Hóu.
His eldest son, Shào, died early.
His second son, Yù, had a serious illness.
His youngest son, Jì, succeeded him,
but had no heir,
and the line became extinct.
In the first year of Yǒng'ān,
an edict stated:
"The late Chancellor Gù Yōng,
with utmost virtue and loyal wisdom,
assisted the state with propriety.
However, his marquisate has ceased to be inherited,
which I deeply lament.
Therefore, let Gù Yōng's second son, Yù, succeed to the title of Marquis of Lǐlíng,
to clearly commemorate his old merits."
Gù Shào, whose courtesy name was Xiàozé,
read widely in books and historical records,
and enjoyed discussing human character.
In his youth, he was as renowned as his maternal uncle Lù Jì,
while Lù Xùn, Zhāng Dūn, and Bǔ Jìng were all considered inferior to him.
From officials of the prefectures and commanderies to scholars from all directions,
people came to visit him,
some to discuss and then leave,
others to form close friendships before parting.
His reputation spread far and wide,
praised by those near and far.
Sūn Quán married his daughter to him, a daughter of Sūn Cè.
At twenty-seven,
he began his career as Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Yùzhāng.
Upon arriving at his post, he first offered sacrifices at the tomb of the worthy elder Xú Rúzi,
and treated Xú Rúzi's descendants with great kindness;
he prohibited licentious and improper sacrifices.
He would send promising junior officials
to study,
select the most advanced among them,
and promote them to important positions.
By promoting the good as an example,
his virtuous influence spread widely.
Initially,
Dīng Xǔ of Qiántáng came from military service,
Zhāng Bǐng of Yángxiàn was born a commoner,
Wú Càn of Wúchéng and Yīn Lǐ of Yúnyáng rose from humble origins.
Gù Shào promoted and befriended all of them,
establishing their reputations.
When Zhāng Bǐng suffered a great loss (of a parent),
Gù Shào personally made the mourning clothes and headbands for him.
When Gù Shào was to go to Yùzhāng,
and had departed and was on a nearby road,
he heard that Zhāng Bǐng was ill.
At that time, hundreds of people were seeing him off.
Gù Shào excused himself from his guests, saying:
"Zhāng Zhòngjié (Zhāng Bǐng's courtesy name) is ill
and unfortunately cannot come to bid farewell.
I regret not seeing him.
I will briefly return to bid him a final farewell;
please wait for me a little while."
Such was his attentiveness to humble scholars,
and his willingness to seek out talent wherever it might be.
These are all similar examples.
Dīng Xǔ later became Military Adviser (Diǎnjūn Zhōngláng),
Zhāng Bǐng became Grand Administrator of Yúnyáng,
Yīn Lǐ became Grand Administrator of Línglíng,
and Wú Càn became Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shàofù).
The world regarded Gù Shào as a discerning judge of character.
He served in the commandery for five years
and died in office.
His sons were Tán and Chéngyún.
Tán (譚) styled Zǐmò (子默),
at the age of twenty, along with Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪) and others, became one of the Four Friends of the Crown Prince.
He was transferred from Middle Palace Secretariat Gentleman to Commandant of the Auxiliary Rectification.
In the Chìwū (赤烏) era,
he replaced Kè (恪) as Left Controller.
Whenever he examined the records,
he never used counting tallies;
he merely counted on his fingers and calculated in his mind,
uncovering all errors and falsehoods.
The subordinate officials were impressed by this.
He was promoted to Commandant of Cavalry.
Xuē Zōng (薛綜) was Minister of the Bureau of Selection,
and he firmly yielded to Tán (譚), saying:
“Tán (譚) has a refined mind and meticulous body;
he penetrates the Dao and comprehends the subtle;
his talent illuminates others;
his virtue accords with the hopes of the multitude.
Indeed, he is not someone whom a foolish subject like myself can surpass.”
Subsequently, he replaced Zōng (綜).
Several months after his grandfather Yōng (雍) died,
he was appointed Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
and replaced Yōng (雍) in overseeing the affairs of the Secretariat.
At this time, Lǔ Wáng Bà (魯王霸) enjoyed great favor,
and was on par with Crown Prince Hé (和).
Tán (譚) submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servant has heard that those who govern a state or a family
must clarify the distinction between the legitimate and illegitimate,
and differentiate the rites for the honored and the humble,
so that there is a hierarchy between high and low,
and ranks are distinctly separated.
If this is so, then the affection of blood relatives will arise,
and the hopes of coveting will be extinguished.
In the past, Jiǎ Yì (賈誼) presented plans for peace and order,
and discussed the power of the feudal lords,
believing that if their power was heavy,
though close, they would inevitably suffer the calamity of rebellion;
if their power was light,
though distant, they would inevitably enjoy the blessing of preservation.
Thus, Huáinán (淮南), a close younger brother,
did not ultimately enjoy the state;
this was lost due to heavy power.
Wú Ruì (吳芮), a distant subject,
transmitted his lineage in Chángshā (長沙);
this was gained due to light power.
In the past, Emperor Wén (文) of Hàn (漢) made Lady Shèn (慎) sit on the same mat as the Empress.
Yuán Àng (袁盎) moved Lady's seat back,
and the Emperor showed anger.
But when Àng (盎) explained the proper etiquette for superior and inferior,
and presented the warning of the ‘human swine,’
the Emperor was pleased and delighted,
and the Lady also understood.
What your servant now presents
is not out of partiality for anyone,
but truly wishes to secure the Crown Prince and benefit Lǔ Wáng (魯王).”
Because of this, Bà (霸) and Tán (譚) had a rift.
At that time, Quán Jì (全寄), the son of Grand Princess's husband, General-in-chief Wèi (衛) Quán Cóng (全琮), was a guest of Bà (霸).
Jì (寄) had always been perverse,
and Tán (譚) did not accept him.
Earlier,
Tán's (譚) younger brother Chéng (承) and Zhāng Xiū (張休) together campaigned north to Shòuchūn (壽春).
Quán Cóng (全琮) was then Grand Commander,
and fought against Wèi (魏) general Wáng Líng (王淩) at Sháopí (芍陂).
His army was at a disadvantage.
The Wèi (魏) soldiers, taking advantage of their victory, overwhelmed and captured the camp of General Qín Huàng (秦晃).
Xiū (休) and Chéng (承) fiercely counterattacked.
They then halted the Wèi (魏) army.
At that time, Cóng’s (琮) sons Xù (緒) and Duān (端) were also generals.
Since the enemy was held,
they advanced and attacked,
and Líng’s (淩) army retreated.
At the time of evaluating merits and awarding honors,
it was believed that the merit of halting the enemy was great,
while the merit of repelling the enemy was small.
Xiū (休) and Chéng (承) were both made generals with miscellaneous titles,
while Xù (緒) and Duān (端) were merely auxiliary generals.
Jì’s (寄) father and son grew more resentful,
and jointly framed Tán (譚).
Tán (譚) was exiled to Jiāozhōu (交州).
In his confinement, he gave vent to his indignation,
and wrote twenty chapters of Xīnyán (新言).
His chapter on "Knowing Difficulty" was likely self-lamenting.
He was exiled for two years,
and died at the age of forty-two
in Jiāozhǐ (交阯).
Chéng (承) styled Zǐzhí (子直).
During the Jiāhé (嘉禾) era, he and his maternal uncle Lù Mào (陸瑁) were both summoned with courtesies.
Quán (權) bestowed a letter upon Chancellor Yōng (雍), saying:
“Your esteemed grandson Zǐzhí (子直)
has an excellent reputation.
Upon meeting him,
he exceeds what I had heard.
I congratulate you on his behalf.”
He was appointed Commandant of Cavalry
and commanded the Yǔlín (羽林) guards.
Later, he became Western Commandant of Wújùn (吳郡).
He and Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪) and others together pacified the Shānyuè (山越),
and separately obtained eight thousand elite soldiers.
He returned and garrisoned at Zhāngkēng (章阬),
was appointed Major of Righteous Manifestation,
and entered the court as an Attendant.
In the Battle of Sháopí (芍陂),
he was appointed General Who Rouses Awe
and went out to lead the Capital Supervisorship.
Several years later, he, his elder brother Tán (譚), Zhāng Xiū (張休), and others were all exiled to Jiāozhōu (交州),
where he died at the age of thirty-seven.
Zhūgě Jǐn (諸葛瑾) styled Zǐyú (子瑜),
was a native of Yángdū (陽都), Lángxié (琅邪).
At the end of the Hàn (漢) dynasty, he fled to Jiāngdōng (江東) to avoid chaos.
When Sūn Cè (孫策) died,
Hóng Zī (弘咨) of Qǔ'ā (曲阿), Sūn Quán’s (孫權) brother-in-law, saw him and was impressed.
He recommended him to Quán (權).
He and Lǔ Sù (魯肅) and others were treated as honored guests.
Later, he became Quán’s (權) Chief Clerk,
and was transferred to Middle Cavalier Commandant.
In the 20th year of Jiàn'ān (建安) (215 CE),
Quán (權) sent Jǐn (瑾) on a mission to Shǔ (蜀) to establish good relations with Liú Bèi (劉備).
He and his younger brother Liàng (亮) met at a public assembly;
they had no private meeting after that.
When speaking with Quán (權) and offering advice or persuasion,
he never spoke harshly or bluntly,
but subtly revealed his demeanor,
roughly stating his intentions.
If there was something not yet agreed upon,
he would set it aside and move to another topic,
then gradually use another matter to create a new opening,
seeking common ground through analogies.
Thus, Quán’s (權) intentions were often resolved.
Zhū Zhì (朱治), Administrator of Wújùn (吳郡),
was a general promoted by Quán (權).
Quán (權) once had a grudge against him,
but had always treated him with respect,
and found it difficult to personally question and rebuke him,
remaining indignant and unresolved.
Jǐn (瑾) divined the reason,
but dared not state it explicitly.
So he requested to privately inquire about his intentions,
and then, in front of Quán (權), wrote a letter
discussing general principles,
and thereby remotely inferred Quán’s (權) thoughts with his own mind.
After finishing,
he presented it to Quán (權).
Quán (權) was pleased,
and said with a laugh:
“My intention is resolved!
Is this not what is meant by ‘Yán Shì’s (顏氏) virtue makes people feel closer to him’?”
Quán (權) was also vexed by Cavalier Commandant Yīn Mó (殷模),
whose crime was immeasurable.
Many subordinates spoke on his behalf,
making Quán’s (權) anger even greater.
He debated back and forth with them.
Only Jǐn (瑾) remained silent.
Quán (權) said:
“Zǐyú (子瑜), why are you alone silent?”
Jǐn (瑾) rose from his mat and said:
“Jǐn (瑾) and Yīn Mó (殷模) and others experienced the collapse of our home province,
and the extinction of all living things.
We abandoned our ancestral tombs,
carried our old and weak,
traversed wild lands,
and returned to your benevolent rule.
Among those who were displaced,
we received the blessing of being nurtured and saved.
I am unable to personally admonish myself
and present even a fraction of what I should,
to the extent that Mó (模) has betrayed your kindness
and fallen into crime.
Your servant is too busy apologizing for my own faults;
I truly dare not speak.”
Quán (權) heard this with sadness,
and then said:
“I will especially pardon him for your sake.”
Afterwards, he followed in the campaign against Guān Yǔ,
and was enfeoffed as Xuānchéng Hóu.
As Suī Nán Jiāngjūn, he replaced Lǚ Méng as Grand Administrator of Nánjùn,
residing in Gōng'ān.
When Liú Bèi marched east to attack Wú,
the King of Wú sought peace.
Zhūgě Jǐn wrote a letter to Bèi, saying:
"I suddenly heard that your banners and drums have arrived at Báidì.
Perhaps some officials are thinking that since the King of Wú seized this province [Jīngzhōu]
and harmed Guān Yǔ,
the resentment is deep and the disaster great,
so it is not advisable to accept peace.
This shows concern for the small,
without paying attention to the large.
Please allow me to discuss for Your Majesty the relative importance [of these matters],
and their scale.
If Your Majesty could suppress your power and reduce your anger,
and temporarily consider my words,
a decision could be made immediately,
without needing to consult with the multitude of ministers again.
How does Your Majesty consider Guān Yǔ's relationship to you compared to that of the former emperor?
How does the size of Jīngzhōu compare to that of the entire realm?
Both should be met with enmity and hatred,
but which should take precedence?
If these calculations are carefully considered,
it will be as easy as turning over one's hand."
At that time, some said that Zhūgě Jǐn had privately sent a trusted person to communicate with Bèi.
Sūn Quán said:
"Between Gū and Zǐyú, there is an oath that will not change even in life or death.
Zǐyú's not failing Gū
is like Gū's not failing Zǐyú."
In the first year of Huángwǔ (222 CE),
he was promoted to Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
oversaw Gōng'ān,
was granted a jié (imperial credential),
and was enfeoffed as Wǎnlíng Hóu.
Yú Fān was exiled due to his unrestrained straightforwardness,
but only Zhūgě Jǐn repeatedly spoke on his behalf.
Yú Fān wrote to a close associate, saying:
"Zhūgě Dūnrén (Zhūgě Jǐn) is benevolent,
he is like Heaven giving life to all things.
Recently, I have been favored by his clear judgment,
which has allowed me to preserve my lot.
My accumulated evil and deep crimes
have made me intensely resented.
Even with the rescue of Qí Lǎo,
I lack the virtue of Yángshé,
and hope for exoneration is difficult."
Zhūgě Jǐn possessed a dignified appearance and profound thoughts;
at that time, people admired his magnanimity and refinement.
Sūn Quán also highly esteemed him,
consulting him on major affairs.
He also specifically consulted Zhūgě Jǐn, saying:
"Recently, I received a memorial from Bóyán (Lù Xùn),
who believes that Cáo Pī is already dead,
and that the people, poisoned and disordered,
should collapse at the sight of our banners,
yet they remain calm.
He heard that they have all selected and employed loyal and virtuous men,
eased punishments,
dispensed benevolence and favor,
lightened taxes and reduced labor,
to please the hearts of the people,
and that their troubles are even deeper than in Cáo Cāo's time.
Gū believes this is not so.
As for Cáo Cāo's actions,
only his killing and punitive expeditions were slightly excessive,
and his alienation of people's flesh and blood,
which was cruel.
As for commanding generals,
few in history compare.
Cáo Pī is ten thousand times inferior to Cáo Cāo.
Now Cáo Ruì is inferior to Cáo Pī,
just as Cáo Pī was inferior to Cáo Cāo.
The reason why he strives to cultivate small favors
must be because his father has recently died,
and he assesses himself as weak and declining.
He fears that the suffering people might collapse suddenly,
hence he forces himself to bend and seek popular support,
wishing only to secure himself.
How could this be the beginning of prosperity?
I hear that he employs people like Chén Chángwén (Chén Qún) and Cáo Zǐdān (Cáo Zhēn) —
some are literary scholars and students,
others are imperial kinsmen and relatives.
How can they command heroic talents and tiger generals to control All Under Heaven?
If authority is not centralized,
then affairs will go awry.
Like Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú in the past,
they were not without strong bonds,
but when they held power,
they ended up harming each other.
This is simply the nature of things.
Moreover, people like Chángwén
were able to uphold goodness in the past
because Cáo Cāo squeezed their heads [with pressure],
fearing Cáo Cāo's authority and dignity,
so they gave their whole hearts and minds,
not daring to do evil.
When Cáo Pī succeeded him,
he was already grown,
and following Cáo Cāo,
he treated them with kindness and affection,
thereby inspiring loyalty.
Now Cáo Ruì is young and weak,
swayed by others.
These Cáo-clan types
will surely seize this opportunity to play tricks and act out,
forming factions and cliques,
each supporting their own.
On such a day,
treachery and slander will rise together,
mutually entrapping and resenting each other,
turning into suspicion and disloyalty.
Once this begins,
the subordinates will scramble for profit,
and the young ruler will not be able to control them.
How can their downfall be delayed?
The reason I know this to be so
is that from ancient times to the present,
how could there be four or five people holding the reins of power
without falling into conflict and tearing each other apart?
The strong will surely bully the weak,
and the weak will surely seek aid.
This is the path to chaos and ruin.
Zǐyú,
you just listen carefully.
Bóyán is usually good at calculations,
but I fear he is a bit short-sighted on this matter."
When Sūn Quán claimed the imperial title,
Zhūgě Jǐn was appointed Dà Jiāngjūn and Zuǒ Dūhù,
and concurrently served as Yùzhōu Mù.
After Lǚ Yī was executed,
Sūn Quán issued another edict rebuking Zhūgě Jǐn and others.
The details are in Sūn Quán's biography.
Zhūgě Jǐn promptly responded to the matter,
with appropriate language and sound reasoning.
Zhūgě Jǐn's son, Zhūgě Kè,
was renowned in his time.
Sūn Quán deeply valued and admired him;
however, Zhūgě Jǐn always disliked him,
believing he was not a son who could preserve the family,
and was constantly worried.
In the fourth year of Chìwū (241 CE),
he died at the age of sixty-eight.
He left a will ordering a plain coffin and burial in everyday clothes,
with simple and frugal arrangements.
Since Zhūgě Kè had already been enfeoffed as a marquis,
his younger brother Zhūgě Róng inherited the title,
took command of the troops,
and was stationed in Gōng'ān.
His subordinates, officers, and soldiers were devoted to him.
When there were no external affairs,
in autumn and winter, they would hunt and practice military skills;
in spring and summer, he would host banquets for guests,
granting leave to officials and soldiers.
Some would travel not less than a thousand lǐ to visit him.
At each gathering, he would inquire among his guests,
each stating their abilities.
Then, he would arrange mats and draw seats closer,
assessing opponents and selecting matches.
Some played board games,
some played shūpú,
some played tóuhú (pitch-pot) or shot bows and pellets.
Groups were divided by category.
Then, sweet fruits were continuously served,
and clear wine flowed slowly.
Zhūgě Róng circulated, observing everything,
tireless throughout the day.
Zhūgě Róng's father and elder brother were plain and simple;
even when on military campaigns,
they wore no elaborate decorations.
But Zhūgě Róng wore brocade and patterned silk,
being exceptionally extravagant and ornate.
When Sūn Quán died,
he was transferred to Fènwēi Jiāngjūn.
Later, when Zhūgě Kè campaigned in Huáinán,
he granted Zhūgě Róng a jié,
ordering him to lead troops into Miǎn [River]
to attack the western forces.
After Zhūgě Kè was executed,
Wúnán Dū Shī Kuān was sent, along with Jiāngjūn Shī Jì, Sūn Yī, and Quán Xī, to apprehend Zhūgě Róng.
When Zhūgě Róng first heard that soldiers were arriving,
he was terrified and hesitant,
unable to make a decision.
When the soldiers arrived and surrounded the city,
he drank poison and died.
His three sons were all executed.
Bù Zhì, courtesy name Zǐshān,
was from Huái'yīn in Líncuì (Lín Huái) Commandery.
During the period of chaos,
he sought refuge in Jiāngdōng.
Alone and impoverished,
he became good friends with Wèi Jīng from Guǎnglíng, who was of the same age.
Both supported themselves by cultivating melons.
During the day, they toiled with their bodies;
at night, they recited classics and commentaries.
Jiāo Zhēngqiāng of Kuàijī
was a prominent clan in the commandery,
whose retainers were unruly and unrestrained.
Zhì and Jīng sought sustenance in his territory,
fearing encroachment,
so they together repaired their blades and offered melons
to Zhēngqiāng.
Zhēngqiāng was then resting within,
detaining them for a long while.
Jīng wished to abandon the visit and leave,
but Zhì stopped him, saying:
"The reason we came in the first place
was that we feared his power;
if we abandon it now
to appear high-minded,
we will only incur enmity."
After a long time,
Zhēngqiāng opened the window and saw them.
He hid behind a low table, sitting inside the tent,
and had mats spread on the ground,
seating Zhì and Jīng outside the window.
Jīng was even more ashamed,
but Zhì's demeanor remained composed.
When Zhēngqiāng had food prepared,
he enjoyed a large table himself,
with stacked dishes of various delicacies,
while giving Zhì and Jīng small plates of rice,
with only vegetables.
Jīng could not eat,
but Zhì ate a great deal until he was full before excusing himself.
Jīng angrily said to Zhì:
"How can you endure this?"
Zhì replied:
"We are poor and lowly,
and so the host treats us as poor and lowly.
This is naturally fitting;
what is there to be ashamed of?"
When Sūn Quán was General of the Gentlemen of Plunder (Tǎolǔ Jiāngjūn),
he summoned Zhì to be Record Keeper (Zhǔjì).
He was appointed Magistrate (Zhǎng) of Hǎiyán,
and later recalled to be East Clerk (Dōngcáo Yuàn) to the General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn).
In the fifteenth year of Jiàn'ān [210 CE],
he was sent out to govern Póyáng as Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu).
Within the year,
he was transferred to be Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Jiāozhōu and General of the Gentlemen of Establishing Martial Might (Lìwǔ Zhōnglángjiāng),
commanding a thousand martial archers (wǔshè lì).
He then traveled south.
The following year,
he was posthumously granted the title of Bearer of the Imperial Credentials (Shǐchíjié) and General of the Gentlemen Who Subdue the South (Zhēngnán Zhōnglángjiāng).
Wú Jù, the Grand Administrator of Cāngwú appointed by Liú Biǎo, secretly harbored disloyal intentions,
appearing compliant outwardly but defiant inwardly.
Zhì lowered himself and used persuasion,
inviting him for a meeting.
He then beheaded and displayed him,
and his prestige greatly spread.
Shì Xiè and his brothers
led their people to submit to his authority.
The submission of the southern lands
began from this point.
The great clans of Yìzhōu, such as Yōng Kǎi, killed Zhèng Áng, the Grand Administrator appointed by Shǔ,
communicated with Xiè,
and sought to submit.
Zhì, acting on imperial authority, dispatched envoys to proclaim grace and accept their submission.
Because of this, he was further appointed General Who Pacifies the Barbarians (Píngróng Jiāngjūn)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Guǎngxìn.
In the first year of Yánkāng [220 CE],
Quán sent Lǚ Dài to replace Zhì.
Zhì led ten thousand righteous warriors from Jiāozhōu out to Chángshā.
It happened that Liú Bèi was advancing eastward,
and the Mán barbarians of Wǔlíng were stirring.
Quán then ordered Zhì to advance to Yìyáng.
Bèi was defeated,
but the commanderies of Líng and Guì were still alarmed and disturbed,
with armed resistance everywhere.
Zhì campaigned around the area
and pacified them all.
In the second year of Huángwǔ [223 CE],
he was promoted to General of the Right (Yòujiāngjūn) and Left Protector of the Army (Zuǒ Hùjūn),
and his title was changed to Marquis of Línxiāng.
In the fifth year [226 CE],
he was granted the Staff of Authority (jiǎjié)
and transferred to garrison at Ōukǒu.
When Quán declared himself emperor,
Zhì was appointed General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn)
and concurrently Governor (Mù) of Jìzhōu.
That year,
he was appointed Superintendent (Dūdū) of Xīlíng,
replacing Lù Xùn in pacifying the two borders.
Soon after, as Jìzhōu was within the Shǔ territories,
he was relieved of his governorship.
At that time, Quán's Crown Prince Dēng was stationed in Wǔchāng,
a person who loved people and esteemed goodness.
He wrote to Zhì, saying:
"Virtuous gentlemen,
it is through you that great transformation flourishes
and the affairs of the time are assisted and managed.
By nature, I am ignorant and obtuse,
not comprehending the ways of the Dao.
Although I sincerely desire to dedicate myself to illustrious virtue
and entrust a part of my duties to gentlemen,
regarding the scholars near and far,
and the propriety of their precedence,
I am still somewhat distant
and unable to understand it thoroughly.
The Classic says: 'Can one love without causing labor?
Can one be loyal without giving counsel?'
This is its meaning,
and is it not what I hope for from gentlemen!"
Zhì then listed the contemporary figures engaged in affairs within Jīngzhōu,
namely Zhūgě Jǐn, Lù Xùn, Zhū Rán, Chéng Pǔ, Pān Jùn, Péi Xuán, Xiàhóu Chéng, Wèi Jīng, Lǐ Sù,
Zhōu Tiáo, and Shí Gàn—eleven people.
He distinguished their conduct
and then submitted a memorial encouraging and praising them, saying:
"Your servant has heard that a ruler does not personally attend to minor matters,
and the hundred officials and various departments each fulfill their duties.
Thus, when Shùn appointed nine sages,
he had no need to exert his mind,
playing a five-stringed zither
and chanting the 'South Wind' poem,
and the world was well-governed without his leaving the hall or temple.
Qí Huán employed Guǎn Zhòng,
even wearing his hair disheveled and riding in a carriage.
Once the state of Qí was well-governed,
he further achieved the 'gathering of the feudal lords to rectify the world' (kuānghé).
In recent times, Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn gathered the Three Heroes (Sān Jié) to establish the imperial enterprise,
while Western Chǔ lost its heroes and failed in its endeavors.
When Jí Àn was in court,
Huáinán abandoned its plots;
when Zhì Dū guarded the frontier,
the Xiongnu retreated.
Therefore, wherever virtuous men are present,
they can repel enemies a myriad of li away;
they are truly the state's sharp instruments,
and the cause of its prosperity or decline.
Currently, the royal transforming influence (wánghuà) has not yet reached north of the Hàn River,
and on the banks of the Hé and Luò Rivers there are still the ugly pretensions of rebels.
This is truly the time to gather heroes, elevate the talented, and appoint the virtuous.
I wish that the sagacious Crown Prince would give this matter serious consideration,
then the world would be exceedingly fortunate."
Later, Lü Yī
of the Secretariat was in charge of collating documents,
and made many accusations.
Bù Zhì submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly hear that the document collators delve into minute details,
blowing on fur to find flaws,
and make severe accusations and deep slanders,
always seeking to entrap people to establish their authority and power.
The innocent and blameless
are unjustly subjected to severe punishment,
which makes the people walk on thin ice,
who among them does not tremble?
In ancient times, judicial officials
were appointed only from among the virtuous.
Thus, Gāo Yáo served as a judge,
Lǚ Hóu commuted punishments,
and Zhāng [Shì] and Yú [Dìngguo] were Grand Ministers of Justice,
and the people suffered no injustice.
The blessings of peace and prosperity
truly arose from this.
Today's minor officials
act differently from the ancients.
Prisons are swayed by bribes,
human lives are treated lightly,
blame is shifted to the superior,
and resentment is swiftly incurred for the state.
If one person sighs in distress,
the kingly way is diminished,
which is extremely hateful and detestable.
'Clarify virtue and be cautious in punishments,'
'the wise consider punishments'
are praised in historical texts.
From now on, in obscure cases,
in the capital, Gù Yōng should be consulted;
in Wǔchāng, Lù Xùn and Pān Jùn [should be consulted].
With an impartial and focused mind,
they must strive to ascertain the truth.
If Bù Zhì's faction is judged by the divine,
what regret would there be in receiving punishment?"
He also said:
"The Son of Heaven takes Heaven as father and Earth as mother,
therefore the palace and all officials
are modelled after the constellations.
If political decrees are implemented
reverently in accordance with the seasons,
and officials are properly chosen,
then yin and yang will be in harmony,
and the seven luminaries will follow their paths.
As of today,
many official positions are vacant,
and even if there are high ministers,
they are not fully trusted.
How can Heaven and Earth not manifest changes under such circumstances?
Thus, the frequent droughts in recent years
are a response to excessive yang.
Moreover, on the fourteenth day of the fifth month of Jiāhé sixth year,
and on the first and twenty-seventh days of the first month of Chìwū second year,
the earth trembled.
The earth is of the yin category,
the symbol of ministers.
The movement indicates a surplus of yin qi,
which is due to ministers monopolizing power.
Heaven and Earth show anomalies
to warn the ruler.
How can one not deeply ponder their meaning?"
He further said:
"Prime Minister Gù Yōng, Grand Commander Lù Xùn, and Grand Minister of Ceremonies Pān Jùn
bear deep worries and heavy responsibilities,
and are committed to demonstrating their sincerity.
Day and night, they are apprehensive,
unable to find peace in sleep or food,
constantly wishing to bring peace to the state and benefit the people,
and to establish long-term plans.
They can be called the heart, backbone, and limbs,
ministers of the state.
They should each be fully entrusted,
and no other official should oversee their responsibilities.
Their achievements should be demanded,
and their shortcomings assessed.
As for these three ministers,
if their thoughts do not extend to something, then so be it;
how dare they monopolize authority and power or deceive their sovereign?"
He also said:
"Dispensing rewards to honor the good,
establishing punishments to awe the wicked,
appointing the virtuous and employing the capable,
and being clear and discerning in laws and methods—
then what achievement will not be accomplished,
what matter will not be resolved,
what sound will not be heard,
what sight will not be seen?
If today the governors of all counties,
each gets the right person,
and together they manage and coordinate,
then how can the various administrations not be prosperous?
I secretly hear that all counties have auxiliary officials,
and a multitude of officials burdens the people,
leading to societal弊.
Moreover, petty individuals, taking advantage of their appointments,
do not strive to serve the public but instead abuse their authority,
offering no benefit to observation or listening,
but rather harming the people.
I foolishly believe they should all be dismissed and reduced."
Sūn Quán also realized his error,
and subsequently executed Lü Yī.
Bù Zhì frequently recommended and promoted those who were suppressed
and rescued those in distress,
submitting dozens of memorials.
Although Sūn Quán could not accept all of them,
he occasionally adopted his words,
and many benefited from his assistance.
In Chìwū ninth year (246 CE),
he succeeded Lù Xùn as Prime Minister.
He still instructed and nurtured his disciples,
never letting go of books,
and his clothing and dwelling were like those of a scholar.
However, the clothing of his wives and concubines within his household was extravagant and luxurious,
for which he was somewhat criticized.
He was stationed in Xīlíng for twenty years,
and neighboring enemies respected his authority and trustworthiness.
He was generous and broad-minded, winning over the masses,
and his joy or anger was not expressed in his voice or demeanor,
yet both his inner and outer circles were awed.
In the tenth year, he died.
His son, Bù Xié, inherited his title
and took command of Bù Zhì's forces,
and was made General Who Stabilizes the Army.
When Bù Xié died,
his son, Bù Jī, inherited the marquisate.
Bù Xié's younger brother, Bù Chǎn,
succeeded to his position as Governor of Xīlíng,
and was made General Who Manifests Military Prowess,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xītíng.
In Fènghuáng first year (272 CE),
he was summoned to be Supervisor of the Palace Guard.
Bù Chǎn had been in Xīlíng for generations.
Suddenly, he was summoned,
and considered himself to have lost his post.
Fearing false accusations and misfortune,
he therefore surrendered the city to Jìn.
He sent Bù Jī and his younger brother Bù Xuán to Luòyáng as hostages.
Jìn appointed Bù Chǎn as Area Commander of All Military Affairs in Xīlíng, General of the Guard, and granted him the honor of San Siz (three high officials),
added the title of Palace Attendant,
given a fake imperial staff, and made him Inspector of Jiāozhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Yídū.
Bù Jī was appointed Overseer of All Military Affairs in Jiānglíng, General of the Left,
added the title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
made Administrator of Lúlíng,
and re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiānglíng.
Bù Xuán was appointed Gentleman of the Household, General Who Spreads Awe,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
General of Chariots and Cavalry Yáng Hù and Inspector of Jīngzhōu Yáng Zhào were ordered to go and rescue Bù Chǎn.
Sūn Hào sent Lù Kàng to the west,
and Yáng Hù and others retreated.
Lù Kàng captured the city,
executed Bù Chǎn and others.
The Bù clan was exterminated,
only Bù Xuán continued the ancestral sacrifices.
Zhōu Zhāo of Yǐngchuān wrote a book praising Bù Zhì and Yán Jùn, etc., saying:
"The reasons why worthy scholar-officials, ancient and modern, have lost their reputations, forfeited their lives, ruined their families, and harmed their countries
are not limited to one,
but to summarize their main downfall,
and aggregate their common ailments,
there are only four.
Being eager to debate is one;
contending for fame and influence is two;
valuing cliques is three;
and being impatient for quick success is four.
Being eager to debate harms others;
contending for fame and influence ruins friendships;
valuing cliques blinds the lord;
and being impatient for quick success leads to moral failings.
If these four are not eliminated,
none can remain whole.
Among gentlemen of the present age, there are indeed
those who can avoid these,
so why should it be only the ancients!
However, when discussing their exceptional distinctiveness,
none compare to the excellence of Gù Yùzhāng, Zhūgě Shǐjūn, Bù Chéngxiàng, Yán Wèiwèi, and Zhāng Fènwēi.
Of the sayings: 'The Master was gentle and skillfully induced people to follow,'
and 'He completes the good in others and does not complete the bad in them,'
Yùzhāng possessed them.
'Looked at from a distance, he appears austere; when approached, he is warm; when he speaks, his words are firm,'
Shǐjūn embodied this.
'Respectful and at ease, dignified but not fierce,'
Chéngxiàng practiced this.
Studying not for salary, with a heart free from ill-gotten gains,
Wèiwèi and Fènwēi trod this path.
Although the actual virtues of these five gentlemen
differed,
with varying degrees of importance,
when it came to their broad principles of action and inaction,
not transgressing the four points,
they were all uniform.
In the past, Dīng Xū came from a humble family,
Wú Càn from a shepherd's background;
Yùzhāng extolled their virtues,
placing them in the ranks alongside Lù [Xùn] and Quán [Zōng];
this ensured that no one remained obscure, and customs became generous.
Shǐjūn, Chéngxiàng, and Wèiwèi, these three gentlemen,
were formerly commoners who were good friends;
various commentators then judged their respective merits and demerits.
Initially,
Wèiwèi was ranked first,
followed by Chéngxiàng,
and then Shǐjūn;
subsequently, they all served an enlightened lord,
managing worldly affairs,
and their talents in advancement and retreat differed,
so their order of fame had to be reversed from the beginning.
This is how ordinary people of the world assess diligence and superficiality.
As for the three gentlemen's shared friendship,
it ultimately suffered no impairment;
was this not the friendship of the ancients!
Moreover, Lǔ Héngjiāng once commanded ten thousand troops,
garrisoned at Lùkǒu,
which was a commendable achievement in his era;
who, capable or incapable,
would not desire it?
But after Héngjiāng's death,
Wèiwèi was chosen to succeed him;
he considered himself unfit to be a commander,
steadfastly declined and refused,
ultimately not taking the position.
Later, he was transferred to the Nine Ministers,
and promoted to preside over the Eight Columns;
his honors were insufficient to display himself,
his salary insufficient to support himself.
As for the other two gentlemen,
both held the rank of supreme general,
reaching the pinnacle of wealth and nobility.
Wèiwèi had no desires to seek,
and the two gentlemen did not recommend him either;
each maintained his aspiration,
preserving their reputation and friendship.
Confucius said: 'The gentleman is proud but does not contend; he is sociable but not partisan.'
This spirit was present in them.
Furthermore, Fènwēi's reputation
was also next to the three gentlemen's;
he was stationed in a region,
received the appointment of a supreme general,
not differing from Shǐjūn and Chéngxiàng.
However, in reviewing state affairs
and discussing contributions,
there were indeed differences in their timing,
hence the distinction in their noble ranks.
Yet, Fènwēi, in such a position,
was clearly able to define his responsibilities,
his heart free from desires of straying from the Way,
his actions free from seeking to expand or shrink his power;
whenever he attended court,
he acted in accordance with ritual,
his words and demeanor were earnest and straightforward,
never failing to be loyal.
Although Shú Sì was a close noble,
he spoke of his worries about his failure;
although Cài Wénzhì was distant and lowly,
he spoke of praising his worthiness.
When his daughter married the crown prince,
he received the ceremony as if it were a condolence,
his indignant attitude
truly reflecting his strong feelings for people;
successes and failures, gains and losses,
all turned out as he had anticipated;
he can be called a man who upheld the Way, foresaw opportunities,
and loved antiquity.
As for managing the state
and commanding armies,
achieving the deeds of a hegemon king
in times of rapid action,
these five were not superior to others.
But in their pure adherence to the Way,
seeking nothing improperly,
rising and falling in their generation,
preserving their reputations and conduct,
they were truly detached from worldly norms,
serving as models.
Therefore, I have briefly discussed their affairs
to show them to later gentlemen."
Zhōu Zhāo, whose courtesy name was Gōngyuǎn,
collaborated with Wéi Yào, Xuē Yíng, and Huá Hé in compiling the Wú Shū.
Later, he became a Zhōngshū Láng,
and was imprisoned for an offense.
Huá Hé submitted a memorial to save him,
but Sūn Xiū did not listen,
and he was consequently executed.
Commentary says: Zhāng Zhāo received a dying command to assist,
and successfully accomplished his meritorious services;
he was loyal, earnest, and upright,
acting never for himself.
Yet, because of his strictness, he was feared;
because of his loftiness, he was alienated;
he was neither appointed Chancellor
nor ascended to the rank of Grand Tutor or Guardian,
but spent his time leisurely in the village,
simply living out his old age.
This illustrates that Sūn Quán's judgment was inferior to his strategy.
Gù Yǒng relied on his established family legacy,
and his wisdom in leadership,
thus he was able to reach the highest honors.
Zhūgě Jǐn and Bù Zhì were both recognized in their time for their virtuous character and principled conduct.
Zhāng Chéng and Gù Shào were open-minded and elder-like,
appreciating people of worth.
Zhōu Zhāo's discussion
praises them highly,
therefore it is recorded in detail.
Tán Xiàn was sincere in his public service,
possessing a loyal and steadfast character.
Xiū and Chéng revised the historical records,
all hoping to do good.
Love and hate contended,
scattering them to the southern frontier;
how sorrowful!
Biographies of Zhāng, Yán, Chéng, Kān, and Xuē, Chapter 8.
Zhāng Hóng, courtesy name Zǐgāng,
was a native of Guǎnglín.
He studied in the capital,
and returned to his home commandery,
where he was recommended as Màocái.
He was invited by the public office,
but declined all offers,
and sought refuge in Jiāngdōng.
When Sūn Cè began his enterprise,
Zhāng Hóng thereupon pledged his allegiance.
Sūn Cè appointed him Zhèngyì Xiàowèi,
and he followed in the campaign against Dānyáng.
Sūn Cè personally took to the battlefield,
and Zhāng Hóng remonstrated, saying:
"The commander-in-chief is the source of strategic planning,
and upon him depends the lives of the three armies.
He should not be reckless,
personally confronting minor bandits.
I wish Your Excellency would value your heaven-bestowed abilities,
and live up to the hopes of the realm,
without causing alarm among those above and below within the country."
In the fourth year of Jiàn'ān (199 CE),
Sūn Cè sent Zhāng Hóng with a memorial to the Xu Palace,
where he was retained as Shìyùshǐ.
Kǒng Róng, the Shàofǔ, and others were all close to him.
When Cáo Gōng heard of Sūn Cè's death,
he intended to attack Wú during the mourning period.
Zhāng Hóng advised against it,
believing that taking advantage of someone's mourning was neither ancient righteousness,
nor, if unsuccessful,
would it merely create enmity and abandon good relations;
it would be better to take the opportunity to treat them generously.
Cáo Gōng followed his advice,
immediately submitting a memorial appointing Sūn Quán as Tǎolǔ Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently Grand Administrator of Kuàijī.
Cáo Gōng wished Zhāng Hóng to assist Sūn Quán in submitting,
and sent Zhāng Hóng out as Dūwèi of the eastern part of Kuàijī.
Later, Sūn Quán appointed Hóng as Chief Clerk.
He followed Sūn Quán on an expedition to Héféi.
Sūn Quán led a force of light cavalry, intending to rush and assault the enemy.
Hóng remonstrated, saying:
"Weapons are instruments of ill omen,
and warfare is a dangerous affair.
Now, Your Excellency relies on the vigor of your prime
and disregards a formidable and violent foe.
Among the three armies,
there is no one whose heart is not chilled with fear.
Even if you cut down generals and capture banners,
and your might shakes the enemy battlefield,
this is the duty of a subordinate general,
not befitting the commander-in-chief.
I hope you will restrain the courage of Bēn and Yù,
and embrace the strategies of a hegemon-king."
Sūn Quán accepted Hóng's words and stopped.
After returning,
the following year, he was about to launch another military expedition.
Hóng again remonstrated, saying:
"From ancient times, the rulers who received the mandate of Heaven,
though aided by the imperial spirits above
and with civil virtue spread below,
also relied on military accomplishments to make their merits manifest.
However, it is valuable to act at the right time;
only then will there be prestige.
Now Your Excellency faces the 'four hundred-year calamity'
and has the merit of saving the endangered.
It is appropriate to temporarily rest the army,
widely open up cultivation and settlement,
appoint the worthy and employ the capable,
strive to promote generosity and benevolence,
and follow Heaven's mandate to execute punishment.
Then you can achieve stability without labor."
Thereupon, Sūn Quán stopped and did not proceed.
Hóng proposed the plan that the capital should be moved to Mòlíng,
and Sūn Quán followed it.
He ordered Hóng to return to Wú to bring his family,
but he fell ill and died on the way.
At the point of death,
he bequeathed a memorial to his son, Jìng, saying:
"From ancient times, those who possessed a state or a family
all wished to cultivate virtuous governance to rival the flourishing ages.
Yet, as for their administration,
many did not leave a fragrant reputation.
It was not that there were no loyal ministers or worthy assistants
who were ignorant of the principles of governance,
but rather that the ruler could not overcome his own inclinations
and failed to employ them.
Indeed, human nature shuns difficulty and seeks ease,
likes conformity and dislikes difference,
which is contrary to the path of good governance.
The proverb says, 'To follow good is like ascending,
to follow evil is like a collapse,'
speaking of the difficulty of goodness.
A ruler, inheriting a foundation built over generations,
occupying a natural position of power,
wielding the authority of the eight handles,
enjoys the pleasure of ease and conformity,
without needing to seek anything from others.
Whereas loyal ministers possess difficult-to-advance methods
and utter words that are unpleasant to hear.
Is it not natural
that they do not get along?
If there is [disunity], then there will be rifts.
Artful sophistry exploits the gaps,
dazzled by minor loyalties,
bound by affection and love,
the worthy and the foolish become mixed up,
and the elders and youngsters lose their proper places.
The source of this
is the disruption of human inclinations.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler understands this,
seeks the worthy as if hungry and thirsty,
accepts remonstrance without weariness,
restrains inclinations and curtails desires,
and sacrifices affection for the sake of righteousness.
Above, there will be no biased or erroneous appointments,
and below, no extravagant hopes.
One should consider carefully,
bear humiliation and conceal defects,
to achieve the greatness of benevolence and comprehensive protection."
He died that year at the age of sixty.
Sūn Quán read the letter and shed tears.
Hóng authored over ten pieces of poetry, prose, inscriptions, and eulogies.
His son, Xuán,
held offices up to Administrator of Nánjùn and Minister of the Household.
Xuán's son, Shàng,
served as a Gentleman-attendant during Sūn Hào's reign.
He was known for his eloquent and quick-witted speech,
and was promoted to Attendant-in-ordinary and Director of the Central Secretariat.
Sūn Hào ordered Shàng to play the zither,
but Shàng replied,
"I have never been able to."
Sūn Hào commanded him to learn it.
Later, during a banquet, when the exquisite subtleties of the zither were discussed,
Shàng incidentally mentioned,
"Jìn Pínggōng ordered Master Kuàng to compose 'Qīngjué,'
but Kuàng said, 'My lord's virtue is thin,
not sufficient to listen to it.'"
Sūn Hào interpreted Shàng's words as likening him to Jìn Pínggōng,
and was displeased.
Later, he was imprisoned for other accumulated offenses,
and this incident was also brought up to interrogate him.
He was sent to Jiàn'ān to build ships.
After a long time,
he was again executed.
Initially,
Qín Sōng, courtesy name Wénbiǎo,
and Chén Duān, courtesy name Zǐzhèng, both from the same commandery as Hóng,
were treated with favor by Sūn Cè along with Hóng,
and participated in his strategies.
They both died early.
Yán Jùn, courtesy name Màncái,
was a native of Péngchéng.
In his youth, he was devoted to study,
skilled in poetry, documents, and the Three Rites,
and also fond of the Shuōwén.
He avoided chaos by moving to Jiāngdōng,
and was close friends with Zhūgě Jǐn and Bù Zhì.
His nature was straightforward, pure, and sincere.
Regarding people,
he gave loyal advice and guided them to goodness,
his aim being to be helpful.
Zhāng Zhāo recommended him to Sūn Quán,
who appointed him as Cavalry Commandant and Attendant-in-ordinary.
When the General Across the River, Lǔ Sù, died,
Sūn Quán appointed Jùn to replace Sù,
commanding ten thousand soldiers
and garrisoning Lùkǒu.
Everyone rejoiced for Jùn,
but Jùn repeatedly declined, saying:
"I am a simple scholar,
unskilled in military affairs.
If I, with my lack of talent, were to occupy this position,
calamity and regret would surely follow."
He spoke passionately,
even to the point of tears,
so Sūn Quán finally acquiesced.
The world praised him for being able to yield genuinely.
When Sūn Quán became King of Wú,
and later claimed the imperial title,
Jùn served as Grand Protector,
and was sent on a mission to Shǔ.
The Chancellor of Shǔ, Zhūgě Liàng, greatly esteemed him.
He did not accumulate his salary or rewards,
but distributed them all to relatives and old acquaintances;
his household was often not well-provided for.
Liú Yǐng of Guǎnglíng, an old friend of Jùn's,
was a profound scholar who lived in his village.
Sūn Quán heard of him and summoned him,
but he declined due to illness.
His younger brother, Lüè, was Administrator of Línglíng.
When Lüè died in office,
Yǐng went to attend the funeral.
Sūn Quán knew he was feigning illness
and urgently dispatched an envoy to arrest him.
Jùn also rushed to inform Yǐng,
telling him to return and apologize to Sūn Quán.
Sūn Quán, in anger, dismissed Jùn,
but Yǐng was spared punishment.
After a long time,
Jùn was appointed Minister of the Household,
and later died.
Jùn authored a Commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety and a Treatise on Tides,
and also debated Guǎn Zhòng and Jì Lù with Péi Xuán and Zhāng Chéng;
all these works are transmitted in the world.
Péi Xuán, courtesy name Yànhuáng,
was a native of Xiàpī.
He also possessed scholarship and good conduct,
and served as Grand Master of the Palace.
He asked his son, Qīn, about the relative merits of the four individuals, Qí Huán, Jìn Wén, Yí, and Huì.
Qīn answered with his own views,
and he and Xuán debated back and forth,
each presenting well-reasoned arguments.
Qīn associated with Crown Prince Dēng,
who praised his literary talent.
Chéng Bǐng, courtesy name Déshū,
was a man from Nándùn, Rǔnán.
He served Zhèng Xuán,
and later, to avoid chaos, he took refuge in Jiāozhōu.
There he discussed the great principles with Liú Xī,
and consequently became widely knowledgeable in the Five Classics.
Shì Xiè appointed him as Grand Scribe.
Quán heard of his reputation as a scholar,
and invited Bǐng with proper etiquette.
Upon his arrival,
he was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
In the fourth year of Huángwǔ,
Quán arranged for Crown Prince Dēng to marry Zhōu Yú's daughter.
Bǐng, then acting as Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
went to Wú to welcome the princess.
Quán personally visited Bǐng's boat,
showing him great honor and respect.
After returning,
Bǐng gently advised Dēng, saying:
"Marriage is the beginning of human relations,
and the foundation of royal education.
Therefore, sagely kings value it highly,
using it to lead the populace
and transform the world through customs.
Thus, the *Shī Jīng* praises 'Guānjū,'
making it the foremost ode.
I hope the Crown Prince will uphold ritual and education in the inner chambers,
preserving what is sung in the 'Zhōu Nán,'
so that moral transformation will flourish above,
and songs of praise will rise from below."
Dēng smiled and said:
"To follow what is good,
and to rectify what is bad,
indeed, I rely on you, Tutor."
He died of illness in office.
He authored *Zhōu Yì Zhāi*, *Shàng Shū Bó*, and *Lúnyǔ Bì*,
totaling over thirty thousand words.
When Bǐng served as Tutor,
the Supervisor of the Imperial Carriages, Zhēng Chóng of Hénán, was also known for his diligent study and upright conduct.
Kàn Zé, courtesy name Dérùn,
was a man from Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His family had been farmers for generations,
but Zé loved learning.
Being poor and without resources,
he often earned money by copying books for others
to afford paper and brushes.
After finishing his copying,
he would have also read and memorized the text thoroughly.
He pursued teachers to discuss and lecture,
comprehensively studying numerous texts,
and was also proficient in calendrical calculations.
Because of this, he became famous.
He was recommended as Xiaolián
and appointed Magistrate of Qiántáng,
then transferred to Magistrate of Chēn.
When Sūn Quán was General of Agile Cavalry,
he was invited to serve as an Assistant in the Western Bureau;
and when Quán declared himself emperor,
Zé was made Grand Scribe.
During the Jiāhé era,
he became Central Secretary,
with the added title of Attendant Official.
In the fifth year of Chìwū,
he was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
retaining his position as Central Secretary.
Zé found that the classical commentaries had too many words,
making them difficult to fully utilize.
So, he judiciously selected from various schools,
editing and simplifying ritual texts and various annotations to instruct the two palaces.
He also devised rules for conduct, entering and exiting, and receiving guests,
and authored *Qiánxiàng Lì Zhù* to rectify the calendar.
Whenever there was a major court debate,
and the classics presented uncertainties,
Quán would consult him.
For his diligent work in classical scholarship,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
By nature, he was humble, respectful, and very prudent.
Even minor officials of the palace or government,
when summoned for questioning,
he would treat with courtesy.
If others had flaws or shortcomings,
he never spoke of them.
His appearance seemed unassuming,
yet there was little he heard that he failed to understand.
Quán once asked:
"Among writings, commentaries, and rhapsodies, which is the finest?"
Zé wished to subtly advise on good governance and chaos,
so he replied that Jiǎ Yì's *Guò Qín Lùn* was the best.
Quán then read it.
Earlier,
when Lǚ Yī's corruption came to light,
officials investigated thoroughly
and proposed the death penalty.
Some suggested that he should be burned and dismembered
to emphasize his heinous crime.
Quán consulted Zé about this.
Zé said:
"In an enlightened age,
such a punishment should not be reinstated."
Quán followed his advice.
Also, when various government departments were troubled
and wished to increase the severity of regulations
to control their subordinates,
Zé always said,
"One should follow the rites and laws."
His harmonizing yet principled approach
was always of this kind.
He died in the winter of the sixth year.
Quán was deeply saddened and lamented his passing,
not eating for several days.
Zé's senior countryman from Dānyáng, Táng Gù, also cultivated himself and accumulated learning,
and was known as a scholar.
He authored commentaries on the *Guóyǔ*, *Gōngyáng*, and *Gǔliáng* traditions,
and regularly lectured to dozens of people.
When Quán became King of Wú,
he appointed Gù as Counselor,
and Lù Xùn, Zhāng Wēn, Luò Tǒng, and others all paid him respect.
In the fourth year of Huángwǔ, he became Imperial Secretary,
and then died.
Xuē Zōng, courtesy name Jìngwén,
was a man from Zhúyì, Pèi Prefecture.
In his youth, he relied on relatives to escape to Jiāozhōu,
and studied under Liú Xī.
After Shì Xiè submitted to Sūn Quán,
Zōng was summoned to be Administrator of the Five Bureaus,
and then appointed Administrator of Hépǔ and Jiāozhǐ.
At that time, the Jiāo region was newly opened,
and Inspector Lǚ Dài led troops to suppress rebellions.
Zōng accompanied him,
crossing the sea to campaign south,
and reaching Jiǔzhēn.
After the task was completed, he returned to the capital
and served as Attendant and Palace Assistant.
When the Western envoy Zhāng Fèng, before Quán, listed the names of Grand Scribe Kàn Zé to ridicule him,
Zé could not reply.
Zōng, who was circulating wine,
then offered a toast and said:
"What is 'Shǔ'?
With a dog it's 'Dú,'
without a dog it's 'Shǔ.'
Eyes askew, body crooked,
insects enter its belly!"
Fèng said:
"Should I not also list your Wú?"
Zōng immediately retorted:
"Without a mouth it's 'Tiān' (heaven),
with a mouth it's 'Wú.'
Ruling over ten thousand states,
the capital of the Son of Heaven!"
At this, everyone present was delighted and laughed,
and Fèng had no reply.
His quick wit and sharp responses were all of this kind.
Lǚ Dài was recalled from Jiāozhōu.
Zōng feared that his successor might not be the right person.
He submitted a memorial, saying:
“Formerly, Emperor Shùn made a southern tour
and died at Cāngwú.
The Qín dynasty established Guìlín, Nánhǎi, and Xiàngjùn commanderies.
Thus, the incorporation of the four states
has a long history.
Zhào Tuó arose in Pānyú,
subduing and winning over the rulers of the Bǎiyuè,
which is south of Zhūguān.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn executed Lǚ Jiā,
opened up nine commanderies,
and established the Inspector of Jiāozhǐ to govern and oversee them.
The mountains and rivers stretch far,
customs are not uniform,
and languages vary;
repeated translation is needed to communicate.
The people are like animals,
without distinction between old and young.
They wear topknots and go barefoot,
with their hair tied through and their garments opening on the left.
The establishment of senior officials,
though present, was as if absent.
Since then,
criminals from the central regions were gradually moved to live among them,
gradually teaching them to read and write,
and giving them a basic understanding of language.
Through the frequent coming and going of envoys,
they observed civility and refinement.
Later, when Xī Guāng became the Administrator of Jiāozhǐ,
and Rèn Yán became the Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn,
they taught them to plow
and encouraged them to wear caps and shoes.
They established marriage officials,
and people began to understand betrothal and marriage.
They established schools
to guide them in the meaning of the classics.
From then on,
for over four hundred years,
there has been some resemblance to Chinese civilization.
Since I first arrived as a guest,
in Zhūyá, outside of the arrangements in prefectures and counties,
all marriages required gathering all households in the eighth month.
When the people assembled,
men and women would choose partners for themselves,
and thus become husband and wife;
parents could not stop them.
In Mǐlíng county of Jiāozhǐ and Dūpáng county of Jiǔzhēn,
it was the custom for a younger brother to marry his elder brother's widow upon the elder brother's death.
This was a common custom,
and senior officials indulged it,
unable to prohibit it.
In Rìnán Commandery, men and women went naked,
feeling no shame.
From this, it can be said
that they were mere insects,
barely having faces.
However, the land is vast, the population large,
and it is perilous and harmful,
easy to cause unrest,
and difficult to bring under good governance.
The state merely restrained them,
showing its might to compel submission.
The rent and taxes from households
were only collected to meet basic needs,

primarily to obtain rare and valuable treasures such as pearls, fragrant medicines, ivory, rhinoceros horn, tortoiseshell, coral, lapis lazuli, parrots, kingfishers, peacocks, and other exotic items, to enrich the imperial collection of precious objects.
It was not necessary to rely on their tribute
to benefit the central state.
However, being beyond the nine domains,
the selection of senior officials
was generally not precise or thorough.
During the Hàn dynasty, the laws were lenient,
and many officials indulged themselves,
hence frequent violations of the law occurred.
The abandonment of Zhūyá
originated from a senior official who, upon seeing their beautiful hair,
shaved it off to make wigs.
As far as I have seen,
Huáng Gài of Nánhǎi, while serving as Grand Administrator of Rìnán,
upon arrival, because the provisions were not abundant,
beat his Chief Clerk to death,
and was subsequently driven out.
Dān Méng, the Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn, hosted a banquet for his wife's father, Zhōu Jīng,
and also invited high-ranking officials.
During the revelry of drinking,
the Commandant of Merit, Fān Xīn, danced and urged Jīng to join.
Jīng refused to rise,
but Xīn still pressed him forcefully.
Méng, in anger, struck Xīn with a staff
within the commandery office.
Xīn’s younger brother, Miáo, led a crowd to attack the office,
shooting Méng with poisoned arrows,
which led to Méng's death.
Shì Xiè, the Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, dispatched troops to suppress them,
but ultimately could not succeed.
Also, the former Inspector, Zhū Fú of Kuàijī,
appointed many of his fellow townsmen, such as Yú Bāo and Liú Yàn, as senior officials,
who oppressed the common people
and forcibly levied taxes.
One yellow fish was collected for one *hú* of rice.
The common people resented and rebelled,
and mountain bandits emerged,
attacking prefectures and commanderies.
Fú fled into the sea,
wandering and perishing.
Next came Zhāng Jīn of Nányáng,
who had a rift with Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu.
His forces were weak and the enemy strong,
and armies were raised year after year.
His generals grew weary and disgusted,
leaving or staying as they pleased.
Jīn exercised little restraint,
lacking sufficient authority and power,
and was thus humiliated and insulted,
eventually being killed.
Afterward came Lài Gōng of Línglíng,
a kind and cautious elder,
but ignorant of current affairs.
Biǎo also sent Wú Jù of Chángshā to be Grand Administrator of Cāngwú.
Jù was a fierce and reckless warrior,
who would not submit to Gōng.
They resented each other,
Jù drove Gōng out,
and sought Bù Zhì.
At that time, there were still many former generals of Jīn, such as Yí Liáo and Qián Bó.
Zhì gradually suppressed them,
and just as order was established,
he was summoned away.
When Lǚ Dài arrived,
there was the upheaval by the Shì clan.
The Yuè army campaigned in the south,
and on the day of pacification,
senior officials were re-established,
the imperial authority was clearly proclaimed,
its prestige extended ten thousand *lǐ*,
and all, great and small, submitted to its influence.
From this, it can be said
that pacifying the borders and comforting the distant peoples
indeed requires the right person.
The responsibility of a regional governor
should certainly be held by one who is pure and capable,
and in these remote, wild regions,
the consequences of good or bad governance are even more profound.
Today, although Jiāozhōu is nominally pacified,
there are still old bandits in Gāoliáng.
The borders of the four commanderies of Nánhǎi, Cāngwú, Yùlín, and Zhūguān are not yet stable,
and they remain dens of bandits and
refuges for rebels and fugitives.
If Dài does not return south,
the new Inspector should be someone meticulous
in overseeing the eight commanderies,
possessing strategy and wisdom,
who can gradually bring Gāoliáng under control.
Grant him prestige and favor,
lend him power and influence,
and hold him accountable for results.
Then perhaps it can be restored.
But if he is merely an ordinary person,
who adheres to common practices,
without extraordinary tactics or unusual skills,
then evils will multiply daily,
and eventually cause lasting harm.
Therefore, the security or danger of the state
depends on whom it employs,
and this must not be overlooked.
I secretly fear that the court might lightly regard this selection,
hence I dare to express my foolish sentiments
to broaden Your Majesty's thoughts."
In the third year of Huánglóng,
Jiànchānghóu Lǜ was appointed Zhèn Jūn Dà Jiàngjūn,
and garrisoned at Bànzhōu.
Zōng was made Chángshǐ under him,
managing all external affairs,
and internally teaching him books.
When Lǜ died,
Zōng entered the court as Zéi Cáo Shàngshū,
then was promoted to Shàngshū Púyè.
At that time, Gōngsūn Yuān surrendered and then rebelled again.
Quán was enraged,
and wanted to personally lead a punitive expedition.
Zōng submitted a memorial, advising:
"A sovereign,
being the head of all nations
and the one upon whom the fate of the world depends,
should, when at home, have heavy gates and drum-and-clapper warnings to guard against the unexpected,
and when traveling, clear the roads and arrange escorts to maintain his majesty.
This is to preserve the blessings of universal peace
and to calm the hearts of all within the four seas.
In ancient times, when Kǒngzǐ was distressed by the times,
he spoke of drifting on a raft across the sea.
Jì Yóu was pleased by this,
but Kǒngzǐ rejected him, saying he was without suitable talent.
When Hàn Yuándì wished to board a tower boat,
Xuē Guǎngdé asked to cut his own throat and stain the imperial carriage with his blood.
Why so?
Because the dangers of water and fire are extreme,
and not places for a sovereign to venture.
The proverb says: 'A son of a thousand jin
does not sit beneath the eaves.'
How much more so for one of ten thousand chariots' dignity?
Now, Liáodōng is a small barbarian state,
without strong city walls,
defensive strategies,
or sharp weapons;
its people are like dogs and sheep without proper governance.
Going there will certainly result in their capture and conquest,
as your enlightened decree states.
However, its land is cold and barren,
crops do not grow well,
the people are accustomed to riding,
and constantly move from place to place.
Upon suddenly hearing of the approach of a large army,
they will assess themselves as no match,
startled like birds and frightened like beasts,
they will flee far and wide.
Even a single person and a single horse
will be impossible to find.
Even if you occupy empty land,
holding it will be useless.
This is the first reason why it should not be done.
Furthermore, there are vast and turbulent waters,
with the difficulty of Chéngshān,
and seafaring is unpredictable,
wind and waves are unavoidable.
In an instant,
people and ships can be separated.
Even with the virtue of Yáo and Shùn,
wisdom would have no place to be applied;
even with the courage of Bēn and Yù,
strength could not be exerted.
This is the second reason why it should not be done.
Moreover, dense fog obscures the sky above,
and salty water steams below,
easily causing running sores to grow,
spreading contamination among people.
Almost all who travel by sea
are afflicted by this ailment.
This is the third reason why it should not be done.
Heaven gave birth to a divine sage
and revealed it with auspicious omens,
intending that you calm the chaos
and bring peace to the people and things;
auspicious signs accumulate daily,
the realm within the seas is on the verge of being pacified,
the rebellious brigands are cruel and tyrannical,
their destruction is imminent.
Once the Central Plain is pacified,
Liáodōng will collapse on its own.
You merely need to fold your hands and wait.
Now, you are going against a certain plan,
seeking extreme and dangerous obstacles,
disregarding the security of the Nine Provinces,
and indulging a moment's anger.
This is neither a weighty strategy for the state,
nor has it ever happened since the creation of the world.
This is truly why your ministers are bowing their heads and holding their breath,
finding no taste in their food,
and no peace on their beds.
I humbly pray Your Majesty restrains your thunderous might,
suppresses your furious wrath,
follows the safety of crossing a bridge,
and avoids the danger of treading on thin ice.
Then your subjects will rely on your blessings,
and the world will be exceedingly fortunate."
At that time, many ministers advised against it,
and Quán consequently did not proceed.
On the Yǐwèi day of the first month,
Quán ordered Zōng to compose a prayer to his ancestors that would not use common text.
Zōng received the edict,
and eventually created a text,
whose sincere words were brilliant.
Quán said:
"Make another two,
so that there are three in total."
Zōng then composed two more prayers,
and their language was all new,
which everyone praised as excellent.
In the third year of Chìwū,
he was transferred to Xuǎn Cáo Shàngshū.
In the fifth year,
he became Tàizǐ Shàofù,
retaining his duties in selection as before.
In the spring of the sixth year,
he passed away.
All the poems, rhapsodies, discussions, and treatises he wrote amounted to tens of thousands of words,
titled Sīzài.
He also compiled Wǔ Zōng Túshù and Èr Jīng Jiě,
all of which are transmitted to later generations.
Zǐ Xǔ,
served as Wēinán Jiāngjūn,
and died of illness on the way back
from a campaign in Jiāozhǐ.
Xǔ's younger brother, Yíng,
whose courtesy name was Dàoyán,
initially served as Mìfǔ Zhōngshū Láng.
When Sūn Xiū ascended the throne,
he became Sànqí Zhōngcháng Shì.
After several years,
he resigned due to illness.
At the beginning of Sūn Hào's reign,
he became Zuǒ Zhífǎ,
then was promoted to Xuǎncáo Shàngshū.
When the crown prince was established,
he also concurrently held the position of Shàofù.
In the third year of Jiànhéng,
Hào recalled and praised Yíng's father, Zōng's, posthumous writings,
and commanded Yíng to continue his work.
Yíng presented a poem which said:
“My ancestors
once served the Hàn dynasty;
for generations unending,
they often held positions at court.
When my father, Zōng,
encountered a difficult era,
the "Mǎo Jīn" (Liu family, referring to the Hàn dynasty) lost its grip,
and the state and family were ruined and disordered.
He sought this land of joy,
hoping to preserve his remnant descendants.
Heaven opened his heart,
and he returned to the Southeast.
Initially, he was a refugee,
suffering at the barbarian frontier.
The Great Emperor established his foundation,
and his grace and virtue were widely bestowed.
He especially received an invitation,
rescuing him from the mud and filth.
He was released from common attire,
received office, and was granted a tally of authority.
He served as the Administrator of Hépǔ,
on the edge of the sea.
He was then transferred to the capital,
and ascended to the vital machinery of government.
The withered revived,
the broken line was reconnected.
From obscurity to prominence,
this was beyond his initial wishes.
Moreover, he was favored and
content with his position.
He again served the Cultured Emperor (referring to Sun Xiū),
who established the Eastern Palace,
and was appointed Shàofù,
his brilliance growing ever greater.
The sagely heir, so bright and clear,
possessed supreme virtue and humility;
his courteous treatment was augmented,
truly generous and abundant.
My lamented former minister (father)
wished to exhaust his loyalty,
but his immense grace remained unrequited;
he passed away from the world.
Alas, I am lowly and humble,
with elder and younger brothers,
fortunate to be born and raised,
descended from Zōng's remaining body.
Though trained in the courtyard,
my dullness is hard to enlighten.
Unable to continue the family legacy,
my ambition was to farm together.
How could I expect the sagely court,
its benevolence flowing abundantly,
to recall my former minister,
pitying his unfulfilled achievements?
It rescued and uplifted him,
bestowing upon him extraordinary honors.
Xǔ, though unworthy, traversed a thousand li,
receiving the command to campaign south.
Banners and implements were prepared,
weapons clanged their sound.
And I, so crude,
truly ignorant and insignificant,
was made to shine upon the former path,
the crucial position for talent;
again serving as Grand Tutor to the Eastern Palace,
continuing to bear the family's glory.
My talent does not reach that of my predecessor,
this is a disgrace and a transgression.
Heaven's virtue is vast and benevolent,
valuing culture and elegance,
mourning the deceased minister,
hoping to preserve his lineage.
How can this foolish descendant
be even remotely similar?
Beholding that former favor,
and considering this ignorant emptiness,
who can bear the shame?
I truly dwell with it.
Day and night, I toss and turn,
reflecting within my heart:
Father and son, brothers,
for generations received grace.
In death, I will repay with tied grass (a metaphor for eternal gratitude);
in life, I vow to sacrifice myself.
Though I may turn to ash and perish,
I cannot repay a ten-thousandth part."
That year,
Hé Dìng (何定) suggested excavating the Shèngxī (聖谿) canal to connect the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) rivers.
Hào (晧) ordered Yíng (瑩) to oversee ten thousand men for the task.
As it proved difficult to accomplish due to numerous rock formations,
the project was abandoned.
He was then appointed as the Commander of the Left Division of Wǔchāng (武昌).
Later, Dìng (定) was executed.
Hào (晧) recalled the Shèngxī (聖谿) affair,
imprisoned Yíng (瑩),
and exiled him to Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
The Right Grand Historian Huá Hè (華覈) submitted a memorial, stating:
"I have heard that the Five Emperors and Three Kings all established historical officials
to record their achievements and virtues,
passing them down through endless generations.
In the Hàn (漢) dynasty, Sīmǎ Qiān (司馬遷) and Bān Gù (班固)
were both generational talents;
their writings are exquisite
and are transmitted alongside the Six Classics.
When Great Wú (吳) received the Mandate,
it established its state in the southern lands.
In the final years of the Great Emperor's reign,
he ordered the Grand Astrologer Dīng Fú (丁孚) and Gentleman Xiàng Jùn (項峻) to begin compiling the Wú Shū (吳書).
Fú (孚) and Jùn (峻) were both not historical talents;
their compilations
are not worthy of record.
During the time of the Young Emperor,
Wéi Yào (韋曜), Zhōu Zhāo (周昭), Xuē Yíng (薛瑩), Liáng Guǎng (梁廣), and I, five individuals, were appointed
to seek out past events.
What we jointly compiled
contained a complete account of origins and conclusions.
Zhāo (昭) and Guǎng (廣) died prematurely,
Yào (曜) betrayed his lord and committed a crime,
Yíng (瑩) was sent out as a general,
and then was exiled again due to an offense.
The book was thus left unfinished
and has not yet been compiled and presented to date.
My talent is meager and inferior,
only suitable for making notes for Yíng (瑩) and others.
If I were to compile it,
I would certainly follow in the footsteps of Fú (孚) and Jùn (峻),
fearing that the foundational achievements of the Great Emperor would fall into obscurity
and the splendid virtues of the current age would be diminished.
Yíng (瑩) is both broadly learned
and especially skilled in writing;
among his colleagues,
Yíng (瑩) is preeminent.
Although many current officials
are well-versed in the classics,
there are few with the talent for historical writing
like Yíng (瑩).
Therefore, I am earnestly concerned for the state's sake.
I truly wish for him to complete this work
to be included at the end of previous histories.
After it is presented,
I would retire to fill a ditch [i.e., die]
with no further regrets."
Hào (晧) then recalled Yíng (瑩)
to be Left Grand Historian.
Soon after,
Miáo Yī (繆禕) of the same commandery, a Minister of the Bureau of Selection, was disliked by lesser men
for his unwavering convictions,
and was demoted to Administrator of Héngyáng (衡陽).
After he accepted the appointment,
he was again impeached and reprimanded for his official duties,
so he submitted a memorial of apology.
He then visited Yíng (瑩) on his way,
which was again reported by others,
saying Yī (禕) was not afraid of his offense
and brought many guests to gather at Yíng (瑩)'s place.
So Yī (禕) was arrested and imprisoned,
then exiled to Guìyáng (桂陽),
and Yíng (瑩) returned to Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Before he arrived,
Yíng (瑩) was recalled
and reinstated to his post.
At that time, many laws and policies were flawed,
and measures were cumbersome and harsh.
Yíng (瑩) frequently submitted proposals
advocating for relaxed punishments and simplified labor,
to benefit and nurture the common people,
and some of his suggestions were implemented.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies.
In the fourth year of Tiānjì (天紀),
when the Jìn (晉) army marched against Hào (晧),
Hào (晧) sent letters to Sīmǎ Zhòu (司馬伷), Wáng Hún (王渾), and Wáng Jùn (王濬) requesting surrender.
The text
was composed by Yíng (瑩).
When Yíng (瑩) arrived in Luòyáng (洛陽),
he was specially received first
and appointed as a Palace Attendant.
His replies to questions and handling of affairs
were all clear and logical.
He died in the third year of Tàikāng (太康).
He authored eight chapters
titled Xīnyì (新議).
The commentary states: Zhāng Hóng (張紘)'s literary style and righteous intentions
made him an excellent talent for his age.
Sūn Cè (孫策) treated him second only to Zhāng Zhāo (張昭),
which truly had its reasons.
Yán (嚴), Chéng (程), and Kǎn Shēng (闞生)
were scholars of their time.
As for Jùn (畯) giving up honors to help an old friend,
was he not a truly noble man!
Xuē Zōng (薛綜)'s learning and counsel
made him a good minister for Wú (吳).
And Yíng (瑩) followed in his footsteps,
indeed possessing his father's style;
however, in a brutal and harsh court,
he repeatedly attained high positions—
a gentleman would find this perilous.
Biography of Zhōu Yú (周瑜), Lǔ Sù (魯肅), and Lǚ Méng (呂蒙), Chapter Nine
