Zhōu Yú (周瑜), courtesy name Gōngjǐn (公瑾), was a native of Shū (舒) in Lújiāng (廬江).
His paternal grandfather Jǐng (景),
and Jǐng (景)'s son Zhōng (忠),
were both Grand Commandants of Hàn (漢).
His father Yì (異)
was the Magistrate of Luòyáng (洛陽).
Yú (瑜) was tall and handsome in adulthood.
Initially,
Sūn Jiān (孫堅) raised an army of righteousness to attack Dǒng Zhuó (董卓),
and moved his family to Shū (舒).
Jiān (堅)'s son Cè (策) was the same age as Yú (瑜),
and they were especially close friends.
Yú (瑜) offered his large house south of the road to Cè (策),
went up to the hall to bow to Cè (策)'s mother,
and they shared everything they had.
Yú (瑜)'s paternal cousin Shàng (尚) was the Administrator of Dānyáng (丹楊),
and Yú (瑜) went to visit him.
At that time, Cè (策) was about to cross east,
and arrived at Lìyáng (歷陽),
sending a swift letter to Yú (瑜).
Yú (瑜) led troops to meet Cè (策).
Cè (策) was overjoyed, saying:
"With you,
I shall succeed!"
They then proceeded to attack Héngjiāng (橫江) and Dānglì (當利),
capturing both.
They then crossed and attacked Mòlíng (秣陵),
defeating Zuó Róng (笮融) and Xuē Lǐ (薛禮),
then descended to Húshú (湖孰) and Jiāngchéng (江乘),
and entered Qū'ē (曲阿).
Liú Yáo (劉繇) fled,
and Cè (策)'s forces already numbered tens of thousands.
He then said to Yú (瑜):
"With these troops, taking Wúhuì (吳會) and pacifying the Shānyuè (山越) is sufficient.
You return and garrison Dānyáng (丹楊)."
Yú (瑜) returned.
Soon after,
Yuán Shù (袁術) sent his cousin Yìn (胤) to replace Shàng (尚) as Administrator,
and Yú (瑜) returned with Shàng (尚) to Shòuchūn (壽春).
Shù (術) wanted to appoint Yú (瑜) as a general,
but Yú (瑜) saw that Shù (術) would ultimately accomplish nothing,
so he requested to be Magistrate of Jūcháo (居巢),
wishing to use this as a path to return east.
Shù (術) permitted it.
He then returned to Wú (吳) from Jūcháo (居巢).
This year
was the third year of Jiàn'ān (建安).
Cè (策) personally welcomed Yú (瑜),
appointed him General of Illustrious Might,
and immediately gave him two thousand soldiers
and fifty cavalry horses.
Yú (瑜) was twenty-four years old at the time,
and everyone in Wú (吳) called him Zhōu Láng (周郎).
Because Yú (瑜)'s kindness and trustworthiness were renowned in Lújiāng (廬江),
he was dispatched to defend Niúzhǔ (牛渚),
and later served as Magistrate of Chūngǔ (春穀).
Soon after,
Cè (策) wished to take Jīngzhōu (荊州),
appointed Yú (瑜) as Central Protector of the Army,
and Administrator of Jiāngxià (江夏),
and followed him in attacking Wǎn (皖),
capturing it.
At that time, they acquired the two daughters of Governor Qiáo (橋公),
both of whom were national beauties.
Cè (策) took the elder Qiáo (橋) for himself,
and Yú (瑜) took the younger Qiáo (橋).
They then advanced to Xúnyáng (尋陽),
defeated Liú Xūn (劉勳),
attacked Jiāngxià (江夏),
then returned to pacify Yùzhāng (豫章) and Lúlíng (廬陵),
and remained to garrison Bāqiū (巴丘).
In the fifth year,
Sūn Cè 薨 [died],
Sūn Quán assumed overall command of affairs.
Zhōu Yú led troops to attend the funeral,
then remained in Wú,
serving as Zhōnghùjūn [Central Protector of the Army] and, with Chángshǐ Zhāng Zhāo, jointly managing all affairs.
In the eleventh year,
he supervised Sūn Yú and others in suppressing the two garrisons of Má and Bǎo,
executing their leaders,
and capturing over ten thousand prisoners.
He then returned to guard Gōngtíng [宮亭].
Huáng Zǔ, the Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià, sent his general Dèng Lóng with several thousand soldiers to invade Cháicāng.
Zhōu Yú pursued and attacked him,
capturing Lóng alive and sending him to Wú.
In the spring of the thirteenth year,
Sūn Quán attacked Jiāngxià,
with Zhōu Yú serving as the Dàdū [Grand Governor] of the vanguard.
In the ninth month of that year,
Cáo Gōng entered Jīngzhōu,
Liú Cóng surrendered with his forces,
and Cáo Gōng acquired his navy.
With several hundred thousand naval and infantry troops,
the generals and officers were all terrified upon hearing this.
Sūn Quán summoned his subordinates [for an audience]
and asked for strategies.
The debaters all said:
“Cáo Gōng is a jackal and a tiger,
yet he claims the title of Chancellor of Hàn,
holding the Son of Heaven to conquer the four directions,
always using the imperial court as his pretext.
To resist him today
would be even more disloyal.
Moreover, the great advantage the general has
to resist Cáo Cāo
is the Yangtze River.
Now Cáo Cāo has obtained Jīngzhōu,
occupying its territory,
and Liú Biǎo’s naval forces—
the `Assault Ships' and `Fighting Ships'—
numbered in the thousands.
Cáo Cāo has launched them all to travel along the river,
and also has infantry,
advancing both by water and land.
This means the strategic advantage of the Yangtze
is now shared with us.
As for the disparity in strength and numbers,
it’s not even worth discussing.
I humbly suggest that the best plan is to welcome him.”
Zhōu Yú said:
“Not so.
Though Cáo Cāo claims the title of Chancellor of Hàn,
in reality he is a traitor to Hàn.
The general, with divine might and heroic talent,
and relying on the achievements of his father and elder brother,
has carved out a domain in Jiāngdōng,
a territory several thousand *lǐ* square,
with elite troops sufficient for use,
and heroes content in their work.
He should still sweep across the land
to eliminate the remnants of corruption for the Hàn dynasty.
How much more so now that Cáo Cāo is bringing death upon himself—
how can we welcome him?
Please allow me to plan for the general: If the northern lands were now peaceful,
and Cáo Cāo had no internal worries,
and could drag out the war for a long time
to contend for our borders,
could he still compete with us for victory on ships and oar-boats?
Now the northern lands are not yet peaceful,
and moreover, Mǎ Chāo and Hán Suì are still in Guānxī,
posing a threat to Cáo Cāo’s rear.
Furthermore, abandoning saddles and horses
and relying on boats and oars
to contend with the Wú and Yuè people
is fundamentally not what the Central Plains excels at.
Also, it is now the height of winter;
the horses have no fodder,
and driving the Central Plains soldiers and masses to travel far across the rivers and lakes,
unaccustomed to the climate,
will certainly cause diseases.
These four points
are the perils of employing troops,
yet Cáo Cāo is recklessly undertaking them all.
It is fitting for the general to capture Cáo Cāo
on this very day.
I request three *wàn* elite soldiers;
I will advance to Xiàkǒu [Summer Mouth]
and guarantee to defeat him for the general.”
Sūn Quán said:
“The old villain has long desired to depose Hàn and establish himself,
only fearing the two Yuán, Lǚ Bù, Liú Biǎo, and me.
Now that these powerful lords have been destroyed,
only I remain.
I and the old villain [Cáo Cāo]
cannot coexist.
Your words that we should attack
are very much in agreement with my own thoughts.
This is Heaven giving you to me.”
At this time, Liú Bèi had been defeated by Cáo Gōng,
and wanted to cross the river south.
He met Lǔ Sù at Dāngyáng,
and together they plotted a plan.
They then advanced to Xiàkǒu,
and sent Zhūgě Liàng to meet Sūn Quán.
Sūn Quán then dispatched Zhōu Yú and Chéng Pǔ and others to join forces with Liú Bèi to resist Cáo Gōng,
and they met at Chìbì.
At that time, Cáo Gōng’s army was already afflicted with disease.
In the initial engagement,
Cáo Gōng’s army was defeated and retreated,
stationing themselves on the north bank of the river.
Zhōu Yú and others were on the south bank.
Zhōu Yú’s subordinate Huáng Gài said:
“Now the enemy is numerous and we are few;
it is difficult to maintain a prolonged fight.
However, observing Cáo Cāo’s fleet, with ships connected bow to stern,
they can be set ablaze and driven away.”
He then took several tens of `Assault Ships' and `Fighting Ships',
filled them with kindling and dry grass,
poured oil into them,
covered them with awnings,
and raised official banners.
He first sent a letter to Cáo Gōng,
deceiving him with an intention to surrender.
He also prepared light boats in advance,
each tied to the stern of a large ship,
and then led them all forward.
Cáo Gōng’s officers and soldiers all craned their necks to watch,
pointing and saying that Huáng Gài was surrendering.
Huáng Gài released all the ships,
setting them on fire simultaneously.
At that time, the wind was strong and fierce,
and it spread the fire to burn all the camps on the shore.
In a moment,
smoke and flames soared to the sky;
many men and horses were burned or drowned to death.
The army then retreated in defeat,
returning to defend Nánjùn.
Liú Bèi and Zhōu Yú and others again pursued them.
Cáo Gōng left Cáo Rén and others to guard the city of Jiānglíng,
and directly returned north.
Zhōu Yú and Chéng Pǔ then advanced on Nánjùn,
facing Cáo Rén,
each separated by the Great River.
Before the armies engaged,
Zhōu Yú immediately sent Gān Níng ahead to occupy Yílíng.
Cáo Rén divided his cavalry to separately attack and besiege Gān Níng.
Gān Níng sent an urgent message to Zhōu Yú.
Zhōu Yú adopted Lǚ Méng’s plan,
leaving Líng Tǒng to guard his rear,
while he himself, with Lǚ Méng, went to relieve Gān Níng.
Once Gān Níng’s siege was lifted,
they crossed to garrison the north bank,
setting a date for a major battle.
Zhōu Yú personally rode his horse to inspect the formation.
He was hit by a stray arrow in his right side.
The wound was severe,
so he returned.
Later, Cáo Rén, hearing that Zhōu Yú was recuperating and had not yet risen,
mobilized his troops and advanced to the formation.
Zhōu Yú then personally roused himself,
inspected the military camps,
and encouraged his officers and soldiers.
Cáo Rén consequently retreated.
Sūn Quán appointed Zhōu Yú as Piānjīangjūn [General of the Vanguard],
and concurrently Grand Administrator of Nánjùn.
He was given Xiàjùn, Hànchāng, Liúyáng, and Zhōulíng as his fiefs,
and garrisoned Jiānglíng.
Liú Bèi, as Zuǒjiāngjūn [General of the Left], concurrently served as Governor of Jīngzhōu,
governing from Gōng'ān.
Liú Bèi went to the capital to meet Sūn Quán.
Zhōu Yú submitted a memorial, saying:
“Liú Bèi, with his heroic and ambitious nature,
and possessing generals like Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi, who are like bears and tigers,
will certainly not long remain subservient to others.
I humbly suggest that the great plan is to move Liú Bèi and place him in Wú,
lavishly build palaces for him,
and provide him with many beautiful women and delights
to entertain his eyes and ears.
Separate these two individuals [Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi],
placing each in a different region,
and allow someone like me to lead them in battle,
and the great task can be accomplished.
Now, carelessly allocating territory to him for his enterprise,
and gathering these three individuals [Liú Bèi, Guān Yǔ, and Zhāng Fēi]
all in the border regions,
I fear that if a dragon gains clouds and rain,
it will ultimately not remain a creature of the pond.”
Sūn Quán, considering that Cáo Gōng was in the north
and one should broadly gather heroes,
and also fearing that Liú Bèi would be difficult to control if abruptly handled,
therefore did not accept the advice.
At that time, Liú Zhāng [劉璋] was the Governor of Yìzhōu [益州].
Outwardly, Zhāng Lǔ [張魯] was encroaching and raiding.
Zhōu Yú [周瑜] then went to the capital to see Sūn Quán [孫權] and said:
"Now Cáo Cāo [曹操] has just suffered a defeat,
and is worried about internal affairs;
he cannot yet unite his forces with yours to act together.
I beg to advance with Fènwēi [奮威] to conquer Shǔ [蜀].
After acquiring Shǔ and incorporating Zhāng Lǔ,
Fènwēi can be left to firmly defend that territory.
We can then form an alliance with Mǎ Chāo [馬超].
I will return and, with you, hold Xiāngyáng [襄陽] to put pressure on Cáo Cāo.
The North can then be contended for."
Sūn Quán agreed to this.
Zhōu Yú returned to Jiānglíng [江陵],
and was preparing for the journey,
but he fell ill and died on the way at Bāqiū [巴丘],
at the age of thirty-six.
Sūn Quán wore plain clothes and mourned,
moving those around him.
When the funeral procession was to return to Wú [吳],
he met it again at Wúhú [蕪湖],
and all the expenses
were provided for by him.
Later, he issued an order saying:
"For the former generals Zhōu Yú and Chéng Pǔ [程普],
if they have retainers,
none shall be interrogated."
Initially, Zhōu Yú was befriended by Sūn Cè [孫策],
and the Grand Imperial Consort also instructed Sūn Quán to treat him as an elder brother.
At that time, Sūn Quán's position was General.
The generals and retainers were rather informal in their etiquette,
but Zhōu Yú alone was the first to show utmost respect
and uphold the duty of a subject.
His disposition was broad and magnanimous,
and he was generally good at judging people;
he was only at odds with Chéng Pǔ.
From a young age, Zhōu Yú had a keen interest in music.
Even after three cups of wine,
if there was a mistake or omission,
Zhōu Yú would always notice it,
and if he noticed it, he would always look back.
Therefore, people at the time sang a ditty:
"If there's a fault in the tune,
Zhōu Láng [周郎] will look."
Zhōu Yú had two sons and one daughter.
His daughter was married to Crown Prince Dēng [登].
His son, Xún [循], married a princess,
was appointed Cavalry Commandant,
had the demeanor of Zhōu Yú,
but died early.
Xún's younger brother, Yìn [胤],
was initially appointed Governor of Xīngyè [興業],
married a distant relative from the imperial clan,
was given a thousand soldiers,
and stationed at Gōng'ān [公安].
In the first year of Huánglóng [黃龍] (229 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng [都鄉].
Later, due to a crime, he was exiled to Lúlíng [廬陵] Commandery.
In the second year of Chìwū [赤烏] (239 CE),
Zhūgě Jǐn [諸葛瑾] and Bù Zhì [步騭] jointly submitted a memorial, saying:
"Yìn, son of the late General Zhōu Yú,
formerly received embellishment,
and was enfeoffed as a general.
He was unable to nurture that fortune,
or think of establishing meritorious service.
Instead, he indulged his desires,
and thus invited crime and punishment.
Your servants humbly believe that Zhōu Yú was formerly favored and trusted,
acting as an inner confidant when within,
and as fangs and claws when without.
He undertook expeditions with mandates,
personally faced arrows and stones,
exhausted his loyalty and gave his life,
regarding death as a return home.
Thus, he was able to defeat Cáo Cāo at Wūlín [烏林],
and drive Cáo Rén [曹仁] from Yǐngdū [郢都],
spreading the nation's power and virtue,
which shook the entire Huáxià [華夏].
The ignorant southern barbarians [Mán Jīng, 蠻荊]
all submitted.
Even Fāng Shú [方叔] of Zhōu [周],
or Xìn [信] and Bù [布] of Hàn [漢],
truly could not surpass him.
Ministers who break enemy formations and fend off difficulties
have always been highly valued by emperors and kings throughout history.
Thus, Emperor Gāo of Hàn [漢高帝] swore an oath when enfeoffing nobles, saying: 'May the Yellow River be like a sash,
Mount Tài [太山] be like a whetstone,
and the nation eternally endure,
extending to its descendants';
this was confirmed with cinnabar writings,
and reinforced with sworn covenants,
stored in the ancestral temple,
and transmitted endlessly.
This was to ensure that the descendants of meritorious officials
would succeed each other for generations,
not merely children and grandchildren,
but even distant offspring.
To repay their virtue and clarify their merits,
so earnestly and diligently,
to such an extent,
was intended to encourage and warn future generations,
so that those who served with their lives
would have no regrets in death.
How much more so since Zhōu Yú's death was not long ago,
and yet his son Yìn has been demoted to a commoner?
This is even more lamentable and grievous.
We humbly believe that Your Majesty is wise and enlightened, who follows ancient precedents,
and is magnanimous in continuing legacies.
We plead on behalf of Yìn,
begging for the remission of his remaining sins,
the restoration of his troops and title,
so that the rooster that has lost its dawn
may crow once more,
and the minister burdened with guilt
may demonstrate his later achievements."
Sūn Quán replied:
"An old meritorious servant, a confidant,
who worked with me,
Gōngjǐn [公瑾] (Zhōu Yú) was indeed such,
and I certainly do not forget him.
In the past, Yìn was young,
initially without merit,
yet he unjustly received elite troops,
and was granted the title of Marquis-General.
This was undoubtedly out of consideration for Gōngjǐn, extending to Yìn.
Yet Yìn relied on this,
indulging in alcoholism and debauchery as he pleased.
Despite repeated warnings,
he showed no signs of repentance.
My relationship with Gōngjǐn
was as between two sovereigns (referring to their close bond).
Would I not wish for Yìn's success?
How could I give up on him?
But Yìn's crimes are pressing,
and it is not yet appropriate to reinstate him immediately.
I intend to let him suffer for a while,
so he can learn from it himself.
Now you two gentlemen diligently invoke Emperor Gāo of Hàn's oath of rivers and mountains.
This makes me feel ashamed.
Although my virtue is not comparable to his,
I still wish to aspire to it,
and the matter is indeed similar.
Therefore, I have not yet followed your recommendation.
As the son of Gōngjǐn,
and with you two gentlemen interceding,
if he can truly reform,
what is there to worry about?"
Zhūgě Jǐn and Bù Zhì's memorial was submitted,
and Zhū Rán [朱然] and Quán Cóng [全琮] also jointly pleaded.
Sūn Quán then agreed.
However, Yìn died of illness.
Zhōu Yú's elder brother's son, Jùn [峻],
also, due to Zhōu Yú's original merits, was made General of the Household,
commanding a thousand officers and soldiers.
When Jùn died,
Quán Cóng memorialized to appoint Jùn's son, Hù [護], as a general.
Sūn Quán said:
"Driving back Cáo Cāo
and expanding to possess Jīngzhōu [荊州]
were all Gōngjǐn's achievements,
and I never forget them.
When I first heard of Jùn's death,
I immediately wanted to appoint Hù,
but then I heard that Hù's character was dangerous,
and appointing him would only cause trouble.
Therefore, I stopped myself.
My thoughts for Gōngjǐn,
how could they ever cease?"
Lǔ Sù [魯肅], courtesy name Zǐjìng [子敬],
was from Dōngchéng [東城], Línqīn [臨淮].
He lost his father when he was born
and lived with his grandmother.
His family was rich,
and he was naturally generous.
At that time, the world was already in chaos,
and Lǔ Sù did not manage family affairs.
He liberally distributed wealth,
and sold off fields,
focusing on aiding the poor and needy and befriending scholars,
and was greatly loved by his hometown and district.
Zhōu Yú was the chief of Jūcháo.
With several hundred men, he deliberately passed by to visit Sù,
and also asked for provisions and supplies.
Sù's family had two granaries of rice,
each containing three thousand hú.
Sù then pointed to one granary and gave it to Zhōu Yú.
Yú increasingly recognized his extraordinary nature,
and thus they became close friends,
establishing a bond like Qiáo and Zhá.
Yuán Shù heard of his reputation
and appointed him as the chief of Dōngchéng.
Sù saw that Shù lacked discipline
and was not worthy of accomplishing great things with,
so he led his old and weak relatives, along with over a hundred lighthearted young men,
south to Jūcháo to join Yú.
When Yú crossed to the east,
Sù accompanied him,
leaving his family in Qū'ā.
Coincidentally, his grandmother died,
and he returned to Dōngchéng to bury her.
Liú Zǐyáng, who was good friends with Sù,
sent Sù a letter saying:
"Currently, heroes are rising throughout the land.
Your talent and ability
are especially suited for these times.
You should quickly return and bring your old mother,
do not stay in Dōngchéng for no reason.
Zhèng Bǎo, who is nearby,
is now in Cháohú,
commanding over ten thousand troops.
He occupies fertile and rich land,
and many people in Lújiāng are flocking to him.
How much more should we?
Observing his situation,
it is also possible to gather a large force.
This opportunity must not be missed.
You should hurry."
Sù replied that he agreed with the plan.
After the burial, he returned to Qū'ā,
intending to go north.
At that time, Yú had already moved Sù's mother to Wú. Sù fully explained the situation to Yú.
Sūn Cè had already passed away at that time,
and Quán was still residing in Wú.
Yú said to Sù:
"In the past, Mǎ Yuán told Guāngwǔ, 'In the world today,
not only does the ruler choose his ministers, but ministers also choose their ruler.'
Now, our lord cherishes the virtuous and values scholars,
embracing the extraordinary and recording the unique.
Moreover, I have heard the secret discussions of former sages,
that those who will succeed the Liú clan
by heaven's mandate
must rise in the southeast.
Judging by the course of events and circumstances,
this aligns with the calendar's count.
They will ultimately establish an imperial foundation
in accordance with the heavenly mandate.
This is the season for brave gentlemen to 'climb dragons and attach to phoenixes,' dashing forth.
I have just realized this;
you need not take Zǐyáng's words to heart."
Sù followed his advice.
Yú then recommended Sù, saying his talent was suited to assist the times,
and that they should widely seek out others like him
to accomplish great deeds,
and he should not be allowed to leave.
Quán immediately met Sù
and was very pleased after speaking with him.
After all the guests had left,
and Sù was also about to depart,
Quán alone called Sù back
and sat with him on a mat to drink.
They then secretly discussed, saying:
"Now the Hàn dynasty is in peril,
and the four quarters are in turmoil.
I, your lonely one, inherit the remaining legacy of my father and elder brother,
and aspire to achieve the accomplishments of Huán and Wén.
Since you have graciously come,
how can you assist me?"
Sù replied:
"In the past, Emperor Gāo, with great effort, wished to honor Emperor Yì but could not
because Xiàng Yǔ was a hindrance.
Today's Cáo Cāo is like Xiàng Yǔ of old.
How can the general achieve the deeds of Huán and Wén?
I secretly estimate
that the Hàn dynasty cannot be restored,
and Cáo Cāo cannot be eliminated quickly.
My plan for the general
is only to form a tripartite division in Jiāngdōng
and observe the opportune moments in the world.
Such a grand strategy
will inherently be without reproach.
Why?
The north indeed has many concerns.
Taking advantage of its many concerns,
eliminate Huáng Zǔ,
then attack Liú Biǎo,
reach the utmost extent of the Long River,
occupy and possess it.
After that, declare yourself emperor
and plan for the world.
This is the achievement of Emperor Gāo."
Quán said:
"Now I am devoting all my strength to one region,
hoping to assist the Hàn only.
This kind of talk is beyond my scope."
Zhāng Zhāo criticized Sù for being unhumble and lacking,
and quite slandered him,
saying Sù was young and crude,
and not yet fit for use.
Quán did not take it to heart,
but valued him even more,
bestowing upon Sù's mother clothes, bed curtains,
and various household items,
making her wealth comparable to her former status.
Liú Biǎo died.
Sù presented his advice, saying:
"Jīngchǔ and our state are neighboring,
with rivers flowing northwards,
externally bordered by the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
and internally blocked by mountains and hills.
It has the fortifications of a golden city,
fertile land extending for ten thousand li,
and a rich and numerous populace.
If we occupy and possess it,
this is the capital for an emperor.
Now Biǎo has just died,
and his two sons have always been at odds.
Among the generals in the army,
each has his own alignment.
Furthermore, Liú Bèi is a hero of the world,
and has a rift with Cāo.
He is a guest of Biǎo,
but Biǎo disliked his ability and could not use him.
If Bèi and they cooperate wholeheartedly,
and all are united,
then it would be appropriate to pacify him
and form a good alliance;
if there is disagreement,
then a separate plan should be made
to accomplish our great enterprise.
I request to be entrusted with the mission of condoling Biǎo's two sons,
and also comforting and rewarding those in charge in their army,
and persuading Bèi to take charge of Biǎo's troops,
uniting in purpose
to jointly resist Cáo Cāo.
Bèi will surely be pleased and obey.
If this can be achieved,
the world can be settled.
If we do not go quickly now,
I fear Cāo will get there first."
Quán immediately dispatched Sù.
When he reached Xiàkǒu,
he heard that Cáo Gōng was already heading towards Jīngzhōu.
He traveled day and night without rest.
By the time he reached Nánjùn,
Biǎo's son Cóng had already surrendered to Cáo Gōng.
Bèi fled in panic,
wanting to cross the river to the south.
Sù went directly to meet him,
and arrived at Dāngyáng Chángbǎn,
where he met Bèi.
He conveyed Quán's intentions,
and explained the strength and solidity of Jiāngdōng,
persuading Bèi to combine forces with Quán.
Bèi was very pleased.
At that time, Zhūgě Liàng was accompanying Bèi.
Sù said to Liàng,
"I am your elder brother Yú's friend,"
and they immediately established a friendship.
Bèi then arrived at Xiàkǒu
and sent Liàng to see Quán.
Sù also returned to report.
At this time, Qúán [孫權] received news that Cáo Gōng [曹公] intended to move east.
He discussed this with his generals,
who all advised Qúán [權] to welcome him,
but Sù [肅] alone remained silent.
Qúán [權] got up to change his clothes.
Sù [肅] followed him under the eaves.
Qúán [權] understood his intention,
and grasping Sù's [肅] hand, said:
"What do you wish to say, sir?"
Sù [肅] replied:
"I observed the discussions of the multitude just now,
and they are solely intent on misleading the General.
They are not fit to plan great affairs with.
Now, I, Sù [肅], may welcome Cāo [操],
but as for the General,
you cannot.
Why do I say this?
If I, Sù [肅], welcome Cāo [操],
Cāo [操] will surely send me back to my home district,
grade my rank and position,
and I would still not lose my post as a junior official,
ride in an ox-cart,
be attended by clerks and soldiers,
socialize with the literati,
and accumulate promotions, ultimately not failing to achieve a provincial or commandery post.
If the General welcomes Cāo [操],
where will you return?
I hope you will quickly decide on a grand strategy,
and not follow the advice of the multitude."
Qúán [權] sighed and said:
"The views held by these people
are greatly disappointing to me.
Now, you, sir, have laid out a grand strategy
that is precisely the same as mine.
This is Heaven bestowing you upon me."
At that time, Zhōu Yú [周瑜] was on a mission to Póyáng [鄱陽].
Sù [肅] advised recalling Yú [瑜].
Thereupon, Yú [瑜] was entrusted with the execution of affairs,
and Sù [肅] was appointed Zànjūn Xiàowèi [贊軍校尉],
to assist in devising strategies.
When Cáo Gōng [曹公] was defeated and fled,
Sù [肅] was the first to return.
Qúán [權] grandly invited his generals to welcome Sù [肅].
As Sù [肅] was about to enter the hall to bow,
Qúán [權] rose to greet him respectfully,
and then said:
"Zǐjìng [子敬],
I dismounted from my horse by holding its saddle to welcome you.
Is this enough to make you illustrious?"
Sù [肅] hurried forward and said:
"Not yet."
When the others heard this,
none were not astonished.
He took his seat,
and slowly raised his whip and said:
"I wish that Your Supreme Highness's prestige and virtue may extend throughout the four seas,
unite the nine provinces,
accomplish the imperial enterprise,
and then summon Sù [肅] with an imperial carriage and soft wheels—
only then will I be truly illustrious!"
Qúán [權] clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
Later, Bèi [備] went to Jīng [京] to meet Qúán [權],
and requested to be made Governor of Jīngzhōu [荊州].
Only Sù [肅] advised Qúán [權] to lend it to him,
to jointly resist Cáo Gōng [曹公].
When Cáo Gōng [曹公] heard that Qúán [權] had granted land to Bèi [備] as his domain,
he was in the midst of writing a letter
and dropped his brush to the ground.
When Zhōu Yú [周瑜] was gravely ill,
he submitted a memorial, saying:
"At present, the world
is engaged in military affairs.
This is what I, Yú [瑜], have worried about day and night in my heart.
I wish that Your Supreme Highness would first consider what has not yet happened,
and only then enjoy peace and joy.
Now, having become an enemy of Cáo Cāo [曹操],
Liú Bèi [劉備] is close by at Gōng'ān [公安].
The borders are adjacent,
and the common people are not yet attached.
It is fitting to obtain a good general to pacify them.
Lǔ Sù's [魯肅] wisdom and strategy are sufficient for the task.
I beg that he be appointed to succeed me, Yú [瑜].
When I, Yú [瑜], fall and die,
all my intentions will be fulfilled."
Immediately, Sù [肅] was appointed Fènwǔ Xiàowèi [奮武校尉],
to succeed Yú [瑜] in commanding the troops.
Yú's [瑜] troops, numbering over four thousand,
and four counties of his enfeoffment,
were all assigned to him.
Chéng Pǔ [程普] was ordered to serve as the Grand Administrator of Nánjùn [南郡].
Sù [肅] initially resided in Jiānglíng [江陵],
and later garrisoned at Lùkǒu [陸口].
His prestige and benevolence spread widely,
and his troops increased by over ten thousand men.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Hànchāng [漢昌] and Piānjiāngjūn [偏將軍].
In the nineteenth year [of Jiàn'ān],
he followed Qúán [權] to defeat Wǎnchéng [皖城],
and was promoted to Héngjiāng Jiāngjūn [橫江將軍].
Earlier,
the Prefect of Yìzhōu [益州], Liú Zhāng [劉璋], had a collapsing administration.
Zhōu Yú [周瑜] and Gān Níng [甘寧] both advised Qúán [權] to seize Shǔ [蜀].
Qúán [權] consulted Bèi [備],
who secretly wished to make plans for himself,
and falsely reported:
"I, Bèi [備], and Zhāng [璋] are related as members of the imperial clan.
I hoped to rely on the heroic spirits [of our ancestors]
to assist the court.
Now that Zhāng [璋] has offended those around you,
I, Bèi [備], am uniquely fearful,
and dare not hear of it.
I wish for him to be treated with leniency.
If this request is not granted,
I, Bèi [備], shall let my hair down and retire to the mountains and forests."
Later, Bèi [備] marched west against Zhāng [璋],
leaving Guān Yǔ [關羽] to guard.
Qúán [權] said:
"That crafty fellow dares to employ deceit!"
When Yǔ [羽] and Sù [肅] were adjacent on the border,
Yǔ [羽] often harbored suspicions,
causing frequent disputes along the frontier.
Sù [肅] always managed him with goodwill.
After Bèi [備] had stabilized Yìzhōu [益州],
Qúán [權] demanded Chángshā [長沙], Línglíng [零陵], and Guìyáng [桂陽].
Bèi [備] did not comply with the order.
Qúán [權] dispatched Lǚ Méng [呂蒙] to lead troops to take them.
Bèi [備] heard of this,
and returned to Gōng'ān [公安] himself,
sending Yǔ [羽] to contend for the three commanderies.
Sù [肅] resided in Yìyáng [益陽],
confronting Yǔ [羽].
Sù [肅] invited Yǔ [羽] to meet,
each party stopping their troops and horses a hundred paces away,
requesting only the generals to meet, unarmed and alone.
Sù [肅] then reproached Yǔ [羽], saying:
"Our state initially, for trivial reasons, lent land to your family
because your family's army was defeated and came from afar,
having nothing to rely on.
Now that you have obtained Yìzhōu [益州],
you have no intention of returning it,
and when we only request the three commanderies,
you still do not obey."
Before he finished speaking,
a man in the assembly said:
"Indeed, land
belongs only to where virtue resides;
how can it be constant?"
Sù [肅] sternly rebuked him,
his words and expression very sharp.
Yǔ [羽] grasped his saber and rose, saying:
"This is a matter for the state itself;
what does this man know?"
He motioned for the man to leave.
Bèi [備] then ceded the Xiāng River [湘水] as the border,
and thereupon the armies withdrew.
Sù [肅] died at the age of forty-six
in the twenty-second year of Jiàn'ān [建安].
Qúán [權] held a mourning ceremony for him,
and also attended his funeral.
Zhūgě Liàng [諸葛亮] also expressed sorrow for him.
When Qúán [權] assumed the imperial title,
he stood before the altar,
and looking at his high officials, said:
"Lǔ Zǐjìng [魯子敬] once spoke of this;
he can be said to have been clear about the course of events."
Sù's [肅] posthumous son, Shú [淑], once grown,
Zhāng Chéng [張承], the Supervising General of Rúxū [濡須], said he would eventually reach a high position.
During the Yǒng'ān [永安] era,
he served as Zhāowǔ Jiāngjūn [昭武將軍], Dūtíng Hóu [都亭侯], and Wǔchāng Dū [武昌督].
During the Jiànhéng [建衡] era,
he was granted the jié [節] (imperial insignia) and
promoted to Xiàkǒu Dū [夏口督].
Wherever he was, he was strict and orderly,
and had administrative competence.
He died in the third year of Fènghuáng [鳳皇].
His son Mù [睦] inherited his peerage [and] commanded his troops.
Lǚ Méng, courtesy name Zǐmíng,
was a native of Fùpí, Rǔnán.
As a youth, he crossed south
and depended on his sister's husband, Dèng Dāng.
Dāng was a general under Sūn Cè
and frequently campaigned against the Shānyuè.
When Méng was fifteen or sixteen,
he secretly followed Dāng to attack bandits.
Dāng looked back and was greatly startled,
shouting at him but unable to stop him.
Upon returning, he told Méng's mother,
who was angry and wanted to punish him.
Méng said:
"It is difficult to remain poor and lowly.
If by chance I achieve some merit,
wealth and high status can be attained.
Moreover, if one does not enter the tiger's den,
how can one obtain a tiger cub?"
His mother took pity on him and let him be.
At that time, an official serving under Dāng belittled Méng for his youth,
saying:
"What can that stripling do?
He is merely offering himself as food for tigers."
Another day, he met Méng
and again insulted him.
Méng was greatly enraged,
drew his knife and killed the official,
then fled,
seeking refuge in the home of the local resident Zhèng Cháng.
Later, he used 校尉 Yuán Xióng to surrender himself,
and Xióng spoke on his behalf during an opportune moment.
Cè summoned and saw him, was impressed by him,
and kept him by his side.
Several years later,
Dèng Dāng died.
Zhāng Zhāo recommended Méng to replace Dāng,
and he was appointed Biébù Sīmǎ.
When Quán took charge of affairs,
he reviewed all the minor generals whose forces were small and poorly equipped,
intending to merge them.
Méng secretly borrowed money
to make crimson uniforms and gaiters for his soldiers.
On the day of inspection,
they were arrayed splendidly,
and the soldiers were well-trained.
Quán saw this and was greatly pleased,
increasing his troops.
He followed Quán in attacking Dānyáng,
achieving success wherever he went,
and was appointed Píngběi Dūwèi,
also administering Guǎngdé Prefecture.
He followed Quán in campaigning against Huáng Zǔ.
Zǔ ordered his commander Chén Jiù to lead a naval force to meet them in battle.
Méng commanded the vanguard,
personally beheading Jiù.
The officers and men, capitalizing on their victory,
advanced and attacked Zǔ's city.
Zǔ heard of Jiù's death,
abandoned the city and fled.
The troops pursued and captured him.
Quán said:
"The success of this campaign
was due to Chén Jiù being captured first."
He appointed Méng as Héngyě Zhōnglángjiàng
and bestowed upon him ten million coins.
That year,
he also, with Zhōu Yú, Chéng Pǔ, and others, decisively defeated Cáo Gōng at Wūlín in the west,
and besieged Cáo Rén at Nánjùn.
The Yìzhōu general Xí Sù came to surrender with his entire army.
Yú memorialized to assign Sù's troops to Méng.
Méng highly praised Sù for his courage and resourcefulness,
and stated that as Sù had come from afar, admiring their culture,
it would be righteous to augment his forces, not to seize them.
Quán approved of his words
and returned Sù's troops.
Yú sent Gān Níng to occupy Yílíng in advance.
Cáo Rén divided his forces to attack Níng.
Níng was in dire straits
and sent a messenger to request aid.
The generals thought their forces were too few to divide.
Méng said to Yú and Pǔ:
"Leave Líng Gōngjì here;
I will go with you.
Relieving the siege and urgent situation
will not take long,
and I guarantee Gōngjì can hold for ten days."
He also persuaded Yú to send three hundred men to cut off the perilous mountain path,
so that if the enemy fled, their horses could be captured.
Yú followed his advice.
When the army arrived at Yílíng,
they engaged in battle that very day,
killing more than half the enemy.
The enemy fled by night.
They encountered the cut-off path,
and all the cavalry abandoned their horses and fled on foot.
The troops pursued and attacked them,
capturing three hundred horses,
which were then loaded onto boats and brought back.
At this, the morale of the officers and men doubled.
They then crossed the river and established a camp,
engaging in combat with the enemy.
Cáo Rén retreated,
and they consequently occupied Nánjùn
and pacified Jīngzhōu.
Upon returning,
Méng was appointed Piān Jiāngjūn,
also administering Xúnyáng Prefecture.
When Lǔ Sù replaced Zhōu Yú,
he was to go to Lùkǒu,
and passed by Méng's camp.
Sù still held Méng in low regard.
Someone advised Sù, saying:
"General Lǚ's achievements and reputation are growing daily;
you cannot treat him with your former attitude.
You should visit him."
So he went to see Méng.
During the height of the drinking,
Méng asked Sù:
"You have been entrusted with a heavy responsibility
and are neighbors with Guān Yǔ.
What strategies
do you have to prepare for the unexpected?"
Sù, without thinking, replied:
"I will adapt to the situation as it arises."
Méng said:
"Although the east and west are now one family,
Guān Yǔ is truly a bear and a tiger.
How can plans not be made in advance?"
He then outlined five strategies for Sù.
Sù then moved from his mat to be closer to him,
patting his back and saying:
"Lǚ Zǐmíng,
I did not know your talent and strategy extended to such a degree!"
He then bowed to Méng's mother
and parted as friends.
At that time, Méng was camped near Chéng Dāng, Sòng Dìng, and Xú Gù.
When the three generals died,
their sons were young and weak.
Quán intended to merge all their troops into Méng's command.
Méng firmly declined,
explaining that Gù and the others had all toiled diligently for the state,
and though their sons were young,
they should not be abandoned.
He submitted his petition three times,
and Quán finally agreed.
Méng then selected teachers for them
to assist and guide them.
His commitment and character were consistently like this.
Wèi's envoy, Xiè Qí of Lújiāng, was the commander of military agriculture at Qíchūn,
stationed at Wǎntián Township,
and frequently raided the border.
Méng sent someone to entice him,
but he did not comply.
So Méng waited for an opportunity to ambush him.
Qí consequently retreated.
His subordinates Sūn Zǐcái and Sòng Háo,
all carrying their elderly and young,
came to Méng and surrendered.
Later, he followed Quán to resist Cáo Gōng at Rúxū,
repeatedly proposing ingenious strategies,
and also advised Quán to build fortifications on both sides of the waterway,
thus making the defenses very strong.
Cáo Gōng was unable to break through and retreated.
Cáo Gōng sent Zhū Guāng to be the Administrator of Lújiāng,
stationing him at Wǎn,
where he greatly expanded the rice fields.
He also ordered idlers to recruit and entice the bandit leaders of Póyáng,
making them serve as internal agents.
Méng said:
"The fields of Wǎn are fertile and rich.
If they have even one harvest,
their forces will surely increase.
If this continues for several years,
Cáo's intentions will be revealed.
They should be eliminated early."
Then he fully explained the situation.
Thereupon, Quán personally led an expedition against Wǎn,
summoning his generals
to ask for strategies.
Méng then recommended Gān Níng to be the Commander of the Ascending Attack,
leading the assault in front,
with Méng following with elite troops.
They launched an attack at dawn,
Méng personally holding a drumstick and beating the drum.
The soldiers all leaped and ascended by themselves,
and the city was captured by mealtime.
Soon after, Zhāng Liáo arrived at Jiáshí,
but hearing that the city had already fallen,
he withdrew.
Quán praised his achievement,
and immediately appointed him Administrator of Lújiāng.
All the men and horses captured were divided and given to him,
and he was separately granted six hundred men for garrison farming at Xúnyáng
and thirty officers.
When Méng returned to Xúnyáng,
before the year was out, bandits rose in Lúlíng.
The other generals attacked but could not capture them.
Quán said:
"Hundreds of fierce birds
are not as good as one osprey."
He again ordered Méng to suppress them.
When Méng arrived,
he executed the chief offenders,
released the rest,
and they became common people again.
At this time, Liú Bèi had Guān Yǔ garrison and defend,
fully possessing Jīngtǔ.
Quán ordered Méng to take the three commanderies of Chángshā, Líng, and Guì from the west.
Méng sent letters to the two commanderies,
and they submitted at the mere sight of his approach.
Only Hǎo Pǔ, the Administrator of Línglíng, defended the city and refused to surrender.
Meanwhile, Bèi personally came from Shǔ to Gōng'ān,
sending Yǔ to contest the three commanderies.
Quán was then stationed at Lùkǒu,
and sent Lǔ Sù with ten thousand men to garrison Yìyáng to resist Yǔ.
He then sent an urgent letter to summon Méng,
ordering him to abandon Línglíng
and quickly return to assist Sù.
Initially,
after Méng had pacified Chángshā,
he was to proceed to Línglíng.
Passing through Énlíng,
he took along Dèng Xuánzhī of Nányáng.
Xuánzhī was an old acquaintance of Hǎo Pǔ,
and Méng intended to use him to entice Pǔ.
When he received the letter to return,
Méng kept it a secret.
That night, he summoned his generals,
instructed them on the strategy,
and announced that they would attack the city at dawn.
He turned to Xuánzhī and said:
"Hǎo Zǐtài heard that there are acts of loyalty and righteousness in the world,
and he also wishes to perform them,
but he does not know the opportune time.
General of the Left is in Hànzhōng,
besieged by Xiàhóu Yuān.
Guān Yǔ is in Nánjùn,
and now His Holiness personally approaches him.
Recently, the Fán army was broken at its original encampment,
and in saving Énlíng,
it was conversely defeated by Sūn Guī.
These are all recent events,
which you have personally witnessed.
They are currently in a desperate situation,
struggling to save themselves from death,
how can they have any remaining strength to manage this place?
Now, our soldiers are elite and sharp,
everyone determined to fight to the death.
His Holiness has dispatched troops,
who are following continuously on the road.
Now, Zǐtài, with a life that hangs by the thread of a day,
awaits a rescue that cannot be hoped for.
It is like a fish in a cow's hoofprint,
hoping to rely on the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
It is clear that it cannot be depended upon.
If Zǐtài could truly unite the hearts of his soldiers
and preserve the defense of an isolated city,
and still delay for a day or two
to await his intended surrender,
that would be acceptable.
Now, I have calculated and deliberated,
and with this attack,
the city will surely be breached
in less than a day.
After the city falls,
what good will his death do,
and what a tragedy it would be
to have his hundred-year-old mother,
white-haired, put to execution!
I estimate that his family has not received outside news
and believes that reinforcements can be relied upon,
which is why he has reached this point.
You may go see him
and explain the advantages and disadvantages."
Xuánzhī met Pǔ,
fully conveying Méng's meaning.
Pǔ was frightened and listened to him.
Xuánzhī came out first to report to Méng,
saying Pǔ would arrive shortly after.
Méng had already instructed four generals,
each to select a hundred men.
When Pǔ exited,
they were to immediately enter and guard the city gates.
A moment later, Pǔ came out.
Méng welcomed him, held his hand,
and together they went down to the boat.
After speaking,
he took out the letter and showed it to him,
then clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
Pǔ saw the letter,
knew that Bèi was in Gōng'ān
and Yǔ was in Yìyáng,
and was ashamed and regretful enough to want to sink into the earth.
Méng left Sūn Jiǎo
to handle the remaining affairs.
On the same day, he led his army to Yìyáng.
Liú Bèi requested an alliance,
and Quán then returned Pǔ and others,
divided the Xiāng River,
and returned Línglíng to him.
Xúnyáng and Yángxīn were made Méng's fiefs.
When the army returned,
they then attacked Héféi.
When they withdrew their troops,
they were ambushed by Zhāng Liáo and others.
Méng and Líng Tǒng defended with their lives.
Later, Cáo Gōng again launched a large expedition to Rúxū.
Quán made Méng commander,
who occupied the previously established fortresses,
and placed ten thousand powerful crossbows on top of them
to resist Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng's vanguard had not yet finished establishing its encampment
when Méng attacked and broke it.
Cáo Gōng withdrew.
Méng was appointed Left Protector of the Army and General of Tiger's Might.
Lú Sù died.
Lǚ Méng was stationed at Lùkǒu in the west.
Lú Sù's army, with over ten thousand men and horses, was entirely transferred to Lǚ Méng.
He was also appointed Grand Administrator of Hànchāng,
and granted a stipend from Xiàjùn, Liúyáng, Hànchāng, and Zhōulíng.
His territory bordered that of Guān Yǔ.
He knew that Guān Yǔ was valiant and formidable,
and harbored ambitions of annexation,
moreover, he occupied the upper reaches of the country,
a situation that could not last long.
Initially,
Lú Sù and others believed that Cáo Gōng was still alive,
and that troubles and difficulties were just beginning,
so it was advisable to assist each other,
and be enemies with him together,
this opportunity must not be lost.
Lǚ Méng then secretly presented a strategy, saying:
"[Now] if the General Who Attacks the Lóu is to guard Nánjùn,
Pān Zhāng is to reside at Báidì,
Jiǎng Qīn is to command ten thousand skirmishers,
moving up and down the Jiāng river,
responding to the enemy's location,
and I, Lǚ Méng, am to occupy Xiāngyáng for the state as a forward base,
if this is done,
what is there to worry about Cáo Cāo,
and what is there to rely on Guān Yǔ?
Moreover, Guān Yǔ and his lord,
pride themselves on their deceitful strength,
and are ever-changing in their alliances;
they cannot be treated as trusted allies.
The reason Guān Yǔ has not yet turned eastward
is because the Supreme One is sagacious and enlightened,
and I, Lǚ Méng, and others are still alive.
If we do not scheme against him while we are strong,
should we suddenly fall ill and die,
and then wish to exert ourselves again,
how could that be possible?"
Sūn Quán deeply adopted his strategy.
He then discussed with him his intention to take Xúzhōu.
Lǚ Méng replied:
"Currently, Cáo Cāo is far away in Héběi,
having recently defeated the Yuáns,
and is pacifying and gathering the people of Yōu and Jì,
he has no time to look eastward.
The garrison troops in Xúzhōu,
are said to be negligible;
it can certainly be conquered by going there.
However, the terrain is connected by land,
where swift cavalry can gallop freely.
If the Supreme One takes Xúzhōu today,
Cáo Cāo will certainly come to contest it within ten days.
Even if it is defended by seventy to eighty thousand men,
one would still harbor worries.
It is better to capture Guān Yǔ,
and fully control the Chángjiāng,
thereby further expanding our strategic advantage."
Sūn Quán particularly considered this statement to be correct.
When Lǚ Méng replaced Lú Sù,
upon his first arrival at Lùkǒu,
he externally redoubled his kindness and generosity,
and fostered good relations with Guān Yǔ.
Later, when Guān Yǔ attacked Fán,
he left troops and generals to guard Gōng'ān and Nánjùn.
Lǚ Méng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Guān Yǔ attacked Fán but left many reserve troops,
he must be fearing that I, Lǚ Méng, would scheme against his rear.
I, Lǚ Méng, have always been ill,
I beg to divide my officers and men and return to Jiànyè,
under the pretext of treating my illness.
When Guān Yǔ hears of this,
he will certainly withdraw his reserve troops,
and send them all to Xiāngyáng.
Then our main army can sail up the river,
marching day and night,
and launch a surprise attack on his empty territory,
thus Nánjùn can be taken,
and Guān Yǔ can be captured."
Thereupon, he feigned severe illness.
Sūn Quán then openly issued a summons for Lǚ Méng to return,
and secretly conspired with him.
Guān Yǔ indeed believed it,
and gradually withdrew his troops to reinforce Fán.
When Wèi dispatched Yú Jìn to relieve Fán,
Guān Yǔ captured Yú Jìn and others entirely,
tens of thousands of men and horses.
He claimed a shortage of provisions,
and unauthorizedly took rice from Xiāngguān.
When Sūn Quán heard of it,
he set out,
first sending Lǚ Méng ahead.
When Lǚ Méng reached Xúnyáng,
he concealed all his elite soldiers in the hold of the ships,
and made plain-clothed men row the boats, disguised as merchants.
They traveled day and night,
and upon reaching Guān Yǔ's riverside outposts,
they captured and bound them all.
Thus Guān Yǔ remained unaware.
They then arrived at Nánjùn,
and Shì Rén and Mí Fāng both surrendered.
Lǚ Méng entered and occupied the city,
and secured all of Guān Yǔ's and his officers' and soldiers' families.
He comforted them all,
and ordered that the army should not disturb any households,
or demand anything.
An officer under Lǚ Méng,
a man from Rǔnán,
took a bamboo hat from a civilian's house
to cover his official armor.
Although the official armor was public property,
Lǚ Méng still considered it a violation of military discipline.
He believed that he could not disregard the law for the sake of a compatriot,
and so, shedding tears, he executed him.
Thereupon, the army was awestruck and terrified,
and nothing was picked up from the roads.
Lǚ Méng daily sent his close attendants to visit and comfort the elders,
asking what they lacked,
providing medicine to the sick,
and clothing and food to the hungry and cold.
Guān Yǔ's treasury and valuables
were all sealed to await Sūn Quán's arrival.
When Guān Yǔ returned,
while on the road,
he repeatedly sent people to communicate with Lǚ Méng.
Lǚ Méng always treated his envoys generously,
allowing them to tour the city,
and inquire about every household,
or personally writing letters to show them proof.
When Guān Yǔ's men returned,
they secretly consulted each other,
and all knew that their families were safe,
and were treated better than usual.
Therefore, Guān Yǔ's officers and soldiers had no will to fight.
Soon after, Sūn Quán arrived.
Guān Yǔ, realizing he was isolated and helpless,
fled to Màichéng.
When he reached Zhāngxiāng in the west,
all his troops abandoned him and surrendered.
Sūn Quán sent Zhū Rán and Pān Zhāng to block his escape route,
and thus both father and son were captured.
Jīngzhōu was then pacified.
Lǚ Méng was appointed Grand Administrator of Nánjùn,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Cánlíng,
and granted one hundred million coins,
and five hundred catties of gold.
Lǚ Méng firmly declined the money and gold,
but Sūn Quán did not permit it.
Before the enfeoffment and titles were bestowed,
Lǚ Méng's illness recurred.
Sūn Quán, who was then in Gōng'ān,
welcomed him and placed him in the inner palace.
He employed every possible means to treat and care for him,
and offered a reward of a thousand pieces of gold to anyone within his domain who could cure Lǚ Méng's illness.
At one point, there was an acupuncture treatment,
Sūn Quán was distressed by it.
He wanted to see his face frequently,
but also feared disturbing him,
so he often peered through a hole in the wall.
When he saw that he could eat a little, he was delighted,
and turned to his attendants, smiling.
Otherwise, he would sigh in exasperation
and could not sleep at night.
When his illness showed improvement,
he issued an amnesty,
and all the officials offered congratulations.
Later, his condition worsened again.
Sūn Quán personally visited him,
and ordered Daoist priests to pray for his life under the stars.
At the age of forty-two,
he eventually died in the inner palace.
At that time, Sūn Quán grieved immensely,
and reduced his daily meals for him.
Before Lǚ Méng died,
he handed over all the gold, jewels, and other gifts he had received to the treasury,
and instructed the chief custodian that upon his death, they should all be returned to the state,
and that his funeral affairs should be kept simple.
When Sūn Quán heard of this,
he was even more saddened and moved.
Lǚ Méng was not diligent in studying texts and histories in his youth.
Whenever he presented important matters,
he would often dictate his memorials and reports orally.
Once, his subordinate affairs were reported to Sūn Quán by Cài Yí, Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià.
Lǚ Méng harbored no resentment.
When Gù Shào, Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng, died,
Sūn Quán asked whom to appoint.
Lǚ Méng then recommended Cài Yí as a capable official.
Sūn Quán smiled and said:
"Do you wish to be like Qí Xī?"
Thereupon, he employed him.
Gān Níng was crude, violent, and fond of killing.
He often displeased Lǚ Méng,
and sometimes disobeyed Sūn Quán's orders.
When Sūn Quán was angry with him,
Lǚ Méng would always plead on his behalf:
"The world is not yet settled,
a fighting general like Gān Níng is hard to find,
it is advisable to tolerate him."
Sūn Quán then treated Gān Níng generously,
and ultimately made use of him.
Méng Bá (蒙霸) inherited the peerage.
He was granted three hundred households to guard the tombs
and fifty qǐng (頃) of land.
Bá (霸) died,
and his elder brother, Cóng (琮), inherited the marquisate.
Cóng (琮) died,
and his younger brother, Mù (睦), succeeded him.
Sūn Quán (孫權), discussing Zhōu Yú (周瑜), Lǔ Sù (魯肅), and Lǚ Méng (呂蒙) with Lù Xùn (陸遜), said:
"Gōngjǐn (公瑾) was heroic and fierce,
with courage and strategy surpassing others.
He defeated Mèngdé (孟德),
opened up Jīngzhōu (荊州),
and was difficult to succeed.
You are now succeeding him.
Gōngjǐn (公瑾) formerly urged Zǐjìng (子敬) to come east
and introduced him to me.
When I dined and conversed with him,
we immediately touched upon the grand strategy for an emperor's enterprise.
This was one moment of joy.
Later, Mèngdé (孟德), capitalizing on his acquisition of Liú Cóng (劉琮),
boastfully declared that he would lead several hundred thousand troops, both naval and land, to advance southward.
I gathered all my generals
to consult on what should be done.
No one offered a suitable response at first.
Even Zǐbù (子布) and Wénbiǎo (文表)
both said that an envoy should be sent with a letter to welcome him.
Zǐjìng (子敬) immediately argued that this was unacceptable
and advised me to quickly summon Gōngjǐn (公瑾),
entrust him with the forces,
and meet and attack the enemy.
This was my second moment of joy.
Moreover, his decisive strategies
far surpassed the ideas of Zhāng Yí (張儀) and Sū Qín (蘇秦).
Although he later advised me to lend Xúandé (玄德) land,
that was one of his shortcomings,
but it is not enough to diminish his two strengths.
The Duke of Zhōu (周公) did not demand perfection from one person,
so I overlook his shortcomings and value his strengths,
often comparing him to Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹).
As for Zǐmíng (子明), in his youth,
I thought he merely did not shrink from hardship or ease,
and was simply brave and resolute.
But as he grew older,
his learning expanded and improved,
and his strategies became extraordinarily brilliant.
He can be ranked next to Gōngjǐn (公瑾),
though his eloquence and inspiring discussions do not quite match his.
His plan to seize Guān Yǔ (關羽)
surpassed Zǐjìng's (子敬).
Zǐjìng (子敬) wrote to me, saying: 'When emperors rise,
they all have those they must eliminate;
Guān Yǔ (關羽) is not worth fearing.'
This was Zǐjìng (子敬) being unable to manage things internally,
but making grand statements outwardly.
I also forgave him
and did not harshly blame him.
However, his military operations,
the establishment of camps, were impeccable.
Orders were executed, prohibitions enforced.
His territories suffered no abandonment or neglect,
and nothing was lost on the roads.
His methods were also excellent."
The commentary says: Cáo Gōng (曹公), with the resources of the Han chancellor,
held the Son of Heaven and swept away the various warlords.
Having newly pacified Jīngchéng (荊城),
he wielded his might over the eastern summer (of China).
At that time, none of the advisors failed to harbor doubts or waver.
Zhōu Yú (周瑜) and Lǔ Sù (魯肅) displayed independent and clear judgment,
standing out among the masses.
They were truly extraordinary talents.
Lǚ Méng (呂蒙) was courageous and had strategic decisiveness,
understanding military calculations.
His deception of Hǎo Pǔ (郝普)
and capture of Guān Yǔ (關羽)
were his most brilliant achievements.
Although he was initially reckless and prone to unwarranted killing,
he ultimately mastered himself
and possessed the magnanimity of a national hero.
How could he merely be a military general?
Sūn Quán's (孫權) assessment
of their merits and demerits was fair and accurate;
hence, it is recorded here.
Biographies of Chéng (程), Huáng (黃), Hán (韓), Jiǎng (蔣), Zhōu (周), Chén (陳), Dǒng (董), Gān (甘), Líng (淩), Xú (徐), Pān (潘), Dīng (丁) — Chapter Ten.
Chéng Pǔ (程普), courtesy name Démóu (德謀),
was from Túyín (土垠), Yòuběipíng (右北平).
He first served as a prefectural and commandery official.
He had a handsome appearance and strategic acumen,
and was skilled in conversation.
He followed Sūn Jiān (孫堅) on campaigns,
suppressing the Yellow Turbans at Wǎn (宛) and Dèng (鄧),
defeating Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) at Yángrén (陽人).
In siege warfare and field battles,
he suffered wounds.
After Jiān (堅) died,
he again followed Sūn Cè (孫策) in Huáinán (淮南).
He participated in the attack on Lújiāng (廬江),
capturing it,
then crossed east together.
When Cè (策) reached Héngjiāng (橫江) and Dānglì (當利),
he defeated Zhāng Yīng (張英), Yú Mí (于麋), and others.
He then took Mòlíng (秣陵), Húshú (湖孰), Jùróng (句容), and Qǔ'ā (曲阿).
Pǔ (普) contributed to all these victories,
and his forces were increased by two thousand men
and fifty cavalry.
He advanced to defeat Wūchéng (烏程), Shímù (石木), Bōmén (波門), Língchuán (陵傳), and Yúkàng (餘亢).
Pǔ's (普) contributions were numerous.
When Cè (策) entered Kuàijī (會稽),
he appointed Pǔ (普) as Commandant of Wújùn (吳郡),
governing Qiántáng (錢唐).
Later, he was transferred to Commandant of Dānyáng (丹楊),
residing in Shíchéng (石城).
He again suppressed the bandits of Xuānchéng (宣城), Jīng (涇), Ānwú (安吳), Língyáng (陵陽), and Chūngǔ (春穀),
defeating them all.
Cè (策) once attacked Zǔ Láng (祖郎)
and was greatly surrounded.
Pǔ (普) and a single cavalryman shielded Cè (策),
spurring their horses and shouting loudly,
using their spears to charge the bandits.
The bandits dispersed,
and Cè (策) was able to escape.
Later, he was appointed Zhonglángjiāng of Dàngkòu (盪寇中郎將)
and concurrently Administrator of Línglíng (零陵).
He followed in the campaign against Liú Xún (劉勳) at Xúnyáng (尋陽)
and advanced to attack Huáng Zǔ (黃祖) at Shāxiàn (沙羨).
He then returned to garrison Shíchéng (石城).
After Cè (策) died,
he, along with Zhāng Zhāo (張昭) and others, jointly assisted Sūn Quán (孫權),
touring the three commanderies
and pacifying those who rebelled.
He also followed in the campaign against Jiāngxià (江夏),
and on the return, passed through Yùzhāng (豫章),
separately attacking Lè'ān (樂安).
After Lè'ān (樂安) was pacified,
he replaced Tàishǐ Cí (太史慈) in guarding Hǎihūn (海昬).
He and Zhōu Yú (周瑜) served as left and right commanders,
defeating Cáo Gōng (曹公) at Wūlín (烏林).
They further attacked Nánjùn (南郡),
driving away Cáo Rén (曹仁).
He was appointed General of the Auxiliary (裨將軍)
and concurrently Administrator of Jiāngxià (江夏),
governing Shāxiàn (沙羨),
and receiving revenue from four counties.
Among the generals who started out earlier,
Pǔ (普) was the eldest,
and people at the time all called him Chéng Gōng (程公).
He was generous
and fond of literati.
After Zhōu Yú (周瑜) died,
he succeeded him as Administrator of Nánjùn (南郡).
When Quán (權) divided Jīngzhōu (荊州) with Liú Bèi (劉備),
Pǔ (普) returned to administer Jiāngxià (江夏).
He was promoted to General Dàngkòu (盪寇將軍)
and then died.
When Quán (權) assumed the imperial title,
he posthumously acknowledged Pǔ's (普) merits
and enfeoffed his son, Zī (咨), as a Tínghóu (亭侯).
Huáng Gài (黃蓋), courtesy name Gōngfù (公覆),
was from Quánlíng (泉陵), Línglíng (零陵).
He initially served as a commandery official,
was recommended as xiàolián (孝廉),
and was appointed to the ducal household.
When Sūn Jiān (孫堅) raised an army of righteousness,
Gài (蓋) joined him.
Jiān (堅) defeated mountain bandits in the south
and drove away Dǒng Zhuó (董卓 in the north.
Gài (蓋) was appointed Biebù Sīmǎ (別部司馬).
After Jiān (堅) died,
Gài (蓋) followed Cè (策) and Quán (權),
donning armor and fighting,
facing blades and storming cities.
When the various Shānyuè were disobedient,
for counties afflicted by banditry and difficulties,
Gài was always appointed as their prefect or chief.
The officials of Shíchéng County
were particularly difficult to control and manage.
Gài therefore appointed two staff officers (yuàn),
who were to separately oversee the various departments.
He instructed them, saying:
"Your prefect (lìng) is without virtue,
and has become an official solely by military achievement,
not known as a civil official.
Now, with the bandits not yet pacified,
there are military duties to attend to.
All matters of documentation are entrusted to you two staff officers.
You are to inspect and oversee the various departments,
and correct any errors or faults.
For all matters handled by the two staff officers,
things entered shall be approved.
If there is any treachery or deceit,
I will certainly not punish you with whips or rods.
You should each exert your utmost effort,
and not be the first to follow the crowd."
Initially, all established their authority,
working diligently day and night.
After a long time,
the officials, seeing that Gài did not inspect documents,
gradually indulged in personal matters.
Gài also suspected laxity externally,
and occasionally reviewed matters.
He found several instances where the two staff officers had not observed the law.
Thereupon, he summoned all the staff officers,
offered them wine and food,
and then brought out the matters to question them.
The two staff officers, finding their excuses exhausted,
all kowtowed and begged for forgiveness.
Gài said:
"I had previously commanded you
that I would certainly not punish you with whips or rods.
I was not deceiving you."
Then he killed them.
The county was struck with terror.
Later, he was transferred to be the chief of Chūn Gǔ,
and then the magistrate of Xúnyáng.
He governed a total of nine counties,
and wherever he went, peace was established.
He was promoted to Dānyáng Dūwèi,
suppressing the powerful and supporting the weak.
The Shānyuè became submissive and attached to him.
Gài's appearance was stern and resolute;
he was skilled at cultivating his troops.
Whenever he launched campaigns,
his soldiers would all vie to be the first.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
he followed Zhōu Yú to resist Cáo Gōng at Chìbì,
proposing the fire attack strategy.
The account is in the biography of Yú.
He was appointed Wǔfēng Zhōnglángjiàng.
When the Mányí of Wǔlíng rebelled,
attacking and besieging cities and towns,
Gài was appointed to lead as the Grand Administrator.
At that time, the county forces numbered only five hundred men.
Feeling that he was outnumbered,
he therefore opened the city gates.
When half of the bandits had entered,
he then attacked them,
beheading several hundred,
while the rest fled,
all returning to their settlements.
He executed the ringleaders,
and pardoned those who had merely followed.
From spring to summer,
the banditry and rebellion were completely quelled.
The various obscure Bā, Lǐ, Yóu, and Dàn tribal chiefs and lords
all changed their ways and reformed their conduct,
offering tribute and requesting an audience.
The county territory was thus pacified.
Later, Yìyáng County in Chángshā was attacked by mountain bandits,
and Gài again pacified them.
He was promoted to Piān Jiāngjūn
and died of illness in office.
Gài was decisive in his official duties,
with no matters left pending.
The people of the state missed him.
When Quán ascended the throne,
he posthumously recognized his merits
and bestowed upon his son, Bǐng, the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
Hán Dāng, courtesy name Yìgōng,
was a native of Lìngzhī, Liáoxī.
(Lìng is pronounced like Láng Dìng反.
Zhī is pronounced like Jù Ér 反.)
Being adept at archery and horsemanship,
and possessing great physical strength,
he was favored by Sūn Jiān.
He accompanied him on campaigns and served with him,
repeatedly facing dangers,
entering enemy lines and capturing prisoners.
He became a Biébù Sīmǎ.
When Sūn Cè crossed eastward,
he followed in attacking the three commanderies,
and was promoted to Xiāndēng Xiàowèi,
given two thousand soldiers
and fifty cavalry horses.
He followed in campaigning against Liú Xún,
defeated Huáng Zǔ,
returned to campaign against Póyáng,
and became the chief of Lè'ān.
The Shānyuè feared and submitted to him.
Later, as Zhōnglángjiàng, he, along with Zhōu Yú and others, resisted and defeated Cáo Gōng.
He also, with Lǚ Méng, attacked and seized Nánjùn,
and was promoted to Piān Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently held the position of Yǒngchāng Tàishǒu.
In the battle of Yídū,
he, along with Lù Xùn, Zhū Rán, and others, jointly attacked the Shǔ army at Zhuóxiāng,
inflicting a great defeat upon them.
He was transferred to Wēiliè Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Dūtíng Hóu.
When Cáo Zhēn attacked Nánjùn,
Dāng defended the southeast.
As commander in the field,
he encouraged his officers and soldiers to unite their hearts and firmly defend.
He also respectfully looked up to the commander-in-chief,
observing decrees and regulations.
Quán praised him.
In the second year of Huángwǔ (223 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Shíchéng Hóu,
promoted to Zhāowǔ Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently held the position of Guānjùn Tàishǒu.
Later, he was also given the title of Dūdū.
He led ten thousand Dǎn Sǐ (dare-to-die) and Jiě Fán (trouble-solving) soldiers
to campaign against the Dānyáng bandits
and defeated them.
He subsequently fell ill and died.
His son, Zōng, inherited the marquisate and command of the troops.
That same year,
when Quán campaigned against Shíyáng,
considering Zōng's grief,
he sent him to guard Wǔchāng.
However, Zōng was dissolute and unruly.
Although Quán did not question him for his father's sake,
Zōng felt internal fear.
He carried his father's coffin,
and with his mother's family, household members, and several thousand troops, fled to Wèi.
Wèi appointed him as a general
and enfeoffed him as Guǎngyáng Hóu.
He repeatedly violated the border
and killed people,
which Quán always gnashed his teeth over.
In the battle of Dōngxīng,
Zōng was the vanguard.
His army was defeated, and he died.
Zhūgě Kè cut off and sent his head,
which was presented to Quán's ancestral temple.
Jiǎng Qīn, courtesy name Gōngyì,
was a native of Shòuchūn, Jiǔjiāng.
When Sūn Cè attacked Yuán Shù,
Qīn followed and served him.
When Cè crossed eastward,
he was appointed Biébù Sīmǎ
and given troops.
He served with Cè throughout his campaigns,
pacifying the three commanderies,
and also followed in pacifying Yùzhāng.
He was then transferred and appointed as Gáyáng Wèi,
and successively served as chief of three counties,
campaigning against and pacifying bandits.
He was promoted to Xībù Dūwèi.
When the bandits Lǚ Hé and Qín Láng and others from Huìjī Yě rebelled,
Qīn led troops to attack them
and successfully captured Hé and Láng.
The five counties were pacified.
He was transferred to Táoyuè Zhōnglángjiàng,
with Jīngjū and Zhāoyáng as his enfeoffed territories.
When Hè Qí campaigned against the Yī bandits,
Qīn commanded ten thousand soldiers
and joined forces with Qí.
The Yī bandits were pacified.
He followed in campaigning against Héféi.
When Wèi general Zhāng Liáo attacked Quán north of Jīn,
Qīn fought bravely and rendered meritorious service.
He was promoted to Dàngkòu Jiāngjūn
and concurrently held the position of Rúxū Dūdū.
Later, he was recalled to the capital
and appointed Yòu Hùjūn,
managing legal disputes.
Quán once entered his inner hall
and saw his mother's simple mosquito net and plain quilt,
and his wife and concubines wearing plain cloth skirts.
Quán sighed at his frugality despite his high position,
and immediately ordered the imperial wardrobe to make a brocade quilt for his mother,
change the bed curtains,
and make all his wife and concubines' clothes of brocade and embroidery.
Initially,
Qīn was stationed at Xuānchéng,
and once attacked the bandits in Yùzhāng.
The magistrate of Wúhú, Xú Shèng, arrested Qīn's garrison officers,
and memorialized to have them executed.
But Sūn Quán, considering that Qīn was far away, did not permit it.
Shèng therefore became uneasy about Qīn.
When Cáo Gōng advanced to Rúxū,
Qīn and Lǚ Méng held the authority to direct the various armies.
Shèng always feared that Qīn would use an incident to harm him,
but Qīn always praised his good qualities.
After Shèng was convinced by his virtue,
commentators praised this.
When Sūn Quán attacked Guān Yǔ,
Qīn led the naval forces into Miǎn,
but on his return,
he fell ill and died on the way.
Sūn Quán wore plain clothes and expressed deep mourning.
He granted Qīn's wife and children
two hundred households from Wúhú and two hundred *qǐng* of land.
His son Yī was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xuānchéng.
He led troops to resist Liú Bèi with distinction,
and upon returning to Nánjùn,
he engaged in battle with Wèi
and died in the line of duty.
Yī had no son.
His younger brother Xiū led the troops,
but later committed a crime and lost his position.
Zhōu Tài, courtesy name Yòupíng,
was a native of Xiàcài in Jiǔjiāng.
He followed Sūn Cè with Jiǎng Qīn as his close attendants,
serving with reverence and respect,
and achieved merit in numerous battles.
When Sūn Cè entered Kuàijī,
he appointed him as Chief of a Separate Command,
and gave him troops.
Sūn Quán loved his character
and requested to keep him for his own use.
When Sūn Cè attacked the mountain bandits of Liù Xiàn,
Sūn Quán stayed in Xuānchéng.
He ordered his soldiers to guard themselves,
numbering fewer than a thousand.
His mindset was still careless,
and he did not establish defensive fortifications.
Suddenly, several thousand mountain bandits arrived.
Sūn Quán had just managed to mount his horse,
but the bandits' blades were already clashing around him,
some striking his saddle.
The multitude could not maintain their composure.
Only Zhōu Tài, in a frenzy of excitement,
threw himself forward to protect Sūn Quán,
his courage doubled that of others.
Because of Zhōu Tài, those around him were also able to engage in battle.
After the bandits dispersed,
he had suffered twelve wounds,
and only revived after a long time.
On that day, had it not been for Zhōu Tài,
Sūn Quán would have been in grave danger.
Sūn Cè deeply appreciated this,
and appointed him Magistrate of Chūngǔ.
Later, he followed in the attack on Wǎn,
and in the campaign against Jiāngxià.
On his return, passing through Yùzhāng,
he was again appointed Magistrate of Yíchūn.
Wherever he served, he collected the taxes and levies.
He achieved merit in the campaign against Huáng Zǔ.
Later, with Zhōu Yú and Chéng Pǔ, he resisted Cáo Gōng at Chìbì,
and attacked Cáo Rén at Nánjùn.
After Jīngzhōu was pacified,
he led troops to garrison Cén.
When Cáo Gōng advanced to Rúxū,
Zhōu Tài again went to engage him.
When Cáo Gōng retreated,
he was left to supervise Rúxū,
and was appointed General Who Pacifies the Barbarians.
At that time, Zhū Rán, Xú Shèng, and others were all under his command,
but none were submissive.
Sūn Quán specially visited the Rúxū Fort for an inspection,
and gathered all the generals,
holding a great feast.
Sūn Quán personally carried wine to Zhōu Tài,
and ordered Zhōu Tài to remove his clothes.
Sūn Quán personally pointed to his scars
and asked about their origins.
Zhōu Tài would then recount the place of each past battle in response.
When he finished,
Sūn Quán had him put his clothes back on,
and the joyful banquet continued late into the night.
The next day,
Sūn Quán sent an envoy to bestow upon him the imperial canopy.
Thus, Xú Shèng and the others became submissive.
Later, when Sūn Quán defeated Guān Yǔ,
desiring to advance and plan for Shu,
he appointed Zhōu Tài as Administrator of Hànzhōng and General Who Inspires Awe,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Língyáng.
He died during the Huángwǔ era.
His son Shào, as a Cavalry Commandant, led troops.
When Cáo Rén advanced to Rúxū,
he fought with distinction,
and also participated in the successful attack on Cáo Xiū.
He was promoted to Deputy General,
and died in the second year of Huánglóng.
His younger brother Chéng led the troops and inherited the marquisate.
Chén Wǔ, courtesy name Zǐliè,
was a native of Sōngzī in Lújiāng.
When Sūn Cè was in Shòuchūn,
Chén Wǔ went to pay his respects.
He was then eighteen years old,
and seven *chǐ* and seven *cùn* tall.
He followed Sūn Cè across the river,
and achieved merit in the campaigns,
being appointed Chief of a Separate Command.
When Sūn Cè defeated Liú Xún,
he captured many people from Lújiāng.
After selecting the elite among them,
he appointed Chén Wǔ as their commander,
and wherever he went, there was no resistance.
When Sūn Quán took control of affairs,
he was transferred to supervise the Five Corps.
He was benevolent and generous,
and many from his hometown and distant travelers sought his patronage.
He was especially cherished and loved by Sūn Quán,
who frequently visited his home.
Having accumulated meritorious service,
he was promoted to Lieutenant-General.
In the twentieth year of Jiàn'ān,
he followed in the attack on Héféi,
and died bravely in battle.
Sūn Quán mourned him
and personally attended his funeral.
His son Xiū inherited his martial spirit.
At nineteen years old,
Sūn Quán summoned and encouraged him,
appointing him Chief of a Separate Command,
and giving him five hundred soldiers.
At that time, many of the new recruits often deserted,
but Xiū managed them adeptly,
losing not a single man.
Sūn Quán admired this,
and appointed him Colonel.
At the end of Jiàn'ān,
when meritorious officials' descendants were recognized,
Xiū was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng,
and appointed Commander to Relieve Troubles.
He died in the first year of Huánglóng.
Dì Biǎo,
courtesy name Wén'ào,
was Sūn Wǔ's illegitimate son.
He was famous in his youth,
and served in the Eastern Palace alongside Zhūgě Kè, Gù Tán, Zhāng Xiū, and others.
They were all close friends.
The Grand Secretary Jì Yàn was also close to Biǎo.
Later, when Yàn incurred guilt,
people at the time all tried to protect themselves,
showing sincerity in their actions but being sparing in their words.
Biǎo alone was not like this,
and gentlemen respected him for it.
He was moved from Crown Prince's Household Administrator to
Commander of the Yi Zhèng.
After his elder brother Xiū died,
Biǎo's mother refused to serve Xiū's mother.
Biǎo said to his mother:
"My brother was unfortunate to die young.
I, Biǎo, now manage the household affairs,
and I ought to serve my legitimate mother.
If Mother can suppress her feelings for my sake,
and obey and serve my legitimate mother,
that would be my greatest wish.
If Mother cannot,
then she must simply move out to live separately."
Biǎo was this just in matters of great righteousness.
Because of this, the two mothers were moved to understanding and lived in harmony.
Biǎo, whose father died on the battlefield,
requested to be employed as a general,
leading five hundred men.
Biǎo wanted to gain the strength of his soldiers,
and wholeheartedly welcomed and treated them well.
All the soldiers loved and attached themselves to him,
and were happy to fight for him.
At that time, there was someone who stole official property,
and suspicion fell on the Wú Nán soldier Shī Míng.
Míng was known to be strong and fierce,
and during his interrogation and torture,
he only wished for death and offered no confession.
The Grand Judge reported this.
Sūn Quán, knowing Biǎo could win the hearts of brave men,
issued an edict to hand Míng over to Biǎo,
to let him ascertain the true situation by his own means.
Biǎo immediately removed Míng's shackles, bathed him,
changed his clothes,
generously provided wine and food,
and joyfully coaxed him.
Míng then confessed,
listing all his accomplices.
Biǎo reported the situation.
Sūn Quán was surprised by this,
and wishing to preserve Biǎo's reputation,
specially pardoned Míng
and executed his accomplices.
Biǎo was promoted to Commander of the Wú Nán Right Division,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Dū Tíng,
to inherit the old peerage.
Biǎo declined all of these,
begging for them to be passed to Xiū's son, Yán,
but Sūn Quán refused.
In the third year of Jiāhé,
Zhūgě Kè became the Administrator of Dānyáng,
suppressing and pacifying the Shānyuè.
He appointed Biǎo as Commander of Xīn'ān,
to assist Kè in his authority.
Initially,
Biǎo had been granted two hundred households of exempted people,
located in Xīn'ān County, Kuàijī.
Biǎo inspected these people,
and finding them all capable and good soldiers,
he submitted a memorial declining the grant,
asking to return them to the officials,
to replenish the elite forces.
An edict stated:
"The late general rendered services to the state;
the state repays him thus.
How can you decline?"
Biǎo then stated:
"Now, to eliminate national bandits
and avenge my father's death,
people are the foundation.
To idly waste these strong and elite men as servants
is not my aspiration."
He immediately selected and took them to augment his divisions.
His actions were reported,
and Sūn Quán greatly praised him.
He ordered the commanderies and counties
to select registered households of weak commoners to fill their places.
Biǎo served in office for three years,
widely inviting surrenders and accepting new recruits,
obtaining over ten thousand soldiers.
When his task was complete and he was about to depart,
it happened that the Pōyáng commoner Wú Jù and others caused unrest,
attacking and capturing cities,
and causing the dependent counties to waver.
Biǎo immediately crossed the border to suppress them.
Jù was defeated,
and subsequently surrendered.
Lù Xùn appointed Biǎo as General of the Vanguards,
further enfeoffing him as Marquis of Dū Xiāng,
and stationed him in Zhāngkēng in the north.
He died at the age of thirty-four.
His family wealth was entirely spent on supporting his soldiers,
and on the day of his death,
his wife and children were left without shelter.
Crown Prince Dēng built a house for them.
His son, Áo, at seventeen,
was appointed Commander of the Separate Division
and given four hundred soldiers.
After Áo died,
Xiū's son, Yán, again became Commander, replacing Áo.
Yán's younger brother, Yǒng,
was a general
and enfeoffed as a marquis.
From the beginning, Shī Míng, grateful to Biǎo,
changed his behavior for the better
and became a capable general,
achieving the rank of general.
Dǒng Xí, courtesy name Yuándài,
was a native of Yúyáo, Kuàijī.
He was eight *chǐ* tall
and possessed extraordinary martial strength.
When Sūn Cè entered the commandery,
Xí welcomed him at Gāoqīan Pavilion.
Cè saw him and was impressed,
appointing him as a thief-investigator in his secretariat.
At that time, the long-standing bandits of Shānyīn, Huáng Lóngluó and Zhōu Bó, gathered several thousand followers.
Sūn Cè personally went to suppress them.
Xí personally cut off the heads of Luó and Bó.
Upon his return, he was appointed Commander of the Separate Division,
given several thousand soldiers,
and promoted to Commander of the Yáng Wǔ.
He followed Cè to attack Wǎn,
then suppressed Liú Xún in Xúnyáng,
and attacked Huáng Zǔ in Jiāngxià.
After Cè died,
Sūn Quán was young
and had just begun to govern.
The Grand Concubine worried about this,
and summoned Zhāng Zhāo and Xí, among others,
asking if Jiāngdōng could be kept safe.
Xí replied:
"Jiāngdōng's terrain
has the fortifications of mountains and rivers,
and the late Governor Tǎonì (Sūn Cè)
bestowed grace and virtue upon the people.
Tǎolǔ (Sūn Quán) inherits the foundation,
and everyone, great and small, obeys his commands.
Zhāng Zhāo manages all civil affairs,
and Xí and others serve as his claws and teeth.
This is a time of favorable geography and harmonious people;
there is absolutely nothing to worry about."
Everyone praised his words.
