The Pōyáng bandits Péng Hǔ and others had tens of thousands of followers.
Xí, along with Líng Tǒng, Bù Zhì, and Jiǎng Qīn, each took a separate division to suppress them.
Wherever Xí went, he defeated them.
Hǔ and the others, seeing his banners,
immediately scattered and fled.
Within ten days, the rebellion was completely pacified.
He was appointed Commander of the Wēi Yuè,
and promoted to General of the Vanguards.
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
Sūn Quán attacked Huáng Zǔ.
Zǔ had two *méngchōng* vessels positioned across the Miǎnkēng,
using large ropes of palm fiber tied to stones as anchors.
A thousand men were on board,
firing crossbows in volleys,
with arrows raining down.
The army could not advance.
Xí and Líng Tǒng were both in the vanguard,
each leading a hundred death-defying men.
Each man wore two layers of armor
and boarded large *gě* boats,
crashing into the *méngchōng* vessels.
Xí personally used a knife to cut both ropes.
The *méngchōng* then drifted with the current,
and the main army was able to advance.
Zǔ then opened the gates and fled,
and the army pursued and beheaded him.
The next day, at a grand assembly,
Sūn Quán raised his cup and offered it to Xí, saying:
"Today's gathering
is due to the merit of cutting the ropes."
Cáo Gōng came out to Rúxū,
Xí followed Sūn Quán and went to meet him.
Sūn Quán ordered Xí to command five turret ships and station them at the mouth of Rúxū.
That night, a sudden storm struck,
and the five turret ships capsized.
The soldiers on both sides scattered into small boats,
begging Xí to let them go.
Xí angrily said:
"I have received the General's appointment
to guard against the enemy here.
How can I abandon my post and leave?
Anyone who dares to speak of this again will be beheaded!"
Thereupon, no one dared to argue.
That night, the ships were destroyed,
and Xí died.
Sūn Quán changed his clothes and attended the funeral,
providing very generous provisions.
Gān Níng, courtesy name Xīngbà,
was a native of Línjiāng, Bājùn.
In his youth, he was spirited and strong,
enjoyed chivalry,
and gathered frivolous young men,
becoming their leader.
They banded together,
carrying bows and crossbows,
wearing feathers and bells.
When people heard the sound of bells,
they immediately knew it was Gān Níng.
When people met him,
or when the chief officials of the subordinate counties
received them with great courtesy, they would socialize happily;
otherwise,
they would release those they led to seize their goods.
They would commit robberies and harm within the jurisdiction of the chief officials,
acting as their bane,
for more than twenty years.
He stopped raiding and plundering,
and read various philosophical works.
He then went to seek refuge with Liú Biǎo,
and consequently lived in Nányáng,
but was not promoted or utilized.
Later, he transferred his allegiance to Huáng Zǔ,
but Huáng Zǔ also treated him as an ordinary person.
Thereupon, he defected to Wú.
Zhōu Yú and Lǚ Méng both recommended him,
and Sūn Quán held him in special esteem,
treating him like an old minister.
Gān Níng presented his plan, saying:
"Now the Hàn dynasty's fortune is daily waning,
Cáo Cāo is increasingly arrogant,
and will eventually usurp the throne.
The land of southern Jīng Province,
with its advantageous mountains and hills,
and circulating rivers,
is truly the western stronghold of our state.
I have already observed Liú Biǎo;
his foresight is not far-reaching,
and his sons are also inferior,
unable to inherit his enterprise and foundation.
Your Highness should plan for it early,
and not let Cáo Cāo get ahead.
For the strategy of this plan,
it is advisable to first take Huáng Zǔ.
Huáng Zǔ is old this year,
very muddled and senile;
his finances and grain are depleted;
his subordinates deceive and manipulate him;
he is keen on profit,
extorting his officers and soldiers.
The officers and soldiers resent him,
and his ships and weaponry
are neglected and unrepaired.
He is lazy in farming,
and the army has no proper ranks.
If Your Highness goes now,
his defeat is assured.
Once Huáng Zǔ's army is defeated,
we can march westward with drums beating,
occupy Chǔ Pass in the west,
and greatly expand our influence.
Then we can gradually plan for Bā and Shǔ."
Sūn Quán deeply accepted his proposal.
Zhāng Zhāo was present at the time,
and countered, saying:
"The region of Wú is precarious;
if the army really goes,
I fear it will certainly lead to chaos."
Gān Níng said to Zhāng Zhāo:
"The state has entrusted you with the responsibility of Xiāo Hé.
You remain here to guard and yet fear chaos.
How can you aspire to emulate the ancients then?"
Sūn Quán raised his cup and toasted Gān Níng, saying:
"Xīngbà,
this year's campaign,
is like this wine,
I have entrusted it to you completely.
You must just strive to develop strategies,
and ensure the defeat of Huáng Zǔ.
Then that will be your achievement.
Why care about Zhāng Zhǎngshǐ's words?"
Sūn Quán then went west,
and indeed captured Huáng Zǔ,
seizing all his officers and troops.
He then gave Gān Níng troops,
who were stationed at Dāngkǒu.
Later, he followed Zhōu Yú to resist and defeat Cáo Gōng at Wūlín.
When attacking Cáo Rén at Nánjùn,
it was not yet taken.
Gān Níng proposed a plan to advance directly and seize Yílíng first.
He went and immediately secured the city,
then entered and garrisoned it.
At that time, he had several hundred soldiers under his command,
and with those newly gained,
they barely numbered a thousand.
Cáo Rén then ordered five or six thousand men to besiege Gān Níng.
Gān Níng endured the attack for several days.
The enemy set up high towers,
raining arrows into the city.
All the officers and soldiers were afraid,
only Gān Níng talked and laughed as usual.
He sent an envoy to report to Zhōu Yú.
Zhōu Yú adopted Lǚ Méng's plan
and led the generals to relieve the siege.
Later, he followed Lǔ Sù to garrison Yìyáng
and resist Guān Yǔ.
Guān Yǔ claimed to have thirty thousand men,
and personally selected five thousand elite soldiers,
to a shallow ford more than ten *li* upstream from the county,
saying he intended to cross by night.
Lǔ Sù discussed this with the generals.
Gān Níng, who had three hundred soldiers at the time,
said:
"You can add five hundred more men to mine,
and I will go confront him.
I guarantee that upon hearing my cough or spit,
Guān Yǔ will not dare to cross the water;
if he crosses, he will be my captive."
Lǔ Sù immediately selected a thousand soldiers and added them to Gān Níng's command.
Gān Níng then went at night.
When Guān Yǔ heard of it,
he stopped and did not cross,
but built a camp with firewood.
This place is now named Guān Yǔ Lài.
Sūn Quán commended Gān Níng's achievement,
and appointed him Administrator of Xīlíng,
governing the two counties of Yángxīn and Xiàzhì.
Later, he followed in the attack on Wǎn,
serving as the supervisor for ascending the city walls.
Gān Níng personally held a rope,
climbed the wall,
leading the officers and soldiers,
and finally broke through and captured Zhū Guāng.
When merits were tallied,
Lǚ Méng was the greatest.
Gān Níng was second,
and was appointed General Who Smashes the Enemy.
Later, Cáo Gōng came out to Rúxū.
Gān Níng served as the vanguard commander,
receiving orders to go out and attack the enemy's forward camp.
Sūn Quán specially bestowed rice wine and various dishes.
Gān Níng then allocated the food and drink to over a hundred men under his command.
After eating,
Gān Níng first poured wine in a silver bowl,
drank two bowls himself,
then poured for his commanders.
The commander bowed down,
unwilling to take it at that moment.
Gān Níng pulled out a sharp sword and placed it on his knee,
scolding him, saying:
"You are recognized by His Highness.
Compared to Gān Níng,
Gān Níng still does not fear death,
why do you alone fear death?"
Seeing Gān Níng's stern expression,
the commander immediately stood up, bowed, took the wine,
and then poured a silver bowl for each soldier.
By the second watch,
they went out silently to attack the enemy.
The enemy was startled and moved,
then retreated.
Gān Níng became even more esteemed,
and his troops were increased by two thousand.
Though Gān Níng was rough, fierce, and fond of killing,
he was frank, sagacious, and strategic.
He thought little of wealth and respected scholars,
and was able to generously provide for his brave soldiers.
His brave soldiers were also happy to fight for him.
In the twentieth year of Jiàn'ān (215 CE),
he followed in the attack on Héféi.
An epidemic broke out,
and the army had already retreated.
Only a thousand or so "tiger warriors" from under Sūn Quán's chariot,
along with Lǚ Méng, Jiǎng Qīn, Líng Tǒng, and Gān Níng,
followed Sūn Quán at the north of Xiāoyáo Jīn.
Zhāng Liáo observed and knew this,
and immediately led his cavalry and infantry to surprise them.
Gān Níng drew his bow and shot at the enemy,
fighting to the death with Líng Tǒng and the others.
Gān Níng sternly asked why the drums and pipes were not playing.
His spirit was resolute and courageous,
and Sūn Quán especially praised him for it.
A kitchen boy of Gān Níng once committed a fault
and fled to Lǚ Méng.
Lǚ Méng feared Gān Níng would kill him,
so he did not immediately return him.
Later, Gān Níng brought gifts to Lǚ Méng's mother.
As they were about to ascend the hall together,
Lǚ Méng brought out the kitchen boy and returned him to Gān Níng.
Gān Níng promised Lǚ Méng he would not kill him.
Soon after returning to his boat,
he tied the boy to a mulberry tree
and personally drew his bow to shoot him dead.
After this,
he ordered his boatmen to add more ropes to the boat,
then took off his clothes and lay down in the boat.
Lǚ Méng was furious,
beat the drums to gather his troops,
and intended to attack Gān Níng's boat.
Gān Níng heard of this,
but purposefully lay still.
Lǚ Méng's mother came out barefoot to admonish Lǚ Méng, saying:
"The Supreme Lord treats you like his own flesh and blood,
and entrusts you with great affairs.
How can you, out of personal anger, wish to attack and kill Gān Níng?
On the day Gān Níng dies,
even if the Supreme Lord does not inquire,
you, as a subordinate, would be acting unlawfully."
Lǚ Méng was known for his extreme filial piety.
Upon hearing his mother's words,
his anger immediately dissipated.
He went to Gān Níng's boat
and called out with a smile:
"Xīngbà,
my old mother is waiting for you to eat;
hurry up!"
Gān Níng wept and sighed, saying:
"I have wronged you."
He returned with Lǚ Méng to see his mother,
and they joyfully feasted all day.
When Gān Níng died,
Sūn Quán grieved deeply for him.
His son, Guī,
was exiled to Kuàijī for a crime,
and died not long after.
Líng Tǒng, courtesy name Gōngjì,
was from Yúháng, Wú Jùn.
His father, Cāo,
was a chivalrous and courageous man.
When Sūn Cè first rose,
Cāo always joined his campaigns,
and often took the lead and faced the sharp edge of battle.
He served as the Chief of Yǒngpíng,
pacified the Shānyuè,
and made the cunning and treacherous restrain themselves.
He was promoted to Commandant of Breaking Raiders.
When Sūn Quán commanded the army,
Cāo followed him to attack Jiāngxià.
Entering Xiàkǒu,
he was the first to scale the walls,
breaking their vanguard.
Advancing alone in a light boat,
he was struck by a stray arrow in mid-river and died.
Líng Tǒng was fifteen years old.
Many around spoke highly of him,
and Sūn Quán, also considering that Cāo died for the state,
appointed Líng Tǒng as a Major of a Separate Command,
acting as Commandant of Breaking Raiders,
and had him take charge of his father's troops.
Later, he followed in an attack on mountain bandits.
Sūn Quán broke a fortified camp and returned first,
leaving behind ten thousand men at the Má Tún camp.
Líng Tǒng and commander Zhāng Yì and others remained to besiege it,
setting a date for the assault.
Before the appointed date,
Líng Tǒng drank with commander Chén Qín.
Chén Qín was fierce, brave, and arrogant,
and as the ritual libator,
he bullied everyone present,
meting out punishments unfairly.
Líng Tǒng resented his insolence
and directly rebuked him, refusing to yield.
Chén Qín grew angry and cursed Líng Tǒng
and his father, Cāo.
Líng Tǒng wept but did not respond,
and the group then dispersed.
Chén Qín, intoxicated and violent,
further insulted Líng Tǒng on the road.
Líng Tǒng could not bear it,
drew his knife and struck Chén Qín,
who died several days later.
When the time came to attack the camp,
Líng Tǒng said:
"Only by dying can I atone for my crime."
He then led and encouraged his soldiers,
personally facing arrows and stones.
The side he attacked
was immediately breached and broken.
The various generals pressed their advantage,
and they utterly defeated the bandits.
Upon returning,
he bound himself and submitted to the military judge.
Sūn Quán admired his resolute bravery,
and allowed him to atone for his crime through his achievements.
Later, Sūn Quán again campaigned against Jiāngxià.
Líng Tǒng served as the vanguard,
sharing a single boat with several tens of his close brave soldiers,
always dozens of *lǐ* ahead of the main army.
He entered the Right Jiāng,
beheaded Huáng Zǔ's general Zhāng Shuò,
and captured all the boatmen.
He returned and reported this to Sūn Quán,
who then led his army, marching day and night,
gathering both land and naval forces.
At that time, Lǚ Méng defeated their naval forces,
while Líng Tǒng was the first to attack their city,
and thus a great victory was achieved.
Sūn Quán appointed Líng Tǒng as Commandant of Enduring Might,
and he, with Zhōu Yú and others, resisted and defeated Cáo Gōng at Wūlín,
then attacked Cáo Rén,
and was promoted to Commandant.
Even while on campaign,
he was close to worthy individuals and welcomed scholars,
thinking little of wealth and valuing righteousness,
possessing the demeanor of a national hero.
He also followed in the defeat of Wǎn,
and was appointed General of the Household who Suppresses Raiders,
and concurrently Administrator of Pèi.
He, with Lǚ Méng and others, took three commanderies in the west,
and returned from Yìyáng.
He followed to Héféi
as Commander of the Right Division.
At that time, Sūn Quán withdrew his army.
The vanguard had already departed,
when the Wei generals Zhāng Liáo and others suddenly arrived at the north of the ford.
Sūn Quán sent men to recall the vanguard troops,
but the troops had gone too far,
and it was impossible to catch up.
Líng Tǒng led three hundred close followers into the encirclement,
protecting and helping Sūn Quán escape.
The enemy had already destroyed the bridge;
of the bridge's components, only two planks remained.
Sūn Quán spurred his horse and galloped across.
Líng Tǒng returned to fight again.
All his attendants died,
and he himself was wounded.
He killed several tens of men.
Estimating that Sūn Quán had escaped,
he then returned.
With the bridge broken and the road cut off,
Líng Tǒng, still in armor, secretly made his way.
When Sūn Quán was already on his boat,
he saw Líng Tǒng and was surprised and delighted.
Líng Tǒng grieved that none of his close followers had returned,
and could not contain his sorrow.
Sūn Quán pulled his sleeve to wipe Líng Tǒng's tears,
and said:
"Gōngjì,
those who are gone are gone.
As long as you are here,
why worry about having no men?"
He was appointed General of the Household,
and his original troops were doubled.
At that time, someone recommended Shèng Xiān from the same commandery to Sūn Quán,
believing him to be a person of great integrity and character,
surpassing Líng Tǒng.
Sūn Quán said:
"It is enough if he is merely like Líng Tǒng."
Later, Sūn Quán summoned Shèng Xiān to arrive at night.
At that time, Líng Tǒng had already gone to bed.
Hearing of it,
he adjusted his clothes and went out the door,
took Shèng Xiān's hand, and brought him in.
His love for good people and lack of malice was like this.
Tǒng believed that there were still many strong and fierce people in the mountains,
who could be enticed with a mix of awe and kindness.
Quán ordered Dōng Zhān to both pacify and attack them.
He commanded the subordinate cities
that whatever Tǒng requested,
should be granted first and reported later.
Tǒng had always loved his soldiers,
and the soldiers also admired him.
He obtained over ten thousand elite soldiers.
When passing through his home county,
he walked into the temple gate,
saw the chief official holding three tablets,
and showed him full respect and courtesy.
To his relatives, old friends,
his kindness and affection increased.
When his affairs were concluded and he was about to depart,
he unfortunately died of illness,
at the age of forty-nine.
When Quán heard of it,
he beat the bed and sat up,
unable to control his sorrow.
For several days, he reduced his meals,
and tears flowed whenever he spoke of him.
He ordered Zhāng Chéng to compose an elegy for him.
His two sons, Liè and Fēng,
were each several years old.
Quán raised them within his palace,
treating them with the same affection as his own sons.
When guests came to see him,
he would call them over and show them, saying:
"These are my tiger cubs!"
When they were eight or nine years old,
he ordered Gé Guāng to teach them to read.
Every ten days, he would allow them to ride horses.
Recalling Tǒng's achievements,
he enfeoffed Liè as a Tínghóu,
and returned his former troops to him.
Later, Liè committed a crime and was dismissed,
and Fēng then inherited his title and led the troops.
Xú Shèng, courtesy name Wénxiàng,
was a native of Jǔ in Lángxié.
Caught in the chaos of war,
he resided as a sojourner in Wú.
He was known for his courage.
When Sūn Quán took control of affairs,
he appointed him Bìebù Sīmǎ,
granted him five hundred soldiers,
and made him the chief of Cháishāng,
to resist Huáng Zǔ.
Zǔ's son, Shè,
once led several thousand men to attack Shèng.
At that time, Shèng's officers and men numbered less than two hundred,
but he resisted and counterattacked them,
wounding and killing over a thousand of Shè's officers and men.
He then opened the gates and sallied forth,
thoroughly defeating them.
Shè thereafter ceased his incursions and no longer became a bandit.
Quán appointed him Xiàowèi and magistrate of Wúhú.
He again performed meritoriously in suppressing the mountain bandits of Nán'ā in Línchéng,
and was promoted to Zhōnglángjiāng,
overseeing the training of soldiers.
When Cáo Gōng advanced to Rúxū,
he followed Quán to defend against him.
The Wèi once launched a large attack across Héngjiāng.
Shèng and the other generals all went to repel them.
At that time, while aboard a méngchōng,
they encountered a swift wind,
and their boats drifted to the enemy shore.
The generals were all terrified,
and none dared to sally forth.
Shèng alone led his troops,
charged up and hacked at the enemy.
The enemy scattered and fled,
suffering some casualties.
When the wind subsided, he returned.
Quán greatly admired his bravery.
When Quán submitted as a vassal to Wèi,
Wèi dispatched Xíng Zhēn to enfeoff Quán as King of Wú.
Quán went to Dūtíng to await Zhēn.
Zhēn displayed an arrogant demeanor.
Zhāng Zhāo was already angered,
and Shèng was filled with indignation.
He turned to his colleagues and said:
"We, Shèng and others, are unable to exert ourselves and risk our lives
to unite Xǔluò for the state
and swallow Bāshǔ,
yet we allow our lord to ally with Zhēn.
Is this not a disgrace!"
Thereupon, tears streamed down his face.
When Zhēn heard this,
he said to his entourage:
"If the generals and ministers of Jiāngdōng are like this,
they will not remain subservient to others for long."
Later, he was promoted to Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed as Dūtínghóu,
appointed administrator of Lújiāng Prefecture,
and granted Línchéng County as his fief.
When Liú Bèi was encamped at Xīlíng,
Shèng attacked and captured various fortifications,
achieving success wherever he went.
When Cáo Xiū advanced to Dòngkǒu,
Shèng, together with Lǚ Fàn and Quán Cóng, crossed the river to resist him.
They encountered a great storm,
and many men and boats were lost.
Shèng gathered his remaining troops
and faced Xiū across the river.
Xiū sent his soldiers to attack Shèng's boats.
Shèng, with few men, resisted many.
The enemy could not overcome him.
Both sides then withdrew their armies.
He was promoted to Āndōng Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Wúhú Hóu.
Later, when Emperor Wén of Wèi launched a major expedition
with the intention of crossing the Jiāng,
Shèng proposed a plan to build an encircling fortification from Jiànyè,
constructing thin palisades,
setting up fake towers on the fortifications,
and floating boats in the river.
The other generals considered it useless,
but Shèng did not listen
and insisted on building it.
When Emperor Wén arrived at Guǎnglíng,
he was astonished at the sight of the fortifications,
which stretched for hundreds of *lǐ*.
As the Jiāng River was also in full flood,
he consequently withdrew his army.
Only then did the other generals submit.
He died during the Huángwǔ reign.
His son, Kǎi,
inherited his title and led his troops.
Pān Zhāng, courtesy name Wénguī,
was a native of Fāgān in Dōngjùn.
When Sūn Quán was magistrate of Yángxiàn,
he first went to follow Quán.
He was dissolute and fond of wine.
Although poor,
he liked to buy on credit.
When creditors came to his door,
he would always say that he would repay them when he became wealthy.
Quán considered him extraordinary and cherished him.
He then ordered him to recruit soldiers,
and he obtained over a hundred men,
whereupon he was made a general.
He achieved meritorious service in suppressing mountain bandits,
and was appointed Bìebù Sīmǎ.
Later, he served as a market censor in Wú,
and theft and banditry ceased.
From this, he became well-known,
and was promoted to magistrate of Xī'ān in Yùzhāng.
When Liú Biǎo was in Jīngzhōu,
the people were often harassed by bandits.
But from the time Zhāng took office,
bandits did not enter his territory.
When the neighboring county of Jiànchāng fell into banditry and rebellion,
he was transferred to lead Jiànchāng,
and given the additional title of Wǔměng Xiàowèi.
He suppressed and pacified the unruly people,
and within ten days, everything was settled.
He gathered the scattered remnants,
obtaining eight hundred men,
and led them back to Jiànyè.
In the battle of Héfèi,
Zhāng Liáo arrived suddenly.
The generals were unprepared.
Chén Wǔ died fighting.
Sòng Qiān and Xú Shèng both fled.
Zhāng, who was positioned behind them,
immediately galloped forward,
crossed his horse, and beheaded two of Qiān's and Shèng's fleeing soldiers.
The soldiers all returned to fight.
Quán greatly admired his bravery,
appointed him Piānjiāngjūn,
and thereupon commanded a hundred officers,
garrisoned at Bànzhōu.
When Quán campaigned against Guān Yǔ,
Zhāng and Zhū Rán cut off Yǔ's escape route.
Upon reaching Línjǔ,
they stopped at Jiáshí.
Zhāng's subordinate, the Sīmǎ Mǎ Zhōng, captured Yǔ,
along with Yǔ's son Píng and commander Zhào Lèi, etc.
Quán immediately divided the two counties of Yídū (to) Wū and Zǐguī to form Gùlíng Commandery,
appointed Zhāng as its administrator and Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed him as Lìyáng Hóu.
When Gān Níng died,
he also absorbed his army.
When Liú Bèi marched out to Yílíng,
Zhāng and Líng Xùn combined their forces to resist him.
Zhāng's subordinates beheaded Bèi's protector-general Féng Xí and others.
The number of those killed and wounded was very large.
He was appointed Píngběi Jiāngjūn and administrator of Xiāngyáng.
Wèi general Xiàhóu Shàng and others besieged Nánjùn.
They divided their vanguard of 30,000 men to build a pontoon bridge,
crossing to Bǎilǐ Zhōu.
Zhūgě Jǐn and Yáng Càn both gathered their troops to relieve the siege,
but did not know where to strike,
while Wèi soldiers continued to cross daily without interruption.
Zhāng said,
“The Wèi forces are currently strong,
and the river is shallow.
We cannot engage them yet.”
So he led his troops
fifty *lǐ* upstream from the Wèi position,
cut several million bundles of reeds,
bound them into large rafts,
intending to set them ablaze and release them downstream
to burn and destroy the pontoon bridge.
Just as the rafts were completed,
waiting for the water level to rise before releasing them,
Shàng withdrew his forces.
Zhāng then took up station at Lùkǒu.
When Quán proclaimed himself emperor,
Zhāng was appointed Right General.
Zhāng was a rough and fierce man;
his prohibitions and orders were strict.
He loved to achieve great deeds.
His command of troops never exceeded a few thousand,
yet wherever he was, it always seemed like ten thousand.
During campaigns, whenever they halted,
he would immediately set up a military market.
Other armies lacked this,
and all relied on him for supplies.
However, his nature was extravagant and indulgent,
which became even worse in his later years.
His attire and possessions exceeded his rank.
If his officers and soldiers were wealthy,
he would sometimes kill them to seize their property,
often disregarding the law.
When the supervisors reported him,
Quán, valuing his achievements, would always pardon him without inquiry.
He died in Jiāhé 3rd year.
His son, Píng,
was exiled to Kuàijī for his misconduct.
Zhāng’s wife resided in Jiànyè,
and was granted land, a residence,
and fifty retainer families.
Dīng Fèng, courtesy name Chéngyuān,
was a native of Ānfēng, Lújiāng.
In his youth, he became a minor officer due to his bravery and prowess,
serving under Gān Níng, Lù Xùn, Pān Zhāng, and others.
He often accompanied them on campaigns,
always excelling in combat.
Each time he beheaded an enemy general and captured a flag,
his body would be covered in wounds.
He was gradually promoted to General of the Household.
When Sūn Liàng ascended the throne,
he was made General Who Defeats the Champions
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng.
When Wèi dispatched Zhūgě Dàn, Hú Zūn, and others to attack Dōngxīng,
Zhūgě Kè led the army to resist them.
All the generals said,
“The enemy heard that the Grand Tutor himself is coming,
so they will surely flee once they land.”
Only Fèng said,
“Not so.
They have mobilized within their borders,
mustering all the Xu and Luò soldiers to launch a major expedition.
They must have a clear plan;
how could they return empty-handed?
Do not rely on the enemy not coming;
rely on our ability to defeat them.”
When Kè landed,
Fèng, along with Generals Táng Zī, Lǚ Jù, and Liú Zàn,
all ascended from the west side of the mountain.
Fèng said,
“Our armies are moving slowly now.
If the enemy occupies advantageous ground,
it will be difficult to contend with them.”
He then cleared a path for the other armies to follow
and led three thousand men from his command to advance directly.
At that time, there was a north wind,
and Fèng hoisted his sails, arriving in two days,
thus occupying Xútáng.
It was cold and snowing,
and the enemy generals were holding a grand feast with wine.
Fèng saw that their vanguard had few soldiers
and said to his men,
“To obtain the title of marquis and rewards
is precisely today!”
He then ordered his soldiers to take off their armor, wear their helmets,
and wield short weapons.
The enemy thereupon laughed at them,
making no preparations.
Fèng unleashed his troops to hack at them,
greatly routing the enemy’s vanguard camp.
When Jù and the others arrived,
the Wèi army collapsed.
He was promoted to General Who Destroys Raiders
and further enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
When Wèi general Wén Qīn surrendered,
Fèng was made General Who Displays Tiger-like Might,
and followed Sūn Jùn to Shòuchūn to welcome him.
He fought with the pursuing enemy army at Gāotíng.
Fèng rode on horseback, holding a spear,
charging into their formation,
beheading several hundred,
and capturing their military equipment.
He was further enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānfēng.
In Tàipíng 2nd year,
Wèi Grand General Zhūgě Dàn, based in Shòuchūn, surrendered,
and the Wèi forces besieged him.
Zhū Yì and Táng Zī were dispatched to relieve the siege,
and Fèng and Lí Fěi were also sent to break the encirclement.
Fèng was the first to charge,
stationing at Líjiāng,
fighting valiantly and achieving merit,
he was appointed Left General.
When Sūn Xiū ascended the throne,
he conspired with Zhāng Bù,
intending to execute Sūn Chén.
Bù said,
“Although Dīng Fèng is not skilled in writing,
his strategies surpass others,
and he can decide important matters.”
Xiū summoned Fèng and informed him,
“Chén wields national authority
and is about to act disloyally.
I wish to execute him with you, General.”
Fèng said,
“The Chancellor’s brothers, friends, and partisans are very numerous.
I fear that public sentiment may differ,
and he cannot be controlled suddenly.
It is best to use the occasion of the Lày Meeting,
with Your Majesty’s soldiers, to execute him.”
Xiū adopted his plan.
During the meeting, he invited Chén,
and Fèng and Zhāng Bù signaled their attendants to kill him.
He was promoted to Grand General
and given the added titles of Left and Right *Dūhù*.
In Yǒng'ān 3rd year,
he was granted the *jié* (credentials) and appointed Governor of Xúzhōu.
In the 6th year,
when Wèi attacked Shǔ,
Fèng led various armies towards Shòuchūn
to create a diversion to aid Shǔ.
Shǔ fell,
and the army returned.
When Xiū died,
Fèng, along with Chancellor Púyáng Xīng and others, followed the advice of Wàn Yù
and jointly welcomed and enthroned Sūn Hào.
He was promoted to Right Grand Commander and Left Army Advisor.
In Bǎodǐng 3rd year,
Hào ordered Fèng and Zhūgě Jìng to attack Héféi.
Fèng wrote a letter to Jìn Grand General Shí Bāo,
creating a rift and sowing discord,
whereupon Bāo was recalled.
In Jiànhéng 1st year,
Fèng again led his forces to fortify Xútáng
and then attacked Jìn’s Gǔyáng.
The people of Gǔyáng, knowing this,
evacuated,
and Fèng gained nothing.
Hào was enraged
and executed Fèng’s vanguard commander.
In the 3rd year,
he died.
Fèng was noble and meritorious,
but gradually became arrogant and conceited.
Some slandered him.
Hào, recalling his previous military conduct,
exiled Fèng’s family to Línchuān.
Fèng’s younger brother, Fēng,
rose to the rank of Rear General
and died before Fèng.
Commentary says: All these generals
were tiger-like ministers of Jiāngbiǎo,
greatly favored by the Sūn clan.
Considering Pān Zhāng’s lack of self-cultivation,
yet Quán was able to overlook his faults and remember his achievements,
it is indeed fitting
that he could hold and defend the Southeast!
Chén Biǎo was from a branch of a general’s family,
yet he could stand shoulder to shoulder with prominent figures from noble families,
distinguishing himself among his peers.
Is this not admirable!
Biography of Zhū Zhì, Zhū Rán, Lǚ Fàn, Zhū Huán, Chapter Eleven
Zhū Zhì, courtesy name Jūnlǐ,
was a man from Gùzhāng, Dānyáng Commandery.
He first served as a county official,
then was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate,
and the province appointed him as an Aide.
He followed Sūn Jiān on campaigns.
In the fifth year of Zhōngpíng (188 CE),
he was appointed Cavalier Commandant (Sīmǎ),
and followed in the suppression of the bandits Zhōu Cháo and Sū Mǎ, among others, in the three commanderies of Chángshā, Línglíng, and Guìyáng.
Having rendered meritorious service,
Jiān recommended Zhì to act as Commandant of the Capital (Xíng Dūwèi).
He then followed in defeating Dǒng Zhuó at Yángrén,
and entered Luòyáng.
He was recommended by memorial to act as Inspector-General (Xíng Dūjūn Xiàowèi),
specially leading infantry and cavalry
to the east to assist the Governor of Xúzhōu, Táo Qiān, in suppressing the Yellow Turbans.
When Jiān passed away,
Zhì supported and assisted Cè,
and joined Yuán Shù.
Later, realizing that Shù's governance and virtue were not firmly established,
he persuaded Cè to return and pacify Jiāngdōng.
At that time, Grand Tutor Mǎ Rìdī was in Shòuchūn;
he appointed Zhì as an Assistant (Yuàn),
and Zhì was promoted to Commandant of Wújùn.
At this time, Wú Jǐng was already in Dānyáng,
and Cè was attacking Lújiāng for Shù.
Thereupon, Liú Yáo feared being absorbed by Yuán and Sūn,
and thus created animosity.
Since Cè's entire household was still in the province,
Zhì dispatched someone to Qū'ā to welcome the Grand Dowager and Quán and his brothers.
He provided for them and protected them,
showing great kindness and care.
Zhì advanced from Qiántáng, intending to reach Wú.
The Administrator of Wújùn, Xǔ Gòng, resisted him at Yóuquán.
Zhì fought with him
and inflicted a great defeat.
Gòng fled south to join the mountain bandit Yán Báihǔ.
Zhì then entered the commandery
and assumed the duties of Administrator.
After Cè defeated Liú Yáo,
he pacified Kuàijī in the east.
Quán was fifteen years old,
and Zhì nominated him as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate.
Later, when Cè passed away,
Zhì and Zhāng Zhāo, among others, jointly upheld and supported Quán.
In the seventh year of Jiàn'ān (202 CE),
Quán recommended Zhì as the Administrator of Wújùn,
acting as General Who Upholds Righteousness (Xíng Fúyì Jiāngjūn),
and allotted Lóu, Yóuquán, Wúxī, and Pílíng as his fiefs,
where he appointed chief officials.
He campaigned against the Yi and Yuè,
assisting in the pacification of the southeast,
and captured and executed remnants of the Yellow Turbans such as Chén Bài and Wàn Bǐng.
In the first year of Huángwǔ (222 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Pílíng,
retaining his commandery office as before.
In the second year (223 CE),
he was appointed General Who Pacifies the State (Ānguó Jiāngjūn),
with a golden seal and purple ribbon, and his fief was transferred to Gùzhāng.
Throughout Quán's successive high positions,
and when he became King of Wú,
whenever Zhì came for an audience,
Quán would always personally welcome him,
holding a tablet and bowing in return.
During banquets and gift-giving,
the grace and respect shown were exceptionally profound.
Even the accompanying officials
were all allowed to present gifts and have private audiences,
such was the extraordinary treatment he received.
Originally,
Quán's younger brother Yì,
was quick-tempered
and acted on his impulses of joy and anger.
Zhì frequently reprimanded him,
enlightening him with principles of righteousness.
Quán's elder cousin, Bēn, Administrator of Yùzhāng,
had a daughter who was married to a son of Cáo Cāo.
When Cáo Cāo conquered Jīngzhōu
and his might shook the southern lands,
Bēn, fearing,
wanted to send his son as a hostage.
Zhì heard of this
and sought to visit Bēn.
He explained the dangers and benefits to him,
and Bēn consequently stopped.
Quán often praised Zhì for his diligent concern for state affairs.
He was by nature frugal and simple.
Though in wealth and high position,
his carriages and clothes were only for service.
Quán treated him with exceptional favor,
personally ordering the supervising military censor (Dūjūn Yùshǐ) to manage the documents of the dependent cities,
while Zhì only administered the taxes of the four counties.
However, many scions of the imperial clan and the four great families of Wú entered service in the commandery.
Commandery officials often numbered in the thousands.
Zhì sent hundreds of them to the king's palace every few years.
Each year, at seasonal times, he presented tribute,
and Quán's reply and rewards were excessively generous.
At this time, the remote areas of Dānyáng
frequently saw treachery and rebellion.
As he was also growing old
and longed for his native land,
he memorialized to be stationed at Gùzhāng
to suppress and pacify the mountain Yuè.
All the elders and old acquaintances
came to his gate.
Zhì welcomed them all,
and drank and feasted with them.
His fellow townsmen regarded it as an honor.
After more than a year in Gùzhāng,
he returned to Wú.
He died in the third year of Huángwǔ (224 CE),
having been in the commandery for thirty-one years,
at the age of sixty-nine.
His son, Cái,
had long served as a commandant leading troops.
After inheriting his father's peerage,
he was promoted to General of the Household (Piān Jiāngjūn).
Cái's younger brother, Jì,
was given Cè's daughter in marriage by Quán,
and also served as a commandant leading troops.
Jì's younger brothers, Wěi and Wànsuì,
both died young.
Cái's son, Wǎn,
inherited the peerage and became a general,
rising to General Who Guards the West (Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn).
Zhū Rán, courtesy name Yìfēng,
was Zhì's sister's son.
His original surname was Shī.
Initially, Zhì had no sons.
When Rán was thirteen,
Zhì petitioned Cè to adopt him as his heir.
Cè ordered Dānyáng Commandery to summon Rán with sheep and wine.
When Rán arrived in Wú,
Cè treated him with great courtesy and congratulated him.
Rán had studied writing with Quán
and formed a bond of affection.
When Quán took charge of affairs,
he appointed Rán as the Chief of Yúyáo.
He was then nineteen years old.
Later, he was promoted to Magistrate of Shānyīn,
and given the additional title of Breaking the Wave Commandant (Zhéchōng Xiàowèi),
supervising five counties.
Quán admired his abilities,
and divided Dānyáng to create Línchuān Commandery,
with Rán as Administrator,
and granted him two thousand soldiers.
At that time, mountain bandits rose in great numbers.
Rán suppressed them,
pacifying them within a month.
When Cáo Cāo marched out to Rúxū,
Rán defended the Dàwù and the garrisons of the three passes,
and was appointed General of the Household (Piān Jiāngjūn).
In the twenty-fourth year of Jiàn'ān (219 CE),
he followed in the campaign against Guān Yǔ.
Separately, he and Pān Zhāng went to Línjǔ and captured Yǔ.
He was promoted to General Who Manifests Military Might (Zhāowǔ Jiāngjūn)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xī'ān Township.
When General Who Manifests Tiger's Might (Hǔwēi Jiāngjūn) Lǚ Méng was gravely ill,
Quán asked:
"If you do not recover,
who can replace you?"
Méng replied:
"Zhū Rán has abundant courage and defense capabilities.
I believe he can be entrusted with the responsibility."
When Méng died,
Quán granted Rán the imperial insignia of authority (Jié),
and stationed him at Jiānglíng.
In the first year of Huángwǔ (222 CE),
Liú Bèi raised an army to attack Yídū.
Rán commanded five thousand men and joined forces with Lù Xùn to resist Bèi.
Rán separately attacked and routed Bèi's vanguard
and cut off his retreat route.
Bèi was consequently defeated and fled.
He was appointed General Who Conquers the North (Zhēng Běi Jiāngjūn)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒng'ān.
The Wèi dispatched Cáo Zhēn, Xiàhóu Shàng, Zhāng Hé, and others to attack Jiānglíng.
The Wèi Wén Dì himself stayed in Wǎn,
to provide them with strategic support,
and they continuously encamped to besiege the city.
Quán sent General Sūn Shèng to lead ten thousand men to guard the sandbar [zhōushàng],
constructing defensive fortifications [wéi wù],
as an external relief force for Rán.
Hé led his troops across to attack Shèng,
but Shèng could not resist,
and immediately retreated.
Hé then occupied the sandbar and maintained the siege,
thus cutting off Rán both internally and externally.
Quán sent Pān Zhāng, Yáng Càn, and others to relieve the siege, but the siege was not lifted.
At that time, many soldiers in Rán's city suffered from dropsy,
and only five thousand men were fit for battle.
Zhēn and the others built earthen mounds,
dug tunnels,
and erected watchtowers,
showering the city with arrows like rain.
The generals and soldiers all turned pale,
but Rán remained calm and fearless,
instead encouraging his officers and men,
waiting for a opportune moment to break through and destroy two enemy camps.
The Wèi had besieged Rán for a total of six months,
and had not yet retreated.
The Magistrate of Jiānglíng, Yáo Tài, led troops guarding the city's north gate.
Seeing the strength of the external forces [outside the city],
and the scarcity of men within the city,
with grain and provisions almost exhausted,
he consequently communicated with the enemy,
plotting to act as an internal informant.
Just as he was about to act,
the matter was discovered,
and Rán executed Tài.
Shàng and the others could not overcome the city,
so they withdrew their attack and returned.
Because of this, Rán's name shook the enemy states,
and he was re-enfeoffed as Dāngyáng Hóu.
In the sixth year [of Huángwǔ],
Quán personally led his troops to attack Shíyáng.
When he later withdrew his army,
Pān Zhāng covered the rear.
During a chaotic night sortie,
the enemy pursued and attacked Zhāng,
and Zhāng could not hold them back.
Rán immediately turned back to resist the enemy,
allowing the forward ships to sail far ahead,
and then slowly departed himself.
In the first year of Huánglóng,
he was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry [Chēqí Jiāngjūn], Right Protector of the Army [Yòu Hùjūn],
and concurrently Governor of Yǎanzhōu.
A short while later,
as Yǎanzhōu was situated in the territory of Shǔ,
he was relieved of his governorship.
In the third year of Jiāhé,
Quán and Shǔ agreed on a date for a major joint offensive.
Quán personally headed towards Xīnchéng,
while Rán and Quán Cóng each received the axe and staff,
acting as left and right commanders [zuǒyòu dūdū].
However, the officers and soldiers fell ill,
so they withdrew without attacking.
In the fifth year of Chìwū,
he campaigned in Zǔzhōng.
The Wèi generals Pú Zhōng and Hú Zhì each led several thousand men.
Pú Zhōng blocked the dangerous defiles,
planning to cut off Rán's retreat,
while Hú Zhì provided backup for Pú Zhōng.
At this time, Rán's commanded troops had already scattered in four directions.
Hearing the news, he had no time to gather them,
so he immediately led eight hundred of his existing soldiers from under his banner to launch a surprise counterattack.
Pú Zhōng fought unsuccessfully,
and Hú Zhì and the others all retreated.
In the ninth year [of Chìwū],
he again campaigned in Zǔzhōng.
The Wèi general Lǐ Xìng and others, hearing that Rán had advanced deep,
led six thousand infantry and cavalry to cut off Rán's retreat.
Rán launched a night attack against them,
and the army returned victorious.
Earlier,
the Gūiyì Mǎ Mào harbored treachery,
which was discovered and led to his execution;
Quán was deeply indignant about this.
Just before his departure, Rán submitted a memorial saying:
"Mǎ Mào is but a mere boy,
yet he dared to betray your kindness.
Your servant now serves under Heaven's might,
and I am confident of victory.
I wish to make what I acquire [from this campaign]
shine far and wide,
filling the Jiāng River with boats,
making it a spectacle worth seeing,
to appease the indignation of all.
I only ask that Your Majesty remembers my former words,
and demands a future fulfillment from your servant."
Quán, at that time, suppressed the memorial and did not release it.
After Rán presented his victory,
all the officials offered their congratulations.
Quán then raised his cup and made music,
and produced Rán's memorial, saying:
"This man previously submitted a memorial,
and I thought it was not certainly achievable.
Now it has indeed turned out as he said,
he can be said to be clear-sighted in discerning affairs."
He sent an envoy to appoint Rán as Left Grand Marshal [Zuǒ Dà Sīmǎ] and Right Army Adviser [Yòu Jūnshī].
Rán's height was less than seven *chǐ*.
His temperament was clear and distinct,
and his inner conduct was pure and upright.
His ornamentation [wéncǎi]
was only applied to military equipment;
everything else was simple and plain.
He was diligent all day long,
always on the battlefield.
In emergencies, his courage was steadfast,
surpassing others.
Even when the world was at peace,
every morning and evening, the drums would beat strictly,
and soldiers in the camp
would all get ready and form ranks.
By doing this, he toyed with the enemy,
making them unaware of what to prepare for,
and thus he always achieved success when he launched an attack.
Although Zhūgě Jǐn's son Róng and Bù Zhì's son Xié each inherited their posts,
Quán specifically had Rán continue to serve as the overall Grand Commander [Dà Dūdū].
Furthermore, Lù Xùn had also passed away.
Among the meritorious officials and famous generals who remained, only Rán survived,
and none could compare to him.
He was ill for two years,
and later his condition gradually worsened.
Quán reduced his meals during the day
and suffered sleepless nights for him.
Imperial envoys carrying medicine and food
were seen continuously on the road.
Whenever Rán sent an envoy to report on the progress of his illness,
Quán would summon him,
personally inquire about his condition,
grant him wine and food upon entering,
and send him off with cloth and silk upon exiting.
Among the meritorious officials from the founding of the dynasty who fell ill,
the ones Quán most deeply cared for
were Lǚ Méng and Líng Tǒng,
and Rán was next to them.
At the age of sixty-eight,
he died in the twelfth year of Chìwū.
Quán wore plain clothes and mourned,
deeply moved by sorrow.
His son Jì inherited his title.
Shī Jī, whose courtesy name was Gōngxù,
was made a Láng due to his father's appointment.
Later, he was appointed Jiànzhōng Dūwèi.
When his uncle, Shī Cái, died,
Shī Jī took command of his troops,
and followed Tàicháng Pān Jùn to subjugate the Wǔxī tribes,
earning renown for his courage and strength.
He was promoted to Piān Jiāngjūn Yíngxià Dū,
and was in charge of bandit suppression.
He upheld the law impartially.
Lǔ Wáng Sūn Bà paid close attention to befriending Shī Jī.
He once visited Shī Jī's quarters,
and invited him to sit.
Wishing to form a bond,
Shī Jī stepped down to the ground and stood,
declining the offer and not accepting it.
After Shī Rán died,
Shī Jī inherited his position,
and was appointed Píngwèi Jiāngjūn
and Lèxiāng Dū.
The following year,
Wèi Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Wáng Chǎng led his troops to attack Jiānglíng City,
but withdrew without success.
Shī Jī wrote to Fènwēi Jiāngjūn Zhūgě Róng, saying:
"Wáng Chǎng has come a long way and is exhausted.
His horses have nothing to eat.
His strength is spent, and he is fleeing.
This is Heaven's help.
Currently, our pursuing force is small.
You can lead your troops to follow,
and I wish to defeat them in the front.
You can then strike them from the rear.
How could this be one person's achievement alone?
We should uphold the principle of 'cutting metal together'."
Zhūgě Róng replied, agreeing with Shī Jī.
Shī Jī then led his troops to catch up with Wáng Chǎng at Jìnán.
Jìnán was thirty *lǐ* from the city.
Shī Jī first won a battle, but Zhūgě Róng did not advance.
Shī Jī later suffered a defeat.
Sūn Quán deeply praised Shī Jī,
and severely rebuked Zhūgě Róng.
Because Zhūgě Róng's elder brother, Dà Jiāngjūn Zhūgě Kè, was highly esteemed,
Zhūgě Róng was not dismissed.
Initially, Shī Jī and Zhūgě Kè and Zhūgě Róng were not on good terms.
After this incident,
the rift deepened even more.
In the first year of Jiànxīng (252 CE),
he was promoted to Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn.
In the spring of the second year (253 CE),
Zhūgě Kè advanced on Xīnchéng,
requesting Shī Jī to join forces,
but left him in charge of Bànzhōu,
and had Zhūgě Róng concurrently hold his position.
In winter,
Zhūgě Kè and Zhūgě Róng were killed.
Shī Jī returned to Lèxiāng
and was granted *jiǎjié*.
In the second year of Tàipíng (257 CE),
he was appointed Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
When Sūn Lín held power,
the high officials harbored doubts and disloyalty.
Shī Jī feared that Wú would certainly fall into turmoil,
and that Zhōngguó would seize the opportunity.
So, he secretly wrote to ally with Shǔ,
making plans for a joint conquest.
Shǔ dispatched Yòu Jiāngjūn Yán Yǔ with five thousand troops
to reinforce the defenses of Báidì,
awaiting Shī Jī's further orders.
In the early years of Yǒng'ān (258 CE),
he was promoted to Shàng Dà Jiāngjūn and Dūhù Dū,
with command from Bāqiū up to Xīlíng.
In the first year of Yuánxīng (264 CE),
he was appointed Zuǒ Dà Sīmǎ.
Initially,
when Shī Rán had completed the mourning rites for his adoptive parents,
he requested to revert to his original surname.
Sūn Quán did not permit it.
In the Wǔfèng era, Shī Jī petitioned to revert to the Shī clan,
and he died in the second year of Jiànhéng (270 CE).
Lǚ Fàn, whose courtesy name was Zǐhéng,
was a native of Xìyáng, Rǔnán.
In his youth, he served as a county official
and possessed a dignified appearance and demeanor.
A certain Liú clan from his town
was wealthy and had a beautiful daughter.
Lǚ Fàn sought her hand.
The girl's mother disliked him
and wished not to give her to him.
But the elder Liú said:
"Looking at Lǚ Zǐhéng, will he remain poor for long?"
And so, they were married.
Later, he fled the chaos to Shòuchūn.
Sūn Cè saw him and was impressed.
Lǚ Fàn then pledged his loyalty to Sūn Cè,
bringing a hundred private retainers with him.
At that time, the Grand Empress Dowager was in Jiāngdū.
Sūn Cè sent Lǚ Fàn to welcome her.
The Xúzhōu Mù Táo Qiān thought Lǚ Fàn was a spy for the Yuán clan
and implicitly ordered the county to arrest and interrogate Lǚ Fàn.
Lǚ Fàn's personal retainers and brave men rescued him and returned.
At that time, only Lǚ Fàn and Sūn Hé constantly followed Sūn Cè,
enduring hardships and not shying away from dangers.
Sūn Cè also treated him as a relative,
always inviting him to ascend the hall
and feast in the presence of the Grand Empress Dowager.
Later, he followed Sūn Cè to attack and defeat Lújiāng,
then returned and crossed the river eastward together.
Upon reaching Héngjiāng and Dānglì,
they defeated Zhāng Yīng and Yú Mí,
took Xiǎodānyáng and Húshú,
and Lǚ Fàn was appointed Húshú Xiàng.
After Sūn Cè pacified Mòlíng and Qǔ'ā
and gathered the remnants of Zé Róng and Liú Yáo's forces,
he increased Lǚ Fàn's troops by two thousand
and fifty cavalry.
Later, he was appointed Wǎnlíng Lìng,
suppressed the Dānyáng bandits,
returned to Wú,
and was promoted to Dū Dū.
At this time, Chén Yǔ from Xiàpī declared himself the Tàishǒu of Wújùn,
stationing himself at Hǎixī,
and colluding with the powerful clan head Yán Báihǔ.
Sūn Cè personally led an expedition against Yán Báihǔ,
while separately sending Lǚ Fàn and Xú Yì to attack Chén Yǔ at Hǎixī,
beheading his general Chén Mù.
He also followed Sūn Cè in attacking Zǔ Láng at Língyáng
and Tàishǐ Cí at Yǒnglǐ.
After the seven counties were pacified,
he was appointed Zhēnglǔ Zhōnglángjiāng,
conquered Jiāngxià,
and returned to pacify Póyáng.
When Sūn Cè died,
he rushed to Wú to mourn.
Later, Sūn Quán again campaigned against Jiāngxià.
Lǚ Fàn and Zhāng Zhāo were left to guard the capital.
When Cáo Cāo arrived at Chìbì,
he and Zhōu Yú and others jointly resisted and defeated him.
Lǚ Fàn was appointed Bì Jiāngjūn
and Tàishǒu of Péngzé,
with Péngzé, Cháisāng, and Lìyáng as his enfeoffed territories.
When Liú Bèi visited Jīng to see Sūn Quán,
Lǚ Fàn secretly requested that Liú Bèi be detained.
Later, he was promoted to Píngnán Jiāngjūn
and garrisoned at Cháisāng.
When Sūn Quán campaigned against Guān Yǔ,
he passed by Lǚ Fàn's residence
and said:
"If I had followed your words earlier,
I would not have had this trouble.
Now I must go and take him.
You guard Jiànyè for me."
When Sūn Quán defeated Guān Yǔ and returned,
he made Wǔchāng his capital,
appointed Lǚ Fàn Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed him as Wǎnlíng Hóu,
appointed him Dānyáng Tàishǒu,
governing Jiànyè,
and overseeing the area from Fúzhōu down to the sea.
His enfeoffed territories were changed to Lìyáng, Huái'ān, and Níngguó.
When Cáo Xiū, Zhāng Liáo, Zāng Bà, and others came to invade,
Lǚ Fàn commanded Xú Shèng, Quán Cóng, Sūn Sháo, and others
to resist Cáo Xiū and his forces with a naval fleet at Dòngkǒu.
He was promoted to Qián Jiāngjūn,
granted *jiǎjié*,
and enfeoffed as Nánchāng Hóu.
At that time, a great storm struck,
causing boats to capsize and people to drown,
with thousands of deaths.
When the army returned,
he was appointed Yángzhōu Mù.
He was fond of pomp and ceremony.
The provincial populace, such as Lù Xùn, Quán Cóng, and noble scions,
all showed him reverence and solemnity,
not daring to be disrespectful or casual.
His residences and attire
were extravagant at the time,
yet he was diligent in his duties and upheld the law.
Therefore, Sūn Quán was pleased with his loyalty
and did not fault him for his extravagance.
Initially, Sūn Cè made Lǚ Fàn responsible for financial management.
When Sūn Quán was young,
if his private retinue had requests,
Lǚ Fàn would always report them
and dared not grant them privately.
At the time, he was resented for this.
When Sūn Quán served as Yángxiàn Zhǎng,
he had private expenditures.
If Sūn Cè sometimes reviewed them,
the Gōngcáo Zhōu Gǔ would immediately fabricate and enter them into the ledgers
to prevent any reprimand.
Sūn Quán was pleased at the time,
but when he later took charge of affairs,
he highly trusted Lǚ Fàn for his loyalty,
but did not use Zhōu Gǔ
because he was able to falsify and alter records.
In the seventh year of the Huángwǔ reign,
Fàn Jiàn was appointed Grand Marshal.
Before his seal and ribbon could be conferred,
he died of illness.
Qúan wore plain clothes and expressed his grief,
sending an envoy to posthumously grant him the seal and ribbon.
When he returned to the capital, Jiànyè,
Qúan passed Fàn Jiàn's tomb and called out,
"Zǐhéng!"
As he spoke, tears flowed,
and he offered a grand sacrifice.
Fàn Jiàn's eldest son had died earlier,
so his second son, Jù, inherited.
Jù, courtesy name Shìyì,
was made a Gentleman by virtue of his father's position.
Later, when Fàn Jiàn became seriously ill,
Jù was appointed Deputy Army Commandant,
assisting in military affairs.
When Fàn Jiàn died,
Jù was promoted to Colonel of the Pacification Army.
He repeatedly suppressed mountain bandits;
in all the rugged, difficult territories
he attacked, he broke them.
He accompanied Grand Minister of the Court Pān Jùn in campaigning against the Wǔxī,
again achieving merit.
When Zhū Rán attacked Fán,
Jù and Zhū Yì broke the outer perimeter of the city.
Upon returning, he was appointed General of the Household,
and entered service as the Right Section Commander of the Horse Pasture,
then promoted to Commandant of Yueqi Cavalry.
In the first year of the Tàiyuán reign,
a great wind blew,
and the Jiāng River overflowed,
gradually submerging the city gates.
Qúan sent men to inspect the water level,
and only Jù was seen having his men bring large boats in preparation for disaster.
Qúan praised him
and appointed him General who Charges the Wèi.
When Qúan became ill,
he made Jù the Right Section Commander of the Crown Prince.
When the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
Jù was appointed Right General.
When Wèi forces advanced to Dōngxīng,
Jù rushed to engage them and achieved merit.
The following year,
Sūn Jùn killed Zhūgě Kè,
and Jù was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry,
managing affairs of the Western Palace.
In the second year of the Wǔfèng reign,
he was granted a staff of authority,
and with Jùn and others, attacked Shòuchūn.
On their return, they met the Wèi general Cáo Zhēn
and defeated him at Gāotíng.
In the first year of the Tàipíng reign,
Jù led his army to invade Wèi territory.
Before reaching the Huái River,
he heard that Sūn Jùn had died,
and that his younger cousin Lín had replaced him.
Jù was greatly enraged,
withdrew his army,
intending to depose Lín.
When Lín heard of this,
he sent a Censor bearing an imperial edict,
commanding Wén Qīn, Líu Zuǎn, Táng Zī, and others to apprehend Jù.
He also dispatched his elder cousin Xiàn with the capital troops to intercept Jù at Jiāngdū.
His attendants urged Jù to surrender to Wèi,
but Jù said,
"I am ashamed to be a traitor."
Thereupon, he committed suicide.
His three kindreds were exterminated.
Zhū Húan, courtesy name Xīumù,
was a native of Wú County in Wú Commandery.
When Sūn Qúan was a general,
Húan served in his staff,
and was appointed Magistrate of Yúyáo.
He arrived when an epidemic was raging,
and grain was scarce and expensive.
Húan divided his virtuous officials,
personally oversaw medicine and medical care,
and provided gruel continuously.
The soldiers and common people were moved and grateful.
He was promoted to Commandant of Charging Raiders,
given two thousand soldiers,
and tasked with organizing the forces of Wú and Kuàijī commanderies,
gathering scattered remnants.
Within a year,
he had assembled over ten thousand men.
Later, mountain bandits in Dānyáng and Póyáng rose up like swarms of bees,
attacking and capturing cities,
killing and plundering officials,
and gathering in strongholds everywhere.
Húan led his generals,
moving to suppress them,
and pacified them all.
He was gradually promoted to General of the Household,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīnchéng Pavilion.
Later, he succeeded Zhōu Tài as Inspector of Rúxū.
In the first year of the Huángwǔ reign,
Wèi sent Grand Marshal Cáo Rén with tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry towards Rúxū.
Rén intended to use his troops to attack and seize the upstream area,
but falsely announced
that he intended to attack Xiànxī to the east.
Húan divided his troops to march to Xiànxī.
After they set out,
he suddenly learned that Rén had advanced to within seventy *lǐ* of Rúxū.
Húan sent an envoy to recall the Xiànxī troops,
but before they arrived, Rén suddenly appeared.
At that time, Húan had five thousand men
under his command and those of his section who were present.
The generals were all apprehensive,
each having fear in their hearts.
Húan exhorted them, saying:
"When two armies face each other,
victory or defeat lies with the general,
not with numbers.
Gentlemen, you have heard of Cáo Rén's military tactics and campaigns,
how does he compare to Húan?
The military treatise that speaks of guests having twice the numbers while hosts have half
refers to both being on open plains,
without city defenses,
and also assumes the bravery and timidity of soldiers are equal.
Now, our enemy is neither wise nor brave,
and moreover, their soldiers are very timid.
They have also marched a thousand *lǐ*,
and both men and horses are exhausted.
Húan and all our armies
occupy a high city,
facing the great river to the south,
and with mountains and hills behind us to the north.
We are rested while they are weary;
we are the host and can control the guest.
This is the posture for a hundred victories in a hundred battles.
Even if Cáo Pī himself were to come,
there would still be no need for worry,
let alone Rén and his ilk!"
Húan then lowered his banners and muffled his drums,
outwardly showing weakness
to lure Rén.
Rén indeed sent his son, Tài, to attack Rúxū city,
and separately dispatched General Cháng Diāo to lead Zhūgě Qían and Wáng Shuāng,
to separately attack Zhōngzhōu on oil boats.
Zhōngzhōu was
where the families of the troops resided. [14án himself led ten thousand men and remained at Tuó'gāo,
serving as a rear guard for Tài and the others.
Húan's troops attacked and seized the oil boats,
or separately attacked Diāo and others.
Húan himself resisted Tài,
burning their camp and forcing them to retreat.
He then beheaded Diāo,
captured Shuāng alive,
and sent him to Wǔchāng.
On the field of battle, over a thousand were killed by beheading or drowning.
Qúan praised Húan's achievement,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Jiāxīng,
and promoted him to General who Arouses Martial Might,
also granting him the concurrent title of Administrator of Péngchéng.
In the seventh year of the Huángwǔ reign,
Póyáng Administrator Zhōu Fáng deceitfully lured Wèi Grand Marshal Cáo Xīu.
Xīu led tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry to Wǎnchéng to receive Fáng.
At this time, Lù Xùn was the commander-in-chief,
while Qúan Cóng and Húan served as left and right commanders,
each leading thirty thousand men to attack Xīu.
Xīu realized he had been deceived,
and was about to withdraw his army,
but, overconfident in his numerous forces,
he sought a decisive battle.
Húan proposed a strategy, saying:
"Xīu was originally appointed due to kinship,
not for his wisdom or bravery as a renowned general.
If he fights now, he will certainly lose;
if he loses, he will certainly flee.
He will flee via Jiāshí and Guàchē.
These two routes are both treacherous and narrow.
If we block the road with ten thousand soldiers,
their entire army can be captured,
and Xīu can be taken alive.
I request to lead my division to cut off his retreat.
If, by the imperial might,
I can offer Xīu himself,
we can then press on with our victory,
advance to take Shòuchūn,
seize Huáinán,
and plan for Xǔ and Luò.
This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity that will last for ten thousand generations;
it must not be missed."
Qúan first discussed it with Lù Xùn,
but Xùn considered it unfeasible.
Therefore, the plan was not implemented.
In the first year of Huánglóng,
Huán was appointed Front General,
and concurrently Governor of Qīngzhōu,
granted a battle-axe of authority.
In the sixth year of Jiāhé,
Lǚ Xí, the Chief Clerk of Lújiāng under Wèi, requested a large army to personally receive him,
intending to open the city gates as a response.
Huán and General Wèi Quán Cóng both led armies to meet him.
Upon arrival,
the plot was exposed,
and the armies had to retreat.
Outside the city was a stream,
about a *lǐ* away from the city,
over thirty *zhàng* wide,
eight or nine *chǐ* deep in some places,
and half that in shallower parts.
All the armies were ordered to cross and leave,
while Huán himself covered the rear.
At that time, Lǐ Yīng, the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng, had his troops and cavalry ready,
intending to wait until the armies were halfway across,
and then launch a sudden attack.
But when he saw Huán's banner and canopy covering the rear,
he dared not sally forth,
such was the awe in which he was held.
At this time, Quán Cóng was the Chief Commander,
and Quán also ordered Partial General Hú Zōng to proclaim imperial edicts,
and participate in military affairs.
Cóng, disappointed that the expedition had yielded no gains,
proposed to divide the generals
and launch some surprise attacks.
Huán, who was always proud,
was ashamed to be part of a subordinate division,
so he went to see Cóng,
asked about his intentions,
and became agitated and angry,
arguing with Cóng.
Cóng wanted to excuse himself,
and then said:
“The Emperor himself ordered Hú Zōng to be the Chief Commander,
and Zōng believes this is appropriate.”
Huán became even more resentful,
and upon returning, sent someone to summon Zōng.
When Zōng arrived at the camp gate,
Huán came out to meet him,
and looked at his attendants, saying:
“I'm letting go,
you all should leave now.”
One person stepped forward
and told Zōng to return.
When Huán came out
and didn't see Zōng,
he knew what his attendants had done,
and then hacked that person to death.
Huán’s aide-de-camp remonstrated with him,
and Huán stabbed the aide-de-camp to death.
Then he feigned a fit of madness
and went to Jiànyè to seek medical treatment.
Quán valued his capabilities
and therefore did not punish him.
He ordered Huán’s son, Yì, to provisionally lead his division,
and had doctors attend to him.
After several months, he sent him back to Zhōngzhōu.
Quán personally went out to bid him farewell,
and said:
“Now that the bandits and enemies still exist,
and the royal path is not yet unified,
I shall conquer the world with you.
I want you to command fifty thousand men and take charge of one front,
to plan for advance and conquest.
I hope your illness will not relapse.”
Huán replied:
“Heaven has bestowed upon Your Majesty a sagely countenance.
When you rule over the four seas,
you place a heavy responsibility on your servant
to eliminate the wicked and rebellious.
My illness will naturally heal itself.”
Huán was by nature protective of his authority
and disliked being subordinate to others.
Whenever he faced the enemy in battle,
if his tactical decisions were not completely his own,
he would become angry and agitated.
However, he valued righteousness over wealth,
and also possessed a strong memory.
He would not forget a person he had met once for decades.
He knew all ten thousand of his troops
and their wives and children.
He cared for and nurtured his officers and soldiers,
and supported his relatives,
sharing his salary and property
with them all.
When Huán’s illness became critical,
the entire camp was filled with sorrow.
At the age of sixty-two,
he died in the first year of Chìwū.
Officers, soldiers, men, and women
all mourned for him.
Moreover, his family had no remaining wealth,
so Quán bestowed five thousand *hú* of salt
to cover the funeral expenses.
His son, Yì, succeeded him.
Yì, courtesy name Jìwén,
was appointed a Gentleman due to his father’s position,
and later was appointed Commandant of Cavalry,
succeeding Huán in leading the troops.
In the fourth year of Chìwū,
he followed Zhū Rán to attack Wèi’s Fánchéng,
devised a plan to break through its outer defenses,
and upon returning, was appointed Partial General.
Wén Qīn, the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng under Wèi, established encampments at Liù'ān,
setting up many garrisons and forts
at strategic points
to attract deserters and defectors,
becoming a menace to the border.
Yì personally led two thousand of his men
and surprised and broke through seven of Qīn’s garrisons,
beheading several hundred,
and was promoted to General Wǔyáng.
Quán discussed tactics and battles with him,
and his replies were satisfactory.
Quán said to Yì’s paternal uncle, General of Agile Cavalry Lǚ Jù:
“I already knew Jìwén's [courage] and resolve,
but seeing him surpasses what I heard.”
In the thirteenth year,
Wén Qīn feigned surrender
and secretly wrote to Yì,
wanting him to personally receive him.
Yì submitted Qīn's letter,
then explained its falseness,
stating that he should not be received immediately.
Quán issued an edict saying:
“Currently, the northern lands are not unified.
Qīn claims he wants to pledge allegiance;
he should be received.
If there is suspicion of deceit,
one only needs to devise a plan to ensnare him,
and deploy heavy troops to guard against him.”
So, Lǚ Jù was sent to command twenty thousand men,
and joining forces with Yì,
they went to the northern border,
but Qīn indeed did not surrender.
In the first year of Jiànxīng,
he was promoted to General Zhènnán.
That year, Wèi sent Hú Zūn, Zhūgě Dàn, and others to emerge from Dōngxīng.
Yì commanded the navy to attack the floating bridge,
destroying it,
and the Wèi army was thoroughly defeated.
In the second year of Tàipíng,
he was granted a battle-axe of authority,
and served as Grand Commander,
rescuing Shòuchūn from siege,
but failed to relieve it.
Upon returning with the army,
he was wrongfully executed by Sūn Chēn.
Critique: Zhū Zhì and Lǚ Fàn were appointed as trusted old ministers.
Zhū Rán and Zhū Huán were renowned for their bravery and ferocity.
Lǚ Jù, Zhū Yì, and Shī Jì all possessed the talent of commanders,
successfully continuing their family legacy.
If Fàn and Huán, who exceeded boundaries,
were able to meet a peaceful end,
then as for Jù and Yì, who did not have such faults yet suffered disaster,
it was because the times they encountered were different.
Biography of Yú, Lù, Zhāng, Luò, Lù, Wú, Zhū, Chapter Twelve
Yú Fān, courtesy name Zhòngxiáng,
was a native of Yúyáo, Kuàijī.
Grand Administrator Wáng Lǎng appointed him as Secretary.
When Sūn Cè conquered Kuàijī,
Fān was at the time in mourning for his father.
Wearing sackcloth, he went to the government office gate.
Lǎng wanted to go out to meet him,
but Fān removed his mourning clothes and entered to see him,
advising Lǎng to avoid Cè.
Lǎng did not heed him,
fought and was defeated,
and fled by sea.
Fān followed and protected him,
reaching Hòuguān in the eastern region.
The Hòuguān chief closed the city gates and refused to receive them.
Fān went and persuaded him,
and then they were admitted.
Lǎng said to Fān:
“You have an elderly mother;
you may return now.”
After Fān returned,
Cè again appointed him as Secretary,
treating him with the courtesy due to a friend,
and personally visited Fān’s residence.
Yú Fān (虞翻) was fond of riding, galloping, hunting, and carousing.
Fān (翻) remonstrated, saying:
"Your Highness employs a multitude gathered like crows,
and drives scattered, attached士 (shì),
all of whom give their utmost strength.
Even Hàn Gāodì (漢高帝) could not surpass this.
But as for lightly going out in disguise,
your attendants do not have time to be strict,
and the officers and soldiers constantly suffer because of it.
A ruler who is not weighty lacks majesty.
Thus, when the white dragon assumed the form of a fish,
it was trapped by Yù Qiě (豫且);
and when Bái (白) released himself,
Liú Jì (劉季) harmed him.
I beg you to pay more attention to this."
Cè (策) said:
"Your words are correct.
However, there are times when I have thoughts,
and sitting idly, I feel depressed.
I have the plans formulated by Bì Chén (裨諶),
which is why I travel."
Fān (翻) was appointed the Chief of Fùchūn (富春).
When Cè (策) died,
all the senior officials wanted to go to attend the funeral.
Fān (翻) said:
"I fear that the mountain people of neighboring counties might commit treachery or disturbance.
If we leave the cities and towns far behind,
it will surely lead to unforeseen dangers."
So he remained and wore mourning clothes to observe the mourning rites.
All the other counties followed his example,
and all were peaceful.
Later, Fān (翻) was recommended as a Màocái (茂才) by the prefecture,
and the Hàn (漢) court summoned him to be a Shìyùshǐ (侍御史).
Cáo Gōng (曹公), as the Sīkōng (司空), also invited him,
but he did not accept any of these appointments.
Fān (翻) wrote to Shàofǔ (少府) Kǒng Róng (孔融),
showing him his commentary on the Yì (易).
Róng (融) replied in a letter, saying:
"Hearing of Yánlíng (延陵)'s mastery of music,
and seeing my lord's study of the Yì (易),
I then knew that the beauties of the southeast
are not merely the bamboo and arrows of Kuàijī (會稽).
Furthermore, observing the phenomena of clouds and objects,
discerning the responses to cold and warmth,
and plumbing their fortunes and misfortunes,
it is in perfect accord with the divine.
One could say you are someone who explores the profound and penetrates the ultimate."
Zhāng Hóng (張紘), the Dūwèi (都尉) of the Eastern Department of Kuàijī (會稽), also wrote to Róng (融), saying:
"Yú Zhòngxiáng (虞仲翔) was previously somewhat attacked by critics,
but his excellent quality is like a precious gem;
carving and polishing it only makes it shine brighter,
and is not enough to diminish it."
Sūn Quán (孫權) appointed him as Qídūwèi (騎都尉).
Fān (翻) frequently offended Sūn Quán (孫權) with his forthright remonstrances,
and Quán (權) was not pleased.
Moreover, his nature was not in harmony with popular customs,
and he incurred much slander and defamation.
Consequently, he was exiled to Dānyáng Jīng Xiàn (丹楊涇縣).
Lǚ Méng (呂蒙), plotting to capture Guān Yǔ (關羽),
feigned illness and returned to Jiànyè (建業).
Knowing that Fān (翻) also possessed medical skills,
he asked him to accompany him,
also wishing to use this as an opportunity for Fān (翻) to be released.
Later, Méng (蒙) led his army westward.
Mí Fāng (麋芳), the Grand Administrator of Nánjùn (南郡), opened the city gates and surrendered.
Méng (蒙) had not yet taken control of the commandery city but was making music on the sandy shore.
Fān (翻) said to Méng (蒙):
"Currently, the only wholeheartedly loyal person is General Mí (麋將軍);
how can all the people in the city be trusted?
Why don't you quickly enter the city and seize its keys and seals?"
Méng (蒙) immediately followed his advice.
At that time, there was a hidden plot in the city,
which fortunately did not proceed due to Fān (翻)'s counsel.
After Guān Yǔ (關羽) was defeated,
Quán (權) had Fān (翻) divine his fate.
He obtained the Jié (節) hexagram, with Duì (兌) below and Kǎn (坎) above,
and the fifth changing line led to Lín (臨).
Fān (翻) said:
"Within two days,
his head will surely be severed."
It turned out exactly as Fān (翻) had said.
Quán (權) said:
"You are not as good as Fúxī (伏羲),
but you can be compared to Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔)."
The Wèi (魏) general Yú Jìn (于禁) was captured by Yǔ (羽)
and imprisoned in the city.
When Quán (權) arrived, he released him
and invited him to meet.
Another day,
Quán (權) rode out on horseback,
leading Jìn (禁) to ride alongside him.
Fān (翻) shouted at Jìn (禁), saying:
"You are a surrendered captive;
how dare you ride alongside my lord!"
He wanted to raise his whip and strike Jìn (禁),
but Quán (權) shouted to stop him.
Later, Quán (權) held a banquet with his officials on a tower-boat.
When Jìn (禁) heard the music, he shed tears.
Fān (翻) again said:
"Are you trying to feign this to escape punishment?"
Quán (權) was displeased and resentful.
After Quán (權) became the King of Wú (吳),
at the end of a joyful banquet,
he personally stood up to offer wine.
Fān (翻) prostrated himself, feigning drunkenness,
and refused to accept it.
When Quán (權) left,
Fān (翻) rose and sat up.
Quán (權) was then greatly enraged
and took a sword, intending to strike him.
All those sitting nearby were terrified,
but only the Grand Minister of Agriculture, Liú Jī (劉基), rose to embrace Quán (權) and remonstrated, saying:
"If Your Majesty, after three cups of wine, kills a good scholar,
even if Fān (翻) is guilty,
who in the world will know it?
Moreover, Your Majesty is known for being able to tolerate the worthy and gather the multitude;
that is why people from all corners look up to you.
Is it permissible to abandon this in one morning?"
Quán (權) said:
"Cáo Mèngdé (曹孟德) still killed Kǒng Wénjǔ (孔文舉);
what is there for me with Yú Fān (虞翻)?"
Jī (基) said:
"Mèngdé (孟德)'s light killing of scholars
was condemned by all under heaven.
Your Majesty personally practices virtue and righteousness,
wishing to rival Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) in greatness;
how can you compare yourself to him?"
Fān (翻) was thus spared.
Quán (權) then instructed his attendants
that from now on, if he spoke of killing after drinking,
no one should actually kill.
Fān (翻) once traveled by boat
and encountered Mí Fāng (麋芳).
Many people on Fāng (芳)'s boat wanted Fān (翻) to make way for him.
The vanguard shouted:
"Make way for the General's boat!"
Fān (翻) sternly said:
"Having lost loyalty and trustworthiness,
how can one serve a lord?
Having surrendered two cities,
and still calling him 'General,'
is that permissible?"
Fāng (芳) closed his door, did not respond, and quickly made way.
Later, Fān (翻) traveled by carriage
and again passed by Fāng (芳)'s camp gate.
The officer closed the gate,
and the carriage could not pass.
Fān (翻) again angrily said:
"When it should be closed, you open it;
when it should be open, you close it.
How can this be appropriate?"
When Fāng (芳) heard this,
he showed a look of shame.
Fān (翻) was blunt and straightforward by nature
and frequently made mistakes when drunk.
Quán (權) and Zhāng Zhāo (張昭) were discussing immortals,
and Fān (翻) pointed at Zhāo (昭) and said:
"They are all dead men,
yet they speak of immortals.
How can there be immortals in this world!"
Quán (權)'s accumulated anger was not just from one incident;
thus, he exiled Fān (翻) to Jiāozhōu (交州).
Although he was in exile for his transgressions,
he tirelessly lectured and studied.
His students numbered several hundred.
He also wrote commentaries on Lǎozi (老子), Lúnyǔ (論語), and Guóyǔ (國語),
all of which have been passed down to posterity.
Initially,
Dīng Lǎn (丁覽) of Shānyīn (山陰)
and Xú Líng (徐陵) of Tàimò (太末)
were either among the county officials
or unrecognized by the masses.
Fān (翻), upon seeing them,
immediately befriended them,
and they eventually achieved prominent reputations.
He lived in the south for over ten years
and died at the age of seventy.
He was returned and buried in his old tomb,
and his wife and children were allowed to return.
Fān (翻) had eleven sons.
The fourth son, Sì (汜), was the most famous.
In the early years of Yǒng'ān (永安),
he rose from Xuǎncáoláng (選曹郎) to Sànqí Zhōng Chángshì (散騎中常侍).
Later, he became Jiānjūn Shǐzhě (監軍使者)
and died of illness while campaigning against Fúyán (扶嚴).
Sì (汜)'s younger brother Zhōng (忠) was the Grand Administrator of Yídū (宜都).
Sǒng (聳) was the Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉),
and was successively promoted to Tíngwèi (廷尉),
and Grand Administrator of Xiāngdōng (湘東) and Héjiān (河間).
Bǐng (昺) was the Tíngwèi Shàngshū (廷尉尚書)
and Grand Administrator of Jìyīn (濟陰).
Lù Jì, courtesy name Gōngjì,
was a native of Wú County in Wú Commandery.
His father, Kāng,
was the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng at the end of the Hàn dynasty.
When Jì was six years old,
he met Yuán Shù in Jiǔjiāng.
Shù offered him oranges.
Jì concealed three in his bosom.
When he left,
he bowed in farewell and they fell to the ground.
Shù said to him,
"Lù Láng, as a guest, why do you conceal oranges in your bosom?"
Jì knelt and replied,
"I wish to take them home and give them to my mother."
Shù was greatly surprised by this.
When Sūn Cè was in Wú,
Zhāng Zhāo, Zhāng Hóng, and Qín Sōng were his chief guests.
They were discussing how the four seas were not yet pacified,
and that it was necessary to use military might to achieve peace.
Jì, being young, was sitting at the end of the seats.
He loudly declared from a distance,
"In the past, Guǎn Yíwú assisted Qí Huánggōng,
uniting the lords nine times,
and bringing peace to the world once,
without using chariots and soldiers.
Kǒngzǐ said, 'If people from afar are not submissive,
then cultivate one's cultural virtue to attract them.'
Now, those discussing do not strive for the method of embracing virtue and morality to win people over,
but only advocate military might.
Though I, Jì, am but a mere child,
I find this deeply unsettling."
Zhāo and the others were astonished by him.
Jì was imposing in appearance,
broadly learned and knowledgeable,
and well-versed in astronomy, calendrical calculations, and mathematics.
Yú Fān, who was older and renowned,
and Páng Tǒng, a notable scholar from Jīngzhōu,
who was also slightly older,
were both good friends with Jì.
When Sūn Quán took control of affairs,
he appointed Jì as a Clerk of Petitions (Zòucáo Yuàn).
Due to his upright conduct, he was feared.
He was then dispatched as the Grand Administrator of Yùlín,
additionally given the title of General of the Household (Piānjiāngjūn),
and supplied with two thousand soldiers.
Jì, having a limp,
and also a mind [intent on] refined scholarship,
it was not his ambition.
Despite having military duties,
he did not abandon his writings.
He composed the *Húntiān Tú* (Diagram of the Celestial Sphere),
and annotated the *Yì* and explained *Xuán* (mysterious studies);
all were transmitted to later generations.
He foresaw his day of demise,
and thus composed a valedictory statement, saying:
"Lù Jì of Wú Commandery, a devoted scholar of Hàn,
young, he diligently studied the *Shī* and *Shū*,
grown, he played with the *Lǐ* and *Yì*.
Receiving the command to campaign south,
he encountered illness and misfortune.
His destined life was not [long],
alas, a sorrowful separation!"
He also said:
"From now on,
beyond sixty years,
chariots will share the same tracks,
and books will share the same script.
I regret not living to see it."
He died at the age of thirty-two.
His eldest son, Hóng,
was the Commandant of the Southern District of Kuàijī.
His second son, Ruì,
was the Commandant of Chángshuǐ.
Zhāng Wēn, courtesy name Huìshù,
was a native of Wú County in Wú Commandery.
His father, Yǔn,
was renowned throughout the province and commanderies for his readiness to part with wealth for scholars.
He served as Sūn Quán's Clerk of the Eastern Bureau (Dōngcáoyuàn)
before he passed away.
Wēn cultivated his integrity in his youth,
and had a remarkably imposing appearance.
Quán heard of him
and asked his high ministers,
"With whom should Wēn be compared today?"
The Grand [Minister of] Agriculture (Dàsīnóng), Liú Jī, said,
"He can be compared to Quán Cóng."
The Grand Astrologer (Tàicháng), Gù Yǒng, said,
"Jī does not fully understand his character.
Wēn has no equal today."
Quán said,
"If that is so,
Zhāng Yǔn did not die without a successor."
When summoned and granted an audience,
his eloquence and responsiveness
made observers lean forward in awe.
Quán changed his demeanor and treated him with greater deference.
When he left,
Zhāng Zhāo grasped his hand and said,
"This old man places his hopes in you,
