you should make them clear."
He was appointed Gentleman-consultant (Yìláng) and Minister of Personnel (Xuǎncáo Shàngshū),
then transferred to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù).
He was greatly trusted and esteemed.
At that time, he was thirty-two years old,
and was sent as Envoy to Shǔ with the title General of the Household Who Assists Righteousness (Fǔyì Zhōnglángjiàng).
Quán said to Wēn,
"It is not fitting for you to travel far,
but I fear that Zhūgě Kǒngmíng does not understand my intention in communicating with the Cáo clan,
therefore I am asking you to go.
If the Shānyuè are all pacified,
I then wish to engage in a major undertaking against [Wèi].
The duty of an envoy
is to accept the mission, not to question the words."
Wēn replied,
"I have no intimate counsel within [the court],
nor special diplomatic skills when dispatched.
I fear I will not achieve the meritorious praise of Zhāng Lǎo,
nor the effectiveness in statecraft of Zǐchǎn.
However, Zhūgě Liàng, being perspicacious and calculating,
will surely understand the appropriateness of the divine strategy's flexibility and restraint.
Furthermore, he has received the benevolent protection of the court.
Inferring Liàng's mind,
there will surely be no doubts or wavering."
When Wēn arrived in Shǔ,
he presented a memorial at the palace gate, saying:
"In the past, Gāozōng, through his period of mourning, revived the Yin dynasty to a second flourishing.
King Chéng, though young, elevated the Zhōu virtue to a state of great peace.
Their achievements covered the entire world,
their renown spread boundlessly.
Now, Your Majesty, with your discerning wisdom,
matches the ancients,
presiding over all affairs with excellent assistants,
shining brightly like the arrayed stars.
Near and far, all who hear of you
are filled with joy and reliance.
The State of Wú diligently exerts its strength,
clearing and purifying the banks of the Jiāng.
We wish to pacify the world with those who possess the Way,
committing our hearts and aligning our plans,
as united as the waters of the Hékǒu.
Military affairs are [difficult] and troublesome,
and we are lacking in manpower for service.
Therefore, enduring the shame of being considered uncouth,
I, your humble servant Wēn, am sent to convey our goodwill.
Your Majesty, who upholds禮儀,
will not casually dismiss this.
Since I entered the distant border,
and even when I reached the nearby suburbs,
I have frequently been honored with warm welcomes,
and imperial edicts of grace have been repeatedly bestowed.
Fearing this honor,
I am filled with trepidation, as if startled.
I respectfully present the sealed letter I carry."
Shǔ greatly valued his talent.
Upon his return,
shortly thereafter,
he was sent to Yùzhāng to organize troops for an expedition.
His mission was not yet completed.
Quán, having secretly harbored resentment against Wēn for praising the administration of Shǔ,
and also disliking his great fame,
which captivated the common people,
feared that he would ultimately not serve his own purpose.
He sought a way to slander him.
It so happened that the affair of Jì Yàn arose,
and he consequently used this to make his move.
Yàn, courtesy name Zǐxiū,
was also a man from Wújùn.
Wēn had brought him in
to be a Selection Registrar (xuǎncáo láng),
and he rose to the position of Minister (shàngshū).
Yàn was stern and upright by nature,
and liked to engage in pure criticism.
Seeing that the government offices and their officials at the time were corrupt and disorderly,
with many unsuitable individuals,
he wished to make clear distinctions between good and bad,
and separate the worthy from the foolish.
He impeached numerous officials,
and scrutinized the selection of officials in the three departments.
Most were demoted from high positions to lower ones,
losing several ranks.
Of those who retained their original positions, not even one in ten did so.
Those who were greedy and corrupt in their positions,
with ignoble aspirations and character,
were all made military officers,
and placed in military camps and offices to house them.
As a result, a multitude of grievances accumulated,
and subtle slanders began to spread.
It was widely reported that Yàn and the Selection Registrar Xú Biāo
acted purely on personal feelings,
their likes and dislikes not guided by public principle.
Yàn and Biāo both committed suicide as a result.
Wēn had always agreed with Yàn and Biāo,
frequently exchanging letters and documents with them,
and communicating news back and forth.
Therefore, Wēn was charged with an offense.
Quán imprisoned him and handed him over to the authorities,
issuing an edict which stated:
“Previously, I ordered Zhāng Wēn to be summoned,
emptying myself to receive him.
Upon his arrival, he was granted prominent positions,
surpassing old retainers.
How could I have expected such a villain,
harboring disloyal intentions?
Previously, Jì Yàn's father and elder brother
had attached themselves to the wicked and rebellious.
I had no reservations,
and therefore promoted and entrusted him with responsibility,
wishing to see what kind of person Yàn was.
Upon observation,
his true nature was indeed revealed.
Yet Wēn formed a life-and-death alliance with him.
Whatever Yàn promoted or demoted,
Wēn was the prime instigator,
mutually supporting each other,
acting as front and back.
If one was not Wēn's partisan,
they would immediately be found fault with,
and criticized harshly.
Furthermore, I previously appointed Wēn to supervise the three commanderies,
to direct officials, retainers, and remnant soldiers.
At that time, fearing trouble,
I wanted him to return quickly,
thus granting him ceremonial halberds
and encouraging him with authority.
But he proceeded to Yùzhāng,
and memorialized to campaign against entrenched villains.
I trusted and accepted his words,
and specifically assigned him five thousand soldiers from the Ràozhàng, Zhàngxià, and Jiěfán divisions.
Later, when I heard Cáo Pī himself advanced from Huái and Sì,
I therefore preemptively ordered Wēn to sally forth if an emergency arose.
Yet Wēn brought all the generals inside
and stationed them in the deep mountains,
disobeying the command.
Fortunately, Pī retreated on his own;
otherwise,
the consequences would have been dire and impossible to fathom.
Moreover, Yīn Lǐ
was originally summoned for divination.
Yet Wēn repeatedly requested to take him to Shǔ,
spreading his fame in a foreign land,
and making much talk about him.
Furthermore, upon Lǐ's return,
he should have returned to his original post,
but Wēn made him guard the Household Affairs Registrar (hùcáo láng) in the Ministry of Personnel;
such appointments
were entirely Wēn's doing.
Also, Wēn told Jiǎ Yuán,
‘I will recommend you to be an Imperial Censor,’
and told Jiǎng Kāng,
‘I will use you to replace Jiǎ Yuán,’
solely to flaunt the national favor as his own influence.
He paraded the national favor as his own power.
Estimating his treacherous heart,
there was nothing he would not do.
I cannot bear to expose him in the marketplace,
so I now banish him back to his home commandery
to serve as a menial clerk.
Alas, Wēn,
you are fortunate to be spared death!”
General Luò Tǒng submitted a memorial arguing for Zhāng Wēn:
"I humbly submit, Your Highness,
that Heaven bestowed upon you brilliant virtue,
and the gods inspired your sagely heart.
You have summoned outstanding talents from all directions,
and placed exceptional individuals in your court.
While many officials have received your profound and generous grace,
Zhāng Wēn also benefited from your most profound favor.
Yet Wēn brought upon himself crimes and censure,
failing to live up to the honorable opportunities given him.
Thinking of this,
it is indeed regrettable and painful.
However, in my dealings,
I have observed and listened on behalf of the state,
and deeply understand his situation.
Therefore, I secretly present my argument.
Wēn truly harbored no ulterior motives in his heart,
nor did he commit any rebellious acts.
He is simply still young,
and his experience in weighty matters is shallow.
Yet he bears a blazing favor,
embodies exceptional talent,
confidently discusses right and wrong,
and offers opinions of praise and criticism.
Consequently, those who sought power envied his favor,
those who contended for fame resented his talent,
the silent disapproved of his discussions,
and those with flaws tried to suppress his opinions.
This is what your ministers ought to discern carefully,
and what this wise court ought to thoroughly investigate.
In the past, Jiǎ Yì
was a minister of utmost loyalty.
Emperor Hàn Wén
was a monarch of great enlightenment.
Yet, with a single word from Jiàng and Guàn,
Jiǎ Yì was sent far away.
Why?
Because those who hated him were deeply entrenched,
and those who slandered him were cunning.
As a result, the world misunderstood him,
and his injustice became manifest to later generations.
Thus, Kǒngzǐ said, 'To be a ruler is difficult,
and to be a minister is not easy.'
Though Wēn's wisdom is not that of strategists,
nor his martial prowess that of fierce tigers,
yet his refined and elegant character,
his heroic and outstanding virtue,
his literary brilliance,
and his debating skill,
make him exceptionally superior to the masses,
shining brightly and illuminating his generation.
No one in his time has been able to match him.
Therefore, when discussing Wēn's talent, it is truly regrettable;
when speaking of his crimes, they are pardonable.
If you could endure your majestic wrath to pardon such profound virtue,
and forgive such worthy talent to strengthen your great enterprise,
it would surely be a splendid glory for this wise court,
and a beautiful sight for all four directions.
The state's stance on Jì Yàn
was not to treat him as a prohibited clan member;
rather, he was treated as an ordinary citizen.
Therefore, he was first employed by Zhū Zhì,
then recommended by the populace,
subsequently entrusted by this wise court,
and also befriended by Wēn.
The righteousness between ruler and minister
is the most important righteousness;
the relationship between friends
is the lightest of relationships.
Since the state found no fault with Yàn regarding the most important righteousness,
Wēn likewise found no fault in befriending Yàn in the lightest of relationships.
While the times favored him from above,
Wēn secretly befriended him from below.
As for wicked people,
if allowed to roam free in mountainous terrains,
they become dangerous bandits;
but if placed in flat lands,
they become strong soldiers.
Therefore, Wēn intended to recruit these wicked people,
to eliminate the harm of dangerous bandits,
and to increase the strength of able soldiers.
However, he stumbled,
and his achievements did not match his words.
Yet, if we compare his dispatch of troops
to that of Xǔ Yàn,
in terms of quantity,
Wēn did not send fewer;
in terms of effectiveness,
Wēn was not inferior;
as for speed,
Wēn was not slower.
Thus, he was able to arrive in the autumn and winter months,
answering the call when there was an alert.
He dared not forget your grace and withhold his effort.
When Wēn arrived in Shǔ,
he praised Yīn Lǐ together with others.
Although a minister should not have foreign relations,
this can also be excused.
'Foreign relations' refers to privately associating without the ruler's command,
or secretly communicating about matters not concerning the state.
If one acts on command,
thereby cultivating good relations for the ruler,
and also expresses one's own feelings,
this is also the way of a minister acting as an envoy.
Thus, when Kǒngzǐ was an envoy to neighboring states,
he observed the ritual of private audiences;
and when Jìzǐ was a guest in the various Huá states,
he also engaged in discussions during banquets.
The ancients had a saying:
'To know a ruler,
observe those he employs.'
Seeing the brilliance of his subordinates
reveals the majesty of their superior.
If Wēn praised Lǐ,
and was able to make the other marvel at him,
it truly served to demonstrate the excellence of our ministers,
to show that the envoy was the right person for the job,
to display the nation's beauty in foreign lands,
and to broadcast the ruler's mandate to other countries.
This is why when Zhào Wénzǐ of Jìn allied with Sòng,
he praised Suí Huì to Qū Jiàn;
and when King Sūn Yǔ of Chǔ was an envoy to Jìn,
he extolled Zuǒ Shǐ to Zhào Yāng.
They also praised the assistants of other nations,
and extolled the ministers of their own country.
The classics and commentaries laud this as glorifying the state,
and do not censure it as engaging in foreign diplomacy.
Wáng Jìng did not worry about the times internally,
nor did he rush to affairs externally.
Wēn impeached him without partiality,
and recommended him without pretense.
Consequently, he and Jìng became great enemies.
This is clear proof of his utmost loyalty.
Jìng's military might
and his capacity for important tasks
both surpassed Jiǎ Yuán and Jiǎng Kāng.
Since Wēn could not allow private feelings to accommodate Jìng,
how could he dare betray his principles to align with Yuán and Kāng?
Moreover, Yuán was not diligent in his duties,
and was incompetent in his work.
Wēn repeatedly confronted him with stern expressions,
and impeached him with harsh words.
If he truly wished to betray his principles and cause trouble,
he would not necessarily have favored Yuán.
All these points,
when compared with the facts, do not align;
when examined by the multitude, they are not proven.
I humbly believe that even if a ruler possesses sagely and wise qualities,
and extraordinary intelligence,
yet with one person's body
to govern millions of people,
from within the layers of palaces
to observe beyond the four borders,
to illuminate the feelings of all subordinates,
and to seek the principles of myriad affairs,
it is still not easy to encompass everything.
Thus, one must listen to and examine the words of subordinates
to broaden the scope of one's brilliant insight.
Now, those who denounce Wēn are earnest,
and those of us who support Wēn are also firm.
Both sides are clever in their words,
and both are sincere in their intentions.
Each claims to act for the state,
and who among them claims to act for private gain?
In a moment of urgency,
it is still difficult to discern immediately.
However, with Your Highness's keen intelligence,
to observe the right and wrong of the discussions,
if you would quietly focus your divine spirit and retain your thoughts,
meticulously examine every detail,
what feelings could remain hidden and unexpressed?
What matters could remain obscure and unclarified?
Wēn is not my close relative,
nor am I one who loves Wēn.
In ancient times, gentlemen
all suppressed personal grievances
to enhance their ruler's discernment.
As they acted thus before,
I would be ashamed to neglect it now.
Therefore, I express my long-held feelings today,
presenting my humble words for your sagely hearing.
This is truly to serve the wise court wholeheartedly,
and not out of concern for Wēn himself."
Sūn Quán ultimately did not accept it.
Six years later,
Wēn died of illness.
His two younger brothers, Zhī and Bái,
also had talent and renown,
and were dismissed along with Wēn.
Luò Tǒng, courtesy name Gōngxù,
was a native of Wūshāng, Kuàijī.
His father, Jùn,
rose to the office of Chancellor of Chén,
and was killed by Yuán Shù.
Tǒng's mother remarried,
becoming a concubine of Huà Xīn.
Tǒng was eight at the time,
and so he returned to Kuàijī with a close relative.
His mother saw him off.
He bowed in farewell and got into the carriage,
but did not look back.
His mother wept behind him.
The driver said,
"Your lady mother is still there."
Tǒng said,
"I do not wish to increase my mother's sorrow,
hence I did not look back."
He served his stepmother with great diligence.
At that time, there was a famine,
and many local villagers and travelers from afar were in distress.
Tǒng reduced his own food and drink for them.
His elder sister, who was kind and virtuous,
was widowed and childless.
She saw Tǒng and felt very sorry for him,
repeatedly asking him the reason.
Tǒng said,
"When gentlemen suffer from insufficient food,
how can I be the only one to eat my fill?"
His sister said,
"If that is truly the case,
why did you not tell me,
but instead suffer like this?"
She then gave Tǒng her private grain,
and also told their mother.
Their mother also esteemed him,
and consequently allowed him to distribute it.
Because of this, his fame became known.
When Sūn Quán, as general, took up the post of Administrator of Kuàijī,
Tǒng, at twenty years old,
was appointed acting Chancellor of Wūchéng.
The households under his administration numbered over ten thousand,
and all praised his benevolent governance.
Quán commended him,
summoned him to be Minister of Merit,
and acting Cavalry Commandant,
and married him to the daughter of his elder paternal cousin, Fǔ.
Tǒng was dedicated to rectifying and observing,
and whatever he heard or saw,
he would not wait until morning to address.
He often urged Quán to honor the worthy and treat scholars courteously,
diligently seeking out what was beneficial and what was detrimental.
On days of feasting and rewards,
he suggested that Quán should speak to each person individually,
inquire about their difficulties,
add personal encouragement,
induce and persuade them to speak,
observe their aspirations,
so that all would feel grateful and indebted,
harboring a desire to repay him.
Quán accepted and adopted his advice.
He was then appointed Central Commander of the Upholders of Loyalty,
leading three thousand Wǔshè guards.
When Líng Tǒng died,
he was again given command of his troops.
At this time, conscriptions and levies were frequent,
exacerbated by epidemics,
causing a depletion of households.
Tǒng submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your servant has heard that rulers of a state
consider holding territory as strength and wealth,
controlling power and favor as honor and nobility,
displaying virtue and righteousness as glory and distinction,
and having descendants for generations as abundant fortune.
However, wealth relies on the people's production,
strength relies on the people's labor,
authority relies on the people's influence,
fortune arises from the people's prosperity,
virtue awaits the people's flourishing,
and righteousness is practiced through the people.
With these six aspects prepared,
then one can respond to Heaven and receive fortune,
preserving the clan and benefiting the nation.
The Shū says: 'Without the ruler, the multitude cannot be at peace,
and without the multitude, the ruler cannot expand in all directions.'
Extending from this statement,
then the people are secure because of the ruler,
and the ruler prospers because of the people—
this is an unchanging principle.
Now, strong enemies are not yet eliminated,
and the realm is not yet in order.
The three armies are endlessly engaged in duties,
and the Jiang borders are under unceasing defense preparations.
Conscriptions and levies have been frequent,
accumulated over many years.
Added to this are the disasters of plague and death,
causing counties to become desolate and empty,
and fields to lie waste.
I hear that in the dependent cities,
the number of households is progressively dwindling,
and there are many disabled and elderly,
with few able-bodied men.
Hearing this,
my heart feels as if it is burning.
Reflecting on the causes,
the common people are ignorant.
They naturally have a disposition to cherish their homeland and be reluctant to move,
and moreover, those who have previously been sent out as soldiers,
if they live, are distressed and without warmth or sustenance;
if they die, their bones are abandoned and never returned.
For this reason, they are especially attached to their roots and dread distant places,
equating it with death.
Whenever there is a conscription,
the weak, the diligent, those with heavy family burdens who stay at home are the first to be sent.
Those with a little wealth
exhaust their families to offer bribes,
heedless of their ultimate ruin.
The nimble ones then flee into dangerous terrain,
joining with groups of evildoers.
The populace is utterly depleted,
crying out in anxiety and distress.
When they are anxious and distressed, they do not engage in productive activities;
when they do not engage in productive activities, they become impoverished;
when they become impoverished, they do not enjoy life.
Therefore, when their stomachs are empty,
rebellious thoughts arise and many defect.
I also hear among the people
that if their residences are small and they can barely support themselves,
when they bear children,
many do not raise them.
Poor soldiers in agricultural colonies
also frequently abandon their children.
Heaven gives them life,
yet parents kill them.
This not only risks violating the harmonious energy,
and disturbing the yin and yang,
but also, Your Highness has established the foundation and founded the state,
an enterprise without end.
Strong neighbors and great enemies cannot be destroyed in an instant,
and constant defense of the borders is not a matter of a few months' garrison.
Yet the soldiers and people are dwindling,
and the next generation is not being raised.
This is not the way to endure for long years
and achieve success.
Indeed, the state having people
is like water having a boat:
when it is calm, it is safe;
when it is turbulent, it is perilous.
The foolish cannot be deceived,
and the weak cannot be overcome.
This is why sagely kings value them,
and fortune and calamity depend on them.
Therefore, they adjust with the people,
observing the times to formulate policies.
At present, the duties of chief officials, who are close to the people,
are merely to acquire provisions,
to deal with immediate emergencies,
and few again govern with benevolence and kindness,
matching Your Highness's all-encompassing benevolence
and diligent solicitude.
Official and popular customs
are daily decaying,
gradually declining.
This situation cannot last long.
Indeed, one cures an illness before it becomes severe,
and removes a problem while it is not yet deep.
I wish Your Highness would, during the brief leisure from myriad affairs,
focus your mind on reflection,
replenish the desolate and empty,
make profound long-term plans,
nurture the remaining people,
enrich the resources of human and wealth,
so as to shine alongside the three luminaries,
and be as revered as Heaven and Earth.
This is your servant Tǒng's great wish,
sufficient for me to die without regret."
Quán was moved by Tǒng's words
and paid deep attention to them.
He then followed Lù Xùn in defeating the Shǔ army at Yídū,
and was promoted to Lieutenant General.
In the early years of Huángwǔ,
Cáo Rén attacked Rúxū,
sending his subordinate general Cháng Diāo and others to raid Zhōngzhōu.
Tǒng and Yán Guī jointly resisted and defeated them.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīnyáng Pavilion,
and later became Commander of Rúxū.
He frequently presented advantageous proposals,
submitting dozens of memorials throughout his career.
All his suggestions were excellent,
but due to their length, not all are included.
He especially emphasized that recruitment by bounty among the people fostered evil and corrupted customs,
creating disloyal and rebellious sentiments,
and urgently needed to be stopped.
Quán discussed this repeatedly with him,
and ultimately implemented it.
He died at the age of thirty-six
in the seventh year of Huángwǔ.
Lù Mào, courtesy name Zǐzhāng,
was the younger brother of Chancellor Lù Xùn.
In his youth, he loved learning and was devoted to righteousness.
Chén Róng from Chén-guó, Púyáng Yì from Chénliú, Jiǎng Zuǎn from Pèi-jùn, Yuán Dí from Guǎnglíng, and others
were all poor but ambitious.
They came to Lù Mào to live and associate with him.
Lù Mào shared his meager provisions and delicacies with them,
and they shared plenty and scarcity together.
When Xú Yuán, from the same commandery,
moved to Kuàijī,
Lù Mào did not know him personally.
However, Xú Yuán, before his death, left a letter
entrusting his orphaned and weak children to Lù Mào.
Lù Mào erected a tomb for him
and took in and guided his sons.
Also, Lù Mào's paternal cousin, Lù Jì, died young.
His two sons and one daughter
were all a few years old or younger.
Lù Mào took them in and raised them
until they grew up before they separated.
When the province and commandery invited him to serve,
he always declined.
At that time, the Secretariat Director Jì Yàn was actively evaluating people, judging good and bad,
and distinguishing between the three bureaus.
He greatly publicized people's hidden faults
to make their disgrace manifest.
Lù Mào wrote to him, saying:
"The sages commend the good and pity the foolish,
forgetting faults and remembering merits,
thereby achieving beautiful transformation.
Moreover, the imperial enterprise is just beginning,
and is about to unify the world.
This is the time when Gāo-Hán abandoned flaws and employed talents.
If good and evil are made to flow separately,
and the monthly evaluations of Rǔ and Yǐng are highly valued,
it can certainly inspire customs and clarify teachings,
but I fear it may not be easy to implement.
It would be better to distantly emulate Zhòngní's universal love,
and moderately follow Guō Tài's broad assistance,
which would be more beneficial to the great Dao."
Jì Yàn was unable to act on this advice
and ultimately met with disaster.
In the first year of Jiāhé,
Lù Mào was summoned by public carriage
and appointed Gentleman of the Household and Minister of the Bureau of Personnel.
Sūn Quán was enraged by Gōngsūn Yuān's cunning and deceitful duplicity
and wished to personally lead an expedition against him.
Lù Mào submitted a memorial, remonstrating:
"I have heard that when sagely kings govern distant barbarians,
they merely keep them in check,
not always seeking to possess them.
Therefore, in ancient times, the territories
were called the 'wild domains,'
meaning they were vague and unstable,
and could not be secured.
Now, Gōngsūn Yuān is a minor villain among the Eastern Yi,
isolated in a corner of the sea.
Although he bears a human face,
he is no different from birds and beasts.
The reason the state spared no wealth and treasures to bestow upon him
was not because it appreciated his virtue and righteousness,
but sincerely wished to entice and fool him,
to secure his horses.
Gōngsūn Yuān's arrogance and cunning,
relying on his remoteness to defy commands,
is merely the usual state of the wild tribes;
why should it be deeply surprising?
In the past, the various Hàn emperors also eagerly dealt with foreign barbarians,
sending envoys and scattering goods,
filling the Western Regions.
Although there were times when they submitted respectfully,
the number of envoys who were harmed
and goods that were confiscated
was countless.
Now, Your Majesty cannot bear this momentary indignation,
and wishes to cross the vast sea
and personally tread upon his land.
Your humble ministers, in our foolish deliberation,
privately consider this to be unsafe.
Why?
The northern bandits and our state
are geographically connected.
Should there be any opportune moment,
they will arrive swiftly.
The reason for crossing the sea to seek horses
and bending to Gōngsūn Yuān's will
was to address an immediate crisis
and remove a deep-seated ailment.
Yet, instead, one abandons the root to pursue the branches,
neglects what is near to govern what is far,
changes strategy out of anger,
and mobilizes the masses out of irritation.
This is what the cunning barbarians wish to hear,
not the best strategy for the Great Wú.
Moreover, the art of war
is to exhaust the enemy with labor,
and await them in comfort,
where the advantages and disadvantages
are often clearly discernible.
Furthermore, Dátǎ Zhǔ is still far
from Gōngsūn Yuān's territory.
When we reach his shore,
our military strength will be divided into three parts:
the strong will advance and attack,
the second will guard the ships,
and the third will transport provisions.
Although there will be many soldiers,
it will be difficult to deploy them all.
Additionally, marching on foot with provisions,
traveling long distances deep into enemy territory,
where the enemy has many horses,
makes interception and harassment unpredictable.
If Gōngsūn Yuān is cunning and deceitful,
and has not cut ties with the north,
on the day the army is mobilized,
they will assist each other like lips and teeth.
If he is truly isolated and without reliance,
he might flee in fear,
and it may be difficult to eliminate him quickly.
If Heaven's punishment is delayed in the northern wilderness,
and the mountain bandits rise up to exploit the opportunity,
I fear this is not a long-term plan for lasting peace."
Sūn Quán did not consent.
Lù Mào again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Military campaigns
were indeed used by previous generations to punish the tyrannical and rebellious,
and to intimidate the four barbarians.
However, such expeditions always took place after the treacherous villains had been eliminated,
and the world was at peace,
when discussions could be held calmly in the imperial court,
with surplus deliberations.
As for a time when the Central Plains are boiling
and the nine regions are entangled,
it generally requires deeply rooting and securing the foundation,
conserving strength and grudging expense,
and striving for self-recuperation,
to await the deficiencies of neighboring enemies.
There has never been a time like this,
when one abandons the near to govern the far,
thereby tiring out the army.
In the past, Wèi Tuó rebelled,
usurping the title of emperor.
At that time, the world was peaceful,
and the common people were prosperous.
The number of armed soldiers
and the accumulation of provisions
could be said to be vast.
Yet, Emperor Wén of Hàn still considered a distant expedition difficult,
and hesitated to mobilize the army,
merely issuing proclamations.
Now, fierce villains have not been eliminated,
and the borders are still alert.
Even if it were the chaos of Chī Yóu or Guǐ Fāng,
one should still differentiate between urgency and delay.
It is not appropriate to prioritize Gōngsūn Yuān.
I beg Your Majesty to restrain your might and rely on strategy,
to temporarily calm the six armies,
to secretly contemplate and plan,
for future considerations.
The world would be exceedingly fortunate."
Sūn Quán read Lù Mào's memorials twice,
and admired his eloquent and incisive arguments,
and so did not proceed with the expedition.
Initially,
Wénrén Mǐn from Lù Mào's commandery was highly regarded in the state and locality,
even more so than Zōng Xiū.
Only Lù Mào thought otherwise,
and later events indeed proved him right.
In the second year of Chìwū,
Lù Mào passed away.
His son, Lù Xǐ, also studied literature
and was fond of evaluating character.
During the reign of Sūn Hào, he served as Minister of the Bureau of Personnel.
Wú Càn, courtesy name Kǒngxiū,
was a native of Wūchéng, Wú-jùn.
When Sūn Hé was county magistrate,
Wú Càn was a minor official.
Sūn Hé greatly admired him.
Later, when Sūn Hé became a general,
he was allowed to select his own senior officials,
and he recommended Wú Càn as Assistant Magistrate of Qū'ā.
He was promoted to Chief Clerk,
and his governance had a good reputation.
Although he rose from humble origins,
he stood shoulder to shoulder and was equally renowned with Lù Xùn and Bǔ Jìng from the same commandery.
When Sūn Quán was General of Chariots and Cavalry,
he summoned Wú Càn to be his Chief Clerk.
He was later dispatched to serve as Magistrate of Shānyīn,
and then returned to become Military Advisor and Commandant.
In the first year of Huángwǔ [222 CE],
Wú Càn, along with Lǚ Fàn, Hè Qí, and others, led a naval force to resist the Wei general Cái Hū at Dòngkǒu.
A great storm arose,
severing the ropes and hawsers of the various ships.
They drifted and were cast ashore,
captured by the Wèi army.
Some capsized and sank.
On the large ships that remained intact,
the people in the water all climbed up and cried out.
Other officers and soldiers, fearing the ships would capsize and sink,
all struck them with spears and halberds, refusing to take them in.
Wú Càn and Huáng Yuān alone ordered their boatmen to take them aboard.
Those around them believed the ships, being heavy, would surely be ruined.
Wú Càn said,
"If the ships are ruined,
we shall all die together!
People are in distress,
how can we abandon them?"
Wú Càn and Huáng Yuān saved over a hundred people.
Upon returning,
Wú Càn was promoted to Grand Administrator of Huìjī,
and invited the recluse Xiè Tán to be his Cóngcáo.
Xiè Tán declined due to illness and did not arrive.
Wú Càn instructed him, saying,
"Indeed, the Yìnglóng is divine in its ability to extend and retract;
the Fènghuáng is esteemed for its auspicious calls.
Why must one conceal one's form beyond the heavens,
or lurk beneath the deepest abyss?"
Wú Càn recruited and gathered a multitude of people,
was appointed Zhāoyì Zhōnglángjiàng,
and with Lǚ Dài, pacified the Shānyuè.
He then entered the court as Túnhú Qīaowèi and Shǎofǔ,
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàifù.
During the crisis of the two palaces,
he spoke out forcefully, upholding righteousness,
clarifying the distinction between the legitimate heir and concubine-born,
wishing to send King Bà of Lǔ to garrison Xiàkǒu,
and ordering Yáng Zhú not to be allowed in the capital.
He also frequently sent news to Lù Xùn.
Lù Xùn was then stationed at Wǔchāng,
and repeatedly submitted memorials to remonstrate.
Because of this, he was slandered and harmed by Bà, Zhú, and others,
imprisoned, and executed.
Zhū Jù, courtesy name Zǐjù,
was a native of Wú County in Wú Commandery.
He had a handsome appearance and great physical strength,
and was also skilled in debate.
In the early part of the Huángwǔ era,
he was summoned and appointed Wǔguān Lángzhōng,
and then made Shìyù Shǐ.
At this time, Jì Yàn, the Shàngshū of the Personnel Department,
abhorred corruption among officials
and wished to purge them.
Zhū Jù believed that the realm was not yet settled,
and that it was fitting to overlook faults for the sake of merit,
casting aside flaws and employing talent.
Raising the pure and degrading the corrupt
would be sufficient to encourage and deter;
if all were demoted at once,
he feared there would be subsequent troubles.
Jì Yàn did not listen,
and ultimately failed.
Sūn Quán sighed over the generals and soldiers,
venting his indignation and lamenting.
He recalled Lǚ Méng and Zhāng Wēn,
believing Zhū Jù possessed both civil and military talents,
and could succeed them.
From then on, he was appointed Jiànyì Qīaowèi,
leading troops to garrison Húshú.
In the first year of Huánglóng [229 CE],
Sūn Quán moved the capital to Jiànyè.
Zhū Jù was summoned to marry a princess,
appointed Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yúnyáng.
He was humble in treating scholars,
lightly regarded wealth, and was fond of giving.
Although his emoluments and rewards were ample, they were often insufficient for his use.
During the Jiāhé era,
large coins were first minted,
each worth five hundred.
Later, Zhū Jù's military division was supposed to receive thirty thousand strings of cash.
The artisan Wáng Suì fraudulently took them.
Lǚ Yī, the Diǎnxiào, suspected Zhū Jù had actually taken them.
He interrogated the responsible officials,
who died under flogging.
Zhū Jù mourned their innocence
and provided them with lavish coffins and burials.
Lǚ Yī then memorialized that Zhū Jù's officials were concealing for him,
hence the generous funeral.
Sūn Quán repeatedly questioned Zhū Jù,
who had no means to clear himself,
and awaited punishment on a straw mat.
Several months later,
Liú Zhù, an officer of the military bureau, realized
and stated that Wáng Suì had taken the money.
Sūn Quán was greatly awakened and said,
"Zhū Jù was wronged,
how much more so the officials and common people?"
He then thoroughly investigated Lǚ Yī's crimes,
and rewarded Liú Zhù a million.
In the ninth year of Chìwū [246 CE],
Zhū Jù was promoted to Piàojí Jiāngjūn.
During the conflict between the two palaces,
Zhū Jù supported the crown prince,
speaking with utmost sincerity,
his righteousness evident in his demeanor,
defending him to the death.
Consequently, he was demoted to Xīndū Jùnchéng.
Before he arrived,
Sūn Hóng, the Zhōngshū Lìng, slandered Zhū Jù.
Taking advantage of Sūn Quán's illness,
Sūn Hóng issued an imperial edict ordering Zhū Jù to commit suicide.
He was fifty-seven years old at the time.
During Sūn Liàng's reign,
his two sons, Xiōng and Sǔn, each again commanded troops.
They were slandered by Quán Gōngzhǔ
and both died.
During the Yǒng'ān era,
his former merits were recalled and recorded.
Xiōng's son, Xuān, inherited the title of Marquis of Yúnyáng
and married a princess.
During Sūn Hào's reign,
Xuān reached the rank of Piàojí Jiāngjūn.
A commentary states: Yú Fān was a straightforward and eccentric man of antiquity,
thus it was difficult for him to avoid trouble in later times.
However, Sūn Quán's inability to tolerate him
shows a lack of broad-mindedness.
Lù Jì to Yáng Xuán
is like Zhòngní to Zuǒ Qīumíng,
or Lǎo Dān to Yán Zhōu;
to take a vessel of sacrifice
and make him guard Nányuè,
is this not to harm such a man!
Zhāng Wēn possessed brilliant literary talent,
but lacked sufficient foresight and caution,
which led to severe misfortune.
Luò Tǒng bravely elucidated great principles,
his words incisive and his reasoning profound,
but he met Sūn Quán when he was closed-minded.
Lù Mào offered earnest and upright remonstrance,
for which gentlemen praised him.
Wú Càn and Zhū Jù suffered hardships and misfortunes,
losing their lives for righteousness.
Alas!
Biography of Lù Xùn, Chapter 13
Lù Xùn, courtesy name Bóyán,
was a native of Wú County in Wú Commandery.
His original name was Yì.
His family was a great clan in Jiāngdōng.
Lù Xùn was orphaned young
and followed his grand-uncle Kāng, the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng, while he was in office.
Yuán Shù had a rift with Kāng
and was about to attack Kāng.
Kāng sent Lù Xùn and his relatives back to Wú.
Lù Xùn was several years older than Kāng's son, Jì,
and managed the household for him.
When Sūn Quán became a general,
Lù Xùn was twenty-one
and began his service in the staff headquarters,
successively serving as secretary in the East and West Cáo departments.
He was then appointed Túntián Dūwèi of Hǎichāng,
and concurrently managed county affairs.
The county suffered continuous droughts for several years.
Lù Xùn opened the granaries to aid the poor,
and encouraged and supervised agriculture and sericulture.
The common people benefited greatly.
At that time, many bandits were hiding in Wú, Huìjī, and Dānyáng.
Lù Xùn presented a practical proposal,
requesting to raise troops there.
Pān Lín, the great bandit leader in the mountains of Huìjī,
had long been a scourge in the region,
and had not been captured for years.
Lù Xùn personally recruited soldiers,
campaigned in the deep and dangerous areas.
All whom he faced submitted,
and his military division already numbered over two thousand men.
When Yóu Tū, the bandit leader in Póyáng, rebelled,
Lù Xùn again went to suppress him.
He was appointed Dìngwēi Qīaowèi,
and his army was stationed at Lìpǔ.
Sūn Quán 權 married his elder brother Sūn Cè's 策 daughter to Lù Xùn 陸遜.
He frequently consulted him on state affairs.
Lù Xùn 陸遜 suggested,
"At present, heroes stand strong,
and wolves eye us covetously.
To defeat enemies and quell chaos
cannot be achieved without a large host.
The mountain bandits are old evils,
entrenched in deep and dangerous terrain.
If our heartland is not pacified,
it will be difficult to plan for distant objectives.
We should greatly enlarge our forces
and select their finest."
Sūn Quán 權 accepted his strategy
and made him Commander of the Right Division under his tent.
At that time, Fèi Zhàn 費棧, a bandit leader from Dānyáng 丹楊, received an official seal and sash from Cáo Gōng 曹公,
inciting the Shānyuè 山越
to act as an internal support for him.
Sūn Quán 權 dispatched Lù Xùn 陸遜 to suppress Fèi Zhàn 費棧.
Fèi Zhàn's 費棧's partisans were numerous, while the attacking force was small.
Lù Xùn 陸遜 then deployed more ceremonial banners,
distributed drums and horns,
and stealthily entered the mountain valleys at night.
They advanced with shouts and drumbeats,
and immediately shattered the enemy.
He then organized the forces of the three eastern commanderies;
the strong were made soldiers,
and the weak were registered as households.
He obtained tens of thousands of elite soldiers.
The old evils were swept away,
and all places he passed through were pacified.
He returned to garrison Wúhú 蕪湖.
Chúnyú Shì 淳于式, the Administrator of Kuàijī 會稽, memorialized that Lù Xùn 陸遜 had wrongly seized civilians,
causing distress throughout the region.
Later, when Lù Xùn 陸遜 went to the capital,
during a conversation,
he praised Chúnyú Shì 淳于式 as an excellent official.
Sūn Quán 權 said,
"Chúnyú Shì 淳ú式 reported against you, yet you recommend him.
Why is this?"
Lù Xùn 陸遜 replied,
"Chúnyú Shì's 淳ú式's intention was to care for the people,
which is why he reported against me.
If I were to further slander Chúnyú Shì 淳ú式 and disturb Your Sagely Hearing,
it would not be conducive to long-term governance."
Sūn Quán 權 said,
"This is truly the act of a magnanimous person;
it is just that others cannot do it."
Lǚ Méng 呂蒙, feigning illness, went to Jiànyè 建業.
Lù Xùn 陸遜 went to see him
and said,
"Guān Yǔ 關羽 is on our border.
How can you leave for so long?
Will there not be cause for worry later?"
Lǚ Méng 呂蒙 said,
"What you say is true,
but my illness is severe."
Lù Xùn 陸遜 said,
"Guān Yǔ 關羽 prides himself on his martial prowess
and looks down upon others.
Having just achieved a great success,
he is arrogant and unrestrained in his ambition.
He is solely focused on advancing north,
not yet suspicious of us.
Hearing of your illness,
he will surely be even less prepared.
If we act unexpectedly now,
we can surely capture and control him.
When you go to see His Supreme Majesty,
you should make a good plan."
Lǚ Méng 呂蒙 said,
"Guān Yǔ 關羽 has always been brave and fierce,
already difficult to contend with,
and moreover, he now holds Jīngzhōu 荊州.
His grace and trust are widely extended,
and having just achieved success,
his courage and influence are even stronger.
He is not easy to scheme against."
When Lǚ Méng 呂蒙 arrived at the capital,
Sūn Quán 權 asked,
"Who can replace you, my lord?"
Lǚ Méng 呂蒙 replied,
"Lù Xùn 陸遜 has profound thoughts and far-reaching plans,
and his talent is sufficient to bear heavy responsibilities.
Observing his strategies,
he can ultimately be entrusted with great tasks.
However, he does not yet have a distant reputation,
so Guān Yǔ 關羽 will not be wary of him;
there will be no such problem.
If you employ him,
you should order him to outwardly conceal himself,
but inwardly observe the opportune moment,
then success can be achieved."
Sūn Quán 權 then summoned Lù Xùn 陸遜,
appointed him General of the Right Division of Cavalry, replacing Lǚ Méng 呂蒙.
When Lù Xùn 陸遜 arrived at Lùkǒu 陸口,
he wrote to Guān Yǔ 關羽, saying,
"Previously, I learned that you observe the opportune moment to act,
conducting your army with discipline,
achieving great victories from small movements.
How magnificent!
The enemy state suffers defeat,
and the advantage is with the allies.
Hearing of your celebration, I clap my hands,
imagining you sweeping across the land,
together supporting the royal order.
Recently, being untalented,
I received my appointment to come west.
I long for your radiant presence,
and wish to receive your excellent counsel."
He also said,
"The capture of Yú Jìn 於禁 and others
has caused joy and admiration near and far.
It is believed that your achievements, General, are sufficient to last through the ages.
Even the army of Jìn Wén 晉文 at Chéngpú 城濮 of old,
or Húaiyīn's 淮陰 strategy of pulling down Zhào 趙,
cannot surpass this.
I hear that Xú Huǎng 徐晃 and others, with few cavalry, have halted their banners,
peeking at your standards.
Cáo Cāo 曹操 is a crafty bandit.
In his anger, he forgets difficulties.
I fear he may secretly increase his forces
to satisfy his ambitions.
Although it is said his army is weary,
he still has fierce warriors.
Moreover, after a battle victory,
one often suffers from underestimating the enemy.
The ancients, relying on tactics,
were even more vigilant after a military victory.
I wish for you, General, to widely plan your strategies
to ensure your complete victory.
I, a mere scholar, am slow and ignorant,
holding a position for which I am unworthy.
I am delighted to be neighbors with your prestige and virtue,
and happy to dedicate myself completely.
Although my strategies may not be perfectly aligned,
they are still worth pondering.
Perhaps, with your enlightened gaze,
you can discern their merit."
Guān Yǔ 關羽 read Lù Xùn's 陸遜's letter
and saw the intent to be humble and rely on him.
He was greatly at ease
and no longer harbored any suspicions.
Lù Xùn 陸遜 fully reported the situation
and elaborated on the essentials for capturing Guān Yǔ 關羽.
Sūn Quán 權 then secretly moved his army upstream,
sending Lù Xùn 陸遜 and Lǚ Méng 呂蒙 as the vanguard.
Upon arrival, they immediately captured Gōng'ān 公安 and Nánjùn 南郡.
Lù Xùn 陸遜 advanced directly,
becoming the Administrator of Yídū 宜都,
was appointed General Pacifying the Borders,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Huátíng 華亭.
Fán Yǒu 樊友, the Administrator of Yídū 宜都 appointed by Liú Bèi 劉備, abandoned his commandery and fled.
The chief officials of all cities and the chieftains of the southern barbarians surrendered.
Lù Xùn 陸遜 requested gold, silver, and copper seals
to provisionally bestow upon the newly surrendered.
This was the eleventh month of the twenty-fourth year of Jiàn'ān 建安 (219 CE).
Lù Xùn 陸遜 dispatched generals Lǐ Yì 李異 and Xiè Jīng 謝旌 and others with three thousand men
to attack the Shǔ 蜀 generals Zhān Yàn 詹晏 and Chén Fèng 陳鳳.
Lǐ Yì 李異 led the naval forces,
and Xiè Jīng 謝旌 led the infantry,
cutting off dangerous strongholds.
They immediately defeated Zhān Yàn 詹晏 and the others,
capturing Chén Fèng 陳鳳 alive.
They also attacked Dèng Fǔ 鄧輔, the Administrator of Fánglíng 房陵, and Guō Mù 郭睦, the Administrator of Nánxiāng 南鄉,
utterly defeating them.
Wén Bù 文布 and Dèng Kǎi 鄧凱, prominent families of Zǐguī 秭歸, gathered several thousand Yi 夷 soldiers,
covering the western flank.
Lù Xùn 陸遜 again dispatched Xiè Jīng 謝旌 to attack and defeat Wén Bù 文布 and Dèng Kǎi 鄧凱.
Wén Bù 文布 and Dèng Kǎi 鄧凱 escaped and fled,
and Shǔ 蜀 made them generals.
Lù Xùn 陸遜 sent men to entice them,
and Wén Bù 文布 led his followers back to surrender.
In total, those killed, captured, and recruited
numbered in the tens of thousands.
Sūn Quán 權 appointed Lù Xùn 陸遜 as Protector of the Right Army and General Pacifying the West,
and advanced his enfeoffment to Marquis of Lóu 婁.
At that time, the scholars from Jīngzhōu 荊州 had recently returned,
and some had not yet found suitable positions.
Lù Xùn 陸遜 submitted a memorial, saying,
"In ancient times, Gāo Zǔ 高祖 of Hàn 漢 received the Mandate
and attracted heroic and extraordinary talents.
Guāng Wǔ 光武 of Hàn 漢 revived the dynasty,
and all the outstanding talents arrived.
As long as one can contribute to the prosperity of the Way and teachings,
distance is not a concern.
Now Jīngzhōu 荊州 has just been pacified,
and its talented individuals are not yet recognized.
I, your humble servant, earnestly
beg for universal grace to cover, carry, extract, and elevate them,
allowing them all to advance themselves.
Then the four seas will crane their necks
and long to return to your great transforming influence."
Sūn Quán 權 respectfully accepted his words.
In the first year of Huángwǔ,
Liú Bèi led a large army to the western border.
Quán ordered Xùn to be Grand Commander and bestowed upon him the imperial credential,
to supervise Zhū Rán, Pān Zhāng, Sòng Qiān, Hán Dāng, Xú Shèng, Xiān Yú Dān, Sūn Huán, and others, with fifty thousand men to resist him.
Bèi advanced from Wūxiá and Jiànpíng, continuously besieging until the border of Yílíng,
setting up dozens of camps.
He used gold brocade and titles as rewards to entice and mobilize various barbarian tribes.
He made General Féng Xí the Chief Commander,
Zhāng Nán the vanguard,
Fǔ Kuāng, Zhào Róng, Liáo Chún, Fù Róng, and others each a separate commander.
He first dispatched Wú Bān with several thousand men to set up camp on flat ground,
intending to challenge them.
All the generals wanted to attack him.
Xùn said:
“There must be a trick here;
let’s just observe.”
Bèi, knowing his plan was unfeasible,
then led eight thousand hidden troops
out from the valley.
Xùn said:
“The reason I did not allow you gentlemen to attack Bān
was because I surmised there must be a cunning reason for it.”
Xùn submitted a memorial, saying:
“Yílíng is a strategic point,
the pass of the state.
Though it is easy to gain,
it is also easy to lose.
Losing it would not only mean the loss of a commandery’s territory,
but Jīngzhōu would also be in peril.
If we contend for it today,
we must ensure success.
Bèi defies Heaven’s constant order,
does not guard his lair,
but dares to deliver himself.
Though I am untalented,
relying on your majestic power,
to attack the rebellious with the obedient,
his destruction is near.
Looking at Bèi’s campaigns before and after,
he mostly failed and rarely succeeded.
Judging from this,
he is not worth worrying about.
Initially, I was concerned that
he would advance both by water and land.
Now, however, he has abandoned his ships for infantry,
setting up camps everywhere.
Observing his deployment,
there will surely be no other changes.
I humbly wish Your Majesty to rest easy,
and not be concerned.”
All the generals uniformly said:
“The attack on Bèi should have been at the beginning.
Now he has been allowed to advance five or six hundred *lǐ*,
and they have been locked in stalemate for seven or eight months.
All the strategic points are now fortified,
so attacking him will surely be unprofitable.”
Xùn said:
“Bèi is a cunning brigand,
who has experienced many things.
When his army first gathered,
their thoughts were focused and keen,
and they could not be challenged.
Now they have stayed for a long time,
without gaining our advantage.
Their troops are weary and their morale low,
and they cannot come up with new plans.
Cornering this bandit
is precisely for today.”
He then first attacked one camp,
but was unsuccessful.
All the generals said:
“It’s just a waste of soldiers.”
Xùn said:
“I already understand the method to defeat them.”
He then commanded each man to carry a bundle of dry grass,
and used fire to attack and capture them.
Once the momentum was established,
he commanded all armies to attack simultaneously,
beheading Zhāng Nán, Féng Xí, and the Hu king Shā Mó Kē, among others,
and destroying over forty of their camps.
Bèi’s generals Dù Lù and Liú Níng were cornered and forced to surrender.
Bèi ascended Mount Mǎ'ān,
and arrayed his troops around himself.
Xùn pressed all his armies to close in from four sides,
and they crumbled and fell apart,
with tens of thousands dead.
Bèi fled by night,
carried by his own messengers,
burning his gongs and armor to cover his retreat,
barely managing to enter Báidì Chéng.
His boats and equipment,
and land and water military supplies,
were all completely lost at once.
Corpses floated,
blocking the river as they drifted downstream.
Bèi was greatly ashamed and indignant,
saying:
“I was humiliated and defeated by Xùn!
Is this not Heaven’s will?!”
Initially,
Sūn Huán had separately attacked Bèi’s vanguard at Yídào,
and was besieged by Bèi,
seeking rescue from Xùn.
Xùn said:
“Not yet.”
The generals said:
“Sūn Āndōng is a member of the ducal clan,
and is now desperately besieged.
How can we not rescue him?”
Xùn said:
“Āndōng has the hearts of his officers and men,
his city is strong, and supplies are ample;
there is nothing to worry about.
Wait until my strategy unfolds;
even if I do not rescue Āndōng,
Āndōng will free himself.”
When his strategy was fully implemented,
Bèi indeed collapsed and fled.
Huán later met Xùn and said:
“Before, I truly resented not being rescued.
Now that it has come to this day,
I realize your strategic planning had its own method.”
When resisting Bèi,
some of the generals were old comrades from Sūn Cè’s time,
or imperial relatives and nobles.
They each boasted and relied on themselves,
not listening to each other.
Xùn drew his sword and said:
“Liú Bèi is famous throughout the land,
feared even by Cáo Cāo.
Now he is within our borders;
this is a formidable opponent.
All of you bear the nation’s grace,
and should unite in harmony,
working together to eliminate this brigand,
to repay what you have received.
But instead, you do not cooperate,
which is not acceptable.
Though I am a mere scholar,
I have received orders from the Lord.
The reason the state has lowered itself to make you all submit to me
is because I have some commendable qualities,
and can endure humiliation and bear heavy responsibilities.
Each of you has your duties;
how can you refuse?!
Military regulations are constant
and must not be violated.”
When Bèi was defeated,
many of the strategies came from Xùn,
and the generals then submitted.
Quán heard of it and said:
“Why did you not report those generals who violated orders from the start?”
Xùn replied:
“I have received profound grace,
and my responsibility exceeds my talent.
Moreover, these generals are either trusted confidantes,
or capable as claws and teeth,
or meritorious officials.
They are all individuals with whom the state should jointly accomplish great affairs.
Although I am dull and weak,
I secretly admire the righteousness of Xiāngrú and Kòu Xún in humbling themselves,
to aid the affairs of the state.”
Quán laughed heartily and praised him,
and additionally appointed Xùn as General Who Stabilizes the State,
and concurrently Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and immediately changed his封 to Marquis of Jiānglíng.
Moreover, once Bèi settled in Báidì,
Xú Shèng, Pān Zhāng, Sòng Qiān, and others eagerly memorialized, saying Bèi could surely be captured,
and requested to attack him again.
Quán asked Xùn about this.
Xùn, along with Zhū Rán and Luò Tǒng, believed that Cáo Pī had assembled a large army,
outwardly claiming to assist our state in attacking Bèi,
but inwardly harbored malicious intentions.
They resolutely decided to return immediately.
Not long after,
the Wèi army indeed emerged,
and they were attacked from three sides.
Bèi soon fell ill and died,
and his son Chán ascended the throne.
Zhūgě Liàng assumed power,
and allied with Quán.
Whenever the circumstances called for it,
Quán would have Xùn speak to Liàng,
and even had Quán’s personal seal carved,
and placed it with Xùn.
Whenever Quán wrote letters to Chán and Liàng,
he would always show them to Xùn first.
If anything was inappropriate in terms of importance or feasibility,
he would immediately have it revised,
and then sealed and sent it with the stamp.
In the seventh year,
Sūn Quán ordered Zhōu Fáng, the Administrator of Póyáng, to trick Cáo Xiū, the Grand Marshal of Wèi.
Xiū indeed led his army into Wǎn,
so Sūn Quán summoned Lù Xùn, granted him the假黃鉞 (jiǎ huángyuè),
and made him Grand Commander
to intercept Xiū.
Once Xiū realized he had been deceived,
he was ashamed of being tricked and enticed.
Relying on his numerous and elite troops,
he then engaged in battle.
Lù Xùn personally commanded the center,
ordered Zhū Huán and Quán Cóng to be the left and right wings,
and the three columns advanced together.
They indeed charged Xiū's ambushed troops,
then drove them away.
Chasing the fleeing and pursuing the routed,
they went straight to Jiáshí,
beheading and capturing over ten thousand men,
and seizing ten thousand horses, mules, donkeys, and carts,
completely depleting his military supplies and equipment.
When Xiū returned,
a carbuncle erupted on his back and he died.
When the various armies returned triumphantly, passing through Wǔchāng,
Sūn Quán ordered his attendants to cover Lù Xùn with the imperial parasol
as he entered and exited the palace gates.
Everything Sūn Quán bestowed upon Lù Xùn
was an imperial item of the highest rarity,
unrivaled at that time.
He was sent back to Xīlíng.
In the first year of Huánglóng,
he was appointed Grand General and Right Protector.
That year,
Sūn Quán made an eastern tour to Jiànyè,
leaving the Crown Prince, the imperial princes, and the nine ministers of the Department of State Affairs.
He summoned Lù Xùn to assist the Crown Prince,
and also to manage matters in Jīngzhōu and the three commanderies of Yùzhāng,
overseeing military and state affairs.
At that time, Lǜ, the Marquis of Jiànchāng, built a duck fighting enclosure in front of his hall,
adding some small decorative touches.
Lù Xùn said sternly:
"Your Lordship should diligently study the classics to improve yourself.
What is the use of this?"
Lǜ immediately demolished it.
Sōng, the Colonel of Archery and the closest to the imperial princes,
had disorderly troops in a drill.
Lù Xùn, facing him, shaved the heads of his subordinate officers.
Xiè Jǐng of Nányáng was skilled in Liú Yì's theory of "punishment first, then ritual."
Lù Xùn admonished Jǐng, saying:
"Ritual has long been superior to punishment.
Yì, with his trivial sophistry, distorts the teachings of the former sages.
All of that is wrong.
You are now serving the Eastern Palace;
you should follow benevolence and righteousness to make your virtuous reputation manifest.
As for such discussions,
there is no need to expound upon them."
Although Lù Xùn was physically away,
his heart was with the state.
He submitted a memorial discussing current affairs, saying:
"Your servant believes that the laws are severe,
and many offenders are commoners.
In recent years,
generals and officials have incurred punishment.
Although their lack of caution is blameworthy,
the world is not yet unified,
and we must plan for advancement.
It is appropriate to be somewhat lenient
to stabilize the sentiments of the lower ranks.
Moreover, state affairs are developing daily,
and capable talents are paramount.
Unless they are
or commit unforgivable offenses,
I beg that they be restored to prominent positions
to display their capabilities and effectiveness.
This is how sagely kings overlook faults and remember merits
to achieve their royal enterprises.
In the past, Hàn Gāo (Emperor Gāo of Hàn) overlooked Chén Píng's transgressions
and utilized his extraordinary strategies,
ultimately establishing his imperial destiny
and leaving achievements for a thousand years.
Indeed, harsh laws and severe punishments are not the grand enterprises of emperors;
punishment without clemency
is not a grand policy for winning over distant peoples."
Sūn Quán wanted to send a detached force to capture Yízhōu and Zhūyá.
He consulted Lù Xùn about both.
Lù Xùn submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your foolish servant believes that with the four seas not yet settled,
the strength of the people is needed
to manage current affairs.
Now, military campaigns have lasted for years,
and the population has visibly dwindled.
Your Majesty, burdened with worries and neglecting sleep and food,
intends to plan for Yízhōu in the distance
to accomplish a great undertaking.
Your servant has repeatedly pondered this
and does not see its benefit.
Attacking over ten thousand *lǐ*,
the winds and waves are unpredictable.
The people are susceptible to the local climate,
which will certainly lead to illness and plague.
Now, to drive the existing population
through barren lands
will only diminish what you wish to increase,
and harm what you wish to benefit.
Moreover, Zhūyá is extremely treacherous,
and its people are like beasts.
Gaining their people is insufficient to accomplish anything,
and lacking their troops will not diminish our forces.
Our existing forces in Jiāngdōng
are sufficient for our current plans.
We should simply accumulate strength before acting.
In the past, Huán Wáng (Sūn Jiān) established his foundation
with less than a single battalion of troops,
yet he opened a great enterprise.
Your Majesty, receiving the mandate,
has expanded and settled the region south of the Yangtze.
Your servant hears that to restore order and suppress rebellion,
troops are needed for intimidation.
Agriculture and sericulture for clothing and food
are the fundamental occupations of the people.
Yet, warfare has not ceased,
and the people suffer from hunger and cold.
Your foolish servant believes that we should nurture and support the soldiers and people,
and lighten their taxes and levies.
Victory among the masses depends on harmony,
and righteousness encourages bravery.
Then the Hé and Wèi regions can be pacified,
and the Nine Provinces will be unified."
Sūn Quán then launched the expedition to Yízhōu,
but the gains did not compensate for the losses.
When Gōngsūn Yuān renounced his alliance,
Sūn Quán wanted to go and subjugate him.
Lù Xùn submitted a memorial, saying:
"Yuān relies on treacherous terrain and strong defenses,
detaining our envoy,
and not presenting the tribute horses.
This is indeed cause for enmity and anger.
The barbarians are disturbing Huáxià (China),
not yet imbued with royal transformative influence.
They flee like birds to the remote borders,
resisting the royal army.
This has caused Your Majesty to be greatly angered,
wishing to trouble your myriad chariots (i.e., you, the emperor) to lightly cross the sea,
disregarding the danger and venturing into the unknown.
Currently, the world is in chaos,
with warlords contending like tigers,
and heroes rising up,
raising their voices and looking with grand ambition.
Your Majesty, with your divine martial prowess,
was born to receive the mandate of the era.
You defeated Cáo Cāo at Wūlín,
vanquished Liú Bèi at Xīlíng,
and captured Guān Yǔ in Jīngzhōu.
These three enemies were the heroes of their generation,
yet you crushed their might.
Where your sagely influence pacifies,
myriad *lǐ* bend like grass.
It is time to pacify Huáxià
and unify the great path.
Now, you cannot tolerate a small grievance
and unleash the wrath of thunder,
violating the warning against standing by the eaves (dangerously close to falling),
and making light of the gravity of your myriad chariots.
This is what perplexes your servant.
Your servant has heard that one who intends to travel ten thousand *lǐ*
does not stop halfway;
one who plans for the four seas
does not sacrifice the great for the small.
Strong enemies are at our borders,
and the wild regions have not yet submitted.
If Your Majesty crosses the sea on a raft for a distant campaign,
it will surely invite opportunism and disturbance.
When sorrow arrives, regret will be too late.
If great matters are achieved in time,
then Yuān will submit without being attacked.
But now, you are reluctant to abandon the troops and horses of Liáodōng,
yet how can you be willing to discard the fundamental enterprise of peace and stability in Jiāngdōng without regret?
I beg you to rest your six armies,
to intimidate the great barbarians,
to quickly settle Zhongxià (the central plains),
and to cast your brilliant light upon future generations."
Sūn Quán adopted his advice.
In the fifth year of Jiāhé,
Quán campaigned north.
He sent Xùn and Zhūgě Jǐn to attack Xiāngyáng.
Xùn dispatched his trusted aide Hán Biǎn to carry a memorial as a report.
On his return,
Biǎn encountered the enemy in Miǎnzhōng,
and was captured by a scouting party.
Jǐn, hearing of this, was greatly alarmed.
He wrote to Xùn, saying:
"The imperial carriage has already returned.
The enemy has captured Hán Biǎn
and knows our situation thoroughly.
Moreover, the water is drying up,
so we should leave immediately."
Xùn did not reply.
Instead, he urged his men to plant turnips and beans,
and played chess and shot arrows with his generals as usual.
Jǐn said:
"Bóyán is full of wisdom and strategy;
he must have a plan."
He came in person to see Xùn,
who said:
"The enemy knows the imperial carriage has returned,
so they have no further worries
and can fully concentrate their forces on us.
They have also secured the strategic positions.
The soldiers' spirits are stirring,
so we must first settle ourselves to calm them,
and implement a deceptive tactic,
before we can withdraw.
If we show signs of retreat now,
the enemy will think we are scared,
and will press upon us,
which would certainly lead to defeat."
So, he secretly made a plan with Jǐn,
ordering Jǐn to oversee the boats and ships,
while Xùn loaded all his troops and horses
to advance towards Xiāngyáng City.
The enemy had always feared Xùn,
and immediately returned to defend the city.
Jǐn then led his boats out.
Xùn calmly arrayed his formations,
projected a formidable presence,
and marched towards the boats;
the enemy dared not interfere.
When the army reached Báiwéi,
Xùn claimed they were stopping to hunt,
but secretly dispatched generals Zhōu Jùn and Zhāng Liáng to attack Xīnshì, Ānlù, and Shíyáng in Jiāngxià.
The market at Shíyáng was prosperous.
When Jùn and the others arrived unexpectedly,
everyone abandoned their goods and rushed into the city.
The city gates became blocked and could not be closed.
The enemy then had to hack down and kill their own people
before they could shut the gates.
They beheaded and captured alive
over a thousand people in total.
Those who were captured alive
were all given protection and care,
and soldiers were not allowed to interfere with or insult them.
For those who brought their families,
they were allowed to settle and inspect them.
If anyone had lost their wives and children,
they were immediately given clothing and provisions,
generously comforted,
and sent back.
Some were so moved and inspired that they came back with others.
The neighboring regions held them in high regard.
Zhào Zhuó, the Cāncáo of Jiāngxià, Péi Shēng, the Bèijiāng of Yìyáng, and the barbarian king Méi Yí, among others,
all led their followers to join Xùn.
Xùn spent his wealth and silk
to provide for them and offer relief.
Moreover, Lù Shì (Lù written as lù) the Administrator of Jiāngxià for Wèi,
who also commanded troops,
often caused trouble on the border,
and had a long-standing disagreement with Wén Pìn's son, Xiū, an old general of the north.
When Xùn heard of this,
he immediately forged a letter of reply to Shì, saying:
"I have received your earnest report.
Knowing of your long-standing feud with Xiū,
which makes it impossible for you both to coexist,
and your desire to surrender,
I have secretly presented your letter to the emperor for his knowledge,
and am preparing troops to welcome you.
You should secretly make ready quickly,
and inform me of a new date."
He placed the letter on the border.
Shì's soldiers found the letter and showed it to Shì.
Shì was terrified,
and consequently sent his wife and children back to Luòyáng.
Because of this, his officials and soldiers no longer trusted him,
and he was subsequently dismissed from office.
In the sixth year,
Zhōu Zhī, a Zhōnglángjiāng, requested to recruit soldiers in Póyáng.
The matter was referred to Xùn for deliberation.
Xùn believed that the people of this commandery were easily stirred up and difficult to pacify,
and should not be recruited,
fearing it would lead to banditry.
However, Zhī insisted on collecting them.
Indeed, the people of the commandery, led by Wú Jù and others, rose in rebellion, killed Zhī,
and attacked and occupied several counties.
The old wicked elements in Yùzhāng and Lúlíng
all joined Jù as bandits.
As soon as Xùn heard,
he immediately attacked and defeated them.
Jù and the others surrendered en masse.
Xùn estimated he had obtained over eight thousand elite soldiers,
and the three commanderies were pacified.
At that time, Lǚ Yī, a Zhōngshū Diǎnjiào,
usurped power,
and arbitrarily wielded authority and influence.
Xùn and Pān Jùn, the Tàicháng, were united in their concern,
and spoke of it with tears.
Later, Quán executed Yī,
and deeply blamed himself,
as recorded in Quán's biography.
At that time, Xiè Yuān and Xiè Kē, among others, each presented proposals for expediency,
wishing to promote beneficial reforms.
The matters were referred to Xùn.
Xùn deliberated, saying:
"A state takes its people as its foundation;
its strength comes from the people's labor,
and its wealth comes from the people's production.
There has never been a case
where the people were prosperous and the state weak,
or where the people were impoverished and the state strong.
Therefore, for a state,
to gain the people is to have order,
to lose them is to have chaos.
If they do not receive benefits,
yet are compelled to exert their utmost effort and achieve results,
that is also difficult.
This is why the 'Shī' (Book of Odes) praises, 'They bless the people and the common folk,
receiving blessings from Heaven.'
I beg your sacred grace
to pacify and relieve the common people.
Within a few years,
the national resources will be somewhat abundant,
and then we can make further plans."
In the seventh year of Chìwū,
he succeeded Gù Yōng as Chancellor.
An imperial edict stated:
"I, being unworthy,
have ascended to the throne in due time.
The royal path is not yet unified,
and villains fill the roads.
Day and night I am filled with apprehension,
unable to rest or sleep.
You, my lord, are endowed with natural intelligence and wisdom,
with illustrious and radiant virtue.
You have commanded the supreme generals,
rectifying the state and quelling difficulties.
Indeed, those who possess achievements that surpass their generation
must receive grand and glorious honors;
those who possess both civil and military talents
must bear the heavy responsibility of the state.
Formerly, Yī Yǐn elevated Tāng,
and Lǚ Shàng assisted Zhōu;
you, my lord, truly combine both internal and external responsibilities.
You, my lord, truly combine both internal and external responsibilities.
Now I appoint you, my lord, as Chancellor.
I shall send the imperial envoy, the Superintendent of the Imperial Clan and Grandee Fù Cháng, to bestow the seal and ribbon upon you.
May you, my lord, further illuminate your brilliant virtue,
cultivate your excellent achievements,
reverently obey the royal commands,
and pacify the four directions.
Alas!
You will oversee the three major affairs,
to instruct all officials.
How can one not be reverent?
May you, my lord, exert yourself!
Your positions as Provincial Governor and Commander-in-Chief overseeing Wǔchāng affairs remain as before."
Previously,
the two palaces were both lacking (in attendants),
and officials inside and outside the court
mostly sent their sons and younger brothers to serve.
Quán Cóng reported this to Lù Xùn,
who believed that if a son or younger brother had talent,
there would be no worry about him not being employed,
and it was inappropriate to privately send them out to seek honor and profit.
If they were not good,
it would ultimately bring disaster.
Furthermore, he heard that the two palaces were rivals in power,
and there would inevitably be partisanship,
which was greatly tabooed by the ancients.
Cóng's son, Jì,
indeed fawned over King Lǔ [Sūn Hé],
and lightly stirred up trouble.
Xùn wrote to Cóng, saying:
"You do not emulate Rìdī,
but rather harbor Ājì,
and ultimately this will bring disaster to your household."
Cóng not only failed to heed him,
but rather became estranged.
When there was discussion about the crown prince's [Sūn Hé's] instability,
Xùn submitted a memorial, stating:
"The crown prince is the legitimate heir,
and should have the stability of a firm rock.
King Lǔ is a vassal,
and his favored rank should be differentiated,
so that both find their proper place,
and those above and below achieve peace.
I respectfully kowtow until my head bleeds to present this."
He sent the memorial three or four times,
and also requested to go to the capital,
wishing to verbally discuss the distinction between the legitimate and illegitimate heir [the crown prince and King Lǔ],
to rectify what was gained and lost.
He was not granted permission,
and Xùn's maternal nephews Gù Tán, Gù Chéng, and Yáo Xìn,
all for being close to the crown prince,
were wrongly exiled.
The Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince, Wú Càn, for frequently exchanging letters with Xùn,
was imprisoned and died.
Quán repeatedly sent imperial envoys to rebuke and blame Xùn,
who, out of indignation and resentment, died
at the age of sixty-three,
leaving no surplus wealth in his home.
Initially,
when Jì Yàn proposed his theory of constructing a new palace,
Xùn advised and warned against it,
believing it would surely lead to disaster.
He also said to Zhūgě Kè:
"For those above me,
I must honor them and rise with them;
for those below me,
I will support them.
Now I observe that your demeanor is contemptuous of those above you,
and disdainful of those below you,
which is not the foundation of peaceful virtue."
Also, Yáng Zhú of Guǎnglíng gained a reputation at a young age,
but Xùn predicted his eventual downfall,
and advised Zhú's elder brother Mù to separate from his clan.
Such was his foresight.
His eldest son Yán died prematurely;
his second son Kàng inherited his title.
During Sūn Xiū's reign,
Xùn was posthumously granted the title Zhāo Hóu.
Kàng, courtesy name Yòujié,
was Sūn Cè's maternal grandson.
When Xùn died,
Kàng was twenty years old.
He was appointed Jiànwǔ Xiàowèi,
commanding Xùn's five thousand troops,
and escorted the funeral east back [to the capital],
where he offered thanks for the imperial favor.
Sūn Quán questioned Kàng about the twenty matters concerning Xùn that Yáng Zhú had reported,
forbade him from receiving guests,
and had imperial envoys interrogate him.
Kàng did not consult anyone,
but answered each matter item by item,
and Quán's anger gradually subsided.
In the ninth year of Chìwū [246 CE],
he was promoted to Lìjié Zhōnglángjiàng,
and exchanged garrisons with Zhūgě Kè at Cháisāng.
When Kàng was about to leave,
he renovated and completed the city walls,
repaired the houses and roofs,
and ensured that the dwelling places and mulberry fruit trees [in the camps]
were not wantonly damaged.
When Kè entered the garrison,
it appeared completely new.
However, Kè's former garrison at Cháisāng
was quite dilapidated,
which made him deeply ashamed.
In the first year of Tàiyuán [251 CE],
he went to the capital to treat an illness.
When he recovered and was about to return,
Quán, with tears, bid him farewell,
saying:
"I previously listened to slanders,
and my great righteousness with your father was not strong,
for which I have wronged you.
All the questions I asked before,
burn and destroy them,
do not let anyone see them."
In the first year of Jiànxīng [252 CE],
he was appointed Fènwēi Jiāngjūn.
In the second year of Tàipíng [257 CE],
when the Wèi general Zhūgě Dàn surrendered at Shòuchūn,
Kàng was appointed Dūdu Cháisāng,
went to Shòuchūn,
defeated the Wèi Yámén Jiāng and Piān Jiāngjūn,
and was promoted to Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn.
In the second year of Yǒng'ān [259 CE],
he was appointed Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn,
and Grand Administrator of Xīlíng,
from Guān Yǔ to Báidì.
In the third year [260 CE],
he was granted the imperial insignia (Jiǎjié).
When Sūn Hào ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhènjūn Dàjiāngjūn,
and concurrently Governor of Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu Mù).
In the second year of Jiànhéng [270 CE],
when Grand Marshal Shī Jì died,
Kàng was appointed Grand Administrator of the military affairs of Xìnlíng, Xīlíng, Yídào, Lèxiāng,
and Gōng'ān,
governing from Lèxiāng.
Kàng heard that many government decrees in the capital were flawed,
and with deep worry and far-reaching concern,
he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that if virtue is equal, the many overcome the few;
if strength is equal, the secure control the precarious.
This is why the Six States were annexed by the powerful Qín,
and Western Chǔ bowed to Gāo of Hàn.
Now the enemy dominates the nine regions,
not just the land west of the pass;
they occupy the nine provinces,
not merely west of the Hónggōu canal.
Our state has no aid from allied nations externally,
and is not as strong as Western Chǔ internally.
Government affairs are declining,
and the common people have not yet....
Yet what the deliberators rely on
is merely long rivers and steep mountains
limiting the borders.
This is a minor aspect of defending the state,
not what the wise prioritize.
Your servant often considers from afar the signs of rise and fall in the Warring States period,
and recently observed the causes of the collapse of the Liú clan.
Examining the classics
and verifying them with current events,
I often pat my pillow in the middle of the night,
and forget to eat during meals.
In the past, when the Xiongnú were not yet destroyed,
Qùbìng declined a mansion;
when the Hàn Way was not pure,
Jiǎ Shēng wept sorrowfully.
How much more so for your servant, who comes from the royal family,
whose lineage has borne glory and favor,
whose personal fate is intertwined with the nation's fortune, sharing its joys and sorrows.
In life and death, separation and union,
my duty allows for no compromise.
Day and night I worry and grieve,
and the thought of this utmost devotion is agonizing.
Indeed, the duty of a servant to his lord is to offend rather than deceive;
the principle of a minister is to sacrifice himself rather than shirk.
I respectfully present seventeen articles regarding current necessities, as follows."
The
seventeen articles are lost from the original,
therefore they are not recorded.
At that time, Hé Dìng 弄權 was wielding power,
and the eunuch officials were interfering in state affairs.
Kàng submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servant has heard that in founding a state and establishing a family,
petty men must not be employed.
To silence slander and correct crookedness [referring to the example of Wǔ Zé Tiān's reign],
the *Táng Shū* offers a solemn warning.
This is why upright men complained and criticized,
and Zhòng Ní sighed.
From the Spring and Autumn period onwards,
down to the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
the root cause of collapse and ruin
has never been other than this.
Petty men do not understand principles and the Dao;
their vision is shallow.
Even if they exert their utmost loyalty and integrity,
they are still not fit for the task,
let alone when their treacherous hearts are inherently deep-seated
and their likes and dislikes easily shift?
If they fear losing [their position],
there is nothing they will not do.
To now entrust them with positions of intelligence and insight,
and grant them the awe of absolute authority,
and yet hope for the emergence of a harmonious and prosperous reputation,
and the establishment of a pure and clean transformation,
is impossible.
Among the current officials,
though truly exceptional talents are few,
yet some are descendants of high-ranking families
who have gradually been nurtured by the Daoist teachings;
others are self-made through integrity and hardship,
their abilities sufficient for use.
They can certainly be appointed to offices according to their talents,
and the multitude of petty men can be suppressed and dismissed.
Only then can the customs be purified,
and the various government affairs be free of defilement.”
In the first year of Fènghuáng,
Bù Chǎn, the Grand Administrator of Xīlíng, seized the city and rebelled,
sending envoys to surrender to the Jìn.
Kàng heard of this
and immediately deployed his various armies,
ordering Generals Zuǒ Yì, Wú Yàn, and Cài Gòng to proceed directly to Xīlíng.
He commanded the army camps to build a formidable circumvallation,
from Chìxī to Gùshì,
internally to besiege Chǎn
and externally to resist the invaders.
He urged them day and night with great urgency,
as if the enemy had already arrived.
The troops suffered greatly from this.
All the generals remonstrated, saying:
“Now, while the three armies are sharp,
we should quickly attack Chǎn.
By the time the Jìn relief arrives,
Chǎn can certainly be captured.
Why bother with a siege,
