and exhaust the strength of the officers and people?”
Kàng replied:
“This city is inherently strong in its strategic position,
and its grain supplies are ample.
Moreover, the defensive fortifications and equipment
were all planned by me long ago.
Now, to turn and attack it [the city],
it cannot be taken quickly.
Furthermore, the northern relief [force] will certainly arrive.
If they arrive and we are unprepared,
with our flanks exposed to attack,
how shall we resist them?”
All the generals wanted to attack Chǎn,
but Kàng always refused.
However, Léi Tán, the Administrator of Yídū, spoke with such earnestness
that Kàng, wanting to placate the crowd,
allowed one assault.
The attack indeed yielded no advantage,
and the siege preparations were then completed.
Yáng Hù, the Jìn General of Chariots and Cavalry, led his army towards Jiānglíng.
All the generals felt that Kàng should not proceed upstream,
but Kàng said:
“Jiānglíng has strong fortifications and ample troops;
there is nothing to worry about.
Even if the enemy captures Jiānglíng,
they will certainly not be able to hold it,
so the loss would be minor.
If Xīlíng becomes entrenched,
then all the barbarian tribes in the Nánshān mountains will be stirred up,
and the worries then
would be too numerous to mention.
I would rather abandon Jiānglíng and rush to Xīlíng,
let alone when Jiānglíng is secure?”
Initially,
Jiānglíng was flat and open,
with convenient roads.
Kàng ordered Zhāng Xián, the Grand Administrator of Jiānglíng, to construct a large weir to block the water,
gradually flooding the flat areas
to cut off rebel incursions.
Hù wanted to use the blocked water
to float boats for transporting grain,
and he loudly declared that he would break the weir to allow his carts to pass.
Kàng, hearing this,
ordered Xián to quickly destroy it.
All the generals were perplexed
and repeatedly remonstrated, but Kàng did not listen.
When Hù reached Dāngyáng,
he heard that the weir had been destroyed,
so he changed from boat to cart transport,
which caused a great expenditure of effort and resources.
Xú Yìn, the Jìn Military Supervisor of Bādōng, led his navy to Jiànpíng.
Yáng Zhào, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, arrived at Xīlíng.
Kàng ordered Zhāng Xián to hold his city securely;
Sūn Zūn, the Grand Administrator of Gōng'ān, to patrol the south bank to resist Hù;
Liú Lǜ, the Naval Supervisor, and Zhū Wǎn, the General Who Guards the West, to oppose Yìn;
and he himself led the three armies,
relying on the circumvallation to face Zhào.
Generals Zhū Qiáo and Yú Zàn, the Camp Commandant, defected to Zhào.
Kàng said:
“Zàn is an old officer in the army;
he knows my strengths and weaknesses.
I have always worried that the barbarian troops are not well-drilled,
and if the enemy attacks the circumvallation,
they will certainly target this spot first.”
That very night, he replaced the barbarian soldiers,
filling their positions with veteran generals.
The next day,
Zhào indeed attacked the place where the former barbarian soldiers had been.
Kàng ordered his army to wheel around and strike them.
Arrows and stones rained down,
and Zhào's troops suffered continuous casualties.
Zhào remained for a month,
but his stratagem failed, and he fled under the cover of night.
Kàng wanted to pursue him,
but he worried that Chǎn was accumulating strength in Xiànglǐng,
waiting for an opportunity,
and his troops were insufficient to divide.
Therefore, he merely beat the drums to alert his troops,
as if he were about to pursue.
Zhào's troops, filled with panic,
all discarded their armor and fled desperately.
Kàng sent light troops to follow them,
and Zhào suffered a major defeat.
Hù and the others all withdrew their armies.
Kàng then captured Xīlíng city,
executing Chǎn's clan and his major generals and officials.
From this point downwards,
tens of thousands of people requested pardons.
After repairing the city and circumvallation,
he returned east to Yuèxiāng.
His demeanor showed no pride,
remaining humble and modest as usual,
and thus he earned the affection of his officers and soldiers.
He was further promoted to Dūhù.
Hearing that Xuē Yíng, the Left Division Supervisor of Wǔchāng, had been summoned and imprisoned,
Kàng submitted a memorial, saying:
“Truly, men of outstanding talent are
the precious treasures of the state and the valuable assets of the altars of soil and grain,
by whom the various government affairs are ordered
and the four gates are peaceful and clear.
Therefore, Lóu Xuán, the Grand Minister of Agriculture; Wáng Fān, the Palace Attendant and Regular Mounted Retainer; and Lǐ Xù, the Chief Steward,
were all outstanding talents of their age,
eminent figures of their time.
Having received initial imperial favor,
they comfortably held their positions,
yet they were all subsequently executed,
some having their families destroyed and ancestral sacrifices ceased,
others cast away to desolate frontiers.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* has the principle of pardoning the worthy,
and the *Chūnqiū* has the righteousness of showing leniency to the good.
The *Shū* says:
‘Rather than kill the innocent,
it is better to err on the side of not punishing according to the law.’
Yet, Fān and others' crimes were not yet definitively established,
when the death penalty was imposed.
Their hearts embodied loyalty and righteousness,
yet their bodies suffered extreme punishment—
is this not grievous!
Moreover, the dead are truly unconscious;
to burn them, melt them, cast them adrift,
and abandon them by the waterside—
I fear this is not the righteous canon of the former kings,
nor what Hú Hóu warned against.
Therefore, the common people are terrified and agitated,
and the officers and people share in their sorrow.
Fān and Xù are forever gone;
regret is now too late.
I sincerely hope, Your Majesty,
that you will pardon and recall Xuán.
And recently, I heard that Xuē Yíng was suddenly arrested.
Yíng's father, Zōng, offered counsel to the late emperor [Sun Quan],
and tutored the Cultured Emperor [Sun Liang].
When Yíng inherited his position,
he internally cultivated his reputation and conduct.
His current offense
is one that can be pardoned.
Your servant fears that the relevant authorities may not have fully investigated the matter,
and if he is again executed,
it will further lose the people's trust.
I beg Your Majesty to bestow your celestial grace,
to pardon Yíng's crime,
to show compassion to the numerous prisoners,
and to clarify the network of laws and punishments.
Then the empire would be exceedingly fortunate!”
At that time, the military campaigns were still ongoing,
and the common people were exhausted.
Lù Kàng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the Yì Jīng values adapting to the times,
and commentaries commend observing opportunities.
Thus, when the Xià dynasty committed many sins, Yīn Tāng employed his army;
when Zhòu indulged in tyranny, Zhōu Wǔ was granted the battle-axe.
If the time is not ripe,
the Jade Terrace will harbor worries of sorrow,
and Mèngjīn will see the army turn back its banners.
Now, instead of striving to enrich the state and strengthen the military,
exerting efforts in agriculture and stockpiling grain,
so that civil and military talents can fully display their use,
and all government offices do not neglect their duties,
making clear promotions and demotions to encourage all officials,
and carefully administering punishments to demonstrate persuasion and deterrence,
instructing all departments with virtue,
and treating the common people with benevolence,
and then, following Heaven and seizing the opportunity,
sweeping across the world –
instead, we listen to generals pursuing fame,
exhausting the army and abusing military power,
with every action costing tens of thousands,
soldiers becoming emaciated and worn out,
the enemy not diminishing,
while we are already gravely ill!
Now we contend for the resources of emperors and kings,
but overlook a hundredfold profit.
This is the deceitful convenience of ministers,
not a sound strategy for the state.
In the past, Qí and Lǔ fought three battles;
the people of Lǔ won twice but perished swiftly.
Why?
Because the balance of power between large and small states was different.
How much more so now, when what our army gains
does not compensate for what it loses?
Moreover, obstructing military action alienates the populace,
a clear lesson from antiquity.
It is truly advisable to temporarily halt small-scale advances and conquests,
to nurture the strength of the soldiers and the people,
observe opportunities and await openings.
Then there will likely be no regrets.
In the spring of the second year,
he was appointed Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) and Inspector of Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu Mù).
In the summer of the third year,
he fell ill,
and submitted a memorial, saying:
"Xīlíng and Jiànpíng
are the outer defenses of the state.
Being located downstream,
they face enemies from two borders.
If the enemy sails downstream,
with a thousand li of ships stem to stern,
rushing like stars and lightning,
they will arrive suddenly.
It will be impossible to rely on aid from other departments to rescue those hanging upside down.
This is a critical juncture for the safety of the state and its altars of soil and grain,
not merely a minor encroachment on territorial borders.
My father, Lù Xùn, once spoke in the western marches,
considering Xīlíng to be the western gate of the state;
though it is said to be easy to defend,
it is also easy to lose.
If it cannot be held,
it is not merely the loss of one commandery,
but then Jīngzhōu will no longer belong to Wú.
If there is any danger,
the entire state should contend for it.
When your servant was previously in Xīlíng,
I walked in Xùn’s footsteps.
I previously requested 30,000 elite troops,
but the [commanders] followed routine
and were unwilling to dispatch them.
Since Bù Chǎn’s rebellion,
there has been even greater attrition.
Now, your servant controls a thousand li,
facing enemies from four directions,
warding off strong adversaries externally,
and managing many barbarian tribes internally,
yet the total available troops number only a few tens of thousands.
They have been weakened and exhausted for a long time,
making it difficult to await changes.
Your servant foolishly believes that the princes are young and immature,
not yet overseeing state affairs.
They should first be appointed tutors and chancellors
to assist and guide their worthy talents,
without using soldiers and horses,
which would impede vital matters.
Moreover, the eunuchs of the Yellow Gate
have opened up recruitment for paid service,
causing soldiers and common people to resent the service,
and runaways to join the recruitment.
I beg that a special imperial edict be issued to review and inspect them,
and dismiss all such recruits,
to supplement the borders that constantly face enemies,
so that the troops under your servant's command reach a full eighty thousand,
reducing various duties and
ensuring trust in rewards and punishments.
Even if Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ were reborn,
they would have no opportunity to display their skill.
If the army is not increased,
and this system is not changed,
yet we desire to achieve great undertakings—this is what your servant deeply laments.
If your servant dies hereafter,
I beg that the western region be placed under my son's command.
May Your Majesty kindly consider your servant's words,
then your servant, though dead, will not perish."
In the autumn, he consequently died.
His son Yàn succeeded him.
Yàn and his younger brothers Jǐng, Xuán, Jī, and Yún jointly commanded Lù Kàng's troops.
Yàn was made Vice General (Bì Jiāngjūn) and Supervisor of Yídào (Yídào Jiān).
In the fourth year of Tiānjì,
the Jìn army attacked Wú.
General of Dragon Might (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) Wáng Jùn sailed downstream to the east,
conquering wherever he went,
ultimately fulfilling Lù Kàng's fears.
Jǐng, courtesy name Shìrén,
was appointed Cavalry Commandant (Qí Dūwèi) for marrying a princess,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Pílíng.
After taking command of Lù Kàng's troops,
he was appointed General of the Household (Piān Jiāngjūn) and Supervisor of Zhōngxià (Zhōngxià Dū).
He was clean-living and fond of learning,
authoring several dozens of works.
On the day Rénxū in the second month,
Yàn was killed by a detachment of Wáng Jùn's army.
On the day Guǐhài,
Jǐng also met his end,
at the age of thirty-one.
Jǐng's wife,
Sūn Hào's younger sister,
was, like Jǐng, the paternal granddaughter of Zhāng Chéng.
Commentary says: Liú Bèi was acclaimed a hero throughout the realm,
feared by his generation.
Lù Xùn, in the prime of his life,
his formidable reputation not yet established,
crushed and defeated him,
everything as he wished.
I marvel at Xùn's strategy,
and also praise Quán's discerning of talent,
which enabled him to accomplish great things.
And Lù Xùn's loyalty was sincere and profound,
worrying for the state to the extent of sacrificing himself.
He was almost a minister of the altars of soil and grain!
Lù Kàng was upright, discerning, resourceful, and capable,
all possessing his father's style,
his excellence carried through generations,
embodying the spirit in miniature.
He can be called one who continued his father's achievements!
Biographies of the Five Sons of the Lord of Wú, Chapter Fourteen
Sūn Dēng, courtesy name Zǐgāo,
was Quán's eldest son.
In the second year of Huángchū in Wèi,
when Quán was made King of Wú,
Dēng was appointed General of the Central East (Dōng Zhōngláng Jiāng)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Wànhù,
but Dēng declined due to illness.
That year,
Dēng was established as Crown Prince,
and tutors were selected and appointed for him,
and outstanding scholars were chosen
to be his companions.
Thus, Zhūgé Kè, Zhāng Xiū, Gù Tán, Chén Biǎo, and others were selected and admitted,
attending him to lecture on the Shījīng and Shūjīng,
and accompanying him on horseback archery outings.
Quán wanted Dēng to read the Hàn Shū
and become familiar with recent history.
As Zhāng Zhāo was a master of teaching,
and Quán was reluctant to trouble him excessively,
he ordered Xiū to receive instruction from Zhāo,
and then return to teach Dēng.
Dēng treated his subordinates
largely with the courtesy of commoners,
sometimes sharing a carriage with Kè, Xiū, Tán, and others,
or sleeping under the same tent.
Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Zhāng Wēn said to Quán:
"The position of Palace Attendant (Zhōng Shùzǐ) is the most intimate,
for direct questions and immediate answers.
It should be filled by outstanding virtues."
Thereupon, Biǎo and others were appointed as Palace Attendants.
Later, feeling that the rituals for shùzǐ were too restrictive,
he again ordered them to tidy their scarves and attend his presence.
In the first year of Huánglóng,
Quán declared himself emperor,
and Dēng was established as Imperial Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
Kè was made Left Protector (Zuǒ Fǔ),
Xiū Right Supporter (Yòu Bì),
Tán Auxiliary Justifier (Fǔzhèng),
and Biǎo Winged Justifier Commandant (Yìzhèng Dūwèi).
These were known as the Four Friends,
while Xiè Jǐng, Fàn Shèn, Diāo Xuán, Yáng Dào, and others were all his guests.
(Dào is pronounced like dào.
) Thus, the Eastern Palace was known for its numerous scholars.
Quán moved the capital to Jiànyè.
He summoned Grand General Lù Xùn to assist Dēng in garrisoning Wǔchāng,
and to oversee affairs of the palace and administration during his absence.
When Dēng went hunting,
he would take the pathways,
always keeping a good distance from fertile fields,
never treading on crops.
When he reached his resting place,
he would again choose a deserted spot,
such was his unwillingness to trouble the people.
Once, when he rode out on horseback,
a projectile passed by.
His attendants sought it out.
There was one man holding a slingshot and carrying pellets.
Everyone thought it was him.
The man denied it and would not submit.
The attendants wanted to beat him,
but Dēng would not allow it.
He ordered them to find the projectile that had passed by,
and compared it, finding it was not of the same kind.
Only then was the man released.
Another time, he lost a golden horse-head cup for holding water.
He found its owner,
who was one of his attendants.
He could not bear to inflict punishment,
so he called and reproached him,
and sent him home permanently,
ordering his close attendants not to speak of it.
Later, when his younger brother, Lǜ, died,
Quán was grieved and diminished by it.
Dēng traveled day and night.
When he reached Lài-xiāng,
he announced his arrival himself,
and was immediately summoned for an audience.
Seeing Quán weeping mournfully,
he thereupon remonstrated, saying:
"Lǜ fell ill and did not recover;
this is fate.
Currently, the northern lands are not unified,
and the four seas are looking on eagerly.
Heaven has exalted Your Majesty,
yet with these thoughts for a lesser loss,
you diminish the meals and provisions of the Grand Officials,
exceeding the rites.
Your servant secretly feels worried and fearful."
Quán accepted his words,
and had his meals increased.
He stayed for more than ten days,
and Quán wished to send him back west.
Dēng deeply pleaded,
stating that he had been away for a long time without performing the morning and evening greetings to his parents,
and that his filial duty was therefore incomplete.
He also spoke of Lù Xùn's loyalty and diligence,
saying there was nothing to worry about.
Quán then kept him there.
In the third year of Jiāhé [234 CE],
Quán campaigned against Xīnchéng,
and made Dēng stay behind to guard,
supervising all remaining affairs.
At that time, the year's harvest was not abundant,
and there were quite a few bandits.
So he presented a memorial to establish new laws and regulations,
by which to defend and protect.
He was very successful in stopping villainy.
Originally,
Dēng's birth mother was of humble status,
but Lady Xú had shown him maternal kindness in his youth.
Later, Lady Xú was deposed due to jealousy and resided in Wú,
while Lady Bù was most favored.
When Lady Bù bestowed gifts,
Dēng did not dare to refuse,
simply bowing and receiving them.
When an envoy from Lady Xú arrived,
he would certainly bathe and wear the clothes she bestowed.
When Dēng was about to be made Crown Prince,
he declined, saying:
"When the root is established, the Way is born.
If you wish to establish a Crown Prince,
you should first establish an Empress."
Quán asked:
"Where is your mother?"
He replied:
"She is in Wú."
Quán fell silent.
He was established as Crown Prince for twenty-one years,
and died at the age of thirty-three.
Approaching death,
he submitted a memorial saying:
"Your servant, being unworthy,
is afflicted with a severe illness.
Reflecting on my own insignificance and frailty,
I fear I may suddenly perish.
Your servant does not spare himself,
but I think of having to leave behind those I provide for and support,
and my bones buried in the earth.
I shall forever cease to attend upon the palace and court,
and behold Your Majesty daily.
While alive, I was of no benefit to the state;
in death, I will cause Your Majesty great sorrow.
This is what chokes me up.
Your servant has heard that life and death are fated,
and longevity and brevity are from Heaven.
Zhōu Jìn and Yán Huí had supreme wisdom and talent,
yet still died young.
How much more so for your servant, who is foolish and crude,
and has exceeded their lifespan.
Born as the heir to the nation,
and enjoying a glorious position in death,
this is already much for your servant.
What is there to grieve or regret?
At present, the great affairs are not yet settled,
and the renegade bandits have not been suppressed.
All the myriad states are eagerly awaiting,
their lives tied to Your Majesty.
Those in danger hope for peace;
those in chaos look up to your rule.
May Your Majesty cast aside and forget about my person,
renounce the lesser kindnesses,
cultivate the doctrines of Huáng-Lǎo,
diligently nourish your divine spirit,
and partake of precious delicacies.
Broaden the scope of your divine wisdom,
to establish an endless enterprise.
Then all under Heaven will be fortunate and rely on you,
and your servant will die without regret.
The Imperial Prince Hé is benevolent, filial, intelligent, and sagacious;
his virtue and conduct are pure and flourishing.
He should be established early,
to secure the hopes of the people.
Zhūgě Kè's talent and strategy are extensive and far-reaching;
his capacity is fit to assist the times.
Zhāng Xiū, Gù Tán, and Xiè Jǐng
are all insightful, discerning, and decisive.
Within the court, they should be entrusted with your closest confidence;
outside, they can serve as your fangs and claws.
Fàn Shèn and Huá Róng are towering in their firm integrity,
possessing the demeanor of national worthies.
Yáng Dǎo is eloquent and quick-witted,
having the talent for specialized diplomatic missions.
Diāo Xuán is generous and broad-minded,
his will to tread the true path.
Péi Qīn is extensively learned,
his literary talent sufficient for use.
Jiǎng Xiū and Yú Fān
have clear principles and integrity.
All these ministers,
some are suitable for the imperial court,
some for generals and commanders.
They are all versed in current affairs,
well-versed in laws and regulations,
upholding fidelity and firm in righteousness,
with an indomitable will.
These are all illuminated by Your Majesty's daily observation,
appointed by your servant to office,
and with whom I have worked closely.
I know their dispositions fully,
and dare to present this information.
Your servant further considers that at present, there are many troubles beyond the borders,
and military campaigns have not ceased.
The six armies should be spurred on,
to plan for advancement.
Armies depend on people as their multitude;
the multitude depends on wealth as its treasure.
I secretly hear that many commanderies and counties are desolate and ravaged,
the people and resources withered and exhausted,
and wickedness and rebellion are germinating.
Therefore, laws and regulations are overly abundant,
and punishments and penalties are excessively severe.
Your servant has heard that in governing, one listens to the people,
and laws and ordinances shift with the times.
It is truly advisable to consult with generals, chancellors, and great ministers to carefully select what is timely and appropriate,
broadly gather public opinions,
relax punishments and lighten taxes,
and equalize and alleviate labor services,
to conform to the hopes of the people.
Lù Xùn is loyal and diligent in these times,
dedicated himself to the nation and worried for it,
frank and upright in public service,
possessing the virtue of selflessness.
Zhūgě Jǐn, Bù Zhì, Zhū Rán, Quán Cóng, Zhū Jù, Lǚ Dài, Wú Càn, Kān Zé, Yán Jùn, Zhāng Chéng, Sūn Yí are loyal to the nation
and thoroughly understand the principles of governance.
They can be ordered to present advantageous suggestions,
abolish harsh and troublesome regulations,
cherish and nurture soldiers and horses,
and comfort and guide the populace.
Within five years,
or at most ten years,
those far away will return,
and those nearby will exert their utmost effort.
Without shedding blood,
the great affairs can be settled.
Your servant has heard, 'When a bird is about to die, its song is mournful;
when a person is about to die, their words are good.'
Therefore, when Zǐnáng was facing death,
he left behind words of warning for his time,
which gentlemen considered loyal.
How much more so for your servant, Dēng,
how could he cease?
May Your Majesty pay attention and accept my words.
Even on the day your servant dies,
it will be as if he lives."
After he passed away, the memorial was reported,
and Quán was even more shattered and moved,
shedding tears whenever he spoke of him.
This year
was the fourth year of Chìwū.
Xiè Jǐng, who was then the Administrator of Yùzhāng,
could not bear his sorrow,
abandoned his post and rushed to the capital,
submitting a memorial to impeach himself.
Quán said:
"You served the Crown Prince,
which is different from other officials."
He sent an imperial envoy to comfort and console him,
allowed him to resume his original position,
and dispatched him back to his commandery.
Dēng was posthumously titled Xuān Tàizǐ.
His sons Fán and Xī
both died young.
His next son, Yīng,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wú.
In the first year of Wǔfèng,
Yīng, due to Dàjiāngjūn Sūn Jùn's usurpation of power,
planned to execute Jùn.
The plot was discovered, and he committed suicide,
and his marquisate was abolished.
Xiè Jǐng, whose courtesy name was Shūfā,
was a native of Wǎn, Nányáng.
In his commandery, he had achievements in governance,
and the officials and common people praised him,
considering him second only to Gù Shào,
with Jǐng being the next best.
He died in office after several years.
Sūn Lǜ, courtesy name Zǐzhì,
was Dēng's younger brother.
From a young age, he was intelligent, astute, and possessed talents and skills,
and Quán cherished and loved him.
In the seventh year of Huángwǔ (228 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jiànchāng.
Two years later,
Chancellor Yōng and others memorialized that Lǜ's nature was intelligent and perceptive,
and his aspirations were renewed daily.
Comparing him to recent Hòu
dynasties, it was fitting to advance his rank and call him a king.
Quán did not permit it then.
After a long time,
Shàngshū Púshè Cún submitted a memorial, saying:
"When emperors and kings rise,
none fail to honor their closest relatives
to glorify the various princes.
Thus, Lǔ and Wèi under Zhōu
were exceptionally favored among the feudal lords.
Gāodì's five kings
were enfeoffed and arrayed in Hàn,
thereby serving as a screen for the imperial court
and guardians for the state.
Marquis of Jiànchāng Lǜ possesses an intelligent and keen nature,
with both civil and military talents.
According to classical institutions,
his title should be formally rectified.
Your Majesty, with modest humility,
has not yet agreed to restore the old system,
which causes distress to officials, both high and low.
At present, treacherous bandits are rampant,
and the sounds of war drums have not ceased.
Our most trusted and vital support, our 'belly and teeth and claws,'
can only be found in our kin and the worthy.
I have discussed this with Chancellor Yōng and others,
and we all agree that Lǜ
should be appointed as Zhènqǐ Jūndà Jiāngjūn,
entrusted with authority over a border region,
to glorify the great enterprise."
Quán then assented to it.
Thereupon, he was granted the imperial insignia and allowed to establish an office,
governing half a province.
As an imperial prince, Lǜ
was young in years,
and people near and far suspected he would not be able to pay attention to matters.
However, when he came to administer affairs,
he followed and upheld the laws and regulations,
and respectfully accepted the advice of his teachers and friends,
exceeding everyone's expectations.
At the age of twenty,
he died in the first year of Jiāhé (232 CE).
He had no son,
so his marquisate was abolished.
Sūn Hé, courtesy name Zǐxiào,
was Lǜ's younger brother.
From a young age, he was loved and favored due to his mother, Consort Wáng.
At fourteen,
a palace guard was established for him,
and Zhōngshū Lìng Kān Zé was appointed to teach him literature and arts.
He was fond of learning and humble towards scholars,
and was greatly praised.
In the fifth year of Chìwū (242 CE),
he was established as crown prince,
then nineteen years old.
Kān Zé was his Tài fù,
and Xuē Zōng was his Shǎo fù.
Cài Yǐng, Zhāng Chún, Fēng Fǔ, Yán Wéi, and others all attended him at ease.
At this time, officials often submitted written queries about affairs,
and Hé believed that deceitful and wicked people
would use these opportunities to sow discord,
giving rise to malicious intent,
which should not be allowed to grow.
He memorialized that this practice should be abolished.
Moreover, Dūdū Liú Bǎo made an accusation against his shùzǐ Dīng Yàn,
and Yàn also accused Bǎo.
Hé said to Yàn:
"Among those with civil and military responsibilities,
how many truly capable individuals are there?
To exploit weaknesses and stir up trouble,
scheming to harm each other,
how could that bring good fortune?"
He then released both of them,
and urged them to be magnanimous.
He often said that contemporary scholars should diligently study and practice scholarly arts,
and learn archery and charioteering
to handle worldly affairs.
Instead, they engaged in socializing and board games, which hindered their careers,
and was not the path to advancement.
Later, when officials attended a banquet,
the topic of board games was discussed.
He considered them to hinder affairs, waste time, and be useless,
wearing out the spirit and harming thought without ever achieving anything significant.
Therefore, they were not a means to advance virtue, cultivate one's career,
or accumulate merits.
Moreover, ambitious individuals cherish every day and spare no effort,
and gentlemen admire the greatest things—
lofty mountains and admirable conduct—
and would be ashamed to fall short.
Indeed, heaven and earth endure for a long time,
but humans reside between them,
like a white steed flashing past a crevice.
Years pass in an instant,
and glory does not return.
The primary concern
lies in the human desires that are hard to relinquish.
If one could truly eliminate useless desires to follow the path of virtue and righteousness,
and abandon non-urgent matters to cultivate the foundation of great achievements,
would not their reputation and conduct
be excellent?
Nevertheless, human nature cannot entirely do without amusement,
and the preference for amusement
also lies in banquets, zithers, books, archery, and charioteering.
Why must it be board games
to find joy?
He then ordered eight of his attendants
to each write an essay to rectify this.
Thereupon, Zhōngshùzǐ Wéi Yào withdrew and presented his discourse,
which Hé showed to his guests.
At the time, Cài Yǐng was fond of board games,
and many officials working in the bureau emulated him,
so this was meant to admonish them.
Thereafter, Consort Wáng and Princess Quán had a rift.
Quán once fell ill,
and Hé performed sacrifices in the temple.
Hé's consort's uncle, Zhāng Xiū, lived near the temple,
and invited Hé to visit his residence.
Princess Quán sent someone to spy,
and then reported that the crown prince was not in the temple,
but had gone specifically to his consort's family to scheme;
she also said that Consort Wáng showed joy
upon hearing that the emperor was ill.
Quán was enraged by this,
Consort Wáng died of grief,
and Hé's favor gradually diminished,
fearing deposition.
Prince Bà of Lǔ's covetousness grew intense.
Lù Xùn, Wú Càn, Gù Tán, and others repeatedly expounded on the principle of legitimate and illegitimate succession,
arguing that it could not be overturned.
Quán Jì and Yáng Zhú, supporters of Prince Bà of Lǔ,
incited slanders daily.
Càn was subsequently imprisoned and executed,
and Tán was exiled to Jiāozhōu.
Quán deliberated for years,
and later imprisoned Hé.
Thereupon, Piāoqí Jiāngjūn Zhū Jù and Shàngshū Púshè Qū Huǎng, leading various generals and officials, muddied their heads and bound themselves,
and for several days went to the imperial palace to plead for Hé.
Quán ascended the Báijué Tower and saw them,
and was greatly displeased,
ordering Jù, Huǎng, and others not to act so rashly.
Quán wanted to depose Hé and enthrone Liàng.
Wúnán Dūdū Chén Zhèng and Wǔyíng Dūdū Chén Xiàng submitted a memorial,
citing Duke Xiàn of Jìn who killed Shēnshēng
and enthroned Xīqí,
causing chaos in the state of Jìn.
Furthermore, Jù and Huǎng steadfastly advised him to stop.
Quán was furious,
and executed Zhèng and Xiàng with their families.
Jù and Huǎng were dragged into the hall,
given a hundred strokes of the staff,
and ultimately Hé was exiled to Gùzhāng.
More than ten officials were punished or exiled for their remonstrances.
Everyone was saddened by this.
In the first month of the second year of Tàiyuán (249 CE),
Hé was enfeoffed as the King of Nányáng,
and sent to Chángshā.
In the fourth month,
Quán died,
and Zhūgě Kè took charge of government.
Kè was the maternal uncle of Hé's consort, Zhāng.
The consort sent the imperial attendant Chén Qiān to Jiànyè to submit a memorial to the empress,
and also to convey her greetings to Kè.
Before leaving,
Kè said to Qiān:
"Please tell the consort
that I am determined to make her surpass others."
This remark was somewhat leaked.
Moreover, Kè had an intention to move the capital,
and ordered the renovation of the Wǔchāng Palace.
People whispered that he intended to welcome Hé.
When Kè was executed,
Sūn Jùn consequently stripped Hé of his imperial seal and ribbon,
exiled him to Xīndū,
and then sent an envoy to bestow death upon him.
Hé bid farewell to his consort, Zhāng.
Zhāng said:
"Good fortune and ill fortune should be shared;
I will certainly not live alone."
She also committed suicide,
and the entire state mourned.
Sūn Xiū stood as emperor.
He enfeoffed Hé's son, Hào, as the Marquis of Wūchéng.
Hào himself returned from Xīndū to his ancestral land.
When Xiū passed away,
Hào ascended the throne.
In that same year, he posthumously honored his father, Hé, with the title "Emperor Wén" (Wén Huángdì).
Hé was re-interred in Mínglíng,
and an estate of two hundred households was established for the tomb,
with a Magistrate (Lìng) and Assistant (Chéng) appointed to guard it.
In the first month of the following year,
Wújùn and Dānyáng's nine counties were again divided to form Wúxīng Jùn,
with its seat of governance in Wūchéng,
and a Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) was appointed.
Sacrifices were offered there in all four seasons.
The relevant officials submitted a memorial stating,
"It is fitting to establish a temple in the capital."
In the seventh month of the second year of Bǎodǐng,
the acting Grand Craftsman (Shǒu Dàjiàng) Xuē Xǔ was dispatched to construct a shrine hall,
which was named Qīngmiào.
In the twelfth month,

the acting Chancellor (Shǒu Chéngxiàng) Mèng Rén and the Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) Yáo Xìn, along with other civil and military officials and two thousand infantry and cavalry from the Central Army, were sent
with the spiritual carriage (língyú) and imperial equipage (fǎjià)
eastward to welcome the spirit from Mínglíng.
Hào granted an audience to Rén
and personally bowed to see him off in the courtyard.
When the spiritual carriage was about to arrive,
Chancellor Lù Kǎi was instructed to offer three kinds of sacrificial animals in the nearby suburbs.
Hào camped overnight outside Jīnchéng.
The next day,
he performed a distant bow (wàngbài) outside the eastern gate.
The day after that,
he bowed at the temple and offered sacrifices,
weeping with profound sorrow.
For seven consecutive days, sacrifices were offered thrice daily,
with musicians and performers providing entertainment day and night.
The relevant officials then submitted a memorial stating,
"Sacrifices should not be too frequent;
frequent sacrifices lead to irreverence.
It is proper to control emotions with ritual."
Only then did the activities cease.
Sūn Bà, whose courtesy name was Zǐwēi,
was Hé's full brother.
Hé was the crown prince.
Bà was made King of Lǔ (Lǔ Wáng),
and he was particularly favored and esteemed,
not differing from Hé.
After a while,
reports of disharmony between Hé and Bà reached Quán's ears.
Quán forbade their mutual visits
and had them devote themselves to intensive study.
The Inspector-General (Dūjūn Shǐzhě) Yáng Dào submitted a memorial, stating:
"I have heard that those who held the world in ancient times
all first clearly distinguished between legitimate and illegitimate heirs,
and enfeoffed their sons and younger brothers,
thereby honoring their ancestors
and serving as bulwarks for the state.
The appointments of the two palaces (Ér Gōng) were lauded throughout the land as appropriate;
this was indeed the foundation for the flourishing prosperity of the Great Wú (Dà Wú).
Recently, I heard that both palaces have cut off all guests,
causing trepidation among those near and far,
and disappointment among all.
I have humbly listened to
and gathered public opinion
from a distance,
and all say that both palaces are intelligent, accomplished, and outstanding.
Since their establishment and formal naming,
three years have passed,
their virtuous conduct is manifest within,
and their excellent reputation shines abroad.
The northwest and other regions
have long heard of and submitted to this.
It is said that Your Majesty should comply with the virtue to which both near and far aspire,
diligently order the two palaces to welcome guests from all directions,
so that foreign lands may hear their reputation
and desire to become Your Majesty's subjects.
Now, Your Majesty has not yet paid attention to this,
but instead has issued a clear edict
to reduce and curtail their guards
and cut off their guests,
preventing tributes and respects from all sides
from being conveyed.
Although this truly reflects Your Majesty's upholding of ancient righteousness,
wishing to have the two palaces focus solely on learning,
no longer concerned with considering minor benefits or listening to trivial matters,
aiming only for reviewing the old and learning the new,
yet this is not the ultimate wish of your humble subjects, who eagerly look forward with longing.
Some say that the two palaces do not adhere to proper standards;
this is what causes me restless nights.
Even if such suspicions exist,
it is still appropriate to rectify and examine them,
and to deliberate secretly,
so that those near and far do not have occasion for dissenting remarks.
I fear that accumulated suspicions will become slanders,
and will spread far and wide over time.
Moreover, the northwest and other regions
are not far from the capital;
divergent opinions
are easily heard and conveyed.
When they are heard and conveyed,
public opinion will arise,
suggesting that the two palaces have committed offenses of disobedience.
I wonder how Your Majesty will explain this?
If there is no way to explain it to foreign lands,
then there is also no way to appease those within the borders.
With doubt lingering internally,
and slander arising externally,
this is not how to cultivate the majestic and
secure the state.
I wish Your Majesty would quickly issue a generous edict
to allow the two palaces to resume their social interactions and ceremonial duties as before.
Then the heavens will be clear, the earth peaceful,
and all nations will be greatly fortunate."
At that time, Quán Jì, Wú Ān, Sūn Qí, Yáng Zhú, and others secretly sided with Bà,
plotting to endanger the crown prince.
When their slanders took effect,
the crown prince was defeated,
and Bà was also granted death.
Zhú's corpse was cast into the Jiāng River.
His elder brother, Mù, having repeatedly admonished and warned Zhú,
was spared capital punishment,
but was still exiled to Nánzhōu.
After Bà was granted death,
Jì, Ān, Qí, and others were also executed,
all for having colluded with Bà to frame Hé.
Bà had two sons,
Jī and Yī.
During the Wǔfèng era,
Jī was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wú (Wú Hóu),
and Yī as the Marquis of Wǎnlíng.
Jī served Sūn Liàng within the palace.
In the second year of Tàipíng,
he stole and rode an imperial horse,
and was arrested and imprisoned.
Liàng asked the Attendant (Shìzhōng) Diāo Xuán,
"What is the penalty for stealing and riding an imperial horse?"
Xuán replied,
"According to the law, the punishment is death.
However, the King of Lǔ (Lǔ Wáng) died early,
so I ask Your Majesty to graciously pardon him."
Liàng said,
"Laws are
for all under heaven to abide by.
How can they be bent for the sake of kinship?
One should think of a way to resolve this; why press me with emotion?"
Xuán said,
"In the past, amnesties varied in scope;
some were for all under heaven,
and there were also amnesties for a thousand li or five hundred li,
extending as far as the emperor's will reached."
Liàng said,
"A discerning person should act thus!"
Thereupon, he issued an amnesty for the palace,
and Jī thus escaped death.
When Sūn Hào ascended the throne,
he recalled the old animosity between Hé and Bà,
stripped Jī and Yī of their titles and lands,
and exiled them with their grandmother, Lady Xiè (Xiè Jī), to Wūshāng County in Kuàijī.
Sūn Fèn
, whose courtesy name was Zǐyáng, was Bā's younger brother.
His mother was called Zhòngjī.
In the second year of Tàiyuán (252 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the King of Qí
and resided in Wǔchāng.
When Quán died,
Grand Tutor Zhūgě Kè did not want the princes to be located in areas along the river with military forces,
so he moved Fèn to Yùzhāng.
Fèn was angry
and did not obey the command,
and repeatedly transgressed the laws and regulations.
Kè submitted a memorial, remonstrating:
"The尊 (Dignity) of emperors and kings
is equal to that of Heaven.
Therefore, the world is their family,
officials are their fathers and elder brothers,
and within the Four Seas,
all are their subjects and concubines.
If an enemy has virtues,
one must promote them;
if a relative has vices,
one must punish them.
This is how one carries out the principles of Heaven and governs all things,
putting the state before oneself.
This is a system established by the sages,
a way that does not change for a hundred generations.
In the early Hàn dynasty,
many princes and imperial relatives became too powerful,
and invariably acted rebelliously.
Above, they almost endangered the altars of grain and soil;
below, relatives killed each other.
Afterwards, they learned from these warnings
and considered it a great taboo.
Since Guāngwǔ,
there have been regulations for the princes:
they were only allowed to entertain themselves within their palaces,
not to govern the people
or interfere with state affairs.
Any communication with them
was strictly forbidden.
Thus, they were able to remain safe
and preserve their blessings and fortunes.
This is the lesson from the successes and failures of previous generations.
Recently, Yuán Shào and Liú Biǎo each had their own territories;
their lands were not small,
and their populations were not weak.
Because they did not distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate heirs,
their ancestral sacrifices were extinguished.
This is something that all, whether wise or foolish,
universally lament.
The late emperor observed ancient warnings and drew lessons for the present,
preventing buds and stopping sprouts,
considering matters for a thousand years.
Therefore, on his sickbed,
he dispatched the various princes,
each to proceed to their respective states.
His imperial edicts were earnest,
and his prohibitions were severe.
The warnings and commands he gave
left nothing unaddressed,
truly wishing above to secure the ancestral temple,
and below to preserve the various princes,
so that for a hundred generations they would succeed each other
without the regret of harming the state or ruining the family.
Your Royal Highness should, above, contemplate Tàibó's will to obey his father;
in the middle, recall the respectful conduct of the King Xiàn of Héjiān and the King Qiáng of Dōnghǎi;
below, suppress your own arrogance and recklessness and take it as a warning.
Yet, I hear that since arriving in Wǔchāng recently,
you have often defied imperial edicts
and disregarded regulations,
arbitrarily dispatching generals' troops to repair and protect your palace.
Furthermore, regarding your attendants and retainers who commit offenses,
they should be reported
and publicly handed over to the authorities.
Instead, you have arbitrarily killed them in private,
and the matters are not clear.
Grand Marshal Lǚ Dài personally received the late emperor's edict
to assist and guide Your Royal Highness,
but you neither heeded nor adopted his words,
causing him distress and fear.
Huá Qí was a close official of the late emperor,
loyal, good, and upright.
What he presented
should have been adopted.
Instead, I hear you were angry with Qí
and spoke of arresting him.
And the imperial secretary Yáng Róng,
who personally received imperial edicts,
and to whom you should be reverent and solemn,
you said, 'I just won't listen to the prohibitions.
What can they do to me?'
When this was heard,
everyone, great and small, was shocked,
and no one felt anything but dread.
A common saying goes: 'A clear mirror reflects one's form;
ancient events reveal the present.'
Your Royal Highness should deeply take the King of Lǔ as a warning,
change your conduct,
be cautious and reverent,
and show utmost respect to the court.
If you do this, there is nothing you cannot obtain.
If you abandon and forget the late emperor's laws and teachings,
and harbor a disrespectful heart,
your ministers would rather fail Your Royal Highness
than dare to fail the late emperor's last will.
We would rather be resented and hated by Your Royal Highness
than dare to forget the majesty of the revered lord
and allow imperial edicts not to be enforced among the vassal officials!
This is the correct principle throughout ancient and modern times,
which Your Royal Highness knows and understands.
Blessings come with a cause;
misfortunes come with a gradual onset.
If the gradual onset is not worried about,
then it will be irreversible.
If the King of Lǔ had only heeded loyal and upright words early,
and harbored feelings of fear and apprehension,
his reign would have been endless.
How could he have met with the disaster of destruction?
Good medicine tastes bitter to the mouth,
but only the sick can bear its sweetness.
Loyal words grate on the ear,
but only the discerning can accept them.
Now, Kè and others are sincerely desirous of removing dangers from their very sprouts for Your Royal Highness,
and expanding the foundation of good fortune.
Therefore, I speak unreservedly,
and wish for your triple consideration."
Fèn was afraid upon receiving the memorial,
and thus moved to Nánchāng.
His hunting and revelry became even more excessive,
and his officials could not endure his commands.
When Kè was executed,
Fèn moved down to Wúhú,
intending to go to Jiànyè to observe the changing situation.
His grand tutor Xiè Cí and others remonstrated with Fèn,
but Fèn killed them.
For this, he was deposed as a commoner
and exiled to Zhāng'ān County.
In the third year of Tàipíng (258 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhāng'ān.
In the second year of Jiànhéng (270 CE),
Sūn Hào's left lady, Lady Wáng, died.
Hào mourned her excessively,
weeping and mourning day and night,
and did not emerge for several months.
Because of this, some in the populace said that Hào had died,
and a rumor spread that Fèn and the Marquis of Shàngyú, Fèng, were to be established.
Fèn's mother Zhòngjī's tomb was in Yùzhāng,
and the Administrator of Yùzhāng, Zhāng Jùn, suspecting this might be true,
cleaned the tomb mound.
Hào heard of this,
had Jùn torn apart by chariots,
exterminated his three clans,
and executed Fèn and his five sons.
The state was abolished.
The commentary states: Sūn Dēng's intentions
were sufficient for abundant and beautiful virtues.
Lǜ and Hé both possessed a disposition for goodness,
and strove to temper themselves.
Some died young,
others did not meet a natural death.
Alas!
Bā, being a concubine's son, interfered with the legitimate heir,
and Fèn did not follow the rules and regulations.
They certainly courted the path of danger and destruction.
However, Fèn's execution
was an undeserved calamity.
Biography of Hè Quán, Lǚ Zhōu, and Zhōnglí, Chapter Fifteen
Hè Qí,
whose courtesy name was Gōngmiáo, was a person from Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
In his youth, he was a county official
and served as the magistrate of Shàn.
A county clerk, Sī Cóng, was a frivolous and rebellious person who committed misdeeds.
Qí wanted to punish him.
The chief clerk remonstrated, saying:
"Cóng
is from a prominent family in the county,
and the Shānyuè are attached to him.
If you punish him today,
the bandits will arrive tomorrow."
Qí was greatly enraged upon hearing this
and immediately beheaded Cóng.
Cóng's clan and associates then gathered together,
numbering over a thousand people,
and raised an army to attack the county.
Qí led the officials and people,
opened the city gates, and launched a sudden attack,
thoroughly defeating them.
His prestige shook the Shānyuè.
Later, the people of Tàimò and Fēngpǔ rebelled.
He was transferred to serve as the magistrate of Tàimò.
He punished the wicked and nurtured the good,
and within a month, all was pacified.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān,
Sūn Cè personally oversaw the commandery,
and selected Qí as an Outstanding Talent and Filial Exemplar.
At that time, Wáng Lǎng fled to Dōngyě,
and Shāng Shēng, the Prefect of Hòuguān, raised troops for Lǎng.
Cè sent Hán Yàn, the Prefect of Yǒngníng, to lead the Southern Commandant (Nánbù Dūwèi)
and command soldiers to attack Shēng.
Qí was appointed Prefect of Yǒngníng.
Yàn was defeated by Shēng,
so Qí again replaced Yàn in leading the affairs of the Commandant.
Shēng feared Qí's prestige,
and sent an envoy to request an alliance.
Qí then explained to him,
detailing the misfortunes and blessings,
whereupon Shēng sent up his seals and ribbons,
and came out of his residence to surrender.
The bandit chiefs Zhāng Yǎ and Zhān Qiáng, etc., were unwilling to see Shēng surrender,
and instead jointly killed Shēng.
Yǎ proclaimed himself Wúshàng Jiāngjūn,
and Qiáng proclaimed himself Tài shǒu of Kuàijī.
The bandits were numerous and Qí's troops few,
insufficient to attack them,
so Qí halted his army and rested his troops.
Yǎ and his son-in-law Hé Xióng contended for power, becoming estranged.
Qí ordered the Yuè people to sow discord among them,
which created suspicion and division,
and they turned their forces against each other.
Qí then advanced to attack,
and in one battle severely defeated Yǎ.
Qiáng's faction was terrified,
and led their followers to surrender.
After Hòuguān was pacified,
Jiàn'ān, Hànxīng, and Nánpíng revolted again.
Qí advanced his troops to Jiàn'ān,
and established a Commandant's office.
This was the eighth year [of Jiàn'ān].
The commandery dispatched five thousand soldiers from its subordinate counties,
each led by their respective county prefects,
all under Qí's command.
The bandit leaders Hóng Míng, Hóng Jìn, Yuàn Yù, Wú Miǎn, and Huá Dāng, five individuals,
each leading tens of thousands of households,
were encamped consecutively in Hànxīng.
Wú had five to six thousand households separately encamped in Dàtán,
and Zōu Lín had six thousand households separately encamped in Gàizhú.
Both (Dàtán) came from Yúhàn.
(Pronounced Gān).
The army attacked Hànxīng,
passing through Yúhàn.
Qí believed that the bandits were numerous and his troops few,
and going deep without reinforcements,
feared being cut off.
He ordered Dīng Fán, the Prefect of Sōngyáng, to stay and guard Yúhàn.
Fán was originally from a neighboring city to Qí's,
and was ashamed to be under his command,
so he refused to stay.
Qí then executed Fán.
Thereupon, the army was shaken with fear,
and everyone obeyed orders.
He then divided his troops to stay and guard,
and advanced to attack Míng and the others,
repeatedly defeating them.
Míng was slain in battle.
Miǎn, Dāng, Jìn, and Yù all surrendered.
He then struck Gàizhú.
As the army approached Dàtán,
(three) [two] generals also surrendered.
In total, six thousand heads were taken in battle and pacification efforts,
and all the famous leaders were captured.
Counties and towns were re-established,
and ten thousand soldiers were levied.
He was appointed Píngdōng Xiàowèi.
In the tenth year,
he further attacked Shàngráo,
and divided it to establish Jiànpíng County.
In the thirteenth year,
he was promoted to Wēiwǔ Zhōnglángjiàng,
and attacked Yī and Shè in Dānyáng.
At that time, the four districts of Wǔqiáng, Yèxiāng, Dōngyáng, and Fēngpǔ had already surrendered.
Qí memorialized to establish Yèxiāng as Shǐxīn County.
Meanwhile, the Shè bandit chief Jīn Qí, with ten thousand households, was encamped on Ānlè Shān,
Máo Gān, with ten thousand households, was encamped on Wūliáo Shān,
and the Yī chiefs Chén Pú and Zǔ Shān, etc., with twenty thousand households, were encamped on Línlì Shān.
Línlì Shān was walled on all four sides,
dozens of zhàng high,
with dangerous and narrow paths
that could not accommodate swords and shields.
The bandits dropped stones from above,
making it impossible to attack.
The army stayed for days,
and the officers and men were troubled by this.
Qí personally went around,
observing the terrain,
and secretly recruited agile soldiers.
He had iron yokes made,
and secretly, in hidden and dangerous places where the bandits were not prepared,
used the yokes to hack out a path along the cliff,
sending men up secretly at night.
Then, many cloths were hung down to help the men below,
and several hundred people ascended.
They spread out on all four sides,
beating drums and blowing horns simultaneously.
Qí held his troops ready.
The bandits heard the drum sounds converging from all sides in the night,
believed that the main army had all ascended,
and were startled, confused, and bewildered,
not knowing what to do.
Those guarding the paths and strategic points
all ran back to rely on the main force.
The main army then ascended,
and severely defeated Pú and the others.
All the rest surrendered.
In total, seven thousand heads were taken.
Qí again memorialized to divide Shè into Xīndìng, Líyáng, and Xiūyáng.
Combining Yī and Shè,
there were a total of six counties.
Quán then provisionally divided them into Xīndū Commandery.
Qí was made Tài shǒu,
established his office in Shǐxīn,
and was promoted to Piānjiāngjūn.
In the sixteenth year,
Láng Zhì, a civilian from Yúháng County in Wú Commandery, gathered his clan and started a bandit rebellion
of several thousand people.
Qí went out to attack them,
and immediately defeated Zhì again.
He memorialized to divide Yúháng into Línshuǐ County.
He was ordered to go to the designated place,
and when he was about to return to the commandery,
Quán came out to bid him farewell along the road,
with music playing and elephants dancing.
He bestowed upon Qí a luxurious carriage and a swift horse,
and stopped his own carriage,
making Qí get into his carriage.
Qí declined, not daring to do so,
so Quán ordered his attendants to help Qí into the carriage,
and commanded the escorting officials, soldiers, and cavalry
to maintain the ceremony as if in the commandery.
Quán looked on and smiled, saying:
"One must exert oneself.
Without accumulating good deeds and diligent effort,
this cannot be obtained."
After about a hundred paces, he turned back.
In the eighteenth year,
the people Páng Cái, Lǐ Yù, Wáng Hǎi, etc., from the eastern part of Yùzhāng, rose up in banditry,
numbering over ten thousand people.
Qí attacked and pacified them,
executing their ringleaders,
and the rest all surrendered.
He selected their strong and robust men as soldiers,
and the rest became county households.
He was promoted to Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn.
In the twentieth year,
he followed Quán to campaign against Héfèi.
At that time, during a sally from the city,
Xú Shèng was wounded and lost his spear.
Qí engaged the enemy in the thick of battle,
recovering Shèng's lost weapon.
In the twenty-first year,
Yóu Tū, a civilian from Póyáng, received seals and ribbons from Cáo Gōng,
and turned the populace into bandits.
Língyáng, Shǐ'ān, and Jīngxiàn all responded to Tū.
Qí, together with Lù Xùn, attacked and defeated Tū,
beheading several thousand.
The remaining factions were terrified and submitted.
The three Dānyáng counties all surrendered.
Eight thousand elite soldiers were levied.
He was appointed Āndōng Jiāngjūn,
ennobled as the Marquis of Shānyīn,
and stationed on the Jiāngshàng,
supervising from Fúzhōu up to Wǎn.
At the beginning of Huángwǔ,
Wèi envoy Cáo Xiū came to attack.
Qí arrived late due to the long journey,
and then stationed himself in Xīnshì to resist.
It happened that the various armies at Dòngkǒu encountered strong winds and were drowned,
losing half their number.
The generals and soldiers lost color.
Fortunately, Qí had not yet crossed,
and his division alone remained intact,
which the generals relied upon for strength.
Qí was by nature extravagant and fond of grandeur,
especially in military matters.
His armor and weapons were exceptionally fine,
his warship was carved and painted crimson,
with a green canopy and crimson screens.
His shields, halberds, and spears
were adorned with flower and melon patterns.
His bows, crossbows, and arrows
were all made from the finest materials.
His covered assault boats (méngchōng) and fighting vessels (dòujiàn)
looked like mountains from a distance.
Xiū and others feared him,
and thus withdrew their army.
He was promoted to Hòujiāngjūn,
and given the axe of authority to lead as Xúzhōu Mù.
Initially,
Jìn Zōng (晉宗) served as a general at Xìkǒu (戲口).
He defected with his troops to Wèi (魏),
and was later appointed as the Administrator of Qīchūn (蘄春).
He planned to attack Ānlè (安樂)
to seize their hostages.
Sūn Quán (孫權) considered this a shameful provocation.
As his army had just been dismissed
and it was the height of summer in the sixth month,
he took them by surprise
and ordered the Chief Controller Mí Fāng (麋芳), Xiān Yú Dān (鮮于丹) and others to attack Qīchūn.
They successfully captured Jìn Zōng alive.
Four years later, he died.
His son, Dá (達), and younger brother, Jǐng (景), both earned good reputations
and became excellent generals.
Quán Cóng (全琮), courtesy name Zǐhuáng (子璜),
was a native of Qiántáng (錢唐) in Wújùn (吳郡).
His father, Róu (柔),
was nominated as Xiàolián (孝廉) during the reign of Emperor Líng (靈帝) of Hàn (漢).
He was appointed as Shàngshū Láng Yòuchéng (尚書郎右丞).
During Dǒng Zhuó's (董卓) rebellion,
he abandoned his office and returned home.
The province invited him to serve as Biéjià Cóngshì (別駕從事),
and an imperial edict then appointed him as Dūwèi (都尉) of Huìjī (會稽) Eastern Commandery.
When Sūn Cè (孫策) arrived in Wú (吳),
Róu raised troops and was the first to pledge allegiance.
Sūn Cè memorialized for Róu to be appointed Dānyáng Dūwèi (丹楊都尉).
When Sūn Quán became Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍),
he made Róu his Chángshǐ (長史),
and later transferred him to be Administrator of Guìyáng (桂陽).
Róu once sent Cóng with several thousand *hú* (斛) of rice to Wú
to purchase goods.
When Cóng arrived,
he distributed it all,
and returned with an empty boat.
Róu was furious.
Cóng kowtowed and said:
"Your foolish son believed that what was to be purchased was not urgent,
but the gentry were facing the hardship of being utterly destitute.
Therefore, I immediately distributed relief
without waiting to report."
Róu was instead greatly impressed by him.
At this time, gentry from the Central Plains fled the chaos and came south.
Those who depended on Cóng for residence numbered in the hundreds.
Cóng spent his family fortune to assist them,
sharing what he had and what he did not.
Thus, his reputation became widely known.
Later, Sūn Quán appointed him Fènwēi Xiàowèi (奮威校尉),
gave him several thousand troops,
and sent him to suppress the Shānyuè (山越).
He then opened recruitment and enlisted
over ten thousand elite soldiers.
He encamped at Niúzhǔ (牛渚),
and was gradually promoted to Piānjiāngjūn (偏將軍).
In the 24th year of Jiàn'ān (建安) (219 CE),
Liú Bèi's (劉備) general Guān Yǔ (關羽) besieged Fán (樊) and Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Cóng submitted a memorial proposing a strategy to attack Guān Yǔ.
At the time, Sūn Quán had already secretly discussed an attack with Lǚ Méng (呂蒙),
and fearing the plan would be leaked,
he therefore shelved Cóng's memorial without a reply.
When Guān Yǔ was captured,
Sūn Quán hosted a banquet at Gōng'ān (公安),
and looked at Cóng, saying:
"You previously made this suggestion.
Although I did not reply to you,
today's victory
is also your achievement."
Thereupon, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yánghuá Tíng (陽華亭侯).
In the first year of Huángchū (黃初) (220 CE),
Wèi (魏) launched a large naval force from Dòngkǒu (洞口).
Sūn Quán ordered Lǚ Fàn (呂範) to oversee the generals in resisting them.
Their military camps were within sight of each other.
The enemy repeatedly launched surprise attacks with light boats.
Cóng always wore armor and carried weapons,
constantly on watch.
After a while,
several thousand enemy troops emerged from the river.
Cóng attacked and routed them,
beheading their general Yǐn Lú (尹盧).
Cóng was promoted to Suínán Jiāngjūn (綏南將軍),
and further enfeoffed as Marquis of Qiántáng (錢唐).
In the fourth year (223 CE),
he was granted the *jié* (節) and appointed Administrator of Jiǔjiāng (九江).
In the seventh year (226 CE),
Sūn Quán arrived at Wǎn (皖)
and sent Cóng with Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) Lù Xùn (陸遜) to attack Cáo Xiū (曹休).
They defeated him at Shítíng (石亭).
At this time, the mountain people of Dānyáng (丹楊), Wú (吳), and Huìjī (會稽) once again became bandits.
They attacked and occupied several subordinate counties.
Sūn Quán divided the strategic areas of the three commanderies into Dōng'ān Jùn (東安郡),
with Cóng as its Administrator.
Upon his arrival,
he clearly established rewards and punishments,
and recruited and enticed defectors.
Within a few years,
he gathered over ten thousand people.
Sūn Quán recalled Cóng to Niúzhǔ,
and abolished Dōng'ān Jùn.
In the first year of Huánglóng (黃龍) (229 CE),
he was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍), Zuǒ Hùjūn (左護軍), and Xúzhōu Mù (徐州牧),
and married a princess.
In the second year of Jiāhé (嘉禾) (233 CE),
he commanded fifty thousand infantry and cavalry to conquer Liù'ān (六安).
The people of Liù'ān all scattered and fled.
The generals wanted to divide their forces to capture them.
Cóng said:
"To take advantage of danger and rely on luck,
with an outcome less than completely certain,
is not in the best interest of the state.
Now, if we divide our forces to capture the people,
the gains and losses will be evenly split.
How can this be called complete success?
Even if we gain something,
it will still not be enough to weaken the enemy or fulfill the nation's expectations.
Should anything unexpected happen,
the losses would be considerable.
Rather than incur guilt,
I would rather bear the responsibility myself,
and not seek glory at the expense of the nation."
In the ninth year of Chìwū (赤烏) (246 CE),
he was promoted to Yòu Dàsīmǎ (右大司馬) and Zuǒ Jūnshī (左軍師).
He was respectful and compliant,
good at understanding expressions and accepting advice.
His words were never harsh or offensive.
Initially,
when Sūn Quán was about to besiege Zhūyá (珠崖) and Yízhōu (夷州),
he always consulted Cóng first.
Cóng said:
"With the might of the Sacred Dynasty,
what direction can it face and not conquer?
However, these distant lands and foreign regions
are separated by perilous seas.
The climate and water are poisonous;
this has been the case since ancient times.
When troops enter and people emerge,
illness is bound to arise,
spreading from one to another.
Those who go may fear they cannot return,
so what gains can be plentiful?
To foolishly deplete the troops on the riverbanks
in the hope of a one-in-ten-thousand profit,
your humble servant finds unacceptable."
Sūn Quán did not listen.
The army campaigned for a year,
and eight or nine out of ten soldiers died from illness and disease.
Sūn Quán deeply regretted it.
Later, when the topic came up,
Cóng replied:
"At that time,
if any of your ministers did not remonstrate,
your servant would consider them disloyal."
As Cóng was both trusted and important,
his relatives and children were all showered with favor and nobility,
receiving thousands of catties of gold.
Yet, he remained humble in his interactions with scholars,
showing no signs of arrogance.
In the twelfth year (249 CE), he died.
His son, Yì (懌), succeeded him.
Later, Yì inherited the lineage and commanded troops.
When rescuing Zhūgě Dàn (諸葛誕) at Shòuchūn (壽春),
he left the city and surrendered first.
Wèi appointed him Píngdōng Jiāngjūn (平東將軍)
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Línxiāng (臨湘).
Yì's nephews, Yī (禕), Yí (儀), and Jìng (靜) also surrendered to Wèi,
and all served as commandery administrators and marquises.
Lǚ Dài (呂岱), courtesy name Dìnggōng (定公),
was a native of Hǎilíng (海陵) in Guǎnglǐng (廣陵).
He served as a county official.
He fled the chaos and crossed south.
When Sūn Quán took charge of affairs,
Lǚ Dài went to the headquarters
and was sent out to serve as Administrator of Wú (吳).
Sūn Quán personally reviewed the county granaries, warehouses, and prisoners.
All administrators and chiefs were present.
Lǚ Dài handled legal cases and interrogations
much to Sūn Quán's satisfaction.
He was summoned and appointed Lùshì (錄事),
then sent out to serve as Chief of Yúyáo (餘姚).
He recruited elite and robust men,
obtaining over a thousand.
At this time, the bandits Lǚ Hé (呂合) and Qín Láng (秦狼) from the five counties of Dōngyě (東冶) in Huìjī (會稽) caused unrest.
Sūn Quán appointed Lǚ Dài as Dūjūn Xiàowèi (督軍校尉),
and sent him with general Jiǎng Qīn (蔣欽) and others to suppress them.
They captured Lǚ Hé and Qín Láng,
and the five counties were pacified.
He was appointed Zhāoxìn Zhōnglángjiāng (昭信中郎將).
In the 20th year of Jiàn'ān [220 AD],
Dū Sūn Mào and ten other generals followed to conquer the three commanderies of Chángshā.
Also, officials from the four counties of Ānchéng, Yōu, Yǒngxīn, and Chálíng jointly entered Yīnshān City,
gathered a multitude to resist Dài.
Dài attacked and besieged them.
They immediately surrendered,
and the three commanderies were completely pacified.
Quán kept Dài to guard Chángshā.
Wú Dàng, the chief of Ānchéng, and Zhōngláng Jiāng Yuán Lóng and others, colluded with Guān Yǔ
and rebelled again.
Dàng occupied Yōuxiàn,
and Lóng was in Lǐlíng.
Quán dispatched Héngjiāng Jiāngjūn Lǔ Sù to attack Yōu,
and Dàng managed to break out and escape.
Dài attacked Lǐlíng,
then captured and executed Lóng,
and was promoted to Lúlíng Tàishǒu.
In the 1st year of Yánkāng [220 AD],
he replaced Bù Zhì as Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ.
Upon arriving at the province,
the bandit leader Qián Bó from Gāoliáng offered to surrender.
Dài, acting on his authority,
appointed Bó as Gāoliáng Xībù Dūwèi.
When the Yí bandits of Yùlín again attacked and besieged commanderies and counties,
Dài campaigned and defeated them.
At this time, Wáng Jīn, a bandit from Zhēnyáng, Guìyáng, gathered a multitude on the border of Nánhǎi,
initiated rebellion and caused harm.
Quán again ordered Dài to suppress him.
He captured Jīn alive,
and sent him to the capital.
The total number of those beheaded and captured alive was over ten thousand.
He was promoted to Ānnán Jiāngjūn,
granted the privilege of a Jié,
and enfeoffed as Dūxiāng Hóu.
When Jiāozhǐ Tàishǒu Shì Xiè died,
Quán appointed Xiè's son, Huī, as Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
and granted him the governorship of Jiǔzhēn Tàishǒu,
while appointing Xiàowèi Chén Shí to replace Xiè.
Dài memorialized to divide the three commanderies south of the sea into Jiāozhōu,
with Jiāngjūn Dài Liáng as Cìshǐ,
and the four commanderies east of the sea into Guǎngzhōu,
with Dài himself as Cìshǐ.
He sent Liáng and Shí to enter the south,
but Huī did not obey the order,
and raised troops to garrison the seaport to resist Liáng and others.
Dài then submitted a memorial requesting to punish Huī for his crime,
and led three thousand troops to cross the sea day and night.
Someone said to Dài:
"Huī relies on generations of favor,
and is supported by the entire province;
he is not to be underestimated."
Dài said:
"Although Huī now harbors rebellious plans,
he does not expect our sudden arrival.
If I secretly move my army swiftly,
and catch him unprepared,
his defeat is certain.
If we delay and do not act quickly,
allowing him to conceive ideas,
to fortify his city and hold out,
then the seven commanderies and the hundred barbarian tribes
will gather like clouds and respond.
Even if there are wise men,
who can devise a plan then?"
So he proceeded,
passed through Hépǔ,
and advanced with Liáng.
When Huī heard of Dài's arrival,
he was indeed greatly terrified,
not knowing what to do.
He immediately led his six brothers, stripped to the waist, to welcome Dài.
Dài beheaded them all and sent their heads away.
Huī's chief generals Gān Lǐ, Huán Zhì, and others, led officials and common people to attack Dài.
Dài bravely fought and utterly defeated them,
and was promoted to Fānyú Hóu.
Thereupon Guǎngzhōu was abolished,
and it reverted to Jiāozhōu as before.
After Dài had pacified Jiāozhōu,
he further advanced to suppress Jiǔzhēn,
beheading and capturing tens of thousands.
He also sent his subordinate officials to proclaim the state's transforming influence in the south,
reaching the kings of Fúnán, Línyì, and Tángmíng beyond the borders,
who each sent envoys to offer tribute.
Quán commended his accomplishments,
and promoted him to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn.
In the 3rd year of Huánglóng [231 AD],
as the southern lands were peaceful and stable,
Dài was recalled to garrison Ōukǒu in Chángshā.
At that time, the Man Yi of Wǔlíng were stirring up trouble.
Dài and Tàicháng Pān Jùn jointly suppressed and pacified them.
In the 3rd year of Jiāhé [234 AD],
Quán ordered Dài to lead Pān Zhāng's troops,
and garrison Lùkǒu,
later moving to Púqí.
In the 4th year [235 AD],
the bandits Lǐ Huán and Lù Hé from Lúlíng, Suí Chūn from Dōngyě, Kuàijī, and Luó Lì from Nánhǎi, all rose up simultaneously.
Chūn immediately surrendered.
Quán again ordered Dài to supervise Liú Zuǎn, Táng Zī, and others to divide and attack them.
and made him lead his forces,
thereby becoming a listed general.
Huán, Lì, and others were all captured and beheaded,
and their heads sent to the capital.
Quán issued an edict to Dài, saying:
"Lì, relying on treacherous terrain, caused rebellion,
leading himself to be executed and his head displayed;
Huán, cunning and deceitful, repeatedly rebelled after surrendering.
Previous campaigns
failed to capture him for years.
Without your strategies and plans,
who could have executed him?
Your loyal and martial integrity
is further demonstrated by this.
With the chief villains eliminated,
the great and small are intimidated.
The remaining minor elements
will be completely eradicated.
From now on,
the state will forever be free from worries about the south,
the three commanderies will be peaceful,
without any alarm or fear.
Moreover, we have gained unruly people to provide labor and taxes.
This is truly something to deeply admire.
Rewards should not exceed a month,
this is a permanent state regulation.
As for what is appropriate by established rules,
you may decide it yourself."
When Pān Jùn died,
Dài replaced Jùn in managing the documents for Jīngzhōu,
and was stationed with Lù Xùn in Wǔchāng,
therefore he supervised Púqí.
Soon after,
Liáo Shì caused rebellion,
attacking and besieging cities and towns.
The various commanderies of Línglíng, Cāngwú, and Yùlín were disturbed.
Dài personally memorialized to proceed immediately,
traveling day and night.
Quán sent an envoy to confer upon Dài the title of Jiāozhōu Mù,
and dispatched various generals such as Táng Zī and others to follow in quick succession.
They campaigned for a year and defeated him,
beheading Shì and those he falsely appointed, such as Línhé Tàishǒu Fèi Yáng,
and wiped out his factions.
The commanderies and counties were all pacified,
and he returned to Wǔchāng.
At this time, he was already eighty years old,
yet his constitution was naturally diligent and vigorous,
and he personally attended to state affairs.
Fènwēi Jiāngjūn Zhāng Chéng wrote to Dài, saying:
"In ancient times, Dàn Shì assisted Zhōu,
and the Er Nán (Songs of the South) were composed.
Now, it is you and Lù Zǐ.
You prioritize loyalty and diligence,
and humbly yield to each other.
Your achievements are perfected through adaptation to circumstances,
and your transforming influence aligns with the Dao.
Gentlemen praise your virtues,
and common people rejoice in your excellence.
Moreover, you are busy with documents,
and guests fill your days.
You do not stop working when tired,
nor complain of weariness from labor.
I also know that when you get on a horse, you leap onto it yourself,
without using the stirrups.
In this, you surpass Lián Pō.
How swift and pleasing you are in everything!
The Yì Jīng says:
'Propriety speaks of respect,
and virtue speaks of abundance.'
How can you embody all these virtues!"
When Lù Xùn died,
Zhūgě Kè replaced Xùn.
Quán then divided Wǔchāng into two sections.
Dài supervised the right section,
from Wǔchāng up to Púqí.
He was promoted to Shàng Dà Jiāngjūn,
and his son Kǎi was appointed Fùjūn Xiàowèi,
to supervise troops at Púqí.
When Sūn Liàng ascended the throne,
Dài was appointed Dà Sīmǎ.
Dài was incorruptible in serving the public,
and his conduct was commendable everywhere.
Initially in Jiāozhōu,
he did not send provisions home for years,
and his wife and children suffered from hunger.
Quán heard of this and sighed,
reprimanding his officials:
"Lǚ Dài traveled thousands of miles
to diligently serve the state,
while his family suffered hardship at home,
and I did not know this earlier.
Where lies the responsibility of my close aides and informants?"
Thereupon, additional money, rice, cloth, and silk were bestowed,
with an annual limit.
Initially,
Lǚ Dài was close to Xú Yuán from Wújùn.
Xú Yuán was fervent and had talent and ambition.
Lǚ Dài knew he could achieve great things,
so he gave him a headscarf and a belt,
and conversed with him.
Later, he recommended and promoted him,
and he served as Yùshǐ.
Xú Yuán was loyal and brave by nature,
and liked to speak frankly.
Whenever Lǚ Dài made mistakes,
Xú Yuán would immediately remonstrate
and publicly discuss them.
When people sometimes told Lǚ Dài about this,
Lǚ Dài sighed and said:
"This is why I value Déyuān."
When Xú Yuán died,
Lǚ Dài wept for him with great sorrow,
saying:
"Déyuān,
you were Lǚ Dài's beneficial friend.
Now, unfortunately,
where will Lǚ Dài hear his faults criticized again?"
Those who discussed it praised this.
In the first year of Tàipíng,
he died at the age of ninety-six.
His son, Kǎi, succeeded him.
His will stipulated that he be interred in a plain coffin,
with a coarse headscarf and a cloth belt,
and that the funeral arrangements
should be kept simple and frugal.
Kǎi carried out all of these instructions.
Zhōu Fáng, courtesy name Zǐyú,
was a native of Yángxiàn in Wújùn.
In his youth, he loved learning
and was nominated as Xiàolián.
He served as the Chief of Níngguó,
then was transferred to Huái'ān.
When Péng Shì, a powerful leader from Qiántáng, and others gathered like ants to form bandits,
Zhōu Fáng was appointed as the Marquis Administrator of Qiántáng.
Within a month,
he beheaded Péng Shì and his confederates,
and was promoted to Dānyáng Xībù Dūwèi.
During the Huángwǔ era,
Péng Qǐ, a powerful leader from Póyáng, rebelled,
attacking and capturing cities within the commandery.
Zhōu Fáng was then appointed as the Administrator of Póyáng.
He collaborated with Hú Zōng to attack and suppress them,
and successfully captured Péng Qǐ alive,
sending him to Wǔchāng.
He was granted the title of Zhāoyì Xiàowèi.
He was instructed to secretly seek out old influential families and famous leaders in the mountains who were known to the northern enemy,
and to trick and provoke Cáo Xiū, the Grand Marshal and Provincial Governor of Yángzhōu for Wèi.
Zhōu Fáng replied
that he feared the local leaders and petty rascals were unreliable,
and that the matter might leak,
failing to lure Cáo Xiū.
He requested to send trusted individuals with seven articles to entice Cáo Xiū:
The first reads:
"Fáng, by a thousand-year stroke of luck,
has become a provincial commoner.
Separated by distant rivers,
my reverence has not yet been demonstrated.
Gazing upon the clouds and scenery,
Heaven truly willed this.
My sincerity is slight,
my position not prominent,
though I harbor fervent longing,
how can I be seen clearly?
A fox dies facing its hill,
human nature longs for its roots,
yet constrained by circumstances,
I violate the ritual of presentation.
Each time I alone crane my neck and look west,
I never fail to lament in waking and sleeping,
tossing and turning restlessly.
Now, taking advantage of this crack and opening,
I can express my long-held aspiration.
If not for divine inspiration,
how could I achieve this!
Unable to bear my eager anticipation,
I entrust my fate from a thousand *lǐ* away.
I respectfully send trusted individuals, Dǒng Cén and Shào Nán, among others, feigning rebellion to present this letter.
The current events and changes
are listed on a separate paper.
May the enlightened Duke and Marquis extend the light of the sun and moon,
illuminating the desires of distant people,
forever allowing those who pledge allegiance to have someone to rely on."
The second reads:
"Fáng is far away in a border region,
separated by rivers and streams.
Benevolence and civilizing influence
have not yet reached me.
Though I express my thoughts from within the valleys,
I fear that with such great righteousness,
I may not be trusted or accepted.
Indeed, things arise from emotion,
and plans are born from changes;
this is consistent throughout antiquity and the present.
Fáng served in the eastern commandery,
his initial wish already granted,
his heart inscribed with a vow to repay,
forever without wavering.
How could I have anticipated that recently I would suffer an undeserved condemnation,
with disaster imminent,
more perilous than throwing an egg?
To advance, there is the propriety of joining or leaving;
to retreat, there is the fault of being slandered and dying unjustly.
Although my aspirations and conduct are humble,
and my existence and demise are but a single matter,
I look upon this as not my proper place,
how can I not feel disheartened!
I dare to follow the ancients,
and thus know where to return,
sincerely expressing my feelings,
revealing my innermost thoughts.
I beg you to bestow the moistness of spring,
to pity and save me in my urgency,
no longer to be suspicious,
and to accept my entrusted fate.
If this matter is divulged,
I will suffer unpredictable punishment.
Firstly, it would harm compassion and damage strategy;
secondly, it would cut off the hearts of those who wish to turn to you.
May the enlightened envoy look far into the past,
pity and commiserate with me,
pay attention to what is pledged,
and quickly grant a secret reply.
Fáng will await your actions,
and expect your response."
The third reads:
"The former Administrator, Wáng Jìng of Guǎnglíng, whom Fáng replaced,
was also once reprimanded
due to the rebellion of the commandery's people.
Wáng Jìng diligently tried to explain himself,
but was never cleared.
Consequently, he formed a secret plan
to pledge allegiance to the North.
Unfortunately, the matter was exposed,
and even infants were executed.
Since Fáng personally witnessed Wáng Jìng's affair,
and moreover observes the contempt the Eastern ruler harbors,
he knows that he will not be treated generously again.
Even if he is temporarily spared,
he will eventually be eliminated.
Now, by ordering Fáng to lead the commandery again,
it is to demand future loyalty.
This is surely meant to kill Fáng.
Though I still breathe,
I am anxious and worried,
not knowing when my life
will end.
A person living in this world
is like a white colt passing a crack,
yet constantly harbors fear and dread;
how can this be expressed!
I can only state my foolishness,
and once again reveal everything.
I fear that due to my low status,
I may not be considered.
I wish the enlightened envoy would give a little detailed consideration
and ponder my words.
The people of this commandery,
though outwardly declared surrendered,
are still in the mountains and wilds,
watching for an opening,
desiring to cause rebellion again.
On the day of rebellion,
Fáng's life will be over.
The Eastern ruler recently secretly deployed his generals,
planning to advance north.
Lǚ Fàn and Sūn Sháo, among others, entered Huái,
Quán Cóng and Zhū Huán hurried to Héféi,
Zhūgě Jǐn, Bù Zhì, and Zhū Rán went to Xiāngyáng,
and Lù Yì and Pān Zhāng, among others, attacked Méi Fū.
