The Eastern ruler's central camp personally covered Shíyáng,
and he separately sent his cousin Sūn Huàn to pacify Ānlù City,
establishing storehouses
and transporting goods and provisions
for military supplies.
He also ordered Zhūgě Liàng to advance towards Guānxī.
None of the generals along the river remained;
only about three thousand soldiers were left to guard Wǔchāng.
If the enlightened envoy, with ten thousand soldiers,
starts from the southern bank of the Huái River,
Fáng will then lead the officials and people from here
to act as an internal response.
The various commanderies in this region
that have previously launched uprisings
and failed just before completion
did so because they lacked external support;
if the Northern army approaches the border,
and sends proclamations to the affiliated cities,
who among the longing people
would not stand on tiptoe in anticipation?
I wish the enlightened envoy would look up to observe the celestial timing,
look down to examine human affairs,
and consult the yarrow stalks and tortoise shells in between,
then it will be evident that my previous words are not empty."
Its fourth point states:
"The dispatched Dǒng Cén and Shào Nán have been part of my household since they were young,
loved and trusted
like my own sons.
Therefore, I specifically ordered them to carry this letter,
using 'rebellion' as a pretense.
We communicated with our eyes and planned in our hearts,
not by speaking aloud.
Even my closest relatives
know nothing of this.
I have also instructed them
that upon reaching the prefecture, they should say they are surrendering,
so that those who wish to rebel and come north can spread the word.
Fáng makes this plan,
leaving it to Heaven.
If it succeeds,
there will be the fortune of survival;
if it accidentally leaks,
then there will be the calamity of annihilation.
Often, in the dead of night, I look up at the sky
and make solemn vows to the stars.
How can such a humble sincerity
reach Heaven?
Yet, with affairs urgent and I being alone and destitute,
I can only appeal to Heaven.
On the day I sent the envoys,
I was between life and death,
my body present but my spirit gone,
my soul bewildered and restless.
I privately fear that the Illustrious Commander may not fully vouch for them,
so Dǒng Cén and Shào Nán, one of them can be kept
as a later guarantee.
One should bring back the instruction.
When the instruction comes back, it should naturally state repentance for rebellion and surrender.
The Eastern Lord has a standing regulation:
those who repent of rebellion and return
are all pardoned for their crimes.
In this way, both sides will be satisfied,
and there will never be any lingering doubts.
When writing this command, looking west,
tears and brush flowed together."
Its fifth point states:
"The people of Póyáng
are truly numerous and stubborn.
If commanded to serve,
they do not immediately obey;
if incited to revolt,
they respond with cheers.
Although they have now surrendered,
their deep-seated resentment is not yet resolved.
Living in mountains and hiding in grass,
their rebellious hearts still exist.
Now the Eastern Lord plans to mobilize a great army,
the whole country will be dispatched,
the riverside will be desolate,
the garrisons and forts will be empty and damaged,
with only the various spies remaining.
If this opportunity is seized to stir up these people,
they can be rallied in an instant.
However, external aid must be relied upon,
with internal and external forces mutually supporting.
Otherwise,
nothing will be achieved.
Now, if the Illustrious Commander advances along the Wǎn route to the riverbank,
Fáng will respond from Lìkǒu on the opposite southern bank.
If you cannot reach the riverbank directly,
you can stop a hundred *lǐ* upstream,
so that the people in this area know the Northern army is there,
and they will then take care of themselves.
The people in this area do not suffer from hunger and cold and are content with war and banditry;
they suffer from punitive expeditions
and are glad to belong to the North.
But if they are poor and in distress when they
initiate an uprising and do not receive timely support,
they will soon suffer disaster.
If the Shíyáng and Qīng, Xú armies follow one another closely,
tying down the opposing forces
and preventing their swift retreat,
that would be excellent, truly excellent.
Fáng was born in the Jiāng-Huái region
and grew up amidst current affairs.
Seeing this advantageous situation,
one hundred undertakings will bring one hundred successes.
Such an opportunity will not come again,
so I dare to lay bare my innermost thoughts."
Its sixth point states:
"The Eastern Lord resents not having captured Shíyáng previously.
Now for this next campaign,
a large new army has been assembled,
and Pān Jùn has been ordered to mobilize the Yi people.
The numbers are very large.
It is heard that regulations have been set in advance,
where weak new recruits will be placed in front,
and good soldiers will be kept in the rear.
On the day of the siege,
it is said they intend to fill the trenches with weak soldiers
to break through immediately.
Although this may not fully happen,
it shows the general intention.
I privately fear that Shíyáng city is small
and cannot hold the opposing forces for long.
Illustrious Commander, please quickly provide relief.
Speed and secrecy are truly essential.
The change of Wáng Jìng
is a recent lesson.
Now Fáng commits his life;
it no longer rests with Heaven,
but precisely with the Illustrious Commander.
If relief arrives,
then success can certainly be achieved.
If relief is not timely,
then I will share the same calamity as Wáng Jìng.
Previously, during Péng Qǐ's time,
it was heard that your banners and pennants were at Fénglóng.
The people of this commandery, great and small, rejoiced
and all wished to make a contribution.
If you had stayed for about a month,
the undertaking would have largely succeeded.
It is a pity you left with lightning speed,
allowing the East to increase its forces and fully concentrate on attacking Péng Qǐ.
Only then was Péng Qǐ defeated.
May the Illustrious Commander deeply consider these words."
Its seventh point states:
"Now that a great undertaking is being launched,
it cannot be encouraged without titles.
I humbly request fifty seals each for generals and marquises,
one hundred seals for *lángjiàng* (Gentlemen of the Household),
and two hundred seals each for *xiàowèi* (Commanders of Detachments) and *dūwèi* (Commanders of Colonel).
These can be provisionally granted to the various leaders
to encourage their aspirations.
I also humbly request several tens of banners and pennants
to serve as markers,
so that the mountain soldiers, officials, and people
can see them with their own eyes,
knowing that the choice of going or staying is already decided,
and that the path of rescue has been clearly set.
Furthermore, there are daily defections and surrenders on both sides;
there are people every day
in the communication between the sides
who always get to know things.
This current great undertaking
requires divine secrecy.
If you review Fáng's letter,
I humbly ask for extreme discretion.
I understand that wisdom has its limits,
and precautions must be profound.
Fáng is filled with worry and apprehension,
and has repeatedly sent messages.
I beg you not to blame or fault me."
Páng then separately submitted a secret memorial, saying:
"To the north, there are fugitive bandits,
firmly entrenched along the Hé and Luò rivers,
who have long delayed the royal punishment.
They have seized control of the northern lands.
I have been unable to offer any extraordinary or excellent plans,
upwards to illuminate and assist the grand transformation,
downwards to express even one ten-thousandth [of my loyalty].
My heart is pounded with worry,
and I sleep fitfully, forgetting to rest.
The sagely court, like Heaven, covers [all],
tolerates my ineffectiveness,
and has graciously issued a superior decree,
commanding me to first entice and capture Zhéi Xiū.
I regret that it has not gone according to plan.
Now, I am to seek out in the prefectural borders prominent mountain valley leaders who are known to the northern bandits,
and have them communicate with the north.
I have profoundly deliberated,
and joy and fear are intertwined.
I secretly fear that such a person cannot be found quickly.
Even if such a person could be found,
I fear they cannot be trusted.
It would be better for me to deceive Xiū;
this would be more convenient for the plan.
This is my long-cherished hope of many years,
encountering a singular opportunity in a thousand years.
I have personally driven myself to the utmost,
exhausting my dull and obscured intellect,
to draft a deception letter to entice Xiū,
as detailed on the separate paper.
I know I do not possess the ancient skills of single or complex stratagems.
Moreover, suddenly receiving this great strategy,
I am flustered and discomfited.
I fear that due to my triviality and foolishness,
I may betray this special favor,
and I am already filled with anxiety.
I have heard that Táng Yáo followed Heaven before Heaven even moved,
and broadly consulted even common folk [like] woodcutters,
thereby achieving great merit.
The court's divine strategy [suggests that]
it wishes to surely bring Xiū into its trap.
With spiritual aid to the sagely plan,
Xiū will surely deliver himself,
enabling the six armies to envelop [him],
leaving no barbarian alive.
The awe-inspiring wind will sweep like lightning,
and the empire will rejoice greatly.
I respectfully submit this memorial to report,
and also present the draft letter.
Fearing my shallow understanding,
I am subsequently filled with trepidation."
The reply authorized its implementation.
Xiū indeed trusted Páng,
and led 100,000 infantry and cavalry,
with provisions filling the roads,
directly entering Wǎn.
Páng also gathered his forces,
and with Lù Xùn, intercepted Xiū.
Xiū's forces shattered and disintegrated,
and tens of thousands were slain or captured.
When Páng first formulated his secret plan,
there were frequently imperial secretaries who came with edicts to question him on various matters.
Páng then went to the gates of the prefectural office [and] the Department of the Palace Gate,
and then cut his hair to apologize,
so Xiū heard of it [and]
no longer harbored doubts.
When the affair succeeded and the army returned,
Quán held a grand banquet for all the generals.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he said to Páng:
"You cut your hair and embraced righteousness,
accomplishing this great task for me.
Your meritorious achievements [and] fame
should be written on bamboo and silk."
He was promoted to Píjiāngjūn and
granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
The bandit leader Dǒng Sì, relying on natural barriers, plundered and robbed,
and Yùzhāng and Línchuān both suffered from his depredations.
Wú Càn and Táng Zī once attacked him with 3,000 soldiers [and] besieged him,
but could not dislodge him for months.
Páng memorialized, requesting to dismiss the troops [and]
be allowed to act at his discretion.
Páng dispatched secret agents,
instructed them with strategies,
and enticed Dǒng Sì to be ambushed and killed.
Dǒng Sì's younger brother was terrified
and surrendered to Lù Xùn at Wǔchāng,
requesting to move to flat lands
and reform himself.
Because of this, several commanderies no longer had cause for worry.
Páng died after thirteen years in the commandery.
He rewarded good and punished evil,
exercising both authority and grace.
His son, Chǔ,
also possessed literary and martial talents.
During the Tiānjì era, he served as Dōngguānlìng and Wúnándū.
Zhōnglí Mù, courtesy name Zǐgàn,
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Hàn Lǔxiàng Yì.
In his youth, he lived in Yǒngxīng,
personally cultivating land,
planting over twenty *mǔ* of rice.
As the harvest approached,
a county resident recognized it [as his own].
Mù said:
"I originally cultivated it because the field was barren, that's all."
He then gave the rice to the county resident.
The county magistrate heard of this,
summoned the resident, and imprisoned him,
intending to punish him according to the law.
Mù pleaded on his behalf.
The magistrate said:
"You emulate Chéng Gōng
and perform righteous deeds yourself.
I, as the people's leader,
must govern according to the law.
How can I set aside public statutes and follow you?"
Mù said:
"This is within the commandery's borders,
and it was due to your kind consideration
that I came to stay here temporarily.
Now, if this person is killed over a small amount of rice,
how can I bear to remain?"
He then packed his belongings
and returned to Shānyīn.
The magistrate personally went to stop him
and released the imprisoned person.
The person was ashamed and afraid,
and together with his wife and children, pounded the taken rice, obtaining sixty *hú* of grain,
and sent it back to Mù.
Mù closed his door and did not accept it.
The person then left it by the roadside,
and no one took it.
Mù gained fame from this.
In the fifth year of Chìwū,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Fǔyì Dūwèi from Lángzhōng,
and then promoted to Nánhǎi Tàishǒu.
He returned to become Chéngxiàng Zhǎngshǐ,
then transferred to Sīzhí,
and promoted to Zhōngshūlìng.
At that time, the mountain people of the three commanderies of Jiàn'ān, Póyáng, and Xīndū rebelled.
Mù was sent out as Jiānjūn Shǐzhě
and pacified them.
The bandit leaders Huáng Luàn and Cháng Jù
sent out their troops
to serve in the military.
He was enfeoffed as Qíntíng Hóu
and appointed Yuèqí Xiàowèi.
In the sixth year of Yǒng'ān [263 CE],
Shǔ was annexed by Wèi.
The Wǔlíng Wǔxī barbarians bordered Shǔ.
At the time, public opinion feared they would rebel.
So, Mù was appointed General Pacifying Wèi,
and concurrently Administrator of Wǔlíng,
and sent to the commandery.
Wèi sent Guō Chún, the magistrate of Hànjiā County, to provisionally serve as Administrator of Wǔlíng.
He led the people of Fúlíng into Shǔ's Qiānlíng border,
stationing them at Chìshā.
He lured and summoned various barbarian tribal chiefs,
some of whom rose up to respond to Chún.
He also advanced to attack Yǒuyáng County,
causing alarm and fear within the commandery.
Mù asked his administrative officers:
"Shǔ in the west has fallen,
and our border is being invaded.
How shall we defend against this?"
They all replied:
"Now, the two counties have treacherous mountains,
and the barbarians are resisting with arms.
We cannot alarm or disturb them with an army.
If we alarm and disturb them, the barbarians will band together.
It is advisable to pacify them gradually.
We can send trustworthy officials to declare our message and offer comfort and consolation."
Mù said:
"No.
The outer territory is invading our inner territory,
deceiving and luring our people.
We should take advantage while their roots are not deep and strike them down.
This is like putting out a fire, where speed is paramount."
He ordered his subordinates to prepare for war quickly.
Any clerks or officials who opposed his plan were subject to military law.
The General Pacifying Barbarians, Gāo Shàng, advised Mù:
"Previously, Grand Regular Pān led five tens of thousands of troops,
and only then did he attack the Wǔxī barbarians.
At that time, the Liú clan maintained alliances,
and the barbarians were mostly civilized.
Now, we lack the support of those days,
and Guō Chún has already occupied Qiānlíng.
For Your Honor to penetrate deep with three thousand troops
is not yet seen as advantageous."
Mù said:
"For extraordinary matters,
how can we follow old ways?"
He immediately led his troops,
advancing day and night.
He traveled along the treacherous mountains,
nearly two thousand *lǐ*.
From the frontier,
he executed over a hundred barbarian ringleaders who had harbored treacherous intentions, along with more than a thousand of their followers.
Chún and his group scattered,
and Wǔxī was pacified.
He was promoted to Supervisor of Gōng'ān and General Manifesting Might,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
He was then transferred to Supervisor of Rúxū.
Again, he was appointed Former General with *jiǎjié* (credentials),
and concurrently Administrator of Wǔlíng.
He died in office.
His family had no surplus wealth,
and the officials and common people mourned him.
His son Yī succeeded him,
taking over the command of troops.
A commentary says: The Shānyuè were prone to rebellion,
difficult to pacify and easy to provoke.
This is why Sūn Quán had no leisure for external defense,
and used humble words with the Wèi clan.
All these ministers
were able to pacify internal troubles
and bring peace to the state and its territories.
Lǚ Dài was pure, diligent, and impartial;
Zhōu Fáng was cunning and often surprising;
Zhōnglí Mù followed the rules of an elder;
Quán Cóng had the talent of his generation,
and was highly valued at the time.
However, he failed to restrain his wicked sons,
and thus incurred criticism and a tarnished reputation.
Biography of Pān Jùn and Lù Kǎi, Chapter 16
Pān Jùn, courtesy name Chéngmíng,
was a native of Hànshòu, Wǔlíng.
At a young age, he studied under Sòng Zhòngzǐ.
Before the age of thirty,
Liú Biǎo, the Administrator of Jīngzhōu, appointed him as the Jīngxià Aide.
At that time, the magistrate of Shāxiàn was corrupt and negligent.
Jùn investigated and executed him,
causing the entire commandery to be shaken with fear.
Later, he became the magistrate of Xiāngxiāng,
and his administration gained much renown.
When Liú Bèi took charge of Jīngzhōu,
he appointed Jùn as Chief Clerk in charge of administration.
When Bèi entered Shǔ,
Jùn was left behind to manage provincial affairs.
Sūn Quán killed Guān Yǔ
and annexed the Jīng territory,
appointing Jùn as Auxiliary Army Lieutenant-General
and entrusting him with troops.
He was promoted to General Manifesting Awe
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Chángqiān Pavilion.
When Quán claimed the imperial title,
Jùn was appointed Minor Prefect,
then advanced to Marquis of Liúyáng,
and later transferred to Grand Regular.
When the Wǔxī Man barbarians rebelled and banded together,
Quán granted Jùn *jié* (credentials)
to supervise all armies in attacking them.
He was trustworthy in rewards and strict in punishments;
the law could not be violated.
The number of those beheaded and captured alive
was in the tens of thousands.
From then on, the various Man tribes declined,
and that region became peaceful.
Before this,
Jùn and Lù Xùn were both stationed in Wǔchāng,
jointly managing the affairs left behind.
He then returned to his former post.
At that time, the Censor Lǚ Yī manipulated power,
impeaching and investigating Chancellor Gù Yǒng and Left General Zhū Jù, among others,
who were all placed under house arrest.
The Palace Attendant Xiè Jī, in a conversation, asked Yī:
"How are Chancellor Gù's affairs?"
Yī replied:
"Not good."
Jī then asked:
"If this lord is dismissed,
who will replace him?"
Yī had not yet answered when Jī said:
"Could it be Grand Regular Pān?"
Yī pondered for a while and said:
"Your words are close to the truth."
Jī said:
"Grand Regular Pān often grinds his teeth at you,
but the distance prevents him from doing anything.
If he replaces Chancellor Gù today,
I fear he will attack you tomorrow."
Yī was greatly frightened
and consequently dismissed the case against Yǒng.
Jùn requested an audience,
going to Jiànyè,
intending to speak frankly and remonstrate strongly.
Upon arrival,
he heard that Crown Prince Dēng had already spoken about it numerous times but was not heeded.
Jùn then invited all officials
and intended to personally kill Yī at the gathering,
taking the blame himself,
to eliminate this menace for the state.
Yī secretly heard of this
and claimed illness, not attending.
Whenever Jùn had an audience,
he never failed to expose Yī's treachery and wickedness.
Because of this, Yī's favor gradually declined,
and he was later executed.
Quán took the blame and reflected on himself,
then reprimanded his ministers.
The account is in the biography of Quán.
In the second year of Chìwū [239 CE],
Jùn died.
His son Zhù succeeded him.
Jùn's daughter was married to Sūn Lǜ, the Marquis of Jiànchāng.
Lù Kǎi, courtesy name Jìngfēng,
was a native of Wújùn’s Wú [County],
and a cousin of Chancellor Xùn.
At the beginning of the Huángwǔ era, he served as the Magistrate of Yǒngxīng and Zhūjì.
Wherever he served, there were records of his good governance.
He was appointed Jianwǔ Dūwèi [Commander of Jianwu],
leading troops.
Although he commanded the army,
he never let go of his books.
He was fond of the Tàixuánjīng,
discussing and expounding its meaning,
and his divinations based on it were always accurate.
During the Chìwū era,
he was appointed Administrator of Dān'ěr.
He campaigned against Zhūyá,
achieving merit by decapitating and capturing many,
and was promoted to Jianwǔ Xiàowèi [Colonel of Jianwu].
In the second year of the Wǔfèng era,
he campaigned against the mountain bandit Chén Bì in Línglíng.
He defeated Bì and achieved victory,
and was appointed Bāqiú Dū [Supervisor of Baqiu] and Piān Jiāngjūn [General of the Vanguard].
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dūxiāng,
and then transferred to be the Wǔchāng Yòubù Dū [Supervisor of the Western Sector of Wuchang].
He joined other generals in marching to Shòuchūn,
and upon his return,
he was repeatedly promoted to Dàngwèi and Suíyuǎn Jiāngjūn [General who Sweeps Away Wei; General who Pacifies the Distant].
When Sūn Xiū ascended the throne,
he was appointed Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn [General who Conquers the North],
granted the imperial credential (jiǎjié), and concurrently held the post of Yùzhōu Mù [Governor of Yuzhou].
When Sūn Hào was enthroned,
he was promoted to Zhènxī Dàjiāngjūn [Grand General who Guards the West],
Dūdū Bāqiú [Overall Supervisor of Baqiu],
and concurrently held the post of Jīngzhōu Mù [Governor of Jingzhou],
and was further enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jiāxīng.
When Sūn Hào made peace with the Jìn,
the envoy Dīng Zhōng returned from the north.
He persuaded Hào that Yìyáng could be attacked.
Kǎi advised against it,
and his words are recorded in the biography of Hào.
In the first year of the Bǎodǐng era,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Chéngxiàng [Left Chancellor].
Hào’s nature was such that he disliked people looking at him.
When the ministers attended him,
none dared to look him in the eye.
Kǎi said to Hào:
“There is no way for a lord and his ministers not to know each other.
If unexpected misfortune suddenly arises,
one would not know where to turn.”
Hào allowed Kǎi to look at him.
Hào moved the capital to Wǔchāng,
causing the people of the Yáng lands to suffer greatly from upstream supply duties,
and this became a burden and distress.
Moreover, many government policies were mistaken,
and the common people were impoverished.
Kǎi submitted a memorial saying: Your servant has heard that a sagacious ruler
finds joy in the joy of his people;
an unsagacious ruler
finds joy in his own pleasure.
He who finds joy in the joy of his people,
his joy lasts longer;
he who finds joy in his own pleasure,
finds no joy and perishes.
The people are
the root of the state;
it is truly fitting to value their sustenance
and cherish their lives.
When the people are at peace, the ruler is at peace;
when the people are joyful, the ruler is joyful.
Recently,
in recent years,
your majesty’s authority has been as destructive as Jié and Zhòu,
your majesty’s wisdom has been obscured by treacherous villains,
and your majesty’s benevolence has been shut off by a multitude of scoundrels.
Without disaster, the people’s lives are exhausted;
without action, the state’s treasury
is empty.
The innocent are punished,
and the undeserving are rewarded,
causing your majesty to incur errors and faults,
and Heaven sends down omens.
Yet, all the dukes and ministers flatter the superior to gain favor,
and oppress the people to seek profit,
leading your majesty to injustice,
and ruining governance with immoral customs.
Your servant secretly grieves over this.
Now, neighboring states are on good terms,
and there are no troubles on the four borders.
It is time to cease corvée labor and nurture the scholars,
to fill the
granaries and treasuries,
and await the opportune time.
Instead, you stir up Heaven’s wrath,
and disturb the myriad people,
causing the people to be uneasy,
and everyone, great and small, to sigh with lament.
This is not the way to preserve the state and nurture the people.
Your servant has heard that good fortune and ill fortune are determined by Heaven,
like a shadow to its form,
or an echo to its sound.
When the form moves, the shadow moves;
when the form stops, the shadow stops.
These destinies are thus
dependent on something,
not on what is said orally.
The reason Qín perished in unifying the world
was solely due to light rewards and heavy punishments,
confused administration and laws,
the people’s strength being exhausted by
extravagance,
their eyes dazzled by beautiful women,
their will corrupted by treasures,
evil ministers in office,
and virtuous scholars hidden away.
The common people were anxious,
and the world suffered from it,
which led to the
calamity of a overturned nest and broken eggs.
The reason Hàn was strong
was that they personally practiced integrity and trustworthiness,
listened to remonstrance and accepted the worthy,
extended benevolence to even woodcutters,
personally invited hermits,
and broadly collected and thoroughly examined
to
formulate their strategies.
This is a clear proof from past events.
More recently, at the decline of Hàn,
the three states stood in a tripod formation.
Cáo lost its discipline,
and Jìn gained its rule.
Furthermore, Yìzhōu was dangerous,
with many strong and skilled soldiers.
By closing the gates and firmly
defending,
it could be preserved for ten thousand generations.
But the Liú clan erred in granting and taking,
and rewards and punishments were misplaced.
The ruler indulged in extravagance,
and the people’s strength was exhausted in non-urgent matters,
which is why it was
conquered by Jìn,
and its ruler and ministers were captured.
This is a clear verification before our very eyes.
Your servant is ignorant of great principles,
his writing is not up to its meaning,
his wisdom is shallow and inferior,
with no further hopes,
and secretly grieves for Your Majesty's empire.
Your servant respectfully reports what his ears and eyes
have heard and seen,
the burdens and harshness experienced by the common people,
and the confusion in criminal law and administration.
I pray Your Majesty cease grand projects,
reduce myriad corvée duties,
strive for leniency,
and abandon harsh governance.
Furthermore, the land of Wǔchāng
is truly dangerous and barren,
not a place for a royal capital to secure the state and nurture the people.
Boats docked there sink and drift,
and dwelling on its hills is steep and perilous.
Moreover,
a children’s rhyme says:
“Better to drink Jiànyè water,
than to eat Wǔchāng fish;
better to return to Jiànyè and die,
than not to stop residing in Wǔchāng.”
Your servant has heard that the constellation Yì changes,
and Yínghuò
acts as an evil omen.
The words of children’s rhymes
originate from the will of Heaven.
To compare peaceful residence with death
is sufficient to show the will of Heaven
and the suffering of the people.
Your servant has heard that a state without three years of reserves
is called a non-state,
yet now there is not even one year’s provision.
This is the responsibility of your ministers.
Yet, all the dukes and ministers, holding positions
above others,
with their salaries extending to their descendants,
have never shown the integrity to dedicate their lives,
or the means to rectify and save the situation.
They merely seek to present small benefits to the ruler,
to gain acceptance and flattery,
poisoning the common people,
and not
planning for the ruler.
Ever since Sūn Hóng raised the righteous army,
cultivation has been abandoned,
and nowhere are there any further inputs.
Moreover, families are divided, fathers and sons serving different duties,
and rations daily
Zhāng,
stored provisions are daily depleted.
The people harbor resentment over dispersion,
and the state faces the gradual exposure of its roots
without anyone to care for them.
The people's strength is exhausted and impoverished,
selling their sons and daughters.
Levies
continue without cease,
daily reaching an extreme of fatigue.
Local chief officials
do not exercise discretion.
Furthermore, there are supervising officials
who do not love the people,
but are eager to wield authority and power.
Everywhere there is harassment,
creating
greater vexation and harshness.
The people suffer from these two burdens,
and their financial resources are depleted twice over.
This is useless and harmful.
I wish Your Majesty would give these people a respite,
showing compassion for the orphaned and weak,
to calm and stabilize
the hearts of the common people.
This is like fish and turtles being freed from poisonous abysses,
and birds and beasts escaping from nets and snares.
The people from the four directions will arrive carrying their children on their backs.
If
this happens,
the people can be preserved,
and the kingdom of the former kings will endure.
Your servant has heard that the five tones make people's ears not sharp,
and the five colors make people's eyes not clear.
These are useless for governance
and harmful to affairs.
Since the time of the former emperor,
when
the empress's palace ladies
and various weavers
numbered less than a hundred,
there were accumulated provisions
and surplus goods.
After the former emperor passed away,
during the reigns of Yòu and Jǐng,
they changed to
extravagance
and did not follow the former emperor's path.
I humbly hear that the number of weavers and other idle attendants
now reaches thousands.
Calculating their output,
it is insufficient for the state's wealth.
Yet, they idly consume official provisions,
year after year.
This is useless.
I wish Your Majesty would consider sending them out to marry,
giving them to men without wives.
If this is done,
it will accord with the will of Heaven above,
and the wishes of the Earth below.
The world
will be exceedingly fortunate.
Your servant has heard that Yīn Tāng selected scholars from merchants,
Qí Huán selected scholars from chariot shafts,
Zhōu Wǔ selected scholars from wood-gatherers,
and the great Hàn selected scholars from servants.
Enlightened
kings and sagely rulers selected scholars based on their virtue,
not being constrained by their humble status.
Therefore, their merits and virtues overflowed,
and their names were recorded in historical annals.
They did not seek out those with pleasing appearances, fine clothes, glib tongues, or ingratiating
manners.
Your servant humbly observes that the current inner favorites
are in positions that are not suited to them,
and their responsibilities do not match their capacities.
They are unable to assist the state or rectify the times,
but instead form factions to support each other,
harming the loyal and concealing
the virtuous.
I wish Your Majesty would select civil and military officials,
each diligent in their office.
Governors and military commanders,
regional defenders outside the capital,
grandees and ministers,
should strive to cultivate benevolent transformation,
assisting Your
Majesty above
and saving the common people below,
each giving their utmost loyalty,
catching every possible oversight.
Then the songs of prosperity will arise,
and the principle of discarded punishments will be clear.
I wish Your Majesty would pay close attention to your servant's foolish
words.
At that time, the general Hè Dìng, who was listed in the palace hall, was fawning, artful, and servile,
highly favored and entrusted with affairs.
Kǎi sternly rebuked Dìng, saying:
"Do you see any of the former ministers who were disloyal to their lords
and disrupted the state's governance,
who were able to die of old age?
Why do you devote yourself solely to flattery and evil,
defiling the imperial ear?
You should reform yourself.
Otherwise,
you will soon face unforeseen disaster."
Dìng greatly resented Kǎi,
thinking of how to slander and harm him.
Kǎi, however, never took it to heart,
but instead devoted himself to public affairs,
with righteousness expressed in his demeanor.
His memorials all pointed to facts without embellishment,
with sincere loyalty emanating from within.
In the first year of Jiànhéng,
he fell ill.
Hào sent the Central Secretariat Director, Dǒng Cháo, to ask what he wished to say.
Kǎi stated:
"Hè Dìng should not be employed.
He should be assigned an external post,
and not entrusted with state affairs.
Xī Xī, a minor official,
initiated the Pǔlǐ fields project,
wishing to revive Yán Mì's old policy,
which also should not be allowed.
Yáo Xìn, Lóu Xuán, Hè Shào, Zhāng Tì, Guō Zhuó, Xuē Yíng, Téng Xiū, and my kinsmen Xǐ and Kàng,
are either pure and upright, loyal and diligent,
or possess outstanding talent and ability.
They are all pillars of the state,
and excellent assistants to the nation.
I wish Your Majesty would give them serious consideration,
consult them on current affairs,
so that each can exert their utmost loyalty,
catching every possible oversight."
He then passed away,
at the age of seventy-two.
His son, Yī,
initially served as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
then was sent out to lead a contingent of troops,
and was appointed as a Major-General.
After Kǎi's death,
Yī entered court to serve as a Palace Steward for the Crown Prince.
Huá Hé, the Right Grand Historian of the State, memorialized to recommend Yī, saying:
"Yī's physique is robust,
and his ability strong and firm.
In terms of talent for command and leadership,
Lǔ Sù was no better.
When he was summoned to return,
he immediately hastened to the capital.
Passing through Wǔchāng,
he did not even glance back.
He took nothing from the weapons or military supplies.
In military affairs, he is decisive,
and in the face of wealth, he is disciplined.
Xiàkǒu
is a vital strategic point for the enemy.
It is fitting to select a famous general to guard it.
Your servant humbly believes
that none is better than Yī."
Previously,
Hào often resented Kǎi for frequently offending him and going against his wishes.
Moreover, Hè Dìng's slanders and fabrications were numerous.
As Kǎi was a prominent minister,
it was difficult to punish him by law.
Furthermore, Lù Kàng was then a great general at the border,
so Hào tolerated him strategically.
After Kàng's death,
Kǎi's family was eventually exiled to Jiàn'ān.
Some say that in the twelfth month of the first year of Bǎodǐng,
Kǎi conspired with the Grand Marshal Dīng Fèng and the Imperial Censor Dīng Gù,
planning to depose Hào and enthrone Sūn Xiū's son when Hào visited the ancestral temple.
At that time, the Left General Líu Píng led the vanguard troops.
Therefore, they secretly spoke to Píng,
but Píng refused and did not consent,
vowing not to reveal it.
Thus, their plan did not succeed.
The Grand Astrologer Chén Miáo reported that Hào's long period of cloudy weather without rain
and the perverse wind currents indicated
an impending conspiracy.
Hào was deeply alarmed and fearful, it is said.
I obtained twenty memorials from Kǎi to Hào from those who came from Jīng and Yáng.
When I extensively asked people from Wú,
many said they had not heard of Kǎi having such a memorial.
Moreover, its language is exceptionally direct and critical,
which Hào would likely not have tolerated.
Some believe that Kǎi kept it hidden in his chest,
not daring to make it public.
When he was severely ill,
Hào sent Dǒng Cháo to visit and ask if he had anything to say,
and Kǎi then entrusted it to him.
The truth is difficult to ascertain,
so it is not included in this chapter.
However, I cherish its pointed criticisms of Hào's actions,
which serve as a warning for future generations.
Therefore, it is transcribed and placed to the left of Kǎi's biography, it is said.
Hào dispatched his trusted aide Zhào Qīn with an oral edict to respond to Kǎi's previous memorial, saying:
"I invariably follow the Former Emperor in my actions.
What is unfair?
What you remonstrate against is wrong.
Moreover, Jiànyè Palace is inauspicious,
so I avoided it.
And the buildings of the Western Palace are dilapidated and crumbling,
so a relocation of the capital must be planned.
Why can it not be moved?"
Kǎi submitted a memorial, saying: "I humbly observe that since Your Majesty assumed power,
the Yin and Yang have been out of harmony,
the five planets have deviated from their courses,
officials have been disloyal,
and corrupt factions have supported each other.
This is due to Your Majesty's failure to adhere to the Former
Emperor's ways.
The rise of a king
is received from Heaven
and cultivated through virtue;
how can it depend on palaces?
Yet Your Majesty, without consulting your high-ranking ministers,
impetuously
drives ahead,
causing the six armies to wander in sorrow and fear.
This defies Heaven and Earth,
and Heaven and Earth respond with calamities,
while children sing their laments.
Even if Your Majesty alone can find peace,
with the common people distressed
and toiling,
how can you govern effectively?
This is the first instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
I have heard that a state's foundation lies in its wise individuals.
Xià killed Lóngfēng,
while Yīn obtained Yī Zhì.
These are clear examples from past generations,
and models for today.
The Palace Regular Attendant Wáng Fān,
being upright and sagacious,
was loyal and outspoken in court.
He was a crucial pillar of the state
and the Lóngfēng of Great Wú.
Yet Your Majesty resented his blunt words,
detested his direct responses,
and had him executed in the palace hall,
his corpse left exposed.
The people within the state are heartbroken,
and those with discernment grieve,
all believing that the Wú state's Fūchā has reappeared.
The Former Emperor cherished the virtuous,
but Your Majesty does the opposite
of this.
This is the second instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
I have heard that prime ministers are the pillars of the state,
and must be strong.
Thus, Hàn had assistants like Xiāo and Cáo,
and the Former Emperor had prime ministers like Gù and Bù.
Yet Wàn Yù,
a man of trivial talent and ordinary character,
who was formerly a household servant,
has been promoted beyond measure to the purple gates.
For Yù, this is already abundant;
for his capacity, it is already overflowing.
Yet Your Majesty cherishes his minor qualities
and ignores broader
interests,
honoring him with a high ministerial post,
surpassing even veteran officials.
The virtuous are indignant,
and the wise are dismayed.
This is the third instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
The Former Emperor loved his people more than infants.
For those without wives, he provided concubines;
for those in single garments, he gave silk;
and uncollected bones, he had them buried.
Yet Your Majesty does the opposite.
This is the fourth instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
In the past, Jié and Zhòu perished due to seductive women,
and Yōu and Lì were plunged into chaos by favored concubines.
The Former Emperor took heed of this
as a personal warning,
and therefore did not keep immoral or corrupt beauties around him,
nor were there numerous
idle women in his back chambers.
Now, the central palace has tens of thousands [of women],
yet it is not fully stocked with empresses and concubines.
Outside, there are many widower
fishers, while women sing lamentations within.
The winds and rains fall unnaturally,
and this is the cause.
This is the fifth instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
The Former Emperor toiled over countless affairs of state,
yet still feared making mistakes.
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you have indulged in pleasures in the back palace,
captivated by women,
causing many state affairs to be neglected,
and subordinates
to harbor deceit.
This is the sixth instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
The Former Emperor greatly valued simplicity and plainness.
His clothes were not gaudy,
his palace had no high towers,
and objects were not elaborately adorned.
Thus, the state was prosperous and the people were content,
and crime did not arise.
Yet Your Majesty levies
and taxes the provinces and commanderies,
exhausting the people's financial resources and labor.
The land is covered in black and yellow [mourning clothes],
while your palaces are adorned in vermilion and purple.
This is the seventh instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
The Former Emperor relied externally on Gù, Lù, Zhū, and Zhāng,
and internally on Hú Zōng and Xuē Zōng.
Thus, all affairs were well-ordered and prosperous,
and the state was pure and solemn.
Now, those outside are not in their
proper positions,
and those within are not the right people.
Chén Shēng and Cáo Fǔ,
petty officials of meager ability,
were discarded by the Former Emperor,
yet Your Majesty favors them.
This is the eighth instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
Whenever the Former Emperor feasted with his ministers,
he restrained the strong wines,
and his subordinates never committed faults of disrespect throughout the day.
All officials and magistrates
fully expressed their views.
Yet Your Majesty
constrains them with forced reverence for your gaze,
and intimidates them with demands for bottomless drinking.
Indeed, wine is for completing rituals,
but excess ruins virtue.
This is no different from the long night's drinking of Shāng Xīn.
This is the
ninth instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
In the past, the Hàn emperors Huán and Líng
favored eunuchs,
greatly losing the people's hearts.
Now Gāo Tōng, Zhān Lián, and Yáng Dù
are lowly palace attendants,
yet Your Majesty rewards them with important
titles
and grants them authority over soldiers.
If difficulties arise along the rivers and islands,
and beacon fires flare up,
then the martial prowess of Dù and his ilk will certainly be unable to repel invaders.
This is the tenth instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
Now, palace women are accumulated in idleness,
and yet eunuchs again run through the provinces and commanderies,
listing common women.
If there is money, they are spared;
if there is no money, they are taken,
causing cries of resentment on the roads,
and mothers and children to part
in death.
This is the eleventh instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
When the Former Emperor was alive,
he also raised the various royal princes.
If a wet nurse was taken,
her husband would be conscripted for service,
but she would be granted money and valuables,
and provided with provisions.
She would be periodically sent home
to see her young child.
Now, however, it is not so.
Husbands and wives are separated in life,
the husband still performs service,
and the child dies thereafter,
leaving the home empty.
This is the twelfth instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
The Former Emperor sighed, saying:
'The state is founded on the people,
and the people depend on food as their heaven,
with clothing as the next priority.
These three,
I hold in my heart.'
Now, however, it is not so.
Agriculture and sericulture are both abandoned.
This is the thirteenth instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
The Former Emperor selected scholars
without regard for their humble origins,
entrusting them with local duties
and testing them through their work.
Those recommended were not undeserving,
and those appointed were not unqualified.
Now, however, it is not so.
The superficial
are promoted,
and partisans advance.
This is the fourteenth instance of not adhering to the Former Emperor.
The Former Emperor's soldiers
were not assigned to other duties,
so that in spring they knew only farming,
and in autumn they knew only harvesting rice.
When there was trouble on the rivers and islands,
they were expected to fight to the death.
Now, the soldiers
are supplied with..."
to the many laborers,
and the provisions and rewards are insufficient,
this is not following the former emperor's fifteenth point.
Now, rewards are for encouraging merit,
and punishments are for deterring evil.
If rewards and punishments are not appropriate,
then scholars and common people will disperse.
Currently, the soldiers along the river,
when they die, they are not mourned;
when they labor, they are not
rewarded.
This is not following the former emperor's sixteenth point.
Now, the local supervisory officials
are already numerous and cumbersome,
and coupled with inner envoys
disrupting things among them,
with one commoner to ten officials,
how can they endure their lot?
In the past, during the reign of Jǐngdì,
the rebellion in
Jiāozhǐ
indeed arose from this.
This is following Jǐngdì's shortcomings,
not following the former emperor's seventeenth point.
Now, the school officials (Jiàoshì)
are the enemies of officials and common people.
In the former emperor's later years,
although there were Lǚ Yī and Qián Qīn,
they were soon all executed
to apologize to the populace.
Now, to again establish
a School Office (Jiàocáo)
and let officials speak freely [about others],
this is not following the former emperor's eighteenth point.
During the former emperor's time,
those in office remained in their positions for a long time,
and then their performance was assessed for promotion or demotion.
Now, officials in the commanderies and counties
sometimes have barely begun governing
before they are summoned or
transferred,
welcoming the new and sending off the old,
causing confusion on the roads,
harming finances and people.
This is especially egregious.
This is not following the former emperor's nineteenth point.
Whenever the former emperor examined a submitted verdict,
he would carefully investigate and review it,
so there were no wrongfully imprisoned in his jails,
and those who died swallowed their lament.
Now, however, this is violated.
This is not following the former
emperor's twentieth point.
If my words can be recorded,
store them in the archives;
if they are false,
punish me for my crime.
I wish Your Majesty would pay attention."
Yìn, courtesy name Jìngzōng,
was Kǎi's younger brother.
He initially served as a Censor (Yùshǐ) and a Bureau Head of Personnel Selection (Shàngshū Xuǎncáo Láng).
Prince Hé heard of his reputation
and treated him with extraordinary courtesy.
It happened that Quán Jì, Yáng Zhú, and others flattered Rúwáng Bà
and contended with Hé,
secretly slandering and framing him.
Yìn was implicated, arrested, and imprisoned.
He suffered extreme torture
but never confessed to anything else.
Later, he served as the Commander-in-chief of Híngyáng (Héngyáng Dūjūn Dūwèi).
In the eleventh year of Chìwū (248 CE),
the Yi and Zéi from Jiāozhǐ and Jiǔzhēn attacked and captured cities and towns,
causing unrest in the Jiāo region.
Yìn was appointed Inspector of Jiāozhōu (Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ) and Colonel Protecting the South (Ānnán Xiàowèi).
Upon Yìn's arrival in the southern border,
he explained the imperial grace and trustworthiness,
diligently promoting recruitment and assimilation.
Huáng Wú and other chieftains from Gāoliáng, with over three thousand households of their followers, all surrendered.
He led his army south,
repeatedly proclaiming his utmost sincerity
and bestowing wealth and silk.
More than a hundred bandit chiefs
and over fifty thousand households,
even those from deep, remote areas who had never been subjugated,
all kowtowed.
The Jiāo region became peaceful and secure.
He was then promoted to General Protecting the South (Ānnán Jiāngjūn).
He again attacked bandits in Cāngwú and Jiànlíng,
defeating them.
He dispatched over eight thousand soldiers in total,
to replenish military supplies.
In the first year of Yǒng'ān (258 CE),
he was summoned to be the Commander of Xīlíng (Xīlíng Dū),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng.
Later, he was transferred [to serve] in Hǔlín.
The Central Secretariat Aide (Zhōngshū Chéng) Huá Hé presented a memorial recommending Yìn, saying:
"Yìn's natural disposition is intelligent and bright,
his talent is comprehensive, and his conduct is pure.
He formerly served in the Personnel Selection Bureau,
and his achievements are well-recorded.
After returning to Jiāozhōu,
he proclaimed the imperial grace,
and displaced people returned and submitted,
making the coastal region peaceful.
Cāngwú and Nánhǎi
annually suffered from [violent] winds and miasmatic vapors.
The winds would break trees
and cause sand to fly and stones to roll;
the vapors would create dense fog
through which even birds would not pass.
Since Yìn arrived in the province,
the winds and vapors ceased,
merchants and travelers moved freely,
the people had no sickness or plague,
and the harvests were abundant.
The provincial capital is near the sea,
and the seawater turns salty in autumn.
Yìn also stored fresh water,
allowing the people to have sweet food.
His benevolent influence spread widely,
touching both humans and spirits.
He thus relied on Heaven's might
to gather the scattered.
When the imperial edict for him to leave arrived,
the people, grateful for his kindness,
forgot their attachment to their land.
The elderly were carried, and the young were led,
willingly following him,
with none wavering,
without needing military escort.
Among all generals who gathered people,
all coerced them with might;
none have been like Yìn, binding them with kindness and trust.
He held his commission in the province
for over ten years,
in a region bordering diverse customs
and where precious treasures are produced,
yet internally he had no concubines adorned with cosmetics and pearls,
and his household had no treasures of patterned armor, rhinoceros horn, or ivory.
Compared to present officials,
such a person is truly rare.
He ought to be in the capital,
a limb of the royal house,
to assist in praising the 'Kāngzāi' hymns of Táng and Yú.
His current post along the river is minor,
not fully utilizing his talents.
There are many who are qualified for the position of Commander of Hǔlín.
If he were recalled to the capital
and favored with a superior post,
then all Heaven's work would be completed,
and all achievements would flourish."
When Yìn died,
his son Shì inherited his title
and became Commander of Cháisāng (Cháisāng Dū) and General Striking Awe (Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn).
In the first year of Tiāncè (275 CE), he and his paternal cousin Yī were both exiled to Jiàn'ān.
In the second year of Tiānjì (278 CE),
he was recalled to Jiànyè
and reinstated as general and marquis.
Commentary says: Pān Jùn was upright and decisive;
Lù Kǎi was loyal, strong, and straightforward.
Both had unyielding integrity
and the character of true men.
Yìn maintained personal purity and accomplished his tasks,
earning renown in the southern lands.
He can be called a good administrator.
Biography of Shì Yí and Hú Zōng, Chapter Seventeen.
Shì Yí, courtesy name Zǐyǔ,
was a native of Yínglíng, Běihǎi.
His original surname was Shì (氏).
He initially served as a county clerk,
then worked for the commandery.
The commandery administrator Kǒng Róng ridiculed Yí,
saying
the character '氏' (Shì)
was '民' (mín, commoner)
without a top stroke,
and could be changed to
'是' (Shì, 'is' or 'right').
So he then changed it.
Later, he joined Liú Yáo
to escape the chaos in Jiāngdōng.
When Yáo's army was defeated,
Yí moved to Kuàijī.
Sūn Quán took over the great enterprise
and courteously summoned Yí through a written decree.
Upon his arrival, he was trusted and appointed
to exclusively manage confidential affairs,
and appointed Cavalry Commandant (Qí Dūwèi).
Lǚ Méng (呂蒙) planned to attack Guān Yǔ (關羽).
Quán (權) consulted Yí (儀) about it.
Yí (儀) approved of his plan
and persuaded Quán (權) to follow it.
He accompanied the campaign to subjugate Yǔ (羽),
and was appointed Zhōngyì Xiàowèi (忠義校尉).
Yí (儀) expressed his gratitude and apology,
and Quán (權) issued an order saying:
"Though I am not Zhào Jiǎnzǐ (趙簡子),
how can you not humble yourself to be Zhōu Shè (周舍)?"
After Jīngzhōu (荊州) was pacified,
and the capital was moved to Wǔchāng (武昌),
he was appointed Bì Jiāngjūn (裨將軍).
Later, he was enfeoffed as Dūtíng Hóu (都亭侯)
and served as Shìzhōng (侍中).
When Quán (權) wanted to entrust him with troops again,
Yí (儀), considering himself untalented,
firmly declined.
In the Huángwǔ (黃武) reign period,
Yí (儀) was sent to Wǎn (皖) to General Liú Shào (劉邵),
with the intention of luring Cáo Xiū (曹休).
When Xiū (休) arrived,
he was greatly defeated.
Yí (儀) was promoted to Piān Jiāngjūn (偏將軍),
entered the palace to oversee Shàngshū (尚書) affairs,
externally managed various offices,
and concurrently handled litigation.
He was also ordered to teach the various princes writing and scholarship.
When the emperor moved east,
Crown Prince Dēng (登) was left to guard Wǔchāng (武昌),
and Yí (儀) was appointed to assist the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince respected him,
first consulting him on matters
before putting them into practice.
He was further enfeoffed as Dūxiāng Hóu (都鄉侯).
Later, he followed the Crown Prince back to Jiànyè (建業),
and was again appointed Shìzhōng (侍中) and Zhōngzhífǎ (中執法),
settling various official matters and handling litigation as before.
The Diǎnjiàoláng (典校郎) Lǚ Yī (呂壹) falsely accused the former Jiāngxià (江夏) Administrator Diāo Jiā (刁嘉) of slandering state policies.
Quán (權) was enraged,
arrested Jiā (嘉) and imprisoned him,
and thoroughly investigated and questioned everyone.
At that time, all those present were terrified of Yī (壹)
and all claimed to have heard the slander.
Only Yí (儀) said he had not heard it.
Thereupon, he was interrogated and cross-examined for several days,
and the imperial edicts became increasingly stern.
The officials held their breath for him.
Yí (儀) replied:
"Now that the blade and saw are at my neck,
how dare I conceal for Jiā (嘉)
and bring about my own destruction,
becoming a ghost of disloyalty!
But I believe that what was heard and known must have a beginning and an end."
He answered the questions based on the facts,
his words unwavering.
Quán (權) then let him off,
and Jiā (嘉) also escaped punishment.
When the Shu (蜀) Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) died,
Quán (權)'s heart was set on Xīzhōu (西州),
and he sent Yí (儀) as an envoy to Shu (蜀) to reaffirm their alliance.
He fulfilled his mission satisfactorily,
and was later appointed Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射).
When the Nán (南) and Lǔ (魯) palaces were first established,
Yí (儀), by his original position, concurrently held the post of Lǔ Wáng Fù (魯王傅).
Yí (儀) was concerned that the two palaces were too close,
so he submitted a memorial saying:
"I humbly submit that King Lǔ (魯王) is naturally endowed with noble virtues,
possessing both civil and military talents.
The current situation demands
that he should guard the four directions
and be a bulwark for the state.
To promote his virtues and reputation,
and widely manifest his awe-inspiring power,
is a good plan for the state,
and what the people within the seas look forward to.
However, my words are crude and rustic,
and I cannot fully express my meaning.
I foolishly believe that the two palaces should have a distinction in rank,
to rectify the order of superior and inferior,
and clarify the foundation of moral education."
This memorial was submitted three or four times.
As a tutor, he was utterly loyal,
constantly offering admonitions;
he was diligent in serving his superiors,
and humble towards others.
He did not manage properties,
nor accept gifts or favors,
and his house was only large enough for himself.
When a neighbor built a grand residence,
Quán (權) looked out and saw it,
and asked who was building the large house.
His attendants replied:
"It seems to be Yí (儀)'s house."
Quán (權) said:
"Yí (儀) is frugal,
so it cannot be him."
Upon inquiry, it was indeed another family.
Such was the trust he commanded.
His clothes were not elaborate,
his meals were not extravagant,
he helped the poor and needy,
and his household had no savings.
When Quán (權) heard of this,
he visited Yí (儀)'s residence,
asked to see his vegetable meals,
tasted them himself,
and sighed in front of him.
He immediately increased his salary and gifts,
and added to his fields and residence.
Yí (儀) repeatedly declined,
feeling distressed by the favor.
He occasionally recommended people,
but never spoke ill of others.
Quán (權) often criticized Yí (儀) for not speaking on matters,
and for not expressing approval or disapproval.
Yí (儀) replied:
"With a sagely ruler above,
and ministers fulfilling their duties,
fearing inadequacy,
I truly dare not offer my foolish and limited opinions
to trouble Your Majesty's ears."
He served the state for several decades
without ever making a mistake.
Lǚ Yī (呂壹) reported various generals, ministers, and high officials,
some of whom were accused of crimes multiple times,
but he never reported Yí (儀).
Quán (權) sighed and said:
"If everyone were like Yí (儀),
why would we need laws?"
When he fell ill,
he left a will for a plain coffin,
to be dressed in everyday clothes,
and to be kept simple and economical.
He died at the age of eighty-one.
Hú Zōng (胡綜), courtesy name Wěizé (偉則),
was a native of Gùshǐ (固始) in Rǔnán (汝南).
He was orphaned young,
and his mother took him to avoid disaster in Jiāngdōng (江東).
Sūn Cè (孫策) was Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽),
and Zōng (綜), at fourteen,
became a Mènxià Xúnxíng (門下循行),
staying in Wú (吳) to study with Sūn Quán (孫權).
After Cè (策) died,
Quán (權) became Tǎolǔ Jiāngjūn (討虜將軍),
appointed Zōng (綜) as Jīncáo Cóngshì (金曹從事),
and he accompanied the campaign against Huáng Zǔ (黃祖),
and was appointed È Zhǎng (鄂長).
When Quán (權) became Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍)
and made Jīng (京) his capital,
he summoned Zōng (綜) back
to be Shūbù (書部),
and with Shì Yí (是儀) and Xú Xiáng (徐詳), they jointly managed confidential military and state affairs.
When Liú Bèi (劉備) descended to Báidì (白帝),
Quán (權), seeing his troops were few,
sent Zōng (綜) to assess the various counties,
obtaining six thousand men.
He established two Jiěfán (解煩) divisions,
with Xiáng (詳) leading the left division and Zōng (綜) leading the right division commander.
The Wú (吳) general Jìn Zōng (晉宗) defected to Wèi (魏).
Wèi (魏) appointed Zōng (宗) as Qīchūn (蘄春) Administrator,
several hundred li from the Jiāng (江),
and he frequently caused trouble.
Quán (權) sent Zōng (綜) with Hè Qí (賀齊) on a swift surprise attack,
capturing Zōng (宗) alive.
Zōng (綜) was further appointed Jiànwǔ Zhōnglángjiāng (建武中郎將).
When Wèi (魏) appointed Quán (權) as Wú Wáng (吳王),
Zōng (綜), Yí (儀), and Xiáng (詳) were all enfeoffed as Tínghóu (亭侯).
In the summer of the eighth year of Huángwǔ (黃武) [229 CE],
a yellow dragon appeared at Xiàkǒu (夏口).
Thereupon Quán (權) assumed the imperial title,
and changed the era name in light of the auspicious sign.
He also made a large yellow dragon standard (Huánglóng Dàyá, 黃龍大牙),
which was always kept in the central army.
The advance and retreat of all armies
depended on its direction.
He ordered Zōng (綜) to compose a rhapsody, which said: "When Heaven and Earth were first established,
the three powers (Heaven, Earth, Man) came into being.
The wolf and bow (constellations) cast their images,
truly symbolizing military prowess.
The sages observed their patterns,
emulated and constructed them,
first making implements,
and
seeking their perfection.
Huáng (黃) and Nóng (農) founded dynasties,
establishing the imperial foundation,
outwardly conforming to the will of Heaven,
inwardly ending the people's calamities.
Gāoxīn (高辛) punished Gòng (共),
Shùn (舜) campaigned against Yǒumiáo (有苗),
Qǐ (啟) had Gān (甘)
As for the
army, Tāng 湯 had Míngtiáo 鳴條.
Zhōu 周 had Mùyě 牧野.
Hàn 漢 had Gāixià 垓下.
None of these were achieved without military force,
which brought peace and established their great undertakings.
The brilliant Great Wú 大吳,
truly by Heaven's endowment of virtue,
with divine martial
prowess as its guide,
reaches the utmost of imperial glory.
Thus, since ancient times,
with Huáng 黃 and Yú 虞 as ancestors,
passing through five generations,
the lineage resided in the lower regions.
Responding to the opportune moment, it received the Mandate,
rising from the southern lands,
to
greatly expand its influence,
and reform our central lands (China).
Therefore, it aligned with Heaven's timing,
and created a divine army,
taking the image of Tàiyī 太一,
with five generals and three gates;
swift as lightning in advance,
slow as clouds in delay,
its movements are disciplined,
concise yet not cumbersome.
The Four Spirits are arrayed,
with the Yellow Dragon in the center,
following the Zhōu 周 system of sun and moon,
it is truly called Tàicháng 太常,
standing out uniquely,
looked upon by the six
armies.
The immortal being is above,
observing the four directions,
the gods truly command it,
bringing auspiciousness to the nation.
When the army desires to change direction,
the Yellow Dragon moves first,
the golden drums do not sound,
silently
it shifts and deploys,
its secret strategies like those of gods,
truly marvelous and mysterious.
In ancient times, in the Zhōu 周 dynasty,
a red crow carried a book.
Now, in Great Wú 大吳,
a yellow dragon spits out a talisman.
This accords with the signs from the Hé 河 and Luò 洛 rivers,
its actions
are always in harmony with the Way,
Heaven aids and man is harmonious,
all say it is excellent.
Shǔ 蜀, hearing of Quán's 權 ascension to the throne,
sent envoys to renew their former good relations.
The alliance text was compiled,
its wording and meaning were excellent,
the details are in Quán's 權 biography.
Quán 權 moved his capital to Jiànyè 建業.
Xiáng 詳 and Zōng 綜 were both appointed Shìzhōng 侍中,
and further enfeoffed as Xiānghóu 鄉侯,
and concurrently as Zǔoyòulǐngjūn 左右領軍.
At that time, a defector from Wèi 魏 or some said Wèi Wú Zhì 吳質, the Dūdū Hébĕi Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn 都督河北振威將軍,
was viewed with some suspicion.
Zōng 綜 then falsely composed a surrender document for Zhì 質 in three sections:
The first states:
"Heaven's order has been broken,
the four seas are collapsing,
all living beings are suffering,
scholars are dispersed,
wherever soldiers and bandits have gone,
towns have no inhabitants,
wind, dust, smoke, and fire,
are everywhere.
Since the Three Dynasties,
the extremity of great chaos
has never been like the present time.
I, your subject Zhì 質, am of meager ambition,
unable to adapt to the times,
bound to my native land,
unable to fly away,
and thus served the Cáo 曹 family in military duties,
residing far in Héshuò 河朔,
separated by the celestial path.
Although I admired your virtue from afar,
and wished to entrust myself to your great destiny,
I was ashamed that I had no means
to express my ambition.
Every time I encountered travelers,
I secretly listened to the news of your civilizing influence,
and humbly learned that Your Majesty's virtue is equal to Heaven's purity,
and bright as the sun and moon.
Your divine martial bearing
is naturally endowed.
You propagate the imperial ultimate,
and your transforming influence spreads for ten thousand *lǐ* 里,
from the Jiāng 江 River southward,
every household receives your benevolent cover.
Heroes and outstanding individuals,
and those who have risen in rank,
all sing with their hearts and praise with their mouths,
joyfully desiring to pledge allegiance.
In the end of the sixth month of this year,
I received news of the auspicious day,
when the dragon rose and ascended the throne,
expanding the great Way,
and setting Heaven's order right,
intending to allow the surviving populace
to behold their true sovereign.
In the past, when King Wǔ 武 of Zhōu 周 attacked Yīn 殷,
the Yīn 殷 people turned their spears.
When Emperor Gāozǔ 高祖 executed Xiàng Yǔ 項羽,
the songs of Chǔ 楚 were heard on all sides.
Compared to today,
those events are not sufficient analogies.
I, your subject Zhì 質, cannot bear my utmost aspirations to Heaven,
and respectfully send my trusted kinsman, Huáng Dìng 黃定 from the same commandery, to respectfully present this memorial,
entrusting him with my surrender and defection,
seeking to reach you with difficulty.
What I wish to present
is listed below."
The second said:
"In the past, Yī Yǐn (伊尹) left Xià (夏) and entered Shāng (商);
Chén Píng (陳平) abandoned Chǔ (楚) and returned to Hàn (漢).
Their achievements were recorded on bamboo and silk,
their names passed down to later generations.
The lords of their time did not call them disloyal and rebellious,
believing that they knew the Mandate of Heaven.
I was once intimately associated with the Cáo (曹) clan.
Outwardly, we were lord and minister,
inwardly, like flesh and blood.
Our bonds of kindness and righteousness were entwined,
with union and no separation.
Consequently, I was entrusted with the responsibility of a distant region,
commanding the armies of Héběi (河北).
At that time,
my aspirations were lofty and grand;
I wished to live and die with the Cáo (曹) clan forever,
fearing only that my achievements would not be established,
and my endeavors would not succeed.
When the Cáo (曹) clan perished [literally, when the Cáo clan came to an end],
and their successor was enthroned,
a child ruler governed,
and slandering words proliferated.
My peers harmed each other through power,
those with different interests found opportunities to speak ill,
and I, by nature, am straightforward and unpretentious,
never subservient to others.
Seeing those several individuals,
I truly felt compelled to confront them.
This was also my fault.
Consequently, I was ensnared by malicious schemes,
invited suspicion,
and was falsely accused of intending to rebel.
Although those who knew the truth vouched for my integrity,
in a chaotic world, slander triumphs,
and lingering suspicion remained.
I constantly feared that one day I would be unjustly harmed without cause,
my heart heavy with anxiety,
like treading on ice and coals.
In the past, Yuè Yì (樂毅) rendered meritorious service to King Zhāo (昭) of Yān (燕) in Qí (齊).
When King Huì (惠) ascended the throne,
he suspected Yuè Yì (樂毅) and deprived him of his command.
Consequently, Yuè Yì (樂毅) left Yān (燕) for Zhào (趙),
his splendid reputation undiminished.
Did he wish to be inconstant in his virtue?
No, he feared that his merits and fame would not be established,
and that disaster would befall him.
In the past, I sent Zhōu Guāng (周光) of Wèi Jùn (魏郡), under the guise of a merchant,
pretending to defect to the south,
to convey secret plans.
At the time, due to the urgency,
I dared not make a formal written memorial,
so I had Guāng (光) transmit it orally.
I believed that the great trend of the world was evident,
and that where the will of Heaven lay,
who else but Wú (吳)?
The people of this region [Héběi],
long to become your subjects,
craning their necks and standing on tiptoe,
only fearing that your army will arrive too late.
If Your Sacred Grace would grant a little trust and acceptance,
I would offer Héběi (河北) to receive the King's army.
My heart is sincere and loyal,
Heaven and the sun bear witness.
But a year has passed since Guāng (光) left,
and I have heard not a whisper.
I wonder if this intention has finally reached you or not?
I look far and sigh,
days and months pass by.
How could Lǔ Wàng (魯望) or Gāo Zǐ (高子) suffice as comparisons!
Moreover, I am treated rather poorly today,
the buzzing of flies [slanderous whispers]
is incessant.
I will certainly suffer this misfortune,
it is only a matter of time.
I privately surmise that Your Majesty has not yet granted clear comfort [to me]
because you must believe that my character is imbued with the principles of benevolence and righteousness,
and that I would not engage in such actions.
You may think what Guāng (光) transmitted
was more false than true,
or perhaps you believe there is some other motive behind this,
not knowing that my character has been implicated by slander and subjected to suspicion,
fearing great harm.
Furthermore, if I were truly guilty,
I would naturally rush to the cauldrons and boiling pots [of punishment],
surrendering myself to await my sentence.
This is indeed what a minister ought to do.
But today, I am innocent,
yet unjustly slandered.
I face the disaster of Shāng Yāng (商鞅) and Bái Qǐ (白起).
Considering the circumstances,
it is appropriate for me to leave.
To die unrighteously,
why should I not leave!
The departure of Yuè Yì (樂毅) and the flight of Wú Qǐ (吳起),
gentlemen lamented their misfortune,
none criticized them.
I pray Your Majesty reflects on the past to understand the present,
and not doubt or wonder at my character.
I also consider that when a minister incurs guilt,
he should, like Wǔ Yuán (伍員), dedicate himself and prove his worth,
and not seek selfish advantage through opportunistic actions.
However, the present and the past,
their circumstances are different.
The north and south are vast,
rivers and lakes separate them.
If I do not take action myself,
how can I escape and be saved!
Therefore, I have forgotten the integrity of a resolute scholar,
and instead contemplate the righteousness of establishing achievements.
Furthermore, I also believe that the successor of the Cáo (曹) clan
is not where the Mandate of Heaven lies.
The government is weak, punishments are chaotic,
power is seized by ministers,
and various generals wield authority independently outside.
Each acts for himself,
none united in heart.
Soldiers are depleted,
the treasury is empty,
discipline is destroyed,
and both high and low are confused.
I imagine that those who have surrendered and defected previously
must have heard this information.
Attacking the weak and obscure [rulers]
should align with the opportune moment of Heaven.
This is truly the time for Your Majesty to advance and conquer,
which is why I, humble as I am, dare to present this plan.
If you now send troops into Huái (淮) and Sì (泗),
and occupy Xiàpī (下邳),
the two provinces of Jīng (荊) and Yáng (揚)
will respond at the sound.
I will sweep down from Héběi (河北) to the south,
the strategic position will be united,
and the foundations firmly established forever.
The troops of Guānxī (關西) will be tied up in their defense.
Qīng (青) and Xú (徐) two provinces will not dare to withdraw their defenses.
The remaining troops in Xǔ (許) and Luò (洛) number less than ten thousand.
Who can come east to contend with Your Majesty?
This is truly a once-in-a-thousand-years opportunity,
how can one not ponder deeply and plan meticulously!
And where I am located,
I already have many horses.
Moreover, the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) regularly bring out horses in the third or fourth month during the time of lush grass.
I estimate that now,
I can obtain over three thousand horses.
When Your Majesty dispatches the army,
it should be at this time,
bringing many cavalrymen to acquire these horses.
These are all things that I have initially known a thing or two about.
Generally, two armies cannot fully ascertain each other's true strength.
But this region [the north] is truly weak now,
easily conquerable.
When Your Majesty takes action,
many will surely respond.
To establish the great enterprise above,
to unite the whole world,
and below, to allow me to achieve extraordinary merit,
this is truly Heaven's will.
If I am not accepted,
this is also Heaven's will.
May Your Majesty reflect on this,
I will not elaborate further."
The third said:
"In the past, Xǔ Zǐyuǎn (許子遠) left Yuán (袁) and went to Cáo (曹).
His plans and calculations were duly accepted,
leading to the defeat of Yuán's (袁) army,
and thus establishing Cáo's (曹) enterprise.
Had the Cáo (曹) clan not believed Zǐyuǎn (子遠),
had they harbored doubt and hesitation,
unresolved in their hearts,
then today the world would belong to the Yuán (袁) clan.
May Your Majesty reflect on this.
Recently, I heard that the border generals Yán Fú (閻浮) and Zhào Jí (趙楫) wished to embrace your great transforming influence,
but their calls were not quickly answered,
leading to their defeat and ruin.
Now I sincerely,
from afar, offer my allegiance.
If you again harbor doubt,
and do not act promptly,
leaving me isolated and cut off,
to suffer this grievous misfortune,
then I fear that all the heroes and valiant warriors in the world who wish to establish merits
will no longer dare to entrust their lives to Your Majesty.
May Your Majesty reflect on this.
Imperial Heaven and Sovereign Earth,
truly hear these words."
After this document circulated,
Zhì (質) had already entered to serve as Attendant Minister.
In the second year,
Yǐn Fān (隱蕃) from Qīngzhōu (青州) defected to Wú (吳).
He submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servant has heard that when Zhòu (紂) was without the Way,
Wéizǐ (微子) was the first to leave;
when Gāozǔ (高祖) was benevolent and enlightened,
Chén Píng (陳平) was the first to join him.
Your servant is twenty-two years old,
abandoning his home territory,
and entrusting his life to one who possesses the Way.
Thanks to the spiritual protection of Heaven,
I have been able to preserve myself and arrive here.
Your servant has been here for some time,
but the officials in charge treat me the same as other defectors,
failing to make a clear distinction,
thus preventing my subtle words and profound insights
from reaching Your Majesty.
I sigh and lament repeatedly,
how can this ever cease?
I respectfully approach the palace gate, kowtow, and submit this petition,
begging to be granted an audience.”
Sūn Quán (孫權) immediately summoned him.
Yǐn Fān (隱蕃) conversed and answered questions,
and presented his views on current affairs,
displaying great eloquence and insight.
Hú Zōng (胡綜) was sitting in attendance at the time,
and Sūn Quán (孫權) asked him what he thought.
Hú Zōng (胡綜) replied:
“Yǐn Fān’s (隱蕃) memorial,
with its grand pronouncements, resembles Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔);
his cleverness, quickness, and sophistry resemble Ní Héng (禰衡);
but his talent is inferior to both.”
Sūn Quán (孫權) then asked what office he would be suitable for.
Hú Zōng (胡綜) replied:
“He is not yet fit to govern the people;
he should first be tested with a minor position in the capital, such as a Dū Niǎn (都輦) official.”
However, Sūn Quán (孫權), seeing Yǐn Fān (隱蕃) eloquently discuss criminal justice,
appointed him as Tíngwèi Jiān (廷尉監).
General of the Left Zhū Jù (朱據) and Grand Judge Hǎo Pǔ (郝普) praised Yǐn Fān (隱蕃) as having the talent of an assistant to a king.
Hǎo Pǔ (郝普) was especially close to him,
often complaining and lamenting his being underestimated.
Later, Yǐn Fān (隱蕃) plotted rebellion,
the plot was discovered, and he was executed.
Hǎo Pǔ (郝普) was reproached and committed suicide.
Zhū Jù (朱據) was put under house arrest,
and only released after some time.
Hú Zōng (胡綜) was appointed Biān Jiāngjūn (偏將軍),
concurrently Zǔo Zhífǎ (左執法),
and was in charge of petitions and lawsuits.
Regarding the affairs of Liáodōng (遼東),
when General Assisting Wú (輔吳將軍) Zhāng Zhāo (張昭) remonstrated with Sūn Quán (孫權) with exceedingly sharp words,
Sūn Quán (孫權) was greatly angered;
Hú Zōng (胡綜) played a crucial role in harmonizing their relationship
and preventing a rift between them.
Hú Zōng (胡綜) had power in this matter.
He was fond of wine;
after drinking, he would shout and express himself fully,
sometimes pushing and pulling wine cups,
or even striking those around him.
Sūn Quán (孫權) cherished his talent
and did not blame him for it.
From the time Sūn Quán (孫權) took charge of affairs,
all official pronouncements, strategic commands,
and diplomatic letters to neighboring states
were generally crafted by Hú Zōng (胡綜).
Initially, due to numerous internal and external matters,
a special regulation was established
that senior officials, upon suffering a bereavement,
were not permitted to leave their posts.
However, there were frequent transgressions.
Sūn Quán (孫權) was troubled by this
and had his court officials deliberate on it.
Hú Zōng (胡綜) argued that the regulation should be made clear,
stating that capital punishment would be applied,
and if it were carried out on one person,
such acts would certainly cease thereafter.
Sūn Quán (孫權) then adopted Hú Zōng’s (胡綜) suggestion,
and from then on, cases of abandoning posts for funerals stopped.
He died in the sixth year of Chìwū (赤烏),
and his son Chōng (沖) succeeded him.
Hú Chōng (胡沖) was gentle and possessed administrative ability;
during the Tiānjì (天紀) era, he served as Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令).
Xú Xiáng (徐詳), courtesy name Zǐmíng (子明),
was from Wúchēng (烏程), Wújùn (吳郡).
He died before Hú Zōng (胡綜).
A review states: Shì Yí (是儀), Xú Xiáng (徐詳), and Hú Zōng (胡綜)
were all capable and enterprising officials during Sūn Quán’s (孫權) time.
Shì Yí (是儀) was pure, diligent, and honest;
Xú Xiáng (徐詳) frequently carried out diplomatic missions;
Hú Zōng (胡綜) possessed literary talent and practical ability;
each was trusted for their respective strengths.
Like the rafters and purlins of a grand mansion,
they supported it!
Biography of Wú Fàn (吳範), Liú Dūn (劉惇), and Zhào Dá (趙達), Chapter 18
Wú Fàn (吳範), courtesy name Wénzé (文則),
was from Shàngyú (上虞), Kuàijī (會稽).
He was known in the commandery for his mastery of calendrical calculations
and his knowledge of meteorological phenomena.
He was nominated as a man of the Way
and went to the capital,
but due to the chaos of the times, he did not proceed.
When Sūn Quán (孫權) rose in the southeast,
Wú Fàn (吳範) dedicated himself to his service.
Whenever there were omens of disaster or good fortune,
he would deduce and describe the situation through calculations.
His methods were often effective,
and thus he became famous.
Initially,
when Sūn Quán (孫權) was in Wú (吳),
he wanted to attack Huáng Zǔ (黃祖).
Wú Fàn (吳範) said:
“This year offers little advantage;
it would be better next year.
Next year, Wùzǐ (戊子),
Liú Biǎo (劉表) of Jīngzhōu (荊州) will also die, and his state will perish.”
Sūn Quán (孫權) then attacked Huáng Zǔ (黃祖)
but ultimately failed to conquer him.
The following year,
the army set out.
When they reached Xúnyáng (尋陽),
Wú Fàn (吳範) observed the omens
and went to Sūn Quán’s (孫權) boat to offer congratulations,
urging the troops to advance quickly.
Upon arrival, they immediately defeated Huáng Zǔ (黃祖),
who escaped during the night.
Sūn Quán (孫權) feared he would be lost,
but Wú Fàn (吳範) said:
“He has not gone far;
we will surely capture Huáng Zǔ (黃祖) alive.”
By the middle of the fifth watch,
he was indeed captured.
Liú Biǎo (劉表) eventually died,
and Jīngzhōu (荊州) was divided.
In the year Rénchén (壬辰),
Wú Fàn (吳範) again reported:
“In the year Jiǎwǔ (甲午),
Liú Bèi (劉備) will gain Yìzhōu (益州).”
Later, Lǚ Dài (呂岱) returned from Shǔ (蜀),
and encountered him at Báidì (白帝).
He spoke of Liú Bèi’s (劉備) troops dispersing,
and nearly half dying,
thus the undertaking would surely fail.
Sūn Quán (孫權) challenged Wú Fàn (吳範) with this,
but Wú Fàn (吳範) said:
“What your servant spoke of was the Way of Heaven,
while what Lǚ Dài (呂岱) saw were merely human affairs.”
Liú Bèi (劉備) eventually gained Shǔ (蜀).
When Sūn Quán (孫權) plotted with Lǚ Méng (呂蒙) to attack Guān Yǔ (關羽),
he consulted his close officials,
most of whom said it was not advisable.
Sūn Quán (孫權) asked Wú Fàn (吳範),
and Wú Fàn (吳範) said:
“You will succeed.”
Later, when Guān Yǔ (關羽) was in Màichéng (麥城),
he sent an envoy to request surrender.
Sūn Quán (孫權) asked Wú Fàn (吳範):
“Will he actually surrender?”
Wú Fàn (吳範) said:
“He has the aura of flight;
his talk of surrender is merely a trick.”
Sūn Quán (孫權) sent Pān Zhāng (潘璋) to block his escape route.
When the scouts returned,
they reported that Guān Yǔ (關羽) had already left.
Wú Fàn (吳範) said:
“Though he has left, he will not escape.”
When asked for the timing,
he said:
“Tomorrow at noon.”
Sūn Quán (孫權) set up a gnomon and a clepsydra to wait.
When noon arrived and he had not appeared,
Sūn Quán (孫權) asked the reason.
Wú Fàn (吳範) said:
“The time is not yet precisely noon.”
A moment later,
a gust of wind stirred the curtains.
Wú Fàn (吳範) clapped his hands and said:
“Guān Yǔ (關羽) has arrived!”
Shortly after,
outside, shouts of “Long live!” were heard,
announcing that Guān Yǔ (關羽) had been captured.
Later, when Sūn Quán (孫權) made peace with Wèi (魏),
Wú Fàn (吳範) said:
“Judging by the omens,
they are coming ostensibly,
