but in reality, they have a scheme;
we should prepare for it.”
When Liú Bèi (劉備) massed his troops at Xīlíng (西陵),
Wú Fàn (吳範) said:
“Later there will be peace and alliance.”
All things eventually transpired as he said.
His divinations and predictions were thus clear and precise.
Sūn Quán 權 appointed Wú Fàn 吳範 as Cavalry Commandant (Jìdūwèi 騎都尉),
and also Administrator of the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐlìng 太史令).
He often consulted him,
wishing to know his divinations.
Wú Fàn 吳範 secretly cherished his art,
and did not reveal its most essential techniques to Sūn Quán 權.
Sūn Quán 權 consequently resented him.
Earlier,
when Sūn Quán 權 was a general,
Wú Fàn 吳範 had once stated that there was "kingly aura" in Jiāngnán 江南,
and that between the years of hài 亥 and zǐ 子, there would be great fortune and celebration.
Sūn Quán 權 said:
"If it truly turns out as you say,
I will make you a marquis."
When Sūn Quán 權 was established as King of Wú 吳,
Wú Fàn 吳範 was attending a banquet,
and said:
"Formerly, in Wúzhōng 吳中,
I spoke of this matter.
Does Your Majesty remember it?"
Sūn Quán 權 said:
"Indeed."
He then called his attendants,
and had them present a marquis's ribbon and seal to Wú Fàn 範.
Wú Fàn 範 knew that Sūn Quán 權 wanted to use this to satisfy his earlier words,
so he immediately pushed it away with his hand and refused it.
Later, when merits were discussed and enfeoffments were granted,
Wú Fàn 範 was made Marquis of Dūtíng 都亭侯.
Just as the imperial edict was about to be issued,
Sūn Quán 權, angered by his possessiveness of his art towards himself,
deleted his name.
Wú Fàn 範 was a man of upright character,
and quite fond of boasting,
but he maintained lifelong relationships with his relatives and old friends.
He had long been good friends with Wèi Téng 魏滕, who was from the same district.
Wèi Téng 滕 once committed a crime,
and Sūn Quán 權's anger and reprimand were very severe,
to the point that anyone who dared to intercede would be put to death.
Wú Fàn 範 said to Wèi Téng 滕:
"I will die with you."
Wèi Téng 滕 said:
"To die without benefit,
what use is such a death?"
Wú Fàn 範 said:
"How can I consider this,
and just sit by and watch you?"
Thereupon, he shaved his head and bound himself, then went to the palace gate,
ordering the bell-bearer to announce him.
The bell-bearer dared not,
saying:
"I will surely die;
I dare not announce it."
Wú Fàn 範 said:
"Do you have children?"
He replied:
"I do."
Wú Fàn 範 said:
"If you die for Wú Fàn 吳範,
I will take care of your children."
The bell-bearer said:
"Yes."
He then pushed through the gate and entered.
Before he finished speaking,
Sūn Quán 權 grew furious,
and wanted to throw a halberd at him immediately.
The bell-bearer hesitated and ran out,
whereupon Wú Fàn 範 rushed in,
kowtowing until his head bled,
his words accompanied by tears.
After a long while,
Sūn Quán 權's anger subsided,
and he pardoned Wèi Téng 滕.
Wèi Téng 滕 saw Wú Fàn 範 and thanked him, saying:
"My parents could give me birth and raise me,
but they could not save me from death.
For a man to know another,
someone like you is enough;
why need more!"
In the fifth year of Huángwǔ 黃武 (226 CE),
Wú Fàn 範 died of illness.
His eldest son had died earlier,
and his younger son was still young,
so his lineage of art was cut off.
Sūn Quán 權 remembered him with longing,
and sought throughout the three provinces for anyone who could master the arts of calculation and divination like Wú Fàn 吳範 and Zhào Dá 趙達,
promising them an enfeoffment of a thousand households.
In the end, no one was found.
Liú Dūn 劉惇, courtesy name Zǐrén 子仁,
was a native of Píngyuán 平原.
Caught in the chaos, he sought refuge elsewhere,
becoming a sojourner in Lúlíng 廬陵, serving Sūn Fǔ 孫輔.
He became renowned in the southern lands for his clear understanding of celestial phenomena and mastery of divinatory calculations.
Whenever there were floods, droughts, or banditry,
he would predict their timing in advance,
and none were ever incorrect.
Sūn Fǔ 輔 was amazed by this,
and made him his military advisor.
Everyone in the army respected and served him,
calling him "Divine Intelligence" (Shénmíng 神明).
During the Jiàn'ān 建安 period (196–220 CE),
Sūn Quán 權 was in Yùzhāng 豫章.
There was a celestial anomaly at the time,
and he asked Liú Dūn 惇 about it.
Liú Dūn 惇 said:
"The disaster is in Dānyáng 丹楊."
Sūn Quán 權 asked:
"What will it be like?"
He replied:
"The guest will overcome the host;
by a certain day, you will receive news."
At that time, Biān Hóng 邊鴻 rebelled,
and it turned out exactly as Liú Dūn 惇 had said.
Liú Dūn 惇 was skilled in all divinatory arts,
especially clear in Tàiyǐ 太乙,
and could deduce and elaborate on its matters,
exhausting its profound subtleties.
He authored over a hundred chapters of books,
and the renowned scholar Diāo Xuán 刁玄 praised them as extraordinary.
Liú Dūn 惇 also treasured his art,
and did not reveal it to others,
which is why the world could not fully understand it.
Zhào Dá 趙達
was a native of Hénán 河南.
In his youth, he studied under Shàn Fǔ 單甫, a Grandee Remonstrant (Shìzhōng 侍中) of the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
He was precise in his thinking,
and believed that there was a "kingly aura" in the southeast,
where one could avoid disaster,
so he escaped and crossed the Jiāng 江 river.
He practiced the art of the Nine Palaces and single calculation,
thoroughly grasping its subtle principles.
Because of this, he could respond to circumstances and achieve results instantly,
answering questions as if divine.
Even calculating flying locusts
and hitting hidden objects,
none failed to be effective.
Someone once challenged Zhào Dá 達, saying:
"Things that fly certainly cannot be verified;
who knows if it's true?
This is probably nonsense."
Zhào Dá 達 had that person take a few *dǒu* (bushels) of small beans,
spread them on a mat,
and immediately stated their number.
When checked, it was indeed accurate.
Once, he visited an old acquaintance.
The acquaintance prepared a meal for him.
After eating, he said:
"In haste, we are short of wine,
and lack fine dishes.
Please don't mind,
what do you think?"
Zhào Dá 達 then took a single chopstick from the tray,
moved it horizontally and vertically a few times,
and then said:
"You have a *hú* (bushel) of fine wine under the east wall,
and also three *jīn* (catties) of venison.
Why do you say you have none?"
At that time, there were other guests present,
who understood the host's sentiment.
The host said, ashamed:
"I wanted to test you, since you are good at divining what is or isn't there,
and indeed it is so effective!"
Thereupon, he brought out the wine and they drank heartily.
There was also a written note with a number in the tens of millions,
which was placed in an empty granary and sealed,
and Zhào Dá 達 was asked to calculate it.
Zhào Dá 達 gave the exact number,
saying:
"It exists in name only, without substance."
His precision was like this.
Dá Bǎo cherished his art.
Even Kān Zé and Yīn Lǐ, both renowned scholars and good gentlemen,
personally humbled themselves to study under him,
but Dá kept it secret and would not impart it.
The Taishǐ Chéng, Gōngsūn Téng, served Dá as a young student,
toiling for many years.
Dá had promised to teach him for a number of years,
but when it came to explaining the technique, he would always stop.
One day, Téng brought wine and provisions,
observed his mood,
knelt and begged him.
Dá said:
"My ancestors obtained this art,
intending to become advisors to emperors.
For three generations, since they entered officialdom,
they never rose above Taishǐ Láng.
I truly do not wish to transmit it again.
Moreover, this art is subtle and profound,
involving 'multiplying the head and dividing the tail' (頭乘尾除),
a method of calculation
that even father and son do not share.
However, seeing your earnest and tireless dedication,
I will truly impart it to you today."
After several rounds of wine,
Dá rose and fetched two volumes of plain silk books,
each as thick as a finger.
Dá said:
"You should copy and read these,
and you will understand it yourself.
I have long neglected them,
and no longer examine them.
Now I wish to review them once,
and I will give them to you in a few days."
Téng went as scheduled,
but Dá pretended to search for the books,
and exclaimed in surprise that they were lost,
saying:
"My daughter's husband came yesterday;
it must have been he who stole them."
And from then on, the matter was dropped.
Initially, when Sūn Quán led armies on campaigns,
he always ordered Dá to make calculations,
and they were all as he predicted.
Quán asked him about his methods,
but Dá never spoke of them.
Because of this, he was held in slight regard,
and his salary and rank did not advance.
Dá often laughed and said to those who practiced celestial prognostication and geomancy:
"One should make calculations behind curtains,
knowing the ways of heaven without leaving the house,
yet you instead expose yourselves day and night to observe qi and omens;
is this not difficult!"
When at leisure and without duties,
he would make calculations to verify them himself.
Then he sighed and said:
"My calculations conclude that my life will end on such and such a date,
and that will be my demise."
Dá's wife had often witnessed his effectiveness,
and hearing this, she wept.
Dá, wishing to appease his wife,
then re-calculated,
saying:
"That was a mistake earlier;
it is not yet time."
Later, he died as predicted.
Quán heard that Dá had books,
sought them but could not obtain them.
He then interrogated his daughter,
and even opened his coffin, but found nothing,
and so the art was lost.
The commentary says: The three men were each skilled in their arts,
and their application of thought was marvelous.
However, a gentleman should devote his mind and spirit
to matters of greater importance and longer vision.
Therefore, those with understanding
abandon the former and embrace the latter.
Biographies of Zhūgě, Téng, and the two Sūn, Púyáng, Chapter Nineteen.
Zhūgě Kè, courtesy name Yuánsùn,
was the eldest son of Zhūgě Jǐn.
He was well-known in his youth.
Upon reaching adulthood, he was appointed Qí Dūwèi.
He, along with Gù Tán and Zhāng Xiū, among others, lectured on the Dao and arts to Crown Prince Dēng,
and all became his friends.
He was transferred from Zhōngshù Zǐ to Zuǒfǔ Dūwèi.
Kè's father, Zhūgě Jǐn, had a long face resembling a donkey's.
Sūn Quán held a grand assembly of officials,
and had someone lead a donkey in,
tying a long tag to its face,
on which was written "Zhūgě Zǐyú."
Kè knelt and said:
"May I beg for a brush to add two characters?"
Permission was then granted, and a brush given.
Kè continued below it:
"'s donkey."
The entire assembly burst into laughter,
and Sūn Quán bestowed the donkey upon Kè.
Another day, when they met again,
Quán asked Kè:
"Between your father and your paternal uncle, who is more worthy?"
He replied:
"My father is superior."
Quán asked for the reason,
and he replied:
"My father knows whom to serve,
my uncle does not,
and for this reason he is superior."
Quán again laughed heartily.
He ordered Kè to serve wine.
When he reached Zhāng Zhāo,
Zhāo already had a flushed face from drinking
and refused to drink,
saying:
"This is not the custom for honoring elders."
Quán said:
"If you can make Duke Zhāng concede,
then he must drink."
Kè challenged Zhāo, saying:
"In ancient times, Grand Master Shàngfǔ (Jiang Ziya), at ninety,
still held the banner and wielded the battle-axe,
and had not yet declared himself old.
Today, in military matters,
the general is behind,
but in matters of wine and food,
the general is first.
How can you say this is not honoring elders?"
Zhāo was left speechless,
and so emptied his cup.
Later, when an envoy from Shǔ arrived,
and all the officials were gathered,
Quán said to the envoy:
"This Zhūgě Kè is very fond of riding.
When you return, tell the Chancellor to send him a good horse."
Kè immediately bowed in thanks.
Quán said:
"Why thank me when the horse has not yet arrived?"
Kè replied:
"Shǔ is Your Majesty's external stable.
Now that there is a gracious decree,
the horse will surely arrive.
How dare I not thank you?"
Kè's quick wit
was always of this kind.
Quán was very impressed by him
and wanted to test him with a task,
ordering him to take charge of Jiédù.
Jiédù managed military provisions and grain,
and the documents were numerous and complex,
which he did not like.
Kè submitted that Dānyáng's mountains were rugged
and its people were strong and spirited.
Although troops had been sent before,
they only managed to gain control of the common people in the outer counties;
the deeper, more remote areas
could not be fully pacified.
He repeatedly requested to be sent out to govern them,
promising to obtain 40,000 armored soldiers within three years.
The general consensus was that Dānyáng's terrain was treacherous and formidable,
bordering the four commanderies of Wú Jùn, Kuàijī, Xīndū, and Póyáng,
spanning several thousand *lǐ* in circumference.
It had tens of thousands of mountains and valleys,
and its secluded inhabitants
had never entered cities or towns
or faced magistrates,
instead relying on weapons and living wild,
growing old in the forests and wilderness.
Fugitives and entrenched criminals
all fled and hid there.
The mountains yielded copper and iron,
from which they cast their own armor and weapons.
Their customs favored martial arts and practiced warfare,
valuing strength and prowess.
They would ascend mountains and brave dangers,
charging into dense thickets
like fish entering deep waters
or monkeys leaping through trees.
When they saw an opening,
they would emerge as bandits,
and each time troops were sent to suppress them,
they would seek out their hidden lairs.
When they fought, they were fierce;
when they were defeated, they scattered like birds.
From previous generations until now,
they had been uncontrollable.
Everyone considered it a difficult task.
Kè's father, Zhūgě Jǐn, heard of this,
and also believed the task would ultimately fail,
sighing:
"Kè will either greatly expand our family's fortune
or greatly disgrace our clan."
Kè strongly presented his case for certain victory.
Quán appointed Kè Fǔyuè Jiāngjūn
and gave him the governorship of Dānyáng,
granting him an honorary guard of three hundred armored horsemen with ceremonial halberds.
After the appointment,
he ordered Kè to prepare his full regalia
and have drums and trumpets play
to escort him home.
At this time, he was thirty-two years old.
When Kè arrived at the commandery,
he then dispatched letters to the chief officials of the affiliated cities in the four commanderies,
ordering each to protect their borders,
clearly establish their units,
and ensure that all common people who had submitted
were settled in encampments.
Then, he divided his internal generals,
stationing troops in remote, defensible areas.
They merely repaired fences
and did not engage in direct combat.
When the enemy's grain was about to ripen,
they would consistently send out troops to cut it down,
leaving no seeds behind.
With the old grain exhausted
and no new harvest,
and the common people settled in encampments
with virtually no income,
the mountain people became hungry and destitute,
gradually emerging to surrender.
Kè then reissued an order, saying:
"The mountain people who abandon evil and embrace transformation
should all be comforted and pacified,
and relocated to outer counties.
No suspicion should be harbored,
nor should they be arrested or detained."
The Prefect of Jiùyáng, Hú Kàng, captured a surrendered man named Zhōu Yí.
Yí was a formerly wicked person
who, due to distress, had temporarily surrendered
but secretly plotted rebellion.
Kàng bound and sent him to the commandery.
Kè, seeing that Kàng had violated his instructions,
executed him publicly,
and reported the situation to the throne.
When the people heard that Kàng was executed for detaining a person,
they knew that the officials simply wanted them to come out.
So, the old and young led each other out.
Within a year,
the number of people matched the original plan.
Kè himself led ten thousand men,
the rest were distributed among his generals.
Quán commended his achievement
and sent the Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk, Xuē Zōng, to comfort the troops.
Zōng first sent a letter to Kè and others, saying:
"The Shānyuè, relying on their remote strongholds,
have not submitted for generations.
When things are relaxed, they are indecisive;
when urgent, they are ruthless.
The Emperor, in a furious display of majesty,
ordered a western campaign.
Divine strategies were inwardly imparted,
and martial might outwardly shook.
Swords were not stained with blood,
armor not wet with sweat.
The chief villains were overthrown,
their factions returned to righteousness.
Mountains and swamps were cleansed,
and ten tens of thousands of barbarians were presented.
No bandits remained in the wilds,
no traitors in the cities.
Not only were the wicked purged,
but military resources were also replenished.
Wild grasses and weeds
transformed into beneficial herbs.
Demons and monsters
became brave warriors.
Though this was truly due to the added prestige of the state,
it was also certainly caused by the Marshal's personal presence and execution.
Although the *Shī* praises the capture of prisoners,
and the *Yì* commends the decapitation of enemies,
how can the Zhōu dynasty's Fāng and Zhào,
or the Hàn dynasty's Wèi and Huò,
be enough to even compare?
Your achievements surpass those of ancient figures,
your merits exceed those of previous ages.
The sovereign is overjoyed,
sighing in admiration from afar.
He is moved by the ancient tradition of the 'four steeds'
and recalls the old ritual of 'drinking to completion.'
Therefore, he sent a high official from the central administration
to welcome you with rewards and gifts,
to honor your splendid achievements
and to comfort your toil."
Kè was appointed General Who Awe the North
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
Kè requested to lead his troops to farm in Lújiāng and Wǎnkǒu.
He then launched a light cavalry raid on Shū,
capturing its people and returning.
He again sent out scouts far and wide
to observe the strategic routes,
intending to seize Shòuchūn.
Quán considered this unfeasible.
During the Chìwū era,
Wèi's Sīmǎ Xuānwáng planned to attack Kè.
Quán was about to dispatch troops to respond,
but an aura-reader deemed it unfavorable.
Thus, Kè was relocated to garrison at Cháisāng.
He wrote a letter to Chancellor Lù Xùn, saying:
"Yáng Jìngshū conveyed a clear discourse,
believing that at present, worthy individuals are scarce,
and those who uphold virtue and conduct are not many.
It is advisable for us to support each other,
acting as interdependent parts of a chariot,
to jointly promote national affairs
and cherish one another.
He also deplored the common tendency of the world to slander and defame each other,
which causes already accomplished individuals
to suffer harm and setbacks;
and those who are about to advance
to feel no joy.
Hearing this, I sighed deeply,
and truly clapped my hands in agreement.
I foolishly believe that a gentleman does not demand perfection from a single person.
Even among Confucius's disciples, numbering about three thousand,
seventy-two were considered outstanding.
As for Zǐzhāng, Zǐlù, Zǐgòng, and the other seventy disciples,
whose virtues were second only to the sage,
they still each had their shortcomings:
Shī Pì was crude,
Cì did not accept his fate.
How much more so for those below them, who could not be without flaws?
Moreover, Confucius did not withdraw from friendship with these few disciples because of their imperfections,
nor did he discard a person's strengths because of their weaknesses.
Furthermore, when selecting officials nowadays,
one should be more lenient than in ancient times.
Why?
Because current affairs are complex and challenging,
and good people are few.
The state's official positions
are often insufficiently filled.
If a person's nature is not wicked,
and their ambition is to exert their efforts,
they should be encouraged and promoted,
allowing them to excel in their assigned roles.
As for minor suitability issues
or private conduct shortcomings,
these should generally be overlooked
and not scrutinized in detail.
Indeed, scholars should not be criticized minutely or harshly.
If they are, even the wise and sagely would not be perfect,
how much less those who are merely passing through?
Therefore, it is said that judging people by the Dao is difficult;
judging people by people is easy.
The wise and foolish can be known.
Since the end of the Hàn dynasty,
Chinese literati and officials, like Xǔ Zǐjiāng and his ilk,
have slandered each other,
sometimes even leading to disaster.
Tracing their origins,
it was not due to great enmity,
but solely because they themselves could not fully conform to ritual,
yet demanded others adhere strictly to righteousness.
If one's own conduct does not conform to ritual,
then others will not be convinced.
If one demands strict righteousness from others,
then others cannot bear it.
Internally, they are not convinced by the other's conduct;
externally, they cannot bear the other's demands.
Thus, they inevitably resent each other.
Once resentment arises,
petty individuals can sow discord between them.
If discord can be sown,
then slanders that come from all directions,
and insidious whispers,
will arrive in a chaotic mix.
Even if a person of utmost clarity and close relation were to handle it,
it would still be difficult for them to resolve it themselves,
how much more so if one has created a rift
and is not yet clear-headed?
This is why Zhāng and Chén came to blows,
and Xiāo and Zhū did not maintain their friendship.
The root cause is merely this.
If one does not overlook minor faults
and constantly criticizes trivial matters,
in the long run, it will lead to familial enmity,
and there will be no one in the entire country whose conduct is considered perfect."
Kè knew that Xùn suspected him of this,
so he elaborated on the principle and endorsed its main idea.
Coincidentally, Xùn died.
Kè was promoted to Grand General,
granted the imperial credential (jiǎjié),
stationed in Wǔchāng,
and took over Xùn's responsibilities in Jīngzhōu.
After a long time,
Quán fell ill,
and the Crown Prince was young.
So, he summoned Kè to be Grand General and Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and the Central Secretariat Director Sūn Hóng to be Junior Tutor.
When Quán's illness worsened,
he summoned Kè, Hóng, as well as Grand Herald Téng Yìn, General Lǚ Jù, and Palace Attendant Sūn Jùn,
entrusting them with the affairs after his death.
The next day,
Quán passed away.
Hóng, who had long been at odds with Kè,
feared being purged by Kè.
He secretly kept the news of Quán's death
hoping to forge an edict to eliminate Kè.
Jùn informed Kè of this.
Kè invited Hóng to discuss matters,
and had him executed during the meeting.
Then, they announced the emperor's passing and donned mourning clothes.
Kè wrote to his younger brother, Gōng'ān Dūdū Róng, saying:
"On the sixteenth day of this month, Yǐwèi,
the Great Emperor abandoned the myriad states.
All, from the highest to the lowest,
are grieving.
As for my father, myself, and my brothers,
we have received extraordinary favors;
we are not merely ordinary subjects.
Therefore, our sorrow is so profound
that our hearts and livers are shattered.
The Crown Prince ascended the imperial throne on Dīngyǒu.
Joy and sorrow are intertwined,
and I know not what to do.
I have received the dying entrustment
to assist the young lord.
I secretly weigh myself
and find my talent is not that of Bólù, yet I bear the trust of Jī Gōng's regency.
I fear I may disgrace the achievements of the Prime Minister assisting Hàn,
and damage the sagacity of the late emperor's entrustment.
Therefore, I am anxious and uneasy,
with myriad concerns.
Moreover, the people resent their superiors,
and everything is observed.
When will things change easily?
Now, with my dull and clumsy disposition,
I occupy the position of guardian.
My difficulties are many, my wisdom scant;
my responsibility is heavy, my plans shallow.
Who will be my 'lips and teeth'?
In the recent Hàn era,
Yān and Gài became entangled,
leading to the affair of Shàngguān.
Finding myself in such a situation,
how can I be at ease?
Furthermore, where my brother is stationed,
it is intertwined with the enemy like dog's teeth.
At this time, you must organize your military equipment,
inspire your officers and soldiers,
and be more vigilant than usual.
Resolve to face a myriad of deaths,
disregarding your own life,
to repay the court,
and not to dishonor your ancestors.
Also, all generals defending their respective borders
are still worried that the enemy barbarians, hearing of the emperor's passing,
might act recklessly and plunder.
The various departments in the border areas
have already received separate strict orders:
the supervising generals under their command
are not to abandon their garrisons presumptuously
and rush here.
Although I harbor feelings of grief and reluctance,
public duty overrides private feelings.
Bóqín wore military attire.
If anyone violates this,
it will not be a minor offense.
To prioritize family over strangers is a clear warning from the ancients."
Kè was then appointed Tài fù.
Thereupon, he abolished the supervision and review of officials,
closed the imperial academy,
remitted outstanding debts,
and eliminated customs duties.
He focused on extending grace and favors,
and everyone was pleased.
Whenever Kè entered or exited,
the common people craned their necks,
eager to see him.
Initially,
in the first year of Huánglóng of Quán, he moved the capital to Jiànyè.
In the second year, he built the Dōngxīng Dī embankment to block the lake water.
Later, when campaigning in Huáinán,
his forces suffered a defeat due to relying on riverine vessels,
and the embankment was subsequently abandoned and not repaired.
In the tenth month of the first year of Jiànxīng, Kè assembled his forces at Dōngxīng
and rebuilt a large embankment.
He constructed two cities on the left and right, leaning against the mountains,
each garrisoned by a thousand men.
He ordered Quán Duān and Liú Lüè to guard them,
then led his army back.
Wèi, seeing Wú forces enter its territory,
felt disgraced by the insult.
It ordered its great generals Hú Zūn and Zhūgě Dàn, among others, to lead seventy thousand troops,
intending to attack and besiege the two forts
and destroy the embankment.
Kè raised forty thousand troops
and rushed to their aid day and night.
Zūn and others ordered their various armies to construct pontoon bridges and cross over,
arraying themselves on the embankment.
They divided their forces to attack the two cities.
The cities were high and steep,
and could not be taken quickly.
Kè dispatched generals Liú Zàn, Lü Jù, Táng Zī, and Dīng Fèng as the vanguard.
At that time, it was cold and snowing.
The Wèi generals were holding a feast.
Seeing Zàn and others with few troops,
who had taken off their armor
and carried no spears or halberds,
only helmets, swords, and shields,
climbing the embankment bare-bodied,
they laughed at them loudly
and did not immediately prepare their troops.
When the Wú soldiers reached the top,
they immediately beat drums, shouted, and hacked wildly.
The Wèi army was startled and scattered,
scrambling to cross the pontoon bridges.
The bridges broke,
and they threw themselves into the water,
trampling each other.
Huán Jiā, the Administrator of Lè'ān, and others perished simultaneously,
with tens of thousands dead.
The former rebel general Hán Zōng, who was a Wèi vanguard commander,
was also beheaded.
They captured thousands of chariots, cattle, horses, donkeys, and mules each,
and supplies piled up like mountains.
They returned triumphantly.
Kè was promoted to Yángdū Hóu,
given the additional title of Jīng-Yáng Zhōumù,
and oversaw all military affairs at home and abroad.
He was bestowed one hundred catties of gold,
two hundred horses,
and ten thousand bolts each of silk and cloth.
Kè subsequently developed a disdain for the enemy.
After his victory in the twelfth month,
he wished to launch another military campaign
the following spring.
All the senior ministers believed that repeated campaigns were exhausting,
and unanimously advised Kè against it.
Kè did not listen.
The Zhōngsàn Dàfū Jiǎng Yán strongly remonstrated
and was forcibly removed.
Kè then wrote an essay to enlighten the assembly, saying:
"Indeed, there cannot be two suns in the sky,
nor two kings on earth.
A king who does not strive to annex the whole world, but instead wishes to extend his legacy to future generations,
has never existed in ancient or modern times.
In the past, during the Warring States period,
the feudal lords, relying on their strong armies and vast territories,
mutually supported each other,
believing this was sufficient to transmit their generations
and that no one could endanger them.
Indulging their desires
and shrinking from hardship,
they allowed Qín to gradually grow powerful,
and thus to annex them.
This is an established fact.
More recently, Liú Jǐngshēng, in Jīngzhōu,
had an army of 100,000,
and wealth and grain piled up like mountains.
But Cáo Cāo was still insignificant.
Instead of competing with him forcefully,
Liú Jǐngshēng sat by and watched him grow strong,
swallowing up all the Yuán clans.
After the North was completely pacified,
Cāo led an army of 300,000 towards Jīngzhōu.
At that time, even if there were wise men,
they could no longer devise plans.
Thereupon, Jǐngshēng's sons
crossed their arms and surrendered,
becoming captives.
When enemy states seek to devour each other,
it is like sworn enemies wanting to eliminate each other.
If one harbors an enemy and allows them to grow,
the disaster will either fall on oneself
or on one's descendants.
One must not fail to plan far ahead.
In the past, Wǔ Zǐxū said: 'Yuè will spend ten years accumulating resources,
ten years training,
and after twenty years,
Wú will surely become a swamp!'
Fūchā, relying on his strength,
dismissed this when he heard it.
Thus, he executed Zǐxū and had no thought of preparing against Yuè,
regretting it only when defeat was imminent.
How could it then be of any use?
Yuè was smaller than Wú,
yet it became Wú's undoing.
How much more so when the enemy is stronger?
In ancient times, Qín only possessed Guānxī,
yet it was still able to annex the Six States.
Now the enemy has all the lands of Qín, Zhào, Hán, Wèi, Yān, and Qí – nine prefectures in total.
These lands are entirely homelands of cavalry
and breeding grounds for scholars.
If we compare Wèi to ancient Qín,
its territory is several times larger.
If we compare Wú and Shǔ to the ancient Six States,
they do not even amount to half of them.
However, the reason we can still resist them today
is simply that Cāo's armies
have just about reached their end,
and those born later have not yet fully grown.
This is precisely the time when the enemy is in decline and not yet at its peak.
Furthermore, Sīmǎ Yì first executed Wáng Líng
and then died himself,
and his sons are young and weak,
yet they hold such great responsibilities.
Even if there are intelligent and strategic men,
they have not yet been able to implement their plans.
Attacking them now
is their time of peril.
The sage's urgency in seizing the opportune moment
truly refers to today.
If we follow the common people's sentiment
and harbor plans for temporary peace,
believing that the natural defenses of the Cháng Jiāng can secure our generations,
without considering Wèi's ultimate fate,
and thereby treating its future lightly based on today's situation,
this is what causes me to sigh deeply.
Since [ancient times],
the focus has been on procreation.
Now, the enemy's population is increasing yearly and monthly,
but they are still young
and cannot yet be used.
If another ten or more years pass,
their numbers will surely double compared to today,
while our state's lands for strong soldiers
will all be exhausted.
Only these existing troops can settle the matter.
If we do not use them early,
but sit idly by and let them grow old,
in another ten or more years,
they will be roughly halved,
and the number of our young men will not even be worth mentioning.
If the enemy's numbers double
while our forces are halved,
even if Yī and Guǎn were to plan for us,
there would be nothing we could do.
Those who do not grasp long-term foresight now
will surely consider these words impractical.
Indeed, to worry in advance before disaster strikes
is certainly what common people deem impractical.
But when the disaster arrives,
and then one bows one's head in despair,
even the wise
can no longer devise a plan.
This has been the problem throughout history,
not just at one particular time.
In the past, Wú initially considered Wǔ Yuán impractical,
so when disaster struck, it could not be saved.
Liú Jǐngshēng could not foresee ten years ahead,
and thus had nothing to bequeath to his descendants.
Now, although I, Kè, lack the talent of a fully-fledged minister,
I have been entrusted with the responsibilities of Xiāo and Huò of Dà Wú.
My wisdom is no different from the common folk,
and my thoughts do not extend far.
If I do not seize this opportunity today to expand the nation's borders,
and then grow old,
while our enemies grow stronger,
and I wish to cut my throat to atone for my failure,
what good would that do?
I hear now that some people believe the common folk are still poor
and wish to let them rest.
These people do not consider the great danger,
but cherish minor toil.
In the past, Emperor Gāo of Hàn already possessed the land of Sān Qín.
Why did he not close the passes and guard the strongholds
to enjoy himself?
Instead, he ventured out to attack Chǔ,
suffered wounds,
had lice in his armor,
and his generals and soldiers were exhausted and distressed.
Did they enjoy the battlefield and forget peace?
It was out of concern that in the long run, both could not coexist!
Whenever I read Jīng Hán's advice to Gōngsūn Shù on a strategy of advance,
and recently saw my uncle's memorial outlining plans to contend with the enemy,
I never fail to sigh with deep emotion.
Restless night and day,
my worries are as I have stated.
Therefore, I have hastily laid out these foolish words
to convey them to a few gentlemen.
Should I perish one morning,
and my strategic plans not be established,
I wish to let future generations know my worries,
for them to consider later."
Everyone regarded Kè's essay as a definitive statement,
and no one dared to challenge it further.
The Administrator of Dānyáng, Niè Yǒu, who was always close to Kè,
wrote to admonish Kè, saying:
"The late Emperor (Dàháng Huángdì) originally had a plan to stop the enemy at Dōngguān,
but the plan was not implemented.
Now, as you, Lord Assistant, support the great enterprise
and fulfill the late Emperor's ambition,
the enemy has come from afar to deliver themselves.
Our generals and soldiers, relying on your prestige and virtue,
will risk their lives to obey orders,
and suddenly achieve extraordinary merit.
Would this not be a blessing from the ancestral temples, spirits, and the altars of earth and grain?
It would be appropriate to temporarily keep our troops at rest, sharpen their morale,
and act when an opportune moment arises.
Now, to rely on this momentum
and wish to launch another large-scale expedition,
the timing is not yet right.
If we simply act on strong intentions,
my private feeling is that it would be unsafe."
Kè added a note after his essay
and wrote back to Yǒu, saying:
"Although your Excellency's reasoning is natural,
you have not grasped the greater scheme.
Study this essay carefully,
and you will be enlightened."
Thereupon, he defied public opinion and launched the army,
mobilizing 200,000 troops from the various commanderies.
The common people were agitated,
and he began to lose popular support.
Gé intended to display his might in Huáinán,
plundering and seizing the people.
However, some generals raised objections, saying:
“If we lead the army deep now,
the people near the border
will certainly flee far away together.
We fear the troops will be exhausted with little gain.
It is better to merely besiege Xīnchéng.
Once Xīnchéng is in distress,
a rescue force will surely arrive.
If they arrive and we then plan against them,
we can achieve a great victory.”
Gé adopted their plan,
turning his army back to besiege Xīnchéng.
The attack and defense continued for months,
but the city could not be captured.
The soldiers were exhausted,
and due to the summer heat, drinking water
caused dysentery and edema.
More than half the men were sick,
and the dead and wounded covered the ground.
The camp officers reported daily that many were sick,
but Gé thought they were feigning
and wanted to execute them.
Thereafter, no one dared to speak.
Gé privately reflected on his miscalculation,
but was ashamed that the city had not fallen,
and his indignation showed on his face.
When General Zhū Yì had something to commend or criticize,
Gé grew angry
and immediately stripped him of his command.
Dūwèi Cài Lín repeatedly presented military plans,
but Gé would not use them.
Cài Lín then spurred his horse and fled to Wèi.
Wèi, knowing the soldiers were tired and sick,
then sent relief troops.
Gé withdrew his army and departed.
The sick and wounded soldiers
staggered along the roads,
some collapsing into pits and ravines,
others captured or seized.
The survivors and the dead alike felt anguish and pain,
and everyone, great and small, cried out in lament.
Yet Gé remained calm and composed.
He stopped by a river islet for a month,
planning to establish fields in Xúnyáng.
When imperial edicts summoning him followed one after another,
he then slowly returned with his army.
From this, the common people were disappointed,
and resentment and criticism arose.
In the eighth month of autumn, the army returned.
With soldiers forming an escort,
he went back to his mansion.
He immediately summoned Zhōngshūlìng Sūn Hēi
and sternly said to him:
“How dare you repeatedly issue edicts without authorization?”
Hēi, terrified, excused himself and left,
then returned home, feigning illness.
After Gé’s campaign,
all the officials whose appointments as magistrates or administrators had been submitted by the offices
were dismissed and new ones selected.
His rule became even more strict and imposing;
he blamed and punished many.
No one who came for an audience
was not filled with apprehension.
He also replaced the palace guards,
employing his close confidants.
He further ordered the troops to be vigilant,
intending to march towards Qīng and Xú.
Sūn Jùn, seizing upon the widespread public resentment
and the general suspicion,
concocted a scheme, alleging Gé intended to stage a coup.
He conspired with Liàng
to arrange a banquet for Gé.
On the night before Gé was to attend,
his spirit was agitated,
and he could not sleep the entire night.
The next morning, as he was about to wash,
he smelled a foul odor in the water.
When an attendant handed him his clothes,
the clothes also smelled.
Gé wondered at this,
changed his clothes and water,
but the smell remained the same.
He felt disheartened and displeased.
When he finished his preparations and rushed out,
a dog tugged at his clothes with its mouth.
Gé said:
“Does the dog not want me to go?”
He returned to his seat,
and after a moment, he rose again.
The dog again tugged at his clothes.
Gé ordered his attendants to drive the dog away,
and then he got into his carriage.
Earlier,
when Gé was about to campaign in Huáinán,
a filial son wearing mourning clothes entered his private quarters.
An attendant reported it,
and Gé ordered him to question the man outside.
The filial son said:
“I didn’t realize I had entered.”
At that time, the guards inside and outside
had also seen nothing.
Everyone found this strange.
After he set out, the central beam of the hall where he sat
snapped.
When he left Xīnchéng and stopped in Dōngxīng,
a white rainbow appeared on his boat.
Upon returning and paying respects at Jiǎnglín,
a white rainbow again coiled around his carriage.
When he was about to attend the banquet,
he stopped his carriage at the palace gate.
Jùn had already hidden soldiers behind the curtains.
Fearing that Gé would not enter in time
and the plot would be exposed,
Jùn himself came out to meet Gé and said:
“If your Excellency is not feeling well,
you can certainly wait for later.
Jùn will duly report to the sovereign.”
He wished to test Gé with this.
Gé replied:
“I must make an effort to enter.”
Sànqí Chángshì Zhāng Yuē, Zhū Ēn, and others secretly wrote to Gé, saying:
“Today’s arrangements are unusual;
we suspect something else is afoot.”
Gé read the letter and went on.
Before he exited the palace gate,
he met Tài Téng Yìn.
Gé said:
“I suddenly have stomach pains and
cannot bear to enter.”
Yìn, unaware of Jùn’s secret plan,
said to Gé:
“You have already turned back and not yet seen His Majesty.
Today, the sovereign has prepared a banquet for you.
You have already reached the gate;
you should make an effort to go in.”
Gé hesitated but then returned,
entering the hall with sword and shoes on,
bowing to Liàng,
and returning to his seat.
Wine was served,
but Gé was suspicious and did not drink.
Jùn then said:
“Your Excellency is not fully recovered from illness,
you must have your usual medicinal wine;
you may take it yourself.”
Gé’s mind was then at ease,
and he drank the wine he had brought himself.
After a few rounds of wine,
Liàng returned to the inner chambers.
Jùn rose to go to the latrine,
removed his long robe,
and put on short attire.
He then came out and said:
“I have an imperial edict to arrest Zhūgě Gé!”
Gé rose in alarm,
but before he could draw his sword,
Jùn’s blade struck down.
Zhāng Yuē, from the side, slashed at Jùn,
only lightly wounding his left hand.
Jùn immediately counter-slashed Yuē,
severing his right arm.
The imperial guards all rushed into the hall.
Jùn said:
“The one we were after was Gé,
and he is now dead.”
He ordered them all to sheathe their blades
and then cleared the area to resume drinking.
Before this,
a children’s rhyme said:
“Zhūgě Gé,
reed mat single garment, bamboo-strip hook-strap,
where shall we seek you, at Chéngzǐ Gé?”
Chéngzǐ Gé
is an inverted pronunciation of Shízǐgāng.
South of Jiànyè there is a long tomb,
named Shízǐgāng,
where people were buried.
Gōuluò refers to
decorated leather belts,
which people of the time called gōuluòdài.
Gé was indeed wrapped in a reed mat, his waist bound with bamboo strips,
and thrown onto this hill.
Kè's eldest son, Chuò,
a Cavalry Commandant,
was involved in a matter concerning the Prince of Lǔ.
Quán sent him back to Kè,
ordering him to be reformed.
Kè poisoned him to death.
His middle son, Sǒng,
was Commandant of Changshuǐ.
His youngest son, Jiàn,
was Commandant of Infantry.
When they heard of Kè's execution,
they loaded their mother into a cart and fled.
Jùn dispatched Cavalry Commander Liú Chéng to pursue and execute Sǒng at Báidū.
Jiàn managed to cross the river,
intending to flee north to Wèi.
After traveling several dozen *lǐ*,
he was apprehended by the pursuing troops.
Kè's nephew, the Marquis of Dūxiāng, Zhāng Zhèn, and Attendant Zhū Ēn, among others,
all had their three clans exterminated.
Initially,
Sǒng repeatedly remonstrated with Kè,
but Kè did not heed him.
He often feared impending disaster.
After Kè's demise,
Zāng Jūn of Lín’huái submitted a memorial requesting his burial, saying:
"I have heard that crashing thunder and flashing lightning
do not last a single morning,
and fierce winds, once unleashed,
rarely persist all day.
Yet, they are still followed by clouds and rain,
which then moisten all things.
This shows that the majesty of Heaven and Earth
cannot endure for days or prolonged periods.
The anger of emperors and kings
should not be indulged to its fullest extent.
As I am foolish and ignorant,
unaware of taboos,
I dare to risk the crime of utter destruction
to implore for the opportune moment for rain.
I humbly reflect that the late Grand Tutor Zhūgě Kè inherited the illustrious reputation of his ancestors.
His uncles and senior relatives encountered the end of the Hàn dynasty's mandate,
and with Jiǔzhōu divided into three powers,
they were entrusted to different regions,
all serving with loyalty and diligence,
promoting and flourishing their family's legacy.
As for Kè,
he grew up in the kingdom,
nurtured by sacred transformation,
achieving renown as a hero.
He served for many years,
with no wicked intentions yet arising.
The late emperor entrusted him with the responsibilities of Yī and Zhōu,
and committed to him all affairs of state.
Kè's inherent nature was stubborn and arrogant,
self-important and disdainful of others.
He failed to respectfully guard the divine regalia
and maintain peace within the state.
He undertook campaigns and exhausted the army,
making three expeditions in less than a year,
wasting soldiers and civilians,
emptying the treasuries.
He usurped the national laws,
changing and replacing them as he pleased.
He used false accusations to coerce the masses,
causing both great and small to hold their breath in fear.
The Central Commander of the Imperial Guard, the Marquis of Dūxiāng, who received the late emperor's testamentary edict,
saw his wickedness
grow worse day by day.
Fearing that he would shake the universe
and endanger the altars of soil and grain,
he roused his righteous indignation,
piercing through the vast heavens.
His planning surpassed divine intelligence,
his courage a hundred times that of Jīng and Niè.
He personally wielded a naked blade,
beheading Kè in the palace hall.
His merit surpassed Zhūxū,
his achievement exceeded Dōngmóu.
The nation's greatest scourge
was eliminated in a single morning.
His head was paraded and displayed,
and the six armies rejoiced and leaped with joy.
The sun and moon shone brighter,
and no dust stirred.
This truly is the spiritual power of the ancestral temples,
confirmed by both Heaven and man.
Now, the three heads of Kè and his sons
have been displayed in the marketplace for days,
viewed by tens of thousands,
with curses rising like a wind.
The great punishment of the state
has left nothing unshaken.
Elders, children,
all have witnessed it.
In human emotions, concerning all things,
extreme joy gives rise to sorrow.
Seeing Kè's former nobility and power,
unmatched in his generation,
holding the highest offices,
enduring for many years in between,
and now his execution and extermination,
no different from wild beasts,
when the viewing is over and emotions turn,
how can one not feel sorrow?
Moreover, a dead person
shares the same realm as the earth.
Digging, hacking, and stabbing
can add nothing further.
May the sacred court emulate Heaven and Earth,
and let its anger not last more than ten days,
allowing his hometown, former officials, and common people
to gather him in the attire of a common soldier,
and grant him a three-inch coffin.
In the past, Xiàng Jí was granted a place for burial,
and Hán Xìn received the favor of interment.
This was the praise Hán Gāo received for revealing divine sagacity.
May Your Majesty uphold the benevolence of the Three Sovereigns,
and extend a compassionate heart,
so that the nation's favor may reach the bones of the executed,
and they may receive unending grace again.
How could this not broadcast Your fame to distant lands
and encourage and deter the world?
Would it not be magnanimous!
In the past, Luán Bù defied orders regarding Péng Yuè,
and I secretly regret that
he did not first request his lord,
but instead acted on his own will with renowned authority.
That he was not punished
was truly fortunate.
Now, I dare not openly proclaim my foolish sentiments
to expose Your heavenly grace.
I humbly prostrate myself with this handwritten petition,
presumptuously presenting it for Your hearing,
begging the sacred court for compassionate consideration."
Thereupon, Liàng and Jùn allowed Kè's former officials to collect and bury him,
and so they searched for him at Shízǐgāng.
Earlier, when Kè withdrew his army and returned,
Niè Yǒu knew he would fail.
He wrote to Téng Yìn, saying:
"When a person is powerful,
mountains and rivers can be uprooted.
But one day, they become weak and shrunken,
and human emotions are myriad.
To speak of it is to sigh with sorrow."
After Kè's execution,
Sūn Jùn became jealous of Yǒu
and wanted to appoint him as Administrator of Yùlín.
Yǒu fell ill and died of worry.
Yǒu's courtesy name was Wéntì,
and he was a native of Yùzhāng.
Téng Yìn's courtesy name was Chéngsì,
and he was a native of Jù, Běihǎi.
His paternal uncle, Tán,
and his father, Zhòu,
were close family friends with Liú Yáo in their home province.
Due to the chaotic times,
they crossed the river to rely on Yáo.
When Sūn Quán was General of Chariots and Cavalry,
he appointed Tán as Right Sīmǎ.
He was praised for his magnanimity
but died young,
without an heir.
Zhòu was skilled at writing prose.
Quán treated him with the courtesy due to a guest.
For military and national documents,
Quán often had him revise and polish them.
He also unfortunately died young.
When Quán became King of Wú,
he remembered past favors
and enfeoffed Yìn as Marquis of Dūtíng.
From a young age, he had integrity and principle,
and a handsome appearance.
At twenty, he married a princess.
At the age of thirty,
he began his career as Administrator of Dānyáng,
then moved to Wújùn and Kuàijī.
He was praised wherever he served.
In the first year of Tàiyuán (248 CE),
when Quán was seriously ill,
Yìn went to the capital
and was appointed Grand Herald,
receiving the testamentary edict along with Zhūgě Kè and others to assist in governance.
Upon Sūn Liàng's ascension,
he was promoted to General of the Guard.
Gē [Zhūgě Kè] was about to lead all his troops to attack Wèi.
Yìn [Téng Yìn] admonished Gē [Zhūgě Kè], saying:
“You, sir, in a time of dynastic transition,
received the trust of Yī [Yī Yǐn] and Huò [Huò Guāng].
Within the court, you stabilized the dynasty;
outside, you crushed strong enemies.
Your fame vibrated throughout the land,
and all under Heaven were shaken.
The hearts of the myriad people
hoped to receive your protection and find peace.
Now, you rashly, after the toils of labor,
raise an army to go on campaign.
The people are weary and their strength exhausted,
and the distant ruler is prepared.
If you attack a city and fail to take it,
and gain nothing from raiding the countryside,
this would be to lose previous achievements and invite future blame.
It is better to lay down arms, rest the army,
and move when an opportune moment appears.
Moreover, warfare is a great matter;
matters are accomplished with the multitude.
If the multitude is not pleased,
how can you, sir, be at peace alone?”
Gē [Zhūgě Kè] said:
“Those who say it cannot be done
are all those who do not see the calculations,
who cling to their homes and seek temporary peace.
And you, my son, also agree with them.
What hope do I have then?
Indeed, with Cáo Fāng being dim-witted and inferior,
and the government being in the hands of private families,
their ministers and people
already have disloyal hearts.
Now, I will rely on the resources of the state
and the prestige of victory in battle.
Then, what place can I go to and not conquer!”
He appointed Yìn [Téng Yìn] as Dūxià Dū [Inspector of the Capital Region],
in charge of overseeing affairs in the capital.
Yìn [Téng Yìn] received guests by day,
and reviewed documents by night,
sometimes staying awake all night.
Sūn Jùn, courtesy name Zǐyuǎn,
was the great-grandson of Sūn Jiān’s younger brother Jìng [Sūn Jìng].
Jìng [Sūn Jìng] begot Gǎo [Sūn Gǎo].
Gǎo [Sūn Gǎo] begot Gōng [Sūn Gōng],
who was a Sànqí Láng.
Gōng [Sūn Gōng] begot Jùn [Sūn Jùn].
From a young age, he was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and was decisive and courageous.
Towards the end of Sūn Quán’s reign,
he was promoted to Wǔwèi Dūwèi [Commander of the Palace Guard],
and served as Zhōngdūhù [Central Protector].
When Quán [Sūn Quán] was on his deathbed,
he received the dying emperor’s trust to assist in governing,
and was made Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn [General of the Palace Guard].
Thus, he was in charge of the imperial guard,
and enfeoffed as Dūxiāng Hóu [Marquis of Duxiang].
After executing Zhūgě Kè,
he was promoted to Chéngxiàng Dàjiāngjūn [Chancellor and Great General],
overseeing all military affairs within and outside the court,
granted a jié [imperial insignia],
and further enfeoffed as Fùchūn Hóu [Marquis of Fuchun].
Téng Yìn, on the grounds of being the father-in-law of Gē [Zhūgě Kè]’s son Sǒng [Zhūgě Sǒng]’s wife, resigned from his position.
Jùn [Sūn Jùn] said:
“The crimes of Gǔn [mythical figure] and Yǔ [legendary king] do not extend to each other.
Why does Marquis Téng [Téng Yìn] act thus?”
Although Jùn [Sūn Jùn] and Yìn [Téng Yìn] were not intimately close internally,
they outwardly tolerated each other.
Jùn [Sūn Jùn] elevated Yìn [Téng Yìn]’s rank to Gāomì Hóu [Marquis of Gaomi],
and they continued to work together as before.
Jùn [Sūn Jùn] originally had no great reputation,
was arrogant, dangerous, and harmful,
and executed many people,
causing the common people to complain.
He also committed adultery with palace women,
and had a private affair with Princess Lǔbān.
In the first year of Wǔfèng [254 CE],
Yīng [Sūn Yīng], the Marquis of Wú, plotted to kill Jùn [Sūn Jùn].
Yīng [Sūn Yīng]’s plot was exposed, and he died.
In the second year [255 CE],
the Wèi generals Wúqiū Jiǎn and Wén Qīn rebelled with their troops.
Jùn [Sūn Jùn], along with Piàojì Jiāngjūn [General of Agile Cavalry] Lǚ Jù and Zuǒ Jiāngjūn [General of the Left] Liú Zàn, attacked Shòuchūn.
They fought against the Wèi people at Yuèjiā.
However, Qīn [Wén Qīn] was defeated and surrendered,
and the army returned.
That year,
an envoy from Shǔ [Shǔ Hàn] came to offer tribute.
General Sūn Yí, [Zhāng Yí, Lín Xún] and others intended to use the gathering to kill Jùn [Sūn Jùn].
The plot was exposed,
and Yí [Sūn Yí] and others committed suicide.
Dozens of people died,
including Princess Lǔyù.
Jùn [Sūn Jùn] wanted to fortify Guǎnglíng.
The court officials knew it was impossible to fortify,
but fearing him, none dared to speak.
Only Téng Yìn advised against it,
but Jùn [Sūn Jùn] did not listen,
and the undertaking ultimately failed.
The following year,
Wén Qīn persuaded Jùn [Sūn Jùn] to campaign against Wèi.

Jùn [Sūn Jùn] ordered Qīn [Wén Qīn], along with Lǚ Jù, Chējì [Jiāngjūn] [General of Chariots] Liú Zuǎn, Zhènnán [Jiāngjūn] [General Who Guards the South] Zhū Yì, and Qián Jiāngjūn [General of the Vanguard] Táng Zī, to enter the Huái and Sì Rivers from Jiāngdū,
with the aim of capturing Qīng and Xú.
Jùn [Sūn Jùn] and Yìn [Téng Yìn] went to Shítou [Stone City].
During the farewell banquet,
Jùn [Sūn Jùn] led about a hundred followers into Jù [Lǚ Jù]’s camp.
Jù [Lǚ Jù]’s troops were well-ordered and disciplined.
Jùn [Sūn Jùn] disliked this,
claimed to have a stomach ache, and left.
He then dreamt that he was attacked by Zhūgě Kè.
Terrified, he fell ill and died,
at the age of thirty-eight,
entrusting the aftermath to Lín [Sūn Lín].
Sūn Lín, courtesy name Zǐtōng,
was of the same ancestry as Jùn [Sūn Jùn].
Lín [Sūn Lín]’s father, Chuò [Sūn Chuò], was Ānmín Dūwèi [Commander for Pacifying the People].
Lín [Sūn Lín] was initially Piān Jiāngjūn [Brigade General].
After Jùn [Sūn Jùn] died,
he became Zhōngdūhù Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn [Central Protector and General of the Palace Guard],
overseeing all military affairs within and outside the court,
and acted as the regent.
Lǚ Jù heard of this and was greatly alarmed.
He and the other commanders jointly signed a memorial,
recommending Téng Yìn as Chéngxiàng [Chancellor].
Lín [Sūn Lín] instead appointed Yìn [Téng Yìn] as Dàsīmǎ [Grand Marshal],
to replace Lǚ Dài stationed at Wǔchāng.
Jù [Lǚ Jù] led his troops back,
and sent someone to inform Yìn [Téng Yìn],
wishing to depose Lín [Sūn Lín] together.
When Lín [Sūn Lín] heard of this,
he dispatched his older cousin Lǜ [Sūn Lǜ] to lead troops to intercept Jù [Lǚ Jù] at Jiāngdū.
He sent imperial envoys to instruct Wén Qīn, Liú Zuǎn, Táng Zī, and others to gather their forces and attack Jù [Lǚ Jù].

He dispatched Zhōngdūhù Zuǒ Jiāngjūn [Central Protector and General of the Left] Huá Róng and Zhōngshū Chéng [Secretary of the Central Secretariat] Dīng Yàn to inform Yìn [Téng Yìn] about taking Jù [Lǚ Jù],
and clearly hinted that Yìn [Téng Yìn] should leave quickly.
Yìn [Téng Yìn] considered himself to be in trouble.
He then detained Róng [Huá Róng] and Yàn [Dīng Yàn],
mustered troops to defend himself,
and summoned Diǎnjūn [Officer in charge of Military Records] Yáng Chóng and Jiāngjūn [General] Sūn Zī.
He informed them that Lín [Sūn Lín] was causing unrest,
and compelled Róng [Huá Róng] and the others to write a letter criticizing Lín [Sūn Lín].
Lín [Sūn Lín] did not listen.
He presented a memorial stating that Yìn [Téng Yìn] had rebelled,
and promised General Liú Chéng with official titles and noble ranks,
ordering him to lead cavalry to quickly attack and besiege Yìn [Téng Yìn].
Yìn [Téng Yìn] again coerced Róng [Huá Róng] and others
to forge an imperial edict to raise troops.
Róng [Huá Róng] and others refused to comply,
so Yìn [Téng Yìn] killed them all.
Yìn [Téng Yìn]’s complexion did not change;
he talked and laughed as usual.
Some advised Yìn [Téng Yìn] to lead his troops to Cānglóngmén [Azure Dragon Gate],
saying that when the generals and soldiers saw the Duke [Yìn [Téng Yìn]] come out,
they would surely abandon Lín [Sūn Lín] and follow the Duke.
It was already past midnight.
Yìn [Téng Yìn] relied on his appointment with Jù [Lǚ Jù],
and also found it difficult to lead troops towards the palace.
So he made an agreement with his subordinates,
and said that Marquis Lǚ [Lǚ Jù] was nearby.
Therefore, they all were willing to die for Yìn [Téng Yìn],
and none dispersed.
At that time, there was a great wind.
By dawn,
Jù [Lǚ Jù] had not arrived.
Lín [Sūn Lín]’s army gathered in force,
and then killed Yìn [Téng Yìn] and dozens of generals and soldiers,
exterminating Yìn [Téng Yìn]’s three clans.
Lín [Sūn Lín] was promoted to Dàjiāngjūn [Great General],
granted a jié [imperial insignia],
enfeoffed as Yǒngníng Hóu [Marquis of Yongning].
He abused his high status and power,
and often behaved disrespectfully.
Initially,
Jùn [Sūn Jùn]’s cousin Lǜ [Sūn Lǜ] was involved in the plot to execute Zhūgě Kè.
Jùn [Sūn Jùn] treated him generously,
promoting him to Yòu Jiāngjūn [General of the Right] and Wúnán Dū [Commander of the Dauntless Troops],
granting him a jié and gài [insignia and ceremonial umbrella],
and placing him in charge of the affairs of the nine ministries.
Lín [Sūn Lín] treated Lǜ [Sūn Lǜ] less favorably than Jùn [Sūn Jùn] had.
Lǜ [Sūn Lǜ] was angered,
and plotted with General Wáng Dūn to kill Lín [Sūn Lín].
Lín [Sūn Lín] killed Dūn [Wáng Dūn],
and Lǜ [Sūn Lǜ] died by taking poison.
The Grand General of Wèi, Zhūgě Dàn, rebelled in Shòuchūn,
and held the city, offering to surrender.
Wú dispatched Wén Qīn, Táng Zī, Quán Duān, Quán Yì, and others leading thirty thousand men to rescue him.
The General Who Guards the South of Wèi, Wáng Jī, besieged Dàn.
Qīn and the others broke through the siege and entered the city.
Wèi deployed over two hundred thousand of its central and regional armies to reinforce the siege of Dàn.
Zhū Yì led thirty thousand men to garrison Ānfēng City,
to support Wén Qīn.
The Inspector of Yǎnzhōu of Wèi, Zhōu Tài, resisted Yì at Yángyuān.
Yì was defeated and retreated,
pursued by Tài,
suffering two thousand dead or wounded.
Chén thereupon raised a large army and garrisoned Huòlǐ.
He again sent Yì to lead Generals Dīng Fèng, Lí Fěi, and others with fifty thousand men to attack Wèi,
leaving the baggage train at Dūlù.
Yì garrisoned Líjiāng,
and sent Generals Rèn Dù, Zhāng Zhèn, and others to recruit six thousand brave men,
to build a pontoon bridge six *lǐ* west of the camp and cross by night,
and to construct a crescent-shaped fort.
They were defeated by the Supervising Imperial Secretary of Wèi, Shí Bāo, and Zhōu Tài.
The army retreated to higher ground.
Yì again built a palisade of wagons to advance towards Wǔmùchéng.
Bāo and Tài attacked Yì.
Yì was defeated and returned.
Meanwhile, Hú Liè, the Administrator of Tàishān of Wèi, with five thousand elite troops, secretly attacked Dūlù by an unexpected route,
and burned all of Yì's supplies.
Chén gave Yì thirty thousand troops and ordered him to fight to the death.
Yì refused to obey.
Chén beheaded him at Huòlǐ,
and then sent his brother Ēn to rescue [Zhūgě Dàn].
Coincidentally, Dàn was defeated, and Ēn returned.
Chén was unable to relieve Dàn,
and lost many officers and men,
and even executed a famous general.
No one did not resent him for this.
Chén became greatly afraid
when Sūn Liàng began to personally manage state affairs
and asked many difficult questions.
He returned to Jiànyè,
claimed illness and did not attend court,
and built a residence south of Zhūquèqiáo.
He sent his brother, General Wēiyuǎn Jù, to enter Cānglóng for palace guard duty,
and his brothers, General Wǔwèi Ēn, General Piān Jiāngjūn Gān, and Commandant of Chángshuǐ Kǎi, to be separately stationed in various camps,
intending to monopolize court power and secure himself.
Liàng harbored suspicion towards Chén.
He then investigated the full details of Rúyù's murder,
and reprimanded Zhū Xióng, the Overseer of Húlín, and Xióng's brother, Zhū Sǔn, the Overseer of the Outer Regions, for not rectifying Sūn Jùn.
He then ordered Dīng Fèng to kill Xióng at Húlín,
and Sǔn at Jiànyè.
Chén entered to remonstrate, but was not heeded.
Liàng then conspired with Princess Lǔbān, Grand Astrologer Quán Shàng, and General Liú Chéng to execute Chén.
Liàng,
Chén's cousin's daughter,
informed Chén of the plot.
Chén led his forces to attack Quán Shàng by night,
and sent his brother Ēn to kill Liú Chéng outside Cānglóngmén.
He then surrounded the palace.
He ordered the Grand Master of Remonstrance, Mèng Zōng, to report to the ancestral temple and depose Liàng,
and summoned the officials to deliberate, saying:
"The Young Emperor is delirious, ill, confused, and chaotic,
and cannot occupy the great position
or succeed the ancestral temple.
We shall report this to the former emperors and depose him.
If any of you gentlemen disagree,
state your differing opinion."
All were terrified and said:
"We obey the General's command."
Chén sent the Palace Secretary Lǐ Chóng to seize Liàng's imperial seal and ribbons,
and announced Liàng's crimes to all far and near.
The Minister of Personnel Huán Yí refused to sign,
so Chén angrily killed him.
The Army Supervisor Shī Zhèng advised Chén to summon and enthrone the Prince of Lángxié, Xiū.
Chén agreed to this,
and sent the Imperial Clan Court Administrator Kǎi with a letter to Xiū, saying:
"Though I, Chén, possess meager talent,
I was entrusted with great responsibility.
I have been unable to assist and guide His Majesty.
In recent months,
he has undertaken many constructions,
befriended Liú Chéng,
indulged in beautiful women,
called forth female officials and commoners,
selected the comeliest among them,
and kept them in the palace.
He took over three thousand sons of soldiers, eighteen years and younger,
and trained them in the imperial park,
day and night continuously,
causing great lamentation.
He ruined over five thousand spears and halberds from the treasury
to make playthings.
Zhū Jù was a loyal minister of the late emperor.
His sons Xióng and Sǔn both inherited their father's foundation
and established themselves with loyalty and righteousness.
The murder of the young princess in the past
was initiated by the empress dowager herself.
The Emperor did not thoroughly investigate the matter's origin,
but immediately killed Xióng and Sǔn.
Remonstrance was not heeded,
and all below hold their breath in fear.
The Emperor built over three hundred small boats in the palace,
adorned with gold and silver,
with artisans working day and night without rest.
Grand Astrologer Quán Shàng,
whose family has received imperial favor for generations,
failed to supervise his imperial relatives,
leading to Quán Duān and others abandoning the city and defecting to Wèi.
Shàng's position is overly weighty,
yet he has never offered a single word of remonstrance to Your Majesty.
Instead, he communicates with the enemy,
allowing news of the state to be transmitted,
which will surely endanger the state.
According to ancient precedents,
the mandate has fallen upon Your Highness.
Therefore, on the twenty-seventh day of this month, we captured Shàng and executed Chéng.
We have made the Emperor the Prince of Kuàijī.
We send Kǎi to respectfully welcome you.
All the officials crane their necks,
standing by the roadside."
Chén sent General Sūn Dān to escort Liàng to his principality,
relocated Shàng to Línglíng,
and moved the Princess to Yùzhāng.
Chén's ambition swelled,
and he insulted both men and gods.
He then burned the Wǔ Zǐxū Temple at the Dàqiáo bridgehead,
and also destroyed Buddhist temples,
beheading the Daoist priests.
When Xiū was enthroned,
he referred to himself as a humble subject from the wilderness
and submitted a memorial to the court, saying:
"I humbly reflect upon myself:
my talent is insufficient for governing the state.
Due to my familial ties,
my position has become that of a supreme minister,
harming the state and damaging the imperial carriage.
My crimes and faults are manifest.
Reflecting on my errors and shortcomings,
I am anxious day and night.
I have heard that Heaven's mandate assists the sincere
and invariably goes to the virtuous.
Thus, when Yōu and Lì lost their proper conduct,
Zhōu Xuān brought about a restoration.
Your Majesty possesses sacred virtue
and inherits the great legacy.
You ought to have excellent assistants
to achieve harmony and prosperity.
Even in the prosperity of Yáo,
he still sought the assistance of Jì and Xiè
to complement his sagely virtue.
The ancients said: 'If one has the ability, take up a position;
if not, desist.'
Although I have exerted myself to the utmost,
it has been of no benefit to the various state affairs.
I respectfully present my seals, tallies, and axes,
and retire to my fields and home
to make way for the worthy."
Xiū granted him an audience and offered words of comfort.
He also issued an edict saying:
"I, being without virtue,
guarded the border abroad.
In this critical juncture,
the various dukes and ministers,
together with myself,
have served the ancestral temple.
I am therefore distressed,
as if treading on thin ice.
The Grand General's loyal strategy arose from within,
supporting the endangered and steadying the tottering,
bringing peace and prosperity to the state.
His achievements are glorious.
In the past, when Emperor Xiàoxuān of Hàn ascended the throne,
Huò Guāng was greatly honored.
Rewarding virtue and merits
is a universal principle throughout antiquity and today.
Let the Grand General be appointed Chancellor and Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
with an income from five counties."
Ēn was made Grandee Secretary and General of the Guards.
Jù was made General of the Right.
Both were enfeoffed as marquises of counties.
Gān was made a General of Assorted Titles and Marquis of a Pavilion.
Kǎi was also enfeoffed as Marquis of a Pavilion.
Chén's family had five marquises,
all commanding the imperial guards.
Their power overshadowed the sovereign,
something unprecedented among the court officials of Wú.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) brought offerings of ox and wine to Sūn Xiū (孫休).
Sūn Xiū (孫休) refused them.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) then brought them to Zhāng Bù (張布), the General of the Left.
In the midst of their drinking,
Sūn Lín (孫綝) uttered words of resentment, saying:
"When the young lord was first deposed,
many advised me to take the throne myself.
I welcomed His Majesty
because I considered him wise and brilliant.
The Emperor would not have been established without me,
but now, when I pay my respects, I am refused,
which makes me no different from any ordinary minister.
I should plan something else."
Zhāng Bù (張布) reported these words to Sūn Xiū (孫休).
Sūn Xiū (孫休) resented it,
fearing that Sūn Lín (孫綝) might cause trouble.
He frequently bestowed rewards upon him,
and further granted him the favor of Attendant-in-ordinary,
sharing the review of documents with Sūn Lín (孫綝).
Someone accused Sūn Lín (孫綝) of harboring resentment, insulting the emperor, and intending to rebel.
Sūn Xiū (孫休) seized the accuser and handed him over to Sūn Lín (孫綝).
Sūn Lín (孫綝) killed him.
Because of this, Sūn Lín (孫綝) became even more fearful.
Through Mèng Zōng (孟宗), he requested to be sent out to garrison Wǔchāng (武昌).
Sūn Xiū (孫休) agreed.
He ordered all of the over ten thousand elite soldiers of the Central Camp under Sūn Lín's (孫綝) command
to pack up,
and all the weapons taken from the armory
to be given to them.
General Wèi Miǎo (魏邈) advised Sūn Xiū (孫休), saying,
"Sūn Lín (孫綝) will surely cause trouble when he is outside."
The Wǔwèi (武衛) officer Shī Shuò (施朔) also reported,
"Sūn Lín (孫綝) intends to rebel; there are signs."
Sūn Xiū (孫休) secretly consulted Zhāng Bù (張布).
Zhāng Bù (張布) and Dīng Fèng (丁奉) plotted to kill Sūn Lín (孫綝) at the assembly.
In the twelfth month, on the Dīngmǎo (丁卯) day of the first year of Yǒng'ān (永安) (258 CE),
a rumor spread in Jiànyè (建業) that there would be trouble at the assembly.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) heard of it
and was displeased.
That night, a strong wind uprooted trees and stirred up sand.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) became even more frightened.
On the Wùchén (戊辰) day, the winter sacrifice assembly was held.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) claimed illness.
Sūn Xiū (孫休) forcefully summoned him,
sending more than ten envoys.
Sūn Lín (孫綝), having no choice,
prepared to enter,
but his followers stopped him.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) said,
"The state has repeatedly issued commands;
I cannot refuse.
You can prepare the troops
and set a fire inside the residence.
This way, I can quickly return."
He then entered.
Soon after, a fire broke out.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) requested to leave.
Sūn Xiū (孫休) said,
"There are plenty of outside troops;
there is no need to trouble the Chancellor."
Sūn Lín (孫綝) rose from his seat.
Dīng Fèng (丁奉) and Zhāng Bù (張布) gestured to their attendants to bind him.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) kowtowed and said,
"I beg to be exiled to Jiāozhōu (交州)."
Sūn Xiū (孫休) said,
"Why did you not exile Téng Yìn (滕胤) and Lǚ Jù (呂據)?"
Sūn Lín (孫綝) again said,
"I beg to be made a government slave."
Sūn Xiū (孫休) said,
"Why did you not make Téng Yìn (滕胤) and Lǚ Jù (呂據) slaves!"
He then beheaded him.
He showed Sūn Lín's (孫綝) head to his followers and said,
"All who conspired with Sūn Lín (孫綝) are pardoned."
Five thousand people laid down their weapons.
Sūn Kǎi (孫闓) took a boat, intending to surrender to the north,
but he was pursued and killed.
His three clans were exterminated.
Sūn Jùn's (孫峻) coffin was unearthed,
his seals and ribbons were taken,
his wooden coffin was chopped up and buried,
because he had killed Lǔ Yù (魯育) and others.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) was twenty-eight years old when he died.
Sūn Xiū (孫休) was ashamed to be of the same clan as Sūn Jùn (孫峻) and Sūn Lín (孫Lín).
He specifically removed them from the clan register,
referring to them as "the late Sūn Jùn (孫峻)" and "the late Sūn Lín (孫Lín)".
Sūn Xiū (孫休) also issued an edict saying:
"Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪), Téng Yìn (滕胤), and Lǚ Jù (呂據) were cruelly harmed by Sūn Jùn (孫峻) and Sūn Lín (孫Lín), brothers, without cause.
This is truly heartbreaking.
They should all be promptly reburied,
and memorial rites held for each of them.
Those who were implicated in Zhūgě Kè's (諸葛恪) and others' affairs and exiled to distant places
are all to be recalled."
Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興), courtesy name Zǐyuán (子元),
was a native of Chénliú (陳留).
His father, Púyáng Yì (濮陽逸),
fled to Jiāngdōng (江東) during the chaos at the end of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
and served as Administrator of Chángshā (長沙).
Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) had a reputation as a scholar in his youth.
During Sūn Quán's (孫權) time, he was appointed Magistrate of Shàngyú (上虞),
gradually rising to the position of Left Registrar of the Ministry of Personnel.
He was sent to Shǔ (蜀) as Colonel of the Five Offices,
and returned to become Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽).
At that time, Wáng Xiū (王休), Prince of Lángxié (琅邪), resided in Kuàijī (會稽),
and Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) formed a deep bond with him.
When Sūn Xiū (孫休) ascended the throne,
he summoned Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) to be Grand Minister of Ceremonies, General of the Guards, and to oversee military and state affairs,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Wàihuáng (外黃).
In the third year of Yǒng'ān (永安) (260 CE),
Commandant Yán Mì (嚴密) proposed developing Dānyáng (丹楊) lake fields
and constructing the Pǔlǐ (浦里) embankment.
An imperial edict commanded all officials to convene for a discussion.
All believed that it would require much labor and the fields would not be guaranteed to yield results,
but Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) alone thought it could be accomplished.
Consequently, all soldiers and common people were gathered to work.
The cost of labor was countless.
Soldiers died,
some even killed themselves,
and the common people greatly resented it.
Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) was promoted to Chancellor.
He colluded with Sūn Xiū's (孫休) favored minister, Zhāng Bù (張布), General of the Left,
leading to widespread disappointment in the country.
In the seventh month of the seventh year (264 CE),
Sūn Xiū (孫休) died.
Wàn Yù (萬彧), Left Commander of the Palace Army, had always been on good terms with Sūn Hào (孫晧), Marquis of Wūchéng (烏程).
He then persuaded Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) and Zhāng Bù (張布).
Consequently, Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) and Zhāng Bù (張布) deposed Sūn Xiū's (孫休) legitimate son and welcomed Sūn Hào (孫晧) to the throne.
After Sūn Hào (孫晧) ascended,
he added Attendant-in-ordinary to Púyáng Xīng's (濮陽興) titles
and made him Governor of Qīngzhōu (青州).
Soon after, Wàn Yù (萬彧) slandered Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) and Zhāng Bù (張布), saying they regretted their previous actions.
On the first day of the eleventh month, when they entered court,
Sūn Hào (孫晧) accordingly arrested Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) and Zhāng Bù (張布),
exiled them to Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
and had them pursued and killed on the way,
exterminating their three clans.
A critique states: Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪)'s talent, vigor, and strategic acumen
were praised by the people of the state.
However, he was arrogant and stingy.
Even the Duke of Zhōu (周公) faced criticism;
how much more so Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪)?
Being conceited and disdainful of others, how could he avoid failure!
If he had personally acted upon the advice in the letters he sent to Lù Xùn (陸遜) and his younger brother Róng (融),
then regret and misfortune would not have befallen him.
What disaster could there have been?
Téng Yìn (滕胤) assiduously cultivated a gentleman's integrity
and followed proper rules.
Yet, during Sūn Jùn's (孫峻) time, he still maintained his high position.
It was an inevitable reason for danger.
Sūn Jùn (孫峻) and Sūn Lín (孫Lín) were vicious rascals who overflowed with evil,
truly not worth discussing.
Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) held the position of Chancellor,
but his considerations were not for the state.
He colluded with the wickedness of Zhāng Bù (張布)
and accepted Wàn Yù's (萬彧) counsel.
His execution and the extermination of his clans were appropriate.
The Biography of Wáng Fān (王蕃), Lóu Hè (樓賀), and Wèi Huá (韋華), Chapter Twenty.
Wáng Fān (王蕃), courtesy name Yǒngyuán (永元),
was a native of Lújiāng (廬江).
He was widely read and knowledgeable,
and also proficient in various arts and skills.
He initially served as a Minister of Personnel,
but left office.
When Sūn Xiū (孫休) ascended the throne,
he, along with Hè Shào (賀邵), Xuē Yíng (薛瑩), and Yú Sì (虞汜), all became Cavalier Attendants-in-ordinary,
and were all granted the title of Commandant of Cavalry.
The public opinion at the time considered them upright.
He was sent as an envoy to Shǔ (蜀),
and the people of Shǔ (蜀) praised him.
Upon his return, he became Inspector of Xiàkǒu (夏口).
In the early reign of Sūn Hào (孫晧),
he again entered court as Attendant-in-ordinary,
holding the same office as Wàn Yù (萬彧).
Wàn Yù (萬彧) had a long-standing relationship with Sūn Hào (孫晧).
Being a commoner, he wielded his influence to disparage others,
claiming Wáng Fān (王蕃) treated him lightly.
Furthermore, Chén Shēng (陳聲), Central Secretary and Sūn Hào's (孫晧) favored minister,
frequently slandered and disparaged Wáng Fān (王蕃).
Wáng Fān (王蕃) had a noble and bright disposition
and could not cater to Sūn Hào's (孫晧) whims or follow his directives.
At times, he would contradict his wishes,
and thus accumulated blame.
In the second year of Gānlù (甘露) (276 CE),
Dīng Zhōng (丁忠) returned from his mission to Jìn (晉).
Sūn Hào (孫晧) held a grand banquet for all his ministers.
Wáng Fān (王蕃) was heavily intoxicated and prostrated himself.
Sūn Hào (孫晧) was suspicious and displeased,
so he had Wáng Fān (王蕃) carried out.
After a while, Wáng Fān (王蕃) requested to return,
but his drunkenness had not subsided.
Wáng Fān (王蕃) possessed a dignified and awe-inspiring nature;
his conduct was composed and unperturbed.
Sūn Hào (孫晧) became furious
and ordered his attendants to behead him below the hall.
General of the Guards Téng Mù (滕牧) and General Who Conquers the West Liú Píng (留平) pleaded for him,
but could not succeed.
Chancellor Lù Kǎi (陸凱) submitted a memorial, saying:
“The Palace Attendant Wáng Fán (王蕃) possessed profound wisdom and clear reasoning.
He understood Heaven and objects,
and was loyal and upright in court.
He was a weighty pillar of the state
and a Lóng Fēng (龍逢) of Great Wú (吳).
Formerly serving Emperor Jǐng (景),
he offered counsel by his side.
Emperor Jǐng (景) admired and praised him,
lamenting that he was an extraordinary talent.
Yet Your Majesty resented his harsh words,
detested his straightforward responses,
executed him in the palace hall,
and left his body exposed.
The people in the commandery were heartbroken,
and all who knew him grieved. ”
Such was his sorrow for Fán (蕃).
Fán (蕃) was thirty-nine years old when he died.
Hào (晧) moved Fán’s (蕃) family to Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
His two younger brothers, Zhù (著) and Yán (延), were both excellent talents.
When Guō Mǎ (郭馬) rebelled,
they refused to serve Mǎ (馬)
and were killed.
Lóu Xuán (樓玄), courtesy name Chéngxiān (承先),
was a native of Qí (蘄) in Péi Jùn (沛郡).
During Sūn Xiū's (孫休) reign, he served as Inspector of Agriculture.
When Sūn Hào (孫晧) ascended the throne,
he, Wáng Fán (王蕃), Guō Zhuō (郭逴), and Wàn Yù (萬彧) all became Palace Attendants.
He was later sent out as Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽),
and then recalled to serve as Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Previously, the palace secretariat staff were chosen by those in charge from among their close associates.
Yù (彧) argued that for such close and confidential positions,
good people should be employed.
Hào (晧) then ordered the relevant officials
to seek out loyal and upright scholars
to fill these positions.
Consequently, Xuán (玄) was appointed Palace Attendant and Commander of the Palace Guard
to oversee palace affairs.
Xuán (玄), as one of the Nine Ministers, carried a sword and stood guard.
He maintained his integrity, led his subordinates,
and acted in accordance with the law.
His responses were sharp and direct,
often contradicting Hào's (晧) wishes,
and he gradually incurred his displeasure and anger.
Later, someone falsely accused Xuán (玄) of meeting Hè Shào (賀邵),
stopping to whisper and laugh loudly together,
slandering political affairs.
He was subsequently summoned for questioning,
and sent to Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Huá Hé (華覈), the Director of the Eastern Archive, submitted a memorial, saying:
“I humbly submit that governing a state
is like managing a household.
Those who manage the fields and wilderness
should all be good and trustworthy.
Furthermore, it is essential to have one person to oversee all the details
and establish the main framework;
only then will all matters be well-ordered.
The Analects say: ‘Was it not Shùn (舜) who governed without effort?
