He merely sat reverently facing south.’
This means that when the right people are entrusted,
one can be at ease and relaxed.
Currently, the realm is unsettled,
and there are many affairs of state.
Matters, large and small,
all must be reported and heard,
frequently brought before Your Majesty,
taxing your sagely thoughts.
Your Majesty has shown interest in ancient studies,
and mastered the arts and literature,
furthermore, you diligently pursue the Way,
adapting your spirit to each season.
It is fitting that you should enjoy peace and quiet to fully develop your divine thoughts,
breathing in the pure and clear,
and reaching the same ultimate state as Heaven.
I have contemplated day and night,
and among all the officials,
in terms of administrative ability,
there is no one more trustworthy
than Lóu Xuán (樓玄).
Xuán (玄) is pure and loyal in public service,
preeminent in his generation.
All admire his integrity,
and none can surpass him.
Indeed, a pure person has a balanced mind and upright intentions,
and a loyal person always follows the righteous path.
Such is Xuán's (玄) nature,
which can be relied upon from beginning to end.
I beg Your Majesty to pardon Xuán's (玄) past faults,
allow him to reform,
promote him to a high ministerial position,
and hold him accountable for his future performance,
allowing him to select personnel for the government,
and assign duties according to talent.
Then Shùn's (舜) effortless governance
can almost be achieved. ”
Hào (晧) resented Xuán's (玄) reputation,
and again exiled Xuán (玄) and his son Jù (據),
entrusting them to Zhāng Yì (張奕), the General of Jiāozhǐ (交阯),
to make them prove themselves in battle,
while secretly ordering Yì (奕) to kill them.
Jù (據) died of illness upon reaching Jiāozhǐ (交阯).
Xuán (玄) himself followed Yì (奕) in suppressing the rebels,
carrying a sword and traveling on foot.
Whenever he saw Yì (奕), he bowed.
Yì (奕) could not bring himself to kill him.
When Yì (奕) suddenly died,
Xuán (玄) was preparing Yì's (奕) coffin
and found the imperial edict in a container.
He then committed suicide.
Hè Shào (賀邵), courtesy name Xīngbó (興伯),
was a native of Shānyīn (山陰), Kuàijī (會稽).
When Sūn Xiū (孫休) ascended the throne,
he was promoted from Cavalier Regular Attendant to Palace Attendant,
and then sent out as Administrator of Wújùn (吳郡).
During Sūn Hào's (孫晧) reign,
he was recalled to serve as Left General of the Army,
then promoted to Prefect of the Central Secretariat,
and concurrently Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
Hào (晧) was brutal and arrogant,
and the government deteriorated daily.
Shào (邵) submitted a memorial of remonstrance, saying:
“The sagely kings of old,
though dwelling deep within the secluded palace, understood affairs a thousand miles away,
and though sitting with folded hands on their sleeping mats,
their brilliance illuminated the eight extremes of the world.
This was due to their ability to employ worthy men.
Your Majesty, with your supreme virtue and noble bearing,
has inherited the imperial enterprise.
It is fitting that you should personally embody the Dao,
reverently uphold the sacred implements,
and commend the worthy and praise the good
to stabilize the various
governmental affairs.
However, in recent years,
the court ranks have been in disarray,
the genuine and false intermingled,
superiors and subordinates appointed without discernment,
and civil and military positions left vacant.
Externally, there are no weighty pillars like mountains,
and internally, there are no officials
to pick up forgotten advice.
Flatterers soar like birds with flapping wings,
meddling with imperial authority,
and pilfering honors and benefits,
while the loyal and good are cast aside,
and trustworthy ministers are harmed.
Consequently, upright scholars
are broken,
while mediocre officials merely flatter,
anticipating intentions and yielding to decrees,
each hoping to seize the opportune moment.
People hold opinions contrary to reason,
and scholars voice perverse theories,
thus causing the clear stream to become turbid,
and loyal ministers to be silenced.
Your Majesty resides above the nine heavens,
hidden within a hundred-layered chamber.
Your words spread like wind,
your commands are followed like shadows.
Surrounded by favored and flattering ministers,
you hear only
agreeable words daily.
You will likely believe that these people are truly worthy
and that the world is already at peace.
What troubles my heart,
how can I not make it known?
I have heard that the rulers who build states delight in hearing their faults,
while chaotic and unruly rulers delight in hearing their praises.
Those who hear their faults see their faults diminish daily and blessings arrive,
while those who hear their praises
see their praises diminish daily and disaster befalls them.
Therefore, ancient rulers
bowed to advance the worthy,
and humbled themselves to seek out faults.
They likened the imperial position to riding a runaway horse,
and considered the tiger's tail as a warning
and caution.
As for Your Majesty,
you enforce strict laws to prohibit candid words,
and dismiss good scholars to obstruct remonstrating ministers,
obscuring the truth of praise and blame,
and burying the words of close favorites.
Formerly,
Gāo Zōng (高宗) sought assistance,
and in a dream found a worthy man.
But Your Majesty seeks them as if forgotten,
and neglects them as if lost.
Hence, the former Palace Attendant Wáng Fán (王蕃), loyal and diligent in public service,
with talent for assistance and governance,
was subjected to great punishment merely for being drunk.
Recently, the Grand Usher Gě Xī (葛奚),
an old minister of the former emperor,
merely spoke some contradictory and
drunken words.
After three cups of wine,
the etiquette
what is not to be feared.
Your Majesty suddenly flared with rage
and called it disrespectful.
Drinking pure wine,
they were poisoned and lost their lives.
From then on,
hearts throughout the realm grieved,
and court officials lost
their way.
Those in office considered retirement a blessing,
and those in residence saw going out as good fortune.
This is truly not how to preserve the grand foundation
and promote flourishing governance.
Moreover, why is Hé Dìng (何定) a petty person who curries favor,
inferior to a servant,
who has no virtue to speak of,
and no use beyond that of a hawk or dog,
yet Your Majesty dotes on his flattery
and lends him your authority?
This allows Dìng (定) to presume upon favor and be unrestrained,
monopolizing power and rewards,
correcting state discussions by mouth,
and manipulating divine mechanisms with his hands,
thereby diminishing the brilliance of the sun and moon above,
and obstructing the path of gentlemen
below.
Indeed, when petty persons seek advancement,
they invariably introduce treacherous benefits.
Dìng (定) idly and rashly initiated a project:
he dispatched border soldiers to drive deer,
set nets in mountains and hills,
cleared away forests
and thickets,
exhausting all the beasts of the nine wilds
and gathering them within a heavy encirclement.
Above, it yields no timely benefit;
below, it incurs expenditure and waste.
Moreover, soldiers are exhausted by transport,
manpower is depleted by driving,
the old and weak suffer from hunger and cold,
and all, great and small, lament.
Your servant secretly observes celestial phenomena:
since recent years, Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽) have been in disarray,
the four seasons have been out of order,
there have been solar eclipses and earthquakes,
and frost has fallen in midsummer.
Referring to the classics,
all these are caused by Yīn (陰) energy overriding Yáng (陽),
and petty persons manipulating power.
Your servant has often read historical records
and verified them
with current events;
the correlation between disasters and auspicious signs
makes me shiver with cold.
In the past, Gāo Zōng (高宗) cultivated himself to dispel the abnormality of the pheasant in the tripod,
and Sòng Jǐng Gōng (宋景公) promoted virtue to avert the change of the Mars planet.
May
Your Majesty, above, fear the reprimands of August Heaven's warnings,
and below, follow the path of the two rulers in averting disaster.
Look far back at the achievements of past generations in appointing the worthy,
and awaken to the mistakes of today's misguided appointments.
Cleanse the court positions,
honor the talented,
dismiss sycophants and villains,
and curb treacherous power.
People of this sort
should not be employed again.
Broadly extend invitations to those long overlooked,
accept frank counsel,
reverently receive Heaven's guidance,
and respectfully uphold the ancestral legacy.
Then the great transformation will spread brightly,
and the hopes of Heaven and man will be fulfilled.
The Analects say:
“When a state prospers,
it regards its people as infants;
when it perishes,
it treats its people as grass and weeds.”
Your Majesty, in the past, concealed your divine brilliance
and hidden virtue in the Eastern Xià (夏).
With your sagely and wise talents,
you ascended to the throne in accordance with Heaven's will.
The four seas stretched their necks in anticipation,
and the eight directions wiped their eyes,
expecting the governance of Chéng (成) and Kāng (康) to flourish at any moment.
Since ascending the throne,
laws and prohibitions have become increasingly harsh,
and taxes and levies more burdensome.
Eunuchs in the palace
are distributed to various prefectures,
arbitrarily initiating projects
and competing to create treacherous gains.
The common people suffer the hardship of the loom,
and the masses are exhausted by endless demands.
The old and young suffer from hunger and cold,
and every household has a starving appearance.
Yet local magistrates,
pressured by fear of culpability,
enforce severe laws and harsh penalties,
tormenting the people to meet quotas.
Consequently, manpower cannot endure,
households are scattered,
and sounds of lamentation
disturb the harmonious atmosphere.
Furthermore, border soldiers along the river,
who should primarily expand territory and borders,
and secondarily
guard the frontier and prepare for difficulties,
ought to be especially well-cared for,
to await the time of need.
However, they are subjected to conscriptions and levies
that come thick and fast,
leaving them without complete coarse garments,
and insufficient food for morning and evening.
Outwardly, they face the hardship of battle;
inwardly, they harbor the sorrow of destitution.
Therefore, fathers and sons abandon each other,
and rebels form lines.
May Your Majesty lighten taxes and abolish vexations,
relieve and assist the poor
and needy,
reduce all non-essential matters,
and abolish restrictive laws.
Then the realm will enjoy their work,
and great governance will universally prevail.
Indeed, the people are the foundation of the state,
and food is the life of the people.
Now the state
has no year's worth of reserves,
and households have no month's worth of provisions.
Yet within the inner palace, more than ten thousand people sit idly and consume.
Internally, there are grievances of separation and emptiness;
externally, there are expenses
of waste.
This leaves granaries empty from disuse,
and soldiers and commoners starving on dregs and husks.
Moreover, the northern enemy watches,
observing the state's rise and fall.
Your Majesty does not rely on your own prestige and virtue,
but on the enemy's not coming;
you disregard the distress and impoverishment of the four seas,
and underestimate
the barbarians as not being a threat.
This is truly not the essential point of a long-term strategy for victory.
In the past, the Great Emperor (Dà Huángdì) toiled with body and mind,
established his foundation in the Southern Xià (夏),
occupied the land along the Jiāngshān (江山),
and expanded territory for ten thousand
lǐ (里).
Although supported by Heaven,
it was truly through human effort.
His remaining good fortune and legacy
have reached Your Majesty.
Your Majesty should strive to enhance your virtuous character
to glorify previous achievements,
love the people and nurture
scholars,
and preserve the ancestral path.
How can you disregard the diligent achievements of your illustrious ancestors,
treat lightly this hard-won great enterprise,
forget the decline of the realm,
and neglect the huge changes of rise and fall?
Your servant has heard that prosperity and adversity are not constant;
good and ill fortune depend on human actions.
The barrier of the long river cannot be relied upon forever.
If we do not guard it,
a single reed boat can cross it.
In the past, Qín (秦) established the title of Emperor,
and occupied the strongholds of Xiáo (殽) and Hán (函).
However, its virtuous governance was not cultivated,
and its laws and policies were harsh and cruel,
poisoning the living people.
Loyal ministers remained silent,
which is why one man's great cry
overthrew the state.
Recently, the Liú (劉) clan occupied the dangers of the three passes
and guarded the solidity of the mighty mountains.
It could be called a golden city and stone chamber,
a legacy for ten thousand generations.
But due to appointing the unworthy,
it was lost in a single morning.
Rulers and ministers
were led by the neck,
all becoming captives.
This is a clear mirror for our generation,
a stark warning before our eyes.
May Your Majesty look far back at past events,
and observe recent changes in the world.
Strengthen the foundation
and root,
curtail personal desires and follow the Dào (道).
Then the governance of Chéng (成) and Kāng (康) will flourish,
and the lineage of the sagely ancestors will be glorious.
When the memorial was presented,
Sūn Hào deeply resented it.
Shào Fènggōng was upright and honest,
feared by those close to the emperor.
They then together slandered Shào and Lóu Xuán, accusing them of slandering and destroying affairs of state.
Both were interrogated and reprimanded.
Lóu Xuán was sent to Nánzhōu,
while Shào was reinstated to his original post.
Later, Shào suffered a stroke (evil wind),
losing the ability to speak.
After several months out of office,
Sūn Hào suspected him of feigning illness.
He was arrested and imprisoned in the wine cellar,
and tortured over a thousand times.
Shào never uttered a single word,
and was ultimately put to death.
His family was exiled to Línhǎi.
An imperial edict was also issued to execute Lóu Xuán’s descendants.
This was the first year of Tiāncè,
and Shào was forty-nine years old.
Wéi Yào, courtesy name Hóngsì,
was a native of Yúnyáng, Wú Jùn.
In his youth, he loved learning
and was skilled at writing.
He began as an assistant to the Chancellor,
then was appointed Magistrate of Xī'ān.
Returning, he became a Gentleman of the Secretariat,
and was promoted to Chief Chamberlain to the Crown Prince.
At that time, Cài Yǐng was also in the Eastern Palace.
He was fond of board games.
Crown Prince Hé, considering it useless,
ordered Wéi Yào to compose an essay on the matter.
His discourse stated: I have heard that gentlemen are ashamed if their achievements are not established in their prime,
and vexed if their names are not recognized after their death.
Thus, it is said, "Study as if you cannot reach your goal,
still fearing you might lose it."
Therefore,
the ambitious scholars of old
lamented the swift passage of years and feared their names would not be established.
Thus, they exerted their minds and refined their conduct,
rising at dawn and sleeping late,
without time for rest.
They measured it by
years and months,
and accumulated it day by day,
like Níng Yuè’s diligence
and Dǒng Shēng’s earnestness,
soaking in the abyss of virtue and righteousness,
and dwelling in the realm of the Dao and arts.
Moreover, with the sagacity of
King Wén of Zhōu (Xībó)
and the talent of the Duke of Zhōu (Jī Gōng),
they still toiled from dusk till dawn.
Thus, they were able to flourish and revive the Zhōu Dao,
leaving a name for myriad generations.
How much more so for subjects and commoners;
how could they
give up?
Looking through history, all those who established meritorious deeds and famous names
had records of extraordinary accumulation,
toiling with their bodies and enduring hardships,
diligently pondering with perseverance.
In times of peace, they did not abandon their work;
in poverty and distress, they did not change their principles.
Thus, Bǔ Shì established his aspirations in farming and herding,
and Huáng Bà received instruction in prison.
Ultimately, they attained the blessings of glory and prominence,
thereby achieving immortal
fame.
Thus, Shān Fǔ was diligent morning and night,
and Wú Hàn never left public service.
How could they have been idle?
Today's people mostly do not apply themselves to classical studies,
but enjoy playing board games,
neglecting duties and abandoning work,
forgetting sleep and food.
They spend whole days and exhaust the daylight,
continuing with lamps and candles.
When
they are at the board, locked in contest,
with victory undecided,
they concentrate their minds and focus their thoughts,
their minds toiling and bodies weary.
Personal affairs are neglected and not attended to;
guests and travelers are ignored and not received.
Even if there are grand
feasts
and the music of Sháo and Xià,
they have no time to notice them.
Sometimes they even gamble away clothing and possessions,
changing their behavior.
The sense of integrity and shame slackens,
and expressions of anger and violence emerge.
However,
their ambition does not extend beyond a single board,
and their endeavors do not go beyond the squares.
Victory over an opponent brings no reward of peerage,
gaining territory brings no actual expansion of land.
The skill is not one of the Six
Arts,
and its use is not for governing the state.
Those who establish themselves do not rely on its techniques;
those selected for office do not follow its path.
If sought in battle formations,
it is not of the same category as Sūn and Wú.
If examined in the realm of Dao and arts,
it is not of the school of Kǒng.
To make deceit and trickery one's business
is not the act of loyalty and trustworthiness.
To make robbery and murder one's name
is not
the intention of the benevolent.
Yet it merely obstructs days and wastes efforts,
ultimately without any benefit.
How is this different from setting up a piece of wood and striking it,
or placing a stone and throwing it?
Moreover, when a gentleman
dwells at home, he toils with his body to provide for his family;
when in court, he exhausts his life to offer loyalty.
Even when facing affairs, he dines late;
how can he indulge in board games?
Therefore,
the conduct of filial piety and brotherly love is established,
and the name of purity and integrity is made manifest.
At present, Great Wú has received the Mandate of Heaven,
but the realm is not yet pacified.
The Sacred Court is diligent and earnest,
committed to finding capable people.
Those with courage and strategy are entrusted with the responsibilities of bears and tigers;
scholars of
refinement are placed in offices like dragons and phoenixes.
All virtues are encompassed,
and both civil and military talents are pursued.
Excellent talents are widely selected,
and outstanding individuals are singled out.
Examination systems are established,
and the rewards of golden
titles are bestowed.
This is truly a glorious gathering of a thousand years,
a fortunate encounter of a hundred generations.
Scholars of this generation
should diligently strive for the ultimate Dao,
cherish their achievements and conserve their efforts,
to assist this enlightened era,
so that their names
may be recorded in historical annals
and their merits in the covenant scrolls.
This is the highest endeavor of a gentleman,
and the most urgent priority of today.
How can a single wooden board compare to the enfeoffment of a state?
How can three hundred dried pieces compare to a commander of ten thousand men?
The imperial robes,
the music of bells and stones,
are sufficient
to encompass the board and trade for board games.
If scholars were to transfer their efforts from board games to poetry and books,
they would have the aspirations of Yán (Huí) and Mǐn (Zǐqiān).
If they applied them to
wisdom and strategy,
they would have the thoughts of Liáng (Zhang) and Píng (Chén).
If they applied them to wealth and goods,
they would have the riches of Yī Dùn.
If they applied them to archery and charioteering,
they would have the readiness of
commanders.
In this way, meritorious fame would be established, and baseness and contempt would be far away.
After [Crown Prince] Hé was deposed, [Wéi Yào] became a Yellow Gate Attendant Gentleman.
When Sūn Liàng ascended the throne,
Zhūgě Kè assisted in governance.
He memorialized for Wéi Yào to be appointed Grand Astrologer,
to compile the Book of Wú.
Huá Hé, Xuē Yíng, and others all participated.
When Sūn Xiū ascended the throne,
he became a Central Secretariat Gentleman
and Libationer of the Academicians.
Sūn Xiū ordered Wéi Yào to follow the precedent of Liú Xiàng
in proofreading and correcting various books.
He also wanted to invite Wéi Yào to lecture,
but General of the Left Zhāng Bù, who was close to the emperor and favored,
often had flawed conduct.
He feared Wéi Yào's presence as a lecturing Confucian scholar,
and also that Wéi Yào's meticulous nature
would cause him to use historical and contemporary examples to caution Sūn Xiū.
He adamantly opposed it.
Sūn Xiū deeply resented Zhāng Bù;
the account is in Sūn Xiū's biography.
However, Wéi Yào ultimately did not enter [the court to lecture].
When Sūn Hào 孫晧 took the throne,
he enfeoffed Gāo Líng Tíng Hóu 高陵亭侯.
He was promoted to Zhōng Shū Pú Yè 中書僕射.
When this office was abolished,
he became a Shì Zhōng 侍中,
regularly overseeing Zuǒ Guó Shǐ 左國史.
At that time, officials everywhere, following instructions, reported auspicious omens.
Hào 晧 questioned Yào 曜 about this.
Yào 曜 replied:
"These are just things from people's baskets and boxes."
Also, Hào 晧 wanted to write an imperial chronicle for his father Hé 和.
Yào 曜 insisted that since Hé 和 had not ascended the imperial throne,
it should properly be titled a biography (zhuàn 傳).
Such instances were not isolated,
and he gradually incurred reproaches and anger.
Yào 曜 became increasingly worried and fearful.
He pleaded that he was old and infirm,
requesting to resign from both the Shì 侍 and Shǐ 史 offices.
He begged to complete the books he was writing,
and have his works separately submitted as his personal undertaking.
Hào 晧 ultimately refused.
At that time, if anyone fell ill,
they were supervised with medicine and care,
and the control over them became even stricter.
Whenever Hào 晧 held a banquet,
it never ended before the day was out.
Regardless of whether they could drink or not, everyone was required to consume seven sheng 升,
and even if they didn't drink it all,
it was poured down until it was finished.
Yào 曜 normally drank no more than two sheng 升 of wine.
Initially, when he was treated with special courtesy,
his amount was often reduced,
or he was secretly given tea in place of wine.
However, as his favor declined,
he was increasingly forced to drink,
and any refusal was considered a crime.
Moreover, after drinking, Hào 晧 would have his attendants challenge and criticize high officials,
mocking them, exposing their private shortcomings,
and finding joy in it.
At times, if there was a fault,
or if someone accidentally violated Hào 晧's taboo name,
they would immediately be arrested and bound,
even to the point of execution.
Yào 曜 believed that outwardly it caused harm,
and inwardly it fostered deep resentment,
preventing harmony;
this was not a good thing.
Therefore, he merely presented difficult questions on classical meanings and discussions.
Hào 晧, believing that he was not complying with imperial edicts
and was not entirely loyal,
thus accumulated previous grievances and anger.
He had Yào 曜 arrested and imprisoned.
This was the second year of Fèng Huáng 鳳皇.
Yào 曜 then submitted a petition through the prison guard, saying:
"Your prisoner is indebted to Your Majesty's grace and compassion,
without comparison.
Yet, I have not even a wisp to repay it.
I have shamed this grace and favor,
and have fallen into the gravest crime.
I contemplate that I shall be reduced to ashes,
and forever abandoned to the Yellow Springs.
My foolish heart, though, earnestly
secretly harbors a thought,
and greedily wishes for it to reach Your Majesty's ears.
Your prisoner once saw ancient calendar commentaries among the people,
whose records contained much that was baseless,
and what was in books was also erroneous.
Your prisoner painstakingly researched biographies and records,
compared similarities and differences,
and collected what he heard and saw,
to compile the Dòng Jì 洞紀.
It begins from Páo Xī 庖犧
and extends to Qín 秦 and Hàn 漢,
totaling three volumes.
It was intended to start from Huáng Wǔ 黃武,
with a separate volume,
but the work is not yet complete.
I also saw the Shì Míng 釋名 compiled by Liú Xī 劉熙.
Indeed, many parts are excellent,
yet the multitude of categories makes it difficult to thoroughly investigate,
so there are occasional successes and failures.
Moreover, regarding titles and ranks,
there are also inaccuracies.
I humbly believe that official ranks,
being what is urgent today,
should not be incorrect.
Your prisoner, forgetting his extreme insignificance,
also compiled one volume each of Guān Zhí Xùn 官職訓 and Biàn Shì Míng 辯釋名,
intending to present them.
They were just newly copied and finished
when, due to my misconduct,
I was imprisoned awaiting my fate.
On the day I perish,
I regret not being able to present them.
I respectfully enclose a list of my works, prepared before my death,
and humbly request that it be submitted to the imperial library,
so that the works may be retrieved from outside,
presented to the court, and heard by Your Majesty.
I am apprehensive of my shallow ignorance,
and fear that it may not accord with Your Majesty's hearing.
I am filled with fear and barely breathing,
and beg for Your Majesty's compassionate consideration."
Yào 曜 hoped to be pardoned by this,
but Hào 晧 was instead surprised by the dirtiness of his document,
and therefore questioned Yào 曜 about it again.
Yào 曜 replied:
"Your prisoner compiled this book,
truly intending to present it.
Fearing errors,
I repeatedly reviewed it,
and did not realize it had become soiled.
Upon being questioned, I shivered with cold,
my body trembling and speech faltering.
I respectfully retract my previous words and kowtow five hundred times,
beating myself with both hands."
Then Huá Hé 華覈 repeatedly submitted memorials to save Yào 曜, saying:
"Yào 曜, having been born in this thousand-year epoch,
was specially recognized with compassion,
and because of his scholarship,
was able to serve as a history official,
a court attendant with sable and cicada ornaments,
receiving heavenly inquiries.
The enlightened court, being benevolent and virtuous,
is careful in its endings and mindful of the distant past.
At the time of receiving the spirits,
Your Majesty shed tears and instructed Yào 曜.
Yào 曜, foolish and unperceptive,
was unable to fully expound upon Your Majesty's great excellence akin to Emperor Shùn 舜,
and instead bound the history official,
preventing the sagely intent from being fulfilled,
and the supreme conduct from being displayed.
This is truly Yào 曜's foolish and ignorant crime deserving of death.
However, I, your servant, earnestly
have seen Yào 曜 diligently study since youth,
never tiring even in old age.
He has delved into the great classics,
reviewed the old and learned the new,
and his knowledge encompasses ancient and modern affairs.
Among external officials, few surpass Yào 曜.
In the past, Lǐ Líng 李陵, a Han general,
was defeated and surrendered to the Xiongnú 匈奴 instead of returning.
Sīmǎ Qiān 司馬遷 did not condemn him,
but spoke on Lǐ Líng's 李陵 behalf.
Emperor Wǔ of Han, recognizing Qiān's 遷 talent as a good historian,
wished him to complete his compilation.
He forbore from executing him,
and the book was finally completed,
to be handed down endlessly.
Today, Yào 曜 in Wú 吳
is also the Sīmǎ Qiān 司馬遷 of Han.
I humbly observe that auspicious omens have repeatedly manifested,
divine signs and heavenly responses
have appeared one after another.
The time for unification
is likely not far off.
After peace is established,
we should observe the times and establish new institutions.
The Three Kings did not adopt each other's rituals,
and the Five Emperors did not perpetuate each other's music.
Simplicity and refinement followed different paths,
and additions and subtractions were distinct.
It would be appropriate to have individuals like Yào 曜, following ancient principles,
make reforms and establishments.
When the Han dynasty succeeded Qin,
there was Shú Sūn Tōng 叔孫通 who established the rites for a generation.
Yào 曜's talent and learning are also second only to Hàn Tōng 漢通.
Moreover, although the Wú Shū 吳書 already has its beginnings,
the encomia (zàn 贊) have not yet been written.
In the past, Bān Gù 班固 wrote the Hàn Shū 漢書,
whose prose was elegant and refined.
Later, Liú Zhēn 劉珍 and Liú Yì 劉毅 and others wrote the Hàn Jì 漢記,
which was far inferior to Bān Gù's 班固,
especially the biographies.
Now, the Wú Shū 吳書 is destined to be transmitted for a thousand years,
ranked among various histories.
Later scholars who judge its merits and demerits
must have talent like Yào 曜.
It truly cannot be allowed to lack an immortal work.
As for your servant's dullness,
I am certainly not the right person.
Yào 曜 is already seventy years old;
his remaining years are few.
I beg that you pardon him one degree of his crime,
and sentence him to lifelong penal servitude,
so that he may complete his literary works,
which will forever serve as a record,
and be passed down for a hundred generations.
I respectfully submit this memorial,
kowtowing a hundred times."
Hào 晧 did not grant permission,
and subsequently executed Yào 曜,
and exiled his family to Líng Líng 零陵.
His son, Lóng 隆,
was also a man of letters.
Huá Hé 華覈, courtesy name Yǒng Xiān 永先,
was a native of Wú Jùn Wǔ Jìn 吳郡武進.
He initially served as Commandant of Shàng Yú Wèi 上虞尉 and Commandant of Agriculture.
Due to his literary talent, he entered the imperial library as Mì Fǔ Láng 祕府郎,
and was promoted to Zhōng Shū Chéng 中書丞.
Shǔ was annexed by Wèi.
Hé went to the palace gate and presented a memorial, saying:
“Lately I heard that the enemy forces gathered like ants and moved towards the western border.
The western border is treacherous and difficult,
so it was thought there would be no danger.
Then it was confirmed that Lù Kàng’s memorial arrived,
stating that Chéngdū was not defended,
our lord had to flee,
and the state was overthrown.
In the past, Wèi was destroyed by the Dí, but Duke Huán saved it.
Now the distance is long,
and it cannot be saved or revived.
Having lost our reliant land,
and abandoned a tributary state,
I, your subject, though mere grass,
secretly feel uneasy.
Your Majesty is sagely and benevolent,
your grace and favor extend afar,
upon hearing such news,
you will surely express sorrow and mourning.
I cannot bear the grief and sadness,
and respectfully present this memorial to inform you.”
When Sūn Hào ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Xúlíng Tínghóu.
In the second year of Bǎodǐng,
Hào began constructing a new palace again.
Its scale was vast and grand,
decorated with pearls and jade,
and the expenses were immense.
At this time, construction began in midsummer,
and agriculture and defense were both neglected.
Hé submitted a memorial, remonstrating: “I have heard that during the reign of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
the nine provinces were peaceful.
The people of Qín were glad to abandon the cruel and harsh government,
and returned to the benevolent and lenient rule of the Liú clan.
Corvée labor was reduced, laws were simplified,
and they began
anew.
Princes and imperial relatives were enfeoffed to protect the Hàn dynasty.
At that time,
everyone considered it as secure as Mount Tài,
an endless foundation.
Yet, Jiǎ Yí
alone believed
there were three things to weep over and shed tears for,
and six things to sigh deeply for.
He then said, ‘How is the current situation different from holding fire under a pile of firewood and sleeping on it,
considering it safe before the fire has even ignited?’
Afterwards, the chaos and rebellions
all happened as he predicted.
Though I am humble and foolish,
and do not understand the great principles,
I secretly use the past events
to measure the present
situation.
Yí said, ‘In a few more years,
the various princes will be strong.
If the Hàn’s grand tutors and chancellors feign illness and resign,
and one attempts to govern with this,
even Yáo and Shùn could not ensure peace.’
Now the great
enemy occupies the land of the nine provinces,
possesses more than half of the population,
is skilled in the remaining arts of warfare,
and rides on their established military might.
They wish to compete with the Middle Kingdom in a scheme of mutual吞噬.
Their
situation is like that of Chǔ and Hàn, which could not coexist,
and not merely like the Hàn princes of Huáinán and Jìběi.
What Yí wished to weep over
is less urgent compared to today,
and the analogy of sleeping
on firewood
with fire beneath is more critical today.
The Great Emperor observed the past generations’ situations and
perceived the present circumstances,
thus greatly expanding agriculture and sericulture,
accumulating immeasurable
reserves,
alleviating the burden of corvée labor on the people,
and diligently nurturing warriors.
Therefore, all, high and low, were grateful
and each thought of sacrificing their lives.
This fortune did not last,
and the myriad states were soon abandoned.
Since then,
powerful ministers have monopolized power,
deceiving the heavens above,
and disobeying public opinion below.
They destroy the foundations of peace and survival,
and seek temporary gain.
They frequently raise armies,
emptying the state treasuries,
resulting in weary troops
and distressed people,
never finding peace.
Those who survive now are but remnants of the injured
and the suffering populace.
This has led to empty military resources,
unfilled granaries,
and insufficient distribution of cloth and silk,
leaving people cold in winter and hot in summer.
Compounded by job losses,
households cannot sustain themselves.
Meanwhile, the north accumulates grain and nourishes its people,
concentrating entirely on the east,
without other concerns.
Shǔ
was our western bulwark,
its land treacherous and secure.
Moreover, it inherited the previous ruler’s art of governance,
so it was thought its defense was sufficient for a long time.
Unexpectedly, in a single day,
it was utterly overthrown.
‘When the lips
are gone, the teeth feel cold’
is what the ancients feared.
The various commanderies of Jiāozhōu,
the southern territory of our state,
Jiāozhǐ and Jiǔzhēn, two commanderies, have already been lost.
Rìnán is isolated and perilous,
its survival difficult to guarantee.
North of Hépǔ,
the people are all unsettled,
and many have deserted and rebelled due to evading corvée.
Yet, garrisons are reduced,
and our prestige and control are diminished.
I constantly fear that in a breath,
there will be another unforeseen
disaster.
In the past, sea pirates watched the eastern counties,
gaining many deserters.
Being accustomed to sea travel,
and emboldened by previous years,
they raid daily.
Now we face threats from front and back,
many difficulties
from head to tail.
This is an critical juncture for our dynasty.
It is indeed appropriate to halt construction projects,
and first prepare for contingencies.
Exert efforts in cultivation,
and provide relief for the hungry and impoverished.
I only fear
that the farming season will pass,
and spring planting will be too late.
When trouble arises,
we will not be prepared.
If we abandon these urgent matters
and devote all efforts to construction,
should an unexpected upheaval of war occur,
we would have to abandon the construction work
and respond to the urgency of beacon fires,
driving a disgruntled populace
to face the peril of bladed weapons.
This is precisely what the great enemy would exploit.
If we merely fortify
and defend,
prolonging the struggle,
then military provisions will surely become scarce.
Before engaging in battle,
the warriors would already be exhausted.
In the time of Tàiwù,
mulberry and grain grew in the court.
He feared and cultivated virtue,
and the omen disappeared, and the Yīn dynasty flourished.
When Yínghuò guarded Xīn constellation,
Sòng considered it a disaster.
Duke Jǐng followed the words of the blind
historian,
and Yínghuò retreated,
and Duke Jǐng lived long.
Cultivating virtue in oneself can move different species,
and words spoken can communicate with spirits and gods.
I, with my foolishness and ignorance,
mistakenly hold a nearby official position,
and cannot widely proclaim benevolent grace to move the spirits.
I feel shame looking up and looking down,
having nowhere to hide.
Retreating and reflecting,
the strange occurrences of Yínghuò and the mulberry and grain
were heavenly warnings to the two rulers.
As for other minor and insignificant omens,
they are merely the work of minor household spirits.
Examining heaven and earth,
there are no other changes.
And auspicious signs and portents
have repeatedly appeared before and after.
A bright pearl has already been sighted,
and white sparrows have subsequently appeared.
The destiny of myriad years
is truly bestowed by spirits.
Taking the nine regions as your residence,
and all under heaven as your home,
not to be ranked with
the people of the households, their relocation is the same.
Furthermore, the palaces of today,
were built by the former emperor (Xiāndì),
who divined the earth and established the foundations,
not as an ill omen.
Moreover, the land of Yángshì is connected to the palace;
if the great undertaking is eventually completed,
and the imperial carriage moves there,
the gods of the gates and paths
will all have to transfer.
Still, I fear that in the long run it may not necessarily be better than the old.
Repeated relocations are not feasible;
to remain would cause
suspicion.
This is why your foolish minister worries day and night.
I have reviewed the Monthly Ordinances (Yuèlìng),
and in the month of mid-summer (Jìxià),
it is not permissible to undertake earthworks,
nor to assemble the various
lords (Zhūhóu),
nor to raise armies or mobilize the populace.
To undertake a great enterprise will surely bring great calamity.
Although the lords (Zhūhóu) are not assembling now,
their armies gathering is no different from their assembly.
In the sixth month, on a wùjǐ
day,
the earth element is in its full vigor;
it is already not to be transgressed.
Furthermore, it is a farming month,
and the season must not be missed.
In the past, Lǔ Yǐnggōng built a wall in Zhōngqiū in summer,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) recorded it,
serving as a warning for
posterity.
Now, to build a palace as a vast foundation for a long reign,
and to transgress the great taboos of heaven and earth,
to repeat what the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) recorded,
and to neglect the most important duty of reverently receiving (the seasons),
your minister, with his foolish
understanding,
secretly finds this unsettling.
I also fear that among the dispersed people summoned,
some may not arrive.
If they are punished, it will disrupt the work and cause trouble;
if not punished, the days and months will drag on.
If all arrive and are gathered,
with a large multitude assembled,
it is rare for there to be no disease.
Moreover, when people's minds are at ease, they think of good;
when suffering, they resent and rebel.
The elite soldiers of Jiāngnán
are difficult for the northern lands to match;
it is desired that ten of our soldiers match
one from the east.
The world is not yet settled;
this is deeply worrisome and regrettable.
If this palace is completed,
and five thousand die or rebel,
then the strength of the northern army will increase by fifty thousand.
If it reaches ten
thousand people,
then it will be an increase of one hundred thousand.
The sick suffer the loss of life,
and the rebels spread ill-will;
this is what makes our great enemy rejoice.
Now we are to contend in strength in the
Central Plains (Zhōngyuán),
to determine who is strong and who is weak.
Precisely at this juncture,
they gain and we lose,
further compounded by toil and distress.
This is what deeply worries heroes and wise strategists.
Your minister has heard that enlightened kings of the past, if their state had no three years' worth of provisions,
would say "the state is not my state."
In times of peace and stability, precautions were taken to this extent;
how much more so when the enemy is strong and great, and we neglect farming and forget
livestock?
Although there has been some planting and cultivation now,
it is heard that the great floods submerged much of it.
The remainder that survived must await weeding and harvest.
Yet the senior officials, fearing deadlines,
are heading to various prefectures above,
personally traversing mountains and
forests,
exerting their full strength in felling timber,
neglecting agriculture and abandoning their duties.
The soldiers and common people, with their wives, children, and weak dependents,
have but meager cultivated land;
if there are floods or droughts, they will have no harvest forever.
The prefectures and commanderies, seeing the rice,
must await an emergency.
The idle multitudes,
rely on official provisions for relief.
If both upper and lower levels are empty and destitute,
and transport and supply are insufficient,
and the northern enemy invades our borders,
even if Zhōu and Zhào were reborn,
or Liáng and Píng reappeared,
they would not be able to devise a clear plan for Your Majesty.
Your minister has heard that when the ruler is enlightened, his ministers are loyal;
when the lord is sagely, his ministers are upright.
Therefore, sincerely,
I humbly brave the imperial wrath,
begging for your compassionate consideration.
The memorial was submitted,
but Hào did not accept it.
Later, he was promoted to Dōngguān Lìng,
and concurrently Right National Historian (Yòu Guóshǐ).
He earnestly submitted a memorial declining the position,
to which Hào replied:
"I have received your memorial.
The Dōngguān is a repository of Confucian scholars,
whose duty it is to lecture on and collate literature and arts,
and to resolve difficult questions.
During the Hàn dynasty, only renowned scholars and great Confucians were appointed to this post.
You request that a more distinguished and capable person be selected.
Upon hearing this,
I consider that you have meticulously studied the ancient texts (féndiǎn),
are broadly read and widely learned;
you can be called one who delights in rites and music, and is earnest in poetry and history.
You should wield your pen and display your literary talent,
to illuminate and assist in the affairs of the time,
surpassing the likes of Yáng, Bān, Zhāng, and Cài.
It is strange that you are so modest,
and greatly undervalue yourself.
You should diligently cultivate your duties,
to surpass the former sages,
and cease your endless objections."
At that time, the granaries had no reserves,
and worldly customs became increasingly extravagant.
Huà Hé submitted a memorial, saying:
"Currently, bandits and enemies are rampant,
and military campaigns have not ceased.
Domestically, there is no accumulation of years of reserves,
and externally, there are no stores to respond to the enemy.
This is what those who govern a state ought to deeply worry about.
The sources of wealth and grain
all come from the people.
Attending to the seasons and diligently farming
is the state's most urgent priority.
Yet, the various officials in the capital,
whose responsibilities differ,
each issue demands from below,
without considering the people's capacity,
and always set short deadlines.
The senior officials, fearing punishment,
press the people day and night,
causing them to abandon their tenant farming tasks,
hurriedly rush to the appointed date,
and deliver the goods to the capital.
Sometimes, these are stored and not used,
simply causing the common people to exhaust their strength and lose time.
When the autumn harvest month arrives,
they supervise the required intake,
depriving them of the time for sowing and planting,
and demanding this year's taxes.
If there are any arrears,
their property is confiscated,
leading to impoverished households
and insufficient food and clothing.
It is appropriate to temporarily halt various labor services
and focus wholeheartedly on agriculture and sericulture.
The ancients said: 'If one man does not plow,
someone may suffer hunger;
if one woman does not weave,
someone may suffer cold.'
Thus, the enlightened kings, in governing the state,
made agriculture their sole priority.
Since the military campaigns began,
it has been nearly a hundred years.
Farmers have abandoned their tasks in the southern fields,
and women laborers have ceased their loom work.
Considering this,
those who eat meager food and suffer long hunger,
and wear thin clothes while treading on ice,
are certainly not few.
Your servant has heard that there are two things the ruler demands from the people,
and three things the people expect from the ruler.
The two demands are: to labor for him,
and to die for him.
The three expectations are: to feed the hungry,
to give rest to the weary,
and to reward the meritorious.
If the people fulfill their two duties but the ruler fails to meet their three expectations,
then resentment arises, and achievements are not established.
Currently, the state treasury is not full,
and the people's labor service is excessive.
The ruler's two demands have been met,
but the people's three expectations have not been reciprocated.
Moreover, the hungry do not wait for fine delicacies before being full,
and the cold do not wait for fox and badger furs before being warm.
Exquisite flavors are for the mouth's enjoyment,
and embroidered patterns are for the body's adornment.
Now, tasks are numerous and labor is heavy,
the people are poor, and customs are extravagant.
All artisans create useless objects,
and women make elaborate ornaments.
They do not diligently work with hemp and ramie,
but instead embroider patterns and ritualistic designs,
imitating one another,
ashamed to be the only one without them.
Even military and civilian households
still follow this trend,
having no internal reserves of grain,
but possessing clothes of fine silk.
As for the wealthy merchants and peddlers,
they further burden themselves with gold and silver,
their extravagance being even more extreme.
The world is not yet at peace,
and the common people are not self-sufficient.
It is fitting to cultivate the sources of the people's livelihood,
and enrich the industries of grain and cloth,
instead of wasting effort on frivolous crafts
and spending days on extravagant matters.
Above, there is no distinction of rank or status,
and below, there is the harm of wasting wealth and resources.
Currently, among officials and soldiers,
some have few or no daughters,
while many have three or four,
and some have one or two.
If we issue a general order that each household with one daughter,
then among one hundred thousand households there would be one hundred thousand women.
If each woman weaves one bolt of cloth per year,
that would be one hundred thousand bolts.
If all within the four borders unite their efforts,
within a few years,
cloth and silk will surely accumulate.
Allow the people to use five colors,
whatever they wish to wear,
but only prohibit embroidered and useless ornaments.
Moreover, beautiful women do not need splendid attire to enhance their charm,
and alluring figures do not need patterned silks to attract affection.
Adornments of five colors
are sufficient for beauty.
If one applies extreme makeup
and dons the most elaborate clothes,
there may not necessarily be no ugly women;
if one abandons splendid attire
and discards embroidered patterns,
there may not necessarily be no beautiful women.
If it is truly as argued,
that having them is useless and abolishing them causes no harm,
why hesitate to temporarily prohibit them to replenish the urgent needs of the state treasury?
This is the foremost priority for alleviating scarcity,
and the fundamental industry for enriching the state.
Even if Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Yīng were reborn,
they could not improve upon this.
Emperors Wén and Jǐng of the Hàn dynasty,
who inherited a peaceful and unified reign,
with the world already settled
and no worries from the four quarters,
still considered carved patterns harmful to agriculture
and brocade embroidery detrimental to women's work,
opening the path to enriching the state
and eliminating the root causes of hunger and cold.
How much more so now, when the six directions are divided,
wolves and jackals fill the roads,
soldiers do not leave the borders,
and armor is not unbuckled?
How can we not expand the sources of wealth
and fill the state treasury's reserves?"
Sūn Hào, seeing that Huà Hé was old,
ordered him to draft a memorial.
Huà Hé dared not.
Sūn Hào again ordered him to compose a draft,
standing and waiting for him.
Huà Hé then composed the text, saying:
"Alas, I, Huà Hé, am a humble minister,
as common as grass.
I encountered Your Majesty's favor and met a sage,
receiving exceptionally profound grace.
Emerging from decaying earth,
like a cicada shedding its skin, I entered the court.
Bathed in the brilliant light of the purple palace,
I rely on its azure jade.
I reverently sip the clear dew,
and bathe in the propitious breeze.
My contributions are as fine as silk or hair,
my debt to the court is as towering as a mountain.
Nourished and enduring ignominy,
my debt of grace accumulates.
My humble self is covered in glory,
my allotted life finds fulfillment.
Wishing to repay this boundless kindness,
I commit myself to the august heavens.
Your sacred grace descends like rain,
pitying and forgiving my faults.
You condescended to order me to draft a response,
your benevolence covering even the lowliest and most foolish.
I dared not disobey the command,
fearing swift retribution.
Venturing to accept the imperial decree,
my soul has departed, but my body remains."
Huà Hé, on various occasions, presented beneficial proposals,
recommended worthy and capable individuals,
and explained away offenses.
He submitted over a hundred documents,
all of which were helpful.
The texts are too numerous to include in their entirety.
In the first year of Tiāncè, he was dismissed due to a minor transgression,
and died a few years later.
The memorials and petitions presented by Wéi Yào and Huà Hé
are all transmitted to the world.
Commentary says: Xuē Yíng praised Wáng Fān for his outstanding character and capacity,
being broad-minded and widely knowledgeable;
Lóu Xuán for his integrity and upright conduct,
and his lucid and logical talent;
Hè Shào for his lofty aspirations and purity,
and his keen and essential understanding;
Wéi Yào for his diligent scholarship and love for antiquity,
his extensive knowledge of various texts,
and his talent for writing history.
Hú Chōng believed that Lóu Xuán, Hè Shào, and Wáng Fān were all refined and brilliant at the same time,
with little difference in superiority or inferiority.
If absolutely forced to rank them,
Lóu Xuán should be first,
and Hè Shào second.
Huà Hé's talent for literature and poetry
surpassed Wéi Yào's,
but his knowledge of classics was inferior.
I observe that Huà Hé repeatedly offered good advice,
with the intent of dedicating himself entirely,
approaching the standard of a loyal minister.
However, these several individuals,
living in a reckless age yet possessing fame and position,
forced their principles to the death,
and were fortunate to escape with their lives.
Your subject, Péi Sōngzhī, submits: I have heard that when wisdom pervades, all principles naturally yield;
when vision is far-reaching, nothing escapes its light.
Though the exhaustion of nature and the probing of the subtle
are profoundly unknowable,
as for the remnants where they reside,
they must touch upon their rough traces.
This is why even a fully accomplished person
is still said to "delight in scrutinizing nearby words,"
and the depth of accumulated virtue
lies in "much knowing of past deeds."
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty's Dào encompasses the profoundest depths,
your spirit transcends all marvelous things,
your glorious light renews daily,
and flourishes ever more resplendently.
Though you penetrate the Fén and Diǎn classics and
delight your heart in the profound and abstruse,
you nonetheless condescend to consider recent times
and broadly observe their rise and fall,
intending thereby to encompass past precedents
and bestow instruction upon future generations.
Previously, your subject received an imperial edict
to collect the differences and similarities of the Three Kingdoms era to annotate Chén Shòu's Guózhì.
Shòu's book is well-organized and observable;
its events are mostly accurate and just.
It is truly a garden for perusal,
a fine history of recent times.
However, its fault lies in its brevity,
sometimes with omissions.
Your subject, following your command, has diligently sought detail,
striving for thoroughness and comprehensiveness.
I have searched for old accounts from above,
and gathered lost materials from all sides.
Although the Three Kingdoms period did not span many years,
its affairs relate to the Hàn and Jìn dynasties.
The beginning and end of what is involved
cover more than a hundred years.
The records and notes are numerous and complex,
often contradictory and mutually exclusive.
Whatever Shòu did not record,
yet whose inclusion is appropriate,
I have taken without exception to supplement his deficiencies.
Or if different accounts describe the same event with divergent wording,
or if the original events are different,
making it difficult to decide,
all are copied in to preserve the different versions.
If, however, there are obvious errors,
and statements unfounded in reason,
then I have corrected the discrepancies to rectify their falsity.
As for the appropriateness of contemporary events and Shòu's minor faults,
I have offered some discussion and debate with my humble opinions.
Since I began this compilation,
nearly a month has passed.
The copying and proofreading are now complete;
I respectfully seal and present it.
I humbly reflect that painting creates patterns with many colors,
and honey is flavored by various pollens,
thus enabling the splendid and plain to have order,
and the sweet to surpass its original essence.
Your subject is truly dull and wanting,
and feels ashamed before these two things.
Though I have exerted myself,
I am utterly devoid of such embellishment.
I am neither as quick-witted as the Huáinán scholar who "composed during a meal,"
nor as subtly inspired as Kuáng Jiǎn's brilliant works.
Lingering without achievement,
I merely defile the brush and ink,
insufficient to requite Your Majesty's sacred decree,
or to slightly atone for my faults and responsibilities.
My shame and fear are profound,
as if plunging into an abyss.
I respectfully prostrate myself with this memorial,
sweating profusely as I do so.
Your subject, Péi Sōngzhī, sincerely, respectfully, fearfully bows his head, bows his head, deserving of death, respectfully submits.
On the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month of Yuánjiā six (429 CE),
presented by Zhōngshū Shìláng and Xīxiāng Hóu, your subject Péi Sōngzhī.
Sīkù Quánshū Zǒngmù Tíyào
Sānguózhì in sixty-five *juàn*,
compiled by Chén Shòu of the Jìn dynasty,
annotated by Péi Sōngzhī of the Sòng dynasty.
Shòu's deeds are fully recorded in his biography in the Jìn Shū,
and Sōngzhī's deeds in his biography in the Sòng Shū.
It comprises thirty *juàn* of the Wèi Zhì,
fifteen *juàn* of the Shǔ Zhì,
and twenty *juàn* of the Wú Zhì.
This work takes Wèi as the legitimate dynasty,
a view first challenged when Xí Záochǐ wrote the Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū.
Since Zhū Zǐ (Zhū Xī),
there has been no one who did not side with Záochǐ and criticize Shòu.
However, judging by reason,
Shòu's error is utterly indefensible;
but judging by circumstance,
Záochǐ's assertion of the Hàn as legitimate was smooth and easy,
while Shòu's desire to assert the Hàn as legitimate would have been difficult and contrary.
This is because in Záochǐ's time, Jìn had already moved south,
and its situation resembled that of Shǔ;
to contend for legitimacy on behalf of a regime in partial peace,
this aligned with the prevailing view of his era.
Shòu, on the other hand, was a minister to Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
and Emperor Wǔ of Jìn inherited the succession from Wèi.
To declare Wèi illegitimate would be to declare Jìn illegitimate.
How could this have been acceptable in his time?
This is similar to how Sòng Tàizǔ's usurpation was close to that of Wèi,
while the Northern Hàn and Southern Táng resembled Shǔ,
hence the scholars of the Northern Sòng all avoided declaring Wèi illegitimate.
After Gāozōng,
the dynasty maintained partial peace south of the Yangtze,
resembling Shǔ, while the Central Plains, the territory of Wèi, was entirely taken by Jīn;
thus, the scholars of the Southern Sòng then arose one after another to declare Shǔ legitimate.
In all these cases, one must consider their respective eras;
they cannot be constrained by a single rule.
Only his mistake of following the precedent of the Shǐ Jì's biographies of Zhōu and Qín,
not beginning with Wèi Wén (Cáo Pī) but with Cáo Cāo,
indeed falls short of the propriety of the Wèi Shū Jì,
which truly should have been avoided.
During the Yuánjiā reign of Sòng,
Péi Sōngzhī received an imperial edict to compile annotations.
His annotations extensively quote various books
and also occasionally include his own opinions.
In broad outline, his approach generally consists of six aspects: First, citing discussions from various scholars
to distinguish right from wrong; second, comparing accounts from various books
to verify discrepancies; third, elaborating on events mentioned in the main text
to detail their intricacies; fourth, supplementing events not found in the main text
to fill omissions; fifth, detailing the lives of persons mentioned in the main text
to provide their biographies; sixth, attaching related persons not found in the main text
under similar categories.
In these annotations, he often indulged in the strange and loved broad knowledge,
which rather marred the work with its disorganization.
For instance, in Yuán Shào's biography, regarding Húmǔ Bān,
who was originally seen because Dǒng Zhuó sent Shào,
the annotation states,
"Bān once saw the Tàishān Fǔjūn and the Hébó;
the event is in the Sōushén Jì,
but much of the account is not included,"
which is already superfluous.
In Zhōng Yáo's biography, a passage from Lù Shì Yìlín is cited,
recording Yáo's intimacy with a ghost woman;
in Jiǎng Jì's biography, a passage from Liè Yì Zhuàn is cited,
recording that Jì's son died and became a Tàishān Wǔbó,
who then summoned his grandson Ā to be the Tàishān Magistrate;
such instances of creating something from nothing and recounting wonders,
numbering over ten places,
are entirely unrelated to the main subject
and deeply detrimental to the methods of historical writing,
truly constituting flaws.
Furthermore, his initial intention also seems to have been to research explanations of words and cite ancient facts,
similar to Yìng Shào's annotations to the Hàn Shū.
Thus, in the Wèi Zhì, Wǔdì Jì, for the character Jǔ (沮) in Jǔ Shòu's name, he notes,
"Jǔ is pronounced like 'zū'";
for the place name Guǎngpíng (獷平), he cites the Xù Hàn Shū Jùnguó Zhì, noting,
"Guǎngpíng is a county name, belonging to Yúyáng";
for Yǒngdào (甬道), he cites the Hàn Shū,
"[Gāozǔ in] the second year fought Chǔ and built a *yǒngdào*";
for Zhuìliú (贅旒), he cites the Gōngyáng Zhuàn;
for Xiānzhèng (先正), he cites the Wénhóu Zhī Mìng;
for the explanation of Wèi (位), he cites the Zuǒ Zhuàn;
for Zhìjiè (致屆), he cites the Shī;
for Suíyuán (綏爰), Shuàibǐ (率俾), and Hūnzuò (昬作), he cites the Shū;
for Jiūqián Tiānxíng (糾虔天刑), he cites the Guóyǔ.
In the Shǔ Zhì, Xì Zhèng's biography, for the essay "Shì Huì,"
every sentence cites ancient events for annotation, extending to several slips of bamboo.
Also, for instance, in Péng Yàng's biography, "gé" (革) is not explained as "old";
in Huà Tuó's biography, "fū" (旉) originally resembles "zhuān" (專);
in Qín Mì's biography, "jí" (棘) and "gé" (革) are different characters;
in Shǎodì Jì, "sǒu" (叟) and "gēng" (更) are different characters,
occasionally containing辨證 (textual criticism).
The sentences in other biographies are not all like this.
However, such instances as the sudden annotation of the surname Liáo (廖) as "bǔjiù qiè" at the beginning of Liáo Lì's biography in the Shǔ Zhì,
or the sudden citation from the Bówù Jì to annotate the character "qiǎng" (繈) in Liáng Mào's biography in the Wèi Zhì,
also occur occasionally.
It seems he intended to do so but did not complete it,
and also cherished what had already been done,
not wishing to delete it;
thus, it is sometimes detailed, sometimes brief,
sometimes present, sometimes absent,
and also rather inconsistent in its style.
Nevertheless, its network is vast and rich;
all the old texts of the Six Dynasties that are now lost
are still glimpsed in their general outlines.
Moreover, many are complete from beginning to end,
unlike Lì Dàoyuán's Shuǐjīng Zhù and Lǐ Shàn's Wénxuǎn Zhù, which are all clipped and fragmented texts.
Therefore, scholars of textual criticism
draw inexhaustible material from it,
and the references they make to it
are even more numerous than to Chén Shòu's original book.
Huáyáng Guózhì, Chén Shòu Zhuàn
Chén Shòu, courtesy name Chéngzuǒ,
was a native of Ānhàn, Bāxī.
In his youth, he studied under Qióu Zhōu, a Sànqí Chángshì.
He specialized in the Shàngshū and the Sān Zhuàn,
and devoted himself to history and the Hàn dynasty.
He was intelligent, alert, and keen,
and his writings were rich and elegant.
He first served as Wèijiāngjūn Zhǔbù and Dōngguān Mìshūláng, and Sànqí Huángmén Shìláng, by state appointment.
After Dàtóng, he was nominated as Xiàolián
and became the Zhōngzhèng of his home commandery.
In Yìbù, after Jiànwǔ,
Zhèng Bóyì of Shǔjùn, Tàiwèi Zhào Yánxìn, and Chén Shēnbó and Zhù Yuánlíng of Hànzhōng, and Wáng Wénbiǎo of Guǎnghàn, all known for their extensive learning and wide knowledge,
compiled the Bāshǔ Qíjiù Zhuàn.
Shòu considered it insufficient for long-term transmission,
so he integrated Bā and Hàn to compile the Yìbù Qíjiù Zhuàn in ten chapters.
Sànqí Chángshì Wén Lì presented a memorial recommending his work.
Emperor Wǔ praised it,
and he was again appointed Zuòzhù Láng.
After the pacification of Wú,
Shòu gathered the histories of the Three Kingdoms,
writing the Wèi, Wú, and Shǔ Sānshū in sixty-five chapters,
titled Sānguó Zhì.
He also wrote the Gǔguó Zhì in fifty chapters.
His evaluation was refined and elegant,
and Zhōngshū Jiān Xún Xù and Lìng Zhāng Huá deeply admired it,
believing that Bān Gù and Shǐ Qiān were not his equals.
He was appointed Píngyáng Hóuxiàng.
Huá also memorialized for him to arrange and compile Zhūgě Liàng's anecdotes into twenty-four chapters.
At that time, Shòu's own collection was also extensive,
so there were some differences.
He was again appointed Zuòzhù Láng.
Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Dù Yù memorialized for him to be appointed Sànqí Shìláng.
An imperial edict stated:
"Yesterday, Shǔ native Shòu Liáng was appropriately staffed.
He can also serve as Shìyùshǐ."
He submitted the Shàngguān Sī Lùn in seven chapters,
based on classical allusions,
discussing what should be inherited and what should be reformed.
He also submitted Shì Huì and Guǎngguó Lùn.
Huá memorialized for him to also hold the position of Zhōngshū Láng,
but Shòu's Wèizhì had displeased Xù,
and Xù did not want him to hold an internal position,
so he memorialized for him to be appointed Chángguǎng Tàishǒu.
His stepmother's will specified no joint burial,
for which he was criticized.
Several years later,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
After the Crown Prince was moved,
he again concurrently served as Sànqí Chángshì.
Emperor Huì said to Sīkōng Zhāng Huá:
"Shòu's talent warrants a permanent position,
not prolonged concurrent service."
Huá memorialized to promote him to the Jiǔ Qīng,
but then he was executed.
Loyal and virtuous officials were ostracized,
and Shòu subsequently died in Luòxià.
His position and reputation did not match his talent,
and people at the time considered it an injustice.
His nephew Fú,
courtesy name Chángxìn,
also had literary talent.
He succeeded Shòu as Zuòzhù Zuǒláng
and served as Shànglián Lìng.
Fú's younger brother Lì,
courtesy name Shúdù,
served as Liángzhōu Biéjià,
and was appointed by Piàojì Jiāngjūn Qíwáng as Yuàn.
He died in Luòxià.
Lì's cousin Jiē,
courtesy name Dázhī,
served as Zhōuzhǔbù,
was nominated as Xiàolián,
and served as Bāozhōng Lìng, Yǒngchāng Xībù Dūwèi, and Jiànníng Xīnggǔ Tàishǒu.
All of them had brilliant literary skills,
and were famous in their time.
In total, Shòu wrote over two hundred chapters,
and Fú, Lì, and Jiē each wrote several tens of chapters.
Many senior figures from the two provinces and literati from Huáxià wrote biographies for them,
generally as described above.
At that time, Lǐ Xiāng Shúlóng of Zītóng was also a brilliant talent,
famous in his era.
He was recommended as Xiùcái
and served as Shàngshū Láng,
and was appointed Jiànpíng Tàishǒu.
He declined due to illness and did not take office,
his intention being to remain in his home province,
so he was appointed Guǎnghàn Tàishǒu.
Initially, he and Shòu were equally renowned
and close friends,
but later their friendship fractured,
and they began to falsely accuse each other.
Discerning people considered this a flaw.
Jìn Shū, Chén Shòu Zhuàn
Chén Shòu, courtesy name Chéngzuǒ,
was a native of Ānhàn, Bāxī.
In his youth, he loved learning
and studied under Qióu Zhōu, a native of the same commandery.
He served in Shǔ as Guān gé Lìshǐ.
and all high officials catered to him,
but Shòu alone refused to bend to him,
for which he was repeatedly reprimanded and demoted.
During his father's mourning,
he fell ill
and had a maid prepare medicine pills.
A guest saw this,
and his fellow villagers spoke ill of it.
When Shǔ was pacified,
he was hindered for several years because of this.
Sīkōng Zhāng Huá admired his talent,
believing that although Shòu did not avoid suspicion,
in light of the circumstances, it did not warrant dismissal.
He was recommended as Xiàolián,
appointed Zuǒ Zuòzhù Láng,
and then transferred to serve as Yángpíng Lìng.
He compiled the collection of Shǔ Minister Zhūgě Liàng
and submitted it.
He was appointed Zuòzhù Láng
and concurrently served as Zhōngzhèng of his home commandery.
He compiled the Sānguó Zhì of Wèi, Wú, and Shǔ,
totaling sixty-five chapters.
People of the time praised his good writing
and considered him a talented historian.
Xiàhóu Zhàn was compiling a Wèi Shū at the time,
but upon seeing Shòu's work,
he discarded his own book and stopped.
Zhāng Huá deeply approved of it
and said to Shòu:
"I will entrust the Jìn Shū to you."
Such was his esteem at the time.
Some say that Dīng Yí and Dīng Yì had great reputations in Wèi.
Shòu said to their sons:
"If you can find a thousand *hú* of rice and give it to me,
I will write excellent biographies for your esteemed fathers."
The Dīngs did not give it to him,
and so he ultimately did not write biographies for them.
Shòu's father was a staff officer for Mǎ Sù.
When Mǎ Sù was executed by Zhūgě Liàng,
Shòu's father was also implicated and had his head shaved.
Furthermore, Zhūgě Zhān looked down on Shòu.
In his biography of Liàng, Shòu stated
that "Liàng's military strategy was not his strong suit,
and he lacked the talent to counter enemies."
He also said
that "Zhān was only skilled in calligraphy,
his reputation exceeding his actual abilities."
Commentators criticized him for this.
Zhāng Huá was about to recommend Shòu as Zhōngshū Láng,
but Xún Xù was jealous of Huá and disliked Shòu,
so he influenced the LíBù
and had Shòu transferred to be Chángguǎng Tàishǒu.
He declined, citing his mother's old age.
When Dù Yù was about to take up his post as commander,
he again recommended him to the emperor,
saying he was suitable for Huáng Sàn.
Because of this, he was appointed Yùshǐ Zhìshū,
but left office due to his mother's mourning.
His mother's dying wish was to be buried in Luòyáng,
and Shòu followed her will.
He was also criticized for not returning his mother to his hometown for burial.
Ultimately, he was reprimanded and discussed negatively.
Earlier,
Qióu Zhōu had once said to Shòu:
"You will certainly achieve fame through your talent and learning,
but you will suffer setbacks.
However, this is not necessarily a misfortune,
so you should be very cautious."
Shòu subsequently suffered disgrace twice,
both as Qióu Zhōu had predicted.
Several years later,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
but had not yet taken office.
He died of illness in Yuánkāng year 7,
at the age of sixty-five.
Liángzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng Shàngshū Láng Fàn Yūn and others submitted a memorial, stating:
"In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn issued an edict saying, 'Sīmǎ Xiāngrú is gravely ill;
send someone to collect all his writings.'
The envoy obtained his posthumous writings,
which discussed the Feng and Shan sacrifices,
and the Son of Heaven was greatly impressed.
We, your ministers, observe that the late Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ Chén Shòu compiled the Sānguó Zhì,
whose words often contained exhortations and warnings,
clearly showing gains and losses,
which is beneficial to public morals.
Although its literary elegance is not equal to Xiāngrú's,
its straightforwardness surpasses it.
We humbly request that it be collected and recorded."
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to the Hénán Yǐn and Luòyáng Lìng to copy his books from his home.
Shòu also compiled the Gǔguó Zhì in fifty chapters and the Yìdū Qíjiù Zhuàn in ten chapters,
and his other writings circulated in the world.
Sòng Shū, Péi Sōngzhī Zhuàn
Péi Sōngzhī, courtesy name Shìqī,
was a native of Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
His grandfather, Mèi,
was Grand Master of Guanglù.
His father, Guīzhèng,
was a Yuánwài Láng.
When Sōngzhī was eight years old,
he had mastered the Lúnyǔ and the Máoshī.
He widely read historical texts and classics,
and conducted himself with simplicity.
At the age of twenty,
he was appointed Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn.
This official served as a guard to the emperor;
during the Tàiyuán reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ of the Jìn dynasty,
distinguished families were selected to participate in consultations.
Initially, Wáng Màozhī of Lángxié and Xiè Yóu of Kuàijī were employed,
both being highly esteemed figures in both the north and south.
His maternal uncle, Yú Kǎi, was in Jiānglíng
and wanted Sōngzhī to go west,
appointing him as the Grand Administrator of Xīnyě.
Due to difficulties, he did not go,
and was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
In the early Yìxī period,
he served as the Magistrate of Gùzhāng, Wúxīng Commandery.
He achieved success in the county,
and was promoted to Shàngshū Cíbù Láng.
Sōngzhī believed that the private stelae erected in his era diverged from facts,
and presented a memorial on the matter, saying:
"The creation of stelae inscriptions
is to illuminate future generations.
Unless one has extraordinary achievements and exceptional virtue,
one cannot truly merit this tradition.
The greatest ones are those whose Way moves far and wide,
and are revered by the world;
the next are those whose conduct is lofty and refined,
and whose remaining deeds are worthy of record.
If one is truly brilliant and promoted to high office,
with notable accomplishments,
and whose transformative influence reaches far,
with benevolent teachings spreading widely,
then what is entrusted to verses and eulogies
relies on being carved and engraved.
If one is not of this category,
then it is almost presumptuous and profane.
With the decay of customs, falsehoods have arisen,
and extravagant embellishments have long been prevalent.
Thus, the inscription for Kǒng Kuī
was 'the deed is his, but the person is not';
Cài Yōng, when composing texts,
often felt ashamed.
But from that time onward,
this trend has become even more widespread.
Any official with a position
is invariably honored with an erection.
Inscriptions rarely contain verifiable truths,
and carving stones has become a common practice for falsehoods,
where truth and falsehood obscure each other,
almost making genuine beauty unappreciated.
Moreover, considering the cost,
it is immeasurable,
and without prohibition,
the abuses will be endless.
I propose that all who wish to erect stelae
should be required to report it to the throne;
only if approved by court deliberation
should it then be permitted.
This way, we can prevent baseless claims
and manifest genuine achievements,
so that generations hence will know they are not虚,
thus inspiring trust and respect,
and spreading the Way to future generations."
From this, all such practices were stopped.
When Gāozǔ launched his northern expedition,
he concurrently held the position of Inspector of Sīzhōu.
He appointed Sōngzhī as the Zhōuzhǔbù,
who was later transferred to Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ.
After the capture of Luòyáng,
Gāozǔ issued an edict saying:
"Péi Sōngzhī is a talent for the imperial court and temples;
he should not long remain in border duties.
I now summon him to serve as Xǐmǎ to the Heir Apparent,
along with Yīn Jǐngrén.
Let him be informed of this."
At that time, there was a discussion about establishing music for the Five Ancestral Temples.
Sōngzhī argued that the music for Consort Zāng's temple should also be the same as the four other temples.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Línglíng,
and then summoned to be Guózǐ Bóshì.
In the third year of Yuánjiā, under Tàizǔ,
after the execution of Sītú Xú Xiànzhī and others,
envoys were dispatched to tour the empire.
Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì Yuán Yú and Sītú Zuǒsī Yuàn Kǒng Miáo were sent to Yángzhōu;
Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng Lù Zǐzhēn and Qǐbù Zhēn Fǎchóng were sent to Jīngzhōu;
Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì Fàn Yōng and Sītú Zhǔbù Páng Zūn were sent to Nányǎnzhōu;
former Shàngshū Yòuchéng Kǒng Mò was sent to the Northern and Southern Yùzhōu;
Fǔjūn Cānjūn Wáng Xīnzhī was sent to Xúzhōu;
Rǒngcóng Púyè Chē Zōng was sent to Qīng and Yǎnzhōu;
Sōngzhī was sent to Xiāngzhōu;
Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng Ruǎn Chángzhī was sent to Yōngzhōu;
former Jìnglíng Tàishǒu Yīn Dàoluán was sent to Yìzhōu;
Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì Lǐ Dānzhī was sent to Guǎngzhōu;
Lángzhōng Yīn Bīn was sent to Liángzhōu and Nánqínzhōu;
former Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Ruǎn Yuánkè was sent to Jiāozhōu;
Fùmǎ Dūwèi Fèngcháoqǐng Pān Sīxiān was sent to Níngzhōu;
all concurrently serving as Sànqí Chángshì.
They were instructed to proclaim the imperial edict, which read:
"In ancient times, kings toured to inspect accomplishments,
and the various lords reported on their duties.
Otherwise, there were rituals of 'existing and inspecting'
and rules for 'visiting and presenting,'
through which the people were observed and policies established,
assignments given and achievements examined,
ensuring communication between superiors and subordinates,
and benefiting all, near and far.
Thus, their achievements shone for ages,
and their Way endured for long years.
I, being ignorant,
have inherited this grand enterprise.
Reverent and fearful in my position,
I am dim in the path of governance,
ever vigilant with worry,
as if standing on the brink of an abyss.
I fear that national customs may decline,
and popular morale become false and withered;
that calamities may cause disharmony,
and floods and droughts harm livelihoods.
Though I diligently attend to numerous affairs
and strive to promote what is fitting,
state matters are indeed vast,
and upon reflection, many deficiencies exist.
Government and penal laws may be misguided,
and I have not yet fully heard of it.
Is it truly that my sincerity has not prevailed,
preventing the hearts of the people from fully expressing themselves?
The shame of a fallen well
rests with me alone.
As the times have been fraught with difficulties,
and the Kingly Way is not yet unified,
the rites of imperial tours
have been abandoned and not restored.
I care for the common people,
never forgetting to be concerned and compassionate.
Now, I send the concurrently appointed Sànqí Chángshì Yú and others to convey orders throughout the four directions,
traveling through commanderies and counties,
personally meeting the Inspectors and officials of Two Thousand Shi,
expressing my utmost sincerity,
widely inquiring about crucial aspects of governance,
observing official administration,
seeking out the grievances of the people,
commending integrity and conduct,
and inquiring about their ailments.
Regarding the merits and demerits of rites and customs,
all shall follow the Zhōu rites.
Each shall write a report
and return to thoroughly memorialize,
so that I may clearly see it as if personally present.
You, grand masters and noblemen, each exert your hearts and diligently serve,
do not slacken your efforts!
If there are those who have far-reaching plans to advise,
or sincere words to offer,
present them to the envoys;
let nothing be hidden or omitted.
I shall respectfully accept good counsel
to rectify deficiencies.
Strive and exert yourselves,
to fulfill my intentions!"
Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之) returned from his mission,
and memorialized, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the Way of Heaven (tiāndào, 天道) extends downwards to assist the bright and luminous,
and that the virtue of a ruler (jūndé, 君德) has broad prevalence as its ultimate goal.
The wise rulers of ancient times
followed their hearts and broadly benefited the people.
Therefore, when cultured thoughts are embodied,
harmony naturally prevails in due season,
and when propriety is practiced in Jiānghàn (江漢),
its civilizing influence extends far.
Thus, they were able to leave behind grand and admirable eulogies,
and expand the flourishing principles of the Zhōu (周) dynasty.
Your humble servant reflects that Your Majesty's divine wisdom (shénruì, 神叡) is profoundly pervasive,
your Way (dào, 道) matches that of remote ages.
Crowned in the magnificent hall,
Your Majesty's heart extends to the eight directions (bābǐao, 八表).
You inquire about the impurity of reverent teachings,
and worry that bright virtues are not widely proclaimed.
You seek clear reports from the common people,
and pity the [widowed and] orphaned.
With a grand proclamation,
Your Majesty's benevolence spreads in all directions,
Your far-reaching plans are manifested in elegant edicts (yǎgào, 雅誥),
and Your gracious instructions (huìxùn, 惠訓) are broadcast to distant regions (xiázōu, 遐陬).
For this reason, all within the realm look up and sing Your praises,
and those from distant lands speaking different languages are all delighted.
None fail to sing and leap for joy,
to engrave the imperial prestige (huángfēng, 皇風) into their hearts.
Some even assist the old and carry the young,
proclaiming their joy by the roadside.
This is truly because Your nurturing influence has flowed forth,
hence they forget its spontaneous origin.
A thousand years' opportunity in a single moment—
this is what it is.
Your servant, mistakenly entrusted with selection and appointment,
unworthily holds a prominent position.
Humbly with my limited abilities,
I think of purifying the eight directions.
I am unable to clearly convey Your Majesty's sacred will (shèngzhǐ, 聖旨),
or solemnly illuminate the moral transformation (fēnghuà, 風化).
My recommendations and demotions are without order,
my discoveries and promotions are based on limited knowledge.
I am ashamed, fearful, and distressed,
not knowing what to do.
I respectfully present twenty-four articles,
and have diligently prepared a report for each matter.
I respectfully note the edict (zhàoshū, 詔書) of the guǐmǎo (癸卯) year,
which states that gains and losses in customs
should entirely follow the rites of Zhōu (周).
Each time, I am to return with a detailed memorial in writing.
I have respectfully prepared a written report on the matters to be appended hereafter."
Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之) understood the true meaning of his mission very well,
and commentators praised him.
He was transferred to be a Central Secretariat Gentleman (zhōngshū shìláng, 中書侍郎) and Grand Arbiter (dàzhōngzhèng, 大中正) of the two prefectures of Sī (司) and Jì (冀).
The emperor (shàng, 上) ordered him to annotate Chén Shòu's (陳壽) Sānguó Zhì (三國志).
Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之) gathered various biographies and records,
and expanded upon unusual accounts.
When it was completed,
he presented it to the emperor.
The emperor (shàng, 上) praised it,
saying:
"This will be imperishable!"
He was sent out as the Administrator (tàishǒu, 太守) of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
where he diligently cared for the common people,
and officials and citizens found him convenient.
He returned to serve as Director of the Palace (tōngzhí, 通直),
then became a Palace Regular Attendant (chángshì, 常侍),
and again took charge as Grand Arbiter (dàzhōngzhèng, 大中正) of the two prefectures.
Soon after, he was sent out as Administrator (tàishǒu, 太守) of Nán Lángxié (南琅邪).
In the fourteenth year [of Yuánjiā (元嘉)],
he retired,
and was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance (zhōngsàn dàfū, 中散大夫).
Soon after, he served as Erudite of the National University (guózǐ bóshì, 國子博士).
He was promoted to Grand Master (dàzhōng dàfū, 大中大夫),
with the Erudite position remaining as before.
He continued Hé Chéngtiān's (何承天) National History (guóshǐ, 國史),
but had not yet begun writing.
In the twenty-eighth year, he died,
aged eighty.
His son, Yǐn (駰),
was Southern Chief Clerk (nánzhōngláng cānjūn, 南中郎參軍).
The essays and treatises written by Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之), and his Jìn Jì (晉紀),
and Péi Yǐn's (裴駰) annotation of Sīmǎ Qiān's (司馬遷) Shǐjì (史記),
all circulated in the world.
